title: GMP-Cor: Quantifying Transcriptional Dysregulation in Antibiotic Tolerance and Persistence
abstract: When cells are exposed to stress, they typically activate stress-response pathways and enter a regulated growth-arrest. But what if the stress overwhelms these pathways? In such cases, cells may enter a disrupted growth-arrest - a poorly adapted, abrupt cessation of growth, characterized by a broad distribution of lag times upon stress removal. This distribution underlies antibiotic persistence during stress recovery. Therefore, gaining a deeper understanding of the disrupted growth-arrest is important for developing more effective antibiotic therapies. In this study, we perform single cell RNA-seq on bacteria in disrupted conditions. We develop GMP-Cor: a metric to quantify dysregulation and analyze gene-gene correlation patterns in sparse single-cell data. We find that gene-gene correlations are significantly reduced in disrupted cells compared to regulated cells, providing direct evidence that this tolerance-enhanced state, along with its increased membrane sensitivity, is associated with global-dysregulation. We demonstrate that GMP-Cor can extend to other biological systems, such as persistent cancer cells, where it separates proliferating from drug-arrested cells.
authors: Gutfreund, A.; Rotem, A.; Ronin, I.; Rosenthal, A. Z.; Agam, O.; Balaban, N. Q.

title: Whole methylome changes in Barrett's metaplasia, dysplasia, and cancer
abstract: The clinical management of Barrett's esophagus (BE) and the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) is dependent on the presence or absence of dysplasia. The histopathological diagnosis of dysplasia is unreliable however, and would benefit from additional diagnostic criteria. Here, we obtained EM-seq whole-genome methylation profiles from 86 samples across the BE/EAC disease spectrum, notably supplementing the scant existing methylation evidence for low-grade and high-grade dysplasia. While the bulk of methylation changes occur in the transition from normal squamous epithelium to intestinal metaplasia (non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus), we identified a smaller set of changes that mark the onset of dysplasia and progression to EAC. Methylation changes were broadly independent of copy number variation. They were tightly anticorrelated with RNA-seq expression for some genes. Deconvolution of the bulk methylation signatures into constituent cell types revealed four sample groupings enriched with a particular cell type (squamous, columnar, lymphoid and erythroid cells), somewhat reflecting existing clinical classifications. We outline potential markers that could improve the diagnosis of metaplasia and dysplasia in EAC.
authors: Liew, Y. J.; Udumanne, T.; Catalan, K.; Ariyavidana, A.; Lee-Ng, K. K. M.; Pascovici, D.; Yang, T.; Kumarasinghe, P.; McLeod, D.; Brown, I.; Bourke, M. J.; Lord, S. J.; Lord, R. V.; Ross, J.

title: Predicting seabird-vessel interactions from bird-borne data alone
abstract: Seabirds often follow fishing vessels to scavenge discards and bait, benefiting from access to food but also facing the risk of bycatch. Exposure to bycatch is commonly assessed by analysing seabird-fishing interactions, typically through the spatiotemporal alignment of seabird and vessel tracking data. However, this approach may underestimate interactions when vessel tracking information is incomplete or unavailable. We tested whether seabird-vessel interactions could be identified using seabird telemetry alone and whether fishing and nonfishing vessels could be distinguished. We analysed GPS, wet-dry, accelerometer and pressure data from 273 Scopoli's shearwaters in the Northwest Mediterranean. We identified 779 vessel-attendance events using seabird GPS, Automatic Identification System (AIS) data and simulation-based tests to distinguish vessel attraction or following from chance encounters. We then trained random forest models to predict vessel-attendance from bird-borne movement and environmental metrics, testing different sensor combinations. Finally, we selected the GPS and environmental model for its performance and compatibility with GPS-only tracking data from 17 radar-equipped shearwaters, whose detectors identified nearby vessels independently of AIS. Models predicting vessel-attendance from seabird movement metrics derived from GPS, wet-dry sensors and accelerometers achieved classification rates above 90% during training. However, when tested on new individuals, 42% of their positive predictions were false-positives. Models combining environmental metrics with either GPS or GPS and wet-dry data achieved classification rates around 75% during training and generalised consistently across individuals, maintaining classification rates of 70% or above. Attendance events involving fishing (n = 482) and nonfishing vessels (n = 297) could not be reliably distinguished. Across 45 trips of radar-equipped shearwaters, the GPS and environmental model discriminated vessel-attendance in hourly bins against AIS detections (AUC = 0.85), supporting assessment of spatiotemporal attendance patterns. At the event level, only 17% of 227 predicted vessel-attendance events were supported by AIS or radar detections. However, radar detected nearby vessels during 19 predicted events lacking AIS support, highlighting the value of complementary vessel detection. This study presents a vessel-independent framework for assessing seabird-vessel interactions based solely on bird-borne data, complementing fisheries monitoring programmes, helping to identify gaps in vessel-tracking systems across poorly monitored marine regions, and informing future assessments of bycatch risk.
authors: Navarro-Herrero, L.; March, D.; Bartumeus, F.; Gonzalez-Solis, J.

title: Maternal diet and genetics shape the human milk metabolome
abstract: Human milk contains a diverse array of metabolites that contribute to infant nutrition, immune development, and microbial colonization. The maternal factors shaping the milk metabolome, and the relative contribution of genetics or diet vs. other factors, remain poorly understood. Here, we profiled 458 milk metabolites in 349 one-month postpartum human milk samples and integrated metabolomic data with maternal diet, clinical, transcriptomic, and genomic measurements. Maternal diet was broadly associated with milk metabolite composition, with significant correlations identified between dietary features and 323 metabolites. Coffee consumption strongly predicted milk quinic acid and 1,3-dimethyluric acid abundance, while high-fiber dietary patterns were associated with metabolites including proline-betaine and N-acetylornithine. Integration of milk transcriptomic and metabolomic data via machine learning identified biologically plausible gene-metabolite pairs, including associations between QPRT expression and quinolinic acid, and DPEP1 and cysteine-glycine dipeptide. Genome-wide association analyses identified nine study-wide significant metabolite quantitative trait loci, including novel milk-specific associations near PDE6A affecting purine metabolites and near GNE affecting free sialic acid. Comparison with plasma metabolite studies demonstrated both shared and milk-specific genetic regulation of metabolites. Finally, we found that of all tested maternal features, diet explained the largest proportion of variation in the milk metabolome. Together, these findings demonstrate that the human milk metabolome reflects both maternal exposures and mammary gland-specific biology. This work establishes a framework for understanding how genetic and environmental factors shape milk composition.
authors: Johnson, K. E.; Duan, Y.; Youssef, A.; Aristizabal-Henao, J. J.; Johnson, A.; Kiebish, M. A.; Nagel, E. M.; Palmsten, K.; Pierce, S.; Wernimont, S.; Bode, L.; Lock, E. F.; Isganaitis, E. M.; Fields, D. A.; Albert, F. W.; Blekhman, R.; Demerath, E. W.

title: A large, distinct family of RNase H fold nucleases associated with numerous defense systems in prokaryotes
abstract: During the last decade, systematic efforts aimed at the characterization of prokaryotic immunity resulted in the discovery of several hundred distinct defense systems in bacteria and archaea. This suggests that the common defense systems were already known and only rare ones remained to be identified. Here we present a genomic census and analysis of a vast family of bacterial and archaeal proteins (known as Domain of Unknown Function, DUF3800) that contain a distinct variant of the RNase H fold and are encoded in a striking 15% of the available complete prokaryotic genomes. Most of these proteins are encoded in defense islands, often in a close association with known defense systems, hence the designation WARD (Weaponized Antiphage RNase- dependent Defense). The WARDs display a broad variety of protein domain architectures and genomic contexts, including a strong link to restriction-modification, CRISPR-Cas, retrons, and non-coding RNAs, suggestive of a substantial diversity in defense mechanisms. We experimentally tested 10 WARDs, mostly, encoded by standalone genes, and found that 9 of these conferred robust protection against diverse phages in Escherichia coli. Therefore, WARDs appear to represent the third most abundant defense system type in prokaryotes.
authors: Wolf, Y. I.; Arshad, K.; Kannatey-Asibu, K.; Theisen, R. Q.; Kitzinger, K. A.; Jain, P. V.; Koonin, E. V.; Makarova, K. S.; Ledvina, H. E.

title: An orphan LuxR regulator controls plant developmental reprogramming during interaction with Novosphingobium resinovorum HR1a
abstract: Rhizoremediation depends on productive plant/pollutant-degrading microorganism interactions, yet the bacterial regulatory mechanisms that shape host responses remain poorly understood. We investigated the role of the previously uncharacterized orphan LuxR874 from the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) degrading bacterium Novosphingobium resinovorum HR1a, in the modulation of plant physiology. Bacterial transcriptomics revealed that LuxR874 controls the expression of genes associated with aromatic and sugar metabolism, and acylCoA related functions. Inactivation of luxR874 altered bacterial responses without affecting root colonization, suggesting that this regulator contributes to the physiological state required to elicit host responses. In gnotobiotic systems, HR1a induced a root phenotype characterized by reduced primary root elongation, increased root thickness, and enhanced root hair formation. These alterations were attenuated in the luxR874 mutant and restored by complementation despite similar colonization levels among strains. Plant RNA-seq analyses revealed extensive host transcriptional reprogramming, including activation of developmental regulators, hormone associated pathways, cell wall remodeling genes, and oxidative stress responses. In contrast, plants inoculated with the luxR874 mutant displayed a weaker transcriptional response resembling the non-inoculated state. Functional analyses supported LuxR874-dependent activation of reactive oxygen species and ethylene related pathways. Our results reveal an unexpected role for an orphan LuxR regulator in coordinating multi-level responses during a rhizoremediation-relevant plant microbe interaction.
authors: Molina, L.; Hurtado, I.; Udaondo, Z.; Segura, A.

title: How the Azadithiolate Ligand Impacts O2-Stability of Group B -Hydrogenase ToHydA
abstract: [FeFe]-hydrogenases are metalloenzymes that catalyze the reversible oxidation and production of H2, making them potential candidates for sustainable energy solutions. However, their practical application is restricted by their extreme O2 sensitivity, which leads to irreversible active site degradation. A newly characterized Group B hydrogenase, ToHydA from Thermosediminibacter oceani, has exhibited exceptional O2-stability even after long-term exposure to air. In ToHydA, the highly conserved proton-transporting cysteine (C212) safeguards the H-cluster from O2-induced degradation by formation of the Hinact state. In this study, we investigate the effects of replacing the azadithiolate (ADT) ligand of [2Fe]H with propanedithiolate (PDT), revealing that this substitution prevents the formation of the Hinact and Htrans states observed in ToHydA WT (bearing the ADT ligand). By combining ATR-FTIR spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we show that a favorable interaction between the nitrogen bridgehead of the ADT ligand and the C212 sidechain is crucial for stabilizing these states. The absence of this interaction in ToHydAPDT (bearing the PDT ligand) prevents the C212 sidechain from approaching the Fed center of [2Fe]H, thereby reducing Hinact accumulation. Moreover, as-isolated ToHydAPDT predominantly exhibits the Hhyd state, which is unusual for [FeFe]-hydrogenases with bound PDT ligand. These findings demonstrate how ligand substitution at the [2Fe]H site of ToHydA affects the structural dynamics, offering detailed molecular insights into the ligand-dependent modulation of [FeFe]-hydrogenases.
authors: Ghosh, S.; Das, C. K.; Naskar, S.; Schäfer, L. V.; Happe, T.

title: PaleoRigor: a bounded research agent with a reproducible evidence trail for paleomicrobiome data processing
abstract: Background: Ancient microbial evidence informs research on past health, diet, and environments, but its scarcity and susceptibility to contamination demand care in selecting and processing data. Language models can now turn a research request into an analysis plan, but an unconstrained planner may reference files that do not exist, apply operations a format forbids, or answer a question the data cannot settle. A planner used on such evidence therefore needs to be bounded, and its decisions recoverable afterwards. Results: We developed PaleoRigor around three commitments. Agent: a language model plans the analysis. Constraint: a validator checks every file reference, format and step dependency before anything runs, execution is restricted to predefined local modules, and a planning contract directs the model to refuse out-of-scope requests with a named reason code rather than answer them. Reproducibility: each run is exported with its plan, intermediate files, checksums and decisions. In a preregistered, frozen held-out evaluation, PaleoRigor passed 23 of 24 runs (95.8%; Wilson 95% confidence interval, 79.8-99.3%): 11 of 12 supported runs and all 12 prespecified boundary decisions. An ablation that removed this planning contract from the same model passed 19 of 24 (79.2%). Repeating the frozen design with a second model configuration yielded 24 of 24 successes for PaleoRigor and 19 of 24 for the ablated arm. Pooled post hoc across both configurations, PaleoRigor passed 47 of 48 runs (97.9%), compared with 38 of 48 (79.2%) for the ablated arms. All 96 run labels were recomputed from retained records and matched. Dataset-level tests matched read counts and compressed-file sizes for six public sequencing records and documented the removal of 114 duplicate sequence entries. A retraction-associated audit illustrated how expert review limited conclusions to file-level evidence. Conclusions: For paleomicrobiome data, pairing a language-model agent with explicit constraints and a reproducible record makes the agent's proposed analysis reviewable before its outputs support a biological claim. PaleoRigor delivers checked inputs, a recorded transformation history and a named reason for each request it refuses, and runs as a local desktop application. It prepares data for specialist analysis; ancient-DNA authentication and biological interpretation remain with the paleobiologist.
authors: Liu, T.; Zhang, H.; Jia, Y.; Ning, K.

title: Sourmash accurately profiles strains from long-read metagenomes preserving gene content
abstract: Background:  Metagenomic strain-level profiling remains challenging because closely related bacterial strains often share more than 99% average nucleotide identity (ANI). However, they can differ substantially in gene content and functional potential. Sourmash uses k-mer sketches with FracMinHash to compare sequencing reads against reference databases, which makes it an interesting approach for strain-level profiling. Because it compares sketches rather than full alignments, it enables fast searches against large reference databases. However, its ability to recover biologically relevant strains and preserve community gene content has not been specifically assessed. Here, we evaluated the performance of sourmash for strain-level identification abundance, functional gene content recovery, and abundance estimations using five mock communities of increasing complexity with known composition. Results. We first assessed whether nucleotide similarity reflects functional similarity between strains. Gene content similarity was generally consistent with ANI but revealed important divergences between closely related strains. For example, Escherichia coli strains sharing more than 98% ANI showed gene content similarities ranging from 20% to 57%, highlighting that nucleotide similarity alone is insufficient to assess functional proximity and consequently the accuracy of strain identification. Above sufficient genome coverage, sourmash identified strains either exactly or with closely related strains sharing highly conserved gene content. These closely related strains provided a biologically relevant representation of the expected functional potential of the mock communities. Gene content recovery was highly accurate, with F1 scores ranging from 0.942 to 0.998 across the five mock communities. Genome abundances estimated against sourmash-identified genomes closely matched the expected community composition: Pearson correlation coefficients ranged from 0.823 to 1 at strain level and from 0.978 to 1 at species level. Conclusions. Our results show that sourmash provides a biologically relevant approach for strain-level characterisation in microbial ecosystems. Even when the exact strain could not be identified, closely related strains retained most of the expected gene content and abundance estimations were accurate, supporting the use of sourmash for downstream functional profiling or metabolic network reconstruction.
authors: Angevin L, Lipovac J, Peterlongo P, Roux E, Vicedomini R.

title: Transmural Single-Nucleus Transcriptomics Nominates Candidate Disease Programs in Human Necrotizing Enterocolitis
abstract: Background & Aims: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a life-threatening disease of premature infants marked by inflammation, ischemia, mucosal injury, and, in advanced cases, necrosis extending into deeper layers of the intestinal wall. Because NEC affects specialized, interacting cells in a developing intestine, we used single-nucleus transcriptomics to build a transmural, cell-type-resolved map and nominate hypothesis-generating disease programs distinct from maturation. Methods: Full-thickness intestinal specimens from fetal/prenatal controls, acute NEC cases, and infant controls were analyzed by single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Fetal and infant samples served as developmental references. Analyses included cell annotation, NEC-versus-infant differential expression, gene ontology (GO), cross-lineage recurrence, cell death signatures, and developmental maturity. Results: We profiled 53,735 nuclei by snRNA-seq and resolved 34 epithelial, stromal, vascular, immune, neuronal, glial, and smooth muscle populations. We used a morphology-based nuclei scoring system for sample selection that predicted high-quality transcript recovery. NEC nuclei were represented across this cellular landscape, with recurrent gene-expression changes suggesting shared inflammatory recruitment, antimicrobial/redox defense, stress adaptation, complement/vascular activation, reduced homeostatic signaling, and cell death-associated regulation. Developmental maturity analysis identified fetal-like expression levels in subsets of NEC-regulated genes. Proliferative crypt populations retained DNA repair/cell-cycle programs with inflammatory, hypoxic, and ER-stress features, while absorptive enterocytes showed reduced digestive, transport, detoxification, and terminal villus-function programs. Secretory-lineage changes implicated goblet mucus-barrier responses with reduced glycosylation, trafficking, and hydration; enteroendocrine changes in epithelial defense, metabolic stress, and neural signaling; and Paneth cell retention of antimicrobial effector transcripts despite altered ER quality control, autophagy, and granule delivery in NEC. Non-epithelial programs implicated stromal Wnt/BMP niche loss, impaired lymphatic drainage/scavenging, macrophage cytokine activation with reduced clearance machinery, neuroglial circuit defects, and altered smooth muscle contraction-relaxation balance. Conclusions: This single nuclear intestinal cell atlas nominates multicellular programs that may govern NEC initiation, progression toward tissue destruction, and resolution toward functional recovery.
authors: Meyer, M. F.; Sweet, C. W.; Breau, K.; Burclaff, J.; Bliton, R. J.; Dodson, H. M.; Cannon, G.; Bougaran, P.; Puri, V.; Frazer, L. C.; Bolzan, L. R.; Rizzuto, C. R.; Sklar, D. E.; Jania, C. title: SeCAT (Sequence Consensus Amplicon Trimming): a simulation-informed Nextflow pipeline for cross-study harmonisation of 16S rRNA metabarcoding datasets
abstract: Global syntheses of 16S rRNA metabarcoding data rely on combining datasets, yet amplicon sequence variants generated with different primer pairs can rarely be compared directly. Existing approaches correct batch effects statistically or aggregate taxonomically; none first establishes whether the sequences are positionally comparable. We present SeCAT (Sequence Consensus Amplicon Trimming), a Nextflow pipeline that maps every study’s variants onto a 16S rRNA full-length reference alignment, determines the largest window shared across studies, and tests by simulation whether trimming to that window degrades community structure before any data are merged. Applied to thirteen marine studies sequenced with three primer sets, twelve converged on a consensus window with a median trimmed read length of 249 bp (9,582 alignment columns). Degradation tests across twelve studies and six taxonomic ranks (72 study-rank combinations) returned 31 passes, 38 cautions and three confirmed failures. Eleven studies (682 samples after filtering) were harmonised (trimmed to the window and merged), collapsing 20,891 primer-specific variants into 12,667 MetaASVs, trimmed sequences deduplicated across studies. Harmonisation preserved community structure at family level (Mantel r = 1.00; Procrustes mZ < 0.001) without adding between-study variance (|ΔRZ| < 0.001). Alpha diversity, including observed richness, was recovered across all levels (intraclass correlations 0.93–1.00), whereas sequence-level congruence was moderate (Procrustes mZ = 0.52), as expected where between-study similarity at sequence level exists only after harmonisation. The harmonised output supports synthesis from aggregated ranks down to exact sequences. By establishing positional comparability before merging, SeCAT opens the archive of primer-fragmented 16S rRNA surveys to sequence-level synthesis.
authors: Terrey D, Huber P, Pereira E, Pelayo MC, Ferguson RMW, Dumbrell AJ, Sweet M, Bani A, Metz S.

title: High-density environmental DNA metabarcoding reveals fine-scale three-dimensional structure of a fish community in a semi-closed bay
abstract: Coastal fish assemblages are influenced by environmental heterogeneity across horizontal and vertical dimensions, yet their fine-scale three-dimensional structure remains poorly understood. We investigated spatial variation in fish assemblages using environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding at 100 stations across three depth layers (300 samples) in Maizuru Bay, a semi-enclosed coastal bay in Japan. Concurrent hydrographic measurements were used to examine associations between fish assemblage composition and environmental conditions. We detected 216 fish species, with mean species richness decreasing from 28.4 at the surface to 16.4 at the bottom. Thirty-three species were detected exclusively below the surface. Fish assemblage composition differed significantly among depth layers and exhibited pronounced horizontal turnover along the bay axis. Although depth, geographic position, and measured environmental variables were associated with assemblage composition, they collectively explained only 13.0% of the variation. The independent contribution of spatial position (2.9%) exceeded those of depth (0.8%) and measured environmental variables (0.9%). These findings demonstrate substantial three-dimensional heterogeneity in coastal fish assemblages that cannot be fully explained by conventional hydrographic measurements. Our study highlights the importance of integrating horizontal and vertical sampling to characterize coastal fish biodiversity and improve marine ecosystem monitoring.
authors: Murakami, H.; Nakadai, R.; Jo, T. S.; Wu, Q.; Kadotani Tomojiri, D.; Masuda, R.

title: A timeline for evolution of metabolism in early microbes
abstract: The metabolism of early microbes shaped our planet's chemistry and enabled more life to evolve. However, it remains uncertain when many forms of metabolism arose and which organisms carried them out. Here we combine machine learning, metabolic networks, and phylogenomics of microbes to date 14 forms of metabolism and 6 other traits. We find that metabolism evolved in three waves, starting >3.4 billion years ago (Ga) with fermentation and sulfur compound respiration. A second wave began ~3.2 Ga with aerobic respiration and growth, while a third began ~1.4 Ga with further specialization. We compared these predictions with independent dates from the geochemical record, and agreement with conservative dates was good (CCC = 0.81 to 0.89). Several forms of metabolism are invisible in the geochemical record, and our approach dates these forms, too. Our results reconcile different lines of evidence for microbial evolution and provide a fuller picture of early Earth.
authors: Hackmann, T.

title: HiSpoT: a novel one-tube dual-barcode PCR method for NGS spoligotyping amplicon library preparation in Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex
abstract: Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious causes of death globally, making rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing essential for effective outbreak tracking and epidemiological surveillance. To address the limitations and high costs of current typing methods, we developed a novel one-tube, dual-barcode PCR method for preparing targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) amplicon libraries for spoligotyping of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), which we termed HiSpoT (High-throughput Spoligotyping by Targeted next generation sequencing). The assay targets 43 conserved spacer oligonucleotides in the CRISPR direct repeat (DR) region and is presented here together with the previously unpublished, difficult-to-design dual-barcode primer set needed to multiplex 96 samples in a single tube. HiSpoT is accurate, fast, high-throughput, and low-cost, eliminating the need for a commercial NGS library preparation kit. Because HiSpoT is PCR-based, the resulting spoligotypes remain directly comparable with the large PCR-based spoligotype databases accumulated over decades, enabling rapid outbreak tracking and biogeographic characterization of the tuberculosis burden of a country, while higher-resolution whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data are obtained. Analysis of 288 clinical MTBC isolates from Israel (2020-2022) demonstrated a broad range of genetic lineages, and comparison of 79 isolates analyzed by both HiSpoT and WGS showed 70% full concordance, with essentially all discrepancies attributable to single-spacer insertion-element disruptions of PCR primer sites. We also present two open-source Google Colab Python tools, Spoligotyping_MTBC_gcl and its condensed HiSpoT_Spoligotyping_v8_ready VIBE variant, freely available on GitHub, which automatically process Illumina paired-end fastq output from HiSpoT or WGS and report binary and octal spoligotypes, spoligo international types (SIT), and MTBC family assignments with accompanying quality-control reports.
authors: Freidlin PJ, Rubinstein M, Fass E, Kutikov I, Zizelski Valenci G, Losev Y, Dveyrin Z, Rorman E, Nissan I.

title: PIrates of the vacuole: phosphoinositide hijacking by T4SS intracellular pathogens.
abstract: Intracellular bacteria equipped with a Type IV Secretion Systems (T4SS), including Legionella pneumophila, Coxiella burnetii, Brucella abortus, and Anaplasma/Ehrlichia species, evolved a convergent strategy of exploiting host cell lipids at every stage of infection, from cholesterol-rich raft-mediated entry to the establishment of replicative vacuoles that evade lysosomal destruction. Indeed, these pathogens actively remodel host cell membranes by deploying T4SS effectors that bind, generate, or deplete specific lipid species, in particular phosphoinositides and cholesterol, to dictate the identity and trafficking fate of their containing vacuole. A remarkable diversity of effectors with lipid-binding or lipid-modifying activities has now been characterized across these pathogens: from the PI4P-centric Dot/Icm effector cascade of Legionella to the cooperating CvpB, CvpE, and Vice triad of Coxiella, and the phosphoinositide-binding immune evasion effector BtpA of Brucella. These pathogens also tap into host lipid droplets for energy and membrane precursors, modulate bioactive lipid mediators such as prostaglandins to curb immune clearance, and present atypical surface lipids to minimize pattern recognition. Advances in lipidomics, including a landmark systematic identification of novel α-helical PI-binding effector folds conserved across Legionella and Coxiella, have shed new light on these processes with unprecedented resolution. This review examines the shared and divergent lipid-subversion strategies of T4SS-bearing intracellular pathogens from an integrated molecular, cellular, and lipidomic perspective, and highlights emerging opportunities for host-directed therapeutic intervention.
authors: Bonazzi M.

title: DirectClean: artifact-aware preprocessing and read rescue for Oxford Nanopore direct-cDNA transcriptome sequencing.
abstract: Oxford Nanopore direct-cDNA sequencing enables full-length transcriptome profiling without PCR amplification, but recurrent chimeric artifacts introduced during reverse transcription and library preparation can compromise isoform reconstruction and gene-fusion analysis. These include foldback inversions, aberrant primer configurations, internal adapter concatemers, and homopolymer-mediated template-switching events. Existing preprocessing strategies primarily address primer-based orientation and adapter detection, leaving several direct-cDNA-specific artifact classes unresolved and often discarding reads that still contain usable transcript sequence. We developed DirectClean, an artifact-aware preprocessing and read-rescue framework integrating strand orientation, artifact removal, and junction-level splitting of recoverable chimeric reads. Benchmarking across four direct-cDNA datasets showed consistently higher read and base retention with DirectClean than with Pychopper. In VCaP, DirectClean retained 65.2% of reads compared with 57.6% for Pychopper, supported additional transcripts, and reduced the chimeric read rate from 30.9% in raw data to 16.9%. Semi-synthetic validation demonstrated accurate rescue of adapter-associated and A/T-rich chimeric reads, and matched real-data analyses showed no enrichment of novel transcript models in split-derived reads relative to matched untouched reads. DirectClean provides a reproducible, openly available framework for artifact-aware preprocessing of direct-cDNA transcriptomes and improves the reliability of downstream isoform and fusion analyses.
authors: Guo Q, Li Y, Yang R.

title: Cell DiffErential Expression by Pooling (CellDEEP) highlights issues in differential gene expression in scRNA-seq.
abstract: Accurate identification of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in single-cell RNA sequencing data remains challenging. Single-cell-specific statistical models often report large numbers of candidate genes but can exhibit inflated false positive rates, whereas pseudobulk approaches improve false discovery control at the cost of reduced sensitivity. To overcome the noise and bias that other tools have, and allow the user to have more control of the DEG process, we present CellDEEP, which uses a cell aggregation (metacell) approach. This tool provides a framework for flexible selection of pooling strategies and parameterization for differential expression analysis. Benchmarking on simulated and real datasets, including COVID-19 and rheumatoid arthritis, shows that CellDEEP often outperforms other methods, consistently reduces false positives compared to single-cell methods and recovers more true positives than pseudobulk methods. Our work shifts the focus from selecting a single 'best' method to an approach that reduces cell-level noise while preserving biological signal, together with transparent validation framework, advancing more reliable differential-expression analysis in single-cell transcriptomics.
authors: Cheng Y, Kettlewell T, Laidlaw RF, Hardy OM, McCluskey A, Otto TD, Somma D.

title: Root microbiota regulates tiller number in rice.
authors: Zhang J, Wang B, Xu H, Liu W, Yu J, Wang Q, Yu H, Wei JW, Dai R, Zhou J, He Y, Zou D, Yang J, Ban X, Hu Q, Meng X, Liu YX, Wang B, Hu B, Wang M, Xin P, Chu J, Li C, Garrido-Oter R, Yu P, Jan van Dijk AD, Dong L, Bouwmeester H, Gao S, Huang A, Chu C, Li J, Bai Y.

title: Amino acid availability influences Staphylococcus aureus interaction with the nasal microbiota in a strain- and community-specific manner.
abstract: BackgroundOnly some individuals carry Staphylococcus aureus in the nose, predisposing them to endogenous infections. While microbial cooperation and competition are known to shape environmental and intestinal microbial communities, their impact on pathogen colonization within the nasal microbiome is largely unknown.ResultsUsing a newly curated nasal strain collection and systematic pairwise interaction analysis, we investigated competitive and collaborative traits between diverse S. aureus strains and nasal communities. Our experiments revealed that nasal species strongly modulate S. aureus growth in a strain- and community-specific manner both in vitro and in gnotobiotic mice. Nutrient-dependent interactions emerged as key drivers. In one example, we found that tyrosine provided by synthetic communities supported proliferation of an auxotrophic S. aureus strain. Screening of a large collection of S. aureus strains identified tyrosine dependency in 8% of strains, with colonization impaired in the absence of supportive communities, indicating broader relevance of this interaction.ConclusionsOur findings reveal distinct metabolic adaptations that enable S. aureus to exploit specific features of resident nasal communities, highlighting complex interspecies networks that influence colonization in the human nose. These insights may inform microbiome-editing strategies to displace S. aureus from the nasal niche. Video Abstract.
authors: Camus L, Franz J, Gerlach D, Lange A, Power JJ, Navarro-Díaz M, Stahl J, Krismer B, Rapp J, Bilici K, Otto M, Klages LJ, Starostin V, Ham S, Kalinowski J, Angenent LT, Link H, Heilbronner S.

title: Breed and housing system shape jejunal transcriptome and digesta microbiota in German Landrace and Saddleback pigs.
abstract: BackgroundSustainable pig farming balances animal welfare, productivity, and social acceptance. Organic systems offer enriched environments for the pigs and represent a model for sustainable production, but require an understanding of how breed, intestinal microbiome, and housing interact. In this study, we compared a commercial breed (German Landrace, GL) and a traditional breed (German Saddleback, GS) reared in different housing systems (Conventional, CON; Organic, ECO). Jejunal mucosa transcriptomes (n = 56) and digesta microbiota (n = 100) were collected from growing pigs at 70 days of life; 54 samples overlapped between the two datasets and were used for all integrated host-microbiome analyses. Data from RNA-seq and 16 S-seq were evaluated through differential expression analysis, microbial community profiling, and DIABLO-based data integration.ResultsJejunal transcriptome variation was influenced primarily by breed. GL pigs exhibited a profile supporting anabolic pathways, including upregulated oxidative phosphorylation, whereas GS pigs showed a profile focused on lipid metabolism and a shift toward energy storage as an adaptation. In contrast, the housing system was the main driver of microbial composition, with ECO housing enriching fermentative taxa such as Lactobacillus and Campylobacter, presumably due to outdoor exposure, while CON housing enriched fewer Lactobacillus but more Clostridium. Breed-Housing combinations analysis revealed distinct adaptive strategies: the modern GL breed responded strongly to housing conditions at both the transcriptional and microbial levels, whereas the traditional GS breed, while also transcriptionally responsive, maintained a more stable microbial community phenotype across environments. Integrated host-microbiome analysis identified a core set of host genes (e.g., PCSK9 and SCD) that were strongly correlated with housing-specific microbes, defining a lipid-inflammation axis.ConclusionBreed and rearing environment jointly shape the porcine jejunal transcriptome and microbiota through distinct strategies. Together, these data provide molecular insight into how traditional and modern breeds differentially respond and potentially adapt to divergent husbandry systems, with implications for health and productivity.Clinical trial numberNot applicable.
authors: Khan HW, Iqbal MA, Reyer H, Trakooljul N, Hadlich F, Oster M, Kuhla B, Keiler J, Wimmers K, Ponsuksili S.

title: The Association of Diet, Intestinal Microbial Starch Utilizers and Butyrate-Producers in Early Life.
abstract: During the first year of life, infant diet changes from liquid to solid food. Resistant starch is one of the first complex carbohydrates available to gut microbiota. With the overall goal to gain mechanistic understanding on the development of microbial starch utilization capacity and its impact on fermentation activity, we investigated the interplay of diet, starch utilizers Ruminococcus bromii and Bifidobacterium adolescentis and the butyrate producer Anaerobutyricum hallii using samples from the longitudinal CARE cohort, and in vitro. Infants started to consume resistant starch at 4 months. While less than one quarter of the infants harboured starch utilizers at 5 months, occurrence increased until the end of year one. In vitro, R. bromii and B. adolescentis degraded resistant starch but only R. bromii released reducing sugars. B. adolescentis formed acetate and lactate. In co-cultures, R. bromii with A. hallii produced more butyrate via reducing sugars than with lactate and acetate from B. adolescentis. At one year of age, infants that harboured both starch utilizer and A. hallii had higher faecal butyrate levels than those without these species. Our results suggest that differences in the mode of resistant starch degradation and cross-feeding contributed to functional redundancy and affected butyrate formation.
authors: Xie J, Frei R, Roduit C, Lauener R, Sasaki M, CK‐CARE Study Group, Schwab C.

title: Targeted Mutagenesis Reveals Noncanonical Genetic Requirements for Carbon Monoxide Oxidation.
abstract: Carbon monoxide (CO) oxidation is a widespread microbial energy metabolism catalysed by MoCu CO dehydrogenase (CODH). Of the two phylogenetically distinct forms (form-I and form-II), only form-I CODH is functionally verified. CODH activity requires maturation of the [CuSMoO2] active site, linked in the carboxydotroph Afipia carboxidovorans OM5 to the genes coxDEF. CODH maturation remains untested outside of this system. Paraburkholderia terrae COX, a recently isolated carboxydovore, encodes both forms of CODH with a reduced and reorganised cox gene cluster. Using targeted mutagenesis, we identify rcoM, coxL, coxF, and coxG as essential for CO oxidation, whereas coxD, coxE, and mocA are non-essential. Deletion of the accessory coxDEF genes produced distinct phenotypes compared to A. carboxidovorans OM5, revealing alternative routes for CODH maturation. Both coxL paralogs were deleted singly and in double knockouts, providing the first molecular evidence that form-II CODH does not contribute to CO oxidation in vivo in these groups of bacteria. Together, these findings show that CODH maturation and function are not universally conserved and caution against inferring CO-oxidising capacity solely from gene presence. Pb. terrae COX emerges as a genetically tractable model for elucidating the diversity and evolution of metalloenzyme assembly pathways in bacteria.
authors: Dawson RA, Hernández M.

title: Microbial Syntrophy Drives Methanogenesis From Residual Hydrocarbons in Anaerobic Oil Sands Tailings.
abstract: Anaerobic oil sands tailings can generate methane for decades as residual naphtha-range and petroleum hydrocarbons sustain microbial metabolism, but how microbial interactions link hydrocarbon turnover to methanogenesis remains poorly resolved. To characterize these microbial associations, we analyse two naphtha-amended anaerobic tailings incubation series using 16S rRNA gene relative abundance, hydrocarbon consumption, and methane production data within a cooperative game-theoretical framework. The abundance-informed Shapley analysis attributes system-level variation to bacterial-archaeal coalitions, highlighting key syntrophic partnerships. Several taxa show inferred contributions to methanogenesis that are disproportionate to their relative abundance, indicating that model-based attribution can differ from abundance ranking. Sensitivity analysis shows that the main methane-attribution patterns remain interpretable across alternative abundance-weighted coefficient formulations. These interaction patterns shift across incubation phases, showing that microbial control over hydrocarbon-dependent methanogenesis changes through time. When incorporated into stochastic forecasting, Shapley-derived reaction intensities improve predictive performance compared with reduced microbial and non-microbial benchmarks. Together, our results indicate that methane production in oil sands tailings can be interpreted through abundance-informed bacterial-archaeal coalition structure, providing a coalition-aware basis for interpreting and forecasting methanogenic hydrocarbon transformation.
authors: Hamidoğlu A, Wang H.
