title: The TCR Motif Atlas: a database of specificities for TCRs recognizing viral, cancer, and autoimmune epitopes.
abstract: T-cell recognition is elicited by the binding between T-cell receptors (TCRs) and epitopes. Many machine learning approaches have been proposed to model TCR-epitope recognition specificity, but most of them act as black boxes. To visualize TCR-epitope recognition specificity, we developed the TCR Motif Atlas (https://tcrmotifatlas.unil.ch). This database builds upon the probabilistic framework of TCR specificity profiles (TSPs) to visualize V and J genes as well as complementarity-determining Region 3 (CDR3) lengths and amino acids enriched in epitope-specific TCRs with respect to baseline TCR repertoires for hundreds of epitopes. An interactive interface enables users to build TSPs based on their own set of TCR sequences to investigate epitope recognition specificity or to explore potential biases in TCR repertoires of known or undetermined specificity. The TCR Motif Atlas further provides links to curated compilations of epitope-specific TCRs and crystal structures of TCR-epitope complexes.
authors: Tadros DM, Shah A, Roessner RA, Racle J, Gfeller D.

title: DectiSomes as broad-spectrum antifungal drugs.
abstract: SUMMARYFungal pathogens represent a significant threat to public health. Aspergillus fumigatus, Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans, and Rhizopus delemar are the primary causative agents for aspergillosis, candidiasis, cryptococcosis, and mucormycosis. They and their closest relatives are responsible for more than 94% of fungal disease-related deaths. All four fungal diseases may lead to meningitis, with mortality rates approaching 99%. They are among the WHO-designated priority fungal pathogens needing new and more effective treatments. In response to this therapeutic gap, we developed DectiSomes-drug-loaded liposomes targeted to fungal cells by host-pathogen receptors. Host-pathogen receptors have many advantages over antibodies as liposome-targeting proteins, including a lack of immunogenicity. Of the pathogen receptors we tested, Dectin-1 and Dectin-2 are the most effective targeting proteins against the fungal pathogens tested. Liposomes loaded with amphotericin B and coated with one of these pathogen receptors bind specifically and strongly to the four pathogens and kill them, reducing the effective dose of amphotericin B by more than an order of magnitude over the untargeted control. DectiSomes are also more effective in murine models of fungal infection. Furthermore, we developed small, malleable versions of DectiSomes with improved drug delivery to the brain and are more effective against cryptococcal meningitis, holding promise for treating all forms of fungal meningitis. Herein, we review our progress and discuss the potential of DectiSomes as a new and effective targeted delivery system for antifungal drugs. In addition, we discuss the challenges associated with fungal diseases and the roadblocks to antifungal drug development and medical mycology research.
authors: Meagher RB, Lewis ZA, Ambati S, Lin X.

title: Is it tuberculosis or chronic pulmonary aspergillosis? Diagnostic challenges, consequences of misdiagnosis, and potential solutions in resource-limited settings.
abstract: SUMMARYChronic pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA) is most often caused by Aspergillus fumigatus and carries significant mortality and morbidity. While the diagnosis of CPA is often delayed, the emergence of CPA among patients with a concurrent or previous history of mycobacterial disease presents a challenge for CPA diagnosis. When patients previously treated for mycobacterial diseases present with new symptoms, it is often unclear whether these symptoms are due to a recurrence of pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB), non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) infection, CPA, co-infection, or another of several other differential diagnoses. Consequently, PTB patients can be misdiagnosed as having smear/GeneXpert-negative PTB. We address these challenges, given the different associated mortality and morbidity of NTM, PTB, and CPA. We proposed a new algorithm to guide clinicians in ruling CPA in or out in both newly diagnosed smear/GeneXpert-negative and NTM patients and those with a previous history of mycobacterial disease. We also recommend follow-up screening of those with a high risk of developing CPA following their PTB/NTM treatment. Implementing screening strategies, such as performing end-of-treatment TB chest X-rays and Aspergillus-specific IgG tests during and at the end of mycobacterial therapy, could facilitate the early diagnosis and treatment of CPA and alleviate associated mortality and morbidity.
authors: Bagheri B, Denning DW, Botha A, Ncube P, Sampson SL.

title: Host genotype-microbiota-metabolome interactions modulate semen quality in Holstein bulls.
abstract: Semen quality is critical for reproductive performance in dairy cattle; however, its microbial, metabolic, and genetic bases remain poorly understood. We integrated rumen microbiota, metabolome, and genome-wide variation from 55 Holstein bulls stratified into relative semen quality high (RSQH) and relative semen quality low (RSQL) groups based on semen quality records to investigate host-microbiome-metabolome interactions associated with fertility. The rumen microbiota was dominated by Bacteroidota, Firmicutes, and Proteobacteria, while Fibrobacter (phylum Fibrobacterota) was enriched in RSQH bulls and positively associated with sperm motility and density. The metabolome distinguished the two groups with 64 discriminatory metabolites, including elevated N-acetyl-L-phenylalanine and prostaglandin H2 in RSQH and sebacic acid in RSQL. Machine learning models were used to prioritize microbial and metabolic features, identifying candidate markers that may contribute to differences in semen quality. Fibrobacter, thromboxane B2, and N1-[4-(cyanomethyl)phenyl]-4-chlorobenzamide emerged as candidate indicators of semen quality, supported by machine learning, high heritability, and genome-wide association study signals. Overall, 511 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were jointly associated with Fibrobacter and these metabolites, including six significantly linked to sperm motility based on GWAS analysis. These SNPs were grouped into two contrasting types, with C1-type variants showing decreasing trends and C2-type variants showing increasing trends in semen quality-related traits. Structural equation modeling revealed that C2-type variants were positively associated with semen traits through microbial and metabolite enrichment, whereas C1-type variants were negatively associated with them. These findings highlight coordinated host genetic, microbial, and metabolic contributions to semen quality in Holstein bulls and provide candidate biomarkers for fertility-related research and breeding.ImportanceImproving bull fertility is important for reproductive efficiency in dairy production, but the biological factors underlying semen quality remain incompletely understood. This study shows that variation in semen quality in Holstein bulls is associated with coordinated differences in rumen microbiota, metabolites, and host genetic variation. In particular, Fibrobacter, thromboxane B2, and N1-[4-(cyanomethyl)phenyl]-4-chlorobenzamide emerged as promising indicators of semen quality. These findings provide a basis for future fertility biomarker research and may support the development of genetics- and microbiota-informed strategies for bull selection and reproductive management.
authors: Ju Z, Jiang Q, Li Y, Zhang Y, Xiao Y, Zhang Y, Wang X, Wei X, Gao Y, Yang C, Liu W, Wang J, Huang J.

title: Atp12 regulates mitochondrial fusion and chronological aging through Fzo1 in Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
abstract: Atp12 is known as a chaperone for mitochondrial ATP synthase assembly, yet its functions and mechanisms in regulating mitochondrial and cellular aging remain elusive. In this study, we demonstrate that Atp12 plays a critical role in regulating mitochondrial dynamics and chronological lifespan (CLS) in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe. We found that Atp12 localizes to mitochondria, and its deletion leads to severe mitochondrial fragmentation, reduced complex II activity, dissipation of mitochondrial membrane potential, and a marked shortening of CLS. Mechanistically, Atp12 acts partially independently of ATP synthase, as the Δatp12Δatp1 double mutant exhibited more severe defects in mitochondrial function and viability than either single mutant, and its mitochondrial morphology resembled that of Δatp12 rather than Δatp1. Transcriptomic and phenotypic analyses identified Fzo1, a mitofusin essential for mitochondrial fusion, as a key downstream target of Atp12 in regulating cellular aging. Further analysis revealed that Atp12 physically interacts with Fzo1 and stabilizes its protein levels. Genetic epistasis experiments demonstrated that Fzo1 insufficiency largely accounts for the mitochondrial fragmentation and functional decline observed in Δatp12 cells, as Fzo1 overexpression effectively rescues these defects. Collectively, these findings uncover a novel function of Atp12 in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis and delaying cellular aging by stabilizing the mitochondrial fusion machinery. Given the evolutionary conservation of Atp12 from yeast to humans, this study provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how the coordination of mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics drives the aging process.IMPORTANCEMitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of cellular aging, but how mitochondria are regulated at the molecular level to influence cellular longevity remains elusive. Here, we reveal that Atp12, a conserved chaperone for ATP synthase assembly, also serves as a stabilizer of the mitofusin Fzo1 to preserve mitochondrial fusion and chronological lifespan in fission yeast. Through direct physical interaction, Atp12 sustains Fzo1 protein levels, thereby maintaining mitochondrial morphology, respiratory function, and cell survival, a function that is largely independent of its canonical role in ATP synthase. This discovery uncovers an unexpected link between a mitochondrial assembly factor and organellar dynamics, establishing the Atp12-Fzo1 axis as a conserved regulatory node that couples mitochondrial quality control to the aging process.
authors: Liu Z, Zhu G, Zeng Y, Deng B, Su Y, Zheng X, Yao R.

title: Molecular basis for bile sensitivity of Escherichia coli with defective LPS O-antigen assembly.
abstract: The periplasmic space between the inner (IM) and outer membranes (OM) of diderm gram-negative bacteria is densely filled with proteins and peptidoglycan cell wall. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is transported through this crowded compartment and then installed at the cell surface. While laboratory-adapted Escherichia coli K-12 strains produce a truncated "rough" LPS, clinical E. coli strains decorate rough LPS with an O-antigen (O-Ag) polysaccharide. At the periplasmic leaflet of the IM, WaaL ligates O-Ag chains onto LPS once it has transited the IM, yielding long "smooth" LPS molecules that are subsequently transported to the OM. Recent reports claim that periplasmic O-Ag chains in ΔwaaL cells disrupt cell envelope integrity to cause bile sensitivity. The presence of long periplasmic O-Ag chains is suggested to stress envelope architecture. Notably, this bile sensitivity is suppressed by disrupting OM-peptidoglycan interactions. Here, we show that even O-Ag repeat units trapped in the cytosol cause bile sensitivity that can be similarly suppressed by disruption of OM-peptidoglycan interactions, despite O-Ag never entering the periplasm. We show that stalled O-Ag chains cause bile sensitivity because they sequester a lipid carrier, limiting its availability for other biosynthetic processes, especially peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis. Indeed, providing more lipid carrier effectively suppressed severe bile sensitivity in ΔwaaL even while increasing the accumulation of long O-Ag chains in the periplasm. Our study clearly shows that periplasmic O-Ag chains do not inherently damage the cell envelope. Rather, stalled O-Ag biogenesis causes a detrimental lipid carrier sequestration that presents as bile sensitivity.IMPORTANCELipopolysaccharide O-antigen (O-Ag) covers the cell surface of wild-type Escherichia coli strains. These long molecules are made inside the crowded periplasmic space and must be accommodated in this compartment. Recent studies reported that long O-Ag chains are toxic molecules in the periplasm, stressing the cell envelope architecture to cause bile sensitivity. We demonstrate that long O-Ag chains in the periplasm are not inherently toxic and that short cytosolic O-Ag repeat units similarly cause bile sensitivity. The accumulation of these O-Ag repeat units or chains acts to sequester an essential lipid carrier, which causes bile sensitivity by impinging on cell wall synthesis. Our study shows that enteric bacteria are vulnerable when lipid carrier availability is reduced, making them more susceptible to the antibacterial effects of bile.
authors: May KL, Muthuraman SM, Grabowicz M.

title: SpoIVA contributes to efficient engulfment through a cytoskeletal-like mechanism during Bacillus subtilis sporulation.
abstract: During endospore (spore) development in bacteria, asymmetric cell division generates two transcriptionally distinct cellular compartments, the mother cell and future spore (forespore). Signaling between these cells leads to sequential and compartmentalized transcription, along with key morphogenetic events, including the phagocytic-like process of engulfment and the recruitment of coat proteins to the engulfing membrane. The SpoIVA ATPase is an essential sporulation protein that assembles into static filaments at the forespore surface during engulfment, where it functions as the basement layer for coat assembly. Here, using Bacillus subtilis, we reveal an additional role for SpoIVA during engulfment. Cytological analysis of a spoIVA null mutant (ΔspoIVA) revealed engulfment defects, such as septal membrane bulges and asymmetric membrane migration, similar to those typically associated with impaired peptidoglycan remodeling during engulfment. Engulfment defects were exacerbated when ΔspoIVA was combined with mutants known to impact engulfment progression and efficiency. Importantly, a spoIVA mutant (K30A) impaired for ATP hydrolysis and filament formation in vitro but partially functional for coat assembly in vivo closely phenocopies the spoIVA null mutant engulfment defects. Based on these data, we propose a model whereby SpoIVA polymerization at the spore surface, independent of coat assembly, plays a mechanical and structural role during engulfment, akin to the cytoskeletal proteins that drive phagocytosis in eukaryotic cells.IMPORTANCEEndospore formation relies on membrane remodeling to generate highly resistant dormant spores in human, animal, and insect pathogens. During engulfment, the mother-cell membrane migrates around the forespore in a phagocytic-like process, while the spore coat is simultaneously assembled. SpoIVA is widely recognized as the ATPase that polymerizes at the forespore surface to nucleate assembly of the multilayered spore coat. Here, we demonstrate that SpoIVA also performs a distinct function during engulfment that is independent of its role in coat formation. Cells lacking SpoIVA, or carrying a polymerization-defective SpoIVA variant, exhibit membrane deformations characteristic of impaired engulfment. We propose that SpoIVA polymers provide structural and mechanical during engulfment, analogous to the role of cytoskeletal systems during eukaryotic phagocytosis.
authors: Fekade B, Gabow S, Coleman K, Bakker S, Graham CLB, Morlot C, Rodrigues CDA.

title: Translational plant microbiome research takes root.
Draft genome sequences of eight fungal strains from arid-agriculture field soil in Arizona, USA.
abstract: We report draft genome sequences for eight fungal isolates, including Aspergillus sp., Aureobasidium sp., Cladosporium sp., Coniochaeta sp., and Fusarium spp. (two strains), Hysteriaceae sp., and Penicillium sp., collected from field soil in an arid-land agriculture site in Arizona, USA, and sequenced by NovaSeq 6000 at ≥30× coverage.
authors: Maro C, Oyekanmi OJ, Spraker J, Lee M-M, Bauer EE, Pauli D, Arnold AE.

title: Population pharmacokinetic modeling of abacavir in HIV-exposed neonates and children with HIV-1 using data from the IMPAACT 2019 and PETITE studies.
abstract: Abacavir (ABC) is one of the primary HIV nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors used in pediatric antiretroviral therapy, yet optimal dosing in neonates and infants is challenging because of rapid developmental changes that influence its pharmacokinetics (PK). In this work, a previously developed pediatric population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) model for ABC was refined to extend its applicability to neonates and young infants by incorporating maturation-related processes and newly available clinical data. PK data from the International Maternal Pediatric Adolescent AIDS Clinical Trials (IMPAACT) 2019 and PETITE studies, which included term neonates (<28 days of life) and infants (<2 years), were integrated into a historical pooled data set of five pediatric studies. Multiple maturation functions and body weight scaling approaches were systematically evaluated to describe developmental changes in ABC disposition. Model performance was assessed using standard goodness-of-fit diagnostics and prediction-corrected visual predictive checks. The final PopPK model incorporated a sigmoid Emax maturation function on oral clearance together with an age-dependent absorption rate constant, providing an accurate description of ABC PK across the full pediatric age range. The updated model successfully captured the higher systemic exposures observed in neonates and infants with immature metabolic capacity during early life. The ABC PK model supports evidence-based dosing guidance for term neonates and young infants.
authors: Kang W-h, Lin Y-W, Chandasana H, Collins J, Bekker A, R Cressey T, Brooks KM, Deprez I, Cheung SYA, Bush M, Mehta R, IMPAACT 2019 Team and PETITE Team.

title: Measles made a stealthy return as another virus took the spotlight.
The Broad Ecological Range of Salmonella enterica Serotype Typhimurium Is Associated With Genomic Diversification.
abstract: Salmonella Typhimurium is a versatile foodborne pathogen with a broad ecological range, making it an ideal model to better understand pathogen adaptations that allow them to infect multiple hosts and persist across environments. Here, we analysed 595 genomes of S. Typhimurium representing three food animal sources (bovine, swine, and poultry) and one non-food animal source (wild birds). We found that S. Typhimurium from food animal sources generally had a more open pangenome and harboured more antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). Notably, swine isolates exhibited the most open pangenome and the highest prevalence of ARGs, patterns that were associated with a greater presence of mobile genetic elements, particularly plasmids. Despite similar core genome sizes, S. Typhimurium from different sources displayed distinct patterns of positive selection in the core genome that varied in frequency and targeted functional categories. In contrast, although accessory genome sizes varied substantially across sources, the frequency of positive selection remained similar. Using machine learning, we identified source-predictive genetic variants, many of which are associated with stress-response functions. These findings suggest that gain and loss of accessory genes and positive selection acting on core genes support differential adaptation in S. Typhimurium, potentially contributing to its broad ecological range.
authors: Ohri L, Chinnareddy S, Goh YX, Zhang H, Deng X, Pruden A, Cheng R, Li S, Liao J.

title: Host Development and Environment Influence the Microbiomes of Aquatic Insects and Riparian Spiders.
abstract: Larval aquatic insects harbour diverse microbiomes critical for physiology and development, yet the effects of metamorphosis combined with environmental exposures on this community remain unknown. Herein we examined bacterial microbiome composition and predicted function across larval and adult stages of three families of aquatic insects and riparian spider predators, collected upstream and downstream of wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) in Ontario, Canada. Insect host developmental stage was the primary driver of microbiome structure. Larval microbiomes were more diverse and showed higher abundances in pathways reflecting active feeding. Larval and adult populations of holometabolous insects shared few ASVs (3.8%-12.6% of the combined ASV pool), whereas a larger proportion was shared in hemimetabolous insects (23.4%). WWTP effluent exposures led to selective microbial filtering rather than broad community restructuring. Macroinvertebrate and spider microbiomes sampled downstream were characterized by higher abundances in bacterial taxa associated with wastewaters and increased xenobiotic degradation pathways. Such impacts on spider microbiomes provide evidence that ecological impacts of effluents cross the aquatic-terrestrial boundary. Lastly, a significant decrease of vertically transmitted endosymbionts (Rickettsiella, Wolbachia) was detected in aquatic insects, representing a pathway through which effluent pollution may affect host fitness without detectably altering overall microbiome diversity.
authors: Esser M, Perrotta B, Kidd K.

title: Functional Genomics of a Zinc-Solubilising Kosakonia cowanii RL-16 and Its Application for Zinc Biofortification in Oryza sativa L.
abstract: Zinc (Zn) is assumed to be the most important micronutrient due to its involvement in different biochemical processes. The daily requirement of Zn for the human body, however, cannot be fulfilled by traditional staple crops such as rice due to its low availability to plants, especially in alkaline soils. The present study was carried out to investigate the potential of indigenous microbial flora, isolated from different agroecological zones, for Zn solubilization and combating Zn deficiency in rice. Out of a total of 135 isolates, RL-16, identified as Kosakonia cowanii, emerged as the most valuable resource for sustainable agricultural applications due to its incredible Zn solubilization potential and additional PGP characteristics. Gene mining of RL-16 revealed the footprints of solubilization of Zn and other nutrients. Under microcosmic conditions, zinc content was significantly improved for the treatment with RL-16 (134.7 mg/kg ± 0.6), compared to the control containing only an insoluble zinc source (107.7 mg/kg ± 1.6). Zinc translocation in seed (ZnSd) was enhanced by the application of RL-16 across both varieties, which was also confirmed by field evaluation. This study demonstrates the whole genome sequence analysis of Kosakonia cowanii and its potential role in Zn biofortification for more targeted and sustainable agricultural practices.
authors: Ikram A, Marghoob MU, Ali H, Hassan N, Zia-Ul-Qamar, Nawaz A, Saqib A, Azam HMH, Sana S, Imtiaz M, Akhtar K, Mubeen F.

title: Industrialization drives convergent microbiome and host physiological shifts in the human metaorganism.
abstract: Understanding how industrialization reshapes the human metaorganism requires integrating microbiome ecology with host physiology across globally diverse populations. Here, we generate multivariate data from the Global Microbiome Conservancy cohort, including gut microbiome, immunoglobulin A (IgA) sequencing, host genotyping, diet, lifestyle, and fecal biomarker profiles, to investigate host-microbiome interactions across gradients of industrialization and geography. We show that industrialization is associated with homogenized microbial compositions, reduced microbial diversity, and lower community stability, independent of host confounders. We further show that industrialization is linked to elevated markers of gut stress, increased IgA secretion, and altered patterns of IgA-bacteria interactions. Finally, we show that microbiome-based disease predictors trained on industrialized populations are uninformative in less industrialized cohorts, highlighting limited cross-population transferability. Together, our results reveal coordinated restructuring of the microbial ecosystem and host physiology and emphasize the need for inclusive, globally representative data to improve translational microbiome applications across diverse human populations.
authors: Poyet M, Rühlemann M, Schaan AP, Ma Y, Moitinho-Silva L, Wacker EM, Jebens H, Patel L, Nguyen LTT, Zimmer A, Plichta D, McDonald D, Stevens C, Agyei A, Afihene MY, Asibey SO, Awuku YA, Badiane AS, Corzett C, Deme A, Dominguez-Rodrigo M, Duah A, Fezeu A, Froment A, Gibbons S, Girard C, Hooker J, Ibrahim F, Iqaluk D, Juimo V, Kettunen P, Lafosse S, Lango-Yaya E, Lee SC, Lehtimäki J, Lim YAL, Mabulla A, Mahachai V, Mohamed RS, Moniz K, Mwikarago IE, Nartey YA, Ndiaye D, Noel M, Onyekwere C, Pin TM, Plymoth A, Roberts L, Ruokolainen L, Rusine J, Segurel L, Shapiro BJ, Sigwazi S, Sistiaga A, Valles K, Vatanen T, Vilaichone RK, Rosenstiel P, Baines J, Franke A, Ellinghaus D, Knight R, Daly M, Xavier RJ, Alm EJ, Groussin M.

title: Convergent genomic evolution of human gut bacteria along an industrialization gradient.
abstract: Whether human-associated environments drive adaptive genome evolution in gut commensal bacteria remains largely unknown. Here, we investigate how genomic adaptation in gut bacteria differs between industrialized and non-industrialized human populations. We generated a collection of isolate genomes spanning diverse host geographies, lifestyles, species, and strains. We first found that, compared with metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), paired isolate genomes recover more functional elements and signals of horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Leveraging isolate genomes from multiple species, we find that strains from industrialized hosts experience an expansion of proteome size and harbor greater pangenome fluidity, driven by recent HGT events. Gene- and variant-level analyses reveal convergent patterns of lifestyle-specific adaptation in functions that are critical for ecological adaptation, such as the stress response, cell-envelope remodeling, and central metabolism. Our results demonstrate that industrialization drives convergent genome evolution in gut bacteria, providing a framework for understanding the mechanisms of microbial adaptation to rapidly changing human environments.
authors: Rühlemann M, Ma Y, Szánthó LL, Waschina S, Moitinho-Silva L, Mews LC, Faus-Camarena J, Jebens H, Costa J, Juimo V, Fezeu A, Agyei A, Afihene MY, Asibey SO, Awuku YA, Duah A, Nartey YA, Ibrahim F, Lim YAL, Tan MP, Onyekwere C, Rusine J, Mwikarago IE, Baines J, Franke A, Szöllősi GJ, Xavier RJ, Alm EJ, Groussin M, Poyet M.

title: Exposure to immune stimuli augments alveolar macrophages to acquire neutrophil antimicrobial molecules to prevent bacterial pneumonia.
abstract: The protective adaptation of innate immune defenses against respiratory pathogens has been linked to previous exposure to immune stimuli; however, the underlying mechanisms of these adaptations are not yet fully understood. Here, we show that pre-exposure to a low dose of non-specific immune stimuli or infection protects against subsequent lethal methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) challenge. This enhanced protection concurs with increased alveolar macrophages (AMs) resulting from a self-renewal process in the lungs. Importantly, these AMs are programmed to acquire neutrophil-released antimicrobial enzymes from the extracellular space to clear MRSA, prevent tissue damage, and rapidly restore lung homeostasis. AM function depends on differential gene expression, including expression of the efferocytosis receptor Mer proto-oncogene tyrosine kinase (MerTK) and the anti-apoptotic regulator Bcl-xL. Thus, our data highlight that AMs acquire neutrophil enzymes as an integral component of innate immune adaptation.
authors: Sharma A, Heffernan LM, Mayandi V, Tumpa ZH, Pirashanna N, Jois SD, Beavers WN, Abuaita BH.

title: Fungal-bacterial interactions.
abstract: The study of fungal-bacterial interactions is an emerging field of biology with relevance for environmental health, medicine, and agriculture, among other sectors. The frequent co-occurrence of fungi and bacteria in many habitats has facilitated the evolution of their symbioses. Both groups are key players in host-associated microbiomes and in nutrient cycling, and these roles often intersect in dynamic ways. Interactions between fungi and bacteria can be mutualistic, commensal, or pathogenic, and they can vary in a context-dependent manner. In mutualistic interactions, fungi and bacteria can exchange nutrients, ameliorate each other's stress, enhance growth, enable dispersal, and facilitate novel niche exploration via metabolite exchange. In contrast, antagonistic interactions frequently involve competition for limited nutrients, such as iron, and active chemical warfare with secreted and bioactive compounds. Bacteria associated with fungi can occur inside of fungal cells (endosymbiotic) or on the surface of fungal hyphae (exosymbiotic). Endosymbiotic bacteria can be further differentiated into facultative symbionts, which retain the ability to enter fungal hyphae but also live independently, and obligate endosymbionts, which are always intracellular and not capable of independent life outside of hyphae. Whereas free-living bacteria can be pathogenic or mutualistic, endosymbiotic bacteria are often regarded as commensals or mutualists, although some can exhibit parasitic attributes in some conditions. A combination of molecular genetics, genomics, and microscopy has been used to study free-living bacteria. In addition to these approaches, fluorescence and electron microscopy have been used as the gold standards to study and differentiate endosymbiotic bacteria based on their intracellular location. More recently, researchers have started using systems-biology approaches to study fungal-bacterial interactions including high-throughput -omics assays. These methods produce expansive datasets that are ideally suited to artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches to tackle long-standing questions about the basic biology and evolution of fungal-bacterial interactions. In this primer we give an overview of fungal-bacterial interactions, including their diversity, community structure, and symbiotic evolution. We highlight two research systems in particular: the intracellular endosymbionts of Mucoromycota fungi and the free-living bacteria associated with edible fungi. We focus on these systems because fungi remain understudied relative to other groups, and only a handful of fungal taxa with their bacterial symbionts are backed by large enough data sets to explore these concepts in detail. Our aim here is not to be comprehensive, but instead to use the most well-understood systems to illustrate emerging principles. We then discuss advances in using AI to infer new aspects of microbial biology and provide suggestions for how these technologies could advance research on fungal-bacterial interactions utilizing existing genomic datasets.
authors: Uehling J, Gohar D, Johnson H.

title: Biodiversity conservation: A fungus-free refuge for Colombia's amphibians.
abstract: New research suggests that the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, a high elevation biodiversity hotspot in northern Colombia, may be one of just a few places left on Earth where amphibian communities have not been affected by the fungal disease chytridiomycosis.
authors: Richards-Zawacki C.

title: Genome evolution: An archaeon stripped bare.
abstract: A newly described archaeon has the smallest genome yet found in its domain, less than half the previous record, stripped of nearly all metabolism and retaining little beyond the machinery to replicate itself. Its biology and evolution remain enigmatic.
authors: van Beveren F, Ettema TJG.

title: Selective profiling of translationally active tRNAs and their dynamics under stress.
abstract: During translation, transfer RNAs (tRNAs) deliver specific amino acids to the ribosome in a coordinated manner with the sequence encoded by the messenger RNA. Despite their central role in protein synthesis, their precise contribution to the modulation of translation remains poorly understood, primarily due to lack of methods to characterize tRNA abundances and their modifications from actively translating ribosomes. Here we develop tRIBO-seq, a simple and robust nanopore-based method to selectively capture ribosome-associated native tRNA populations (ribo-tRNAs) from actively translating ribosomes, providing tRNA abundance, modification and fragmentation information from a single experiment. Using tRIBO-seq, we find that ribo-tRNAs, but often not total tRNAs, are significantly altered on stress. Notably, we find that tRNAome alterations strongly vary depending on the stress type; while viral infection and leucine deprivation leads to changes in ribo-tRNA abundances, methionine starvation causes a dramatic loss of methyl-based tRNA modifications. By contrast, we find that arsenite exposure does not alter tRNA abundances nor modification patterns, but rather causes major fragmentation events in selected subsets of ribo-tRNAs. Altogether, tRIBO-seq offers a robust and reproducible approach to map the full tRNA landscape-capturing tRNA abundance, modification and fragmentation patterns-across both total and actively translating tRNA populations, revealing the dynamics of the tRNAome with unprecedented resolution, in a single experiment.
authors: Monti M, Yilmaz H, Del Piano A, Arnoldi M, Bonomo I, Llovera L, Sarabando J, Ribeiro D, Soares AR, Clamer M, Novoa EM.

title: Conserved synaptic modifications by humanized tau through diverse isoform- and mutation-specific intracellular interactions
abstract: Mutations in the microtubule-binding protein tau are considered causal for a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively referred to as primary tauopathies. Specific tauopathies are associated with different mutations, distinct tau isoforms, manifest in unique cellular and circuit-wide patterns of degeneration, and present with specific clinical symptoms and trajectories. The mechanisms that link variations in the primary tau protein structure to distinct forms of neural circuit dysfunction remain largely unknown. Here, we created an orthogonal viral resource to systematically examine the impact of expressing humanized tau isoforms harboring different disease-relevant mutations in excitatory pyramidal cells from the mouse prelimbic cortex. We used these reagents to show that expression of mutant humanized tau (hTau) as either of two isoforms produced very similar patterns of circuit-specific synaptic disconnection on cortical projection neurons. However, mass spectrometry revealed that the interactomes of these different tau species varied markedly as functions of isoform, mutation, and subcellular location. We validated the functional relevance of increased hTau interactions with mitochondrial proteins in induced neurons differentiated from Ngn2-iPSCs expressing different hTau constructs. These results suggest different disease-relevant hTau proteins likely use distinct mechanisms to drive a highly stereotyped form of synapse loss in cortical neurons.
authors: Nickerson, E.; Pomeroy-Tuck, J.; Pratt, S.; Rodriguez, C.; Zhao, T.; Stodola, T.; Hoffman, B.; Maser, R.; Bloss, E.

title: Structural basis of ribosomal RNA repair by RtcB2
abstract: Ribotoxins disable ribosomes by cleaving ribosomal RNA, but how repair enzymes recognize and restore these damaged machines remains unclear. Here, we report three cryo-electron microscopy structures of the RNA ligase RtcB2 bound to damaged Escherichia coli 30S subunits. An extended interface stabilizes the ribosomal head and decoding-center scaffold while positioning the cleaved 3'-phosphate end within the catalytic pocket. Two structures contain enzyme-linked guanosine monophosphate, whereas the third captures its transfer to the RNA. RNA activation accompanies RtcB2 reorientation and entry of the 5'-hydroxyl-containing segment into an adjacent cleft. Comparisons with assembled ribosomes reveal structural barriers to substrate access. These structures connect recognition of a damaged ribosome to chemical activation of its RNA for repair.
authors: Tian, Y.; Zhou, Q.; Yu, Q.; Huang, Y.; Zhang, W.; Huang, J.; Yu, T.; Zeng, F.

title: Histopathological and virus-associated features of Boid Inclusion Body Disease in Boa constrictor
abstract: Boid inclusion body disease (BIBD) is a reptarenavirus-induced fatal disease of boid snakes that, while diagnosed with ease due to the pathognomonic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (IB), is not yet fully characterized pathomorphologically and with regards to its pathogenesis. The present study retrospectively investigated a random cohort of 50 captive male and female boa constrictors of variable age (neonate to 25 years) for histopathological changes and in situ viral protein (nucleoprotein, NP, and glycoprotein 2, GP2) expression patterns. IB formation and NP expression were scored semiquantitatively. The vast majority of snakes (42/50; 84%) exhibited histopathological changes; these mainly (39/42; 93%) represented inflammatory processes that most frequently affected the gastrointestinal tract. Overall, IB and NP scores were significantly higher in the more recent cases (2020-2025) compared to the older cases (2000-2003). NP scores did not differ between age groups or sex, but were lower in animals with clinical signs and higher in those with histopathological changes. No statistically significant association was found between NP scores and inflammatory processes, neither in general nor in individual organs. GP2 expression, as an indicator of virion assembly, was less consistent than NP expression and generally restricted to individual cells with and without IBs. There was no histological evidence of overt damage in infected cells. Jointly, the results indicate different phases of restrictive and systemic viral replication that are not directly associated with pathological processes and/or clinical signs.
authors: Bogner, M.; Dervas, E.; De Neck, S.; Hepojoki, J.; Baggio, F.; Hetzel, U.; Kipar, A.

title: The Application of 3D Cryo-Volume Electron Microscopy to Visualize and Quantify the Photosynthetic Filamentous Cyanobacterium Anabaena
abstract: Cryogenic volume electron microscopy (cryo-vEM) is a rapidly developing nanoscale imaging approach that enables three-dimensional datasets of vitrified cells and tissues at intermediate resolutions without treatment with chemical fixatives or metal contrasting agents. Our goal was to evaluate the suitability of cryo-vEM for whole cells of photosynthetic organisms such as cyanobacteria. Two species of Anabaena, a filamentous cyanobacterium, were captured on poly-L-lysine-coated grids, vitrified by plunge-freezing into liquid ethane, and mapped by secondary electron and integrated fluorescence light microscopy to identify target cells. Cells of interest were coated with platinum, trenched with xenon, and 3D volumes collected by alternating argon milling and through-lens detector (TLD) imaging on a Thermo Scientific Hydra plasma focused ion beam scanning electron microscope. Volumes were segmented via 2.5D U-Net models, then quantified in Dragonfly 3D World. Block-face images revealed the cell wall, thylakoids, phycobilisomes, carboxysomes, cyanophycin and polyphosphate granules. Whole-cell 3D rendering allowed quantification of carboxysomes, cyanophycin granules, and measurement of thylakoid thickness and spacing in A. inaequalis and Anabaena sp. UTEX 2576. Thus, cryo-vEM provided interpretable whole-cell ultrastructure of cyanobacteria without chemical pre-treatment, and its compatibility with cryo-fluorescence and in situ cryo-ET enables contextual multi-scale perspectives from whole cells to molecular structures.
authors: Angermeier, A. R.; Rotkina, L. G.; Lebow, C.; Chiu, W.; Burch-Smith, T. M.; Czymmek, K. J.

title: Stochastic gene expression drives state switching and phenotypic heterogeneity in RNA repair
abstract: Bacterial populations often exhibit variability in cellular responses to antibiotics which can affect treatment success and survival outcomes. This heterogeneity suggests that genetically identical cells can occupy different states of susceptibility within the same population. Better understanding of these dynamic responses is essential for determining how cells respond to stress and survive antibiotic-induced damage. In this work, we investigate heterogeneity in antibiotic responses driven by the Rtc RNA repair system in E. coli. We develop a stochastic model of Rtc-mediated RNA repair to identify the drivers of heterogeneity at the single-cell level. We observe bimodality in cellular translational capacity and a transient memory in predicted responses to RNA damage, demonstrating how intrinsic stochasticity in Rtc-regulation can lead to phenotypic heterogeneity. Classifying single-cell trajectories, we predict drivers of state switching between the resistant and susceptible states, finding that stochastic expression of the rtc regulator determines entry into a resistant cell state, while dilution drives the system back into a susceptible state. These results indicate that heterogeneity in RNA repair emerges from stochastic switching between states, offering a route to understanding how individual cells survive in the presence of translation-targeting antibiotics.
authors: Hindley, H. J.; Lara Molina, R.; Weisse, A. Y.

title: GPBench: A benchmark framework for genomic prediction
abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) has emerged as a powerful data mining strategy for disease risk assessment and molecular breeding. GP leverages genome-wide genetic variations and phenotypic information through a computational model to estimate genetic potential or disease risk. However, the field of GP still faces several major challenges: (i) dataset bias and insufficient representativeness; (ii) the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and a systematic benchmarking framework; (iii) heavy reliance on empirical expertise for experimental result interpretation, which hinders large-scale and systematic analysis. These issues make it difficult to conduct systematic cross-species evaluation and comparison of GP methods, and their authentic applications. To address these challenges, we established a standardized and extensible GP benchmark framework-GPBench. We first collected and harmonized public datasets from 16 species, covering animals, plants, and microorganisms, comprising 57 traits, 40,821 samples, and 493,821 single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Then, using the standardized datasets, the framework evaluates 21 GP models and provides a unified assessment across four dimensions: effectiveness, sensitivity, robustness, and scalability. Furthermore, we developed a large language model-based intelligent analysis system to facilitate the interpretation of GP experiments and model recommendations. GPBench provides the community with a fair, unified, and scalable platform (https://www.sdu-idea.cn/GPBench/) and an open-source library for comparing and optimizing GP methods, ultimately accelerating the application of GP in life sciences and biomedical research.
authors: Zhang X, Luo H, Li G, Zhang X, Wang S, Liu L, Guo M, Tan Q, Domeniconi C, Chen J, Wang J, Yu G.

title: The  Braarudosphaera bigelowii  genome reveals cellular remodeling around a nitrogen-fixing organelle
abstract: Braarudosphaera bigelowii hosts the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial organelle UCYN-A, or the nitroplast, but the absence of a reference genome has limited investigation of the genomic features accompanying this association. Here, we present nuclear and organellar genome resources for the cultured  B. bigelowii strain FR-21. The assembly comprises a 472.1-Mb nuclear genome together with representative nitroplast, chloroplast, and mitochondrial genomes of 1.49 Mb, 107 kb, and 44 kb, respectively. The four genomic compartments have strongly differentiated GC compositions, consistent with their distinct evolutionary origins.  The large nuclear genome does not appear to reflect a corresponding expansion of protein-coding capacity. Repeat annotation indicates that approximately 77% of the nuclear assembly is repetitive, leaving approximately 108 Mb of nonrepetitive sequence containing roughly 16,000 predicted protein-coding genes. Phylogenomic analysis places  B. bigelowii within the expected diversity of haptophytes, indicating that its unusual diazotrophic lifestyle is not associated with an anomalous phylogenetic position.  Comparative analysis of nitrogen metabolism genes reveals extensive remodeling of host nitrogen acquisition and assimilation.  B. bigelowii lacks major components required for nitrate and nitrite assimilation and has reduced capacity to use urea, cyanate, and several internally recycled nitrogen sources. In contrast, ammonium transport and the glutamine synthetase-glutamate synthase pathway are retained. This combination suggests reduced flexibility in nitrogen use and a host metabolism increasingly centered on ammonium supplied by the nitroplast.  B. bigelowii also encodes an expanded set of flavodoxin and cryptochrome genes. Eleven of 14 flavodoxin candidates and 21 of 39 cryptochrome candidates contained motifs linked to nitroplast targeting. Together with previous evidence that some of these proteins are abundantly imported into the nitroplast, these expansions point to host-encoded roles in nitroplast redox metabolism and diel regulation.  These genome resources establish a foundation for investigating nitroplast protein import, host-organelle metabolic integration, and the genomic consequences of acquiring an intracellular nitrogen-fixing compartment. They further show that the evolution of the  B. bigelowii -UCYN-A relationship involved substantial remodeling of genome architecture and nitrogen metabolism in both partners.
authors: Coale TH, Füssy Z, Cornejo-Castillo FM, Mak WKE, Turk-Kubo KA, Hagino K, Zehr JP.

title: Recruitment of intrasegmental and propriospinal interneuron networks of forelimb motor circuitry in chronic cervical contusion spinal cord injury
abstract: Cervical spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts descending supraspinal input and spinal networks controlling upper extremity motor function, making recovery of arm and hand function a major priority for affected individuals. The vast majority of regenerative strategies have been studied during the acute and sub-acute phases following SCI, while therapeutic testing remains limited for chronic injury, when persistent barriers significantly limit circuit remodeling. We asked whether pharmacologic enhancement of neuronal-intrinsic axon growth capacity through PTEN inhibition could promote forelimb motor recovery and circuit plasticity in a rodent model of chronic cervical SCI. Following C5 hemi-contusion, female rats underwent behavioral testing of forelimb motor function and received PTEN antagonist peptide (PAP) beginning at a chronic time point, and the trans-synaptic tracer, pseudorabies virus (PRV), was injected into ipsilesional triceps to trace forelimb-associated motor circuitry. PAP selectively improved forelimb usage during cylinder paw-preference testing, but not strength, sensorimotor, or gait-related forelimb measures. PAP increased recruitment of PRV-traced local-projecting and propriospinal interneuron networks. In addition, PAP enhanced synaptic input to these recruited propriospinal interneurons, raising the possibility that spared descending pathways may contribute to recovery through spinal relay circuits. Lastly, we mapped the supraspinal connectome providing descending input from brainstem to the lower motor neurons innervating forelimb muscle, and we determined how this connectome was impacted both by SCI and PAP. Together, these findings show that, even in chronic SCI, pharmacological PTEN inhibition can promote forelimb functional recovery and significant circuit remodeling, with spinal interneuron networks emerging as a key site of PAP-induced plasticity.
authors: Crowther, K.; Harbeck, A.; Middlesworth, M.; Bosch, M.; Lyttle, M. A.; MacGibbon, C.; Jaffe, D. A.; Michel-Flutot, P.; Fitchett, E.; Li, S.; Lepore, A. C.

title: Proteome-Wide Serology Identifies Secreted IgD against RSV Fusion Glycoprotein as a Signature of Broadly Elevated Antibody Response
abstract: Serological evaluation of antibody response using conventional indirect immunoassays cannot capture the full depth, diversity, and functional complexity of human polyclonal antibodies. Here, we developed mass spectrometry-based Proteome-Wide Serology (ProWiSe) assays for the identification and absolute quantification of antigen-specific human antibodies across isotypes, subclasses, and variable-region repertoires. Using ProWiSe, we measured the depth and diversity of serum antibodies to multiple antigens of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a pathogen associated with repeated reinfections and skewed immune response. IgG1 antibodies targeting the fusion glycoprotein F (RSVF) dominated the antibody response, with a background-corrected median level of 1,700 ng/mL across 214 healthy maternal serum samples from the general population. ProWiSe identified reproducible co-enrichment of complement component 1q complexes, revealed the usage of several dozen IGHV variable-region germline genes in the anti-RSVF polyclonal response, and suggested limited IGHV repertoire diversity in some individuals. In addition to IgG1, we discovered a complex antibody response characterized by significantly elevated levels of nearly all human immunoglobulin isotypes and subclasses, including previously unexplored IgG4 and IgD. The identification of high-affinity IgD against prefusion and postfusion RSVF, but not against other antigens studied, was the most unexpected observation, occurring in 52% of the healthy maternal serum samples. ProWiSe unambiguously identified the secreted IgD isoform P01880-1 and supported the IgD paradox of preferential {lambda} light-chain usage in secreted IgD. Detectable anti-RSVF IgD levels ([≥]0.11 ng/mL) correlated with broadly elevated antibody responses across all other isotypes and subclasses, except IgE. ProWiSe assays offer a versatile platform for quantitative serological diagnostics, exploration of depth, diversity, and dynamics of polyclonal antibody response, and discovery of rare antibody isotypes.
authors: Turner, Z.; Tang, W.; Rais, Y.; Drabovich, A. P.

title: COSMOS: integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics for mosquito-borne disease
abstract: By 2050, almost half of the global population will be at risk of mosquito-borne disease. Effective response requires monitoring both pathogen transmission and vector abundance, yet these are typically assessed using separate assays with limited taxonomic breadth. Here we present COSMOS (COmprehensive Sequencing for MOSquito-borne disease), a targeted metagenomics workflow designed to reconstruct pathogen genomes and mosquito community composition directly from mixed field-collected samples. Over three annual rounds of a major Australian surveillance program, we evaluated >120,000 mosquitoes in 219 traps, with 98.7% agreement with surveillance data across seven monitored arboviruses, and additional detections of Sindbis virus and the state's first detection of encephalitic Little Sussex virus. Of 137 viral detections, 101 yielded near-complete genomes (>90% coverage) at median 95x depth. Using an accompanying computational workflow, COSMOS quantified mosquito composition, matching entomological estimates of reported vector species (CCC 0.78-0.89). Joint analysis of virus and vector composition identified structured mosquito communities associated with spatial and temporal environmental variation, allowing the ecological context of arbovirus detections to be characterised. Detections during the Murray Valley encephalitis virus outbreak in 2023 were concentrated within a narrowly defined mosquito-community space corresponding to rural communities dominated by the inland S-AUS sub-lineage of Culex annulirostris. Integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics provides ecological and evolutionary context for arbovirus activity within a single scalable workflow for surveillance and outbreak response.
authors: Forster, A. J.; Khan, A. A.; Garrett, E.; Toi, C.; Suster, C. J.; Haniotis, J.; Dang, K.; Watson, J.; Doggett, S.; Chen, S. C.-A.; Watts, M. R.; Kok, J.; Sintchenko, V.; Payne, M.; Webb, C.; Rockett, R. J.; Golubchik, T.

title: Factors affecting microbial community composition in Split Lake, MB, Canada
abstract: Split Lake is a large freshwater lake in northern Manitoba, Canada, that receives major inflows from the Nelson River, Burntwood River, and Grassy River. In 1976, during the Churchill River Diversion (CRD) project, most of the water in the Churchill River was diverted into the Nelson River via the Rat River, and the Burntwood River, creating a large inflow pressure in the lower Nelson area, including Split Lake. Decades after its implementation, the Churchill River Diversion still influences ecological and environmental processes in the area. In this study, metabarcoding of the 16S rRNA gene was employed to characterize the microbial community structure of the lake. Environmental factors (temperature, pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen) and cyanotoxin levels were also assessed.  The objectives of this study were to establish a baseline for microbiota across the lake and examine how environmental variables affect microbial population dynamics. The study was conducted in the summer of 2024, encompassing 14 sites on Split Lake and 2 sites on Assean Lake, an adjacent waterbody with minimal influence from hydroelectric infrastructure. Split Lake was found to harbor six distinct microbial clusters, with turbidity and dissolved oxygen levels correlating with different aquatic regimes within the lake. The predominant taxa in Split Lake included Actinobacteria hgcI clade and  Cyanobium . Microcystin concentrations measured throughout the study were always below the Maximum Acceptable Concentration (MAC) set for Canadian federal drinking water standards.
authors: Vidanage T, Tataskweyak Environmental Monitoring Agency, Collins RE.

title: Particle-Associated Prokaryotic Community Structures in the Bering and Chukchi Seas
abstract: Free-living and particle-associated bacteria play distinct roles in the cycling of organic matter, but how these lifestyles are partitioned in the highly productive, rapidly warming Bering and Chukchi Seas is largely unknown. During the Arctic Shelf Growth, Advection, Respiration and Deposition Rate Experiments (ASGARD) cruise in June 2017, a period of anomalously warm sea surface temperatures, we collected 78 samples at three depths (surface, middle, and bottom) at 12 process stations and sequentially filtered them onto 20 {micro}m, 3 {micro}m, and 0.2 {micro}m filters. Using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and hierarchical clustering of amplicon sequence variant (ASV) relative abundances, we resolved four sample clusters. Although pore size was not used to build the clusters, communities separated into a free-living cluster associated mainly with Anadyr Water (FL1; 0.2 {micro}m fraction) and three particle-associated clusters (PA1-PA3; 3 and 20 {micro}m fractions), several of which were enriched in Bacteroidia. Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacteroidia were present in all size fractions, with Gammaproteobacteria most biased toward the free-living fraction. Community structure did not differ with depth, consistent with the shallow, weakly stratified shelf, and distance-based redundancy analysis identified salinity as the sole significant environmental factor distinguishing communities. These results suggest that lifestyle and water-mass origin, rather than depth, structure size-fractionated bacterial communities on the Pacific Arctic shelf, and that freshening and changes in bloom dynamics could reshape particle-associated communities in this region.
authors: Shibue, R.; Collins, R. E.

title: GOParsimony: parsimonious saltation across the Gene Ontology digraph for efficient functional annotation
abstract: Background. The Gene Ontology (GO) is standardly probed by biological researchers keen to discern the functional tendencies of their gene/protein data sets. However, lists of GO terms are often ontically overwhelming, and need to be filtered to remove redundancy. Methods for such filtering either employ predefined lists of terms that may not actually be relevant to a specific gene/protein set, or apply arbitrary thresholds, such as for semantic distance (i.e., GO term dissimilarity). Methods. Here, I introduce the tool GOParsimony, which is designed to avoid such issues and to pick out the most parsimonious (i.e., simplest, most concise) explanation for the functional tendencies of any set of proteins/genes. It achieves this by saltating across the GO digraph, assigning and updating cascades of term precedence until convergence. The set of GO terms assigned precedence = 1 is the most parsimonious set. Hierarchical clustering with other GO terms with higher precedence levels can be investigated for clues about functional modules. Results. GO term precedence graphs and two-dimensional heatmaps of GO terms and genes/proteins are output, along with other plots that can be cross-referenced for functional insights. In test analyses for five example data sets from budding yeast and human, GOParsimony consistently produces reduced GO term lists that have greater significance and low or intermediate coverage of the space of significant GO terms, when compared to other distributed methods in default mode. GOParsimony can be obtained at: https://github.com/pmharrison/GOParsimony .
authors: Harrison, P. M.

title: Tn-Seq-based identification of genes that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates
abstract: Microbial biofilms, whether surface-associated or in the form of aggregated microbes, cause a variety of persistent infections due to their inherent tolerance to antibiotic treatment. Current knowledge of the mechanistic basis of biofilm-associated antibiotic tolerance is fragmented, and the relative importance of previously identified factors remains unknown. We developed a Tn-Seq-based workflow that enables simultaneous assessment of the relative antibiotic tolerance of thousands of individual clonal bacterial aggregates, each established by a single transposon mutant. Using this genome-wide Tn-Seq analysis approach, we identified several factors and pathways that play a role in antimicrobial tolerance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa aggregates. The majority of these factors are important for aggregate-associated tolerance to specific antibiotics, whereas some factors play a role in aggregate-associated tolerance regardless of the class of antibiotic. This methodology provides a framework that can be adapted to investigate aggregate-associated tolerance for other bacterial species and in response to different antimicrobial agents and stressors.
authors: Goltermann, L.; Gualdi, S.; Rybtke, M.; Shahryari, S.; Liang, Z.; Lin, S.; Kragh, K. N.; Eberl, L.; Tolker-Nielsen, T.

title: Metabolic engineering of Saccharomyces cerevisiae for improved polyphosphate production
abstract: Finite high-grade phosphate rock reserves and rising legislative demand for phosphorus recycling create a need for processes converting phosphorus-containing residual streams into valuable products. Microbial synthesis of inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) could complement its energy-intensive chemical manufacturing while enabling phosphorus recovery in a value-added product with applications ranging from food processing to flame retardants and fertilizer. After orthophosphate (Pi) starvation and refeeding, Saccharomyces cerevisiae naturally accumulates polyP as a cellular Pi reserve, but the current multistage process complicates industrial implementation. Here, we identified metabolic interventions that uncouple polyP accumulation from Pi starvation by systematic evaluation of 57 engineered S. cerevisiae CEN.PK113-7D strains. Constitutive activation of the PHO regulon produced the strongest increase in polyP, whereas disruption of inositol pyrophosphate synthesis, Pi import, or the vacuolar transporter chaperone complex impaired accumulation. This pattern indicates that efficient polyP accumulation depends on coordinated activation of Pi acquisition and vacuolar polymerization. Notably, deletion of PHO80 converted a transient starvation response into a constitutive production phenotype, enabling high polyP accumulation during growth. Optimization of the growth medium increased the polyP content further, and efficient use of the supplied Pi was demonstrated, while electron microscopy paired with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy supported increased vacuolar storage. During aerobic exponential fed-batch cultivation, pho80{Delta} simultaneously formed biomass and polyP, reaching a polyP content of 22.1% of cell dry weight and a titer of 8.2 g/L, both expressed as KPO3 equivalents. These findings establish S. cerevisiae pho80{Delta} as a promising platform for biological polyP production and phosphorus recovery.
authors: Baier, M.; Karmainski, T.; Buhl, E. M.; Deitert, A.; Eerlings, R.; Voelker, F.; Brans, L.; Deis, E.; Demling, P.; Blank, L. M.

title: Inferring modularity in genotype-phenotype maps using patterns of epistasis and pleiotropy
abstract: Methods for inferring the relationship between genotype and phenotype often search for low-dimensional structure, motivated by the hypothesis that genetic loci can be organized into a small number of groups representing biological processes. These methods typically group genetic loci based on which other loci they interact with (epistasis) or based on how their effects covary across environmental conditions (patterns of pleiotropy). Here, we present two complementary methods that combine epistasis and pleiotropy to infer modular structure. The first, Sparse, Low-dimensional, Epistatic Decomposition (SLED), parametrizes the genotype-phenotype map in terms of a small number of modules: loci contribute sparse additive and epistatic effects to modules, and modules contribute sparse additive and epistatic effects to multiple phenotypes. The second method, Graph Tensor Decomposition (GTD), represents the epistatic interactions in each environment as a combination of shared basis graphs, each capturing a pattern of epistasis that recurs across environments. Since GTD does not use additive effects, learned graphs are not restricted to include only loci whose additive effects covary across environments. We validate SLED and GTD on synthetic data, then apply both methods to an experimental dataset consisting of the growth rates of yeast segregants from an F1 cross, measured across 101 environments with a hub-and-spoke structure. We evaluate the biological structure of the inferred modules and show that both models generalize well to held-out environments. Finally, we compare the modules inferred by SLED, GTD, and a previously established method that infers sparse modular structure from a locus-by-environment matrix of additive effects (SSD) and find that all three methods yield highly similar modular architectures. This suggests that the genetic architecture underlying this dataset is consistent across additive effects (SSD), epistatic effects (GTD), and both jointly (SLED). Together, our methods provide a framework for combining two sources of information, epistasis and pleiotropy, to infer interpretable low-dimensional structure in genotype-phenotype maps, expanding on previous work that has traditionally treated each independently.
authors: Lawson, N.; Brophy, G.; Holmes, C. M.; Seigal, A.; Desai, M. M.; Petti, S.

title: Effects of Reduced Watering Regimes on Hops Growth and Rhizospheric Microbial Communities
abstract: Marked by shifts in historic climatic patterns, the effects of climate change have begun to disrupt biological life worldwide. In agricultural systems, the abiotic effects of climate change such as increased temperatures and reduced rainfall extend beyond crop yield and can be felt at the ecological level through microbial community shifts associated at the interface of the root/soil matrix, known as the rhizosphere. Shifts in rhizospheric community composition have been known to greatly impact crop health, making common garden studies examining the totality of climate related impacts on crops of the utmost importance. Using a combination of both phenotypic and metabarcoding data collected from the rhizosphere, we present a multi-month drought tolerance experiment using the cash crop Humulus lupulus (hops) and five of its cultivars; Cascade, Centennial, Chinook, Comet and CTZ. Statistical analyses of phenotypic data revealed that hops displayed a differential impact on reduced watering strategies while rhizospheric data revealed more consistent patterns of association between microbes and cultivar type. We hope results from our study can be used to further expand our knowledge on the impact of future climate change and necessary reduced watering strategies on agricultural systems, providing insight into potential mechanisms of response for drought tolerance in crop systems.
authors: McElwee-Adame, A.; Mulligan, C.; Kibury, K.; Glynn, Z.; Golshani, M.; Alkhafaji, A.; Vourlitis, G.; Sethuraman, A.

title: Characterization of intermolecular base pairing using AMT crosslinking in mammalian cells during oxidative stress
abstract: Intermolecular base pairing is essential for normal gene regulation but can also cause neurodegeneration when dysregulated. Despite its importance, intermolecular base pairing remains poorly characterized in cells. We coupled AMT crosslinking with RNA pulldown to probe intermolecular base pairing in mammalian cells under oxidative stress, a state that drives G3BP1/2-dependent stress granule assembly, translational repression, and increased exposure of RNA sequences available for intermolecular interactions. AMT captured intermolecular base pairing interactions among reporter RNAs in vitro and the known interaction between the U3 snoRNA and pre-18S rRNA in cellulo. Although detection sensitivity was limited for endogenous mRNAs, we found that base pairing among inducibly expressed reporter mRNAs is sensitive to RNA sequence, oxidative stress, and G3BP1/2. Furthermore, chemical probing revealed that base accessibility to DMS within non-translated regions of candidate RNAs remains similar between stressed and unstressed cells, and those lacking G3BP1/2, indicating that RNAs remained state under these conditions. Our findings establish an approach for studying RNA base pairing in cells and suggest that intermolecular base pairing may act together with RNA structure to preserve RNAs during oxidative stress.
authors: Liao, J. N.; Betances, I.; Shen, E.; Trcek, T.

title: Model-Agnostic Decomposition of the Difference in Mean Response Between Two Groups via Game-Theoretic Attribution with Minimum-Switching-Distortion Coupling
abstract: The difference in mean response between two groups can arise from differences in covariate-response relationships, covariate distributions, or both. We propose a model-agnostic decomposition (MAD) of this difference into structure and composition effects. We formulate a cooperative switching game with a model-switch player and individual covariate-switch players, organized into model and covariate unions. MAD employs the Owen value, whose quotient game yields the aggregate structure and composition effects and whose internal game allocates the aggregate composition effect across covariates, and thereby inherits its fair allocation properties. In the internal game, partial covariate switches create hybrid covariate vectors whose joint distributions are not determined by the group-specific covariate distributions alone. To resolve this indeterminacy, we propose a minimum-switching-distortion (MSD) coupling, formulated as an optimal-transport problem. The MSD coupling satisfies admissibility conditions of identity at coincidence, transposition equivariance, and coordinate equivariance, and its sparse support reduces allocation cost. Because MAD imposes no particular functional form, it accommodates machine-learning models that adapt to complex nonlinear and interactive relationships, thereby yielding more accurate decompositions. Simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of MAD and the MSD coupling in terms of decomposition accuracy, coupling admissibility, and computational cost. As an illustration, we decompose the difference in mean body mass index between UK and US males aged 30-70 years using microbiome data, at the aggregate level and across microbial genera.
authors: Koh, H.

title: Accelerating antibiotic discovery from Earth's isolated habitats through protein language models and microfluidics
abstract: The antibiotic potential of Earth's isolated habitat microbiomes remains largely unexplored. Accessing this resource requires reliable prioritization across divergent peptide sequences and efficient experimental validation. Here we present MicroSPEAR, an end-to-end framework for antimicrobial peptide (AMP) discovery integrating SPEAR, a sequence-structure-aware ensemble predictor, with MicroGrad, a microfluidic testing platform. SPEAR generalized to low-homology peptides and prioritized potent candidates despite training on binary activity labels. MicroGrad simplified liquid handling and shortened susceptibility testing from approximately 18 h to 4 h. Applied to a catalogue derived from 4,480 metagenomes spanning 15 isolated habitat types, SPEAR identified 383,027 non-redundant candidate AMPs, 63.1% of which lacked detectable homologues in reference databases. Of 85 synthesized candidates, 79 exhibited antibacterial activity at [≤]64 M;. Mechanistic analyses revealed distinct modes of membrane disruption. Four broad-spectrum candidates with low toxicity significantly reduced bacterial burdens in a mouse thigh infection model. MicroSPEAR connects underexplored microbial diversity with experimentally validated antibiotic leads and provides a foundation for lab-in-the-loop discovery.
authors: Kang, Z.; Zhou, Q.; Zhang, H.; Liu, J.; Liu, K.; Zhou, K.; Zhang, Y.; Wang, Y.; Chen, P.; Liu, B.-F.; Ning, K.

title: Developing synthetic auxin-based trans-kingdom signaling
abstract: Synthetic trans-kingdom signaling systems with tunable transduction properties provide a unique avenue to explore how communication between organisms coordinate behaviors without the confounding complexity of natural systems. However, existing trans-kingdom signaling systems suffer from either toxic signal molecules, a need for rare precursors for signal generation, or transduction machinery which is either species-specific or cannot be easily tuned. This limits their capacity to be broadly applied across kingdoms and their utility as a model system to study trans-kingdom interactions. In this work we elucidate the design principles for a trans-kingdom signaling system based on the plant phytohormone, Indole 3-Acetic Acid (auxin), that overcomes these challenges. We demonstrate how auxin biosynthesis can be engineered into a model sender organism, the cyanobacteria Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942, and how this signal can be tuned with low leak and high dynamic range. We also show these signals can be connected to gene expression using tunable synthetic auxin-responsive signaling systems across multiple kingdoms. We demonstrate that S. elongatus generated auxin signals can tune gene expression in co-cultured Saccharomyces cerevisiae via auxin-induced degradation. Additionally, we show that when the S. elongatus are associated with the roots of the model plant, Arabidopsis thaliana, the auxin they generate can control gene expression via auxin-responsive synthetic transcription factors expressed from the plants genome. Taken together, our results demonstrate the design principles for a tunable auxin-based trans-kingdom signaling system that can be broadly applied across species.
authors: Furnish, M.; Kokarakis, E. J.; Kopycienski, D.; Thune-Larsen, B.; Ducat, D. C.; Khakhar, A.

title: V-SWITCH: A single-vector OFF-to-ON fluorescent reporter of live RNA virus infections
abstract: Fluorescent reporters of viral infection are powerful tools for studying viral pathogenesis and host-pathogen interactions. Here, we present V-SWITCH, a highly modular, single-vector, cell-based OFF-to-ON fluorescent reporter that enables robust detection of viral infection in living cells. V-SWITCH is based on a split mNeonGreen (mNG) system employing a release-and-capture mechanism. In the "OFF" state, the mNG3A(1-10) fragment is anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum via a Sec61 transmembrane domain, while the mNG(11) fragment, fused to BFP, is constitutively expressed in the nucleus. Upon infection, the viral protease cleaves a protease cleavage site (PCS) adjacent to the mNG3A(1-10) fragment, liberating it for translocation into the nucleus. There, it complements mNG(11) to reconstitute fluorescence. The constitutive BFP serves as both an expression control and a nuclear segmentation marker for image analysis. Each module in this dual-cassette design is flanked by unique restriction sites allowing rapid swapping of virus-specific PCS, split fluorophores, membrane anchors, and promoters. We demonstrate the versatility of the V-SWITCH reporter for several viruses (Dengue virus, Zika virus, West Nile virus and Human Coronavirus OC43) in several cell lines (A549, BJ-5 fibroblasts, HEK293T and HeLa). Reporter activation enables clear discrimination of infected and uninfected cells by flow cytometry and reveals time-dependent and heterogeneous infection dynamics by live-cell imaging at single-cell resolution. Importantly, we demonstrate the potential of V-SWITCH to support both rapid functional screening for host factor dependencies, as well as high-throughput compound screening to enable antiviral discovery and comparative evaluation of therapeutic strategies across multiple viruses and cell types.
authors: Cid-Rosas, M.; Grunberg, M.; Matia, A.; Lee, S.-C.; Woosley, H.; Pradeep, S.; Kanwar, S.; Khadka, S.; Mehta, S. B.; Huttenhain, R.; Turon-Lagot, V.; Arias, C.

title: Parallel and lineage-dependent mitonuclear evolution in threespine stickleback
abstract: Mitochondrial function depends on interactions between proteins and RNAs encoded by the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. Repeated adaptation to similar environments may favor parallel changes in nuclear genes supporting mitochondrial function, while maintaining compatibility with different mitochondrial backgrounds may favor population-specific responses. Threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) repeatedly colonized freshwater habitats from ancestral marine populations carrying standing genetic variation. We tested whether these colonizations resulted in parallel evolution of nuclear oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) genes and whether these responses coincided with evidence of mitonuclear evolutionary coupling. Several divergent mitochondrial lineages were distributed across populations with limited geographic correspondence. Mitochondrial ribosomal proteins and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases exhibited elevated nonsynonymous divergence and polymorphism relative to their cytosolic counterparts. We also identified positive evolutionary rate covariation between mitochondrial and nuclear genes that comprise OXPHOS Complex IV, suggesting that evolutionary coupling is concentrated in particular functional modules. Many nuclear OXPHOS genes displayed large allele-frequency changes that were parallel across freshwater populations in Alaska and British Columbia, while the magnitude of differentiation differed between regions. Mitochondrial lineage was associated with a smaller, locus-specific component of nuclear OXPHOS variation, concentrated in Complex I genes. Notably, the genes with large freshwater-associated evolutionary shifts were largely distinct from those displaying mitonuclear rate covariation. In this context, the gene cox4i1 emerges as a candidate connecting repeated freshwater adaptation with molecular variation at the mitonuclear interface. Together, these findings suggest that freshwater adaptation drives broadly parallel nuclear OXPHOS evolution across heterogeneous mitochondrial backgrounds, while evidence of mitonuclear evolutionary coupling is more localized.
authors: Yu, C.; Bolnick, D. I.; Weber, J. N.

title: Genome-scale metabolic models reveal phylogenetic conservation of amino acid fermentation-linked metabolic traits in soil bacteria
abstract: Soil microorganisms drive biogeochemical cycling of carbon, nitrogen, and other elements, but the partitioning of metabolic fluxes among taxa remains poorly understood, limiting our ability to link community composition to ecosystem function. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) offer a mechanistic framework to connect taxa and their metabolic pathways to these fluxes. However, heterogeneity of soil communities has hampered recovery of high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), constraining application of flux balance analysis (FBA) to soil metagenomes and skewing available GEMs towards cultured model organisms. This gap limits our understanding of soil microbial physiology and responses to disturbance. Here, we present a collection of GEMs for 550 MAGs (497 bacterial, 53 archaeal) recovered from 94 soil samples across the continental United States. As an example application, we used FBA to estimate uptake and secretion of 44 commonly exchanged metabolites and tested whether these fluxes are phylogenetically conserved. While the overall bacterial phylogenetic signal was weak (median r = 0.029), eight metabolites showed significant conservation: amino acids (L-methionine, L-leucine, L-isoleucine), fermentation intermediates (pyruvate, acetaldehyde, ethanol), and amino acid degradation by-products NH  3 and CO  2 . Most bacterial MAGs were predicted to import branched-chain amino acids, and a subset also secreted pyruvate and ethanol, identifying candidate cross-feeding interactions. Thus, fermentation-linked traits may be phylogenetically conserved and predictable from community composition, whereas most other metabolites showed no detectable signal. Ultimately, this resource enables genome-resolved prediction of soil microbial metabolisms, from cross-feeding and carbon-use efficiency to community responses to disturbance, providing a mechanistic bridge between microbial taxonomy and ecosystem-scale biogeochemistry.
authors: Song YC, Ayala-Ortiz C, Stratton KG, Chakrawal A, Graham EB.
