title: Tyrosine hydroxylase deletion in Ntsr1 neurons confers resistance to diet-induced weight gain: an energy-balance analysis
abstract: High-fat diet (HFD) disrupts circadian feeding rhythms and promotes diet-induced obesity (DIO), but the neural mechanisms linking diet to energy balance remain unclear. Previously, we demonstrated that dopamine production in neurotensin receptor 1 (Ntsr1)-expressing neurons was required for HFD-induced daytime overfeeding and DIO. Here, we tested whether DIO resistance in Ntsr1Cre;Thflox conditional knockout (cKO) mice was explained by altered energy expenditure. We replicated resistance to HFD-induced weight gain and assessed food intake, indirect calorimetry, activity, body temperature, fecal energy, fecal nonesterified fatty acids, and the gut microbiome. Indirect calorimetry on standard chow diet (SCD) was confounded by reduced intake and body weight loss, whereas HFD-fed cKO mice consumed food readily and resisted weight gain. Unlike our previous study, daytime feeding was not suppressed; instead, cKO mice were slightly and variably hypophagic on HFD but not SCD. DIO resistance was not accompanied by increased energy expenditure, activity, or body temperature. Rather, cKO mice showed reduced energy expenditure and activity and lower body temperature on both diets. In the replication cohort, HFD fecal output was lower in cKO mice, whereas the independent bomb-calorimetry cohort showed no genotype difference in fecal mass; fecal energy density and nonesterified fatty acid concentration were unchanged. Preliminary analysis of the microbiome was consistent with an obesity-resistant gut profile. Together, these findings indicate that the feeding phenotype is diet- and experiment-dependent and that DIO resistance is not explained by increased energy expenditure, activity, thermogenesis, or detectable changes in fecal energy or fat content.
authors: Wu, R.; Gomez, A.; Wong, J.; Gordillo, R.; Kamitakahara, A. K.; Steele, A. D.

title: TestNet-PA: Sampling-Zero-Aware Inference of Microbial Presence-Absence Networks
abstract: Microbial presence-absence networks, also referred to as co-occurrence networks, characterize patterns of coexistence and incompatibility among taxa. However, sequencing-based presence--absence analysis can be compromised by pervasive 'sampling zeros' in microbiome data, causing widely used methods such as Fisher's exact test to identify spurious co-occurrence dependence. To our knowledge, no existing method is designed to account for sampling zeros in this setting. We introduce TestNet-PA, a method for testing pairwise microbial co-occurrence dependence. TestNet-PA models each observed zero as arising from a mixture of 'structural' and 'sampling' zeros, with the mixing probabilities governed by library size and relative abundance. Because the relative abundance underlying an observed zero is unobserved, we impute it by borrowing information from other samples. We then construct a quasi-likelihood and develop an EM algorithm to infer dependence between the underlying true presence--absence statuses. Extensive simulations based on real gut, vaginal, and oral microbiome data templates showed that TestNet-PA consistently controlled the FDR while maintaining good sensitivity. By contrast, Fisher's exact test generally yielded inflated FDR. Analyses of the three real microbiome datasets further illustrated how accounting for sampling zeros can affect the inferred co-occurrence networks.
authors: Mao, Y.; Hu, Y.-J.

title: Isocaloric restriction of a high-fat diet under TAK-242 administration: metabolic and gut microbial responses in mice
abstract: High-fat feeding promotes obesity in mice largely by increasing energy intake, so diet composition and energy intake are hard to separate without pair-feeding. We previously showed that isocaloric restriction normalizes body weight, glycemia and plasma lipids but not visceral adiposity, adipose inflammation or the fecal microbial community. We hypothesized that, during administration of the TLR4 signaling inhibitor TAK-242, matching energy intake to that of low-fat controls would normalize adiposity, intestinal barrier gene expression and the fecal microbial community. Male C57BL/6 mice (n = 8 per group) received a low-fat diet, a high-fat diet ad libitum, or a high-fat diet pair-fed to controls from week 0 or week 5 for 12 weeks; TAK-242 (3 ug/g, three times weekly) was given to every group from week 0.4, with no vehicle-injected arm. Intake did not differ among groups during a three-week low-fat acclimation (P = .88); over the 12 weeks on the assigned diets the ad libitum high-fat group ate 5.5% more than controls (P = .50). Over the full trajectory the ad libitum high-fat group gained 0.48 g/week more than controls (group x week, P = .012); both pair-fed groups had lower fasting glucose than that group. Adipocyte diameter, visceral fat proportion, ileal barrier genes, CCK-induced satiation and microbial alpha diversity did not differ significantly among groups. Adipose Ccl2 expression differed (P = .043, exploratory), as did fecal community composition (PERMANOVA P = .022), although no pairwise contrast survived correction. Energy restriction did not return the microbial community toward the low-fat profile.
authors: Jeong, E.; Chae, S.; Eun, S.; Chai, H.; Lee, S.

title: Energetic and functional development of soil food webs along secondary succession
abstract: 1. As ecosystems develop, aboveground biomass and belowground organic matter accumulate, while energy turnover declines. This trend is largely supported by vegetation studies, but remains unexplored for soil food webs that channel the majority of energy in terrestrial ecosystems. 2. Here, we tested whether successional theory applies to soil food webs across size-based compartments, ranging from microfauna (nematodes) to macrofauna (soil arthropods and earthworms), along a secondary succession in southwestern China, using an energy-flux approach. To assess whether forest restoration by planting follows natural succession, we also compared spruce and larch plantations with secondary birch forest of the same successional stage. 3. Supporting expectations of reduced energy turnover, the results showed an increasing animal biomass-to-energy flux ratio and a functional shift from herbivory-dominated (green) to detritivory-dominated (brown) energy channelling along succession. Soil food web compartments showed contrasting trends: macro-food webs shifted towards bacterial energy channels with decreasing predation, while micro-food webs maintained similar bacterial/fungal energy flux ratios and tended towards increasing predation. The larch plantation supported lower animal biomass than the secondary birch forest, whereas the spruce plantation did not differ. We further found that energy flux correlated positively with microbial biomass and soil animal diversity, but negatively with litter biomass during succession. 4. Overall, we expand successional theory by revealing the transformations in energy use and pathways within soil food webs along secondary succession, thereby advancing understanding of ecosystem functioning and guiding ecosystem restoration. Our results further suggest that tree plantations do not necessarily replicate the belowground development of natural succession, which should be considered in ecosystem restoration.
authors: Zhang, A.; Tu, C.; Wang, Y.; Li, J.; Zhou, Z.; Luo, R.; Hohberg, K.; Chen, Z.; Zhu, B.; Pang, X.; Eisenhauer, N.; Potapov, A.

title: Aging, HIV Status, and Sex Differentially Influence Antiretroviral Therapy Disposition Pathways in Rectosigmoid Tissue and Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells
abstract: People living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are increasingly surviving into older age due to the effectiveness of antiretroviral (ARV) therapy (ART), creating a growing population in whom age-related changes may influence treatment outcomes. Although aging is known to affect drug disposition, the molecular mechanisms by which aging alters ARV pharmacology remain incompletely understood, particularly within tissue compartments, including the rectosigmoid region of the colon, that serve as sites of HIV transmission and persistence. To address this knowledge gap, we used proteomics by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to evaluate the impact of age and HIV status on proteins and pathways relevant to ARV disposition in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and rectosigmoid colon tissue obtained from young (18-50) HIV-seronegative adults, older (65-80) HIV-seronegative adults, and older virally suppressed people living with HIV. We found that aging and HIV infection differentially influenced proteins predominantly within nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) pathways, in rectosigmoid tissue and PBMC. HIV-associated effects to the proteome were more prominent in PBMC, whereas aging produced broader alterations in ARV disposition-related proteins in rectosigmoid tissue, including proteins involved in drug transport, intracellular drug activation, dephosphorylation, and nucleotide homeostasis. Several age-associated changes were further influenced by biologic sex, suggesting that aging may not affect ARV disposition uniformly across populations. To place these findings within a broader context, pathway analyses were performed that identified extensive tissue-specific remodeling associated with aging and HIV infection involving drug disposition, immune regulation, cellular metabolism, and disease-related pathways. Notably, aging was associated with alterations in pathways relevant to nucleotide metabolism and gastrointestinal tissue function, suggesting that processes beyond traditional drug transport and metabolism pathways may contribute to variability in ARV disposition with advancing age. Together, these findings identify aging as an important modifier of pathways that regulate ARV disposition within compartments relevant to HIV transmission and persistence. While the clinical consequences of our findings are unknown, these data provide a mechanistic foundation for future studies investigating whether age-associated changes influence the effectiveness of ART and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in older adults.
authors: Wilkins HN, White CJ, Zheng R, Mamun LA, Eberhard CD, Fuchs EJ, Hoffmann J, Gupta E, Orsburn B, Hendrix CW, Bumpus NN, Williams DW.

title: Microglial AhR Drives Sex-Biased Amyloid Pathology
abstract: Microglia integrate local and systemic signals that can modify their response to amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}), but the molecular pathways connecting these signals to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), a sensor of microbiota- and host-derived metabolites, as a microglial regulator of amyloid pathology. Sustained administration of the AhR agonist indoxyl-3-sulfate (I3S) exacerbated cortical A{beta} deposition and plaque-associated neuritic damage in APPNL-F mice. Conversely, constitutive AhR deficiency reduced amyloid burden, promoted plaque compaction, and preserved behavioural performance, whereas inducible deletion of AhR in microglia was sufficient to reduce plaque accumulation. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that AhR loss reprogrammed microglia toward phagolysosomal and A{beta}-recognition states and enhanced microglial A{beta} uptake, with markedly stronger effects in females. APPNL-F mice also exhibited sex-dependent remodelling of the gut microbiota and tryptophan-derived metabolites. Circulating indole-3-aldehyde (IAld) robustly activated AhR and was associated with cortical amyloid pathology. AhR-activating bioactivity was increased in mouse serum, cortex and faecal extracts and was higher in serum from the COGNIBIO12 analytical subcohort than in independently recruited cognitively unimpaired H2H participants. Among amyloid-positive patients, higher serum AhR bioactivity was associated with lower CSF A{beta}42 concentrations. Together, these findings identify microglial AhR as a metabolically responsive regulator linking systemic ligand availability, biological sex, and microglial control of amyloid pathology.

title: Genome-resolved metatranscriptomic analysis of arsenic demethylation and detoxification in a methanogenic rice paddy soil
abstract: Microbial methylation and demethylation of arsenic in rice paddy soils influence the speciation and toxicity of arsenic in rice, with implications for human health and rice yields. Here, we combine genome-resolved metatranscriptomics with arsenic speciation analysis in methanogenic paddy soil incubations to elucidate microbial pathways regulating As demethylation, with emphasis on: (i) evaluating links between methyltransferase gene transcription by methylotrophic methanogens and arsenic demethylation; and (ii) assessing how toxicity-induced microbial responses regulate As demethylation and the resulting distribution of As species. Experiments with dimethylarsinic (DMAs) and 2-bromoethanesulfonate as a methanogenesis inhibitor confirm an important role of methanogens in anaerobic arsenic demethylation. Amendment of the methylotrophic substrate trimethylamine accelerated arsenic demethylation and induced an association between arsenic demethylation rates and the transcription of diverse methylotrophic methyltransferases. Six Methanosarcina metagenome assembled genomes dominated methyltransferase transcription and concurrently transcribed genes involved in multiple (methyl)arsenic oxidation and efflux pathways, illustrating a link between putative demethylation and arsenic detoxification at the genome level. Paddy soil incubations also demonstrated toxicity-driven feedbacks between DMAs concentrations and demethylation rates, wherein higher DMAs concentrations inhibited methanogenesis and decreased pseudo first-order demethylation rate constants. These findings provide new insights into links between methylotrophic methanogenesis and arsenic demethylation in anaerobic conditions, with implications for biogeochemical control of arsenic speciation in rice paddy soils.
authors: Yoon, H.; Vega, M. A. P.; Reid, M. C.

title: Polar Marine Microbial Communities as Reservoirs of Polyester Degrading Enzymes
abstract: Background: Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is one of the most widely used plastics and a major contributor to marine pollution. While the diversity of PET hydrolases (PETases), which degrade PET into mono(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (MHET), terephthalate (TPA) and ethylene glycol, has been documented in temperate and tropical waters, their potential presence in polar oceans remains unascertained. Results: Here, we systematically screened polar and non-polar marine metagenomes using Hidden Markov models (HMM) generated using experimentally validated PETases. We identified >680 putative PETase-like sequences, with Antarctic and Arctic candidates enriched in high-fidelity motifs associated with PETase-like activity. Phylogenetic and structural analyses defined a high-confidence PETase-like clade comprising both Type I and Type II enzymes, differing in thermostability-related features and PET-binding motifs. Experimental assays confirmed polyesterase activity in 5/9 candidates from this clade, including polar-derived variants active at 14-25{degrees}C. Downstream enzymes for PET consumption were also widespread, detecting 209 putative MHET hydrolases and 442 TPA-catabolyzing enzymes. Further, we reconstructed 112 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) carrying at least one enzyme of the PET degradation pathway, 89 of them carrying a PETase-like gene. Notably, 15 MAGs encoded multiple PETase-like enzymes, nine of them from polar datasets, and one polar MAG harbored a complete PETase-MHETase-TPA pathway, suggesting the genomic potential for a fully integrated degradation potential in cold-adapted taxa. Conclusions: Together, these results demonstrate that polar oceans act as previously overlooked reservoirs of taxonomically and functionally diverse plastic-degrading enzymes. The enrichment of PETase-like enzymes and downstream pathways in polar microbial communities expands the global biogeography of plastic biodegradation and highlights cold-active enzymes as promising candidates for developing low-temperature plastic bioremediation strategies.
authors: Grinen, A.; Cifuentes-Anticevic, J.; Buscaglia, M.; Vergara-Barros, P.; Verdejo, A. N.; Perez-Lara, R.; Worden-Aracena, D.; Gatica Vargas, F.; Engelberger, F.; Ramirez-Sarmiento, C. A.; Diez, B.

title: Stochasticity in Metabolism: Oxidative Stress Response Phenotypes As Emergent Consequences of Network Topology
abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are ubiquitous yet elusive due to their reactivity and short half-lives, making simulation essential for mechanistic insight. Traditional ROS modeling has been confined to small ODE frameworks limited by kinetic-parameter scarcity. Here, we recast ROS dynamics as a flux-balance analysis (FBA) optimization problem using COBRA and CPLEX, augmenting the Escherichia coli iJO1366 genome-scale model with 84 spontaneous oxidation, 14 redox, and 9 detoxification reactions, targeting three ROS species: hydroxyl radicals, superoxide, and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). We also formalize five fundamental rules of oxidation biology in the form of mixed-integer linear constraints, allowing us to dynamically incorporate reaction rate constants and let complex behavior emerge from first principles. Among these phenomena is the bimodal killing pattern under H2O2 stress, first announced over 40 years ago and never computationally recapitulated until now. We observe it by stochastically sampling our models with GapSplit, simulating bet-hedging and partitioning solutions into growers, persisters, and non-survivors. In our simulations, this killing effect arises solely from the metabolic network topology during random exploration of alternative metabolic configurations. The conservation of steady state creates a stochastic bias for detoxification when central carbon metabolism reaches its metabolic capacity to deal with ROS, causing the famous survival recovery phase. The recovery phase is thus part of Mode 1 metabolism, characterized by spare detoxification capacity and fulfilled by the Ahp reaction in E. coli. Mode 2 has no spare detoxification. We anticipate this to be an overlooked universal principle.
authors: Mihnev, A.; Luong, D.; Porat, J.; Chang, R. L.

title: Thalassolituus haligoni sp. nov., BB40, a model species for non-cyanobacterial diazotrophs within Oceanospirillales isolated from a Fjord-like Inlet in Kjipuktuk
abstract: Marine non-cyanobacterial diazotrophs (NCDs) are recognized as globally distributed, however, few representatives have been isolated in pure cultures. As a result, understanding the physiology, growth rate, substrate preference and dinitrogen (N2) fixation capabilities proves difficult. Thalassolituus haligoni. sp. nov., BB40 was isolated from a fjord-like inlet within Kjipuktuk (Halifax), Nova Scotia. The fully sequenced genome displayed all necessary genes required for N2 fixation, and various carbon uptake pathways. The gram-negative flagellated rod shape bacterium displayed significantly higher growth rates in medium amended with nitrate (NO3-) or ammonia (NH3), compared to dissolved N2, as the sole nitrogen source. Biological N2 fixation rates were detectable across all conditions, measuring a range from 9.34 x 10-6 to 1.4 x 10-1 fmol N cell-1 day-1. Growth of the isolate was successful between 4 oC up to 35 oC, with a Topt of 20 oC for N2, and between 27 - 30 oC for fixed nitrogen (NO3- and NH3). The closest relatives to T. haligoni, were found to be the uncultured Arc-gamma-03 (99% average nucleotide identity (ANI)) and Oceanobacter antarcticus (97% ANI). T. haligoni also displays versatile capabilities for growth on various carbon, and nitrogen sources, and antibiotics. Collectively this study provides an in-depth physiological assessment of an Oceanospirillales diazotrophic species which we presently have limited knowledge of.
authors: LaRoche, J.; Rose, S. A.; Bertrand, E. M.; Duffy, S. L. G.; Tolman, J.; Ludovic, P.; Chaillou, G.

title: Altered neurodevelopment, CSF volume, and emotional reactivity following postnatal Zika virus infection in infant macaques
abstract: Although congenital Zika virus (ZIKV) syndrome is well-characterized, the neurodevelopmental consequences of postnatal infection are understudied. We used a rhesus macaque (RM) model to investigate the consequences of postnatal ZIKV infection on brain and behavior. Male and female infant RMs infected with ZIKV at 1 month of age were compared to sex-, age-, and rearing-matched controls: uninfected and treated with Poly-IC as an innate immune control. ZIKV-infected infants showed poor state control in early infancy and increased hostility during an acute stressor. They displayed sex-specific behavioral alterations during caregiver separation though attachment bonds were preserved. MRI at 3 months revealed larger total cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volume, reduced visual processing region volumes, and sex-specific brain structural alterations: males exhibited amygdala hypertrophy, whereas females had volumetric reductions in temporal-limbic and temporal-auditory cortices. These findings indicate that postnatal ZIKV infection is associated with alterations in sensory, social and emotion-regulatory systems and in CSF volume, that may warrant long-term monitoring of exposed children.
authors: Desai, N. P.; Love, K. F.; van Schoor, A.; Freeman, S.; Ali, M.; Richardson, R.; Kovacs-Balint, Z. A.; Tobar Mosqueira, R. A.; Lebovic, R. L.; Acevedo-Polo, J. H.; Vlasova, R. title: Do plasmid-dependent phages enable the survival of costly plasmids?
abstract: Plasmids store auxiliary genes that address environmental challenges such as antibiotics. In the short term, plasmid loss can be advantageous to hosts if plasmid benefits are temporary but costs are permanent. However, this loss can proceed to plasmid extinction, with access to plasmid-derived benefits permanently lost. We consider a worst-case scenario: a plasmid that yields benefits only infrequently, imposes heavy costs that cannot be alleviated, and whose host population faces a competitor that cannot acquire the costly plasmid. Thus, horizontal transmission of this plasmid is detrimental to the host population when the plasmid does not provide benefits. Using population models, we demonstrate that -- counterintuitively -- plasmid-dependent phages can enable high-cost plasmid survival. Phage predation pins the plasmid at low abundance, effectively neutralizing the plasmid cost at the population level and boosting persistence time. When the costly plasmid becomes beneficial, it spreads and survives by vertical transmission until benefits subside.
authors: Yuly, J. L.; Avallone, M.; Abad, L.; Wingreen, N. S.

title: RoDPAA: A Robust Dissimilarity-Based Principal Angle Analysis Framework for Multi-View Microbiome Data Integration
abstract: Multiview microbiome studies profile the same participants across body sites or molecular layers, but integration is hampered by sparse, compositional data, modest sample sizes and methods that recognize only exact sharing. We present RoDPAA (Robust Dissimilarity-based Principal Angle Analysis), a framework that represents each view through any data-appropriate dissimilarity, such as Bray--Curtis, without log-ratio transformation or likelihood assumptions. RoDPAA aligns view-specific signal subspaces through principal angles, captures complete and partial sharing, and tests by permutation how many components are shared, using only eigendecomposition and little tuning. In Gaussian simulations, RoDPAA matched JIVE and MOFA given true ranks, ran faster and alone recovered the shared dimension in every replicate. In two inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) cohorts with sparse, zero-inflated data, Bray--Curtis-based RoDPAA recovered shared structure that was stable to prevalence filtering, whereas log-ratio-based alternatives were not. Its leading microbiome--metabolome factors, learned without disease labels, were the only ones associated with IBD.
authors: Xu, Y.; Wang, Y.

title: Proteome-wide discovery of novel diagnostic antigens for coccidioidomycosis
abstract: Coccidioidomycosis, commonly called Valley Fever (VF), caused by Coccidioides spp., is an understudied fungal disease that accounts for a substantial fraction of pneumonias in endemic areas. Diagnosis remains challenging because the mainstay of diagnosis is serology, and current assays have modest sensitivity in early infection. Discovery of new antigens could improve serologic detection early in disease. Here, we use PepSeq, a DNA-programmable serology platform, to represent the complete proteome of Coccidioides within a library of 244,000 DNA-barcoded peptides. By profiling antibody reactivity at the protein and epitope levels in VF patients, naturally infected pigtail macaques, and healthy controls, we identify numerous previously-unrecognized antigens and epitopes, including some shared between humans and macaque responses. When translated into a pooled peptide ELISA, we show that a subset of identified antigens can discriminate VF cases from controls in an independent cohort with high accuracy (AUC = 0.91). These findings establish high-dimensional peptide serology as a scalable approach for fungal antigen discovery and identify new targets for improved VF diagnosis.
authors: Elko E, Ryle L, Nelson GA, Sarbo NG, Harms CE, Kelley E, Fredericks MN, Keim P, Knox K, Kala M, Fuller DH, Settles EW, Barker BM, Magee DM, Lake DF, Grys TE, Thompson GR, Altin J, Ladner JT, Mead HL.

title: Near real-time data on the human neutralizing antibody landscape to influenza virus in summer of 2026 shows antigenic advance of H3N2 subclade K region D mutants and H1N1 D.3.1.1 Sa mutants
abstract: Human seasonal influenza evolves rapidly, necessitating twice yearly decisions about whether to update the strains in the vaccine. To help inform this decision, we have been using high-throughput sequencing-based neutralization assays to make twice yearly measurements of how recent human sera neutralize current human H3N2 and H1N1 strains. Here we provide the third installment in this series of measurements by reporting 52,268 titers representing neutralization of 148 viral strains by 355 human sera collected between April and August of 2026. Our measurements show that new H3N2 subclade K strains with mutations in antigenic region D and new H1N1 subclade D.3.1.1 strains with mutations in antigenic region Sa (such as G155E) have reduced neutralization by human sera, with notable heterogeneity in the impact of some of these mutations across sera from different individuals. This paper is accompanied by an interactive summary (https://jbloomlab.github.io/flu-seqneut-2026/summary.html) that enables detailed exploration of the results, and all titer data are publicly available for further analysis to aid vaccine antigen selection and studies of viral evolution.
authors: Kikawa, C.; Butler, A.; Huddleston, J.; Turner, S. A.; Peck, H.; Englund, J. A.; Lacombe, K.; Busch, M.; Lanteri, M. C.; Stone, M.; Spencer, B.; Greninger, A. L.; Smith, D. J.; Wallace, S.; Marshall, H. S.; Tosif, S.; Hensley, S. E.; Barr, I. G.; Bloom, J. D.

title: Integrated omics analysis reveals reorganization of nitrogen and lipid metabolism in a toluene-degrading bacterium in the gas phase
abstract: Gas-phase bioprocesses, in which microbial cells are immobilized on solid carriers exposed to the gas phase, enable efficient conversion of poorly water-soluble compounds for biodegradation and bioproduction. However, operation without a surrounding bulk aqueous medium can constrain the replenishment of water and nonvolatile nutrients. The metabolic mechanisms that sustain cellular activity in these low-water environments remain largely unknown. Here, we elucidated the metabolic alterations in the highly adhesive bacterium Acinetobacter sp. Tol 5 degrading toluene in the gas and aqueous phases. Polyurethane carriers bearing cells from independent cultures were assigned to the gas phase or to two aqueous media, nitrogen-depleted basal salt medium and phosphate-buffered saline, so that the conditions differed only in phase and nutrient availability. In cells actively degrading toluene, integrated metabolomics, lipidomics, and transcriptomics (97 metabolites, 108 lipids, and 3,899 genes) revealed a metabolic state specific to the gas phase. Under gas-phase conditions, amino acid and nucleotide degradation was enhanced while the intracellular glutamate pool was maintained at a high level, and citrulline specifically accumulated. Membrane lipids were remodeled, and the storage lipid triacylglycerol was consumed, suggesting that it serves as an endogenous carbon and energy source and may also contribute to metabolic water production under nutrient- and water-limited gas-phase conditions. These findings highlight nitrogen metabolism and lipid mobilization as features of gas-phase adaptation, providing a rational basis for designing robust gas-phase bioprocesses and selecting suitable microbial chassis.
authors: Inoue, S.; Naobayashi, T.; Tokiyoshi, K.; Yoshimoto, S.; Tsugawa, H.; Hori, K.

title: R-pyocin-mediated selection restores aminoglycoside sensitivity in a pan-drug resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate
abstract: The global escalation of antibiotic resistance is a critical threat necessitating innovative strategies to provide new therapeutic options and restore the efficacy of conventional drugs. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exemplifies this challenge by utilizing a robust genomic resistome to persist in clinical settings. Here, we demonstrate that R-pyocins (phage-like bactericidal particles) can be leveraged not as conventional biocides but as precise selective forces to drive an evolutionary trap. We subjected the laboratory strains PAO1 and PAK and the clinical pan-drug-resistant (PDR) wound isolate MRSN 6220 to R-pyocin selective pressure. Under sustained R-pyocin pressure, every pyomelanogenic variant we recovered evaded R-pyocin killing through large-scale chromosomal deletions spanning 250-388 kbp. These deletions encompass a conserved region harboring the galU gene (essential for LPS synthesis), the hmgA gene (yielding a pyomelanogenic brown phenotype), and the mexXYZ multidrug efflux operon. While the loss of galU confers broad cross-resistance to R-pyocins by likely truncating the LPS receptor, the concurrent excision of mexXY induces profound collateral sensitivity to aminoglycosides. These deletions also eliminate critical virulence factors and biofilm clusters, including the hcnABC, exoY, phzABCDEFG, and cup operons. In a Galleria mellonella model, the resulting brown mutants were non-lethal, and in infected murine wound tissue treated ex vivo with gentamicin they exhibited a significant 3-log reduction in bacterial load, whereas the pan-drug-resistant ancestor did not. This work establishes a framework for utilizing R-pyocins as evolutionary steering agents that couple the acquisition of R-pyocin resistance to the reversion of multidrug resistance into an attenuated, biofilm-deficient, and clinically manageable state.
authors: Estrada, I.; Campbell, D.; Welch, G. S.; Smith, P.; Goldberg, J. B.; Rumbaugh, K. P.; Diggle, S. P.

title: LplA-mediated rescue of lethal myopathy and cardiomyopathy in mitochondrial lipoylation-deficient mammalian caused by Lipt1
abstract: Inherited mitochondrial metabolic disorders impair cellular energy generation and often lead to fatal metabolic crises. Mitochondrial lipoylation defects represent a severe case of such disorders that can lead to lethality but lacks effective treatment so far. In this study, we generated a viable mouse model with muscle-specific deficiency of the lipoyltransferase coded by Lipt1 to provide an in vivo preclinical model that overcomes embryonic lethality. Using this model, we examined a bacterial lipoate protein ligase A (LplA)-mediated gene therapy via adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery. By introducing LplA alongside lipoic acid supplementation, we reconstituted a salvage pathway that bypasses the mammalian endogenous lipoylation pathway. The intervention rescued premature lethality, recovered motor function and reversed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in the Lipt1-deficient mouse model. Mechanistically, AAV-LplA reconstitutes mitochondrial protein lipoylation and oxidative phosphorylation in situ. This energetic rescue suppresses phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-Akt hyperactivation, thereby restoring autophagic clearance and subsequently contributing to the recovery of the pathological phenotype. This study established AAV-LplA as a promising gene-delivery strategy for rescuing lethal mitochondrial lipoylation disorders.
authors: Yu, J.; Hu, Z.; Liu, Z.; Yang, R.; Zeng, A.

title: Sequential pathways preserve kinetochore integrity in meiosis
abstract: Kinetochores connect chromosomes to spindle microtubules, but how their integrity is maintained as they are remodelled during meiosis remains poorly understood. Here, we identify three distinct pathways linking centromeric chromatin to the outer kinetochore in budding yeast, mediated by the Ctf19 complex (Ctf19cCCAN), Mif2CENP-C and binding of Okp1CENP-Q-Ame1CENP-U to the Cse4CENP-A essential N-terminal domain (END). Although partially redundant during mitosis, all three connections are required during meiosis, with distinct temporal requirements. The assembled Ctf19cCCAN and Mif2CENP-C-dependent pathways maintain kinetochore integrity from meiotic entry, while Cse4CENP-A-Okp1CENP-Q-Ame1CENP-U binding becomes critical during prophase and the meiotic divisions. We further show that Ipl1Aurora B maintains kinetochore integrity independently of Ctf19cCCAN and provide evidence for an outer kinetochore-associated Ipl1Aurora B pool. Strikingly, Cse4CENP-A phosphomimetic mutations that restore kinetochore integrity upon Ipl1Aurora B depletion instead exacerbate defects in cells lacking Ctf19cCCAN. Our findings suggest that phosphorylation of the Cse4CENP-A N-terminal domain (NTD) by Ipl1Aurora B may regulate the use of alternative centromere-kinetochore connections to adapt to the changing requirements of meiosis.
authors: Hamaia, M. C.; Spanos, C.; Borek, W. E.; Marston, A. L.

title: Comparison of PMA-treated DNA and RNA-based 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing for viable bacterial profiling in patients with Cystic Fibrosis.
abstract: Abstract16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing remains the most widely used technique in microbiome studies. However, conventional 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing cannot distinguish DNA from live versus dead bacteria, which can be important for understanding bacterial community dynamics and guiding therapy in cystic fibrosis (CF). Two commonly used strategies to target viable communities are propidium monoazide (PMA) pretreatment of DNA and RNA-based (cDNA) sequencing. However, their direct comparison in CF sputum has not been systematically evaluated.We analysed 41 sputum samples collected during clinical stability (n=26) or exacerbation (n=15). Paired aliquots underwent PMA-treated DNA extraction or RNA extraction followed by cDNA synthesis, and were subjected to 16S rRNA gene (V4) sequencing. We then compared the bacterial community structure, ecotype, and predicted functional profiles between the two methods.PMA-treated samples exhibited higher alpha diversity (p<0.0001) and lower dominance (p=0.0001) than RNA-based profiles, along with significant differences in beta diversity (R2=0.04, p=0.017). These differences were seen primarily in stable samples, contrary to high concordance in exacerbation samples. Seven community types were identified, dominated either by CF pathogens (Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus, Burkholderiaceae) or diverse oral commensals (Streptococcus, Neisseria, Veillonella, Prevotella). Pretreatment-associated cluster shifts occurred mainly in stable communities enriched with Prevotella and Veillonella (PMA-enriched) or Staphylococcus (RNA-enriched). Functional prediction revealed that 28.22% of KEGG Orthology identifiers differed significantly between methods, particularly pathways related to membrane transport, energy metabolism, and quorum sensing.Overall, RNA-based sequencing provides 16S rRNA amplicon profiles comparable to PMA-treated DNA, especially in pathogen-dominated exacerbation samples, and may represent a practical alternative for viable microbiota assessment in CF airway studies.

title: Towards a conceptual framework of microbiome-mediated host defense
abstract: Lay SummaryMicrobiomes are essential for the health of plants and animals, contributing to nutrient acquisition, metabolic regulation, and host health. Disruptions in the composition or function of these microbial communities, referred to as dysbiosis, are frequently associated with declining host health. Although plant and animal microbiomes have traditionally been studied in separate disciplines, growing evidence suggests that common ecological and molecular principles underpin microbiome assembly, stability, and host defense across both systems. In this perspective, we bring together recent advances in animal, plant and soil microbiomes research to explore how interactions between microorganisms and their hosts contribute to health. Particular attention is given to microbial metabolites and effector molecules, which can mediate communication, recognition, and functional reorganization within microbial communities. We propose that these interactions are driven by recognition-based processes analogous to immune modulation across animals, plants, and soils, enabling microbial communities to sense health threats and coordinate protective responses. By integrating concepts across kingdoms and ecosystems, we propose a conceptual framework in which disease-protective functions emerge from dynamic interactions among microorganisms and their hosts. This perspective postulates that microbiomes possess community-level, immune-like properties, offering a unifying conceptual basis for understanding how complex microbial ecosystems contribute to health and resilience across kingdoms and ecosystems.

title: Bioimaging and comparative genomics for characterization of surface-bacteria isolated from a blood bank facility
abstract: Blood banks represent highly controlled healthcare environments where microbiological surveillance has traditionally focused on Blood products rather than environmental microbial reservoirs. Despite their crucial role in transfusion safety, the ecology of surface-associated microorganisms remains poorly understood. This cross-sectional study characterized culturable bacteria recovered from Blood-bank surfaces. We combined scanning electron microscopy, culture-based microbiology, phenotypic characterization, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, and whole-genome sequencing to investigate whether surfaces within a public blood bank facility (BBF) constitute reservoirs of environmentally derived bacteria with putative traits potentially relevant to environmental survival. Samples collected from a public BBF in Tucumán, Argentina yielded 36 culturable bacterial isolates, predominantly Gram-positive taxa together with a limited number of opportunistic Gram-negative species. Several isolates showed reduced susceptibility to various groups of antimicrobials; furthermore, several strains exhibited strong biofilm formation, production of amyloid-like fibers, motility, and hemolytic activity. Whole-genome sequencing of six representative isolates supported previous species affiliations, identified genes related to antimicrobial resistance, adhesion, biofilm formation, stress adaptation, and cytotoxicity, highlighting the importance of integrating genomic and phenotypic analyses. Notably, BS-018 showed a low ANI to the reported comparison genome, but its taxonomic assignment remains unresolved. Blood bank surfaces function as localized environmental conditions favoring bacteria with potential persistence-associated traits. This study identified environmental bacterial isolates exhibiting phenotypic and genomic characteristics potentially relevant to biosafety surveillance. Our results support incorporating integrated bioimaging, phenotypic characterization, and environmental surveillance with genomic resolution into infection prevention strategies and transfusion biosafety programs.
authors: Virginia Helena Albarracín

title: Lower triglyceride-glucose index is independently associated with multidrug-resistant organism infection in patients with pyogenic liver abscess: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: BackgroundThe triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, a surrogate marker of insulin resistance, has been linked to various infectious outcomes. However, no prior research has explored its independent association with multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO) infection among patients with pyogenic liver abscess (PLA). This retrospective cohort study aimed to investigate the relationship between TyG index and MDRO infection identified at or during the index admission in hospitalized PLA patients.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study of 440 PLA patients. The association between the TyG index and MDRO infection was evaluated using univariate and multivariate logistic regression, adjusting for a comprehensive panel of confounders, including severity of illness proxies. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were constructed to determine the predictive value of the TyG index, and restricted cubic splines (RCS) were used to examine the dose–response relationship. Interactions were examined via subgroup analysis, and adjusted odds ratios (ORs) accompanied by 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were depicted in a forest plot.ResultsMDRO infection was identified in 40 (9.1%) patients, including one patient that was simultaneously infected with both ESBL-KP and E. coli. After full multivariate adjustment (Model III), continuous TyG index exhibited a significant inverse independent association with MDRO infection: per standard deviation (SD) elevation of TyG index, the adjusted OR (aOR) was 0.470 (95% CI: 0.298–0.742). Relative to the lowest TyG tertile (T1, reference group), patients in the second (T2) and third (T3) tertiles presented markedly reduced MDRO odds, with aORs of 0.244 (95% CI: 0.095–0.628) and 0.241 (95% CI: 0.089–0.655), respectively. RCS modeling showed a declining relationship without statistically significant non-linearity (non-linear p-value = 0.233); because a non-significant non-linearity test does not establish linearity, and MDRO rates were similar in T2 (5.4%) and T3 (6.7%), the pattern is best characterized as threshold-like, with risk concentrated in the lowest TyG range. The TyG index yielded modest predictive accuracy for MDRO infection, with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.629. Subgroup interaction analyses detected no significant effect modification across all stratified clinical subgroups (all interaction p-values ranged from 0.146 to 0.864 in adjusted models).ConclusionAmong PLA patients, reduced TyG index independently correlates with elevated risk of MDRO infection. These novel findings reveal an inverse association of uncertain mechanism between host metabolic status and MDRO infection risk in PLA.
authors: Cuilan Tang

title: Accuracy of CRISPR/Cas-based nucleic acid detection for HIV-1: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background and aimsHIV continues to pose a substantial worldwide public health burden, and achieving the UNAIDS 95–95-95 goals depends on diagnostics that are reliable, rapid, and inexpensive. Because of its exceptional specificity and adaptable design, the CRISPR-Cas platform has emerged as an attractive option for nucleic acid detection. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we assessed the diagnostic accuracy of CRISPR-Cas-based assays for HIV-1, aiming to clarify their suitability for point-of-care testing and resource-limited settings.MethodsWeb of Science, PubMed, and CNKI were searched through August 12, 2026. We included original studies that applied CRISPR-Cas assays to detect HIV-1 nucleic acids and reported sufficient data to construct 2 × 2 tables (TP, FP, FN, TN), with RT-qPCR for HIV-1 RNA or qPCR for HIV-1 DNA serving as the reference standard. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, and SROC curves were generated using a bivariate random-effects model. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression were performed to investigate heterogeneity.ResultsNine studies met the inclusion criteria. The pooled sensitivity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.90–0.98) and the pooled specificity was 0.98 (95% CI 0.93–1.00), with an AUC of 0.99. The I2 statistic revealed low heterogeneity (11.82% for sensitivity and 8.91% for specificity). Publication bias was not statistically significant (Deeks’ test, p = 0.925). When stratified by Cas protein, Cas12a yielded a sensitivity of 0.97 and a specificity of 0.98, while Cas13a showed a sensitivity of 0.93 and a specificity of 0.99. However, each subgroup comprised only four to five studies, and between-subgroup differences were not formally examined. The use of fluorescence readout did not significantly influence accuracy (p > 0.05). Studies using RPA/RAA amplification achieved accuracy comparable to the overall pooled estimates.ConclusionIn selected studies, CRISPR-Cas-based assays showed high sensitivity and specificity for HIV-1, but clinical equivalence to qPCR remains unproven. When combined with RPA/RAA isothermal amplification, it holds promise as a rapid, accurate point-of-care testing (POCT) tool. Nevertheless, limited studies and methodological concerns highlight the need for further multicenter validation and real-world implementation data.Systematic review registrationThis systematic review and meta-analysis was registered with the Open Science Framework (OSF). The registration DOI is 10.17605/OSF.IO/AUTV8.
authors: Xiangying Zhang

title: Nitidine chloride alleviates DSS-induced ulcerative colitis in mice by modulating inflammation-intestinal barrier crosstalk and gut microbiota-metabolite interactions
abstract: IntroductionZanthoxylum nitidum (Roxb.) DC. is a traditional Chinese medicine widely used to treat digestive disorders. Nitidine chloride (NC) and its isomer chelerythrine chloride (CC) are the major bioactive benzophenanthridine alkaloids of Zanthoxylum nitidum, differing only in the methoxy substitution site on their molecular skeletons. However, whether this structural difference alters their pharmacological activities remains unclear.MethodsThis study established a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced ulcerative colitis (UC) mouse model to compare the therapeutic phenotypes of NC and CC and further elucidate the protective mechanisms of NC.ResultsAlthough both compounds alleviated UC, NC exhibited slightly superior effects in attenuating body weight loss and restoring several organ indices. Mechanistic analysis revealed that NC exerted protective effects against UC via dual regulation of inflammation-intestinal barrier crosstalk and gut microbiota-metabolite interactions. Specifically, NC disrupted the vicious crosstalk loop between intestinal inflammation and mucosal barrier damage. On the one hand, it suppressed excessive inflammatory responses by modulating pro-inflammatory cytokines and anti-inflammatory IL-10 in serum and colonic tissues, as well as downregulating colonic COX-2 expression. On the other hand, it restored intestinal barrier integrity by reducing serum levels of intestinal permeability markers diamine oxidase (DAO) and D-lactate, and upregulating tight junction proteins (Claudin-1, ZO-1) and MUC2. These effects blocked inflammatory infiltration induced by barrier leakage. Furthermore, 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolomics analysis showed that NC remodeled the dysregulated gut microbiota-metabolite interaction network in UC mice. NC significantly enriched beneficial intestinal bacteria such as Akkermansia and Limosilactobacillus. It also restored metabolic homeostasis of core pathways including glycerophospholipid metabolism, arachidonic acid metabolism, and branched-chain amino acid metabolism. Spearman correlation analysis further verified the close associations between differential microbial taxa and serum metabolites upon NC intervention. Moreover, network pharmacology and molecular docking provided preliminary in silico insights into potential target interactions of NC and CC.ConclusionCollectively, this study revealed that NC alleviated DSS-induced UC in mice by modulating inflammation-intestinal barrier crosstalk and gut microbiota-metabolite interactions. These findings provide pharmacodynamic mechanisms and experimental evidence supporting NC as a promising natural lead compound for anti-UC research, and lay a pharmacodynamic foundation for the modern development of Zanthoxylum nitidum.
authors: Hui-Peng Song

title: Alterations in oral metabolomics and microbiomics across CRC progression and identification of potential metabolic biomarkers
abstract: BackgroundOral microbiota can enter the gut via the oral-gut axis, leading to alterations in intestinal microbiota and their metabolites, which promote colorectal cancer (CRC). Relevant studies have shown that improving the detection rate of colorectal adenomas and performing timely removal can significantly reduce the incidence and mortality of CRC. Therefore, this study aims to elucidate changes in oral microbiota and their associated metabolites during the progression of CRC, clarify the relationship between these alterations and the onset and development of CRC, and identify potential metabolic biomarkers.ResultsWe performed LC–MS/MS metabolomic profiling and 16S rRNA gene sequencing analyses on oral samples from 23 patients with CRC, 19 patients with colorectal adenomas (CRA), and 22 normal controls (NC). Metabolomic analysis revealed significant differences in metabolites among the NC, CRA, and CRC groups. Notably, Tauro-b-muricholic acid exhibited a progressive increasing trend from NC to CRA and then to CRC. Metabolites associated with CRC were significantly enriched in the Glycerophospholipid metabolism pathway, as well as in pathways related to infections and autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and leishmaniasis. ROC curve analyses of metabolites between CRC vs. NC and CRC vs. CRA yielded AUC values of 0.95 and 0.91, respectively, suggesting its potential value in exploratory studies of noninvasive CRC diagnosis. Regarding microbiome analysis, both α-diversity and β-diversity analyses indicated significant differences in microbial community composition among the NC, CRA, and CRC groups. LEfSe analysis further identified that, compared with the NC group, g__Veillonella, g__Actinomyces, g__Leptotrichia, and g__Stomatobaculum were significantly enriched in CRC group. Compared with the CRA group, g__Selenomonas and g__Megasphaera were significantly enriched in CRC group. Correlation analyses between microbiota and metabolites demonstrated that the potential metabolite biomarkers enriched in CRC were significantly positively correlated with the aforementioned differential taxa.ConclusionThis study, through integrated metabolomic and microbiome analyses, demonstrated that both oral metabolites and oral microbiota are altered during the development of colorectal cancer. It highlighted potential early-driver metabolites across stages of colorectal carcinogenesis and identified novel candidate biomarkers from the oral metabolome for early, non-invasive risk screening of colorectal cancer.
authors: Fang Liu

title: Ethnobotanical survey and antibiofilm evaluation of medicinal plants used for the control of tomato bacterial wilt caused by Ralstonia solanacearum
abstract: IntroductionTomato is an important economic activity for rural populations in Burkina Faso. However, tomato wilt, caused by Ralstonia solanacearum is a serious threat to tomato yields. However, market gardeners use toxic pesticides to combat pests and plant diseases. The aim of this study was to identify medicinal plants traditionally used to treat crop diseases, so as to assess the plant’s potential to inhibit biofilm formation in R. solanacearum.MethodsAn ethnobotanical survey was conducted in the Northen region of Burkina Faso. We collected information on the chemical and biological treatment methods used by market gardeners. Five most frequently cited plants were selected for a biological study. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), antibiofilm activity against R. solanacearum were assessed. The total polyphenol and flavonoid contents of the extracts were quantified.ResultsA random sample of 103 volunteer market gardeners were interviewed. Seven plants and twenty-one pesticides were identified for treating crop diseases, grouped into seven (7) major chemical families. The avermectins were the most frequently cited and with the carbamates are classed as very hazardous. The plants most cited were A. indica (32.03%), N. tabacum (9.7%), K. senegalensis (9.7%), O. americanum (9.7%) and C. chinense (9.7%). O. americanum exhibited the most significant antibacterial activity, against strains 1743(12.5 mg/mL), OH19 (12.5 mg/mL) and B28 (25 mg/mL). Other extracts showed MIC values ≥50 mg/mL against all strains except OH19 for N. tabacum (25 mg/mL) and K. senegalensis (12.5 mg/mL). In addition, A. indica (63.33%), O. americanum (56.53%), C. chinense (54.8%), and N. tabacum (51.73%) presented the significative antibiofilm activities. K. senegalensis extract, which lack flavonoids, have shown no significant antibiofilm effect. O. americanum extract, rich in flavonoids (1. 93 ± 0.61 μg QE/100 mg) exhibited a significant antibiofilm inhibition.ConclusionThe significant antibiofilm effect of C. chinense, O. americanum, A. indica, and N. tabacum suggests that these plants are a promising alternative in the fight against R. solanacearum.
authors: Martin Kiendrebeogo

title: Histone H3.3 subvariant H3mm15 is required for normal spermatogenesis by regulating gene expression
abstract: AbstractHistone H3 variants play a fundamental role in chromatin regulation, contributing to gene expression. While the functional diversity of H3.3 subvariants remains largely unexplored, we identified H3mm15 as a testis-expressed H3.3 subvariant that regulates meiotic transcription. Using RNA sequencing and variant-specific reverse-transcription quantitative PCR, we demonstrate here that H3mm15 is expressed predominantly in the testis. Loss of H3mm15 leads to seminiferous tubule disorganization and altered expression of spermatogenesis-related genes. Chromatin profiling reveals that H3mm15 is relatively enriched at promoter-proximal regions compared with H3.3, despite its lower overall chromatin incorporation and lower nucleosomal stability. Functional assays show that H3mm15 has a more moderate impact on transcriptional responses to stimuli than H3.3. Although H3mm15 forms a less stable nucleosome, its reduced stability does not confer enhanced transcription by RNAPII in vitro. Our findings suggest the existence of an H3.3 sub-barcode mechanism, in which structurally distinct H3.3 subvariants differentially regulate chromatin states and contribute to gene regulation during spermatogenesis.

title: A novel mechanism for morphological change during bacterial sporulation based on programmed peptidoglycan degradation.
abstract: Many bacteria form spores to endure unfavorable conditions. While Firmicutes generate endospores through cell division, sporulation in non-Firmicutes remains less understood. The Gram-negative bacterium Myxococcus xanthus undergoes sporulation through two distinct mechanisms: rapid sporulation triggered by chemical induction and slow sporulation driven by starvation, both occurring independently of cell division. Instead, these processes depend on the complete degradation of the peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall by two lytic transglycosylases (LTGs), LtgA and LtgB. Remarkably, LtgB programs the pace of PG degradation by LtgA during rapid sporulation, ensuring a controlled process that prevents abrupt PG breakdown and the formation of non-resistant pseudospores. In addition to regulation between LTGs, PG degradation is also influenced by its synthesis; cells exhibiting increased muropeptide production often circumvent sporulation. These findings not only reveal novel mechanisms of bacterial sporulation but also shed light on the regulatory network governing PG dynamics.
authors: Ramirez Carbo CA, Irazoki O, Venkatesan S, Chen LJS, Morales HA, Garcia Avila AJ, Cheung HL, Cava F, Nan B.

title: StableProt: Structure-Aware Deep Learning for Protein Thermostability (Tm) and Environmental Adaptation (OGT) Prediction
abstract: Predicting protein melting temperature (Tm) and organismal optimal growth temperature (OGT) is essential for enzyme engineering, biocatalyst design, and metagenomic bioprospecting, yet computational prediction faces several fundamental bottlenecks: sequence-only representations miss tertiary packing; dual-task coupling induces destructive gradient conflict; natural database skew (>87% mesophiles) drives mesophilic collapse; and existing tools produce uncalibrated point predictions. To address these challenges, we present StableProt, a structure-aware framework that couples amino acid sequences with Foldseek 3Di structural tokens via a frozen SaProt backbone to capture 3D contacts. Disjoint heads condition thermodynamic stability on ecological context without gradient conflict, while targeted 14% mesophilic subsampling expands thermophile representation to eliminate mesophilic collapse. Calibrated ensemble modeling reduces calibration error to 1.92%, providing dependable 95% confidence intervals. Evaluating models across 10{degrees}C temperature intervals reveals severe baseline collapse at thermal extremes, whereas StableProt maintains robust accuracy across regimes. On ProThermDB and zero-shot FireProtDB, StableProt achieves state-of-the-art probabilistic accuracy (CRPS = 4.52{degrees}C and 8.71{degrees}C) while recovering 92.0% of hyperthermophiles ([≥]80{degrees}C), and in prospective validation, its calibrated intervals capture both enzyme stability (75.3% coverage) and host environmental growth temperatures (78.1% coverage). StableProt is freely accessible as an interactive web server at https://stableprot.dixitlab.org/.
authors: Behera, B. P.; Dixit, A.

title: Temperature effects on life history strategies for rapid growth potential of leaf epiphytic bacteria
abstract: AbstractPhyllosphere bacteria, occupying both epiphytic and endophytic habitats, constitute a critical plant-atmosphere interface. However, their community assembly and life-history strategies (LHSs) in response to temperature increase remain poorly understood. Here, we compared leaf phyllosphere bacterial communities with those in other plant compartments across four representative plant species from an alpine meadow on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. By combining observations along an elevational gradient with a controlled warming experiment, we found that temperature was closely associated with the deterministic assembly of leaf phyllosphere bacterial communities. Elevated temperature corresponded to shifts in taxonomic composition, diversity, assembly process, cross-compartment bacterial source, and co-occurrence network. Furthermore, elevated temperature was associated with a shift toward r-strategists in leaf phyllosphere bacterial LHSs, evidenced by higher ribosomal RNA operon (rrn) copy numbers for rapid growth potential and corroborated by genome assemblies of four warming-responsive epiphytic isolates and metagenomic sequencing. Based on 880 public 16S rRNA gene datasets from 45 locations on six continents, we identified a global increase in the rrn copy number in leaf epiphytic bacterial communities across diverse plant species, which was associated with elevated temperatures and enhanced diurnal fluctuation. Finally, we proposed a concept of four LHSs (growth, stress tolerance, competition, and resource acquisition) based on functional inference from 16S rRNA data, supported by the assembled epiphytic bacterial genomes and metagenomes. Collectively, our findings established a trait-based framework for understanding responses of leaf phyllosphere bacteria to future warming.

title: Free-living autotrophs drive a carbon fixation peak within the Orca Basin chemocline while heterotrophs dominate total activity from seawater to brine
abstract: AbstractDeep hypersaline anoxic basins (DHABs) are stratified, polyextreme environments found within enclosed and semi-enclosed seas worldwide. Here, we quantified microbial activity in Orca Basin, the largest known DHAB, to investigate carbon cycling across its steep chemical and salinity gradients. We measured total anabolic activity and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) fixation as a function of metabolic lifestyle (autotroph or heterotroph) and spatial niche (free-living or particle-associated) using dual-isotope labeling experiments and single-cell analysis by nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry (nanoSIMS). Activity was detected within all ten depths investigated from seawater to hypersaline brine, including by most cells within the brine. DIC fixation and total anabolic activity peaked within the oxic-anoxic interface, notably separate from the peak in cell and particle density deeper in the halocline. Autotrophs drove the peak in DIC fixation, but heterotrophs drove that of total activity; autotrophs were more abundant than heterotrophs at this depth but on average smaller and slower growing. Particle-associated heterotrophs, but not autotrophs, were significantly more active than their free-living counterparts within the interface. Heterotrophic communities derived an average of 4% to 10% of their biomass from DIC across the vertical transect, contributing just 2% of total DIC fixation within the peak but the majority within overlying seawater. Metagenomic analysis of catabolically active, sorted cells indicated members of at least five phyla were active within the oxic-anoxic interface, including putatively autotrophic Thermoproteota. These data provide high-sensitivity microbial activity measurements in Orca Basin and highlight the widespread viability of the resident microbiome.

title: A thermokinetic genome-scale metabolic model of the dominant archaeon Haloquadratum walsbyi reveals physicochemical constraints shaping carbon use
abstract: AbstractHypersaline ecosystems are among the most physicochemically extreme habitats on Earth, where high ionic strength, low water activity, and nutrient limitation impose energetic constraints on microbial metabolism. Despite these conditions, hypersaline lakes sustain stable microbial communities in which haloarchaea frequently dominate carbon turnover and energy fluxes. Understanding how microbial metabolism operates under such physicochemical constraints is therefore essential for explaining carbon processing in these ecosystems. Here, we reconstruct the first genome-scale metabolic model (GSMM) of the haloarchaeon Haloquadratum walsbyi, a globally distributed microorganism that dominates NaCl-saturated thalassohaline microbial communities. Owing to its known global dominance, metabolic processes in this organism are likely to exert a strong influence on nutrient processing in hypersaline systems. We hypothesize that physicochemical constraints of hypersaline environments restrict the set of energetically feasible metabolic states available to this organism, thereby shaping carbon assimilation strategies in these ecosystems. The reconstruction integrates genome reannotation, sequence homology, structural inference, and extensive manual curation, resolving functional assignments for 212 previously uncharacterized proteins. The resulting network comprises 1,313 metabolites and 1,873 reactions. Model simulations indicate that glycerol- and pyruvate-supported metabolism remain energetically feasible under hypersaline physicochemical assumptions used. Comparison with an independent transcriptomic dataset showed expression of genes associated with the predicted glycerol pathway, providing qualitative support for its physiological relevance. By extending the GSMM with a non-ideal, energy-dependent thermokinetic model, this study provides a mechanistic link between genomic potential, environmental constraints, and the formation of metabolic niches in hypersaline microbial ecosystems.

title: Marine bacterial taxonomy and metabolic exchange control the fate of extracellular glycolate carbon
abstract: AbstractHeterotrophic bacterial metabolism is a globally critical component of the marine carbon cycle, but its progression within a complex network of compounds and organisms challenges our ability to quantify carbon fate. Currently unresolved are the genomic underpinnings that control the path of carbon through microbial food webs and the role of metabolic exchange in these dynamics. We hypothesized that genomes could predict which members initially affect carbon fate for a given compound. We also posited that exchange of breakdown products generated from that compound further alters the path of carbon through the ecosystem. Our experiments featured simplified organic matter and microbial communities that examined glycolate metabolism in a diverse set of sixteen heterotrophic marine bacterial isolates. Stable isotope probing and imaging mass spectrometry alongside genomic analyses and microscopy revealed relationships between taxonomy and carbon fluxes. Nine of thirteen strains genomically capable of glycolate metabolism directly assimilated and respired glycolate carbon in monoculture. We then co-cultivated glycolate-incorporators with non-incorporators and found several non-incorporators assimilated more glycolate carbon into biomass than incorporators. Carbon use efficiency, reflecting partitioning of carbon into biomass versus carbon dioxide, was distinct across co-cultures and ranged from 0.01 - 3.15% depending on the co-culture mixtures. These results suggest glycolate carbon fate is not driven solely by microbial taxa genomically capable of assimilation but rather by metabolic interactions that further impact the efficiency of carbon transfer. Quantifying these effects is critical to refine conceptual and numerical models of heterotrophic organic matter processing.

title: Periphyton-associated combined restoration promotes microbial restructuring and phosphorus cycling in gleyed paddy soil
abstract: AbstractPersistent reductive stress and soil acidification impose strong environmental filtering in gleyed paddy soils, suppressing microbial activity and limiting phosphorus (P) bioavailability. Inspired by natural soil-water interface dynamics, we developed a restoration strategy combining slow-release CaO2, periphyton development, and phosphate-solubilizing bacteria (PSB) to alleviate habitat constraints and reactivate endogenous P cycling under field conditions. Slow-release CaO2 provided initial oxidative and alkalizing conditioning, effectively elevating soil pH and reducing total reducing substances (TRS). This initial habitat amelioration was accompanied by periphyton proliferation and a marked reduction in within-treatment community heterogeneity (microbiome convergence). Co-occurrence network analysis revealed topological realignments, with PSB taxa (Bacillus and Pseudomonas) occupying module hubs and periphytic microalgae acting as connectors between photoautotrophic and heterotrophic guilds. Metatranscriptomic profiling demonstrated coordinated upregulation of complementary P-cycling pathways, including pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)-dependent inorganic P solubilization and organic P mineralization (phoD, pqq, phn, and bpp). These functional transcripts were positively correlated with soil pH, phosphatase activities, and available P, but negatively correlated with TRS. Overall, this integrated conditioning strategy alleviated environmental filtering and was associated with coupled multi-guild functional responses, ultimately boosting endogenous P-cycling potential in degraded paddy soils. These findings suggest that a functional complementary framework may help inform microbiome-assisted restoration of constrained agricultural soils.

title: Biological insights and methodological challenges learned from working with a diverse heterotrophic marine bacterial library
abstract: AbstractOrganized collections of bacterial strains can help bridge the gap between studying model organisms and communities, through comparative experiments between genetically and phenotypically diverse strains. Yet, to date, few studies discuss in a detailed and systematic manner the processes of collecting and maintaining bacterial strain libraries. Here, we aim to address this gap by describing the establishment and initial characterization of a library of 62 marine heterotrophic bacteria, selected to represent a significant fraction of the genome-encoded functional diversity and a wide range of known phytoplankton-bacteria interactions. We systematically document the practical and methodological challenges of collecting, verifying, and phenotyping a diverse marine bacterial library; aspects of comparative microbiology that have received comparatively little detailed, systematic treatment to date. Cultured strains contain up to hundreds of mutations compared with the reference genomes, with non-synonymous mutations in rpoB and/or rpoC genes observed in ~15% of the cultures. Most strains grow well at 25°C, but the dependence of growth rate on temperature and the width of the temperature niche varies between strains in a systematic manner. We describe steps towards designing a universal, defined, minimal media for marine bacteria, revealing that growth inhibition on amino acids and peptides by carbohydrates is widespread. Cell counts obtained from flow cytometry and colony plating differ systematically, as do different methods to assess motility. Finally, we discuss traits potentially related to microbial interactions such as hemolysis, biofilm formation, and antibiotic resistance. Gammaproteobacteria such as Alteromonas, Pseudoalteromonas, and Vibrio reveal consistently robust growth, and activity, perhaps explaining why these clades are well-explored. Explicitly discussing the insights and challenges of working with strain libraries will pave the way to robust, reproducible, and generalizable mapping of bacterial traits across diversity.

title: Linking historical and current hydrothermal conditions with microbial functional potentials for soil Carbon, Nitrogen, and Phosphorus cycling
abstract: AbstractSoil microbial communities regulate carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P) cycling by producing extracellular enzymes that decompose organic matter and release nutrients. Yet how historical and current hydrothermal conditions jointly relate to the abundance of gene-encoded potential enzymes for soil C, N, and P cycling remains poorly resolved. We developed a predictive and interpretable machine-learning (ML) framework that integrates soil metagenomes across the continental United States with historical and contemporary hydrothermal metrics and soil physicochemical properties to quantify relative abundances of gene-encoded potential enzyme functional classes involved in soil C, N, and P cycling and to assess their associations with hydrothermal conditions. Our results showed that present hydrothermal conditions influenced gene-encoded functional potentials only when combined with historical hydrothermal context, revealing four association patterns. Both current and historical soil moisture were strongly linked to gene-encoded functional potential for N mineralization and transformation, usually in a U-shaped pattern. Soil thermal conditions positively related to gene functional potential for N acquisition. Conversely, gene-encoded functional potential for C and P acquisition was mainly associated with historical hydrothermal conditions and was affected by local soil nutrients. These patterns likely reflect the trade-off in microbial resource allocation between mitigating hydrothermal stresses and acquiring nutrients. These results provide a gene-level, continental-scale framework linking hydrothermal history and present conditions to the testable microbial functional allocation hypothesis. These outcomes enable more explicit representation of microbial association with long-term environmental change and their consequences for soil C, N, and P cycling in biogeochemical and Earth system models.
