title: PFM: perturbed flow matching for structure-based drug design
abstract: AbstractMotivationTarget-specific 3D molecular generation is a promising approach for structure-based drug design. However, existing diffusion-based methods are generally restricted to marginal distributions with closed-form solutions, limiting the flexibility of generative process design, especially for the forward noising process. As a result, these methods may be less effective in modeling the complex distributions underlying pocket-conditioned molecular generation.ResultsWe develop Perturbed Flow Matching (PFM), a flow-matching-based framework for protein pocket–conditioned 3D molecular generation. PFM employs a perturbed conditional probability path that incorporates both pocket binding-site information and coupled atom type–coordinate information, enabling more effective generation of molecules in protein binding environments. On CrossDocked2020, PFM achieves competitive structural quality and the best average Vina score among the evaluated unguided methods (-7.12); PFM-G further improves the score to -8.70 with tailored classifier-free guidance. Experiments on additional molecular datasets further confirm the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed framework.Availability and implementationhttps://github.com/kurisu92725/PFM

title: CellSavior: an open-source framework for improved cell calling in targeted single-cell DNA sequencing
abstract: AbstractMotivationSingle-cell DNA sequencing (scDNA-seq) has emerged as a key approach for studying complex genomic variation, including tumor heterogeneity. Despite its increasing commercial availability, exemplified by the Tapestri platform, analytical reproducibility remains limited due to reliance on proprietary and non-transparent pipelines. Among preprocessing steps, cell calling is particularly critical, as it determines which barcodes correspond to true cells rather than background noise and directly shapes all downstream analyses. However, existing methods typically rely on empirical thresholding and exhibit inconsistent performance across datasets. These limitations underscore the need for a robust and generalizable cell calling framework for reliable scDNA-seq analysis.ResultsWe developed CellSavior, an open-source cell calling algorithm with an integrated downstream pipeline that produces standardized outputs. CellSavior employs an ensemble clustering strategy across multiple distance metrics, combined with confidence-weighted merging, to generate a consensus classification that reduces bias and improves robustness. Across 33 public and in-house single-cell DNA sequencing datasets, CellSavior recapitulated cell annotations generated by commercial software (CellFinder) in 31 cases (93.9%). In the remaining discordant cases, CellSavior yielded more biologically interpretable annotations, rescuing previously undetected clusters enriched for key hotspot genomic alterations.AvailabilityThe source code for CellSavior is freely available at https://github.com/dauer-tgilab/CellSavior; DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22744146.Supplementary informationSupplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: DTBNet: Multimodal 3D Geometric Perception with Hierarchical Attention for Robust Drug–Target Interaction and Binding Affinity Prediction
abstract: AbstractMotivationAccurate prediction of drug-target interactions (DTIs) and binding affinity (DTA) constitutes a core challenge in accelerating drug discovery. While existing computational methods have made progress, most models struggle to capture critical physicochemical interactions in 3D space due to reliance on 1D sequences or 2D graph structures, and exhibit limited generalization in cold-start scenarios. This study proposes DTBNet, a unified prediction framework integrating multimodal geometric perception and hierarchical attention. The framework constructs heterogeneous embeddings combining local chemical details with global biological information by incorporating protein 3D geometric features and multilevel drug representations. During cross-modal interaction, atom–residue cross-attention first captures pair-specific local associations, followed by group-level multi-head self-attention that integrates complementary chemical-semantic, global structural, and local geometric interaction representations.ResultsExperiments on benchmark datasets (Davis, KIBA, PDBBind) demonstrate that compared with the optimal baseline models, DTBNet achieves up to 19.8% reduction in mean squared error and 8.0% improvement in Pearson correlation coefficient, maintaining optimal performance in drug cold-start, target cold-start, and completely novel pairing scenarios, showcasing robust cross-domain adaptability. Independent validation on GPCR targets achieves RMSE 0.783, confirming real-world applicability. Visualization analyses reveal DTBNet precisely identifies interaction sites between key transmembrane helical domain residues and drug aromatic rings, with attention distribution highly consistent with experimentally resolved binding conformations. These results establish DTBNet as a new performance benchmark through 3D geometric perception and dynamic attention mechanisms, providing interpretable molecular insights for structure-based rational drug design and demonstrating broad potential in virtual screening and target discovery.AvailabilityThe source code and data are available at https://github.com/wyx2012/DTB_Net.Supplementary informationSupplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: MIRAGE-DTA: conflict-aware multimodal evidence arbitration for drug–target affinity prediction
abstract: AbstractMotivationMultimodal drug–target affinity (DTA) models can incorporate molecular, protein, assay and textual evidence whose availability and reliability vary under missing modalities, cold-start entities and assay distribution shift.ResultsWe present MIRAGE-DTA, a reliability-oriented evidence-arbitration layer that complements DTA encoders by keeping current-sample and training-set retrieval evidence as two explicit chains, carrying modality masks into fusion, retrieving training-only neighbors, and resolving disagreement with an interaction gate and validation-selected anchor. Across BindingDB_Kd, DAVIS, KIBA and a 2010–2024 CHEMBL_ASSAY benchmark with 35,238 interactions, experiments tested cold-start, missing-modality and assay/temporal shift settings. Under 35% sequence/text missingness on CHEMBL_ASSAY, 10-seed paired evaluation showed that MIRAGE-DTA reduced expected calibration error relative to late fusion by 0.0524, 0.0923 and 0.1018 on assay-cold, target-cold and temporal splits. Risk at 80% coverage was significantly lower on target-cold and temporal splits and numerically lower on assay-cold. A complementary complete-evidence direct-pChEMBL regression analysis also showed lower RMSE for the two-branch model than for current-only and retrieval-only regressors across assay-cold, target-cold and temporal splits. Ranking remained broadly competitive, with a modest trade-off on the temporal split, indicating that the principal benefit lies in calibrated and selective prediction under incomplete or shifted evidence. Shortcut audits quantified neighbor-overlap effects and showed that temporal retrieval was not driven by repeated compounds or near-duplicate scaffolds.Availability and implementationSource code is available at https://github.com/wushen1103-collab/mirage_drug_miniprototype and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22695984; data come from public sources.

title: Depth-dependent responses of soil microbial communities and co-occurrence networks to solar photovoltaic panel installation along a soil profile in a hyper-arid desert
abstract: IntroductionPhotovoltaic (PV) power generation is expanding rapidly in arid regions, but its belowground ecological effects across soil profiles remain poorly understood.MethodsHere, we examined soil bacterial and fungal communities across three microhabitats (bare land, between PV panels, under PV panels) and five soil layers (0–100 cm) at a PV station in Xinjiang, China. Bacterial 16S rRNA gene and fungal ITS amplicon sequencing was integrated with functional prediction, community assembly analysis, and co-occurrence networks.ResultsPV panel installation significantly altered microbial taxonomic composition and potential functions, with Pseudomonas and functions related to methanol oxidation and nitrogen fixation enriched in PV zones, while nitrate reduction and hydrocarbon degradation were more abundant in bare land (BL). These effects weakened with increasing soil depth. Bacterial α-diversity did not change significantly, but bacterial community structure differed significantly between PV zones and BL; fungal community structure differed only in the 0–20 cm and 20–40 cm soil layers. Bacterial assembly shifted from deterministic homogeneous selection in BL to more stochastic processes in PV zones, accompanied by increased dispersal limitation, suggesting weakened deterministic environmental filtering and reduced dispersal under PV panels, whereas fungal assembly remained stochastic-dominated. Bacterial co-occurrence networks decreased in size and complexity with soil depth. PV-zone co-occurrence networks were more modular but more vulnerable than BL, while fungal networks were smaller and relatively stable.DiscussionThese findings reveal depth-dependent and microhabitat-specific microbial responses to PV installation, with bacteria more sensitive than fungi, and provide a scientific basis for assessing the ecological impacts of large-scale PV deployment in arid desert ecosystems.

title: Transitional ecosystem states in coastal waters undergoing changing oxygen conditions revealed by coupled geochemical and microbial dynamics
abstract: BackgroundCoastal oxygen depletion is a major driver of changes in sediment biogeochemistry and microbial functioning. However, oxygen states vary over space and time, which results in temporal dynamics that are so far under explored. This study examined three sites with differing oxygen regimes across a year to investigate how temporal oxygen variability shapes surface sediment microbial communities and activity.MethodsCoastal Baltic Sea surface sediments were sampled over one year at three sites with differing long-term oxygen regimes—one site that was predominantly oxic, one with predominantly low-oxygen conditions, and one intermediate site with fluctuating oxygen availability. Sediment biogeochemistry, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, and metatranscriptomic analyses were combined to assess temporal changes in microbial community composition and transcriptional activity.ResultsThe results showed that long-term oxygen history was the primary factor structuring both microbial community composition and transcriptional profiles. The shallow site was characterized by mostly oxygenated conditions and exhibited relatively stable communities and transcriptional activity over time. The deep site was predominantly characterized by long-term low-oxygen conditions and was dominated by anaerobic metabolic patterns. In contrast, the intermediate site, that was exposed to more pronounced fluctuating oxygen conditions, showed the highest temporal variability in both community composition and RNA transcripts. This site also displayed stronger shifts in transcriptional activity over time, indicating a higher sensitivity of microbial processes to environmental variability compared to the other sites.ConclusionThese results suggested that transitional oxygen habitats represented dynamic ecological states where microbial communities and functions rapidly responded to changing environmental conditions. Overall, oxygen availability strongly structured both microbial composition and activity in coastal sediments, with transitional habitats exhibiting enhanced temporal variability. These findings further indicated that environments experiencing fluctuating oxygen conditions may be particularly responsive to ongoing environmental change in coastal systems.

title: Esophageal microecology: unraveling the mechanisms underlying esophageal cancer and precancerous lesions
abstract: Esophageal cancer is a common and lethal digestive malignancy worldwide. Despite advances in imaging and endoscopy, most patients are diagnosed at intermediate or advanced stages and have poor long-term outcomes. Perturbations of the oral, esophageal, and intestinal microbiota have emerged as potential risk factors for esophageal cancer and its precursors, although studies remain highly heterogeneous in populations, sampling methods, and analytical strategies. This review synthesises current evidence on the microecological features of the normal esophagus, with a primary focus on esophageal squamous intraepithelial neoplasia (ESIN)—synonymous with dysplasia—and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Barrett’s esophagus (BE) and esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) are also examined selectively for comparative purposes to highlight distinct microenvironmental trajectories. We examine potential microbiota-mediated mechanisms, including chronic inflammation, immune modulation, metabolic alterations, genotoxicity, bacteria–fungus interactions, and bacteriophage-driven remodelling of host–microbe networks, and discuss translational opportunities to improve clinical outcomes.

title: Exploratory randomized trial of the bacterial lysate Qipian in stable COPD: peripheral inflammatory, gut and airway microbiota, and fecal metabolomic changes
abstract: IntroductionTo explore Qipian-associated changes in clinical symptoms, systemic inflammation, microbiota, and metabolomic profiles in patients with stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).MethodThis exploratory study enrolled 40 patients with stable COPD who completed 12 weeks of follow-up (Qipian group: n = 22; control group: n = 18). Key assessments included: pulmonary function (FEV1/FVC, FEV1, FEV1%, FVC, FEF25−−75%), clinical symptoms (mMRC dyspnea scale, CAT questionnaire), inflammatory markers, gut and airway microbiota analysis (16S rRNA sequencing for α/β-diversity and taxonomic profiling), untargeted metabolomics (LC-MS-based differential metabolite screening and KEGG pathway enrichment).ResultAfter treatment, the mMRC and CAT scores in the Qipian group showed a decreasing trend compared to the control group (P = 0.156 and P = 0.055). No statistically significant differences were observed in pulmonary function parameters (all P > 0.05). Inflammatory analysis revealed a significant reduction in NLRP3 expression in the Qipian group compared to controls (P < 0.001). IL-13 expression decreased significantly compared with pre-treatment levels (P = 0.034), accompanied by a reduction in serum IL-13 protein levels. Microbiome profiling demonstrated that, compared to the control group, the β-diversity of the gut microbiota in the Qipian group significantly separated after treatment, with an increased relative abundance of potentially beneficial taxa, including Limosilactobacillus and Lactobacillus, and a decreased abundance of potentially pathogenic-associated taxa, including Escherichia-Shigella and Streptococcus. Similarly, the β diversity of the airway microbiota was significantly distinct, showing increased relative abundance of potentially beneficial or commensal-associated taxa such as Veillonella and Prevotella, and decreased abundance of potentially pathogenic-associated taxa such as Streptococcus. Metabolomic profiling identified significant upregulation of L-glutamic acid and L-glutamine. Exploratory correlation analyses suggested associations among selected metabolites, microbiota taxa, and inflammatory markers.ConclusionIn this exploratory randomized controlled trial, Qipian was associated with non-significant trends toward symptom improvement and with changes in selected inflammatory markers, gut and airway microbiota, and gut metabolites in patients with stable COPD. These findings suggest Qipian-associated biological changes along the gut–lung axis, involving microbial community remodeling, microbiota-related metabolic alterations, and changes in NLRP3/caspase-1- and IL-13-related inflammatory signaling. However, the clinical outcomes did not reach statistical significance, and these findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory evidence of clinical efficacy.Trial RegistrationChinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2100054037. registered on 07 December, 2021.

title: Harnessing waste-derived amendments for microbially mediated acid mine drainage remediation: from mechanisms to process optimization and machine learning
abstract: Acid mine drainage (AMD) remains a persistent environmental challenge, creating a need for treatment strategies that combine sustained contaminant control with resource-efficient use of residual materials. Waste-derived amendments may couple residue valorization with microbially mediated treatment of AMD, particularly mine-tailings leachate, but direct evidence combining variable waste-derived donors with heterogeneous collected leachate remains limited, and machine-learning (ML) models have rarely been validated across amendment batches, reactors, or sites. This review therefore evaluates amendment functions, microbial and geochemical mechanisms, operational constraints, and the role of ML in process development. A targeted narrative synthesis was conducted using publisher webpages, PubMed, and institutional repositories through 17 September 2026. Evidence was organized into four application settings: collected tailings-leachate treatment, source-zone tailings amendment, other real mine waters, and synthetic AMD; modeling studies were assessed separately for transferability. Representative studies show that performance is strongly endpoint-dependent. In 460-day field reactors containing organic substrates, sulfate removal was 26–35 mol% and Zn removal reached 88–95 mol%, whereas Mn removal was only 2–6 mol%. In a 172-day ethanol-fed reactor treating successive tailings leachates, sulfate removal reached 84.7 ± 6.9%, most metal removals approached 100%, and Mn removal was approximately 80%. A 17-run brewery-wastewater modeling study reported within-study R2 values of 0.97 and 0.99, demonstrating predictive feasibility but not transferable or autonomous control. The review is limited by selective rather than exhaustive searching, incomplete access to some full texts, and heterogeneity in influent chemistry, treatment boundaries, and sampling periods, which precluded pooled analysis. Overall, waste-derived amendments can support sulfate reduction, alkalinity generation, biomass retention, and metal partitioning, but strong metal removal can coexist with incomplete sulfate conversion and element-specific limitations. Future progress requires continuous and field-scale validation, matched mass balances, disturbance testing, residual-stability assessment, and ML used as constrained decision support rather than as a substitute for mechanistic and prospective operating evidence.

title: Season dominates and housing system conditionally modulates the gut microbiota of red pandas
abstract: The gut microbiota critically influences host nutrition and immunity, yet the combined effects of housing systems and season on endangered bamboo-feeding mammals remain unclear. We analyzed the gut microbial diversity, community structure, and potential metabolic functions of captive and free-range red pandas (Ailurus styani) across winter–spring and summer–autumn seasons. Season emerged as the primary driver of microbial richness and community structure, with higher richness in winter–spring and greater seasonal amplitude in free-range than captive red pandas. Housing effects were significant only in summer–autumn, when free-range individuals showed higher Shannon/Simpson diversity and distinct community separation from captives. Dominant phyla were Firmicutes (65.17%) and Proteobacteria (26.76%). Differential enrichment included Streptococcus in captive summer–autumn, Lactococcus/Leuconostoc in free-range summer–autumn, Escherichia-Shigella/Staphylococcus in captive winter–spring, and genus 1174-901-12 (an uncultured genus within the family Ruminococcaceae) in free-range winter–spring. Based on KEGG prediction, free-range individuals exhibited stronger seasonal functional potential differences; they were enriched in 17 pathways, including amino acid metabolism and energy metabolism, in winter–spring, and shifted toward carbohydrate metabolism and membrane transport in summer–autumn, with additional enrichment in xenobiotics biodegradation and metabolism pathways. In contrast, the functional potential shift in captive individuals was relatively limited. In summary, seasonal variation dominated the structural remodeling of the gut microbiota in red pandas, while housing system acted as a conditional regulatory factor whose effect was significantly amplified in summer–autumn. This study suggests that the free-range pattern may help maintain gut microbiota diversity, structural stability, and metabolic functional potential. This study provides a microecological basis for gut health management in endangered bamboo-eating mammals.

title: Research progress on the mechanisms of microbial degradation of antibiotics and attenuation of antibiotic resistance genes during composting
abstract: Antibiotics and their resistance genes (ARGs) commonly coexist in organic solid waste, posing significant ecological and public health risks. Composting is a crucial biological process for mitigating such composite pollution. This review elucidates the microbial mechanisms driving the simultaneous removal of antibiotics and ARGs in composting systems. Specifically, it details how parent antibiotic compounds are transformed through enzymatic degradation and co-metabolic pathways, thereby alleviating selection pressure on drug-resistant bacteria. Microbial strategies that interfere with the transmission and persistence of ARGs, including the inhibition of horizontal gene transfer and the degradation of extracellular DNA, are highlighted. Furthermore, this review introduces the core concept of “synergistic attenuation,” emphasizing the coupled relationship between antibiotic degradation and ARG suppression. It also summarizes the application of multi-omics techniques (e.g., metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and metabolomics) in validating these complex mechanisms. Finally, it outlines future directions for enhancing this synergistic process through targeted regulation of microbial community structure and function, providing a theoretical foundation and innovative insights for optimizing composting as an efficient and low-risk organic waste treatment technology.

title: Microbial control of ocular homeostasis and disease: mechanisms, metabolites, and therapeutic opportunities
abstract: The relationship between microbiota and ocular disease is reshaping current views of eye health. Ocular homeostasis depends not only on local tissues but also on interactions among several systems. These systems include the ocular surface microbiota, gut microbiota, systemic immune and metabolic networks, the blood–eye barrier, and the neurovascular unit. Commensal microbial signals can preserve epithelial integrity, barrier immunity, wound repair, immune tolerance, vascular stability, and neuroprotection. Dysbiosis can convert this regulatory network into a source of ocular injury. This occurs through several mechanisms, such as lipopolysaccharide exposure, loss of short chain fatty acids, disturbed tryptophan, bile acid, and lipid metabolism, Th17 and Treg imbalance, complement activation, microglial reprogramming, and molecular mimicry. These regulatory interactions operate along an integrated, multi-compartment spatial network. Locally, the exposed ocular surface and contiguous periocular niches calibrate epithelial renewal and barrier immunity. Systemically, intestinal microbial communities regulate intraocular vascular integrity and neuroimmune tone through circulating metabolites, pathogen-associated molecular patterns, and immune cell trafficking. Low-biomass intraocular signals and the ocular virome provide additional layers of local immune governance. Disruption of this compartmentalized network characterizes ocular surface diseases, uveitis, diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, and retinal degeneration. Therapeutic strategies are consequently shifting from empirical antimicrobial eradication toward targeted microbiota-directed interventions, including postbiotics, metabolite supplementation, and barrier-reinforcing platforms. Characterizing these host-microbial circuits may guide the development of therapies that restore ocular health by stabilizing local and systemic microenvironments.

title: The phageome in critical illness: bacteriophage–bacteria interactions, resistome dynamics, and pathogen domination in the intensive care unit
abstract: Critical illness disrupts microbial communities through antimicrobial exposure, altered nutrient supply, tissue injury, and loss of anatomical barriers. Bacterial profiling has linked these disturbances to pathogen domination and infection, but bacteria participate in ecosystems that also contain bacteriophages, eukaryotic viruses, and mobile genetic elements. This narrative review examines how the phageome may influence microbial ecological transitions during critical illness, including changes in colonization resistance, pathogen domination, and the potential progression to invasive infection. We integrate recent human observations with experimental evidence on phage predation, lysogeny, bacterial defense, spatial organization, and resistance-gene mobility. Longitudinal respiratory viromics and circulating phage DNA studies provide direct clinical entry points, whereas much of the mechanistic evidence originates from healthy volunteers, inflammatory disease cohorts, cultured communities, and animal models. These evidence levels support an ecological framework but do not establish a universal phage-mediated pathway to ICU infection. Phages can suppress susceptible pathogens, remove protective commensals, select resistant bacterial phenotypes, or support lysogen fitness. Their contribution to antimicrobial resistance extends beyond resistance genes encoded within phage genomes to transduction, phage–plasmid exchange, and indirect effects on conjugation and community composition. Interpretation requires separating viral detection from productive infection, bacterial DNA packaging from successful transfer, and relative abundance from absolute expansion. We propose a compartment-aware longitudinal research framework combining viral-particle and bulk metagenomics, bacterial strain resolution, functional validation, and prospectively adjudicated clinical events. The immediate clinical opportunity is to determine whether phage measurements add actionable information to bacterial surveillance; therapeutic manipulation remains a downstream application requiring ecological and clinical validation.

title: Fusobacterium nucleatum regulates SLC7A11, inhibits ferroptosis and leads to oxaliplatin resistance in colorectal cancer
abstract: BackgroundFusobacterium nucleatum (F. nucleatum), a pathogenic bacterium associated with colorectal cancer (CRC), has been increasingly linked to chemoresistance. While ferroptosis is recognized as a contributor to chemotherapy resistance mechanisms, the regulatory role of gut microbiota in this process remains poorly characterized.MethodsTo explore the potential relationship between gut microbiota dysbiosis and CRC recurrence, 16S rRNA sequencing was performed on CRC tissues, revealing a positive correlation between the high abundance of F. nucleatum in CRC tissue and tumor recurrence. Experimental validation confirmed F. nucleatum-mediated oxaliplatin (L-OHP) resistance both in vitro and in vivo. Analysis of the transcriptome of cells co-cultured with F. nucleatum identified an association between ferroptosis and F. nucleatum infection. Furthermore, in vitro analyses quantified malondialdehyde, ferrous iron, glutathione, and oxidized glutathione levels to assess potential ferroptosis modulation under L-OHP exposure.ResultsMechanistically, F. nucleatum inhibits ferroptosis and promotes L-OHP resistance through the overexpression of SLC7A11. This effect is mediated by the TLR4/AP-1 signaling pathway, as confirmed by chromatin immunoprecipitation quantitative PCR (ChIP–qPCR) and dual-luciferase reporter assays, which showed enhanced binding of AP-1 c-Jun to the SLC7A11 promoter following F. nucleatum infection. Clinical data further supported the association between the TLR4/AP-1/SLC7A11 axis, F. nucleatum abundance in tumor tissue, and CRC recurrence.ConclusionThese findings establish a direct role of F. nucleatum in L-OHP resistance through ferroptosis inhibition. Therapeutic targeting of F. nucleatum and ferroptosis pathways may thus offer novel strategies to mitigate chemotherapy resistance and improve the prognosis of CRC patients.

title: Protection against lethal pneumonic plague by intramuscular F1V vaccine incorporating a colloidal TLR4-TLR7 dual adjuvant
abstract: Yersinia pestis is a facultative intracellular bacterium that causes plague, which manifests in bubonic form and the more severe pneumonic and septicemic forms. There is no FDA-approved vaccine for plague, and those used in the past for human prophylaxis were suboptimal against aerosol infection or nonencapsulated strains. To provide broad protection against Y. pestis, further optimization of vaccine formulations is essential. In a lethal aerosol challenge model using nonencapsulated Y. pestis in BALB/c mice, we compared an existing benchmark vaccine to a similar formulation using novel TLR4-TLR7 dual adjuvant KUP101A in place of TLR9 adjuvant CpG 2006. In addition, we compared vaccination through the subcutaneous (SC) and intramuscular (IM) routes, and we compared vaccination using KUP101A with or without additional alum adjuvant. Two vaccine doses were given four weeks apart, and four weeks later mice were challenged via whole-body aerosol exposure. KUP101A compared favorably to CpG for conferring protection after Y. pestis challenge and led to significantly lower bacterial burden in tissues. This was observed despite similar humoral immunity and Th1/Th2 phenotype, and less evidence of splenic T cell memory than was seen with CpG. Alum was necessary for the protective effect of KUP101A, similarly to CpG. Finally, we saw evidence that IM vaccination was preferable to SC for inducing Th1 polarization, based on the ratio of serum IgG2a to IgG1 and splenocyte cytokine secretion. This study demonstrates that KUP101A is a promising adjuvant with a favorable safety profile for future Y. pestis vaccine development.

title: Increasing prevalence of a mupirocin- and fusidic acid-resistant MSSA CC121-t1994 clone in pediatric skin and soft tissue infections: 8-year longitudinal study at an Spanish Hospital
abstract: IntroductionSkin and soft tissue infections (SSTI) in pediatric patients have increased in recent years, and mupirocin and fusidic acid are important therapeutic options.Materials and methodsAll 217 Staphylococcus aureus isolates recovered from pediatric SSTIs in a Spanish hospital during January 2018-october 2025 were characterized (one isolate/patient). The phenotypes and genotypes of antimicrobial resistance, virulence genes and genetic lineages were analyzed along three time periods (2018–2021, 2022–2023 and 2024–2025).ResultsMost of 217 isolates were methicillin-susceptible (MSSA, 91.2%), and these MSSA belonged to 14 clonal-complexes (CC), being CC121 (54.5%) the most prevalent followed by CC30 (11.6%) and CC45 (7.1%). Ten spa-types were found among MSSA-CC121 isolates, being t1994 predominant (75.0%), followed by t1077 and t272. Seventeen of the 19 MRSA isolates identified belonged to the lineages CC8, CC30, and CC5. Most of MSSA-CC121 isolates carried eta and/or etb (98/108, 90.7%), and this prevalence was even higher among CC121-t1994 isolates (93.8%). The tst gene was mainly detected among MSSA-CC30/CC22. The prevalence of MSSA-CC121 isolates increased during the 8-year study (21.6%/2018–2021, 50.6%/2022–2023, 65.2%/2024–2025), associated with an enrichment of spa-t1994 (9.8%/2018–2021, 59.6%/2024–2025), and a decrease in CC30 prevalence. High frequencies of mupirocin-resistant (MUPR, mostly mediated by mupA) and fusidic-acid-resistant (FAR, mostly mediated by fusB) were observed among S. aureus (43.8 and 30.9%, respectively), and resistance to both (MUPR-FAR) was found in 29.5% of isolates, most of them MSSA-CC121 (95.3%). A significant increase in the rate of MUPR-FAR isolates was observed along the years, both among S. aureus (5.9%/2018–2021, 28.6%/2022–2023 and 43.8%/2024–2025) and CC121 isolates (27.3%/2018–2021, 53.8%/2022–2023 and 63.8%/2024–2025) (p < 0.05). The prevalence of impetigo cases among the pediatric SSTIs increased along the years (2018–2021: 37.3%; 2022–2023: 68.8%; 2024–2025: 80.9%); in addition, a significant increase was observed in the prevalence of MSSA-CC121 and MSSA-CC121-MUPR-FAR in impetigo cases along the years (p < 0.05).Conclusiona MUPR-FAR MSSA-CC121-t1994 clone, harboring mupA, fusB and exfoliatin genes, was increasingly detected among pediatric SSTIs in this hospital-based study, especially in impetigo cases, what deserves careful monitoring for its control.

title: Antimicrobial peptide–drug conjugates: rational design, pharmacological evaluation, and translational perspectives
abstract: Antimicrobial peptide–drug conjugates (APDCs) combine peptide and antibiotic functions within a single covalent construct. APDCs share design features with antibody–drug conjugates, but the field lacks an integrated account of how such conjugates should be designed and evaluated. This review examines that process from scaffold selection to translational precedent. Design decisions are treated as medicinal chemistry: which antimicrobial peptide scaffold to start from and how to stabilize it, which payload to carry, whether the linker should be cleavable, conditionally stable, or non-cleavable, and whether engaging one or two targets yields a better antibacterial profile. Pharmacological evidence is then assessed for representative vancomycin, β-lactam, aminoglycoside, and fluoroquinolone conjugates, with experimentally demonstrated mechanisms distinguished from those that are indirectly inferred, computationally predicted, or hypothesized. In series reported through July 2026, conjugation produced large MIC reductions relative to inactive or resistant parent antibiotics, including in vancomycin-resistant enterococci, and in some cases restored activity against strains refractory to both parent molecules; comparisons with active standards of care were limited. By contrast, pharmacokinetic characterization is nearly absent, immunomodulatory and anti-biofilm mechanisms are only beginning to be dissected, in vivo efficacy has been reported for only seven APDC programs, and no dedicated toxicology study was identified. Two adjacent programs—the approved siderophore cephalosporin cefiderocol and the discontinued antibody–antibiotic conjugate DSTA4637S—serve as translational precedents, illustrating the manufacturing, safety, and regulatory hurdles an APDC must clear. Within these constraints, experimentally validated artificial-intelligence-assisted sequence design may support peptide modules for future APDCs, although our literature search did not identify an AI-designed APDC.

title: Gut microbial characteristics associated with pegylated interferon treatment response in chronic hepatitis B: insights into the gut–liver axis
abstract: BackgroundPegylated interferon (Peg-IFN) treatment response varies considerably among patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB). The role of the gut microbiota in this heterogeneity remains unclear. This study aimed to characterize gut microbial features associated with Peg-IFN response and explore their potential relevance to the gut–liver axis.MethodsA total of 64 patients with CHB who completed 24 weeks of Peg-IFN-based therapy were enrolled in this study. Fecal samples collected at week 24 were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Microbial characteristics and clinical factors associated with treatment response were evaluated, followed by development of an integrated classification model.ResultsAmong the 64 patients, 38 were classified as responders and 26 as non-responders. Responders exhibited distinct gut microbial profiles, characterized by increased microbial richness (p = 0.014), altered community composition (p = 0.045), and different microbial interaction patterns. Dorea abundance was enriched in responders and independently associated with treatment response. Multivariable logistic regression identified lower baseline HBsAg levels (OR = 0.562, p = 0.048), higher platelet counts (OR = 1.020, p = 0.007), and increased Dorea abundance (OR = 3.876, p = 0.008) as independent factors associated with response. Restricted cubic spline analysis supported a significant association between Dorea abundance and response probability. The Virological–Host–Microbial (VHM) triad model integrating these factors demonstrated promising apparent discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.790) and calibration in the development cohort.ConclusionDistinct gut microbial ecological patterns are associated with Peg-IFN treatment response in CHB, with Dorea representing a characteristic microbial feature. This study provides a multidimensional framework for understanding heterogeneity in interferon responsiveness and highlights the potential relevance of the gut–liver–immune axis.

title: Survival and genomic mutations of long-term Pseudomonas fluorescens cultures: an in vitro model to study persistence in food production environments
abstract: BackgroundMicrobial persistence in food production environments poses a significant challenge to food safety, as bacteria can survive cleaning and disinfection procedures by existing in dormant states and forming biofilms.MethodsWith the aim to investigate the long-term adaptive strategies three strains (CECT378, ps_20, and ps_77) belonging to the Pseudomonas fluorescens subgroup (Pf) were maintained in minimal medium for two years under nutrient starvation at 4 °C and 22 °C were characterized. Active cells (CFU), the PMAxx-derived genome-copy/CFU ratio, used as an indirect indicator of the presence of viable but non-culturable (VBNC) cells and persister cells were monitored across multiple time points. Whole-genome sequencing data from 330 clones recovered from cultures maintained at both temperatures were analyzed to investigate genomic adaptation during long-term survival.ResultsThe strains maintained high cell densities (~107–108 CFU/mL) throughout the experiment, with the active state predominating. The number of persister cells increased progressively over time, particularly at 4 °C, whereas the PMAxx-derived genome-copy/CFU ratio remained generally low, suggesting a limited potential contribution of VBNC cells. Whole-genome sequencing revealed strain-dependent mutation accumulation patterns,with dN/dS ratios below 1 in CECT378 and ps_20 and above 1 in ps_77. Convergent mutations were identified across strains in genes regulating biofilm formation, RNA polymerase subunits (rpoS, rpoA), two-component systems (BarA/uvrY, cbrA), and genes previously associated with the WS (wrinkly spreader) phenotype (nlpD, PgaA, DGCs genes).ConclusionThe results suggested that transcriptional regulation could play a central role in the long-term survival of the species. Finally, biofilm adaptation may represent an important strategy for coping with stress and survival, with important implications for food safety management.

title: Evidence-gated integration of microbiome, metabolome, and host transcriptome data reveals a gap between reproducible signals and cross-layer mechanistic evidence in hepatocellular and colorectal cancer
abstract: IntroductionMicrobiome multi-omics studies frequently identify microbial, metabolic, and host transcriptional associations, but their reproducibility and support for connected biological mechanisms remain uncertain. We evaluated these relationships in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and colorectal cancer (CRC) using an eight-dimensional, non-compensatory evidence-gating framework.MethodsNine public HCC datasets spanning microbiome, metabolome, and host transcriptome profiles were analyzed alongside CRC microbial and metabolomic data and separate host transcriptomic datasets. Analyses included cross-cohort replication, participant-matched taxon–metabolite associations, host transcriptional responses, sensitivity testing, and independent evidence scoring. Complete mechanistic eligibility required support across all eight evidence dimensions.ResultsIn HCC, 13 genera showed concordant directions and nominal significance across conventional leave-one-cohort-out analyses, but none met the adjusted external validation criterion. Six longitudinal plasma feature-window signals and 12 differential liver metabolites were identified without cross-specimen concordance under false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Three hepatic transcriptional programs replicated across independent bulk datasets, but none of the four HCC candidate families met all eight evidence requirements. In CRC, four bacterial species replicated in held-out disease-feature testing. Paired microbial and fecal metabolite profiles from 347 participants yielded 18 replicated taxon–metabolite associations, of which 10 met robustness criteria and eight retained support after joint-taxon adjustment. The Peptostreptococcus stomatis–glycocholate association replicated in held-out testing (adjusted residual r = 0.315, q = 0.00232) and remained significant after joint-taxon adjustment (β = 0.209, q = 0.0144) and unified-partition analysis with global Benjamini–Hochberg correction (held-out q = 0.0303). Reanalysis of glycocholic acid (GCA) treatment transcriptomic data identified increased SOX14, ZDHHC9, and CD274 expression, although the three-gene response score yielded an exact permutation P = 0.10. Independent assessments agreed on all 48 evidence ratings (quadratic-weighted κ = 1.000).DiscussionEvidence gating distinguished reproducible molecular associations from complete cross-layer mechanistic support. The P. stomatis–glycocholate association, accompanied by complementary GCA-responsive host transcription, represents a candidate for further investigation rather than an established microbial–metabolite–host mechanism.

title: A study on the sources of HIV-1 transmission in Haikou, China: insights from molecular genetics and field epidemiological investigations
abstract: ObjectiveThis study aimed to integrate molecular network analysis, Bayesian phylogenetic modeling, and field epidemiological investigation to systematically trace the sources of HIV-1 transmission in Haikou, China.DesignA longitudinal molecular surveillance program was implemented between 2021 and 2024, combined with a cross-sectional field epidemiological investigation.MethodsSubtype-specific local sequence databases were constructed from nationwide sequences. Molecular clusters containing both local and external sequences were subjected to phylogeographic analysis under a Bayesian relaxed molecular clock and a Skygrid model to infer transmission origins. Complementing the molecular analyses, field epidemiological investigations were carried out among a subset of participants to assess self-reported transmission sources.ResultsAmong the 1,125 pol sequences, CRF01_AE (35.64%), CRF07_BC (38.58%), CRF65_cpx (7.20%), and CRF55_01B (4.53%) were the four most prevalent subtypes, with local clustering rates of 36.65%, 33.64%, 86.42%, and 54.90%, respectively. Phylogeographic analysis identified Guangdong as the primary origin of HIV-1 introductions into Haikou for all four subtypes, followed by Beijing (CRF01_AE_C1 and CRF65_cpx) and Shanghai (CRF07_BC). CRF01_AE showed bidirectional transmission between Haikou and Sanya, and between Haikou and Dongfang; CRF07_BC and CRF65_cpx both disseminated from Haikou to six other cities in Hainan. Field epidemiological investigations revealed that 52.33% (236/451) of participants had acquired HIV outside Haikou, with Guangdong being the primary source (16.95%, 40/236), followed by Sichuan (5.93%, 14/236). Within Hainan, Sanya accounted for the largest share (7.63%, 18/236).ConclusionBy integrating molecular and epidemiological evidence, this study advances the tracing of HIV-1 transmission sources and underscores the critical need for cross-regional prevention strategies targeting mobile populations.

title: Gut microbiota–driven immunometabolic reprogramming in inflammatory bowel disease: a comprehensive review of impaired inflammation resolution and relapse susceptibility
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is clinically characterized by alternating periods of relapse and remission. Even after clinical or endoscopic remission has been achieved, dysbiosis, metabolic abnormalities, impaired barrier function, and residual immune activation may persist, indicating that control of inflammation does not necessarily equate to complete restoration of mucosal homeostasis. Recent studies have shown that IBD-associated dysbiosis not only alters microbial composition but also reshapes mucosal nutritional, redox, and metabolic niches through short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan derivatives, bile acids, and other host–microbial co-metabolic signals, thereby inducing immunometabolic reprogramming in macrophages, T cells, B cells, group 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s), and intestinal epithelial cells. Persistent metabolic abnormalities may restrict the transition of immune cells from inflammatory effector states toward clearance, tolerance, and tissue-repair states, while also disrupting efferocytosis, regulatory T-cell (Treg) stability, immunoglobulin A (IgA)- and ILC3-associated mucosal defense, and epithelial mitochondrial function and regeneration. These alterations may consequently impair inflammation resolution and result in incomplete mucosal repair. Even after overt inflammation has subsided, residual abnormalities in the microbiota, immunometabolism, and epithelial barrier may maintain a fragile mucosal homeostatic state that is highly susceptible to perturbation, lowering the threshold for inflammatory reactivation and increasing susceptibility to relapse. This review focuses on the bidirectional crosstalk between the gut microbiota and immunometabolism, systematically summarizing its roles in impaired inflammation resolution, insufficient restoration of mucosal homeostasis, and IBD relapse. We further discuss potential therapeutic strategies, including microbiota reconstruction, restoration of microbial metabolic functions, immunometabolic modulation, and epithelial repair, with the aim of providing a mechanistic framework and new therapeutic perspectives for sustained remission and relapse prevention in IBD.

title: Bioaccumulation of the pathogenic bacterium Vibrio alginolyticus by the mussel Brachidontes pharaonis in the Gulf of Suez, Red Sea, Egypt
abstract: IntroductionThe bivalve Brachidontes pharaonis (Fisher, 1871) is a filter-feeding mussel widely used as a coastal bioindicator and may accumulate Vibrio alginolyticus, a ubiquitous marine bacterium with pathogenic potential, from surrounding seawater. Despite its ecological relevance in the Gulf of Suez, the dynamics of this host–bacterium association remain poorly characterized. This study therefore investigated whether B. pharaonis accumulates V. alginolyticus from Gulf of Suez seawater and evaluated the ecological significance of this host–habitat association. MethodsSeawater and mussel samples were collected seasonally from three sites along the Gulf of Suez, Egypt, between 2021 and 2022. ResultsV. alginolyticus abundance in seawater was quantified using quantitative PCR (qPCR), while its presence in mussel tissues was determined by end-point PCR, and occurrence patterns in both compartments were analyzed in relation to physicochemical variables. V. alginolyticus was consistently detected in seawater across all sites, with concentrations ranging from 1.59 to 3.27 × 109 gene equivalent (GE)/µL, showing modest seasonal increases in summer and marked inter-site heterogeneity. The site with intermediate mussel abundance (Kabanon) exhibited the highest bacterial prevalence in tissue (73% overall, peaking at 57% in summer), with no associated mass mortality, suggesting a mild, non-pathogenic accumulation regime. Notably, bacterial dynamics in mussel tissue, mussel-free bacteria, and seawater bacteria appeared to respond divergently to physicochemical parameters, indicating potential compartment-specific drivers. DiscussionThese findings indicate that B. pharaonis accumulation of V. alginolyticus may be better explained by a host–habitat interaction than by a pattern proportional to mussel density, with prevalence approximately twofold higher at the intermediate-abundance site; however, this interpretation remains to be experimentally validated. The partial decoupling of mussel-associated assemblages from water-column communities points to host-selective filtration and microhabitat heterogeneity as possible ecological drivers, underscoring the value of B. pharaonis as a sentinel species for Vibrio monitoring in coastal ecosystems.

title: Shifts in rumen prokaryotic communities of grazing beef cows with divergent feed efficiency in response to seasonal grazing
abstract:
Background
                Cow–calf operations represent a major component of beef production, typically relying on seasonal grazing of perennial forages. While understanding the role of the rumen microbiome in improving feed efficiency in grazing systems is essential for sustainable beef production, most studies have focused on cattle in confined systems such as feedlots. There is limited understanding of how rumen microbial communities change across feeding regimens in cow-calf operations with seasonal grazing. This study characterized rumen prokaryotic communities of beef cows across four feeding regimens, drylot (DL), planted pasture (PP), summer native rangeland (SNR), and fall native rangeland (FNR) within a year-round cow–calf production cycle, aiming to determine their relationships with feed efficiency.
              
                Results
                Prokaryotic communities in rumen samples collected from breeding beef cows under DL, PP, SNR, and FNR were assessed using metataxonomic sequencing and quantitative PCR. Feed efficiency was evaluated using residual feed intake adjusted for backfat thickness (RFIf) under DL. The microbial profiling and quantification revealed significant shifts in microbial composition and diversity across the four regimens. Bacterial diversity was highest in DL and declined during grazing, while archaeal diversity increased in SNR compared to PP and FNR. Several taxa were differentially enriched under distinct feeding regimens: Thermobifida, Saccharomonospora, Corynebacterium, and Methanoculleus thermophilus appeared only in DL, while Patescibacteria and Olsenella were more abundant during grazing. Further analysis of microbial fermentation profiles revealed that concentrations of major volatile fatty acids (VFAs) were higher in PP than in the other regimens. Heritable bacteria (p-251-o5 and Pirellula) were enriched in native rangelands and negatively correlated with VFA concentrations. In FNR, the abundance of the dominant bacterial taxon Christensenellaceae R-7 group increased, while Prevotella declined. Differential abundance analysis identified RFIf-associated taxa, including Eubacterium cellulosolvens group, Colidextrobacter, and Methanosphaera sp. ISO3–F5 regardless of feeding regime variation.
              
                Conclusions
                This study provides a comprehensive assessment of rumen prokaryotic dynamics across seasonal feeding regimens in cow-calf production, revealing varied shifts between bacteria and archaea. We further identified feeding regimen-specific associations between microbial taxa and feed efficiency, suggesting diet-microbiome interactions influencing grazing cow’s feed efficiency. These findings enhance the understanding of host-microbe interactions in confined and grazing environments, offering insights for sustainable beef production strategies.

title: Widespread Microbial Suppression and Functional Shifts in Wastewater Treatment Microbiomes Under Climate Warming
abstract:
Climate warming may fundamentally reshape engineered microbiomes. Global‐scale modelling reveals widespread microbial suppression, weakened community interactions and altered ecosystem functions in wastewater treatment plants, providing early warning of climate‐driven ecological vulnerabilities.

ABSTRACT
Climate warming is expected to reshape microbial communities, yet its impacts on engineered microbial ecosystems remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a deep‐learning framework to assess microbial responses to climate warming across global wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs). Under a +1.5°C warming perturbation, ~77% of analyzed microbial taxa showed predicted declines in relative abundance, accompanied by decreased weights in ~54% of reconstructed microbial associations. Keystone taxa were also predominantly predicted to decline, suggesting potential changes in community association structure under warming. From an exploratory ecological perspective, warming‐associated increases in viral abundance may further contribute to microbial suppression through enhanced viral pressure on key taxa. Taxonomically inferred functional profiles suggested warming was also associated with broad shifts in ecological functional profiles, including potential impairments in nutrient cycling. Notably, increases in methanogenesis‐associated taxa coupled with reduced methane oxidation suggested a potential imbalance in methane cycling. Together, these findings indicate that climate warming may substantially reshape the composition, interactions and ecological functioning of WWTP microbiomes. Our study provides a global assessment of climate‐associated risks in engineered microbial ecosystems and offers a basis for developing climate‐resilient wastewater management strategies.

title: Long‐Term Acclimation and Membrane Lipid Remodelling Enable Anaerobic Oxidation of Methane at Low‐pH by ‘Ca. Methanoperedens vercellensis’
abstract:
Anaerobic methanotrophic archaea from the genus ‘Ca. Methanoperedens’ are slow‐growing microorganisms utilizing a range of electron acceptors such as nitrate. A granular enrichment culture of ‘Ca. Methanoperedens vercellensis’ remains metabolically active during stepwise acidification of the medium down to pH 5.65, whereas its activity is inhibited by immediate acid stress. Long‐term acclimation potential of the biomass is enabled by remodelling of membrane lipid composition, a viable strategy for survival in acidic ecosystems.

ABSTRACT
Anaerobic methanotrophic archaea are key members of the methane cycle, preventing emissions of the potent greenhouse gas into the atmosphere. Previous studies of freshwater anaerobic methanotrophs targeted their activity at circumneutral pH whereas molecular ecology studies detected anaerobic methane oxidizers in acidic environments such as peatlands. However, it remains unclear whether they can adapt to low pH and sustain an effective biological methane filter under acidic conditions. Here, we show that a granular enrichment culture of the freshwater methanotroph ‘Ca. M. vercellensis’ remains metabolically active down to pH 5.65 with appropriate acclimation time while it loses activity when experiencing immediate acid stress. Population‐wide acclimation is required to support anaerobic methane oxidation at lower pH. Archaeal lipid analyses revealed an increased abundance of zwitterionic intact polar lipids over anionic lipids. This coincided with structural changes in biomass granules while methane oxidation rate and enrichment proportion of ‘Ca. M. vercellensis’ remained stable. These results demonstrate that ‘Ca. M. vercellensis’ remains metabolically active at lower pH values, despite increased maintenance energy requirements and the need for cytoplasmic pH homeostasis. Furthermore, they highlight that stress adaptations in slow‐growing microorganisms requires long‐term observation. Our findings provide new insights into methane cycling in acidic ecosystems.

title: Paralogous guanine deaminases acquired from bacteria by horizontal gene transfer promote purine homeostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans
abstract:
by Sushila Bhattacharya, Lisa Fischer, Evrim Fer, Jennifer Snoozy, Grace N. Hagedorn, Marco Herde, Betül Kaçar, Claus-Peter Witte, Kurt Warnhoff

Disruptions in purine metabolism contribute to a range of human diseases, from rare genetic disorders such as Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and xanthinuria to common conditions including gout and cancer. To better understand the metabolic networks that regulate purine homeostasis, we developed a Caenorhabditis elegans model of xanthine dehydrogenase (xdh-1) deficiency. Remarkably, xdh-1 mutant animals form rare xanthine stones, recapitulating a hallmark of human xanthinuria. To uncover genetic regulators of purine homeostasis, we performed a forward genetic screen for mutations that exacerbate xanthine stone formation in xdh-1 mutants. This approach identified multiple loss-of-function alleles in a previously uncharacterized gene, which we named gda-1. We show that gda-1 encodes an intestinal guanine deaminase that mediates a key enzymatic step in purine catabolism. The C. elegans genome also encodes a paralog, gda-2, which shares guanine deaminase activity but is expressed in distinct tissues. While gda-2 can compensate for gda-1 loss in guanine metabolism, the two genes exhibit non-redundant roles in regulating xanthine accumulation and stone formation. Interestingly, our evolutionary analyses suggest that gda-2 was acquired by nematodes via horizontal gene transfer from bacteria. These findings reveal a spatially regulated purine catabolism pathway in C. elegans and suggest that acquisition of bacterial genes has shaped a core nematode metabolic network.

title: Ultrafast alignment-free detection of viral genome variation with bronko
abstract: As viral sequencing datasets continue to grow, traditional alignment-based variant calling pipelines are becoming computationally prohibitive. To address these challenges, we developed bronko, an ultrafast alignment-free framework for detecting viral variation directly from sequencing data. The novel computational approach implemented in bronko allows scaling to massive viral sequencing datasets and has four key components: i) a locality-sensitive bucketing function to rapidly identify single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) relative to reference(s), ii) a direct k-mer count pseudo-mapping approach that approximates a pileup without alignment, iii) a greedy de novo assembly algorithm to reconstruct mutation-dense regions and indels and iv) a streaming-based sliding window outlier test to estimate baseline noise across the genome and precisely differentiate real minor variants from noise. Together, these components yield near-linear computational complexity with respect to sequencing depth, enabling bronko to process thousands of viral samples rapidly on modest hardware. Our results are threefold: 1) On simulated amplicon sequencing, bronko recovers variants with higher precision and comparable recall to existing tools while running up to one to three orders of magnitude faster; 2) bronko generates sequence alignments directly from sequencing data, with SNP content nearly identical to that of whole-genome alignment while also running in a fraction of the time, and 3) applying bronko to longitudinal sequencing data from chronically infected SARS-CoV-2 patients revealed consistent patterns of intrahost diversification and adaptive mutations over time. Altogether, these results demonstrate bronko's potential as a scalable tool for large-scale viral genomic analyses, overcoming longstanding computational barriers for intrahost and interhost characterization of viral variation.

title: Short-read sequencing benchmarking with donor-specific assemblies
abstract:
Background
                     High-throughput short-read sequencing has become a core technology for genomics, but the rapid expansion of available platforms has made it increasingly important to benchmark them under standardized conditions. A major challenge is that conventional reference-based comparisons confound true sequencing errors with inherited variation and reference bias, making it difficult to isolate platform-intrinsic performance.
                  
                     Results
                     We benchmark nine short-read chemistries across seven DNA sequencers using two highly characterized benchmark samples, HG002 and COLO829BL, together with donor-specific assemblies to measure sequencing errors against sample-matched genomic references. This strategy separates authentic platform errors from biological divergence and reveals substantial differences in substitution, indel, read-position, and sequence-context error profiles. Element AVITI UltraQ and Roche SBX-D show the lowest substitution error rates, whereas Ultima and Roche chemistries exhibit the strongest indel-associated biases. We find pronounced platform-specific effects in low-complexity regions and trinucleotide contexts, including homopolymer-associated errors and context-dependent substitution skews that are directly relevant to rare-variant detection. In addition, we show that donor-specific references are essential for unbiased base-quality recalibration because they minimize reference bias and more faithfully support cross-platform comparison and low-frequency variant-calling thresholds.
                  
                     Conclusions
                     Donor-specific assembly-based benchmarking provides a robust framework for measuring true short-read sequencing errors and comparing platforms on a common, sample-matched basis. Our results establish a comprehensive reference for the community and show that authentic error profiles can guide platform selection, quality filtering, and improved detection of rare somatic variation.

title: Community benchmarking of generative models for privacy-preserving synthetic bulk RNA-seq data generation
abstract:
Background
                The synthesis of anonymized data derived from real-world cohorts offers a promising strategy for regulatory-compliant and privacy-preserving biological data sharing, potentially facilitating model development that can improve predictive performance. However, the extent to which generative models can preserve biological signals while remaining resilient to adversarial privacy attacks in high-dimensional omics contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, the CAMDA 2025 Health Privacy Challenge launched a community-driven effort to evaluate synthetic and privacy-preserving data generation for bulk RNA-seq cohorts.
              
                Results
                Building on this initiative, we systematically benchmark 11 generative methods across two cancer cohorts (~ 1,000 and ~ 5,000 patients) over 978 landmark genes. Methods are evaluated across distributional fidelity, downstream utility, biological plausibility and empirical privacy risk, with emphasis on trade-offs between vulnerability to membership inference attacks and other evaluation dimensions. Expressive deep generative models achieve strong predictive utility and differential expression recovery, but are often more vulnerable to membership inference risk under the evaluated threat model. Differentially private methods improve resistance to attacks at the cost of reduced utility, while simpler statistical approaches offer competitive utility with moderate privacy risk and fast training.
              
                Conclusions
                Synthetic bulk RNA-seq quality is inherently multi-dimensional and shaped by trade-offs between utility, biological preservation and privacy. Our results indicate that model architecture drives distinct trade-offs across these axes, suggesting that model choice should align with dataset characteristics, intended downstream use and privacy requirements. Privacy risk should also be assessed using multiple complementary attack methods and, where possible, mitigated through formal differential privacy protection.

title: A global post-transcriptional regulator directs Acinetobacter baumannii carbon preference and gut colonization
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multidrug-resistant pathogen that colonizes the gut, increasing the risk of subsequent infection and transmission. Recent work showed that A. baumannii catabolizes ornithine, a non-preferred carbon source, to colonize the gut. However, the mechanisms of carbon preference were unknown in A. baumannii. Here, experimental evolution identified the conserved RNA-binding protein CsrA as a regulator of carbon preference in A. baumannii, a previously unreported CsrA function. RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-Seq) revealed hundreds of CsrA-associated transcripts. A. baumannii CsrA directly bound and repressed expression of the ast arginine/ornithine catabolic operons. The Pseudomonas aeruginosa CsrA homolog RsmA repressed arginine/ornithine catabolic operon expression, suggesting this CsrA function extends to other bacterial taxa. Finally, CsrA was required for competitive fitness during A. baumannii gut colonization. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized role for a global regulator in A. baumannii carbon preference and persistence in the gut, a critical reservoir for multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: Characterization of Lactobacillus rhamnosus-Derived Extracellular Vesicles and Their Cellular Cytoprotective Effects Against Trimethylamine-Induced Oxidative Stress in Caco-2 Cells
abstract: Dietary trimethylamine (TMA) underwent gut microbiota-mediated catabolism and subsequent hepatic oxidation to generate trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a key metabolic factor linked to vascular and colorectal diseases. While the systemic effects of circulating TMAO were heavily investigated, the direct localized cellular interactions of its precursor, TMA, at the intestinal epithelial level required further elucidation. This study characterized extracellular vesicles isolated from Lactobacillus rhamnosus (Lr-EVs) and evaluated their cytoprotective potential in an in vitro human intestinal Caco-2 cell model under TMA-induced stress. Exposure to a high concentration of TMA (20 mM) significantly reduced Caco-2 viability to 78.8%, triggered intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and compromised tight junction integrity as observed via the disruption of Zonula Occludens-1 (ZO-1) alignment. Co-treatment with Lr-EVs (100-300 g/mL) counteracted this cellular toxicity, enhancing cell survival up to 172%. Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that Lr-EVs suppressed the transcriptional upregulation of the pro-inflammatory gene IL-1{beta}, restored the expression of the metabolic regulator SIRT1, and stabilized transcript levels of key mitochondrial-encoded electron transport chain genes (ND6, CYTB, CO1, and ATP6). Additionally, Lr-EVs exhibited intrinsic radical scavenging activities in cell-free ABTS and DPPH assays. These preliminary in vitro findings demonstrated that Lr-EVs mitigated TMA-induced cellular injury, oxidative stress, and junctional disruption at the transcriptomic level, supporting further investigation of probiotic-derived EVs as prospective cell-free functional ingredients.

title: Structural basis of virion assembly in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infecting mycobacteriophage SWU1
abstract: The rising threat of drug-resistant tuberculosis has renewed interest in bacteriophage therapy as an urgently needed alternative. Rational engineering of these viruses, however, requires an atomic-level understanding of virion architecture. Mycobacteriophage SWU1 belongs to subcluster A2, one of the few mycobacteriophage lineages known to infect Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis). Using single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), we resolved essentially the entire SWU1 virion architecture by localized reconstruction of four modules, the capsid, portal vertex, tail and baseplate, at resolutions of 3.62 [A], 3.51 [A], 3.70 [A] and 3.22 [A], respectively. The T=7 capsid comprises 415 copies of an HK97-fold major capsid protein and lacks any decoration protein in density. The 12-fold portal reconciles its C5-C12 mismatch with the capsid vertex through defined, non-equivalent subunit contacts. The baseplate carries a 13-fold tail-fiber ring on a 6-fold hub, a geometry without precedent among characterized phages, established here by symmetry-free reconstruction. These findings provide the critical insights into the assembly and infection of SWU1, laying a structural foundation for the future optimization of phage-based anti-TB therapeutics.

title: Metagenomic Insights into the Fecal Microbiome, Resistome, and Mobilome of Beef Cattle in Cow-Calf Operations in Florida, United States
abstract: Food-producing animals are a focus of One Health approaches to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as reservoirs of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria (ARB) and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). We hypothesized that microbial composition, ARGs profiles, and mobile genetic element (MGE) profiles would differ by operation size and animal age group. Fecal samples from 162 cows and calves were combined into 54 composite samples, each comprising three animals of the same age group. Across operation sizes, Bacillota (51.4-64.9%), Bacteroidota (12.0-17.3%), Pseudomonadota (10.3-16.5%), and Actinomycetota (3.3-10.9%) were predominant phyla. Alpha diversity did not differ among operation sizes; however, cows exhibited greater observed richness, Shannon diversity, and Simpson diversity than calves (all P < 0.001). Microbial composition did not differ significantly among operation sizes (PERMANOVA, R{superscript 2} = 0.065, P = 0.609) but differed significantly between cows and calves (R{superscript 2} = 0.200, P < 0.001). Seventy-five ARGs representing 14 resistance classes were identified. Normalized ARG hit rates were higher in small operations (0.444) than in medium (0.278) and large operations (0.222; P = 0.088), whereas calves exhibited a higher estimated marginal mean normalized ARG hit rate than cows (0.383 vs. 0.247 hits/million reads; P < 0.001). Of 1,054 curated ARG hits, 23.9% occurred on predicted plasmid contigs, 0.9% on predicted viral contigs, and 7.1% on contigs containing insertion sequences. Overall findings demonstrate differences in fecal microbiome diversity and ARG abundance between cows and calves and indicate that predicted plasmids are associated with a notable proportion of ARG hits in Florida beef cow-calf operations.
authors: Ali, A., K. Edison, L., Bittar, J. H. J., Denagamage, T., Lee, A. C. Y., Jeong, K. C., Hernandez, J. A., Kariyawasam, S.

title: Genomes2Genes: A Progressive Cactus Gene Analysis Pipeline
abstract: Whole-genome alignments are fundamental resources in comparative genomics, because they place genes and their surrounding sequences in a shared evolutionary context. Progressive Cactus aligns large numbers of genomes without a reference genome and reconstructs ancestral sequences along the input phylogeny. However, its Hierarchical Alignment Format output has mainly been used for visualization, phylogenomics, and pangenome studies, and gene-level analyses of these alignments remain difficult. Here, we present Genomes2Genes, a pipeline that converts Progressive Cactus graph-based alignments into validated coding sequence alignments of extant species and their reconstructed ancestors. The pipeline extracts exon alignment blocks, handles atypical genomic jumps, stitches exons into transcripts, and reports start codons, stop codons, and frameshifting indels across species, with validation steps throughout and a base-by-base audit of the final alignments. It catches both biological and technical artifacts and can be run on any part of the genome. We anticipate that this pipeline will be useful in identifying and removing problematic regions used in the potential reconstruction of species or gene phylogenies. We developed and tested the pipeline on a whole-genome alignment of 21 Brassicaceae species and 2 outgroups and found that, among 45,491 lineage-specific genes, the pipeline supported 22,376 candidate de novo genes, of which 1,811 had complete evidence of enabler mutations. Genomes2Genes is publicly available and extends whole-genome alignments to gene-level questions in comparative genomics and evolutionary biology.
authors: Sanders, S. C., Casola, C.

title: Telotrons: spliceosomal introns composed of telomeric repeats
abstract: Spliceosomal intron numbers vary widely across eukaryotes, but the only established mechanism for large bursts of intron gain is the spread of transposable introner elements. We describe telotrons, spliceosomal introns composed predominantly of telomeric repeats. In a survey of 10,310 eukaryotic genome assemblies, we identified 7,008 introns with >85% telomeric repeat coverage and an additional 44,423 with >50% to [≤]85% coverage, in 25 genomes spanning haptophytes, dinoflagellates, a cryptophyte, stramenopiles, the apicomplexan Eimeria, and the nematode Mesorhabditis. Most telotrons carry GT-AG or GC-AG splice boundaries, and RNA-seq supports their splicing. Their repeat orientations are consistent with telomerase extension of broken DNA ends, and intron absence at corresponding positions in orthologs supports widespread de novo gain. In Eimeria and Mesorhabditis, telotrons instead occupy positions where orthologs carry ordinary introns, suggesting modification of existing introns. Telotrons thus point to telomerase as an endogenous driver of structural innovation through intron creation and remodeling.
authors: Kramer, A. M., Corbett-Detig, R.

title: Lifestyle-mediated shifts in the gut microbiome and host genetics modulate gene expression in intestinal organoids
abstract: Industrialization-associated shifts in the gut microbiome have been linked to disease, but the mechanisms by which microbial communities influence host gene regulation remain poorly understood. We developed a live microbiome-colonic organoid (colonoid) co-culture system to investigate genotype-dependent host responses to gut microbial community variation. Colonoid 2D monolayers from healthy donors were co-cultured with live gut microbial communities from individuals living urban or rural lifestyles, followed by RNA-sequencing. Urban and rural microbiomes elicited largely shared transcriptional responses, however they induced distinct host genetic effects on gene expression. We identified 511 host genes with microbiome-dependent allele-specific expression (ASE) which were involved in epithelial architecture, cell-matrix interactions and structural integrity. Notably, 149 host genes had distinct allelic effects between Urban and Rural microbiomes (urban-rural condition specific ASE or cASE), revealing genotype-dependent host responses to lifestyle-associated microbiomes. Urban-rural cASE was associated with microbial community composition, predominantly involving Prevotella and Bacteroides species. Targeted Prevotella copri spike-in recapitulated Prevotella-associated allelic effects at specific loci, including one in the IBD-associated autophagy gene, ATG4B. Together, these findings establish an experimental framework to investigate genotype-by-microbiome interactions, and demonstrate that lifestyle-mediated shifts in the microbiome modify host cis-regulatory genetic effects on gene expression.
authors: Nirmalan, S., Arif, S., Garlicki, G., Alazizi, A., Hutchins, K., Poyet, M., Groussin, M., Carbonetto, P., Pique-Regi, R., Blekhman, R., Luca, F.

title: MaaD-TAD: an all-atom model of the duplicated PRAMEF/HNRNPCL chromatin domain built from sequence homology
abstract: In the nucleus, the placement of genes in the 3D fold of DNA affects how they function. Models of this fold use two kinds of data: contact maps constructed from Hi-C, and nucleosome maps showing where DNA is wound around nucleosomes. Over evolution, sections of the genome were copied, creating near-identical regions. Reads from these regions cannot be assigned to one copy and are discarded, leaving "void regions" in both maps. We tested MaaD-TAD, a pipeline that models topologically associating domains (TADs) at the atomic level, on the PRAMEF/HNRNPCL locus on human chromosome 1. This challenging locus spans 652 kb, with only 15% of its nucleosome positions known and most contact data missing. To test our hypothesis that copies with similar sequence lie close in space, i.e. homology as a surrogate for proximity, we constructed a map of sequence homology in place of Hi-C and used CSynth to fold it into a 3D path. We then lengthened the path to fit a chromatin fibre, and refined the model by adding cohesin complexes, which stabilize chromatin structure. Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex through which a loop of chromatin is threaded; the loop is commonly anchored by CTCF proteins bound on either leg. Using known databases, we placed CTCF sites in our model and joined three to their copies with cohesin rings; in each pair the sites face each other, as loop anchors do. The final model holds 3,359 nucleosomes and about 55 million atoms. Micro-C, an advanced, higher-resolution form of Hi-C, provided data on two other duplicated regions that support our hypothesis: matching copies touched 1.2 to 1.9 times more often than expected. Our approach provides a novel method to reconstruct DNA regions with absent contact data and, to our knowledge, the first all-atom model of a complete TAD.
authors: Santos, J. R. L., MacIsaac, M., Moon, E. B., Befus, A. D., Marcet-Palacios, M.
