title: Systematic promoter perturbation reveals limitations of AlphaGenome gene expression predictions
abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) models promise to facilitate the interpretation of noncoding variants by predicting their effects on gene regulation directly from genomic sequence. However, whether these models recapitulate fundamental principles of transcriptional biology remains unclear. Here, we tested whether AlphaGenome recognizes the expected consequences of promoter disruption on predicted gene expression. We systematically perturbed annotated promoter elements in silico for 2,111 promoter-gene pairs using dinucleotide shuffling, GC-adjusted random base substitution, and N-masking. We then compared AlphaGenome-predicted CAGE and RNA-sequencing signals across 20 tissues for reference and promoter-disrupted sequences. While CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions were strongly correlated for reference sequences, promoter disruption markedly reduced predicted CAGE activity, with N masking producing reductions of approximately three orders of magnitude. By contrast, the predicted RNA-sequencing signals were substantially less affected, resulting in an uncoupling of two molecular readouts of gene expression. Exon-level analyses showed that AlphaGenome predicted reduced RNA-sequencing signal when exonic sequences are within the disrupted region, but frequently failed to propagate this effect to downstream exons. This divergence between the CAGE and RNA-sequencing readouts was apparent from the second exon onward and was more pronounced in longer genes. Although alternative transcription initiation and shared downstream exons may explain individual cases, it is unlikely to account for the systematic discordance between CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions. These findings indicate that AlphaGenome can recognize the local loss of promoter activity without consistently capturing its consequences across the corresponding transcript. More broadly, our results show that predictions from individual S2F output tracks do not necessarily reflect a coherent model of transcription. Systematic biological benchmarking and experimental validation therefore remain essential before such predictions can be used to prioritize or classify noncoding variants in research or diagnostic settings.
authors: Sreenivasan, V. K. A., Aksu, E. D., Spielmann, M.

title: Integrating bacterial genomics and host transcriptomics links Burkholderia pseudomallei variation to melioidosis mortality and neutrophil responses
abstract: Bacterial genetic variation contributes to the outcome of infection, but its relationship with host immune responses is rarely investigated in the same patients, limiting the biological interpretation of pathogen-associated disease severity. Here, we integrated pathogen genomics, clinical outcomes and host transcriptomics to investigate host-pathogen interactions in melioidosis, a frequently fatal infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. We analysed prospective clinical data from 2,142 patients, whole-genome sequences from 2,101 infecting isolates and 646 paired host blood transcriptomes across five cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. Infections were typically dominated by a single strain, with limited within-host diversification, supporting the use of an infecting isolate genome to investigate pathogen-associated clinical outcomes. Bacterial genome-wide association studies identified one locus associated with binary mortality at genome-wide significance. Incorporating patient age, sex, body mass index and Charlson Comorbidity Index increased this to four, while modelling time to death as a continuous phenotype identified seven loci. Integration with paired host transcriptomes linked mortality-associated bacterial genetic variation to imputed signatures of increased immature neutrophils and reduced neutrophil degranulation. An intergenic region upstream of the polyketide synthesis locus BPSS1006-BPSS1011 was additionally associated with downregulation of host genes involved in myeloid-cell signalling and cell proliferation pathways. These findings connect naturally occurring B. pseudomallei genomic variation associated with mortality to distinct host immune signatures, providing insight into pathogen-host interactions underlying severe melioidosis and a framework for investigating the contribution of pathogen genetic diversity to clinical outcomes.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Personalised Gene Expression Prediction Improves Cell-Type-Specific Association Testing
abstract: Linking genetic variation to disease requires accurate prediction of its effects on gene expression in relevant cell types. Sequence-to-function models offer a way to predict these effects and, with training on personal genomes, have begun to capture inter-individual expression differences. However, effect sign accuracy remains limited, and predictive uncertainty is unquantified. Here we introduce ATTICUS, which combines personalised sequence representations with uncertainty-aware expression prediction. ATTICUS transfers regulatory information learned in bulk expression pretraining to cell-type-specific expression prediction without requiring genotypes paired with single-cell expression data. Across blood and brain cell types in OneK1K and ROSMAP, ATTICUS approximately doubles expression prediction correlations relative to scPrediXcan and substantially improves sign accuracy. Moreover, ATTICUS enables uncertainty-aware transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). Applied to systemic lupus erythematosus and Alzheimer's disease, ATTICUS identifies more associations, with greater cell-type specificity and stronger directional concordance, and reduced statistical inflation. Together, our results demonstrate that personalised training makes predictions more directionally consistent, and uncertainty propagation improves the calibration of TWAS and the prioritisation of disease genes. ATTICUS provides a framework for both, enabling the use of single-cell expression datasets without matched genotypes to inform uncertainty-aware TWAS, expanding their use in prioritising disease-associated genes and cell types.
authors: Styll, P., Di, Y., Cai, N.

title: Segment-dependent phylogenetic resolution reveals geographic and host sampling gaps in Oropouche virus genomes
abstract: Background. Oropouche virus (OROV) has been reported in areas beyond its historical Amazonian range since 2023, accompanied by rapid growth in publicly available genomic data. However, the extent to which these data provide reliable phylogenetic and epidemiological resolution, and whether that resolution differs among genome segments, has not been systematically examined. Methods. Nucleotide sequences annotated under Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense were retrieved from NCBI Virus (accessed 13 May 2025) and filtered to retain records at least 70% of the reference length for each segment, yielding 898 S, 831 M, and 832 L sequences. Segments were aligned independently with MAFFT, and maximum-likelihood phylogenies were inferred with IQ-TREE using ModelFinder and ultrafast bootstrap approximation. Trees were annotated with collection date, country, and host in iTOL. Results. Phylogenetic resolution differed among segments. Contemporary Brazilian sequences formed a largely unresolved region in the S segment tree, whereas the M and L trees resolved recent clusters to differing degrees. Resolution did not track segment length: the M tree resolved contemporary structure more strongly than the longer L tree, and total tree length was approximately 3.5 times greater in the M tree despite near-identical taxon sampling. Sequences collected before 2010 were recovered in supported clusters in all three segment trees, although their configuration differed by segment. These sequences were also predominantly non-Brazilian and non-human, preventing collection date, geographic origin, and host from being separated as explanations for the observed clustering. The species-level query also retained three reassortant viruses, which may influence segment-specific topologies; sequences annotated to the United States were Iquitos virus rather than OROV. Two Italian sequences clustered with Cuban sequences across all three trees, concordant with published travel histories. Conclusions. Publicly available sequences contain phylogenetic structure that differs among the S, M, and L segment trees, but interpretation is constrained by uneven temporal, geographic, and host sampling and by the inclusion of reassortant species in a species-level dataset. The concentration of sequences from Brazil and human hosts, together with limited representation of non-human hosts, restricts inference about OROV diversity and ecology. Broader and more balanced genomic surveillance would improve the ability to resolve OROV evolutionary and transmission patterns.
authors: Siam, R., Elbehery, A. H. A.

title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica) reveals extensive centromeric satellite arrays
abstract: We present a chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly from Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica). The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes of 322 Mb and 295 Mb, with 89.7% and 95.6% respectively, each scaffolded into 7 chromosomes. Assembly completeness is high (BUSCO 97.8% in each haplotype), with 34,213 and 29,684 annotated protein-coding genes for haplotypes one and two, respectively. The chromosomes contain extensive centromeric satellite arrays that cover up to half of some chromosomes. Their precise functional boundaries remain undetermined.

title: Rapid environmental DNA detection with isothermal amplification methods: a comparison with the real-time quantitative PCR in the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita).
abstract: Species detection relying on environmental DNA (eDNA) traditionally relies on Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). This amplification technique takes in general a minimum of one hour and requires in most cases access to specialized laboratories and equipment. Isothermal amplification techniques, originating from clinical research, are emerging as rapid and field-deployable alternative methods. Yet, whether their sensitivity, specificity, and cost/time-efficiency are comparable to the traditional real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) remains to be assessed. In this work, we compare the performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with qPCR to detect the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita) from aquatic filtrations. This objective was achieved in three steps. First, we developed LAMP and RPA primers specific to the target species based on its mitochondrial genome. Second, we amplified DNA extracts from E. calamita and from tissues of closely related species using real-time fluorescence detection with LAMP, RPA, and qPCR commercially available protocols to evaluate and compare the sensitivity and specificity of the three methods. Finally, we validated all protocols on eDNA extracts recovered from water samples from ponds surveyed by field scientists. We show that RPA had a sensitivity equivalent to that of the qPCR, while LAMP sensitivity was ten times lower. All our assays amplified the species DNA in eDNA samples where the species was observed by field scientists. Through this work, we thus propose a robust methodology for implementing isothermal amplification assays for eDNA applications and show that RPA is a good alternative to qPCR for detecting conservation-priority species (i.e. protected or invasive species) when time and lab facilities are constrained.
authors: Chieux, A., Guerrieri, A., Bellemain, E., Boyer, F., Merzi, T., Tablerlet, P., Iribar, A., Zinger, L., Bonin, A.

title: Genome assembly and characterization of two Brazilian soybean cultivars contrasting for stink bug resistance
abstract: Brazil's tropical soybean germplasm still has few genomic resources: only one assembly of a Brazilian cultivar is available at NCBI. Here we describe chromosome-level de novo assemblies of two contrasting cultivars: IAC-100, described as resistant to phytophagous stink bugs, and CD-215, susceptible. We sequenced high molecular weight DNA using 10x Genomics linked reads, assembled the reads with Supernova, anchored the assembly to the Williams 82 reference with RaGOO and corrected structural errors with REAPR. The assemblies span 1.057 and 1.061 Gb, with scaffold N50 values of 53.6 and 54.2 Mb (48.0 and 47.7 Mb excluding gaps), and recover more than 97% of conserved plant genes assessed by BUSCO. Homology-based projection of the reference protein-coding genes generated 46,774 and 46,620 gene models. Comparing the proteomes of the two cultivars, we identified 2,002 divergent isoforms in 1,427 loci, classified by sequence divergence, length variation, combined divergence and non-conserved homology. These data expand the genomic resources for tropical soybean germplasm, still underrepresented in public databases, and for studies of insect resistance.
authors: Godoy Filho, M. A. d., Viana, J. P. G., Santos, L. B. d., Wei, W., Santos, M. d. F., Pinheiro, J. B.

title: A genomic prediction framework for growth traits in black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) breeding programmes
abstract: Background Genomic prediction has been applied in livestock, plant and aquaculture species to accelerate genetic gain. However, its application and potential still remain unexplored in farmed black soldier fly (BSF), an emerging globally important insect production species. Due to the diversity of BSF feed sources, selection strategies need to be evaluated across various feedstocks and production environments to aid in building genomic selection into BSF breeding programmes. In this study, 2,083 BSF larvae from the base population were reared on three diets (SYK: Soy-okara, BSG: brewers' spent grain and FVW: fruit and vegetable waste), and 536 from the F7 population were reared on a chicken starter feed diet. Larvae were phenotyped for four growth traits (LBW, larval body weight; LL, larval length; LW, larval width; LSA, larval surface area) and genotyped across 4,680 SNPs. Genomic prediction was evaluated using seven methods under additive (A) and additive-dominance (AD) models, considering across- and within-diet effects, genotype by diet (G x D) interactions, differences amongst reference and test generations, and SNP densities. Results Performance varied across all scenarios, with LBW showing higher predictive ability (PA) among the growth traits. Accounting for dominance generally improved PA. Multivariate models accounting for G x D performed similarly to, or marginally better than, within-diet predictions. Cross-diet prediction was more variable and generally lower than within-diet prediction, showing reduced transferability across untested nutritional environments. Reducing the SNP density from 4,680 to 3,000 SNPs maintained comparable PA; however, PA decreased below 3,000 SNPs. Across multiple generations, predictive performance declined, resulting from reduced genetic connectivity and possible genotype-by-environment (G x E) interactions between the reference and testing populations. Conclusions Overall, these results provide an application-based framework for genomic prediction in BSF in semi- or commercial production settings. Results also highlight the importance of the genetic model, representative reference populations, and appropriate marker densities for genomic selection.
authors: Gowda, K. B., Massault, C., Jerry, D. R., Zenger, K. R.

title: SPACE-Tag Enables High-Throughput Spatial Chromatin Profiling With CUT&Tag
abstract: Spatial epigenomics maps chromatin states within intact tissues, yet current methods remain limited by accessibility and scale. We developed SPACE-Tag, a spatial CUT&Tag framework that converts epigenetic marks-associated DNA into polyadenylated RNA through T7 based linear amplification, enabling direct integration with standard spatial transcriptomic workflows. Applied to the mouse brain, SPACETag resolved activating and repressive chromatin landscapes, recovered region-specific gene regulatory programs across anatomical domains, and showed strong correlation with existing bulk and single cell reference data. We generated an integrated multimodal atlas of the aging mouse brain, profiling five histone modifications and the transcriptome in parallel across the adult lifespan to establish the largest spatial multimodal dataset to date. This analysis uncovered sharp regional divergence with aging in the brain: fiber tracts showed widespread transcriptional downregulation, often without nearby chromatin state transitions, whereas the isocortex showed coordinated chromatin transcriptome changes, including an H3K4me1 peak module that increased with age, was enriched at super-enhancers and linked to upregulation of neuronal plasticity regulators. These findings highlight the power of multimodal and high throughput spatial genomics in uncovering the divergent regulatory logic that governs tissue-specific vulnerability and resilience in the aging brain.
authors: Yan, C., He, R., Fernandez, S., Pleska, M., Maniatis, S., Raimondi, I., Vickovic, S.

title: Disparities in avian genomic resources highlight gaps across the Global South
abstract: Avian genomes have proliferated rapidly in recent years while expanding our knowledge of genomic evolution. However, evaluating bird sampling across the tree of life and across their distributions is necessary to assess their contributions to global bird diversity and diversification patterns. We evaluated all available avian genome assemblies across geography, taxonomy, conservation status, and time. The 1,712 species with at least one genome assembly represent only ~15% of recognized avian diversity. Although all orders were represented, 24 bird families (all restricted to the Global South) lacked any genome assembly, and only ~37% (N= 2,397) of recognized genera had genomic representation. Nearly 78% of the most evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered (EDGE) lineages lacked a genome. Genomic resources are concentrated in temperate regions of the Global North, whereas species-rich tropical regions in Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia remain severely underrepresented relative to their diversity. Even after accounting for conservation status, evolutionary distinctiveness, and ecology, Global South species had roughly fourfold lower odds of having a genome than Global North species. Notably, the post-2021 surge in genome sequencing has counter-intuitively widened this gap. Together, our results highlight persistent gaps in genomic resources across the Global South and the need to collectively address these global knowledge gaps via collaborative efforts.
authors: K. L., V., Arvind, C., Goyal, N., Warudkar, A., Reddy, S., Robin, V. V.

title: Cell-free expression and NGS-powered substrate profiling reveal a thermostable metagenomic meganuclease from an extreme environment with novel specificity
abstract: AbstractAs an alternative to historical enzyme isolation, metagenomic databases (e.g. MGnify) provide information on vast unculturable microbial diversity, including extreme environments, and constitute an enormous source of functional proteins. Conservative mining of these data by close sequence homology alone tends to identify merely different versions of known enzymes. Here we present a discovery strategy for meganucleases based on wider capture of less homologous enzymes in metagenomic databases, and incorporating metadata with their homology. We use cell-free expression to bypass host incompatibility and the need for purification, along with deep sequencing for experimental assessment of substrate specificity and cleavage pattern, thereby circumventing classical gel-based profiling. Specifically, we discovered the temperature-stable (>55°C), intron-encoded LAGLIDADG meganuclease I-MG11 that recognizes a GC-rich 17 base pair sequence to generate 4-nt palindromic 3′-overhangs—the first monomeric meganuclease to produce such overhangs. Co-folding models of I-MG11 bound to DNA provide a structural context for enzyme–DNA interactions, highlighting differences from other monomeric LAGLIDADG meganucleases (e.g. I-SceI) shaped by InDels (insertion–deletions) in the DNA-binding region that may cause specificity changes. Our strategy streamlines general bona fide identification and annotation of meganucleases, while the unique properties of I-MG11 expand the toolbox of molecular genome engineering.

title: Microfluidic concatemer sequencing unveils cooperative and competitive enhancer clusters in gene regulation
abstract: AbstractChromatin looping plays a pivotal role in eukaryotic gene regulation; however, technical limitations have hindered the comprehensive characterization of higher-order interactions among genomic loci. As a result, key questions, such as whether enhancers function cooperatively or competitively at the single-molecule and ensemble levels, remain largely unresolved. Here, we present Drop-t, a novel microfluidics-based method that enables systematic profiling of higher-order chromatin architecture at both the single-molecule and population scales. We demonstrate that Drop-t is not only resistant to common ligation-induced DNA entanglements, which frequently cause nanopore clogging, but also provides greater relevance for elucidating regulatory mechanisms compared to existing ligation-free approaches. Using Drop-t, we uncovered extensive, previously underappreciated non-specific enhancer–promoter interactions (EPIs) and showed that these may influence transcriptional variability by competing with specific EPIs. Notably, we identified two major gene classes, dictator genes and leader genes, based on whether their promoters are predominantly regulated by competitive or cooperative specific EPIs, respectively. Together, our findings established Drop-t as a powerful tool for decoding the higher-order organizational principles of chromatin architecture and their impact on transcriptional regulation and variability.

title: Transcription factor 3 cooperates with CXXC finger protein 1 to regulate histone H3K4 trimethylation and developmental competence in mouse oocytes
abstract: AbstractDuring oogenesis, the establishment of oocyte-specific gene expression relies on epigenetic and transcriptional remodeling. Both histone modifications and transcription factors are crucial for the oocyte to acquire developmental competence; however, the mechanisms involved remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify transcription factor 3 (TCF3), an E-protein family member, as a key maternal regulator of oocyte developmental potential. Oocyte-specific deletion of Tcf3 results in female infertility, characterized by impaired meiotic maturation and early embryonic arrest at the two-cell stage. These defects are associated with defective maternal mRNA clearance and disrupted establishment of the H3K4me3 landscape in maturing oocytes. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that TCF3 directs H3K4me3 deposition at target gene promoters through interaction with CXXC finger protein 1 (CXXC1), the core subunit of the SETD1 histone methyltransferase complex. Importantly, this TCF3–CXXC1 interaction depends on their DNA-binding activity, highlighting the specificity of TCF3 in coordinating with CXXC1 to regulate maternal target genes, such as Pabpn1l. Together, our findings uncover a transcription factor-driven mechanism of epigenetic reprogramming that is essential for the maternal-to-zygotic transition.

title: Allele-selective targeting of uromodulin by antisense oligonucleotides reduces aggregates and kidney damage in a mouse model of autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease
abstract: AbstractAutosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD) arises from gain-of-toxic-function mutations in the UMOD gene coding for uromodulin, the most abundant protein excreted in normal urine. Mutant uromodulin accumulates in the cells lining the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle, leading to intracellular aggregates, cellular stress, and kidney damage. Here, we demonstrate that an antisense gapmer oligonucleotide (ASO) designed against the representative c.553C > A (p.R185S) UMOD mutation produced allele-selective silencing of the mutant messenger RNA and protein in kidney cells. Short-term administration of a murine ASO analogue in the established Umod  R186S/+ mouse model of ADTKD suppressed uromodulin and lowered tubular damage, whereas a non-targeting scrambled control was inactive. After a 4-week treatment, ASO accumulation in the Umod  R186S/+ kidneys reached ∼320 000 copies per TAL cell, quantified using a sensitive splint-ligation assay. The ASO treatment suppressed premature mutant uromodulin and its toxic aggregates in Umod  R186S/+ kidneys, whereas it had no effects on wild-type uromodulin in Umod  +/+ kidneys. Notably, the ASO improved tubular function and decreased kidney tubulointerstitial inflammation in Umod  R186S/+ mice. This work offers a roadmap for antisense therapy to treat ADTKD-UMOD and substantiates the therapeutic potential of ASOs in disorders of the kidney tubule.

title: Archaeal histones coordinate conserved DNA sequence motifs to promote CRISPR adaptive immunity
abstract: AbstractArchaea and bacteria acquire resistance to viruses by integrating fragments of foreign DNA at the beginning of a CRISPR locus. In the archaeon Pyrococcus furiosus, histones bind the leader to promote specific integration at the first CRISPR repeat. However, it remains unknown whether archaeal CRISPR leaders contain conserved DNA sequence motifs required for integration. Here, we analyze 542 archaeal CRISPR leaders found across Thermococcales and Methanococcales. We identify 36 motifs found up to 500 bps upstream of archaeal CRISPR loci. Scrambling or truncating novel motifs or histone binding sites found 100–400 bps upstream of the P. furiosus CRISPR modestly decreases integration efficiency. However, mutation of motif T2, which overlaps with the proximal histone site and is adjacent to the CRISPR, ablates both histone-mediated and histone-independent integration. Mutations tiled across T2 reveal that a pyrimidine at position −3 of the leader is required for histone-independent integration, and basepairs −4 to −19 are required for histone-mediated integration. T2 is found in most Thermococcales, and a similar sequence is found in most Methanococcales leaders, suggesting this motif may be a broadly conserved element that facilitates CRISPR adaptive immunity across taxonomic orders. These data shed light on the sequence requirements for histone-mediated DNA integration

title: The anti-phage defense system GAPS4 is a double-edged sword that sensitizes bacteria to DNA-damaging agents
abstract: AbstractThe arms race between bacteria and bacteriophages (phages) gave rise to multiple layers of antagonistic mechanisms, many of which remain unexplored. Here, we investigated the widespread anti-phage defense system GAPS4. We found that GAPS4 forms a heterotetrameric complex containing active PD-(D/E)xK phosphodiesterase domains. It is triggered upon sensing DNA damage, leading to genomic DNA degradation and cell suicide. We further demonstrated that this activation mechanism renders GAPS4 a double-edged sword, sensitizing bacteria to various DNA-targeting antibacterial agents. Collectively, our findings reveal a possible evolutionary trade-off between anti-phage defense and immunity against interbacterial antagonism.

title: Nutrition-Gut Microbiota Axis in PDAC: Research Progress from Nutritional Abnormalities and Microbial Dysbiosis to Clinical Interventions
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy with insidious onset and poor overall prognosis, representing one of the most challenging tumors in the digestive system. In recent years, advances in tumor nutrition, gut microbiome research, and immuno-metabolic studies have led to the recognition of PDAC as a systemic disease. It is driven not only by local tumor changes but also by host nutritional status, pancreatic exocrine and endocrine dysfunction, systemic inflammation, intestinal barrier integrity, and microbial dysbiosis. Patients with PDAC commonly experience weight loss, sarcopenia, cachexia, micronutrient deficiencies, and disturbances in glucose and lipid metabolism. These changes arise from multiple factors, including inadequate dietary intake, impaired digestion and absorption, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, persistent inflammation, metabolic reprogramming, and treatment-related effects. At the same time, PDAC patients show clear alterations in gut microbiota composition and function, including reduced microbial diversity, loss of beneficial symbiotic bacteria, overgrowth of opportunistic pathogens, and impaired short-chain fatty acid metabolism. Nutritional abnormalities and microbial dysbiosis are not separate phenomena; they interact closely through the nutrition-gut microbiota axis and together contribute to PDAC development, treatment response, and clinical outcomes. As a result, nutritional assessment, body composition analysis, composite nutritional/immunological scores, and specific nutrition-related biomarkers are gaining importance for risk stratification and prognosis. Perioperative nutritional support, pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy, targeted nutrient interventions, and microbiota-directed strategies have also demonstrated promising clinical potential. This review summarizes changes in nutritional status and gut microbiota in PDAC, the value of nutrition-related biomarkers, and current intervention strategies targeting the nutrition-gut microbiota axis, to support more precise assessment and integrated management of the disease.

The DS had lower forage biomass and concentrations of several nutrients, whereas DS sheep had higher OMI, lower dietary plant diversity and greater representation of Rosaceae (p < 0.05). Faecal bacterial communities differed between groups. Plant-family composition, rather than dietary alpha diversity, was associated with bacterial variation; Rosaceae and Tamaricaceae showed the strongest associations (r
2 = 0.929 and 0.836, respectively; p = 0.001). Selected bacterial genera were associated with Rosaceae (Mantel R = 0.59, p = 0.001). Among 3819 detected metabolites, 1177 differed between groups and were mainly enriched in flavonoid- and phenylpropanoid-related pathways (adjusted p < 0.05). These findings reveal coordinated associations among diet, faecal microbiota and metabolites and identify plant-family composition as a key correlate of habitat-related microbial and metabolic variation.

title: Bioremediation of Chlorpyrifos Contaminated Soil: Microcosm Investigation and 16S rRNA Gene Amplicon Sequencing
abstract:
This study characterized biofilm‐forming bacterial strains Pseudomonas aeruginosa MD3 and Bacillus toyonensis LD07 immobilized on sugarcane bagasse. This highly porous bio‐product demonstrated exceptional phenotypic plasticity and robust bioremediation efficacy, achieving 99% chlorpyrifos degradation at 4500 ppm. Metagenomic analysis confirmed significant ecological shifts, validating this system for xenobiotic remediation.

ABSTRACT
This study describes the isolation and characterization of two biofilm‐forming bacterial strains, Pseudomonas aeruginosa MD3 and Bacillus toyonensis LD07, capable of degrading chlorpyrifos. These isolates demonstrated remarkable phenotypic plasticity, maintaining biofilm formation across varying pH, temperature and salinity levels. To maximize microbial stability and metabolic efficiency, sugarcane bagasse was utilized as a support matrix. Analytical characterization (EDX, BET and XRD) confirmed that the bagasse possesses a highly porous architecture, serving as a protective scaffold and an auxiliary carbon source for synergistic co‐metabolism. A bio‐product formulated via solid‐state fermentation on this matrix exhibited exceptional bioremediation efficacy, eliminating 99% of chlorpyrifos at an extreme concentration of 4500 ppm within 35 days. Furthermore, 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing of coffee‐growing soils across different treatments (natural control, pesticide‐stressed and 10% bio‐product amended) with accession numbers PRJNA1529359 revealed distinct shifts in microbial community dynamics. While the taxonomic landscape was broadly dominated by Bacillota, Pseudomonadota and Actinomycetota, the bio‐product amendment caused P. aeruginosa and B. toyonensis to become the dominant taxa. Ultimately, these insights underscore the viability of cost‐effective agricultural by‐products for cell immobilization and highlight metagenomics as a powerful predictive framework for monitoring the remediation of anthropogenically stressed ecosystems.

title: Single‐Cell Identification of Bacterivorous Mixotrophs in a Freshwater Habitat
abstract:
A workflow diagram showing the taxonomic identification of bacteria‐consuming mixotrophs from natural environments, achieved through fluorescence‐activated single‐cell sorting and microscopic observation. The single‐cell approach allows us to establish a clear connection between biodiversity and functional activities in aquatic environments with high resolution.

ABSTRACT
The nutritional strategy of phago‐mixotrophy among pigmented eukaryotes has been widely recognized and characterized across various taxonomic lineages. While their ecological role as bacterivores in different aquatic environments is acknowledged, establishing a clear connection between phago‐mixotrophic activities and taxonomy within natural communities remains challenging. In this study, we utilized a combination of microscopy and fluorescence‐activated single‐cell sorting techniques to investigate the diversity and temporal variations of bacteria‐feeding mixotrophs in a freshwater habitat. We identified four groups of mixotrophs using both methods: Pedinellales (Dictyochophyceae), Cryptomonas (Cryptophyceae), Dinobryon (Chrysophyceae) and a single‐chloroplast bearing group within Chlorophyta. Together, these groups accounted for 58%–96% and 54%–95% of total mixotrophs detected by microscopy and cell sorting, respectively. Samples collected in different seasons demonstrated that Pedinellales and Chlorophyta were more abundant in spring and summer/autumn, while Dinobryon was only present in winter when temperatures were lowest and light intensity was moderate. Our findings, with 6 classes and 12 genera identified as bacterivorous mixotrophs, highlight the promising potential of single‐cell techniques in aquatic microbiology. This approach reveals the taxonomic identity and feeding activities of phago‐mixotrophs in situ, thereby enhancing our understanding of their functional ecological roles within microbial food webs.

title: Riboflavin Metabolism Links Metabolic State to Biofilm Development, Cell‐Envelope Homeostasis, and Antimicrobial Susceptibility in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
abstract:
Using functional genomics, CRISPRi‐mediated perturbation and targeted overexpression, coupled with metabolic perturbation, phenotypic characterization and systems‐level analyses, we uncover riboflavin metabolism as a signalling axis linking cellular metabolism to biofilm‐associated community behaviour in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Its modulation remodels the cell envelope, alters antibiotic susceptibility and reveals metabolic control of persistence with therapeutic potential.

ABSTRACT
Biofilm formation and phenotypic drug tolerance contribute to the persistence and treatment challenges associated with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tb). Although M. tb lacks canonical quorum‐sensing systems, it exhibits coordinated metabolic and cell‐envelope adaptations during biofilm development, suggesting the existence of alternative mechanisms linking cellular metabolism to multicellular behaviour. Here, using a combination of functional genomics, metabolic perturbation and systems‐level analyses, we identify riboflavin metabolism as a regulatory axis influencing biofilm development and antimicrobial susceptibility in M. tb. CRISPRi‐mediated knockdown and targeted overexpression of riboflavin biosynthetic genes markedly altered biofilm architecture, cell morphology, envelope ultrastructure, membrane permeability and lipid composition, with ribA2 and ribF emerging as potential metabolic vulnerabilities. Exogenous riboflavin enhanced biofilm formation, whereas the riboflavin antimetabolite roseoflavin suppressed this phenotype. Notably, cell‐free supernatants from late‐stage cultures, accumulated higher levels of riboflavin and restored biofilm formation in a riboflavin‐biosynthesis‐deficient strain, supporting a diffusible regulatory function beyond the established metabolic roles of riboflavin‐derived FMN and FAD. Integrated transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses revealed coordinated reprogramming of biofilm‐associated regulatory pathways, cell‐envelope lipid metabolism and the F420 biosynthetic network, accompanied by increased susceptibility to anti‐tuberculosis drugs. Molecular docking further identified potential interactions of riboflavin with regulatory proteins associated with biofilm and stress‐response pathways. Together, these findings establish riboflavin metabolism as a previously underappreciated regulatory layer connecting microbial metabolism, biofilm development, cell‐envelope homeostasis and drug tolerance. This metabolic axis provides a potential framework for developing microbial biotechnology‐based strategies to interfere with biofilm‐associated persistence and improve the efficacy of anti‐tuberculosis therapeutics.

title: Impact of training data on deep learning–based RNA 3D structure quality assessment
abstract: AbstractAccurate reference-free assessment of predicted RNA 3D structures is essential for large-scale RNA modeling, yet the impact of training data on deep learning–based quality predictors remains poorly understood. Here, we present a systematic cross-training analysis of three deep learning predictors for RNA 3D structure quality assessment, each originally developed on distinct training sets. By retraining each predictor on alternative (nonnative) datasets—including RNA3DQA, a new set created specifically for this project—and evaluating performance on independent RNA-Puzzles benchmarks, we systematically assess the relative contributions of model architecture and training data composition. Our results reveal pronounced differences in cross-dataset generalization, with predictors often performing better when trained on nonnative datasets than on their native ones. Notably, the impact of the training datasets varied across predictors, with RNA3DQA yielding the overall best accuracy and ranking stability results specifically for the ARES model. Native training sets yielded better performance for RNA3DCNN and lociPARSE. These findings demonstrate that the characteristics of the training data play a dominant, model-dependent role in shaping the performance and robustness of reference-free RNA 3D structure quality assessment methods. We conclude with practical recommendations for designing transferable training datasets and for benchmarking deep learning–based quality predictors in RNA structural bioinformatics.

title: scYOU: a multi-scale yoked optimization and unsupervised framework for analysis of cellular heterogeneity and complex-associated protein module recovery
abstract: AbstractAdvances in high-resolution proteomic technologies are enabling systematic characterization of cellular heterogeneity and protein functional programs at increasing depth. However, existing computational approaches typically focus on either cell-level organization or protein-level structure, lacking a unified framework that jointly models both entities. Here we present scYOU, a multi-scale yoked optimization and unsupervised framework that simultaneously captures cellular heterogeneity and protein functional organization through a dual-channel neural network architecture. scYOU learns cell and protein embeddings in parallel while coupling the two views through a supercell-constrained alignment strategy. Supercells are constructed based on high-order expression similarity and define grouping structures over cells. A dual-channel alignment objective is imposed at the reconstruction level, such that reconstructed expression profiles of cells within the same supercell are encouraged to converge, whereas those from different supercells remain separable. On the protein side, Gene Ontology–derived functional similarity priors regularize protein embeddings to preserve molecular biological consistency. Across diverse benchmark datasets, scYOU achieves strong and relatively consistent clustering performance together with improved embedding separability, while the learned protein representations support embedding-guided refinement of existing interaction networks and the recovery of complex-associated protein modules. These results establish scYOU as a structurally coupled, multi-level representation learning framework for proteomic data, and highlight the importance of jointly modeling cellular heterogeneity and protein functional modules within a unified computational paradigm. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/anchor-hue/scYou.

title: spaDWGCN: a spatial distance weighted graph convolution network for accurate spatial tissue structure identification
abstract: AbstractThe continuous development of spatial transcriptomics enables us to obtain gene expression matrices alongside spatial coordinate labels for cells or spots, providing tools for understanding spatial tissue microenvironments and spatially resolved cell–cell interactions. Although numerous methods have been developed to identify spatial tissue architecture, most of them adopt binary adjacency matrices that treat all neighboring cells equally, and few comprehensively incorporate distance information into both graph construction and feature representation. Here we introduce spaDWGCN, a spatial distance weighted graph convolutional network algorithm that takes cellular gene expression and microenvironment composition as inputs. This approach introduces fine-grained distance weighting at two levels: replacing the conventional 0–1 binary adjacency matrix with a distance-weighted adjacency matrix at the graph level, and substituting the neighbor count matrix with a distance-weighted microenvironment composition matrix at the feature level. Furthermore, spaDWGCN jointly models gene expression and microenvironment composition through separate graph convolutional network branches and trainable fusion, integrating transcriptional patterns with their local neighborhood context within a unified framework. Experiments on spatial transcriptomics multi-platform datasets, including MERFISH, STARmap, Stereo-seq, Slide-seqV2, and 10× Visium, demonstrate that this distance-weighted strategy achieves competitive performance in spatial domain identification and other downstream analyses.

title: In vitro culture and draft genome assembly of Monographella maydis predict a molecular driver of its sexual fitness in maize tar spot disease
abstract:
Background
                     Tar Spot Complex (TSC) is a devastating foliar disease of maize that threatens global food security, causing yield losses of up to 50%. While the disease is initiated by Phyllachora maydis, the “fisheye” necrosis that intensifies disease severity is attributed to Monographella maydis. Historically, the precise role of M. maydis has remained elusive due to a lack of reliable in vitro culture systems and genomic resources. This study reports the first successful isolation and reproducible in vitro culture of M. maydis, identifying V8 agar as an optimal medium for mycelial growth and sporulation.
                  
                     Results
                     Using PacBio long-read sequencing technology, we generated a high-quality 39.8 Mb genome assembly for M. maydis, predicting 10,228 protein coding genes, 227 non-coding RNAs, 175 tRNAs and 45 rRNAs. Functional annotation identified a diverse repertoire of secreted proteins, likely involved in the tar spot disease pathosystem. Phylogenomic analysis confirmed that M. maydis is distinct from P. maydis, supporting a synergistic rather than evolutionary relationship between the two fungi. Furthermore, the identification of a conserved adenosine deaminase-acting-on-tRNA residue (H352) suggests potential for A-to-I RNA editing during sexual reproduction. Finally, we report the use of ITS1 and ITS4 primer pair for successful detection of M. maydis from infected leaf tissues.
                  
                     Conclusion
                     This study establishes the first robust in vitro culture system and high-quality reference genome for Monographella maydis, providing foundational resources for investigating its biology and role in the tar spot disease complex. These genomic and molecular tools will facilitate future studies on fungal pathogenicity, host–pathogen interactions, and the development of improved disease management strategies.

title: CADE: a reference-free workflow for coefficient-sensitivity analysis in bulk transcriptomic differential expression
abstract:
Background
                     Bulk differential-expression (DE) coefficients can change when disease alters cell-type abundance, but matched single-cell references are often unavailable in small or rare-disease studies. Existing marker-covariate adjustments can produce an adjusted DE table, yet they do not directly report which gene-level coefficients are stable, attenuated, amplified or representation-sensitive after composition adjustment. Coefficient-sensitivity analysis deliberately asks a narrower question than deconvolution: for each gene, how much does the reported group effect change once marker-derived composition weights are added to the model, in which direction does it change, and is that change stable to marker choice and to the coordinate representation of the weights? The output is a per-gene ranking of coefficient stability, not an estimate of cell-type fractions.
                  
                     Results
                     We developed CADE (Composition-Aware Differential Expression), an R workflow that estimates marker-derived relative composition weights, fits paired unadjusted and composition-adjusted limma models, and computes a per-gene Composition Confounding Index (CCI). CADE reports signed coefficient-change labels, marker-dropout bootstrap rank stability (repeatedly omitting markers and re-ranking genes, to show which rankings persist), label-permutation calibration, denominator-threshold diagnostics, stabilised-denominator output and isometric log-ratio coordinate-sensitivity analysis. Genes whose classification depends on the coordinate representation of the composition weights are explicitly identified. In the controlled synthetic composition-bias benchmark, CADE preserved recovery of cell-intrinsic DE genes under composition bias, including AUROC 0.996 at 100% synthetic bias versus 0.902 for unadjusted limma. Marker-derived weights recovered PBMC ground-truth relative composition with mean r = 0.993, and a macrophage activation syndrome pseudobulk evaluation against scRNA-seq-derived composition showed mean r = 0.779, with all seven mappings that had a usable scRNA-seq reference showing p < 0.001 (of eight preset categories; Neutrophils had no reference in this ground truth). In familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis PBMCs (GSE26050; n = 11 versus 33 controls), CADE illustrated the separation of low-CCI from model-sensitive coefficients within a targeted immune, iron and ferroptosis panel.
                  
                     Conclusions
                     CADE provides a reference-free, reproducible workflow for characterising how sensitive bulk transcriptomic DE coefficients are to marker-derived composition adjustment. It reports coefficient stability and does not estimate absolute cell fractions. The FHL analysis is used as a small-cohort worked example, and disease-specific findings remain hypothesis-generating.

title: CAcnesDB: a database of Cutibacterium acnes with integrated functional insights derived from multi-modal genome annotation
abstract: AbstractCutibacterium acnes is a predominant member of the human skin microbiome, generally as a beneficial or a benign inhabitant, which under specific conditions transforms into a pathogen, causing acne and associated inflammatory responses. While there is a wealth of data on the microbiology and genomics of the microbe, there is a lack of comprehensive annotation of the proteins coded by the genome, slowing progress in understanding its unique metabolic versatility and survival in host hypoxic sebaceous niches. We configured an integrated pipeline for functional annotation of the C. acnes genome, combining gene calling, domain and ontology mapping, KEGG pathways assignment, proteome-scale structural modeling, predicting pockets and associating the small-molecule metabolites based on binding site similarity to facilitate structure-to-function annotation. Structural predictions using ColabFold covered nearly the full proteome, with 83.7% of models showing high confidence. To infer protein function, ligand-binding sites in the C. acnes modeled proteome were predicted using a consensus of three independent algorithms, PocketDepth, SiteHound, and Fpocket. Small molecule ligands were mapped to the resulting pockets through structural comparison of the pockets with known small-molecule binding sites in PDB where there was direct or indirect evidence for such binding, resulting in the C. acnes predicted ligandome (CApL) comprising 693 protein-ligand pairs across 534 proteins. CAcnesDB is a comprehensive database of the C. acnes genome, hosting functional annotation from multiple levels of input and analyses, covering 2297 protein-coding genes.

title: Estimating rates of SARS-CoV-2 lineage spread using graph spectra from genetic sequence data
abstract:
by Emma E. Goldberg, Michael D. Kupperman, Ruian Ke

The modern enormous scale of viral genomic data, as exemplified by SARS-CoV-2, presents unique opportunities for epidemic inference and real-time monitoring. A key challenge is to wade through the extremely large stream of sequence data in order to identify small subsets of sequences that may represent rapid population growth of newly emerged lineages. To address this challenge, we developed a new approach that combines techniques in graph theory and machine learning. We represent distances between small subsets of sequences as graph Laplacians and identify from them features of rapid population growth. From early sequence data collected in the US and the UK between 2021 and mid-2022, we identified two features—genetic diversity and graph connectivity—that allow us to reliably estimate growth rates of newly emerged lineages. To test our model, we used data collected from mid-2022 to end-2024 and accurately inferred the growth rates of lineages that appeared during this period. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for data collected in 2023 when the sequencing efforts were relatively high (thousands of sequences per day) in the US and the UK, our model correctly identified the most rapidly expanding lineages when they were still at low frequencies. Overall, our work provides a scalable and adaptable tool to estimate the growth rate of newly emerged SARS-CoV-2 lineages.
authors: Ruian Ke

title: Improved light conditions sustain pelagic primary production in western Wadden Sea despite biomass declines under major nutrient reductions
abstract:
Abstract
Pelagic microalgae supply the major part of labile and readily accessible organic carbon in coastal systems, making long‐term monitoring of phytoplankton blooms and primary production (PP) essential for assessing the Wadden Sea's carrying capacity. Over the past three decades (1990–2023), our phenology analysis indicates that both the spring and summer‐autumn phytoplankton blooms declined in peak magnitude, and secondary blooms shifted later in the season (≈ 40 d over 34 years). These changes coincided with strong reductions in riverine nutrient loads (TN −64%; TP −93%), which were positively correlated with summer phytoplankton biomass. We leveraged one of the longest and methodologically consistent coastal PP time series to identify major patterns and drivers for the western Wadden Sea. Limitation analysis for 2012–2023 showed that phosphorus was the primary limiting nutrient, with silicate co‐limitation during spring peaks and nitrogen limitation emerging later in the season. Estimated pelagic PP (mgC m−2 d−1) during the main growth period (May–September) remained relatively stable over 2012–2023, despite a 56% decline in phytoplankton biomass (mg Chl‐a m−3). This stability reflects a compensatory increase (170%) in derived phytoplankton growth rates (gC gC−1 d−1), likely facilitated by improved early‐season light conditions (≈ 17% increase in March–April). The compensatory balance between declining biomass and increasing growth appears fragile. If nutrient loads further decline and/or light conditions shift beyond the optimum range, the compensatory growth may become insufficient to offset biomass declines. The result would be reduced pelagic primary production and a lower carrying capacity of the ecosystem.

title: Fish gut microbiota mediate pollutant-induced lipid toxicity via bidirectional biotransformation and dysbiosis
abstract: AbstractThe gut microbiota acts simultaneously as a target of environmental pollutants and as a driver of their biotransformation, but how these two roles jointly determine host toxicity remains insufficiently defined. Using zebrafish as a One Health model, we show that dietary exposure to environmentally relevant levels of triphenyl phosphate (TPHP), an organophosphate flame retardant, causes intestinal lipid accumulation, barrier disruption, and PPAR pathway dysregulation. By combining antibiotic-treated zebrafish models, stable isotope-assisted metabolomics, and multiomics profiling, we found that the gut microbiota transforms TPHP through a bidirectional network. It reactivates host-derived glucuronidated metabolites via deconjugation and ferments TPHP carbon skeletons into small-molecule metabolites, including L-phenylalanine and N-acetyltyramine, that are integrated into host lipid and energy metabolism. The functional disruption of the microbiota abolishes these metabolite signals, supporting a key role of the gut microbiota in TPHP biotransformation. Metagenomics identifies specific bacterial taxa (such as Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, and Aeromonas) and hydrolytic enzyme families responsible for these transformations. Our findings suggest that the gut microbiota functions beyond a passive target of pollutant exposure: it expands the metabolic fate of TPHP and generates pollutant-derived metabolic signals that intersect with host lipid homeostasis, collectively mediating the observed lipotoxicity through host–microbe interactions. This work provides a mechanistic framework for incorporating gut microbiome dynamics into chemical risk assessment under the One Health paradigm.

title: Aerobic preference in the marine protist Paradiplonema papillatum having anaerobic genomic potential
abstract:
Background
                     The diplonemid Paradiplonema papillatum is a marine planktonic protist with predicted complex and versatile metabolism. Investigation of carbohydrate metabolism and capacity for anaerobic life strategy revealed a disparity between its genomic and actual physiological preference. Despite possessing the genetic toolkit that should allow it to thrive in anoxic environment, P. papillatum primarily relies on aerobic metabolism, which it finely tunes in response to nutrient availability.
                  
                     Results
                     Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle serves as a key regulatory switch. The NAD+- and NADP+-dependent IDH paralogues maintain the cycle’s plasticity, as this enzyme can support both the standard oxidative TCA cycle and its reductive branch, depending on metabolic requirements. The TCA cycle provides reduced cofactors, which branches into both canonical and non-canonical pathways when nutrients are abundant. This branched respiration is supported by ubiquinones UQ8 and UQ9, whose biosynthetic pathway is a mosaic of a genes of different evolutionary origins. In addition to oxidative phosphorylation, P. papillatum can synthesize ATP in the propionate cycle and the acetate:succinate coenzyme A (CoA) transferase/succinyl-CoA synthetase cycle via substrate-level phosphorylation.
                  
                     Conclusions
                     Our results highlight the complex regulation of mitochondrial metabolism in the diverse and abundant diplonemids and provide insight into the physiological strategies of marine planktonic microeukaryotes.

title: Integrated Phenotypic and Genome-Informed Characterization of Environmental Aspergillus Isolates With Potential for Citric Acid Production.
abstract: Aspergillus species are widely used in industrial biotechnology, particularly for citric acid production. This study characterized environmental Aspergillus isolates from Côte d'Ivoire with potential for citric acid production using an integrated phenotypic and genome-informed approach. Isolates recovered from banana rhizosphere soil and decomposing fruits and vegetables were screened for aflatoxin-associated reactions using the ammonia vapor assay and for acidification on bromocresol green-supplemented Czapek-Dox agar. Selected isolates were analyzed by whole-genome sequencing, Kaiju taxonomic profiling, and EggNOG-mapper functional annotation. Citric acid production was quantified under solid-state fermentation using a calibrated colorimetric assay. Among 110 fungal isolates recovered, 24 Aspergillus isolates were grouped into seven morphotypes. Four isolates (E1-E4) showed acidification activity and no detectable aflatoxin-associated reaction under the assay conditions. Morphological and whole-genome taxonomic analyses conservatively affiliated E1-E3 with the Aspergillus niger species complex, whereas E4 remained taxonomically unresolved. E2 showed the highest proportion of reads assigned to A. niger reference sequences (92%) and the greatest representation of predicted functions associated with citrate metabolism and carbohydrate degradation. During solid-state fermentation, E2 exhibited the highest measured citric acid concentration under the tested conditions. Comparative genomic analyses also showed greater similarity among E1-E3 than with E4. Overall, E2 emerged as the most promising candidate for further citric acid production studies, supporting the value of combining quantitative phenotypic assessment with genome-informed characterization of environmental fungal isolates.
authors: Kouman WE, Kacou OBC, Kambou S, Fofana O, Angaman DM.

title: The bacterial swarming factor SwrD belongs to a diverse family of proteins that form hexameric rings.
abstract: Prokaryotic swarming is a collective surface-associated behavior that supports rapid colonization, biofilm formation, and host interactions. Swarming requires enhanced flagellar motor (FM) torque generation under high-load conditions. In many bacteria, this adaptation is achieved through increased stator unit recruitment and coordinated transcriptional regulation of motility genes. Genetic studies have implicated several relatively poorly characterized proteins in swarming, including SwrD, a component of the fla-che operon whose loss impairs torque generation in Bacillus subtilis. Intriguingly, SwrD is conserved in spirochetes that experience high viscous loads but do not exhibit canonical swarming, suggesting a broader functional role in FM regulation. Here, we structurally and biophysically characterize SwrD from B. subtilis and the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. In both cases, we show that SwrD assembles into a hexameric ring-like structure featuring a highly charged, disordered peripheral tail. Whereas SwrD displays structural similarities to periplasmic lipoproteins and DNA-binding proteins, lipidation regions and DNA interaction motifs of these other proteins are not conserved in SwrD. Deletion of swrD in B. subtilis results in pronounced swarming defects and altered expression of fla-che operon transcripts. In silico interaction analyses further identify the stator protein MotA as a high-confidence SwrD interactor, but this interaction could not be validated biochemically. Conserved SwrD residues mediate subunit contacts or locate to the hexamer periphery where they may mediate functionally important interactions.
journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
authors: Nair D, Zhang K, Khala A, Li C, Crane BR.

title: Quorum Sensing and Biofilm Regulation in ESKAPE Pathogens: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Targets, and Translational Challenges.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an emerging global health threat responsible for antibiotics being ineffective, leading to persistent infections, increased mortality, and healthcare costs. ESKAPE (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species) pathogens have a higher priority worldwide for the development of therapeutic approaches other than traditional antibiotics. Quorum sensing (QS) links population-dependent gene expression with a mechanistic understanding of bacterial communication, virulence regulation, and biofilm-associated persistence. Major QS systems across ESKAPE pathogens are Agr and accessory gene regulator networks in Gram-positive bacteria; LuxS/AI-2 signaling; the LuxI/LuxR-family systems in Gram-negative bacteria; the Las, Rhl, and Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) networks in P. aeruginosa; and the AbaI/AbaR system in A. baumannii. This review focuses on QS regulatory mechanisms in ESKAPE pathogens and discusses the novel approaches to target QS-associated virulence and biofilm formation. A review of the literature on QS signaling pathways, biofilm regulation, and anti-QS therapies was performed with special focus on combating strategies like plant-derived phytochemicals, synthetic QS inhibitors, enzymatic quorum quenching, probiotics, and combinations of QS-targeted agents with conventional antibiotics. QS systems are involved in virulence regulation, adhesion, biofilm maturation, and bacterial persistence. Plant-based compounds such as flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and polyphenols have been shown to have potential to interfere with QS-related processes. Synthetic inhibitors, quorum-quenching enzymes, probiotics, and antibiotic combination strategies are also promising approaches. By integrating QS regulation with virulence, biofilm biology, and antimicrobial response across ESKAPE pathogens, this review provides a comparative framework to guide future target prioritization, diagnostic development, and evaluation of adjunctive anti-virulence strategies. Mechanistic validation, standardized cross-pathogen comparisons, and long-term resistance-evolution studies are needed to establish the therapeutic readiness and clinical value of these approaches.
authors: Saini J, Gautam S, Sharma D, Khanduri A, Venugopal D.

title: In vitro antibacterial and antibiofilm activity of phycocyanin against Klebsiella pneumoniae: effects on growth kinetics and antibiotic susceptibility.
abstract: BackgroundThe increasing clinical burden of antimicrobial-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, together with its capacity for biofilm formation and persistence, has intensified the search for alternative and adjunctive antimicrobial strategies. Phycocyanin is a cyanobacteria-derived phycobiliprotein with emerging biological and antimicrobial properties; however, its activity against K. pneumoniae, particularly across planktonic, biofilm, and antibiotic-response phenotypes, remains insufficiently characterized.MethodsKlebsiella pneumoniae ATCC 700,603 was used as the experimental strain, and phycocyanin obtained from Sigma was evaluated for antibacterial and antibiofilm activity. Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) were determined by broth microdilution and subsequent subculture, respectively. Bacterial growth kinetics were monitored for 72 h under sub-inhibitory phycocyanin exposure, while direct antibacterial activity was evaluated using an agar well diffusion assay. Biofilm formation was assessed using the crystal violet microtiter-plate method. Changes in antibiotic inhibition-zone diameters following sub-inhibitory phycocyanin exposure were evaluated using ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and imipenem. All experiments were performed in triplicate.ResultsPhycocyanin exhibited measurable antibacterial activity against K. pneumoniae, with MIC and MBC values of 10 and 20 mg/mL, respectively. Growth-kinetic analysis showed comparable bacterial growth during the initial hours, followed by sustained attenuation of growth in phycocyanin-exposed cultures from approximately 6 h onward. In the agar well diffusion assay, inhibition-zone diameters increased in a concentration-dependent manner, from approximately 7 mm at the lowest tested amount to 12 mm at the highest. Phycocyanin also inhibited biofilm formation in a concentration-dependent manner, with maximum inhibition reaching 41.3% at the highest tested concentration. Following sub-inhibitory phycocyanin exposure, increased inhibition-zone diameters were observed for ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and imipenem, with the greatest changes generally occurring after 24 h of exposure.ConclusionsPhycocyanin demonstrated antibacterial and concentration-dependent antibiofilm activity against K. pneumoniae ATCC 700,603 and altered the bacterial antibiotic-response phenotype following sub-inhibitory exposure. The observed effects on bacterial growth, biofilm formation, and antibiotic inhibition-zone diameters suggest that phycocyanin may have potential as an adjunctive antimicrobial or antibiofilm agent. However, these findings do not establish pharmacodynamic synergy or reversal of antimicrobial resistance. Further studies using quantitative combination assays, resistant clinical isolates, mechanistic approaches, and in vivo models are required to determine the translational relevance of these effects.
journal: International microbiology : the official journal of the Spanish Society for Microbiology
authors: Bahrami A, Taheri M, Alikhani MY, Nouri F.

title: Peptide candidates and host-pathogen protein interactions against WSSV and Vibrio spp. in farmed penaeid shrimp: A scoping review of CADD strategies.
abstract: This scoping review highlights the advancements in the computational discovery of peptide candidates and the modeling of host-pathogen protein interactions, spanning from the discovery of physiological AMPs to rational design mediated by computational tools, which have become a pivotal asset in addressing major shrimp farming pathogens such as WSSV and virulent Vibrio spp. strains. In this context, biocomputational studies hold strategic potential for mitigating sanitary crises in modern aquaculture. By analyzing 23 articles (2015-2026), a transition from traditional biochemical isolation to in silico prospecting was identified. The results also reveal a marked concentration of this output in Asia (22/23; 95.7% of the corpus), led by India and China (7/23; 30.4% each). Methodological convergence toward protein-protein docking (HADDOCK/ClusPro) combined with Molecular Dynamics simulations (GROMACS) was also observed. Notably, envelope proteins (VP28, VP26, and VP39) prevail as antiviral targets, while membrane lysis and the blockade of PirA/PirB toxins dominate antibacterial strategies. A consistent gap was identified: none of the 23 included studies reported electronic reactivity (DFT), QSAR-based toxicity prediction or ecotoxicological analyses, so that the chemical stability of these candidates in aquatic environments and their effects on the associated microbiota were not assessed in this literature. We conclude that the future of the field depends on the integration of drug delivery systems (e.g., chitosan), thermodynamic rigor via MM-PBSA, and the expansion of methods that ensure environmental biosafety and translational viability, aiming to consolidate these compounds as viable pharmacological agents.
authors: Bastos LRN, de Sousa DS, Salmito-Vanderley CSB, Marinho ES.

title: DNA methylation of nuclear donor cells and cloning efficiency in cattle.
abstract: Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) efficiency remains low, largely due to incomplete epigenetic reprogramming of donor-cell nucleus by the enucleated oocyte during early embryonic development. In this study, we investigated DNA methylation patterns across candidate genomic regions in six bovine skin fibroblast lines, including three classified as high- and three as low-efficiency lines based on a large number of embryo transfers. Repetitive elements, including α-Satellite and Satellite I DNA, did not differ significantly in methylation between groups. Likewise, no significant differences in methylation were observed in the METTL14 region. In the XIST DMR1, methylation patterns varied substantially among animals, largely due to the aberrant methylation profile observed in one cell line from the low-efficiency group, highlighting inter-individual epigenetic variation among animals. In Oct4 region 1, methylation levels tended to be higher in the high-efficiency group. The H19/IGF2 ICR showed differences between groups of fibroblast lines, with a higher proportion of unmethylated alleles in the low-efficiency group. The IGF2R/AIRN ICR exhibited higher methylation levels in the high-efficiency group. Because IGF2R/AIRN is not imprinted in fibroblasts, this differential methylation pattern may represent an additional epigenetic barrier to oocyte-mediated nuclear reprogramming. These findings identify the IGF2R/AIRN ICR as a candidate locus associated with SCNT efficiency and suggest that donor-cell epigenetic features may influence nuclear reprogramming following nuclear transfer. Understanding how distinct genomic regions respond to reprogramming may provide further insight into the molecular mechanisms the low efficiency of SCNT.
authors: Moura AO, Caetano AR, Pimenta LKL, Rumpf R, Franco MM.

title: African swine fever virus histone-like protein A104R subverts host antiviral defenses by suppressing the nuclear translocation of IRF3 and STAT1.
abstract: A104R of African swine fever virus (ASFV), putative histone-like protein, is known to be involved in essential processes such as viral DNA replication, repair, and transcription. Although it has been revealed that the deletion of A104R affects ASFV pathogenicity for live attenuated vaccine development, the molecular mechanism underlying those effects remains unclear. Here, we report a novel molecular mechanism of A104R that suppresses karyopherin-α (KPNA) mediated antiviral responses. A104R competitively bound to the major nuclear localization signal (NLS) region on KPNA3 and KPNA4, thereby disrupting their interaction with interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3). A104R also bound to the unique C terminal nonclassical NLS region of KPNA6 and competitively inhibited the interaction between KPNA6 and phosphorylated signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1). Therefore, A104R inhibited the nuclear translocation of IRF3 and phosphorylated STAT1, thereby suppressing type I interferon (IFN) signalling and IFN-mediated antiviral responses. Consequently, ectopic expression of A104R enhanced DNA virus replication and suppressed IFN production by inhibiting the IRF3-mediated type I IFN signalling pathway and suppressed the interferon-β (IFN-β)-mediated antiviral responses. Taken together, these results highlight that A104R plays a dual role in suppressing IFN response and IFN-mediated antiviral responses. This mechanism provides new insight into the A104R induced ASFV pathogenesis, which provide a critical implication for a better understanding of the ASFV pathogenesis.
authors: Gamage N, Rathnapala P, Cha JW, Haluwana DK, Subasinghe A, Weerawardhana A, Lee JS.

title: CD3scFv-Engineered AAV Capsid Drives Superior In Vitro and In Vivo CAR-T Cell Generation and Leads to Complete Eradication of CD19+ Tumors.
abstract: Adeno-associated viruses (AAV) are emerging vectors for in vivo delivery of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) therapies. Natural AAV serotypes were previously considered unsuitable due to their poor transduction of non-activated human T cells. To overcome this limitation, we inserted an anti-CD3 single-chain variable fragment (CD3scFv) into one of the three AAV capsid proteins (VP1, VP2, or VP3) to specifically target and activate human T cells. This strategy preserved normal vector production yields, while enabling specific T cell targeting. Using AAV6 as a representative serotype, our lead candidate AVO-100 achieved more than 200-fold higher transduction efficiency of primary human T cells compared to unmodified counterpart. In vitro, AVO-100-mediated CD19-CAR delivery resulted in efficient CAR expression and killing of CD19+ Raji lymphoma cells in co-culture assays. In vivo, a single intravenous dose of AVO-100 at 2×108 vector genomes (vg) per subject using NSG mice bearing Raji xenografts, prompted complete tumor eradication and significantly prolonged survival, whereas control untreated animals succumbed to a progressive disease. These results demonstrate that site-selective CD3scFv insertion into a single AAV capsid protein provides a robust, versatile platform for improved T cell transduction and effective in vivo CAR-T cell generation, offering a promising off-the-shelf approach for treating B cell malignancies.
journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
authors: Chen H, Hoang T, Smith A, Shahim T, Ho CY, Selemenakis P, Luo N, Ahmad M, Aqdas A, Chen M.

title: Characteristic metabolite emergence and coordinated multi-omics reprogramming in a four-member synthetic Streptomyces consortium during rice straw deconstruction.
abstract: Efficient bioconversion of rice straw is often constrained by the structural complexity of lignocellulose and the limited functional capacity of individual microbial strains. In this study, a mixed Streptomyces consortium composed of four lignocellulose-degrading isolates was constructed and evaluated for rice straw conversion. Compared with the corresponding monocultures, the consortium showed superior growth, higher lignocellulolytic enzyme activities, and enhanced straw degradation when rice straw was used as the sole carbon source. Untargeted LC-MS metabolomics further revealed a distinct metabolic profile in the mixed culture and identified three characteristic metabolites, annotated as Crotamiton, 3-Acetylpyridine, and Harmaline, which accumulated dynamically during fermentation. Transcriptomic analyses demonstrated extensive co-culture-induced reprogramming and recurrent enrichment of pathways related to ribosome, oxidative phosphorylation, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and carbon metabolism. Integrated metabolomic-transcriptomic analysis further identified 21 candidate genes associated with the three characteristic metabolites, and their coordinated upregulation was supported by RT-qPCR. Proteomic comparison between straw- and glucose-grown mixed cultures showed preferential accumulation of proteins involved in transport and membrane function, hydrolase activity, substrate processing, and redox/respiration under straw conditions. Importantly, field-scale composting experiments using 400 kg straw piles further confirmed the superiority of the mixed consortium, which promoted lignin and cellulose degradation, accelerated compost maturation, and reproduced the accumulation trends of the three characteristic metabolites under practical conditions. Collectively, these results indicate that cooperative interactions within the consortium establish a coordinated multi-omics functional state favorable for efficient rice straw deconstruction, providing a promising basis for microbial consortium design in agricultural straw valorization and composting applications.
authors: Jiao Y, Li X, Bai Y, Wu Q, Zhou G, Ding H, Wei Z, Zhao Y.

title: Acridine Derived Photosensitizers for Fungal Photoinactivation and Their Limited Clinical Applicability.
abstract: This narrative review evaluates what published experiments establish about acridine-derived photosensitizers for fungal photoinactivation, with emphasis on imidazoacridinones and literature published through July 2025. Selected derivatives reduced the number of colony-forming planktonic Candida cells under direct blue-light illumination. Compounds absorbing in the same spectral region produced different colony-count reductions; their activity also varied with cellular accumulation and irradiation conditions. These culture results do not establish efficacy against infection. Blue excitation penetrates tissue poorly, limiting its use against fungi at depth. Host-cell testing of C1330 used a tetrazolium-reduction (MTT) metabolic assay in human keratinocytes. This assay did not determine whether treated cells could still form colonies and cannot establish host safety or selective fungal killing. Claims of cell killing require assessment of colony-forming survival in fungi and colony-forming mammalian cells. Separate acridine-orange studies examined coatings applied to fungi immobilized on quartz and light-triggered release from liposomal films containing triclosan. These surface and release experiments do not establish treatment of infected tissue. Evidence for mature-biofilm killing, sustained fungal control, and preferential fungal injury remains inadequate. The reviewed imidazoacridinones are therefore unlikely to have a useful clinical role on the available evidence: their blue excitation limits tissue penetration, and fungal killing at exposures that preserve host-cell survival has not been demonstrated.
authors: Joulaei M, Soleimanzadeh Khayat M, Zafari J, Jouni FJ.
