title: Temporal dynamics of cytokine expression, oxidative stress, and endocrine dysfunction following Escherichia coli-induced epididymo-orchitis in rats.
abstract: Bacterial epididymo-orchitis (EO) can compromise male reproductive function, but the temporal relationships among testicular inflammatory, oxidative, and endocrine changes remain incompletely characterized. This study examined these changes after Escherichia coli inoculation in rats. Ninety adult male Wistar rats were allocated to untreated control and 100-μL and 200-μL bacterial-inoculum groups and evaluated at 24 h and 1, 2, 3, and 4 weeks (n = 6 per group per time point). Histological, immunohistochemical, immunofluorescent, biochemical, hormonal, and molecular assessments characterized testicular injury, marker-positive cell distributions, immune cell accumulation, redox status, cytokine expression, and Leydig cell-associated endpoints. Changes in TAC, MDA, CAT, GSH, GSSG, and IL-10 were reported at 24 h, whereas significant SOD suppression and pro-inflammatory cytokine upregulation were reported from 1 week. The assayed steroid-related transcripts were reported to decrease at 24 h; reduced Leydig cell lipid-associated fluorescence and serum testosterone were apparent from 1 week. CD68-positive cell accumulation was greatest during the early period, particularly at 1 week, whereas CD45-positive leukocyte density peaked at 3 weeks. Testicular injury was accompanied by reduced THY-1- and NANOG-positive cell densities. Differences between inoculum-volume groups varied by endpoint and time point. These findings describe temporal associations among testicular injury and redox, inflammatory, and endocrine changes; they do not establish a causal sequence, functional spermatogonial stem cell depletion, or impaired fertility. The timing of potential clinical interventions requires separate validation.
authors: Nomanzadeh A, Razi M, Hasanzadeh S, Hobbenaghi R.

title: A Pilot Surveillance Program to Identify Emerging SARS-CoV-2 Variants in International Travelers Arriving at a Major International Airport: Prospective Cohort Evaluation.
abstract: BackgroundTesting arriving international travelers for COVID-19 paired with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) may identify new introductions of SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern in California, enabling a timely public health response. Traveler genomic surveillance may be a way to improve gaps in worldwide disease genomic surveillance.ObjectiveThis paper aimed to describe a pilot surveillance program to identify SARS-CoV-2 variants in arriving international travelers at San Francisco International Airport (SFO).MethodsThe California Department of Public Health implemented a pilot program at SFO to voluntarily test arriving international travelers for COVID-19 from June 2021 to November 2021 to identify SARS-CoV-2 variants. Arriving international travelers were offered self-collect COVID-19 antigen tests upon arrival at SFO. Travelers with positive COVID-19 antigen tests or with COVID-19 symptoms were recommended to self-collect and mail an additional specimen for diagnostic molecular testing. WGS of SARS-CoV-2 was performed on RNA extracts from positive tests to identify variants.ResultsIn total, 2.1% (19,008/892,558) of all arriving international travelers at SFO from 133 different countries of departure enrolled in the program. The COVID-19 test positivity among this group was 0.7% (33/5038), and the weekly test positivity range, 0% to 1.5%, was lower than the weekly test positivity across the state of California during the same time frame. Arriving international travelers departing from Turkey (3/145, 2.1%), Mexico (7/602, 1.2%), and the United Kingdom (6/626, 1.0%) had the highest test positivity. Of the 14 positive molecular tests, 10 (71.4%) were sequenced, and all were found to belong to the SARS-CoV-2 Delta B.1.617.2 lineage, the most prevalent SARS-CoV-2 variant in California and worldwide at the time.ConclusionsVoluntary testing of arriving international travelers paired with WGS was operationally and logistically feasible. Although the number of sequenced positive COVID-19 specimens in this program was limited, the lessons learned from this pilot informed improvements to subsequent iterations of traveler viral genomic surveillance in California and highlighted the potential value of traveler viral genomic surveillance to support early identification and characterization of emerging infectious diseases entering a region.
authors: Foote EM, Bouchard EL, Baylis EF, Getabecha S, Arunleung P, Salas M, Gautham G, Morales C, Wadford DA, Jacobson K.

title: The underappreciated role for phase variation and quasi-clonality in microbial populations.
abstract: Phase variation is a well-established phenomenon in some bacteria, where it generates heritable phenotypic variants within a population. These states, while reversible, are stable across generations, giving rise to quasi-clonal populations even when starting from a single bacterium. Underlying mechanisms include variation in short homopolymeric or heteropolymeric sequence repeats, DNA inversions mediated by site-specific recombination, reversible insertions and deletions, and switching between alternative methylation states. Although phase variation occurs in diverse bacteria, its contribution to phenotypic heterogeneity remains overlooked and use of the term is often absent in describing this phenomenon.
authors: Dyzenhaus S, Gray-Owen SD, Lan F.

title: The last gift cohort: advancing HIV reservoir research through single-cell and spatial approaches.
abstract: Purpose of reviewDespite effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), persistent HIV reservoirs remain the primary obstacle to achieving an HIV cure. Understanding persistence requires defining not only reservoir size but also the identity and state of infected cells and their anatomical microenvironments - features that blood-based bulk measurements cannot resolve. We synthesize published findings from the Last Gift end-of-life cohort, in which longitudinal sampling and tissue donation via rapid autopsy have advanced our understanding of HIV persistence across anatomical compartments. We then highlight how integrated single-cell and spatial profiling can link proviral features to host-cell states and local tissue neighborhoods, helping to define the cellular and microenvironmental niches that sustain persistence.Recent findingsThe Last Gift studies have mapped HIV DNA and envelope diversity across up to 33 anatomical compartments, inferred lymphoid and gastrointestinal tissues to be dominant sources of viral dispersal, shown that >85% of expanded proviral clones are shared across tissues, and recovered inducible, replication-competent virus from parietal-cortex microglia. Single-cell profiling has resolved heterogeneous microglial transcriptional and chromatin states containing rare HIV RNA or accessible proviral DNA and has identified a transcriptomic definition of cells expressing HIV RNA despite viral suppression on ART. Additionally, mass cytometry of viral sensors and restriction factors has defined tissue- and cell subset-specific antiviral programs, including restriction-factor profiles in lymph-node follicular helper T-cells predicted to favor HIV persistence. In parallel, imaging-based spatial transcriptomics with custom HIV probes, immunoPET/CT-guided tissue sampling, and duplex RNAscope/DNAscope have made direct localization of viral nucleic acids within annotated tissue neighborhoods technically feasible. No single assay, however, establishes proviral intactness, transcriptional activity, cellular identity, spatial position, and neighborhoods at once.SummaryReservoir measurements should be reported by what each assay can establish rather than as interchangeable estimates of reservoir size. Cohorts such as the Last Gift, which yield matched blood and multiorgan tissue from the same donor with longitudinal clinical context, are well suited to applying direct proviral characterization, single-cell phenotyping and spatially resolved viral detection in parallel on the same specimens. This combination defines the resolution - intact provirus, in an identified cell, in a defined tissue niche - that cure trials should increasingly be expected to measure.
journal: Current opinion in HIV and AIDS
authors: Stephens VR, Beliakova-Bethell N, Wanjalla CN.

title: Contact-induced molecular reorganisation in a model Escherichia coli lipid membrane.
abstract: The nanoscale composition, molecular organisation and mechanics of biological membranes underpins their function for cellular compartmentalisation, signalling, and mechanical integrity. Eukaryotic membranes can readjust their molecular content and structural organisation in response to specific interactions or changes in their environment, including through the formation of more ordered and solid-like nanodomains - lipid rafts. Recent studies have shown that bacterial membranes also possess significant lipid diversity and can form functional microdomains reminiscent of eukaryotic lipid rafts, despite lacking sterols and sphingolipids. In all cases, the role of biochemical interactions between lipids has long been recognized as determinant for the membrane molecular organisation and physical properties. In this study, we explore how non-specific physical contacts between a model lipid membrane mimicking the composition of the inner membrane of Escherichia coli and different substrates affect membrane molecular organisation and physical properties at the nanoscale. Using atomic force microscopy, we track the evolution of the membrane when kept a few degrees above its transition temperature. The sample is fully immersed in a solution mimicking the ionic composition of the standard E. coli growth media and placed in a sealed chamber to prevent changes in the interfacial hydration layer between the membrane and substrate. Aside from the expected role of the substrate on the lipid phase transition, we observe a slow substrate-dependent molecular reorganisation of the membrane following a spinodal-like behaviour. Over a period varying between minutes for rougher substrates to hours for atomically flat substrates, mechanically stiffer yet still fluid nanodomains emerge. Concomitant changes in height difference between lipid nanodomains are consistent with a substrate-biased lipid flip-flop mechanism resulting in compositional asymmetry between leaflets. The results support previous theoretical predictions and demonstrate that membrane-surface interactions may be sufficient to passively drive molecular reorganisation in bacterial membranes, with consequences for membrane function and mechanics, including in processes like osmotic pressure regulation.
authors: Tormena N, Pilizota T, Voïtchovsky K.

title: Yhk8 as a genomic modifier of copper susceptibility in yeast.
abstract: Copper is essential for life as an enzymatic cofactor and antioxidant participant, but in excess, it is toxic to all living organisms, including yeast. Because this toxicity varies by genetic background, we investigated the underlying modifier loci using a panel of four genetically diverse strains-Sake (SA), North American (NA), West African (WA), and Wine/European (WE)-and their segregants. Copper sulfate (CuSO4) susceptibility, quantified by the maximum growth rate (µMax), was strain-dependent, with resistance decreasing in the order SA > WE > WA > NA. Furthermore, cellular growth was inversely correlated with intracellular superoxide levels measured via dihydroethidium staining. By analyzing µMax in 96 segregants from an SA x NA cross exposed to CuSO4, we performed quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping and prioritized 16 candidate modifiers. Functional validations in a Yhk8 deletant resulted in impaired growth and elevated superoxide levels upon copper exposure. Finally, bioinformatics structural predictions support that Yhk8 is a putative drug/proton antiporter with functional analogy to human SLC47A1, containing a predicted copper-binding site. Together, these findings support Yhk8 as a key genetic modifier of copper response in yeast.
journal: Biometals : an international journal on the role of metal ions in biology, biochemistry, and medicine
authors: Olguín V, Contreras S, Arriagada F, Saavedra J, Szenfeld B, Cubillos FA, Klein AD.

title: Integrative Multiomics Analysis of the Angiogenesis-EMT Interface in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
abstract: Angiogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) are key hallmarks that contribute to the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), but whether the two programs vary simultaneously across tumors and how much of this reflects tumor composition remain unclear. We scored predefined, non-overlapping 20-gene angiogenesis and EMT signatures with a rank-based method in 342 primary oral cavity tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA-OSCC). The two programs were strongly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.809, P = 2.7 x 10^-80), and 2,396 bridge genes were associated with both programs across the transcriptome. The bridge genes were enriched in pathways associated with focal adhesion and extracellular matrix-receptor interaction. In the cellular case, fibroblast and endothelial marker scores were prominent and correlated with the program scores. The coupling was attenuated but remained positive after joint adjustment for tumor purity and stromal and immune scores (partial rho = 0.406) and with an epithelial-restricted EMT score (rho = 0.710). Further correlation was performed with a partial EMT (pEMT), which shows a significant positive correlation (rho = 0.59) and an inverse correlation with tumor purity (rho = -0.70). 146 final gene candidates were found using multi-omic evidence and candidate-level testing on the external cohort GSE30784; after adjusting for inferred cell fractions, 101 of these candidates supported the dual program. For thorough characterization, three candidates with an emphasis on OSMR, MICAL2, and LHFPL2 were chosen. Additional CPTAC data were used to confirm protein-level support, which was strongest for MICAL2. No significant connection was seen between the Interface score and overall survival (hazard ratio per 1-SD increase, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.78-1.08). These results describe a coordinated angiogenesis-EMT transcriptional state in OSCC that is attenuated but retained after accounting for tumor composition, and nominate candidate genes for experimental study.
authors: Das S, Natarajan E, Singh R, Shaikh R.

title: Multi-omics integration reveals candidate genes and molecular mechanisms associated with resistance to sugarcane smut
abstract: Sugarcane smut, caused by the fungus  Sporisorium scitamineum (Syd.), is one of the main diseases affecting sugarcane and is capable of causing severe yield losses in susceptible varieties. Given the limitations of classical breeding, mainly due to the genetic complexity of sugarcane cultivars, molecular and omics approaches have gained increasing prominence for studying the genetic basis of traits such as disease resistance. In this context, we investigated sugarcane resistance to smut through the integration of association mapping methods and transcriptomics. A panel of 155 genotypes was genotyped with 33,335 SNP markers and inoculated with  S. scitamineum generating three phenotypic variables. These data were jointly analyzed through genome-wide association analyses to identify marker-trait associations. In addition, transcriptomic analyses were performed using publicly available datasets from four studies evaluating sugarcane responses to smut. The integration of these multi-omics data enabled the identification of candidate genes involved in structural reinforcement, immune signaling, redox homeostasis, genome maintenance, and cellular adaptation. These findings provide valuable molecular resources for functional validation and breeding strategies aimed at developing sugarcane cultivars with enhanced smut resistance.
authors: Thomazim D, Pimenta RJG, Santos LdF, Moraes AdCL, Sforça DA, Anjos LOS, dos Anjos IA, da Silva FB, Pinto LR, de Souza AP.

title: Biosynthesis-Integrated Editing of Bacterial Cellulose Enables Sequence-Programmable Biointerfaces
abstract: Abstract  Structural polysaccharides self-assemble into densely packed fibrils, providing a molecular foundation for the hierarchical organization and mechanical integrity of biological materials. However, the same interchain interactions that stabilize these structures severely restrict chemical accessibility, making molecular editing after assembly a formidable challenge. Here, we integrate regiochemical editing into bacterial cellulose biosynthesis using azido-glucose analogues substituted at C2, C3, or C6. The resulting cellulose materials exhibit regioisomer-dependent differences in crystallinity, fibrillar organization, and mechanical properties, while precursor feeding further modulates crystallinity. The incorporated azide groups remain chemically accessible after assembly, enabling DNA conjugation and rolling-circle amplification to construct sequence-programmable aptamer interfaces. By varying the aptamer sequence, the same cellulose platform can be reprogrammed for either selective cell capture and release or HGF-mimetic regulation of endothelial behavior. This work establishes a biosynthesis-integrated strategy that connects molecular editing during cellulose formation with hierarchical material organization and subsequent biological programming.
authors: Yang G, Tang G, He Q, Zou S, Wang H, Huang G, Yin W, Shi Z, Chen Z, Yin L, Chen G.

title: PM₂.₅-Associated Variation in Airborne Antimicrobial Resistance Gene Abundance During Winter Smog Episodes in Urban Pakistan (2022–2023)
abstract: Abstract    Airborne particulate matter (PM₂.₅) is a major component of winter smog and has been increasingly recognized as a potential carrier of microbial contaminants, including antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). However, limited data are available on the distribution of airborne ARGs associated with PM₂.₅ in urban environments of Pakistan.  Objective  This study aimed to quantify the relative abundance of clinically relevant ARGs in PM₂.₅-associated bacterial communities across three cities of Pakistan and to evaluate their association with air pollution and meteorological conditions.  Methodology  PM₂.₅ samples were collected from Lahore, Islamabad, and Okara during the winter months (November–December 2022 and 2023). External DNA (eDNA) associated with particulate matter was extracted and analysed using quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR). The relative abundance of selected ARGs (  sul1, blaTEM, blaCTX-M-32, blaNDM-1, vanA, vanRA, tnpA, intI1  , and  blaTEM-F  ) was determined using the 2^(-ΔCt) method and normalized against the 16S rRNA gene. Environmental parameters, including PM₂.₅ concentration, Air Quality Index (AQI), temperature, and humidity, were also assessed.  Results  Lahore exhibited the highest pollution levels, with PM₂.₅ concentrations reaching 276.6 ± 27.4 µg/m³ and AQI values up to 289.3 ± 42.7. PM₂.₅ showed strong positive correlations with AQI (r = 0.92) and relative humidity (r = 0.91) and a negative correlation with temperature (r = − 0.38). Distinct spatial variation in ARG relative abundance was observed across the study sites. The  blaNDM-1  gene demonstrated the highest relative abundance, particularly in Lahore (0.077) and Islamabad (0.056), while  vanA  showed a comparatively higher abundance in Okara. Other ARGs, including  blaTEM-F, sul1  , and  intI1  , exhibited variable distribution patterns across cities, indicating heterogeneous environmental resistome profiles.  Conclusion  The findings reveal significant spatial variability in airborne ARG relative abundance associated with PM₂.₅ and highlight the influence of environmental conditions on resistome distribution. These results underscore the importance of monitoring airborne antimicrobial resistance in polluted urban environments and provide baseline data for future environmental and public health assessments.
authors: Khan MI, Amin A, Khalid N, Ahmed I.

title: Demographic variation of viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus among Round Gobies in the St. Lawrence River.
abstract: ObjectiveWe investigated the demographic dynamics of viral hemorrhagic septicemia virus (VHSV) infections in wild Round Goby Neogobius melanostomus from the nearshore habitats of the upper St. Lawrence River from 2018 to 2022. We examined viral prevalence and titers between Round Goby sexes and age-classes to identify how demography correlates with prevalence and amplification of this pathogen within this host species.MethodsReverse-transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction was used to detect and quantify viral N-gene genetic material in pooled organ (i.e., liver, kidney, spleen) and brain tissues of wild Round Gobies that were collected from the upper St. Lawrence River. Age and sex were assigned to each individual to elucidate how patterns of infection prevalence and amplification vary depending on demography within this host species.ResultViral hemorrhagic septicemia virus was detected by reverse-transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction in 49.62% of the sampled Round Gobies, with significant variation in prevalence and titers observed across demographic groups. Sex-based VHSV prevalence was 15.87% in females and 55.95% in males, and infected fish of both sexes contained similar median viral titers. Age-based prevalence increased with age, ranging from 14.29% in age-1 fish to 68.35% in age-4 fish, whereas viral titers were highest in age-2 fish and decreased with age thereafter.ConclusionRound Gobies exhibit a high prevalence (49.62%) of VHSV infections. However, the pathogen is distributed unevenly among demographics within this species. Both sex and age interact with the infection status of an individual.
authors: Haws AL, Getchell RG, Farrell JM.

title: Single-Nucleus Transcriptomics Reveals Cell Type Specific Defence Responses and Identifies AhWRKY40 as a Key Regulator of Peanut Resistance to Sclerotium rolfsii.
abstract: Peanut stem rot caused by Sclerotium rolfsii is a devastating soil borne disease that severely constrains peanut production worldwide. Despite its economic importance, highly resistant peanut cultivars are still largely unavailable, and the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying peanut resistance remain poorly understood. We obtained a total of 29,308 high-quality nuclei, annotated five major cell types, and detected 52,819 expressed genes. Comparative analysis revealed widespread transcriptional reprogramming and a predominance of downregulated genes in response to pathogen infection, accompanied by a substantial reduction in cell abundance across all cell populations. Notably, epidermal cells harboured the highest proportion of disease resistance genes. Pseudotime trajectory analysis further demonstrated that S. rolfsii infection altered cellular transcriptional states and induced cell type specific immune reprogramming. Integrative analyses combining gene coexpression, pseudotime dynamics, virtual knockout, and transgenic validation consistently identified AhWRKY40 as a key regulatory factor associated with disease resistance. Overexpression of AhWRKY40 enhanced resistance to S. rolfsii and was accompanied by increased accumulation of jasmonic acid (JA) and salicylic acid (SA), suggesting its involvement in hormone-mediated defence responses. Collectively, our study provides new insights into the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying peanut resistance to stem rot, identifies AhWRKY40 as a promising candidate gene for disease resistance, and establishes a valuable resource for functional genomics and molecular breeding to improve southern blight resistance in peanut.
authors: Sun Z, Liu H, Hong Y, Umer MJ, Wang W, Liu P, Shen H, Pu X, Zhang J, Sun D.

title: Profiling of RNA 8-oxoG marks in Escherichia coli identifies critical intrinsic characteristics that contribute to 8-oxoG accumulation in bacteria.
abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are environmentally ubiquitous and have pervasive impacts on cellular homeostasis. RNA is vulnerable to oxidative chemical alterations from myriad endogenous and exogenous sources. The most common chemical modification resulting from ROS exposure to RNA is 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine (8-oxoG). While 8-oxoG modifications are known to impact mRNA processing, understanding the broader biological impact of 8-oxoG requires knowledge of how these modifications accumulate. In this work, we assessed the disparate enrichment of 8-oxoG modifications within RNAs in the E. coli transcriptome using an RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing technique with a high-affinity 8-oxoG antibody (8-oxoG-RIP-Seq). Our investigation of the RNA 8-oxoG enrichment landscape uncovered intrinsic RNA characteristics that correlate with 8-oxoG enrichment. These findings suggest intrinsic characteristics of RNA, most notably relative abundance, CDS length and G‑nucleotide composition, significantly influence RNA 8-oxoG accumulation. We harnessed these properties to construct a simple multiple linear regression model that predicts RNA 8-oxoG accumulation, which we validated in E. coli. This model was subsequently applied to predict 8-oxoG‑enriched RNA species in four other bacterial species spanning a wide range of oxidative stress tolerances; these predictions suggest that 8-oxoG accumulation is species dependent, with limited overlap in RNAs and functional pathways that are more susceptible to 8-oxoG accumulation. Further evaluation of this model in the extremophile D. radiodurans revealed a substantial reduction in predictive power. Overall, these findings better inform understanding of RNA 8-oxoG patterns in bacteria and have broader impacts towards advancing knowledge of the connection between RNA oxidation and cellular homeostasis.
authors: Burroughs MR, Quiñones-Diaz BI, Grismore KB, Contreras LM.

title: Inhibitory Effect of Trichoderma harzianum Strain A3.1 Against Fusarium Species Causing Fig Root Rot.
abstract: To identify the causal pathogen of fig root rot in Artux, Xinjiang, China and screen high-efficacy biocontrol agents, diseased fig root tissues were used as research materials. Pathogen isolation, morphological characterization, molecular identification and pathogenicity assays were sequentially performed to characterize the disease-causing fungus, followed by screening of antagonistic microorganisms. The results demonstrated that the pathogen responsible for fig root rot was Fusarium kazakhstanicum. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of F. kazakhstanicum causing fig root rot on Ficus carica in China. A highly effective antagonistic fungal strain designated A3.1 was isolated from the rhizosphere soil of healthy fig trees, and was identified as Trichoderma harzianum based on morphological traits and molecular phylogenetic evidence. Dual-culture assays revealed that T. harzianum A3.1 achieved a mycelial growth inhibition rate of 72.5% against F. kazakhstanicum. Light microscopic and scanning electron microscopy observations further illustrated that T. harzianum A3.1 severely disrupted the hyphal architecture of the pathogen, causing hyphal deformation and granular deposits at the contact sites. This strain possesses great application prospects for biocontrol against the pathogen causing fig root rot, and this research lays a foundation for developing environmentally sustainable control strategies of fig root rot in Xinjiang, China.
authors: Sijia Z, Guorong L, Deng X, Halifu S.

title: Mapping HIV reservoir geography: lessons for cure from the Last Gift rapid autopsy cohort.
abstract: Purpose of reviewDeep tissue reservoirs remain a major barrier to HIV cure. Their anatomical distribution and connectivity are difficult to study in living people. We examine how the Last Gift rapid-autopsy cohort clarifies reservoir connectivity, persistence behind anatomical barriers, and variation within organs, and consider the implications for cure.Recent findingsTissue studies reveal HIV reservoirs that are interconnected across yet differ between and within anatomical sites. Viral sequence analyses suggest that blood links tissue reservoirs, with gut and lymphoid tissues acting as hubs of viral dispersal. Recovery of replication-competent HIV from brain microglia during suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART) provides direct evidence of a resident brain reservoir. Even within the gastrointestinal tract, HIV DNA burden and transcriptions vary by region, with different microbiome associations in the small and large bowel.SummaryHIV reservoir geography supports durable ART-free remission as a practical goal. Achieving this goal will likely require combination therapies with complementary functions and tissue access. Because tissue heterogeneity limits what negative biopsies can establish, remission should be assessed through carefully monitored analytical treatment interruption and long-term follow up.
journal: Current opinion in HIV and AIDS
authors: Birabaharan M, Immer A, Gomez AN, Valdes D, Smith DM.

title: Multifaceted roles of 3C-like protease in porcine enteric coronavirus immune evasion and antiviral targeting.
abstract: Porcine enteric coronaviruses, including porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV), porcine transmissible gastroenteritis virus (TGEV), porcine deltacoronavirus (PDCoV), and swine acute diarrhea syndrome coronavirus (SADS-CoV), have resulted in significant economic losses for the global swine industry and have raised substantial public health concerns due to their potential for cross-species transmission and zoonotic risk. As positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses, these coronaviruses possess genomes that encode a set of nonstructural proteins essential for viral replication. Among these, the 3C-like protease (3CLpro) is highly conserved and plays an indispensable role in processing viral polyproteins. The 3CLpro exhibits a characteristic three-domain architecture featuring a conserved Cys-His catalytic dyad, with its dimerization being critical for catalytic activity. This protease specifically cleaves key molecules involved in the signaling pathways of innate immunity and programmed cell death. Despite sequence variations among α-, β-, γ-, and δ-coronaviruses, the catalytic core and substrate-binding pockets of 3CLpro remain structurally conserved, rendering this protease an ideal target for broad-spectrum antiviral agents. Targeting 3CLpro presents a promising strategy for combating porcine coronavirus infections. This review summarizes the structural characteristics, catalytic mechanisms, specific cleavage of host proteins, and the potential for antiviral drug development related to porcine coronavirus 3CLpro, aiming to provide a theoretical basis for elucidating its multifunctional roles in viral replication and immune regulation.
authors: Huang Y, Tian C, Cui H, Zheng L, Chen H, Zhang Y, Zhao Y, Ma S.

title: Fructobacillus fructosus isolated from palm wine: functional screening and safety evaluation as a potential probiotic.
abstract: Fructobacillus fructosus, a specialized fructophilic lactic acid bacterium from traditional fermented ecosystems, remains largely unexplored for its functional probiotic properties. This study established a robust, experimentally validated in vitro baseline of the probiotic potential and safety profile of the Fructobacillus fructosus strain MRS-3 isolated from traditional palm wine. The taxonomic identification was confirmed by 16 S rRNA gene sequencing and phylogenetic analysis. In vitro screening assays were used to evaluate the gastrointestinal survivability (acid/bile tolerance) and cell surface traits (autoaggregation, hydrophobicity, and Caco-2 cell adhesion) of the isolate. Baseline biological safety was quantitatively determined using minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values against reference breakpoints and a hemolysis assay. Strain MRS-3 was confirmed as Fructobacillus fructosus (GenBank: PV123975.1) by 16 S rRNA gene sequencing and exhibited growth across a broad range of pH, salt concentrations, and temperatures. It demonstrated tolerance to acidic and bile salt conditions, with viable counts ranging from 5.3 to 5.9 and 5.4 to 5.98 log CFU/mL, respectively. The strain showed high auto-aggregation (94.8%) and cell-surface hydrophobicity toward xylene (90%), toluene (90.9%), and hexane (76%), together with co-aggregation with selected indicator strains and measurable adhesion to Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cells. No hemolytic activity was observed, and inhibition zones were observed in the antibiotic susceptibility study under the experimental conditions spanning 18 to 27 mm. The results obtained strongly support the potential of Fructobacillus fructosus MRS-3 isolated from palm wine as a safe and functional probiotic candidate. This study provides a critical empirical baseline for the genus, demonstrating that its phenotypic traits merit future targeted in vivo validation.
authors: Sudarsini B, Indira M.

title: Single-Cell Transcriptome-Wide Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization Analysis Reveals Immune Cell-Specific Mechanisms in Alzheimer's Disease
abstract: Objective:  To integrate single-cell expression quantitative trait locus (sc-eQTL), Alzheimer's disease (AD) genome-wide association study (GWAS), and Bayesian colocalization analyses, in order to systematically identify candidate causal genes and potential immune mechanisms that specifically regulate AD risk in peripheral immune cells. Methods: Using the cis-eQTLs of 14 peripheral blood immune cell types from the OneK1K single-cell eQTL dataset as exposure data and the AD GWAS (GCST90565439) as outcome data, a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis was performed. Weak instrumental variables were removed using F-statistics, and approximately independent genetic instruments were obtained by linkage disequilibrium pruning. For significant gene-cell type associations, compareCluster functional enrichment, Bayesian colocalization, and phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) were further performed, and the 1M-scBloodNL dataset was used for replication validation. Results: The MR analysis identified 187 gene-cell type associations significantly associated with AD risk, involving 161 candidate causal genes. Among them, 141 genes showed significant associations in only a single immune cell type, suggesting that AD-related immune genetic regulation has marked cell type specificity. Functional enrichment analysis showed that the significant genes in different immune cell types were enriched in biological processes including MHC class II antigen presentation, phagocytosis, membrane invagination, and positive regulation of T cell activation. Colocalization analysis indicated a strong shared genetic signal between TNF expression in CD4+SOX4+ T cells and AD risk (PP.H4 = 0.833). In the 1M-scBloodNL replication analysis, several candidate genes showed consistent direction and nominal significance. The PheWAS results suggested that the significant phenotypic associations of the TNF instrumental variable were mainly concentrated in immune- and hematology-related traits, with no genome-wide significant neurological phenotypic associations observed. Conclusion: This study suggests that single-cell eQTL-MR combined with colocalization analysis can be used to dissect the cell type-specific genetic regulatory mechanisms of peripheral immunity in AD. The genetically predicted expression of TNF in CD4+SOX4+ T cells may represent an important immune-related signal for AD risk, but further validation in independent populations and functional experiments is still required.
authors: Si Y, Si Y.

title: High Neuronal PAS Domain Protein 2 Expression Associated with Poor Prognosis, Tumor Immune Infiltration, and Adenosine Pathway Markers in Lung Cancer.
abstract: This study aims to explore the clinical significance of neuronal PAS domain protein 2 (NPAS2) in lung cancer, its relationship with the tumor immune microenvironment, and its potential upstream non-coding RNA (ncRNA) regulatory network. By analyzing transcriptomic data and clinical information from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database, prognostic genes were identified, and NPAS2 expression was analyzed in lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma to determine its associations with patient survival and immune cell infiltration. Immunohistochemical analysis was also performed to compare NPAS2 expression between lung cancer tissues and adjacent non-tumor tissues. NPAS2 expression was elevated in tumor tissues, with higher expression associated with reduced overall survival. This association remained significant in multivariate Cox regression analysis (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.11687, P = 0.0252). In the analyzed dataset, a diagnostic model incorporating NPAS2, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), marker of proliferation Ki-67 (MKI67), and tumor protein p63 (TP63) yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.987. Immune infiltration analysis revealed that in lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma, NPAS2 expression was positively correlated with CD4⁺ T cell and neutrophil infiltration, as well as with the expression of the immune checkpoint molecule sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-like lectin 15 (SIGLEC15). Additionally, NPAS2 expression was positively correlated with the adenosine pathway markers CD39 and CD73. Bioinformatics analysis further identified a potential regulatory axis of NORAD/AC087477.2-hsa-miR-106a-5p/hsa-miR-17-5p-NPAS2. These results suggest that NPAS2 may be a candidate biomarker for lung cancer diagnosis and prognosis assessment and may be associated with tumor immune cell infiltration and adenosine-related immune regulatory processes. However, further functional experiments and clinical validation are needed to clarify its potential molecular mechanism and clinical application value.
authors: Dai J, Reyimu A, Song X, Zhou W.

title: Formal Description of Cladocopium proximale sp. nov., a Coral Photosymbiont From the C1 Radiation.
abstract: Coral reefs are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth and rely on endosymbiosis with Symbiodiniaceae, a diverse family of dinoflagellates essential for coral nutrition and which also play an important role in thermal tolerance. Despite their ecological importance, resolving species boundaries within Symbiodiniaceae remains challenging, partly due to limited phylogenetic signal in commonly used genetic markers and the absence of broadly accepted criteria for species delimitation. Refining taxonomic resolution is therefore critical for understanding symbiont diversity, distributions, and evolutionary relationships. In this study, we delimit two closely related Cladocopium species using a meta-haplotype framework applied to two hypervariable loci-the ITS2 region and the psbA non-coding region (psbAncr). Slowly evolving markers failed to differentiate Cladocopium proximale (SCF049; described here) from its sister species C. proliferum. In contrast, consistent genetic differences between the two taxa were detected across both hypervariable regions. Together with morphological differences, these results support the recognition of C. proximale and C. proliferum as distinct species. Our results highlight the value of combining multiple hypervariable markers to improve taxonomic accuracy in Symbiodiniaceae, providing a stronger basis for understanding how symbiont diversity and ecological differentiation may influence coral resilience and responses to environmental change. More broadly, closely related Symbiodiniaceae such as these provide important systems for examining speciation processes, including potential ecological differentiation and reproductive compatibility.
authors: Terzi G, van Oppen MJH, Seveso D, Nitschke MR.

title: Genome-Wide Characterization of HERV-Derived RNA Regulatory Potential in the Human Transcriptome.
abstract: Human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs) comprise nearly 8% of the human genome, and their long terminal repeats (LTRs) are well-established sources of transcriptional regulatory elements. However, their contribution to RNA-level regulatory features remains largely unexplored. Here, we present a genome-wide characterization of the RNA regulatory potential of 53,176 HERV internal regions and 560,594 LTRs. We found 16.2% more predicted RNA-binding protein motif occurrences in HERV internal regions than expected after controlling for dinucleotide composition. At the subfamily level, overall motif abundance was elevated in HERVH but remained close to expectation in HERVK (HML-2). Conserved retroviral protein domains incorporated into transcripts were mostly located in exceptionally long terminal exons, approximately 7-fold longer than those of other multi-exon transcripts. HERV internal sequence overlapped 4,074 annotated long noncoding RNA genes and accounted for more than 80% of the gene body of 144, most of them functionally unannotated. Finally, 6,583 unique antisense LTRs at transcript termini formed SPARCS-like candidate configurations that could support antisense RNA pairing; protein-coding genes carrying them in 3' untranslated regions showed enrichment for immune signaling and recombination-related terms. These results provide a genome-wide framework of candidate HERV-derived RNA regulatory features and transcript architectures for experimental testing.
authors: Montserrat-Ayuso T, Pujol A, Esteve-Codina A.

title: The transcription factor SiROCX coordinates a stage-specific xylan- and cellulose-degrading secretome during immune-compatible colonization of monocot roots by Serendipita indica.
abstract: Intracellular accommodation of beneficial fungi requires controlled remodelling of host cell walls while avoiding excessive activation of plant immune responses. During colonization of monocot roots, the endophytic fungus Serendipita indica induces a suite of carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) targeting xylan and cellulose, but how this program is transcriptionally controlled in basidiomycetes is unknown. Here, we combined co-expression network analysis of time-resolved colonization transcriptomes with DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq) of module-associated transcription factors. This identified SiROCX, a Zn2Cys6 transcription factor of an Agaricomycetes-specific Roc1/ROCX lineage, whose DAP-seq-defined regulon is enriched in CAZyme genes. Inducible overexpression of SiROCX activated representative targets, enriched the secretome in CAZymes and enhanced xylanase and cellulase activities on xylan and delignified alcohol-insoluble residue (dAIR) of barley roots under in vitro conditions. Premature activation of this program during barley colonization was associated with early induction of a host immune marker despite comparable fungal biomass, consistent with a role for temporal control in maintaining symbiotic compatibility. Together, these findings identify SiROCX as a major regulator of a host-adapted cell wall-degrading secretome and reveal an Agaricomycetes-specific regulatory module that coordinates host cell wall remodelling with immune-compatible symbiotic colonization.
authors: Armbruster L, Brands M, Baumgart L, Dreesmann F, Leson L, Peltz N, Ramírez V, Zhang Y, Nassr T, Langen G, Pauly M, Zuccaro A.

title: Laryngeal Cancer Microbiome Study Reveals Parvimonas and Campylobacter as Potential Therapy Targets.
abstract: ObjectiveLaryngeal cancer accounts for 40% of head and neck malignancies and 1% of all cancer-related deaths worldwide. We evaluated the laryngeal cancer microbiome to identify cancer-specific genera as potential treatment targets.MethodsA prospective study was conducted using 57 laryngeal mucosal samples from 24 treatment-naive laryngeal cancer patients and 33 patients who were undergoing otolaryngological surgery unrelated to oral or laryngeal diseases (01/2023-09/2025). DNA was extracted and amplified in triplicate, targeting the V3/V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene, followed by paired-end 2 × 300 bp sequencing on the Illumina NextSeq 2000. Amplicon sequence variants were identified via DADA2 and assigned to genera using a naive Bayes classifier. Two samples with zero classified read pairs were excluded.ResultsMost patients were male (87.5% cancer, 66.7% controls) and smokers (83.3% cancer, 54.5% controls). Cancer patients' core laryngeal microbiomes uniquely contained Parvimonas (3.67%; 95% CI: 0.70%-6.64%), and Campylobacter (1.12%; 95% CI: 0.60%-1.63%), while control patients' uniquely contained Corynebacterium (2.97%; 95% CI: 0.00%-7.67%) and Alloprevotella (1.34%; 95% CI: 0.64%-2.04%). Cancer samples were significantly enriched in 19 genera, notably Peptococcus (2.93, q = 0.0003), Campylobacter (1.68, q = 0.009), and Parvimonas (2.02, q = 0.03), compared to controls.ConclusionsLaryngeal cancer patients' samples displayed microbial dysbiosis, with enrichment of microbes present in gastrointestinal cancers, cervical cancer, and inflammatory states; they also exhibited loss of immunoprotective taxa. These findings support that microbiome profiling can distinguish malignant mucosa and guide future studies targeting genera increased in cancer, including Parvimonas and Campylobacter.Level of evidence: 3
authors: Lad H, Shah A, Thompson ER, Javid S, Chee RH, Zaransky S, Dhanda A, Mudhar A, Lamichhane S, Chua AT, Bono K, Bono J, Kaye R, Johnson WE, Cugini C, Yan K.

title: Relevance of the Avalon Assemblage as an Astrobiological Analog for Icy Ocean Worlds.
abstract: We discuss the astrobiological potential of Earth's first animals--the nearly 600-million-year-old Avalon assemblage--and the relevance that these ancient communities may have for the search for life on icy or cold water worlds. The Avalon assemblage originated on deep, dark, salty, and cold seafloors with intriguing similarities to hypothesized icy ocean world habitats. These fossils provide an opportunity to study the signatures of entire communities of organisms that lived under conditions unlike those on Earth today. We discuss how information gleaned from the Avalon assemblage applies to the search for life on icy ocean worlds and explore how the physicochemical nature of their habitat could provide insights for astrobiology search strategies. Although the focus in astrobiology is on microbial communities, complex macroscopic life modifies its environment in ways and at scales that microbes cannot. The Avalon assemblage allows investigation of the circumstances under which such life emerged, clarifying the role of stochastic and probabilistic processes in evolution. Avalonian communities and their paleoenvironments capture the ecosystems of a world in transition from microbe- to animal-dominated, illuminating the potential changes driven by these first animals-and their potentially detectable biosignatures. We close by framing questions that can leverage insights from the Avalon assemblage for biosignature detection and identify research opportunities for further exploration.
authors: Cantine MD, Journaux B, Griffiths HJ, Mitchell EG, Ostrander CM, Cothren HR, Jones U.

title: Advances in assessing donor organ quality and perioperative risk for kidney transplantation.
abstract: Kidney transplantation faces persistent challenges in accurately evaluating donor organ quality and predicting long-term outcomes, with traditional assessment methods demonstrating limited predictive capacity. The increasing utilization of marginal-quality donor organs has intensified the need for sophisticated evaluation strategies. Machine perfusion technology has transformed organ preservation from mere static storage to a dynamic platform potentially enabling real-time monitoring, assessment, and interventions during the preservation period. Molecular profiling technologies such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics could provide refined biomarkers for donor kidney assessment across several phases of kidney transplantation. The first window arises during donor evaluation. Techniques such as high-resolution molecular typing, genetic profiling, epigenomic markers, and artificial intelligence-enhanced imaging provide additional information compared to traditional scoring systems. During organ preservation, a second window emerges, allowing additional, isolated assessment of the organ after procurement but before transplantation. Machine perfusion systems enable sampling of perfusate and tissue for multi-omics analysis to characterize injury or function, although most candidate biomarkers remain at the discovery or early validation stage. After transplantation, donor-derived cell-free deoxyribonucleic acid, urinary chemokines, and advanced imaging modalities offer non-invasive early detection of graft injury. Clinical translation of these new techniques faces substantial challenges: most studies are single-center and have small sample sizes, assay standardization remains incomplete, and evidence linking biomarker-guided decisions to improved long-term graft survival is lacking. Machine learning may enhance risk stratification but remains largely unvalidated in prospective trials. Future progress requires a shift from short-term endpoint prediction to long-term outcome validation through multicenter studies, standardized protocols, and equitable implementation strategies.
authors: Zuo Y, Lantinga VA, Orozco-García E, Ogurlu B, Moers C.

title: Epigenetic regulation of macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) by DNA methylation during Vibrio anguillarum infection in Ruditapes philippinarum.
abstract: To investigate the effects of Vibrio anguillarum infection on the expression of macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) and DNA methylation of its promoter in the Manila clam Ruditapes philippinarum, we analyzed MIF sequence homology and phylogenetic relationships, temporal expression patterns after V. anguillarum infection, and promoter DNA methylation profiles, and used a dual-luciferase reporter assay to validate the regulatory effect of methylation on promoter activity. The results showed that the conserved domain of R. philippinarum MIF exhibited the highest homology with those of Meretrix meretrix and Mercenaria mercenaria. qRT-PCR analysis showed that MIF expression was significantly upregulated 12 h after V. anguillarum infection, peaked at 48 h (approximately 5.64-fold higher than the level at 0 h), and then returned to basal levels. Bisulfite sequencing PCR (BSP) analysis showed that MIF promoter methylation levels decreased significantly at 24 h and 48 h after infection, with the most pronounced demethylation observed at CpG 3, CpG 9, and CpG 11. Promoter methylation levels were significantly negatively correlated with MIF expression (R = -0.7552, P = 0.0062). The dual-luciferase reporter assay showed that in vitro methylation treatment significantly decreased MIF promoter activity. These results suggest that V. anguillarum infection may upregulate MIF expression by inducing promoter demethylation, thereby contributing to the host immune response. This study provides a reference for understanding the immune regulatory mechanisms underlying the resistance of R. philippinarum to V. anguillarum infection from an epigenetic perspective.
authors: Huang T, Li J, Nie H.

title: Structural Diversity and Functional Roles of the Internalin Family Proteins in Listeria monocytogenes.
abstract: Listeria monocytogenes is an important foodborne intracellular pathogen that can cause listeriosis in humans and animals, with a relatively high mortality rate. Internalin (Inl) family proteins are critical virulence factors of L. monocytogenes and play essential roles in bacterial adhesion, host cell invasion, tissue colonization, immune evasion, and systemic infection. In recent years, with the continuous advancement of genomics, structural biology, and host-pathogen interaction studies, an increasing number of internalin family members and their biological functions have been identified. Different internalins exhibit significant differences in receptor recognition, tissue tropism, and pathogenic mechanisms. This review systematically summarizes the structural characteristics and classification of the internalin family in L. monocytogenes, with particular emphasis on recent advances in the functions of major family members, including InlA, InlB, InlC, InlK, InlF, InlP, InlL, and InlJ, in intestinal invasion, penetration of the placental and blood-brain barriers, intracellular survival, immune evasion, biofilm formation, and host interactions. Furthermore, recent research hotspots in the functional characterization of internalin proteins are discussed, along with their potential applications in elucidating virulence mechanisms, vaccine development, and targeted prevention and control strategies. This review aims to provide a theoretical reference for further investigations into the pathogenic mechanisms of L. monocytogenes and the development of novel prevention and control strategies.
authors: Leng Q, Ma Y, Xia X, Qin X, Hirata T, Dong Q, Li Z.

title: Broad vaccine protection against globally diverse influenza A/H5Nx viruses.
abstract: Influenza A/H5Nx viruses continue to diversify and undergo gene reassortment as they infect avian and mammalian hosts worldwide. The severity of human infections varies substantially between different H5 clades and neuraminidase (NA) reassortants, creating unpredictable pandemic risk. Existing H5 vaccines, typically based on a single hemagglutinin (HA) strain, cannot keep pace with this natural variation. To address this problem, we computationally engineer HA, NA, and M2 antigens representing the global antigenic space of circulating H5Nx viruses, prioritizing N1 and N6 subtypes associated with the highest threat in humans. The resulting digitally immune-optimized mRNA vaccine, DVX-panH5Nx, elicits broad HA neutralization and NA inhibition across divergent clades in mice and ferrets. Compared to WHO candidate vaccine viruses (CVVs), DVX-panH5Nx confers superior protection against antigenically distinct H5N1 challenges spanning two decades of viral evolution, demonstrating that computationally designed multivalent antigen vaccines can overcome natural influenza diversification and provide a scalable strategy for pre-pandemic preparedness.

title: Precision recreation and multiplex stacking of disease-resistance alleles in tomato using optimized prime editing.
abstract: Prime editing enables precise modification of plant genomes and provides a means to recreate beneficial alleles underlying agronomically important traits. However, efficient and multiplexable prime editing systems remain limited in dicot crops. Here, we developed optimized prime editing systems for tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) and applied them to engineer and stack disease-resistance alleles. Using three tomato prime editors, TomPE2, TomPE6c, and TomPE7, we recreated a naturally occurring resistance-associated deletion identified in pepper by precisely deleting two leucine residues from the CYSTM-domain proteins SlBs5 and SlBs5L. The resulting tomato lines exhibited enhanced resistance to Xanthomonas, demonstrating that a resistance allele can be functionally recreated across related crop species. In parallel, introduction of premature stop codons into the susceptibility gene SlDMR6 conferred resistance to both Xanthomonas and Pseudomonas syringae. Transcriptome profiling revealed distinct defense states: Slbs5/Slbs5L plants predominantly exhibited enhanced pathogen-induced defense responses, whereas Sldmr6 plants showed elevated basal defense. Comparison of prime editor architectures and culture temperatures revealed differences in editing activity and precision, with TomPE6c producing the highest proportion of precise edits. We further developed a modular multiplex prime editing system capable of simultaneously modifying multiple loci, enabling resistance alleles and regulatory variants to be combined within a single generation. The engineered alleles were stably inherited, and resistance phenotypes were maintained under elevated temperature conditions. Together, these results establish prime editing as an effective platform for precise recreation, engineering, and multiplex stacking of disease-resistance alleles and provide a framework for accelerating resistance breeding in crops.
authors: Khadka N, Adero M, Gupta A, Yang B.

title: Development of a tryptophan-based dual selection system to investigate S-layer spatial organization during cytokinesis in Sulfolobus acidocaldarius.
abstract: Sulfolobus acidocaldarius is a thermoacidophilic archaeon used as a model system for studying fundamental cellular processes and for emerging biotechnological applications. However, the limited availability of selectable markers restricts advanced genetic manipulation in this organism. Here, we report the development of a tryptophan auxotrophy-based selection system in S. acidocaldarius. A ΔtrpBA mutant was constructed in the ΔpyrE background strain using a classical pop-in/pop-out recombination strategy. The resulting mutant exhibited little impairment of growth in rich medium, likely due to exogenous tryptophan supplied by complex nutrients, but failed to grow in a newly developed defined Brock-based amino acid dropout medium lacking tryptophan. Exploiting both uracil and tryptophan auxotrophies, we achieved dual-plasmid co-transformation and co-expression of the surface layer proteins and a dominant-negative mutant of the AAA-ATPase Vps4, revealing the accumulation of surface layer lattice forming protein SlaA at the midzone of division-arrested cells and its membrane anchor SlaB. Together, these results provide evidence for spatial regulation of S-layer assembly during archaeal cytokinesis while expanding the genetic toolkit available for S. acidocaldarius.
authors: Foo S, Baum B.

title: Genes in the Light: A Scoping Review of Bacterial Transcriptional Responses to Visible Range Radiation Across Wavelength and Dose.
abstract: Non-phototrophic bacteria do not use light for energy, yet many detect visible radiation and reorganise gene expression accordingly. Two routes are involved: dedicated photoreceptors (flavin-binding BLUF and LOV domains, biliverdin-binding bacteriophytochromes and cobalamin-binding CarH/LitR regulators), and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated when endogenous porphyrins and flavins absorb light, which trigger an oxidative-stress programme without any photosensory protein. This scoping review maps which genes change expression under visible light (400-700 nm) and how responses vary with wavelength, dose and context. We searched Elicit, PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PMC, performed citation chasing, and charted 70 core primary studies. Blue light (400-470 nm) is reported to produce the largest transcriptional changes in most direct comparisons. Blue-light responses are frequently but not universally characterised by induction of oxidative-stress defences and repression of carbohydrate metabolism, virulence determinants and quorum-sensing systems; important exceptions exist, including up-regulation of type III secretion genes in Pseudomonas syringae. Red and far-red light (620-760 nm) elicits substantial change chiefly in species encoding bacteriophytochromes. Temperature determines whether photoreceptor-dependent regulation occurs at all: in Listeria monocytogenes and Acinetobacter baumannii it operates at environmental temperatures and is attenuated or reversed at 37 °C. Dose-response data and functional validation are scarce, and dosimetry is reported in incompatible units; standardised dosimetry, time-resolved designs and phenotypic confirmation are the principal needs.
authors: Yousuf Azeemi ST, Azeemi S, Shaukat SF, Mahmood K.

title: Editing of SpNRAMP3, SpCAX3, and SpHMA3 differentially affects cadmium concentrations and growth responses in Sedum plumbizincicola.
abstract: Sedum plumbizincicola is a Cd/Zn hyperaccumulator with exceptional Cd tolerance and shoot accumulation capacity. Here, bioinformatic analysis, subcellular localization, heterologous expression in yeast, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing were combined to characterize the role of SpNRAMP3 in Cd homeostasis and tissue Cd allocation and its functional relationships with SpCAX3 and SpHMA3. SpNRAMP3 encodes a protein with 11 predicted transmembrane domains and shows a localization pattern consistent with tonoplast association; it is expressed in roots, stems and leaves and displays Cd-responsive expression. Heterologous expression of SpNRAMP3 in yeast increased cellular Cd accumulation and conferred Cd hypersensitivity. Two independent SpNRAMP3-edited lines showed greater Cd sensitivity and lower Cd concentrations in young leaves, supporting a role for SpNRAMP3 in Cd homeostasis, growth response, and tissue Cd allocation. Heterologous expression of SpCAX3 also altered cellular Cd accumulation and Cd sensitivity in yeast. Compared with the wild type, the spnramp3spcax3 double-edited lines showed 72.5-79.8% lower Cd concentrations in young leaves and reduced relative growth inhibition under Cd stress, whereas the spnramp3sphma3 lines showed 28.2-58.6% lower Cd concentrations in young leaves but substantially greater growth inhibition. These results suggest that SpHMA3 primarily mediates vacuolar Cd sequestration, whereas SpNRAMP3 and SpCAX3 may contribute to Cd homeostasis and tissue Cd allocation through distinct but functionally connected processes. These proteins may act together to support Cd hyperaccumulation and hypertolerance in S. plumbizincicola. This study provides a framework for understanding Cd homeostasis and tissue Cd allocation in hyperaccumulator plants and identifies candidate targets for genome-editing-based improvement of phytoremediation.
authors: Wu X, Zhang Y, Mo Y, Liu H, Wu L, Ren H, Zhang Y, Xu W.

title: Classical guinea pig coat phenotypes are associated with variants in  FGF5  and  CELSR1
abstract: ABSTRACT  Classical Mendelian coat phenotypes in the domestic guinea pig,  Cavia porcellus , were central to early studies of mammalian genetics, yet their molecular bases remain unresolved. Long fur is characterized by elongated hair, and rough coat by whorled patterns of fur orientation. Here, we performed genome-wide association mapping using exome and whole-genome sequencing data to identify the genetic basis of both phenotypes. Mapping of long fur identified a locus containing  FGF5 and resolved the association to a premature stop codon, independently confirming a previously proposed candidate variant. Mapping of rough coat identified a locus containing  CELSR1 , an atypical cadherin and core component of the planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway, resolving the association to an in-frame proline insertion in its extracellular domain. The variant is associated with a dominant rough-coat phenotype, unlike previously characterized recessive mouse  Celsr1 alleles, which produce a similar hair-patterning phenotype only when homozygous. The mouse alleles are also associated with severe developmental abnormalities, including open neural tube, which are not observed in rough-coat guinea pigs. This dominant, tissue-specific phenotype suggests that the insertion alters CELSR1 function in a previously undescribed manner. Consistent with this possibility, the rough-coat variant localized normally to cell-cell junctions in cultured mouse keratinocytes and retained its ability to recruit Fzd6 and Vangl2, demonstrating preserved molecular interactions involved in PCP junction assembly. These findings resolve the molecular basis of two classical guinea pig coat phenotypes and identify a naturally occurring, dominant  CELSR1 allele associated with a mode of PCP disruption distinct from previously characterized alleles.
authors: Halley M, Bierle CJ, Hsieh P, Zaidi A, Albert FW, Cetera M.

title: Bacterial and host cell-specific delivery of BMP, GrpE, and pMGA antigens via attenuated Salmonella confers bivalent protection against Mycoplasma gallisepticum and Salmonella Gallinarum in chickens.
abstract: Mycoplasma gallisepticum and Salmonella Gallinarum (SG) are economically important bacterial pathogens affecting poultry production, yet no single vaccine addresses both pathogens simultaneously. We engineered a recombinant SG vaccine strain, JOL3203, based on the dual-expression plasmid pJHL270, incorporating functionally distinct prokaryotic and eukaryotic cassettes to deliver two complementary Mycoplasma gallisepticum antigens from a single immunization regimen. The bacterial cassette under the Ptrc promoter expressed a multi-epitope chimeric antigen derived from conserved B-cell, MHC class I, and MHC class II epitopes of the BMP, GrpE, pMGA1.2, and pMGA1.3 proteins. The host cell cassette under the CMV promoter expressed a domain-based fusion antigen incorporating the N-terminal 400 residues of the BMP family protein, the C-terminal 250 residues of GrpE, and immunodominant pMGA epitopes. This dual-expression strategy was designed to promote antigen presentation through both exogenous and endogenous processing pathways, thereby stimulating complementary CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T-cell responses. In silico analyses predicted high antigenicity, favorable structural quality, and strong interaction with chicken TLR2-2. Expression was confirmed by western blotting at 32 kDa in bacterial lysates and 83 kDa in infected chicken bone marrow-derived macrophages, with transcription validated by RT-PCR. JOL3203 achieved 100% survival in safety evaluations versus 83% mortality in the wild-type SG group, with minimal systemic dissemination and histopathological changes. Vaccination elicited robust Mycoplasma-specific systemic IgY, mucosal IgA, expanded CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell populations, upregulated MHC class I and II expression, and a balanced Th1/Th2 cytokine profile of IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-4. Following intratracheal challenge, vaccinated birds showed significantly reduced tracheal colonization by color-changing unit assay, decreased mucosal thickening, and improved average daily weight gain versus PBS controls. JOL3203 further conferred 100% survival against lethal SG challenge compared with 75% mortality in PBS controls, with significantly reduced hepatic and splenic bacterial burdens. These findings demonstrate that the pJHL270 dual-expression platform provides a safe and effective strategy for simultaneous protection against Mycoplasma gallisepticum and SG while supporting its broader application as a modular live-vector vaccine platform for poultry.
authors: Bakhsh M, Kwon J, Gabasa DME, Depasupil AM, Cabarles JC, Lee JH.

title: Temporal changes in Zika virus populations during infection of three Aedes mosquito species.
abstract: Zika virus (ZIKV) is a mosquito-borne flavivirus transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus, although other species are potential vectors. ZIKV quasispecies may change during mosquito infection, but their dynamics across mosquito species remain poorly understood. We compared ZIKV quasispecies in experimentally infected Ae. aegypti, Ae. albopictus, and the potential vector Ae. japonicus. Viral genomes from pooled samples representing different mosquito body parts and infection periods were analysed by next-generation sequencing, and variant frequencies were evaluated using multivariate analyses. We identified 333 nucleotide variants in the viral open reading frame, including 142 nonsynonymous substitutions. Variant frequency patterns were significantly associated with mosquito species and infection period, whereas no significant associations were detected with body part or viral titre. Subset analyses revealed an association with infection period in Ae. japonicus, but not in the combined Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus dataset, although differences in sampling periods limited interspecies comparisons. Three nonsynonymous substitutions were shared among species: T442I and I446T in the envelope (E) protein near the N444 glycosylation motif, and Q2893K in NS5. T442I and I446T frequencies generally increased during infection in Ae. albopictus and Ae. japonicus, whereas they initially increased but declined at the final sampling point in Ae. aegypti. Q2893K remained relatively stable. T442I and I446T also increased during serial passage in Ae. albopictus-derived C6/36 cells. These recurrent frequency increases are consistent with positive selection, although their functional significance remains undetermined.
authors: Shimooka M, Miki K, Sasaki R, Eshita Y, Orba Y, Sawa H, Muramatsu Y, Uchida L.

title: Functional characterization of MfJAZ1 from Medicago falcata as a negative regulator of cold tolerance in transgenic Arabidopsis.
abstract: Jasmonate ZIM-domain (JAZ) proteins are essential transcriptional repressors in the jasmonic acid (JA) signaling pathway, crucial for coordinating plant growth and stress responses. However, the specific function of MfJAZ1 in regulating cold tolerance in Medicago falcata remains unclear. In this study, MfJAZ1 was cloned from M. falcata cv. Hulunbuir. The encoded protein localizes to the nucleus and its expression is induced by low temperature, drought, salt, alkali, and abscisic acid treatments. Under low temperature treatment, Arabidopsis plants overexpressing (OE) MfJAZ1 exhibited a lower survival rate than the wild-type (WT), accompanied by decreased catalase (CAT) activity and increased malondialdehyde (MDA) content, whereas the atjaz1 mutant showed the opposite trend. Complementation of the atjaz1 with MfJAZ1 largely restored these physiological indices to WT levels. Furthermore, under cold stress, the expression levels of cold-responsive genes were lower in OE plants than in WT, and significantly lower than those in atjaz1. A 933 bp promoter fragment of MfJAZ1, isolated via genome walking, contains cis-elements related to light, hormone, and stress responses. Yeast one-hybrid (Y1H) and Luciferase (LUC) assays suggested a potential association between MfClpP and the MfJAZ1 promoter. Yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) and Bimolecular Fluorescence Complementation (BiFC) assays demonstrated that MfFdC2 interacts with the TIFY domain of MfJAZ1 protein. However, the specific functional significance of the direct transcriptional targets of MfJAZ1 and its interaction with MfFdC2 remains to be determined. Collectively, these results suggest that overexpression of MfJAZ1 negatively regulates the cold tolerance of Arabidopsis by diminishing antioxidant enzyme activity and suppressing the expression of cold-responsive genes. Our findings have laid the foundation for future research on the functional significance of MfClpP-MfJAZ1-MfFdC2 during cold stress.
authors: Chai L, Qian K, Yang H, Liu Y, Chen M, Sun J, Nurbiya M, Zhang P.

title: Genetic susceptibility to anterior cruciate ligament rupture in females: a systematic review of female-stratified candidate-gene evidence and the absence of genome-wide studies.
abstract: ObjectiveTo systematically synthesise and critically appraise genetic association studies reporting female-stratified evidence for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture.DesignSystematic review.Data sourcesWeb of Science, Scopus, Ovid MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 21 December 2025, which was the predefined search date for this review.Eligibility criteria for selecting studiesHuman genetic association studies reporting female-stratified ACL rupture outcomes or extractable female-only data were included. Studies reporting combined-sex analyses without extractable female data were excluded. Due to predefined heterogeneity in phenotypes, populations and genetic models, findings were synthesised narratively.Results19 studies met the inclusion criteria, predominantly small candidate-gene case-control designs. Importantly, these publications did not represent 19 independent cohorts. The largest prospective cohort included 790 women at risk at baseline, of whom 58 sustained an incident ACL injury and 732 remained without incident injury. COL5A1 rs12722 was the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant. Positive single-variant estimates principally concerned CC homozygotes under a recessive model and arose from South African samples with documented participant reuse. Separate allelic associations were also reported. Independence of this signal was limited by probable cohort overlap, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence. Evidence for other collagen, proteoglycan, inflammatory and extracellular matrix remodelling genes was inconsistent. No female-stratified genome-wide association studies were identified.ConclusionsCOL5A1 rs12722 is the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant, but independent replication is not established. Positive recessive estimates concern CC homozygotes and should not be extended to heterozygotes. Small samples, participant reuse, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence limit certainty. Female-stratified associations do not establish sex-specific effects. Evidence derives predominantly from women of European ancestry, and generalisability to other ancestries remains unknown. Current findings do not support genetic screening for ACL rupture risk in female athletes; adequately powered, female-stratified genomic studies with rigorous phenotyping and independent replication across diverse ancestries are needed.
authors: Edmonds CJ, Browne GJ, Khan WS, McDonnell SM.

title: Designing sustainable systems: sustainability assessment of bio-based products and processes
abstract: In this webinar, we will introduce the EU’s Safe and Sustainable by Design (SSbD) framework and its application through NORCE biotechnology case studies, alongside an eco-design framework combining process simulation and evolutionary multi-objective optimization for sustainable decision-making. We will also explore CO₂ emissions from (bio)chemical processes, focusing on wastewater treatment, solvent incineration and energy consumption, as well as bacterial communities in microalgal production systems and their relationship with microalgal strains, growth conditions and scale-up.

title: Nucleotide metabolism and cervical cancer: A comprehensive study of molecular subtypes and therapeutic targets.
abstract: Cervical cancer (CC) is among the most prevalent malignancies in women worldwide. Tumor progression involves profound metabolic reprogramming, in which nucleotide metabolism sustains deoxyribonucleic acid/ribonucleic acid synthesis and proliferation; however, its role in CC remains unclear. Transcriptomic and clinical data of CC patients were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas. Nonnegative matrix factorization classified patients into molecular subtypes based on nucleotide metabolism-related genes and compared their survival, immune infiltration, somatic mutations, and drug sensitivity. Mfuzz soft clustering identified subtype-associated expression patterns. Gene set variation analysis scoring, differential expression analysis, and Gene Ontology/Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment of differentially expressed genes were then performed. Prognostic models were constructed using multiple machine learning algorithms, and the model with the highest concordance index (C-index) was selected. Patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups and assessed using multivariate Cox regression, Kaplan-Meier, and time-dependent receiver operating characteristic analyses. Immune checkpoint inhibitor response was predicted using the tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion algorithm, and molecular docking was performed between core genes and candidate compounds. Nonnegative matrix factorization revealed 5 subtypes with distinct outcomes: cluster 2 showed the worst prognosis, whereas clusters 3 and 4 had favorable survival. TTN, KMT2C, HUWE1, and PIK3CA were frequently mutated across subtypes. B cells, regulatory T cells, CD8+ T cells, and M2 macrophages were enriched in clusters 3 and 4. VX-680, CIL70, and BRD-K01737880 exhibited significantly lower IC50 values in the poor-prognosis group. Seven key genes (SERPINE1, CAV1, SOD2, SLC16A1, XDH, CYP27B1, and NAGS) were identified by Mfuzz clustering. Forty-two differentially expressed genes between the high- and low-score groups were predominantly enriched in xenobiotic response, nutrient sensing, small-molecule catabolism, inflammatory response, tumor necrosis factor signaling, apoptosis, and hypoxia. The generalized boosted regression model achieved the highest C-index, with 1-, 3-, and 5-year area under the curves of 0.62, 0.67, and 0.61, indicating modest discrimination. Tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion analysis indicated reduced immune checkpoint inhibitor responsiveness in the high-risk group. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding between core genes and candidate compounds, providing hypotheses for experimental validation. This study delineates the associations of nucleotide metabolism-related genes with molecular classification and prognosis in CC and identifies potential biomarkers, candidate therapeutic agents, and a prognostic model providing complementary assessment value.
authors: Li F, Bao C, Liu Y, Liu B, Zhai F.

title: Integrated Multi-Omics Profiling of Thymoma Identifies Subtype-Specific Remodeling and Myasthenia Gravis-Associated Targets.
abstract: Thymoma is a rare thymic epithelial tumor strongly associated with myasthenia gravis (MG), yet the tumor intrinsic molecular states underlying this link remain unclear. Here, we profiled paired thymoma and distant nontumorous thymic tissues using untargeted metabolomics, lipidomics, and label-free quantitative proteomics, integrating these layers with MG status, clinicopathologic data, immunohistochemistry, and external transcriptomic validation from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohort. Thymomas exhibited a reproducible metabolic and lipidomic signature characterized by coordinated alterations in amino acid and nucleotide metabolism alongside structured changes in lipid subclasses that support membrane remodeling. Proteomic profiling distinguished tumors from distant nontumorous thymic tissue and identified three exploratory proteomic groups with distinct pathway patterns tightly coupled to lipid metabolic shifts. Integrated analyses identified HMGCS1 and SCP2 as subtype-enriched, lipid-linked hubs and uncovered an MG-associated molecular module comprising creatine, MePC(37:4), ACP5, AP1S1, NECTIN4, and fatty acid pathways. AP1S1 showed an independent association with the overall survival in the TCGA thymoma cohort. A derived 13-lipid panel showed high discrimination in an internal evaluation, supporting its potential as a candidate signature for further validation. This tissue-based multi-omics study systematically maps coordinated molecular remodeling in thymoma, highlighting HMGCS1, SCP2, and AP1S1 as prioritized candidates for future mechanistic and translational research.
authors: Sun Y, Mao J, Sun X, Cao W, Liu J, Zhang G, Xu X, Wang R, Huo W, Zuo J.
