title: Functional convergence of soil fungal communities with biotic homogenization in a biodiversity hotspot
abstract: Abstract    Aims  Soil fungal communities playcritical roles in ecosystem functions. However, soil fungal communities are becoming homogenization under human disturbance although the functional consequences remain poorly understood.  Methods  Here we investigated soil fungal community composition, diversity, and functional guild structure acrossagroecosystems, grasslands, and forests in four isolated valleys of the Mountains of Southwest China, a globally recognized biodiversity hotspot. We characterized the patterns of biotic homogenization and the relative abundance of functional guilds. Community assembly processes were inferred using the iCAMP framework.  Results  Agroecosystems harbored 30.3% higher phylotype richness than grasslands but exhibited significantly lower β-diversity (3.25% and 4.71% lower than grasslands and forests, respectively) and higher biotic homogenization degrees. Agroecosystems hosted more abundant plant pathogens than forests and grasslands (by 361.5% and 354.0%, respectively) and more saprotrophs (by 91.3% and 72.8%), but substantially fewer ectomycorrhizal fungi (93.3% lower than forests). Soil fungal communities in agroecosystems showed the highest importance of homogeneous selection, whereas heterogeneous selection was lowest, consistent with the homogenization pattern. The richness and abundance of plant pathogens and saprotrophs increased whereas those of ectomycorrhizal fungi decreased with biotic homogenization. Bin-level assembly analysis revealed that the assembly processes were associated with functional guilds. Soil total phosphorus, nitrate, and C:P ratio were key environmental drivers of homogenization and functional guild shifts.  Conclusions  These findings demonstrate that agricultural activities drive fungal community convergence through environmental filtering, with cascading effects on functional guilds that may compromise ecosystem multifunctionality and long-term soil health.
authors: Yan B, Sun Y, Li L, He G, Zhang M, Fang H, Shi L.

title: Human parvovirus B19-associated Evans syndrome with fulminant hematologic onset mimicking thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: a case report
abstract: Abstract    Background  Human parvovirus B19 infection rarely presents with severe bicytopenia and multiorgan involvement. Acute presentations with fulminant immune-mediated cytopenia closely mimic severe thrombotic microangiopathies (TMAs) like thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), making early diagnosis highly challenging.  Case presentation  A 65-year-old male was admitted with hematemesis and melena. Suspecting thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or other thrombotic microangiopathies, emergency plasma exchange and continuous renal replacement therapy were immediately initiated. Crucially, pre-treatment samples for ADAMTS13 and metagenomic next-generation sequencing were collected prior to these interventions. Following rapid clinical deterioration requiring endotracheal intubation, intravenous methylprednisolone was initiated. Initial platelet and hemoglobin levels were 3×10⁹/L and 90 g/L, which subsequently plummeted to nadirs of 1×10⁹/L and 46 g/L. Immunohematological tests identified immune-mediated cytopenia: a weakly positive direct antiglobulin test for IgG, positive C3, and spherocytes. ADAMTS13 activity was normal. The pre-treatment metagenomic next-generation sequencing exclusively detected parvovirus B19 (21632 reads), shifting the diagnostic focus to B19-associated Evans syndrome. Following comprehensive therapy, the patient demonstrated a progressive regenerative erythropoietic response. He was successfully extubated, with platelets recovering to 174×10⁹/L and hemoglobin to 86-87 g/L.  Conclusions  Parvovirus B19 should be actively considered in adults presenting with fulminant immune-mediated bicytopenia mimicking TTP. Procuring critical etiological and immunohematological samples prior to plasma exchange is essential to establish an accurate final diagnosis.
authors: Xie Z, Zou X, Zhang L.

title: From Access to Appropriate Use: Reimbursement Design for Pathogen Nucleic Acid Diagnostics across Six Health Systems, 2014–2026
abstract: Abstract  Background  Pathogen nucleic acid diagnostics answer questions that culture, antigen detection and serology cannot answer within the treatment-decision window — slow-growing and fastidious organisms, paucibacillary disease, and genotypic resistance — yet are persistently reimbursed below that value; we ask whether that mismatch is transitional or structural. Methods  We compare six health systems (China, the United States, Germany, France, England, Japan) under a most-different-systems design, tracing three index technology classes defined by target scope — single-pathogen detection with or without a resistance-conferring variant; multi-pathogen targeted detection by multiplex or isothermal amplification or panel enrichment with sequencing; and untargeted metagenomic sequencing of the primary specimen — through a three-gates framework (approval, price assignment, coverage) using primary policy documents, 2014–2026, under confidence-tiered verification. Results  All six systems impose the same three gates, but the binding gate differs: China's price-item gate is being removed by the 2026 national price-item guideline (trial), which standardises item definitions but not price levels, so the binding constraint migrates to insurance listing rather than disappearing; the United States binds at clinical-utility evidence; Germany at coverage. A "double squeeze" of inpatient diagnosis-related-group bundling and outpatient price compression (Medicare's ratcheted PAMA repricing, repeatedly deferred; China's volume-based procurement cuts of 47–77%; Japan's FY2014 256-item fee cut) suppresses adoption of cost-effective tests. Five innovation carve-outs echoing the coverage-with-evidence-development concept underperform for diagnostics: Germany's inpatient innovation channel (NUB) integrated 105 of more than 3,400 methods into regular payment in 2005–2020 (single peer-reviewed source); Medicare's molecular-panel coverage policy excludes metagenomic sequencing from its scope, with no affirmative coverage elsewhere. Regulatory review itself ranges from months (Japan's targets; US 510(k) goals) to multiple years (China's Class III elapsed times; EU notified-body backlogs). For metagenomic sequencing, Gate 1 is a laboratory-accreditation regime rather than product review, and the longest lags sit at the approval–payment interface (median 5.7 years from FDA authorisation to nominal Medicare coverage in a 2016–2019 cohort; diagnostics' lags were shorter). Conclusion  The reimbursement gap is structural and is best explained by the externalisation of diagnostic value across budget silos; closing it requires diagnostic-specific payment design coupled to prescriber competency in test selection.
authors: Shen C, Li D, Chen H.

title: A history of type 2 diabetes results in immune dysregulation and failure to contain a fatal fungal infection
abstract: Abstract    Glucose metabolism enables antimicrobial defences, but it also contributes to pathogen proliferation and immune evasion. A key disease of glucose metabolism, type 2 diabetes (T2D), leads to worse outcomes of  Candida albicans  infections with poorly understood mechanisms. Here we used genetic and dietary animal models of T2D and show that, following bloodstream  C. albicans  infection, T2D animals develop strongly exacerbated disease across several T2D aetiologies. Obesity alone (without overt hyperglycaemia) is sufficient to worsen  C. albicans  disease, but it does not fully recapitulate the severity in T2D hosts that are both obese and overtly hyperglycaemic. Mechanistic analyses showed that a convergence of pathogen and host factors leads to poor outcomes in T2D.  C. albicans  exploits poor host glycaemic control through activation of a transcriptional program for glucose utilisation to drive pathogen proliferation. This, combined with dysregulated immunity characterised by increased pro-inflammatory responses and reduced interferon and NK cell signatures, leads to host failure in restricting fungal growth. We further show that life-long metabolic dysregulation, rather than blood glucose levels at infection, drives poor infection outcomes. Our study illuminates host and pathogen mechanisms leading to worse fungal infection in T2D, provides a rich multi-omics resource for understanding fungal infection in metabolic diseases, and suggests that long-term control of metabolic dysregulation, rather than acute lowering of glucose, is essential for improving survival.
authors: Traven A, Stölting H, Ghoshal A, Weerasinghe H, Wu Y, Rusu P, Multari D, Jeppe K, Barlow C, Schittenhelm R, O’Sullivan K, Mu A, Rose A.

title: Fine Mapping of QTL cqSW.A07 for Thousand-seed Weight in Brassica rapa L.
abstract: Abstract    • Background:  Thousand-seed weight serves as a crucial factor influencing rapeseed yield and has historically been a major focus in breeding initiatives for rapeseed. Thus far, quantitative trait locus analyses concerning thousand-seed weight have predominantly been conducted in  Brassica napus  , with similar investigations in  Brassica rapa  being limited. In this study, precise QTL mapping of the thousand-seed weight trait in  Brassica rapa  was conducted by constructing and analyzing residual heterozygous lines. • Results:  This study utilized reduced-representation genome sequencing on 230 F₂ resulting from a cross between the Brassica rapa varieties Dahuang and Haoyou 11. Using these data, a high-density genetic linkage map was established, measuring a total length of 730.585 cM with an average inter-marker distance of 0.015 cM. A significant QTL, identified as  cqSW.A07  , was located on A07 within a 1.44 Mb interval. To refine the mapping of  cqSW.A07  , linked markers were developed, and residual heterozygous lines were generated, narrowing the region to 115.06 kb. Gene expression analysis indicated that  BraA07g035320.3C  is a probable candidate gene associated with  cqSW.A07  . Sequence analysis of the two alleles revealed 31 amino acid differences. • Conclusions:  In this study, the  cqSW.A07  for thousand-seed weight in  Brassica rapa  was mapped to 115.06 kb, and the annotated gene  BraA07g035320.3C  , which may influence the thousand-seed weight was identified. These results provide a molecular basis for high-yield breeding of  Brassica rapa  .
authors: Zhao H, Zhao Z, Zhao Z, Xu L, Li Y, Zhang Y, Pan Y, Liu H, Du D, Tang G, Xiao L.

title: Genome-Wide Identification of the Potato MAPKKKK Gene Family Reveals StMAPKKKK1 as a Positive Regulator of Salt and Drought Tolerance
abstract: Abstract    Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase kinases (MAP4Ks/MAPKKKKs) reside at the apex of MAPK signalling cascades, yet their roles in potato abiotic stress responses remain unexplored. Here, we identified eight  StMAPKKKK  genes via genome-wide identification in potato. StMAPKKKK1 protein was strongly induced by salt and drought stress and localized to the plasma membrane and cytoplasm. Yeast two-hybrid (Y2H), bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), and split-luciferase complementation (SLC) experiments show that StMAPKKKK1 physically interacts with StMAPKK2. To assess its function, we generated  StMAPKKKK1-  overexpressing (OE) and RNA interference (RNAi) lines in potato cultivar  'Atlantic'  . OE lines exhibited improved growth, with higher plant height, biomass, and leaf number, whereas RNAi lines were more sensitive than non-transgenic (NT) controls under both salt and drought stress conditions. Higher activities of ascorbate peroxidase (APX), catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and peroxidase (POD), as well as proline and total chlorophyll contents, along with lower levels of hydrogen peroxide (H  2  O  2  ) and malondialdehyde (MDA) were observed in OE lines. In contrast, RNAi lines showed opposite trends for all above-mentioned parameters. These results indicate alleviated oxidative damage, enhanced osmotic adjustment, and better pigment retention. This study presents the first functional characterization of the  StMAPKKKK  family in potato and establishes  StMAPKKKK1  as a positive regulator of salt and drought tolerance, acting at least partially through interaction with StMAPKK2 and activation of the antioxidant defense system.
authors: zhu X.

title: B-cell activation markers and cancer risk in people with HIV: An integrative case-control and Mendelian randomization analysis.
abstract: Early and continuous antiretroviral therapy (ART) reduces cancer risk in people with HIV (PWH), yet residual risk potentially driven by persistent B-cell activation remains. We used observational and genetic triangulation to evaluate whether baseline B-cell biomarkers are associated with subsequent cancer risk. We conducted: (i) a nested case-control study within the INSIGHT trials (158 cases and 313 matched controls) assessing B-cell biomarkers (sCD23, sCD27, sCD30, CXCL13) in PWH; and (ii) two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) to evaluate likely causal relationships between these proteins and 23 cancer types using general-population genome-wide association studies. Median time from study entry to cancer diagnosis was 2.9 years. In PWH, CXCL13 was associated with overall cancer risk (highest tertile vs. lowest tertile OR 2.36, 95% CI 1.24-4.5), driven by infection-related cancers (N = 82; OR 4.81, 1.76-13.1) and lymphoma (N = 36; OR 9.92, 1.58-62.2). The CXCL13 association remained robust among virally suppressed participants (P = 0.018). sCD30 was also associated with infection-related cancers (OR 2.77, 1.09-7.03). sCD23 showed a linear association with infection-related cancer (OR per SD 1.42, 1.01-2.00), though tertile-based analyses were non-significant. In the general population, MR meta-analyses showed null associations for these biomarkers across 23 cancer types (P > 0.05). Our study links B-cell markers with cancer risk in PWH, identifying CXCL13 as a marker of infection-related cancer risk despite effective ART, highlighting a "residual inflammatory gap" for modern risk stratification. The lack of causal MR signals suggests these proteins are markers of HIV-associated immune activation rather than universal etiological factors for cancer.

title: S-nitrosoglutathione reductase deficiency is associated with altered recovery from repeated climate stress across generations in Arabidopsis thaliana.
abstract: Climate change exposes plants to recurrent and interacting stresses, yet the extent to which these effects persist across generations, and the mechanisms involved, remain unclear. Here, we compared Arabidopsis thaliana wild type (WT, Col-0) plants with gsnor1-3 (hereafter, gsnor-ko), a mutant deficient in S-nitrosoglutathione reductase (GSNOR), an enzyme involved in nitric oxide homeostasis. Plants were propagated for three successive generations (G1-G3) under control, drought, elevated CO2, O3, heat (warm temperature), and combined treatment scenarios, followed by two recovery generations under control conditions (G4-G5). We quantified rosette growth, photosynthetic traits, seed production, and transcriptome dynamics by RNA-seq. Across environments, gsnor-ko exhibited reduced vegetative growth and reproductive output compared with WT. Transcriptomic responses were strongly scenario- and generation-dependent, with the largest differential expression shifts observed under heat and combined-treatment (combination) conditions. Compared with WT, gsnor-ko showed greater transcriptome similarity across generations and among genes differentially expressed in response to the same treatment. Functional enrichment and candidate-gene analyses identified pathways/components linked to DNA methylation, heterochromatin maintenance, histone ubiquitination, m6A RNA regulation, and methyl-donor metabolism. Together, these findings are consistent with a model in which GSNOR activity contributes to transcriptomic recovery after repeated climate stress, whereas GSNOR deficiency is associated with recurrent or reconfigured stress-associated transcriptional states at G1, G3, and G5, suggesting epigenetically associated regulatory reconfiguration.

title: L-Threonine production from acetate by metabolically engineered Corynebacterium glutamicum using a pH-controlled fed-batch process.
abstract: Acetate has a considerable potential as a non-food feedstock for microbial bioproduction, yet its use for amino acid production remains underexplored. Here, we developed a process for L-threonine production from acetate as the sole carbon source with Corynebacterium glutamicum by integrating rational, genome-based metabolic engineering with pH-coupled fed-batch cultivation. The engineered strain AT-3 carried five chromosomal mutations that alleviated feedback inhibition of key enzymes and redirected carbon flux toward the aspartate pathway. Substrate supply was controlled using a custom Visual Basic-based feeding script that automatically adjusted the acetic acid feed in response to online pH measurements. Robust process performance was maintained during a tenfold scale-up from 100-mL DASbox to 1-L DASGIP bioreactors. The optimized process achieved an L-threonine titer of 10.04 g/L and a yield of 0.086 g/g acetate. This study provides a basis for further studies on the development and improvement of acetate-based amino acid production process. KEY POINTS: • Plasmid-free C. glutamicum strains produce L-threonine in acetate minimal medium • pH-controlled acetic acid feed in bioreactors improved L-threonine production • Acetate-based production of feed amino acids avoids competition with human food.
authors: Broschard P, Endt N, Wirtz A, Glitz C, Baumgart M, Bott M.

title: OsPIL1 modulates growth-yield-blast resistance trade-offs involving OsINV3 and jasmonate signaling.
abstract: Phytochrome-interacting factor-like proteins coordinate plant growth and defense, but the influence of genetic background on their functions in rice remains unclear. We characterized OsPIL1 in japonica cv. Lijiangxintuanheigu (LTH) and examined its association with OsINV3 in LTH and indica cv. Acuce. Although the cultivars shared identical OsPIL1 coding sequences, OsPIL1 overexpression restricted growth, reduced yield-related traits, and increased blast susceptibility in LTH, contrasting with previously reported effects in Acuce. In uninoculated LTH plants, overexpression increased peroxidase activity and several defense-related transcripts but reduced reactive oxygen species and jasmonate accumulation. Following Magnaporthe oryzae inoculation, OsPIL1 knockout lines showed enhanced resistance, lower fungal biomass, and elevated defense outputs. Exogenous jasmonate alleviated symptoms in wild-type, knockout, and overexpression plants, indicating that this protection did not strictly require functional OsPIL1. Transcriptome profiling linked OsPIL1 perturbation to photosynthesis, phenylpropanoid metabolism, and defense signaling. OsPIL1 overexpression was associated with reduced OsINV3 expression in stems of both cultivars, whereas leaf responses depended on cultivar and developmental stage. Combined loss of OsPIL1 and OsINV3 enhanced resistance in LTH but reduced resistance in Acuce, accompanied by differences in downstream gene expression. These findings establish contrasting phenotypic outcomes of OsPIL1-associated networks in two rice backgrounds and identify candidate relationships for investigating growth and defense coordination.
authors: He P, Chen X, Chao Z, Yang S, Deng J, Yang J.

title: Molecular Profiling and Precision Oncology for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer in Latin America: Unique Epidemiology, Persistent Barriers, and Paths Toward Equity.
abstract: AbstractNon-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) represents a critical public health crisis in Latin America (LA), the leading cause of cancer-associated mortality across the region. Although global incidence rates are shifting, the burden in low- and middle-income countries is projected to increase significantly by 2030. Beyond the impact of tobacco, LA faces unique challenges derived from environmental exposures and diverse genetic ancestry that shape a molecular landscape distinct from other regions. This has resulted in a high prevalence of actionable drivers, particularly EGFR mutations, positioning a large segment of the population as ideal candidates for precision medicine approaches. However, current efforts to address this epidemic fall short of regional needs, as the potential of precision oncology remains largely unrealized due to multilevel systemic and economic barriers. Despite the scientific potential of targeted therapies to drastically improve survival, LA has not broadly or expeditiously adopted these strategies. A profound implementation gap is characterized by a reliance on inefficient single-gene testing, fragmented regulatory frameworks, and severe infrastructural limitations. Consequently, only a minimal proportion of the regional patient population benefits from recent advances, whereas the majority continue to receive empirical chemotherapy with significantly inferior survival outcomes. Addressing these disparities requires a steadfast focus on systemic transformation, ranging from establishing centralized genomic hubs to implementing structured educational programs. Standardizing care through molecular tumor boards (MTBs) and harmonizing regulatory pathways are essential steps in translating research into clinical benefits. In this review, we discuss the unique molecular epidemiology of the region and the challenges of treatment implementation, focusing on the urgent need to integrate new technologies to ensure equitable access to precision oncology. LA has one of the highest potential population-level benefits from precision oncology in NSCLC; however, systemic barriers prevent this molecular opportunity from translating into equitable survival gains (Graphical abstract).Graphical abstract
journal: Journal of immunotherapy and precision oncology
authors: Picón CR, Borea R, Rizzo MM, Minatta JN, Amorin RI, Pandolfi JB, Cardona AF, Arrieta O, Enrico D, Voza A, Denninghoff V, Rolfo C.

title: Computational tools for biomarker identification in inborn errors of metabolism: A rapid systematic review.
abstract: Inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs) are a heterogeneous group of rare genetic diseases characterized by enzymatic, transporter, or cofactor deficiencies that disrupt metabolic homeostasis. Biomarker identification is central to their diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic monitoring, but phenotypic heterogeneity and limited patient cohorts pose persistent challenges. Computational tools, including genome-scale metabolic modeling, systems biology, and quantitative systems pharmacology, are emerging and aiming to address these limitations. This work aimed to identify, characterize, and synthesize the available evidence on computational tools for predicting or identifying metabolic biomarkers in individuals diagnosed with IEMs. A rapid systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed and EMBASE for studies published within the last ten years in English or Spanish. Eligible studies applied computational methodologies, such as in silico modeling, constraint-based modeling, machine learning, or metabolic network analysis, for biomarker discovery, prediction, or validation in IEMs. Three reviewers performed selection independently, resolving discrepancies by consensus. Of 955 records identified, 13 studies met the eligibility criteria. They were classified into four categories: machine learning and artificial intelligence approaches for predictive modeling and risk stratification; genome-scale and constraint-based modeling to simulate enzymatic deficiencies and identify candidate biomarkers; systems biology and network-based modeling for pathway-level signatures and diagnostic visualization; and quantitative systems pharmacology frameworks to model therapeutic response and biomarker trajectories. When combined with conventional methods, computational tools may improve the mechanistic interpretability, scalability, and multi-omics integration during biomarker identification for EIMs. However, most approaches remain exploratory, and prospective clinical validation is limited. Future efforts should prioritize hybrid modeling, standardized reporting, and clinical integration.
authors: Saldaña DA, Echeverri-Peña OY, Alméciga-Díaz CJ.

title: Small molecules targeting SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid reveal a conserved RNA-binding vulnerability across human coronaviruses.
abstract: SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 exemplify the persistent threat posed by coronaviruses, with their capacity for zoonotic spill over, rapid transmission, and severe disease resulting in substantial morbidity, mortality, and socio-economic burden. The repeated emergence of highly pathogenic coronaviruses highlights the urgent need for broad-spectrum therapeutic strategies. The nucleocapsid (N) protein, essential for RNA binding, genome packaging, and viral replication, remains a highly conserved yet underexplored antiviral target. Sequence alignment revealed 90% identity between SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV N proteins, and 48.1% identity between SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV N proteins. In our earlier work, we identified two small molecules, ceftazidime and sennoside A, that bind the N-terminal domain of the SARS-CoV-2 N protein and inhibit nucleic acid binding, and identified their binding sites using NMR chemical shift perturbation assays. Here, we observed that several residues involved in inhibitor binding are conserved across betacoronaviruses, suggesting a shared druggable vulnerability. We have purified recombinant N proteins from SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2, and demonstrated by electrophoretic mobility shift assays that both compounds significantly reduced RNA binding. Their inhibitory concentrations (IC50) were determined using fluorescence polarization. The docking analyses indicated that both inhibitors target the RNA-binding pocket of the N-NTD, consistent with a conserved mechanism of action. Collectively, our findings reveal a conserved RNA-binding vulnerability in coronavirus N proteins and highlights the pan-coronavirus therapeutic potential of these inhibitors.
authors: Singh S, Gupta GD.

title: Acute nicotine exposure produces a spatially organized transcriptional response in mouse olfactory cortex
abstract: Nicotine acts on nicotinic receptors throughout the forebrain. Most molecular studies of its effects, however, have focused on reward circuitry and have used bulk tissue, which cannot show which cells respond or how responding cells are arranged relative to one another. We previously found that a single nicotine exposure activates hippocampal astrocytes through the astrocyte-expressed kinase AKT2. Here we asked which cells respond to nicotine in the anterior olfactory cortex, a cholinergic-modulated region that encodes odor associations, and whether their astrocytic surroundings change. Male mice received a single intraperitoneal injection of nicotine or saline, and coronal sections spanning the anterior olfactory nucleus, piriform cortex and adjacent isocortex were sequencing 24 h later using Visium HD. Differential expression on nucleus-based segmentation was concentrated in olfactory excitatory neurons. Pathways centered on calcium-handling, synapse-assembly and extracellular-matrix programs, together with a lasting reduction of the immediate-early gene Egr1. Within the piriform region, the response localized to a continuous population of superficial pyramidal neurons expressing Cartpt and Penk. These neurons upregulated synapse-assembly, receptor-regulation and proteoglycan programs without changes to cell-type proportions. Nicotine also reduced expression of Sparcl1, which encodes astrocyte-secreted synaptogenic protein hevin, within one cell diameter of these neurons. Our study shows that a single nicotine exposure leaves a spatially organized transcriptional program on olfactory circuitry, centered on one neuronal population and the tissue at its border. These results identify candidate cells, genes and tissue locations for testing how nicotine alters sensory cue circuits.
authors: Griffioen MK, Lombardi A, Milstead R, Borski C, Zou S, Stitzel J, Ehringer MA, Hoeffer CA.

title: In Silico Drug Repurposing: Integrating Network Pharmacology and Structure-Based Virtual Screening to Accelerate Preclinical Drug Development
abstract: De novo drug discovery requires over a decade of research and $1.5 billion to $2.5 billion in investment per approved molecule, yet more than 90% of candidates fail during clinical trials due to unforeseen toxicity or poor efficacy. In silico drug repurposing offers a faster, cost-effective alternative by finding new therapeutic uses for regulatory-approved or clinical-stage molecules. However, individual computational methods have clear blind spots. Network biology identifies disease-related genes but lacks atomic-level detail on how a drug physically binds to a receptor. Conversely, standalone molecular docking often produces false-positive hits and relies on an outdated single-target mindset. This review provides a practical blueprint for combining network pharmacology with structure-based virtual screening (SBVS) in preclinical drug repurposing. We first outline how disease genomics databases (DisGeNET, GeneCards) and protein–protein interaction (PPI) networks (STRING) pair with graph-theory tools in Cytoscape (cytoHubba, MCODE) to pinpoint central hub proteins. Next, we detail how to screen curated chemical libraries (DrugBank, ChEMBL) against these prioritized targets using AutoDock Vina and AlphaFold structures. We also explain why approved drugs still require indication-specific pharmacokinetic checks in SwissADME and ADMETlab 3.0, followed by 100–500 ns explicit-solvent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations in GROMACS and MM-PBSA/GBSA free-energy rescoring. Finally, we review recent preclinical applications across infectious, neurological, and oncological diseases and discuss how deep-learning tools like DiffDock and AlphaFold 3 are reshaping virtual screening.
authors: Nayem AA, Tarikul Islam Tusher S, Deb S.

title: Anti-PBP2a Vaccines and Immunotherapies Against Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus: Current Evidence, Challenges, and Perspectives
abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major antimicrobial-resistant pathogen worldwide and a high-priority target for new therapeutic strategies. Methicillin resistance is primarily mediated by the mecA gene, which encodes penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2a), a transpeptidase with reduced affinity for β-lactam antibiotics. Because PBP2a plays a key role in bacterial survival under β-lactam pressure, highly specific to Methicillin-resistant Staphylococci, and immunologically recognizable, it represents an attractive target for immunotherapeutic approaches. This review summarizes current knowledge of PBP2a structure, biological function, and immunological relevance, focusing on vaccine and antibody-based strategies. Studies employing DNA vaccines, recombinant proteins, multi-epitope constructs, and passive immunization have demonstrated protective immune responses and reduced bacterial burden in animal models of MRSA infection. Monoclonal antibodies targeting PBP2a have also shown prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy, including activity independent of Fc-mediated effector functions, suggesting direct interference with PBP2a function. Their potential use in rapid immunodiagnostic assays for methicillin resistance is also discussed. Emerging strategies, including antibody engineering, glycoengineering, antibody-drug conjugates, mucosal vaccination, and combination therapies with antibiotics, may further enhance clinical applicability. Although evidence remains preclinical, PBP2a represents a promising target for active and passive immunization against Methicillin-resistant staphylococci.
authors: Senna JP, Boechat JPC.

title: Activity of aztreonam-avibactam and comparators against difficult-to-treat resistant Enterobacterales from United States medical centres (2020-24) <sup>†</sup>.
abstract: BackgroundThe occurrence of infections caused by Gram-negative bacteria with difficult-to-treat resistance (DTR) is rapidly increasing, generally requiring the use of recently approved, last-resort antimicrobial agents or old compounds that are more toxic and/or less effective. We evaluated the activity of aztreonam-avibactam and comparators against DTR Enterobacterales.MethodsA total of 42 295 Enterobacterales isolates were consecutively collected (one per patient) from 85 US medical centres in 2020-24 and susceptibility tested by Clinical Laboratory Standards Institute broth microdilution. The collection included 450 carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) and 284 DTR isolates, which were screened for β-lactamases by whole genome sequencing.ResultsAztreonam-avibactam was active against 98.2% of DTR (minimum inhibitory concentration for 50%/90% of the collection, 0.25/1 mg/L) and 97.1% of CRE isolates and retained potent activity (≥90.0% susceptibility) against DTR isolates non-susceptible to ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam and/or cefiderocol. Cefiderocol was active against 92.8% of DTR isolates, whereas ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam and the aminoglycosides exhibited limited activity against these organisms. Aztreonam-avibactam and cefiderocol were active against 97.8% and 84.4% of DTR metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) producers, respectively. The most common carbapenemase genes identified among DTR isolates were bla KPC (57.7% of isolates) and bla NDM (29.9%). An MBL gene was observed in 31.7% of DTR and 25.1% of CRE isolates.ConclusionsAztreonam-avibactam retained potent activity against DTR Enterobacterales from US medical centres, and its activity was not adversely affected by clinically relevant carbapenemases or resistance to agents used to treat multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales. The activities of other β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations and cefiderocol were compromised by the increased occurrence of MBL producers.
authors: Sader HS, Kimbrough JH, Debabov D, Papp-Wallace KM, Castanheira M.

title: Whitefly hijacks host NtWRKY6 to activate NtRGL2 and suppress gibberellin signaling.
abstract: BackgroundPiercing-sucking insects severely impair crop productivity by suppressing the growth of host plants. Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) infestation induces a pronounced dwarf phenotype associated with reduced gibberellin (GA) signaling; however, the underlying molecular mechanism remains largely unknown. Here, we investigated the role of the hormone-responsive transcription factor, NtWRKY6, in mediating whitefly-induced inhibition of host growth.ResultsSilencing of NtWRKY6 significantly restored bioactive GA₃ accumulation and alleviated whitefly-induced growth inhibition, whereas NtWRKY6 overexpression further aggravated GA deficiency and dwarfism. Using DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq) as a discovery screen, together with yeast one-hybrid and dual-luciferase assays, we identified NtRGL2, a DELLA-encoding negative regulator of GA signaling, as a direct transcriptional target of NtWRKY6. Intensive whitefly feeding induced NtRGL2 expression in wild-type plants, but this induction was largely abolished in NtWRKY6-silenced plants, demonstrating that NtWRKY6 is required for the whitefly-mediated activation of NtRGL2. Furthermore, silencing NtRGL2 substantially mitigated the inhibitory effects of whitefly infestation on GA₃ accumulation and plant growth, confirming its critical role downstream of NtWRKY6.ConclusionOur findings reveal a previously unrecognized regulatory module in which whitefly infestation exploits the host transcription factor NtWRKY6 to promote NtRGL2 expression, a change consistent with enhanced DELLA-associated repression of GA signaling and suppression of host growth. This study reveals a molecular mechanism by which a piercing-sucking insect modulates host phytohormone homeostasis to alter plant development, providing new insights into plant-insect interactions and potential targets for sustainable pest management. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: Ren J, Yang Y, Liu X, Wu J, Zhao S, Shi J, Dai M, Liu Y, Li M, Guo L, Li Q, Sun X, Li Y, Zhao H.

title: Fragment-based hit-to-lead optimization and preliminary mechanistic investigation of fungicidal thioester derivatives.
abstract: BackgroundPlant pathogenic fungi cause substantial crop yield losses worldwide, and chemical fungicides remain indispensable for maintaining crop productivity and food security. However, the widespread use of fungicides with similar chemical structures and modes of action has accelerated the development of cross-resistance, highlighting the urgent need for novel fungicidal scaffolds.ResultsA total of 48 thioester derivatives were designed and synthesized. Among them, compound B22 exhibited the highest antifungal activity against Rhizoctonia solani, with a half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) value of 0.124 μg mL-1, showing approximately tenfold greater potency than fenfuram (EC50 = 1.480 μg mL-1), although it was less active than fluxapyroxad (EC50 = 0.041 μg mL-1). At 100 μg mL-1, compound B22 also showed 79.2% protective control against rice sheath blight under greenhouse conditions. Scanning electron microscopy revealed pronounced morphological abnormalities in R. solani hyphae following B22 treatment. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses indicated substantial perturbations in energy metabolism-related processes, while a preliminary biochemical assay showed that B22 inhibited porcine heart succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) activity. Molecular docking further suggested that B22 could be accommodated in the SDH-binding pocket through hydrogen-bonding and cation-π interactions.ConclusionBioactivity screening and antifungal mechanism studies suggested the potential of thioester derivatives as promising candidates for the development of novel fungicidal agents. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: Cheng L, Hu S, Wu B, Wang C, Jiang Q, Zhou C, Cheng J.

title: Regulation of the 22-nt antiviral silencing pathway in tomato by two RNA viruses.
abstract: RNA silencing plays a central role in plant antiviral defence, in which viral RNA is processed into small RNAs (sRNAs) that guide Argonaute-mediated cleavage of viral transcripts. Among these, 22-nucleotide (nt) sRNAs are unique in their ability to trigger secondary sRNA production, thereby amplifying transitive silencing. In tomato, this 22-nt antiviral pathway is strongly activated upon virus infection through the upregulation of DCL2b, yet the underlying mechanism has remained unclear. miR6026, generated by DCL2b and targeting DCL2b itself, forms a feedback loop that fine-tunes this response. Here we show that tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) and tomato bushy stunt virus (TBSV) activate DCL2b transcription via the Dof16 transcription factor. Transcription of MIR6026 is also activated by both TMV and TBSV, while viral infection promotes DCL2b relocalization towards the cytoplasm, preventing pri-miR6026 processing into mature miR6026. This redistribution is associated with reduced phosphorylation of DCL2b at Tyr69, which weakens its interaction with importin-α and limits its nuclear localization. Notably, Arabidopsis DCL2 exhibits a similar virus-induced relocalization pattern, highlighting a conserved mechanism that enhances antiviral silencing during infection while minimizing off-target effects on host genes under normal conditions.
authors: Li J, Li Q, Yang Q, Zheng Y, Li H, Yang L, Yu Z, Zhang R, Wei N, Li F, Wang Z.

title: Expanding the Clinical and Molecular Spectrum of Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis Associated With Biallelic Variants in LSR.
abstract: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC) comprises autosomal recessive disorders causing early-onset cholestasis that may progress to cirrhosis and liver failure. Although more than 13 genes are associated with PFIC, some patients remain genetically undiagnosed. LSR, encoding lipolysis-stimulated lipoprotein receptor, has recently emerged as a candidate gene. LSR contributes to tricellular tight-junction integrity and epithelial barrier function. We report four additional patients from three unrelated families with biallelic LSR variants, expanding the reported clinical and molecular spectrum. Features included intractable pruritus, cholestasis with normal or mildly elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), progressive hepatic dysfunction and variable extrahepatic findings, including growth failure, neurodevelopmental delay, seizures and microcephaly. Two patients died from end-stage liver disease. Review of published cases suggests a predominantly progressive cholestatic phenotype with variable syndromic features. These findings support consideration of LSR variants in unresolved PFIC and the value of comprehensive genomic testing.
authors: Kafley P, Dhakad A, Sarma MS, Kar A, Ammu Omana V, Nigam N, Mishra R, Srivastava A, Dalal A, Vaikom Hariharan S, Moirangthem A.

title: Hypoxia orchestrates the natural history of inflammatory bowel disease: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) arises from a dynamic interplay between epithelial dysfunction, immune activation, microbial dysbiosis and tissue remodelling. Although hypoxia was initially regarded as a consequence of intestinal inflammation, it is now recognized as an active regulator of epithelial, immune and stromal responses that coordinate disease progression. Here, we propose that hypoxia acts as a biological organizer linking oxygen sensing to the transition from intestinal homeostasis to chronic inflammation and structural tissue damage. We use this term in a mechanistic rather than a hierarchical sense: oxygen availability is a shared upstream constraint on epithelial, immune, microbial and stromal programmes, not a single initiating event. This review integrates evidence connecting oxygen sensing with epithelial barrier integrity, immunometabolism, microbial ecology and stromal remodelling, with emphasis on advances in single-cell transcriptomics, spatial biology and microbiome research. Physiological low-oxygen gradients support epithelial metabolism, barrier integrity and immune tolerance, whereas persistent inflammatory hypoxia drives oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming and maladaptive epithelial-immune-microbial interactions. Hypoxia also contributes to spatially distinct epithelial, immune and stromal niches that may sustain chronic inflammation and fibrotic progression. Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids and succinate, together with iron metabolism and ferroptosis, further link oxygen sensing to tissue injury, adaptation and repair. These findings position hypoxia-responsive signalling as a pharmacologically actionable network rather than a downstream consequence of inflammation. Targeting selected components may promote mucosal healing and limit structural disease progression, although successful translation will require cell- and isoform-selective modulation, adequate tissue exposure and careful assessment of long-term safety.
authors: Luque MVS, Moreno ASA, Angarita-Planchez ME, Múnera-Rodríguez AM, López-Enríquez S, Casado-Jurado D, de Miguel M, Palomares F.

title: Self-assembled carboxymethyl cellulose/graphene oxide and chitosan ultra-high oxygen barrier layer on bio-based flexible films for lamb non-contact preservation.
abstract: A high-performance natural nanocomposite coating was developed to enhance the barrier properties of bio-based films for meat packaging. The flexible substrate consisted of a bio-based PLLA and graphene oxide (GO)-grafted poly(butylene itaconate) (GO-g-PLBI) copolymer. A high-barrier coating was assembled on this substrate via layer-by-layer (LbL) self-assembly of chitosan (CS) and a carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC)/GO composite. This approach enhanced the dispersion of GO, the mechanical strength, antibacterial activity, UV shielding and oxygen (O2) barrier properties of the film. Additionally, the CMC/GO composite exhibited a stronger hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions with CS. Consequently, the film exhibited higher CS and CMC/GO loadings along with superior water resistance. Notably, alternating the deposition of CS and CMC/GO composite for 9 bilayers led to a dramatic decrease in the O2 transmission rate from 41.9 to 0.05 cm3 m-2·d-1, while maintaining considerable translucency. In the non-contact packaging of chilled lamb, the film's outstanding O2 barrier facilitated the rapid formation of a low-O2, high-CO2 headspace, which was driven by the synergistic effects of meat tissue oxidation and microbial metabolism. Hence, this film achieved better preservation performance for fresh lamb when compared with conventional PA/PE film, as evidenced by improved microbiological quality, physicochemical properties, and texture.
authors: Zhang J, Dong T, Liu H, Zhang Y, Wu Y, Guo J, Li Y, Yun X.

title: Identification and functional characterization of cGAS, STING and MAVSL in amphioxus Branchiostoma japonicum.
abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon (IFN) genes (STING) pathway is an evolutionarily conserved nucleic acid-sensing mechanism in animals, but the identities and signaling relationships of its components in cephalochordates remain incompletely understood. Here, candidate cGAS, STING and mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein-like (MAVSL) homologs were identified in Branchiostoma japonicum. The full-length cDNAs encode proteins of 658, 267 and 546 amino acids, respectively. Sequence analyses identified an N-terminal AT-hook-containing region and a C-terminal Mab21/NTase domain in the candidate cGAS protein, a predicted TMEM173/cyclic dinucleotide-binding domain in the candidate STING protein, and a caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD)-containing candidate MAVSL protein in which a C-terminal transmembrane domain was not detected. Transcripts of all three genes were detected in multiple tissues, with the highest levels in the notochord. After exposure to LPS, poly(I:C), or poly(dA:dT), transcript levels changed transiently. In HEK293T cells, the candidate proteins localized to the cytoplasm, and fluorescent signals for cGAS or STING overlapped with those of MAVSL. Overexpression experiments showed higher IFNα, IRF1, Mx1, Viperin and ISG15 transcript levels after co-expression with candidate MAVSL than after expression of the individual proteins in HEK293T cells. These results provide molecular and heterologous expression evidence for cGAS, STING and MAVSL components in amphioxus.
authors: Deng Y, Du Y, Yuan J, Liu R, Chen J, Fan B, Li X, Li B, Nie P, Song X.

title: PRKN-independent mitophagy regulators in dopaminergic neurons identified by genome-wide CRISPR screening.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the development of PD. PRKN/Parkin is known to play an essential role in mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy. Indeed, mutations and inactivation of this gene are associated with hereditary and idiopathic forms of PD. Despite extensive studies on PRKN-dependent mitophagy, the molecular regulators of PRKN-independent mitophagy in dopaminergic neurons remain incompletely understood. We generated a PRKN knockout iPSC-derived dopaminergic neuronal line expressing the fluorescent mitophagy biosensor mito-SRAI, which reports the delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes as an increase in the TOLLES/YPet fluorescence ratio. We used this cell line to conduct a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen to reveal genetic regulators involved in PRKN-independent mitophagy. Dozens of genes were identified whose knockout increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in an uncoupler-dependent manner. Of these, several genes emerged as candidates with potential therapeutic implications, one of which was Cathepsin F (CTSF). CCCP treatment increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in neurons with siRNA-mediated CTSF knockdown, and CTSF knockdown partially preserved the proportion of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons after paraquat exposure. These results suggest that CTSF is a candidate regulator of PRKN-independent mitophagy and that this lysosomal enzyme may represent a potentially druggable candidate target for PD.
authors: Nishimura T, Kunisada Y, Li HL, Highfill CA, Nagasawa K, Tsujihata Y.

title: Rules of the road for loop-extruding motors: loading, unloading, and crowding.
abstract: Loop extrusion by structural maintenance of chromosome (SMC) complexes has emerged as a key mechanism of genome organization across domains of life, yet the rules that govern where these motors load, unload, and become enriched remain poorly understood. The canonical model treats cohesin as loading and unloading uniformly but stopping at extrusion barriers. Chromosome architecture is then shaped by where extruding complexes stop. Accumulating evidence broadens this view by uncovering cases of (i) targeted SMC loading across metazoa, plants, and fungi, (ii) sites of specific SMC release, and (iii) domains of crowded loop extrusion. Together, these new Rules of the Road shift the focus from where extruders stop to where they start, end, and dwell-with implications for development, gene regulation, and genome stability.
authors: Mirny LA, Zhegalova I, Galitsyna A.

title: A single-residue deletion in H9N2 hemagglutinin uncouples viral burden from disease severity.
abstract: H9N2 avian influenza viruses are characterized by significant genetic diversity. Deletions within the hemagglutinin (HA) receptor-binding domain represent a notable, albeit rare, evolutionary trajectory. Here, we systematically characterized the multifaceted impact of a single-amino-acid deletion at residue 227 of HA (designated HAΔ227), a naturally occurring deletion within the 220-loop that overlaps a key antigenic epitope, using isogenic reverse genetics H9N2 viruses. Paradoxically, the HAΔ227 imposed a fitness cost and was associated with enhanced HA receptor-binding avidity, reduced apparent virion-associated NA activity, altered HA/NA functional balance, attenuated viral replication in vitro, and reduced respiratory shedding in vivo. Notably, despite this compromised replicative fitness, infection with the mutant virus was associated with an altered host immune response in chickens, characterized by elevated levels of interferon-γ (IFN-γ), interleukin-10 (IL-10), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1). These altered immune responses were associated with more severe pulmonary lesions, indicating a dissociation between disease severity and viral RNA load. Furthermore, the deletion increased the pH threshold for HA-mediated membrane fusion and substantially altered antigenic relationships. Collectively, our findings identify HA residue 227 as a functionally important site at which a single-residue deletion is associated with a phenotypic trade-off between replicative capacity and disease severity: reduced replicative fitness accompanied by altered inflammatory responses and greater tissue injury. This study highlights the potential phenotypic significance of a rare deletion in influenza virus HA and demonstrates that viral burden alone may not adequately predict disease severity.
authors: Sun Y, Zhu Y, Zhang P, Sheng S, Gai L, Li S, Zhang F, Cao P, He A, Wang W, Li X, Cong Y.

title: Domain Swapping Reveals Direction-Dependent Compatibility of Fungal Polyketide Synthase-Nonribosomal Peptide Synthetase Off-Loading Domains.
abstract: Two fungal natural products, hirsutellone and didymellamide, are proposed to be biosynthesized from closely related β-ketoamide intermediates despite producing structurally distinct cyclic products. This unusual biosynthetic relationship raises the question of whether the corresponding polyketide synthase-nonribosomal peptide synthetase (PKS-NRPS) off-loading domains are functionally interchangeable. Here, we identified and characterized HirA, a PKS-NRPS involved in hirsutellone biosynthesis, and used it together with AsolS, a PKS-NRPS involved in didymellamide biosynthesis, as a model system to investigate the compatibility of fungal PKS-NRPS off-loading domains. Heterologous expression in Aspergillus oryzae established that HirA produces a β-ketoamide intermediate possessing a nonaketide polyketide chain closely related to that generated by AsolS. Reciprocal domain swapping revealed asymmetric compatibility: artificial fusion of the HirA-derived reductase domain to the AsolS assembly line supported productive processing of the AsolS-derived intermediate, whereas reciprocal fusion of the Dieckmann cyclase domain yielded the C18-derived product at a low level but did not produce the expected tetramic acid derivative. These results demonstrate that off-loading activity can be retained following domain swapping between distinct fungal PKS-NRPS systems, but the extent of productive processing is strongly direction-dependent. Taken together, our findings identify direction-dependent compatibility and fusion-site dependence as important constraints for engineering fungal PKS-NRPS off-loading domains.
authors: Sato S, Ugai T, Yamane M, Liu X, Oikawa H, Minami A.

title: Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses prioritize candidate genes associated with lysosomes and ferroptosis in rheumatoid arthritis synovium.
abstract: ObjectivesTo prioritize candidate genes associated with lysosome-related and ferroptosis-related annotations in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) synovium and characterize their expression across synovial cell populations.MethodsPublicly available bulk and single-cell transcriptomic data from patients with RA and osteoarthritis (OA) were integrated with curated lysosome-related genes (LRGs) and ferroptosis-related genes (FRGs). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) shared by both gene sets were identified. Gene-set expression scoring and high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA) were used to characterize cellular expression patterns and prioritize candidate genes. Candidate-gene expression was assessed in external datasets and by exploratory quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR).ResultsMyeloid cells and fibroblast-like synoviocyte (FLS) populations showed relatively high expression scores for the shared gene set. Intersection analysis of the shared DEGs and selected co-expression module genes identified four candidates: VAMP2, HRAS, GRN, and BGN. External datasets supported lower VAMP2 expression in RA than in OA. Exploratory qRT-PCR analysis of synovial samples from four patients with RA and four patients with OA showed a consistent expression difference.ConclusionIntegrated transcriptomic analyses prioritized VAMP2 as a candidate gene associated with lysosome-related and ferroptosis-related annotations in RA synovium. External datasets and exploratory qRT-PCR supported its lower expression in RA. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish a causal role for VAMP2 in lysosomal regulation or ferroptosis. Key Points • Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses prioritized four candidate genes associated with lysosome-related and ferroptosis-related annotations. • Myeloid cells and FLS populations showed relatively high expression scores for the shared gene set. • External datasets and exploratory qRT-PCR supported lower VAMP2 expression in RA, prioritizing it for further functional investigation.
authors: Yan G, Yan H, Yu P, Xiang Y, Yang G, Zhang Y, Long L, Huang X.

title: Gene-metabolite-cardiac associations in the Chronic Kidney Disease in Children (CKiD) study.
abstract: BackgroundCharacterizing gene-metabolite-cardiac associations in childhood chronic kidney disease (CKD) has the potential to identify new research directions or therapeutic targets for mitigating the excessive cardiovascular risk in childhood CKD.MethodsThe Chronic Kidney Disease in Children (CKiD) is a prospective cohort that recruited children with eGFR 30-90 ml/min/1.73 m2 across 54 North American centers. Predictor and outcome variables included genotypes, metabolite levels, left ventricular mass index (LVMI) z-score, and left ventricular filling pressure (E/e'). Multivariable linear regression analyses assessed metabolite associations with either LVMI z-score or E/e', adjusting for age, sex, CKD duration, glomerular etiology, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system blockade, hypertension, anemia, dyslipidemia, eGFR, and proteinuria. Significance was based on the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate Results556 unique participants with 574 metabolites and ~8.4 million SNPs were included. Sphingomyelin (d18:2/d18:1) and hypotaurine were associated with LVMI z-score. Isobutyrylglycine and 3beta-hydroxy-5-cholestenoate were associated with E/e'. Multiple genetic variants associated with these metabolites at p ConclusionsWe identified metabolites associated with cardiac markers in children with CKD. We identified genetic associations with variability in these metabolites. Collectively, these gene-metabolite associations suggest roles for inflammation, increased oxidative stress, mitochondrial and energy dysmetabolism, and gut microbial dysbiosis in mediating cardiac pathology in childhood CKD. A higher resolution version of the Graphical abstract is available as Supplementary information.

title: Antimicrobial Nanoparticles Against Resistant Bacteria and Biofilms: From Material Design to Clinical Translation
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and biofilm-associated infections continue to compromise the effectiveness of conventional antibiotics, highlighting the need for complementary therapeutic approaches. Nanoparticle-based systems offer two distinct but potentially convergent strategies: direct antibacterial activity and improved delivery of antimicrobial agents. This narrative review critically examines inorganic, organic, and hybrid nanoplatforms, including metal and metal-oxide nanoparticles, carbon-derived materials, mesoporous silica, polymeric carriers, lipid-based systems, and stimuli-responsive formulations. Their mechanisms of action, physicochemical determinants of efficacy, and potential applications against multidrug-resistant bacteria and biofilm-associated infections are discussed. Particular attention is given to the distinction between bacterial resistance, tolerance, and persistence, as well as the challenges associated with nanoparticle penetration, antimicrobial synergy, and reproducible antibacterial activity. Although preclinical findings demonstrate considerable therapeutic potential, translation into clinical practice remains limited. Inhaled liposomal amikacin illustrates the clinical relevance of indication-specific nanodelivery, while emphasizing that therapeutic benefits cannot be generalized across nanoparticle formulations. Major challenges include cytotoxicity, bacterial adaptation, biodistribution, stability in biological environments, manufacturing scalability, regulatory requirements, and environmental safety. Future research should prioritize standardized characterization, clinically relevant infection models, robust comparisons with conventional treatments, and integrated assessments of safety and resistance evolution. Within a One Health framework, nanoparticle-based technologies may contribute to more effective antimicrobial therapies, provided that their development is guided by demonstrable clinical benefits, responsible antimicrobial use, and consideration of their broader environmental impact.
authors: Ferraz MP.

title: A Transcriptome-Inferred Binucleation State of CD10⁺ (MME⁺) Macrophages Consistent with Incomplete Cytokinesis: Morphology–Metabolism Coupling and a “Don’t-Eat-Me” Immune-Evasion Profile
abstract: Background:  Binucleated and multinucleated macrophages (cells carrying two or more nuclei in one cell body) occur in granulomas and tumors, yet their origins beyond cell–cell fusion, and the macrophage role of CD10 (MME), remain unresolved. We asked who CD10⁺ macrophages are, whether their binucleation reflects incomplete cytokinesis (failure of the final separation step of cell division), and how this state relates to phagocytic immune evasion. Methods: Analyzing 20,000 lung adenocarcinoma myeloid cells (GSE131907), we applied a three-axis discrimination rule (molecular-output level, lineage concordance, G2/M activity), a six-module prediction model, and a 35-molecule eat-me/don’t-eat-me panel. Results: CD10⁺ cells comprised 16.2% of myeloid cells (87.6% C1QC⁺ tumor-associated macrophage (TAM)-derived, predominantly normal-lung-derived alveolar macrophages) and split by origin into scavenger and inflammatory–pro-angiogenic types (Type-1 and Type-2). Transcriptome-inferred binucleated candidates constituted 27.0% of CD10⁺ cells with G2/M programs directionally elevated (consistent with incomplete cytokinesis over fusion; attenuated after library-size control); the state and its key contrasts replicated in tumor-restricted cells and an independent NSCLC atlas. The lysosome module showed the largest association (unadjusted Δ = +0.222; persists after library-size control, residual Δ = +0.068); the classifier reached an AUC of 0.77 (same-cohort, not externally validated). These cells also showed a transcript-level shift of the don’t-eat-me/eat-me balance centered on CD47 (Δ = +0.127; calreticulin unchanged)—itself both an anti-phagocytic checkpoint and a multinucleation participant. Conclusions: We hypothesize that lysosomal stress drives cytokinesis failure and barrier co-assembly, nominating the CD10⁺ binucleated state as a testable node of phagocytic immune evasion for combination checkpoint targeting.

title: Design and Validation of Multiplexed Respiratory RT-LAMP assay for the differentiation of SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A and Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in COVID-19 Pandemic Samples from Western Kenya.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the importance of widespread, accessible viral surveillance to ensure pandemic-preparedness. The rapid diagnosis of respiratory infections is crucial not only for effective patient management but also to inform ongoing surveillance for the detection of outbreaks. Reverse transcriptase-Loop mediated isothermal amplification (RT-LAMP) assays are an attractive alternative to reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for rapid, decentralised testing in resource limited settings due being rapid and low cost. Here we present the design and evaluation of a multiplexed RT-LAMP assay for the simultaneous detection of SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A and Respiratory Syncytial Virus via the incorporation of fluorescently labelled LAMP probes. Mid-nasal swabs collected from 175 participants on the day of enrolment in the MALCOV Cohort study in Kisumu, Kenya were used in the evaluation of the RT-LAMP assay. Overall, 114 SARS-CoV-2, six Influenza A, two Influenza B and zero RSV samples were identified in the cohort by the Allplex SARS-CoV-2/FluA/FluB/RSV RT-PCR kit (Seegene Inc) reference test, in addition to 53 negatives. Sensitivity and specificity of the RT-LAMP assay (SARS-CoV-2/FluA/RSV) when compared to RT-PCR was 82.64% [CI95%:74.70-88.92%] and 100% [CI95%:93.40-100%] at 40 minutes for all samples respectively. The mean time to a positive result was 11minutes, highlighting the speed of this technology compared to the more commonly used RT-PCR. RT-LAMP enables rapid multi-pathogen detection with comparable diagnostic accuracy to RT-PCR.
authors: Greenland-Bews C, Suwara MI, Voto IAP, Shah S, Achieng M, Badoum ES, Barsosio HC, Brazal-Monzo H, Canizales J, Drabko A, Hannan L, Kabore JT, Lesosky M, Marlais T, Matthewman J, Nebie I, Onyango ED, Ouedraogo A, Otieno K, Serme S, Sirima SB, Soulama BI, Tangara B, Tiono AB, Wu W, Soulama I, Rehak M, Kariuki S, Drakeley C, ter Kuile FO, Allen DJ, Adams ER, Gillies EA, Edwards T.

title: A four-gene diagnostic panel for distinguishing primary progressive multiple sclerosis from HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis.
abstract: Primary Progressive Multiple Sclerosis (PPMS) and HTLV-1-Associated Myelopathy/Tropical Spastic Paraparesis (HAM/TSP) are clinically overlapping progressive myelopathies characterized by spastic paraparesis and autonomic dysfunction. However, they originate from fundamentally distinct pathogenic processes: autoimmune demyelination in PPMS versus chronic retroviral-driven neuroinflammation in HAM/TSP. Current diagnostic approaches are frequently inadequate, as HTLV-1 screening is often omitted in non-endemic regions and positive serology in endemic areas does not rule out concomitant PPMS, highlighting the urgent need for complementary molecular diagnostic tools. In this study, we developed an integrative bioinformatics framework combining network analysis, differential expression profiling, and machine learning to identify a transcriptional signature capable of distinguishing PPMS from HAM/TSP. Disease-specific gene modules were identified through cross-dataset preservation analysis and module-trait correlations. Random Forest classification with recursive feature elimination was employed to derive a parsimonious Diagnostic Risk Score (DRS), which was validated on an independent external cohort under a frozen-threshold, leakage-free design. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) revealed striking topological divergence between the two diseases: HAM/TSP exhibited a consolidated network architecture with a single dominant module, whereas PPMS displayed a highly fragmented topology with numerous smaller modules. Cross-dataset preservation analysis identified 11 PPMS-specific and 63 HAM/TSP-specific candidate biomarker genes. Machine learning refinement reduced this to a 4-gene signature comprising ZFAND1, MAPRE2, TBK1, and LPAR6, which achieved robust classification performance in cross-validation (macro-averaged accuracy: 0.982; macro-averaged F1-score: 0.987; AUC-ROC: 0.995) and robust performance on external validation (macro-averaged accuracy: 0.975; macro-averaged F1-score: 0.937; AUC-ROC: 0.800). The 4-gene signature captures distinct biological dimensions: ZFAND1 marks proteostatic stress from viral inflammation, TBK1 excludes the HTLV-1 interferon signature, MAPRE2 reflects a HAM/TSP-associated cytoskeletal program, and LPAR6 links inflammatory signaling to oligodendrocyte maturation. This multidimensional architecture explains the panel's high accuracy and offers mechanistic insights. The proposed approach offers a practical, transcriptome-based adjunct to current diagnostic methods, with potential to guide therapeutic stratification and reduce misdiagnosis of PPMS and HAM/TSP.
authors: Zarei Ghobadi M, Afsaneh E, Mozhgani SH.

title: Deciphering the molecular discrepancies in halogenated disinfection byproducts formation between autochthonous and allochthonous precursors in natural eutrophic water.
abstract: Pre-chlorination of eutrophic waters releases algal organic matter, yielding highly toxic halogenated disinfection byproducts (Xn-DBPs). However, the molecular discrepancies between autochthonous and allochthonous Xn-DBP precursors remain poorly understood in eutrophic waters. An interpretable machine-learning framework was developed to classify precursor formulae into operationally defined autochthonous and allochthonous categories using molecular descriptors derived from FT-ICR MS. XGBoost had the best overall classification performance among all tested models and excellent discrimination on an independent external validation dataset. N/C and H/C were identified as the two most influential features in the six-feature XGBoost model by the SHAP analysis. Within our datasets, higher N/C and H/C values (H/C ≥ 1.25) tended to contribute positively to autochthonous precursor predictions, and these patterns are model-specific and do not constitute standalone source-diagnostic thresholds. A total of 48 autochthonous and 58 allochthonous precursors yielded 25 and 68 Cln-DBPs, respectively. Autochthonous precursors exhibited significantly higher N content and potential bioavailability, but lower carbon skeleton unsaturation than allochthonous precursors (p n-DBP source control by highlighting the potential health risks posed by eutrophic waters with high autochthonous DOM inputs, which preferentially form nitrogenous, bioaccumulative Xn-DBPs.
authors: Wu S, Wei W, Fu QL, Fujii M, Dong H, Ma R, Yang X, Fu P, Wang Y.

title: Carbon-iron co-enrichment on rice rhizoplane is associated with Fe plaque crystallization and persistent Cd immobilization: A five-year field study.
abstract: Cadmium (Cd) contamination in paddy soils threatens rice safety, yet the longevity of amendment-based immobilization remains uncertain. Here, a five-year field experiment investigated Cd migration across the soil-root-rice continuum after a single application of lime or oyster shell powder (OS). Both amendments reduced brown-rice Cd in the first year, but only OS maintained the effect; after five years, grain Cd remained at 0.11 mg kg⁻¹ , below the food-safety limit of 0.20 mg kg⁻¹ and lower than the control (0.23 mg kg⁻¹) and lime treatment (0.20 mg kg⁻¹). Sequential extraction and cross-niche metagenomic analyses revealed pronounced carbon-iron (C-Fe) co-enrichment at the rhizoplane under OS treatment. OS increased operationally defined poorly crystalline Fe-associated fractions and extractable organic C, accompanied by greater Cd partitioning within rhizoplane Fe-associated pools. Metagenomic analyses further revealed enrichment of carbohydrate-active enzyme families and Cd-resistance-associated genes at the OS rhizoplane. These findings indicate that persistent rhizoplane C-Fe associations are associated with enhanced Cd retention at the root-soil interface and may contribute to the long-term performance of oyster shell amendment under field conditions.
authors: Kong F, Yuan ZF, Wang Z, Jia H, Yang Z, Zhang Q, Xu M, Lu S.

title: Integrative analysis of two contrasting peanut cultivars reveals stress-specific polyamine biosynthesis signatures associated with tolerance to cold, drought and combined stress.
abstract: Cold and drought frequently co-occur during peanut development in high-latitude regions. Polyamine (PA) homeostasis, encompassing putrescine (Put), spermidine (Spd) and spermine (Spm), is critical for plant stress tolerance, yet its role under combined stress remains elusive. We identified 22 PA biosynthesis genes encoding arginine decarboxylase (ADC), agmatine deiminase (AIH), N-carbamoylputrescine amidase (CPA), ornithine decarboxylase (ODC), S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase (SAMDC), Spd synthase (SPDS) and Spm synthase (SPMS) in peanut, with 12 and 11 homologs in its two diploid progenitors. They showed strong conservation in phylogeny, motifs, gene structure and protein architecture, despite putative losses of AdSAMDC3, AdSAMDC4 and AiSAMDC1. Cis-regulatory element and expression analyses indicated broad roles in peanut development and stress responses. Comparative analyses of tolerant cultivar NH5 and sensitive cultivar FH18 showed that combined stress caused the greatest growth inhibition, with cold predominating. NH5 exhibited less damage and better recovery, accompanied by stronger and more sustained induction of PA biosynthesis genes and enzyme activities, as well as greater Put and Spm accumulation during both stress and recovery. Integrative analyses using Mantel tests and PLS-DA revealed stress-specific regulatory signatures: cold was primarily associated with SPMS-mediated Spm biosynthesis, drought with ODC-mediated Put biosynthesis, and combined stress with coordinated ADC/ODC-mediated Put production and SPMS-mediated Spm accumulation. AhSPMS1 was a common discriminant across all three stresses, whereas AhADC1, AhODC1, AhCPA1, AhAIH1 and AhSAMDC1 contributed in a stress-dependent manner. These findings establish a comprehensive framework for PA biosynthesis in peanut and identify candidate genes and metabolites for improving tolerance to cold, drought and their combination.

title: Prioritizing Osteoporosis-Associated Candidates Through Multi-Omics Mendelian Randomization, Transcriptomic Modeling, and in vitro Validation.
abstract: BackgroundGut microbiota, immune traits, and circulating metabolites may contribute to skeletal biology. We integrated genetic association analyses, transcriptomic profiling, and cell experiments to prioritize osteoporosis-associated molecular candidates.MethodsTwo-sample Mendelian randomization (MR), gene prioritization, and three GEO datasets comprising 110 samples were integrated. MR estimates were recalculated while retaining outcome-associated instruments, followed by false-discovery-rate correction. Exploratory classifiers and a five-gene nomogram were evaluated internally. Protein expression and osteoclast formation were examined in control and RANKL-treated RAW264.7 cells in three independent experiments per group. Supplementary validation repeated normalization, screening and tuning within training folds.ResultsAmong 2,329 IVW tests, the metabolite exposure indexed by GCST90200621 was associated with osteoporosis after multiplicity adjustment (odds ratio 1.296, 95% confidence interval 1.155-1.454; within-domain adjusted P = 0.0135). No colocalization record had PP.H4 above 0.5. The transcriptomic workflow prioritized CCR1, TRMT2A, FADS2, FBXL14, and TTLL12. The original nine-gene RF analysis had an internal test-partition AUC of 0.805. Expression of all five proteins increased during RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis. Additional nested validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.528; cross-study performance remained limited. Fixed-five-gene ridge sensitivity analysis yielded a mean internal AUC of 0.756, conditional on prior gene selection.ConclusionIntegrating genetic and transcriptomic analyses with cell experiments prioritized five osteoporosis-associated candidates whose protein expression increased during osteoclast differentiation. These complementary findings provide a focused basis for biological follow-up; predictive and gene-specific functional applications require further validation.
authors: Sun L, Ni S, Yang K, Zhu X, Tang J, Shi H, Sun X, Ding H.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic and DNA Methylation Analysis Identifies KRT6B and CHI3L2 as Candidate Shared Biomarkers of Psoriasis and Cutaneous Melanoma.
abstract: BackgroundDifferent studies have drawn inconsistent conclusions on whether psoriasis increases the risk of cutaneous melanoma (CM). Although shared gene expression or methylation pathways between the two diseases have been independently reported, suggesting a potential molecular basis for their comorbidity, whether expression and methylation synergistically contribute to their pathogenesis remains unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to identify common methylation-regulated genes (co-MRGs) as potential biomarkers for the association between psoriasis and CM.MethodsTranscriptomic and DNA methylation data of psoriasis and CM, comprising 53 cases and 55 normal controls in total, from GEO and ArrayExpress were used as the main dataset. Differential expression and differential methylation analyses were performed on the main dataset using limma and DMRcate; co-MRGs were further identified. TCGA-GTEx data (472 CM cases and 326 normal controls) served as the external validation dataset to validate the expression regulation of the identified co-MRGs in CM. Network analyses were based on the main dataset; immune infiltration and survival analyses were based on the validation dataset; and IHC analyses were based on the HPA database.ResultsThree co-MRGs (KRT6B, CHI3L2, and TSPAN8) were identified. KRT6B was hypomethylated/upregulated in psoriasis but hypermethylated/downregulated in CM, with enrichment in epidermal development and keratinization. CHI3L2 was hypomethylated and upregulated in both, exhibiting superior diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.867). TSPAN8 was hypermethylated/downregulated in both. KRT6B trended toward poor CM prognosis, whereas CHI3L2 high expression correlated with better survival. HPA-based IHC validation confirmed differential expression of KRT6B and CHI3L2.ConclusionThis study identified two novel promising candidate co-MRG biomarkers, KRT6B and CHI3L2, providing preliminary evidence for a shared molecular link between psoriasis and CM. However, limitations remain, as psoriasis and CM data were derived from separate datasets, and further experimental validation is required.
authors: Gao L, RenChen X, Li H, Li B.

title: Identification and validation of circadian rhythm-related diagnostic biomarkers for endometriosis through integrating machine learning and single-cell analysis.
abstract: BackgroundEndometriosis (EMs) is a chronic inflammatory disease, and the lack of candidate molecular biomarkers remain a major clinical challenge. Circadian rhythm disruption plays a non-negligible role in EMs. However, the diagnostic potential of circadian rhythm-related biomarkers remains insufficiently validated.MethodsWe performed weighted gene co-expression network analysis to screen for endometriosis-related hub modules. Four machine learning algorithms were used for feature selection in the training cohort, and the resulting diagnostic model was evaluated in three independent GEO validation cohorts. To evaluate the immune microenvironment, we applied MCPcounter, CIBERSORT, and single-sample gene set enrichment analysis. Single‑cell RNA‑seq data were processed with Seurat for cell clustering and annotation, cell‑cell communication networks were constructed using CellChat, and pseudotime trajectory analysis was performed with Monocle.ResultsSMC2, SUV39H2, and TIMELESS were identified as candidate molecular biomarkers, demonstrating favorable diagnostic performance across three independent validation sets. Computational immune infiltration analysis suggested higher enrichment scores for B cells and CD8+ T cells, along with lower scores for Tregs and NK cells in EMs samples. Single-cell analysis revealed an increased proportion of mesenchymal cells in EMs samples and altered cell-cell communication involving BMP, CHEMERIN, and GRN signaling pathways. Pseudotime analysis further suggested transcriptional relationships among distinct stromal cell populations.ConclusionThis study identified SMC2, SUV39H2, and TIMELESS as candidate tissue-based molecular biomarkers for EMs and revealed alterations in stromal cell populations and immune-related features associated with the disease.
journal: European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology
authors: Chen D, Xu L, Cheng L, Su A.
