title: Dynamic CD4⁺ T-Cell eQTLs Reveal Gene Regulatory Networks Associated with Atopic Dermatitis.
abstract: Background and objectiveAtopic dermatitis (AD) is a complex immune-mediated disorder in which aberrant activation of CD4⁺ T cells plays a critical pathogenic role. We integrated dynamic CD4⁺ T cell expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data with Mendelian randomization (MR) to dissect the causal effect of transcriptional changes on AD risk.MethodsThis study integrated dynamic CD4⁺ T-cell eQTL analysis, two-sample MR, colocalization analysis, single-cell transcriptomic, pseudotime, cell-cell communication and protein-protein interaction (PPI) analyses, with virtual single-cell knockout further used to evaluate gene regulatory effects in AD. We systematically analyzed gene expression and genetic variation in CD4⁺ T cells from 119 individuals of European ancestry across multiple activation time points (0 h, 16 h, 40 h, and 5 days).ResultsWe performed two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) integrating dynamic CD4⁺ T-cell eQTL, OneK1K, eQTLGen, and FinnGen R12 AD cohort data. The analysis identified 298 genes significantly associated with AD (FDR ConclusionWe demonstrate that understanding the dynamic characteristics of CD4⁺ T cells is crucial for AD, and prioritize genes for future research into its pathogenesis.
authors: Chen J, Bai B.

title: A rare co-infection of Colletotrichum truncatum and Nocardia cyriacigeorgica in a renal transplant recipient.
abstract: Opportunistic infections caused by uncommon pathogens are increasingly reported in renal transplant recipients receiving prolonged immunosuppressive therapy. We report the first case of co-infection with Colletotrichum truncatum and disseminated Nocardia cyriacigeorgica in a renal transplant recipient. A 52-year-old woman presented with right arm and thigh swellings. Microbiological examination of the pus from thigh lesion demonstrated Colletotrichum truncatum, confirmed by sequencing of internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region of ribosomal DNA, whereas aspirate from the arm swelling revealed partially acid-fast branching filamentous bacilli, identified as Nocardia cyriacigeorgica by MALDI-TOF MS. Chest imaging showed pulmonary nodules which yielded N. cyriacigeorgica from fine-needle aspirate, confirming disseminated nocardiosis. The patient was treated with a successive combination of antibiotic therapy (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ceftriaxone followed by amoxicillin-clavulanate, meropenem, linezolid, minocycline and tedizolid) for Nocardia species and itraconazole for C. truncatum. Complete resolution of pulmonary lesions was achieved after a year of therapy, but persistence of cutaneous lesions required surgical removal. This case highlights the importance of prompt microbiological diagnosis, and individualized treatment strategies in managing rare opportunistic co-infections in renal transplant recipients.
authors: Kaur H, Kumar D, Ahmad H, Sharma A, Kaur R, Kundu R, Singh H, Muthu V, Agnihotri S, Rudramurthy SM.

title: Identification and validation of an ion homeostasis-related diagnostic gene signature for tuberculosis and exploratory analysis of SLC24A2.
abstract: BackgroundTuberculosis (TB) remains a major global public health problem. Ion homeostasis is involved in the regulation of host anti-infection immunity, but the potential value of ion homeostasis-related genes (IHRGs) in the molecular diagnosis of TB has not been fully evaluated.MethodsDifferentially expressed IHRGs were screened based on GEO transcriptomic datasets; candidate diagnostic genes were identified by combining the LASSO and Boruta algorithms; a multivariable logistic regression model was constructed; and its discriminative performance and stability were evaluated through internal cross-validation, penalized regression, and independent external cohorts. In addition, ssGSEA, GeneMANIA, GSVA, and molecular docking analyses were performed to explore the potential biological implications of the representative candidate gene SLC24A2.ResultsA total of 8 candidate diagnostic genes were screened out: CCL28, CCR2, CCR6, CD52, FAM20A, KEL, SLC24A2, and XCL1. The model showed an apparent AUC of 0.997 in the training set, a nested cross-validation AUC of 0.862 for the combined LASSO and Boruta screening strategy, and an AUC of 0.986 in the GSE34608 external validation cohort. Further analysis indicated that the original model suffered from unstable parameter estimation and numerical saturation of predicted probabilities in part of the external validation data. SLC24A2 was upregulated in the three datasets and was associated with some immune-related gene sets and signaling pathway scores. Molecular docking analysis suggested a potential interaction between Calcitriol and SLC24A2.ConclusionIn this study, 8 ion homeostasis-related candidate diagnostic genes were identified, and exploratory analyses of the potential biological role of SLC24A2 and its interaction with candidate compounds were performed. These findings provide a preliminary basis for further validation of molecular diagnostic markers for TB and subsequent research on potential therapeutic targets.
authors: Li M, Sun C, Chen L, Wu C, Liu Q.

title: Identification of Endoplasmic reticulum Homeostasis-associated diagnostic biomarkers for Sarcopenia through integrated Bioinformatics and Experimental Validation.
abstract: Sarcopenia is an age-related skeletal muscle disorder characterized by progressive loss of muscle mass and function, yet reliable biomarkers for early diagnosis remain limited. Emerging evidence suggests that disruption of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) homeostasis contributes to skeletal muscle aging, however, the diagnostic relevance of ER stress- and reticulophagy-related alterations in sarcopenia remains poorly understood. In this study, three skeletal muscle transcriptomic datasets (GSE25941, GSE28422, and GSE38718) were integrated following batch-effect correction to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between sarcopenic and control samples. DEGs were intersected with ER stress and reticulophagy related gene sets to obtain sarcopenia-associated candidate genes. Subsequently, three machine-learning algorithms, including least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), random forest (RF), and support vector machine (SVM), were applied to identify key hub genes. Functional enrichment analyses, transcription factor (TF)-miRNA regulatory network construction, protein-chemical interaction analyses, external validation, nomogram development, and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) verification were performed. A total of 236 DEGs were identified, comprising 34 upregulated and 202 downregulated genes. Intersection analysis with 1,772 ER stress and reticulophagy related genes yielded 10 candidate genes, from which five hub genes (ACTC1, NPY, CDKN2B, GADD45G, and GRIA1) were consistently identified by machine-learning analyses. Functional enrichment analysis indicated significant involvement in extracellular matrix organization, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, mitochondrial translation, and respiratory electron transport pathways. Regulatory network analyses further revealed potential interactions with multiple transcription factors, miRNAs, and chemical compounds. In the independent validation cohort (GSE1428), ACTC1 showed strong individual discriminative performance, NPY and GADD45G showed moderate performance, whereas GRIA1 showed limited discrimination and CDKN2B showed near-chance individual performance, whereas the combined gene signature exhibited improved discriminative ability. A predictive nomogram was established. Moreover, qRT-PCR analysis of human skeletal muscle biopsy specimens confirmed significantly increased expression of ACTC1, NPY, CDKN2B, and GRIA1, together with decreased expression of GADD45G in sarcopenic muscle tissues compared with controls (all p < 0.05). Collectively, our findings identified a five-gene signature associated with ER stress and reticulophagy related molecular networks in sarcopenia. Although these genes are not established core regulators of ER stress or reticulophagy, they exhibited promising diagnostic value and may reflect ER homeostasis-related molecular alterations during skeletal muscle aging, providing novel biomarkers and potential insights into the molecular basis of sarcopenia.
authors: Shi L, Yan H, Lu J, Yu W, Li Y, Zhang Z.

title: Polystyrene microplastic and bisphenol A Co-exposure drives oxidative collapse, neuroendocrine disruption, apoptotic activation, and hepatopancreatic pathology in Pontogammarus maeoticus.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) and bisphenol A (BPA) are widespread emerging aquatic pollutants that may pose ecological risks to sensitive invertebrates; however, their combined chronic effects on neuroendocrine regulation, apoptotic signaling, and hepatopancreatic integrity in endemic Caspian crustaceans remain uncharacterized. This study assessed the 30-day chronic toxicity of polystyrene microplastics (PS-MPs, 7.26 µm; 0.05 and 5 mg L⁻¹), BPA (50% LC₅₀), and their combination (5 mg L⁻¹ PS-MPs + 50% LC₅₀ BPA) in Pontogammarus maeoticus using a multi-biomarker approach. Combined exposure produced the highest mean CYP450 level, although it did not differ significantly from MP2 or BPA alone, and the highest cleaved/pro-caspase-3 ratio. Heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) increased in all exposed groups, peaking under combined exposure at a level not significantly different from BPA alone. SOD activity increased, whereas catalase and total antioxidant capacity were lowest under co-exposure. Crustacean hyperglycemic hormone (CHH), measured as a relative immunoreactive value, was highest in the combined group, and acetylcholinesterase (AChE) activity was significantly reduced under the higher PS-MP concentration, BPA, and co-exposure. Reproductive hormones (17β-estradiol and testosterone) decreased in exposed groups, with the lowest values under co-exposure, and hepatopancreatic lesions were most severe in the combined treatment. Overall, co-exposure was empirically associated with stronger oxidative, apoptotic, endocrine, and histological responses than most single exposures. Because BPA adsorption onto PS-MPs and tissue residues were not measured, a carrier-mediated interaction remains a plausible but unproven hypothesis. These findings support further evaluation of P. maeoticus as a candidate bioindicator of plastic-associated pollution in the Caspian Sea.
authors: Vahdatiraad L, Heidari B, Zarei S, Hadavand BS.

title: A time-resolved single-nucleus atlas of cochlear aging reveals biphasic inflammaging and Tbx2-dependent inner hair cell maintenance.
abstract: BackgroundAge-related hearing loss (ARHL) is the most prevalent sensory deficit in older adults, yet its molecular progression remains poorly resolved. Few cochlear single-cell studies have integrated cell-cell communication, gene regulatory network (GRN) reconstruction, and cross-cohort bulk validation into one temporal framework.MethodsWe reanalyzed publicly available single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from C57BL/6 J mouse cochleae at 3, 12, and 24 months and cross-validated against two independent bulk microarray cohorts. Ligand-receptor interactions were inferred and validated at the ligand-expression level. GRNs were reconstructed and perturbed in silico; and feature selection extracted cross-scale inflammatory features.ResultsARHL did not follow a linear decline. A cochlea-wide type I interferon response peaked at 12 months and resolved by 24. Apolipoprotein E followed a three-phase trajectory, baseline, compensatory upregulation, collapse, across spiral ganglion neurons, inner hair cells (IHCs), macrophages, and fibrocytes. SLIT-ROBO axon-guidance signaling shut down in these cells, alongside neurotrophic and Notch withdrawal. In silico perturbation identified T-box transcription factor 2 (Tbx2) as a protective GRN node: knockout drove 81.2% of IHCs toward aging and overexpression 74.6% toward youth. A 13-gene inflammatory panel showed midlife activation and end-stage exhaustion in macrophages, mirroring the interferon peak.ConclusionThese findings support a two-stage ARHL model, midlife immune activation followed by end-stage synaptic, lipid, and axon-guidance collapse, positioning the midlife window and Tbx2-dependent IHC maintenance as candidate intervention targets, pending in vivo validation.
authors: Zhao H, Wang Y, Wang Q, Ma X, Zhao K, Zhai X, Wang R, Han M, Cui L, Sun Y.

title: Single-cell and spatial analysis of inflammation-associated resistance in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
abstract: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) is frequently associated with chronic inflammation and a complex stromal microenvironment, yet the cellular and molecular features underlying heterogeneous responses to neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy remain unclear. Here, using Flex-based single-cell transcriptomic profiling of post-treatment ICC specimens from responders and non-responders, together with multiplex immunohistochemistry and animal model validation, we delineate a coordinated, inflammation-associated multicellular state linked to treatment non-response. Non-response tumors showed enrichment of SPINK1⁺ epithelial cells, inflammatory cancer-associated fibroblasts, SPP1⁺ and inflammatory macrophage states, and immunosuppressive or inflammation-associated CD4⁺ T-cell programs. Across epithelial, stromal, and immune compartments, IL6-JAK-STAT3-related inflammatory signaling emerged as a recurrent feature of resistance. Computational cell-cell communication analysis predicted increased communication probabilities between iCAFs and SPINK1⁺ epithelial cells and between InfMp and CD4Tem cells in non-response tumors, nominating TNF-TLR2, HMGB1-TLR2, AGT-CYBB, and TNF-ICAM1 as candidate ligand-receptor associations. Tissue-level validation confirmed increased SPINK1 expression, inflammatory macrophage features, and elevated p-STAT3 signals in non-response tumors. Combined PD-1 blockade and JAK1/2 inhibition showed enhanced antitumor activity in both a hydrodynamic injection-based cholangiocarcinoma-like mouse model and a humanized huPBMC-NOG-dKO mouse model bearing ICC-X1 xenografts. In the hydrodynamic model, the combination was also accompanied by reduced p-STAT3 activity and enhanced T-cell infiltration and granzyme B expression. Together, these findings identify a coordinated, multicellular inflammatory state associated with non-response to neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy in ICC and nominate JAK-STAT signaling as a convergent, therapeutically actionable vulnerability. The antitumor activity observed with combined JAK1/2 inhibition and PD-1 blockade further supports evaluating this inflammatory signaling axis as a therapeutic target to improve immunotherapy responsiveness in ICC.
journal: Drug resistance updates : reviews and commentaries in antimicrobial and anticancer chemotherapy
authors: Tang X, Huang H, Shen X, Kong G, Zhang W, Yu J, Wu C, Wu J.

title: Integrated Molecular Detection and Epidemiological Investigation of Brucella abortus in Dairy Cattle and Farm Workers During a Brucellosis Outbreak.
abstract: BackgroundBrucellosis is a highly contagious zoonotic disease caused by bacteria belonging to the genus Brucella that can infect a wide range of domestic and wild animals. A recent brucellosis outbreak was reported at a dairy farm in the peri-urban region of Khanewal District, Punjab, Pakistan.ObjectiveIn response, this study aimed to improve understanding of the dynamics of Brucella abortus infection in cattle and dairy farm workers in the local context.MethodsIn November 2024, a total of 83 cattle, representing six different breeds, along with blood samples from 11 farm workers directly involved in handling these animals, were sampled. Relevant epidemiological data were also collected to support the investigation. To detect Brucella infection in cattle, both the Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) targeting the IS711 gene were employed.ResultsAll sampled cattle tested seropositive for Brucella antibodies by RBPT, indicating widespread exposure to Brucella. Molecular detection through partial IS711 sequence amplification revealed that 48% of the cattle and 45% of the farm workers (5 out of 11) tested positive for Brucella spp.InfectionSubsequent DNA sequencing and BLAST analysis confirmed the presence of B. abortus in both cattle and humans. The obtained IS711 sequences closely matched those previously reported in ruminants and humans in China. Data analysis further showed that cows were more susceptible to B. abortus infection compared to bulls (p = 0.01). However, no significant association was observed between infection status and cattle breed, age, presence or absence of ectoparasites, or history of abortion (for all p > 0.05).ConclusionThe present study provides evidence of B. abortus detection among cattle at the investigated dairy farm in Khanewal. The findings should be interpreted within the context of the studied farm, as the purposive sampling of a single dairy farm does not permit extrapolation to the wider cattle population of Khanewal District or Pakistan. Further multi-farm studies involving geographically diverse cattle populations are warranted to determine the broader occurrence and epidemiological pattern of B. abortus.
authors: Asif M, Obaid MK, Naeem M, Muqaddas H, Ullah S, Khan A, Mahmood N, Ren Q, Alqahtani FM, Said MA, Dabiellil F, Iqbal F.

title: Circadian Rhythm-Associated Diagnostic Biomarkers Reveal Immune Dysregulation and Molecular Subtypes in Recurrent Pregnancy Loss.
abstract: BackgroundRecurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) is a clinically complex reproductive disorder involving impaired maternal-fetal communication and immune imbalance. Circadian rhythm disturbance has recently attracted attention in reproductive failure, but its diagnostic relevance and possible connection with immune dysregulation in RPL remain insufficiently defined.MethodsGSE165004 was used as the discovery cohort, and GSE26787 was used as an independent small cohort for preliminary evaluation. Circadian rhythm-associated genes were collected from GeneCards. Differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and ssGSEA-based circadian rhythm scoring were integrated to identify RPL-associated circadian transcriptional alterations. Candidate genes were further evaluated by protein-protein interaction analysis, functional enrichment, receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, nomogram construction, immune infiltration assessment, molecular subtype identification, and ceRNA regulatory network prediction.ResultsRPL samples showed a significantly lower circadian rhythm-associated gene score than control samples, indicating reduced circadian-associated transcriptional activity. Three genes, GJA1, UCP2, and GSN, were identified as circadian rhythm-associated candidate diagnostic biomarkers for RPL. In the discovery cohort, the AUC values of GJA1, UCP2, and GSN were 0.80, 0.77, and 0.81, respectively. Their diagnostic performance was further evaluated in an independent small cohort, where the AUC values were 0.72, 0.80, and 0.92, respectively. GSN showed a significant expression difference between RPL and control samples in the independent cohort, whereas GJA1 and UCP2 did not reach statistical significance. Immune infiltration analysis revealed changes in fibroblast, neutrophil, macrophage, Treg, T helper cell, and interferon-related signatures. Consensus clustering based on the three biomarkers classified RPL samples into two molecular subtypes with different immune-stromal characteristics, coagulation-related activity, and metabolic features. The ceRNA network contained 3 diagnostic mRNAs, 43 predicted miRNAs, and 61 upstream lncRNAs.ConclusionGJA1, UCP2, and GSN may represent circadian rhythm-associated candidate biomarkers for RPL. Their expression patterns may reflect circadian-immune dysregulation and molecular heterogeneity. These findings provide a circadian rhythm-based perspective for understanding RPL pathogenesis and nominate candidate molecules for future diagnostic and mechanistic validation.
journal: American journal of reproductive immunology (New York, N.Y. : 1989)
authors: Chen Y, Li Y, Wang S, Wang Y, Feng X.

title: Hypoxia Signatures in Renal Cell Carcinoma: From HIF-Mediated Omics Remodeling to Precision Diagnostics.
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC), particularly clear cell RCC (ccRCC), exhibits extensive metabolic, signaling, and microenvironmental remodeling associated with dysregulated VHL-HIF signaling. HIF activation in RCC may arise from VHL loss under normoxic conditions and from genuine tumor hypoxia due to inadequate oxygen availability; these states can converge on overlapping downstream programs but are biologically distinct. This review examines proteomic, phosphoproteomic, metabolomic, and emerging spatial and single-cell studies that characterize hypoxia- and VHL-HIF-associated molecular alterations in RCC. Particular emphasis is placed on protein-level changes in metabolism, angiogenesis, extracellular matrix remodeling, signaling, and immune regulation, as well as on how these measurements complement transcriptomic data. The review further distinguishes mechanistic molecular signatures from candidate diagnostic, prognostic, predictive, pharmacodynamic, and treatment-selection biomarkers. Evidence for circulating proteins and metabolites is discussed together with available measures of diagnostic performance, analytical validation, and clinical validation. Finally, the potential of integrated discovery and targeted mass-spectrometry approaches to support clinically useful multianalyte biomarker panel development is considered, while highlighting the challenges of tumor heterogeneity, assay reproducibility, cohort validation, and clinical utility.
authors: Mahalinga M, Rai AB, Prasad TSK.

title: Proximity Labeling: An Empowering Tool for Deciphering Molecular Mechanisms.
abstract: Proximity labeling (PL) has become a widely used approach for studying protein-protein interactions (PPIs) and addressing limitations of conventional techniques in capturing transient, weak interactions, and physiological protein networks within living systems. Over the past decade, core PL enzymes, notably APEX2, BirA* (BioID), and TurboID, have been iteratively engineered, with reported improvements in temporal resolution, targeting specificity, and biocompatibility. This review summarizes how PL technologies have developed and describes the enzymatic properties, catalytic mechanisms, and reported performance trade-offs of the commonly used tools. We then survey applications of PL in neuroscience, cardiology, oncology, and infectious disease, where it has been used to map compartment-specific proteomes and spatiotemporally regulated networks, including neural activity-driven PPIs, tumor microenvironment cross-talk, and host-pathogen interfaces. Many of the resulting candidates await orthogonal validation. We also describe recently reported conditional PL systems with optical, calcium- or oxygen-dependent control. Finally, we discuss open questions and possible directions for PL development, including enzyme-directed evolution, multisignal responsive regulation, cross-omics integration, and translational applications. This review is intended as a practical reference for researchers to support the selection and application of PL platforms in specific experimental contexts from mechanistic studies to the identification of candidate therapeutic targets.
authors: Liang H, Chen S, Gan K, Chai R, Bi Z.

title: From Mechanical Perturbation to Pathological Locking: Temporal-Mechanical Evolution of the Postsynaptic Density After Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: BackgroundTraumatic brain injury (TBI) induces persistent cognitive deficits, yet conventional biochemical and structural models often fail to explain synaptic signal collapse in the absence of overt tissue rupture.ResultsHere, we present a hypothesis-generating mechanobiological framework that positions postsynaptic density (PSD)-a multivalent protein condensate governed by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)-as a primary locus of synaptic mechanovulnerability. We argue that TBI-induced synaptic pathology is not merely a quantitative loss of molecular components, but a progressive, staged material state transition of the PSD network. This pathological evolution initiates with hyperacute mechanical deconstruction, leading to physical scaffold decoupling and nanoscale receptor misalignment. It then advances through an acute mechano-metabolic crisis characterized by enzymatic scaffold cleavage and impaired re-condensation, ultimately culminating in a chronically locked, low-dynamic "solidified" state. Furthermore, post-injury extracellular matrix stiffening and the mechanical exposure of cryptic epitopes trigger aberrant microglial pruning via mechanosensors such as Piezo1, permanently dismantling neural circuits. Because the supporting evidence is heterogeneous, we explicitly grade each element of this model as established directly in TBI, supported in non-TBI synaptic systems, extrapolated from reconstituted condensates, or hypothetical.ConclusionsBy bridging macroscopic biomechanics with nanoscale molecular pathology, this review highlights a critical conceptual gap and proposes "mechano-therapeutics" as a hypothesis-generating concept rather than an established treatment avenue. We suggest that strategies targeting the physical properties of the synapse, such as stabilizing scaffold oligomerization, modulating mechanotransduction pathways, and restoring physiological tissue stiffness, are candidate directions whose feasibility, delivery, cell-type specificity, timing, and safety must first be established in preclinical models before any clinical translation to rescue synaptic homeostasis and cognitive function after TBI.
authors: Jia Y, Cao Z, Xue H, Feng Z, Ma Z, Tian Z, Li X, Luo P.

title: Revealing the Action Mechanism of WISP2 in Miscarriage Based Multi-Omic Analysis and Experimental Validation.
abstract: Recurrent miscarriage (RM) is a major unresolved issue in reproductive medicine. Although WISP2 is known to participate in multiple cellular processes, its function in trophoblast biology and pregnancy maintenance remains unknown. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing on chorionic villus tissues from RM patients and normal controls to identify cell-type-specific transcriptional alterations, which led to the identification of WISP2 as a candidate gene in the SCT/EVT subpopulation. Fetal membrane samples (chorion) were obtained from Qingdao Women and Children's Hospital's Surgical Outpatient Department: 20 RM patients and 20 healthy controls. Using qRT-PCR, Western blot, and immunohistochemistry to detect gene and protein expression. HTR-8 cells were used to construct WISP2 overexpressing cells, and MTT, wound healing and Transwell experiments were performed for functional experiments. Eleven cell classes in the sample were demonstrated by single-cell analysis. Among these cells were DSCs and SCT/extravillous trophoblasts (EVT). The level of WISP2 is low in SCT/EVT cells from RM patients. In chorionic villus tissues, both WISP2 and E-cadherin were significantly upregulated in the RM group relative to the control group (all p  0.05), suggesting that WISP2 promotes an epithelial-like phenotype accompanied by ERK pathway activation. In summary, WISP2 is dysregulated in RM and suppresses trophoblast invasion and EMT in vitro, suggesting a potential role in RM pathogenesis, though in vivo validation is required.
authors: Leng Z, Yan B, Wang F, Bian X, Huang Y, Lv H, Jiang Z, Sun X.

title: Analysis and Identification of Candidate Genes Associated with M1 Macrophage Infiltration and Glycolysis in Breast Cancer.
abstract: Macrophage polarization and glycolytic reprogramming contribute to the breast cancer microenvironment. However, the genes associated with these features and their clinical relevance remain poorly defined. Breast cancer transcriptomic datasets were analyzed using immune deconvolution, single-sample gene set enrichment analysis, and weighted gene coexpression network analysis. We identified 101 genes shared by the M1 macrophage-associated, glycolysis-related, and differentially expressed gene sets. Eight genes showed suggestive genetically predicted associations with BC risk. Machine learning selected seven consensus genes. In TCGA-BRCA, six genes differed significantly between tumor and normal tissue, but only five changed in the same direction as in GSE65194. In the 56 paired clinical tissues, ADAM15, PPP1R14B, and XPO5 were upregulated in tumors, whereas FAM172A and PPM1M were downregulated. ADAM15, PPP1R14B, and XPO5 were preferentially expressed in M1-like TAMs, whereas FAM172A and PPM1M showed higher expression in M2-like TAMs. In BMDMs, overexpression of ADAM15, XPO5, or PPP1R14B, as well as knockdown of PPM1M or FAM172A, increased the proportion of CD80-positive cells and ATP, glucose uptake, and lactate production. Five genes showed significant associations with overall survival. Functional enrichment analyses implicated immune regulation, extracellular matrix organization, and metabolic pathways.
authors: Zhang L, Wu L, Xu C, Fang C, Tian X, Zhu K.

title: Integrative transcriptomic analysis and preclinical validation identify lansoprazole as a therapeutic candidate for preeclampsia.
abstract: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy disorder with often severe consequences across the maternal-fetal dyad and limited treatment options. We performed an integrated meta-analysis of six placental transcriptomic datasets to identify a preeclampsia-specific gene expression signature, revealing dysregulated pathways related to hypoxia, immune dysfunction, and metabolism. Multivariate INTegrative (MINT) analysis was used to establish a smaller predictive signature with potential utility for identifying circulating biomarkers for earlier preeclampsia diagnosis and monitoring disease progression. This preeclampsia signature queried against a transcriptomic database of more than 1,000 compounds identified lansoprazole, a widely used proton pump inhibitor with an established safety profile, as the top-ranked compound based on its ability to reverse the preeclampsia-associated gene expression signature. Protective benefits of lansoprazole were confirmed using a murine model of immune-mediated fetal wastage where treatment overturned elevated soluble FLT1 levels with significantly improved pregnancy outcomes. These findings support further investigation of lansoprazole as a potential therapy for preeclampsia.
authors: Appierdo R, Pham G, Yin O, Tang AS, Shao TY, Severance AL, Yilmaz B, Einhaus J, Wong RJ, Vallania F, Gherardini PF, Helmer-Citterich M, Gaudillière B, Oskotsky TT, Stevenson DK, Way SS, Sirota M.

title: Role of LGALS9 and human milk oligosaccharides in modulating immune responses in food allergy: Insights from network pharmacology and molecular simulations.
abstract: BackgroundFood allergy is a growing global health concern, and effective strategies for restoring immune tolerance remain limited. Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) have potential immunomodulatory effects, but their molecular targets and mechanisms in food allergy are not fully understood.ObjectiveThis study aimed to identify potential protective genes associated with food allergy and to investigate the possible role of LGALS9 in HMO-related immune regulation.MethodsNetwork pharmacology was used to identify overlapping targets between food allergy-associated genes and four selected HMOs: 2'-fucosyllactose, 3'-sialyllactose, lacto-N-neotetraose, and lacto-N-tetraose. Mendelian randomization analysis was performed to assess the association between candidate gene expression and food allergy. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis was used to examine LGALS9 expression across immune cell populations and treatment-response groups. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were conducted to evaluate predicted interactions between LGALS9 and the four HMOs. In vitro BMDC-naïve CD4+ T-cell co-culture assays were further used to assess T-cell differentiation and cytokine secretion.ResultsNetwork pharmacology identified 16 overlapping targets between the four HMOs and food allergy-associated genes. Mendelian randomization analysis showed a significant inverse association between LGALS9 expression and food allergy, supporting a potential protective role. Single-cell analysis of a peanut allergy oral immunotherapy cohort showed that LGALS9 expression was significantly higher in healthy controls than in the patient groups, particularly in Treg cells. Molecular docking suggested that all four HMOs could interact with the selected LGALS9 binding site, with lacto-N-tetraose showing the most favorable docking-derived binding score. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that the predicted complexes remained structurally stable over the simulated period without major conformational changes in LGALS9. In vitro assays showed that HMO-treated BMDCs promoted CD25+Foxp3+ Treg differentiation and increased IL-10 secretion.ConclusionThe integrated computational, transcriptomic, genetic, and in vitro findings identify LGALS9 as a potential HMO-associated immunoregulatory target in food allergy. However, direct functional studies are still required to determine whether the immunomodulatory effects of HMOs are dependent on LGALS9.
authors: Chen S, Ai K, Liu Y, Xiong Z, Zhong W, Yang A, Wu Z, Chen H, Li X.

title: Machine learning-guided multimodal analysis of APAF1-associated tumor microenvironment features prioritizes morellic acid for gastric cancer.
abstract: BackgroundGastric cancer (GC) exhibits substantial molecular heterogeneity and a complex tumor microenvironment (TME). Apoptotic protease-activating factor 1 (APAF1) is a core component of mitochondrial apoptosis; however, its association with immune characteristics, spatial heterogeneity and compound discovery in GC remains poorly defined.MethodsThe bulk transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics with machine learning-based modeling, immune deconvolution and spatial niche analysis were integrated to characterize APAF1-associated features in GC. Machine learning-guided computational screening combining molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations was used to prioritize morellic acid (MA). The biological effects of MA and the involvement of APAF1-associated signaling were evaluated through in vitro and in vivo assays using APAF1-targeting siRNA and shRNA, respectively.ResultsAPAF1 expression was increased in GC, particularly in early-stage tumors and was independently associated with improved overall survival after multivariable adjustment (HR = 0.681, 95% CI: 0.494-0.940, P = 0.0196). However, its standalone prognostic discrimination was limited, with time-dependent ROC analyses showing poor predictive performance. Tumor-versus-normal ROC analysis demonstrated differential expression between GC and normal tissues (AUC = 0.875, 95% CI: 0.823-0.918). Single-cell and spatial analyses revealed that APAF1 expression was associated with distinct immune-cell patterns and tumor spatial niches. Machine learning-guided computational screening prioritized MA as a candidate compound. MA inhibited GC cell proliferation and migration (IC50: 1.807 ± 0.16 to 6.216 ± 0.23 μM) and suppressed tumor growth in vivo, achieving tumor inhibition rates of 79.32 ± 7.69%, 92.37 ± 4.21%, and 92.19 ± 2.99% at low, medium and high doses, respectively. APAF1 silencing attenuated MA-associated changes in cleaved Caspase-3 activation and GSDME-NT accumulation, suggesting the involvement of APAF1-associated cell-death signaling.ConclusionAPAF1 is associated with distinct tumor microenvironment characteristics and clinical features in GC, supporting its potential relevance to tumor biology beyond its canonical role in mitochondrial apoptosis. The novelty of this study lies in extending the investigation of APAF1 beyond its canonical apoptotic function by integrating machine learning with multimodal transcriptomic and spatial analyses to characterize APAF1-associated TME features and computationally prioritize MA. All the findings provide a cross-scale framework linking APAF1-associated tumor biology with candidate compound screening and MA-related cell-death responses in GC.
journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
authors: Jia B, Yan B, Li S, Yang J, Cheng Z, Zhou X, Song W, Hong X, Chen S, Wu Z, Sheng H, Yang Y, Xu F, Wang J.

title: Geographical flavor fingerprinting of Thelephora ganbajun: an integrated analysis of volatile and non-volatile metabolomics, transcriptomics, and environmental factors.
abstract: The geographical variation in the distinctive flavor of Thelephora ganbajun remains poorly understood. We integrated electronic-nose profiling, volatile and non-volatile metabolomics, transcriptomics, nutritional measurements, and environmental data from seven Yunnan origins. Flavor profiles differed across origins: Yimen had the highest total free amino acid content, while Fengqing and Shiping showed stronger earthy and green aroma attributes, respectively. Relative odor activity values highlighted 73 putatively annotated volatiles as potential aroma contributors, including 1-nonen-3-one, 1-octen-3-ol, and 1,3,5-trithiane. Differential non-volatile metabolites were enriched in tryptophan metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, and sesquiterpenoid and triterpenoid biosynthesis. Fourteen candidate genes showed expression patterns associated with selected non-volatile metabolites. Geographical and climatic variables, along with soil available phosphorus and potassium, were associated with pathway variation. These findings provide a basis for characterizing geographical flavor differences and evaluating regional flavor quality in T. ganbajun.
authors: Song L, Yang S, Yang S, Yan R, Wang F, Zhao Q, Zheng H, Gui M.

title: Integrated multi-omics analysis of flavonoid metabolism in soybean seeds of different colours reveals candidate regulatory networks associated with anthocyanin and isoflavone accumulation.
abstract: Soybean seed colour reflects divergence in flavonoid metabolism and is an important quality attribute for edamame and functional food ingredients. The transcript-metabolite patterns associated with anthocyanin and isoflavone accumulation across colour phenotypes remain incompletely characterised. We compared one black-seeded (B), one green-seeded (G), and one yellow-seeded (Y) accession using commercial colorimetric assays, widely targeted metabolomic profiling, and RNA sequencing. Whole-seed assays showed higher total anthocyanin contents in B and G than in Y and a higher total flavonoid content in B than in G and Y. B also showed higher relative abundances of several delphinidin derivatives, proanthocyanidins, and catechins. Selected cyanidin and pelargonidin derivatives were more abundant in Y, whereas daidzein and several triterpenoid saponins were more abundant in G. Transcriptome comparisons identified accession-associated differences in flavonoid-pathway genes, including members of the CHS, CHI, and DFR families. Several flavonoid-related transcripts and metabolites showed parallel patterns across the three accessions. Exploratory DIABLO analysis revealed coordinated variation among the phenotype, metabolite, pathway-gene, and transcription-factor datasets and retained 20 transcription factors across two model components. RT-qPCR mean patterns were broadly similar to the RNA-seq results for some selected genes. Together, these findings reveal distinct flavonoid profiles and associated transcriptional patterns among the three soybean accessions, providing candidate metabolites, genes, and transcription factors for further functional and biochemical investigation.
authors: Qin Y, Chen W, Chen Y, Huang X, Tang F, Guo X, Wei Q, Qin X, Yan H, Chen S, Bai X, Liang J, Wei R.

title: Temporal patterns of melanopsin-evoked calcium signaling engage NF-κB-associated transcriptional and phosphoproteomic responses.
abstract: Cells use oscillatory calcium (Ca2+) signals to regulate diverse biological processes, with temporal dynamics providing a potential layer of intracellular information. We used optogenetic activation of the Gαq-coupled photoreceptor melanopsin to impose defined slow or fast temporal stimulation patterns in human non-excitable cells, evoking oscillatory Ca2+-associated signaling while preserving receptor-proximal signaling. Fast, regular melanopsin stimulation induced stronger nuclear factor κB (NF-κB)-associated tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and interleukin-8 (IL8) expression than temporally irregular stimulation, while TNF and IL8 showed partly distinct responses to stimulation frequency. Transcriptomic analysis identified an MYC-associated gene expression program despite unchanged MYC transcript levels. Integration of transcriptomic and phosphoproteomic datasets identified candidate kinase networks involving PRKDC, CHEK2, and ATM, potentially linking temporally patterned signaling to cell-cycle and stress-response pathways. Together, these findings show that distinct temporal patterns of melanopsin-evoked signaling are associated with distinct transcriptional and phospho-signaling responses, highlighting temporal dynamics as a feature of intracellular information processing.
authors: Nikpour P, Varas-Godoy M, Tenghamn J, Uhlén P, Smedler E.

title: Single-cell heterogeneity of adipose eosinophils is shaped by sex and RELMα and linked to macrophage communication networks in obesity.
abstract: Eosinophils are immune cells with terminal effector functions in type 2 immune responses, yet recent findings suggest that they exhibit functional plasticity and heterogeneity dependent on tissue-specific cues. Building on our prior functional study showing that the immunoregulatory protein RELMα and eosinophils contribute to female protection from high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity, we used single-cell transcriptional profiling to study adipose eosinophil states at higher resolution. We identify six transcriptionally distinct eosinophil clusters whose relative abundance differs by sex, helminth infection, and RELMα status. Adipose tissue from females or helminth-infected mice is enriched for eosinophil clusters with type 2/homeostatic-associated transcriptional programs, whereas males and RELMα-deficient mice have increased representation of inflammatory/MHCII-associated clusters together with an altered predicted macrophage-eosinophil communication networks. Spectral flow cytometry and adipose tissue in situ hybridization independently support eosinophil heterogeneity and candidate chemokine-receptor interactions. Through single-cell regulatory network inference and clustering analysis, we further identified transcription factor regulons unique to the specific eosinophil clusters, including sex-differential and HFD-enriched regulatory programs supported by target-gene expression patterns. Collectively, these data provide a framework for describing adipose eosinophil heterogeneity within a previously established RELMα-macrophage-eosinophil axis and identify candidate transcriptional and communication programs for future functional testing.
authors: Ruggiero-Ruff RE, Qiu X, Vance L, He Y, Coss D, Godzik A, Nair MG.

title: Polysaccharide-based conjugate systems for probiotic encapsulation and colon - targeted release: A review.
abstract: Oral probiotics face viability challenges during processing, storage, and gastrointestinal transit. This critical review provides a unified analytical framework for polysaccharide-based conjugated probiotic encapsulation, bridging synthesis chemistry, delivery mechanisms, and industrial feasibility. Covalent modification and network-forming routes, including Maillard glycation, chemical crosslinking, enzymatic crosslinking, radical-mediated grafting, and thiol-based functionalization, are compared with non-covalent assembly and energy-assisted processing in terms of network architecture, thermal resistance, and scalability. Colon-targeted release mechanisms, including pH-responsive swelling, enzymatic degradation, microbiota fermentation, and multi-stimuli architectures, are critically evaluated. Practical applicability in commercial matrices like yogurt, kefir, honey, and ice cream is discussed alongside processing and regulatory considerations. While conjugated matrices offer superior gastric protection and controllable release, critical gaps remain in release kinetics, long-term storage data, residual crosslinker safety, and strain-specific variability. Translational readiness requires integrating AI-driven predictive design, life cycle assessment, and standardized gastrointestinal simulation protocols.
authors: Ekrami M, Gashtasbi S, Roshani-Dehlaghi N, Samieitousi S, Emam-Djomeh Z.

title: Development of a One-Step RT-LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12b Assay for Rapid On-Site Detection of Dabie Bandavirus.
abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), caused by Dabie bandavirus (DBV), has rapidly spread to multiple countries worldwide since its discovery in 2009, posing a serious threat to global public health security. SFTS is a tick-borne disease, and people living in mountainous and hilly areas are at increased risk of infection, which highlights the urgent need for rapid, accurate, and field-applicable diagnostic strategies for DBV. In this study, LAMP primers and CRISPR sgRNA were designed based on the conserved region of the DBV L segment. A one-pot, one-step molecular assay integrating reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification (RT-LAMP) with CRISPR/Cas12b technology was established after systematic optimization of key parameters. The assay operates under isothermal conditions at 60 °C, delivering results within 40 min. Analytical evaluation demonstrated a limit of detection of 25.6 RNA copies per reaction. No cross-reactivity was observed with Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Chikungunya virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, Dengue virus, and Zika virus. Clinical validation using 42 specimens showed complete concordance with gold-standard qRT-PCR, achieving 100% sensitivity (30/30) and 100% specificity (12/12). For point-of-care application, fluorescence visualization was incorporated into the CRISPR/Cas-based detection workflow, enabling straightforward result interpretation. This integrated RT-LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12b platform provides rapid and specific detection of DBV through a simplified workflow that does not require complex instrumentation, supporting its potential application in resource-limited environments.
authors: Guo J, Wu T, Qiao Q, Zhu X, Zhao K, Cui L, Huo X, Ge Y.

title: Transcriptomics-based drug repositioning in a neurocysticercosis rat model identifies putative therapeutic candidates reported to mitigate neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration
abstract: Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is a major cause of epilepsy and neurological symptoms in low- and middle-income countries. Although antiparasitic treatment targets the parasite, it often fails to fully resolve symptoms and can exacerbate brain tissue damage. Using a rat model of NCC and transcriptomic profiling, we assessed the effects of infection and treatment on brain gene expression to uncover disease molecular pathways and identify putative therapeutic candidates through in silico drug repurposing. We analyzed transcriptomic profiles at two stages of infection (4- and 6-month post-infection (MPI)), and after treatment at 6 MPI (6 MPI + T). At 6 MPI, fewer immune-related genes and pathways were enriched compared to 4 MPI, likely due to MAPK pathway repression, but immune activation increased significantly after treatment, possibly due to cyst degeneration. Drug repositioning identified 30 candidate drugs. Among these, vorinostat, ciclosporin, papaverine, valproic acid, and chlorpromazine have been reported to mitigate neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. Taken together, these results provide a molecular rationale for drug repositioning in neurocysticercosis; however, further experimental validation in larger cohorts is required to confirm the therapeutic potential of the identified candidates.

title: Study of the relationship between transposable elements and microRNAs in the development of glioblastoma for its targeted therapy.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GB) differs from other malignancies in its pronounced aggressiveness, drug resistance (including with modern chemotherapy and anti-PD-1 immunotherapy), high mortality, and the involvement of transposable elements (TEs) in its development. This is reflected in the high frequency of detection of TE-driven chromothripsis in GB samples (39%). Chromothripsis affects chromosomes 7, 9, and 12, with amplification of the EGFR and MDM2/CDK4 oncogenes. GB is characterized by the expression of multiple transcripts and peptides derived from specific TEs and stimulating an antitumor immune response. At the same time, LINE1 and a number of long terminal repeat-containing retroelements have been described as having a tumor-promoting effect on GB. Therefore, a differentiated approach to treating GB is promising, with inhibition of TEs involved in carcinogenesis and simultaneous activation of the safest and most immunogenic TEs (viral mimicry). For this approach, it has been proposed to use microRNAs derived from TEs and represented in the MDTE database. A review of the scientific literature identified 43 such microRNAs with tumor suppressor properties. However, additional experimental and clinical studies are needed for their possible use before these molecules can be considered as therapeutic targets. Twenty oncogenic microRNAs derived from TEs were also identified. Interactions of these microRNAs with long noncoding RNAs and circular RNAs in GB pathogenesis are also described.
authors: Mustafin R.

title: Draft genome sequence of a potential new species of Mesorhizobium isolated from Neltuma juliflora, a tropical legume in Costa Rica
abstract: We present the draft genome of the Mesorhizobium sp. LEGMi-168a strain isolated from Neltuma juliflora (Sw.) Raf. (Fabaceae, Caesalpinioideae) in Costa Rica. It exhibited an average nucleotide identity (ANI) of 91.88% and a digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH) value of 49.90% compared to its closest relative, Mesorhizobium captivum van Lill et al. 2024 (VK22ET). Furthermore, the phylogenetic tree based on the 16S rRNA suggests that the strain belongs to a clade alongside Mesorhizobium shonense Degefu et al. 2013 (DSM 29846T) and Mesorhizobium sp. M1B.F.Ca.ET.045.04.1.1. However, the phylogenomic analyses suggest that this strain does not fall within any currently described species clade. Functional in silico annotation identified the presence of genes related to nodulation capacity (nodA, nodB, nodC, nodD, nodN, and nodO) and others associated with nitrogen fixation (fixU, nifA, nifB, nifE, nifH, nifN, nifQ, and nifW). The differences in ANI and dDDH values, combined with the phylogenomic position relative to known species observed in the in silico analysis, suggest that strain LEGMi-168a represents a potential new species. In this study, we presented the draft genome sequence of strain LEGMi-168a and provided genomic and phylogenetic evidence supporting its potential status as a novel Mesorhizobium species. The genome sequence provided a resource for future comparative, taxonomic, and symbiosis related studies of Mesorhizobium associated with leguminous plants.
authors: Campos-Parra D, Jiménez-Fallas g, Mendoza-Guido B, Rojas-Jimenez K.

title: Culture-negative peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis rates are decreased with water lysis but not 16S rRNA gene sequencing.
abstract: ObjectivesA successful peritoneal dialysis (PD) programme should aim to have low peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis (PDAP) rates. Identification of the microbial organism enables targeted antibiotic treatment and allows for a root cause analysis to be performed. Culture-negative (CN) peritonitis presents a more challenging scenario whereby empirical treatment for Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms is commenced for 14 days, with Gram-negative cover discontinued based upon clinical response. In accordance with ISPD recommendations, we conducted a clinical quality improvement project in 2018 to decrease our culture-negative PDAP.MethodsFrom 2018 to 2021, our department had 336 cases of PDAP. The introduction of a water-lysis step and the application of 16S rRNA gene sequencing were implemented to reduce culture-negative PDAP.ResultsThere were 336 cases of PDAP between 2018 and 2021. In total, 135 cases occurred prior to the initiation of the water lysis step and 201 cases occurred after the introduction of the water lysis step and 16S rRNA sequencing. The rate of culture-negative PDAP prior to our change in PD effluent culture methodology was 33% (45/135); following changes to include a water lysis step and an increase in sample volume, the rate of culture-negative PDAP significantly fell to 20% (41/201) (p p = 0.61).ConclusionsIntroduction of water lysis of peritoneal effluent significantly decreased culture-negative peritonitis rates, thus increasing organism identification and allowing for targeted antimicrobial therapy.
journal: Peritoneal dialysis international : journal of the International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis
authors: Nadarajah L, Butler I, Ciesielczuk H, Lambourne J, Fan S.

title: Genomic and plasmid-level identity between an environmental Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate from India and the high-risk clinical clone HS11286: a comparative genomic analysis of the K. pneumoniae species complex
abstract: Abstract    Background  Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of multidrug-resistant infection, and its persistence in environmental reservoirs is increasingly recognized as a One Health concern. Objectives  To characterize the genomic relatedness of clinical and environmental K. pneumoniae species complex isolates from India to the internationally significant high-risk clinical strain HS11286. Methods  Eleven publicly available  K. pneumoniae  species complex genomes from clinical, river, lake, raw milk, and soil sources were typed using Kleborate and compared by pan-genome (Panaroo) and core-genome phylogenetic analysis (IQ-TREE), average nucleotide identity (fastANI), plasmid replicon typing (PlasmidFinder), and accessory-genome Jaccard similarity. Results  One river water isolate, DCP2, shared sequence type ST11, capsule locus KL103 and O-locus OL2α.1 with HS11286, with a whole-genome average nucleotide identity of 99.99%, the highest pairwise value in the dataset. The two isolates formed a fully supported sister pair (bootstrap = 100) with near-zero branch length, shared an identical complement of five plasmid replicon types at matching sequence identity, and carried the same nine resistance gene classes, including KPC-2 and rmtB. Accessory-genome Jaccard similarity between HS11286 and DCP2 was 0.9956, with 436 accessory genes shared exclusively by this pair. Conclusions  DCP2 and HS11286 represent the same clonal lineage, sharing near-identical core, accessory and plasmid genomic content despite different countries and years of isolation, providing genomic evidence that environmental water can harbour, and potentially disseminate, high-risk clinical K. pneumoniae clones.
authors: Ayesha N, Nair SSD.

title: Effects of a dispersin-containing detergent on the quantitative and qualitative composition of bacterial communities in household washing machines.
abstract: For energy saving purposes, lower washing temperatures are increasingly used in domestic washing processes. In addition, consumers often use liquid detergents, which lack bleach and are less effective against microorganisms. As a result, biofouling in machines and unpleasant odors may develop. Dispersin-amended detergents were recently shown to modify bacterial community composition in washing machines and to reduce laundry malodor. In this study, Oxford Nanopore sequencing of full-length 16S rRNA gene amplicons and quantitative PCR were used to qualitatively and quantitatively examine bacterial communities in two machine parts - sump water and pump sump - after washing with either a dispersin-amended detergent or the same detergent without dispersin. DNA was extracted from all samples in a standardized manner. Full-length 16S rRNA gene sequences (~1.5 kb) revealed the presence of less malodour-associated taxa, such as Rhizobium and Agrobacterium, in machines washed with the dispersin-containing formulation. qPCR showed that biosoil increased markedly after washing without dispersin particularly in the pump sump, whereas it remained nearly unchanged or decreased after washing with dispersin. Overall, the dispersin-amended detergent demonstrated higher cleaning efficiency and prevented biosoil formation, highlighting the potential of dispersin to improve hygiene in domestic laundering.
authors: Seyednikkhoo S, Weide M, Egert M.

title: Comprehensive fecal metabolomics and 16S rRNA gene sequencing for the exploration of the mechanism of sodium cantharidinate in the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a complex malignancy characterized by metabolic and immune dysregulation. Current treatments are limited by insufficient efficacy and severe side-effects. Sodium cantharidinate (SC) is a derivative of cantharidin demonstrated significant antitumor effects, but the mechanism remains unclear. In this study, Murine hepatoma Hepa1-6 cells were implanted in C57BL/6 mice to establish an orthotopic HCC model, and SC was administered intravenously via the tail vein for 14 days. The serum was collected for biochemical analysis, while fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolomics were used to assess gut microbiota profiles and metabolic alterations following SC treatment. Spearman's correlation coefficient was employed to assess the relationships between gut microbiota at the genus level and fecal metabolites. SC treatment significantly suppressed orthotopic tumor growth, reduced the liver weight/body weight ratio, improved serum biochemical parameters, and alleviated histopathological abnormalities. Fecal microbiological analysis revealed that SC reduced the abundance of Muribaculaceae and Adlercreutzia and increased the abundance of Bacteroides and Alistipes. Meanwhile, metabolomic profiling revealed alterations in lipid and purine metabolism involving leukotriene B4, lysophosphatidic acid (LysoPA), and xanthine, which were significantly associated with changes in the relative abundances of gut microbial taxa. Collectively, these findings demonstrated that SC suppressed HCC progression and was associated with coordinated alterations in gut microbial composition and fecal metabolic profiles.
journal: Journal of pharmaceutical and biomedical analysis
authors: Wang Q, Lu D, Xu L, Liu X, Wang P, Liu L, Li X, Zhang J.

title: Rapid and reliable DNA extraction method for the quantification of X- and Y- chromosome-bearing spermatozoa in ram semen.
abstract: Accurate determination of X and Y chromosome-bearing spermatozoa ratios is a useful tool for reproductive management and livestock breeding efficiency. However, the highly condensed chromatin structure of spermatozoa presents a significant challenge for genomic DNA extraction, and current standard protocols are time-consuming. This study aimed to optimise ovine semen DNA extraction for the application of quantifying X and Y chromosome-bearing spermatozoa. A frozen ovine semen sample was divided into four groups (suspension of 30 ×106 spermatozoa cells). Three cell lysis methods; 1) 1 h + 10 µL DTT (dithiothreitol) (n = 8), 2) 1 h + 20 µL DTT (n = 7), and 3) 3 h + 20 µL DTT (n = 7), were designed to evaluate the genomic DNA (gDNA) compared to the 24 h + 10 µL of DTT (n = 8) (standard DNA extraction method). Quantitative Polymerase Chain Reaction (qPCR) SYBR Green assay was used to measure gDNA copy number from the extraction group using the housekeeping gene 18S rRNA. The ratio of X and Y chromosome-bearing spermatozoa was assessed using a qPCR TaqMan assay of Y-specific (SRY) and X-specific (PLP) genes. A gBlock was developed for each 18S rRNA, Y-specific (SRY) and X-specific (PLP) gene to generate the standard curve of both SYBR Green and TaqMan assays. The reference method of 24 h + 10 µL of DTT yielded the highest copies of extracted gDNA (3,040,919.6 copies ± 2,325,479.6), which was significantly greater than all other methods (P < 0.05). Meanwhile, Y:X ratio differed significantly among methods (P < 0.05) by the 24 h + 10 µL DTT and the 1 h + 10 µL DTT treatments yielded comparable Y:X ratios (1.32 ± 0.32 and 1.30 ± 0.21, respectively), indicating no significant difference between these methods. In contrast, 1 h + 20 µL DTT and 3 h + 20 µL DTT resulted in lower Y:X ratios (0.97 ± 0.22 and 0.97 ± 0.17). These findings indicated that the interaction between the DTT concentration and incubation period is critical for releasing spermatozoal DNA. Moreover, the amount of DTT is likely to affect the decondensation of X- and Y-chromosome-bearing spermatozoa differently. In conclusion, optimising the semen DNA extraction method, the 1 h + 10 µL DTT method is less time-consuming and reliable, making it suitable for routine laboratory verification of sperm sex ratio.
authors: Saengruang N, Barton X, Rungruangsak J, Tobe SS, Bruce M, Oskam C, Irons PC.

title: Performance of the BIOFIRE® Joint Infection Panel in the diagnosis of osteoarticular infections in adults and children in Santiago, Chile
abstract: Abstract    Purpose  To evaluate the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of the BIOFIRE® Joint Infection multiplex PCR panel compared to conventional culture and 16S rRNA sequencing for the diagnosis of acute osteoarticular infections (OAI) in a Latin American setting. Methods  A prospective study was conducted between August 2022 and January 2024 at two tertiary hospitals in Santiago, Chile, involving a dual cohort of 124 adults and 32 children. A total of 156 samples (synovial fluid and osteoarticular tissue) were analyzed. JI panel's performance was compared against a Composite Reference Standard (CRS) consisting of standard-of-care culture and universal 16S rRNA PCR with sequencing. Results  Staphylococcus aureus  was the predominant pathogen identified in both cohorts (49.3% by culture vs. 46.8% by JI). For all on-panel microorganisms, the JI panel demonstrated an overall sensitivity of 90.9% (95% CI: 81.3–96.6%) and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 92.4% (95% CI: 84.2–97.2%). In the pediatric population, the panel achieved a specificity of 95.2% and an NPV of 95.2%. Notably, the JI panel maintained high performance in 20.5% of patients with prior antibiotic exposure and successfully identified polymicrobial infections that were missed or underreported by traditional cultures. Conclusions  The JI panel is a rapid, highly accurate tool for the microbiological documentation of OAIs in real-world clinical settings in Latin America. Its high NPV and rapid turnaround time (65 minutes) support its integration into diagnostic stewardship algorithms to optimize early and optimal antimicrobial therapy, particularly in pediatric cases and patients with suspected fastidious or culture-negative infections.
authors: Benadof D, Acuña M, Leiva Y, Yohannessen K, Martínez Á, Oyarzun A, Aldunate JT, Clement P, Bohle C, Vilches V.

title: Association of tonsillar Pseudomonas identified by 16S rRNA sequencing with clinical remission after tonsillectomy in IgA nephropathy: a machine learning approach.
abstract: BackgroundEmerging evidence suggests that mucosal immune responses in the tonsils may be associated with clinical features of immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN). This study characterised the tonsillar microbiota implicated in IgAN using 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing.MethodsWe retrospectively analysed tonsillar tissues from 20 patients with biopsy-proven IgAN and 19 patients with recurrent tonsillitis (RT) who underwent tonsillectomy. The microbiota composition was determined via 16S rRNA sequencing, and the disease-associated genera were identified using the Boruta feature selection algorithm. Their associations with clinical outcomes after tonsillectomy were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, Kaplan-Meier analysis, and log-rank tests.ResultsA total of 194 and 190 genera were detected for IgAN and RT. The α-diversity did not differ significantly between the groups, but the β-diversity analysis revealed distinct microbial community structures (p ConclusionThis study reveals distinct tonsillar microbiota profiles between patients with IgAN and those with RT and shows that tonsillar Pseudomonas enrichment was associated with favourable outcomes after tonsillectomy. These findings suggest that tonsillar Pseudomonas may be associated with clinical remission after tonsillectomy in IgAN.

title: Uterine microbiota across cytological severity of subclinical endometritis in Simmental cows: a full-length 16S rRNA nanopore study.
abstract: Subclinical endometritis (SE) reduces fertility in dairy cows without clinical signs. In this cross-sectional study we compared the uterine microbiota of cows with SE and cytologically healthy cows, and examined how it varies across cytological severity, using full-length 16S rRNA nanopore sequencing. Uterine cytobrush samples were collected 48 to 62 days postpartum from Simmental cows in 24 herds and graded cytologically (score 0 to 3) using thresholds defined a priori. Of 137 cows with a valid score, 105 were included in the primary analysis after 24 cows with fewer than 1000 bacterial reads and eight cows with discordant diversity were excluded. Alpha diversity was higher in cows with SE than in cytologically healthy cows (mean Shannon 3.26 vs 3.03; p: 0.026) and was significantly correlated with the score (ρ: 0.22; p: 0.027), but did not differ among the three SE scores. Community structure differed between the groups (Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA R2: 0.036; p: 0.014), and pairwise comparisons showed significant differences between score 0 and scores 1 and 3, but not among the SE scores. Genera with a higher relative abundance in SE included gut-associated anaerobes such as Paeniclostridium and Mogibacterium, whereas genera with a higher relative abundance in healthy cows were environmental taxa that also dominated the negative control. The differences between healthy and SE cows were not significant when herd or sequencing library was accounted for. Herd explained 46% of the variation in community structure (p: 0.001). Classical uterine pathogens were rare, and Trueperella spp. were detected only at trace levels. Full-length 16S sequencing across four grades of cytological severity showed that diversity and community structure differed between cytologically healthy and SE cows but not among the SE scores, that this difference was not significant after adjustment for herd or sequencing library, and that herd had a significant effect on the uterine microbiota.

title: Bacterial dysbiosis in sinonasal fungal ball: a paired 16S rRNA gene sequencing study
abstract: Abstract    Purpose  Sinonasal fungal ball is usually classified as a non-invasive fungal disease. However, the bacterial changes that accompany the lesion are still not well defined. This study compared bacterial community structure and predicted functional potential between the affected sinus and the contralateral healthy side in patients with sinonasal fungal ball. Methods  Using high-throughput 16S rRNA gene sequencing, 29 paired sinus samples were analysed, including fungal ball diseased-side samples (FBDS) and matched healthy-side samples (FBHS). The cohort included 25 maxillary sinus fungal ball pairs and 4 sphenoid sinus fungal ball pairs. Taxonomic composition, alpha diversity, beta diversity, genus-level differential abundance, co-abundance networks, and PICRUSt-predicted KEGG functional profiles were compared. Results  FBDS and FBHS had distinct bacterial profiles. FBDS showed enrichment of Proteobacteria, Bacteroidetes and Fusobacteria, reduced alpha diversity, altered Bray-Curtis structure, and greater dispersion. Sixteen robust differential genera were identified, including FBDS-enriched  Achromobacter  and FBHS-enriched  Ochrobactrum, Desulfovibrio, Lactobacillus, Lentzea, Sphingomonas, Staphylococcus  and  Corynebacterium  . FBHS also showed a denser co-abundance network. PICRUSt predicted FBDS enrichment in lipopolysaccharide/glycan biosynthesis and translation-related pathways, whereas FBHS was linked to xenobiotic degradation and lipid metabolism. Most findings persisted in maxillary-only analysis. Conclusion  Sinonasal fungal ball was associated with local bacterial dysbiosis on the affected side. The main features were reduced diversity, altered community composition, higher inter-individual variation, a simpler co-abundance structure, and different predicted functional potential. These findings suggest that fungal ball disease may involve localized bacterial ecological remodeling, not only fungal colonization.
authors: Shi P, Wang Y, Zhang Y, Yang T, Zhou J, Zeng Y, Dong S, Li Y, Wei H.

title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals distinct metabolic signatures and gut microbiome alterations across the pediatric obesity spectrum.
abstract: Pediatric obesity drives extensive metabolic remodeling across gut and systemic compartments, yet integrated multi-omics characterization across the full obesity spectrum remains incomplete. We studied 57 Mexican children stratified by BMI into normal weight (NW, n = 15), overweight (Ow, n = 8), and obese (Ob, n = 34) groups using liver enzyme profiling, untargeted fecal and serum metabolomics, 16S rRNA gut microbiome sequencing, and antimicrobial resistance assessment. Demographic parameters were comparable across groups (p = 0.632), minimizing confounding. Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) showed the strongest obesity association (25.5 ± 6.0 vs. 15.0 ± 3.0 U/L in NW; p ρ = 0.92) and Tyzzerella with vulpecholate (ρ = 0.94)-mapping to mechanistic pathways linking SCFAs, bile acids, tryptophan-indole derivatives, and aromatic amino acids to obesity pathogenesis. These findings identify GGT as a sensitive pediatric metabolic biomarker and provide mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets for early intervention.

title: Detection of vector-borne organisms in domestic cats in the United States and Canada (2019 - 2025) with analysis of Hepatozoon variants.
abstract: Published large-scale vector-borne organism (VBO) PCR prevalence studies in domestic cats are limited. The prevalence of VBOs in feline blood samples submitted for PCR testing by a veterinary diagnostic laboratory between January 2, 2019, and December 23, 2025 (n = 7581) was determined. Feline blood samples were tested for Anaplasma, Apicomplexa, Babesia, Bartonella, Cytauxzoon, Ehrlichia, hemotropic Mycoplasma, and Rickettsia. VBOs were detected in 1373/7581 (18.1%) blood samples, with Mycoplasma haemominutum (8.87%) and Bartonella henselae (5.99%) being the most prevalent. Hepatozoon spp. were identified in 40 (0.58%) cats, prompting further genetic and epidemiologic characterization. Sequence analysis of a 182-bp fragment of the Hepatozoon 18S rRNA gene from 40 PCR-positive cats identified seven haplotypes with the highest sequence similarities to Hepatozoon silvestris, Hepatozoon felis, and bobcat-associated Hepatozoon spp. Phylogenetic analysis resolved the variants into major groups clustering with H. silvestris, H. felis, and nondomestic felid-associated Hepatozoon spp. Most Hepatozoon-positive cats originated from the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic regions of the United States (34/40; 85.0%), of which seven infections (7/40; 17.5%) involved cats undergoing blood donor screening. Overall, PCR testing confirmed infection with a VBO in approximately one in five cats tested in the U.S and Canada. Hepatozoon infections were more common than previously recognized, underscoring the value of Hepatozoon-specific PCR in feline VBO diagnostic testing.
authors: Martinez ME, Clarke SB, Wilson JM, Leber ME, Hall CV, Gin TE, Birkenheuer AJ, Breitschwerdt EB, Qurollo BA.

title: Reversal of gut dysbiosis-related arachidonic acid deficiency alleviates Parkinsonian motor deficits and neuroinflammation.
abstract: Gut microbiota dysbiosis has been increasingly implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), but the relationship of microbiota-associated metabolic alterations to PD remains poorly understood. This study investigated the association between gut microbiota dysbiosis and arachidonic acid (AA) dysregulation in PD and evaluated whether modulation of AA homeostasis could ameliorate Parkinsonian phenotypes. Gut microbial alterations were characterized by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and serum metabolic changes were assessed using untargeted metabolomics combined with microbiota-metabolite correlation analysis. Marked gut microbiota dysbiosis was observed in PD mice and was accompanied by reduced serum AA levels. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) increased serum AA levels and improved motor performance, providing functional support for a link between gut microbiota alterations and disrupted AA homeostasis. In addition, exogenous AA supplementation attenuated motor dysfunction and neuroinflammation. Collectively, these findings support a functional association among gut microbiota dysbiosis, altered AA homeostasis, and Parkinsonian phenotypes, suggesting that modulation of gut microbiota composition or AA availability may represent potential strategies for alleviating PD-associated motor dysfunction and neuroinflammation.

title: Molecular Survey of Meat-Borne Zoonotic Protozoa in Food Animals and Poultry in Bangladesh.
abstract: BackgroundMeat-borne protozoan parasites, including Toxoplasma gondii, Sarcocystis spp. and Neospora caninum, present significant veterinary and public health concerns due to their potential transmission through meat.ObjectivesThis study provides the first molecular survey of these parasites in meat-producing animals and poultry in Bangladesh.MethodsWe analysed 236 meat samples from 74 cattle, 114 goats and 48 backyard chickens using PCR assays targeting the REP-529 gene for T. gondii, 18S rRNA for Sarcocystis spp. and NC-5 for N. caninum. Positive samples were sequenced and compared with global isolates.ResultsT. gondii was detected in 7.0% of goats and 2.08% of chickens but not in cattle. Sarcocystis spp. affected 45.9% of cattle, 62.3% of goats and 4.17% of chickens. N. caninum was detected in 25.7% of cattle, 28.9% of goats and 16.67% of chickens. In cattle, Sarcocystis spp. and N. caninum infections were significantly associated with the rearing system and health status, respectively. In goats, Sarcocystis infection was associated with age. DNA sequence analysis identified three Sarcocystis species: S. cruzi in cattle and S. capracanis and S. tenella in goats. Notably, a S. capracanis-like sequence was also unexpectedly detected in chickens.ConclusionsThe detection of zoonotic T. gondii and high prevalence of Sarcocystis spp. and N. caninum indicate foodborne risk and environmental contamination. These findings urge the need for improved farm biosecurity, safe meat handling and One Health-based surveillance in Bangladesh.

title: Dysregulation of selected lncRNAs and Hippo/EMT-associated genes in hepatocellular carcinoma patients.
abstract: Background and aimLiver cancer remains the sixth most common malignancy and the third leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, with hepatocellular carcinoma accounting for most cases. Long non-coding RNAs regulate hepatocarcinogenesis by modulating proliferation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and invasion. This study aimed to characterize the expression of three such transcripts (MALAT1, NEAT1, NKILA) and two protein-coding genes of the Hippo/EMT axis (YAP1, SNAI1) in a single-center Romanian cohort of hepatocellular carcinoma patients and to interpret the resulting pattern in relation to the existing literature.MethodsTumoral and non-tumoral liver tissue samples were obtained from patients with non-metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma undergoing surgical resection. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol, reverse-transcribed, and quantified by SYBR Green-based qRT-PCR on a QuantStudio 7 Flex platform. Relative expression was calculated by the ΔΔCt method, normalized to B2M and 18S rRNA, and compared between the two groups using GraphPad Prism; p Results39 tumoral and 39 non-tumoral tissue samples were analyzed. MALAT1 (p = 0.0008), YAP1 (p = 0.0016), and SNAI1 (p = 0.0365) were significantly overexpressed in tumoral tissue, whereas NEAT1 was significantly reduced (p = 0.0320). NKILA showed no significant difference between groups (p = 0.3592). Effect sizes were graded, with the strongest separation for MALAT1 and YAP1 and more modest differences for SNAI1 and NEAT1.ConclusionMALAT1, YAP1, and SNAI1 overexpression in hepatocellular carcinoma was confirmed in a single-center cohort from Romania, including predominantly early-stage subjects. The reduction of NEAT1 diverges from most prior reports and may reflect isoform-specific detection or the molecular abnormality of the cirrhotic tissue comparator. Future work should incorporate isoform-specific assays, etiology-stratified cohorts, and outcome correlation.

title: Effects of ultrasound on the component, anti-inflammatory activity of adlay seed polyphenols and the mechanism of alleviating colitis.
abstract: Adlay (Coix lacryma-jobi L.) seeds are rich in polyphenols with diverse bioactivities. Ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) was used to prepare adlay seed polyphenols extract (ASP), and the effects of ultrasonic intensity on the composition and in vitro anti-inflammatory activity of ASP were evaluated by UPLC-QTOF-MS and a cellular inflammation model. The anti-colitis mechanism of ASP obtained at the optimal ultrasonic power was further validated in dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis mice. Fourteen major phenolic compounds were identified in ASP. Moderate-intensity ultrasound at 300 W significantly increased the phenolic constituents of ASP by 61.01%, mainly kaempferol, ferulic acid, and coniferyl alcohol, and enhanced its anti-inflammatory bioactivity. In DSS-induced mice, ASP intervention preserved intestinal barrier integrity, suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines, and promoted anti-inflammatory cytokine secretion. 16S rRNA sequencing further showed that ASP restored gut microbial homeostasis by decreasing pro-inflammatory Escherichia-Shigella (57.14%) and Bacteroides (45.83%) and enriching beneficial Lachnospiraceae_NK4A136_group (68.49%), supporting recovery of basal metabolic function and intestinal epithelial repair. Transcriptomic profiling and qPCR validation confirmed that ASP alleviated colitis by suppressing aberrant activation of the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway. Collectively, UAE enhanced the anti-inflammatory bioactivity of ASP, providing a basis for its development and application in colitis intervention.
