title: Citrullination of fibrinogen induced by Porphyromonas gingivalis serve as a key pathway in breaking immune tolerance in rheumatoid arthritis.
abstract: ObjectiveThis study investigates how Porphyromonas gingivalis (P. gingivalis) breaks immune tolerance to citrullinated antigens in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and characterizes the immunogenicity of citrullinated fibrinogen generated by its secreted peptidylarginine deiminase (PPAD).MethodsSubgingival microbiota from ACPA-positive/negative RA patients and healthy controls were profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing and qPCR. Collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mice were orally colonized with wild-type P. gingivalis W83 or a PPAD-knockout strain, with arthritis severity, histopathology, and immune responses assessed. An in vitro citrullination system was used to produce modified fibrinogen, whose binding to ACPA, macrophage activation, and in vivo immunogenicity were evaluated.ResultsP. gingivalis was enriched in ACPA-positive RA patients, correlating with anti-CCP titers and disease activity. Wild-type, but not PPAD-knockout, P. gingivalis exacerbated CIA, boosting anti-CCP levels and splenic B cells. Fibrinogen was the primary substrate upregulated for citrullination in gingiva. The resulting citrullinated fibrinogen formed immune complexes with ACPA that drove M1 macrophage polarization via the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB pathway. In vivo, this modified protein induced anti-CCP antibodies and aggravated arthritis; proteolytically cleaved fragments demonstrated even greater immunogenicity.ConclusionBy secreting PPAD to citrullinate oral fibrinogen, P. gingivalis initiates systemic autoimmunity and promotes ACPA-positive RA. This work strengthens the mucosal origin hypothesis and provides new targets for early intervention.

title: Fecal neuraminidase correlates with inflammatory signatures and microbiome shifts in preclinical Crohn's disease.
abstract: The mucus layer, rich in mucin glycoproteins, serves as a critical barrier to microbial invasion. Neuraminidases cleave terminal sialic acids from mucin glycans, a process that may influence mucus integrity, epithelial exposure to microbial antigens, and mucosal immune responses, making fecal neuraminidase activity a biologically relevant functional readout of host-microbe interactions in the context of Crohn's disease (CD) pathogenesis. We evaluated whether fecal neuraminidase activity is associated with future CD risk and examine its relationships with inflammatory and microbial signatures relevant to early disease development. Within the prospective GEM cohort, 69 individuals who later developed CD were matched to 69 healthy first-degree relative controls. Fecal neuraminidase activity was measured using a fluorometric assay. Conditional logistic regression assessed its association with future CD risk. Partial Spearman correlations evaluated relationships with 446 serum proteins (OLINK), followed by pathway enrichment analysis, and with fecal calprotectin (FCP) and gut microbial composition (16S rRNA sequencing). Fecal neuraminidase activity was positively associated with future CD (OR = 1.541; 95% CI: 1.05-2.25; p = 0.026). Proteins correlated with neuraminidase activity were enriched in immune and inflammatory pathways. Neuraminidase activity was positively correlated positively with FCP (p ≤ 0.05), and its association with future CD was attenuated after adjustment for FCP. Fourteen microbial taxa were significantly correlated with neuraminidase activity (q ≤ 0.05). Fecal neuraminidase activity's relationships with inflammatory markers and microbial taxa support its potential relevance as a functional marker of host-microbe alterations during preclinical CD.

title: Chronic exposure to sulfur species, sodium metabisulfite and methionine, causes gut microbial dysbiosis and impairs intestinal health in adult zebrafish model.
abstract: Sulfur species (SS) are well documented for their toxicity in respiratory and dermal systems; however, their effects on the gastrointestinal (GI) microbiome remain largely unexplored. This research investigated the impact of prolonged exposure to high concentrations of sodium metabisulfite (SM) and L-methionine (MET), administered individually and in combination, on gut microbial composition and intestinal health in zebrafish. High concentrations of SM and MET, particularly in combination, significantly reduced somatic growth and intestinal weight and altered the GI microbiome, as confirmed by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing. The highest combination group showed the greatest relative enrichment of the family Enterobacteriaceae and the genus Enterobacter compared with the control. This dysbiosis-like condition coincided with elevated intestinal sulfide levels, increased total SS accumulation, and lower relative short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) levels. High SS exposure also impaired intestinal digestive enzymatic activity and triggered oxidative stress, evidenced by reduced antioxidant defenses. Histopathological evaluation further confirmed structural injury to the intestinal mucosa, including goblet cell hyperplasia. At the transcriptional level, high SS exposure dysregulated intestinal pro-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic gene expression and upregulated ptgs2a/COX-2 protein expression. Conversely, MET at low individual doses did not show these adverse changes and was instead associated with greater relative abundance of the commensal bacterium Cetobacterium and higher relative SCFA levels. It was also associated with higher antioxidant and digestive enzyme activity, lower MDA levels, and lower baxa expression. In conclusion, these results provide evidence that prolonged exposure to excess SS drives Enterobacteriaceae-dominated gut dysbiosis, redox imbalance, and mucosal inflammation in adult zebrafish.
journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Toxicology & pharmacology : CBP

title: Oil biodegradation and marine oil snow formation in Arctic seawater microcosms at 4 °C
abstract: Hudson Bay is a sub-Arctic inland sea characterized by seasonal sea-ice cover, which governs marine circulation, biological productivity, and ecosystem structure. In recent decades, the duration of sea-ice cover has declined, resulting in longer ice-free seasons that are expected to elevate marine activity and environmental exposure to anthropogenic disturbances. As such, the potential for oil spill incidents associated with increased marine operations is expected to rise. To understand microbial biodegradation dynamics associated with marine oil snow (MOS), seawater microcosms amended with diesel fuel were incubated at 4 °C for 6 weeks. We amended all our microcosms with UV-weathered Churchill diesel fuel at 1% (v/v). 16S rRNA sequencing of the incubations revealed a decline in overall microbial diversity and a dramatic increase in specialized oil-degrading taxa, with  Pseudomonas and  Pseudoalteromonas being the main taxa involved, as both effectively degrade hydrocarbons under ambient and stimulated conditions. Biostimulation with nutrients (NaNO  3 , KH  2 PO  4 ) and an alternative dispersant at 0.1% (v/v) resulted in a greater abundance of MOS aggregates and rapid enrichment of oil-degraders. Simple n-alkanes exhibited the highest biodegradation loss relative to complex polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs); however, biostimulation did not substantially enhance their degradation. Additionally, UV weathering resulted in a 22% loss of PAHs, which is three times higher than the UV loss observed for n-alkanes. Biostimulated samples exhibited an elevated transfer of high molecular weight alkanes and PAHs from the oil into the aqueous phase, accompanied by a rapid enrichment of oil-degrading taxa.

title: Microbial, Metabolic, and Inflammatory Features Associated with Delayed Diabetic Wound Healing in Mice.
abstract: IntroductionDiabetic ulcers are characterized by delayed tissue repair, persistent inflammation, and wound microenvironment remodeling, yet the systemic and local molecular features associated with impaired diabetic wound healing remain incompletely defined.MethodsIn this exploratory pilot study, we profiled gut microbiota (16S rRNA sequencing), wound-tissue metabolites (liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, LC-MS), and local gene expression (reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction, RT-qPCR) in a mouse model of diabetic ulcers. Three biological replicates per group (n = 3 mice/group) were included in each analytical platform.ResultsCompared with non-diabetic wound controls, diabetic mice showed delayed healing alongside altered gut microbial structures, including enrichment of Clostridiales and Mucispirillum and depletion of Lactobacillus. Wound metabolomics tentatively identified candidate metabolic shifts involving molecules such as 16-oxopalmitate and indoleacetaldehyde. Locally, candidate pro-inflammatory genes (Il1b, Tnf, Nos2, Mmp9) were upregulated, whereas candidate repair-associated markers (Arg1, Vegfa) were decreased. Correlation analysis further connected selected diabetes-associated microbial changes with local wound metabolic remodeling, revealing exploratory associations among gut microbial features, wound metabolites, and local inflammatory/repair-related gene expression in delayed diabetic wound healing.DiscussionIn view of very small sample size (n = 3 per group), these findings provide hypothesis-generating preclinical evidence relevant to diabetic wound microenvironment remodeling, and indicates specific microbial, metabolic, and gene-expression targets for larger validation studies.

title: Cervicovaginal microbiome modulates HPV genotype-specific clearance/persistence: role of bacterial dysbiosis in cervical carcinogenesis.
abstract: ObjectivesThis study focuses on the distinct epidemiological features of high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) genotypes in Asian populations: HPV52/56/58 show uniquely high prevalence and strong correlation with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, but their detection rates drop sharply in invasive cervical cancer, a pattern clearly different from the persistent dominance of HPV16/18 throughout malignant progression.MethodsTo further elucidate the potential host-microbe interactions underlying these epidemiological observations, we integrated a 16S rRNA-sequenced cross-sectional discovery cohort and an independent longitudinal validation cohort from a Chinese population, with strict experimental quality control throughout the workflow.ResultThe preliminary analytical results demonstrate that a Lactobacillus-dominant cervicovaginal microbiome (CVM) is significantly and positively associated with HPV viral clearance, while enriched abundance of Gardnerella, Saccharofermentans and Atopobium exhibits a robust correlation with persistent HPV52/56/58 infection. Three undercharacterized microbial taxa-Chryseobacterium, Sphingobacterium and Enhydrobacter are closely linked to sustained HPV16/18 prevalence across advanced disease stages, and show negative correlation with the above obligate anaerobes, which aligns with the sharp decline of HPV52/56/58 in tumor tissues. A hormone-linked Chryseobacterium enrichment were also identified, a taxon with previously reported progesterone-degrading functional properties.ConclusionWhile further longitudinal studies are required to establish causal relationships, our results indicate that CVM dysbiosis may modulate the natural history of these high-burden HPV genotypes, and provide a foundational rationale for subsequent development of genotype-specific, microbiota-targeted cervical disease intervention strategies.

title: A homogeneous acidic polysaccharide from Guangxi-cultivated Alpiniae Oxyphyllae fructus attenuates DSS-induced ulcerative colitis by remodeling the amino acid metabolism-microbiota-barrier axis.
abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic intestinal inflammatory condition with limited management options, driving interest in food-derived bioactive polysaccharides as potential dietary interventions. Alpiniae Oxyphyllae Fructus (AOF), an edible and medicinal plant traditionally used for gastrointestinal health, is widely cultivated in Guangxi, China; however, polysaccharides from Guangxi-grown AOF have not been systematically characterized, and their structure-activity relationships in UC remain undefined. In this study, a homogeneous acidic polysaccharide (AOFP-3) was isolated from Guangxi-cultivated AOF and structurally characterized. Its anti-UC activity was evaluated in a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model by integrating untargeted metabolomics, targeted amino acid profiling, 16S rRNA sequencing, and immunohistochemistry. AOFP-3 was identified as a highly branched acidic heteropolysaccharide (Mw 19.728 kDa) rich in galacturonic acid (53.38%), with a putative backbone of alternating →4)-α-D-GalpA-(1 → and →4)-α-D-GalpA-6-OMe-(1 → residues. In DSS-induced UC mice, AOFP-3 dose-dependently alleviated weight loss, colon shortening, histopathological damage, and inflammation. Mechanistically, AOFP-3 treatment was associated with restoration of amino acid homeostasis, particularly involving branched-chain amino acids and the alanine/glycine-serine-threonine metabolic axis, with remodeling of the gut microbiota (enrichment of Akkermansia and Lactobacillus and suppression of Staphylococcus and Enterococcus) and repair of both physical (Occludin, Claudin-1, ZO-1) and chemical (MUC-2, goblet cells) barriers. These findings establish a structural and mechanistic basis for the bioactivity of Guangxi-grown AOF polysaccharides and support their further investigation as functional food ingredients for gut health promotion.
authors: Xiang Y, He C, Yuan H, Wang E, Yan Z, Li Z, Liu C, Zhang Y, He J.

title: Chronic exposure to diclofenac and meloxicam from early development elicits endpoint-specific adult responses in marine medaka (Oryzias melastigma).
abstract: Adult responses to prolonged exposure to diclofenac (DCF) and meloxicam (MEX) remain insufficiently characterized in marine fish. Marine medaka (Oryzias melastigma) were exposed to nominal concentrations of DCF (0.01-10 μg/L) or MEX (0.1-10 μg/L) from 3 to 4 h post-fertilization to 6 months post-fertilization, with exploratory equimass co-exposures at 0.1 + 0.1 and 10 + 10 μg/L. Adult assessments used three replicate tanks per treatment and included organismal and somatic endpoints, with intestinal 16S rRNA gene profiling and cardiac data-independent acquisition proteomics in selected treatments. No somatic endpoint differed significantly from the solvent control in either sex after multiple-comparison adjustment. Intestinal community composition differed overall among treatments. DCF at 10 μg/L reduced Chao1 richness and Shannon diversity, whereas MEX at 0.1 or 10 μg/L did not differ significantly from the control in either index. Direct DCF-MEX comparisons at 10 μg/L detected no significant differences in sex-specific somatic endpoints or alpha-diversity indices after Holm correction. Cardiac proteomics compared DCF (0.01 and 10 μg/L) and MEX (10 μg/L) treatments with the solvent control. Over-representation analysis identified Lysosome enrichment in all three treatment-control comparisons after pathway-level Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Gene set enrichment analysis identified positive enrichment of Lysosome, Other glycan degradation, and Sphingolipid metabolism in all three comparisons (false discovery rate < 0.05). These findings identify a shared cardiac proteomic signature associated with lysosomal substrate processing, although its implications for intracellular turnover and cardiac performance remain unresolved. The study supports comparative assessment of chronic pharmaceutical responses across biological endpoints.

title: Cryptosporidium Infection Is Associated with Gut Microbiome Alterations in Bangladeshi Children and Families.
abstract: BackgroundCryptosporidium spp. are enteric protozoa associated with moderate-to-severe diarrhea and impaired growth in children worldwide. However, the relationship between Cryptosporidium infection and gut microbiome remains poorly understood.MethodsWe investigated gut microbiota dynamics associated with Cryptosporidium infection in a longitudinal cohort of 84 children and family members in Bangladesh. Fecal samples (n=233) were collected pre-infection, during infection, and post-infection. Microbial profiling was performed using 16S rRNA sequencing, with taxonomic classification and abundance estimation conducted via Cosmos ID-HUB. Associations between infection status, microbial diversity, and taxa abundance were evaluated using multivariable models adjusting for age and sex.ResultsMost Cryptosporidium infections were subclinical (96.1%), with 3.86% presenting diarrhea. In individuals ≥ 3 years of age, gut microbial α-diversity decreased during infection (p-value range = 0.01-3.68x10-10) and increased following recovery (p-value range = 0.0017- 0.0019). During infection, Roseburia and Megaspheara were reduced relative to both pre- (q-value = 0.011 and 0.02) and post-infection (q-value =2.34 x10-5 and 0.001). In addition, Prevotella (q-value = 0.03) and Leuconostoc (q-value=0.04) were reduced relative to pre-infection. Shigella abundance increased during infection (q-value =3.4x10-5) and persisted post-infection (q-value=9.0x10-6). In children ≤ 3 years of age, α-diversity increased during infection compared to pre-infection (p-value=0.045). α-diversity and β-diversity during the post-infection period were associated with lower weight for age z scores.ConclusionsCryptosporidium infection is associated with dynamic and persistent alterations in the gut microbiome, even in the absence of diarrhea, which may be related to impaired child growth, and deserve deeper analysis as promising potential targets for microbiota-mediated interventions.

title: Effects of Maternal Ligature-Induced Periodontitis on Brain in Offspring.
abstract: The combined effects of chronic maternal periodontitis on offspring gut microbiome and brain outcomes remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of maternal oral microbiome disruption on brain function and gut microbiome in offspring. Periodontitis was induced in 11- to 12-wk-old parous C57BL/6J mice by maintaining ligatures around both sides of the maxillary second molars for 4 wk, followed by breeding with naïve male mice. Maternal oral and gut microbiome, as well as the offspring gut microbiome, was analyzed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Male offspring were evaluated at 7 to 8 wk of age via a set of analyses, including behavioral tests, microbiome profiling, RNA sequencing, immunohistochemistry for glial cell populations, and in vivo calcium imaging. Cerebellar DNA methylation was assessed at embryonic day 18.5 to examine early epigenetic alterations. Maternal periodontitis significantly reduced microbial diversity in the maternal oral microbiome and altered the composition of the maternal gut microbiome. In offspring, α-diversity was reduced in the gut microbiome. Behavioral analyses revealed impaired social interaction and reduced spontaneous locomotion, while motor coordination and memory-related behaviors were preserved. RNA sequencing identified region-specific changes in gene expression, particularly in the cerebellum, highlighting its vulnerability to maternal inflammatory conditions. DNA methylation analysis revealed epigenetic alterations during the fetal stage, suggesting early programming effects. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated a significant increase in astrocyte density in the cerebellum and frontal cortex, whereas oligodendrocytes and microglia were unaffected. Furthermore, calcium imaging revealed disrupted neuronal synchrony among Purkinje cells without significant changes in individual neuronal activity parameters. Maternal oral microbiome disruption induces coordinated alterations in maternal and offspring microbiomes and leads to persistent neurobehavioral, molecular, and cellular changes in offspring. These findings provide new insights into the link between maternal oral health and offspring neurodevelopment, highlighting the potential role of microbiome-mediated mechanisms in shaping brain function.

title: Using brewing industry byproducts to create feed additives for aquaculture-raised rainbow trout under thermal stress.
abstract: The aquaculture industry helps meet the seafood demands of a rapidly growing human population. The goal of this study was to determine the effects of feed additives, generated from byproducts of the beer brewing industry, on the growth rate, production parameters, and intestinal bacterial composition of aquaculture-raised rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss). Two prevalent brewery byproducts, brewer's spent yeast (BSY) and brewer's spent grain (BSG), were converted into high-value fish feed additives. To increase nutritional value of the byproducts, BSY was treated with exoenzymes, and BSG was used to cultivate black soldier fly (BSF; Hermetia illucens) larvae, which was treated with proprietary chitinases. During a seven-week trial using a recirculating aquaculture system, 22.15 ± 0.24 g (mean ± standard error) fish were randomly separated with 12 fish/tank in quadruplicate for each of the six diets (48 fish per diet), and tanks were randomly assigned diets. Survival rates were recorded daily, and fish were weighed every two weeks to track growth rates, adjust feed amounts, and calculate feed efficiency at the tank level. Fish intestinal mucosa swabs were collected at the beginning and end of the trial to analyze changes in the bacterial communities. Due to a malfunction in the chiller that maintained cool water temperatures, temperature and dissolved oxygen became substantial chronic (two week) and then acute (12-24 hr) stress factors near the end of the trial. Therefore, the research focus shifted to understand the impacts of thermal and oxygen stress on fish fed these novel feed additives. Clear changes in the structure of the bacterial intestinal community were observed in the fish between the start and end of the study as evaluated by 16S rRNA gene analysis. Results suggest that fish fed three of the experimental diets benefitted by having higher survival rates and growth rates when subjected to the unplanned stress.
authors: Layton AR, Pough Ii JD, Kuhn DD, Stevens AM.

title: Knowledge gap in vertebrate genetic diversity in a northern remanent of neotropical rainforest.
abstract: Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve is one of the last remaining areas of primary tropical rainforest in Mexico. This fragile ecosystem heavily reduced by human perturbations is part of the Mesoamerican hotspot. The reserve harbors many endemic species. Thus, identifying, cataloging, and studying the biodiversity of this ecosystem has been of utmost importance. A promising approach for fast species identification to assess biodiversity is the use of DNA barcoding techniques. However, these techniques are limited by reliable DNA databases. Using novel Perl scripts, we generated a barcoding database to assess mitochondrial sequence availability in public databases for 903 vertebrate species that inhabit the reserve. Of these, 39 species had no sequences, 189 had complete mitochondrial genomes sequenced and the rest were partially sequenced. We studied over 80,000 sequences spanning 16 mitochondrial genomic markers and found 5 well-studied markers (COI-5P, CYTB, ND2, 16S rRNA and 12S rRNA) with more than 50% species coverage. The COI-5P region and CYTB were the best studied and most recommended markers for barcoding studies, and 7 additional markers have been preferred for one or more specific taxonomic groups. The remaining markers were almost exclusively sequenced as part of whole mitochondrial genomes. The best-known taxonomic group was mammals while the least known was reptiles. We also evaluated the sequencing frequency distribution for endemic, threatened and trade-restricted species driving interests in ecological research. In general, most species within each group were less sequenced when compared to the mean of all species, skewed by a few highly sequenced species of ecological interest. The most sequenced species are trade-restricted species, especially threatened species. This is driven by ecology-based research in the area. Finally, our results highlight a lack of barcoding research in local and endemic species of the Mesoamerican hotspot focusing on specific species but ignoring the wider range of biodiversity.
authors: Martínez Cano DJ, Reynoso VH, Vázquez-Cruz ML, Alvarado-Robledo EJ, Ángeles-López YI, Zarza E.

title: Chronic Arsenic Exposure Induces Hepatocyte Proliferation in Rats via the Gut-Liver Axis: Interventions With Fecal Microbiota Transplantation and/or Arsenic Withdrawal.
abstract: Arsenic (As) contamination in groundwater has been reported in many countries and is a major risk factor for liver injury. While the impact of arsenic exposure on gut microbiota and its role in liver diseases through the gut-liver axis has been documented, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. In this study, we established a chronic arsenic exposure rat model by administering sodium arsenite (NaAsO2) at concentrations of 30 and 100 mg/L through drinking water until 62 weeks of age. Subsequently, high As-exposed rats were subjected to fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), arsenic cessation, or combined FMT and arsenic cessation interventions for 2 months. Liver pathological changes, hepatocyte proliferation, intestinal microbiota composition, fecal butyrate levels, and the expression of butyrate-related molecular markers were evaluated using hematoxylin-eosin staining, immunohistochemistry, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, gas chromatography, and quantitative real-time PCR. Chronic arsenic exposure increased hepatocyte proliferation, as evidenced by elevated PCNA and Ki-67 expression in liver tissues. Microbiota analysis revealed that arsenic exposure significantly altered gut microbial community structure and reduced the abundance of butyrate-producing bacteria, particularly Lachnospiraceae and Blautia. Consistently, fecal butyrate levels showed a decreasing trend after arsenic exposure. Furthermore, arsenic exposure significantly suppressed hepatic miR-22 expression, accompanied by increased expression of Sirt1 and Ctnnb1 and decreased expression of Gsk3b, suggesting activation of a proliferation-related signaling pathway. Intervention with FMT and/or arsenic cessation partially restored gut microbiota composition, alleviated miR-22 suppression, and improved arsenic-induced molecular alterations. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that chronic arsenic exposure promotes hepatocyte proliferation through disruption of gut microbiota and reduction of microbiota-derived butyrate, which may regulate the miR-22/Sirt1 signaling pathway. Restoration of intestinal microbiota by FMT or cessation of arsenic exposure may provide potential strategies for mitigating arsenic-induced hepatic abnormalities.
authors: Wang K, Liu Y, Wang L, Xu Y, Gu Z, Sun R, Wei C, Zhao Q, Li B, Yan X, Qiu Y.

title: Gamma irradiation concerning genetics of Ralstonia solanacearum and export quality in potatoes.
abstract: BackgroundPotato brown rot, caused by Ralstonia solanacearum, is an important quarantine disease that can seriously affect tuber quality and limit the movement and marketability of potatoes. Gamma irradiation may help control the pathogen after harvest, but the dose used can also affect the nutritional value and quality of potato tubers.PurposeWe aimed to study the genetic diversity of the potato brown rot pathogen, Ralstonia solanacearum, using molecular markers. We also evaluated how irradiation affects the physicochemical properties of treated and untreated potato tubers.Materials and methodsCommercial potato varieties were collected from major potato-growing areas of Bangladesh for pathogen isolation and irradiation studies. Forty-two bacterial isolates were characterized on TTC medium and examined using PS-1/PS-2 PCR, 16S rRNA sequencing, phylotype-specific PCR, and mutS amplification. After irradiation, the tubers were assessed for weight loss, ascorbic acid, anthocyanin, carotenoid, total soluble solids (TSS), and mineral content.ResultsVirulent isolates produced the expected 553-bp PS-1/PS-2 amplicon. Sequence analysis placed a representative isolate close to Asian Ralstonia reference strains, while phylotype-specific PCR generated a 213-bp product corresponding to phylotype IV. The pathogen-specific 553-bp amplicon remained detectable up to 5.5 kGy but was not detected at 6 kGy under the conditions used in this study. A reduction in mutS band intensity was also observed following irradiation. The effects of irradiation on tuber quality varied with cultivar and dose. Ascorbic acid and carotenoid contents generally decreased with increasing irradiation dose, whereas anthocyanin and TSS remained comparatively stable. Mineral concentrations were generally higher in irradiated tubers than in untreated samples.ConclusionGamma irradiation reduced the detectability of the pathogen-specific PCR target, although this does not confirm complete pathogen inactivation. Irradiation conditions require optimization to balance pathogen suppression and nutritional quality. Further viability testing and genomic characterization are recommended.
authors: Haque MM, Haque M, Hasna MK, Khalil MI, Mortuza MF, Hossain MA, Paul NR, Akter S, Mehedi MNH.

title: Associations of gut microbial and serum metabolic features with metabolic comorbidities in patients with NAFLD.
abstract: IntroductionNon-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) coexists with dyslipidemia or impaired fasting glucose (IFG), but gut microbial and serum metabolic features remain incompletely characterized.ObjectivesWe aimed to compare gut microbial beta diversity, taxonomic profiles, predicted microbial functions, and serum metabolites across healthy controls (HCs) and NAFLD subgroups; evaluate omics-based classifiers and exploratory integrated classifiers distinguishing subgroups from HCs; and assess metabolic responses to Dialister invisus supplementation in mice.MethodsFecal microbiota and serum metabolites were profiled by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and targeted UPLC-MS/MS, respectively, in 41 HCs and 222 NAFLD patients. Patients were stratified into three subgroups by dyslipidemia and IFG: NAFLD_N (neither dyslipidemia nor IFG), NAFLD_DLP (dyslipidemia without IFG), and NAFLD_IFG (IFG irrespective of lipid status; HbA1c/OGTT unavailable). Random-forest classifiers were developed for each omics layer and for post hoc integrated multi-omics panels to distinguish each NAFLD subgroup from HCs, with performance evaluated in the held-out set. Dialister invisus was administered to high-calorie diet-fed mice, and metabolic and hepatic outcomes were assessed.ResultsNAFLD patients showed lower Dialister invisus abundance and higher abundance of the GTDB placeholder taxon Phascolarctobacterium_A sp900545025, with increased predicted menaquinone biosynthetic potential. Microbial and serum metabolite profiles differed significantly among subgroups. Microbiome classifiers achieved AUROCs of 0.71, 0.58, and 0.73 in the held-out internal evaluation, whereas metabolome classifiers achieved AUROCs of 0.89, 0.83, and 0.93 for NAFLD_N, NAFLD_DLP, and NAFLD_IFG. Post hoc integrated panels yielded descriptive AUROCs of 0.92, 0.89, and 0.96 in that subset. Dialister invisus supplementation reduced body weight, serum ALT, AST, triglycerides, fasting blood glucose, and ipGTT AUC in high-calorie diet-fed mice.ConclusionThis study identifies shared gut microbial and serum metabolic alterations across NAFLD patients irrespective of IFG or dyslipidemia, alongside subgroup-specific signatures. The Dialister invisus findings support its potential role in metabolic regulation and warrant mechanistic investigation.

title: Staphylococcus aureus-derived xanthine exacerbates allergic rhinitis-induced olfactory dysfunction through promoting Th17 cell differentiation and IL-17A production.
abstract: ObjectivesAllergic rhinitis (AR) is frequently accompanied by olfactory dysfunction (OD), yet the role of microbial metabolites in this process remains poorly elucidated. This study aimed to investigate how xanthine, a metabolite derived from Staphylococcus aureus (Sa), exacerbates AR-induced OD by promoting Th17 cell differentiation and IL-17A production.MethodsMulti-omics analyses, comprising metabolomics, proteomics and 16S rRNA gene sequencing, were performed on AR patients and mouse models with AR. Sa was cultured and key metabolites in its supernatant were detected using untargeted metabolomics. AR mice were nasally challenged with Sa supernatant or xanthine, and comparisons were made with mice with chronic AR and OD. The therapeutic potential of an anti-IL-17A neutralising antibody was assessed in AR mice stimulated with Sa supernatant or xanthine.ResultsPurine metabolism was significantly enriched, and xanthine levels were elevated in AR patients and mouse models, particularly those with OD. Airway microbial dysbiosis in AR mice was characterised by increased Staphylococcus abundance, and the Sa infection pathway was enriched in patients with AR. Untargeted metabolomics of Sa supernatant revealed increased xanthine levels and enrichment of purine metabolism. Nasal challenge with Sa supernatant or xanthine significantly exacerbated OD. Mechanistically, xanthine promoted Th17 cell differentiation and IL-17A production. Notably, IL-17A neutralisation effectively alleviated xanthine-exacerbated OD, indicating a pivotal role for the IL-17A pathway in this process.ConclusionSa-derived xanthine aggravates AR-induced OD by driving Th17 cell differentiation and IL-17A production. These findings highlight the xanthine-IL-17A pathway as a potential therapeutic target for improving olfactory function in AR.
authors: Hu Y, Wang W, Yang T, Song X, Wang Y, Cheng Y, Mou Y, Ren C, Song X.

title: Effects of high-concentrate feeding and yeast culture supplementation on cecal fermentation, microbiota, metabolite profiles, and mucosal responses in lambs.
abstract: ObjectiveAlthough yeast culture (YC) has been widely studied for its beneficial effects on ruminal fermentation, its effects on cecal microbial, metabolic, and mucosal responses under high-concentrate feeding remain unclear. This study evaluated cecal fermentation, microbial, metabolic, and mucosal responses to high-concentrate feeding and YC supplementation in lambs.MethodsForty-five three-month-old Du × Han F1 male lambs were assigned to three dietary treatments for 60 days: a control diet with a concentrate-to-roughage ratio of 1.3:1 (CON), a high-concentrate diet with a ratio of 1.7:1 (HC), or the HC diet supplemented with 0.5% YC. At the end of the trial, six lambs from each treatment were selected for terminal sampling. Cecal fermentation, mucosal histology, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, and quantitative real-time PCR were evaluated.ResultsCompared with the CON group, HC feeding decreased cecal pH, acetate, isovalerate, valerate, and the acetate-to-propionate ratio and was accompanied by mucosal injury, lower expression of tight junction-related genes, and higher expression of inflammatory cytokines. Alpha diversity did not differ among treatments, whereas overall microbial community structure and cecal metabolic profiles varied among groups. YC supplementation increased cecal pH and improved selected fermentation indices, particularly valerate concentration and the acetate-to-propionate ratio. It also ameliorated mucosal lesions, increased the expression of ZO-1, Occludin, Claudin-1, and Claudin-4, and decreased TNF-α and IL-1β expression. Candidate differential metabolites identified between the YC and HC groups were associated with pathways including cholesterol metabolism, primary bile acid biosynthesis, bile secretion, ABC transporters, and AMPK signaling. Exploratory correlation analysis identified nominal associations between selected bacterial genera and candidate differential metabolites related to lipid, organic acid, and bile acid metabolism.ConclusionYC supplementation partially alleviated high-concentrate diet-associated alterations in cecal fermentation and mucosal injury, accompanied by changes in barrier-related gene expression, cecal microbiota, and metabolite profiles.
authors: Cheng Y, Niu M, Pan Y.

title: A cohort study of the bacterial faecal microbiota development post-weaning in healthy piglets in pig herds with different intestinal health status.
abstract: BackgroundWeaning of piglets in commercial production involves a sudden separation from the sow and an abrupt switch to a grain-based feed. During this phase of gut microbiota adaptation, disease-associated bacteria, such as enterotoxin-producing Escherichia coli, can proliferate, causing post-weaning diarrhoea (PWD). An observational cohort study of the faecal microbiota development during the first three weeks post-weaning in apparently healthy piglets from three farms was conducted. Four sample series were made, where Farm 1, which had no clinical signs of PWD, was sampled twice. Farm 2 had intermittent PWD problems, and Farm 3 used high-dose zinc oxide (ZnO) after weaning. Rectal swab samples were collected before weaning and on days 3, 7, 10, 14 and 21 after weaning. The bacterial faecal microbiota was assessed using 16S rRNA V3-V4 variable region sequencing.ResultsOf the identified amplicon sequence variants, 99% and 84% could be classified at the phylum and family level, respectively. Firmicutes and Bacteroidota were the two dominant phyla in all study groups. In Farm 2, with intermittent PWD problems, the relative abundance of Proteobacteria was significantly higher compared to the other study groups (P ConclusionsA difference between the gut microbiota of piglets before and after weaning was found in all study groups. Weaning led to an imbalance in gut microbiota and changes to the faecal consistency, even in piglets without clinical PWD. The faecal microbiota composition differed between study groups and across the study period, also between repeated samplings of the same farm. The higher relative abundance of Proteobacteria in the herd with intermittent PWD problems could be a contributing factor to the recurring issues with PWD in this herd. The use of ZnO seemed to have delayed the maturation of the microbiota, although further studies are needed to confirm this. Overall, the results show that no single microbiota composition can predict weaning without gut disturbances.
authors: Klahr Fritz M, Rosendal T, Leijon M, Sannö A, Wallgren P, Sjölund M.

title: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii-associated 18β-glycyrrhetinic acid protects against sepsis via ABCC1-mediated suppression of MAPK/NF-κB signaling.
abstract: Gut microbiota dysbiosis is increasingly recognized as a modifiable determinant of sepsis susceptibility and outcomes, yet protective commensals and microbiota-associated metabolites with actionable host mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Here, fecal 16S rRNA sequencing of septic and non-septic patients revealed a marked depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii during sepsis. Oral administration of F. prausnitzii improved survival and alleviated multiorgan injury in mice subjected to cecal ligation and puncture. Untargeted metabolomics and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry identified 18β-glycyrrhetinic acid (18β-GA) as a major metabolite enriched in F. prausnitzii culture supernatants, and exogenous 18β-GA recapitulated key protective effects in vivo. In lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages, 18β-GA reduced pro-inflammatory mediator expression and suppressed mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation. Proteomics-guided prioritization and complementary pharmacological and genetic validation implicated ATP-binding cassette subfamily C member 1 (ABCC1) as a mediator involved in the protective effects of 18β-GA. Genetic silencing of ABCC1 attenuated the anti-inflammatory effects of 18β-GA, while pharmacological inhibition of ABCC1 by probenecid (PBN) and MK-571 partially reproduced the protective effects of 18β-GA. Collectively, these findings identify a F. prausnitzii-18β-GA-associated ABCC1 regulatory axis that contributes to the control of septic inflammation and highlight microbiota-derived metabolites as potential modulators of host inflammatory responses.IMPORTANCESepsis is a life-threatening syndrome with limited effective therapies beyond supportive care. Gut microbiota disruption is increasingly recognized as an important contributor to sepsis, but the protective microbes, effector metabolites, and host pathways involved are not well understood. Here, we show that F. prausnitzii is markedly depleted in sepsis and that supplementation with this commensal improves outcomes in experimental sepsis. We further identify 18β-glycyrrhetinic acid as a microbiota-associated metabolite with anti-inflammatory and organ-protective activity and implicate ABCC1 as a functionally relevant host target. Our findings provide mechanistic insight into how protective commensals can influence sepsis progression and support microbiome-informed, host-directed therapeutic strategies.

title: The Integration Methodology of Metabolomics, Bioinformatics and Western Blot to Investigate the Mechanism of the Jiawei Erzhi Formula in Treating Postmenopausal Osteoporosis based on Intestinal Microecology.
abstract: IntroductionPostmenopausal Osteoporosis (PMOP) is a prevalent disorder characterized by estrogen deficiency-induced bone loss, microstructural deterioration, and increased fracture risk. Jiawei Erzhi Formula (JWEZF) has shown therapeutic potential in PMOP. Clinical observations indicate that JWEZF not only improves bone outcomes but also alleviates constipation in certain patients, suggesting a modulatory effect on intestinal microecology. Based on the gut-bone axis, the present study explored the potential mechanisms of JWEZF in treating PMOP from a gut microecology perspective.MethodsOvariectomized (OVX) SD rats were used as a PMOP model, with a focus on intestinal microecology. The comprehensive analytical approach encompassed bioinformatics, 16S rRNA microbial sequencing, fecal non-targeted metabolomics, targeted bile acid quantification, immunohistochemistry, and Western blot validation.ResultsBioinformatics identified 27 potential signaling pathways associated with steroid and bile acid metabolism. Microbial sequencing demonstrated that JWEZF restored intestinal microecological homeostasis by regulating the abundance of key bacterial taxa, including Lachnospiraceae. In the Model group, Bacteroidetes increased to 34.89%, and Firmicutes decreased to 53.10%, whereas JWEZF treatment partially restored these proportions. Metabolomics revealed differential metabolites primarily linked to bile acid biosynthesis, steroid synthesis, and steroid hormone synthesis pathways. Quantitative bile acid analysis showed that JWEZF treatment was associated with normalization of abnormal fecal bile acid profiles. The GLP-1-positive staining area decreased in the Model group (1.14 ± 0.77%) compared with the Sham group (3.97 ± 0.96%) and increased after JWEZF treatment, particularly in the High-dose group (3.92 ± 1.02%). Western blot analysis showed that TGR5 protein expression was reduced in the Model group (0.20 ± 0.05) and increased following JWEZF treatment.DiscussionThese findings indicate that JWEZF treatment was associated with coordinated changes in gut microbiota composition, fecal bile acid metabolism, and intestinal TGR5/GLP-1-related markers. The results, together with correlation analyses integrating microbial, metabolomic, and signaling-marker datasets, support the potential involvement of a gut microbiota-bile acid-TGR5/GLP-1 regulatory axis. However, the evidence remains associative and requires functional validation.ConclusionJWEZF alleviates PMOP by modulating gut microbiota composition and bile acid metabolism, with potential involvement of TGR5/GLP-1 signaling in regulating bone metabolism.
authors: Ding Y, Hou C, Liu J, Liu X, Li Y, Liu E, Chen X.

title: Exploration of Low-Abundance Tundrisphaera and Tissue 3-Hydroxybutyric Acid (β-HB) in Gastric Cancer Lymphovascular Invasion: A Multi- Cohort Multi-Omics Study with Clearly Defined Evidence Boundaries
abstract: Abstract  Background  Lymphovascular invasion (LVI) is one of the early routes of gastric cancer dissemination. Tissue-associated microorganisms and ketone-body metabolism may be associated with aggressive disease, but parallel between-group differences cannot establish a microbial–metabolic mechanism. This study integrated a discovery cohort with paired gastric tissue 16S rRNA and targeted metabolomics data, together with public transcriptomic, single-cell, methylation, dependency, and perturbation resources. Methods  Clinical LVI labels were available for 66 gastric cancer cases, of which 65 had both 16S and metabolomics data (32 LVI-negative [V0] and 33 LVI-positive [V1] cases). We evaluated microbial diversity, community composition, genus-level differences, and a random forest classifier with rigorous control of information leakage, and implemented a mutually exclusive two-stage descriptive genus screen. The strict tier required a mean relative abundance of ≤ 0.01% in V0 and ≥ 0.05% in V1, and a pseudocount-adjusted fold change of ≥ 10; genera that did not meet the strict-tier criteria entered a relaxed additional tier, which required a V1 cumulative genus-table count of ≥ 20 and a ≥ 10-fold increase in mean abundance. DepMap and LINCS analyses were used only to prioritize experimental candidates. title: De Novo transcriptome assembly and functional annotation in non-model organisms.
abstract: Advances in RNA sequencing have established transcriptomics as a key approach for investigating gene expression, regulation, and functional diversity across both model and non-model organisms. In the absence of high-quality reference genomes, de novo transcriptome assembly remains essential, yet its accuracy and reproducibility depend heavily on the choice and integration of computational strategies. This review provides a comprehensive and structured framework for de novo transcriptome reconstruction and functional annotation in non-model systems, integrating current best practices across quality control, assembly, redundancy reduction, and annotation workflows. We systematically compare short-read, long-read, and hybrid assembly approaches, and evaluate multi-layered annotation strategies combining homology-based, domain-based, and ontology-driven methods. We further highlight emerging developments, including long-read transcriptomics, machine learning-assisted annotation, orthology inference, and multi-omics integration, which improve transcriptome completeness and biological interpretability. Key limitations in current workflows are critically examined, including database biases, incomplete annotations, and challenges in isoform resolution, particularly in underrepresented taxa. By consolidating methodological advances with practical recommendations, this review proposes a reproducible and scalable roadmap for transcriptome analysis in non-model organisms. We also discuss future directions, including the development of inclusive reference databases, AI-driven annotation frameworks, and open, containerized infrastructures aligned with FAIR principles to support global transcriptomics research.
authors: Habib N, Rfaki A, Al Idrissi N, Nejjari C, Belyamani L, Ghazal H.

title: PartiDesign: A structure-sequence co-design paradigm for practical all-to-all biomolecules design
abstract: Engineering interactions among biomolecules offers a route to creating new biological functions. Although unified models have advanced biomolecular structure prediction and design, efficient and controllable generation across molecular modalities remains challenging. A key challenge is to couple three-dimensional structure generation with sequence or chemical-identity design across chemically diverse systems. Here, we introduce PartiDesign, a unified structure-sequence co-design model that extends the partially latent framework of La-Proteina to proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules. PartiDesign jointly generates molecular structures and their corresponding sequences or chemical identities, while providing fine-grained control over secondary structure, chemical bonding and amino acid preferences. Across diverse benchmarks for the de novo design of proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules against specified targets, PartiDesign achieved the highest estimated successful-design throughput among the evaluated methods on most benchmarks under the adopted compute-budget protocols. Its configurable constraints further support cyclic peptide and antibody design, allowing generation to be tailored to specific structural and chemical requirements. PartiDesign was developed using 128 Huawei Ascend 910B accelerators, each with 64 GB of memory. The source code is available at https://github.com/MegaGatlingPea/PartiDesign-official, and a freely accessible web server at https://cadd.zju.edu.cn/partidesign/ enables users to generate binding partners without programming expertise. Together, these capabilities provide a versatile and accessible framework for all-to-all biomolecular design, with applications in molecular engineering and drug discovery.
authors: Jin Z, Zhang X, Kang Y, Hou T.

title: The Genome Lab: designing a simpler interface for genome assembly and annotation
abstract: Background:  Galaxy is a web-based platform for analysing data, particularly biological data such as DNA. While genome assembly and annotation is a typical starting point for users, navigating this process can be challenging: many factors affect which tools and settings are appropriate, and researchers with genomes to analyse often have deep taxonomic expertise but less bioinformatics experience. Methods To better present relevant resources, we built the Genome Lab: a domain-specific interface for genome assembly and annotation. Informed by user experience considerations, the design targets discoverability and navigation, and is intended to reduce the effort required to find resources and to understand the genome assembly process. Applying six key design decisions, we gave the Lab a clear, simple layout showing an organised set of tools and workflows, so that new users can get started quickly and experienced users have their frequently required resources at hand. Results We present a worked example of genome assembly and annotation, carried out the way a researcher might use the Genome Lab. Working from Nanopore sequencing reads, the curated path produced a genome assembly, a completeness assessment and gene models, viewed in a genome browser. Conclusions The Genome Lab has been implemented as a generic framework that other communities have since used to build Labs for their own domains, on Galaxy Australia and elsewhere. A curated, domain-specific interface provides a simpler entry point for researchers new to the field. We describe the design decisions, the framework and a worked example, which may help other groups build a similar interface for their own domain.
authors: Syme A, Hyde C, Thang WM, Mok W, Price G.

title: Folding without glutamine: Proteome-scale removal of a canonical amino acid.
abstract: All known life uses a canonical alphabet of 20 amino acids, yet which residues are structurally essential remains untested at proteome scale. Isoleucine was recently eliminated from ribosomal proteins in Escherichia coli, establishing that amino acid alphabet reduction is feasible. Here we ask whether an entire amino acid can be eliminated from a proteome, and develop a computational framework to identify the best target. Using two independent approaches - ProteinMPNN structure-based probabilities and multiple sequence alignment conservation - we define "keep-score" as the fraction of positions where the native residue is optimal. Both methods converge on an unexpected candidate: glutamine has the lowest keep-score, with proline and glycine the highest - counter to substitution-matrix intuition. Glutamine's low keep-score is not explained by a single obvious substitute; glutamate is preferred in only 14% of replacements. Removing this target proteome-wide, we replaced every glutamine across 4,148 proteins with ProteinMPNN-optimal alternatives and modeled the resulting sequences with AlphaFold2. The recoded proteome maintained native-like structures: 85.5% of models exceeded a TMscore of 0.8, indistinguishable from the 85.9% baseline for rebuilt native sequences. Orthogonal validation - ESMFold predictions, Rosetta energy calculations, and conformational ensemble comparisons - revealed no evidence of systematic misfolding attributable to glutamine removal. As a consistency check, a glutamine-free TEM-1 β-lactamase designed with ProteinMPNN conferred ampicillin resistance in E. coli, indicating fold preservation can extend to biological function. Evolutionary evidence further supports these findings: 24% of E. coli proteins have glutamine-free orthologs in prokaryotic genomes, and glutamine ranks lowest in keep-score in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. These results show that an entire amino acid can be removed from a proteome with folds broadly preserved, establishing keep-score as a general framework and glutamine as the primary candidate for recoding. Crucially, this reflects a computational analysis of structural replaceability, not a demonstration of biological dispensability.
authors: Garciarrubio A, Ramos-Cerrillo B, Morett E, Segovia L.

title: Prediction of Intrinsic Disorder in Protein Sequences Using the Fast and Accurate flDPnn2 Method.
abstract: Many proteins, particularly in eukaryotes, contain intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in their sequences. IDRs lack a stable tertiary structure under physiological conditions, yet they are essential for a broad range of cellular functions. They can be efficiently and accurately identified with computational methods. We focus on flDPnn2, which is an improved version of its predecessor, flDPnn. Results from the recently completed third Critical Assessment of Protein Intrinsic Disorder Prediction (CAID3) show that these improvements led to relatively high prediction accuracy and low runtime, with flDPnn2 taking only 15 s to predict a 1,000-residue-long sequence. Comparative evaluation on CAID3 also revealed that flDPnn2 is the fastest among the most accurate disorder predictors. We provide a practical guide for flDPnn2 users, explaining how to collect and interpret results produced by flDPnn2 via its freely available web server at https://biomine.cs.vcu.edu/servers/flDPnn2/. We also include a case study that provides a helpful illustration for these explanations. The flDPnn2 web server supports batch submission of up to 50 FASTA-formatted protein sequences and provides results in multiple formats, facilitating convenient analysis and interpretation. © 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC. Basic Protocol 1: Using the flDPnn2 web server to predict protein intrinsic disorder.
authors: Wang K, Hu G, Kurgan L.

title: A population-based resource for the prioritization of rare variants of unknown significance in clinical genomics
abstract: Rare diseases represent a major public health challenge because they are often associated with severe phenotypes, yet many causal variants remain undiscovered. Founder populations provide a unique opportunity to identify disease-causing variants through the local enrichment of rare alleles. Using whole-genome sequencing data from individuals in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean population, enriched variants were identified and their founder status was assessed through identity-by-descent sharing. Variant impact was evaluated using functional prediction tools without relying on prior clinical classification. A total of 131 founder variants of interest were identified, most of which would likely have been overlooked by conventional approaches based on existing clinical annotations. We developed a web-based platform that facilitates clinician access to the latest interpretation of their genetic variants of interest. These findings demonstrate that potentially pathogenic variants can remain undetected even in extensively studied founder populations. More broadly, they highlight the value of population structure-based approaches for uncovering rare disease variants and improving the characterization of genetic disease risk across human populations.
authors: Tremblay S, Moreau C, Morin G, Laprise C, Girard SL.

title: Variant Classification of a Non-Protein Coding Gene: ACMG/AMP Specifications for  RMRP  from the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel
abstract: Purpose  This study, conducted by the Clinical Genome Resource Severe Combined Immunodeficiency Disease Variant Curation Expert Panel (ClinGen SCID-VCEP), aimed to adapt the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) framework for germline variant interpretation in  RMRP . Unlike the protein-coding genes for which the framework was primarily developed,  RMRP encodes a non-protein-coding RNA. Biallelic pathogenic variants in  RMRP cause cartilage–hair hypoplasia, which can include severe combined immunodeficiency disease and other immune abnormalities.  Methods  An  RMRP -focused SCID-VCEP subgroup reviewed all 28 ACMG/AMP evidence criteria using population databases, published clinical and experimental data, computational predictions, and expert consensus. Each criterion was retained, modified, or designated as not applicable based on  RMRP biology and disease mechanisms. The resulting specifications were pilot tested using 27 variants selected from ClinVar and research laboratory data.  Results  Fifteen ACMG/AMP criteria were determined to be applicable to  RMRP , while 13 were considered not applicable. Several criteria were modified to evaluate nucleotide-level effects on transcriptional regulation, critical promoter regions, and RNA secondary structure. The specifications also incorporated  RMRP -specific recommendations for population frequency, functional evidence, variant phase, segregation, and phenotype. Application of the specifications classified 6 variants as pathogenic, 10 as likely pathogenic, 7 as variants of uncertain significance, and 4 as benign. Previously pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants remained within the pathogenic spectrum, and all previously benign variants remained benign. Variants with conflicting ClinVar interpretations were resolved as either likely pathogenic or uncertain. PM1, PM3, and PP4 were the primary criteria supporting pathogenic classifications.  Conclusion  The SCID-VCEP specifications provide a standardized approach to the classification of germline  RMRP variants in cartilage–hair hypoplasia and demonstrate how the ACMG/AMP framework can be adapted for a disease-associated non-protein-coding RNA gene. These specifications support the development of variant interpretation frameworks for other clinically relevant non-protein-coding genes.

title: gcat, its_a_scam: modular tools for single cell data processing and per-cell quality control
abstract: Motivation  The era of designing bioinformatic pipelines using open source tools is giving way to monolithic, and often proprietary, tools designed for end-to-end analysis, especially in the context of single cell data. While these tools are convenient for going from sequencing data to an almost complete data analysis “in a few clicks”, they can strongly limit data use beyond standard analyses. Results  We developed  Gene and Chromosome Analysis Toolkit (gcat) and  It’s a scam To Sell Another Single Cell Analysis Method (  its_a_scam ) for modular processing and quality control of single cell genomic data, freeing users from their reliance on proprietary tools. gcat is a C++ library for parsing genomic data and working with it over genomic coordinates.  its_a_scam is built on top of gcat and provides a suite of tools for a wide range of single cell data processing and quality control.  its_a_scam can be used in conjunction with commonly used open source tools for scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq count matrix generation, and for performing per-cell quality control directly from alignment files. These alignment-level per-cell metrics can be used for quality control of each cell or to understand celltype differences post-clustering or post-annotation. Using a peripheral blood mononuclear cell Multiome dataset, we show that the count matrices generated with the aid of  its_a_scam are highly concordant with those generated by proprietary pipelines. The alignment metrics further demonstrate celltype differences in aligned genomic regions, metagene profiles, and genebody coverage. The modular nature of  its_a_scam allows users to integrate it into their existing pipelines, while also enabling analysis beyond current pipelines.  Availability  gcat (distributed as gcatlib) and  its_a_scam are open source and available at  https://github.com/rishvanth-kp/gcatlib and  https://github.com/rishvanth-kp/its_a_scam . Detailed documentation is available at  https://gcatlib.readthedocs.io/ and  https://its-a-scam.readthedocs.io/ .
authors: Prabakar RK, Meyer HV.

title: Long-Read Reference Transcriptomes for Five Species of Rosaceae Tribe Spiraeeae: A Resource for Investigating Sequence Divergence, Species-Associated Expression Variation, and Leaf-Developmental Candidate Genes.
abstract: Species in the Rosaceae tribe Spiraeeae occupy diverse habitats and vary strikingly in growth form and leaf morphology. Still, no reference transcriptomes have been published for the tribe, and its transcriptome-level variation is uncharacterized. We generated long-read (PacBio Iso-Seq) reference transcriptomes of five species spanning three genera: Petrophytum caespitosum (Nutt.) Rydb., Spiraea lucida Douglas ex Greene, Spiraea splendens Baumann ex K. Koch, Aruncus dioicus (Walter) Fernald var. dioicus, and Aruncus aethusifolius (H.Lév.) Nakai. We then quantified expression across 20 individuals using 3'-tag RNA sequencing (TagSeq) to characterize expression patterns, ortholog sequence divergence, and gene repertoire. Multivariate analyses (principal component analysis [PCA] and hierarchical clustering) resolved replicates into three groups corresponding to the sampled genera. Because the material combined field-collected and potted plants, we treat expression comparisons as descriptive and do not attribute them to genetic control of interspecific differences. Pairwise analyses revealed extensive transcriptional divergence between genera, including thousands of differentially expressed transcripts in comparisons such as A. aethusifolius vs. P. caespitosum. Functional enrichment highlighted variation in transport and catabolism, plastid organization, and biotic-stress responses, implicating both metabolic and organelle-associated processes. Transcription factor families, particularly bHLH and bZIP, varied most among differentially expressed transcripts. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA) recovered modules correlated with species identity; because between-species variation dominates this dataset, we treat these as descriptive summaries of coexpression structure and do not regard them as independent evidence of species-specific regulatory programs. Because reads were quantified against a reference assembled from species-specific contigs, mapping rates were higher within species (70.5%-85.1%) than across species (25.1%-77.0%), and between-species expression comparisons are interpreted with this asymmetry in mind. Sequence-level analysis of orthologous transcript pairs indicated that protein-coding genes are predominantly under purifying selection. A small fraction (2.7%-5.0% of retained pairs) showed Ka/Ks > 1, but these were concentrated at low synonymous divergence, where ratio estimates are unstable; we therefore treat them as screening-level candidates for rapid divergence, enriched for stress-response, membrane-trafficking, and ion-transport annotations, and we make no claim of positive selection. These results provide a comparative transcriptomic framework for Spiraeeae and identify candidate transcripts and protein-coding differences for future studies of ecological and morphological variation in Rosaceae.
authors: Mafakheri AM, Potter D.

title: iTB-DRS: a multi-stage feature selection framework to identify Mycobacterium tuberculosis drug-resistance using single-nucleotide polymorphisms.
abstract: Rapid and accurate prediction of Mycobacterium tuberculosis drug resistance is crucial for effective tuberculosis control. However, data from genome-wide association studies are often characterized by high dimensionality and many redundant features, posing significant challenges to prediction models. To address these challenges, we propose a novel computational framework called iTB-DRS, which employs a hierarchical multi-stage feature selection strategy. The workflow begins with data encoding followed by a four-step selection mechanism, including (i) filtering noise using a Mean Decrease Accuracy based on Random Forest; (ii) ranking features by Maximum Information Coefficient to capture nonlinear association; (iii) performing pairwise predictive evaluation to identify SNP-SNP combinations with increased joint predictive value; and (iv) optimizing feature subsets through backward feature elimination. Finally, a set of Random Forest classifiers is trained to predict drug resistance to different drugs. When using an independent data set, iTB-DRS generally outperformed RF, LASSO + RF, and mRMR + RF baselines across multiple drug metric combinations. Simultaneously, the developed framework achieved good predictive accuracy on the training data set close to that of the computational pipeline TB-Profiler frequently used to predict Mycobacterium tuberculosis lineage and drug resistance. However, a performance gap between these two predictive tools emerged on the independent data set for several second-line drugs, which is mainly due to the catalog-based prior knowledge used by TB-Profiler. Taken together, the data obtained showed that iTB-DRS provides a low-complexity and interpretable solution that balances predictive accuracy and computational feasibility, offering a complementary research tool for genomic surveillance and candidate-marker discovery.IMPORTANCEDrug-resistant tuberculosis poses a significant threat to global health, narrowing the range of effective treatment options and increasing mortality rates. Rapid identification of drug resistance is crucial for selecting appropriate treatments during therapy. However, existing genomic tools often rely on predefined mutation catalogs, which may not fully capture complex or emerging resistance patterns. Therefore, studies on the development of novel effective methods for prediction of drug-resistant tuberculosis are of great importance. Here, we introduce a data-driven computational framework abbreviated as iTB-DRS that predicts Mycobacterium tuberculosis drug resistance using whole-genome sequencing data and a multi-stage feature selection strategy. Unlike catalog-based tools that use embedded prior knowledge, the proposed framework can be retrained on newly accumulated data to evaluate mutations and drugs not represented in existing catalogs. This flexibility positions iTB-DRS as a complementary, hypothesis-generating tool for genomic surveillance rather than a stand-alone replacement for validated catalog-based clinical software.
authors: Chen Y-X, Andrianov AM, Gabrielian A, Rosenthal A, Tuzikov AV.

title: Conversational Multi-Agentic Network-Driven Disease Module Identification and Drug Repurposing Prediction With ChatDRex: Platform Development Study.
abstract: BackgroundRepurposing approved drugs offers a time- and cost-effective alternative to traditional drug development. However, in silico prediction of repurposing candidates is challenging and requires the effective collaboration of specialists in various fields, including pharmacology, medicine, biology, and bioinformatics. Fragmented, specialized algorithms and tools often address only narrow aspects of the overall problem. Heterogeneous, unstructured data landscapes require the expertise of specialized users. Hence, diverse data sources might not integrate smoothly across workflows.ObjectiveWe aimed to develop an integrated, natural language-driven system that enables domain experts to conduct complex network-based drug repurposing analyses by integrating heterogeneous biomedical data sources and specialized bioinformatics methods within a unified workflow.MethodsWith ChatDRex, we present a conversation-based, multi-agent system that facilitates the execution of complex bioinformatic analyses aiming for network-based drug repurposing prediction. It builds on the integrated systems medicine knowledge graph NeDRexDB. ChatDRex provides natural language access to its extensive biomedical knowledge base. It integrates bioinformatics agents for network analysis, literature mining, and drug repurposing. These are complemented by agents that evaluate functional coherence for in silico validation. Its flexible multi-agent design assigns specific tasks to specialized agents, including query routing, data retrieval, algorithm execution, and result visualization. A dedicated reasoning module keeps the user in the loop and allows for hallucination detection.ResultsChatDRex operationalizes complex network-based drug repurposing workflows through conversational interaction, integrating biomedical knowledge access with algorithm execution and validation-oriented assessments. Its modular multi-agent architecture enables scalable task specialization across retrieval, analysis, validation, and visualization, while the reasoning module provides transparency and safeguards against unreliable outputs.ConclusionsBy enabling researchers with limited computational expertise to control complex analyses with natural language, ChatDRex could democratize access to bioinformatics as an important resource for drug repurposing. It could enable clinical experts to generate hypotheses and explore drug repurposing opportunities, ultimately accelerating the discovery of novel therapies and advancing personalized medicine and translational research.
authors: Süwer S, Bagemihl K, Baier S, Dicunta L, List M, Baumbach J, Delgado-Chaves FM, Maier A.

title: SQANTI-evidence: isoform-resolved, evidence-tiered structural annotation of unannotated genomes from long-read RNA-seq
abstract: Long-read RNA sequencing captures full-length transcripts, yet current annotation pipelines fail to properly curate the data for gene prediction. We present SQANTI-evidence, a novel software that annotates a genome from long reads alone, without the need for a reference annotation or protein database. SQANTI3-curated transcripts enter the annotation as observed, with isoforms and untranslated regions; AUGUSTUS predicts genes at loci without read support. In benchmarks, the curated layer was the most precise gene set in five of seven species, recovered twice as many exact isoforms as BRAKER in mammals and placed 3′ ends nearest the poly(A) site. We annotated 13 ERGA datasets.
authors: Atienza López P, Conesa A.

title: Whole-proteome structure/function prediction in uropathogenic E. coli reveals previously missed host-microbe and microbe-phage interaction pathways.
abstract: The rapid advancement of high-throughput sequencing technologies has vastly increased the number of known protein sequences, but the experimental characterization of their structures and functions lags behind. This gap in knowledge impedes our understanding of biological mechanisms of these proteins, hinders the interpretation of high-throughput experiments, and exposes a significant challenge in modern biology: deducing the structural and functional information of proteins based on their sequences. Most computational approaches rely on homology with well-annotated proteins, yet many proteins lack identifiable homologues, reducing the power of this approach. Here, we integrated cutting-edge protein structure and function prediction methods to develop a complete sequence-structure-function pipeline that predicts structures and functions based on primary sequences. We applied this pipeline to predict the structure and function of all proteins in Escherichia coli UTI89, a model strain of uropathogenic E. coli. Based on the predicted functions, we performed enrichment analysis on the whole genome and revealed the possible roles and related biological mechanisms of poorly annotated proteins in this organism. Moreover, the performance of our pipeline was further validated through detailed case studies of the UTI89_C0931 and ybtS genes. Finally, we compiled the UTI89 structure and function database (https://seq2fun.dcmb.med.umich.edu/UTI89), offering it as a crucial resource to aid researchers in elucidating the roles of unannotated proteins. This database aims to bridge critical knowledge gaps in microbial pathogenicity and resistance, enhancing our capacity to tackle emerging health threats.
authors: Peng C, Schreiber H, Zhang C, Liu Q, Hultgren S, Freddolino L.

title: Gene library deep sequencing for protein superfamily profiling.
abstract: Unraveling protein function at scale remains challenging. Gain-of-function (GOF) screens harnessing open reading frame (ORF) libraries enable systematic annotation of proteins that drive cell behavior and drug action. However, non-uniform gene coverage and undesired coding sequence variations compromise ORF library integrity and constrain the obtainable biological insight. In contrast, sequencing methods for characterizing current and next-generation ORF libraries remain limited. Here, we developed the scalable library deep sequencing workflow PPLseq (pooled plasmid library sequencing) for cost-effective, barcode-free ORF sequencing with single-nucleotide resolution. In a prototypical superfamily library of >300 human G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), PPLseq validated ORF identities and revealed sequence and coverage variation. Integration of PPLseq into high-throughput gene engineering facilitated assembly of a new GPCR fusion library. Systematic imaging-based phenotyping identified robustly expressed yet understudied receptors. Collectively, these results demonstrate broadly applicable, accessible, and accurate genetic library sequencing in library-to-phenotype profiling toward deeper insights into proteome function.
authors: T Sabapathy R, Henry-Cocks K, Feng J, Marri S, Granado GB, Janovjak H.

title: Seven-Gene Signature and Immune Microenvironment as Determinants of Survival Rate in Colorectal Carcinoma.
abstract: Backgrounds: Colorectal cancer (CRC) prognosis remains difficult due to molecular heterogeneity and interaction between tumor cells and the immune microenvironment. This study aimed to identify transcriptomic and immune-cell patterns associated with overall survival (OS) and to develop an integrated prognostic model to improve risk stratification. Methods: RNA-sequencing was performed on 131 primary CRC samples and matched normal tissues. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified and functionally characterized through gene ontology, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment, and protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis. Immune-cell composition was estimated using CIBERSORTx deconvolution and evaluated for its association with OS. Prognostic DEGs were screened using univariate Cox regression and Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) analysis to construct a risk score. The model was validated in the Cancer Genome Atlas Database (TCGA)-COAD (colon cancer) and READ (rectal cancer) cohorts. A nomogram integrating molecular and clinicopathological variables were generated. Results: A total of 5589 DEGs were identified between CRC and normal tissues, enriched in pathways related to cell cycle, Tumor Protein P53 (TP53), WNT Family Member (WNT), Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (JAK/STAT), calcium signaling, metabolism, and immune regulation. PPI analysis highlighted ten upregulated hub genes involved in mitotic spindle formation and chromosomal stability. Immune infiltration analysys indicated that higher proportions of plasma cells (p = 6.9 × 10- 4), naïve B cells (p = 0.019), resting CD4+ memory T cells (p = 0.02), M0 macrophages (p = 0.0077), and activated dendritic cells (p = 1.89 × 10- 5) were associated with improved OS, whereas monocytes (p = 0.012), neutrophils (p = 0.041), activated mast cells (p = 0.0066), and M2 macrophages (p = 0.014) were linked to poorer survival. A seven-gene signature including aspartate beta-hydroxylase (ASPH), bradykinin receptor B1 (BDKRB1), calcium voltage-gated channel auxiliary subunit beta 1 (CACNB1), C-C motif chemokine receptor 8 (CCR8), cyclic nucleotide gated channel subunit alpha 3 (CNGA3), microtubule associated protein 1A (MAP1A) and oxytocin receptor (OXTR) stratified patients into high- and low-risk groups with significant OS differences. The model demonstrated strong predictive performance (AUC: 0.84 at 1 year) and was validated in TCGA cohorts. Multivariate analysis confirmed the risk score as an independent prognostic factor. The integrated nomogram accurately predicted 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival (C-index = 0.757; 95% CI 0.724-0.791). Conclusions: We developed and validated a seven-gene immune-related prognostic signature that, combined with clinicopathological parameters, provides a robust tool for individualized survival prediction and may guide precision management in CRC patients.
authors: Rallo V, Massidda M, Wen X, Deiana M, Maschio A, Shen J, Ninniri MC, Piras D, Carru C, Coradduzza D, Muroni MR, Cossu-Rocca P, Scanu AM, Angius A, Miglio MR.
