title: Local fractal dimension as an indicator of functional reorganization in molecular interaction networks
abstract: Changes in protein abundance incompletely describe how molecular perturbations reshape cellular organization. Here we introduce DIFFRACT, a framework that integrates quantitative proteomics with protein-protein interaction networks to identify reorganization through changes in local fractal dimension. Molecular associations define effective distances between connected proteins, allowing the geometry of their surrounding network neighborhoods to be compared across conditions. Analyses across four organisms (  E. coli, A. thaliana ,  C. elegans , and  H. sapiens ) and three interaction resources (STRING, BioGRID, and IntAct) establish heterogeneous local scaling, while controlled perturbations demonstrate sensitivity to regional changes and invariance to uniform distance rescaling. Applied to RAVER1-deficient A549 cells, DIFFRACT identifies components associated with established RNA-regulatory functions and candidate roles in tRNA biology, mitochondrial organization and ciliogenesis. Selected RNA-regulatory and ciliary themes are not significantly enriched by abundance-ranked gene set analysis, supporting complementary information from network geometry. Selected functional annotations also recur in HEK293T cells. Guided by the ciliary predictions, we show that RAVER1 depletion increases the proportion of ciliated A549 cells 2.57-fold and increases cilium length. DIFFRACT thus connects changes in molecular network geometry to experimentally testable biological responses, extending the interpretation of proteomic perturbations beyond differential abundance.
authors: Hause F, Wedler-Geyer A, Lederer M, Fuchs T, Ihling CH, Tänzler D, Keil R, Sorokin O, Wussow S, Sinz A, Hüttelmaier S.

title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of the cigarette beetle Lasioderma serricorne reveals genomic adaptations to stored-product niches
abstract: Abstract    Background  Lasioderma serricorne  (Coleoptera: Ptinidae) is a globally significant stored‑product pest renowned for its exceptional adaptability to diverse substrates, including toxin‑rich tobacco. Despite its economic importance and ecological relevance, the genomic basis of its adaptation to stored‑product niches remains largely unexplored. Results  Here, we present a chromosome‑level genome assembly of  L. serricorne  generated through an integrative approach combining PacBio HiFi, Hi‑C, and NGS sequencing. The 188.96 Mb genome is anchored into 11 pseudochromosomes with a scaffold N50 of 19.11 Mb and a BUSCO completeness of 97.1%, representing a high‑quality reference for this species. Comparative genomic analyses across 20 Coleoptera species with a Neuroptera outgroup revealed that 41 gene families have undergone significant expansion in the  L. serricorne  lineage, with prominent enrichments in detoxification pathways (including insecticide metabolism and response to toxic substances) and carbohydrate metabolism. Among these, the ELL (elongation factor for RNA polymerase II) gene family exhibits a remarkable lineage‑specific expansion to 89 copies, suggesting enhanced transcriptional responsiveness to environmental stressors. Furthermore, positive selection analysis identified 88 genes under adaptive evolution along the  L. serricorne  branch, including  ABCC10  (ATP‑binding cassette transporter),  MAN1B1  (glycosyl hydrolase), and  CPT1A  (carnitine palmitoyltransferase), which harbour lineage‑specific amino acid substitutions potentially linked to nicotine tolerance and metabolic adaptation. Conclusions  These genomic features collectively illustrate how  L. serricorne  has evolved to exploit stored‑product environments through expansions of detoxification and digestive gene repertoires, alongside adaptive changes in energy metabolism. This reference genome provides a foundational resource for understanding the genetic mechanisms of pest adaptation and for developing novel management strategies.
authors: Zhang J, Li W, Liu X, Xu J, Liu X, Qian Y, Han Y, Jiao T, Lu J.

title: BioGraphX-Sol: A Structure-Free, Fully Interpretable Protein Solubility Predictor Exceeds AlphaFold3-Based Methods and Reveals Nine Universal Cross-Species Determinants
abstract: Abstract  Protein solubility is a critical determinant of recombinant expression yield, yet current state-of-the-art predictors often rely on either AlphaFold3-predicted structures or large ensembles of protein language models, limiting accessibility and interpretability. We present BioGraphX-Sol, a sequence-only predictor that constructs biophysically grounded constraint graphs directly from amino acid sequences to extract 200 physicochemical features spanning graph topology, IDP and polymer physics, aggregation-hotspot geometry, and novel surface- and terminal-conditioned descriptors, without requiring 3D coordinates, multiple sequence alignments, or pretrained models. On the standard eSOL benchmark, the XGB+ESM post-hoc ensemble essentially matches ProtSATT in predictive performance ($R^2 = 0.5451$ vs.\$R^2 = 0.5450$), despite training only 1.44M neural parameters and requiring no structure prediction. The physics-only XGBoost configuration ($R^2 = 0.499$, ROC--AUC $= 0.873$) exceeds FGNNSol ($R^2 = 0.487$, ROC--AUC $= 0.867$), which combines AlphaFold3-derived 3D coordinates with ESM-C embeddings and structural descriptors across roughly 1,831 input dimensions, showing that explicit 3D structure prediction is unnecessary when the relevant physicochemical information is correctly encoded. A post-hoc $\alpha$ sweep quantifies the physicochemical-to-evolutionary information balance at approximately 59\%/41\%, providing, to our knowledge, the first quantitative decomposition of information sources for protein solubility prediction. In zero-shot transfer to \textit{S.\cerevisiae}, the physics-only XGBoost achieves the highest ROC--AUC ($0.8524$) and PR--AUC ($0.9246$) among all evaluated methods. Permutation-importance analysis identifies nine universal solubility determinants exhibiting consistent directional effects across \textit{E.\coli} and \textit{S.\cerevisiae} (9/9 agreement). The physics-only configuration requires no GPU at inference and runs efficiently on standard CPU hardware, supporting the Green AI principle that compact, interpretable representations grounded in domain knowledge can provide a viable alternative to parameter scaling.
authors: Saeed A.

title: DECODER-SC: A single-cell algorithm for quantifying transcription factor-target regulatory discordance.
abstract: Existing transcription factor (TF) activity inference methods quantify regulatory potential but do not evaluate whether inferred TF activity is concordant with downstream target-gene expression. To address this limitation, we present DECODER-SC, a single-cell algorithm that quantifies TF-target regulatory discordance from single-cell RNA-sequencing data. DECODER-SC integrates direction-aware regulatory logic using DoRothEA activation and repression annotations, weighted discordance scoring, and permutation-based statistical inference to compute TF-level, interaction-level, and cell-level discordance metrics. Benchmarking against AUCell, VIPER, and TF-target correlation baseline demonstrated that discordance profiles capture regulatory structure not explained by activity magnitude or simple expression co-variation. Ablation analysis supported the contribution of activator/repressor-aware modeling to discordance detection, while robustness analyses demonstrated highly stable TF rankings across multiple threshold settings. Orthogonal Perturb-seq validation demonstrated a reproducible IRF1 discordance signal across experimental units (effect = 0.0643, 95% CI = 0.0441-0.0845, BH-adjusted P = 0.0235). Leave-one-target-out and VIPER-based sensitivity analyses confirmed that discordance classifications are robust to target-level circularity and alternative TF-activity inference (97.76% and 73.42% agreement, respectively). Replicate-aware sample-level analysis further showed that cell-level proliferation and pathway associations were exploratory rather than statistically independent. Application of DECODER-SC across multiple single-cell transcriptomic datasets identified recurrent regulatory discordance patterns associated with malignant progression, stress-adaptive transcriptional programs, and transitional cellular states. DECODER-SC expands current single-cell regulatory analysis by enabling systematic quantification of TF-target discordance across heterogeneous cellular populations.
authors: Haider A, Rasul I, Al Farraj DA, Aboul-Soud MAM, Giesy JP, Majid A, Li C.

title: Multi-omics data integration in bioinformatics: methods, applications, and the path toward biological reasoning.
abstract: High-throughput technologies now make it possible to simultaneously generate genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data. Spatial and single-cell platforms, in turn, provide cellular and spatial information in greater detail. Relying on a single omics method captures only a fraction of this complexity and often overlooks interactions across different layers. Despite these advances, clinical applications remain limited. This review examines integration strategies, along with their applications in various diseases, and the machine learning methods used to implement them. Rather than focusing solely on predictive performance, the aim is to support biological reasoning by formulating testable hypotheses, drawing causal inferences, and gaining insights that can guide clinical decisions. A reanalysis of a publicly available chronic lymphocytic leukemia dataset revealed that one data type was missing in approximately one-third of patients. When early and intermediate integration were combined with simple zero imputation, agreement dropped to chance and near-chance levels. In contrast, late integration, which does not require data imputation, was largely unaffected by this issue. This demonstrates that findings regarding integration strategies cannot be considered in isolation from how missing data are handled. The review also covers approaches that directly address missing data. Major barriers to clinical application include confounding batch effects, unreliable feature attribution when features are correlated, and deficiencies in clinical quality assurance. This review proposes four criteria to help identify models that not only ensure statistical validity but also genuinely support biological reasoning: mechanistic specificity, causal grounding, failure transparency, and decision relevance.
authors: Kabartan Çökeli E, Cerrahoğlu F.

title: RNAflash: Fast and Sensitive Structure-aware RNA Homology Detection and Alignment
abstract: Abstract  RNA homology search plays a crucial role in RNA structure prediction, facing a trade-off between sensitivity and speed. Here we present RNAflash, a two-stage framework that combines RNA language model-based retrieval with structure-informed reranking and alignment. A retrieval bi-encoder RNAflash-R trained through contrastive learning first retrieves candidate RNA sequences from a large pre-encoded database. Then, its cross-encoder RNAflash-A reranks and aligns the retrieved RNA candidates via jointly trained prediction heads, using predicted secondary structures to refine nucleotide correspondence scores. Across held-out Rfam families, RNAflash retrieved RNA homologs more sensitively than sequence-based methods, and produced alignments comparable to those of structure-based methods. In large-scale searches of RNAcentral, RNAflash generated multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) with stronger coupling and covariation signals than sequence-based and Infernal pipelines, while performing search and MSA construction 3.7-fold faster than non-iterative Riboseek and over 100-fold faster than Infernal and RNAcmap. The lightweight variant RNAflash-L achieves sub-second average search times per query while producing higher-quality MSAs than nhmmer and non-iterative Riboseek. The results show that RNAflash makes sensitive RNA homology search and MSA construction more scalable, and provides an efficient source of MSAs for downstream RNA structure prediction.
authors: Pan X, Chen B, Wang S, Zhu W, Xue Y, Shen H.

title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction.
abstract: RNA language models have achieved strong performance across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by hierarchical structure, making structural information important for pre-training. Existing approaches often depend on noisy annotations or task-specific objectives that can limit generalizability. Here we present structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model trained on 21 million RNA sequence-structure pairs by integrating base-pairing interactions into masked language modelling through a pair-matching operation. We also introduce MUSES, a multi-source ensemble of secondary structures designed to mitigate predictor bias, and a dynamic masking ratio that balances structure-guided and nucleotide-level masking. structRFM learns joint sequence and structure representations as sequence-level, nucleotide-level and pairwise features for broad downstream adaptation. It ranks highly in zero-shot homology classification and establishes new benchmarks for secondary-structure prediction. Its tertiary-structure adaptation, Zfold, consistently improves both three-dimensional predictions and their extracted secondary structures, with performance comparable to AlphaFold31 across CASP15-natural, CASP16 and RNA-Puzzles. structRFM also improves performance on function-prediction tasks and generalizes to newly released RNA families and long non-coding RNAs. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight multimodal RNA language models for robust structural and functional inference. The complete 21-million-pair dataset, model weights and source code are openly available to support multimodal RNA foundation-model development.
authors: Zhu H, Li R, Chang A, Chen H, Zhang F, Tang F, Ye T, Li X, Gu Y, Xiong P, Zhou SK.

title: Unsupervised prioritization of gene-regulatory variants with isolation forests
abstract: Most common variants occur in non-coding genomic regions. Numerous expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) can influence nearby gene expression. Across diverse traits and diseases, many genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci have been shown to colocalize with eQTLs, supporting gene-regulatory causal mechanisms. However, linkage disequilibrium (LD) obscures the identification of the causal variant(s), necessitating prioritization by functional annotations. Previously published variant prioritization tools relied on the machine-learning-based combination of diverse feature types like evolutionary conservation and chromatin information, whereas more recent deep learning tools learn and describe gene-regulatory DNA sequence grammar. However, the latter approaches often generate a large number of scores per variant. We designed a novel unsupervised machine-learning approach based on isolation forests to integrate the predictions from the broadly used Enformer deep learning model into a single gene-regulatory predictive score for each common variant. Our novel approach eQTL prediction with isolation forests (eQIF) demonstrates strong performance in predicting eQTLs and gene-regulatory GWAS variants. We show that top eQIF variants are located in evolutionarily conserved transcription factor binding site (TFBS) footprints, and that the frequency of top eQIF variants within overrepresented TFBS motifs recapitulates the motif information content. eQIF predictions are precomputed for 9,421,183 common variants and publicly available. Abstract Figure  Graphical Abstract. eQIF is a novel score for predicting the gene-regulatory impact of variants. eQIF is based on the top 20 principal components (PCs) from the publicly available precomputed Enformer deep-learning chromatin predictions overlapping common gnomAD variants. The PCs were provided to an isolation forest to learn global density within the multi-dimensional feature space. After training the model, it was applied to predict a global anomaly score (eQIF) for all gnomAD variants. eQIF was finally used for fine-mapped variant classification, functional variant discovery and precise prioritization of highly informative TFBS positions. authors: Schmidt AW, Rosendahl J, Laumen H, Ossowski S.

title: The genetic architecture of human DNA methylome variation
abstract: Population DNA methylome analyses remain largely confined to reference-defined genomic space despite extensive human genetic diversity. A central challenge is therefore to define comparable methylation phenotypes across diverse genomes and map the genetic architecture of methylome variation. Here, using 460 haplotypes from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2, we develop two complementary pangenome-based frameworks: one compares methylation within homologous regions while retaining haplotype-specific structural configuration and CpG content; the other represents CpG island (CGI) variation at homologous loci as sequence-resolved alleles. We identified 47,039 CGI alleles, including 8,040 absent from CHM13; 62% were attributable to structural variants and 31% to small variants. Through local genealogies, we reconstructed CGI gain, loss and turnover, revealing how present-day methylation differences align with CGI evolutionary trajectories. We found that genome-wide, methylation variability was buffered against genetic diversity across more than 90% of the genome, with exceptions at extreme nucleotide diversity and locally around structural variants. Our methylation framework enabled population-scale allele-aware methylation quantitative trait locus (mQTL) mapping into non-reference and structurally complex sequence, where mQTL-associated intervals were enriched. mQTLs linked methylation to transcriptomic phenotypes, population differentiation and complex traits, supporting 8% of population differentially methylated regions and colocalizing with more than half of genome-wide association study loci. Together, our study redefines human methylome analysis and our findings reveal a genome-wide architecture of genetic-epigenetic coupling, reshaping how methylation variation is interpreted across human development and disease.
authors: Liu T, Macias-Velasco JF, Zhuo X, Lin J, Porubsky D, Zhang W, Li D, Tomlinson C, Belter EA, Dong Z, Dong S, Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC), Eichler EE, Wang T.

title: A practical resource for multi-omics data integration in microbial systems.
abstract: The increasing availability of microbial multi-omics datasets has created new opportunities to explore complex biological systems. However, exploration remains limited by the lack of accessible, reproducible workflows that integrate multiple omics layers and deliver easily interpretable visualizations of functional and pathway-level insights. Here, we present an R-based workflow for integrated analysis and network-based interpretation of microbial multi-omics data. The workflow enables microbiologists to analyse transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic datasets either individually or in combination, apply univariate and multivariate approaches for biomarker discovery and generate interpretable visualizations of functional and pathway-level signatures. Implemented as a multi-step R Markdown workflow, the resource leverages established open-source tools, including mixOmics for biomarker identification and omics integration and clusterProfiler for functional enrichment analysis. Functional integration is then performed on the enrichment results themselves rather than on individual features. By combining functional annotations from distinct omics layers, strains or conditions into a unified network, it enables simultaneous visualization of functional connectivity and of the sources from which each response was recovered, so that conserved and condition-specific responses can be identified directly rather than reconciled across separate outputs. A dedicated Shiny application makes this framework fully dynamic, allowing users to interactively filter, interpret and prioritize shared and condition-specific biological responses. We demonstrate its utility using a publicly available Streptococcus pyogenes dataset, revealing both shared and strain-specific functional responses to human serum. This resource provides an adaptable framework for systematic multi-omics analysis, improving accessibility and reproducibility and facilitating functional interpretation of microbial responses to diverse environments.
authors: Mujchariyakul W, Hachani A, Stinear TP, Lê Cao KA, Howden BP, Walsh CJ, Guérillot R.

title: Gene Embedding Hub: a standardized resource for human gene representations
abstract: Gene embeddings are vector representations of gene identity that provide machine-learning models with information from diverse biological sources. However, their use is hindered by a lack of standardization: inconsistent identifiers, formats, and preprocessing conventions. In this work, we present a unified resource of 67 human gene-embedding sets derived from protein, DNA and RNA sequences, biomedical text, bulk expression data, single-cell expression models, functional data, biological networks, knowledge graphs, regulatory genomics and multimodal models, covering up to 20,097 GENCODE-annotated protein-coding genes. The collection includes both published precomputed embeddings and representations generated or extracted from publicly available models and biological data. Each embedding set is organized in a folder containing the embedding matrix, the Ensembl gene identifiers, machine-readable metadata, and processing documentation. We validate the resource by measuring global and local similarity, cross-embedding consensus, and cross-embedding predictability. The collection is designed to allow community-contributed embeddings that meet predefined technical and documentation requirements, enables comparison of gene representations across modalities and provides standardized embeddings for training and downstream applications.
authors: Tabares D, Bohl M, Boeva V.

title: Silent methodological failures in AI-assisted science: benchmarking large language model agents for virtual gene knockout analysis
abstract: Abstract  Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in computational biology, yet their reliability in executing complex scientific workflows remains poorly characterized. Here, we benchmarked five LLM agents (DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM 5.1, HY3 Preview, Kimi K2.6, and Minimax M2.7) on virtual gene knockout analyses using four computational frameworks across two single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets. All agents successfully completed the assigned workflows, but their quantitative outputs varied substantially: execution times spanned a 31fold range (61 − 1,920 s), while cross-model coefficients of variation reached 142.1%. Notably, four of five agents (80%) exhibited “silent methodological failures,” generating computationally valid, error-free code that produced biologically implausible results. Among the evaluated agents, GLM 5.1 showed the most balanced performance across computational efficiency and biological plausibility. These findings demonstrate that successful code execution alone does not ensure scientific validity and highlight cross-model concordance and biological validation as important quality-control strategies for Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted computational biology workflows.
authors: Wang B, Li J, Zhang S.

title: NORMA 3.0: aesthetic and group-aware visualization and analysis of annotated biological networks
abstract: Summary  Interpreting a biological network often rests on the relationship between its connectivity and the functional groups annotated on it, such as pathways, complexes, or enriched terms. For example, whether a group forms a cohesive module, how groups overlap, and which proteins connect them. These relationships are often hard to assess visually when groups are numerous or overlap, and most tools represent membership only by node color. NORMA 3.0 is a complete client-side rewrite of its predecessors, delineating and laying out groups with convex hulls, bubble sets, or fog clouds. Multi-group nodes are rendered as pies and directed, and parallel edges retain their evidence channels. Eighteen 2D and nine 3D layouts are scored by silhouette width, outline intrusion and overlap, and benchmarked for group separation and run time. The implementation also includes edge bundling, network importers for six databases, 21 topological measures, group-level and enrichment statistics, comparison of up to ten networks, export of high-resolution images, and an Application Programming Interface. Availability and implementation  NORMA 3.0 is freely available at  https://normaviz.org . The source code is available at  https://github.com/PavlopoulosLab/NORMA .  Contact  pavlopoulos@fleming.gr Supplementary information  Supplementary data are available at  Bioinformatics online.
authors: Baltoumas F, Karatzas E, Koutrouli M, Galaras A, Aplakidou E, Chasapi IN, Chasapi MN, Lazanas P, Lamari E, Pržulj N, Georgakopoulos-Soares I, Pavlopoulos GA.

title: A chromosome-level genome of the king penguin (Aptenodytes patagonicus): a resource for linking genotype to fitness in a long-lived vertebrate.
abstract: The king penguin (Aptenodytes patagonicus) is a long-lived seabird of the Southern Ocean that is emerging as a promising model in the wild for studying evolution. We present a high-quality, haplotype-resolved 1.35 Gb chromosome-level genome of an adult female king penguin - 'Pen/Se-guin' - assembled using PacBio HiFi long-reads and Hi-C proximity data. A total of 95% of the assembly is assigned to 34 chromosomes (32 autosomes, plus the Z and W chromosomes). The primary haplotype has a BUSCO completeness of 97.2%, and across both haplotypes the assembly has a k-mer completeness of 99.7% and a quality value of 63.8. We also assembled a circularised mitogenome (20,520 bp) containing the avian tandem duplication. Repetitive sequence annotation showed that 16.3% of the genome comprises repetitive elements, with LINEs representing the most abundant transposable element class (5.6%). Gene prediction using an extensive multi-tissue RNA-seq dataset resulted in 18,081 predicted protein-coding genes, of which 17,081 were functionally annotated, with a BUSCO completeness of 98.4% and an OMArk completeness of 97.3%. Compared with the previous draft genome, the presented genome shows a 30-fold increase in assembly contiguity and a substantially improved genome annotation, exceeding the standards of the Earth BioGenome Project and Vertebrate Genomes Project. This genome provides a foundation for ongoing and future studies using the king penguin to investigate genotype-fitness relationships, ageing, life-history evolution, and adaptation.
authors: Paris JR, Nitta Fernandes FA, Santos CA, Pointon DB, Wood JMD, Obiol JF, Salces-Ortiz J, Fernández R, Cristofari R, Le Bohec C, Trucchi E.

title: Benchmarking Structural Variant Detection in Whole-Exome Sequencing of 67 Multiple Myeloma Cell Lines
abstract: Background:  Although the majority of structural variant (SV) workflows have been derived based on whole genome sequencing (WGS) data, they continue to be applied to whole exome sequence (WES) data for which many studies have evaluated their performance in cancer. An equally important consideration that has not been well studied is the impact of cancer context specific features among WGS-derived SV callers applied to WES data. Similar to personalized medicine, not all SV callers are alike and optimal for use with all cancer types and sequence data types. In addition to sequencing related data features, cancer types have embedded features withing the sequencing data that should be considered. Herein, we performed an analysis of SV heterogeneity among WGS-derived SV callers to WES data in multiple myeloma (MM), a cancer known for its genetically heterogeneous nature. Using WES data derived from a panel of 67 Multiple Myeloma (MM) cell lines, we evaluated seven WGS-derived SV detection tools (Delly, SvABA, BreakDancer, Smoove, LUMPY and Manta) for their ability to identify cytogenetically known genetic abnormalities and to characterize overall differences in the number, length, type, and runtime of SVs called among them. Results. Among the seven tools, Smoove and Manta both had the shortest runtime, processing files in less than 2 minutes, in contrast to tools that required more than two hours to run such as SvABA and Pindel. Smoove was the only SV caller to identify a range of SV types, while SvABA was the most restrictive, calling only breakends. All tools differed in the length of SVs called, with SvABA's unfiltered output including the shortest length of less than 10 base pairs (bps), and Delly and BreakDancer's output including the longest, with SVs of less than 1,000 bps. At the chromosome level, SvABA's unfiltered output and Delly's output included 78% and 27.5% of known SVs, respectively, with the remaining tools (including SvABA's filtered output) achieved recall rates of less of less than 10%. By comparison, at the genomics coordinate level, no tool identified more than 20% of known SVs. Conclusions. As all evaluated SV detection tools achieved poor recall rates on this comprehensive catalog of MM cell lines, this study implies SVs detected by WGS-based SV callers on WES data should be confirmed experimentally before being declared legitimate. Heterogeneity in these tools' output lends support to their combined use in practice. Considering that many clinical grade sequencing panels continue to expand their repertoire of rearrangements with therapeutic implications, our results prompt the potential need for cancer type-matched workflows to evaluate the calling of such rearrangements.
authors: Pugalenthi LS, Nanduri R, Hong R, Ylagan M, Prasad R, Arasappan D, Kowalski-Muegge J.

title: RPFace: From biased structural benchmarks to generalizable RNA-protein interface prediction
abstract: Modeling protein-RNA complexes with co-folding and docking methods is routine, yet these methods are evaluated on benchmarks whose composition mirrors the deposited structures on which they were trained or tuned, leaving open whether their reported performance reflects true generalization. Here, we focus the evaluation on the region that carries the biological signal: the binding interface. For the first time, we construct and release a fair benchmark that stratifies protein-RNA data into distinct structural and experimental groups, providing a more stringent test of generalization than aggregate averages. On this benchmark, we find that accuracy of detecting the binding site using co-folding methods is concentrated in ribosomal complexes and varies systematically with factors such as experimental modality. For docking methods, it is reliable only when the input conformations are already close to the bound state, and it is inconsistent across RNA classes. Both families of methods fail to transfer to in vivo CLIP experiments. To address this gap, we introduce RPFace, to the best of our knowledge the first model that jointly predicts the binding preference of every protein residue and every RNA nucleotide directly from sequence, requiring no experimental structure, template, or multiple sequence alignment. RPFace combines an ensemble of predicted secondary structures with a multi-modal embedding-enrichment scheme that fuses representations from RNA foundation models and structure prediction models. Unlike existing approaches, it is a very small and fast model that delivers stable performance across structural and experimental conditions, is robust to conformational change, and generalizes to in vivo datasets without extensive pretraining. As a result, RPFace matches the state-of-the-art methods on protein interfaces with no evolutionary information, and outperforms them on RNA interfaces, with the largest gains in zero-shot settings despite using only sequence information. The model, code, and data are available at Github.
authors: Hashemi Aghdam H, Shukueian Tabrizi S, Cicek AE.

title: Joint protein-DNA language modeling enables prediction and engineering of DNA recognition specificity
abstract: Protein-DNA recognition specificity underlies transcriptional regulation, DNA replication, chromatin remodeling and genome editing. Protein-DNA recognition depends on both interacting sequences, yet language models that learn this cross-molecular dependence explicitly during pretraining remain limited. Here, we developed the Protein-DNA Language Models (PDLMs), interaction-aware language models that jointly represent protein and DNA sequences. PDLMs were built by continued pretraining from ESM2 with masked language modeling on paired protein-DNA sequences. A shared encoder places amino acids and nucleotides in the same molecular context, enabling conditional sequence scoring and transferable pair representations. We further introduced a domain-aware masking strategy that increased masking probability within DNA-binding domains to strengthen learning of interaction-relevant regions. Across downstream tasks, PDLMs improved protein-DNA pair classification relative to independent-encoder baselines and supported prediction of mutation-associated binding changes. Zero-shot scoring recovered known changes in DNA-recognition specificity and prioritized variants with higher editing activity. Learned representations also supported cross-study prediction of base editor activity. After fine-tuning on transcription factor binding data, PDLMs predicted DNA motifs directly from protein sequences. Together, PDLMs provide a framework for interaction-aware biomolecular language modeling, with potential applications in protein engineering and genome editing.
authors: Xiong Y, Ren J, Wei X, Li X, Li J, Wei W.

title: RPI-Zero: Zero-shot RNA-Protein Interaction Prediction
abstract: In vivo protein-RNA interactions are mapped almost exclusively by CLIP-seq, which profiles one protein in one cell type per experiment and needs a specific antibody; only about 10% of the roughly 2,000 human RNA-binding proteins have been assayed, and the Protein Data Bank holds around 5,000 protein-RNA complexes, a quarter of them ribosomes. Sequence-based prediction could extend coverage to unprofiled, newly discovered, or designed molecules, but existing predictors are not built for that case. One family trains a separate model per protein and cannot move beyond proteins with CLIP data; the other scores pairs but targets a single RNA class. Most are evaluated with random splits and randomly paired negatives that leave near-identical sequences on both sides of the split, and many require structure or read only short windows, discarding the context around a binding site. Their accuracy falls sharply when whole molecules are held out. We address this with two contributions. First, a strict benchmark of 2.1 million examples built from 11.6 million peaks of CLIP experiments targeting 209 proteins, taken from four public databases, in which each RNA is a spliced transcript with nucleotide-level labels, and sequence-similarity clusters are assigned whole to training, validation, and test sets, giving separate slices for unseen RNAs, unseen proteins, and unseen pairs. Negatives are matched to positives in length and in the number of other proteins binding the transcript, removing the shortcut by which a model predicts binding from how popular a transcript is without reading the protein. Second, RPI-Zero, a sequence-only model that reads any full-length protein and RNA jointly in up to 4,096 tokens, so the RNA representation is conditioned on the protein, and describes every protein as a mixture of shared motif prototypes, placing unseen proteins in the same terms as training ones. One model covers all proteins and RNA classes, uses no structure, and needs no interaction data for a new molecule. Compared with five state-of-the-art methods, it achieves the highest score in eight different metrics on unseen RNAs, unseen proteins, and unseen pairs. The model and data are available at https://github.com/ciceklab/RPI-Zero and https://zenodo.org/records/23748141, respectively.
authors: Eren K, Esendemir EI, Shukueian Tabrizi S, Hashemi Aghdam H, Cicek AE.

title: Physiological mapping and prediction reveal stress-responsive translation initiation landscapes
abstract: Translation initiation defines the protein output of the transcriptome, but its physiological dynamics in cells and tissues remain incompletely characterized. Here we develop TISCA2, an inhibitor-free method that captures eIF5B-associated initiating ribosomes to map translation initiation sites genome-wide. By directly identifying start sites rather than inferring translation from elongating-ribosome periodicity, TISCA2 improves the detection of short and overlapping translons. Translation of a subset of TISCA2-identified translons is supported by N-terminal proteomics and HLA-I immunopeptidomics. The arsenite-induced integrated stress response broadly redistributes start-site usage, reducing upstream initiation in favor of downstream initiation. TISCA2 further reveals tissue-specific initiation landscapes in vivo, with increased detection of downstream candidate start sites in the testis. Finally, we develop IncepTIS, a sequence-based deep learning model that predicts position-resolved and condition-dependent initiation landscapes. IncepTIS-guided optimization generates de novo mRNA 5′ leaders with stress-responsive initiation patterns. Together, TISCA2 and IncepTIS provide an experimental and computational framework for mapping, predicting and engineering translation initiation in mammalian cells and tissues.

title: Decoding Cell-type Specific Gene Regulation with CellReg3D by Integrating DNA Large Language Models and 3D Genome Structure
abstract: Gene regulation is a core biological mechanism crucial for organismal growth and development. Recent advances in deep learning, coupled with increasing computational resources, have enabled large-scale modelling of gene regulatory processes. While numerous models have been proposed, effectively capturing long-range genomic interactions remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce CellReg3D, a multiscale and multi-modal deep learning framework designed to model cell-type-specific gene regulation by integrating local sequence patterns with long-range genomic interactions. Existing approaches often overlook the contribution of 3D genome architecture and face limitations in combining sequence-based features with chromatin interaction data. Specifically, CellReg3D overcomes these gaps by leveraging a DNA language model to encode sequence-level information and incorporating Hi-C-derived 3D chromatin interactions to capture chromatin spatial organization. We demonstrate that CellReg3D effectively learns epigenetic patterns and chromatin activity states, achieving state-of-the-art performance in predicting epigenetic marks and gene expression profiles across multiple cell types. Using interpretable methods, we illustrate how the model identifies cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms and prioritizes functional non-coding variants. Furthermore, we apply CellReg3D to enhance the interpretation of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and uncover novel potential gene regulatory interactions. Overall, CellReg3D offers a integrative framework for decoding regulatory genomics, unifying sequence and 3D genome structure data to advance variant prioritization, disease mechanism discovery, and personalized functional genomics.
authors: Wang X, Zhang Y, Chen S, Imoto S, Webb GI, Vasilakos AV, Li F, Wang K, Song J.

title: Predicting single-molecule chromatin distribution from DNA sequence
abstract: Genome regulation unfolds through dynamic and stochastic single-molecule events. Deep learning models that read gene regulatory activities from DNA sequences have markedly advanced our ability to predict cell-population-level averages. However, they cannot capture the full spectrum of heterogeneity and dynamics at the single-molecule level, which directly reflect the underlying mechanisms of genome regulation. Here, we introduce a sequence-to-distribution (S2d) framework that directly models the entire probabilistic distribution of single-molecule chromatin states from DNA sequence alone. We used this framework to train Mola, a model of single-molecule chromatin accessibility. We harness Mola to investigate sequence-based regulatory code and mechanisms for multiple aspects of chromatin regulation at the single-molecule level. By quantifying sequence-driven nucleosome regulation, we reveal distinct modes of transcription factor engagement with nucleosomes, including a novel nucleosome-trapping factor, ZNF146. We characterized the sequence determinants governing the +1 nucleosome after transcription start sites and identified YY1 as the strongest +1 nucleosome-positioning factor. Leveraging long-context single-molecule modeling, we further discovered a shared sequence basis for the co-accessibility of regulatory elements and the co-footprinting of transcription factors. Joint prediction of DNA methylation and accessibility reveals a sequence-driven bimodal state mediated by methylation-sensitive transcription factors. Beyond static single-molecule snapshots, the S2d framework can generate pseudo-dynamic trajectories of chromatin states and propose a roadmap toward genome-wide chromatin dynamics. Moreover, we showed that Mola can predict and interpret the effects of genetic variants at the single-molecule level, revealing how sequence changes reshape distal regulatory coordination. Together, this sequence-to-distribution framework lays the foundation for understanding how genomic sequence encodes stochastic and dynamic genome regulation, and how genetic variation changes it, one molecule at a time.
authors: Wang R, Jin J, Pott S, Zhou J.

title: Evolutionary Evidence in Human Disease Variant Interpretation: A Mechanism-First Framework for Comparative Genomics
abstract: Interpreting human disease-associated variants remains challenging because no single evidence type reliably establishes whether a sequence change disrupts a disease-relevant mechanism. Comparative genomics is widely used to address this problem, particularly through evolutionary conservation and constraint, yet the biological meaning and evidentiary value of comparative signals can vary substantially across genes, variants and disease mechanisms. This critical narrative review examines when evolutionary evidence genuinely improves human disease variant interpretation and when it can mislead. We evaluate conservation and constraint across coding and noncoding sequences in relation to evolutionary distance, orthology, alignment quality, population variation, gene-disease validity, phenotype, functional assays, transcriptomics and structural information. We argue that evolutionary evidence should be treated as a conditional evidence layer rather than a direct indicator of pathogenicity. We further identify evidentiary dependence as an underappreciated source of overconfidence, because conservation measures and computational predictors such as CADD, REVEL and AlphaMissense may draw on overlapping evolutionary data, annotations or clinical labels. To address these limitations, we propose a mechanism-first framework that begins by defining the relevant disease mechanism and transcript, then selects comparative evidence according to the biological claim being tested and evaluates whether additional evidence provides genuinely independent information. The framework also considers lineage-specific function, regulatory turnover, ancestry, reference bias, structural variation, pangenomes and emerging sequence-based models. We conclude that evolutionary evidence is most informative when it helps resolve a specific mechanistic question, identifies variants for functional investigation, or strengthens a coherent interpretation, rather than serving as a shortcut from sequence similarity to clinical causality.
authors: Abdulrahim LA, Ayua JN.

title: Natural genetic diversity modulates structural stability changes caused by pathogenic variants in small proteins
abstract: Clinical genomics relies heavily on linear reference genomes such as GRCh38, often ne-glecting natural sequence diversity that can modify variant expressivity and drive diagnostic health disparities. Meanwhile, variant interpretation is moving toward direct biophysical evidence of disrupted protein function, yet how natural genetic backgrounds modulate variant-induced protein stability changes remains uncharacterized. Here, we present a physics-based computational and data processing framework to evaluate how global sequence diversity alters the predicted thermodynamic impact of pathogenic mutations. Focusing on small human proteins (  ≤ 100 residues), we reconstructed natural DNA haplotypes from 1000 Genomes Project data and introduced ClinVar pathogenic variants, yielding both natural and pathogenic protein haplotypes that were structurally modeled and energetically relaxed. Across 271 tested variants in 46 genes, structural stability changes (ΔΔ  G ) for 168 variants (62%) differed significantly depending on the underlying natural haplotype background (Kruskal-Wallis, Bonferroni-adjusted  p < 0.01). These background-sensitive variants spanned 43 of the 46 genes (93%), suggesting that thermodynamic modulation by natural sequence context is a pervasive phenomenon across the human proteome. Accounting for haplotype context in protein stability profiling is therefore essential for equitable, ancestry-aware precision medicine.
authors: Niemeijer T, Swertz MA, van der Velde KJ.

title: Quantitative imaging of native tissue architecture combined with deep multi-omics reveals the spatial biology of kidney aging
abstract: Aging alters tissue architecture and metabolism in spatially heterogeneous ways, yet the connections between these measurable structural and compositional phenotypes and underlying molecular changes are largely unknown. Here, we introduce NORIGAMI (NoRI-Guided AI for Multimodal Integration), a pipeline combining Normalized Raman Imaging (NoRI), deep learning, quantitative morphology, deep proteomics, and metabolomics to investigate renal aging. Unlike conventional histology, NoRI provides label-free, scattering-corrected measurements of absolute total protein and lipid mass concentrations (mg/mL). In 32 male rats aged 9, 18, 21 and 25 months, NORIGAMI predicted the chronological age of held-out rats from NoRI images (mean absolute error 0.78 months; R² = 0.97), and whole-tissue images outperformed models trained on isolated tubules. Quantitative imaging identified 41 age-associated morphological and compositional features (FDR < 0.05), revealing anatomically heterogeneous and non-linear changes in lipid droplet concentration, droplet size, cytoplasmic lipid concentration and tubular architecture. Deep molecular profiling quantified 11,485 proteins and 269 metabolites, revealing coordinated declines in differentiated proximal tubule (PT) identity and oxidative metabolism, selective increases in basement-membrane collagen-IV chains, and increasing molecular heterogeneity with age. A protein clock, built mainly from extracellular-matrix and heparan-sulfate proteins, predicted age with a mean absolute error of 1.6 months. Old kidneys diverged along a dominant injury-remodeling axis, seen separately in the proteome, in kidney RNA from 54 other rats and in the metabolome, in which tubular-injury and immune proteins, including the NAD  + -consuming enzyme CD38, rise as differentiated-tubule proteins and NAD  + fall. NORIGAMI subsequently linked NAD  + -associated molecular changes to candidate quantitative features of tubular geometry and protein–lipid organization in exploratory analyses, while complementary KIM-1-centered analyses identified overlapping candidate morphological associations involving epithelial injury and, possibly, lipid handling and yielded additional molecular candidates for mechanistic validation. Collectively, these findings suggest that declining tubular metabolic function, altered lipid organization and injury-associated molecular programs represent interconnected features of renal aging. NORIGAMI provides a framework for identifying the quantitative structural manifestations of molecular aging and generating spatially informed, experimentally testable hypotheses about tissue dysfunction.
authors: Trim WV, Diakova M, Sonnett M, Petrova K, Zhang B, Oh S, Donne R, McEwen C, Salmon H, Gadi A, Shavlakadze T, Chouchani ET, Glass DJ, Kirschner MW.

title: Cell IO: a database linking single-cell transcriptomes to literature-derived knowledge of cell functions and perturbations
abstract: Abstract  Single-cell transcriptome databases tell us which genes a cell type expresses, but what a cell type does, and what happens to it when a gene is perturbed, remains scattered across the literature. Cell IO (https://cell-io.riken.jp/) links these two kinds of knowledge through Cell Ontology identifiers. Its transcriptome layer re-processes 10x Chromium single- cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq experiments of human, mouse, and rat from the Sequence Read Archive with a uniform pipeline, annotates clusters with Cell Ontology terms restricted by the tissue of origin, and stores the cell type composition and UMAP embedding of every experiment (currently 14,931 experiments and 82.9 million cells). Its literature layer holds 895,258 claims extracted with a large language model and verified in a second pass from open-access abstracts, review articles, and gene perturbation studies in immunology and neuroscience, each with the verbatim sentence, highlighted entity spans, evidence strength, and ontology-normalized cell, gene, and context. The web interface lets users search cell types by name, synonym, or identifier, find the experiments in which a cell type is most abundant, inspect the composition and embedding of each experiment, read and filter the claims about a cell type by knowledge base, direction, evidence strength, and organism, and identify cell types whose functional characterization is missing from part of the literature. Cell IO is freely available without registration.
authors: Ozaki H.

title: Emzing: A Deep Learning-Enabled Software Suite for End-to-End Analysis of High-Resolution LC-MS Metabolomics Data.
abstract: High-resolution LC-MS-based metabolomics requires transforming noise-dominated raw data into quantitative feature tables and, ultimately, biologically meaningful insights. In practice, this process is fragmented across multiple tools and involves extensive parameter tuning and manual curation. Emzing is a web-based, vendor-agnostic platform that integrates end-to-end analysis, from raw data interrogation to statistical interpretation, within a unified environment. Emzing introduces data-driven, deep learning-based methods for signal extraction and feature quantification, formulating peak detection as a supervised learning problem in both spectral and chromatographic domains. A data-driven noise estimation strategy replaces fixed intensity thresholds, improving sensitivity to low-intensity signals. Feature correspondence across samples is established using robust retention-time alignment and graph-based grouping, while correlation-driven feature tagging assigns isotopes, adducts, and in-source fragments. Metabolite annotation (MSI level 2) combines spectral denoising with composite scoring of MS/MS spectra against reference libraries. Emzing further integrates processing with downstream statistical and machine learning-based analyses to facilitate reliable biological interpretation. Interactive visualization across all stages enables transparent curation and rapid iteration from initial results to publication-quality outputs. The use of pretrained models in inference mode, together with a reduced parameter space, supports reproducible analysis. Emzing improves true-feature recovery, quantitation accuracy, and reproducibility on benchmark data sets while reducing reliance on manual intervention. Scalability is demonstrated through Emzing Vault, a repository containing over 110 reprocessed public domain data sets.
authors: Singh A, Nandi K, Dubey P, Santhosh NK, Banerjee S, Nakrani P, Sunder AV, Sahasrabuddhe D, Wangikar PP.

title: Personalized Prediction of Venetoclax-Associated Tumor Lysis Syndrome in Acute Myeloid Leukemia Using Drug Exposure, Genetic Polymorphisms, and Clinical-Laboratory Characteristics.
abstract: BackgroundTumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is a life-threatening complication of venetoclax (VEN) for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Existing TLS risk tools were developed for CLL/SLL and need validation in AML. This study aims to integrate drug exposure, genetic polymorphisms and clinical indicators to build a personalized machine learning model for TLS risk in AML patients on VEN, and establish a standardized management flowchart.Methods186 AML patients on VEN therapy were prospectively enrolled. Key predictors were identified via univariate and multivariate regression. Four algorithms-logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and XGBoost-were compared to select the optimal predictive model. Model performance was evaluated using area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). SHAP interpretability analysis was employed to reveal feature contributions. Finally, an online TLS risk calculator was developed, and a standardized management workflow was established.ResultsAmong 186 patients, 39 (21.0%) developed TLS. The final model included four core covariates: VEN peak plasma concentration (Cmax), VEGFA rs3025039 genotype, ECOG performance status, elevated baseline WBC count. Among algorithms, XGBoost performed best, with validation set AUC=0.861, accuracy=0.811, specificity=0.831, sensitivity=0.7, F1=0.667, and Brier score=0.124, indicating good calibration. DCA and PRC curves confirmed high clinical utility. Based on this model, an online TLS calculator for risk stratification and personalized intervention, as well as a standardized management protocol, was successfully developed.ConclusionThe interpretable XGBoost model developed in this study can effectively predict TLS risk associated with VEN therapy in AML patients. The online prediction tool developed based on this model facilitates precise risk stratification, helping to avoid overtreatment of low-risk patients while optimizing resource allocation and significantly improving the safety of targeted therapy for AML.
authors: Wang C, Lin X, Yang Y, Peng M, Wu F, Zhou J, Xie H, Wang S, Liu M.

title: Implementation of an Internalized Hemolysis Assessment Approach in Targeted Bottom-Up Proteomics for the Purpose of Blood Plasma Sample Quality Control.
abstract: Mishandling of samples during blood plasma preparation may lead to biases in proteomic analysis and misinterpretation of data. An earlier study by Geyer et al. (2019) described proteins that may indicate poor plasma sample quality. Following this work, we have imitated a triangular strategy for biomarker discovery, established a targeted quantitative method for panels of hemolyzed and coagulated plasma sample markers proposed in the previous study, and validated it in our own model experiment. We have developed a scale for estimating the degree (rate) of hemolysis based on several protein markers and investigated the feasibility of using an internal control approach to detect hemolysis in targeted proteomic analysis. We propose including our plasma sample quality assessment and associated sample exclusion criteria into standard MRM analyses to provide more reliable data for proteomic research.
authors: Vakaryuk AV, Butenko IO, Kitsilovskaya NA, Kovalenko AV, Gremyacheva VD, Kozhemyakin GL, Lebedeva AA, Baraboshkin NM, Fedorov OV, Kurilova OV, Gorbunov KS, Kolesnikova IV, Davydova LA, Govorun VM.

title: In silico identification of drug compounds to arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase of Proteus mirabilis to combat its antibiotic resistance using an integrated bioinformatics: subtractive proteomics, molecular docking, MD simulation and DFT studies.
abstract: Proteus mirabilis is a major opportunistic Gram-negative pathogen causing complicated urinary tract infections (UTIs), particularly in catheterized patients. Although several antibiotics, including streptomycin, erythromycin, and sparfloxacin, remain effective against some infections, the growing spread of multidrug-resistant P. mirabilis strains has created an urgent need to identify new therapeutic targets and treatment options. Using a subtractive proteomics approach, this study identified potential therapeutic targets in P. mirabilis. Among the 417 essential pathogen-specific proteins, 11 were identified as druggable, virulence-associated, and antibiotic resistance-related proteins, making them promising novel therapeutic targets against P. mirabilis. Among them, nine are enzymatic proteins involved in crucial biological pathways such as glycan and amino acid biosynthesis, energy metabolism, cellular signaling, and genetic information processing. The protein-protein interactions (PPIs) and hub gene analysis revealed arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase (API) as a primary target; structure-guided virtual screening identified five hits, ferric derisomaltose, hyaluronic acid, acarbose, rutin, and dihydrostreptomycin that exhibit binding affinities ranging from -13.540 to -10.616 kcal/mol with P. mirabilis arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase (PmAPI), suggesting their potential as anti-P. mirabilis agents towards infectious disease control. The density functional theory (DFT) studies and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations interaction analysis on PmAPI with potent hits clearly showed reactivity of the hits and stable binding with PmAPI during the 500-ns MD simulation.
authors: Sureshan M, Mohan NV, Sriram N, Jothi A, Sadiq SP, Vilwanathan R, Sivaraman T, Trivedi RK.

title: A naturally occurring recombinant PRRSV with a JXA1-derived nsp9 fragment is associated with enhanced virulence in piglets.
abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) nonstructural protein 9 (nsp9), the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, has been implicated as a critical virulence determinant of highly pathogenic PRRSV (HP-PRRSV) through reverse genetics studies with engineered chimeric viruses. However, field isolates that naturally carry such nsp9-centric recombination events-thereby serving as potential in vivo models-remain exceptionally rare. Here we report the isolation and characterization of a novel PRRSV strain TJ25928 from a farm in China experiencing a severe PRRS outbreak. TJ25928 possesses the characteristic 131-amino-acid deletion pattern of NADC30-like strains and phylogenetically belongs to Lineage 1.8. Recombination analysis revealed a distinct configuration: the backbone of TJ25928 is derived from NADC30-like strains, while a discrete fragment within the nsp9 coding region (nt 7856-8923) is derived from JXA1-like HP-PRRSV. The boundaries of this nsp9 fragment overlap substantially with the nsp9 segment previously implicated in fatal virulence in engineered chimeric viruses. In piglet challenge experiments, TJ25928 induced significant febrile response (8-12 days post-infection), pronounced growth suppression (approximately 28% reduction in total weight gain at 21 days post-infection), and 33.3% (1/3) mortality. TJ25928 represents an important example of a field isolate that naturally carries the nsp9 recombination configuration previously studied by reverse genetics, providing a valuable natural model for future investigations into the role of nsp9 in PRRSV virulence. These findings underscore the pathogenic potential of nsp9 recombination events in the field and offer a useful tool for future mechanistic studies on PRRSV virulence.
authors: Zhu RY, Li J, Meng LZ, Zhu YT, Sun W, Ma JJ, Li JL, Li YX, Mo BL, Zhang SQ, Wang J, Miao ZR, Shi Y, Cheng XJ, Zhao J, Ren ZH, Sun YF.

title: Tools for in vivo labelling of ALFA-tagged proteins in C. elegans .
abstract: Understanding protein function requires tools to visualize and manipulate proteins in vivo . NanoTags, short epitope tags that are recognized by single-chain antibodies, are an emerging method for versatile in vivo labelling and manipulation of endogenous proteins. The short (13 amino acid) ALFA tag has been shown to allow labelling of endogenous proteins in several model systems, including C. elegans . Here we describe the generation and validation of transgenes to facilitate global and tissue-specific visualization of ALFA-tagged endogenous proteins in C. elegans . We propose a modular NanoTag system as a powerful approach for investigating protein functions in vivo in C. elegans .
authors: Topalidou I, Lehrbach N.

title: Strain-resolved comparative genomics and functional characterization of culturable lactic acid bacteria from Guizhou sour soup
abstract: Abstract    Guizhou sour soup is a traditional fermented food and a reservoir of diverse lactic acid bacteria (LAB), yet the strain-resolved genomic architecture and functional heterogeneity of its culturable LAB remain poorly defined. We established a large culture collection and integrated comparative genomics with targeted analyses of bile salt hydrolase (BSH), exopolysaccharide/capsular polysaccharide (EPS/CPS) loci, genomic safety, and in vitro phenotypes to evaluate strain-level diversity and identify traits relevant to functional strain selection. Among 1,741 culturable isolates recovered from red and white sour soups, Lactobacillales accounted for 85.69% and 95.24%, respectively. Whole-genome sequencing of 172 isolates, comprising 92  Lacticaseibacillus paracasei  , 30  Lactiplantibacillus plantarum  , and 50  Limosilactobacillus fermentum  , revealed open pan-genomes with distinct species-level functional architectures.  L. paracasei  showed the greatest accessory-genome contribution,  L. plantarum  the highest mean normalized BSH representation, and  L. fermentum  distinct oxidative-stress- and amino-acid-associated profiles. No antimicrobial resistance or virulence-associated genes were detected at the applied screening thresholds. BSH analyses showed lineage-specific sequence variation but conserved catalytic Cys2 and ligand-proximal architecture, whereas EPS/CPS loci varied among species and strains. Cholesterol removal was strongly strain- and condition-dependent:  L. paracasei  R1156 reached 71.69 ± 4.84% in standard MRS, while  L. plantarum  R2345, R2037, R1621, and R203 maintained 56.85–64.32% removal under 0.1% bile salts, exceeding the reference strain  Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus  GG (LGG). These findings establish a strain-resolved genomic and phenotypic resource and demonstrate the value of integrating comparative genomics with direct phenotypic screening for rational selection of food-associated LAB for further biotechnological evaluation.
authors: bai f, wang n, liu y, wen q, hu c, zhu s, mou r, yang r, han y, luo p.

title: NPlasmid-seq: Cas9-encoded terminal signatures enable molecule-level nanopore quality control of vector and IVT-template plasmids
abstract: Consensus-based plasmid quality control can overlook structural heterogeneity within a preparation. We developed NPlasmid-seq, a Cas9-guided nanopore workflow that encodes sample identity through paired terminal signatures generated at predefined backbone positions, without sample-specific oligonucleotide barcodes. We cleavage-validated 24 sgRNAs. In five representative assigned read bins, each bin showed its strongest sequence agreement with its cognate reference. Contaminant detection was evaluated with a single class-specific classifier applied both to computational read mixtures and to physical DNA mixtures, placing the two designs on a common scale. In computational read mixtures of 5,000 reads, a contaminant was detected in all 20 independent subsamples at each of 0.2%, 0.5%, 1% and 5% abundance and in 13 of 20 subsamples at 0.1%; precision was 1.000 in all 100 subsamples, with no false-positive calls among 493,200 reads from the declared target plasmid. In physical DNA mixtures carried through cleavage, pooled library preparation and sequencing, a contaminant was detected in all six samples prepared at 0.5 mol% input and all six at 1 mol%. Observed read fractions did not distinguish the 0.5 and 1 mol% input levels. Instead, they differed systematically by 4.0-fold between preparation pools, a larger effect than the difference between the two input levels. We therefore interpret the workflow as a detector, not a quantifier, of sub-percent contamination. Read-level analysis identified a recurrent 93-bp deletion in 61.7% of reads from a preparation that had passed consensus-based quality control. Sanger genotyping of 24 colonies identified deletion-type profiles in 10 colonies and intact-type profiles in three. The remaining 11 colonies showed double peaks at the diagnostic locus, consistent with coexistence of both sequence forms within individual clones. In in vitro transcription template plasmids, longer poly(A) tracts were associated with higher multimeric-read fractions. Across ten matched A90 culture pairs, propagation at 30 °C reduced these fractions relative to 37 °C (paired t-test, P = 0.0098). These measurements describe recovered read populations, not absolute molecular abundances. NPlasmid-seq therefore complements consensus validation by revealing sequence and structural heterogeneity within a preparation and by identifying a culture condition associated with a lower multimeric-read fraction.
authors: Xu Y, Wen W, Sun D, Yin Y, Ma X, Ren J, Zhang S, Chang J, Pang S, Wang S, Zhang X, Zhang J.

title: Amino Acid Metabolic Flexibility: A Framework for Locating Anabolic Resistance in Aging and Obesity-Related Insulin Resistance
abstract: Anabolic resistance, a reduced muscle protein synthetic response to protein or exercise, is reported in older adults and in people with obesity and insulin resistance. Yet it is still measured with one readout: the increment in muscle protein synthesis over a few hours after a single dose. This review makes four contributions. First, it identifies five impasses: single doses confound sensitivity with maximal responsiveness; most of an ingested meal goes untracked; breakdown is rarely measured; individual reproducibility is unknown; and acute responses are not validated predictors of muscle mass. Second, it proposes amino acid metabolic flexibility as a disposal framework in which an attenuated response can arise through four routes: reduced delivery, impaired sensing and translation, competing oxidative disposal, and impaired antiproteolysis. Third, it treats exercise as a probe as well as a stimulus, because whether prior exercise corrects a deficit helps to locate it. Fourth, applying the framework to aging and obesity-related insulin resistance suggests that similar synthetic phenotypes arise through different routes and yields a testable hypothesis: that insulin resistance diverts absorbed amino acids toward oxidation. A multidomain, repeated-measures design to test these predictions is outlined.
authors: Nunes EA.

title: SCAN: a cross-species single-cell transcriptome resource for domestic animals-revealing divergent spermatogenesis in avian and mammalian systems.
abstract: BackgroundDespite the astonishing growth of livestock single-cell transcriptome data, its full potential is severely limited by the lack of specialized functional databases and annotation tools. The ability to systematically integrate, standardize, and deeply interpret livestock single-cell data remains very limited.ResultsThis study constructed SCAN, a high-quality resource platform integrating over 2.1 million single-cell datasets from six livestock species (Sus scrofa, Gallus gallus, Bos taurus, Bos grunniens, Ovis aries, and Oryctolagus cuniculus) and a representative model organism (Danio rerio). This dataset covers 33 tissue types and 155 cell types, providing differential gene expression profiles for each cell type. Based on this platform, we developed standardized analysis pipelines and visualization tools, and established a livestock marker gene library and a high-quality chicken single-cell annotation reference dataset (CARD). In addition, to demonstrate the utility of the platform, we used SCAN to perform a cross-species single-cell comparison of spermatogenesis between avian and mammalian species. The analysis showed that the early stages of spermatogenesis were relatively conserved across species, whereas differences increased at the later stages; chicken SPT and sperm were significantly enriched in catabolism-related pathways. These observations suggest that the late stages of chicken spermatogenesis may employ a metabolic strategy distinct from that of mammals, but the underlying mechanisms remain to be validated by functional experiments.ConclusionsThis study provides a unified and standardized resource platform (SCAN) for livestock single-cell data, greatly facilitating data access, cell annotation, and downstream biological exploration, thereby enabling downstream biological discovery-as exemplified by the spermatogenesis study presented in this research. The SCAN database is freely and permanently available at http://www.scanimalsdb.bio-zz.cn .
journal: Journal of animal science and biotechnology
authors: Li Y, Wei Q, Li G, Li R, Li Z, Wang X, Zhang L, Guo Y, Sun G, Li W, Li Z, Tian Y, Kang X, Tian Z, Wang G, Wang Y, Liu Q.

title: What's in a name? The case of family B1 G-protein coupled receptor (GPCRS) genes.
abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) of Family B1 constitute a sequence-conserved yet functionally diverse group of peptide hormones and neuropeptide receptors that regulate key physiological processes across Metazoa. In vertebrates, five major receptor subfamilies have been characterized, and standardized gene nomenclature guidelines have been established based on functional evidence and evolutionary signal. In contrast, the diversity, evolutionary history, and classification of Family B1 GPCRs in invertebrates remain poorly understood, despite evidence for highly variable and often expanded receptor gene repertoires. The extensive genomic diversity of invertebrates means there is substantial sequence divergence from vertebrate homologues, highlighting the need for a standardized and evolutionarily informed nomenclature system. Here, we conducted a comprehensive comparative genomic and phylogenetic analysis of Family B1 GPCRs across a wide range of metazoan lineages, including non-bilaterians, protostomes, and deuterostomes, to assign receptor members within a unified evolutionary framework. Our results indicate that Family B1 GPCRs originated early in metazoan evolution, with ancestral receptor forms present in cnidarians prior to the protostome-deuterostome divergence. Subsequent evolution was shaped by lineage-specific gene duplications, losses, and the emergence of distinct receptor subfamilies in bilaterians. Protostomes display extensive diversification, including lineage-specific receptor groups, whereas deuterostomes retain a more conserved repertoire, with the emergence of canonical vertebrate subfamilies GCGR, PTHR and SCTR. We propose an evolution-informed framework for the classification and naming of Family B1 GPCRs that prioritizes phylogenetic relationships over functional annotation alone. Specifically, we propose the renaming of Cluster A receptors to protostome CALCR-like receptors (p-CALCRL) and Cluster B receptors to GPSR-like receptors (GPSRL). The proposed renaming improves gene annotation accuracy, facilitates cross-species comparisons, and advances understanding of the evolutionary dynamics of peptide signalling systems across Metazoa.
authors: Cardoso JCR, Alberto T, Saque M, Bentes J, Carrera E, Maia B, Ramos D, Yanez-Guerra L, Power DM.

title: Tools for genetic mapping and gene identification in Caenorhabditis briggsae
abstract: The nematode Caenorhabditis briggsae serves as an important companion species for Caenorhabditis elegans for comparative studies. Because C. briggsae exhibits androdioecious reproduction and ease of laboratory culture similar to C. elegans, it has long been used for genetic studies in cross-species comparisons of mutant phenotypes to uncover the evolution of gene function. Here, we provide an updated toolkit for C. briggsae genetic experiments, leveraging the resource of recently improved C. briggsae genome sequence assemblies with variant mapping tools and gene identification methods. We identify and validate a set of indel variants between CGC2 (AF16) and two divergent strains, HK104 and VX34. We then use these variants to genetically map 10 previously isolated mutations and identify the impacted genes using high-throughput sequencing. We combine these new genes with others curated from the literature into an updated map with 73 genes, providing an enriched resource for C. briggsae genetic studies.
authors: Lyu H, Jhaveri NS, O'Connor LM, Tanny RE, Freytag K, Genova C, Gupta B, Andersen EC, Chamberlin HM.

title: Protify: A Benchmarking Platform Revealing Task Dependence and Homology Leakage in Protein Language Model Evaluation
abstract: Protein Language Models (pLMs) have become essential tools for computational protein analysis, and the rapid proliferation of architectures, training objectives, and pretraining corpora has produced a diverse and expanding model landscape. Evaluation practices, however, remain fragmented: studies use different datasets, preprocessing pipelines, and reporting conventions, so results rarely transfer between publications. Here we introduce Protify, an open-source platform that standardizes pLM benchmarking across zero-shot, supervised, and transferlearning settings through a unified, low-code interface. Protify currently supports 35 pretrained models and 61 curated datasets and it is easy to add custom versions of each. Leveraging Protify's high throughput pipelines, we benchmarked 23 models on ProteinGym, discovering that DPLM3B is currently the top-performing self-supervised encoder. Another large-scale supervised evaluation across 32 diverse tasks, spanning enzyme classification, gene ontology annotation, protein-protein interaction, subcellular localization, and other functional properties, found that no single pLM dominated: 14 different models took the top score on at least one dataset, and the margins between the best and second-best models fell within run-to-run variability. On enzyme optimal pH prediction, a general-purpose probe pipeline matched or exceeded EpHod, a specialized model selected from 11,550 training runs, after 50 hyperparameter trials (R2 = 0.482 versus 0.425). Under a homology-controlled split of the same data, every pooled-embedding probe collapsed to near-zero R2, and only a transformer probe over full residue embeddings recovered appreciable signal (R2 = 0.248). Model rankings therefore depend as much on evaluation design as on the models themselves. Protify makes those design choices explicit, controlled, and replayable, and is freely available at https://github.com/Gleghorn-Lab/Protify.
authors: Rafailidis N, Hallee LP, Peleg T, Horger C, Haviland L, Gleghorn JP.

title: An information-theoretic framework for inferring T cell dynamics from single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing.
abstract: Single-cell T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire sequencing enables simultaneous profiling of gene expression and TCR sequences, providing a coregistered measure of T cell phenotypic diversity and clonal dynamics. However, principled probabilistic frameworks for joint modeling of clonotype and phenotype have remained limited. Here we introduce TCRi, a hierarchical Bayesian information-theoretic framework that infers the joint probability distribution between genetic clonotype and transcriptional phenotype from paired single-cell transcriptomic and TCR sequencing data. TCRi treats phenotype assignment as a probabilistic inference problem: a variational autoencoder embeds single-cell expression into a structured latent space, and a hierarchical Bayesian model learns clonotype-specific phenotype distributions through principled information-sharing across clonotypes, patients and covariates. From these distributions, TCRi computes information-theoretic quantities: clonotypic entropy, phenotypic entropy, phenotypic flux and mutual information between clonotype and phenotype. When TCRi was applied to four real-world datasets comprising 167,118 CD8 T cells from patients with cancer treated with anti-PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint blockade, mutual information emerged as a robust discriminator of therapeutic response.

title: Polyphosphate and Disordered Hfq Regions Drive DNA Compaction through Conformation-Dependent Interactions.
abstract: The RNA-binding protein Hfq and inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) were previously suggested to promote DNA compaction of AT-rich regions by forming heterochromatin-like structures, yet the underlying molecular mechanism remains unclear. Here, we combine coarse-grained and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the interplay between Hfq, polyP, and DNA. Under physiological conditions, polyP electrostatically interacts with the distal faces of multiple Hfq hexamers, clustering them near DNA and leaving the proximal faces available to interact with the DNA minor groove via the disordered N-termini, thereby promoting compaction. While this mechanism shows limited dependence on DNA sequence, it is highly sensitive to environmental conditions. Under high-salt conditions, electrostatic interactions are screened, weakening polyP-Hfq association and limiting Hfq clustering, while stabilization of non-canonical DNA conformations exposes hydrophobic surfaces. These changes shift the mode of Hfq interaction with DNA toward its distal face and disordered C-termini, favoring hydrophobic interactions and reducing compaction. Together, our findings reveal a conformation-dependent switch in Hfq-DNA interaction modes governed by cellular conditions, providing a molecular framework for environment-responsive genome organization in bacteria.
authors: Navon Y, Levy Y.
