title: DoAggregate: a pipeline for aggregation testing for rare-variant on a gene and pathway level
abstract: Motivation  Aggregation tests overcome the classical limitation of rare variant analysis in cohort study design. Choosing the right statistical test remains one of the biggest challenges. Existing tools fall short in offering a comprehensive solution that includes automatic data processing, testing across all genes, as well as exploration of broader genetic regions such as pathways and Gene Ontology (GO) terms. Most aggregation tests only report p-values and basic statistics, lacking in the presentation of cohort level statistics and comparison of results across whole genome or exome scales. Results  We introduce DoAggregate, an innovative, scalable pipeline designed to address these challenges. DoAggregate enables users to perform aggregation tests across genes, pathways, and GO terms. It leverages Excalibur, an ensemble approach combining 36 distinct aggregation methods. The pipeline enhances data analysis by presenting over-representation analysis and aggregation results in detailed Excel sheets, complete with annotations and plots to facilitate nuanced interpretation and comparison. Applied to public exome data from the 1000 Genomes Project, DoAggregate tested 10,447 genes, 49 over-represented pathways and 36 over-represented GO terms in a single run, returning annotated, cohort-level results for each region. Availability and implementation  DoAggregate source code, documentation and installation instructions as well as test data sets and results are freely available at  https://github.com/boutrys/DoAggregate and released under the MIT license. The repository contains the serial implementation (R package), the parallel implementation for Slurm-based computer clusters and the web application.  Supplementary information  Supplementary data are available online.
authors: Boutry S, Van Marcke C, Limaye N, Smits G, Brouillard P, De Bortoli M, Pairet E, Saadat A, Helaers R, Fellay J, Lenaerts T, Vikkula M.

title: Matched-Control Benchmarking of Quantum Machine Learning Models for Hierarchical Protein Function Prediction
abstract: Abstract  Predicting protein function requires assigning hierarchical Gene Ontology (GO) terms to sequences with limited experimental annotation. We tested whether quantum machine learning improves this task when each model is compared with a classical control matched to its architecture or input representation. Five quantum models spanning variational circuits, quantum features, and fidelity kernels were evaluated on 40,000 proteins from the CAFA6 training release, using frozen 480-dimensional ESM-2 embeddings, 180 GO terms, and an internal cluster-disjoint train–validation–test split. Kernel bandwidths were selected through a training-only concentration screen (Gate-0), which also estimated shots required per kernel entry. Across five seeds, the standalone quantum models scored below their matched controls by 0.0023–0.0847 in aspect-mean maximum F-measure; the 48-layer re-uploading kernel was admitted in only two seeds and lost in both. Freezing the variational circuit did not reduce performance. Late fusion of quantum and classical predictions improved on cosine nearest neighbours by 0.0034, but kernel-level mixing selected a purely classical weight, and the fused score (0.6697) remained below that of a classical RBF nearest-neighbour model (0.6719). Finite-shot simulations preserved this ordering, although the quantum kernel ridge model was sensitive to shot noise. These results provide no evidence of a standalone quantum advantage on this benchmark. The fusion gain is consistent with complementary prediction errors, but its mechanism remains to be tested against a matched classical ensemble.
authors: Majidi F.

title: Fast Protein Crystal detection and classification using Detectron2 and gaussian mixture models for continuous Bioprocessing
abstract: Abstract  The fast and accurate detection of protein crystals is essential in the biopharmaceutical industry. This work presents a unified approach that integrates Detectron2-based instance segmentation with optimized image pre-processing and Gaussian Mixture Model clustering. Protein crystallization underpins structural biology and drug discovery, yet manual inspection of microscopy images is time-consuming, subjective, and error-prone. We developed an automated end-to-end pipeline for crystal detection and characterization on microfluidic platforms. The dataset contains 1,860 images, with 382 annotated, for instance segmentation. Baselines including YOLOv3 and edge-based methods, struggle in high-density conditions and produce false positives from artifacts. Models Detectron2 Mask R-CNN ResNet-101–FPN, achieving a high average statistical metric, the Dice Score of 0.90 while maintaining a false-positive rate below 5\%, as confirmed through expert validation. A GMM module in PCA-reduced features identifies four clusters with weights [0.5926, 0.1650, 0.2252, 0.0172], reflecting morphology patterns. The framework enables accurate crystal measurement and morphology analysis, achieving 92\% agreement with expert annotations and fewer than 5\% false-positive detections during validation, thereby reducing observer-dependent bias and supporting high-throughput crystallisation screening. Improves reproducibility and efficiency, supports data-driven structural biology, and rational drug design, enabling faster protein structure determination and therapeutic discovery..
authors: Kuhn R, Horacek F, Kumari P, Patel MN, Adedokun O, Bano S, Pancholi K.

title: scRM: A single-cell foundation model trained on scRNA-seq reads
abstract: Single-cell foundation models currently learn from gene count matrices, which are discretized, species-specific summaries that discard the RNA sequence, splice-site usage, 3  ′ UTR isoform identity and the mutational information present in the underlying sequencing reads. Here we introduce single-cell raw data pretraining, a framework that trains foundation models directly on sequencing reads, requiring no read alignment or count matrix, allowing any trained model to be applicable to arbitrary species.  Our first model in this framework, the single-cell read model scRM, pairs two transformer encoders with a hierarchy of attention pools and contains 1.2 million parameters. We trained it as a JEPA on 3,000 mouse neuron cells on a single H100 in one hour, and benchmarked it zero-shot against leading single-cell foundation models with orders of magnitude more parameters and training cells. Our results show that our lightweight model reaches the performance of existing models on all tasks, and exceeds every one of them on perturbation detection tasks whose detection requires sequence-level detail. To our knowledge, scRM is the first single-cell foundation model trained on sequencing reads, demonstrating that raw data pretraining is not only feasible but competitive at a fraction of the computational cost. We anticipate that scaling this framework and exploring alternative architectures will unlock biological information inaccessible to count models and extend the dataset-specific pretraining it already makes possible. The source code is available at  https://github.com/altoslabs/scRM .
authors: He D, Patro R, Nassar M, Wu H, Yan Q, Xu G, Torkenczy K, Liu J, Tyanova S.

title: A new tool for quantifying mitochondrial RNA processing intermediates reveals increased levels of immature mRNA species under oxidative stress
abstract: Summary  Mitochondrial gene expression in mammals requires the processing of polycistronic transcripts into mature RNAs, generating multigene maturation intermediates. Yet these species and their potential association with mitochondrial stress remain poorly characterized. We analyzed intact RNA species in healthy mouse hearts through direct RNA sequencing and identified polyadenylated mitochondrial transcripts containing complete mRNA sequences with uncleaved tRNA extensions, which we termed immature mRNAs (imRNAs). Guided by these findings, we developed a new computational tool to estimate imRNA levels using conventional short-read RNA-seq datasets. Analysis of mouse hearts deficient in mitochondrial superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), a model of mitochondrial oxidative stress, revealed selectively elevated levels of imRNAs retaining 5’ tRNA extensions, without increases in those with 3’ tRNA extensions. Comparative analyses of several mouse models with defects in mitochondrial respiration, transcription, translation, or proteostasis did not reproduce this pattern. A mouse model of mitochondrial import stress with reduced ROS generation exhibited decreased levels of imRNAs retaining 5’ tRNA extensions. Conversely, human induced pluripotent stem cells treated with rotenone, which elevates mitochondrial ROS, showed increased levels of imRNAs retaining 5’ but not 3’ tRNA extensions, reproducing the pattern observed in SOD2-deficient mouse hearts. These findings identify an imRNA signature potentially associated with mitochondrial oxidative stress. The presence of imRNAs described here suggests that widely used transcriptome analysis pipelines may count these species as mature mRNAs, overestimating mitochondrial mRNA levels and overlooking defects in RNA maturation. By enabling retrospective analysis of processing intermediates, our tool provides access to previously unexamined information in existing RNA-seq datasets.
authors: Ozkurede U, Rajhans S, Accornero F, Liu JC.

title: Genomic signatures of reproductive isolation are decoupled from floral divergence in a long-standing hybrid zone.
abstract: A central goal in evolutionary biology is to understand how species boundaries are maintained despite gene flow. Two North American wildflower species with divergent floral syndromes, Penstemon davidsonii (bee syndrome) and P. newberryi (bird syndrome), have formed hybrid zones in the eastern Sierra Nevada for at least 85 years. We combined multiple approaches to test whether divergent floral syndromes enforce reproductive isolation as predicted by classic models of pollinator-driven ecological speciation. The two parent species exhibited strong divergence across multivariate trait space and have maintained genomic differentiation despite persistent hybridization. Floral hue, a key component of pollination syndrome, mapped to a single genomic region containing two candidate genes with large effects on anthocyanin pigment composition. Pollinator visual models indicated that genetic variation at this region affects detectability to hummingbirds, but not bees. Genomic cline analyses identified many significantly steep clines, suggesting a polygenic basis to reproductive isolation. Surprisingly, these barriers appear unrelated to floral isolation; the major floral hue locus exhibits a strikingly shallow genomic cline and elevated heterozygosity, suggesting pervasive gene flow. Our results reveal that conspicuous trait divergence can be decoupled from reproductive barriers, challenging assumptions about how reproductive isolation is maintained in hybridizing populations.
journal: Evolution; international journal of organic evolution
authors: Stone BW, Williams NH, Depatie TH, Radford ZJ, Mosley AM, Wessinger CA.

title: Cytoplasmic ATR orchestrates PRRSV and EBOV replication organelle assembly via vimentin phosphorylation.
abstract: The ataxia telangiectasia-mutated and Rad3-related (ATR) kinase is a well-established master regulator of the DNA damage response and replication stress. In this study, we uncover an unexpected, conserved role of ATR in promoting the replication of two distinct RNA viruses-an arterivirus and a filovirus-through vimentin phosphorylation. Acute pharmacologic inhibition or knockdown of ATR robustly suppress viral replication and sharply reduce the formation of double-membrane vesicles and membrane-less condensates that serve as replication organelles (ROs) for these divergent viral classes. Notably, although ATR is recruited to cytoplasmic ROs throughout the viral life cycle, it acts specifically at the replication stage without affecting viral attachment, entry, or egress. We further show that ATR directly interacts with and phosphorylates vimentin within ROs, driving vimentin rearrangement and delineating RO boundaries. Mechanistically, ATR-dependent phosphorylation of vimentin at Ser459 is indispensable for RO formation during infection by both PRRSV and EBOV. Together, these findings reveal a conserved ATR-vimentin signaling axis that promotes RO biogenesis across diverse RNA viruses, defining a noncanonical function of cytoplasmic ATR in orchestrating the assembly of both membrane-bound and membrane-less replication compartments via vimentin phosphorylation.
authors: Xu C, Xia Y, Cao Z, Xu X, Xiang Y, Li F, Li P, Chiu S, Cai G, Wang X.

title: Positive promotion effect of negative potential on propanethiol degradation in microbial electrolytic cells.
abstract: Volatile organic sulfur compounds (VOSCs) are typical odorous pollutants that are difficult to abate. The effective removal of VOSCs by microbial electrolytic cells (MECs) is a promising strategy for reducing mitigation. This work employed propanethiol (PT) as a representative contaminate and explored the performance of MEC by controlling anodic potentials at -0.4, -0.2, 0, 0.2, 0.4 V (vs. Ag/AgCl). The results indicated that the potential of -0.2 V and -0.4 V increased PT removal by 8.2% and 13.9%, while sulfate conversion rose by 6.7% and 12.6%, demonstrating the prominent enhancement of negative polarization for PT remediation. Low-negative bioanode potentials of -0.4 V and -0.2 V drove high sulfur-to-sulfate conversion of 51.2% and 45.3%, highest protein/polysaccharide ratio of 1.37 and outer-membrane c-type cytochromes content of 36.7 μmol/cm3. Moreover, microbial community analysis showed that the abundance of functional species of Acinetobacter sp. and Thiobacillus sp. were increased. Furthermore, the observed nanowires together with metagenomic evidence further demonstrated that negative potentials exerted positive effects on microbial electroactivity. Overall, this study elucidates bioanode potential driven PT degradation of in MECs, providing valuable implications for abatement of VOSCs via bioelectrochemical systems.
authors: You J, Liu Z, Li Z, Ji Z, Yu J, Qu M.

title: TRACE: a framework for traceable biomedical resource construction demonstrated through single-cell glaucoma data
abstract: The growing availability of public omics datasets presents opportunities for biomedical research, yet constructing research question-driven resources from distributed studies remains challenging due to heterogeneous data, incomplete metadata and limited documentation of curation decisions. Here, we present TRACE (Traceable Resource Assembly and Curation Ecosystem), a general framework that links systematic knowledge discovery, data curation and resource delivery while preserving provenance throughout resource construction. We demonstrate TRACE through TRACE-scGlaucoma, a curated single-cell transcriptomics resource for glaucoma and optic nerve biology. Systematic screening identified 57 eligible studies, of which 42 provided accessible datasets comprising approximately 3.3 million cells. The resource provides harmonised metadata, standardised cell-type annotations and reusable expression objects while retaining original study information and curation provenance. We demonstrate its analytical utility through cellular enrichment of glaucoma GWAS-associated genes, comparing candidate drug-repurposing signals across distinct biological contexts and assessment of cell-type annotation reliability. TRACE provides a systematic and traceable approach to transforming fragmented public datasets into reusable biomedical resources, supporting reproducible analyses and future extensions across disease areas and data modalities.
authors: Liang X, Jayakumar R, Strbenac D, Torkel M, Bian B, Lee E, Gu J, Phan VTN, Crowston J, Yang JYH, Shim H.

title: Mapping the regulatory wiring of endothelial cell differentiation reveals a critical role for Hippo mechanosignaling
abstract: At each step of development, stem cells encounter a branching decision to differentiate into one type of cell or another. This decision is executed through the action of competing gene programs that specify different cellular identities. Consequently, creating a comprehensive map of the gene programs that drive each branching step of human cell differentiation remains a long-sought goal of developmental and stem cell biology. Here, we introduce a framework combining genome-wide CRISPR screens, single-cell readouts, and gene program inference to systematically discover and characterize regulators of cell differentiation. This framework includes a method for CRISPR perturbations paired with single-cell RNA-seq called circular capture Perturb-seq (CC-Perturb-seq), which improves gRNA detection from split-pool combinatorial indexing protocols and enables perturbing many candidate regulators to map their effects on gene programs. We applied this framework to map how human pluripotent stem cells differentiate into arterial endothelial cells (ECs), and identified 174 regulators that promote or inhibit EC differentiation. By tracking gene programs across three stages of differentiation, we resolved when and how regulators divert cells toward alternative fates. This map revealed an unexpected requirement for the Hippo mechanosignaling pathway in EC specification. During lateral mesoderm differentiation, Hippo mechanosignaling was required to activate ETV2, the master transcriptional regulator of endothelial identity. Inhibiting Hippo blocked ETV2 even in the presence of VEGF and diverted progenitors to a mesenchymal fate in vitro. Likewise, Hippo signaling was required for maximal etv2 expression in developing zebrafish embryos. Conversely, pharmacologically activating the Hippo pathway increased the purity of both arterial and venous EC differentiation in vitro. Our framework thus identifies novel regulators of endothelial cell differentiation, improves stem-cell differentiation protocols via manipulation of mechanosignaling, and provides a generalizable platform for mapping the regulatory wiring of human development.

title: Bacillus cereus MHI 86 and Bacillus thuringiensis 5-29 both produce the antilisterial bacteriocin thuricin S – analysis of antimicrobial spectrum, stability, and producer strain suitability, including cytotoxicity evaluation
abstract: Abstract    Thuricin-like bacteriocins are known for their potent antibacterial properties. This study characterizes thuricin S from  Bacillus (B.) cereus  MHI 86 and  B. thuringiensis  5–29 previously isolated from foods. Cell-free supernatants and partially purified thuricin S exhibited antibacterial activity against Gram-positive species, including  Listeria  and  Bacillus  . Thuricin S production started at mid exponential growth phase. Minimum inhibitory concentrations against  L. monocytogenes  were 5.73 µg/mL (MHI 86) and 10.77 µg/mL (5–29). Both genomes harbor thuricin S-encoding open reading frames. From 8 h of growth, transcription of the bacteriocin gene cluster was consistently detected with most prominent bands at 120 bp. Accordingly, antibacterially active peptides were found at ~ 3.1 kDa, consistent with the size of thuricin S. Ultra-performance liquid chromatography-electrospray ionization mass spectrometry confirmed the molecular mass of the partially purified peptides as 3137.6 Da. The bacteriocins were active at neutral and acidic pH (3–7) and up to 80°C. In conclusion, this study is the first to provide a comparative characterisation of thuricin S in two different  Bacillus  spp. It sheds light on the genetic and transcriptional basis of thuricin S production, as well as its growth and production kinetics, antimicrobial activity, molecular weight, stability, and associated toxin production and cytotoxicity. Notably, thuricin S can be used as a natural agent against  L. monocytogenes  to control post-pasteurisation contamination.
authors: Batman SG, Kittler S, Plötz M, Dräger G, Jessberger N.

title: Physicochemical Characterization, Cytotoxicity, and Antimicrobial Activity of Polymeric Nanoparticles for Ocular Delivery of Norfloxacin
abstract: Abstract    Ocular infections, can lead to severe complications, and may result in vision loss, if not treated effectively. Norfloxacin (NFX), a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic, acts by inhibiting bacterial DNA replication and transcription and is effective against drug-resistant pathogens commonly associated with serious ocular infections. However, its poor water solubility limits its therapeutic potential for ocular delivery. In this study nanoparticles was formulated with Eudragit® RS 100 (ERS100) and Polycaprolactone (PCL) to enhance the ocular bioavailability of NFX. The nanoparticles were prepared using the spray-drying method. According to the characterization studies the optimized formulation exhibited a particle size of 383.43 ± 8.01 nm, a low PDI of 0.135 ± 0.01, and a positively charged zeta potential of + 34.97 ± 0.22 mV, indicating excellent stability and favorable interaction with the negatively charged ocular surface, which may enhance the ocular bioavailability of NFX. Cytotoxicity studies using the MTT assay on the human retinal pigment epithelial cell line (ARPE-19) confirmed the ocular safety of the nanoparticles, as their IC  50  values vastly exceeded their minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs), indicating a broad therapeutic safety margin. Antimicrobial efficacy was further confirmed through disk diffusion and MIC assays. Based on the obtained results, it can be concluded that ERS100–PCL-based nanoparticles have strong potential as an effective ocular delivery system for NFX in the treatment of severe ocular infections.
authors: ÖZDEMİR İ, AYKAÇ K, ÖZMEN CK, ŞENEL B, SOYER P, BAŞARAN E.

title: Ecological and Molecular Basis of Capripoxvirus Cross-Host Transmission: From Transmission Networks to Adaptive Evolution.
abstract: BackgroundCapripoxvirus (CaPV), comprising sheeppox virus (SPPV), goatpox virus (GTPV) and lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV), represents a growing transboundary threat to global livestock, with expanding geographic distribution and increasingly prominent cross-species transmission in mixed farming systems.ObjectivesThis review systematically examines the multifaceted drivers of CaPV spillover from ecological, molecular and evolutionary perspectives.MethodsThis review integrates ecological, molecular and evolutionary analyses, incorporating mathematical modelling and summarising advances in CRISPR/Cas-based diagnostics.ResultsEcologically, a tripartite network involving habitat sharing, landscape permeability (e.g., forest farmland edges) and arthropod vectors is proposed; mathematical modelling identifies vector-to-host ratio and vaccination coverage as critical modulators of outbreak severity. Molecularly, genetic plasticity in terminal genomic regions (e.g., ankyrin family) and host range genes (HRGs) such as M062R, M159, and LSDV012 enable antagonism of host restriction factors including SAMD9, IFIT1 and PKR, with the C7L superfamily playing a pivotal role in breaching species barriers. Evolutionarily, recombination-driven diversification, immune selection pressure and genetic bottlenecks collectively shape adaptive radiation and frequent host jumping events. Advances in CRISPR/Cas-based diagnostics are summarised. However, live attenuated vaccines show limitations in safety and efficacy.Conclusions and clinical relevancePersistent challenges include ecological surveillance, molecular discrimination of the three species and vaccine-wild type recombination risks. By integrating these disciplines, this review offers a comprehensive framework for understanding CaPV cross-species transmission and supports the design of precision control strategies targeting ecological and molecular vulnerabilities.
authors: He Z, Zhang J, Kuang S, Li S, Chen J, Yang J, Ma Z, Ding J, Zhang B, Zhang Y.

title: Beyond occurrence: matrix-dependent microbial ecological responses to pharmaceutical and personal care products between water and surface sediments in an urbanized river-bay continuum.
abstract: Pharmaceutical and personal care products (PPCPs) are ubiquitous in urbanized estuarine and coastal systems, yet their associations with microbial communities and functional potential under environmentally realistic exposure conditions remains poorly understood, particularly across contrasting environmental matrices. Here, 36 PPCPs were systematically characterized over a year across water and surface sediments in the Shenzhen River-Bay system to elucidate their contamination patterns, ecological risks, and associations with microbial communities. PPCPs exhibited pronounced matrix-specific spatiotemporal dynamics, with concentrations reaching 4354.35 ng/L in water and 1497.25 ng/g dw in surface sediments during autumn. Distinct compositional profiles between the two matrices further revealed contrasting exposure patterns along the river-bay continuum. Integrated risk prioritization identified seven priority PPCPs, with distinct risk profiles emerging between water and surface sediments. Notably, PPCPs exhibited stronger independent associations with microbial community variation than major environmental parameters in both matrices, highlighting their ecological relevance at environmentally realistic concentrations. Moreover, PPCP-microbe-function relationships displayed pronounced matrix dependence: PPCPs showed significant positive direct associations with carbon-, phosphorus-, and sulfur-related functional potential in water and nitrogen-related functional potential in surface sediments. Collectively, these findings reveal associations among PPCPs, microbial communities, and nutrient-related functional potential across environmental matrices, highlighting the need to account for matrix-specific environmental contexts alongside contaminant concentrations in ecological risk assessment.
authors: Deng Y, Chen X, Zou J, Tang T, Sheng Y, Tang S, Zhang X.

title: Sub-Inhibitory Plant-Derived GRAS Compounds and the Salmonella Type III Secretion System: A Critical Review and a Genotype-Informed Path Forward.
abstract: Plant-derived compounds that are generally recognized as safe (GRAS) suppress Salmonella virulence gene expression at concentrations that do not inhibit growth. A recent comprehensive review covered this phenomenon broadly across membrane, efflux, quorum-sensing, and biofilm mechanisms. The present review takes a narrower view and examines one axis, the Type III Secretion System (T3SS) that translocates effector proteins during host-cell invasion. At growth-curve-confirmed sub-inhibitory concentrations, eugenol, thymol, carvacrol, and cinnamaldehyde downregulate T3SS-associated transcripts. In the most well-studied cases, this downregulation also extends to effector proteins. That evidence is summarized here and placed alongside the adjacent quorum-sensing, biofilm, and sub-MIC antibiotic literature, together with reporting gaps in PCR primer background and amplicon efficiency that limit how far some of these results can be pushed. Two questions relevant to pre-harvest control, with poultry production as the primary applied context, remain largely unaddressed. The first is whether the magnitude of virulence suppression varies predictably across genetically diverse Salmonella strains at two main resolutions: serovar and SNP-variation within a serovar. The second question is whether structure-guided computational screening can expand the candidate pool beyond the four essential oil constituents that dominate this review. To define potential targets for such screens, the 30 Salmonella T3SS structures currently available in the Protein Data Bank are summarized here by functional class. Answering both questions would move the field toward genomically informed, strain-specific compound selection as a precision pre-harvest intervention.
authors: Li X.

title: CgSTAT1 regulates the production of multiple immune effectors in anti-bacterial immune response in oyster.
abstract: Signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) is the critical component of the JAK/STAT signaling pathway. In the present study, a STAT homologue (termed CgSTAT1) was characterized from oyster Crassostrea gigas. The open reading frame of CgSTAT1 cDNA was of 2982 bp encoding a polypeptide of 993 amino acid. The mRNA transcripts of CgSTAT1 were observed in all tested various tissues, with the highest level in hemocytes. After Vibrio splendidus stimulation, the mRNA expression of CgSTAT1 was significantly up-regulated in hemocytes, and CgSTAT1 translocated from hemocyte cytoplasm into nucleus. In CgSTAT1-knockdown oyster, the mRNA expressions of CgIL17-2, CgIL17-6, CgTNF-1, CgDefh2 and CgNOS in hemocytes were significantly decreased after V. splendidus stimulation. The bacterial clearance ability in cell-free hemolymph of STAT1-RNAi oyster decreased significantly, and the NO concentration also declined. These results collectively demonstrated that CgSTAT1 played important roles in regulating the anti-bacterial immune response by triggering the expression of immune effectors.
authors: Wang L, Wu Z, Sun J, Yang W, Mu S, Liu Z, Li X, Song L.

title: Vernalization-associated induction of BdFUL2 and its contribution to flowering time in Brachypodium distachyon.
abstract: The genome of grass model plant Brachypodium distachyon has four FRUITFULL (FUL) genes. Among them, only the function of BdVRN1/FUL1 in flowering time has been elucidated, the functions of other three BdFUL proteins remain largely unknown. In this study, we investigated the involvement of BdFUL2 in response to vernalization firstly. Similar to BdVRN1, we found that the H3K4me3 level and the expression of BdFUL2 are regulated by vernalization. Then, the contribution of BdFUL2 to flowering time was identified under long day conditions by generating RNA interference lines. Consistent with late flowering phenotype, the expression of several flowering related genes was altered in BdFUL2 RNA interference plants, such as BdFT1, BdFT2, BdVRN2. The results of electrophoresis mobility shift and yeast one hybrid experiments showed that BdFUL2 can directly bind to BdFT2 promoter. Furthermore, we verified the interaction between BdFUL2 and BdVRN1 by BIFC and CO-IP. Additionally, we found that BdFUL2 is associated with gibberellin synthesis. Our findings extend the understanding of the function and mechanism of FUL transcription factors in flowering time.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Li H, Su Y, Fan J, Sun X.

title: C-Terminal Dimerization Enables Assembly of Ebola Virus VP30 Oligomers with transcriptional support activity.
abstract: Ebola virus VP30 is a multifunctional phosphoprotein essential for initiating viral transcription. VP30 functions as a homo-oligomer, where oligomerization is critical for its transcriptional-support activity. While a tetra-leucine motif in the N-terminal region (amino acids (aa) 100-105) mediates oligomerization, the structural determinants and functional relevance of a VP30 dimerization motif in the C-terminus remained poorly defined. Using a novel high-resolution (1.43 Å) crystal structure and biochemical approaches, we identified residues 142ITLL145 in the VP30 C-terminal domain (CTD) as key contributors to VP30 dimerization. Alanine conversions of these residues (VP30-CTD142-145A) disrupted CTD dimerization, as demonstrated by native mass spectrometry, size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering, and split-GFP complementation assays. Notably, VP30-CTD functions as a dominant-negative inhibitor of full-length VP30 in a minigenome assay, whereas the dimerization-deficient mutant VP30-CTD142-145A does not. Critically, introduction of these mutations into full-length VP30 completely abolished viral transcription in minigenome assays. Recombinant EBOV carrying the VP30 dimerization mutations could not be rescued in cell culture, demonstrating that VP30-CTD dimerization is essential for viral replication. Together, these findings establish that CTD-mediated dimerization is essential for VP30's transcriptional support activity and virus propagation, identifying VP30 dimerization as a previously uncharacterized determinant of the viral replication cycle. Importantly, the dimerization interface is conserved among filoviruses, suggesting it represents a broadly conserved and potentially targetable vulnerability for antiviral intervention.
authors: Veeck C, Werner AD, Mais CN, Hartlieb B, Bange G, Becker S.

title: Surface engineering of cell-derived particles for targeted delivery of genome editors.
abstract: Genome editing technologies hold significant promise for the treatment of genetic disorders, but safe and efficient delivery remains a major barrier to their clinical translation. Cell-derived particles, including extracellular vesicles (EVs) and virus-like particles (VLPs), have emerged as promising non-viral delivery platforms, offering biological compatibility and the capacity to package and deliver genome editors as ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes in a transient manner that reduces the risk of off-target editing. The surface composition of these vehicles is shaped by their biogenesis pathway and their cell of origin, which in turn govern their cellular tropism. Through various engineering strategies, including producer cell engineering, viral-glycoprotein pseudotyping, and post-isolation surface modifications, this tropism can be expanded or redirected toward cell types and tissues beyond the liver. Here, we review the biology underlying cell-derived particle surface composition and the targeting strategies employed to engineer cell-type specificity.
authors: DeAgazio C, Singh A, Banskota S.

title: Pandemic-Driven Shifts in RSV Diversity, Evolution, and Global Spread
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic dramatically disrupted the seasonal circulation of RSV, with subsequent heterogeneous global resurgence. We aimed to characterize how pandemic-era disruptions restructured global RSV transmission dynamics, evolutionary patterns, and drivers of reemergence. We show that RSV-A and RSV-B genetic diversity underwent profound pandemic-associated suppression followed by heterogeneous resurgence. The post-pandemic period was characterized by pronounced changes in diversity, with the emergence of novel RSV-A genotypes (A.D.3 and A.D.5.2) and the expansion of the RSV-B, B.D.E.1 genotype. The recovery of RSV-B deviated strongly from neutral expectations and positive selection was detected at 20 sites in the G glycoprotein, F fusion protein, and M2-2 regulatory protein. Phylogeographic reconstruction revealed a sharp decline in international viral spread during the pandemic, followed by increasing persistence. Europe consistently served as the predominant global source, followed by Western Pacific and North America. Air-travel volume was the strongest predictor of dissemination (log coefficient >0.68 for both subtypes). Post-pandemic RSV resurgence represented fundamental epidemiological restructuring shaped by a population bottleneck, positive selection and major impact of air-travel. These findings underscore the need for robust genomic surveillance to track the global circulation of lineages, and to monitor effectiveness of pharmaceutical interventions given the emergence of new genotypes. One Sentence Summary  Air Mobility and Diversifying Selection Shape Post-Pandemic RSV Global Diversity
authors: Gustani-Buss E, Weinberger DM, Grubaugh ND, Colizza V, Shao Y, Suchard M, Evers A, Mazur NI, Wildenbeest JG, Lebbink RJ, van Zoggel HJ, Bont L, Lemey P.

title: MET inhibition exploits conserved regulatory dependencies in malignant rhabdoid tumors
abstract: Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are lethal, yet genomically simple childhood cancers characterised by universal SWI/SNF dysregulation. Despite this shared molecular framework, the regulatory programs sustaining MRTs and how they wire actionable dependencies, remain poorly defined. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omic profiling and spatial transcriptomics across anatomically and molecularly diverse MRTs, generating a comprehensive multimodal MRT dataset at single-cell resolution. We leveraged this resource to identify candidate tumor-specific dependencies, which were subsequently functionally validated in vitro and in vivo in matched patient-derived models. We found that distinct malignant subpopulations are spatially patterned in complex environmentally shaped topologies, consistent with reciprocal interactions with stromal and immune compartments contributing to intratumoral transcriptional diversity. We identified recurrent transcriptional metaprograms conserved across patients and molecular subtypes, including a previously undescribed shared core rhabdoid program, as well as a metaprogram characterized by extracellular matrix interactions, and preferentially localized in tumor-stroma intermixed neighborhoods, supporting identification of niche conditioning cues. Mechanistically, we identified regulatory wiring driving these metaprograms, with the core shared rhabdoid programme coordinated by a circuit centred on TCF12, ZNF148 and CHD2. Guided by target nominations from our integrated analyses, we performed a curated drug screen using patient-derived MRT models and validated HGF/MET signaling as a selective vulnerability in extrarenal rhabdoid tumors. Pharmacologic MET inhibition was cytotoxic in sensitive models and induced a complete response in vivo using a clinically approved compound. Importantly, MET expression in primary tumors correlated with response, supporting biomarker-guided patient stratification for immediate clinical translation. Collectively, our findings define the molecular architecture of MRTs, reveal conserved regulatory programs beyond anatomical and molecular subtypes, and highlight a targetable signaling axis with immediate translational potential, establishing a framework for precision therapy in this lethal pediatric malignancy. Highlights  Comprehensive multimodal atlas of malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) integrating single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and in vivo functional validation in matched patient-derived models. Recurrent malignant transcriptional metaprograms are conserved across MRT subtypes and are spatially zonated within tumors, highlighting plasticity in response to environmental cues. A core rhabdoid regulatory circuit centred on TCF12/ZNF148/CHD2 coordinates the principal shared malignant program. Drug screening and functional validation identify core regulatory circuit-linked HGF/MET axis dependence in a subset of MRTs. Treatment with a clinically approved MET inhibitor induces striking complete response in vivo in MET-high tumors, supporting MET IHC-guided patient selection and immediate therapeutic translation.

title: Design and Recombinant Production of Proline-rich Antimicrobial Peptide 385P
abstract: Abstract    The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance has increased the search for alternative agents with novel mechanisms of action. Here, we established an end-to-end framework for the rational development of proline-rich antimicrobial peptides (PrAMPs), integrating computational motif discovery, peptide design, recombinant production, and biological characterization. Conserved motifs from highly active PrAMPs were identified and ranked using MEME and rationally assembled to generate the 36-amino acid peptide 385P. A C-terminal hexahistidine-tagged construct (r385P) was successfully produced in  Pichia pastoris  GS115 and confirmed by SDS-PAGE, Western blotting, and His-tag ELISA. r385P exhibited broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, with MICs of 4–32 µg/mL against Gram-negative bacteria, 2–32 µg/mL against Gram-positive bacteria, and 64 µg/mL against  Candida albicans  and  Candida glabrata  , with the highest antibacterial activity against  Listeria monocytogenes  and  Acinetobacter baumannii  . r385P exhibited strong antibiofilm activity, achieving 83.83% inhibition against  Escherichia coli  O157:H7 at MIC/2 and complete inhibition against  Staphylococcus aureus  at MIC. FICI assays revealed antibiotic- and species-dependent interactions, including synergy with kanamycin against  Klebsiella pneumoniae  (FICI = 0.375) and consistent additive interactions with tetracycline. r385P retained full antimicrobial activity after exposure to 50–200 mM NaCl and 1–4 h of trypsin treatment, while MICs increased two- and four-fold following exposure to 65 and 95°C, respectively. Hemolysis remained below 4% at 256 µg/mL, while MRC-5 cell viability was 71% at 320 µg/mL. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the potential of conserved-motif assembly as a practical strategy for developing functionally robust PrAMP candidates.
authors: Kesmen Z, Canpolat M, Herdem D.

title: HLA-B*57 as a Dominant Genetic Determinant of HIV-1 Elite Control: Comparative Reanalysis of MHC Variant Associations in European andAfrican-American Cohorts A reanalysis of published genomic association data
abstract: Abstract  Background  HIV-1 elite controllers (EC) maintain undetectable viral loads without antiretroviral therapy; a phenotype strongly linked to variation in the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC). HLA-B*57:01 is the most replicated genetic association with elite control in individuals of European ancestry, with HLA-B*57:03 identified as its counterpart in African-ancestry populations. Whether the structure of this association – its dose-dependence and independence from other MHC signals – has been characterized consistently across both ancestries has not been addressed in accessible form. Methods  Using published allele/carrier frequencies from Rahmouni et al. (2025, 2023), we analyzed a European cohort (543 elite controllers, 3,272 uninfected controls) and an African-American cohort (759 HIV-1-seropositive individuals enriched for elite controllers, cs1 + cs2, ICGH consortium). For the European cohort, we performed: (1) primary HLA-B*57 association testing, (2) a nine-variant MHC panel analysis, (3) a viral-load trend test, and (4) an HLA-B*57-Stratified Association Analysis. For the African-American cohort, we tested enrichment of rs1131446 (the HLA-B*57:03 tag SNP) relative to its background frequency in the general African population (1000 Genomes AFR, n = 661). All tests used Fisher's exact test with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction where applicable. title: Turnip crinkle virus coat protein determines whether salicylic acid promotes or restricts infection
abstract: Abstract  Turnip crinkle virus (TCV) coat protein (CP) coordinates virion assembly, immune recognition, and RNA silencing suppression, but how these functions shape disease remains unclear. We redirected CP from the nucleus by appending an identical nuclear export signal to either terminus. Despite similarly reducing nuclear CP accumulation, N- and C-terminal modifications produced opposing effects on disease, viral accumulation, particle formation, and HRT-mediated recognition, indicating that sustained nuclear CP is dispensable for these outcomes. Transcriptomic and biochemical analyses revealed that disease severity closely tracked salicylic acid (SA) accumulation. Genetic disruption of SA biosynthesis reduced chlorosis and necrosis, establishing SA as a driver of TCV-associated disease. However, SA had CP-dependent effects on viral accumulation, promoting WT and N-NES infection while restricting C-NES. The R6A CP mutant uncoupled disease from viral burden, inducing SA and severe symptoms despite reduced accumulation. Thus, CP determines SA induction and whether an SA-rich environment favors or restricts TCV.
authors: Rademacher D, Kingsolver B, Dawane A, May J.

title: Toxic mercury, aquatic ecosystem collapse, and the ancient Lowland Maya.
abstract: Environmental impacts endured by the Lowland Maya during the Classic Period (250 to 920 CE) included droughts, deforestation, and soil erosion. Recent studies on mercury (Hg) pollution and cyanotoxins suggest that degraded water quality was also a stressor for the Pre-Columbian Maya. Hg in the Maya region is related to use of both elemental mercury and mineral cinnabar (HgS), the latter used as a red pigment. Questions, however, remain concerning the toxicity of Hg or the consequences of prehistoric Hg exposure on ecosystem and human health. Here, we show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation. Sediments also have evidence of aquatic food web collapse (algae, bacteria, cyanobacteria, ostracods, snails, and nonbiting midges), coincident with the time of high Hg concentrations, confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.
authors: Waters MN, Wooten SL, Abrook AM, Brenner M, Curtis JH, Langdon PG, Medina-Gonzalez RM, Paradeisis-Stathis S, Vachula RS.

title: A biofilm-derived peptide as an underwater adhesive.
abstract: Wet adhesives that perform under water have broad applications in industrial and biomedical settings. To date, molecular designs for underwater adhesives have largely been inspired by marine animals including mussels and barnacles. Here, we propose bacterial biofilms as an alternative source of inspiration for underwater adhesives. Specifically, we demonstrate the application potential of a peptide derived from biofilms formed by the notorious pathogen Vibrio cholerae. We characterize the ability of this biofilm-derived peptide to adsorb onto various surfaces and to glue wet surfaces by using a combination of confocal microscopy, molecular dynamics simulations, atomic force microscopy, lap shear tests, and spectroscopic tools. We further show that the peptide can coaggregate with microspheres acting as an effective flocculant. Our results open new design possibilities for underwater adhesives inspired by natural biofilms.
authors: Huang X, Liszczyk ED, Prasad R, Mitchell ME, Wang Z, Liu Y, Saluja S, Wang M, Jackson RA, Dahl P, Eguiluz RA, Malvankar N, Yan ECY, Olson R, Zhou HX, Yan J.

title: Massively parallel self-assembly of suspendable microcompartments for functional cell screening.
abstract: Modern biology increasingly demands platforms that can compartmentalize and analyze single cells and cell-cell interactions at massive scale, yet existing compartmentalization strategies based on microfluidics suffer from critical limitations. Emerging lab-on-a-particle technologies such as nanovials enable anchored single cells or small groups of cells to be isolated and assayed in a fully suspendable and parallelized manner using standard instrumentation, although their open architectures can result in loss of growing or un-attached cells. Here, we introduce capped nanovials: self-assembling hydrogel compartments formed by docking spherical capping particles into bowl-shaped nanovials. We routinely achieve capping of >80% of all nanovials in a sample and >90% sorting yield by flow cytometry, making the capped nanovial system well-suited for preparing and running large-scale assays. Furthermore, we demonstrate stable clonal expansion of single mammalian, yeast, and bacterial cells; growth-based selections of >10,000 colonies; enhanced signal-to-noise in secretion assays; and high-purity selection of antibody-secreting cells based on activation of co-encapsulated T cell reporters (>30-fold signal, up to 100% selection purity). By combining the simplicity of a well plate with the functional precision of droplet microfluidics without requiring oil or custom instrumentation, capped nanovials realize accessible, high-throughput, and high-resolution experimentation.
authors: Mellody M, Nakagawa Y, Arnheim A, Shang L, Soo C, Tsubamoto N, Taylor S, Ghosh R, Ho M, Guenther AM, Shastry S, Luk W, Morales I, Liang J, de Rutte J, James RG, Di Carlo D.

title: Explainable computational framework for subtype classification and biomarker identification in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma using machine learning.
abstract: The precise classification of basal, classical, atypical, and mesenchymal subtypes of Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma (HNSCC) is crucial for advancing precision oncology. Our research aims to develop an explainable subtype classification model for HNSCC.These molecular subtypes have been previously defined; reliable and meaningful computational methods for the classification of molecular subtypes and prioritization of molecular biomarkers for each subtype do not exist. We developed an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model that classifies molecular subtypes based on combined transcriptomic profiles from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA-HNSC) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GSE65858). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to quantify the importance of genes for model predictions. Subsequently, genes with high predictive importance were analyzed in protein-protein interactions using STRING, and hub genes were identified by Maximum Clique Centrality (MCC) and used for the identification of candidate biomarkers for each of the subtypes. We employed machine learning methods such as Random Forest (RF), Logistic Regression (LR), Decision Tree (DT), AdaBoost (AB), Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Gaussian Naive Bayes (GNB), XGBoost (XGB), and Gradient Boosting (GB). The XGBoost model achieved an accuracy of 95% after hyperparameter tuning and cross-validation. Biologically relevant subtype-specific biomarkers associated with each molecular subtype were identified. To highlight the potential biological functions of these biomarkers, pathway analysis was performed. Further assessment of these genes, such as survival analysis and druggability, showed promise for the development of targeted therapies.
authors: Rajan A, Biji CL, Sinha MG, Oviya IR.

title: Bioremediation potential assessment of the developed Microalgae-Bacterial Biofilm using 3D-printed PLA carriers.
abstract: The high energy demand of conventional wastewater treatment and the depletion of freshwater resources call for cost-effective and sustainable treatment solutions. Microalgae-based systems have gained attention due to their dual role in nutrient removal and biomass valorization. This study investigates a Coupled Microalgae-Bacterial Biofilm (CMBB) system for the bioremediation of primary-treated domestic wastewater, developed by immobilizing an indigenous microalgae-bacterial consortium on in-house-designed three-dimensional (3D) printed polylactic acid (PLA) carriers. After 5 days of enrichment, each carrier accumulated 231 ± 7.83 mg of biomass. The carriers were evaluated in laboratory-scale batch reactors (1.2 L working volume; n = 3) at 50%, 75% and 100% surface-area coverage over a 7-day treatment cycle. The 75% coverage gave the highest organic removal: after a hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 5 days it removed 87.21 ± 2.1% of total COD, 81.82 ± 2.15% of soluble COD (sCOD) and 69.32 ± 3.2% of BOD5, and BOD5 removal rose to 76.14% after day 7. At all coverages, ammoniacal nitrogen was removed by 95-98%, nitrate by about 65-69% and phosphate by about 83% within 7 days. Nitrate did not accumulate, which indicates that nitrogen removal was dominated by assimilation into algal-bacterial biomass, possibly together with simultaneous nitrification-denitrification, rather than by nitrification alone. Effluent tCOD fell below the 80 mg/L irrigation-reuse limit within 3 days at 75% and 100% coverage, and BOD5 fell below 30 mg/L by day 7. Under the same experimental conditions, the attached biofilm performed efficiently in removal of tCOD, sCOD and BOD5 than free (suspended) consortium cells. Combining indigenous consortia with engineered 3D-printed carriers is a promising low-energy route to decentralized wastewater treatment, nutrient recovery and water reuse; pilot-scale validation under field conditions is the next step.
authors: Singh B, Dhir A, Rout PR, Mamane H, Sharma SG.

title: Epigenetic and transcriptional control of sexual development in the multicellular Sordariomycete fungi.
abstract: SUMMARYMany Sordariomycete fungi produce flask-shaped perithecia that encapsulate meiotic cells and facilitate dispersion of sexual spores. Perithecial development represents a striking example of complex multicellularity in fungi, requiring coordinated gene regulation through transcriptional, chromatin-based, and post-transcriptional mechanisms. This review summarizes recent work to dissect sexual development in several well-studied fungi: Neurospora crassa, Sordaria macrospora, Podospora anserina, and Fusarium graminearum. Studies with these fungi have uncovered interconnected regulatory mechanisms that coordinate fruiting body development. Transcription factor networks control differentiation of perithecial tissues and cell types. Chromatin regulators, such as histone chaperones, ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers, acetyltransferases, and Polycomb Repressive Complex 2, impact major developmental transitions. In addition, post-transcriptional mechanisms that operate during sexual development play critical regulatory roles. Recoding of the transcriptome by A-to-I mRNA editing is specific to perithecia and is essential for sexual development of N. crassa and F. graminearum. Finally, sex-specific genome defense pathways protect genome integrity and are essential for the completion of meiosis in some species. We summarize recent advances and highlight the remarkable regulatory complexity underlying fruiting body development in Sordariomycete fungi. In addition, we identify key open questions for future research.
authors: Deaven AM, Lewis ZA.

title: Transgene expression kinetics and replication potential of recombinant adenovirus serotype 4 in a mouse model and its use as a herpes simplex virus vaccine.
abstract: Human adenovirus serotype 4 (Ad4) is used as a replication-competent oral vaccine that safely and effectively prevents Ad4 respiratory illness in US military personnel. Recombinant Ad4 vaccine candidates elicit mucosal and systemic immune responses against respiratory viruses in hamsters, nonhuman primates, and humans. Although evaluation of Ad4 vaccine candidates in mice would be extremely useful given the number of immunologic tools available, this has been limited by concerns about reduced viral replication in these animals. Here, we generated recombinant Ad4 vectors that express either luciferase (Ad4-Luc), green fluorescent protein (Ad4-EGFP), or herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) glycoprotein D (Ad4-gD2) to identify transgene expression kinetics, the presence of Ad4 vector replication, and HSV-2 immune responses and protection against HSV-2 infection. Local luciferase activity was observed from 7 h to 20 days after intranasal inoculation of BALB/c and humanized mice. Subsequent inoculations with Ad4-Luc showed reduced luciferase expression in BALB/c mice but robust expression in humanized mice, suggesting an immune response to the vector in wild-type mice. Ad4 DNA production, but not luciferase activity, was reduced in the lungs of BALB/c mice treated with cidofovir before inoculation with Ad4, implying that Ad4 replicated, albeit at a low level, in the lungs. Intranasal vaccination of mice with Ad4-gD2 resulted in HSV-2-neutralizing antibodies in the serum and, after HSV-2 intravaginal challenge, reduced disease scores, increased survival, and reduced shedding. Overall, the BALB/c mouse model is semi-permissive to Ad4 mucosal infection, but transgene expression is sufficient for the study of Ad4-based vaccine candidates.ImportanceMucosal surfaces serve as the primary site of infection and shedding for many viral pathogens. Immune responses at mucosal sites provide protection, but few mucosal vaccines are licensed. The oral replication-competent adenovirus serotype 4 (Ad4) vaccine is used to prevent respiratory illness in military recruits, has an extraordinary record of safety and efficacy, and has been tested as a recombinant platform for other viruses. Further development of this vaccine platform has been partially hindered by the perceived inability to evaluate vaccine candidates in mice. Here, we characterize recombinant Ad4 transgene expression kinetics and viral replication after inoculation at various sites and show protection against herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) genital disease in mice after intranasal vaccination. We show that Ad4 can induce protective efficacy, even in a semi-permissive mouse model, suggesting this is a promising vector for HSV-2 and potentially other viral pathogens.
authors: Vostal AC, Maciorowski D, Readler JM, Pytel IS, Patamawenu A, Cooney C, Roeder PM, Roenicke R, Van't Veer F, Kim T, Ober E, Yi Y, Gu J, Harrison M, Kim B, Liu G, Dowdell K, Hostal A, Wang K, Connors M, Cohen JI.

title: Introducing SARS-CoV-2 wastewater surveillance in Lebanon.
abstract: Wastewater surveillance (WWS) gained global attention during the COVID-19 pandemic as an early warning system to continuously monitor SARS-CoV-2 and its evolving variants. The aim of this study is to detect and sequence SARS-CoV-2 in wastewater from an area in Lebanon that hosts vulnerable groups of Lebanese residents and refugees. A total of 188 wastewater samples were collected from 18 manholes between 20 February 2023 and 31 May 2023. Viral RNA extraction, RT-PCR, and genomic sequencing were performed. Eighteen percent of collected samples were SARS-CoV-2-positive. Omicron BA.2 was the only circulating variant in February. An overlap between Omicron BA.2 (33.33%) and B.1.1-like sublineages, including C.26 (16.67%), B.1.1.207 (16.67%), B.1.1.214 (16.67%), and C.2.1 (16.67%) was detected in March. In April, while Omicron circulation decreased to 12.5%, a BA.1 and BA.2 recombinant (XM) was detected. The lack of disaggregated data sets and case-specific SARS-CoV-2 reports from the study site residents limited our ability to perform correlation and comparative analyses between wastewater and national clinical data. However, wastewater samples showed higher positivity rates during most of the months prior to national surges of cases. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating WWS in public health interventions to complement clinical and epidemiologic surveillance.ImportanceWastewater surveillance (WWS) is a valuable environmental surveillance tool that facilitates the real-time detection of circulating viruses and emerging variants. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to significant acceleration in the use of WWS as an early warning system for detecting SARS-CoV-2 and monitoring community transmission. This is the first study introducing SARS-CoV-2 community-based WWS in Lebanon. The findings of this study highlight the importance and feasibility of implementing WWS in a limited-resource setting to complement epidemiological surveillance in monitoring trends of SARS-CoV-2 at the population/community level.
authors: Bou Hamdan M, Mroweh M, Abou Hassan F, Germani A, Dejong J, El-Jardali F, Melhem NM, CAEP Study Group.

title: Recombinant Fusion of Polyglutamic Acid Enhances Cell-Penetrating Peptide-Mediated CRISPR-Cas9 Delivery.
abstract: Genome editing has been revolutionized by Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein 9 (Cas9) technology. However, efficient intracellular delivery of Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) remains a major challenge, particularly in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods. Integrating viral vectors carry a risk of insertional mutagenesis, whereas physical methods such as electroporation are not well suited for in vivo or clinically relevant applications. Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) offer a promising alternative for direct RNP delivery, although their efficiency is often limited by endosomal entrapment and limited cytosolic release. In this study, we developed two recombinant CPP-fused Cas9 proteins, polyglutamate (PE)-trans-activator of transcription (TAT)-nuclear localization signal (NLS)-Cas9 (PETATCas9) and TAT-NLS-Cas9 (TATCas9), designed to improve solubility, membrane penetration, RNP complex formation, and nuclear targeting. PE tag in PETATCas9 was introduced to optimize charge balance and reduce nonspecific electrostatic interactions between TAT and guide RNA (gRNA), thereby enhancing RNP stability and delivery performance. Both recombinant proteins were expressed, purified, and assembled with gRNA into functional RNP complexes for delivery into SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. The optimized CPP-Cas9 RNP system enabled efficient intracellular delivery and glucosylceramidase beta 1 (GBA1) gene editing in SH-SY5Y cells. These findings establish PETATCas9 as a scalable, transient, nonviral, and self-delivering RNP platform for CRISPR-based genome editing in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods.
authors: Sharma A, Seo Y, Park TS.

title: An ancestral T2 RNase provides insights into the origin and evolution of self-incompatible S-RNase.
abstract: With the evolution of true floral structures, angiosperms have become the most diverse and successful plant group, a success largely attributed to the genetic diversity generated by self-incompatibility. The canonical S-RNase (class III T2 RNase)/F-boxes locus that mediates gametophytic self-incompatibility is present across multiple lineages of core eudicots, and its origin has been traced back to the last common ancestor of core eudicots. However, because class III T2 RNases are completely absent from non-eudicot taxa, the origin of this S-RNase/F-boxes locus remains elusive. Here, we identify a rare class TI T2 RNase (EVM0017713)/F-boxes locus in the basal eudicot Akebia trifoliata as a candidate S-locus for late-acting self-incompatibility, sharing molecular features with the S-RNase/F-boxes locus. The class TI T2 RNase subfamily exhibits a continuous gradient transition from class I to class III T2 RNase subfamilies in terms of phylogenetic distribution, molecular structural characteristics, physicochemical properties, and gene structure. Crucially, the class TI EVM0017713/F-boxes locus is ancient and collinear with the S-RNase/F-boxes loci. These results suggest that the class TI T2 RNase/F-box locus may represent an ancestral form of the S-RNase/F-box system, offering new insights into the origin and evolution of plant self-incompatibility.
authors: Yang H, Li J, Zhong S, Han R, Yi X, Chen C, Hu X, Li Q, Luo P.

title: Tongue Microbiota in Children with Geographic Tongue: A Pilot Case-Control Study.
abstract: This study aimed to explore the characteristics of tongue microbiota in children with geographic tongue (GT) and provide microecological evidence for elucidating the occurrence and progression mechanism of GT. 16S rDNA high-throughput sequencing combined with bioinformatic analysis was adopted to compare the species differences of tongue microbial communities between children with GT and healthy children. The microbial richness of tongue coating in children with GT was markedly lower than that in healthy children (p Prevotella, Veillonella, and Actinomyces, while the tongue coating of children with GT was predominated by Neisseria, Pasteurellaceae, and Streptococcus. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes functional pathway enrichment analysis demonstrated an overall downregulation trend of metabolic functions in tongue coating microbiota of children with GT, with main differential pathways in histidine metabolism and teichoic acid biosynthesis. These results indicate that the onset of GT is highly correlated with abnormal enrichment of Neisseria, Pasteurellaceae, and Streptococcus. Imbalance of the tongue coating microbial communities may be involved in the development of GT.
journal: Omics : a journal of integrative biology
authors: Yuan D, Huang X, Lin Y, Ye W, Liao L.

title: Dynamic GelMA/Oxidized Hyaluronic Acid Hydrogels Enable Acid-Accelerated Localized Delivery of Photothermal Melatonin-Derived Carbon Dots for Infected Bone Repair.
abstract: Infected bone defects remain difficult to reconstruct because bacterial persistence, acidic stress, excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), inflammatory dysregulation, and impaired osteogenesis reinforce one another. Here, sulfur-doped melatonin carbon dots (DM-CDs) were synthesized from melatonin and d-cysteine and immobilized within a gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA)/oxidized hyaluronic acid hydrogel (GH-DM) through dynamic Schiff-base interactions. Sulfur-containing surface states endowed DM-CDs with strong 808 nm absorption, an approximately 50% photothermal conversion efficiency, stable heating cycles, and NIR-amplified antibacterial activity. The melatonin-derived surface simultaneously scavenged ROS, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, and was associated with increased Nrf2 and Sirt1 transcript levels together with recovery of CAT and SOD activities in mouse bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs). Under acidic conditions, dynamic imine interactions were associated with modestly accelerated DM-CD release, whereas NIR irradiation provided an external means to amplify local heating and antibacterial performance. GH-DM reduced planktonic bacterial viability and biofilm biomass, decreased cell-associated Staphylococcus aureus signals, and enhanced BMSC osteogenic differentiation, as shown by ALP activity, matrix mineralization, and increased RUNX2, ALP, COL1, and OCN expression. Mouse BMSC RNA sequencing revealed enrichment of collagen-containing extracellular-matrix programs and attenuation of NF-κB, IL-1β, IL-6, and osteoclast-differentiation-related signatures. Separate LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 experiments supported attenuation of a pro-inflammatory state and increased IL-10 expression. In infected femoral defects, GH-DM plus NIR markedly reduced bacterial burden and improved trabecular regeneration, with no detectable major-organ histopathology or abnormalities in the measured hematological, hepatic, and renal indices. These findings support a locally delivered carbon-dot hydrogel with acid-accelerated release that coordinates infection control, redox protection, inflammatory regulation, and bone regeneration.
authors: Xie E, Wu Y, Wang A, Liu X, Cang D, Zou G, Yin J.

title: Proteolytic feedback of quorum sensing promotes infection by  Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: ABSTRACT  Quorum sensing (QS) enables bacteria to coordinate collective behaviors in response to population density. However, the mechanisms by which QS circuits are reset or attenuated remain poorly understood. In  Pseudomonas aeruginosa , the LuxR-type transcription factor RhlR controls virulence gene expression at high cell density, requiring both its cognate acyl-homoserine lactone signal and the accessory protein PqsE for full activity. Here, we show that RhlR abundance is actively controlled by ATP-dependent proteolysis through a self-limiting negative feedback loop. We identify an N-terminal degron within RhlR that is protected from protease recognition by PqsE binding and is required for degradation by both the Lon and the ClpP1-ClpP2 protease complex. Removal of this degron stabilizes RhlR, advancing the timing of QS-regulated gene expression, enhancing biofilm formation, imposes a competitive fitness cost  in vitro , and reduced virulence in an acute mouse lung infection. Mechanistically, RhlR directly activates transcription of  clpP2 , encoding a subunit of the protease complex required for its own degradation, establishing a self-limiting negative feedback loop. Disruption of RhlR DNA binding stabilizes the receptor through dual effects on reduced  clpP2 expression and increased PqsE availability via the loss of RhlR- dependent repression of  pqsE . Together, these findings reveal proteolytic turnover as an underappreciated regulatory layer of QS-activation and establish a mechanism for how receptor turnover may facilitate the transition away from high-cell density states.
authors: Mallery CP, Fernandes SE, Schumacher ML, Pope AN, Dillow H, Mendoza AG, Jorth PA, Paczkowski JE.

title: Marine oil snow formation in microcosm incubations of artificial seawater at 4 °C
abstract: Abstract   An oil spill in the Arctic would have far-reaching impacts on the environment, the biota, and the Inuit communities that depend on this unique ecosystem for their livelihoods. Due to the rapid retreat of sea ice in the region, the Arctic is becoming more vulnerable to oil spills. Since microorganisms are the first responders to oil contamination, understanding their behavior is critical for designing bioremediation approaches tailored to Arctic conditions. In this study, we conducted microcosm experiments at 4 °C in the dark to simulate an Arctic oil spill, using crude oil and diesel as hydrocarbon sources. Biostimulation was tested with the addition of nutrients NaNO  3 and KH  2 PO  4 , and soy lecithin–Tween 80 dissolved in ethanol as an alternative dispersant. Microcosms were placed on tube rollers at 3 rpm to mimic natural wave action and run with appropriate controls to assess microbial community shifts. Our objectives were to characterize the early microbial succession associated with oil degradation and marine oil snow (MOS) formation, and to determine how nutrients, dispersants, oil type (crude vs. diesel), photochemical aging (fresh vs. weathered), and oil concentration influence these processes.  We observed that the combined effect of nutrients and dispersant resulted in rapid MOS formation, occurring as early as 30 minutes after the initial setup. Microbial taxa exhibited varying tolerance to different concentrations of the same oil, and the dominant hydrocarbon degraders in fresh diesel treatments were distinctly different from those in weathered diesel. Furthermore, the nutrient–dispersant treatment promoted an earlier succession of oil-degrading taxa compared to nutrient-only or dispersant- only treatments. Together, these results highlight the importance of cold-adapted microbial communities in driving early oil degradation and MOS formation in Arctic waters, and they provide insights relevant to the development of Arctic-specific bioremediation strategies.
authors: Vidanage T, Collins RE.

title: Resolving Gene-Metabolism Links through Multi-Metabolite mQTL Commonality Analysis
abstract: High-throughput metabolomics detects so many compounds that most studies use only a fraction of them, focusing on the few metabolites with an annotated structure or substructure. Metabolite genome-wide association studies of specialized metabolism detect many metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs), but most associated metabolite features remain unannotated, limiting gene discovery. In leaves of 362 tomato accessions under control and water-deficit conditions, only 13 of the 826 metabolite features associated with 77 reproducible mQTLs were annotated with good confidence. To study the mQTLs with the largest impact, we developed commonality analysis, an approach that does not depend on well-studied pathways. Commonality analysis uses biologically defined groups, such as the features associated with one mQTL, to infer relatedness between metabolites. By identifying the fragments, neutral losses or mass transformations that are common in a group, it links the group to a substructure, pathway or reaction, and can extend annotation within the group. Most high-impact mQTLs had a significantly distinct fragment commonality, whose outstanding fragments suggested the pathway involved and its candidate gene. We demonstrate the approach in three representative mQTLs: (i) common fragments pointed to a sinapoyl-hexose pathway and a serine carboxypeptidase-like candidate acyltransferase; (ii) common fragments marked the features associated with a purine permease as nitrogen-containing, which isotope labeling then supported; (iii) a common 2.02 Da transformation pointed to a double-bond reduction and a putative reductase. Overexpression of each gene reproduced the commonality patterns, supporting the candidate genes and showing that the approach also applies to experimentally defined metabolite groups.
authors: Rosental L, Zach YY, Lapidot-Cohen T, Weil S, Tabachnik C, Sternlicht E, Niger T, Borovikova-Sheinker A, Panda S, Rogachev I, Shahaf N, Ouyang B, Aharoni A, Dong S, Sade N, Brotman Y.

title: cGAS integrates Toll-like receptor signaling in platelets to promote thromboinflammation
abstract: Thromboinflammation is driven by innate immune signaling and promotes tissue injury during sepsis. Activation of platelets by bacterial products and alarmins amplifies inflammation, coagulation, and thrombotic dysfunction. However, the mechanisms by which these diverse inflammatory signals converge to elicit common platelet responses remain largely undefined. Mitochondria are key integrators of cellular stress responses and can activate innate immune pathways through the release of mitochondrial DNA and engagement of the DNA sensor cGAS. We therefore hypothesized that stimulation of innate immune receptors generates endogenous cGAS ligands within platelets, providing a unifying mechanism by which distinct inflammatory cues converge on cGAS-STING signaling. Here, we demonstrate that activation of TLR4, TLR1/2, and TLR5 engages a platelet-intrinsic mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis that promotes platelet activation. In a model of endotoxemia, genetic deletion of cGAS reduced platelet activation, thrombocytopenia, pyroptosis and the early systemic inflammatory response. Platelet transfer experiments further established that platelet-intrinsic cGAS is sufficient to amplify inflammatory responses  in vivo . Mechanistically, we demonstrated that cytosolic accumulation of mtDNA and activation of cGAS-STING signaling pathway in platelets are dependent on mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) and correlated with the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species. In contrast, canonical platelet agonists activated platelets independently of cGAS and failed to induce substantial cytosolic mtDNA accumulation. Importantly, this signaling architecture was conserved in human platelets, where TLR1/2-mediated activation required MCU- and STING-dependent signaling, whereas responses to thrombin receptor-activating peptide and collagen-related peptide remained largely unaffected. Together, these findings identify cGAS as an intracellular signal integration node that allows diverse innate immune receptors to converge on a common platelet activation pathway through sensing of mitochondria-derived DNA, allowing a rapid platelet response to microbial products.
authors: Bidias AR, Arsenault L, Fleury S, Welman M, Osouf M, Germain M, Pernet E, Lordkipanidzé M, Pepin G.

title: Runs That Succeed and Are Wrong: An Audit of Silent Failures in a Multi-Omics Platform’s Validation Runs
abstract: Bioinformatics pipelines can finish with a success status, write parseable summaries and report wrong results. We audited the 42 validation runs of a multi-omics Nextflow platform that the author built, reading the summary archived for each run; every summary records the status “success”. Of the runs, 14 carry a confirmed silent failure in one of five classes, each traced to code. Bulk RNA-seq of fly, Arabidopsis and yeast was quantified against a default human transcript index, and fly and bacterial variants were annotated with the human SnpEff database. The proteomics pipeline’s false discovery rate (FDR) filter aborted on an option that OpenMS had renamed, and a shell fallback passed the unfiltered list on, as we reproduced in the OpenMS build behind its container. Metabolomics features were matched across samples on exact rounded keys, so that the matrix paired almost none of the features that replicate injections of one reference plasma share. And a spatial run filed as a brain section processed bronchoalveolar-lavage reads from another study. In the validation’s later round, its model judge gave the maximum score on every metric to answers that repeated the failures’ signatures: the expected answers came from the same summaries, and the metrics measure agreement with them, not whether a summary is true. A mapping-rate floor, which only five of the failed runs report, catches three. Checks written after the failures were known flag all 13 failures of the four classes they target, as they must, since a failure counts as confirmed only when its summary shows the signature; no check looks for reads from another study. Only clean runs test the checks, and no provenance, identity or invariant check flags any of the nine clean runs, a result that allows a false-positive rate as high as 34 percent; the checks behind eight of the 13 detections never ran on a clean run. On the run outputs, the checks catch the same failures and, after a fix to the audit’s strain table that had flagged a control, flag no clean run. How well the checks detect failures they were not written for is untested.
authors: Palanikumar N.

title: Transition-Based Analysis Distinguishes Stage-Associated and Subtype-Specific lncRNA Signatures in Breast Cancer
abstract: Molecular profiling of cancer samples has traditionally emphasized protein-coding genes and microRNAs, whereas long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) remain challenging to characterize because of their generally low expression levels and poorly understood biological functions. Thousands of lncRNAs are expressed in cancer, but their contributions to tumor heterogeneity and clinical characterization have largely been overlooked. Here, we systematically analyzed lncRNA expression in the breast cancer cohort from TCGA. We developed a transition-based framework to distinguish lncRNAs consistently expressed across samples from those exhibiting statistically significant expression differences between consecutive clinical stages. Using a stringent (|z|>3) threshold, we identified four sets of transition-associated lncRNAs (Tr-lncRNAs) with directional expression changes across clinical stages. An orthogonal analysis identified subtype-associated lncRNAs (St-lncRNAs) based on maximal expression variance, distinguishing Luminal A, Luminal B, HER2-positive, and basal-like tumors. The 30 most informative lncRNAs revealed that subtype-associated patterns remained broadly consistent across clinical stages. Genomic-context analyses revealed frequent antisense relationships between lncRNAs and their counterpart protein-coding genes, raising the possibility of regulatory interactions. In addition, statistical integration of Ribo-seq evidence with translation-initiation criteria identified several lncRNA encoding micropeptides, which could expand the repertoire of candidate cancer antigens. Finally, ST8SIA6-AS1, MAPT-IT1, and LINC01087 were associated with patient survival across independent breast cancer studies. Together, these findings establish a framework for distinguishing stage-associated expression changes from subtype-associated patterns and prioritizing understudied transcripts as candidate indicators of breast cancer characteristics and progression.
authors: Zok S, Linial M.
