title: Characterization of Pulmonary Tropism, Expression Kinetics and Safety of the Novel Adeno-Associated Virus-LungM3 Vector.
abstract: This study investigated the lung-targeting characteristics, dose- and time-dependent effects, and safety of a novel engineered adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector, AAV-LungM3. In vitro, mouse primary lung organoids were transduced with AAV-LungM3 at doses of 103, 104, and 105 vector genomes (vg)/cell, and transduction was evaluated by fluorescence detection. For in vivo validation, C57BL/6 mice received intratracheal injection of AAV-LungM3 at doses of 0.5 × 1011, 1.0 × 1011, and 2.0 × 1011 vg. Flow cytometry was performed to assess the dose-dependent transduction specificity and efficiency of AAV-LungM3 in type I alveolar epithelial cells (AT1 cells) and type II alveolar epithelial cells (AT2 cells). Using the favorable dose determined by the dose-response assay, the temporal changes in AT2 cell transduction specificity and efficiency were further monitored over a 4-week period. In addition, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, detection of peripheral blood inflammatory factors, and analysis of plasma biochemical indicators were used to evaluate early-phase safety. In vitro transduction increased in a dose-dependent manner. In vivo assays revealed that the AT2 cell transduction specificity of AAV-LungM3 decreased gradually with increasing viral dose, whereas its transduction specificity for AT1 cells increased. Nevertheless, no significant differences in the transduction efficiency of AT1 cells and AT2 cells were observed among all dose groups. Longitudinal monitoring indicated that week 2 was the preferred time point for AAV-LungM3 transduction. In conclusion, under the tested conditions, AAV-LungM3 exhibited targeting specificity to AT2 cells and favorable in vivo expression with no observed toxic effects, serving as a potential delivery platform for pulmonary gene therapy.
authors: Nie H, Du J, Feng X, Fan J, Wang R, Li Q, Cao K, Gao C, Liu W, Jiang J, Wang Z, Zeng L.

title: Genetic architecture of bone strength and composition in White Leghorn laying hens.
abstract: BackgroundSkeletal issues such as fractures and poor bone quality are increasingly recognized for their negative impacts on animal welfare and the economic challenges they bring to the poultry industry. Previous pedigree-based analyses in White Leghorn laying hens have reported moderate heritabilities for cortical and medullary bone composition traits (ranging from 0.18 to 0.41) and strong genetic correlations (0.69 to 0.90) with tibia breaking strength and density. This study uses genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to identify genetic markers associated with bone strength and composition traits, aiming to advance our understanding of the genetic architecture of bone quality in White Leghorn laying hens.ResultsWe identified a set of markers on chromosome 20 (11.55-12.29 Mb) in strong LD with each other (r2 > 0.8), significantly associated with humeral stiffness, and overlapping with humeral strength and tibial cortical thickness. These markers were located within the previously identified QTL on chromosome 20 for bone biomechanical strength and body weight. This region harbors a bone morphogenetic protein 7 gene (BMP7) with a known role in skeletogenesis and growth in chicken. Genetic markers with the strongest suggestive association with organic and mineral contents, and total amount of carbonate in bone mineral MinCO3 1415 in tibia medullary bone were detected on chromosome 1 (173.5-173.6 Mb). This region contains the long non-coding RNALOC107052041 (LncFAM), which has previously been mapped within growth-related QTL and its polymorphisms have been associated with body weight and skeletal dimensions in chickens. Finally, more accurate heritabilities were estimated for thermogravimetry measurements of bone compositional traits as compared to infrared spectroscopy, with medullary organic and mineral contents being the most heritable (~0.19) and highly correlated with tibia density (0.7).ConclusionsThis study identified genomic loci associated with variation in bone quality traits, providing candidates for functional validation and for future evaluation of their potential to improve the prediction of bone strength in laying hens.
authors: Kurta K, Wilson PW, Andersson B, Schmutz M, Cavero D, Enrich-Essvein T, Crespo-Lopez L, Rodriguez-Navarro AB, Dunn IC, de Koning DJ, Johnsson M.

title: Antiviral Cytokine Signaling in Insects: Functional Parallels with Vertebrate Interferon Antiviral Immunity.
abstract: The absence of homologs for interferons and their receptors in insect genomes has long suggested that insects lack inducible antiviral responses. However, recent accumulating evidence calls this view into question. In this review, we summarize key findings and recent advances in this emerging field. Several secreted factors that respond to viral infection have been identified in insects, including Vago and Vago-like proteins; among these, members such as CxVago and BmVago activate downstream antiviral responses through the JAK/STAT pathway. Homologs of vertebrate interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) including CH25H, NFIL3, MxL1, and viperin have also been demonstrated to possess antiviral activities in insects. These findings outline a functional cascade of "virus-induced secreted factor - receptor recognition - signal transduction-antiviral effector" suggesting the presence of antiviral cytokine signaling in insects that is functionally parallel to the vertebrate IFN system. Although this field remains in its infancy, the available evidence has laid a foundation for future investigations. Further studies are needed to systematically identify novel antiviral cytokine molecules, validate functional receptors, and elucidate downstream signaling networks and effector mechanisms.
authors: Huang Y, Swevers L, Feng M.

title: Analysis of pathological changes and virus-susceptible cells in the testes following MPXV infection in a rhesus macaque model.
abstract: Monkeypox virus (MPXV) is an emerging public health threat, with increasing epidemiological and clinical evidence supporting sexual transmission, including detection of viral DNA in semen. However, the pathogenic mechanisms of MPXV within the male reproductive system remain poorly defined. We employed a rhesus macaque model to investigate MPXV-induced testicular alterations. Combining bulk RNA sequencing, histopathological analysis and immunofluorescence staining, we characterized testicular pathology, viral antigen distribution, and host responses during the early stage of infection. We found that MPXV did not induce marked inflammation or widespread cell death, and seminiferous tubule architecture remained largely intact during infection. Furthermore, within seminiferous tubules, Sertoli cells showed higher proportion of MPXV antigen co-localization than spermatogonia and spermatocytes, whereas in the interstitium, vascular endothelial cells and immune cells, including macrophages and T cells, showed prominent MPXV antigen detection, consistent with a potential contribution of hematogenous dissemination to testicular involvement. MPXV infection was associated with downregulation of the Sertoli cell marker SOX9 and alterations in tight junction-associated proteins, suggesting changes in Sertoli cell characteristics and BTB-associated molecular features. Transcriptomic analysis revealed changes in interferon-related antiviral pathways and complement-related gene expression, with C1q-positive signals detected in both interstitial and seminiferous tubular regions. In addition, changes in spermatogenesis-related gene expression were observed, which may reflect alterations in the spermatogenic microenvironment. Collectively, this study provides a quantitative characterization of early MPXV-testis interactions and cellular tropism across multiple testicular cell types in a non-human primate model, and provides insights into the pathological and immune responses associated with MPXV infection.
authors: Chang JT, Lin KQ, Liu LB, Yang W, Fan DY, Xue J, Wang PG, An J.

title: Enantioselective biodegradation of the pyrethroid (±)-alpha-cypermethrin by the bacteria Priestia megaterium CBMAI 2842 isolated from citrus culture.
abstract: Intensive use of pesticides to control agricultural pests has raised environmental concerns, making it necessary to adopt efficient strategies for treating contaminated areas. In this study, we evaluated the biodegradation potential of the bacterium Priestia megaterium CBMAI 2842, isolated from orange leaves, toward (±)-α-cypermethrin. Biodegradation assays were carried out in the presence of 100 mg·L-1 (±)-α-cypermethrin at 32 °C for 1, 3, 5, and 10 days, with monitoring by high-performance liquid chromatography with UV-Vis detection. P. megaterium CBMAI 2842 showed biodegradation potential, promoting 51% and 48% degradation of (±)-α-cypermethrin after 5 and 10 days, respectively, in a non-supplemented system (without nutrient broth). With nutrient broth supplementation, biodegradation increased, reaching 75% after 5 days. Chiral HPLC/UV-Vis analyses indicated no enantiomeric selectivity between 1 and 3 days of incubation in the non-supplemented system. However, after 5 and 10 days, preferential degradation of the (+)-(1R,cis,αS) enantiomer was observed, resulting in enrichment of the residual (-)-(1S,cis,αR) enantiomer, with enantiomeric excesses of 26% and 12%, respectively. In the nutrient-broth-supplemented system, after 5 days, higher biodegradation and a high enantiomeric excess (e.e. = 94%) were observed for the enantiomer (-)-(1S,cis,αR). Additionally, integrating untargeted metabolomics with bioinformatics tools, including MetaboAnalyst and GNPS feature-based molecular networking, enabled the putative annotation of metabolites with the exploration of metabolic changes and pathways associated with bacterial biodegradation. Additionally, the tentative annotation of eleven metabolites by gas and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry enabled the proposal of an α-cypermethrin biodegradation pathway, expanding knowledge about the environmental fate of these compounds and identifying an efficient biocatalyst., i.e., P. megaterium CBMAI 2842 for decontamination processes.

title: Generalists and specialists in industrial wastewater treatment system: Niche differentiation shapes distinct bacterial diversity and assembly patterns.
abstract: Microbial habitat generalists and specialists coexist in environment and exert distinct influences on community dynamics. However, a knowledge gap remains regarding the assembly patterns and ecological functions of these two groups in full-scale industrial wastewater treatment plants (IWWTPs). Here, we explored the ecological characteristics of generalists and specialists from 11 IWWTPs, including 3 different wastewater types and 4 WWTP compartments. Owing to niche breadth differences, generalists and specialists differ substantially in community diversity, assembly processes, r-K life strategy selection, and ecological functions. The generalists exhibited higher niche breadth, community alpha diversity / compositional similarity, and weaker dispersal limitation. In contrast, specialists showed the opposite trend. The generalists and specialists exhibited distinct r-K life strategy preference, which specialists tended to be r-strategists, while generalists tended to be K-strategists. Moreover, some genera including Hyphomicrobium, Thauera, Acinetobacter were identified as biomarkers which could distinguish different IWWTPs. The generalists and specialists showed stronger positive associations with pollutant removal in anoxic and oxic tank, respectively. Functional differences between these two groups existed in different environmental conditions. Our study enhances the ecological understanding on IWWTPs bacterial generalists and specialists and provide a foundation for further studies on the community regulation strategy.
authors: Chen W, Wei J, Chen D, Su Z, Xiong F, Li Y, Wen D.

title: Advancing terpenoid biosynthesis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae: Synthetic biology approaches for efficient longifolene production.
abstract: The sustainable microbial production of high-value terpenoids like longifolene represents a critical frontier in green manufacturing, yet it is often hindered by systemic metabolic inefficiencies in microbial hosts. To address this, we present a comprehensive systems metabolic engineering framework in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that integrates three complementary modules to overcome the key bottlenecks of enzyme catalysis, cofactor supply, and precursor availability. First, we enhanced the catalytic module by employing the RII dimerization/docking domain-RI anchoring disruptor (RIDD-RIAD) peptide-mediated enzyme assembly and structure-guided Pinus sylvestris longifolene synthase (psTPS) variant screening, 'which improved whole-cell longifolene production under the tested conditions. Second, to resolve nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) cofactor imbalance, we engineered a dual-regeneration system by introducing an exogenous formate dehydrogenase (FDH) and simultaneously amplifying endogenous pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) flux. Third, we reprogrammed central carbon metabolism by integrating the non-oxidative glycolysis (NOG) pathway and deleting the transcriptional repressors DOS2 and YNR063W, and was associated with a larger steady-state cytosolic acetyl-CoA pool, the essential terpenoid precursor. This multi-pronged strategy culminated in a highly optimized strain that achieved a titer of 92.84 mg/L in shake-flask cultures. Critically, the process was successfully scaled to a 5 L bioreactor under fed-batch conditions, yielding 4181.51 mg/L total longifolene at 204 h (3484.79 mg/L extracellular and 696.72 mg/L cell-associated), the highest total titer among the microbial reports identified in Supplementary Table S4. Differences in product recovery and cultivation protocols limit direct process comparisons. Our work demonstrates that coordinated optimization of enzyme assembly, cofactor regeneration, and carbon-flow reprogramming can substantially improve longifolene biosynthesis in S. cerevisiae. This study provides a longifolene-focused case study for modular pathway optimization, while broader application of this strategy to other terpenoids or natural products will require further pathway-specific validation.
authors: Zhang W, Xin Y, Li S, Shen X, Zhang J, He H, Xiang S, Ba L, Liu Y.

title: Informatics for the Planet: Integrating Species, Ecosystems, and Geophysical Data to Manage the Health of Earth Systems.
abstract: UnlabelledBiomedical and health informatics has traditionally focused on human-centric clinical data to support individual patient care and health systems. However, contemporary health challenges driven by climate change, biodiversity loss, and ecological degradation demand an expanded paradigm that addresses interdependencies among human, animal, and environmental health. This editorial introduces a new JMIR Medical Informatics section called "Planetary Health Informatics"-an essential evolution extending informatics praxis beyond human health care and toward Earth's interconnected systems. JMIR Medical Informatics is launching a call for papers for this new section dedicated to advancing planetary health informatics (PHI) theory, methods, and applications for a sustainable future shaped by humans' impact on Earth. We invite authors to submit work that explores how PHI integrates species, ecosystem, and geophysical data to address critical global challenges, including metagenomic disease surveillance, climate-related hazard forecasting, environmental pollution monitoring, and health infrastructure decarbonization. By synthesizing broader ecological frameworks, we present a road map for transforming fragmented data streams into planetary-scale intelligence.
authors: Gray K, Benis A, Dueholm Müller S, Winkel K, Borda A.

title: A Plasmodium knowlesi A1-H.1 transcriptome time course focusing on the late asexual blood stages.
abstract: The zoonotic parasite Plasmodium knowlesi is closely related to Plasmodium vivax, the second leading cause of human malaria. P. knowlesi line A1-H.1 can be maintained in human erythrocytes and is an experimental model for P. vivax biology. We present the first transcriptome time course of the intraerythrocytic developmental cycle (IDC) of P. knowlesi A1-H.1 grown in human normocytes. Bulk RNA-sequencing was performed at five IDC stages using tightly synchronised cultures, enabling identification of constitutively expressed genes and stage-specific biomarkers, and investigation of temporal expression patterns of multigene families. Comparative analysis with P. vivax orthologues revealed strong genome-wide conservation of temporal expression. Analysis of invasion-associated genes and ApiAP2 transcription factors identified genes with conserved expression patterns for which P. knowlesi is likely a good model to study the P. vivax gene. To support comparative analyses, we developed an open-access interactive webtool to explore and visualise P. knowlesi - P. vivax - P. falciparum orthologue expression across the IDC (https://interactive.itg.be/app/pk-orthologue-expression-viewer). This time course dataset provides a reference transcriptome framework for P. knowlesi A1-H.1 and a resource for comparative Plasmodium biology. The interactive webtool facilitates rapid identification of candidate genes with conserved temporal expression, streamlining functional studies in which P. knowlesi A1-H.1 serves as a model for P. vivax.
authors: De Meulenaere K, Díaz-Delgado D, Monsieurs P, Sauve E, Cortés A, Knuepfer E, Rosanas-Urgell A.

title: Liver concentrations of JNJ-73763989 siRNA triggers in patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB): The INSIGHT study panel 3 results.
abstract: BackgroundJNJ-73763989 is a 2:1 combination of 2 N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated short interfering RNAs (siRNA) targeting the S (daplusiran) and X (tomligisiran) regions of the hepatitis B virus genome. In phase 2b studies, 48 weeks of JNJ-73763989-based combination treatments led to dose-dependent reductions in viral markers, including hepatitis B surface antigen. The objective of the INSIGHT study Panel 3 was to quantify intrahepatic concentrations of the siRNAs in human livers during and after treatment.MethodsIn the open-label, single-arm, single-center study, participants with chronic hepatitis B received 48 weeks of treatment with JNJ-73763989 200 mg every 4 weeks and nucleos(t)ide analog, with optional pegylated interferon α2a 180 µg weekly added after Treatment Week (TW) 40. Core liver biopsies were collected at TW12, TW40, and at Follow-up Week (FUW) 24.ResultsLiver biopsies were available from all 4 participants at TW12 and from 3 at TW40 and FUW24. Between TW12 and TW40, liver concentrations of daplusiran and tomligisiran increased 1.5- to 2.6-fold, consistent with intrahepatic accumulation. Twenty-eight weeks after the last injection of JNJ-73763989, the triggers were still measurable in 2 of 3 participants with 4.5- to 15-fold reduced concentrations from peak levels; the estimated liver half-life ranged from approximately 2.9 to 16.1 weeks.ConclusionsIn this first study to assess liver concentrations of GalNAc-siRNA in humans with sequential biopsies, long persistence of JNJ-73763989 triggers in human livers may partially explain the prolonged suppressive effect on viral parameters observed in phase 2 studies.
authors: Asselah T, Vilgrain V, Kakuda TN, Ediage EN, Snoeys J, Menasria Benazzouz S, Jezorwski J, Kim L, Lenz O, Guinard-Azadian C, Biermer M.

title: Rifamycin use and gut microbial antibiotic resistance genes in cirrhosis: Results from a double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) carriage is associated with poor outcomes in patients with liver cirrhosis, which is worsened by repeated antibiotic exposure and hospitalizations. While the semi-synthetic rifamycin derivative, rifaximin, has recently been linked to ARG expansion preclinically, the effects of rifamycin SV MMX (RiVM) on the gut resistome remain unknown. We evaluated longitudinal resistome changes with RiVM in cirrhosis. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled RIVET trial (15 RiVM, 15 placebo) included compensated cirrhosis patients who underwent shotgun metagenomic sequencing before/after 30 days of therapy. ARGs were annotated using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database. The longitudinal resistome was evaluated using univariable and multi-variable methods (LEfSe, paired-Wilcoxon testing, and MaAsLin3), and machine learning (ML) was used to determine ARG changes at subject and group levels. RiVM induced minimal perturbation of the gut resistome, without significant change in ARGs versus after FDR adjustment. Complementary approaches (univariable and multivariable) identified a trend towards lower vancomycin resistance ARGs, including vanW and vanT operon-associated genes, after RiVM exposure. In contrast, several Enterobacteriaceae-associated multidrug efflux regulators (including evgS, emrK, and mdtA) showed nominal increases post-rifamycin that did not withstand FDR. Group-level ML demonstrated limited discrimination between groups; however, within-subject longitudinal models achieved improved classification performance. No increase in infections or treatment-related safety concerns was observed. We conclude that rifamycin MMX was not associated with infections and did not enrich antimicrobial resistance genes compared to placebo in a small randomized 30-day clinical trial in patients with compensated cirrhosis. There was a tendency towards reduced vancomycin resistance and ARG reduction after rifamycin exposure. Registration: NCT04082780 www.clinicaltrials.gov.
authors: Bajaj JS, Davis BC, Puri P, Gallagher ML, Fagan A, Obolewicz H, Mousel T, Boja SH, Sikaroodi M, Gillevet PM.

title: Disruption of OsNLP4-mediated nitrate signaling alters root exudate composition and root-associated bacterial communities in rice.
abstract: OsNLP4 is a master regulator of nitrate signaling, but its ecological role in the root-associated bacterial communities is unknown. This study investigated how OsNLP4-mediated nitrate signaling influences root-associated microbial composition and root exudate metabolism. We found that the osnlp4 mutants exhibited distinct root-associated bacterial communities compared to the WT under non-nitrogen-fertilized conditions, with a significant enrichment of Bradyrhizobium and other bacterial taxa with potential roles in nitrogen cycling. Isolated Bradyrhizobium strains showed increased colonization in the osnlp4 mutant. Metabolomic analysis revealed increased secretion of sugars and phosphoric acid, along with a lower C:N ratio, in the osnlp4 mutant root exudates. Bacterial growth and chemotactic responses differed between WT- and osnlp4-derived root exudates, and sugars enriched in osnlp4 exudates elicited chemotactic responses in isolated Bradyrhizobium strains. These metabolic changes were associated with differential bacterial responses to WT and osnlp4 root exudates and may contribute to the altered root-associated bacterial community. Taken together, our results suggest that OsNLP4 links nitrate signaling and nitrogen metabolism with root-associated bacterial community assembly. Disruption of OsNLP4 reprograms root exudation and reshapes root-associated microbial communities, highlighting an association between nitrate signaling, nutrient allocation, and root-associated bacterial community assembly in rice.
authors: Yasuda M, Yoshida T, Yoshida A, Masuda S, Shibata A, Shirasu K, Kameoka H, Endo M, Fujiwara T, Sato S, Minamisawa K, Hayashi M, Ohkama-Ohtsu N, Okazaki S.

title: Identification of auxin response factor ARF27 as a regulator of maize root morphogenesis.
abstract: Auxin is a central phytohormone that mediates root development. This study investigated the genetic basis of auxin-mediated primary root growth in Zea mays (maize) seedlings, which is not well-understood in this key cereal crop. To address this knowledge gap, 618 accessions from the Wisconsin Diversity panel were leveraged for a genome wide association study (GWAS) followed by reverse genetics and in silico gene regulatory network reconstruction (GRN). The GWAS identified several candidate genes associated with variation in root growth responses, including RAMOSA2 and multiple members of the AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR (ARF) gene family. Maize AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR27 (ZmARF27), an ortholog of Arabidopsis ARF7 and ARF19, was prioritized for functional characterization. A reduction in ZmARF27 levels led to short primary roots, insensitivity to exogenous auxin, and altered transcriptional responses. Reconstruction of an ZmARF27 GRN included known maize classical root development genes, such as ROOTLESS CONCERNING CROWN ROOTS, numerous auxin pathway genes, and genes associated with cell wall biogenesis. Altogether, this study identifies ZmARF27 as a novel genetic driver of auxin-mediated root growth and gene expression in maize.
authors: Dash L, Draves MA, Khangura RS, McReynolds MR, Muench RL, Cowling CL, Song G, Dilkes BP, Walley JW, Kelley DR.

title: Integrative bioinformatics and experimental validation of the prognostic and functional relevance of XDH and ITPA in non-small cell lung cancer.
abstract: Purine metabolism has been implicated in tumor biology and immune regulation, but the clinical and biological relevance of purine metabolism-related genes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains incompletely defined. Transcriptomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project, together with TCGA clinical data, were analyzed to identify differentially expressed purine metabolism-related genes and assess their prognostic associations. Immune infiltration was evaluated using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA), and single-cell transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to characterize the cellular context of candidate genes. Stemness features and drug sensitivity were assessed using transcriptome-based computational models. XDH and ITPA protein expression was examined by Western blotting and immunohistochemistry (IHC) in an independent NSCLC cohort and in cell models. Stable knockdown of XDH or ITPA was performed in H1299 cells, with key functional findings further evaluated in A549 cells. Cisplatin sensitivity was assessed using cell-viability dose-response assays in H1299 and A549 cells. Several purine metabolism-related genes were upregulated in NSCLC and associated with overall survival (OS). XDH and ITPA showed higher protein expression in tumor tissues and were associated with adverse clinicopathological features and poorer survival. Higher expression of these genes was also associated with altered immune infiltration patterns. The messenger RNA-based stemness index (mRNAsi) was associated with ITPA and XDH expression in different directions, whereas higher XDH expression was associated with higher predicted half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values for cisplatin. Knockdown of XDH or ITPA attenuated proliferative, clonogenic, migratory, and invasive phenotypes in H1299 cells, with key findings reproduced in A549 cells. XDH knockdown also reduced the experimentally determined cisplatin IC50 in both H1299 and A549 cells. XDH and ITPA may represent candidate prognostic and functionally relevant purine metabolism-related genes in NSCLC. The integrated clinical, computational, and cellular findings support their association with NSCLC progression-related phenotypes, while the underlying molecular mechanisms and broader clinical applicability require further investigation.
authors: Zhang W, Song J, Zhu H, Wang Y, Wang H, Li X.

title: Human senataxin uses distinct peripheral elements to unwind R-loops and act on RNA polymerase II
abstract: ABSTRACT  Persistent R-loops and paused or stalled RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) elongation complexes can threaten genome stability. Senataxin (SETX) contributes to R-loop resolution and RNAPII regulation, but their intimate connection during transcription makes the individual contributions of these activities difficult to distinguish in cells. To determine whether these activities rely on the same molecular features, we investigated the structure and biochemical properties of the SETX helicase domain (SETX-HD). Cryo-EM defines the conserved helicase core and RNA-binding channel of SETX-HD, while biochemical analyses identify distinct roles for two peripheral elements: a previously uncharacterised C-terminal RNA-binding domain (CT-RBD) and the prong subdomain. In reconstituted mammalian transcription assays, SETX-HD promotes passage beyond a defined RNAPII pause and elongation-complex dissociation on the same template. The CT-RBD stabilises RNA engagement and is required for efficient R-loop unwinding, whereas its deletion preserves both RNAPII-associated activities. Conversely, replacing the native SETX prong with its fungal Sen1 counterpart preserves R-loop unwinding but impairs both RNAPII outcomes. These reciprocal separation-of-function effects establish that a common SETX-HD RNA-translocation core depends on distinct peripheral elements for R-loop unwinding and action on mammalian RNAPII. This separation provides a direct route to determine how these activities contribute to SETX function in cells.
authors: Lanicek M, Sedova K, Hasanova Z, Porrua O, Sebesta M.

title: A candidate  HNRNPU  –  CHD2  RNA-processing axis in neurodevelopmental disease
abstract: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in  HNRNPU , which encodes a nuclear RNA-binding scaffold protein, cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy, intellectual disability and brain malformations, but the programs that link  HNRNPU dosage to neuronal dysfunction remain poorly defined. We depleted  HNRNPU in Human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T) cells, profiled gene expression and alternative splicing, intersected the two datasets, and asked which of the resulting genes already carried a neurodevelopmental annotation. Knockdown produced 5,643 differentially expressed genes and 21,728 high-confidence splicing events; 1,222 genes changed at both levels, and two pre-specified neurodevelopmental panel genes were among them:  CHD2 and  DYRK1A . In K562 eCLIP experiments, 107 reproducible  HNRNPU peaks were detected across the  CHD2 gene body, and three of the four regulated exons introduce a reading-frame shift whose premature termination codon lies far upstream of the final exon junction, predicting nonsense-mediated decay. Public K562 knockdown data reproduced the rise in  CHD2 mRNA and the same skipped-exon change, and  CHD2 depletion in the neural line SH-SY5Y altered cell-cycle, DNA-repair and neural gene programs. HNRNPU therefore constrains a frameshift-prone splicing switch in  CHD2 , a candidate route from  HNRNPU haploinsufficiency to loss of functional  CHD2 if these transcripts are degraded.  Highlights  HNRNPU depletion changes  CHD2 expression and exon inclusion in human cells.  eCLIP places  HNRNPU on  CHD2 RNA, consistent with direct control of its splicing.  Three  CHD2 exons are frameshift-prone, predicting loss of full-length  CHD2 .
authors: Tang H, Xiao Z, Wang R, Babarinde IA, Huang S, Hutchins AP, Ma G.

title: Antibiotics drive immunometabolic rewiring of human immune responses
abstract: Antibiotics are routinely evaluated for their antimicrobial activity, potential host toxicity, and disruption of the microbiome. Certain antibiotics can also impact cell-intrinsic host processes, including evolutionarily conserved processes in the mitochondria. These raise the possibility that antibiotics can directly impact host immunity, which relies on mitochondrial function for their immunometabolic activation. However, the immunological consequences of most antibiotics in current use have not been systematically examined. Here, we performed a comprehensive analysis of the effects of clinically used antibiotics on activation of primary human immune cells. We uncovered an underappreciated antibiotic-specific modulation of immune function in healthy individuals and infectious disease patients. Focusing on the immunomodulatory antibiotic ciprofloxacin, we found altered mitochondrial gene expression across multiple immune populations, driving distinct, lineage-specific responses and heightened sensitivity of T-cells. Ciprofloxacin impaired primary human T-cell expansion and activation and altered mitochondrial function and metabolism. We further demonstrated immunomodulatory effects of selected antibiotics in response to inactivated bacteria and during live viral infection. Finally, to test the implications of our findings in vivo, we showed that immune activation is altered shortly after a single dose of antibiotic administration in mice. This work established a widespread impact of antibiotics on immune-cell function, and identified mitochondrial perturbation as one underlying mechanism, with implications for host-pathogen interactions and antimicrobial therapy.
authors: Hen-Avivi S, Bossel Ben-Moshe N, Avera R, Adin I, Kitsberg Y, Lyskov SK, Navon S, Zalmanovich A, Yardeni T, Ben-Ami R, Avraham R.

title: Activity of Aztreonam-Avibactam and Comparators against Difficult-To-Treat Resistant (DTR) Enterobacterales from European Medical Centres Stratified by Infection Type and Country (2021– 2025)
abstract: Abstract  Background: Difficult-to-treat resistant (DTR) isolates, defined as bacterial isolates expressing nonsusceptibility to all first-line agents, is a major problem worldwide. We evaluated the activity of aztreonam-avibactam and comparators against DTR Enterobacterales from European medical centres. Methods: 30,345 Enterobacterales isolates were consecutively collected from 41 European medical centres in 19 countries in 2021–2025. Isolates were susceptibility tested by broth microdilution and MIC interpreted according to EUCAST breakpoints. The collection included 1113 DTR isolates, defined as a carbapenem-resistant isolate (MIC ≥4 mg/L for meropenem and/or imipenem) not susceptible to fluoroquinolones. All DTR isolates were screened for β-lactamase genes by whole genome sequencing. Results were stratified by infection type and country. Results: Aztreonam-avibactam was active against 99.6% of DTR (MIC50/90, 0.25/0.5 mg/L), and exhibited consistent activity against DTR isolates from all infection types. Cefiderocol was active against 78.8% of DTR isolates; ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam, and the aminoglycosides exhibited limited activity against these organisms. The frequency of DTR was higher among isolates from pneumonia (6.6%) compared to other infection types (2.3–3.4%) and varied from 0.0% (Switzerland) to 19.7% (Poland) among countries. DTR susceptibility to aztreonam-avibactam ranged from 94.4% (France) to 100.0% (14 countries). Aztreonam-avibactam retained potent activity against DTR isolates nonsusceptible to ceftazidime-avibactam (99.2% susceptible), meropenem-vaborbactam (99.6% susceptible), and/or cefiderocol (97.8% susceptible). The most common carbapenemase identified among DTR isolates was NDM (41.2% of DTR), followed by OXA-48–like (38.2%), and KPC (34.3%). Moreover, 99.6% of metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) producers were susceptible to aztreonam-avibactam and 68.2% were susceptible to cefiderocol. Conclusions: Aztreonam-avibactam retained potent activity against DTR Enterobacterales from European medical centres and its activity was not adversely affected by clinically relevant carbapenemases or resistance to agents currently used to treat multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales. The activities of other β-lactamase inhibitor combinations and cefiderocol were compromised by the increased occurrence of MBL producers.
authors: SADER HS, MENDES RE, PEREZ K, STONE G, PAPP-WALLACE KM, CASTANHEIRA M.

title: Glucocorticoid regulation of the human noncoding genome.
abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs) are widely used anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive agents known to induce substantial changes in gene expression, yet their effects on noncoding RNAs such as long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) or microRNAs (miRNAs) remain poorly characterized. Here, we present the first comprehensive and systematic analysis of GC regulation of the noncoding genome across nine human primary cell types from both hematopoietic and nonhematopoietic lineages. In vitro GC treatment was applied to each cell type, with transcriptomic profiling (total RNA-seq and small RNA-seq) at 2 and 6 h posttreatment. We identify more than 2000 GC-responsive noncoding transcripts, including 654 annotated lncRNAs, 1376 novel lncRNAs, and 39 miRNAs. The noncoding RNA response to GCs is highly cell type dependent: 80% of GC-responsive lncRNAs and 97% of miRNAs are unique to a single cell type. Hematopoietic cells exhibit a greater magnitude of lncRNA induction compared with nonhematopoietic cells. Notably, GC treatment uncovers dozens of facultative, stimulus-dependent lncRNAs. GC-responsive transcripts span diverse lncRNA classes, with enrichment of host lncRNAs. In contrast, only a limited number of miRNAs are GC responsive. GC regulation of transcript abundance for miRNAs and their host lncRNAs appears to be independent. Our results, which are accessible through an interactive web application, establish a framework for studying how noncoding transcription contributes to physiological and clinical heterogeneity in GC responses. The newly identified GC-responsive noncoding transcripts could represent biomarkers of GC exposure, determinants of GC sensitivity or resistance, or candidate regulators of tissue-specific GC effects.
authors: Tran T, Kwiat R, Cao Q, Kuhn S, Howe KN, Gadkari M, Franco LM.

title: Viral haplotype reconstruction from long reads with virCHap.
abstract: Resolving genomes at the haplotype level for viral populations is crucial for understanding the prevalence of viral diseases and for the development of effective therapeutic treatments. However, viral haplotype reconstruction still presents challenges, such as an unknown number of strains, high interstrain similarity, repetitive regions, and difficulties in abundance estimation. Here, we develop virCHap, a new reference-based haplotype phasing algorithm for viruses, which applies graph partitioning followed by iteratively quantifiable cluster merging on long-read sequencing data. Benchmarking on simulated and real data sets demonstrates that virCHap outperforms current tools in terms of recall, accurate abundance estimates, and read clustering accuracy. On a simulated large-genome VZV experiment, virCHap has a 96% recall, 13.6% higher than the second-best method, and has the most accurate abundance estimates. On a real five-strain PVY data set, virCHap has a precision exceeding 94.4%, a recall of >97%, and a read clustering accuracy of 93.4%, outperforming the second-best method by 33%. On a real six-strain SARS-CoV-2 data set, virCHap achieves >96.7% accuracy, and the most accurate abundance estimates within the spike (S) gene.
authors: Gao Y, Liu B, Li G, Yu T.

title: Dynamic balance of sparse flux vectors for efficient simulation of culture dynamics and metabolic network reduction.
abstract: Dynamic Flux Balance Analysis (DFBA) enables simulation of microbial culture dynamics under changing environmental conditions but remains computationally expensive for tasks such as parameter calibration and bioprocess control when applied to genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs). To address this, we introduce Dynamic Flux Vector Balancing (DFVB), a mathematical reformulation that solves an equivalent problem using a pre-computed sparse basis of flux solutions. This new algorithm enables an automatic, simulation-based network reduction. We show that DFVB exactly reproduces the DFBA culture dynamics in large-scale GEMs, while reducing the number of active reactions by up to 70% and accelerating simulations by up to threefold. Also, it identifies inactive reactions more accurately than Flux Variability Analysis (FVA) when compared to transcriptomic data profiles. Furthermore, during kinetic parameter estimation in two fermentation scenarios, DFVB achieved equal or superior calibration accuracy compared to standard DFBA. By circumventing solution degeneracy, DFVB yielded dynamic predictions with reduced uncertainty, despite inherent parameter identifiability limits. Together, these results position DFVB as a scalable and efficient alternative to DFBA, easing the integration of GEMs for bioprocess simulation and optimization.
authors: García IT, Torrealba C, Luna R, Pérez-Correa JR, Saa PA.

title: Multi-Environment Genomic Analysis Reveals Limited Concordance Between Sorghum Leaf Blight Incidence and Severity.
abstract: Leaf blight caused by Exserohilum turcicum constrains sorghum production in semi-arid environments. Disease incidence and severity are related, but their relationship need not imply shared resistance loci. Records from five locations in Niger and Senegal comprised 1339 paired plot observations. Field-stratum-adjusted accession values were estimated before rank-based inverse-normal transformation. The primary population contained 100 accessions evaluated in at least four locations; all 102 genotype-matched accessions were included in a sensitivity analysis. Genome-wide efficient mixed-model association (GEMMA) score tests used leave-one-chromosome-out kinship matrices, and trait-level p-values were combined with the aggregated Cauchy association test (ACAT) and the Simes procedure. Adjusted incidence and standard severity were moderately correlated (Pearson r = 0.429); the correlation was lower after conditioning severity on incidence (r = 0.066). Across 567,758 single-nucleotide polymorphisms, ACAT had a genomic inflation factor of 1.014 and a minimum p-value of 2.64 × 10-5. No marker passed the Benjamini-Hochberg 10% false-discovery-rate criterion for either trait or either combination; likelihood-ratio analyses also produced no discoveries at this threshold. Incidence-severity association-profile concordance was weak (Pearson r = 0.127; Spearman ρ = 0.094). Top-ranked overlap was 5.65-fold at 1% and 2.24-fold at 5% relative to the marker-count expectation, a descriptive comparison that does not account for linkage disequilibrium. ACAT and Simes rankings were similar (ρ = 0.895). Ten top-ranked, genotype-equivalence-aware, linkage-disequilibrium-clumped regions are presented as exploratory candidates. Phenotypic association was therefore stronger than detectable sharing of marker-association evidence. Limited sample size and sensitivity to phenotype definition, field composition and test choice constrain locus-level conclusions.
authors: Ahn E, Baek I, Prom LK, Kim MS, Meinhardt LW, Magill C.

title: Transcriptomic profiling of goats' systemic immune response to Haemonchus contortus infection during primary and secondary infection.
abstract: Haemonchus contortus is an economically important gastrointestinal nematode affecting small ruminants globally. Understanding immune responses during primary and secondary exposure may inform improved control strategies. This study investigated systemic immune transcriptional responses in Boer goat buffy-coat samples during early (D5) and late (D21) primary and secondary infections using RNA sequencing (N = 6; 3 animals/pool). Data were analysed using CLC Genomics Workbench, with functional enrichment assessed using STRING and immune pathways examined using KEGG. Differential gene expression analysis (p-value ≤0.05) identified 252 and 330 upregulated genes during primary infection and 373 and 269 during secondary infection at D5 and D21, respectively. Primary infection was characterised by a neutrophil-associated, pro-inflammatory signature involving CXCL8-CXCR1/2, CSF3R/CSF2R, IL-6-STAT3/5, and MYD88-MAPK signalling. Secondary infection showed early Th2-associated signatures at D5, including STAT6, IL4, and IL13 upregulation. However, canonical Th2-associated genes were not upregulated at D21, GATA3 and STAT4 were downregulated in both infections, indicating time-dependent responses. Additional changes involved IL-10/IL-10R, IL-4R/IL-13RA1, SOCS, and DUSP signalling. Functional enrichment identified Th2-associated immunity, complement activation, and leukocyte migration, antigen processing and presentation, B-cell receptor, and T-cell receptor signalling. These findings indicate temporally distinct systemic responses to primary and secondary exposure, rather than sustained helper-T-cell polarization. These signatures may be reflective of altered leukocyte composition, cell-specific transcriptional regulation, or both. Overall, these findings identify candidate immune pathways and signatures associated with immune responses to H. contortus in both naïve and previously exposed hosts, and may lay a foundation for future vaccine and genetic-resistance studies.
authors: Ndaba BS, Faber E, Marufu MC, Pretorius A, Tshilwane SI.

title: Recombinant depolymerase DP21 from Klebsiella phage GADU21 exerts Dual-Antibiofilm and biofilm-disrupting activity against multiple bacterial species.
abstract: Phage-derived depolymerases are promising antibiofilm enzymes. In this study, intact and disintegrated GADU21 phage were first tested for their ability to disrupt mature biofilm using the crystal violet assay. Disintegrated phage was more active on biofilms than intact phage. The dp21 gene encoding the depolymerase was then amplified from GADU21, cloned into pET30a, and expressed in E. coli BL21. Purified rDP21 (∼105 kDa) was characterized for antibiofilm activity at different pH values, residual activity following thermal pre-incubation, and Mg2+ dependence, with biofilm degradation and prevention capacity also shown by SEM and CLSM. rDP21 exhibited antibiofilm activity at pH 4-10 and retained partial activity after pre-incubation at temperatures up to 70 °C. Importantly, rDP21 did not affect planktonic growth of the tested bacteria, supporting a matrix-targeting rather than bactericidal mode of action, while significantly reducing preformed biofilm biomass and inhibiting biofilm formation by P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae, E. coli, P. mirabilis, S. epidermidis, S. aureus and E. faecalis by 58-59%, 49-50%, 46-47%, 30-34%, 33-31%, 30-24%, and 26-33%, respectively. SEM and CLSM images confirmed pronounced disruption of biofilm. These properties support its potential use as an effective antibiofilm agent.
authors: Salih Doğan H, Orbayoğlu GA, Karaynir A, Ali S, Doğan Y, Yalçin M, Hoşbul T, Bozdoğan B.

title: Disentangling the Genetic Relationship Between Sleep and Epilepsy.
abstract: ObjectiveA bidirectional relationship between sleep and epilepsy is well recognised, yet the biological mechanisms linking them remain poorly understood. Both have a genetic basis, with genome-wide association studies (GWAS) capturing polygenic contributions. By leveraging GWAS summary statistics, we aimed to investigate their shared genetic architecture.MethodsWe analysed seven sleep traits (morningness chronotype, sleep duration, habitual short/long sleep, insomnia, daytime napping/sleepiness) with common epilepsy types (focal epilepsy and genetic generalised epilepsy [GGE]). For each trait pair, we estimated genome-wide genetic correlation, tested bidirectional causality, quantified polygenic overlap, performed gene-trait associations to identify putative pleiotropic genes, estimated local genetic correlations and investigated whether regions of significance were driven by shared causal variants using colocalisation and fine-mapping.ResultsGenome-wide analyses supported a positive genetic correlation between higher GGE risk and habitual short sleep, with extensive polygenic overlap (75%-97%) across seven sleep traits. Gene-trait analyses identified RMI1 as a putative sleep-epilepsy candidate, with 13 additional sleep-associated genes linked to monogenic epilepsies (e.g., KANSL1, GRIN2A). Locus-specific analyses identified 16 genomic loci of interest (13 sleep-GGE, 3 sleep-focal epilepsy). Morningness-GGE shared the largest number of locus-specific associations. No significant causal relationships were identified, and causal variants did not colocalise.InterpretationOur findings support complex shared genetic contributions between sleep and epilepsy, with distinct patterns for focal compared to generalised epilepsy. These differences may help explain syndrome-specific sleep-wake associations, including seizure timing and predisposition. By localising shared loci and highlighting specific overlapping genes, we provide a foundation for future research into the mechanisms underlying epilepsy-sleep comorbidities.
journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology
authors: Le KN, Jackson VE, Stirling RE, Gerring ZF, Stevelink R, Berkovic SF, Scheffer IE, Karoly PJ, Bahlo M, Oliver KL.

title: The genetic basis of extra-lobed leaves in ivyleaf morning glory (  Ipomoea hederacea  )
abstract: Intraspecific leaf shape variation is common among angiosperms. Ivyleaf morning glory (  Ipomoea hederacea ) has become a useful system for studying the genetics and ecology of leaf shape variation as this species exhibits two leaf shapes: leaves with entire margins, and 3-lobed leaves. It is known that these phenotypes are controlled by a single locus, and differ in their ecophysiology, geographic distribution, ecology, and fitness. However, while lobed individuals producing leaves with 1-2 extra lobes have also been regularly observed, the genetic basis, if any, of these phenotypes has not been described. To investigate the genetic basis of extra-lobing, we compared phenotypic distributions of leaf shapes of an F2 generation to Mendelian ratios for a single locus trait and conducted a bulked segregant analysis to uncover quantitative trait loci. Our results suggest that producing extra-lobed leaves has a complex genetic basis and that there are multiple QTLs underlying this phenotype containing potential candidate genes involved with auxin distribution and leaf development. Whether these extra-lobed phenotypes also differ in terms of their physiology and ecology remains unexplored.  Article summary  Ivyleaf morning glory exhibits two main leaf shapes, heart-shaped entire leaves and 3-lobed, controlled by a single Mendelian locus. However, within the lobed genotypes, there are occasional individuals that produce leaves with extra lobes. We examined whether there was a simple genetic basis to producing extra lobes, and if so, does it have the same genetic basis as the other leaf shapes, or are different regions in the genome responsible? After planting 500 individuals in a greenhouse and collecting phenotypic and genomic data, we found that extra-lobing is heritable, does not have a simple Mendelian basis, but may be influenced by multiple QTLs.
authors: Henry MR, Hernandez DJ, Li MC, Glasgow E, Peake AL, Stinchcombe JR.

title: Revamped transposon-induced hepatocellular carcinoma model reveals deep similarities of cancer-driver landscapes across mice and humans
abstract: Genome-scale cancer-driver discovery is limited by statistical uncertainty in driver calling and by experimental constraints on mutations available for selection. We developed 3×fOnc3—a three-frame Sleeping Beauty (SB) mutagenesis system designed to broaden functional perturbations and reduce integration biases of traditional SB screens—and tested it in vivo in mouse liver. Within 12 months, 60% of mice developed heterogeneous hepatocellular tumors. Tumor-selected integrations were interpreted against an empirical reference from SB-based therapeutic gene delivery to hepatocytes, enabling correction for gene targetability. Background-aware filtering prioritized 315 driver candidates, including 243 protein-coding genes. Tumors were multiclonal, and identical integration-marked lineages expanded differently across lesions, supporting context-dependent clonal expansion. SB hits within young L1 subfamily members were selectively enriched in tumors. Human orthologues of candidate drivers were enriched for Cancer Gene Census genes and protein-altering pan-cancer mutations. Together, 3×fOnc3 reveals a background-corrected driver landscape linking driver selection to clonal tumor evolution and cross-species cancer relevance.
authors: Imre G, Mátés-Nagy A, Raya M, Verebi OO, Hudoba L, Faragó A, Latinovics D, Karkas R, Germán P, Kálmán P, Migh E, Pettkó-Szandtner A, Kolacsek O, Füredi A, Horváth P, Orbán T, Nagy I, Mátés L.

title: Structure of  Bacillus cereus  ZmaM, a peptidase-ABC transporter that secretes and activates zwittermicin A
abstract: Bacteria engage in microbial warfare by secreting toxic molecules. These toxins can serve as therapeutics or drug discovery starting points, motivating investigations of their production. Bacteria that produce these toxins must protect themselves, and a common strategy is to synthesize an inactive prodrug that is activated upon secretion. Some prodrugs are capped with  N -acyl-ᴅ-asparagine motifs, which are removed by two types of prodrug peptidases. Type I peptidases are membrane-bound S12 hydrolases; type II peptidases have an additional C-terminal half-ABC transporter module. Recent structures of a type I peptidase revealed how its transmembrane domain completes the substrate-binding site, but little is known about type II peptidases. Here, we show that the  B. cereus type II peptidase ZmaM is responsible for both the export of prezwittermicin and its activation into zwittermicin. The structure of homodimeric ZmaM reveals a central type IV ABC transporter flanked by peptidase modules. The periplasmic hydrolase domains interact over the transporter’s open outer vestibule. Mutations to intermodule interfaces impact both peptidase and ATP hydrolysis activities, indicating the peptidase and transporter modules are interdependent. Together, our findings reveal an evolutionary strategy to coordinate toxin activation with its export and inform future efforts to harness these systems in biotechnology.
authors: Zavala GE, Velilla JA, Walsh RM, Patel M, Mennes K, Rafat W, Aguilar Ramos MA, Daniel-Ivad M, Ramírez-Guadiana FH, Rudner DZ, Balskus EP, Gaudet R.

title: Genetic transformation and fluorescent protein expression in the biomaterial-producing fungus Fomes fomentarius.
abstract: BackgroundFungal-based materials are currently studied as renewable and sustainable alternatives to fossil-based materials used in construction, packaging, textile, and fashion industries. The polypore fungus Fomes fomentarius produces a range of lightweight, durable, and flexible materials from diverse plant residual streams. Genetic engineering of this fungus is an important technological objective, both from fundamental perspectives and to optimize performance characteristics of F. fomentarius materials.ResultsWe provide proof of principle that F. fomentarius can be genetically transformed. Hyphae produced high amounts of protoplasts using standard protocols. These protoplasts were transformed using nourseothricin selection and a nourseothricin N-acetyl transferase resistance marker (natR). Expression of natR was successful using a F. fomentarius translation elongation factor promoter. Stable, multicopy, and non-targeted integration of exogenous cassettes with recipient genome was confirmed by diagnostic PCR and Southern blotting. Preliminary attempts at genome editing based disruption of a putative ku70 encoding gene were, however, unsuccessful. We validated expression of two fluorescent proteins using a Schizophyllum commune H2B promoter using qRT-PCR and fluorescent microscopy. These data confirm functionality of mCherry and eGFP in F. fomentarius and suggest these proteins can be used for future protein localisation studies. Finally, we report DNase activity in F. fomentarius which we hypothesize may be a significant technical challenge for genetic transformation of this fungus.ConclusionF. fomentarius can be genetically transformed using the promoters, marker, and nourseothricin selection system developed in this study. Expression of both eGFP and mCherry is a significant step towards cell biological and gene functional analyses using fluorescent microscopy. We have laid the foundations for overexpression studies, and, additionally, identified several challenges which need to be overcome for targeted genetic engineering in this important material producing fungus.
authors: Regner C, Zillessen J, Hoberg F, Elsner S, Cairns TC, Freidank-Pohl C, Meyer V.

title: Roadmap for inferring metabolic regulation using multiomics, machine learning, and genome-scale modeling.
abstract: Machine learning and genome-scale metabolic modeling have accelerated the discovery of metabolic-regulatory relationships in model microbes and mammalian cells. This review provides a roadmap for integrating omics with computational methods for studying systems-level transcriptional, post-translational, and allosteric regulation. Developing methods to infer and integrate multiple regulatory mechanisms simultaneously is essential for discovering novel modes of metabolic regulation and precise engineering of metabolic networks.
authors: Schildcrout R, Rhoads N, Chandrasekaran S.

title: Nanobody-Modified Outer Membrane Vesicles Attenuate Alzheimer's Disease-Like Neurodegeneration by Modulating Mitophagy-Associated Phenotypes and cGAS-STING-Related Inflammatory Signaling.
abstract: This study examined anti-transferrin receptor (TfR) nanobody-functionalized bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) as an engineered platform for improving Alzheimer's disease (AD)-like neuronal injury. Escherichia coli-derived OMVs were characterized for morphology, size distribution, surface charge, protein features, nanobody loading, residual endotoxin levels, endotoxin-associated inflammatory responses, and repeated-exposure immune-safety readouts, and were evaluated in neuronal-related cells and APP/PS1 mice. Engineered OMVs showed receptor-associated uptake and preferential brain-delivery signals, increased HT-22 cell viability, reduced apoptosis, and elevated mitophagy-associated markers including LC3-II, PINK1, and Parkin. OMV treatment also reduced cytosolic mtDNA abundance, DNA/cGAS colocalization, phosphorylation of STING/TBK1/IRF3, and inflammatory-marker expression. PINK1 or Parkin knockdown partially weakened OMV-associated mitochondrial and inflammatory readouts, whereas pharmacological autophagy modulation supported a contribution of autophagy-related processes without establishing selective PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy in vivo. In APP/PS1 mice, OMV administration improved Morris water maze and rotarod performance and alleviated neuroinflammatory and histological injury-related changes. Overall, anti-TfR nanobody-modified OMVs were associated with enhanced receptor-related delivery, mitophagy-linked phenotypes, reduced cytosolic mtDNA/cGAS-STING-related inflammatory signaling, and improved AD-like outcomes, supporting further delivery-system optimization and mechanistic validation.
authors: Xiao J, Yang Z, Li J, Xiong Q, Xia X, Hao L, Ling Z, Pang K, Zhou C, Wu H.

title: Multisensing photoreceptors: a cross-kingdom perspective.
abstract: Photoreceptors are classically depicted as monochromatic switches governed strictly by light. However, emerging biophysical and structural insights reveal that these proteins act as dynamic, multisensory hubs across kingdoms of life. Drawing primarily on plant and fungal systems, where mechanisms are most extensively characterized, this review synthesizes how photoreceptors integrate ambient temperature and cellular oxidative state alongside photon flux, with cross-kingdom examples extending this framework to bacteria. Thermal energy modulates dark reversion rates, quaternary assembly, and photobody phase separation, whereas reactive oxygen species alter the photocycle and trigger structural shifts through direct redox sensing. Under a 'stress-first' evolutionary model, ancestral stress-sensing scaffolds could be retrofitted with chromophores via exaptation, providing a unified biophysical rationale for how cells decode complex, fluctuating environments.
authors: Schuhmacher L, Landmark A, Fischer R.

title: Biochar-mediated N-Fe redox coupling for Cd immobilization and N<sub>2</sub>O mitigation in flooded paddy soil.
abstract: Coupled soil N and Fe redox processes influence heavy-metal mobility and greenhouse-gas emissions. As an electron shuttle, biochar can directly mediate N and Fe redox transformations. However, how this function regulates electron allocation within N-Fe redox processes and whether this regulation contributes to Cd immobilization and N2O mitigation remains unclear. Here, anaerobic incubation experiments combined with electrochemical characterization, electron allocation analysis and metagenomic analysis were conducted in Cd-contaminated paddy soils. Nitrate addition suppressed Fe(III) reduction and amorphous Fe oxide formation in the control treatments, indicating competition between nitrate and Fe(III) reduction. In contrast, biochar increased Fe(III) and nitrate reduction rates by 18-402% and 53-258%, respectively. Biochar also enhanced soil electron-transfer rate and capacity, enriched electroactive microorganisms and extracellular electron-transfer functional genes. The electron allocation analysis showed that biochar increased total quantified electron consumption and suggested that biochar may alleviate competition between nitrate and Fe(III) reduction. Enhanced Fe(III) reduction increased Fe(II) production and may have promoted nitrate-associated Fe(II) oxidation, with amorphous Fe oxide contents increasing by 9-63%. These Fe transformations redistributed Cd into Fe/Mn oxide-bound fractions and decreased CaCl2-extractable Cd by 29-55%. Within the nitrate reduction pathways, biochar increased absolute electron consumption by dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), while decreasing that by denitrification. These changes were accompanied by 10-49% higher NH4+ concentrations and 13-19% lower cumulative N2O emissions. These findings highlight the role of biochar-mediated electron transfer in regulating electron allocation within coupled N-Fe redox processes, providing novel insights into concurrent Cd immobilization and N2O mitigation in paddy soils.
authors: Si T, Chen X, Wang S, Bian R, Liu X, Zhang X, Joseph S, Mao Y, Li L, Pan G.

title: Sulfur-iron-driven autotrophic constructed wetlands for coupled nitrogen removal and phosphorus transformation under low carbon-to-nitrogen ratio conditions.
abstract: Constructed wetlands are widely used for nitrogen removal, yet their performance in low carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) wastewater is often constrained by insufficient electron donors. Autotrophic denitrification provides a carbon-independent alternative, but systems relying on single inorganic substrates frequently exhibit limited electron supply and unstable nutrient transformation. Here, a sulfur-iron-slag-based constructed wetland (SCW) was developed to investigate nitrogen removal and its linkage with phosphorus dynamics under progressively decreasing C/N conditions. The system achieved consistently high nitrate removal (>93%) and a maximum total nitrogen removal efficiency of 79.22%, substantially outperforming a conventional sand-based wetland (53.58%) at a C/N ratio of 0.67. Enhanced nitrogen removal was associated with the sulfur-iron functional medium and sustained autotrophic denitrification. However, phosphorus showed a contrasting response: although aqueous P release decreased with continued operation, the SCW remained a net aqueous P source throughout the reported period, accompanied by redistribution of solid-phase P toward Fe/Al-associated and Ca-associated fractions. Microbial and metagenomic analyses revealed the enrichment of sulfur-oxidizing and autotrophic denitrifying taxa together with shifts in nitrogen- and sulfur-related functional-gene profiles, consistent with enhanced sulfur-associated autotrophic potential. Functional gene profiles further indicated that electron transfer processes governed the integration of multi-element biogeochemical cycles rather than isolated increases in individual pathways. Overall, this study elucidates process-level coupling between enhanced autotrophic nitrogen removal and dynamic phosphorus transformation, providing mechanistic insights and practical guidance for optimizing constructed wetlands treating low-C/N wastewater.
authors: Zhao L, Zhang Y, Tian T, Huang Y, Gu Y, He X, Tang J, He S.

title: Inarigivir exhibits RIG-I-independent antiviral activity against HBV DNA replication in vitro by inhibiting viral polymerase activity.
abstract: Inarigivir (SB 9200) is a linear dinucleotide antiviral drug designed to act as a RIG-I agonist, activating cellular innate immune responses. Clinical trials in hepatitis C virus (HCV) patients have confirmed the innate immune-activating antiviral activity of Inarigivir. In hepatitis B virus (HBV) patients, clinical trials using Inarigivir have demonstrated significant reductions in HBV DNA and RNA levels, although heterogeneous drug-induced liver injury has been observed at higher doses. To further explore Inarigivir's mechanism of action against HBV, we characterized its antiviral effect in various hepatocyte-derived cell lines, including transiently transfected HepG2 and Huh7 cells, inducible HBV stable cell lines HepAD38 and HepDES19, and HBV-infected human hepatocytes. Our results show that Inarigivir inhibits HBV DNA replication in a dose-dependent manner without affecting HBV RNA levels or pgRNA encapsidation. HBV RNA immunoprecipitation assays revealed that Inarigivir does not affect viral polymerase binding to pgRNA, while the in vitro endogenous polymerase reaction (EPR) assays demonstrated that Inarigivir inhibits HBV DNA synthesis catalyzed by polymerase within the capsid. Additionally, we provided several lines of evidence indicating that Inarigivir's antiviral effect is independent of the RIG-I signalling pathway in hepatocyte-derived cells. Taken together, our study demonstrates a RIG-I-independent antiviral mechanism of Inarigivir by inhibiting HBV DNA replication as a dinucleosidic non-chain-terminating reverse transcriptase inhibitor.
authors: Zhang JJ, Colledge D, Jurado A, Sun N, Zhang H, Jackson K, Sozzi V, Li X, Eyre NS, Beard MR, Iyer R, Afdhal N, Guo H.

title: Single-probe, amplification-free multiplex mRNA PNA-FISH maps bacterial gene expression in intact three-dimensional biofilms
abstract: Biofilms are spatially structured communities in which local microenvironments drive physiological differentiation, yet mapping gene expression inside intact three-dimensional biofilms remains challenging. Bacterial spatial transcriptomics methods typically rely on tiled probe sets, sequential hybridization rounds, or signal amplification. Here, we show that a single short, directly labelled peptide nucleic acid (PNA) probe per target is sufficient to quantify bacterial mRNA  in situ without amplification. With all probes designed for a common hybridization condition, a transcript panel is resolved in one hybridization on a standard confocal microscope, in unmodified cells while preserving biofilm architecture. Benchmarked against the biphasic cycle of  Legionella pneumophila , multiplex mRNA PNA-FISH recovers the expected transcriptional switch and agrees quantitatively with RT-qPCR in planktonic and biofilm populations. In flow-cell biofilms, it shows that sessile populations do not recapitulate the planktonic program and that transcriptional differences follow cellular aggregation state rather than depth.
authors: Barbosa A, Smith HJ, Parker A, Jones CJ, Goeres DM, Azevedo NF, Cerqueira L.

title: Machine learning guided design of strong transcriptional activation domains
abstract: Summary  Artificial intelligence has accelerated the design of structured proteins, but it remains difficult to design functional intrinsically disordered proteins because of weak structural constraints and poorly defined sequence-to-function relationships  1 . Activation domains (ADs), transcription factor regions that recruit coactivators, are an excellent test case for the  de novo design of intrinsically disordered sequences. ADs are one of the oldest groups of functional intrinsically disordered sequences  2 and designed ADs have applications in synthetic biology, biotechnology, and agriculture. We computationally generated 500,000 candidate sequences that resembled known ADs and predicted AD function with extant machine learning models, including three neural networks. From high-scoring sequences, we selected 18,750 for experimental validation in yeast. Surprisingly, >90% of the 16,770 well-measured sequences function as ADs. Sequences predicted to be active by multiple models were stronger, motivating development of a fast and accurate consensus AD predictor, MADRIGAL. A number of our designed ADs retain functionality across fungi, plants, and human cells. This work illustrates a generalizable paradigm for incorporating sequence-to-function models into the design loop to efficiently generate functional intrinsically disordered sequences.

title: Therapeutic vulnerabilities of the drug-resistant fungal meningitis pathogen  Cryptococcus neoformans
abstract: SUMMARY  Treatment options are limited for the priority fungal pathogen  Cryptococcus neoformans . We describe CRISPR-insert, a scalable gene inactivation method for global interrogation of drug targets. Genome-wide screens using this methodology combined with machine learning predict 1,297 essential genes under liberal criteria. Unexpectedly absent from this list is  FKS1 , encoding the target of echinocandin drugs to which  C. neoformans is resistant. Contrary to longstanding literature, targeted deletion shows that  FKS1 is not essential. Solid-state NMR reveals that  fks1 Δ mutants lack β-1,3-glucan, arguing against compensation by another synthase. We experimentally test essentiality predictions for genes lacking human orthologs, identifying high-priority drug target candidates. To uncover targets for combination therapies, we establish genome-scale quantitative genetic interaction mapping. We use this method to uncover synthetic lethal dependencies of echinocandin resistance determinants, including the druggable calcineurin and Cdc50-Apt1 pathways. CRISPR-insert illuminates therapeutic vulnerabilities of an invasive fungal pathogen.
authors: Huang MY, Hecht P, Cesar K, Ciranni M, Wei AL, Boucher MJ, Briner SL, Lortal L, Nayak V, Ankur A, Wang T, Doering TL, Pastore VP, Madhani HD.

title: Metagenomic insights into kapok-driven nitrogen-cycling hotspots enhancing soil biological resilience in tropical agroforestry systems
abstract: Abstract    Intensive rice monoculture in tropical regions is increasingly vulnerable to soil degradation, low nitrogen use efficiency (NUE), and amplified nutrient losses under climate change extremes, necessitating sustainable, biologically driven management strategies. This study evaluated the role of traditional kapok–rice agroforestry, integrating the native red silk-cotton tree (  Bombax ceiba  ), in regulating soil nutrient dynamics, nitrogen (N) mineralization, microbial biomass, extracellular enzyme activities, and microbial community composition across five rice growth stages (tillering, booting, heading, maturity, and fallow) compared to rice monoculture systems in Changjiang County, Hainan, China. Using a paired-plot design with three independent replicate fields per system, we compared kapok-integrated soils against adjacent rice monoculture controls. Kapok-integrated soils exhibited markedly enhanced fertility relative to monoculture, with soil organic matter increasing by up to 42%, total N by 44–49%, and available N, P, and K by 63%, 133%, and 93%, respectively, at the maturity stage, compared to monoculture controls. Microbial biomass carbon and nitrogen peaked at 397.17 and 362.40 mg kg  − 1  , accompanied by significantly higher N-acquiring enzyme activities (N-acetylglucosaminidase and leucine aminopeptidase), indicating intensified microbial functioning. Nitrogen mineralization potential (N  o  ) and cumulative mineralized N were substantially greater (63.42 and 67.46 mg kg  − 1  over 90 days), reflecting improved N retention and cycling capacity under agroforestry management. These enhancements were linked to distinct microbial community shifts dominated by Pseudomonadota, Actinomycetota, Ascomycota, and Bacillariophyta, suggesting increased functional stability and adaptive capacity under climate-sensitive conditions. Overall, kapok–rice agroforestry strengthens soil biological processes, enhances nitrogen cycling, and improves ecosystem resilience, demonstrating its potential as a nature-based, low-input management strategy to mitigate soil degradation and sustain productivity in tropical rice systems under climate change extremes.
authors: ALI S, Xiang W, Ren M, AHMED W.

title: A Candidate Genomic DNA Reference Material for PCR-Based Detection of Brucella spp.: Intralaboratory Characterization and Preliminary Application in LAMP Assays
abstract: Analytical standardization of Brucella molecular assays requires reference materials with assigned values and defined uncertainty. We produced and characterized intralaboratory a candidate genomic DNA reference material from Brucella abortus RB51 for PCR-based detection of Brucella spp., and evaluated its preliminary use in fluorescence-based and colorimetric LAMP assays. DNA was extracted, assessed by qPCR and dPCR, and diluted to two levels. Homogeneity and stability were evaluated by duplex qPCR targeting ctrA and nikR, whereas property values were assigned by duplex dPCR. qPCR efficiencies were 95.3% for ctrA and 92.1% for nikR. The material fulfilled the homogeneity criterion, with relative homogeneity uncertainties between 0.37% and 1.41%. Assigned values (levels 1 and 2) were 32 989 ± 5 475 and 285 ± 47 copies/µL for ctrA, and 29 722 ± 3 263 and 286 ± 42 copies/µL for nikR. Short-term stability at 4 °C was supported for 8 weeks and was included in the uncertainty budget. ctrA-based LAMP assays were optimized at 67 °C for 45 min and amplified reproducibly in both formats. Amplification was consistent from 2411 to 6.34 copies/µL. This material provides a metrologically characterized tool for quality control, method verification, and optimization of PCR- and LAMP-based assays for Brucella spp.

title: Extended DNA damage-induced G2/M arrests lead to aberrant mitoses through accumulation of securin.
abstract: The stochastic nature of DNA damage dictates various scenarios of stress survival among different cells. We used time-lapse microscopy to perform single-cell level analyses of yeast populations with double-stranded DNA breaks and nonfunctional telomeres. Activation of the DNA damage signalling resulted in a broad distribution in the duration of G2/M arrests. Strikingly, the longer arrests correlated with aberrant mitoses caused by miscoordination of nuclear division and cytokinesis, leading to cell death. Chk1-dependent phosphorylation of Pds1 (securin), an inhibitor of sister chromatid separation in mitosis, was responsible for this phenomenon. Securin progressively accumulated during G2/M arrests, leading to grossly delayed or missed nuclear divisions. This phenotype could be suppressed by slowing down the progression of mitotic exit via LTE1 deletion or by lowering securin levels. Our results demonstrate that in cells taking too long to complete DNA repair, the DNA damage checkpoint promotes aberrant mitoses and cell death, thereby eliminating cells with a higher chance of genomic instability.
authors: Dubenko A, Jnied M, Kotenko O, Makovets S.

title: NRF2 plays a significant role in the suppression of genotoxicity during aging whereas its protective role for acute UVB genotoxicity is limited to MIS response in mouse skin epidermis.
abstract: Our body is continuously exposed to endogenous and exogenous sources of oxidative stress arising from physiological metabolism and environmental factors such as ultraviolet (UV) radiation. These stresses generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) that can induce genotoxicity through oxidative DNA damage. To evaluate the contribution of NRF2, which is a master transcription factor regulating cellular antioxidant responses, to the suppression of oxidative stress-induced genotoxicity in the skin, we examined Nrf2-deficient mice regarding mutagenic responses to two separate biological situations: acute UVB exposures and the chronic process of aging. Analyses were performed using transgenic mice carrying the bacterial lacZ gene as a mutational reporter. No significant differences were detected between Nrf2-deficient and wild-type mice in mutagenicity, induced mutation spectrum, and mutation distribution within the reporter gene after acute UVB exposure, whereas the dose-response kinetics of UVB-induced mutation in the phase called "mutation induction suppression" (MIS) differed significantly between genotypes, with a more pronounced MIS response observed in the Nrf2-/- epidermis. Little contribution of ROS to genotoxicity was observed after the acute exposure. Notably, however, the age-dependent accumulation of mutations was significantly elevated in the Nrf2-deficient epidermis compared to the wild-type. These findings indicate that NRF2 plays a protective role for the skin, not by directly preventing genotoxicity, but by promoting tissue recovery after acute UVB damage and, more importantly, by suppressing the genotoxic effects of physiologically produced ROS in a chronic aging process.
authors: Ikehata H, Yamamoto M.
