title: Activity of omadacycline and comparator agents against rapidly growing mycobacteria by broth microdilution and whole genome sequencing.
abstract: Pulmonary infections caused by rapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM), such as Mycobacteroides abscessus, are challenging to treat, highlighting the need for new therapeutic options. This study evaluated the in vitro activity of omadacycline against RGM and investigated the influence of tetracycline resistance mechanisms on its in vitro activity. In vitro susceptibility to omadacycline and comparator antimicrobials was assessed by broth microdilution against 476 geographically diverse RGM isolates from the United States. Omadacycline minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) distributions were compared between cystic fibrosis (CF) and non-CF RGM isolates. Variation in the TetR-TetX operon and the rrl, rrs, and erm(41) genes was evaluated by whole genome sequencing. Omadacycline exhibited low MIC values across all RGM species (MIC50/MIC90: 0.25/0.5 µg/mL). CF isolates showed a modest shift toward higher omadacycline MIC values (P = 0.001). The activity of comparator antimicrobials varied by species, whereas omadacycline was consistent and comparable to tigecycline. The TetR-TetX operon was present in all sequenced isolates, with variable amino acid sequences across species. These variations did not significantly affect omadacycline or tigecycline activity, whereas doxycycline and minocycline remained largely inactive regardless of TetR-TetX variation. The rrs A1408G mutation was identified in 6% of M. abscessus isolates, and rrl mutations were identified in 4% of isolates. The T28C erm(41) sequevar was present in 80% of M. abscessus subsp. abscessus and 100% of M. abscessus subsp. bolletii, whereas 100% of M. abscessus subsp. massiliense exhibited a truncated erm(41). Omadacycline consistently demonstrated potent in vitro activity across RGM species regardless of TetR-TetX operon variation, supporting its potential role in treating RGM infections.ImportanceRapidly growing mycobacteria (RGM) are a group of bacteria that often resist common antibiotics, making the infections they cause hard to treat. In this study, we tested omadacycline, a newer antibiotic in the tetracycline class, against a large collection of these bacteria collected from patients across the United States. We found that omadacycline showed consistent activity against different RGM species, requiring low concentrations to inhibit bacterial growth in laboratory testing. These findings support further evaluation of omadacycline as a potential treatment option for patients with RGM infections, which can be challenging to manage.
authors: Calado Nogueira de Moura V, Gillaspie JJ, Anastasiou DM, Serio AW, Strong M, Khare R, Daley CL.

title: Genome sequence of the endophyte Bacillus halotolerans Adn01R isolated from Agropyron desertorum roots.
abstract: We report the draft genome of endophytic Bacillus halotolerans Adn01R isolated from roots of Agropyron desertorum. Sequencing on Illumina NextSeq (1.4 M paired-end reads) and assembly with SPAdes yielded a 4.15-Mb genome (43.71% guanine-cytosine [GC], N50 4.14 Mb, 98× coverage). The assembly shows 99.8% BUSCO completeness and 4,298 genes.

title: Ineffectiveness of permethrin in human scabies treatment: A multicenter study of kdr gene mutations.
abstract: BackgroundScabies remains a widespread parasitic skin disease with increasing reports of treatment failure associated with permethrin, the first-line therapy. Emerging evidence suggests that genetic variation in the voltage-gated sodium channel (VGSC) may be associated with reduced susceptibility to pyrethroids, although its contribution to clinical treatment failure in human scabies remains incompletely characterized.ObjectivesTo investigate the presence and frequency of knockdown resistance (kdr) gene mutations associated with permethrin treatment failure in S. scabiei collected from patients in multiple centres across Europe and Africa.MethodsMite samples were obtained from patients with clinically diagnosed scabies in France, Belgium, Tunisia and Madagascar between 2023 and 2025. Genomic DNA was extracted and PCR amplification of the voltage-sensitive sodium channel (VSSC) gene was performed, followed by bidirectional sequencing to identify single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Detected mutations were analysed and correlated with clinical treatment outcomes.ResultsOut of 61 suspected cases, 45 were confirmed as scabies infestations. Molecular analysis identified three mutations-M918L, G733D and S916S-in 25 (55.5%) specimens, which were detected in patients with documented permethrin treatment failure. In contrast, 20 out of 45 patients without these mutations experienced successful treatment outcomes. M918L was the most frequent and widely distributed mutation. These genetic findings were consistent with the observed treatment ineffectiveness. This study is the first to report these mutations in Belgium, Tunisia and Madagascar.ConclusionsThis pilot multicentre study identified an association between specific VGSC polymorphisms and documented permethrin treatment failure in human scabies. M918L, G733D and S916S represent candidate resistance-associated variants, whereas the functional significance of the synonymous S916S substitution requires further investigation. Regarding the multifactorial nature of scabies treatment, the increasing occurrence of VGSC nucleotide substitutions highlights an emerging challenge in scabies management and underscores the urgent need for ongoing resistance monitoring, molecular surveillance and the development of alternative therapeutic strategies.
journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
authors: Akhoundi M, Saegeman V, Goeteyn V, Chouaieb H, Lahouel M, Denguezli M, Fathallah A, Raharisoa A, Brun S, Barquero J, Durand R, Izri A.

title: ADAR-mediated RNA editing of Influenza A virus genomes may be age-dependent and inversely correlates with viral load.
abstract: BackgroundSeasonal influenza epidemics cause significant mortality, especially among the elderly. Influenza A virus triggers the host innate immune system through various mechanisms. Human enzymes belonging to the group of RNA-acting adenosine deaminases (ADARs) play a role in the innate antiviral immune response, partly by inducing mutations in viral RNA. The effect of this mechanismin influenza A virus infection remains unexplained in humans.ObjectiveThe aim of this study was to assess the clinical impact of ADAR-induced mutations on influenza A virus in hospitalised patients.MethodsFull-genome deep sequencing of Influenza A virus was performed on respiratory samples from 75 hospitalised, Influenza A(H3N2) virus infected patients, aged 41 to 95 years. ADAR-associated mutations in minor viral subpopulations were analysed in relation to demographic and clinical factors.ResultsADAR-associated mutations showed a significant inverse correlation with viral load (p p = 0.0051), especially in patients older than 75 years. The association between ADAR-associated mutations and viral load was independent of age, inflammation, and disease severity (p ConclusionsWe found an association between ADAR-induced mutations and viral load, which may indicate an antiviral function of ADAR on influenza A virus. The lower mutation rate and associated higher viral load in the elderly suggest an age-dependent reduced ADAR activity, which may contribute to increased disease severity.
authors: Widström J, Fingal J, Ringlander J, Lindh M, Andersson M, Wahllöf M, Rydell GE, Bustamante Jaramillo LF, Kann M, Westin J.

title: Decoding anterior-posterior patterning cues into embryo-wide binary fate decisions through recruitment-mediated targeting.
abstract: Developmental pattern formation requires patterning cues to be converted into discrete, gene- and cell-specific regulatory outputs, but how this conversion is achieved remains unclear. We address this problem in Caenorhabditis elegans anterior-posterior patterning, where quantitatively asymmetric Wnt/β-catenin cues, namely anterior-enriched POP-1/TCF and posterior-enriched SYS-1/β-catenin, are decoded into binary, switch-like fate decisions. We show that these cues are resolved into embryo-wide binary regulatory outputs through ZIP-7/DBP, a transcription factor with stage-specific, lineage-wide posterior-exclusive expression that is essential for multiple posterior fate decisions. We define a model for this cue-to-decision decoding. At the zip-7 promoter, the transcription factor ZIP-8/NFIL3, which begins to be expressed during mid-embryogenesis prior to ZIP-7 onset, provides an activating input while recruiting POP-1 and SYS-1. POP-1 restrains this activity anteriorly, whereas the POP-1-SYS-1 complex promotes it posteriorly, thereby generating a binary pattern of zip-7 transcription. This recruitment-mediated promoter control couples Wnt/β-catenin cues to gene-specific transcriptional regulation and enables flexible spatiotemporal control of cue-dependent transcription. Genome-wide analyses further suggest that recruitment-mediated cotargeting may extend beyond zip-7 and point to additional candidate factors with similar recruitment functions, supporting a scalable framework for decoding patterning cues into context-specific regulatory decisions.
authors: Xiao L, Cong Y, Qi H, Bai Y, Ma X, Zhou Z, Huang X, Wang Y, Du Z.

title: Food-derived resveratrol confers multigenerational host defense against PA14 via p38 MAPK and DAF-16 signaling in C. elegans.
abstract: Food-derived bioactive compounds are promising candidates for enhancing host immune defense. Here, we established an integrated screening strategy combining immunodeficiency-related gene mining, compound-target mapping, food-derived component annotation, and drug-likeness evaluation to identify candidate immunomodulators. Highly relevant immunodeficiency-associated genes were screened from GeneCards, and active compounds targeting these genes were retrieved from ChEMBL (pChEMBL ≥ 6). These compounds were cross-referenced with the food-derived components from FooDB, followed by network-based target analysis and rule-based drug-likeness filtering. Using this pipeline, resveratrol was prioritized as a representative candidate. In the Caenorhabditis elegans-Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 infection model, resveratrol significantly improved host survival, with 0.5 mM showing the strongest protective effect. This concentration also enhanced body length, locomotion, and lifespan without causing developmental delay. Fluorescence analysis suggested that resveratrol improved lysosomal and mitochondrial homeostasis and reduced infection-associated cellular damage. Integrated transcriptomic analysis and genetic validation demonstrated that resveratrol-mediated protection required intact p38 MAPK signaling and DAF-16 activity, and resveratrol promoted DAF-16 nuclear localization. Moreover, parental resveratrol treatment enhanced PA14 resistance in untreated offspring through both maternal and paternal lineages, with the heritable effect persisting for at least three generations. These findings identify resveratrol as a food-derived candidate with host-protective activity that promotes pathogen resistance and induces heritable host defense through p38 MAPK- and DAF-16-dependent mechanisms, highlighting the potential of dietary interventions for immune modulation and transgenerational health benefits.
authors: Wen Y, Shan S, Fu J, Yao J, Zhao C.

title: The NS4B A119T mutation of dengue virus 2 confers adaptation to mammalian cells and increased pathogenicity in AG129 mice.
abstract: Mouse-adapted dengue virus type 2 (DENV2), designated the AG-P10 strain, was established through serial blind passages between AG129 mice and mosquito C6/36 cells. Compared with the parental strain INDIA/09-74, the AG-P10 strain exhibited increased virulence in AG129 mice, leading to rapid body weight loss and earlier mortality. In vitro characterization of the AG-P10 strain demonstrated significantly enhanced viral replication and larger focus formation in mammalian Vero and A549 cells but not in mosquito-derived C6/36 cells, suggesting host-specific adaptation. Whole-genome sequencing of the AG-P10 strain identified two nonsynonymous mutations, A119T in NS4B and E802Q in NS5. Through an analysis of recombinant viruses, we determined that the A119T mutation alone is sufficient to confer enhanced pathogenicity in AG129 mice and increased viral replication in Vero and A549 cells, suggesting its potential role in viral adaptation and pathogenesis. The DENV2 with the A119T mutation, as well as the AG-P10 strain, thus provides a robust animal model for developing antiviral therapeutics and vaccines against DENV and for investigating the molecular mechanisms governing DENV2 replication and virulence.
authors: Tabata K, Itakura Y, Uemura K, Mulavu M, Yamashita M, Matsushita T, Kusakabe S, Toba S, Sasaki M, Saito S, Gonzalez G, Hall WW, Sawa H, Sato A, Orba Y.

title: Identification and Validation of Hub Genes Associated With Periodontitis and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
abstract: BackgroundAccumulating evidence suggests a close relationship between periodontitis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE); however, the shared molecular mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. This study aimed to identify candidate genes and molecular features shared between periodontitis and SLE through integrative bioinformatics analysis and clinical validation.MethodsGene expression profiles were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database, and differentially expressed genes (DEGs) shared between periodontitis and SLE were identified. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses were performed, followed by protein-protein interaction (PPI) network construction and hub gene screening. The expression patterns of the hub genes were evaluated in independent validation datasets, and their discriminatory performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Immune cell infiltration and its correlations with hub gene expression were further investigated. Transcription factor-microRNA regulatory networks and candidate compounds were computationally predicted. Finally, quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) was performed to validate hub gene expression in clinical samples.ResultsA total of 124 overlapping DEGs were identified, from which five hub genes-CCL3, LY96, FOS, MMP9, and PTGS2-were selected. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses indicated that the overlapping DEGs were predominantly associated with inflammatory and immune-related biological processes and signaling pathways. All five hub genes showed consistent expression patterns in the independent periodontitis validation dataset, whereas FOS, LY96, and PTGS2, but not CCL3 and MMP9, showed consistent differential expression in the independent SLE validation dataset. ROC analyses demonstrated varying discriminatory performance across the analyzed datasets. Immune infiltration analysis revealed differences in estimated immune cell profiles in both disease datasets, and computational prediction identified candidate regulatory interactions and compounds for further investigation. qPCR validation in clinical samples (n = 15 per group) showed significantly increased expression of all five hub genes in gingival tissues from patients with periodontitis and PBMCs from patients with SLE compared with their respective healthy controls.ConclusionThis study identified CCL3, LY96, FOS, MMP9, and PTGS2 as candidate genes associated with periodontitis and SLE. FOS, LY96, and PTGS2 showed consistent expression patterns across datasets, whereas CCL3 and MMP9 exhibited dataset-dependent variation in SLE. Clinical qPCR validation showed increased expression of all five genes in both disease cohorts. These findings provide insight into the shared molecular features of periodontitis and SLE and warrant further validation in larger, independent, and clinically well-characterized cohorts.
authors: Li Y, Xu X, Wu Z, Li F, Zhang J.

title: [Genetic analysis of a child with Frontometaphyseal dysplasia 1 due to variant of FLNA gene and literature review].
abstract: ObjectiveTo explore the clinical characteristics and genetic etiology of a child with Frontometaphyseal dysplasia 1 (FMD1) due to variant of FLNA gene.MethodsA child who presented at the Department of Endocrinology, the Third Xiangya Hospital of Central South University in July 2025 with a 6-year history of prominent supraorbital ridges was selected as study subject. Clinical data of the child were collected. Peripheral venous blood samples were collected from the child and his parents for the extraction of genomic DNA. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was carried out, and candidate variant was validated by Sanger sequencing. Pathogenicity of the variant was rated based on guidelines from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). Structure of the mutant protein was predicted using AlphaFold and PyMOL software. Literature retrieval was performed using Chinese and English keywords "FLNA gene" and "frontometaphyseal dysplasia". The clinical manifestations and inheritance patterns of previously reported cases with the variant were analyzed. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the hospital (Ethics No.: 25971).ResultsThe child exhibited multiple skeletal deformities including prominent supraorbital ridges, micrognathia, hearing loss, scoliosis, long bone curvature, broad and flat deformities of the thumbs and great toes, and joint contractures. Additionally, he was complicated with congenital urinary tract obstruction. WES revealed that he has harbored a hemizygous missense variant c.3557C>T (p.Ser1186Leu) in exon 22 of the FLNA gene, which showed a strong correlation with his clinical phenotype. Sanger sequencing confirmed this variant to be de novo in origin. Based on the ACMG guidelines, the FLNA c.3557C>T (p.Ser1186Leu) variant was classified as pathogenic (PS4_Moderate+PM2_Supporting+PM6+PP1_Strong+PP2+PP3). Protein structural modeling suggested that this variant could reduce local hydrogen bonds, which may weaken local anchoring force. Literature review has retrieved 8 articles (1 in Chinese) related to FMD1 due to the FLNA c.3557C>T variant. Together with the present case, a total of 14 patients (13 males and 1 female) were included. All patients showed obvious supraorbital hyperplasia (100.0%). Other common manifestations included wrist/distal joint contracture (14 cases), micrognathia (10 cases), scoliosis (10 cases), and spatulate thumbs/toes (9 cases). Other manifestations included hearing loss (8 cases), permanent tooth agenesis (8 cases), long bone bowing (8 cases), hypertelorism (8 cases). Urinary tract malformations (3 cases) and cardiovascular malformations (2 cases) were relatively rare. Analysis of the inheritance pattern showed that 2 of the 14 patients carried de novo variants, and the remaining 12 patients were from 9 families, with their mothers as heterozygous carriers (one mosaic).ConclusionThis study has diagnosed a child with FMD1 due to a hemizygous c.3557C>T (p.Ser1186Leu) missense variant of the FLNA gene, which expanded the mutational spectrum of FMD1.

title: [Genetic analysis of a family with PAX2-related nephropathy].
abstract: ObjectiveTo explore the genetic etiology of a fetus with bilateral renal dysplasia and oligohydramnios detected by prenatal ultrasound.MethodsFetal tissue and peripheral blood samples from the couple were collected for trio-whole exome sequencing (trio-WES). Candidate variant was verified by Sanger sequencing. Conservation of the variant site was analyzed via multi-species sequence alignment, and protein structural changes were predicted by homology modeling. Wild-type PAX2 and its mutant construct were separately overexpressed in cells to compare their regulatory activity towards downstream target genes. This study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of the hospital (2021-38).ResultsThe fetus was found to harbor a heterozygous c.203T>C (p.Ile68Thr) missense variant of the PAX2 gene, which was inherited from its mother, and the variant arose de novo in the maternal grandfather. The variant was not recorded in normal population databases and located in a highly conserved paired domain, which could alter the local conformation of the protein. In vitro experiments showed that, compared with the wild type, the mutant PAX2 had significantly reduced transcriptional activation ability on target genes C3 and NAIP, with a differential regulatory effect on CD55. Based on the guidelines from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG), the variant was classified as likely pathogenic.ConclusionThe novel c.203T>C variant of the PAX2 gene probably underlay the bilateral renal dysplasia in this fetus. Above finding has expanded the mutational spectrum of the PAX2 gene and provided molecular evidence for genetic counseling and prenatal diagnosis for the family.

title: [Genetic analysis and prenatal diagnosis for a Chinese pedigree affected with X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia due to variant of EDA gene].
abstract: ObjectiveTo explore molecular basis for a Chinese pedigree affected with X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (XLHED).MethodsA Chinese pedigree presenting at the Northwest Women's and Children's Hospital in October 2023 was enrolled in this study. Clinical data were retrospectively analyzed. Peripheral blood samples were collected from the proband and his family members for genomic DNA extraction. Whole exome sequencing (WES) was carried out to screen for candidate pathogenic variants. Sanger sequencing was used to validate these variants within the pedigree, followed by pathogenicity assessment of the candidate variants. Chorionic villus sampling was conducted during the first trimester for prenatal diagnosis in two pregnant relatives (the proband's mother and maternal aunt). This study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of the hospital (Ethics No.: 2024-027).ResultsThe proband, a 7-year-old boy, exhibited classic features of XLHED including hypodontia and sparse hair. Genetic analysis identified a hemizygous c.572_573insC (p.Gly192Argfs*48) frameshift variant in exon 4 of the EDA gene. Both the proband's mother and maternal aunt were heterozygous for this variant but remained asymptomatic. Segregation analysis traced the variant to the proband's maternal grandfather, who displayed a phenotype similar to that of the proband. Based on the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines, the variant was classified as pathogenic (PVS1+PP4+PM2_Supporting). The variant was unreported previously. Subsequent chorionic villus sampling confirmed that neither fetus had carried the same variant, and postnatal follow-up revealed normal phenotypes in both infants.ConclusionThe c.572_573insC (p.Gly192Argfs*48) variant of the EDA gene probably underlay the XLHED in this pedigree. Above finding has expanded the mutational spectrum of the EDA gene and facilitated the prenatal management. The lack of clinical expression in female heterozygous carriers underscores the importance of accurate risk assessment in genetic counseling for pedigrees affected with XLHED.

title: Redirecting Metabolic Flux to Minimize By-Product Formation Enables Efficient De Novo Biosynthesis of Chlorogenic Acid in Escherichia coli.
abstract: Chlorogenic acid (CGA) is an important natural hydroxycinnamic acid ester with diverse biological activities, including antioxidant, antibacterial, and potential antitumor properties. However, efficient microbial titer of CGA remains challenging because of insufficient hydroxylation efficiency, by-product accumulation, and limited host tolerance. Herein, an efficient and sustainable microbial platform for de novo CGA biosynthesis was constructed in Escherichia coli. Enhancement of the NAD(H) biosynthetic pathway increased intracellular reducing power and increased hydroxylation efficiency. A synergistic hydroxylation module consisting of the p-coumarate 3-hydroxylase from Saccharothrix espanaensis (SeC3H) and the flavin reductase from Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PaHpaC)was further introduced to promote the conversion of p-coumaric acid (pCA) to caffeic acid (CA) and redirect metabolic flux toward CGA biosynthesis. Rational engineering of 4-coumarate-CoA ligase from Arabidopsis thaliana (At4CL) increased substrate selectivity and decreased the formation of the major by-product p-coumaroylquinic acid (pCQA). In addition, transcriptomic analysis identified lsrG, a gene associated with the AI-2 quorum-sensing system, as a beneficial target whose overexpression further enhanced CGA titer. The final engineered strain produced 7220.3 mg/L CGA in a 50 L fed-batch fermentation. The strategies developed herein may provide an effective metabolic engineering framework for the sustainable biosynthesis of CGA and other aromatic natural products.
authors: Su Y, Chen Q, Chen J, Zhang S, Yu Y, Qin Z, Zeng W, Zhou J.

title: A Mechanistic Viral Host Perturbation Score (VHPS) Reveals Shared and Virus-Specific Transcriptional Programs Across Human Respiratory Infections.
abstract: BackgroundAcute viral infections trigger overlapping but virus-specific blood transcriptional responses; however, current analyses rarely quantify the mechanistic depth of activation across pathways, regulators, and immune cell compositions.MethodsRNA-seq data from GSE157240 were reanalyzed to infer transcription factor (TF) activity using DoRothEA/decoupleR, signaling pathway activity using PROGENy, and stress pathway and transcriptional perturbation breadth metrics. These four components were integrated into a viral host perturbation score (VHPS), a proof-of-concept framework designed to quantify the magnitude of host transcriptional perturbation. Differential expression analysis, Gene Ontology enrichment, module scoring, and CIBERSORTx-based immune deconvolution were used to compare respiratory and systemic viral infections.ResultsVHPS-stratified viruses along an axis of host transcriptional perturbation, with DNA viruses showing the highest median perturbation, followed by dengue and enterovirus/rhinovirus, whereas influenza A and other respiratory RNA viruses were intermediate and healthy controls were lowest. Upregulated genes revealed virus-specific and shared signatures, and immune/stress GO terms showed stronger T cell and interferon enrichment for respiratory viruses. A 26-gene "shared respiratory antiviral" module correlated with VHPS and TF/stress components but not PROGENy activity. Immune deconvolution revealed virus-specific leukocyte remodeling, with marked Treg depletion and elevated neutrophils in respiratory viruses, monocyte skewing in dengue, and the lowest Treg fractions in DNA viruses.ConclusionsTogether, VHPS and immune deconvolution delineate shared and virus-specific regulatory programs in acute viral infections, but the generalizability of VHPS requires evaluation in independent datasets.
authors: Sanabani SS.

title: Regulation of endogenous dsRNA: strategies for self-tolerance.
abstract: Cells must continuously distinguish cellular-derived RNA from pathogenic RNA to mount effective antiviral responses while avoiding harmful autoinflammation. Cytoplasmic RNA-sensing receptors, including RIG-I-like receptors, PKR, OAS-RNase L and ZBP1, detect RNA primarily through molecular features such as structure (double- versus single-stranded), modification state and subcellular localization rather than sequence. While these are characteristics of viral nucleic acids, mammalian genomes generate abundant self-derived double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), including from transposable elements, antisense transcription and RNA processing intermediates, which exist in the cytoplasm. This review describes our current understanding of how cells achieve self-tolerance through the active regulation of endogenous RNA. These mechanisms comprise epigenetic silencing of repetitive elements, RNA modifications (such as A-to-I editing and m6A), precise splicing, regulated nuclear export and decay, circRNA buffering, protein shielding and dedicated RNA degradation pathways. Insights from rare inherited monogenic interferonopathies and murine models illustrate how perturbations in these pathways lead to inappropriate activation of cytoplasmic RNA sensors and inflammatory disease when cellular dsRNA is mistakenly recognized as non-self. We highlight how dysregulated dsRNA homeostasis contributes to common autoimmune and neuroinflammatory disorders. Understanding how cells regulate endogenous dsRNA is crucial for defining disease mechanisms and developing new therapeutic strategies.
authors: Heraud-Farlow J, Chan YP, Davidson S, Walkley C.

title: What Is the Evidence for Silver Resistance in Chronic Wounds? A Systematic Review of Prevalence and In Vitro Studies.
abstract: Silver-containing wound dressings are among the most widely used topical antimicrobial interventions in chronic wound management. Amid escalating antimicrobial resistance and increasing scrutiny of antiseptic stewardship, there is growing debate regarding the prevalence and clinical relevance of bacterial resistance to silver, yet the available evidence has not previously been systematically evaluated with a specific focus on chronic wound populations. This review aimed to evaluate the published evidence on the prevalence of silver resistance in bacteria isolated from chronic wounds and to summarise experimental evidence on the capacity of wound-associated isolates to acquire reduced silver susceptibility in vitro. We searched MEDLINE, Embase and Scopus in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, identifying 2190 records, of which five publications met eligibility criteria. Two publications investigating overlapping isolates were consolidated, yielding four independent datasets. Three prevalence datasets reported markedly different rates: studies from the United Kingdom and Sweden identified low phenotypic resistance (0 of 112 and 1 of 56 isolates) and sil gene prevalence (< 2% in both), while a study from Bangladesh reported substantially higher phenotypic resistance (31.5%) and sil carriage (30.9%). Regional differences in antibiotic use offer a plausible explanation but were not directly tested in any included study and concordance between genotypic and phenotypic resistance was poor throughout. Two in vitro induction studies produced divergent results by endpoint: reduced planktonic susceptibility reverted towards baseline once silver exposure was withdrawn, whereas substantial increases in biofilm eradication concentration in Pseudomonas aeruginosa persisted. Prevalence was low where examined, but three datasets from three countries cannot establish the global burden of silver resistance in chronic wounds and critical gaps remain in geographic representation, methodological standardisation and validated breakpoints. Current evidence is insufficient to support changes to guidelines or policy in either direction.
authors: Radzieta M, Tehan P, Bergamin E, Schwarzer S, Nygren E, Hamberg T.

title: Enantiomer-Dependent Modulation of Lithium Uptake and Accumulation in Plants by Foliar Application of Chiral SeNPs.
abstract: The rapid expansion of lithium-based new energy technologies has led to substantial lithium inputs into soil, potentially threatening human health through the consumption of lithium-accumulated agricultural products. Therefore, efficient strategies are urgently needed to mitigate the uptake and accumulation of lithium in plant fruits. Nanotechnology offers promising avenues for enhancing stress resilience and improving the quality of crops grown in contaminated soils. Here, we found that lithium was distributed unevenly among tissues (leaves: 1365, roots: 508, stems: 112, and fruits: 24 mg kg-1) of eggplants grown in lithium-contaminated soil. Notably, foliar spraying of selenium nanoparticles with levorotatory chirality (l-SeNPs) effectively reduced fruit lithium content and promoted its accumulation in the leaves, roots, and stems, in which vacuolar compartmentalization was the primary pathway for tolerance to high lithium content, whereas the dextrorotatory enantiomer showed no such effects. Mechanism investigation elucidated that l-SeNPs can reinforce antioxidant defense systems of eggplant under lithium stress through a microbiome-metabolome-transcriptome bridging cascade, in which l-SeNPs substantially affected rhizosphere bacterial and metabolic networks along with minor changes in the bioavailability of lithium in rhizosphere soil. This study sheds light on the superiority of nanoscale chirality in modulating lithium uptake and accumulation in plants grown in metal-contaminated soil, providing strategies for agromining of lithium.
authors: Tong M, Lin C, Xu Z, Yang X, Li L, Wang Y, Jiang G.

title: Psychoactive Pollutant Impacts Baseline Immune Traits but Not Behavior and Microbiome in a Fish.
abstract: Pharmaceutical pollution is an increasing global threat to freshwater ecosystems. Psychoactive drugs, such as antidepressants, are of particular concern because they affect evolutionarily conserved neuroendocrine pathways in nontarget organisms. As these pathways regulate interconnected biological systems, understanding the ecological consequences of pharmaceutical exposure requires an integrative approach. Here, we investigated the effects of 28-day exposure to control (freshwater), low (4.2 ± 0.3 ng/L), and high (637.5 ± 173.84 ng/L) fluoxetine concentrations on behaviors, baseline immune traits, and skin mucus microbiome composition in the Murray River rainbowfish (Melanotaenia fluviatilis). Fluoxetine exposure did not impact fish behavior, including activity, freezing behavior, shelter use, or microbiome composition. In contrast, immune traits were significantly altered. Both fluoxetine concentrations reduced total white blood cell (WBC) count, while only fish exposed to the low concentration showed reduced lymphocyte counts and elevated neutrophil counts, consistent with a stress-associated WBC redistribution response. Our findings show that different, but interconnected, biological systems can differ in their sensitivity to pollutants and suggest that immune traits may be an early, sensitive indicator of exposure to psychoactive pharmaceuticals. These findings highlight the importance of integrating multiple biological end points to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of the ecological consequences of pharmaceutical contamination.
authors: Melhado G, Eastment RV, Marques FZ, Aich U, Peters A, Wong BBM.

title: The GndA Microprotein Promotes Cell Growth during Heat Shock in Escherichia coli.
abstract: Hundreds of bacterial small open reading frames (sORFs) encoding microproteins of fewer than 50 amino acids have recently been identified. Biological functions have been ascribed to an increasing number of microproteins, some of which play roles in bacterial stress responses. In this work, we provide evidence that GndA, a frameshifted 36-amino acid microprotein encoded in an internal open reading frame overlapping the 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (6PGD) coding sequence (CDS), functions in the response to heat shock. We demonstrate independent contributions of GndA and 6PGD to cell growth at a high temperature. GndA is hydrophobic and associates with the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and the inner membrane. Consistent with a role in cellular homeostasis, GndA mutations alter the transcriptional response to heat shock. These results demonstrate that GndA promotes bacterial cell growth at high temperatures independently of the 6PGD protein that it overlaps. GndA thus expands the paradigm of bacterial microproteins that function in cellular stress responses.
authors: Mohsen JJ, Bertolotti NR, Jiang K, Mohsen MG, DeRosa CM, Dewani N, Quinto L, Dabdoub G, Erkalo B, Landajuela A, Karatekin E, Isaacs FJ, Slavoff SA.

title: Stacking Up: The Expanding Catalog of Filament-Forming Enzymes.
abstract: Enzyme filamentation has emerged as a widespread and functionally important mode of macromolecular organization. Once viewed as an unusual property of a few metabolic enzymes, reversible filament formation is now known for more than 50 enzymes across bacteria, archaea, plants, fungi, and animals. This review summarizes recent progress in the field, expanding substantially on our 2019 analysis and incorporating more than 300 new publications. We survey the known filament-forming enzymes, their catalytic activities, biological contexts, filament architectures, and available structural information from X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, and in cellulo imaging approaches. Filamenting enzymes span five major enzyme classes and function in metabolism, stress responses, signaling, replication, and host defense. In many cases, polymerization occurs at critical metabolic branch points and appears to regulate enzyme activity, allostery, substrate channeling, localization, or sequestration. Distinct filament geometries, including linear stacks, solenoidal coils, tubes, and rings, are associated with specific functional outcomes and cellular roles. We also highlight emerging in cellulo structural studies of enzyme filaments, summarizing the insights they provide into filament organization and cellular assembly when available. Together, these findings highlight enzyme filamentation as a common mode of macromolecular organization with consequences for structure, assembly, and function in diverse biological contexts.
authors: Horton NC.

title: Exploring Key Microbial Enzymes as Targets for Benzimidazole Derivatives: Synthesis, SAR, and Therapeutic Relevance.
abstract: The benzimidazole pharmacophore has become a key theme in the identification and advancement of innovative antimicrobial agents owing to its resemblance with the purines (nucleotides), which make it responsible for better interaction with the targeted enzymes and receptors. This review thoroughly gives a complete overview in current developments of benzimidazole derivatives as antimicrobial agents. In the present review, we have collected information from various published reports on benzimidazole derivatives as anti-bacterials by inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase, peptide deformylase, glucosamine-6-phosphate synthase, dihydrofolate reductase, enoyl acyl carrier protein reductase, dehydrosqualene synthase, dihydropteroate synthase, and peptidyl transferase, and as antifungal agents by inhibiting lanosterol 14α-demethylase. The current review explored the synthesis, structure-activity relationship (SAR), and mechanistic studies of benzimidazole derivatives as antimicrobial agents in the past 11 years (2015-2026). The aim is to assemble the current research reports and to give a generalized view to the medicinal chemists for the design of potent antimicrobials.
authors: Yadav G, Jain R, Kumar Y.

title: The bisbenzimide compound ridinilazole has antiviral activity against vaccinia and mpox viruses.
abstract: Mpox remains a significant global public health threat, highlighting the need for new antiviral therapies. Ridinilazole is a symmetric bisbenzimide developed for the treatment of Clostridium difficile infection that has recently been shown to inhibit human cytomegalovirus. Here, we investigated its antiviral activity against orthopoxviruses (OPXV). Ridinilazole potently inhibited vaccinia virus replication in primary human foreskin fibroblasts, with an IC50 of 21 nM and minimal cytotoxicity. Importantly, ridinilazole also reduced infectious monkeypox virus (the causative agent of mpox) yields in primary fibroblasts by more than 150-fold. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that ridinilazole did not affect early viral gene expression or viral DNA replication, but significantly reduced the expression of late viral genes at both transcript and protein levels. These findings identify ridinilazole as an effective inhibitor of OPXV replication and support its potential repurposing as a novel therapeutic for mpox.
authors: El-Jesr M, Eke L, Strang BL, Maluquer de Motes C, Sumner RP.

title: The Sweetpotato Black Rot Pathogen Ceratocystis fimbriata.
abstract: Black rot, caused by the soilborne fungus Ceratocystis fimbriata, is a major postharvest disease of sweetpotato (Ipomoea batatas) worldwide. Recent genomic and epidemiological studies have advanced our understanding of the interactions among host, pathogen and environment that influence disease development. Here, we review current knowledge of the pathogen's biology, epidemiology, virulence and management, and identify priorities for future research.TaxonomyClass: Sordariomycetes; Subclass: Hypocreomycetidae; Order: Microascales; Family: Ceratocystidaceae; Genus: Ceratocystis; Species: Ceratocystis fimbriata.Host rangeCeratocystis fimbriata sensu stricto is the sweetpotato-associated species. The broader host range historically attributed to C. fimbriata reflects the C. fimbriata sensu lato species complex, which included host-associated lineages now recognized as distinct Ceratocystis taxa.Disease symptomsLatent infections of storage roots evolve into firm, greenish-black cortical lesions bearing protruding perithecia; foliar wilting and stunting can occur in the field.Disease controlIntegrated measures, including pathogen-free slips, gentle harvesting, curing, cold storage, sanitation, fungicide dips and emerging microbial biological control strategies, provide partial control; host resistance remains an important breeding target.Useful websiteshttps://plantpathology.ces.ncsu.edu-diagnostic fact sheets; https://vegetables.tennessee.edu-Southeastern U.S. Vegetable Handbook.
authors: Avila K, Parada-Rojas CH, Mascarenhas J, Quesada-Ocampo LM.

title: Global Carriage of Antimicrobial Resistance Genes and Virulence Factors Among Physicians in Cirrhosis Care
abstract: Abstract  Cirrhosis patients are at high risk for drug-resistant infections, which may be transmitted between patients and healthcare providers. In this study, we used shotgun metagenomics to characterize the fecal microbiome of physicians in cirrhosis care (n = 55) across 9 countries. Our results indicate physicians from low- or middle-income countries carry greater antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) diversity corresponding to increased taxonomic richness. Physicians carried a low prevalence of clinically relevant ARGs or virulence factors (VFs), regardless of country of practice or patient exposure. Further comparison of fecal microbiomes between a subset of cirrhosis patients and physicians’ fecal samples collected from the same medical facility in the United States indicated that cirrhosis patients carried a far greater burden of high-risk VFs and ARGs. Collectively, this study provides evidence that most physicians in cirrhosis care are unlikely to be a primary reservoir of drug-resistant pathogens, although further surveillance of healthcare workers is warranted.
authors: Sommer AJ, Sikaroodi M, Fagan A, Davis BC, Khoruts A, Gillevet PM, Bajaj JS.

title: Identification of Non-Invasive Tumor-specific Biomarkers for Hepatocellular Carcinoma through Multi-transcriptomics Data Integration
abstract: Abstract  Background  Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most prevalent primary liver cancer and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Early detection is critical for improving patient outcomes; however, current surveillance modalities exhibit insufficient sensitivity for early-stage disease. While tissue biopsy remains the diagnostic gold standard, its invasive nature limits its routine application. This study seeks to identify non-invasive blood-based biomarkers for HCC through transcriptomic analysis. Methods  We analyzed transcriptomic datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), focusing on HCC tissues, plasma, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) and differential expression profiling were employed to identify candidate biomarkers, with key genes prioritized using STRING network analysis. Additionally, exosomal miRNA profiles were integrated to capture systemic regulatory signatures. Pathway enrichment analysis was conducted via Reactome 2024 to identify consistently dysregulated "tissue fundamental pathways" across liver datasets, which were then compared with blood-derived pathways. Candidate genes within these pathways were analyzed to define potential blood-based biomarker panels. Results  We identified 11 plasma-derived genes (e.g., RPS27A, CCND1, HSP90AB1, POLR2F, H2BC13, H2BC14, POLR2C, POLR2L, NPM1, FEN1, XRCC6), 6 PBMC-derived genes (e.g., JUN, POLR2H, CUL1, DICER1, AURKA, CCNA1), and 9 exosomal miRNAs (e.g., hsa-miR-671-5p, hsa-miR-184, hsa-miR-425-5p, hsa-miR-193a-5p, hsa-miR-103a-3p, hsa-miR-371a-5p, hsa-miR-874-3p, hsa-miR-663a, hsa-miR-18a-5p) significantly correlated with HCC. Many identified biomarkers align with established cancer hallmark pathways, underscoring their mechanistic relevance. Notably, several of these genes (e.g., JUN, POLR2C) and miRNAs (e.g., miR-874-3p) have not been previously reported in association with HCC, highlighting their potential as novel biomarker candidates. Conclusion  This integrative multi-transcriptomic analysis has unveiled novel, clinically relevant blood-based biomarkers for HCC, providing a promising foundation for sensitive, non-invasive detection strategies. Prospective validation in clinical cohorts is crucial for advancing the translation of these findings into early diagnostic protocols.
authors: Golshan Z, Fadakar H, Salehi S, Najafi Y, Akbari S, Momeni M, Gholaminejad A.

title: Blast percentage confounds transcriptome to drug-response associations in Beat AML: DHODH and sorafenib as a worked example
abstract: Abstract  Beat AML pairs ex vivo dose response for 125 compounds with transcriptomes from the same patients and is widely mined for markers of drug sensitivity. Those analyses adjust for general drug sensitivity, differentiation state, proliferation and genotype, but not for the blast content of the specimen, and a recent four-cohort study concluded that such an adjustment was not warranted. Across 12,000 gene-by-drug pairs, 35 per cent of the associations significant under the usual adjustment set lost significance when blast percentage was added, against 3.7 per cent gained. The pairs came from 800 genome-wide genes and the 15 most tested compounds, with the sample set fixed per drug so that nothing turns on a change in n. Blast percentage correlated with both transcript abundance and residual drug response. The comparable figures for tumor purity in solid tumors are about 14 and 11 per cent. A worked example shows the cost to a candidate marker. Under the usual model DHODH expression was the strongest correlate of sorafenib response among the genes tested, sorafenib ranked first of 125 drugs (rho − 0.259, FDR 6.5 × 10⁻⁷) and the empirical p against an expression-matched genome-wide null was below 0.001. With blast percentage added, rho fell to − 0.186 (n 414), sorafenib to rank four and the empirical p to 0.012. What survived was selective: five of the six other FLT3-directed compounds showed nothing. Blast percentage belongs in the adjustment set for these analyses. It is already in the diagnostic record and costs nothing to include.
authors: Ekmekci CG.

title: Integrative Evolutionary and Structural Analysis of GBA1 Provides Insights Into Mutation-Specific Effects Associated With Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: GBA1 encodes lysosomal acid β-glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase [GCase]), a key lysosomal enzyme and one of the most important genetic factors in Parkinson's disease (PD). Yet how different GBA1 variants influence PD-related molecular pathology remains incompletely understood. Here, we integrated phylogenetic, comparative sequence, structural, docking, and molecular dynamics analyses to identify evolutionarily constrained features of GBA1 that may influence its interaction with α-synuclein (SNCA) and thereby contribute to PD pathogenesis. Phylogenetic reconstruction indicated that GBA1 originated early in bilaterian evolution and was maintained as a single-copy gene in the sampled taxa, consistent with strong functional constraint. Sequence-based analyses across sarcopterygian lineages further supported pervasive purifying selection, especially within the TIM barrel catalytic domain. Comparative structural analyses highlighted a conformationally sensitive segment spanning Residues 379-389, which includes catalytic and neighboring residues and showed recurrent involvement in both mammalian evolution and PD-associated mutant proteins. Docking and molecular dynamics simulations of wild-type and mutant GBA1-SNCA complexes indicated that PD-associated substitutions can remodel hydrogen-bond networks and influence the conformational landscape of the GBA1-SNCA complex in a mutation-specific manner. Although no statistically significant differences in global structural or energetic properties were detected, individual variants exhibited distinct patterns of conformational deviation, flexibility, and interaction dynamics relative to wild type. In particular, Residues 387-389 emerged as part of a structurally responsive region linked to altered GBA1-SNCA association. Together, these findings highlight candidate structural determinants for future experimental studies of GBA1-associated neurodegeneration.
authors: Mustafa S, Abbasi AN, Mughal KA, Batool F, Malik MF, Khalid RR, Abbasi AA, Bao Y.

title: Improving Whole-Cell Taxifolin Production Performance Through Growth-coupled Directed Laboratory Evolution of Flavanone 3-hydroxylase in Escherichia coli.
abstract: The unique hydroxylation pattern confers dihydroflavonols with multiple beneficial functions to human health. The bioproduction of dihydroflavonols is strictly driven by flavanone 3-hydroxylase (F3H. This study focused on producing taxifolin, a typical high-value dihydroflavonol. We established taxifolin synthesis route by substituting the plant-derived flavonoid 3'-hydroxylase (F3'H) with prokaryote-derived two-component 4HPA3H system (HpaB and HpaC). Kinetics of the production indicated that F3H is the rate-limiting node. A directed library evolution (DLE) method was proposed to debottleneck this route. The tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle was rebuilt in Escherichia coli to couple DLE with cell growth. Very high transformation efficiency was achieved after medium optimization, thus facilitating the mutant library building. A library, theoretically containing 42360 mutants, was built and underwent a 4-day DLE. Among the randomly picked out mutants, SlF3Hv01 showed significantly accelerated catalytic rate. The whole-cell containing SlF3Hv01 produced 301.28% more taxifolin (93.82 mg/L) at 22 h and 29.73% more taxifolin (119.87 mg/L) at 46 h than that containing the wild type. This study built an E. coli chassis and developed an easy-to-manipulate DLE method to improve the taxifolin production. It can also be expanded to improve the performance of whole-cell catalyst or microbial cell factory containing other α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase.
authors: Xu J, Fan Y, Chang J, Guo Z, Dou W, Xu Y, Wang S, Zhang W, Wang W, Lv Y, Xu P.

title: Comparison of Wildtype and Recombinant Adeno-Associated Virus (AAV) Production Reveals Distinct Productivity and Content Ratio Profiles.
abstract: Recombinant adeno-associated virus is a leading viral vector for gene therapy. However, recombinant adeno-associated virus production systems have low titer and content ratio (ratio of genome-containing to total adeno-associated virus capsids), making it difficult to generate the large number of vector genomes required for clinical or commercial use. In contrast, wildtype adeno-associated virus achieves over ten-fold higher titer compared to recombinant adeno-associated virus and a content ratio of over 95% full. Despite the higher productivity of wildtype adeno-associated virus, the mechanisms behind its productivity remain poorly understood. In this study, we developed and characterized a novel wildtype adeno-associated virus production platform in suspension human embryonic kidney cells across varying multiplicities of infection of adeno-associated virus to adenovirus. The impact of cellular viral genome delivery mechanisms and the interplay between adeno-associated virus and its adenoviral helper were investigated by comparing infection-based systems with transfection-based and infection-transfection hybrid systems. Wildtype and hybrid infection systems had remarkably different host cell growth profiles and viral gene expression patterns, and achieved over a log-fold higher titers and 45% higher content ratios, reaching 8.1 × 1012 vector genomes/mL culture and 72.2% full, compared to recombinant transfection systems (1.63 × 1011 vector genomes/mL and 26.9% full).
authors: Alfieri S, Lee KH.

title: Skin-Protective Effects of Marinophyll, a Carotenoid From Marine Erythrobacter sp. SDW2.
abstract: BackgroundPrevious studies have highlighted that marine organisms, such as microalgae and marine bacteria, exhibit significantly higher and more sustainable biosynthetic yields of unique carotenoids compared to terrestrial sources. These advantages in production efficiency have sparked significant interest in developing materials derived from marine origins. Marinophyll, natural carotenoids extracted from marine sources, have demonstrated potential in managing oxidative stress and inflammation linked to various skin conditions.Materials and methodsHaCaT keratinocytes were treated with various concentrations of Marinophyll and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) to assess cell viability and intracellular ROS production. Antioxidant enzyme expression, including Nrf2, HO-1, and SOD2, was evaluated using RT-PCR and immunocytochemistry. The anti-inflammatory effects of Marinophyll were investigated in HaCaT cells treated with IL-4 and Poly I:C, and skin barrier repair was assessed in human skin explants using immunofluorescence staining. The skin explants were obtained from healthy adult donors (aged 43-57 years) undergoing elective breast reduction or abdominoplasty surgery, with informed consent and approval from the relevant ethics committee. All tissues were provided by Seoul National University Bundang Hospital.ResultsThe results showed that Marinophyll reduced intracellular ROS production in H2O2-exposed HaCaT cells. Additionally, Marinophyll significantly upregulated the mRNA and protein expression of Nrf2, HO-1, and SOD2 in HaCaT cells. Pretreatment with Marinophyll reduced the levels of inflammatory cytokines IL-1α and IL-1β induced by IL-4 and Poly I:C. In human skin explants, Marinophyll enhanced filaggrin expression, contributing to improved skin barrier function.ConclusionMarinophyll demonstrates significant antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and skin barrier-enhancing properties, making it a promising candidate for therapeutic applications in managing oxidative stress and inflammation-associated skin disorders.
journal: Skin research and technology : official journal of International Society for Bioengineering and the Skin (ISBS) [and] International Society for Digital Imaging of Skin (ISDIS) [and] International Society for Skin Imaging (ISSI)
authors: Kim H, Kyung S, Lee KE, Nho YH, Ryu J, Park M, Choi YJ, Kang S.

title: Comparison of Faecal Anaerobic Fungi of Cows and Goats Offered Similar Diet.
abstract: BackgroundAnaerobic fungi (AF) are key contributors to fibre degradation in ruminants, yet their host-associated patterns remain poorly understood. The aim of this study was to compare the diversity and composition of AF in faeces of goats and cows offered similar diet and to evaluate the influence of animal species on the gut mycobiome.MethodsA total of 15 female goats (Blond Adamellan) and 16 female cows (Brown Swiss) kept on an organic farm were fed pasture and hay. The fungal structure in faeces was examined by high-throughput sequencing using the D2 LSU region.ResultsAlpha diversity measurements revealed significantly lower species richness and evenness in goats compared to cows. Beta diversity analysis showed statistical dissimilarities and distinct community structures between the two ruminant species confirming host-specific clustering. Taxonomic composition differed significantly, cow samples were dominated by Caecomycetaceae and Neocallimastigaceae, particularly the genera Orpinomyces, Caecomyces and Cyllamyces. Goat samples were dominated by Anaeromyces, Caecomyces and according to relative abundance they formed two distinct clusters with highly similar fungal profile. Differential abundance analysis further highlighted the enrichment of Anaeromyces, unclassified genus within Caecomycetaceae, Feramyces and Pecoramyces in goats, whereas Caecomyces and Piromyces were more abundant in cows.ConclusionThese findings underscore the strong influence of host phylogeny on the faecal anaerobic fungal community.
authors: Mahayri TM, Serra A, Luthar J, Roubalová R, Moniello G, Mattiello S, Celozzi S, Mrázek J, Fliegerová KO.

title: Okgyeamides A-C: Cyclic Pentapeptides with Distinct Tyr-Trp C-C and C-N Cross-Links from a Cave-Derived Streptomyces sp.
abstract: Okgyeamides A-C (1-3), cyclic pentapeptides with a YPWIP sequence and distinct Tyr-Trp C-C and C-N cross-links, were isolated from cave-derived Streptomyces sp. SOG2-3 KCTC19252P. Their structures were characterized by NMR, HRESIMS, advanced Marfey's and GITC analyses, DP4+ calculations, and ECD analysis. Genome analysis identified a candidate precursor-P450 locus, okgA-okgB, consistent with a ribosomal origin. Okgyeamide A (1) showed ABTS radical-scavenging activity under the conditions tested.
authors: Kim RH, Park S, Park S, Cho YJ, Ban YH, Bae M.

title: Genetic Prioritization of BTN3A2 Reveals an Interferon-Responsive T-Cell Program in Dermatomyositis Through Single-Cell Mendelian Randomization and Multi-Omics Integration.
abstract: Dermatomyositis (DM) is a complex autoimmune disorder characterized by genetic susceptibility and dysregulated immune activation. However, the relationship between genetic variation and specific immune cell states remains poorly understood. We aimed to identify genetically supported immune-cell-specific molecular programs underlying DM and investigate their biological relevance. We integrated immune-cell-specific single-cell expression quantitative trait loci (sc-eQTLs) from the OneK1K cohort with DM genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics using two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR). Candidate genes were replicated using an independent sc-eQTL dataset and prioritized by Bayesian colocalization. Multi-tissue validation was performed using skeletal muscle transcriptomics, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC), and skin single-cell RNA sequencing, protein expression data, clinical phenotypes, virtual knockout analysis, and gain-of-function analyses of BTN3A2. We identified 204 immune cell-specific eGenes associated with DM and prioritized four high-confidence genes, including HLA-DRB1, HLA-C, Lnc-HLA-B-2, and BTN3A2. BTN3A2 showed robust colocalization across multiple CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell subsets and was further supported by muscle transcriptomic data. BTN3A2 was consistently upregulated in both DM muscle tissues and PBMCs and was broadly expressed across T-cell, NK-cell, and B-cell populations. BTN3A2+ T cells exhibited enhanced cytotoxic, activation, antigen-presentation, and interferon-responsive programs, which were reproduced in circulating PBMCs and lesional skin T cells. BTN3A2 expression was negatively correlated with MMT8 scores, while in silico knockout analysis implicated interferon-stimulated and antiviral pathways. Integrating cell-type-specific genetic evidence with multi-tissue immune profiling identified BTN3A2 as a genetically supported candidate associated with DM and an interferon-responsive T-cell state, providing novel insights for future mechanistic investigation.

authors: Jin J, Di Y, Zhang X, Sun S, Chen M, Guo Z, Wang H, Dai S.

title: Fungal ADP-ribosylation: an emerging signalling pathway in adaptation and virulence.
abstract: ADP-ribosylation is a posttranslational modification conserved across all domains of life and some viruses. While it is well established as a critical signalling mechanism in humans and is widely exploited as a therapeutic target in cancer, its roles in other kingdoms, particularly Fungi, remain poorly understood. Despite this, recent advances highlight the importance of fungal ADP-ribosylation in the regulation of key cellular maintenance processes such as DNA damage and oxidative stress responses, morphogenesis, growth, and proliferation. Here, we summarise our current understanding of fungal ADP-ribosylation and how it supports stress adaptation and virulence. While many aspects of fungal ADP-ribosylation remain unexplored, emerging discoveries underscore its importance in fungal biology and hint at a great potential for future antifungal therapies.
authors: Gosciniak JMM, Rack JGM.

title: Engineering Mosaic T7 Bacteriophages for Dual Peptide Display to Enable Cellular Targeting and Ligand-Directed Protein Capture.
abstract: Integrating molecular recognition, tracing, and interactome capture within a single nanoparticle could allow for probing, manipulation, and control of complex biological systems. Achieving such multifunctionality within a single well-defined nanostructure remains challenging. T7 bacteriophage-based biological nanoparticles provide a robust and genetically programmable scaffold; however, conventional T7 display systems typically accommodate only one exogenous peptide species per phage particle, limiting multifunctional and combinatorial applications. Here, we describe a mosaic phage platform that enables the simultaneous display of two peptides on separate T7 coat protein subunits. By combining genome-encoded and plasmid-driven expression of peptide-fused capsid proteins, the system provides a modular route for assembling multifunctional phage nanoparticles. We generated mosaic T7 phages co-presenting the neuropilin-1 (NRP-1)-binding peptide RPARPAR alongside either a HA-tag or a Twin-Strep (Tstrep) tag affinity handle. These engineered phages specifically target NRP-1-expressing cells and enable immunofluorescence visualization and pull-down of NRP-1 from complex lysates. Furthermore, a random peptide T7 phage library co-displaying the constant lung-homing peptide RPARPAR shows preferential pulmonary accumulation in vivo, demonstrating utility for combinatorial targeting and tissue-directed phage selection. Collectively, this dual-display approach expands phage display by enabling cell targeting, visualization, molecular interactome probing, and in vivo tissue homing within a single genetically encoded nanoparticle platform.
authors: Marchetti L, Põšnograjeva K, Lingasamy P, Pleiko K, Ilves I, Teesalu T.

title: Genome-wide scan and fine-mapping nominate ANAPC4 as a candidate modulator of Chinese Holstein heifer puberty timing.
abstract: Dairy fertility strongly affects farm sustainability because young cows must be raised for many months before they begin producing milk. Age at first service (AFS) is a key driver of reproductive efficiency and rearing costs in dairy systems. We analyzed Chinese Holstein heifers to dissect the genetic architecture of AFS and nominate functional candidates. After low-coverage whole-genome sequencing and genotype imputation, a total of 7 964 217 SNPs were retained for genome-wide association study (GWAS) and window-based variance partitioning. Among the seven traits evaluated-AFS, age at first calving (AFC), first-to-last insemination interval in heifers (IFLh), number of services per conception in heifers (NSh), conception rate in heifers (CRh), birth weight of heifers (BiWh), and gestation length in heifers (GLh)-AFS exhibited the highest heritability, with a moderate estimate of h 2=0.276. Three candidate regions prioritized by significance and additive variance jointly explained 0.91% of the genetic variance. On BTA6, the association peak spans ZCCHC4 and ANAPC4; notably, ANAPC4 contributes to estrogen-induced oocyte maturation. In blood, cis-expression quantitative trait loci mapping and co-localization analysis provided strong evidence that the GWAS locus colocalizes with ANAPC4 expression, with the posterior probability of shared causality (PP.H 4) reaching 0.921. SuSiE fine-mapping pinpointed the association to a ~30 kb region comprising a 20 variant credible set that segregates into two high linkage disequilibrium haplotypes (H0 and H1), with the H1H1 genotype linked to elevated ANAPC4 expression and a ~2.1 day reduction in AFS. Motif analyses suggested allele-specific TF-binding differences between haplotypes consistent with regulatory effects. Taken together, these findings pinpoint a fine-mapped regulatory haplotype that upregulates ANAPC4 expression and is associated with earlier AFS, providing actionable markers for genomic selection to advance heifer puberty timing and improve farm profitability.
authors: Pan CL, Ma LG, Cao XS, Wang QY, Wang LL, Wang J, Wang A, Li R, Wang XH, Ma Y, Liu GL, Zhu K, Lv XZ, Zhang ZB, Jiang Y.

title: PIH1D2 Loss-of-Function Directs Ciliary and Cell Cycle Defects Resulting in Left Isomerism With or Without Biliary Atresia.
abstract: Background & aimsLaterality disorders are rare congenital conditions caused by disruption of left-right embryonic patterning, often associated with ciliary dysfunction. Despite the identification of numerous causative genes, the molecular basis remains unresolved in many patients. We aimed to identify the genetic cause of left isomerism heterotaxy in two unrelated patients, and investigate the functional consequences of the implicated gene.MethodsGenome sequencing was performed in both patients. Candidate variants were validated by RNA and protein analyses in patient-derived fibroblasts. To study the functional consequences, we conducted RNA-seq, cell cycle assays (flow cytometry, EdU incorporation, Ki-67 staining), rescue experiments with the wild-type gene, and primary ciliogenesis studies.ResultsBoth patients harboured biallelic loss-of-function variants in PIH1D2, a gene not previously associated with human disease. Transcript analyses confirmed aberrant splicing, and immunofluorescence staining revealed loss of PIH1D2 expression in Patient 1's primary fibroblasts. RNA-seq demonstrated dysregulation of pathways related to cell cycle regulation and developmental signalling. Patient fibroblasts showed impaired cell cycle re-entry from G0 following serum starvation and reduced S-phase progression. Wild type PIH1D2 overexpression partially rescued these defects. Furthermore, patient cells exhibited significantly reduced primary ciliogenesis compared to controls.ConclusionsOur findings establish PIH1D2 as a novel disease gene for left isomerism heterotaxy, with biliary atresia observed in one of the patients. Loss of PIH1D2 impairs ciliogenesis and cell cycle progression, providing a mechanistic link between ciliary defects and abnormal left-right patterning. These results expand the spectrum of cilia-related laterality disorders and identify PIH1D2 as a critical regulator of human development.
journal: Liver international : official journal of the International Association for the Study of the Liver
authors: Kurolap A, Chai Gadot C, Shalata A, Eshach Adiv O, Amir Y, Lando BL, Stehling F, Hershkovitz T, Osman K, Habib C, Mintz H, Steinberg R, Hochberg A, Hamiel U, Mory A, Marom D, von Hardenberg S, Singer A, Auber B, Baris Feldman H.

title: Molecular Epidemiology of Varicella-Zoster Virus Among Patients From Two French Tertiary Care Hospitals: Differential Distribution of Clades According to Demographic Criteria.
abstract: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) nomenclature currently recognizes seven established clades (designated 1-6 and 9). A geographical segregation of VZV clades has been shown, with Clades 1, 3, and 6 predominating in Europe, Americas, and Australia, Clade 2 in Japan and East-Asia, and Clades 4 and 5 in Asia and Africa. This distribution of VZV clades is dependent on the importation of viral strains, because of immigration and travels, and the implementation of varicella vaccine. The surveillance of VZV epidemiology is therefore necessary. VZV genotyping strategies rely on evaluating a panel of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) across the different open reading frames (ORFs) of the viral genome. We described retrospectively the VZV clade distribution among 339 patients in Pitié-Salpêtrière (Paris) and Bordeaux University hospitals from 2018 to 2023. Clade 1 was detected in 27.1%, Clade 3 in 37.2%, Clade 5 in 31.9%, and other clades in 3.8% of the patients. The distribution of clades did not differ according to sex, immune status of the patients, and clinical presentation of VZV infection. However, patients infected with Clade 5 were statistically younger than those infected with other clades, especially European-born patients. This epidemiological characteristic of VZV Clade 5 may have multifactorial etiology, including the combination of viral, host, and environmental factors.
authors: Fernandez J, Cheminet M, Mazarguil L, Gay M, Fauchois A, Tumiotto C, Burrel S, Boutolleau D.

title: Carbon Catabolite Repression and Quorum Sensing Interplay in Marine Fish Spoilage: An Integrated Metabolic Perspective.
abstract: Bacterial quorum sensing (QS) systems pose a significant challenge to the preservation of protein-rich marine fish, as coordinated spoilage behaviors such as biofilm formation and volatile amine production are activated under specific metabolic conditions. Despite well-characterized spoilage organisms, the regulatory logic linking metabolic state to QS-driven collective behaviors remains incompletely understood. Thus, the goals of this review were to synthesize current knowledge on how carbon catabolite repression (CCR) gates QS-dependent spoilage programs in marine fish; examine the molecular mechanisms by which global regulators (cAMP-CRP, Crc/CrcZ, CcpA, (p)ppGpp-RpoS) interface with QS circuitry; and describe how this mechanistic understanding can be translated into anti-virulence preservation strategies that mislead metabolic sensors or disrupt quorum communication. In particular, this review focuses on the ecological manifestations of CCR-QS crosstalk in key spoilage genera and the latest progress in integrating metabolic modulators with QS inhibitors within stimuli-responsive smart packaging. Finally, current challenges limiting the systematic application of this metabolic perspective in the fish industry are discussed, including unresolved molecular interfaces in nonmodel spoilage organisms and methodological bottlenecks in spatially resolved analysis. It is important to note that while the proposed CCR-QS framework is strongly supported by direct mechanistic evidence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, its molecular details remain largely unvalidated in most major marine fish specific spoilage organisms (SSOs). Nevertheless, this framework offers a testable conceptual scaffold that integrates nutrient-driven growth kinetics with QS-mediated social behavior, providing a mechanistic basis for designing next-generation precision preservation strategies.
journal: Comprehensive reviews in food science and food safety
authors: Li X, Zeng Y, Liu Z, Jia F.

title: Investigation of Torque Teno Virus Loads as a Marker of Immunosuppression in Pediatric Chronic Renal Failure: A Pilot Study.
abstract: BackgroundTorque Teno Virus (TTV), family Anelloviridae, is a small, non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus that has not been linked with any specific human illness but nevertheless constitutes a major component of the human virome. An association between TTV loads and the immune status of the host with reference to other viral infections, immunosuppression therapy, and acute rejection is reported in adult and pediatric kidney transplant recipients. We sought to investigate the feasibility of TTV as a surrogate marker of the degree of immunosuppression in pediatric kidney transplant patients.Methods185 children attending the Nephrology clinic in Children's Health Ireland at Temple Street were studied over a four-year period from September 2019 until November 2023, ranging from 0 to 17 years of age. Patients were enrolled from pre-transplant undergoing kidney replacement therapy (n = 12), from post-transplant (n = 124) groups, and from patients with chronic renal failure (n = 20) (without kidney replacement therapy), all of which were compared to controls (n = 35). TTV loads were quantified using a standardized TTV R-gene kit.ResultsTTV loads were significantly higher compared to controls from 3 months post-transplantation onward (p ConclusionThese findings suggest that both immunosuppressive status and gender-related factors contribute to TTV kinetics after transplantation and should be considered when interpreting TTV as a biomarker of immune function. Larger studies are required to confirm our findings.
authors: Kelly E, Awan A, Wildes D, De Gascun CF, Drew RJ, Heggenstaller A, Riordan M, Hassan J.

title: Revolutionizing the tomato cultivation: advances and frontiers in virus-resistant tomato breeding.
abstract: Plant viruses are major pathogens that significantly reduce the quality and yield of tomato crops. The most influential viruses belong to the genera Crinivirus, Begomovirus, Tobamovirus, and Potyvirus. Tomato breeders have successfully incorporated virus-resistance genes, such as Ty, Sw, Tm, and Pot 1, from wild germplasms into cultivated varieties. However, the challenge remains that most resistance genes confer only qualitative resistance, making them vulnerable to new viruses, recombination, and mixed infections. To our knowledge, this review is the first to systematically compare the synergy and complementarity among three antiviral breeding strategies-conventional R-gene pyramiding (e.g. Ty, Sw, Tm), RNA interference (RNAi)-based transgenics, and CRISPR/Cas genome editing-in tomato. We also innovatively incorporate the emerging genus Amalgavirus into the antiviral framework and propose targeted countermeasures against its escape mechanisms, including synthetic NLR decoys and Cas13-mediated transcriptional degradation. Using the three breeding methodologies, we concluded by outlining the difficulties and offering recommendations for future improvements in tomato antiviral breeding.
authors: Khaskheli MA, Raza A, Jueping S, Hassan MA, Janiad S, Sabir S, Khaskheli RA, Khan MA, Zeb A, Hayyat Q, Wang Y.

title: Formulation-specific effects of commercial proteases combined with cleaning-relevant chemicals on Escherichia coli K-12 biofilms.
abstract: AimsThis study evaluated whether commercial proteases with distinct acidic and neutral-to-alkaline compatibility profiles could modify the effects of cleaning- and sanitation-relevant chemicals on Escherichia coli K-12 biofilms.Methods and resultsPepsin, acid-stable Aspergillus niger protease, native Bacillus subtilis protease, and an alkaline protease for detergent applications (APD) were characterized for apparent pH and temperature optima and stability, then tested alone and with sodium hypochlorite, sodium hydroxide, phosphoric acid, nitric acid, acetic acid, lactic acid, and EDTA. Planktonic minimum inhibitory concentration, crystal violet biomass, and TTC-reduction assays were used. Proteases alone did not completely inhibit planktonic growth at 0.1%, and protease addition produced only limited MIC decreases. Selected cotreatments improved inhibition of biofilm formation, particularly at submaximal chemical concentrations, but generally did not decrease residual CV-stainable biomass in preformed biofilms. Selected cotreatments also reduced TTC-reduction signals without proportional decreases in CV-stainable biomass.ConclusionsProtease-assisted effects were formulation-, biofilm-stage-, and assay-dependent. These findings support formulation-specific screening of protease-chemical combinations based on the intended biofilm-control stage, compatibility with the cleaning chemistry, and performance relative to the corresponding chemical treatment.
authors: Park N, Anjum N, Rodriguez Monge V, Bastarrachea LJ, Brandao J.

title: From SELEX to sequencing: uncovering enriched aptamers with next-generation sequencing and bioinformatics.
abstract: MotivationThe combinatorial chemistry process called systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) enables the selection of aptamers against different targets. The integration of next-generation sequencing (NGS) into SELEX workflows represents a powerful strategy to enhance the identification and prioritization of target-binding aptamers. In this study, we present an optimized computational approach for the NGS-based analysis of enriched aptamer pools generated through SELEX. It encompasses sequencing library preparation, sequence data preprocessing, clustering, multiple sequence alignment, phylogenetic analysis, and secondary structure prediction.ResultsTo identify target-specific aptamers, two comparative analysis strategies were implemented. In the first strategy, sequences detected in the negative selection pool were removed from the positive selection pool to eliminate nonspecific binders, resulting in six distinct sequence clusters. In the second approach, all sequences were retained, and cluster distributions were compared between the positive and negative selection pools, identifying seven clusters in the positive and six in the negative pool. Phylogenetic relationships and structural predictions enabled the selection of promising candidates, which were prioritized based on secondary structure, sequence abundance, and genetic distance from nonspecific binders. Binding specificity was assessed through dot blot assays, confirming that the selected aptamers exhibited strong specific binding to the target protein. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the NGS-guided workflow for aptamer discovery and highlight its value in streamlining candidate selection for downstream functional validation.Availability and implementationThe data underlying this article will be shared on reasonable request to the corresponding author.
authors: Girbas MG, Müller J, Schlensak C, Avci-Adali M.
