title: Transcriptomic response of the head kidney and gill of lumpfish (Cyclopterus lumpus) to Moritella viscosa infection.
abstract: Moritella viscosa, the causative agent of winter ulcer disease, infects several cold-water marine fish species, but its pathogenesis and associated host responses in lumpfish (Cyclopterus lumpus) remain poorly understood. Here, we established a systemic infection model and characterized disease progression, tissue pathology, bacterial recovery, and transcriptional responses following intraperitoneal challenge with M. viscosa J311. Cumulative mortality reached 66.67%, 48.39%, and 30.51% following challenge with 3.1 × 108, 3.1 × 107, and 3.1 × 106 CFU dose-1, respectively, with an estimated LD50 of 8.1 × 107 CFU dose-1. Infection resulted in ulcerative lesions, systemic bacterial recovery, and histopathological alterations in multiple tissues. Transcriptomic analysis of head kidney and gill at 10 days post-infection following challenge with 3.1 × 106 CFU dose-1 identified 731 and 217 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), respectively, with only 41 shared DEGs. The head kidney exhibited broad regulation of acute-phase and inflammatory responses, iron homeostasis, protease-associated processes, transport, and metabolism. In contrast, the gill response involved complement regulation, inflammatory and leukocyte-trafficking processes, and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. Greater bacterial recovery from the gill despite a broader transcriptional response in the head kidney demonstrated distinct tissue-specific responses during systemic infection. Gill mmp9 induction, downregulation of collagen-related transcripts, enrichment of fibrillar collagen-associated processes, and lamellar damage further supported substantial ECM remodeling. These findings provide new insight into tissue-specific responses and pathogenesis during M. viscosa infection in lumpfish.
authors: Cao T, Gnanagobal H, Vasquez I, Chakraborty S, Hossain A, Paramanathan T, Boyce D, Santander J.

title: A pectic polysaccharide from Lonicera japonica alleviates DNCB-induced atopic dermatitis-like inflammation associated with gut microbial and metabolic alterations and reduced cutaneous JAK2/STAT3 activation and Th17 responses.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceLonicera japonica Thunb. (Jin Yin Hua) is a traditional medicinal herb widely used in East Asia for inflammatory disorders and is commonly included in herbal prescriptions for atopic dermatitis (AD). WLJP-025p, a homogeneous pectic polysaccharide isolated from Lonicera japonica, has shown anti-inflammatory and anti-AD potential, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear.Aim of the studyThis study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic effect of WLJP-025p on DNCB-induced AD-like dermatitis in mice and to investigate associated changes in epidermal barrier dysfunction, Th17/IL-17 A-associated inflammation, JAK2/STAT3 signaling, and gut microbial and metabolic profiles.Materials and methodsAn AD-like mouse model was established in BALB/c mice by repeated application of 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene (DNCB). WLJP-025p was orally administered at 30 or 60 mg/kg during the challenge phase, and topical dexamethasone was used as a reference anti-inflammatory control. Disease severity was assessed by skin appearance, dermatitis score, ear thickness, serum biomarkers, and histopathological examination. Skin barrier and inflammation-related proteins were evaluated by immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, Western blotting, and flow cytometry. Colonic injury was examined by hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Alcian blue-periodic acid-Schiff (AB-PAS) staining. Fecal metagenomic and metabolomic analyses were conducted to characterize gut microbial and metabolic changes.ResultsWLJP-025p significantly alleviated DNCB-induced AD-like lesions, as evidenced by reduced erythema, scaling, excoriation, ear swelling, dermatitis scores, epidermal hyperplasia, and mast cell infiltration. WLJP-025p decreased serum IgE, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-17 A levels. It restored filaggrin (FLG) expression and suppressed thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) expression in skin lesions, indicating improved epidermal barrier function. WLJP-025p also reduced the proportions of splenic CD3+CD4+IL-17 A+ T cells and suppressed cutaneous IL-17 A-related inflammatory mediators, including CCR6 and CCL20. These changes were accompanied by decreased phosphorylation of JAK2 and STAT3 in lesional skin. In addition, WLJP-025p alleviated DNCB-associated colonic injury and was accompanied by changes in gut microbial and metabolic profiles.ConclusionWLJP-025p exerted protective effects against DNCB-induced AD-like dermatitis. Treatment was accompanied by restoration of epidermal barrier-related markers, reduced JAK2/STAT3 activation and Th17/IL-17 A-associated inflammatory signaling, improved gut barrier integrity, and alterations in gut microbial and fecal metabolite profiles. These findings indicate that oral WLJP-025p treatment is associated with concurrent intestinal and cutaneous changes in this AD-like model.
authors: Jin M, Hu Y, Ding M, Cheng J, Liu M, Liu X, Bai X, Fan X.

title: Serum torque teno virus levels are strongly associated with stages of non-advanced HIV-1 infection at diagnosis.
abstract: ObjectivesTorque teno virus (TTV) is a ubiquitous component of the human blood virome and its replication is tightly controlled by the host immune system. TTV levels have therefore been proposed as a surrogate marker of immune competence. In people with HIV-1 infection (PWH), higher TTV levels have been associated with advanced infection. We investigated TTV levels in individuals diagnosed with non-advanced HIV-1 infection. TTV viral load (VL) was compared between primary and chronic infection to assess whether it could reflect immune dysfunction not captured par CD4+ T-cell counts.MethodsWe conducted a monocentric cohort study including adults newly diagnosed with HIV-1 infection. All participants were antiretroviral therapy-naïve with HIV-1 viremia. Individuals with advanced HIV-1 infection were excluded. HIV-1 infection stage was determined using immunoblot-based laboratory staging according to Fiebig classification. TTV DNA was quantified in serum samples using a qPCR assay. Associations with HIV-1 infection stage were assessed using logistic regression analysis.ResultsA total of 126 PWH were included. Primary HIV-1 infection accounted for 42.1% of diagnoses and chronic infection for 57.9%. Overall, TTV DNA was detected in 61.1% of participants. TTV detection was more frequent in chronic infection than in primary infection (82.2% vs 32.1%, p+ T-cell counts. In multivariable analysis, HIV-1 VL and TTV VL were independently associated with HIV-1 infection stage. High TTV VL (≥4 log copies/mL) was strongly associated with chronic infection.ConclusionsIn individuals diagnosed with non-advanced HIV-1 infection, TTV levels differed markedly between primary and chronic infection despite similar CD4+ T-cell counts. These findings suggest that TTV VL could reflect alterations in immune competence not captured by conventional immunological markers and may represent an additional biomarker to assess immune status in PWH.
journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
authors: Alidjinou EK, Coulon P, Tetart M, Guigon A, Viget N, Meybeck A, Hober D, Robineau O.

title: Life-history strategies of soil microorganisms and their interactions with plant diversity: a review.
abstract: Faced with the global challenges of biodiversity loss and soil function degradation across ecosystems, deciphering the synergistic mechanisms between soil microorganisms and plant diversity is essential for supporting ecological restoration and sustainable development. This study reviews the evolutionary progression of microbial life-history strategies, from the r-K dichotomy to the CSR/CSO and YAS frameworks, and onward to multidimensional modern frameworks, revealing their central role in driving microbial ecological adaptation. Focusing on the evolution and drivers of microbial life-history strategies, this work synthesizes plant-microbe interactions in grassland ecosystems, which are globally extensive, highly responsive to management and climate, and central to restoration practice. Evidence from forests and croplands is used only where it clarifies a general mechanism or its boundary of applicability. It further addresses these relationships within grassland ecosystems, elucidating the coevolutionary dynamics between plants and microorganisms and the divergent microbial life-history strategies shaped by dominant plant functional groups including grasses and legumes. This review synthesizes current evidence linking microbial life-history strategies with plant diversity and functional-group composition in grasslands. It discusses how plant inputs, soil resource availability, environmental stress, and management practices may shape microbial traits and plant-microbe interactions. By distinguishing experimentally supported mechanisms from observational associations and conceptual hypotheses, this review identifies potential applications in grassland restoration and highlights the methodological limitations that must be addressed before microbial life-history strategies can be used as operational indicators of restoration outcomes.
authors: Rundong C, Jie S, Jiamin W, Mengyao Z, Haitao Z, Xuebing Y, Shengnan S.

title: Portable micro-spectrometric LAMP platform for rapid semi-quantitative pathogen detection in food safety.
abstract: This study reports the development of an integrated, portable analytical platform combining a micro-spectrometer with loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for the rapid, on-site detection of Vibrio vulnificus. The system, controlled by LinkIt 7697 microprocessors, achieves precise thermal regulation within ±0.32 °C at 64 °C and features a customized optical path for real-time fluorescence monitoring. Utilizing calcein as a metal-sensitive fluorescent indicator, the device captures the spectral shift and intensity enhancement resulting from the displacement of manganese ions during DNA synthesis. Unlike traditional photodiode-based sensors, the integrated micro-spectrometer enables full-spectrum analysis at 1-min intervals, providing superior discrimination between true positive signals and background autofluorescence. Experimental results demonstrate successful detection of Vibrio vulnificus genomic fragments within 40 min, achieving a detection limit of 0.1 pg/μL, with data automatically synchronized to a cloud database for remote epidemiological surveillance. The combination of high-fidelity spectral acquisition and isothermal chemistry offers a robust, cost-effective solution for food safety monitoring and point-of-care testing in resource-limited environments.
authors: Liao PK, Kijamnajsuk P, Lubis SA, Wardani AK, Chen JJ.

title: Seed Morphogenesis: Genetic Architecture, Regulatory Mechanisms, and Breeding Opportunities.
abstract: Seed morphogenesis determines seed size, shape, tissue organization, and developmental patterning, which influence crop yield and quality. This review compiles the genetic architecture, regulatory mechanisms, and breeding strategies for seed morphogenesis in major crops. Functionally validated genes and QTLs are cataloged with clear inclusion criteria to distinguish direct evidence for the causal gene from candidate genes identified by GWAS and linkage mapping. Developmental and environmental signals converge through hormonal crosstalk and epigenetic control, including Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) mediated histone modifications, DNA methylation, chromatin remodeling, and non-coding RNAs to shape seed morphogenesis. Six central regulatory modules govern seed morphogenesis: endosperm proliferation and cellularization, seed coat development, embryo patterning, hormonal integration, cell cycle and expansion control, and ncRNAs. Conserved and species-specific pathways are compared across Arabidopsis, cereals, and legumes, demonstrating that embryo patterning (LAFL, WOX, HD-ZIP III) is highly conserved, while endosperm development (MINI3/IKU2, AGL62) and seed coat development (SHP1/SHP2, STK, MYB5) are divergent, highlighting the need for species-specific frameworks. Modern technological advances such as high-throughput phenotyping, multi-omics, and CRISPR/Cas9 enable module-level functional validation. Breeding programs can deploy validated module genes through MAS, GS, and genome editing. Despite these advances, phenotyping, G × E interactions, pleiotropy, and the functional validation gap in underutilized crops remain unresolved. These gaps can be overcome by shifting from single-gene level manipulation to network-level engineering, integrating multi-omics and systems biology to translate module-level discoveries into improved seed morphogenesis.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Waqas M, Nadeem M, Shahid MQ, Daowu H, Shopu H, Xiongming D.

title: Sex-stratified genome-wide association analyses reveal sexually dimorphic genetic architecture of backfat thickness in pigs.
abstract: Sex influences the genetic architecture of complex traits, but its role in regulating backfat thickness (BFT) in pigs remains unclear. Here, we performed sex-combined and sex-stratified genome-wide association analyses in 2920 Duroc pigs (1460 females and 1460 entire males) using 6,320,080 imputed variants. Compared with the conventional sex-adjusted GWAS, sex-stratified analyses identified sex-specific loci, including a female-driven association region locus on SSC13 (~15.4 Mb) and a male-specific locus on SSC11 (~7.6 Mb), and revealed distinct allele-frequency and effect-size distributions between sexes. Candidate genes underlying these loci included RBMS3, MEDAG, TEX26, HSPH1 and B3GLCT. Moreover, sex-stratified genomic prediction achieved higher prediction accuracy, increasing prediction correlations from 0.652 to 0.723 in males and 0.757 in females, with cross-validated correlations increasing from 0.545 to 0.596 and 0.629, respectively. Collectively, these findings reveal the genetic basis of sexual dimorphism in BFT and provide new insights into the genetic dissection of dimorphic traits and livestock breeding.
authors: Ling C, Tian Y, Xiao H, Huang Y, Zhao S, Xiao S, Zhang Z.

title: Study on the mechanism of a Benzamide compound exerting anti - Staphylococcus aureus effect by inhibiting the purine metabolism pathway.
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is a major human pathogen responsible for a wide range of infections, and there remains a critical need for new antibacterial agents. In this study, we identified a bioactive benzamide compound b18, which exhibited anti- S. aureus activity with a MIC of 50 μg/mL. Importantly, b18 showed no cytotoxicity toward the normal human liver cell line HL7702, indicating a favorable safety profile. Scanning electron microscopy analysis revealed that b18 treatment caused pronounced morphological damage to the bacterial cells. To explore the underlying mechanism, we performed transcriptome sequencing combined with PPI analysis and KEGG pathway enrichment. Integrated with molecular docking simulations, these results suggest that b18 may potentially target GuaA and interfere with the purine metabolism pathway. Our findings highlight b18 as a promising lead compound, with GuaA proposed as a candidate target within purine biosynthesis, offering a potential strategy for combating S. aureus infections. Further biochemical validation is required to verify these predictions.
authors: Yan G, Liu G, Zhou R, Cao Z, Wang Y, Yan S, Xing Y, Wang T, Liu M, Gao Y, Lv H, Feng G, Jia R, Zhou M.

title: Clinical and immunological correlates of CXCR4 coreceptor use in people with HIV-1 receiving antiretroviral therapy in the Netherlands: a multicentre cohort study.
abstract: BackgroundCXCR4-using (X4) viruses are associated with faster disease progression in untreated HIV-1 infection, although their clinical, virological, and immunological correlates during suppressive antiretroviral therapy are not well characterised. We aimed to assess the associations between X4 coreceptor use and clinical outcomes, HIV persistence, and immunological profiles in people with HIV-1 receiving suppressive antiretroviral therapy.MethodsIn this multicentre cohort study, asymptomatic adults with HIV receiving suppressive antiretroviral therapy were enrolled from four HIV treatment centres in the Netherlands between Oct 16, 2019, and Oct 27, 2021 and followed up for 2 years. Clinical data were obtained from structured questionnaires and electronic health records. HIV-1 coreceptor use was predicted from triplicate env sequencing with Geno2pheno, and participants were classified as having CCR5-using (R5), X4, or mixed virus. HIV-1 subtype was assigned using env and pol sequences. Total and intact HIV DNA in CD4+ T cells were quantified using multiplex digital PCR. Plasma proteomics, bulk peripheral blood mononuclear cell transcriptomics, and high-dimensional flow cytometry were used for systems-level profiling. Associations between predicted coreceptor use and clinical outcomes, HIV-reservoir measures, and immunological profiles were assessed using adjusted regression models and discovery and validation cohorts.FindingsCoreceptor use was assigned in 1724 participants; 1222 had R5 virus, 336 had X4 virus, and 166 had mixed classifications. Primary clinical analyses included 1494 participants, of whom 1172 were in the R5 group and 322 were in the X4 group. Compared with the R5 group, the X4 group had a lower CD4+ nadir, a higher prevalence of previous AIDS-defining events, poorer immunological recovery, and more comorbidities, particularly type 2 diabetes and non-affective psychiatric disorders. The median total HIV DNA was 1051 copies per 106 CD4+ T cells in the X4 group versus 599 copies per 106 CD4+ T cells in the R5 group, and the median intact HIV DNA was 23 copies per 106 CD4+ T cells versus 15 copies per 106 CD4+ T cells. No significant differences were observed in plasma inflammatory proteins. Participants in the X4 group had higher frequencies of activated CD4+ T cells and PD-1+ regulatory T cells, and transcriptomic analyses identified downregulation of two validated transcripts involved in transcriptional repression and lipid hydrolysis.InterpretationAmong people with HIV receiving suppressive antiretroviral therapy, infection with X4 virus was associated with markers of more advanced previous HIV disease, impaired immune recovery, larger HIV reservoirs, and selected comorbidities despite viral suppression. Coreceptor use might therefore help to contextualise clinical, virological, and immunological heterogeneity in treated HIV-1 infection and could be relevant to future HIV cure studies.FundingViiV Healthcare.
authors: Mehta K, Otten T, Rios-Vazquez V, Delporte M, Verschoore M, Blomme EE, Rokx C, Stalenhoef J, Berrevoets MAH, van Lunzen J, Netea MG, Gerlo S, van der Ven AJ, Vandekerckhove L, Rutsaert S.

title: KRAS<sup>G12D</sup>-targeted therapy sensitivity depends on interferon signaling activation in pancreatic cancer.
abstract: KRASG12D is a predominant driver in pancreatic cancer, yet the basis of intrinsic resistance to KRASG12D-targeted therapy remains poorly defined. Integrated genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics profiling across 242 patient-derived organoids (PDOs) and matched tumor tissues reveals a KRASG12D-mutant subset intrinsically resistant to KRASG12D-targeted therapeutics, characterized by marked downregulation of innate immune signaling pathways. Functional validation demonstrates that suppressing interferon signaling in sensitive models induces resistance, whereas activation of interferon signaling, particularly interferon beta (IFN-β), increases sensitivity in resistant models. Combining IFN-β with KRAS inhibitors (MRTX1133, HRS-4642, and RMC-6236) exhibits synergistic antitumor effects in intrinsically resistant pancreatic cancer. Mechanistically, sustained MYC activity is associated with attenuated sensitivity to KRAS inhibition and correlates with repressed interferon signaling, suggesting a potential role in promoting intrinsic resistance. These findings identify interferon signaling as a candidate determinant of KRAS-targeted therapy response and support interferon-based combinations as a potential strategy for intrinsically resistant pancreatic cancer.
authors: Zhang Y, Tang S, Zhang Y, Liu J, Shi X, Li Y, Li Y, Wang H, Zhong C, Sun M, Li W, Zhu Y, Yang W, Zhao Y, Guo S, Wu Z, Wang L, Jin G, Gao D.

title: In vitro and In silico Inhibitory Investigations of elastase release in fMLF/CB-Induced human neutrophils of ısolated naphtopyrones from marine fungi Aspergillus Niger.
abstract: In this study, the secondary metabolites produced by Aspergillus niger associated with the tunicate Microcosmus vulgaris collected from the Aegean Sea (Turkiye) were explored. Five known naphtopyrones, rubrofusarin B (1), flavasperone (2), aurasperone B (3), fonsecinone D (4), aurasperone A (7), and two known disaccharides, α,α-trehalose (5) and β,β-trehalose (6) were isolated. Compounds were elucidated using 1D and 2D NMR spectroscopy and by comparing coupling constants and optical rotation values with literature data. Compounds (1-4) were evaluated for the first time in vitro anti-inflammatory activity via human neutrophil elastase (HNE) release induced by fMLF/CB. The most potent compound was aurasperone B (10 µM) with 20.33% inhibition, following fonsecinone D (10 µM) with 11.83% inhibition, compared to the standard genistein (3 µM) with 31.57% inhibition. Molecular docking of compounds (1-4 and 7) against HNE (PDB ID: 1H1B) indicated efficient enzyme inhibition by interactions with key residues of the active site. Aurasperone B (3), which exhibits the second highest binding affinity, and fonsecinone D (4) are discovered potential candidates for further biological and pharmacological studies to validate their therapeutic potential.
authors: Torun Z, Ebada SS, Osman HM, Korinek M, Konuklugil B.

title: Inferring the multi-host fitness landscape of endive necrotic mosaic virus from cross-inoculation experiments.
abstract: Fitness landscapes offer a compact representation of adaptation, yet are rarely inferred from sparse multi-environment data. We present a Bayesian approach to infer an effective multi-host phenotypic fitness landscape from cross-inoculation assays by linking successful infection probabilities to Fisher's geometrical model and to an explicit decomposition of establishment routes. The model estimates (i) the distance matrix among host-specific phenotypic optima, (ii) target-host permissiveness through the widths of fitness peaks, (iii) target-specific differences in the efficiency with which phenotypic suitability translates into successful infection, and (iv) the conditional probabilities that successful infections are attributed to direct establishment, rescue from standing variation in the source inoculum, or de novo rescue in the target host. We apply the approach to an experimental evolution dataset for endive necrotic mosaic virus evolved on five Asteraceae hosts and challenged in a full cross-inoculation design. The inferred landscape can be visualized as a phenotypic map of the host community, revealing pronounced heterogeneity in target-host permissiveness and a geometry broadly concordant with host phylogeny. By grounding assay-derived distances in an explicit mechanistic model, the approach provides a parsimonious representation of multi-host constraints that can be used to discuss establishment barriers and potential springboard hosts in heterogeneous communities. More broadly, it offers a general method for inferring effective fitness landscapes from sparse multi-environment data.
authors: Roques L, Papaïx J, Martin G, Forien R, Lenormand T, Soubeyrand S, Berthier K, Moury B.

title: Yra2 regulates proteolysis of Cse4 to prevent its mislocalization to non-centromeric regions for chromosomal stability in budding yeast.
abstract: Restricting the centromere-specific histone H3 variant Cse4 (CENP-A in human) to centromeric chromatin ensures faithful chromosome segregation. Mislocalization of overexpressed Cse4/CENP-A to non-centromeric regions contributes to chromosomal instability (CIN), an important hallmark of many cancers. Hence, defining mechanisms that prevent mislocalization of Cse4 is clinically significant. Here we report a role for YRA2 (Yeast RNA Annealing Protein 2) in ubiquitin mediated proteolysis of Cse4 to prevent its mislocalization for chromosomal stability. YRA2 was identified in a genome-wide screen for gene deletions that exhibit synthetic dosage lethality (SDL) upon overexpression of CSE4 (GALCSE4). We determined that yra2Δ strains exhibit increased Cse4 stability, enriched Cse4 chromatin association, reduced Cse4 ubiquitination, Cse4 mislocalization, and CIN. Defects in interaction of E3 ubiquitin ligase Psh1 with Cse4 contributes to stability of Cse4 in yra2Δ strains. Consistent with these results, overexpression of PSH1 suppresses GALCSE4 SDL in yra2Δ strain. Yra2 mediated proteolysis of Cse4 is separable from its RNA related functions as GALCSE4 SDL was not observed in yra2F96A,F108A strain with mutations in Yra2 RNA recognition motif. Furthermore, poly(A)+ RNA export mutants in YRA1 (yra1-2) and MEX67 (mex67-5), that interact with Yra2, do not exhibit GALCSE4 SDL and defects in RNA export are not observed in yra2Δ cells. We determined that evolutionarily conserved C-terminal ChTOP domain of Yra2 with an intact N-terminal RNA binding domain exhibits GALCSE4 SDL and defects in Cse4 proteolysis. In summary, we have defined a role for Yra2 in preventing mislocalization of Cse4 by facilitating its proteolysis for chromosomal stability.
authors: Mishra PK, Ohkuni K, Raymond P, Hicks EM, Costanzo M, Boone C, Zenklusen DR, Basrai MA.

title: Genomic dissection of environmental responsiveness and cross-environment productivity in fenugreek.
abstract: Dissecting the genetic basis of genotype × environment interaction (G × E) is important for breeding crops with stable or responsive performance across production environments. Using previously published seed-yield data from 107 Egyptian fenugreek accessions evaluated under two contrasting field environments, we investigated whether yield potential and environmental responsiveness share a common genetic basis. Seed yield per plant was measured in Giza (SYP_G; reference environment) and Wadi El-Natrun (SYP_W; contrasting environment). Nine derived indices were calculated to characterize environmental responsiveness, productivity, and stability: relative performance index (RPI), yield plasticity index (YPI), stress tolerance index (STI), log response ratio (LRR), mean productivity (MP), harmonic mean (HM), tolerance index (TOL), stress susceptibility index (SSI), and AMMI stability value (ASV). The near-zero correlation between SYP_G and SYP_W (r = 0.107) indicated substantial genotype reranking across environments, while several response indices were closely related to SYP_W and therefore predominantly reflected environment-dependent yield expression. Phenotypic analyses also identified contrasting performance strategies, ranging from highly responsive accessions, such as G15 (RPI = 3.629), to highly stable accessions, such as G41 (YPI = 0.001). These phenotypes were integrated with 38,142 SNPs using univariate association-mapping approaches. In addition, SYP_G and SYP_W were subjected to multivariate association-mapping. Association mapping identified one genome-wide-significant SNP for STI and several suggestive loci showed concordant associations across mapping methods. Within the current panel, marker coverage, and significance thresholds, most adaptation-index associations did not overlap previously reported yield loci; however, dDocent_Contig_39939_66, previously associated with seed yield in this panel, also showed cross-method suggestive associations with RPI and TOL. Comparative genomic analysis of three legume reference genomes supported two gene-linked candidate loci associated with STI: a cation/H⁺ antiporter and an importin subunit beta-1. The same analysis classified two of the strongest statistical signals, including the sole genome-wide-significant locus, as repetitive or transposable-element sequences rather than single-copy genes. These findings demonstrate that statistical association strength does not necessarily establish a coding-gene basis for loci identified using reference-free ddRAD markers. Within the current population size and marker coverage, environmental responsiveness and productivity appeared partially distinct but biologically connected components of environment-dependent yield performance. The results provide a genomic and phenotypic framework for prioritizing fenugreek germplasm for further evaluation while emphasizing the need for independent-population, multi-season, and functional validation of the identified candidate loci.
authors: Aljabri M, Abd El-Wahab MMH, Dobeie AM, El-Soda M.

title: Repurposing Etravirine as a PlcA-Targeting inhibitor to block autophagic escape of Listeria monocytogenes.
abstract: The rapid rise of antibiotic resistance underscores the urgent need for anti-infective strategies that circumvent classical bactericidal approaches. Host-directed antivirulence therapies, which target host defense pathways or pathogen virulence rather than essential viability, may reduce selection pressure and delay resistance, but potent small-molecule examples remain limited. Here we identified a drug repurposing candidate against the intracellular pathogen Listeria monocytogenes (L. monocytogenes) by targeting its phosphatidylinositol-specific phospholipase C PlcA, a key virulence factor involved in autophagy escape. Using a compound-microarray high-throughput binding platform, we discovered that the approved HIV non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor Etravirine directly bound PlcA and inhibited its phosphatidylinositol-hydrolyzing activity without affecting bacterial growth or plcA transcription. In infected cells, Etravirine restored PtdIns3P levels, increased MAP1LC3/LC3 (microtubule associated protein 1 light chain 3) recruitment and autophagic flux, promoted lysosomal delivery, and reduced infection-induced cellular damage. Etravirine also enhanced basal autophagic flux and induced an autophagy-associated transcriptional program. These effects were reproduced in RAW264.7 macrophages and were attenuated by 3-MA. In mouse infection models, Etravirine reduced bacterial burdens and inflammatory pathology and improved survival. Biophysical, hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS), docking, mutational, and preliminary analogue analyses supported a putative Etravirine-binding region near the PlcA myo-inositol-binding pocket. Together, these findings establish Etravirine as a PlcA-targeting antivirulence candidate that also strengthens host autophagy-associated restriction of L. monocytogenes.
authors: Li G, Sheng Q, Liu J, Yang H, Dou X, Zhong Y, Wang Z, Zhang J, Deng Y, Xu L, Wang J, Deng X, He C, Wang Q, Qiu J.

title: Harnessing engineered laccase and functional carrier materials for efficient dye degradation: From mechanism to application.
abstract: Laccases are copper-containing oxidases that have been widely investigated for the decolorization and degradation of synthetic dyes, including azo, anthraquinone, triphenylmethane, indigo and thiazine dyes. However, their application in dye-containing wastewater remains constrained by enzyme instability under complex effluent conditions, limited oxidation of some recalcitrant or high-redox-potential dyes, mediator dependence, and poor recovery and reuse of free laccase. This review discusses recent progress in laccase-catalyzed dye degradation from a mechanism-to-engineering perspective, linking dye-structure-dependent degradation pathways with laccase discovery, recombinant expression, protein engineering and immobilization strategies. Particular attention is given to comparative evidence across dye classes, fungal and bacterial laccases, engineered variants generated through rational design, directed evolution and semi-rational mutagenesis, and immobilized laccase systems based on nanomaterials, biopolymers, magnetic carriers and porous supports. In addition, the review distinguishes laboratory model dye systems from simulated and real wastewater applications, highlighting the need for more cautious interpretation of decolorization efficiency, degradation evidence and process feasibility. Finally, we outline future prospects for laccase applications in dye degradation, including the mining of novel laccases from extreme environments, artificial intelligence-assisted laccase design, and developing new nano-scale carrier materials, which will be essential for enhancing laccase performance and broadening its application scope.
authors: Zhang Y, Yu M, Zhang Y, Chen C, Yang X, Kang Y, Wu S, Liu Y, Zhou Z, Qian L.

title: Concurrent detection of low-pathogenic H9N2 avian influenza virus and Salmonella spp. in a poorly performing commercial layer flock in Bangladesh.
abstract: Avian influenza virus (AIV) remains a major threat to poultry production in Bangladesh, where both highly pathogenic (HPAIV) and low-pathogenic (LPAIV) subtypes circulate. Although HPAIV is typically associated with high mortality, H9N2 LPAIV often causes mild clinical disease but has been associated with reduced egg production and economic losses in commercial poultry. This study describes the concurrent detection of H9N2 and Salmonella spp. in a 33-week-old Hy-Line Brown commercial layer flock in Moulvibazar, Bangladesh, in which a marked decline in laying performance was observed. A total of 50 birds were sampled for virological and bacteriological investigations. Oropharyngeal swabs were tested by real-time reverse transcription PCR (rRT-PCR) targeting the influenza A virus matrix (M) gene, followed by H9- and N2-specific assays. Cloacal swabs were cultured using selective enrichment and plating methods, and presumptive Salmonella spp. isolates were confirmed by PCR targeting the invA gene. Among the sampled birds, concurrent H9N2 and Salmonella spp. were detected in 11/50, while no birds were positive for H9N2 alone; Salmonella spp. alone was detected in 3/50 birds. The investigated flock exhibited markedly reduced egg production, remaining at 0% through 25 weeks of age and reaching a maximum of only 71.72% at 46 weeks, compared with the breed-standard value of 88%, while cumulative mortality reached 23.4% by 46 weeks, substantially exceeding the breed standard. These findings document the concurrent detection of H9N2 and Salmonella spp. and poor laying performance in the investigated flock. Given the single-flock design, absence of an H9N2-only comparison group and a contemporaneous healthy control flock, and incomplete assessment of other infectious and farm-level factors, the findings do not establish a causal relationship or determine whether Salmonella spp. contributed to the observed production losses. Further controlled and longitudinal studies involving multiple flocks and appropriate comparison groups are warranted to clarify the respective contributions of H9N2 and bacterial coinfections to production losses in commercial layer flocks.
authors: Kayesh MEH, Akimul MK, Hosen M, Anower AKMM, Karim MR.

title: Dissecting cell-type-specific genetic associations between colorectal cancer liability and thrombotic risk in peripheral blood immune cells.
abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a major complication of colorectal cancer (CRC), but whether CRC-associated thrombotic susceptibility includes cell-specific inherited regulatory components in peripheral blood remains unclear. To investigate associations between CRC genetic liability and VTE-related outcomes within peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) regulatory contexts. We integrated CRC GWAS, FinnGen VTE-related outcomes, and TenK10K PBMC single-cell eQTL data across 28 immune cell types using cell-stratified Mendelian randomization (csMR). Prioritized signals were further examined in single-cell RNA-seq datasets and bulk transcriptomes. Conventional MR showed no clear evidence that CRC liability increased VTE, DVT, or PE risk, and LD Score regression detected no significant genome-wide genetic correlation. In contrast, csMR identified nominal, cell-context-dependent associations. B intermediate cells were prioritized across VTE (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.03-1.32), DVT (OR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.08-1.57), and PE (OR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.07-1.49), while CD14 + monocytes and CD4 + central memory T cells received additional support from downstream single-cell analyses. Gene-level analyses prioritized LAMA5, LIMA1, and TRIM28 in these respective cell contexts. In bulk blood, RPS21 showed consistent disease-associated expression patterns and discriminated VTE patients from healthy controls in an external dataset (AUC, 0.865; 95% CI, 0.800-0.923). These findings suggest that genetic overlap between CRC liability and thrombotic phenotypes may be localized to selected PBMC regulatory contexts rather than broadly detectable genome-wide. Among the prioritized signals, B intermediate cells showed the most consistent csMR associations across VTE, DVT, and PE. The cell-gene pairs, together with RPS21, warrant independent genetic, functional, and prospective validation as candidates for studying peripheral immune regulation and blood-based markers of CRC-associated thrombosis.
authors: Ying J, Ling T, Fang Z, Zhang C, Bao Y, Tang J.

title: GhMYB63 activates the IDA‑like peptide gene GhIDL1 to promote boll abscission in cotton.
abstract: Key messageGhMYB63-induced GhIDL1 promotes cotton boll abscission through a conserved IDA/IDL-like peptide pathway involving EPIP-dependent activity and candidate GhHAE/GhHSL2 receptor kinases. Premature boll abscission severely limits cotton yield, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the role of the IDA-like peptide-encoding gene GhIDL1 and its upstream regulator during boll abscission in upland cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.). RNA-seq analysis revealed that GhIDL1 expression was induced in the abscission zone (AZ) following stigma removal. Virus-induced gene silencing of GhIDL1 increased the force required for boll detachment, delayed abscission, enhanced boll retention, and reduced the expression of cell wall-remodeling genes (GhPG, GhCEL1). Conversely, ectopic expression of GhIDL1 accelerated floral organ abscission in Arabidopsis and complemented the abscission-defective ida-2 mutant. Deletion analysis further showed that the N-terminal signal peptide and conserved C-terminal bioactive motif were required for functional complementation. Yeast one-hybrid, electrophoretic mobility shift, and dual-luciferase assays demonstrated that the R2R3‑MYB transcription factor GhMYB63 binds to the GhIDL1 promoter and enhances its activity. In cotton, silencing GhMYB63 reduced GhIDL1 transcript abundance, and silencing GhMYB63 alone or together with GhIDL1 decreased boll abscission. Structural modeling, together with simultaneous silencing of GhIDL1, GhHAE, and GhHSL2, implicated GhHAE and GhHSL2 as candidate receptors in GhIDL1-associated signaling. These findings support a GhMYB63-GhIDL1 regulatory model in cotton boll abscission, providing potential targets for genetic improvement of cotton yield.
authors: Jia M, Geng C, Han S, Xue L, Li Y, Zhao X, Cheng X, Lv S, Liu L, Jiang J.

title: The development of a digital PCR approach for the detection of fecal contamination using Bacteroidales and vertebrate mtDNA probes.
abstract: Fecal contamination of food such as fruits and vegetables remains a major public health concern. The United States (US) Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that 48 million people get sick from foodborne illness every year. The quality of farm produce is affected by pathogens from feces or environmental factors that might affect their growth, harvest, and distribution. Rapid and reliable detection methods are therefore essential for identifying contamination sources and improving food safety monitoring. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based methods provide a sensitive and specific approach for detecting bacterial DNA in food samples, including fecal-associated microbial markers such as Bacteroides or other host-associated targets. The goal of this study was to develop a method using digital PCR to detect fecal (Bacteroides) contamination on agricultural produce (strawberries) and to compare these results with standard real-time PCR-based methods. Fecal samples from cattle, rodents, poultry, and other animals were collected, and bacterial DNA (Bacteroides) from these samples was collected and analyzed, and the resultant procedures could detect femtogram levels of bacteria in a sample. To determine the origin of the fecal contamination, mtDNA primers and probes were next developed for multiple vertebrate species using either single or multiplex PCR. These assays were developed, optimized, and validated to detect concentrations as low as 10 copies/µL mtDNA of sample, making these procedures useful in determining the origin or source of fecal contamination of produce.
authors: Etim S, Raha D, Sanchez AN, Ghemrawi M, Duncan G, McCord B.

title: Pleiotropic functions of HogA, a Hog1‑like paralog of SakA, in Aspergillus niger RAF106.
abstract: The high-osmolarity glycerol (HOG) mitogen-activated protein kinase Hog1 is a conserved core regulator governing stress responses in various fungi. However, the comprehensive physiological functions of Hog1-type MAPKs remain poorly characterized in Aspergillus niger, a fungus widely applied in industrial fermentation and frequently responsible for post-harvest food spoilage. This study identified HogA, a Hog1-like paralog of SakA, from Pu-erh tea-derived A. niger RAF106 and characterized its functions through multiple phenotypic and transcriptional analyses. Deletion of hogA did not affect vegetative mycelial growth but drastically suppressed conidiophore differentiation and conidial production. The ΔhogA mutant displayed defective cell wall ultrastructure and greater hypersensitivity to Congo red, H2O2, and NaCl than the wild-type and complemented strains. In addition, loss of hogA significantly attenuated the fruit spoilage capability of A. niger on apples. Moreover, deletion of hogA led to altered enzyme activities: moderately reduced activities of pectinase, xylanase, and β-xylosidase, and elevated activities of α-amylase, glucoamylase, and β-glucosidase. These phenotypic changes coincided with altered expression of phenotype-related genes and decreased antioxidant enzyme activities. Collectively, this study confirms that HogA acts as a pleiotropic regulator orchestrating fungal development, multi-stress adaptation, carbohydrate hydrolase activities, and fruit decay, providing a promising genetic target for engineering industrial A. niger with high enzyme yield and robust stress resistance.
authors: Liu XB, Wang J, Wang YS, Xie LY, Liu T, Song XB, Fang X, Shi QS, Xie XB, Zhou G.

title: Bi-Allelic PRKCZ Loss-of-Function Variants and Adult-Onset Retinitis Pigmentosa.
abstract: ImportanceInherited retinal diseases are genetically heterogeneous disorders, with retinitis pigmentosa (RP) representing the most common form; although more than 90 genes have been implicated, many RP cases remain molecularly unsolved.ObjectivesTo describe an adult-onset RP phenotype associated with loss-of-function variants in PRKCZ, profile the clinical features of this disorder, and investigate the underlying disease mechanism.Design, setting, and participantsIn this case series study, genomic analyses were performed in individuals with unsolved childhood- and adult-onset retinal disease recruited through international research and diagnostic programs. Detailed clinical characterization was conducted in affected individuals. In vitro analyses were carried out to validate the genomic findings using primary and transduced cell-based experimental approaches. Genomic analyses were performed from October 2023 to December 2025; functional studies were carried out from January 2024 to May 2026.ExposureBi-allelic likely pathogenic variants in a novel RP disease gene candidate, PRKCZ.Main outcomes and measuresThe primary outcome was genetic, clinical, and functional effects of bi-allelic PRKCZ inactivating variants associated with adult-onset RP. A detailed ophthalmologic assessment was conducted to characterize the clinical phenotype. Functional analyses in patient-derived fibroblasts and transduced cell lines were performed to validate the consequence of disruptive variants on PRKCZ transcript processing and PKCζ function.ResultsAmong approximately 4500 individuals with unsolved childhood- and adult-onset retinal disease tested, 6 bi-allelic PRKCZ variants were identified in 13 affected individuals from 10 unrelated families, 5 of which were predicted to lead to loss of function (frameshift, nonsense, or splice-altering variants). Six of 13 affected individuals (46%) were female. Most cases carried a recurrent frameshift variant (c.139_140del; p.Met47Valfs*19). All variants selectively affected the long PRKCZ transcript encoding the N-terminal Phox and Bem1 (PB1) domain. Clinically, PRKCZ-associated RP showed adult onset (18-49 years), progressive night blindness, peripheral visual field constriction, and eventual central vision loss. Four individuals exhibited adult-onset sensorineural hearing loss. Functional studies in patient-derived fibroblasts demonstrated selective loss of the long PRKCZ isoform, impaired ciliogenesis, and altered mitochondrial organization, which were validated in stable PRKCZ knockdown cell lines. Structural modeling and coimmunoprecipitation assays indicated that the missense variant was associated with the disruption of PB1 domain-mediated protein-protein interactions.Conclusions and relevanceIn this case series study, bi-allelic inactivating variants in PRKCZ were associated with adult-onset RP with an isoform-specific mechanism involving the long retinal-enriched transcript. These findings expand the genetic spectrum of RP and highlight PRKCZ as a potentially clinically relevant gene implicated in adult-onset retinal degeneration.

title: Ca2+-Driven Nanodomain Enrichment And Plasma Membrane Proteome Remodelling Govern Plant Response To Bacterial Outer Membrane Vesicles.
abstract: Phytopathogenic outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) can elicit protective immune responses and can be utilised for crop protection. Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo), a Gram-negative bacterium that causes Bacterial Blight of rice, releases OMVs. However, the role of Xoo-OMVs in the Xoo-rice interaction remains unexplored. We investigated the early signalling events underlying the plant's response to Xoo-OMV to gain insight into plant-pathogen interactions. We observed that Xoo-OMVs trigger a rapid, unique Ca2+ signal in rice that is essential for evoking an immune response. By imaging and proteomic analysis of the rice plasma membrane (PM), we found that this Ca2+ signal is required for Xoo-OMV-induced nanodomain enrichment and aggregation of defence response-associated proteins in rice PM. The specific protein assembly in the PM helps the plant defend itself against Xoo. In the absence of the early Ca2+ signal, rice cannot respond effectively to Xoo-OMVs, resulting in a compromised immune response. Collectively, our study shows that rice responds to Xoo-OMVs via Ca2+-signal-induced nanodomain assembly and protein reorganisation at the PM, preparing the plant for an imminent pathogen invasion.
authors: Mondal I, Das H, Behera S.

title: High-quality draft genome sequences of two soil-isolated Micrococcales: Cellulomonas iranensis DSM 14785T and Oerskovia jenensis DSM 46000T.
abstract: We report high-quality draft genome sequences from two bacterial type strains from the order Micrococcales that were originally isolated from Eurasian soils. The Cellulomonas iranensis DSM 14785T genome is 3.98 Mbp with 3,630 predicted genes, while the Oerskovia jenensis DSM 46000T genome is 4.45 Mbp with 4,031 predicted genes.
authors: Hludzinski A, Vail S, Pukal R, Ritter S, Ivanova NN, Seshadri R, Escobar M.

title: Finding the Goldilocks zone: modulating glycoprotein cleavage and fusogenicity optimizes the efficacy of a candidate Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus vaccine.
abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is the etiologic agent of a highly lethal hemorrhagic disease spread by ticks throughout Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, for which no FDA- or EMA-approved vaccines or therapeutics exist. A lack of fundamental understanding of the molecular mechanisms of CCHFV assembly, egress, and entry has challenged the development of medical countermeasures. Herein, we investigated the molecular basis of replicative efficacy of a highly protective recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus vaccine bearing the CCHFV glycoprotein complex (rVSV-GPC). We identified key amino acid residues associated with rVSV-GPC adaptation and showed that these could be transferred to a divergent CCHFV genetic background to afford a new vaccine vector with enhanced protective efficacy against heterologous viral challenge. We show that the key amino acid substitutions enhance rVSV-GPC infectivity via multiple distinct biochemical and cell-biological mechanisms. Our mechanistic studies provide the first evidence that SKI-1 cleavage at the GP38-Gn boundary modulates the pH threshold of CCHFV membrane fusion and points to a critical role for virion-associated GP38 and GP38-Gn interaction in regulating the pre-fusion conformation of the glycoprotein spike during virion biogenesis, egress, and cell entry.ImportanceHerein, we investigated the molecular basis of replicative efficacy of a highly protective rVSV-GPC vaccine candidate. We identified key amino acid residues associated with rVSV-GPC adaptation, including two novel residues, and showed that a minimal set of these could be transferred to a divergent CCHFV genetic background to afford a new vaccine vector with enhanced protective efficacy against heterologous viral challenge. Our work provides important new information to refine VSV-vectored CCHFV vaccines, to assess which critical GPC adaptations might benefit other vaccine modalities such as subunit and RNA, and to aid in the development of vaccines against divergent orthonairoviruses. Our findings also shed new light on the basic biology of CCHFV. We show that the key amino acid substitutions enhance rVSV-GPC infectivity via multiple, distinct biochemical and cell-biological mechanisms. Most notably, we provide the first evidence that SKI-1 cleavage at the GP38-Gn boundary modulates the pH threshold of viral membrane fusion. This points to an unanticipated role for virion-associated GP38 and GP38-Gn interaction in protecting and regulating the pre-fusion conformation of GPC during CCHFV biogenesis, egress, and cell entry.
authors: Berrigan J, Monticelli SR, Spealman P, Cohen CA, Batchelor TG, Wang A, McFadden E, Bakken RR, Slough MM, Wirchnianski AS, Mittler E, Cross RW, Geisbert TW, Erasmus JH, Hawman DW, McLellan JS, Herbert AS, Chandran K.

title: Spatial Gene Expression in Fungi: mRNA Localization, Condensates, and Beyond.
abstract: Polarized growth and cellular asymmetry are broadly conserved properties of fungal life, from transient bud-site selection in unicellular yeasts to sustained hyphal extension in filamentous and coenocytic species. While vesicle trafficking, cytoskeletal organization, and cell-wall remodeling are well-established contributors to these processes, the role of mRNA localization is only beginning to be fully appreciated. In this review, we examine how the spatial regulation of mRNAs and their translation contributes to fungal polarity, morphogenesis, and environmental adaptation. We discuss current knowledge around three interconnected layers contributing to mRNA localization: active cytoskeletal transport-actin-based in compact yeasts and microtubule-based in long hyphae; partitioning into biomolecular condensates such as P-bodies and Whi3-mRNA assemblies; and cytoplasmic-scale architectural features including bulk flow, nuclear positioning, and nuclear heterogeneity that become increasingly important in multinucleate and coenocytic systems such as arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Together, these mechanisms establish spatial gene expression as an integral component of fungal polarity, with implications for fungal development, host-pathogen interactions, and ecological adaptation, and for our broader understanding of polarized growth in eukaryotic cell organization.
authors: Otterdijk SV, Wang Z, Arends R, Tutucci E.

title: Marine microbial-derived cytotoxic alkaloids: a comprehensive review of structures, bioactivities, chemical syntheses, and biosynthetic advances (2000-2025).
abstract: The distinctive physicochemical conditions of marine habitats foster a diverse range of microbial resources. Microbially-derived alkaloidal metabolites, characterised by novel structures and potent bioactivities, have become increasingly important as sources of lead compounds for anticancer drug development. This review systematically classifies cytotoxic alkaloids obtained from marine microorganisms, outlines the structural traits of various alkaloid groups, evaluates their antiproliferative activity against various human cancer cell lines along with potential mechanisms, and summarises progress in chemical synthesis and biosynthetic investigations. Finally, it discusses the application prospects and existing challenges of these alkaloids in anticancer drug development, thus offering a data reference for exploring and utilising marine microbial-derived anticancer drug candidates.
authors: He X, Xu T.

title: Structures of MyD88 and its oncogenic mutant reveal DNA binding with implications for cytosolic DNA sensing
abstract: MyD88 is a universal adaptor that connects to Toll-like receptors and interleukin-1 receptors through its Toll/IL-1R homology (TIR) domain and activates inflammatory signaling via its death domain (DD). However, how MyD88  TIR serves as the platform for these functions and if it has additional functions remain unclear. Here, we report cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of MyD88  TIR and its cancer-specific mutant L252P (previously L265P) mainly in ring and spiral forms, respectively. Both assemblies are formed by antiparallel double-filaments, using canonical TIR interfaces within each strand but unique surfaces between the strands, and position MyD88  DD at the same sides of the assemblies for self-oligomerization and pathway activation. Surprisingly, these WT or L252P filaments are bound to dsDNA using the concave sides of the rings and the spirals. In vitro assays and cellular studies establish that MyD88 directly binds dsDNA and promotes inflammatory cytokine expression, particularly pro-IL-1β, following dsDNA transfection or viral infection. Notably, these responses are unaffected by deficiency of UNC93B1, the essential chaperone required for trafficking endosomal nucleic acid-sensing TLRs. Structure-guide MyD88 mutant that disrupts dsDNA binding specifically compromises dsDNA-induced transcriptional program while maintaining TLR signaling. RNA-seq further reveals that MyD88 plays a crucial role in inducing gene expression upon dsDNA sensing and that about half of cGAS-dependent genes are also MyD88-dependent. Together, our structural, biochemical and genetic data support the findings that MyD88 directly engages with cytosolic dsDNA and cooperates with cGAS to promote the full innate immune transcriptional response.
authors: Fontana P, Tufan AB, Günther P, Goldberg E, Dörfler S, Vora SM, Schirokauer L, Paulo JA, Oh HS, Gygi SP, Knipe DM, Wu H.

title: A Synthetic Virology Platform for Rapid Prototyping of Influenza A Virus mutants
abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) remains a significant public health threat, with the need for effective vaccines and antiviral therapies remaining a high priority.  In vitro testing is paramount in studying novel IAV viruses and their immunogenicity. To address this need, we developed a synthetic virology approach to rapidly prototype and test IAV mutants with altered antigenic sites. By strategically inserting restriction sites within an ambisense plasmid, we generated a tool where we can seamlessly replace either 1) the full hemagglutinin (HA), 2) the HA globular head domain to generate head/stalk chimeras or 3) the five canonical antigenic sites. The cloning inserts can be computationally designed and artificially synthesized, enabling rescue of synthetic Influenza A viruses. Using this platform we rescued IAV H1N1, H3N2 & H5N1, and went on to prototype their respective antigenic site mutants & chimeric IAVs using viral genome sequence alone. This platform could be useful for generating vaccine seed strains or to study anti-viral immunity.  Abstract Figure  Figure 0. Abstract Figure
authors: Murti JR, Schön K, Angeletti D.

title: Integrated Genomic and Immune Profiling Reveals PIK3CA-Mutant HPV16-Positive Cervical Cancer as a Clinically Aggressive and Immunologically Distinct Subtype in Patients from Eastern India
abstract: Background  HPV16-driven cervical cancer (CaCx) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among Indian women. Identifying population-specific genomic and immune determinants may improve therapeutic strategies. Methods  We performed whole-exome sequencing on 49 HPV16-positive cervical tumors and matched blood samples. Available RNA-seq data from 29 out of 49 tumors were integrated, to identify recurrent mutations, altered pathways, and immune microenvironment features. Results  We identified 6,462 somatic mutations enriched in cancer-related pathways, particularly PI3K-Akt signaling.  PIK3CA was the most recurrently mutated gene (42%), significantly higher frequency (p Conclusion  PIK3CA mutations define a molecularly aggressive, immunologically distinct subtype of HPV16-positive CaCx in Indian patients, underscoring their potential for targeted therapeutic interventions.
authors: Ghosh A, Ghosh A, Sinha A, Mathai S, Bhaumik J, Mukhopadhyay A, Majumder S, Maitra A, Biswas NK, Mondal K, Majumder PP, Sengupta S.

title: Chemical profiling and antioxidant potential of the ethanolic extract of the Odontotermes formosanus fungus comb: an integrated LC–MS/MS and computational study
abstract: Abstract    Fungus combs of fungus-growing termites are complex symbiotic matrices formed through termite feeding and digestion of plant substrates, followed by continuous transformation by symbiotic  Termitomyces  fungi and associated microorganisms. Although extracts from the fungus combs of some fungus-growing termite species have been reported to exhibit antioxidant activity, the chemical composition and biological properties of the fungus comb of  Odontotermes formosanus  remain poorly characterised. In the present study, untargeted liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) was used to characterise the ethanolic extract of the  O. formosanus  fungus comb (OFCE), and its antioxidant activity was evaluated using 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical-scavenging and ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assays. As an exploratory extension, ageing-related database targets were used as a biological context, and target prediction, network analysis, molecular docking, and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations were integrated to prioritise selected putative annotations and predicted ligand–target relationships. Azelaic acid and N-acetyltryptophan were among the candidates prioritised for further evaluation. Under the computational models and simulation conditions used, the two epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)–ligand complexes exhibited conformational compatibility and maintained relatively stable conformational states during portions of the simulations. Collectively, these findings indicate that the  O. formosanus  –  Termitomyces  fungus-comb system contains a chemically diverse pool of ethanol-extractable small molecules accompanied by measurable antioxidant activity, thereby providing candidate leads for subsequent structural confirmation, source attribution, quantitative analysis, and activity validation.
authors: Liu J, Kang R, Dong J, Wang W, Li Z, Huang J, Fan Q, Ming L, Liu H, Jiang W, Dong Z.

title: Divergent climatic, geographic, and taxonomic associations of human gut resistome burden and composition across 34 countries
abstract: Abstract    Background  Understanding how antimicrobial resistance (AMR) relates to gut microbial community structure is essential for interpreting the human gut resistome in its ecological context.  Methodology  We investigated the relationships between resistance burden, resistance-class composition, and microbial taxonomic profiles in 98 healthy young adults from 34 countries, recruited among first-year medical students. Country-level pooled shotgun metagenomics was integrated with individual-level 16S rRNA gene sequencing.  Results  At the country-pool level, clustering of resistance-class profiles identified three clusters (RCPC1-RCPC3). RCPC1 combined the highest AMR burden with greater relative abundance of taxa reported as potentially pathogenic, genotoxic, or aerotolerant. This cluster also showed a higher representation of putative short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, indicating that elevated resistance burden can coexist with taxa associated with beneficial metabolic functions. At the individual level, clustering of 16S-based predicted metabolic pathways identified four clusters (PMC1-PMC4) sharing a broadly conserved functional background. Country-level analyses further distinguished factors associated with resistance abundance from those associated with resistance-class composition. Mean annual temperature showed an exploratory positive association with AMR abundance, corresponding to approximately 22% higher abundance per 10°C increase after adjustment for continental grouping and pool size. PM2.5 exposure showed a threshold-like pattern across WHO-defined tiers. Neither environmental variable was associated with resistance-class composition, whereas countries assigned to the Asian group showed enrichment of macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin resistance.  Conclusion  Resistance burden and composition capture complementary features of the gut resistome and should be interpreted alongside microbial community structure. Higher resistance burden can coexist with putatively beneficial taxa, highlighting the limits of single-metric assessments and the potential value of integrated resistome-taxonomic profiling for One Health surveillance.
authors: Mikolás M, Dávid P, Szilágyi-Rácz A, Szilágyi-Tolnai E, Fauszt P, Alsayahien A, Abousharabia I, Gashi N, Szabó Z, Pham T, Bíró S, Stündl L, Remenyik J, Paholcsek M.

title: Allelic tuning of PtoRLK609 kinase activity shapes adaptive xylem remodeling in Populus tomentosa.
abstract: Climate change poses unprecedented challenges to perennial trees. However, the molecular mechanisms by which trees achieve long-term adaptive xylem remodeling remain poorly understood. Here, using transcriptomics and population genomics in 302 Populus tomentosa accessions sampled from three climatically distinct subpopulations, we identified receptor-like kinases (RLKs) associated with climate-related variation in xylem lignification. Among 49 candidates, the wall-associated kinase PtoRLK609 showed among the strongest signatures of population differentiation, a pattern consistent with climate-associated selection. Two major PtoRLK609 haplotypes, defined by four linked missense variants, showed marked geographic differentiation, with PtoRLK609Hap2 reaching fixation or near-fixation in northern populations that experience drier and cooler climates, and was associated with elevated lignin content. PtoRLK609 phosphorylates the transcription factor PtoERF105 at Ser171, which promotes its nuclear accumulation and enhances activation of the lignin biosynthesis genes PtoLAC4 and PtoCCoAOMT1, as well as the vessel development regulator PtoVND7. The PtoRLK609Hap2 protein variant showed higher kinase activity and more efficient phosphorylation of PtoERF105 than PtoRLK609Hap1, linking natural protein variation to differential transcriptional output. Consistent with this mechanism, gain- and loss-of-function analyses showed that PtoRLK609 promotes secondary cell wall lignification, elevates the syringyl-to-guaiacyl (S/G) ratio, increases vessel density, and is associated with better maintenance of stem water status under controlled water deficit. These findings characterize a PtoRLK609-PtoERF105 phosphorylation module associated with xylem remodeling and identify an RLK locus that is a strong candidate for contributing to climate-associated divergence in perennial trees.
authors: Qi W, Wen Z, Huang W, Ren T, Xiao L, Fang Y, Li Y, Yuan X, Cheng W, He W, Quan M, Du Q, Ingvarsson PK, El-Kassaby YA, Zhang D.

title: Yersinia enterocolitica 2/O:9 outbreak in France linked to raw cow milk cheese, 2024.
abstract: Enteric yersiniosis represents the fourth most frequently reported bacterial foodborne zoonosis in Europe and has been responsible for several outbreaks. Infections are primarily caused by Yersinia enterocolitica and, to a lesser extent, by Yersinia pseudotuberculosis. Investigation of an outbreak caused by Y. enterocolitica bioserotype 2/O:9 with isolates belonging to a single genomic cluster (0-3 alleles distances mismatch between isolates) identified common exposure to a raw cow's milk cheese, leading to an international product recall. The outbreak affected 167 confirmed cases between 17 September 2024 and 07 March 2025 in France and 5 cross-border cases. Y. enterocolitica isolates belonging to the same genomic cluster were detected in the cheese at the cheese factory and in a milking machine filter of a milk producer. This investigation is a reminder of the risks associated with raw milk cheese consumption. We emphasize the need for producers of milk to identify and prevent critical contamination points for Y. enterocolitica.

title: Porcine astrovirus induces endoplasmic reticulum stress-mediated autophagic degradation of MAVS to inhibit type I interferon production.
abstract: Porcine astrovirus (PAstV) infection predominantly results in diarrhea and encephalitis in suckling piglets, yet the underlying pathogenic mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, the PAstV1-GX1 strain, previously isolated, was utilized to infect PK-15 cells. The results demonstrated that PAstV infection induced pronounced endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, as evidenced by the upregulation of HSPA5/GRP78 expression, and macroautophagy/autophagy, indicated by the increased conversion of MAP1LC3/LC3 from LC3-I to LC3-II and decreased expression of SQSTM1/p62. Pharmacological mitigation of ER stress effectively suppressed autophagy, suggesting that PAstV facilitates autophagy via ER stress. Further mechanistic investigations identified that PAstV infection selectively activated the EIF2AK3/PERK-EIF2S1/eIF2α-ATF4 pathway within the unfolded protein response, establishing this pathway as the pivotal upstream signal mediating autophagy. Through the screening of viral proteins, the capsid protein was identified as the primary viral component responsible for inducing ER stress and autophagy. This protein was concurrently localized to both mitochondria and the ER, where it interacted with the MAVS (mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein). The capsid protein facilitated the degradation of MAVS via the autophagy pathway and an apoptosis-related pathway in a non-classical, caspase-3-independent manner, thereby suppressing the production of type I interferons. Modulating ER stress, autophagy, or apoptosis greatly impacted the capsid protein's suppression of type I interferons. This suggested that the capsid protein hindered type I interferon production by triggering ER stress, which activated autophagy and possibly apoptosis, resulting in MAVS degradation. title: Integrating plasma-derived circulating proteins with multi-omics approaches to identify potential therapeutic targets for esophageal adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background: Esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) is a complex disease often preceded by Barrett's esophagus. Objective: This study aimed to identify potential drug targets and support early prevention and treatment. Method: We integrated cis-protein quantitative trait loci (cis-pQTLs) and genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from 35 559 individuals using Mendelian randomization to infer causal relationships, with FDR correction applied. To assess tissue relevance, the source cis-pQTL instruments were examined across three GTEx v8 esophageal tissues, followed by tissue-informed single-variant Wald analyses of CD55 and NDST1. Gene ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway analyses, along with protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, were used to explore biological functions and interactions. Overlapping genes were identified through differential expression analysis using the GEO database. Key feature genes were screened using XGBoost and Lasso regression, and diagnostic performance was evaluated by ROC curve AUC in both training and validation sets. Immune infiltration analysis explored the tumor microenvironment, and molecular docking assessed drug potential. Results: We identified 28 plasma proteins causally linked to EAC. KEGG analysis revealed enrichment in oxidative stress and inflammation-related pathways. Transcriptomic validation confirmed three overlapping genes. CD55 and NDST1 emerged as key markers with strong diagnostic accuracy after Lasso and XGBoost screening. Most significant esophageal SNP-tissue associations were directionally concordant with the corresponding plasma pQTL effects, and the tissue-specific Wald estimates for CD55 and NDST1 were consistent with the primary plasma-based findings. Immune infiltration analysis showed significant changes in immune cell composition in EAC, particularly natural killer cells, plasma cells, and mast cells. Drug prediction and docking supported the druggability of these targets. Conclusion: CD55 and NDST1 are promising therapeutic candidates for EAC. Drugs based on these genetic findings could improve clinical trial success rates and reduce costs.
journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
authors: Zhu A, Sun H, Cheng C, Zhou Y, Huang S, Chen Z, Huang S, Feng Y.

title: Sono-enzymatically engineered tannic acid/doxycycline-lignin nanoparticles enable self-assembled bioactive chitosan hydrogels for chronic wound healing.
abstract: Chronic wounds remain a major clinical challenge due to their multifactorial pathology, characterised by excessive proteolytic and oxidative enzyme activity, persistent inflammation, bacterial infection, and biofilm formation. Here, we report a green, nano-enabled hydrogel fabricated through the in situ self-assembly of thiolated chitosan (TCS), driven by tannic acid/doxycycline-functionalised lignin nanoparticles (PLD NPs). Doxycycline was incorporated at a sub-inhibitory concentration (12.5 μg/mL), enabling PLD NPs (0.5 mg/mL) to inhibit matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity by approximately 50 % without inducing antibacterial effects. Dynamic interactions between the polymer network and NPs produced injectable, self-healing hydrogels capable of stimuli-responsive NPs release under chronic wound-like conditions, including variations in pH, hydrogen peroxide, and lysozyme. Ex vivo evaluation using human chronic wound exudates demonstrated potent inhibition of MMP and myeloperoxidase activities by 73 % and 80 %, respectively. The hydrogels further exhibited strong antimicrobial and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, achieving 4.8- and 4.3-log reductions in bacterial viability while preventing 73 % and 65 % of biofilm formation, respectively. In vitro studies confirmed excellent biocompatibility with human keratinocytes and fibroblasts, together with up to 82 % cellular antioxidant activity and enhanced fibroblast migration. Importantly, in an in vivo full-thickness S. aureus-infected mouse wound model, the hydrogels achieved complete wound closure within 18 days, outperforming commercial antiseptic treatments. Overall, this work demonstrates a multifunctional hydrogel platform that simultaneously modulates the chronic wound microenvironment, controls infection and biofilm formation, reduces oxidative stress, and promotes tissue regeneration, offering a promising strategy for advanced chronic wound management.
authors: Ahmadi R, Ramon E, Todorova K, Petrova Z, Hinojosa-Caballero D, Tzanov T.

title: Impacts of combined nanoplastic and cadmium pollution on nitrogen removal performance in constructed wetlands.
abstract: Nanoplastics (NPs) and cadmium (Cd) frequently co-occur in aquatic environments and can accumulate in constructed wetlands, potentially impairing nitrogen removal. Here, polystyrene (PS-NPs) and polylactic acid nanoplastics (PLA-NPs) were used to evaluate the impacts of NPs-Cd co-contamination on wetland performance and microbial ecology. Co-exposure, particularly with PLA-NPs, significantly decreased NH₄⁺-N, total nitrogen, and COD removal efficiencies. In Phase II, NH₄⁺-N removal efficiency in the PLA-1000 system decreased by 8.49 % compared with the control. PLA-NPs exerted stronger inhibition on plant photosynthetic pigments, while PS-NPs induced higher lipid peroxidation (MDA). The combined stress of PLA-NPs and Cd adversely affected Nitrospirota and suppressed key metabolic pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation and pyruvate metabolism, while enhancing bacterial secretion systems linked to pathogenicity. Functionally, PLA-NPs + Cd reduced the relative abundance of nitrite oxidoreductase-encoding genes, whereas both PS-NPs + Cd and PLA-NPs + Cd decreased the relative abundance of nitrate reductase-encoding genes. Overall, co-contamination promotes nitrogen accumulation and may alter nitrogen transformation pathways, highlighting the ecological threat of biodegradable nanoplastics in wetland systems.
authors: Yu G, Luo C, Zheng D, Sun B, Chen H.

title: Machine learning and in vivo evidence identify CCNB2 as a candidate biomarker of 2-aminobenzothiazole-induced hepatotoxicity in Carassius auratus.
abstract: 2-Aminobenzothiazole (NTH), a tire wear-derived contaminant ubiquitously detected in aquatic ecosystems, has been linked to neurotoxicity and cardiotoxicity in zebrafish, yet its hepatotoxic potential remains poorly characterized. Here, we integrated in silico toxicity prediction, in vivo exposure experiments in crucian carp (Carassius auratus), transcriptomics, machine learning, and molecular simulations to characterize NTH hepatotoxicity and identify candidate genes. Fish exposed to nominal concentrations of 0.5 and 5 mg/L NTH for 15 days exhibited dose-dependent hepatic injury, including steatosis, inflammatory infiltration, dyslipidemia and elevated transaminases. Transcriptomic analysis revealed a dose-dependent shift from disruption of ribosome biogenesis and RNA processing at the low dose to enrichment of cell cycle, DNA replication, and p53 signaling pathways at the high dose. Consensus screening with nine machine learning algorithms on the rat DrugMatrix liver cohort, followed by consistency assessment in an independent mouse cohort, consistently identified CCNB2 as a cross-species conserved candidate gene associated with hepatic exposure response, showing a non-monotonic dose-response pattern in NTH-exposed fish. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations and MM-PBSA free-energy estimates predicted a plausible binding pose for NTH in a putative CCNB2 pocket. Collectively, these findings characterize the hepatotoxicity of NTH and identify CCNB2 as a candidate gene associated with the hepatic exposure response, which may inform hazard characterization pending functional and independent experimental validation.
authors: Zhang Y, Zhang Y, Shao T, Chu W.

title: ROS-associated aerobic methane formation by Shewanella oneidensis coupled with algal organic matters as methyl donors: An overlooked methane emission pathway in eutrophic waters.
abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS)-associated aerobic methane (CH4) formation provides a compelling explanation for the CH4 paradox in oxic waters. However, the microbial heterogeneity and ecological relevance of this process remain largely unexplored. This study investigated aerobic CH4 formation by Shewanella oneidensis, a bacterium with specialized iron metabolism and ROS-regulation capabilities. The potential of algal organic matters (AOM) to provide methylated precursors for this process in eutrophic lakes was also evaluated. The results revealed that aerobic CH4 formation by S. oneidensis depended on iron concentration, with higher CH4 production at 50 μM than at 5 μM. However, CH4 formation was insensitive to the initial iron valence owing to rapid Fe2+/Fe3+ interconversion. Oxic and hypoxic conditions differentially modulated intracellular ROS homeostasis, thereby influencing CH4 formation. Transcriptomic analysis revealed specific reprogramming in response to oxygen availability. Compared with AOM from the early exponential phase (OD680 = 0.5), AOM from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii during the late stationary (OD680 = 2.2) and decline (OD680 = 1.3) phases resulted in 3.77 and 4.26 times the CH4 levels, respectively. This suggests that algal senescence may represent a critical period for CH4 emissions. Incubations with Lake Taihu overlying water and sediment further confirmed the contribution of natural methylated precursors and indigenous microbial communities to ROS-associated CH4 formation. Overall, this study establishes a ROS-associated pathway linking algal-derived methyl substrates to aerobic CH4 formation in eutrophic lakes. These findings provide environmentally relevant evidence to elucidate the CH4 paradox in oxic waters.
authors: Ding J, Zhu R, Sun H, Wu Y, Yin C, Li L, Zeng RJ.
