title: Functional analysis of NANOS protein variants identified in men with infertility employing zebrafish embryos
abstract: Study question  Are vertebrate NANOS proteins associated with human fertility, and can a rapid  in vivo assay in zebrafish be established to evaluate the biological activity of human  NANOS variants?  Summary answer  Combining a rapid  in vivo assay we developed for Nanos protein activity and patient-derived genetic data, we identified  NANOS variants that could contribute to male infertility.  What is known already  Male infertility affects approximately 17% of the population, but linking specific gene variants to this condition remains challenging. NANOS proteins are essential regulators of germ cell development in different model organisms; however, a rapid and robust  in vivo assay for evaluating their activity in the context of human male infertility is currently lacking.  Study design, size, duration  Exome/genome data from 3,338 men included in the Male Reproductive Genomics (MERGE) cohort were examined in this study. Of these, 2038 men showed severely impaired spermatogenesis but were otherwise healthy. Ninety-Six men with intact spermatogenesis were included in the study as controls. Additionally, the study included a targeted analysis of  NANOS variants in 44 patients from the IMIGC cohort.  Participants/materials, setting, methods  The exome/genome data were screened for rare, stop-gain, frameshift, splice site, as well as missense variants in  NANOS1 ,  NANOS2 , and  NANOS3 . Human amino acid substitutions were introduced at the corresponding positions in the zebrafish proteins. Ectopic co-expression of wild-type Dnd1 and Nanos3 in zebrafish embryos induces a germ cell-like fate in somatic cells, resulting in severe developmental defects and embryonic lethality. Based on this principle, we established a rapid  in vivo assay in which wild-type Dnd1 was co-expressed with wild-type or variant Nanos2 and Nanos3 proteins in live zebrafish embryos, expecting early embryonic death if a variant protein is functional. This assay was used to evaluate the activity of  NANOS2 and  NANOS3 variants identified in men with infertility.  Main results and the role of chance  In human exome/genome sequencing data, we identified one heterozygous missense variant in NANOS2 and two heterozygous missense variants in NANOS3. The function of the variants was examined in the zebrafish using the  in vivo assay we developed. Co-expression of wild-type Dnd1 with selected Nanos2 or Nanos3 variants identified in infertile men resulted in defects in induction of the germ cell-like phenotype, demonstrating the power of the biological readout for evaluating the potential effects of patient-derived variants on NANOS protein activity. Together, our analysis enabled the evaluation of single nucleotide variants, whose impact on protein function is difficult to predict, and allowed us to distinguish variants with little or no effect on protein function from those that strongly reduce activity and may potentially contribute to infertility.  Limitations, reasons for caution  The assay requires access to zebrafish embryos and basic imaging equipment. Although the functional conservation of NANOS proteins between zebrafish and humans is supported by previous studies, species-specific differences may influence protein activity. Therefore, the zebrafish assay should be considered one component of a broader framework for evaluating  NANOS variants as contributing factor for infertility.  Wider implications of the findings  Using  NANOS2 and  NANOS3 as examples, we demonstrate that integrating clinical genetic data with functional cell and developmental biology can help establish links between candidate disease genes and human fertility. This strategy may apply to other germline-specific genes whose ectopic expression produces measurable developmental phenotypes in zebrafish embryos. title: Refining the genetic architecture of myocardial infarction through integrative post-genome-wide association study functional genomics analysis.
abstract: MotivationMyocardial infarction is a leading cause of death worldwide and has a strong genetic component. Genome-wide association studies have identified many associated loci, but the genes and variants through which most of them act remain unclear. We aimed to refine the genetic architecture of myocardial infarction by integrating complementary post-association evidence.ResultsA meta-analysis of the Million Veteran Program and UK Biobank (62 129 cases and 828 364 controls) identified 135 genome-wide significant risk loci, five of them potentially novel. Gene-based analysis yielded 333 significant genes, fine-mapping prioritized 613 high-confidence variants, and Bayesian colocalization identified 39 significant gene-tissue signals across 25 eligible loci. Combining all evidence highlighted 10 high-confidence candidate genes, including PHACTR1 and SLC22A3, with enrichment for lipid metabolism, mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, angiogenesis and chromatin remodeling. Repeating the pipeline with a stricter allele frequency threshold retained 129 loci and full support for 8 of the 10 genes.Availability and implementationInput summary statistics are publicly available from the European Bioinformatics Institute genome-wide association study catalog (accessions GCST90475932 and GCST90473536); derived results are provided in the supplementary data.
authors: Islam MS, Mollah MMH, Ahsan MA, Ali M, Pal NK, Faysal MF, Mollah MNH.

title: BDCA2-dependent phagocytosis enables strain-specific activation of plasmacytoid dendritic cells by lactic acid bacteria.
abstract: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) detect microbial DNA via endosomal Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9), yet the mechanisms by which they selectively internalize specific bacteria remain unclear. We demonstrate that type I interferon (IFN-I) responses to lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are entirely dependent on phagocytosis and exhibit pronounced strain specificity. Among tested strains, Lactococcus lactis strain Plasma (LC-Plasma) was efficiently phagocytosed and potently induced IFN-α in both primary human pDCs and CAL-1 cells, whereas closely related strains showed minimal uptake and cytokine production. Phagocytosis was essential for TLR9-dependent IFN-α secretion. Transcriptomic and functional analyses identified BDCA2, a galactose-binding C-type lectin receptor, as a key mediator of LAB uptake. Blocking BDCA2 significantly impaired both phagocytosis and cytokine responses. BDCA2-Fc fusion proteins bound strongly to LAB. Glycan profiling identified glycan signatures associated with highly phagocytosed Lactococcus strains. These findings define BDCA2-dependent phagocytosis as a critical determinant of strain-specific LAB recognition by human pDCs.
authors: Hori S, Hirose Y, Matsuo-Dapaah J, Zheng J, Tsuji T, Fujita H, Nanao M, Tsuji R.

title: Integrative Reanalysis of Public Intracellular and Vaccine-Challenge Transcriptomes, Informed by Single-Cell and Metabolomic Atlases, Refines Antigen Prioritisation for Next-Generation Veterinary Brucella Vaccines
abstract: Brucellosis is the most widespread bacterial zoonosis and a leading cause of abortion and infertility in cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. The live vaccines licensed for livestock (B. abortus S19 and RB51, B. melitensis Rev.1) give incomplete protection, retain residual virulence and induce antibodies that are indistinguishable from those of field infection, and no human vaccine is licensed. Antigen discovery for safer subunit and mRNA alternatives has proceeded one candidate at a time, so it remains unclear which immunogenic proteins are abundant in the intracellular niche that protective immunity must recognise. We reanalysed four public data layers: dual RNA-sequencing of intracellular B. abortus and infected murine macrophages (GSE100914), splenic transcriptomes from vaccinated and challenged mice (GSE254248), and single-cell (PRJCA054635) and metabolomic (ST003696, ST003692) atlases. Intracellular residence induced 704 genes and repressed 249, enriching translation functions 2.9-fold. Omp28/BP26 was the second most abundant intracellular transcript (35,652 TPM; log2FC 4.25), whereas the lipoproteins omp16, omp10 and omp19 were 116-637-fold less abundant. Vaccination left a germinal-centre and TCF1+ memory imprint rather than an effector-cytokine signature. A composite score combining abundance, induction and surface exposure reorders the candidate panel, placing Omp28/BP26 and omp2b above current candidates and defining concrete priorities for veterinary vaccine development.
authors: Zhao Y, Cheng H, Zhou S, He L, Xiu C, Huang B, Lu X.

title: Reciprocal MDK-THRB lipid-oxidation transcriptional programs in MASH-associated hepatocellular carcinoma: a two-cohort human transcriptomic analysis.
abstract: PurposeMidkine (MDK) and thyroid hormone receptor beta (THRB) have each been implicated separately in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). THRB drives hepatic fatty-acid beta-oxidation (FAO). We tested whether MDK and the THRB-linked FAO program are reciprocally related in human liver tissue.MethodsWe analyzed two independent human cohorts on different platforms. TCGA-LIHC provided 374 tumor and 50 adjacent non-tumor RNA-seq samples. GSE164760 provided 53 NASH-HCC, 74 NASH, 29 non-tumoral NASH adjacent to HCC, 8 cirrhotic and 6 healthy microarray samples. We quantified MDK, THRB and a curated 21-gene hepatic FAO composite score. Tests included Mann-Whitney, Spearman, Kruskal-Wallis, Jonckheere-Terpstra and genome-wide correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction.ResultsMDK was higher in tumor tissue in both cohorts (TCGA-LIHC p = 1.0 × 10-24, GSE164760 p = 8.1 × 10-13). The FAO composite was correspondingly lower (p = 7.0 × 10-10 and p = 7.1 × 10-6). THRB itself was lower in GSE164760 (p = 3.9 × 10-3) but not in TCGA-LIHC (p = 0.509). MDK correlated negatively with THRB and with the FAO composite in both cohorts. The strongest association was MDK versus FAO composite (rho=-0.45 in each cohort). Within-group analysis showed that the THRB to FAO composite correlation persisted in almost every subgroup. The MDK correlations weakened in three smaller subgroups. Across the five GSE164760 disease states, MDK, THRB and the FAO composite each differed significantly (Kruskal-Wallis p -5) and each followed a significant monotonic trend (Jonckheere-Terpstra one-sided p -3).ConclusionA reciprocal MDK-high and FAO-low transcriptional signature is reproducible across two independent human cohorts and across the MASH-to-HCC spectrum. These human tissue data support THRB agonism as a candidate therapeutic rationale in MASH-HCC that warrants prospective validation.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05104-3.
authors: Muniappan V, Dwivedi K, Sakila S, Sejpal J, Varadhan P, Santhosha K, Ramachandiran S, Muruganantham B, Venkatesh R, Gunasekaran B, Lokaiah T, Mishra SK, Darshan Y, Rajput S.

title: Biological Mechanisms Underlying the Adverse Health Consequences of Human Circadian Misalignment from Night Shift Work.
abstract: Purpose of reviewThe waking and working times of night shift workers are displaced relative to the natural light/dark cycle, putting behavioral patterns in misalignment with the circadian regulation of biological processes. This state of circadian misalignment constitutes a circadian health problem, with widespread negative consequences for metabolic, cardiovascular, and mental health, as well as elevated risk of cancer. Scientific advances over the past decade have shed light on key aspects of the underlying biological mechanisms. With a focus on recent human studies, this paper reviews novel insights into what drives the adverse health consequences of circadian misalignment due to night shift work.Recent findingsMisalignment between the central circadian pacemaker and externally driven behavioral patterns during night shift work produces a rapid uncoupling of peripheral rhythms, reflected in the cargo of exosomes and other signaling mechanisms, and causes conflict between central and peripheral regulatory mechanisms. This endogenous internal desynchrony has been shown to be linked to shifted meal timing and, in part, may be mediated by the gut microbiome. Endogenous internal desynchrony leads to insulin resistance - a manifestation of metabolic dysfunction. It perturbs the cardiometabolic and immune systems, and also erodes mental health. At the cellular level, mistimed DNA repair mechanisms leave residual DNA damage after exposure to a night shift schedule - which, over time, may result in genomic instability and ultimately carcinogenesis.SummaryA systems biology perspective serves to elucidate how the effects of endogenous circadian disruption from night shift work increase the risk of acute and chronic illnesses. Internal desynchrony, endogenous in nature, is a common underlying cause. Time-restricted eating may help to address metabolic dysfunction due to night shift work; countermeasures for other negative health outcomes, including cancer and mental health disorders, remain to be developed.
authors: Lundholm KR, Satterfield BC, Banks S, Liu PY, Kombala CJ, Hurtado-Alvarado G, Greer AJ, Muck RA, Layton MA, Du D, Gaddameedhi S, Van Dongen HPA.

title: Determinants of orthoflavivirus tropism in humans: from cellular entry to organ-specific pathogenesis.
abstract: Orthoflaviviruses, including dengue virus, tick-borne encephalitis virus, West Nile virus, Zika virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, and yellow fever virus, cause a wide spectrum of diseases in humans despite sharing a similar genomic organization. These viruses pose a growing global threat as they are spreading widely, treatment options remain limited, and both climate change and expanding mosquito populations increase the risk of outbreaks worldwide. This review summarizes the determinants of their human tropism, the capacity to infect specific cell types, tissues, and organs. We synthesized current knowledge on how viral factors, including host factor utilization and immune cell trafficking, shape tropism across multiple layers. Central to this process are sequential host barriers that govern infection, including viral attachment, internalization, and replication. Understanding these determinants is essential for informing strategies to mitigate the global burden of these medically important pathogens.
authors: Russow JA, Bertzbach LD, Ip WH, Pfaender S.

title: Whole genome sequences of four potential indigenous probiotics strains isolated from sediment of Sundarbans mangrove and wild black tiger shrimp (Penaeus monodon) from the Bay of Bengal, Bangladesh.
abstract: Here, we report the whole genome sequences of four potential indigenous probiotic strains: Photobacterium ganghwense MSR_IP16, Bacillus subtilis MSR_IP31, and two Bacillus velezensis (MSR_IP55 and MSR_IP80) isolated from sediment of Sundarbans mangrove and brood shrimps from the Bay of Bengal, Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh. Genome assemblies ranged from 3.9 to 5.3 Mb with 19-44 contigs, respectively.
authors: Ahmmed S, Rohomania T, Rahman MS.

title: Shared Genetic Architecture Between Mental Disorders and Heart Failure Subtypes: A Comprehensive Multitrait Genome-Wide Analysis.
abstract: BackgroundMental disorders and heart failure frequently co-occur, but their shared genetic architecture remains incompletely understood.MethodsProspective Cox regression analysis in the UK Biobank (UKB) quantified the risk of incident heart failure associated with mental disorders. Linkage disequilibrium score regression estimated genetic correlations, while multitrait genome-wide association and cross-phenotype association analyses identified candidate pleiotropic loci. Statistical fine mapping and gene-level association analyses prioritized candidate variants and genes. Bayesian colocalization assessed evidence for shared candidate variants, and exploratory Gene Ontology biological-process overrepresentation analysis provided descriptive biological context. Single-cell RNA sequencing and genetically informed spatial mapping (gsMap) provided cellular and spatial context for prioritized genes. Geneformer-based in silico perturbation analysis was performed using a cardiac cell atlas of dilated cardiomyopathy to prioritize candidate pleiotropic genes and identify cardiac cell states showing predicted embedding shifts.ResultsProspective UKB analyses demonstrated that mental disorders, such as posttraumatic stress disorder, depression, and bipolar disorder, were associated with a higher risk of incident heart failure. Multitrait analysis identified 607 pleiotropic variants, with fine-mapping and colocalization converging on prioritized candidate loci, including TMEM18, NKX2-2, and XRN2. Single-cell expression profiling and spatial mapping provided context at the cellular and tissue levels for the prioritized genes. Geneformer-based in silico perturbation prioritized FOXP1 and TMEM106B as leading pleiotropic candidate genes on the basis of their predicted changes in downstream gene embeddings in cardiac cellular contexts.ConclusionsThis study identifies shared genetic architecture between mental disorders and heart failure and prioritizes candidate pleiotropic genes associated with both. Transcriptomic and in silico perturbation analyses provide exploratory cellular, spatial, and cardiac functional context. Functional validation is required before mechanistic or therapeutic interpretation.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
authors: Yan S, Chai K, Yang J, Cui J, Wang H.

title: A plasmid-encoded H-NS protein selectively binds its own plasmid.
abstract: H-NS is an abundant nucleoid-associated protein found in Enterobacterales species. Some conjugative plasmids encode H-NS homologs, which are thought to facilitate plasmid maintenance and reduce the fitness costs associated with plasmid carriage. Here, we characterize HppXCROD2, an H-NS homolog encoded by the IncX4 plasmid pCROD2 of Citrobacter rodentium. Our data indicate that HppXCROD2 has a strong preference for binding pCROD2 over the chromosome, or other plasmids. By contrast, chromosomally encoded H-NS displays no preference for plasmid sequence. When expressed from a heterologous plasmid in Escherichia coli, HppXCROD2 showed similar DNA-sequence preference to chromosomally encoded H-NS. Moreover, HppXCROD2 binding to a sequence from pCROD2 was much lower when that sequence was cloned in a laboratory plasmid. Thus, HppXCROD2 preferentially binds DNA in the context of the plasmid where it is encoded, a phenomenon we term "cognate plasmid specificity." We propose that cognate plasmid specificity occurs through recognition of plasmid-specific DNA topology generated by plasmid-encoded topoisomerases. Cognate plasmid specificity may insulate regulation of plasmid genes from the effects of host DNA, while minimizing disruption of host chromosome regulation due to plasmid carriage.IMPORTANCEMany bacteria carry conjugative plasmids, mobile DNA molecules that spread traits such as antibiotic resistance. Some conjugative plasmids encode proteins related to the bacterial DNA-binding protein H-NS. We show that an H-NS-like protein from the IncX4 plasmid pCROD2 binds almost exclusively to the plasmid from which it originates, while largely ignoring the host chromosome. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism that allows plasmids to regulate their own genes with high specificity while minimizing interference with host gene expression.
authors: Stringer AM, Rodríguez-Valverde D, Ruiz-Perez F, Santiago AE, Wade JT.

title: Paralytic shellfish toxin production in Alexandrium minutum (Dinophyceae): Insights from omics integration using toxigenic and nontoxigenic recombinant progeny.
abstract: Paralytic shellfish toxins (PSTs) are produced by certain species of cyanobacteria and dinoflagellates. Part of the PST biosynthetic pathway has been elucidated in cyanobacteria, and the implication of some sxt genes has been confirmed by experimental studies. Contrary to cyanobacteria, knowledge about PST biosynthesis in dinoflagellates is more limited and generally restricted to comparative studies with the cyanobacterial pathway. To investigate the specificity of the PST pathway in dinoflagellates, 16 toxigenic and nontoxigenic Alexandrium minutum strains from a recombinant cross were compared, without prior assumption about genes or metabolites involved in PST synthesis, using an integrative approach combining untargeted metabolomic and transcriptomic data. Among the 60 most distinguishing transcripts between toxigenic and non-toxigenic strains, only three sxt genes were present: sxtA4, sxtG, and sxtI. In contrast, non-sxt homologs were detected as highly discriminant between these two phenotypes. More specifically, a phyH homolog may act as the analog of the sxtS gene observed in cyanobacteria. Moreover, we identified four putative synthetic PST intermediates. Among these, Int-C'2 correlated with the toxic phenotype, whereas three others were detected in both toxigenic and nontoxigenic strains, suggesting that these strains may share some parts of the biosynthetic pathway. Finally, our analyses identified both horizontally gained sxt genes and endogenous genes, including the candidate gene phyH, as candidate components of the PST biosynthetic pathway in A. minutum.
authors: Mary L, Quere J, Latimier M, Artigaud S, Hégaret H, Le Gac M, Réveillon D.

title: Genome-wide association analysis identifies candidate miRNA-targeted genes associated with spatial grain size and weight variation in barley.
abstract: Grain homogeneity in size and weight is crucial for improving grain quality. Reducing spatial variability in grain size and weight across the spike is important for increasing grain uniformity, quality, and breeding barley with consistent yield. However, there is limited knowledge on the molecular genetic basis of grain shape in temperate cereals, including barley. Therefore, we studied grain size and weight along the barley spikes, comparing apical vs. basal grains in both two- and six-rowed spikes and central vs. lateral grains in six-rowed spikes. Regardless of row type, the basal part of the barley spike has more uniform grains. The grains from two-rowed barley had significantly wider and higher thousand-kernel weight, while grains from six-rowed barley were longer with increased grain area. The results showed a clear basal-to-apical gradient in grain size and weight, which implies genetic control of the variation. Gene-based analysis identifies a family of miRNA-regulated transcription factors, SQUAMOSA PROMOTER BINDING PROTEIN-LIKEs (HvSPLs) and APETALA2/Ethylene Responsive Factor (HvAP2/ERF), that are associated with grain size-related traits in barley, establishing a novel connection between positional grain characteristics and miRNA-driven regulation mechanisms in a temperate cereal. The results provide an important foundation for uncovering the biological functions of HvSPLs and HvAP2/ERF, which hold important potential for regulating agronomic traits and for understanding their roles in temperate cereals like barley. Genetic variation in miRNA-targeted HvSPL and HvAP2/ERF genes will provide more natural trait-enhancing alleles for crop breeding.
authors: Alqudah AM, Thabet SG, Chatterjee M, Alqahtani MDH, Sehmisch S, Lantos E, Krebes C, Börner A.

title: Crystal structure of tyrosine-tRNA synthetase from Helicobacter pylori G27.
abstract: Helicobacter pylori, a major cause of gastric ulcers and cancers, infects nearly half of the world's population. The crystal structure of a potential H. pylori structure-guided drug-discovery target, tyrosine-tRNA synthetase (HpTyrRS), has been determined by the Seattle Structural Genomics Center for Infectious Disease (SSGCID). HpTyrRS is an enzyme that catalyzes the ATP-dependent attachment of tyrosine to tRNA. HpTyrRS was produced and crystallized, and its structure was determined at 2.2 Å resolution. HpTyrRS has a prototypical bacterial TyrRS topology and forms dimers in solution. HpTyrRS shares a conserved binding cavity for a previously identified Staphylococcus aureus TyrRS inhibitor (SB-219383). The reported structure and analysis establish HpTyrRS as a potential target for structure-guided drug discovery and repurposing.
journal: Acta crystallographica. Section F, Structural biology communications
authors: Igbalajobi D, Taylor JE, Gao R, Ayanlade J, Zigweid R, Subramanian S, Udell H, Edwards TE, Abendroth J, Lorimer D, Myler PJ, Staker B, Ndip EM, Asojo OA.

title: A Rapid Lithium Ion-Based Transformation Method for Kluyveromyces lactis.
abstract: Kluyveromyces lactis is a budding yeast host useful for recombinant protein production; however, its transformation often relies on electroporation due to the perceived low efficiency of chemical methods, thereby limiting throughput. In this study, we developed a robust, small-scale chemical transformation protocol (using 15 μL of competent cells) that achieves high efficiency, particularly with linear DNA. No significant differences in efficiency were observed between lithium chloride and lithium acetate, nor across concentrations ranging from 0.1 to 1.0 M, for making cells competent. The addition of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) during heat shock enhanced colony counts, while ethanol inhibited the process. When PCR fragments containing the optimized pan-genomic autonomous replication sequence (PanARS-OPT) were used for transformation, the transformation efficiency was approximately 7-fold higher than that of circular plasmids, yielding over 105 transformants/μg DNA. This high efficiency with linear DNA can be due to a potent non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) activity in K. lactis. This rapid, "one-tube" method eliminates the need for plasmid construction and specialized equipment, offering a tool for rapid and high-throughput genetic engineering in K. lactis.
authors: Tsugama D, Zuo Z.

title: Steinernema chainatense n. sp., a new entomopathogenic nematode (Nematoda: Steinernematidae) from Thailand.
abstract: A new entomopathogenic nematode, Steinernema chainatense n. sp., was isolated during sampling in a cassava field in Chai Nat Province, Central Thailand. A combination of morphological, morphometric, and molecular traits places the new species within the longicaudum clade of the glaseri-group. Infective juveniles (IJs) of S. chainatense n. sp. are characterised by a body length of 871 (798-939) μm, a maximum body diameter of 27 (24-30) μm, and a lateral field with eight equally developed ridges at mid-body and a formula of 2, 6, 8, 2. First-generation males are characterised by large, brown spicules, 88 (80-95) μm long, with a well-developed velum. The male genital papillae number 25 in total, comprising 12 pairs and a single midventral papilla. The internal transcribed spacer (ITS) and D2-D3 sequences differ from those of other members of the longicaudum clade by 3.6-10.4% and 1.5-3.5%, respectively. Phylogenetic analysis based on the ITS region of rDNA indicates a close relationship between S. chainatense n. sp. and S. taiwanensis, S. adamsi, S. guangdongense, and S. longicaudum, with S. taiwanensis as its sister taxon. The bacterial symbiont of S. chainatense n. sp. is the recently described Xenorhabdus thailandensis. These morphological and molecular differences support the recognition of S. chainatense n. sp. as a distinct species.
authors: Půža V, Nermuť J, Skoková Habuštová O, Pansri S, Vitta A.

title: New abscisic acid analogues produced via genome mining-guided heterologous expression.
abstract: Abscisic acid (ABA), a pivotal phytohormone, was traditionally considered to be synthesized via the carotenoid pathway exclusively in plants. In our recent work, a dedicated ABA biosynthetic gene cluster (ablt) was discovered from the marine-derived fungus Alternaria alternata JJY-32 by genome mining. Heterologous expression of the ablt cluster in Aspergillus nidulans A1145 led to the production of two new analogues of ABA, designated as abaterpene A (1) and abaterpene B (2), along with six known sesquiterpenes. Further step-wise gene co-expression analysis demonstrated that ablt3 and ablt5 are necessary and sufficient for the production of compounds 1 and 2. The structures were determined using comprehensive 1D and 2D NMR data and assisted by ECD calculations.
authors: Liu G, Ge X, Lan D, Tong X, Shang X, Wang W, Che Q, Zhu T, Li D, Zhang G.

title: Magnetic Resonance Reveals Radical Stability in Native Biofilms and Its Role in Bacterial Resistance.
abstract: Bacterial cells embedded in biofilms exhibit enhanced antimicrobial resistance compared with planktonic cells, contributing to persistent infections and failure of conventional antibiotic treatments. This resistance is influenced by the extracellular matrix (ECM), a heterogeneous network of polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids surrounding embedded cells. However, how the ECM regulates the accessibility of redox-active small molecules remains poorly understood. Here, we combine electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), solid-state NMR (ssNMR), and dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) ssNMR to determine how native Pseudomonas fluorescens Pf0-1 colony biofilms differentially reduce nitroxide radicals across morphologies. EPR reveals that radical reduction depends on biofilm morphology, hydration, and ECM composition. Wild-type biofilms exhibit slower nitroxide reduction than planktonic cells, while isolated ECM and dehydrated biofilms show negligible reduction, highlighting the importance of cellular accessibility. ssNMR identifies preferential spatial proximity of nitroxides to ECM polysaccharides and lipids, while DNP ssNMR reveals increasing polysaccharide content across biofilm morphologies that correlates with slower reduction kinetics. These findings support a model of protection in which the ECM provides the barrier to nitroxide access, and cellular reduction is the final step. Our integrated magnetic resonance approach provides molecular insight into how biofilm composition and structure determine the fate of therapeutically relevant redox-active small molecules.
authors: Mandato A, Hunter H, Srinivasa S, Byeon CH, Tunc A, Wells MK, Scott FJ, Mentink-Vigier F, Kim W, Saxena S, Akbey Ü.

title: De novo structural mining and engineering of TadA deaminases for high efficiency adenine base editors.
abstract: Conventional enzyme discovery relies primarily on sequence homology and phylogenetic relationships, limiting the identification of functionally related but sequence-divergent proteins. Here, we developed a structure-guided mining framework integrating AlphaFold2-predicted structures with Foldseek-based three-dimensional alignment to identify previously uncharacterized TadA scaffolds with conserved folds and divergent sequences. Two candidates, eMaTadA and eErTadA, were engineered into functional adenine base editors (ABEs) by fusion to Cas9 nickase. The resulting editors mediated robust A-to-G editing with high product purity and restricted bystander editing. Under expression-stratified and activity-matched conditions, eMa-ABE and eEr-ABE showed reduced guide-dependent DNA off-target editing relative to ABE8e, while orthogonal R-loop assays revealed lower SpCas9-independent deamination of exposed single-stranded DNA (ssDNA). In human CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, eMa-ABE achieved up to approximately 80% editing at established HBG1/2 promoter targets and induced fetal hemoglobin expression following erythroid differentiation. Lipid nanoparticle delivery corrected approximately 50% of ATP7B P992L alleles in mouse liver, with no detectable increase in editing at the examined computationally predicted off-target loci. Furthermore, embedding eMaTadA within Cas9 expanded the editing window from A3-A9 to A3-A14 and enabled efficient start-codon-mediated gene inactivation. Collectively, this study establishes a structure-guided strategy for discovering and engineering sequence-divergent deaminases and expands the molecular diversity and therapeutic potential of the ABE toolkit.
journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
authors: Chen B, Nong B, Lin S, Yang Y, Yu Y, Tan W, Zhu T, Pei Y, Xu W, Wu Y, Ma X, Yu J, Huang W, Hu Y, Songyang Z.

title: Multi-Dataset Transcriptomic Screening Identifies Myosin VI as a Prognostic Biomarker Linked to Migration in Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Distant metastasis remains a principal determinant of mortality in prostate cancer (PCa), yet markers associated with metastatic potential at an early stage remain scarce. Here, cross-cohort mining of public transcriptomic data was combined with in vitro loss-of-function experiments to nominate and characterize candidate prognostic and metastasis-associated markers in PCa. Six independent cohorts-the Cancer Genome Atlas prostate adenocarcinoma cohort (TCGA-PRAD) and five Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) series-were analyzed separately for differential expression between tumor and adjacent normal tissue, with Benjamini-Hochberg control of the false discovery rate (FDR) applied within each dataset before cross-dataset comparison. This analysis identified 81 consensus differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Candidates were prioritized by protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and exploratory Kaplan-Meier survival screening. The two leading genes were re-examined using the Tumor Immune Estimation Resource (TIMER) database, where only myosin VI (MYO6) remained associated with shorter overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.35, P = 0.0385). Lentiviral short hairpin RNA (shRNA) silencing of MYO6 in PC-3 and DU145 cells reduced migration and invasion, whereas colony-formation and MTS assays showed a concurrent increase in proliferation, a dissociation compatible with a "go-or-grow" trade-off. Immunoblotting after MYO6 silencing showed higher E-cadherin and Claudin-1 and lower N-cadherin, whereas Vimentin changed in the opposite direction, indicating a partial rather than complete epithelial shift. These findings identify MYO6 as a prognostic and metastasis-associated candidate in PCa and support the broader applicability of this screening framework for biomarker nomination in other tumor types.
authors: Tian R, Zhang W, Wang J, Han X, Sun Y, Ma H, Liang L.

title: Molecular characterization of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales from Peshawar City, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan.
abstract: Background/objectivesThe dissemination of multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales poses a critical public health challenge, particularly in resource-limited regions with high antimicrobial use and limited surveillance. We analysed the phenotypic and genotypic resistance profiles of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales collected in 2023 from three tertiary care hospitals in Peshawar, Pakistan.MethodsWe performed antimicrobial susceptibility testing on 32 Enterobacterales isolates suspected of carbapenemase production using disk diffusion, gradient diffusion, and broth microdilution according to EUCAST guidelines. We conducted whole-genome sequencing to identify resistance genes, sequence types, and mutations associated with reduced susceptibility to novel β-lactams.ResultsThe collection comprised 16 Escherichia coli, 13 Klebsiella pneumoniae, and 3 Proteus mirabilis isolates. The predominant carbapenemase gene was bla NDM-5 (90.6%), frequently combined with bla OXA-48-like variants (46.9%). ESBL genes, mainly bla CTX-M-15, were common (78.1%), while CMY-type AmpC β-lactamases were detected in 28.1% of isolates. Insertions in the PBP3-encoding gene ftsI and CMY co-production were associated with elevated aztreonam-avibactam MICs in E.coli. Reduced cefiderocol susceptibility was observed mainly among NDM-producing E. coli ST2 isolates carrying cirA disruption and ftsI insertions. All isolates remained susceptible to colistin, most of them to gentamicin (84.4%), and exhibited wild-type MIC-distributions for tigecycline, and eravacycline. Genomic analysis identified clustering of high-risk clones, suggesting ongoing local transmission. Notably, 11/13 K. pneumoniae ST147 isolates carried multiple virulence-associated genes consistent with hypervirulence.ConclusionsHigh-risk NDM-producing Enterobacterales with increasingly complex resistance and virulence mechanisms are circulating in Pakistan, including determinants compromising last-line β-lactams. Strengthened genomic surveillance is essential to guide therapy and limit further spread.
authors: Mancini S, Ullah I, Seth-Smith HMB, Kolesnik-Goldmann N, Hinic V, Roloff T, Egli A, Ali Syed M, Nolte O.

title: Comparative analysis of central nervous system persistence of morbilliviruses across host species reveals shared features with subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.
abstract: BackgroundSubacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare but always fatal neurological complication of measles, associated with persistent measles virus (MeV) infection of the central nervous system (CNS). MeV is detected in the brains of deceased SSPE patients as hypermutated viral genomes, which often contain premature stop codons in the matrix (M) gene and encode a hyperfusogenic fusion (F) protein. As a result, infected cells in the CNS cannot produce virions but rather transmit the viral ribonucleoprotein from cell-to-cell in a slow but progressive manner, which ultimately results in widespread MeV infection of the brain. However, our understanding of the pathogenesis of SSPE is constrained by the lack of animal models combined with a clinically silent incubation period of several years.Main textIn a recent publication in PNAS, Daniel Roji et al. analysed animal morbillivirus sequences detected in the brains of persistently infected hosts, including a lynx (canine distemper virus, CDV), two seals (phocine distemper virus, PDV) and a dolphin (cetacean morbillivirus, CeMV). The authors describe that the morbillivirus sequences detected in these animals contained unique mutational signatures. The CDV, CeMV and one of the PDV sequences encoded nonfunctional M proteins and hyperfusogenic F proteins, reminiscent of the mutational profile of MeV detected in SSPE patients. Therefore, the authors conclude that human and animal morbilliviruses associated with chronic neurological infections share key genotypic and phenotypic traits, and that thorough analysis of naturally occurring animal morbillivirus infections could improve our understanding of SSPE pathogenesis.ConclusionThe comparison of neurological complications associated with human and animal morbillivirus infections as described by Daniel Roji et al. provides a unique One Health approach to understanding the drivers of SSPE. These findings may support the development of early diagnostics or an animal model for SSPE, providing an opportunity to test novel intervention strategies.
authors: de Swart RL, de Vries RD.

title: Functional verification of bacteriochlorophyll biosynthetic genes distributed in pink-pigmented facultative methylotrophs.
abstract: Pink-pigmented facultative methylotrophs (PPFMs), represented by the genera Methylobacterium and Methylorubrum, are ubiquitous bacteria commonly found in nutrient-poor environments such as plant leaf surfaces. Comparative genomics has revealed that many PPFMs possess genes for bacteriochlorophyll (BChl) biosynthesis; however, whether these genes support functional phototrophy has remained largely unknown. Here, we systematically investigated BChl production and its physiological function in PPFMs. Among 43 Methylobacterium/Methylorubrum type strains examined, 36 produced BChl, demonstrating that BChl production is widespread despite substantial diversity in the culture conditions required for its induction. In Methylorubrum extorquens AM1, BChl production required light and specific carbon substrates, and light stimulated the expression of BChl biosynthetic genes. In contrast, Methylobacterium phyllosphaerae CBMB27 produced BChl under standard growth conditions, with a modest transcriptional response to light. Comparison of intracellular ATP levels between the wild-type and the ΔbchZ strains demonstrated BChl-dependent ATP production in Methylobacteriumphyllosphaerae CBMB27, but not in Methylorubrumextorquens AM1. Under carbon-limited conditions, this BChl-dependent ATP production conferred a measurable growth advantage. These findings demonstrate that BChl-mediated phototrophy is physiologically functional in at least a subset of PPFMs, and suggest that the regulation and ecological roles of BChl production have diversified among species.
authors: Iguchi H, Miyabe G, Orita I, Tani A.

title: Genetic diversity, selection signatures, and breed-specific SNP marker identification in Baerchuke sheep.
abstract: Indigenous sheep genetic resources are important for breeding improvement and germplasm conservation. Baerchuke (BECK) sheep, an indigenous breed from Xinjiang, China, is valued for its meat quality and environmental adaptability, but its genomic characteristics remain poorly understood. Here, 343 BECK sheep were genotyped using a 50 K SNP chip and integrated with genomic data from six indigenous Xinjiang sheep populations. Population genetic analyses revealed moderate genetic diversity and close genetic affinity between BECK and Bayinbuluke sheep. Selection signature analyses identified 26 candidate genes, including ZNF385B, TSHZ2, and FCHSD2, with potential roles in growth and muscle-related biological processes. In addition, the HITSNP approach identified 343 breed-informative SNP markers with high informativeness and low redundancy that effectively differentiated BECK from the other populations examined. This study provides the first systematic genome-wide characterization of BECK sheep and provides genomic resources for germplasm conservation, breed identification, and future marker-assisted breeding.
authors: Yang H, Rouzi M, Su P, Zhao Y, Andersson G, Bongcam-Rudloff E, Aimaiti M, Jiang L, Han J, Yang M.

title: Co-housing Alters Gut Microbiota and Disease Severity in Experimental Pemphigoid Disease.
abstract: Pemphigoid diseases (PD) are autoimmune blistering disorders in which alterations of the skin and gut microbiota have been reported, yet how microbial variation relates to disease severity remains unclear. Using a bullous pemphigoid-like mouse model, we compared genetically identical C57BL/6J mice from two breeding facilities that differed in their baseline microbiota. Mice from Charles River developed markedly milder disease than in-house-bred animals. Co-housing partially homogenized their gut microbiota, shifting in-house mice asymmetrically toward the Charles River community, coinciding with reduced disease severity in co-housed in-house mice. The skin microbiota showed more modest and less consistent shifts, potentially reflecting its lower biomass and higher technical noise. Lower gut microbial diversity and enrichment of pro-inflammatory taxa like Turicimonas muris and Muribaculum intestinale were linked to more severe disease, whereas taxa such as Lactobacillus intestinalis and Parabacteroides distasonis correlated with protection. A gut taxon belonging to Scatocola was identified as a candidate negative predictor of disease severity in correlation and machine-learning analyses. Together, these findings support an association between natural variation in the gut microbiota and autoimmune skin inflammation and identify candidate microbial taxa that warrant further functional validation.
authors: Liu X, Patzelt S, Ma Y, Cepic A, Dikmen HO, Bieber K, Groussin M, Poyet M, Ibrahim S, Schmidt E, Baines JF.

title: [Translated article] What's new in spinal instrumentation-related infections.
abstract: Infections associated with spinal instrumentation represent one of the most complex complications in spine surgery and frequently involve biofilm-forming pathogens that compromise the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapies. Diagnosis - particularly in chronic cases - requires the use of advanced microbiological techniques, such as implant sonication, next-generation metagenomic sequencing, and prolonged culture incubation. Therapeutic strategies depend on the chronicity of the infection and the stability of the implant, ranging from surgical debridement with retention of osteosynthesis material to staged delayed re-instrumentation. Empirical antibiotic therapy should be initiated promptly and subsequently adjusted according to microbiological results. Prevention remains a fundamental pillar and includes strict perioperative optimization. Favorable outcomes rely on early detection, a multidisciplinary team approach, and individualized surgical and antimicrobial management based on accurate clinical and radiological assessment.
journal: Revista espanola de cirugia ortopedica y traumatologia
authors: Ortega-Yago A, Rubio P, Ulldemolins P, Baeza-Oliete J, Bas P, Bas T.

title: Applications of artificial intelligence in parasitology: A holistic perspective from diagnosis to therapeutics.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated to address challenges in parasite detection, disease surveillance, and therapeutic development. This narrative review examines current and emerging AI applications in parasitology across diagnostics, drug discovery, genomics, epidemiology, education, and public health decision-making, with particular emphasis on diagnostic applications. Machine learning and deep learning methods support automated parasite detection, classification, and quantification in microscopic images, alongside medical image analysis and arthropod identification. Applications are discussed for malaria, leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis, cystic echinococcosis, soil-transmitted helminth infections, and intestinal protozoal infections. Beyond diagnosis, AI-assisted approaches support compound screening, drug repurposing, toxicity prediction, and prioritization of potential therapeutic targets. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses also offer opportunities to investigate parasite biology and predict drug resistance. Surveillance models may inform outbreak forecasting and targeted control, although their operational value requires evaluation in the intended settings. Educational applications remain emerging, and the benefits of digital learning should be distinguished from those attributable specifically to AI. Across these domains, performance on curated datasets does not establish clinical utility or generalizability. Major barriers include limited representative datasets, insufficient external and prospective validation, infrastructure constraints, and concerns regarding privacy, bias, and accountability. Future progress requires reproducible evaluation, experimental validation of therapeutic candidates, and assessment of clinical and public health benefits. AI is therefore best positioned as a complementary tool that supports parasitological expertise, with responsible implementation guided by transparency, equitable access, and human oversight.
authors: Uslug M, Celik F, Simsek S.

title: Plant-derived high-C:P amendments enhance legacy phosphorus utilization in phosphorus-enriched greenhouse soil via stoichiometric regulation and microbial functional coupling.
abstract: Long-term intensive fertilization has accumulated large legacy phosphorus (P) pools in greenhouse vegetable soils, while substituting chemical fertilizers with livestock manure may exacerbate soil P loading. We evaluated pakchoi growth and legacy P utilization in an acidified, P-enriched greenhouse soil, comparing an unfertilized, unamended control (CK) with equal-carbon inputs of low-C:P, high-P chicken manure (OF) and high-C:P, low-P plant-derived amendments: alkali lignin (AL), straw (ST), and alkali-lignin-modified straw (AST). Compared with the OF, shoot dry weight was 47.0% and 12.4% higher under ST and AST, respectively, while shoot P uptake increased by 80.2% and 76.8%. OF produced an apparent P surplus, whereas ST and AST generated negative apparent P balances, indicating current-season amendment P inputs could not offset shoot P removal and supporting enhanced legacy P utilization without further accumulation of available or labile inorganic P. Plant-derived amendments increased soil C:P and pH, generally enhanced C- and N-acquiring enzyme activities, and reduced ecoenzymatic vector angles, alleviating relative microbial P-acquisition limitation. Metagenomic and random forest analyses showed that enhanced P acquisition was not primarily linked to a single P-cycling process, but more closely associated with resource stoichiometry and soluble N status, alongside coordinated restructuring of microbial C degradation, N transformation, and P-cycling functions. Overall, AL most strongly ameliorated acidity but elicited weak plant responses; ST produced the strongest biomass response, while AST maintained comparably high P acquisition and markedly improved soil pH. These high-C:P amendments provide a low-P alternative to high-P manure inputs, offering a strategy for reduced-P management and legacy P utilization.
authors: Wang Y, Fan H, Yang X, Wang Z, Shang J, Zhang Q.

title: Antiviral activity of tannic acid against porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus and transcriptomic identification of TNFAIP3 as a candidate proviral host factor.
abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) causes enormous economic losses to the global swine industry. Given the extensive viral diversity and the limited heterologous cross-protection of current vaccines, antiviral strategies with broad activity against diverse PRRSV strains are urgently needed. This study investigated the anti-PRRSV activity of tannic acid (TA), a plant-derived polyphenol. TA potently inhibited PRRSV replication in both MARC-145 cells (half-maximal inhibitory concentration [IC50] = 5.34 μM; selectivity index [SI] = 12.59) and primary porcine alveolar macrophages (IC50 = 4.22 μM; SI = 42.65) and exhibited broad activity against multiple lineages of PRRSV-2. Mode-of-action assays revealed that TA primarily exerts virucidal and post-entry inhibitory effects. RNA sequencing-based transcriptomic analysis of TA-treated, PRRSV-infected cells identified differentially expressed genes significantly enriched in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and interleukin-17 (IL-17) signaling pathways. Among five candidate genes selected for small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated functional validation, knockdown of TNF alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3, also known as A20) most significantly suppressed PRRSV replication. PRRSV infection markedly upregulated TNFAIP3 expression, and TA reversed this upregulation in a dose-dependent manner. TNFAIP3 silencing reduced viral RNA levels, nucleocapsid (N) protein expression, and infectious titers, with the most pronounced effect during early infection. Collectively, the findings identify TA as a potent anti-PRRSV polyphenol and reveal TNFAIP3 as a candidate proviral host factor that is upregulated during PRRSV infection, providing insights into virus-host interactions and potential targets for host-directed antiviral strategies.
authors: Liu R, Liu T, Miao C, Zhou Q, Gao P, Zhang Y, Ge X, Han J, Guo X, Zhou L, Yang H.

title: Convergent Biogenic Magnetite Formation from Diverse Iron (Oxyhydr)oxide Precursors Drives Cr(VI) Reduction via an Environmental Battery Mechanism.
abstract: Iron (oxyhydr)oxides mediate electron flux across coupled biogeochemical cycles in anoxic environments, yet whether their biogenic transformation feeds back to reshape interfacial electron transfer efficiency remains unresolved. Here, five structurally distinct iron (oxyhydr)oxide precursors (ferrihydrite, goethite, magnetite, wüstite, and hematite) were exposed to anaerobic sulfur-oxidizing bioreactors under Cr(VI) stress, and their transformation trajectories were tracked using synchrotron EXAFS spectroscopy, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, DFT calculations, and metagenomic profiling. Mineral bioavailability decreased in the order ferrihydrite > goethite > magnetite > wüstite > hematite, a hierarchy governed by lattice iron-leaching energetics quantified via DFT (Efev from -8.96 eV for ferrihydrite to 5.76 eV for hematite). Despite this wide disparity in precursor lability, all biotransformation trajectories converged on magnetite as the thermodynamically stable end point. In the ferrihydrite system, biogenic magnetite reached 60% of the final solid phase and operated as an in situ "environmental battery" (storing and releasing electrons through reversible Fe(II)/Fe(III) lattice cycling), lowering interfacial charge transfer resistance and producing a 4.77-fold higher pseudo-first-order Cr(VI) reduction rate constant than the mineral-free biotic control (C-S). Metagenomic analysis revealed mineral-specific restructuring of the microbial community toward a tightly coupled sulfur-iron redox network. These results reframe precursor mineralogy from a determinant of intrinsic reactivity to a kinetic regulator of biogenic electron-buffer formation, providing a mechanistic basis for mineral-informed bioremediation design.
authors: Chen N, Yuan Y, Zhan Y, Cao W, An N, Xiao Q, Feng C, Liu T, Wu S, Guo H.

title: Exploring the antibiofilm potential of marine Streptomyces sp. VITNABS17 against biofilm forming Klebsiella pneumoniae: an in vitro and in silico approach.
abstract: Biofilm-associated bacterial infections pose a significant challenge in clinical settings due to their persistence and reduced susceptibility to current antimicrobials, underscoring the need for novel antibiofilm agents. This study aimed to evaluate the antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of cell-free extracts from marine Streptomyces sp. using integrated in vitro and in silico approaches. Initial antibacterial screening by agar well diffusion assay identified VITNABS17 as the most active isolate, exhibiting a broad antibacterial spectrum against the tested bacterial pathogens. Evaluation of biofilm formation by tube method revealed K. pneumoniae as the strongest biofilm-forming pathogen. The ethyl acetate extract of VITNABS17 reduced K. pneumoniae biofilm biomass by 66.2 ± 0.22% at 20 mg/mL, while the minimum biofilm inhibitory concentration (MBIC) was 1 mg/mL, corresponding to 55.50% inhibition. GC-MS analysis revealed a diverse metabolite profile, with diethyl phthalate identified as the most abundant compound. Molecular docking predicted binding affinities of -6.0 kcal/mol for MrkA and -4.4 kcal/mol for LuxS, indicating potential interactions of diethyl phthalate with biofilm-associated protein targets. The potential isolate was identified as Streptomyces sp. VITNABS17 by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Overall, these findings provide preliminary evidence for the antibiofilm potential of VITNABS17 and warrant further investigation into the identification and characterization of its active metabolites.
authors: Bose N, Sarkar A, S Babu A, Rao KVB.

title: Anti-Bacterial and Anti-Biofilm Activities of Cell-Free Supernatant of Lactobacillus johnsonii Against Salmonella Typhimurium.
abstract: Salmonella Typhimurium is a predominant foodborne pathogen whose robust biofilm-forming capacity poses a persistent challenge to food safety and public health. This study investigated the inhibitory effects of cell-free supernatant (CFS) derived from Lactobacillus johnsonii on biofilms and characterized the transcriptional responses associated with CFS exposure using RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). L.johnsonii CFS retarded bacterial growth at high concentrations. Moreover, CFS at various concentrations significantly inhibited biofilm formation in both S. Typhimurium strains, SL1344 and 14028, with maximum inhibition rates of 88.22% and 79.32%, respectively. CFS treatment markedly reduced metabolic activity, surface hydrophobicity, and auto-aggregation, meanwhile impaired bacterial motility and disrupted the architectural integrity of the biofilms. Furthermore, the CFS effectively prevented biofilm formation on various food and food-contact surfaces. RNA-seq analysis revealed that CFS treatment significantly altered the transcriptional profiles of Salmonella, with differentially expressed genes mainly enriched in ribosome, carbon metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, secondary metabolite biosynthesis, and microbial metabolism in diverse environments. These findings demonstrate the antibiofilm potential of L. johnsonii CFS under laboratory conditions and indicate its potential in controlling Salmonella contamination in food industry.
authors: Zhang M, Zhu W, Wang A, Li H, Zhao S, Wang W, Xia X, Ren X.

title: Mucosal disease associated with BVDV-1b and BVDV-1e in cattle in Southern Brazil.
abstract: Bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) is an important pathogen of the global cattle industry. Fetal infection during the period of immunotolerance may result in the birth of persistently infected (PI) animals. In such animals, the emergence of or superinfection with cytopathic variants may trigger mucosal disease (MD). The objective of this study was to characterize the anatomopathological and virological aspects of two cases of MD. Animal 1, a 24-month-old presented with diarrhea, weight loss, lameness, sialorrhea, and oral and cutaneous lesions. Animal 2, a four-month-old, exhibited weight loss, intermittent diarrhea, and dehydration. Both animals were submitted to necropsy, and tissue samples from all organs were collected for histopathological evaluation. For BVDV detection, serum samples were subjected to RT-PCR and amplified products were submitted to Sanger sequencing and phylogenetic analysis. Liver and spleen fragments were used for viral isolation in MDBK cell cultures. Immunohistochemistry using the panpestiviral monoclonal antibody 15C5 was performed to detect BVDV antigen. Anatomopathological examination of Animal 1 revealed ulcerative glossitis, erosive stomatitis, erosive and ulcerative esophagitis as well as erosive and ulcerative rumenitis, erosive abomasitis, and ulcerative and crusting dermatitis affecting the nasal planum and the distal limb region. In Animal 2, ulcerative rumenitis, erosive abomasitis, and lymphoid depletion in the ileal Peyer's patches were observed. Both animals were positive for BVDV in immunohistochemistry and classified as BVDV-1e and BVDV-1b based on phylogenetic analysis. Viral isolates from both cases induced cytopathic effect between 48 and 96 h post-inoculation. This study demonstrates distinct lesion patterns in unrelated cases of MD associated with BVDV-1e and BVDV-1b in cattle, constitutes the first report of typical MD associated with these subgenotypes in Brazil.
authors: Marian L, Baumbach LF, Withoeft JA, Ferreira AB, Hilbe M, Rocha EV, Wisser CS, da Costa UM, Canal CW, Casagrande RA.

title: MXene-polydopamine-cyanobacteria photobioelectrochemical biosensor for atrazine detection in environmental waters.
abstract: A cyanobacteria-based photobioelectrochemical biosensor was developed for the first time using Synechococcus elongatus whole cells immobilized on a Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene electrode modified with an electropolymerized polydopamine (PDA) layer. This surface created a biotic-abiotic interface that facilitated light-driven electron transfer for the sensitive screening of photosystem II (PSII)-inhibiting herbicides in environmental waters, using atrazine (ATZ) as a model analyte. The biosensor was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The detection strategy relies on the inhibition of PSII photosynthetic activity, which produces a concentration-dependent decrease in photocurrent. Under optimized conditions, the biosensor achieved a limit of detection (LOD) of 1.92 nM (0.414 ppb), a linear range of 5-200 nM, and a sensitivity of 177.71 nA decade⁻¹ cm⁻². Interference studies demonstrated class selectivity toward PSII-inhibiting herbicides (e.g., DCMU, simazine, desethylatrazine), with negligible response ( 95% for 1 day and approximately 93% at day 2. However, a 61% signal loss was observed by day 5 (stored at 4 °C), highlighting an operational limitation inherent to whole-cell biological systems. The biosensor was successfully applied to determine ATZ in groundwater, river water, and seawater, delivering accurate recoveries (99.75-103.9%) and offering a green alternative for on-site environmental monitoring.
authors: Silva CCG, Bueno ML, Falone MF, de Lima LF, de Araujo WR, Zanoni MVB, Beluomini MA.

title: Integrated GWAS and linkage analysis to reveal genetic loci for maize ear traits.
abstract: Maize ear architecture is a critical determinant of grain yield, yet its genetic basis remains incompletely understood. This study aims to explore novel genetic variations generated by radiation-induced mutagenesis, systematically dissect the genetic basis of key maize ear traits and develop molecular markers capable of effectively distinguishing germplasm with contrasting ear phenotypes. We conducted an integrated genomic analysis of four key ear traits (ear length (EL), diameter (ED), ear row number (ERN), and kernel number per row (KNR)) using two radiation-mutagenized populations: 1355 multi-background radiation-induced mutant lines (RMLs) derived from three elite inbred lines (ZH6218, T32, and ZNC442), and 626 radiation-induced mutant lines derived from the ZH6218 background (ZF6218), grown in two environments. Phenotypic evaluation revealed substantial variation, with ED and ERN showing high heritability, while KNR exhibited stronger genotype-environment interactions. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identified 53 suggestive QTNs, including three pleiotropic loci associated with both ED and KNR. Linkage mapping in ZF6218 uncovered 36 segregation distortion loci (SDLs), with eight novel loci contributing to ear morphology. Notably, a prominent KNR-associated SDL (SDL-KNR8.2) co-localized with a GWAS peak (S08_18815086), narrowing the candidate interval to 575 kb on chromosome 8 harboring 22 genes. Spatiotemporal expression profiling suggested three distinct gene clusters: early apical, intermediate elongation, and late differentiation, implicating hierarchical control of meristem development. In silico candidate gene analysis identified a C/T SNP in the second exon of Zm00001d008757 that is significantly associated with KNR variation, which may serve as a candidate marker for breeding selection. These findings provide a theoretical basis and candidate resources for understanding maize ear development, and warrant further validation before application in molecular breeding.
authors: Wu Z, Jiang X, Jiang Y, Tu L, Liu P, Guo X, Wang A, Zhu Y, Lu X, Chen Z, Wu X.

title: Molecular Characterization of Feline Leukemia Virus from Cats in Shelters in the Metropolitan Region of Recife, Pernambuco, Northeast Brazil.
abstract: This research aimed to conduct an epidemiological-molecular study of feline leukemia virus (FeLV) infection in cats from shelters in the Metropolitan Region of Recife (MRR), Pernambuco, Northeast Brazil. Blood samples from 260 cats from 18 shelters located in 5 municipalities within the MRR were analyzed. DNA samples from peripheral blood were subjected to Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) to detect FeLV proviral DNA. PCR-positive samples were sequenced and analyzed using BLAST software for phylogenetic tree construction. The prevalence of infection in cats was 9.6% (25/260). Among the 18 sampled shelters, 33.3% (6/18) had cats positive for FeLV. It was observed that 60% (3/5) of the investigated municipalities had felines positive for FeLV infection. Among the positive cats, males accounted for 52% (13/25) and females for 48% (12/25). Of the 22 sequenced samples, 18 sequences were used as queries for an online BLAST search to build a dataset. This study is pioneering in the state of Pernambuco and demonstrates the prevalence of FeLV infection in felines living in shelters in the Metropolitan Region of Recife, PE. Based on these results, we recommend vaccinating any cat with outdoor access in the study region. Understanding the prevalence of FeLV in Pernambuco provides insights into the local situation and helps develop effective hygienic-sanitary programs in feline shelters in the MRR, contributing to increased awareness of responsible pet ownership and reducing FeLV transmission among community felines.
authors: da Silva Farias CK, Duarte PM, da Silva Junior WJ, Januário CAB, Carvalho Maia RC, de Carvalho OV, Pinheiro Junior JW.

title: Genome-wide DNA Methylation Difference Between Sexes in Juveniles and Epigenetic Regulation of Sexual Development in Intersex Crabs Eriocheir sinensis.
abstract: Epigenetic regulation of sexual development is widely documented in model species, yet data for commercial invertebrates remain limited. Here, we used whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) to profile genome-wide DNA methylation and identify differentially methylated regions (DMRs) between the female and male juveniles at stage III in the Chinese mitten crab Eriocheir sinensis. Global methylated cytosines accounted for approximately 1.44% and 1.45% of all cytosines in the female and male genomes, respectively. Among the CpG, CHG, and CHH contexts, CpG showed the highest mean methylation levels, at 8.15% in females and 8.08% in males. A total of 21,038 nominally significant DMRs were identified between sexes, with 11,557 (55%) hypermethylated DMRs in males. Notably, the methylation level of the ZW chromosome was the highest compared to the ZZ chromosome and the autosomes, suggesting sex-biased epigenetic modification within the ZW/ZZ sex determination system. On autosomes, the hypermethylated DMRs in females were mainly detected in the gene body regions of Sex lethal, Male-specific lethal 3, Feminization-1c, and Feminization-1a. On the ZW chromosome, 233 DMRs were hypermethylated in females, whereas 161 were hypermethylated in males. Furthermore, in the intersex crabs (ZW) bearing male first gonopods, the promoter of LOC113817324 exhibited intersex-specific hypermethylation in the ovary, whereas intronic methylation of the Serine/threonine-protein kinase (ATR) remained low, mirroring the pattern observed in normal male (ZZ) testes. These findings reveal sex- and intersex-associated DNA methylation patterns in E. sinensis and provide candidate epigenetic loci for further investigation of sexual development.
authors: Zhang YQ, Lai XL, Liu XY, Yang JX, Tang MJ, Wu XG, Qiu GF.

title: Low variability in the capsid gene of a generalist densovirus across lepidopteran hosts and geographic regions.
abstract: Viruses are ubiquitous in all ecosystems, and insects can serve as model host systems for understanding their geographic range and host specificity. Lepidoptera are relatively easy to collect and rear and are known to harbor diverse groups of viral pathogens. Much of the research on viruses in Lepidoptera has focused on baculoviruses, but this is beginning to change with better sequencing techniques. In this study, we use genetic tools to characterize the host and geographical range of the Junonia coenia densovirus (JcDV) (Family Parvoviridae, subfamily Densovirinae, genus Protoambidensovirus, specific epithet lepidopteran1). Using host tissue and larval frass, we screened 25 lepidopteran families from 11 locations across North and Central and South America for JcDV. We detected JcDV in the frass from 11 families of Lepidoptera, originating from both Neotropical and Nearctic biogeographic realms. To characterize genetic variation in the viruses detected, we conducted Sanger sequencing of a segment of the viral capsid gene in ten frass samples and from an additional 56 individual lepidopteran cadavers from three families in the Papilionoidea superfamily. Across all sequences obtained, the average sequence identity to the Oxford reference genome sequence was 99.85% and within our samples 99.77%. Compared to the reference, we found 18 nucleotide changes which were characterized into ten JcDV haplotype variants. These differences conferred seven amino acid substitutions and were not predicted by sample type (frass or cadaver tissue), geographic location, or lepidopteran host family. Ultimately, we conclude that JcDV is a widespread virus to which many lepidopteran families are exposed in their natural environment, and the capsid gene of JcDV is genetically well-conserved across geographic space and lepidopteran host species.
authors: McKeegan KJ, Muchoney ND, Peechatt V, Dyer LA, Teglas MB, Smilanich AM.

title: Pan-pediatric brain tumor microRNA networks define immune microenvironment states and responses to CAR T-cell therapy
abstract: Pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors remain a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in children, yet molecular programs that shape their immune microenvironments and response to immunotherapy remain poorly defined. Because microRNAs (miRNAs) coordinately regulate gene expression across multiple pathways, we hypothesized that miRNA programs may capture broader immune states than individual immune-regulatory molecules. We integrated small RNA and bulk transcriptomic profiles from diffuse midline glioma, medulloblastoma, ependymoma, and low-grade glioma to identify miRNA programs associated with tumor immune states. Across tumor histologies, dysregulated miRNAs were associated with T-cell, natural killer cell, antigen-presentation, and myeloid programs. Diffuse midline glioma exhibited a distinct miRNA program associated with reduced lymphocyte signatures and increased suppressive myeloid features. Longitudinal profiling of immunocompetent glioma models during B7-H3 CAR T-cell therapy revealed dynamic remodeling of miRNA and immune transcriptional programs. Human tumor-associated miRNAs were significantly enriched among miRNAs associated with CAR T response  in vivo . Functional interrogation of miR-149 demonstrated enhanced CAR T-cell expansion and sustained antitumor activity during repeated antigen stimulation. Together, these data define miRNA programs associated with immune states across pediatric CNS tumors and identify miR-149 as a candidate regulator of CAR T-cell function, providing a genomic framework for developing miRNA-directed strategies to improve CAR T-cell therapy.  Importance of Study  Pediatric CNS tumors exhibit distinct immunomodulatory microRNA signatures that are associated with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and are altered following B7-H3 CAR T-cell therapy. Identification of therapy-responsive microRNAs conserved across preclinical models and patient samples provides potential targets for simultaneously modulating multiple suppressive pathways and improving immunotherapy outcomes in pediatric brain tumors.
authors: Coleman K, Corbett R, Yi Z, Song B, Sickler A, Babaei A, Rokita JL, Haydar D.

title: Inference and validation of causal genetic interactions in aging human fibroblasts
abstract: In the past hundred years, the fraction of fatalities due to age-related disease has risen from an envied minority of cases to the leading cause of death and economic morbidity in the developed world. Despite notable advances in understanding aging, its intrinsic complexity has prevented major therapeutic break-throughs. This complexity extends across all systems and scales in an organism, leaving a ‘fingerprint of aging’ across every aspect of cell and tissue behavior whose interrelationships are difficult to untangle. Compounding this problem, human aging is observed largely through cross-sectional rather than longitudinal data. Whether such data retain sufficient dynamical information to reveal causal interactions is unclear. Here we show that they can. Using convergent cross mapping (CCM), a method for identifying causal interactions in nonlinear dynamical systems, we reconstruct directed genetic interactions from age-ordered, cross-sectional transcriptomic data—recovering dynamics from populations rather than individuals. Applied to dermal fibroblasts from 490 GTEx donors, CCM identifies a genome-scale causal network whose topology, together with age-dependent changes in gene expression, predicts candidate drivers of aging. We tested these predictions experimentally by single-gene overexpression in fibroblasts from 55-year-old donors. Single-cell RNA sequencing confirmed 53.8% of testable CCM-predicted causal interactions, showing that dynamics reconstructed from cross-sectional populations contain experimentally recoverable information about gene-gene interactions. This 53.8% additionally exceeded that produced by multiple comparanda methods and a random null. We then asked whether this information could identify interventions that reverse cellular aging. Independent transcriptomic and high-dimensional morphological assays show that CCM-selected perturbations shift old fibroblasts toward states characteristic of young cells. These two measures of rejuvenation are strongly correlated, and the strongest interventions cause a majority of 55-year-old cells to resemble cells from 25-year-old donors. Thus, causal dynamics can be recovered from cross-sectional population data and used to identify interventions in aging. More generally, the results suggest a way to distinguish genes that change with age from genes that drive those changes, providing experimentally testable targets for altering the aging phenotype.
authors: Krieger MS, Milanova D, Thompson D, Cochran NR, Wang T, Pokharel B, Ford RP, Gheorghe AH, Gilpin W, Freund Y, Sugihara G, Church G.

title: Dual recognition of phage SSB triggers DRT4 for antiphage defense
abstract: Defense-associated reverse transcriptase 4 (DRT4) protects bacteria against phages through single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) synthesis and activation of an effector RNase. How precisely phage recognition is coupled to RNase activation remains unclear. Here, we combine structural, biochemical, and genetic analyses to define the requirements for DRT4 activation. Cryo-electron microscopy structures capture DNA synthesis and provide a structural basis for preferential purine incorporation. Screening against the BASEL phage collection reveals protection against diverse phages and identifies the Bas17-encoded ssDNA-binding (SSB) protein gp44 as a DRT4 trigger. We show that DRT4 requires both recognition of its ssDNA product and direct protein-protein interactions of gp44 for RNase activation. Together, our findings support a previously unrecognized “two-factor authentication” model in which ssDNA-mediated recruitment of a phage SSB cooperates with specific protein interactions to license abortive infection for antiphage defense.
authors: Jasnauskaitė M, Cibulskis A, Kazlauskaitė K, Skorupskaitė A, Juozapaitis J, Mikšys A, Tomkuvienė M, Malinauskaitė L, Pausch P.

title: Hidden Players: Latent Viruses Can Modulate Plant Disease Outcomes in Coinfection Contexts
abstract: ABSTRACT  Latent viruses are ubiquitous components of plant viromes and are likely the rule rather than the exception in natural host populations. Yet, despite their prevalence, little is known about how they influence the outcome of infections by acute viruses. Here, we used a factorial design to test the effects of two latent secoviruses, apple latent spherical virus (ALSV) and Arabidopsis latent virus 1 (ArLV1), on infections by the acute viruses tobacco rattle virus (TRV) and turnip mosaic virus (TuMV). Coinfections were evaluated across eight  Arabidopsis thaliana genotypes, including wild-type and mutants impaired in RNA silencing, DNA methylation and hormone-signaling pathways. Latent-virus effects on both viral accumulation and disease severity were highly dependent on the combination of host and viral genotypes. Hormonal pathways played a prominent role in mediating these interactions, with recurrent responses involving jasmonic acid, salicylic acid and ethylene signaling. ALSV generally attenuated disease severity and acute-virus accumulation, whereas ArLV1 produced both antagonistic and synergistic outcomes depending on host background. Notably, ArLV1 coinfection increased TuMV-induced disease severity in some genotype, an effect never observed with ALSV. These results demonstrate that latent viruses can substantially modify disease expression and viral fitness and highlight the need to account for the pre-existing virome when predicting plant disease outcomes, viral emergence, and epidemiological dynamics.
authors: Lafforgue G, Elena SF.

title: When the forest speaks again: in-depth genomic analysis of serotyping failure reveals geographic extension of sylvatic DENV-2 in southeastern Senegal, 2026
abstract: In August 2026, eight febrile patients in the Kédougou and Tambacounda regions of Senegal tested positive by pan-flavivirus and pan-dengue RT-PCR but could not be assigned to a serotype. In-depth genome sequencing identified sylvatic dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2, genotype VI). These findings indicate the re-emergence and geographic spread of DENV-2/GVI beyond its historical focus.
authors: Dieng I, Efire AS, Sagne SN, Ndione MHD, Camara D, Doukanda SFM, Dia N, Diallo B, Barry MA, Fall G, Faye O.

title: GWAS of Lyme disease identifies five loci and discovers a connection with post-infectious diseases
abstract: Lyme disease is a vector-borne bacterial infection with marked heterogeneity in susceptibility and clinical manifestations. We investigated the genetic architecture and clinical heterogeneity of Lyme disease using genetic and longitudinal health data from FinnGen and the Estonian Biobank. Genome-wide association analyses included 37,571 individuals with Lyme disease and 670,567 controls (N = 708,138), complemented by sex-stratified analyses and temporal phenotyping in FinnGen. The overall GWAS meta-analysis identified three genome-wide significant loci at  SCGB1D2 ,  TLR1/TLR6 , and  HLA-DQA1 . Sex-stratified analyses identified additional genome-wide significant signals at  CPE in males (β = −0.077, P = 2.99 × 10⁻⁸) and the  TYMP-CPT1B locus in females (β = −0.064, P = 4.98 × 10⁻⁸). The  TLR1/6 association was more pronounced in males (β = −0.141, P = 2.16 × 10⁻¹²) than in females (β = −0.060, P = 1.21 × 10⁻⁵).  Temporal phenotyping showed enrichment of neurological, musculoskeletal, and dermatological manifestations after Lyme disease diagnosis, with associations generally attenuating over time. Bell palsy showed the strongest association at 1-6 months (OR 11.49, P = 2.37 × 10⁻⁷⁹), while joint pain was also enriched during this interval (OR 1.74, P = 1.95 × 10⁻²³). Early associations with joint pain and Bell palsy were stronger in males than in females. These findings expand the genetic architecture of Lyme disease, implicate innate immune sensing through the  TLR1/TLR6 locus, and antigen presentation through the HLA associations. Overall, the results highlight a strong polygenic signal with Lyme disease and a connection with other post-infectious clinical manifestations.
authors: Strausz S, Romppanen E, Haapaniemi H, FinnGen, Estonian Biobank Research Team, Health Informatics Research Team, Saxena R, Sinnott-Armstrong N, Abner E, Ollila HM.
