title: On-site slaughter and dressing in retail chicken outlets: Escherichia coli contamination and antimicrobial resistance on food-contact surfaces in Dhaka Division, Bangladesh
abstract: Abstract    Background  The retail poultry-processing environment is a critical reservoir for multidrug-resistant (MDR)  Escherichia coli  , posing significant zoonotic and public health risks. In Bangladesh, there is limited regulatory oversight on antibiotic application in poultry production, leading to frequent and indiscriminate use which allows resistant bacteria to persist on processing surfaces and potentially enter the human food chain, posing significant public health risks. This study assessed the prevalence, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profiles, and genetic determinants of  E. coli  isolated from retail chicken outlets in Dhaka Division. Methods  A total of 180 swab samples were collected from knives, cutting tables, and dressing machines across six outlets in Savar, Sreepur, and Dhamrai upazilas from July to October 2025.  E. coli  was isolated using selective culture, biochemically confirmed via VITEK®2, and molecularly validated by PCR targeting the malB gene. Susceptibility to twelve antimicrobial agents was determined by disc diffusion and interpreted against CLSI criteria, and isolates were screened by PCR for blaOXA-1, sul1 and sul3. Results  Of 180 samples, 90 (50%) yielded  E. coli  , with knives showing the highest contamination (57.9%), followed by tables (47.6%) and dressing machines (45.0%). Resistance was most frequent to ampicillin (96%), trimethoprim (96%), azithromycin (93%), nalidixic acid (89%) and tetracycline (89%); meropenem remained active against 93% of isolates. The Spearman correlation analysis revealed strong positive associations among β-lactam antibiotics, moderate correlations between β-lactams and aminoglycosides, and negative correlation between ciprofloxacin and meropenem, suggesting both co-selection and independent resistance mechanisms among the studied isolates. Multiple Antibiotic Resistance (MAR) indices ranged from 0.00 to 0.83, with 93.3% exceeding 0.2, indicating significant selective pressure from antimicrobial exposure. Molecular analysis revealed sul-3 (26.7%) and blaOXA-1 (23.3%) as predominant resistance genes, with 13.3% of isolates harboring multiple determinants. Conclusion  E. coli  was present on half of all food-contact surfaces at comparable frequency across implements, and most isolates were resistant to multiple antimicrobial classes. Contamination was distributed across the dressing station rather than concentrated on any single implement, so hygiene measures targeting one item are unlikely to suffice. The gap between phenotypic resistance and the genes screened indicates further determinants warranting genomic investigation.
authors: Rihad M, Ammar NHM, Shahadat MN, Islam S, Roy UK, Hossain MR, Siddique AB, Sarkar S, Hossain MA.

title: Germplasm evaluation and different control strategies against Rhizoctonia solani in potato
abstract: Abstract    Black scurf and stem canker caused by the soil-borne basidiomycete  Rhizoctonia solani  (teleomorph  Thanatephorus cucumeris  ) remain major constraints to potato production worldwide. This study combined morphological and ITS-based molecular characterisation of  R. solani  isolates from black-scurf-affected tubers in Faisalabad, Pakistan, with screening of 50 potato germplasm entries and comparative evaluation of four chemical fungicides, six plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR),  Trichoderma harzianum  and six aqueous plant extracts. Five isolates (Rs1-Rs5) were confirmed as  R. solani  by ITS sequencing and deposited in GenBank (PZ952552-PZ952556). Neighbour-Joining phylogeny placed them within the  R. solani  /  T. cucumeris  clade. Germplasm responses ranged from resistant (FD3536, FD63-1, FD78-36; disease incidence 6–8%) to highly susceptible (Simply Red = 93%).  In vitro  , Cabrio Top and Antracol completely inhibited mycelial growth at 50 and 100 ppm.  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  (OR741775) produced 100% growth inhibition and  P. putida  (PX496465) 89.6–93.6%;  T. harzianum  (PZ955200) gave 45.4–47.8% inhibition in dual culture. Among extracts,  Azadirachta indica  at 15% yielded the highest inhibition (41.9%). In a subsequent pot trial on the susceptible cultivar Kashmir,  P. aeruginosa  ,  P. putida  , Cabrio Top, Antracol, Miravis Duo,  T. harzianum  ,  A. indica  and  Calotropis procera  reduced disease incidence and severity to zero;  P. aeruginosa  and  P. putida  also produced the highest tuber numbers (10 and 9 per plant). Multivariate analyses confirmed the superiority of selected  Pseudomonas  strains. The results identify useful host resistance and effective chemical and biological agents that can contribute to integrated management of potato black scurf.
authors: Usman M, Ehetisham-Ul-Haq M, Kamran M, Abbas A, Ahmad U, Ehsan S, Arif UB, Abbas H.

title: 3-Methylpentanoic Acid Controls Wheat Blast Disease by Disrupting Cell Wall Integrity and Putatively Targeting UDP-Glucose 4-Epimerase.
abstract: Wheat blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae Triticum (MoT), is a devastating fungal disease threatening global food security. The emergence of fungicide-resistant MoT populations necessitates safe, eco-friendly alternatives. This study evaluates the biorational potential of 3-methylpentanoic acid (3-MP), a volatile organic compound (VOC) produced by Bacillus safensis NI2B against MoT. In vitro assays demonstrated that 3-MP inhibits MoT mycelial growth, conidiogenesis, conidial germination, and appressorium formation in a dose-dependent manner, achieving complete suppression at 100 to 125 µM. Furthermore, detached leaf, seedling, and spike assays revealed robust preventive and curative efficacy, indicating strong translational potential for wheat blast management. Mechanistic analyses indicated reduced fungal cellular viability following 3-MP treatment, as confirmed by fluorescein diacetate staining. In silico molecular screening and dynamics simulations predicted that 3-MP putatively interacts with UDP-glucose 4-epimerase (UGE), a key enzyme in galactose metabolism and cell wall integrity. 3-MP binds stably within the NAD+-associated Rossmann fold of UGE, sterically hindering substrate access and perturbing NAD+ orientation. RT-qPCR expression analysis was consistent with this model, showing a biphasic response characterized by early induction followed by significant repression of UGE transcripts, which aligns with disrupted UDP-glucose metabolism and impaired cell wall biosynthesis. Collectively, this study establishes 3-MP as a potent biocontrol agent and provides preliminary mechanistic insights into its antifungal activity associated with UGE perturbation. These findings offer a promising molecular framework for developing VOC-based integrated pest management strategies against wheat blast. [Formula: see text] Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). title: Molecular evidence of spotted fever group Rickettsia and Lyme disease- and relapsing fever-associated Borrelia, and the absence of scrub typhus-associated Orientia in ixodid ticks from contrasting habitats in Peninsular Malaysia.
abstract: Tick-borne pathogens are emerging across Southeast Asia, but their diversity and ecological drivers in Malaysia remain poorly understood. We screened 539 ixodid ticks collected from natural forests, marginal habitats, and oil palm plantations in Peninsular Malaysia for Rickettsia spp., Borrelia spp., and Orientia tsutsugamushi using PCR and phylogenetic analyses. Overall, 10.61% (7/66) of tick pools tested positive for bacterial pathogens. Rickettsia was detected in 4.55% (3/66) of pools from Dermacentor auratus and Amblyomma cordiferum, whereas Borrelia was detected in 6.06% (4/66) of pools from A. cordiferum, Haemaphysalis hystricis, and Ixodes granulatus. Orientia tsutsugamushi was not detected. Phylogenetic analyses placed the detected Rickettsia within ancestral and spotted fever groups and the detected Borrelia within Lyme disease and relapsing fever clades. Positive detections suggested habitat-specific patterns, with Borrelia identified only in forest-derived tick pools, Rickettsia detected in both forest and marginal habitats, and none of the targeted pathogens detected in plantation-derived pools. This study provides comparative molecular evidence of zoonotic tick-borne bacteria across contrasting landscapes in Peninsular Malaysia, establishing a baseline for future surveillance and underscoring the need to investigate how land-use change may influence pathogen transmission at the human-wildlife interface.
journal: International journal for parasitology. Parasites and wildlife
authors: Taufik AS, Husin NA, AbdulHalim AA, AbdulRahim MHS, Jiliun EA, Mufasirin, Hastutiek P, Ya'cob Z.

title: Ecological niche partitioning and urbanization-driven restructuring of flea-borne pathogen communities in stray carnivores of Peninsular Malaysia: discovery of uncharacterised Bartonella lineages.
abstract: BackgroundFlea-borne bacteria are emerging zoonotic pathogens of increasing public health importance, yet their ecological distribution, community structure, and genetic diversity across contrasting landscapes in Southeast Asia remain poorly understood. This study investigated flea infestation, flea-borne bacterial pathogens, and their ecological associations in stray cats and dogs across urban, peri-urban, and rural landscapes of Peninsular Malaysia.MethodsA total of 296 stray cats and dogs were examined for flea infestation, and all recovered fleas (n = 636) were identified morphologically and screened individually for Bartonella spp., Rickettsia spp., and Orientia tsutsugamushi using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays followed by Sanger sequencing and phylogenetic analysis. Risk factors associated with flea infestation, Bartonella spp. and Rickettsia spp. occurrence were evaluated using generalized linear models (GLMs), generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs), and Firth's penalized logistic regression, respectively. Pathogen community structure was assessed using alpha diversity indices, non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS), permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA), and tripartite ecological network analysis.ResultsOverall flea infestation prevalence was 32.09% (95/296), with infestation significantly higher in cats (39.44%) than dogs (13.25%) (χ2 = 10.672, df = 1, p = 0.001). All 636 fleas exhibited complete host-associated segregation, with Ctenocephalides felis (n = 485) occurring exclusively on cats and C. orientis (n = 151) exclusively on dogs. Flea-borne pathogens were detected in 71.86% (457/636) of fleas, comprising Bartonella henselae, B. clarridgeiae, B. koehlerae, several uncharacterized Bartonella lineages, Rickettsia felis, and R. asembonensis. Urban landscapes were associated with significantly higher Bartonella prevalence in C. felis (70.05%), whereas C. orientis was overwhelmingly dominated by R. asembonensis (94.04%). Ecological analyses demonstrated significant landscape-associated variation in pathogen community composition among C. felis populations but not C. orientis. Phylogenetic analysis identified a distinct, well-supported clade of previously uncharacterized Bartonella lineages (bootstrap = 100%). No O. tsutsugamushi was detected in any flea sample.ConclusionsFlea-borne pathogen communities in Peninsular Malaysia are structured by strong host-vector associations and ecological landscape, with peri-urban environments supporting greater pathogen diversity and urban landscapes demonstrated higher detection of Bartonella in C. felis. The discovery of previously uncharacterized Bartonella lineages expands the known diversity of flea-associated Bartonella in Malaysia and highlights the importance of integrating molecular epidemiology with community ecology to improve surveillance of emerging flea-borne zoonoses.
authors: Alison JT, Taufik AS, Jahfar AI, AbdulHalim AA, Husin NA, Izwan-Anas N, Mansor MS, Ya'cob Z.

title: Network Pharmacology and Molecular Docking on the Mechanism of Epimedium in the Treatment of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease.
abstract: IntroductionTo investigate the mechanism of Epimedium in the treatment of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) using network pharmacology and molecular docking approaches.MethodsThe active components and corresponding targets of Epimedium were screened from the Traditional Chinese Medicine Systems Pharmacology (TCMSP) database. COPD-related disease targets were obtained from the OMIM and GeneCards databases. All target genes were standardized using the UniProt database. Protein-Protein Interaction (PPI) networks, Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment, and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses were performed using the ClusterProfiler R package and the STRING database. The herb-compound-target network and the target-pathway network were constructed in Cytoscape to identify core compounds, key targets, and major pathways. Finally, molecular docking between the core targets and the active compounds was performed using AutoDock Vina.ResultsA total of 23 active components and 223 corresponding targets of Epimedium were identified in the treatment of COPD. The core targets included TP53, IL1B, AKT1, TNF, and IL6. GO enrichment analysis indicated that biological processes were primarily enriched in responses to lipopolysaccharide, molecules of bacterial origin, epithelial cell proliferation and injury repair, and regulation of apoptotic signaling pathways. KEGG pathway enrichment yielded 200 signaling pathways; after excluding irrelevant pathways, the most significantly enriched pathways were predominantly associated with inflammation and immune regulation, including the PI3KAkt, TNF, IL-17, AGE-RAGE, and p53 signaling pathways. Molecular docking results demonstrated that the active compounds of Epimedium exhibited favorable binding affinities with IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF.DiscussionThese findings suggest that Epimedium exerts therapeutic effects against COPD through a multicomponent, multi-target, and multi-pathway regulatory mechanism. The integrated network pharmacology and molecular docking analyses indicate that modulation of inflammatory and oxidative stress-related pathways may represent the principal molecular basis underlying its pharmacological activity, providing mechanistic support for future experimental validation.ConclusionEpimedium exhibits the multi-component, multi-target, and multi-pathway characteristics of traditional Chinese medicine. Its therapeutic effects in COPD are mediated through active ingredients such as quercetin, kaempferol, and luteolin, which regulate core targets including IL-1β, IL-6, TNF, and TP53, and modulate inflammation- and immune-related pathways such as PI3K-Akt, AGE-RAGE, and IL-17. These actions collectively contribute to anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative stress effects, regulation of pulmonary apoptosis, and inhibition of pulmonary vascular and airway remodeling. This study tried to apply network pharmacology and molecular docking to elucidate the multi-target synergistic mechanism of Epimedium in the treatment of COPD, providing a theoretical basis for subsequent experimental validation and drug development.
authors: Pan C, Wang Y, Li Y, He Z, Chen H, Li Z, Fu H, Zhuang S, Liu J.

title: Combined nitrate and oxygen dosing restores phosphorus retention and suppresses sulfide without mobilizing legacy sediment metals in a eutrophic urban lake.
abstract: Lake Schäfersee (Berlin, Germany), a eutrophic urban lake with a regularly anoxic, sulfidic hypolimnion and metal-contaminated sediments, has been treated since 2017 by hypolimnetic dosing of calcium nitrate (Ca(NO3)2) and oxygen-saturated water. We monitored inorganic nutrients, dissolved organic carbon, sulfide, (semi)metals, and the sediment microbial community. Ca(NO3)2 additions produced transient NO3-N peaks confined to the hypolimnion, and concentrations in the epilimnion stayed -1. Bottom-water redox potential turned positive after dosing. Relative to untreated years, hypolimnetic O2 increased, while H2S fell by 82%, PO4-P by 87%, and NH4-N by 72%; pore-water DOC declined by a third within 14 days of dosing. Despite cadmium, chromium, copper, lead and zinc exceeding sediment quality guidelines, no sustained mobilization to the water body occurred, lead stayed below the drinking-water limit. Sediment community composition followed seasonal bottom-water oxygenation rather than treatment status, and methanogenic Methanothrix declined. Microcystis was present in the sediment, but neither the mcyA gene nor microcystin-LR was detected in the water column. Combined Ca(NO3)2 and oxygenated water improved water quality without mobilizing legacy metals or promoting toxigenic cyanobacteria, offering a potential alternative to dredging or aluminum and lanthanum dosing where nitrogen, metal, and cyanobacterial dynamics are monitored.
authors: Burgold R, Klemz R, Wassmann H, Martínez-Ruiz EB, Wagner A, Kaupenjohann M, Szewzyk U, Cooper M.

title: Fine-Scale Population Structure, High Gene Flow and Local Adaptation in Australasian Snapper (Chrysophrys auratus) in New Zealand.
abstract: Understanding how populations are structured and adapt to their local environment is critical for developing effective management strategies. We used the commercially and culturally valued marine teleost Chrysophrys auratus (the Australasian snapper) as an exemplar of a high-gene-flow species to study genetic structure, population connectivity, and local adaptation. We performed whole-genome sequencing of 382 individuals across 13 sample locations, covering the range of the species in New Zealand. We find that snapper consist of two genetic clusters with low levels of genetic differentiation (F ST = 0.0031): a northeastern (NE) and a southwestern (SW) cluster, with genetic discontinuities around the Tauroa and Mahia Peninsulas. We further observe widespread admixture and dispersal events, which are indicative of ongoing gene flow, in particular around the areas of the genetic discontinuities near the Tauroa and Mahia Peninsulas. Selection scans identified 25 regions of interest (ROIs) throughout the genome. The haplotype-based statistic XP-nSL was used to identify which genetic cluster each ROI was most likely under selection, 12 and 13 ROIs for the NE and SW clusters, respectively. The identification of candidate genes with similar molecular functions provided tentative evidence of polygenic adaptation to local environments. Finally, we discuss how monitoring genetic variation contributes to fisheries management by maintaining genetic diversity and resilience in commercial fish. These insights into genetic structure, connectivity, genetic diversity, and local adaptation are critical for protecting species under increased pressure from anthropogenic threats like fishing and climate change, and are thus directly applicable to fisheries management.
authors: Oosting T, Star B, Wellenreuther M, Ritchie PA.

title: Proteo-transcriptomic insights into the venom composition of the ectoparasitoid Eupelmus urozonus.
abstract: BackgroundEctoparasitoid venoms are 'cocktails' of bioactive molecules injected during oviposition to paralyze the host and remodel its physiology and immunity, but for many species of agro-ecological interest, the composition remains poorly defined. In this study, we aimed to describe the venom repertoire of Eupelmus urozonus in an integrated manner by combining transcriptomics of the venom glands and proteomics of the venom.ResultsThe assembly and annotation of the transcriptome, based on BLAST and Gene Ontology, revealed a strong representation of functions related to ion binding and biosynthetic processes, with top hits indicating a marked homology with Nasonia vitripennis. In parallel, LC-MS/MS analysis of venom proteins (from SDS-PAGE bands digested in-gel and queried against a database constructed from the transcriptome, with peptide ion score >18 and a minimum of four such peptides per protein) confidently identified 316 venom proteins; 75 of these have a predicted signal peptide and are therefore classified as predicted secretory components. The main functional classes include hydrolases, proteases, and related inhibitors, as well as stress- and transport-associated proteins. Overall, the venom includes putative immunomodulatory and metabolic factors with lineage-specific innovations, and a significant proportion of proteins are unannotated or potentially species-specific.ConclusionThese results provide a solid basis for the functional validation of new candidate effectors and suggest that the venom of E. urozonus represents a reservoir of bioactive molecules with potential biotechnological applications, particularly in the context of sustainable pest management strategies. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Linking functional biodiversity, natural enemies, and insect microbiomes for sustainable biological control of agricultural pests.
abstract: Global agricultural pests continue to threaten crop productivity. Rising chemical resistance, environmental concerns, and the need for a sustainable food supply have increased interest in ecologically oriented pest control strategies. Furthermore, biological control has emerged as an essential component of sustainable agriculture, where habitat diversification and functional biodiversity can increase natural enemies' abundance, activity, and pest suppression. Recent studies indicate that insect microbiomes are essential for nutrition, immunity, growth, ecological adaptations, and interactions between insects and their natural enemies. Recent research suggests that microbial communities could impact host vulnerability to predators, parasitoids, and entomopathogenic fungi (EPF), which might subsequently influence biological control. Despite these progressions, functional biodiversity, natural enemy ecology, and insect microbiome research have historically developed as relatively separate fields of study. This review aims to synthesize current knowledge on ecological interactions among functional biodiversity, insect microbiomes, and biological control in agricultural systems. We examined the impact of habitat diversification on beneficial insects, the composition and functional role of microbiomes in relation to insect fitness, and the influence of microbial communities on the interaction between pests and biological control agents (BCAs). We then examined recent findings that have shown that environmental conditions, shaped by biodiversity, might affect microbiome assembly through mechanisms such as environmental microbial reservoirs, habitat complexity, and landscape-scale processes. We propose an integrated approach in which functional biodiversity directly influences biological control through ecological interactions and indirectly through the microbiome's effects on pest-natural enemy interactions. We state that biodiversity, microbiomes, and biological control are interconnected processes that should be regarded as integral components of agroecosystem functionality. Microbiome ecology may offer a new opportunity to enhance sustainable pest suppression and reduce chemical inputs in conservation biological management. Future research should focus on multitrophic, field-based, and mechanistic investigations that advance microbiome-informed biological control strategies for resilient and climate-smart agriculture. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: Haider K, Abbas D, Kabir K, Ali MS, Ismail AM, Sufian M.

title: Discovery of novel alleles in Kartagener's syndrome.
abstract: Kartagener's syndrome (KS) is a rare, typically autosomal recessive ciliopathy and a subtype of primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), characterized by situs inversus, bronchiectasis, and chronic sinusitis. KS accounts for approximately 50% of PCD cases and results from impaired motile cilia function. Defective embryonic nodal ciliary beating leads to stochastic left-right axis determination and situs abnormalities. Although numerous genes have been implicated in PCD, up to 30% of cases remain genetically unresolved, and studies specifically focused on KS cohorts remain limited. Here, we performed whole exome sequencing in 17 adult patients from a Turkish KS cohort to identify pathogenic variants and novel candidate genes. Variants were prioritised based on sequencing quality, population allele frequency, and predicted functional impact, and included single-nucleotide variants, small insertions/deletions, and copy-number variations. The restriction of the cohort to individuals with situs inversus provided a phenotype-specific context for variant interpretation, as genes not typically associated with left-right axis determination were less likely to account for disease in this study population. Pathogenic or potentially disease-associated variants were identified in multiple established PCD genes, including DNAH5, DNAI1, DNAI2, DNAAF1, DNAAF3, CFAP300, and ODAD1, with several novel alleles detected. In one patient lacking biallelic variants in known PCD genes, expanded analysis identified heterozygous variants in the cilia-associated genes DLEC1 and DNAAF9 together with a hemizygous copy number loss in EZR, a gene known to affect motile cilia function. The possible relevance of these concurrent findings warrants further investigation in genetically unresolved cases. Overall, analysis of this KS-specific cohort demonstrated a high diagnostic yield, expanded the variant spectrum associated with Kartagener's syndrome, and further supported the utility of phenotype-driven genomic analysis in genetically heterogeneous ciliopathies.
journal: Mammalian genome : official journal of the International Mammalian Genome Society
authors: Coskunpinar EM, Sifoglu D, Tasolar FET, Yildirim H, Cetinkaya E.

title: Creating the first synthetic plastid genome in plants.
abstract: Over the last decade, there has been a shift in biotechnology from genome reading (sequencing) to genome writing (engineering). While significant progress has been made in prokaryotes and yeast, genome writing remains in its infancy in plants. Unlike their complex nuclear genomes, the compact and biotechnologically attractive plastid genome represents an ideal target to launch plant genome writing at scale.
authors: Lenaghan SC, Bock R, Dunkelmann DL, Karas BJ, Mordaka PM, Pfotenhauer AC, Purton S, Smith AG, Stewart CN.

title: Cyclic lipopeptide nano-assemblies induce mitochondrial apoptosis and suppress migration in hepatocellular carcinoma cells with mitochondrial perturbation and Snail2 downregulation.
abstract: Cyclic lipopeptides represent a promising class of bioactive molecules with potential anticancer applications. Here, we investigate the anti-hepatoma activity and mechanism of B-Lb, a cyclic lipopeptide featuring a heptapeptide backbone and a unique fatty acid tail. Our study reveals that the fatty acid tail is indispensable for B-Lb's bioactivity, as its removal or substitution abolishes cytotoxicity and alters self-assembly morphology. B-Lb undergoes concentration-dependent self-assembly into nanorods, a process directed by its hydrophobic tail. In vitro, B-Lb potently inhibits the proliferation of SMMC-7721 hepatocellular carcinoma cells (IC50 = 5.852 μM), an effect associated with mitochondrial apoptosis. B-Lb-induced cytotoxicity was accompanied by mitochondrial perturbation, including changes consistent with mPTP opening, a reduced Bcl-2/Bax ratio, and marked alterations in mitochondrial morphology. Furthermore, B-Lb suppresses cell migration by downregulating the pro-metastatic transcription factor Snail2. In a murine xenograft model, B-Lb (30 mg/kg) demonstrates robust antitumor efficacy, inducing significant tumor necrosis and reducing Ki67 proliferation index without causing treatment-associated body-weight loss, suggesting acceptable gross tolerability under the tested conditions. Exploratory differential protein expression analysis further suggests potential alterations in glycolysis, cytoskeletal integrity, and nucleic acid homeostasis associated with the response to B-Lb. Collectively, our findings establish B-Lb as a potent, self-assembling cyclic lipopeptide that acts on multiple facets of hepatoma cell biology, including proliferation, mitochondrial integrity, and migration, highlighting its potential as a novel therapeutic candidate for hepatocellular carcinoma.
authors: Lu JY, He BS, Wang DH, Li YQ, Guo Z, Huang WT.

title: Epigenetics of HFRS: Linking immunity, pathogenesis, and vaccine-induced protection.
abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV), is an important public-health concern, particularly in Asia. Clinical manifestations range from febrile illness to vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, haemorrhage and acute kidney injury. The mechanisms underlying variation in disease severity and the variability and durability of vaccine-induced immunity remain incompletely understood. Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin regulation and non-coding RNA-mediated regulation, can influence antiviral immunity and immune-cell function in several biological settings; however, their specific contributions to HFRS remain insufficiently characterised. This structured narrative review examines hantavirus-specific evidence alongside relevant findings from other viral infections and vaccination settings, focusing on inflammatory responses, endothelial dysfunction, regulatory non-coding RNAs, trained immunity and potential applications in vaccinology. Experimental HTNV studies and clinical investigations of regulatory RNAs have identified candidate pathways associated with hantavirus-host interactions; however, these findings do not establish that epigenetic mechanisms determine HFRS severity or clinical outcomes. Similarly, preclinical hantavirus vaccine studies and early clinical evaluations provide evidence regarding immunogenicity and safety but do not demonstrate epigenetic mediation of protective immunity. Findings from Andes virus (ANDV), associated primarily with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), and other viral systems are therefore considered comparative or contextual evidence, not directly generalizable to HFRS. This review identifies critical knowledge gaps and outlines how longitudinal, cell-resolved epigenomic profiling, functional validation and integrated multi-omics could clarify causal mechanisms, explain interindividual variation in disease outcomes and vaccine responses, and establish the potential translational value of epigenetic biomarkers and interventions.
authors: Singh HO, Tatte VS, Kaushal H.

title: Identification of Novel Enzymes Regulating ADP-Ribosylation of Uracil and Thymine in Nucleic Acids.
abstract: ADP-ribosylation (ADPr) is a conserved modification that regulates a wide range of cellular processes. Although proteins are the best-characterized substrates of ADPr, recent studies have demonstrated that nucleic acids can also be modified. However, the enzymes responsible for installing and removing nucleic acid ADPr, as well as its biological functions, remain poorly understood. Here, we identify human PARP15 as an ADP-ribosyltransferase that robustly modifies uracil bases in single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) and confirm that human TARG1 reverses PARP15-catalysed ADPr. We further identify the first phage-encoded hydrolase capable of efficiently removing both uracil- and thymine-linked ADP-ribose from nucleic acids. Biochemical analyses provide proof-of-principle evidence that uracil ADP-ribosylation (U-ADPr) may modulate vertebrate antiviral responses, whereas we provide new evidence that thymine ADP-ribosylation (T-ADPr) functions as a molecular signal in bacterial-phage warfare. Together, our findings expand the known repertoire of nucleic acid ADP-ribosylation, define key enzymes regulating pyrimidine ADPr dynamics, and suggest a conserved enzymatic framework for pyrimidine ADPr in immunity across evolution.
authors: Lu Y, Deeksha W, Zhu K, Ahel J, Huang Y, Tang L, Schuller M, Filippov DV, Liu Q, Mikoc A, Ahel D, Ahel I.

title: ISG-15 promotes de novo HBV infection after pediatric liver transplant via IL-18/STAT1 from HBcAb-positive donors.
abstract: Introduction and objectivesLiver transplantation is the main therapy for pediatric end-stage liver disease, but use of hepatitis B core antibody-positive (HBcAb+) grafts increases the risk of de novo hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. We examined whether ISG-15 promotes de novo HBV through IL-18/STAT1 signaling.Patients and methodsWe retrospectively analyzed clinical data and conducted proteomics analysis. Liver biopsy specimens were randomly selected from eight pediatric recipients who developed de novo HBV infection and from 10 pediatric recipients who did not develop de novo HBV infection, after liver transplantation was performed between 2018 and 2019. In proteomic comparisons between the de novo and non-de novo HBV groups, we identified 5027 proteins, including 221 differentially expressed proteins. Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment analyzes were conducted to evaluate functional associations.ResultsDifferentially expressed proteins were primarily involved in the immune response, viral defense, and cell adhesion processes. In vitro experiments using small interfering RNA and plasmid transfection to knock down and overexpress ISG-15 in hepatoblastoma (HepG2.2.15) cells demonstrated that ISG-15 overexpression significantly enhanced cell proliferation and migration, whereas ISG-15 knockdown inhibited these biological processes. Treatment with the STAT1 inhibitor fludarabine and the agonist 2-nitropropane further confirmed that ISG-15 promotes HBV replication by regulating the IL-18/STAT1 signaling axis.ConclusionsThe findings of this study provide experimental evidence that can help in understanding the role of ISG-15 in HBV infection and offer potential targets for clinical intervention to prevent de novo HBV infection after liver transplantation using HBcAb-positive grafts.
authors: Fulati F, Zhang Z, Gao W, Dong C.

title: Bovine leptospirosis: Pathogenic species and serovars of Leptospira associated with dairy cows.
abstract: Leptospirosis is an economically important zoonotic bacterial infection of livestock that causes abortions, stillbirths, infertility, and loss of milk production. Bovine leptospirosis occurs worldwide and is caused by infection with pathogenic bacteria in the genus Leptospira that can colonize the kidney or genital tract of both males and females to maintain disease transmission via shedding in urine, the reproductive tract, or via vertical transmission to a fetus. Cattle are a reservoir host for L. borgpetersenii serovar Hardjo but can also shed other pathogenic species and serovars associated with bovine infection and zoonotic transmission. In this observational study, urine samples (n = 384) were collected from dairy cows in a California slaughterhouse to test for the presence of pathogenic Leptospira. In total, 56 urine samples (15%) were positive, with 55 (14%) positive by lipL32 rtPCR and 24 (6%) positive by culture. Characterization of cultured isolates identified L. borgpetersenii serovar Hardjo (n = 18), L. interrogans serovar Pomona (n = 5), and L. interrogans serovar Copenhageni (n = 1). Leptospira targeted amplicon sequencing analysis of 32 lipL32 PCR-positive but culture-negative urine samples identified 23 as positive for L. borgpetersenii, one as positive for a mixed infection comprising L. borgpetersenii and L. santarosai, and 4 as positive for L. santarosai; 4 remained undefined. Phylogenetics identified a new genotype of L. borgpetersenii that was not readily amenable to culture using current medium formulations. The identification of species and serovars of Leptospira currently circulating in cattle is critical for efficacious surveillance, diagnostic, and prevention strategies.

title: Comparative shelf life of pasteurized camel and bovine milk from a single commercial source: Bacterial community succession, predicted functional potential, and casein integrity.
abstract: In this exploratory single-source comparison, the tested pasteurized camel milk (CM) remained microbiologically acceptable for longer than the tested bovine milk (BM), but the microbiological basis of that difference has not been established. We followed pasteurized CM and BM through refrigerated storage at 4°C using aerobic and lactic acid bacteria (LAB) enumeration, pH and titratable acidity, SDS-PAGE protein profiling, and 16S rRNA gene (V3-V4) amplicon sequencing on the DNBSEQ platform, with functional potential inferred by PICRUSt2. Aerobic counts in CM stayed below the detection limit until d 92, crossed the 5 log cfu/mL limit set by the Gulf Standard on d 99, and reached 5.33 log cfu/mL on d 100. BM crossed the same limit on d 35, and its LAB population climbed to 10.8 log cfu/mL by d 37. LAB were never recovered from CM. A core of 132 operational taxonomic units (OTUs) persisted across all 6 CM sampling points, yet the community was not static: Pseudomonadota accounted for 64.9% of the initial community and was displaced by Bacillota, which reached 100% at d 20 and 67.8% at d 102, with pulses of transient OTUs at d 70 and 80. LEfSe associated fresh CM with Enterobacteriaceae and d 102 with Macrococcus and Staphylococcaceae. Predicted chemotaxis and flagellar assembly pathways rose at d 102, although the predicted differences were not supported statistically. Casein bands faded in CM after d 21 while BM proteins stayed intact, indicating that proteolysis, not bacterial growth, sets the practical storage limit for CM.
authors: Hamed NS, Ulusoy BH, Kamal-Eldin A, Ayyash M.

title: Intermittent illumination enables reversible carbon buffering by Rhodopseudomonas palustris for enhanced methane recovery from food waste anaerobic digestion.
abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) of food waste (FW) is vulnerable to acidification when fermentation outpaces syntrophic oxidation and methanogenesis. To address this temporal imbalance, we introduced Rhodopseudomonas palustris (R. palustris), which can assimilate fermentation-derived volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and store carbon as polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs). Intermittent illumination reduced VFA accumulation and end-cycle H2 partial pressure, while yielding the highest mean daily methane production (589.0 mL d-1) and fraction of carbon recovered as methane (37.2 %). A pure-culture assay showed that PHA accumulated during illumination and declined in darkness, indicating reversible intracellular carbon storage and remobilization. The PHA turnover pattern paralleled reactor methane dynamics, which was consistent with a temporal association between carbon storage and downstream methanogenesis. Intermittent illumination yielded the lowest NADH/NAD+ ratio while maintaining high ATP availability. Community analysis revealed a more balanced distribution of functional guilds between the liquid and reactor-wall fractions, while metagenomic analysis indicated functional potential for PHA turnover and methanogenesis. Together, these findings support a carbon-buffering model in which light-dark cycling is associated with transient carbon storage and subsequent remobilization, potentially improving the temporal coupling between acidogenesis and methane formation and enhancing AD stability and methane recovery.
authors: Zhang W, Li X, Zhang X, Zhang W, Gu L, Chen Y, Ai H.

title: High light alters biomacromolecule composition and enhances exopolysaccharide production in Porphyridium aerugineum.
abstract: Microalgae of the genus Porphyridium are valuable bioresources for producing sulfated exopolysaccharides (EPS) with industrial potential, yet their productivity under high light (HL) stress is underexplored. Here, the HL acclimation of the red alga Porphyridium aerugineum (550 μmol/m2/s) was investigated through time-course physiological assays, ultrastructural imaging, and multi-omics profiling. HL significantly enhanced biomass accumulation and EPS yield (3.5-fold) despite reduced photosynthetic efficiency. These data indicate altered biomass composition, with proteins and intracellular carbohydrates declining (by 40.7% and 36.5% on day 20 relative to LL, respectively), neutral lipids reduced, and cell walls more compact. Moderate ROS elevation and upregulated proline and ascorbate peroxidase under HL suggest a well‑regulated oxidative stress response, while monosaccharide analysis revealed a slight increase in glucuronic acid content, potentially benefiting EPS bioactivity. Multi-omics revealed coordinated downregulation of photosynthesis and nitrogen assimilation (NRT2, NR), enrichment of the ribosome pathway (indicating accelerated protein turnover for nitrogen recycling), and post-transcriptional buffering of carbon fixation. Based on these multi-omics data, UGPase, GBSS1, and a bZIP transcription factor are proposed as candidate targets for future strain improvement. These findings suggest that HL can be used to enhance EPS production in P. aerugineum, providing a potential basis and candidate targets for microalgal biorefineries.
authors: Ji L, Yuan Y, Xu L, Sun L, Zheng G, Fan J.

title: Genetic dissection of rapid proteolysis identifies TXNDC15 as a key factor of ERAD and lipid homeostasis.
abstract: Biological systems face a constantly changing environment and must swiftly respond to stimuli; yet how cells sense and adapt to environmental and physiological cues is incompletely understood. Short-lived proteins can be rapidly induced upon perturbation, enabling swift activation of adaptive cellular responses. Here, leveraging genome-wide data on protein-transcript correlation, we systematically searched for rapid proteolysis substrates whose abundance reflects the activity of the underlying proteolytic machinery. Focusing on the candidate substrate ABHD2, we performed CRISPR-based genetic screens to dissect its degradation. These screens identified TXNDC15 as an essential factor in MARCHF6-mediated ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD). Mechanistically, TXNDC15 supports substrate exit and degradation from the ER via a catalysis-independent mechanism. Loss of TXNDC15 remodels the ER proteome and lipid homeostasis. Together, our work defines a missing component of ERAD and provides a generalizable strategy to decode post-translational regulatory circuits.
authors: Liu Y, Yaochai MY, Liu S, Alwaseem H, Birsoy K.

title: Photorhabdus CipA and CipB spontaneously demix into distinct, isolable cytosolic crystals through orthogonal self-assembly in mammalian cells.
abstract: Crystalline inclusion proteins CipA and CipB from Photorhabdus luminescens serve as versatile scaffolds for clustering genetically fused heterologous proteins into light-refractile inclusion bodies in bacteria. Although various Cip-fusion proteins have been tested in microbial systems, the phase separation behaviors and biochemical attributes of Cip and Cip-fusion proteins in eukaryotic cellular environments remain poorly understood. This study demonstrates that CipA and CipB undergo crystallization in the cytosol of human embryonic kidney cells. Shortly after transfection, CipA and CipB become the most abundant proteins in mammalian cells and produce prominent cytosolic crystals often exceeding 10 μm in side length. Co-expression of CipA and CipB drives spontaneous demixing into two distinct crystal populations, and their orthogonality is maintained even when an unrelated third protein crystallizes in the same cytosol, permitting three crystal types to coexist simultaneously. Intracellular crystals are readily isolable from cells, and once purified, these crystals are stable in vitro at physiological pH. CipA and CipB crystals, however, exhibit distinct pH-dependent solubilization behaviors, differing in both dissolution kinetics and oligomeric profiles. When fused to GFP, both CipA and CipB enable Cip-GFP fusions to phase separate into condensate-like cytosolic protein droplets. While Cip-mCherry fusions do not drive spontaneous self-assembly, Cip-mCherry can still be efficiently recruited into Cip-GFP-generated condensate droplet only when their Cip-scaffold identity is matched. Although fused cargo types influence the phase separation threshold of individual Cip-fusion proteins, the findings support Cip as robust orthogonal self-assembly platforms for producing programmable cytosolic protein assemblies in mammalian cells.
authors: Hasegawa H, Wang S, Pelegri-O'Day EM.

title: Transcriptome, metabolite profiling and functional genomics provide molecular insights into sweetpotato sprouting.
abstract: Short dormancy period of sweetpotato (Ipomoea batatas) storage roots causes significant economic losses. To unravel the molecular mechanism of sweetpotato sprouting, a comparative transcriptome was performed using storage roots incubated under non-sprout (15 °C) and sprout favouring conditions (25 °C). Our analysis revealed that 7404 genes were differentially expressed between non-sprouting and sprouted storage roots incubated at 25 °C. Further, we observed that gibberellin (GA) biosynthesis gene IbGA3OXIDASE and abscisic acid (ABA) catabolism gene ABA 8'-HYDROXYLASE were upregulated by > 10-fold and > 40-fold, respectively, at the onset of sprouting. Metabolite profiling showed increased GA and cytokinin levels, but reduced ABA content in the sprout initials. Based on conserved expression patterns of phytohormone-related genes during sprouting in potato tubers and sweetpotato storage roots, two genes that were downregulated during sweetpotato sprouting - IbPYL4 (ABA receptor) and IbGA2OXIDASE (GA catabolic enzyme) - were independently overexpressed in potato. Transgenic potato plants overexpressing IbPYL4 or IbGA2OXIDASE exhibited low percentages of tuber sprouting and reduced sprout length. Furthermore, knockdown of the ABA 8'-HYDROXYLASE gene (ABA catabolism) significantly reduced sprout length in sweetpotato storage roots compared to wild-type plants. Overall, our study suggests that selective candidate genes (ABA 8'-HYDROXYLASE, IbPYL4, IbGA3OXIDASE, and IbGA2OXIDASE) could be targeted for developing sweetpotato genotypes with enhanced shelf-life.
authors: Patil AB, Vyawahare AB, Barvkar VT, Gawade NS, Barbole RS, Joshi RS, Kadoo NY, Kondhare KR.

title: Association of IL-6 and IL-10 serum levels with genetic variants in diabetic neuropathy: Clinical findings from a Bangladeshi patient cohort.
abstract: BackgroundDiabetic Neuropathy (DN) is a prevalent complication of diabetes linked to chronic inflammation. Interleukin-6 (IL-6) and Interleukin-10 (IL-10) are key cytokines implicated in DN pathogenesis. This study investigates the association of IL6 and IL10 gene polymorphisms and serum levels with DN in the Bangladeshi population.Materials and methodsA case-control study was conducted with 225 participants: diabetic patients with DN (n = 75), diabetic patients without DN (n = 75), and healthy controls (n = 75). Genomic DNA was extracted for genotyping IL-6 (rs1800796) and IL-10 (rs1800896) SNPs via PCR. Serum cytokine levels were measured using ELISA.ResultsSerum IL-6 levels were significantly higher in the DN group than in the other study groups (p ConclusionThese findings support further investigation of serum IL-6 as a potential candidate biomarker for diabetic neuropathy, whereas the independent contribution of the investigated IL-6 and IL-10 polymorphisms remains uncertain. Larger prospective studies with independent external validation are required before clinical application can be considered.

title: Reverse vaccinology for development of vaccine against Aeromonas hydrophila infection in nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus).
abstract: Aeromonas hydrophila is one of the main pathogens of Tilapia and has a wide range phenotype, making it difficult to prevent by a unique vaccine. And turning the majority of the treatment using antibiotics. The aim of this work was to predict vaccine candidate with potential efficacy to protect Oreochromis niloticus against Aeromonas hydrophila, applying bioinformatics tools in a reverse vaccinology approach. It was obtained 35 A. hydrophila genomes in the São Francisco Valley in Petrolina/PE/Brazil, as well as 24 A. hydrophila and 02 O. niloticus complete genomes available in Genbank. After identification of core genes of Aeromonas hydrophila and a subtractive genomics analysis between the O. niloticus genome and A. hydrophila genome, 32 of the 178 resulting proteins, were considered likely vaccine targets as they showed a high adherence probability (> 0.51) in the Vaxign tool. After BLAST analysis against the database of essential genes (DEG), 18 proteins showed defined criteria e-value (≤ 10- 6) and a relevant similarity with the proteins of pathogenic species from the genus Aeromonas. Were selected 10 proteins, based on the criteria of portability adhesion, molecular mass between 19 and 80 kDa and presence of one or no transmembrane helix. The analyses identified nine proteins [secreted (n = 8) and PSE (n = 1)] with immunological and novel properties as candidates for vaccine targets. Finally, in vitro/in vivo tests will be necessary to experimentally validate the results of this search.
journal: Brazilian journal of microbiology : [publication of the Brazilian Society for Microbiology]

title: The role of 2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase (OAS) proteins in HIV infection: innate antiviral immunity, viral persistence, and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) establishes persistent infection despite robust innate immune responses and effective antiretroviral therapy, highlighting the importance of host antiviral mechanisms in regulating viral replication and persistence. Among interferon-stimulated genes, 2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase 1 (OAS1) is a key antiviral effector that senses viral double-stranded RNA and activates the OAS-RNase L pathway. Beyond its canonical antiviral activity, emerging evidence implicates OAS1 in immune regulation, viral latency, neuroinflammation, and retroviral disease progression. This review examines the genomic organization, structural diversity, isoform-specific functions, genetic variation, and interferon-mediated regulation of the OAS protein family, emphasizing OAS1 in HIV infection. Experimental and clinical studies indicate that type I and type III interferons induce OAS1 in macrophages, dendritic cells, epithelial and endothelial cells, microglia, and lymphocytes, contributing to HIV restriction through RNase L activation and enhanced innate antiviral responses. OAS signalling may also support mucosal antiviral defence, regulate viral burden and chronic immune activation, influence interferon responsiveness during combination antiretroviral therapy, and contribute to central nervous system protection. Conversely, dysregulated OAS1 expression has been associated with HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders. Genetic polymorphisms and alternative splicing generate functional diversity in OAS1, potentially influencing antiviral activity, individual susceptibility, and clinical outcomes. Collectively, available evidence positions OAS1 as a multifunctional antiviral and immunoregulatory component of host defence that may influence multiple aspects of HIV pathogenesis. Further investigation into OAS1 activation, genetic variation, isoform-specific functions, and immune modulation may facilitate biomarker discovery and support the development of host-directed therapeutic strategies against persistent retroviral infections.
authors: Akbarin MM, Farjami Z, Soltani M, Álvarez HR.

title: Ginsenoside Rg3 attenuates hyperuricemia-associated AKI by upregulating CPT1A and suppressing NLRP3/Caspase-1/GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis.
abstract: Hyperuricemia-associated acute kidney injury (HUA-AKI), a frequent complication of chronic hyperuricemia, is driven by oxidative stress, inflammation, and pyroptosis in renal tubular epithelial cells. Ginsenoside Rg3, a principal bioactive compound derived from Panax ginseng, possesses anti-inflammatory and metabolic regulatory activities; however, its therapeutic effects and underlying mechanisms in HUA-AKI remain elusive. In this study, an HUA-AKI mouse model was established via intraperitoneal injection of potassium oxonate combined with oral hypoxanthine, and an in vitro model using uric acid (UA)-stimulated HK-2 cells. Rg3 treatment markedly improved renal function, reduced tubular injury, and alleviated oxidative stress without altering serum UA levels. Transcriptomic profiling identified 229 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) reversed by Rg3, and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis revealed significant inhibition of the NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome and pyroptosis pathways, alongside upregulation of the carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A)-mediated fatty acid oxidation pathway. Western blotting, immunohistochemistry, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) confirmed that Rg3 upregulated CPT1A expression and suppressed activation of NLRP3, cleaved caspase‑1, gasdermin D N‑terminal fragment (GSDMD‑NT), as well as the release of interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18 in both mouse kidney tissues and HK-2 cells. Notably, co-administration of the CPT1A inhibitor sodium taurocholate (STC) partially abolished the renoprotective effects of Rg3, as demonstrated by restored cell viability, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release, re‑elevation of pyroptosis-related proteins and cytokines, and reappearance of membrane pore formation and rupture under transmission electron microscopy. Collectively, our findings suggest that Rg3 may ameliorate HUA‑AKI, at least in part, through CPT1A upregulation and subsequent suppression of the NLRP3/caspase-1/GSDMD axis, positioning Rg3 as a promising therapeutic candidate for HUA-AKI.
journal: In vitro cellular & developmental biology. Animal
authors: Zhao N, Song W, Zhang M, Wang R, Liu W, Shao J, Wang D.

title: In vitro and in vivo activity of OSUAB-0284, a preclinical candidate for Staphylococcus aureus infections.
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus remains one of the world's deadliest pathogens. OSUAB-0284 (284) is a novel, small-molecule anti-staphylococcal agent targeting bacterial type II topoisomerases. 284 inhibited supercoiling by DNA gyrase and decatenation by topoisomerase IV with similar (balanced) potency (IC50 values of 0.80 and 0.15 μM, respectively) and promoted the accumulation of single-strand DNA breaks mediated by DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Cryo-electron microscopy of 284 in ternary complex with 20-bp DNA and S. aureus DNA gyrase elucidated the binding mode. 284 displayed impressive activity against a panel of 100 recent clinical isolates of S. aureus, with a minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC90) of 0.25 μg/mL. Spontaneous frequency of resistance studies indicated a very low rate of resistance selection (-10). In vitro studies of absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity and in vivo pharmacokinetics studies in mice and rats revealed favorable properties for further development. 284 was efficacious in a thigh infection model using neutropenic mice, with twice-daily oral doses ≥50 mg/kg demonstrating ~1 log10 reduction in bacterial colony-forming units. Preliminary safety studies in rats demonstrated that 284 was well tolerated up to the highest tested oral dose of 1,000 mg/kg. 284 is currently in preclinical development as a novel anti-staphylococcal therapy.

title: A stable atypical H2S-negative, non-motile Salmonella Infantis variant from a human isolate associated with a barA stop-gain mutation.
abstract: Salmonella enterica serovar Infantis (S. Infantis) is an increasingly important food-borne pathogen, and detection in broiler flocks via the standardized EN/ISO 6579-1:2017 is of utmost importance. Phenotypic characteristics, such as the production of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and swarming behavior, are essential for detection. However, the occurrence of atypical variants lacking such phenotypic characteristics bears a risk to public health. In this study, we characterized an Austrian human-derived S. Infantis strain showing, in addition to the normal colony phenotype (NCP), also an atypical colony variant (ACV) lacking H2S production and motility. Both phenotypes proved stability, and no differences were found in cell morphology. In comparison to NCP, ACV demonstrated altered biofilm formation on Congo Red agar, and showed lower streptomycin resistance. The genomic analysis revealed a total of 21 mutations specific to ACV, including a stop-gain mutation in barA. Using gene network analysis, a connection between barA and operons relevant for H2S production, ttr, and phs was found. As barA is a well-known regulator with established roles in motility, the observed truncation provides a plausible regulatory basis for the stable H2S-negative, non-motile phenotype. Furthermore, mutations in barA have been linked to persistent Salmonella infections in humans, supporting our findings. Importantly, such atypical variants might go undetected in the mandatory control programs.IMPORTANCEPhenotypic characteristics, such as the production of hydrogen sulfide and motility, are essential for culture-based detection of Salmonella. This study shows that Salmonella Infantis can lose these key diagnostic features through regulatory mutations, enabling escape from routine surveillance while maintaining infection potential. As the present mutation is known to contribute to bacterial persistence in the host, our findings highlight a dual clinical concern of diagnostic evasion and possible adaptation to host survival. This work demonstrates a critical limitation of phenotype-dependent diagnostics and underscores the need for surveillance strategies that can detect atypical but clinically relevant Salmonella variants.
authors: Fesina D, Palmieri N, Kranzler M, Brandstetter M, Kornschober C, Bilic I, Hess M, Hess C, Drauch V.

title: Atypical E3 ligase HOIL1 promotes MDA5 signaling and ester-linked ubiquitination of LGP2.
abstract: The RIG-I-like receptors, RIG-I and MDA5, are innate sensors of RNA virus infections that are critical for mounting a robust antiviral immune response. Heme-oxidized IRP2 ligase 1 (HOIL1), a component of the linear ubiquitin chain assembly complex (LUBAC), is essential for interferon induction in response to viruses sensed by MDA5, but not viruses sensed by RIG-I; however, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. LUBAC contains two atypical E3 ubiquitin ligases, HOIL1 and HOIP. While HOIP generates "linear" polyubiquitin chains, HOIL1 catalyzes ester-linked ubiquitination of serine and threonine residues and glucosaccharides. Here, we show that HOIL1 E3 ligase activity is critical for MDA5-dependent interferon induction, whereas HOIP E3 ligase activity plays a minor role. Mechanistically, HOIL1 E3 ligase activity was required for MDA5 translocation to mitochondrion-associated membranes and the formation of MAVS aggregates. We further identified LGP2, a positive regulator of MDA5 oligomerization, as a HOIL1-interacting protein and substrate for ester-linked ubiquitination. In mice, loss of HOIL1 or its E3 ligase activity markedly impaired early interferon responses following infection with viruses sensed by MDA5. While HOIL1 deficiency resulted in increased viral burden and reduced survival, loss of HOIL1 ligase activity alone did not, indicating that HOIL1 exerts additional functions during antiviral immunity. Collectively, these findings establish ester-linked ubiquitination by HOIL1 as a critical mechanism regulating MDA5 signaling.IMPORTANCEThe rapid and robust production of interferon is critical for controlling viral infections. Cytoplasmic RNA sensors, RIG-I and MDA5, detect infection with distinct groups of viruses, leading to the transcriptional induction of interferon. However, inappropriate production of interferon triggered by aberrant MDA5 activation by cellular RNAs causes severe inflammatory disorders. Here, we report that the ubiquitin ligase activity of heme-oxidized IRP2 ligase 1 (HOIL1) is critical for the production of interferon in response to viruses that are sensed by MDA5 in cells and mice. We identify the third RIG-I-like receptor, LGP2, as a substrate for ester-linked ubiquitination by HOIL1, and show that, like LGP2, HOIL1 ubiquitin ligase activity is required for the efficient oligomerization of MDA5 and the initiation of downstream signaling leading to the induction of interferon. These findings reveal a new regulator of MDA5-driven interferon production and identify a potential therapeutic target for MDA5-mediated inflammatory diseases.
authors: Cheng D, Zhu J, Chathuranga WAG, Chakraborty S, Liu G, Lacoursiere RE, Pruneda JN, Gack MU, MacDuff DA.

title: The physical state of the nucleus tracks its function across eukaryotes
abstract: The nucleus is consistently less dense than the surrounding cytoplasm, a difference proposed to arise from selective nuclear import. The functional significance of low nuclear density, however, remains unknown. Because density is a bulk property of the cell, acute perturbations inevitably have pleiotropic consequences. We therefore turned to the natural experiments offered by the tree of life where nuclei vary in genome size, chromatin organisation, import selectivity and transcriptional state, and asked whether low nuclear density is tied to particular nuclear architectures or functions. Using dinoflagellates, Giardia and ciliates, we show nuclear density is uncoupled from genome size. In ciliates, two nuclei in one cytoplasm reach opposite densities relative to it, governed by nuclear import rather than transcription. We thus conform nuclear import as a major determinant of nuclear density and reveal nuclei that break the low-density rule.
authors: Pleitner M, Biswas A, Uhlich J, Reber S.

title: A reproductive hierarchy controls mating fates among sibling yeast gametes
abstract: Mating strategies shape inbreeding, gene flow and genetic diversity, yet their outcomes remain challenging to quantify. In  Saccharomyces , population-genomic models predict mating predominantly between sibling meiotic products, with rare selfing and outcrossing. Here we developed an integrated framework combining multicolor flow cytometry, time-resolved imaging and mathematical modelling to directly quantify mating across scales. Bulk measurements revealed coexisting strategies whose frequencies vary with density, genotype and environment. A minimal stochastic model uses these population-level patterns to infer probabilistic hierarchies among mating modes, which single-tetrad analyses independently support. These reveal divergent and interdependent reproductive trajectories among sibling gametes, with one pair typically mating first and reshaping opportunities for the others. Temporal heterogeneity in germination and mating further diversifies reproductive outcomes and shapes compatibility, as experimental synchronization overcomes temporal reproductive barriers, enabling hybridization. Together, reproductive strategy emerges from heterogeneous gamete fates, raising the possibility that sibling diversification constitutes reproductive bet-hedging.
authors: Vischioni C, Barré BP, Vittorelli N, De Chiara M, Pompei S, Vulin C, Luneau JS, Tomasiak K, Tellini N, Laugier S, Khaiwal S, Mitri S, Llorente B, Cosentino Lagomarsino M, Fischer G, Liti G.

title: The effects of DNA repair factor-Cas9 fusions on homing gene drive performance
abstract: CRISPR-based homing gene drives achieve super-Mendelian inheritance by converting wild-type alleles into drive alleles through homology-directed repair (HDR). However, competing end-joining repair can generate resistance alleles that limit drive spread. Although fusing Cas9 to DNA repair-associated proteins has improved HDR in conventional genome editing systems, its effectiveness in gene drives remains unclear. Here, we systematically evaluated in  Drosophila melanogaster eight Cas9 fusion constructs previously reported to improve HDR in other systems. Although none of the fusion constructs significantly increased HDR-associated signals in S2 cells, several candidates retained relatively high activity comparable to standard Cas9. These candidates were then tested  in vivo across multiple split drive systems, regulatory elements, target loci, and parental sexes. Cas9-POLD3 significantly increased female drive inheritance in contexts with low baseline efficiency or substantial nonfunctional resistance formation, likely by increasing effective cutting rate and potentially also by biasing repair outcomes toward drive conversion. Cas9-Geminin degron generally maintained germline drive performance while reducing embryo resistance. Together, these findings identify Cas9-POLD3 and Cas9-Geminin degron as complementary, context-specific tools for enhancing drive conversion and limiting embryo resistance, respectively. These results highlight the importance of matching fusion modules to the regulatory and genetic context of individual drive systems.
authors: Wu Y, Xu X, Liang N, Xia Y, Tan AY, Yang J, Yang X, Champer J.

title: Cold-active acetyl esterase from Stropharia rugosoannulata and its synergistic effects with xylanase.
abstract: Acetyl esterases play an important role in the deacetylation of hemicellulose. This study aimed to identify and characterize a novel carbohydrate esterase family 16 (CE16) acetyl esterase from the saprophytic fungus Stropharia rugosoannulata and evaluate its potential for enhancing the enzymatic depolymerization of natural lignocellulosic substrates under mild conditions. A putative CE16 family gene was identified through genomic mining and heterologously expressed in Escherichia coli. The recombinant enzyme, SrAEA, was purified and biochemically characterized. The synergistic effect of SrAEA with xylanase was evaluated on beechwood powder, corncob powder, and rice bran. SrAEA exhibited optimal catalytic activity at 20 °C and pH 7.0, defining it as a cold-adapted enzyme. Structural analysis showed that it possesses a non-canonical Ser-His-Asn catalytic triad and a conserved SGNH-hydrolase fold. The enzyme exhibited the highest catalytic efficiency toward the short-chain substrate 4-methylumbelliferyl acetate, with no detectable activity on longer-chain substrates. Sequential treatment with SrAEA and xylanase increased reducing-sugar release in a substrate-dependent manner. These findings identify SrAEA as a fungal CE16 acetyl esterase with activity at 20 °C and show that its sequential use with xylanase can increase reducing-sugar release under the tested conditions. Its process utility and energy requirements remain to be evaluated.
authors: Liu G, Wang Y, Yang J, Han Z.

title: Field‑Based Dissection of Stomatal Anatomy and Conductance Reveals Stable QTL Under Drought and Heat in Wheat.
abstract: Stomatal traits balance carbon gain with water loss, yet their breeding potential in wheat remains underexploited. This study investigated physiological and anatomical stomatal responses across 2 years of large-scale field trials under water-limitation and warming treatments. Across both seasons, stomatal conductance (gs) declined under stress, reflecting strong environmental constraint on gas-exchange (water-limitation: -26.9%; warming-treatment: -13.8%). Partitioning responses by surface identified the adaxial surface as the dominant contributor to gs variation and the most stress responsive. Despite increases in theoretical anatomical gas-exchange capacity (gsmax), stomatal conductance efficiency (gse) declined, indicating decoupling between anatomical capacity and realised conductance. Drought reduced stomatal size while increasing density whereas warming increased size and density, yet both responses maintained gas-exchange capacity. Moderate-to-high heritability was observed for anatomical traits (water-limitation: 0.13-0.57; warming-treatment: 0.42-0.71), contrasting with lower, less stable heritability for gs (water-limitation: 0.13-0.41; warming-treatment: 0.13-0.50). Genome-wide-association-mapping identified 60 putative QTLs, predominantly for anatomical traits. Candidate loci on chromosomes 7B, 2B, 3B and 5 A emerged as pleiotropic genomic intervals influencing stomatal anatomy across environments. These findings indicate that wheat maintains anatomical gas-exchange capacity while dynamically regulating realised conductance under stress, highlighting anatomically stable stomatal traits as promising breeding targets for climate resilience and yield stability.
authors: Chaplin E, Tanaka E, Merchant A, Sznajder B, Trethowan R, Salter W.

title: The transcription factor CgGCN4 coordinates carbon-nitrogen metabolism to improve glycerol and ethanol biosynthesis under low-nitrogen stress in yeast.
abstract: Nitrogen limitation suppresses growth and target metabolite synthesis of industrial yeast, and the key transcription factor coordinating carbon-nitrogen balance in Candida glycerinogenes remains unclear. This work identified CgGCN4 as the core effector of nitrogen starvation response: screen nitrogen-starvation responsive transcription factor in C. glycerinogenes; characterize physiological function via overexpression and antisense repression in glycerol-producing yeast; test cross-species function by heterologous expression in S. cerevisiae for ethanol fermentation application. qRT-PCR reveals nitrogen starvation activates three nutrient-sensing pathways, with CgGCN4 showing the highest transcript level (4.2). At 84 h fermentation, CgGCN4-OE consumes 250.2 g/L glucose, yields 122.6 g/L glycerol and reaches OD600 of 45.6, outperforming wild type. Transcriptomics demonstrates CgGCN4 co-upregulates glycolysis, TCA and amino acid synthesis to balance C/N metabolism. Its conserved function is validated in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In 5 L fed-batch culture, engineered Sc-BNA-MG produces 67.7 g/L ethanol (10.1% higher than control), with intracellular NAD(H) pool rising by 27.5% at 6 h. CgGCN4 serves as a cross-species regulatory hub mitigating low-nitrogen stress, a promising target for yeast factory engineering.
authors: Wang M, Zhuge B, Jiang D, Wang Z, Zong H.

title: A novel shark VNAR antibody-based immunotoxin targeting ERα36 disrupts non-genomic estrogen signaling and tumor metabolic reprogramming in breast cancer.
abstract: ERα36, a membrane-associated splice variant of estrogen receptor α, mediates rapid non-genomic estrogen signaling and is frequently overexpressed in aggressive and therapy-resistant breast cancers. Although ERα36 represents a promising therapeutic target, its clinical exploitation remains limited due to the lack of high-affinity and highly specific targeting ligands capable of recognizing its extracellular domain. In this paper, we constructed a shark-derived variable new antigen receptor (VNAR) phage display immune library and isolated two high-affinity VNAR single-domain antibodies (FR6 and TH4) targeting distinct epitopes on ERα36. The TH4 VNAR was further engineered by fusion with a truncated Pseudomonas aeruginosa exotoxin (PE24) to generate a recombinant immunotoxin (TH4-PE24), characterized by (1) high specificity and affinity for ERα36 (KD = 0.751 nmol/L), (2) potent and selective cytotoxicity against ERα36-positive breast cancer cells (IC50 = 1.54 nmol/L), (3) a dual mechanism involving ERα36 degradation and suppression of PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK signaling pathways, and (4) significant in vivo antitumor efficacy in xenograft models without observable systemic toxicity. With this immunotoxin, we further investigated how ERα36 targeting could remodel tumor metabolism. ERα36-mediated metabolic regulation in breast cancer is a new research direction with many aspects unknown. We found that TH4-PE24 treatment led to extensive metabolic reprogramming, including disruption of nucleotide metabolism, ABC transporters, and central carbon metabolism. Overall, we report a novel shark VNAR-based immunotoxin platform that can achieve precise and potent antitumor effects by targeting the previously intractable membrane receptor ERα36. The modular design features make it translational for various other studies, such as targeting additional immune checkpoint molecules and developing next-generation precision therapeutics against membrane receptors that are inaccessible to conventional antibody modalities. The schematic diagram illustrates the screening of shark-derived variable new antigen receptors (VNARs) targeting estrogen receptor α, the identification and functional characterization of antigen-binding epitopes, and the construction of a VNAR-based immunotoxin, together with its in vitro and in vivo antitumor efficacy and safety evaluation. Estrogen receptor α36 (ERα36) is a membrane-associated splice variant of estrogen receptor α that primarily mediates non-genomic estrogen signaling. Owing to the α-helical structure of its C-terminal 27 amino acids, ERα36 has long been considered difficult to target with functionally active antibodies. Shark VNARs possess a unique and extended CDR3 region, enabling the recognition of complex and conformational epitopes. Taking advantage of this structural feature, we achieved functional targeting of ERα36 and identified two VNARs that recognize distinct linear and conformational epitopes, respectively. Among them, the conformational epitope-recognizing VNAR, TH4, was further employed to construct a novel immunotoxin. This immunotoxin not only suppresses ERα36 expression in breast cancer cells but also inhibits AKT and ERK signaling pathways, leading to reduced breast cancer cell proliferation and attenuation of tumorigenicity in ERα36-positive breast cancer.
authors: Xi XZ, Zhu LL, Xiang Z, Yin L, Chen GL, Wang YQ, Liu XC, Gu YC, Wang Q.

title: Strategy Sets the Scene: Genetic architecture of linalool resistance in Botrytis cinerea.
abstract: Botrytis cinerea is a necrotrophic fungal pathogen that infects thousands of plant species. During infection, these diverse plant hosts produce different specialized metabolites that can inhibit pathogen growth and shape pathogen fitness. However, the genetic architecture of pathogen resistance toward individual host defense metabolites remains poorly understood. To address this question, we exposed 83 B. cinerea isolates to the metabolite linalool and quantified physiological and structural responses. Exposure revealed extensive phenotypic diversity across isolates. Population structure analysis using genome-wide SNP data showed little genetic subdivision despite diverse hosts and geographic location. Genome-wide association identified 98 genes of interest associated with membrane transport and stress response regulation. Genetic associations were stronger for morphological traits than for physiological traits, suggesting that hyphal architecture may have a complex genetic architecture contributing to linalool resistance. Together, these results establish natural variation in linalool response and provide candidate loci for understanding how generalist pathogens respond to host-derived chemical defenses.
authors: Madrigal M, Moseley JC, Kliebenstein DJ, Dowell JA.

title: DREM: integrating resistance and domain probabilities to prioritize plant immune receptors
abstract: ABSTRACT  Plant resistance (R) genes, key players in the immune system, have traditionally been identified with HMM-based tools relying on sequence homology, whose sensitivity decreases for divergent or non-canonical resistance proteins. Here, DREM (Deep Resistance gene Evaluator Model) is presented as a deep learning framework that learns the compositional properties of resistance proteins from sequence alone rather than searching for predefined motifs. The framework combines two bidirectional long short-term memory networks with attention: a binary resistance classifier and a multi-label classifier of resistance domains. Validation on experimentally characterized proteins from RefPlantNLR recovered 99.8% of sequences, and on 15,000 held-out proteins DREM outperformed the deep learning predictor PRGminer (Matthews correlation coefficient 0.938 vs 0.820), with about two-thirds fewer classification errors. Across five plant proteomes, DREM identified 4,046 High Confidence or Candidate proteins; canonical domain architecture was confirmed in 75.5%, whereas 992 carried strong DREM signals without detectable Pfam domains, and 54 of 55 characterized nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) loci ranked within the top 1.7% of their proteomes. Unlike domain-gated pipelines such as R-Predictor, DREM also recovered experimentally validated atypical NLRs, RPW8 proteins and non-receptor resistance genes. Attention did not concentrate on canonical ATP-binding motifs, consistent with the model drawing on sequence information beyond conserved domain signatures. Lightweight and applicable to complete proteomes, DREM complements domain-based annotation with a calibrated ranking. It links genome-wide prediction to the selection of resistance genes for functional validation, including atypical receptors missed by profile-based tools.
authors: Dublino R, Carandente V, Sperlì G, Ercolano M.

title: Genotype imputation improves GWAS resolution and facilitates candidate gene identification in pearl millet
abstract: Pearl millet (  Cenchrus americanus ; syn.  Pennisetum glaucum (L.) R. Br.) is an important cereal crop mainly grown in semi-arid areas. However, in pearl millet, genes underlying many agronomic traits remain unknown. Our previous genome-wide association study (GWAS) was based primarily on genotype data derived from restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (RAD-seq), which contained a high proportion of missing genotypes and may have limited mapping resolution. To address this limitation, we used whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-derived genotype data from 21 elite lines as a reference panel to impute missing genotypes in the RAD-seq-derived dataset. Genotype imputation reduced the proportion of missing genotypes from 82.42% to 0% and increased the mean density of non-missing genotypes from 569.61 to 1,158.09 genotypes/Mb. Leave-one-out validation yielded a mean genotype concordance of 89.9 ± 4.6%. GWAS using the imputed dataset showed more localized association signals for several traits. Homologs of rice  SHORT INTERNODES1 , Arabidopsis  FLOWERING LOCUS Y , and rice  EPIDERMAL PATTERNING FACTOR 2 were identified as candidates for genes regulating culm height, days to panicle emergence, and awn growth, respectively. These results demonstrate that reference-panel-based genotype imputation can increase the utility of reduced-representation genotype datasets and facilitate candidate gene identification in pearl millet.  Key message  Imputation of missing genotypes in RAD-seq-derived genotype data using a WGS-derived reference panel improved GWAS resolution and facilitated candidate gene identification for agronomic traits in pearl millet.
authors: Kambara K, Gupta SK, Tsugama D.
