title: Transcriptomic, untargeted metabolomic, and gut microbiota studies on the anticoccidial activity of the combination formula in broilers.
abstract: Coccidiosis, a devastating intracellular parasitic disease, poses a significant threat to the poultry industry. Traditional control methods, which involve the inclusion of anticoccidial drugs in feed, have raised concerns over veterinary drug residues. Consequently, there is a pressing need to identify suitable alternatives or complementary strategies to anticoccidial drugs, with plant-derived natural products emerging as a promising candidate. Our laboratory has previously identified a combination formula that demonstrates good anticoccidial activity. However, the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. This study aims to elucidate the mechanism of action of this formula using a multi-omics approach, including transcriptomics, untargeted metabolomics, and gut microbiota analysis. Cecal transcriptomic analysis revealed significant enrichment in pathways, such as lysosomes, ribosomes, oxidative phosphorylation, and sphingolipid metabolism following treatment with the combination formula. Untargeted metabolomic profiling indicated a pronounced enrichment in the gut IgA generation immune network pathway, with retinoic acid identified as a key differential metabolite. Gut microbiota sequencing analysis suggested that the combination formula modulates the gut microbiota of infected broilers towards a composition resembling that of healthy broilers. Collectively, these results suggest that the combination formula exerts its anticoccidial effects through the regulation of differential gene clusters, metabolites, and microbiota. The results of this study have provided us with a deeper understanding of the good anticoccidial effects of the combination formula.ImportanceEimeria tenella is a significant parasitic protozoan that poses a substantial threat to the development of the poultry industry. The combination formula, a synergistic blend of plant-derived natural products, has been identified in our laboratory for its good anticoccidial effects. In this study, we employed non-targeted metabolomics, transcriptomics, and gut microbiome sequencing to elucidate the mechanism of action against coccidiosis. Our results revealed a multitude of differential gene clusters and metabolites. Furthermore, the gut microbiota structure of the cecal content in the treated group more closely resembled that of the healthy control group.
authors: Geng T, Yang H, Liu Y, Zhao J, Zhou Y.

title: Bioinspired Mechano-Chemical Titanium Interfaces With Potential for Infection-Resistant Osseointegration.
abstract: Bacterial colonization and insufficient osseointegration remain major challenges for titanium-based orthopedic and dental implants. Here, we developed a bioinspired mechano-chemical titanium interface by combining an anodization-derived micro-/nano-pitted topography with a polydopamine-citric acid-quercetin (PCQ) functional layer. Inspired by dragonfly-wing micro-/nanostructures, the resulting OPT@PCQ interface exhibited hierarchical topography, enhanced hydrophilicity, and preserved overall mechanical response. OPT@PCQ showed favorable cytocompatibility and significantly promoted osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells, with increased alkaline phosphatase activity, matrix mineralization, and RUNX2, COL1A1, and OCN expression. It also displayed pronounced antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, accompanied by bacterial morphological deformation and reduced viability. Transcriptomic analysis of S. aureus revealed broad perturbation of central carbon metabolism, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, ribosome-associated processes, and stress-response pathways. In vivo, OPT@PCQ promoted wound closure and markedly enhanced new bone formation and trabecular reconstruction in a noninfected rat femoral defect model. Qualitative hemolysis assessment and major-organ histology provided preliminary evidence of hemocompatibility and systemic biosafety under the tested conditions. Collectively, these findings support OPT@PCQ as a multifunctional titanium interface with potential for infection-resistant osseointegration; however, direct validation in an infected bone-defect model remains necessary.
authors: Lu H, Chen R, Chen Y, Zhu M, Liu H, Xu Z, Jian M, Jin K, Wang H, Liu T, Wang J, Zou J, Qiao Y.

title: Hybrid membrane vesicle-enabled sonodynamic therapy using ciprofloxacin for treating biofilm-associated infections.
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections on indwelling medical devices pose significant clinical challenges due to antibiotic resistance and poor drug penetration. Sonodynamic therapy (SDT) is a promising strategy utilizing ultrasound to activate sonosensitizers for generating reactive oxygen species (ROS). However, the lack of safe and effective sonosensitizers and bacterial-targeting delivery systems limits its application in treating biofilm infection. To address these limitations, we developed antibiotic ciprofloxacin-loaded hybrid membrane vesicles (CIP@HMVs), where ciprofloxacin acts as a safe sonosensitizer and HMVs serve as a detoxified bacterial-targeted delivery system. HMVs were engineered by fusing Pseudomonas aeruginosa-derived outer membrane vesicles (PAEVs) with macrophage membrane vesicles (MMVs), creating a dual-functional nanoplatform with homotypic bacteria-targeting and detoxification capabilities. CIP@HMVs exploited ciprofloxacin's sonosensitizer properties to generate singlet oxygen (1O2) under ultrasound, while HMVs enhanced bacterial uptake in P. aeruginosa. This enabled synergistic bactericidal effects against planktonic bacteria via membrane disruption and intracellular ROS burst, achieving a 5.7-log bacterial reduction in catheter biofilms in vitro. Crucially, HMVs neutralized PAEVs' LPS toxicity in vitro and demonstrated negligible systemic toxicity in vivo. In a murine catheter-infection model, CIP@HMVs under ultrasound achieved 99.8% bacterial eradication and reduced inflammation. This bacterial-targeting sonodynamic platform provides a transformative strategy for treating device-associated biofilm infections with high efficacy and biosafety.
authors: Xiao X, Yan M, Yang L, Li Q, He L, Yuan Z, Guo Y, Zhong X, Ding X.

title: In silico analysis of SCO, an almost undescribed family of β-lactamases.
abstract: Introductionβ-lactamases rank amongst the most common mechanisms of antibiotic resistance, accounting for thousands of different variants. Current genomic tools have resulted in an exponential growth of new variants, most of which, as is the case for SCO, remain undescribed or non-characterised. This study aimed to detect new variants of SCO in GenBank records.Material and methodsThe amino acid sequence of SCO-1 was compared with what is present in GenBank. Only amino acid sequences with >85% identity were considered. No synthetic or partial sequences were included in the analyses.ResultsEleven different SCO variants were detected, 9 of which had previously not been designated as specific variants. Several of the modifications suggested the possible expansion of substrates towards 3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins or the resistance to inhibitors, while others might impair SCO functionality. SCO β-lactamases were detected in 6 bacterial families accounting for 14 genera.ConclusionsThe presence of undescribed SCO variants in GenBank is reported, and the need to establish the exact substrate profile of new variants is highlighted.
journal: Revista espanola de quimioterapia : publicacion oficial de la Sociedad Espanola de Quimioterapia
authors: Ruiz J.

title: Genetic Variants Associated with Placental Abnormalities in Stillbirths
abstract: Background  Placental insufficiency (PI), characterized by impaired placental function, is a leading cause of stillbirth. Although rare coding variants are known to cause a subset of stillbirths, their contribution to PI is poorly understood. Methods  We conducted a secondary analysis of stillbirth cases (N=292) of the Stillbirth Collaborative Research Network study with exome sequencing available on postmortem placental or fetal samples. PI was defined by standardized placental pathological lesions (e.g., maternal vascular malperfusion) and prespecified clinical criteria for placental dysfunction. Candidate gene-based rare-variant burden analysis was performed using the Sequence Kernel Association Test-Optimal framework, focusing on evolutionarily constrained developmental and placental-function genes. Primary analysis compared stillbirths with and without placental vascular malperfusion. Similar comparisons by clinical PI and other placental pathological lesions were conducted in secondary analysis. Results  Stillbirths with PI phenotypes demonstrated different patterns of genetic variation than stillbirths without PI. Specifically, we observed nominal differential enrichment of constrained variants in biologically prioritized placental-function genes, regulating extravillous trophoblast invasion and spiral artery remodeling (  CTNND2 ,  PHACTR1 ,  SLIT1, VEGFA ), placental angiogenesis (  IGF2R ,  TEK ), mitochondrial homeostasis (  OPA1 ), and fetal growth (  DLK1 ,  GNAS ). Secondary analyses on specific placental pathological lesions suggested recurrent enrichment of genes within similar placental developmental pathways.  Conclusions  We observed nominal differential enrichment of constrained developmental and placental-function genes in stillbirths with PI compared to stillbirths without PI. The observed genetic signals across PI phenotypes suggest shared biological pathways underlie placental dysfunction. Our findings advance genotype-phenotype characterization and help prioritize candidate pathways for larger collaborative genomic and functional studies to improve stillbirth risk stratification and prevention.
authors: Workalemahu T, Nicholas TJ, Quinlan AR, Yang X, Griffin LB, Leisher S, Blue NR, Arthurs AL, Page JM, Branch DW, Camp NJ, Jorde LB, Roberts CT, Giordano JL, Wapner R, Kingdom J, Gibbins KJ, Parast MM, Reddy UM, Silver RM.

title: Dietary Enhancement for Iron Deficiency and Anaemia Treatment (DEFeAT): study protocol for a randomised controlled trial to assess the effect of a mineral-enriched powder on iron deficiency in women of reproductive age
abstract: Background: Iron deficiency (ID) and iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) have global and severe health implications, and disproportionately impact women of reproductive age. Current methods of supplementing diets with iron are challenged by poor adherence and palatability, reducing effectiveness of these treatment strategies. The aim of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of a novel home beverage fortification with a mineral-enriched powder, designed to enhance bioavailability and ease of use, for the treatment of ID in women of reproductive age. Methods: This single-centre, randomised, double-blinded placebo-controlled trial will enrol 150 eligible biologically female participants with ID. Participants will be randomly assigned to the active intervention (iron/zinc-enriched powder) or control group (placebo powder) over 6 months. Primary outcomes will include change in serum ferritin (SF) concentrations and proportion of participants who remain iron deficient at 6-months. Secondary outcomes will include change in SF and haemoglobin (Hb) concentrations across timepoints, and levels of metabolites and key circulating pro-inflammatory biomarkers, changes in dietary intakes, self-reported perceptions of health, barriers to use of the powder, adherence and palatability, safety outcomes, and cost-effectiveness. Exploratory outcomes will assess the gut microbial metagenome and metabolome. Discussion: Fortification, an effective approach for the prevention of ID/IDA, has advantages over some methods of supplementation because it uses low levels of iron, minimising unpleasant side effects, does not risk toxicity, and has high acceptability and compliance rates. This mineral-enriched powder uses electrolytic iron and zinc sulphate monohydrate of a small particle size, which is less irritating to the gut, and facilitates bioavailability. Findings from the study will be shared with those affected by and involved in treating these conditions, as a novel intervention that is both effective and acceptable among women of reproductive age would help to improve treatment compliance, and ultimately, reduce ID/IDA burden. Trial registration: This trial is registered at clinicaltrials.gov (  NCT05990166 ): https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/  NCT05990166 , August 2023.
authors: Burns JL, Scott H, Mbuagbaw L, Miller CH, Sheyholislami H, Clouthier BA, Fontaine-Bisson B, Connor KL.

title: Plant microbiomes have a greater effect than plant size on flowering and growth in  Asclepias syriaca
abstract: Plants strike a delicate balance between growth and defense. The calculus of how to defend against herbivores, and maximize growth and reproduction, can differ between annuals and perennials. Annuals have a live fast, reproduce young strategy; while perennials may maximize fecundity over years. Milkweed, a herbaceous perennial, is a mix of these two strategies. On one hand, a single individual milkweed ramet is functionally a herbaceous annual and vulnerable to herbivory. On the other hand, below ground connections allow plants to share resources and persist for multiple years, perhaps lowering the cost of localized herbivory. Here, we study the impact herbivory on the leaf and soil microbiome on milkweed growth and flowering in a naturally occurring population. Specifically, using milkweed populations at three different sites in Virginia, following individual ramets throughout the growth and flowering season, we quantified the soil and leaf microbiome through metagenomic shotgun sequencing. After controlling for plant size and plant genotype, we asked how the microbiome composition was related to flowering time and growth. We find that the leaf microbiome is a strong predictor of plant growth rate, but not flowering. Conversely, we find that the soil microbiome and plant size predict flowering probability. We found no evidence that herbivory altered the leaf or soil microbiome composition. Together these results provide evidence that plant microbiomes also influence growth and fecundity in natural populations of milkweed. These results also provide evidence that the leaf microbiome in milkweed is robust and stable in the face of significant herbivory. This study expands our knowledge of the contribution of plant microbiomes to plant demography in a clonal perennial plant.
authors: Puzey JR, Munkres I, D’Orgeix C, Dalgleish HJ.

title: From Omics Data to Biological Context: The CURIE AI Engine. Illustrated with the Transcriptomic Response to Bacterial Pneumonia
abstract: High-throughput sequencing necessitates robust computational tools to contextualize complex transcriptomic data. In this study, we analyzed RNA-Seq data from peripheral blood of bacterial pneumonia patients and healthy controls (GEO: GSE161731) to investigate systemic molecular responses to infection. Differential gene expression analysis identified significantly upregulated genes in pneumonia. We used GANGO for Gene Ontology (GO) term enrichment and BioFunctional for hierarchical exploration, providing an initial overview of affected biological processes. To deepen interpretation, we leveraged CURIE (  www.curieai.tech ), an AI platform that cross-references GO terms with scientific literature. CURIE generates narrative explanations, linking molecular mechanisms, experimental evidence, and publications to each biological process, moving beyond simple enrichment. Our combined analysis revealed a coordinated upregulation of pathways involved in DNA repair and replication, transcriptional activation, RNA processing, translation, ribosome biogenesis, mitochondrial respiration, and cofactor binding. By integrating these findings within a broad, literature-supported framework, we highlighted how multiple cellular compartments and processes collaborate to mount an effective response to infection-induced stress. This study underscores the potential of combining classical statistical enrichment with AI-based interpretation for a holistic understanding of host-pathogen interactions at the transcriptomic level.
authors: Castellani G, Rodriguez-Mena A, Tarragó-Claramunt X, Madarnás-Gómez V, Torres-Favier Y, Méndez-Viera J, Monleón-Getino A.

title: Multi-omics reveals selective metabolic remodeling with trace element supplementation in chronic kidney disease
abstract: Introduction  Chronic kidney disease (CKD) generates metabolically heterogeneous stress across circulating, microbial, and renal compartments. Trace element supplementation may engage redox and metabolic pathways and selectively modulate responsive metabolic programs. Objectives  To define the metabolic branch selectivity, renal regional distribution, and tissue correlates of responses to a trace element cocktail (TEX) through an integrated clinical-to-mouse multi-omics framework, and to organize these findings into an experimentally testable model. Methods  In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 80 adults receiving maintenance hemodialysis received standard care plus TEX (20 mL/day; n = 40) or standard care plus matched placebo (n = 40). Longitudinal clinical outcomes were analyzed using participant random-intercept models. Endpoint plasma metabolomics and fecal metagenomics included healthy controls (n = 10) and voluntary trial subsets (placebo, n = 12; TEX, n = 20). Mice with 5/6 nephrectomy underwent targeted tryptophan metabolite profiling, renal spatial metabolomics, histopathology, and molecular analyses. Results  Longitudinal monitoring showed no overt treatment-related laboratory safety signal. Plasma metabolomics identified treatment-associated differences (false discovery rate Conclusion  This study establishes branch selectivity and renal regional specificity as defining features of TEX-associated metabolic remodeling in CKD. The integrated evidence defines a spatially organized, kynurenine-centered metabolic–renal response architecture comprising host kynurenine-branch remodeling, anatomically patterned renal metabolic responses, and selective structural, tubular, and mitochondrial/redox phenotypes, with kynurenine–mitochondrial/redox coupling as the central mechanistic proposition. Trial registration  International Traditional Medicine Clinical Trial Registry, ITMCTR2026000263; retrospectively registered on 3 February 2026, after completion of recruitment and follow-up.
authors: Piao J, Jin M, Yin F, Quan Z, Gao Z, Cui Z.

title: A coding CAG repeat expansion in  EP400  causes Spinocerebellar Ataxia
abstract: Several polyglutamine-encoding repeat expansions cause spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs) and other movement disorders. SCAs are genetically heterogeneous with a substantial diagnostic gap. We used genome sequencing data from 266 individuals of European and Asian ancestry and screened genome-wide for repeat expansions using STRling, a dedicated repeat expansion caller. The cohort comprised patients with movement disorders, predominantly dystonia and ataxia, as well as unaffected participants. Further, we screened another 436 individuals with ataxia and 427 ethnically matched controls through fragment analysis of the most promising candidate locus in  EP400 . We applied targeted long-read sequencing to expansion carriers and one control individual to resolve the sequence structure of the repeat locus. Finally, we used microsatellite markers in chromosome 12q24.32–33 to test for a common founder.  A genome-wide outlier analysis in STRling revealed a polyglutamine-encoding repeat expansion (GRCh38 chr12:132,062,525–132,062,590) in the E1A binding protein p400 (  EP400 ) gene in two patients with ataxia. Through screening of additional ataxia patients, we identified in total 18 patients from 14 families with heterozygous repeat expansions in  EP400. All expansion carriers were from Serbia. The repeat number in affected individuals ranged from 37 to 55, whereas the longest control allele had 32 repeats. We demonstrated that non-expanded alleles carried a CAA interruption within the 5′ CAG tract – this interruption was lost in expanded alleles. Expansion carriers have pure SCA with onset mainly in their 40s and 50s. There is an inverse correlation between the number of repeats and age at onset. The  EP400- encoded protein plays an essential role in chromatin remodeling, epigenetic regulation and DNA repair. Pathogenic sequence variants in  EP400 have previously been implicated in a neurodevelopmental disorder.  Our study identifies repeat expansions in  EP400 as a novel and frequent cause of ataxia in Serbian patients. This finding further increases the diagnostic yield of ataxia testing and warrants investigation in ataxia patients worldwide. We add  EP400 to the growing list of ataxia-associated repeat loci, which warrants inclusion in diagnostic ataxia panels.

title: Characterization of  de novo  structural variants in trios with orofacial clefts
abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are larger genetic rearrangements such as deletions, duplications, and insertions and other forms of structural alterations. Given their large size, they can have an outsized effect on phenotype, however, the contribution of SVs to the genetic architecture of orofacial clefts (OFCs) is not well understood. In this study, we sought to better understand the contribution SVs to OFC risk by characterizing  de novo SVs (dnSVs) in 1,549 probands with an OFC. Overall, we called 375 dnSVs in 307 probands (0.242 dnSVs per genome). The dnSV rate per genome was highest among individuals with cleft lip (CL, 0.29), followed by cleft lip and palate (CLP, 0.25) and cleft palate only (CP, 0.20), though differences across subtypes were not statistically significant. There were also no differences between sex or syndromic status, but we did identify a significant difference in the rate of duplications across OFC subtypes (p=0.005). Compared to CP (0.028), duplication rates were significantly higher for both CL (0.121; p = 0.003) and CLP (0.096; p = 0.002), suggesting a potential etiologic mechanism for CL/P. We systematically curated each dnSV to classify its potential for influencing OFC risk by examining the genes and regulatory elements disrupted by the SV and evidence for their role in craniofacial development or OFCs. We identified 22 dnSVs in regions associated with recurrent genomic disorders, including seven deletions and one duplication of the well-established OFC risk locus 22q11.2. Additionally, we identified 12 large (>1Mb) SVs, with eight meeting criteria for a likely pathogenic classification based on total gene involvement, and seven dnSVs disrupting well-known genes associated with autosomal dominant forms of OFC. The most notable was  SATB2, for which we found four dnSVs, all in individuals with CP. Next, by combining evidence from recurrent dnSVs and  de novo single nucleotide variants with Hi-C contact maps and predicted chromatin states from developing craniofacial tissues, we found new candidate genes for OFC risk including  FHAD1 ,  NBEA ,  NR3C2 , and  SPHKAP . Overall, dnSVs classified as likely pathogenic accounted for putative molecular diagnoses in approximately 1.67% of the cohort, with an additional 0.96% having variants of unknown significance with plausible risk for OFCs. Our results support dnSVs as an important component of OFC etiology and suggest their inclusion in analyses may improve diagnostic yield for affected individuals.

title: Identification of bromodomain family genes across the cotton genome and the enhancement of plant growth and development by GhBRD34
abstract: Abstract    Background  Bromodomain (BRD)-containing proteins are important regulators of plant growth, development, and responses to environmental stress. However, the understanding of their specific biological functions and molecular mechanisms in cotton is limited. Results  Here, we performed a genome‑wide survey and identified 69 GhBRD family members, which are located on 24 chromosomes of the upland cotton genome. Analysis of the promoter regions revealed several conserved cis-acting elements that play roles in light signaling, abiotic stress responses, and phytohormone signaling. Available transcriptome datasets revealed that four of these genes (  GhBRD1  ,  GhBRD33  ,  GhBRD34  , and  GhBRD68  ) exhibited consistently high expression across different tissues, suggesting that these genes participate in various aspects of plant growth and development. When  GhBRD34  was silenced through virus‑induced gene silencing in upland cotton, plant growth and development were markedly suppressed, resulting in reduced plant height and a relatively small leaf area. Conversely,  GhBRD34  overexpression in  Arabidopsis  not only promoted growth and development but also rendered the plants more sensitive to drought conditions. Conclusions  Our findings lay a solid foundation for future studies aimed at dissecting the molecular pathways through which  GhBRD34  influences growth, development, and drought responsiveness in upland cotton.
authors: Wu H, Liu X, Li Y, Yan Q, Wei Y, Li C, Liu H, Xie L, Wang X, Ma K.

title: Computational Identification of Secreted Molecular Candidates for Perivascular Hydrogel Delivery in Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
abstract: Background:  Perivascular hydrogel wrapping combines circumferential mechanical reinforcement with sustained local release of therapeutic payloads and is an emerging preclinical strategy for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). Because no hydrogel-intervention transcriptome is publicly available, the molecular payloads best suited to extra-adventitial delivery remain undefined. This study used human AAA transcriptomes to prioritize secreted molecules that could be loaded into a perivascular hydrogel. Methods. Differential expression was performed with limma on human AAA datasets (GSE57691, with small and large AAA; GSE7084, AAA wall; GSE47472, AAA neck), and the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were intersected with the Human Protein Atlas predicted secreted-protein set (1,902 genes). Candidates were examined by Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment, STRING protein-protein interaction, single-sample gene-set enrichment analysis with immune correlations, single-cell localization (GSE166676), and cross-species comparison with mouse AAA (GSE12591). Results. The AAA molecular program was already established in small AAA, with no significant additional transcriptomic change between small and large lesions. Intersecting the DEGs with the secretome yielded 82 candidate secreted proteins (16 up-regulated and 66 down-regulated in small AAA). Up-regulated drivers (IL1B, IL6, TNF, CCL3L1, CXCL1, CXCL5) correlated with M1 macrophages, NLRP3, and MMP9, whereas down-regulated protective factors (FRZB, TIMP4, SPARCL1, SMOC2, IGFBP5, GPX3) localized to vascular smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts. NELL2 was the only novel secreted protein robustly up-regulated across datasets. Cross-species agreement with the angiotensin II mouse model was poor. Conclusions. This computational study identifies a tiered list of secreted molecules potentially suitable for perivascular hydrogel-cell delivery against AAA: inflammatory drivers to antagonize, lost protective factors to replenish, and novel targets such as NELL2 to validate. The mechanical supportive effect of hydrogels cannot be assessed by transcriptomics, and the candidates require biomaterial, animal, and safety experiments.
authors: Cheng H.

title: Multi-omics Genetic Prioritization and Cross-species Analysis of Mitochondrial Genes in Trigeminal Neuralgia.
abstract: To identify mitochondrial genes associated with trigeminal neuralgia (TN) and characterize their expression in patient blood and experimental trigeminal nerve injury. We integrated methylation, expression, and protein quantitative trait loci with FinnGen TN genome-wide association data, focusing on MitoCarta3.0 genes. Summary-data-based Mendelian randomization, heterogeneity testing, colocalization, and tissue-specific analyses prioritized candidates. An exploratory case-control expression analysis measured candidate-gene expression by reverse-transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction in pretreatment blood from 12 patients with TN and 12 controls; experimental analyses examined blood and selected tissues from six rats with infraorbital nerve chronic constriction injury (ION-CCI) and six sham-operated rats. Longitudinal behavioral testing characterized the injury model. NIT2, HDHD3, and GRHPR overlapped across the three molecular screens. Colocalization supported NIT2 in the anterior cingulate cortex (PP.H4 = 0.949) and GRHPR in tibial nerve (PP.H4 = 0.818). All three genes showed increased expression in patient blood (all false-discovery-rate q < 0.001). HDHD3 and GRHPR also increased in rat blood (both q = 0.0188), and GRHPR increased in the injured infraorbital nerve (q = 0.0076). Genetically predicted higher GRHPR expression was associated with lower TN risk. Human genetics and cross-species expression analyses identify mitochondrial candidates associated with TN and trigeminal nerve injury. The protective genetic direction and injury-associated expression of GRHPR support a hypothesis of compensatory metabolic adaptation in trigeminal pain.
authors: Wei Y, Lan Z, Xie Y, Yi Z, Du X, Jiang Z.

title: Investigating the presence of microbiota-based phenotypes in irritable bowel syndrome.
abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is heterogenous disorder of gut-brain interaction, with a key role for the dysregulated host-gut microbiota interplay. IBS subtyping is based only on symptoms of bowel habits, reflecting limited insight into underlying biological mechanisms. This study aimed to define microbiota-based IBS phenotypes and to compare these to traditional stool-based subtyping. The study utilized data from the Maastricht IBS cohort. Gut microbiota composition was analysed using shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Faecal volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were measured by gas chromatography mass spectrometry. Dietary intake and gastrointestinal and mental health symptoms were assessed using a food frequency questionnaire, the Dutch Healthy Diet-15 index, the gastrointestinal symptom rating scale, and hospital anxiety and depression scores, respectively. Machine-learning approaches were applied to identify microbiota-based phenotypical clusters, which were compared with established Rome III subtypes, and associated with faecal VOCs, gastrointestinal symptom severity, diet and mental health. 178 IBS patients and 134 healthy controls were included. Gut microbiota composition distinguished IBS patients from healthy controls with an AUCROC 0 · 8. This discriminatory profile was not associated with Rome III subtypes, while statistically significant associations were found with faecal VOCs profiles (i.e.R= 0 · 67,p= 4 · 46e-4) and symptom severity scores of abdominal pain (p= 0 · 05), reflux (p= 0 · 03), diarrhoea (p= 0 · 01) and depression (p< 0 · 001). Dietary associations varied across clusters. These results suggest that gut microbiota profiling might provide a basis to define relevant IBS endotypes. Further exploration and validation efforts into this direction are needed using longitudinal studies to refine IBS patient stratification ultimately.

title: A DNA nanostructure-enabled photothermal hydrogel for synergistic antibacterial therapy and infected wound repair.
abstract: Bacterial infection is a major cause of delayed wound healing, while overuse of antibiotics has accelerated the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Developing multifunctional antibacterial biomaterials that eradicate bacteria without relying on conventional antibiotics is therefore highly desirable. Herein, we report an injectable polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based hydrogel incorporating gold nanorods (ARs) and a DNA nanostructure-mediated silver and antisense oligonucleotide delivery system (A-C@Ag) to achieve synergistic antibacterial therapy and enhanced skin regeneration. The hydrogel is formed by rapid thiol-maleimide crosslinking of PEG precursors containing AR@A-C@Ag, providing excellent injectability, biocompatibility, and mechanical stability. Upon near-infrared irradiation, the AR generates mild photothermal heating to directly damage bacteria and simultaneously promotes the on-demand release of Ag+ and antisense oligonucleotides from the DNA nanostructure, resulting in markedly enhanced antibacterial activity against both Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli by facilitating bacterial membrane disruption. In a S. aureus-infected full-thickness wound model, AR@A-C@Ag/Gel under NIR irradiation significantly accelerated wound closure by efficiently eliminating bacteria, suppressing inflammation, promoting angiogenesis and collagen deposition, and facilitating the regeneration of skin appendages. This work demonstrates that integrating DNA nanostructure-enabled drug delivery with mild photothermal therapy represents an effective strategy for constructing antibiotic-free antibacterial hydrogels for infected wound repair.
authors: Chen J, Zhao Q, Li T, Zhang X, Pu Y, He B.

title: Opines: origins, roles, structures with a nomenclature proposal, and syntheses.
abstract: Covering: 1927 to 2026.Although discovered almost a century ago, opines represent an ever-growing family of natural products, derived from a variety of organisms, including bacteria, fungi, plants, and marine invertebrates. Opines exhibit a wide variety of structures and play numerous biological roles, some of which have had significant implications in molecular biology, notably in the development of genetically modified organisms (GMOs) and in plant evolution with the recent discovery of natural GMOs. The opines structurally related to N-alkylated α-amino acids are useful chiral building blocks for the pharmaceutical and fine chemical industries, and some of the enzymes involved in their biosynthesis are now being exploited in these industries for drug development. This review first traces the history of opines from 1927 up to now in term of both chemical and biological views; then a new classification with clearer names is proposed mostly based on structural grounds. The various syntheses of opines are described and discussed according to this proposed classification, together with their known applications in biology, chemical biology and chemistry. Finally, several possible directions are highlighted as a roadmap for future research.
authors: Otten L, Pale P.

title: Diabesity: an old term, a modern challenge - multi-omics and precision anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in type 2 diabetes.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity are closely interconnected but heterogeneous conditions in which treatment response, safety, body weight, glycemic control, and long-term clinical outcomes vary substantially between individuals. This narrative review evaluates emerging anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with coexisting T2DM and obesity and examines the translational role of multi-omics in future precision treatment selection. Distinct from reviews focused primarily on obesity pharmacotherapy or omics-based disease stratification, the present review emphasizes the interface between contemporary drug mechanisms, T2DM-associated metabolic heterogeneity, candidate molecular signatures, and the level of evidence required for clinically actionable prescribing. We summarize evidence for approved and investigational oral incretin therapies, dual and triple receptor agonists, amylin-based strategies, established antidiabetic drugs, and adjunctive approaches targeting body composition. Throughout the review, we distinguish established clinical evidence from mechanistic rationale, candidate biomarkers, exploratory associations, and hypothetical future precision applications. We also separate metabolic efficacy endpoints, such as body weight and HbA1c, from intermediate cardiometabolic risk markers and from cardiovascular or kidney outcomes demonstrated in dedicated outcome trials. At present, no genomic, metabolomic, lipidomic, proteomic, microbiome, or integrated multi-omics signature has been clinically validated to select a specific anti-obesity medication for patients with T2DM and obesity. Major unresolved issues include the need for prospective biomarker validation, direct comparative trials, standardized assays, externally validated and calibrated prediction models, preservation of skeletal muscle health and physical function, long-term safety, treatment durability, affordability, and equitable implementation. Multi-omics should therefore be viewed as an investigational framework for generating and testing precision-treatment hypotheses rather than as a basis for routine prescribing.

authors: Hoffmann K, Pucek WF, Skrzypek W, Kierzkowski F, Ratajczak P, Maggio V, Rizzo M, El-Tanani M, Rabbani SA, Bhongade B, Satyam SM, Talath S, Rangraze IR, Wali AF, Ibraheem W, El-Tanani Y, Ispas S, Bryl W, Paczkowska A.

title: Enrichment of the Conserved RY-Repeat Cis-Element in Maize upon Ustilago maydis Infection and Its Interaction with the Candidate Secreted Protein UMAG_06102.
abstract: Ustilago maydis causes corn smut diseases by forming tumors on maize. Effectors of U. maydis could regulate host gene transcription. However, there is remaining uncertainty about the mechanisms underlying the regulation of transcription reprogramming of maize genes by U. maydis to facilitate disease progression. Here, we conducted systemic enrichment analysis of cis-elements in maize genes induced by infection with U. maydis. Yeast library screening and gene expression analysis were used to identify candidate proteins that could interact with the RY-repeat-containing promoter regions. Knocking out and genetic variation analysis were also deployed to study the role of fungal protein binding to RY-repeat during U. maydis infection. The conserved plant cis-element RY-repeat in maize was enriched in response to U. maydis. UMAG_06102, a candidate secreted protein of U. maydis, showed a Y1H-detected interaction with the RY-repeat-containing region of ZmSWEET11 promoter in a yeast-one-hybrid system. Knocking out UMAG_06102 was associated with the reduced expression of ZmSWEET11 and a decrease in virulence. Moreover, the genetic variation of the RY-repeat of ZmSWEET11 was likely associated with the disease incidence of U. maydis on maize. Our results suggested that U. maydis could influence the host gene expression through the enrichment of the RY-repeat of ZmSWEET11, thus impacting tumor formation on host tissues.
authors: Ruan X, Pan X, Wang Q, Gao X.

title: Non-Coding Structural Variants in Regulatory Regions and High Polygenic Burden May Jointly Contribute to Early-Onset Familial Hashimoto's Thyroiditis.
abstract: Background/objectivesMultigenerational families with unusually early disease onset provide a unique opportunity to investigate the genetic architecture underlying the missing heritability of complex diseases. Here, we investigated the genetic basis of apparent autosomal dominant early-onset Hashimoto's thyroiditis (HT) in a multigenerational pedigree using whole-exome sequencing (WES) in 9 individuals and PacBio HiFi long-read whole-genome sequencing (LR-WGS) in four family members spanning three generations.MethodsWES identified a rare disease-segregating TPH2 missense variant, while LR-WGS identified approximately 2000 structural variants (SVs) shared by the three sequenced affected relatives and absent from the unaffected father.ResultsAffected-lineage-shared SVs were significantly enriched within established hypothyroidism GWAS loci (447 observed vs. 292.6 expected overlaps; p = 6.99 × 10-4), with prominent clusters at the NFATC1-ATP9B and PDCD6-AHRR loci. Integrative analyses incorporating regulatory annotation, GWAS overlap, and exploratory proteomic profiling highlighted candidate regulatory SVs affecting enhancers and long non-coding RNAs within the TPH2/TRHDE, TPO/LALTOP, and TSHR loci. Exploratory proteomic profiling was consistent with involvement of the NFATC1-ATP9B and PDCD6-AHRR loci and identified AXIN1 as an additional candidate locus. Parallel polygenic risk score (PRS) analysis showed that the three affected sequenced family members ranked above the 95th percentile of the HT PRS distribution.ConclusionsTogether, these findings are consistent with a multi-hit genetic model in which elevated polygenic burden and multiple regulatory structural variants may jointly contribute to early-onset familial HT. The observed enrichment of affected-lineage-shared SVs within established hypothyroidism GWAS loci further suggests that regulatory structural variation may contribute to previously unexplained non-coding genetic susceptibility.
authors: Boraska Perica V, Barić Žižić A, Sladić S, Vuletić M, Listeš I, Kaličanin D, Žnidar V, Čikeš Čulić V, Torlak Lovrić V, Punda A, Škrabić V, Barbalić M.

title: Rapid On-Site Detection of Clarithromycin in Water Using an Evanescent Wave Fluorescence Immunosensor.
abstract: Clarithromycin (CLA), a widely used macrolide antibiotic and contaminant of emerging concern (CEC), is frequently detected in aquatic environments. Its residues can induce bacterial antibiotic resistance, threatening public health and ecosystems. In this study, we constructed an evanescent wave fluorescence immunoassay for the rapid detection of clarithromycin. It detects CLA in water quickly, sensitively, and in a portable format. The sensor combines evanescent wave fluorescence with an indirect competitive immunoassay. It uses a CLA-bovine serum albumin (BSA) conjugate on an optical fiber bioprobe, along with a Cy5.5-labeled anti-clarithromycin monoclonal antibody (Ka = 7.40 × 109 L/mol) as the signal reporter. After optimization, the assay gave a linear range of 7.50-77.45 μg/L. The LOD was 1.67 μg/L, and the LOQ was 7.50 μg/L. The functionalized fiber bioprobe also held up well in repeated use. It stayed stable for over 200 regeneration cycles, with an RSD of 5.63%. The entire automated detection workflow was completed within 20 min without manual intervention. Real-sample validation was performed using tap water and river water spiked at 10, 30, and 60 μg/L, yielding recoveries ranging from 87.13% to 104.84%, with relative standard deviations below 13.08%. These results were corroborated by ELISA. These attributes, combined with the instrument's portability and the probe's regenerability, render this biosensor a promising analytical platform for on-site environmental monitoring of clarithromycin residues.
authors: Zhang W, Liu Y, Liu J, Long F, Li H, Zhang X, Shi Y, Li C.

title: Near-infrared pre-irradiation is associated with a distinct transcriptional signature in rat gastric irreversible electroporation: an exploratory genome-wide analysis.
abstract: Near-infrared (NIR) pre-irradiation before irreversible electroporation (IRE), or NIRE, augments apoptosis in rat stomach, but its transcriptional correlates are unknown. We profiled rat gastric corpus from four arms on the Rat Gene 2.0 ST array (n = 3 per arm; light only n = 1) in an exploratory design. Under nominal criteria (fold change at least 1.5, uncorrected p < 0.05), IRE and NIRE altered 1175 and 1365 transcripts versus control and 334 differed between NIRE and IRE. With limma moderated statistics the control contrasts gave 172 and 318 transcripts at FDR < 0.05, but none reached FDR < 0.05 for NIRE versus IRE (minimum 0.198, Nqo2), and unsupervised ordination did not separate the arms (PERMANOVA p = 0.10, an exact test floor). Against the IRE response, 64% of that signature comprised changes induced by IRE that NIRE attenuated or reversed; only 7% was amplification. Competitive gene-set tests gave a nominal, uncorrected signal for the metallothionein family (p = 0.036) and a trend toward lower NRF2/ARE targets (p = 0.057), the latter reflecting an absent IRE-associated antioxidant induction rather than suppression below control; no set survived correction, and a heat-shock panel was unchanged (p = 0.66). These are descriptive, hypothesis-generating observations that nominate candidate programs for validation; they do not establish a mechanism.
authors: Jeon HJ, Kim HB, Choi HS, Lee JM, Kim ES, Keum B, Jeen YT, Chun HJ.

title: Cross species metabolic complementation of vitamin K2 biosynthesis determines emergent suppression of tomato Fusarium wilt.
abstract: Multi-omics approaches have revealed a cross-species functional emergence phenomenon leading to emergent suppression of Fusarium wilt. We show that a three‑species consortium exhibits emergent suppression of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici (Fol) that is absent in single or pairwise cultures. This antifungal activity arises from coordinated activation of two phylogenetically distinct vitamin K2 biosynthesis pathways-the Men pathway (primarily Bacillus) and the Mqn pathway (Paenibacillus)-whose complementary actions enhance K2 production and directly inhibit the pathogen. A structural analogue, vitamin K3, recapitulates this effect, offering translational potential. Our findings establish that emergent microbiome functions depend on interaction‑triggered latent metabolic activation, not constitutive exchange or additive effects.
authors: Zhao L, Li Y, Zhao J, Jousset A, Dini-Andreote F, Tan L, Guan X, Xu Y, Wei Z.

title: Chitinase biosynthesis and antifungal chitin bioconversion by Streptomyces mutabilis Ssg through statistical optimisation: an agro-industrial waste valorisation approach.
abstract: Chitin valorisation through enzymatic bioconversion offers a sustainable route for converting biowastes into value-added bioactive products. In this study, the chitinolytic strain Ssg, showing close phylogenetic affinity with Streptomyces mutabilis, was evaluated for chitinase production in a waste-integrated submerged fermentation system based on crustacean-derived colloidal chitin and supplemented with date seed and orange-peel powders as low-cost co-substrates. The isolate showed a high chitinolytic index of 17.20 ± 0.70. Plackett-Burman screening identified substrate composition and incubation time as key determinants of chitinase production, while Box-Behnken optimisation revealed significant interaction effects and identified the best-performing combination. At 10 g/L date seed powder, 4.08 g/L orange peel powder, and 72 h of incubation, chitinase activity reached 3196 ± 1.73 U/mL, closely matching the predicted value of 3198.01 U/mL. Optimisation increased enzyme production 7.6-fold and reduced fermentation time from 6 days to 72 h. Specific activity also increased from 4870 ± 170 to 13,620 ± 105 U/mg, reflecting stronger chitinolytic performance of the optimised preparation. Both the Optimised Cell-Free Supernatant and the crude chitin hydrolysate exhibited comparable antifungal activity against Aspergillus brasiliensis and Fusarium sp., with a slight advantage for the hydrolysate. The strongest response was observed against Fusarium sp. with the crude chitin hydrolysate, showing an inhibition zone of 24.00 ± 1.00 mm and mycelial growth inhibition of 38.75%. Microscopic observations revealed hyphal deformation and structural disorganisation. Overall, this study establishes a waste-integrated strategy for high-level chitinase production and supports the potential of the Ssg system for chitin bioconversion and biocontrol-oriented applications.
authors: Missouri A, Khaldi A, Benine ML, Bassou D, Kebbouche Gana S, Bensedjad A, Laraki M, Megherbi A, Boumegoura A, Emiliani G, Boucif M, Kaissar FZ.

title: The key amino acids (cysteine and histidine) across BVDV-1 N<sup>pro</sup> sequence that affect autoprotease activity and inhibition of IFN-β synthesis.
abstract: The N-terminal protease (Npro) of bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) possesses two major biological functions, namely autoprotease activity and antagonism of interferon (IFN) synthesis, both of which are important for viral replication and immune evasion. Given the high mutation rate of the BVDV genome, whether mutations in Npro affect these functions remains largely unknown. Because cysteine and histidine residues are critical determinants of Npro activity, we systematically investigated the roles of all cysteine and histidine residues in regulating autoprotease activity and IFN antagonism. Synonymous codon substitutions involving cysteine or histidine residues did not affect the autoprotease activity of Npro. In contrast, analyses of nonsynonymous substitutions revealed that, in addition to the previously identified catalytic residues His49 and Cys69, His40, His99, and the zinc-binding residues Cys112, Cys134, and Cys138 were also essential for efficient autoprotease activity. By comparison, substitution of His148 had no detectable effect on either autoprotease activity or IFN antagonism. Functional dissociation analyses demonstrated that mutations at Glu22 and His49 enhanced IFN-β antagonism while abolishing autoprotease activity, whereas the Cys69 mutation abolished autocleavage but retained IFN suppression. In contrast, certain substitutions at His130 and Cys161 selectively impaired IFN antagonism without affecting autocleavage, indicating that these two functions are partially separable. Notably, mutations at His40, His99, Cys112, Cys134 and Cys138 markedly impaired both autoprotease activity and IFN antagonism, suggesting that these residues represent common functional determinants of the two activities. Sequence alignment of Npro proteins from different BVDV-1 strains identified naturally occurring non-conservative variations at positions 40, 130 and 148. Further analyses showed that the naturally occurring His40Arg and His130Pro substitutions significantly affected both autoprotease activity and IFN antagonism, supporting a functional association between Npro autocleavage and IFN suppression. In contrast, His148Arg, His148Asn, and His148Gln substitutions had no detectable effect on either activity. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that cysteine and histidine residues play critical roles in regulating both autoprotease activity and IFN antagonism of BVDV-1 Npro. Mutations at specific residues differentially affect these functions, highlighting the importance of conserved cysteine and histidine residues in maintaining the multifunctional properties of Npro.
authors: Ren XT, Hong JS, An LL, Wang T, Ma XX.

title: PLCB3 as a causal regulator linking ferroptosis and immune remodeling in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
abstract: BackgroundHeart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a complex syndrome lacking effective targeted therapies, but its causal genes and mechanisms remain poorly defined.ObjectiveTo investigate the role of PLCB3 and its association with ferroptosis in HFpEF.MethodsWe integrated transcriptomic data and genome-wide association studies (GWAS) data and employed differential expression analysis, mendelian randomization (MR), summary data-based mendelian randomization (SMR), and colocalization analysis to identify key genes associated with HFpEF. Furthermore, functional validation was performed using a HFpEF mouse model and siRNA mediated PLCB3 knockdown in AC16 cardiomyocytes. Cell viability, reactive oxygen species (ROS), lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis related protein expression were subsequently assessed to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying PLCB3-mediated ferroptosis.ResultsPhospholipase C beta 3 (PLCB3) was identified as a candidate causal gene for HFpEF. PLCB3 expression was significantly reduced in HFpEF cardiac tissue and a mouse model induced by high-fat diet and l-NAME. Knockdown of PLCB3 decreased cell viability and induced ferroptosis, as indicated by reduced GPX4 and FTH1 expression, increased ACSL4 levels, and elevated lipid peroxidation and reactive oxygen species. These effects were significantly reversed by the ferroptosis inhibitor Ferrostatin-1. In vivo, ferroptosis-related markers were similarly altered in HFpEF mice. In addition, immune infiltration analysis revealed significant differences in multiple immune cell populations between HFpEF and controls. Single-cell eQTL-based MR analysis further suggested that PLCB3 expression is associated with specific immune cell subsets, including B cells, CD4+ naïve T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells.ConclusionPLCB3 is a potential regulator of HFpEF and may contribute to disease progression through its role in regulating ferroptosis and immune alterations. These findings provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms of HFpEF and suggest that targeting PLCB3 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy.
authors: Zhu H, Qin C, Yang J, Luo S, Guo Y.

title: Methanogenic archaea Methanobrevibacter smithii and Methanosphaera stadtmanae promote mucosal homeostasis and protect from colitis.
abstract: The intestinal microbiota is a critical determinant of mucosal homeostasis, yet the functional contributions of Archaea-which constitute up to 10% of the anaerobic community-remain largely undefined. Here, we provide evidence that the human methanogens Methanobrevibacter smithii (MSm) and Methanosphaera stadtmanae (MSt) promote colonic health. Transcriptomic analysis of germ-free mice reveals that MSm and MSt induce distinct colonic programs important for epithelial integrity. Using gnotobiotic and antibiotic-treated specific-pathogen-free mouse models, we show that MSm and MSt reinforce the epithelial barrier, characterized by increased goblet cell expansion, mucus thickening, and enhanced epithelial regeneration. Furthermore, methanogens expand Foxp3+ regulatory T cell (Treg) populations without inducing pro-inflammatory TH17 responses. Notably, MSm and MSt protect against dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis. While MSt-mediated protection requires adaptive immunity, MSm retains partial efficacy in lymphocyte-deficient mice, revealing nonredundant protective mechanisms. These findings indicate that methanogenic archaea promote mucosal integrity during host association and suggest that methanogens may hold therapeutic potential for inflammatory bowel disease, though translation to human disease remains to be established.
authors: Byrd EE, Harris BW, Zhang H, Warren WE, Kolli SH, Putelo AM, McGinty MT, Solga MD, Rutkowski MR, Kendall MM.

title: Conformational flexibility of the nitrogenase-like reductase CfbC/D involved in coenzyme F<sub>430</sub> biosynthesis.
abstract: The nitrogenase-like reductase CfbC/D catalyzes the six-electron reduction of the tetrapyrrole macrocycle of Ni2+-sirohydrochlorin a,c-diamide during the biosynthesis of coenzyme F430, an essential cofactor for biological methane formation and consumption. The individual dimeric protein components, CfbC2 and CfbD2, form a complex to allow for electron transfer from the [4Fe:4S] cluster in CfbC2 to the [4Fe:4S] cluster in CfbD2 and onto the substrate. The overall process is ATP-dependent. Although CfbC/D belongs to the family of nitrogenase-like enzymes, there are several intriguing differences between CfbC/D, other nitrogenase-like enzymes and nitrogenase itself. In contrast to the other enzymes, CfbC/D exhibits a simpler molecular architecture, forming a heterotetrameric CfbC2D2 assembly. Furthermore, the interaction of the CfbC and CfbD components does not depend on the presence of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Here we report cryoelectron microscopy structures of the CfbC/D complex prepared in the absence and presence of substrates. These structures not only shed light on the molecular architecture of the CfbC/D complex but also reveal a high degree of structural flexibility within the CfbD2 component, which undergoes a large conformational change in the presence of an ATP analog and the tetrapyrrole substrate. The interplay of CfbD with its reductase CfbC also strongly suggests an evolutionary pathway toward the modern nitrogenase from methanogenic archaea.
authors: Zhang L, Schuhmacher F, Kussler A, Einsle O, Layer G.

title: Restoration of full length filamin C is sufficient to prevent FLNC deficient cardiomyopathy in mice.
abstract: Filamin C (FLNC) is an essential cytoskeletal protein required for cardiomyocyte structural integrity and mechanotransduction. Truncating FLNC variants cause haploinsufficiency associated with dilated and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies, yet no therapies currently address the underlying defect of FLNC deficiency. Gene replacement is challenging because the approximately 8.2-kb FLNC coding sequence exceeds the packaging capacity of conventional adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors. Here, we engineered a triple-AAV strategy optimized for full-length FLNC reconstitution in the heart. Screening in HEK293 cells identified GP41-1 and IMPDH as a compatible orthogonal pair for efficient full-length FLNC reconstitution. In tamoxifen-inducible, cardiomyocyte-specific Flnc knockout mice, systemic delivery of optimized MyoAAV2A vectors restored full-length FLNC expression and re-established sarcomeric localization following cardiomyocyte FLNC depletion. A total vector dose of 1 × 10¹³ genome copies/kg restored FLNC to approximately endogenous abundance, preserved systolic function and ventricular dimensions, limited cardiac enlargement, attenuated fibrotic remodeling and prevented premature death. FLNC replacement also attenuated pathological transcriptional remodeling and compensatory changes in cytoskeletal and junction-associated proteins. These findings demonstrate that systemic split-intein-mediated reconstitution of full-length FLNC can preserve cardiac structure and function in vivo, providing preclinical support for a mutation-independent therapeutic strategy for FLNC-associated cardiomyopathy.
authors: Jiang Z, Feng W, Chen Z, Bogomolovas J, Li M, Ye M, Gu Y, Zhou X, Chen J.

title: Glutamate coordinates with Lactobacillus amylovorus to attenuate intestinal damage induced by deoxynivalenol.
abstract: Deoxynivalenol (DON) is a prevalent trichothecene mycotoxin that threatens intestinal health, yet its effects on gut microbiota remain poorly understood. Here, Lactobacillus amylovorus isolated from Ningxiang pigs showed strong acid and bile tolerance but significantly impaired growth under DON exposure. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that DON disrupted amino acid metabolism in L. amylovorus, particularly glutamate metabolism. Among the amino acids tested, only glutamate supplementation restored bacterial growth under DON exposure. Futhermore, co-supplementation with glutamate and L. amylovorus alleviated DON-induced intestinal injury by improving intestinal barrier integrity and serum amino acid homeostasis in mice. Intestinal transcriptomics showed that differentially expressed genes were mainly enriched in the nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathway. Co-supplementation modulated NF-κB signaling, restored glutamate metabolism, reduced IL-1β and IL-6 levels, and increased Bcl2, Btk, and Cd40 expression. Correlation and protein-protein interaction analyses further suggested a potential association between B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2) and glutamic-pyruvic transaminase 2 (GPT2), a key enzyme in glutamate metabolism. Overall, glutamate cooperates with L. amylovorus to alleviate DON-induced intestinal injury, potentially through coordinated regulation of glutamate metabolism and NF-κB signaling.
authors: Zeng Y, Guo Y, Yuan L, He Y, Han Q, Yin Y, Zhou X.

title: Seasonal variation in the content of β-asarone and related phenylpropenes and their associated transcriptomic profiles in Acorus calamus.
abstract: Acorus calamus L. is a monocotyledonous medicinal plant possessing bioactive compounds, including β-asarone, which exhibits anti-microbial, neuroprotective, and antioxidant effects. However, the biosynthetic pathway of β-asarone in A. calamus remains poorly understood. This study investigated seasonal changes in the accumulation of β-asarone and related phenylpropenes and their associated transcriptome. Leaf, root, and rhizome samples were analyzed by gas chromatography, and leaf samples representing periods with the lowest and highest levels of β-asarone and its related phenylpropene (Z)-methylisoeugenol were selected for comparative transcriptome analysis. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway enrichment analysis revealed distinct gene expression patterns during β-asarone accumulation, including the downregulation of most phenylpropanoid biosynthetic genes and upregulation of the genes encoding 4-coumarate-CoA ligase and caffeoyl-CoA O-methyltransferase. Conversely, these genes exhibited different expression patterns during the periods of high (Z)-methylisoeugenol accumulation. This study suggests that β-asarone biosynthesis involves different pathways from predicted phenylpropene routes and provides insights into the seasonal regulation of specialized phenylpropanoid metabolism in A. calamus.
authors: Ganbat O, Kashimoto N, Matsumoto M, Ogawa T, Koeduka T, Ulziibat B, Okazawa A.

title: Map-based cloning of the susceptibility locus conditioning bs6 resistance in pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) encoding mutant alleles of pseudokinase proteins.
abstract: Key messageThe bs6 resistance gene against bacterial spot was identified by map-based cloning in pepper (C. annuum L.). The recessive bs661 locus of pepper Capsicum annuum L. var. 61R (Ca61R) conditions a non-hypersensitive resistance trait, characterized by a slightly swollen, pale green, photosynthetically active leaf tissue, following Xanthomonas euvesicatoria Race 6 (XeR6) infection. In contrast, C. annuum cv. Feherozon (CaFo) is susceptible to XeR6. Map-based cloning of the bs661 locus revealed that the bs661 locus encodes three predicted proteins, pbs661npk, pbs661n, pbs661pk in Ca61R which are the counterpart of the three wild type predicted proteins, pBs6FoNPK, pBs6FoN and pBs6FoPK in CaFo, respectively. Sequence analysis revealed that the pBs6FoNPK protein showed 35% identity and 53% similarity to the ZRK4 pseudokinase (pAtZRK4) identified in Arabidopsis thaliana, which possesses N-terminal and C-terminal (pseudokinase) domains. The pBs6FoN and pBs6FoPK proteins resemble the N-terminal and C-terminal domains of the pBs6FoNPK protein, respectively, thus, they also contain pseudokinase domains/sequences. In Ca61R, pbs661npk and pbs661n are truncated counterparts of pBs6FoNPK and pBs6FoN, respectively, as a consequence of a single-nucleotide insertion that causes frameshifts and premature stop codons, whereas pbs661pk differs from pBs6FoPK by a single amino acid, a serine to alanine substitution at position 133. These three proteins are considered functionless. The ORF of pBs6FoN, pBs6FoPK and pbs661n, pbs661pk, respectively, are encoded by a single transcript in both parental plants. For this reason the translation of pBs6FoPK was ambiguous, however, the expression of pBs6FoN-dsRed fusion protein demonstrated that pBs6FoPK in fact can be translated. The three wild type proteins (pBs6FoNPK, pBs6FoN and pBs6FoPK) were independently responsible for ETS (effector-triggered susceptibility), because all three genes had to be in mutant configuration to manifest the resistant phenotype, in addition, any one of the three was able to reverse the resistant phenotype to susceptibility. Functional analysis using virus-induced gene silencing and transient genetic complementation demonstrated that the three CaFo proteins contribute redundantly to XeR6 susceptibility. Silencing either Bs6FoNPK, Bs6FoN and Bs6FoPK alone did not alter susceptibility, whereas simultaneous silencing of these genes conferred resistance. Conversely, the individual expression of pBs6FoNPK, pBs6FoN, and pBs6FoPK, in the resistant Ca61R background each restored susceptibility. These results demonstrate that the three Bs6 proteins act redundantly to promote XeR6 susceptibility and that loss of function of all three corresponding proteins was required for the recessive resistance phenotype conferred by bs661.
journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik

title: An exploratory study of the effect of metformin on the whole blood transcriptome of nondiabetic older adults with age-related macular degeneration.
abstract: Metformin has received increasing attention for benefits beyond blood glucose lowering. The purpose of this study was to identify changes in whole blood transcriptome from a course of metformin in a randomized trial (NCT02684578) of nondiabetic older adults with age-related macular degeneration (AMD). We included patients who were ≥ 55 years of age, nondiabetic, and had geographic atrophy due to AMD. We excluded patients with metformin use for another reason, reduced renal or liver function, or other vitreoretinal diseases. Participants were randomized to metformin or control. The metformin group was prescribed 1000 mg metformin twice daily for 18 months. All eligible patients were approached for consent to blood sample collection. We performed metagenomic sequencing on whole blood samples and conducted differential expression analysis. Fifteen patients underwent blood collection, with eight in the metformin group and seven in the control group. No individual gene achieved statistical significance of difference between groups after correction for multiple comparisons. As a secondary, hypothesis-generating analysis, canonical pathway analysis found downregulation of interferon α/β signaling (P = 0.003, z score = -2.4), cell junction organization (P = 0.03, z score = -2.2), and epithelial mesenchymal transition pathways in the metformin group (P = 0.02, z score = -2.2). There was possible inhibition of upstream proinflammatory molecules and activation of anti-inflammatory molecules by metformin. In this small sub-study of a randomized trial, no gene was significantly changed after metformin exposure. Pathway enrichment analysis identified signals potentially consistent with metformin-associated modulation of "inflammaging" and other biological pathways which require validation in larger cohorts.
authors: Chen X, Zhang YS, Yan D, Doan T, Shen LL, Taha AT, Yang D, Psaras C, Callander JK, Xin NY, Shivkumar A, Fawzi AA, Yiu G, Telander DG, Leung LB, Flaxel C, Newman JC, Keenan JD, Stewart JM.

title: Marine microbial arginase: a metabolic therapeutic strategy for oral squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) represents a significant clinical burden, with limited advancements in metabolic-targeted therapies. Arginase is a metalloenzyme that plays an essential role in the hydrolysis of L-arginine into urea and L-ornithine. In recent years, arginase enzyme also shows promising role in therapeutic especially in anti-cancer therapy through arginine deprivation therapy (ADT). Among many tumors that are arginine-auxotrophic due to downregulation of ASS1 are hepatocellular carcinoma, melanoma, and subsets of oral cancers, and are therefore susceptible to depletion of extracellular arginine. Although recombinant human arginase has advanced to preclinical and clinical trials, issues such as immunological reactions and limited stability have sparked interest in alternative sources. Marine microorganisms, especially from deep-sea environments, are known to produce unique and stable enzymes with high catalytic efficiency and are less prone to protein denaturation. As a result of their remarkable stability in harsh conditions and variety of structures, marine microbial arginases have emerged as the top candidates for investigation. In addition to remaining active at varying pH, salinity, and temperatures, these enzymes offer a versatile platform for protein engineering and therapeutic optimisation. This review focuses on the biochemical and structural properties of arginase, compares microbial and human forms, and explores the mechanisms of its antitumor action, including tumor cell growth inhibition, angiogenesis modulation, and immune suppression within the tumor microenvironment. Additionally, it identifies developments in marine bioprospecting, combination strategies with immunotherapy, and nanoparticle-based delivery as major trends influencing future research.
authors: Priya R, Ragul G, Ritika G, Kannan K, Ganapathy D, Pitchiah S.

title: Tissue expression of aquaporin-5 and cytochrome c as potential forensic biomarkers of drowning: Evidence from an experimental rat model.
abstract: Determining whether a person died from drowning remains a major forensic challenge, particularly in cases involving advanced decomposition where only skeletal remains are available. Traditional methods, such as diatom analysis and macroscopic autopsy findings, often lack sufficient specificity and reliability. Although several molecular biomarkers have been investigated, none has yet demonstrated sufficient accuracy for routine forensic application. This prospective experimental study evaluated a novel dual-biomarker approach using Aquaporin 5 (AQP5), a water channel protein, and Cytochrome c (CYCS), an apoptosis-related protein, as potential indicators of drowning. Thirty-eight adult Wistar rats were randomly assigned to experimental drowning groups or non-drowning control groups (exposed to freshwater from Boračko and Jablaničko lakes. Lung, femoral bone, and dental tissues were collected postmortem, and AQP5 and CYCS concentrations were quantified using commercially available ELISA kits. Statistical analyses included the Shapiro-Wilk test and the Mann-Whitney U test, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. AQP5 expression in dental tissue differed significantly between drowning and control groups in both freshwater environments (p = 0.0184 and p = 0.0235), whereas no significant differences were observed in lung or bone tissues. CYCS expression did not differ significantly between drowning and control groups in any tissue examined. These findings suggest that AQP5 expression in dental tissue may represent a promising supplementary biomarker for the forensic diagnosis of drowning, particularly in cases where only skeletal remains are available. Further validation in human tissues and larger experimental cohorts is warranted.
authors: Dervišević E, Osmanović H, Katica M, Bešić A, Čelebičić M, Goletić T, Terzić I, Šabić E, Selmanagić A, Spahović H, Dervišević M, Montanari E, Montana A.

title: Temporal regulation of metabolic processes in the marine diazotroph Crocosphaera watsonii WH8501.
abstract: Marine diazotrophic cyanobacteria play a crucial role in oceanic nitrogen cycling, supporting primary production and ecosystem balance. Crocosphaera watsonii WH8501 exemplifies this capability by temporally separating photosynthesis and diazotrophy. To investigate the regulatory mechanisms underlying this process, we employed mass spectrometry-based proteomics in a high-resolution diel culturing experiment, revealing tightly coordinated protein abundance patterns. Unsupervised clustering of diel protein abundance profiles identified six groups of co-regulated proteins characterized by distinct temporal expression patterns and functional categories. Cluster 1 contained nitrogen fixation and amino acid biosynthesis proteins that peaked at night, while cluster 2 included glycogen metabolism and photosynthetic dark reaction proteins that were most abundant during the night and day-night transition, supporting carbon consumption and energy production. Clusters 3 and 4 were enriched in proteins involved in photosynthesis, cell division, and lipid synthesis, with maximal abundance around midday. Cluster 5 comprised peptide biosynthesis proteins that peaked later in the day and may facilitate nitrogenase complex formation. Cluster 6, expressed during the day-night transition, revealed coordinated nitrogenase assembly, with Fe-S cluster proteins preceding peak nitrogenase iron protein abundance, suggesting a temporally ordered sequence of enzyme maturation. Distinct temporal patterns in iron trafficking to heme and Fe-S cluster biosynthetic systems further indicated tightly regulated allocation of iron to metalloproteins across the diel cycle. Together, these results reveal the intricate temporal coordination that enables Crocosphaera to balance nitrogen fixation and photosynthesis within a single cell and underscore the central role of diel regulation in sustaining these globally important processes.IMPORTANCEMarine diazotrophic cyanobacteria play an essential role in global nitrogen cycling and ocean productivity. In this study, we investigate the temporal regulation of Crocosphaera watsonii metabolism using high-resolution proteomics under diel culturing conditions. Our analysis resolves six distinct clusters of protein abundance patterns across the light/dark cycle, reflecting intricate coordination of nitrogen fixation, photosynthesis, carbon allocation, and iron homeostasis. Notably, we identify temporally ordered assembly of nitrogenase subunits, including precursory expression of Fe-S cluster proteins and indications of tightly controlled iron trafficking systems. These findings provide new mechanistic insight into how unicellular diazotrophs synchronize key metabolic processes under natural diel cycles.
authors: Gauglitz JM, Inomura K, Bittremieux W, Moran DM, McIlvin MR, Saito MA.

title: Genetically regulated molecular mediators of phenotypic heterogeneity in autism spectrum disorder
abstract: Background  Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) shows wide phenotypic variation, from adults without intellectual disability and with low support needs to minimally verbal children with intellectual disability and severe behavioral symptoms. Genetic studies of this heterogeneity have focused mainly on high-impact de novo variants and polygenic scores; here we investigate, at the molecular level, the role of common variants. Materials and methods  We analyzed genotypic and phenotypic data from 9,332 individuals with ASD in the SPARK cohort. We considered 31 traits: six latent factors derived from the Social Communication Questionnaire and the Repetitive Behavior Scale-Revised, 22 co-occurring diagnoses, parent-reported IQ range, age at diagnosis, and age at first walking. We performed within-case genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and, for the 10 traits with evidence of SNP heritability, association analyses with genetically predicted gene and protein expression, splicing, and enhancer activity in brain and blood (xWAS). Nominated genes were tested for enrichment in biological processes, brain cell types, and developmental stages. xWAS-derived transcriptional signatures were compared with chemical perturbation signatures from CMap/LINCS L1000 to prioritize candidate drugs. Results  GWAS identified seven genome-wide significant loci for five traits, including loci near  GABRG3 and  TENM2 associated with co-occurring sleep, feeding or toileting problems. xWAS identified seven gene–trait associations involving three phenotypes (FDR Conclusion  Combining within-case GWAS with xWAS nominates candidate genes mediating common-variant effects on ASD heterogeneity, provides biological insight, and suggests candidates for phenotypically stratified drug repositioning.
authors: Marinelli C, Amaolo A, Marnetto D, Provero P.

title: Programmable Surface Receptor-Mediated Cell Targeting with Designer Antibody-Routed Nanoparticles (DARTs)
abstract: Precise  in vivo delivery remains a massive barrier to therapeutic genome editing. Recently, major strides have been made towards cell type-specific delivery, with potential to improve the safety profiles of future gene therapies. However, programming such targeted tropism is limited by the minimal repertoire of scFv sequences, nanobodies, and viral fusogens that enable cell-type specificity, and the slow, iterative design-build-test cycle required to identify and optimize them. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by developing the  d esigner  a ntibody-routed (DART) platform: a modular, plug-and-play tool that decouples delivery vehicle production from tropism engineering. By presenting generic, bioorthogonal antibody-binding interfaces on the surfaces of enveloped particles, the DART system enables conjugation of those particles with off-the-shelf antibodies that direct cell entry without requiring genetic or chemical manipulation.  D esigner  a ntibody-routed virus-like particle  s (DARTs) leverage this facile conjugation method to interrogate and identify transduction-competent surface antigens across cell types. They enable combinatorial targeting and the discovery of antigens that synergistically enhance transduction. Finally, DARTs function in the fetal murine nervous system, empirically identifying CD56 as a previously uncharacterized surface antigen enabling editing in hard-to-transduce neural populations. Overall, the DART platform provides a universal tool for rapidly profiling unique, targetable antigens and leveraging them for precision editing applications.
authors: Roth GV, Gengaro IR, Ahmadian N, Gao K, Wang D, Xu S, Chavez M, Finn P, Wang A, Qi LS.
