title: New insights into the Cenangiaceae: Marsonomyces, gen. nov., the first case of true polyspory in Helotiales, and taxonomic revisions in Neomelanconium.
abstract: The new genus Marsonomyces is proposed to accommodate two new species, M. pinicola and M. salicacearum, collected between 1990 and 2020 at four locations in Europe (Germany, the Netherlands, Poland) and Macaronesia (Tenerife). The most striking characteristics of the genus are large, long-cylindrical, ~128-spored asci with inamyloid, thin-walled, hemispherical apices and minute, allantoid ascospores aggregating prior to discharge in a large, elongated spore cluster. The observed polyspory is a result of seven nuclear divisions prior to spore wall formation. Phylogenetic rDNA and multigene analyses suggest placement in the family Cenangiaceae, in sister position to a clade comprising Encoelia/Velutarina, Cenangiopsis, and Trochila. This relationship is supported by morphological traits, such as brown, coriaceous, drought-tolerant apothecia growing on xeric branches, erumpent from bark (but also superficially on wood), the presence of refractive vacuolar bodies in the living paraphyses, the absence of an ionomidotic reaction, and allantoid ascospores. The two new species are morphologically very similar but can be distinguished by wider spores, the presence of hairs and occurrence on gymnosperms in M. pinicola, and the presence of rhomboid crystals and occurrence on angiosperms in M. salicacearum. Marsonomyces represents the first known case of true polyspory within the Helotiales. A possible parasitism on perithecia and pycnidia of unidentified Diaporthales is discussed. Another fungicolous member of Cenangiaceae, Hymenobolus kmetii, was investigated. Morphological reexamination of the holotype confirmed its conspecificity with Mycosphaerangium quercinum. The phylogenetically closely related genera Mycosphaerangium and Neomelanconium share numerous morphological characteristics. Consequently, Mycosphaerangium is synonymized with the older Neomelanconium, and the new combinations N. kmetii, N. magnisporum, and N. tetrasporum are proposed.
authors: Baral HO, Polhorský A, Quijada L.

title: Stony coral symbioses show variable responses to future ocean conditions.
abstract: Coral reefs support over a quarter of marine species and nearly a billion people worldwide but are also among the ecosystems most threatened by anthropogenic impacts. There is long-standing debate about whether coral symbioses will be disrupted or respond adaptively under future ocean conditions. Using a factorial 2.5-year future-ocean mesocosm experiment across eight coral species representing the major coral lineages, we tracked symbiont community shifts within replicate fragments from the same individual coral. Some corals exhibited stochastic divergence, whereas others showed deterministic shifts in symbiont community composition. Heat stress generally reduced symbiont diversity and promoted predictable restructuring, consistent with deterministic adaptation to moderate thermal stress but stochastic accumulation of diversity under extreme conditions. We propose that adaptive and stochastic responses represent endpoints along a continuum of host-orchestrated symbiont sorting. This study bridges coral reef ecology with broader host-microbiome theory, offering an integrated perspective on how symbiotic systems may respond to environmental change.
authors: de Souza MR, Bruce J, Cros A, Jury CP, Drury C, Toonen RJ.

title: Identification and validation of biomarkers associated with mitochondrial dynamics dysfunction in Parkinson's disease based on GEO datasets.
abstract: BackgroundParkinson's disease (PD), the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, is characterized by an unclear etiology and a lack of specific early diagnostic biomarkers. This study investigated novel biomarkers associated with mitochondrial dynamics (MD) dysfunction in PD.MethodsTranscriptomic data from the Gene Expression Omnibus database (training set: GSE6613, n = 72; validation set: GSE99039, n = 438) and 23 MD-related genes (MDRGs) were integrated. Differentially expressed genes were screened using the limma package. Three machine learning algorithms (random forest, support vector machine, and generalized linear model) were employed to construct diagnostic models. Feature importance analysis identified key candidate biomarkers, which were preliminarily validated in clinical samples via reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Functional enrichment, immune infiltration, and compound prediction analyses were subsequently performed.ResultsCysteinyl leukotriene receptor 2 (CYSLTR2) and alpha‑tocopherol transfer protein‑like gene (TTPAL) were identified as MDRG score-correlated biomarkers. In the validation set, CYSLTR2 was significantly downregulated (log2FC = -1.25, P ConclusionThis study identified CYSLTR2 and TTPAL as novel candidate biomarkers associated with MD dysfunction in PD, providing novel targets for mechanistic investigation and therapeutic exploration.

title: Dynamic virulence decomposition disentangles host and pathogen contributions over the course of infection.
abstract: Decomposing virulence into host and pathogen effects is key to understanding how virulence is generated during infection, and how host and pathogen contributions evolve over time. Conventional virulence decomposition is, however, not designed to quantify how these contributions vary throughout an infection. Building on conventional virulence decomposition, we developed a dynamic framework that integrates disease space analysis to quantify these changing contributions. We applied this framework to existing data from house finches (Haemorhous mexicanus) experimentally infected with the emerging bacterial pathogen, Mycoplasma gallisepticum, examining two biologically meaningful infection phases: an early phase dominated by innate immune responses and a later phase in which the adaptive immune response is fully activated. Our analyses revealed that virulence components evolved differently across infection phases, with pathogen exploitation, per-parasite-pathogenicity (PPP), and host resistance each exhibiting distinct trajectories. These findings corroborated several known evolutionary patterns, while also revealing the evolution of increased PPP in this system. In contrast, the apparent evolution of host tolerance inferred from aggregated peak measurements was not supported by phase-specific analyses, demonstrating that aggregated and phase-specific measures can provide different mechanistic insights into virulence. By linking conventional virulence decomposition with disease space analysis, our dynamic virulence decomposition framework provides a general approach for quantifying how host and pathogen processes shape virulence over the course of infection.
authors: Franz M, Bonneaud C.

title: The effect of varying levels of irrigation on Tuber melanosporum mycelia and the ectomycorrhizal fungal community in a black truffle orchard in British Columbia, Canada.
abstract: The French black truffle is the prized fruiting body of the ectomycorrhizal fungus Tuber melanosporum Vittad. Optimizing the growth of T. melanosporum while mitigating ectomycorrhizal fungal competitors are important goals for producers, particularly in novel growing regions. We investigated the influence irrigation on (1) the abundance of T. melanosporum extramatrical mycelium and (2) the communities of ectomycorrhizal fungi in soil and roots in an 8 year old T. melanosporum-Quercus robur L. orchard located in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada that had yet to produce truffles. Irrigation treatments were characterized by high (- 30 kPa mean soil water potential), moderate (- 80 kPa), or low (non-irrigated) soil moisture. Soil samples were collected monthly from July to September 2021, at 50 cm and 100 cm from the base of trees. Droplet digital PCR was used to estimate the abundance and distribution of T. melanosporum extramatrical mycelia in the soil. The ectomycorrhizal fungal community in soil and on mycorrhizal root tips were examined using PacBio Sequel II. Moderate irrigation had 17% more DNA than low irrigation, and high irrigation had 39% less DNA, but neither treatment was significantly different from the low irrigation treatment. Still soil DNA content decreased exponentially and significantly with soil water content (p < 0.001). Irrigation treatments did not affect the fungal community composition or richness, though several species of Scleroderma were found in high frequency. To our knowledge, this is the first study of a North American T. melanosporum truffle orchard in which a management variable (irrigation) was manipulated.
authors: Loverock LB, Mezzini S, Carl S, Berch S, Hannam K, Jones MD, Durall DM.

title: Modern breeding of root, tuber, and bulb crops to enhance food and nutritional security.
abstract: Key messageUnlocking the molecular mechanisms and pathways of underground storage organ development and nutrient and non-nutrient traits may provide more avenues to tailor elite germplasm enriched with these characteristics in root, tuber, and bulb crops. Biofortified cassava, potato, and sweet potato provide food and nutritional security to millions of people in Africa, Asia, and Latin American regions. Root and tuber crops provide food and nutritional security to millions of people in Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean, while garlic and onions, in addition to strong therapeutic potential, are widely used in food preparation to add flavour and taste. Root, tuber, and bulb (RTB) crops are a good source of carbohydrates, minerals, and bioactive compounds. However, these crops also possess a variety of allergens and toxic compounds, limiting their consumption. Here, we synthesized i) the contribution of RTB crops on food and nutrition security in the Global South, ii) the various types of allergens and toxic compounds detected in these crops, iii) catalogue germplasm resources across national and international genebanks, iv) document the range of genetic variation in edible organs morphology, nutrient and non-nutrient traits, v) discuss advances in high-throughput phenomics to monitor variability, vi) assess population structure and diversity in germplasm pool, vii) list genomic regions (QTL) and genes (both functionally characterized and candidate genes and QTL) associated with storage organs (roots or tubers) morphology, nutrient and non-nutrient traits, viii) uptake, transport, and storage of minerals in edible vegetable organs and their effects on consumers, and ix) advances in genetic improvement of nutritionally enhanced (nutrient and non-nutrient traits) and productive germplasm through crossbreeding and biotechnological interventions. Assessing and exploiting functional diversity, combined with the use of functionally characterized genes and associated markers for storage root growth/thickening, and nutrient and non-nutrient traits, can be deployed in breeding programs to improve these characteristics in RTB crops. Numerous candidate genes and genomic regions (or quantitative trait loci) reported herein must be functionally validated before being deployed in crop breeding programs. A greater emphasis should be placed on genetically and phenotypically characterizing RTB germplasm, and on combining empirical breeding with molecular tools to enhance precision, efficiency, and rapid genetic gain. Millions of rural households in parts of Africa, Asia, and Latin America are currently benefiting from the commercialization of provitamin A-enriched cassava, potato, and sweet potato. The development of orange-fleshed sweet potato cultivars with higher levels of provitamin A was awarded the ''World Food Prize'' in 2016. There are more opportunities to enhance nutrition status and food security through improvement of root, tuber, and bulb crops.
journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
authors: Ortiz R, Dwivedi SL, Pelikan A, Goldman IL.

title: PEDV NSP5 promotes immune evasion by recruiting TRIM28 to degrade DDX3X.
abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) has emerged as the predominant swine enteric coronavirus, causing vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration, and high mortality in piglets. Members of the DEAD-box family play critical roles in viral infection, yet their roles in PEDV infection remain undefined. Furthermore, it is unknown whether PEDV and its proteins regulate the expression of these DEAD-box proteins. In this study, reverse transcription quantitative PCR was used to examine the gene expression changes of 15 DEAD-box family members in the intestinal tissues of one-month-old PEDV-infected piglets. We found that the expression of DEAD-box helicase 3 X-Linked (DDX3X) was upregulated following PEDV infection, a result that was similarly observed in cellular experiments. Overexpression and knockdown of DDX3X significantly inhibited or promoted PEDV replication, respectively. Moreover, the use of specific DDX3X inhibitors demonstrated that DDX3X primarily restricts PEDV RNA accumulation. Our study also showed that DDX3X enhances RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) signaling by promoting the phosphorylation of TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1), and Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) proteins. Co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence assays further demonstrated the association and colocalization of DDX3X with TBK1 and IRF3, potentially contributing to its antiviral function. We constructed all PEDV proteins and identified that NSP5 reduces DDX3X levels via ubiquitination. Additionally, we discovered that tripartite motif-containing protein 28 (TRIM28) interacts with DDX3X and mediates its K48-linked ubiquitination. Knockdown of TRIM28 significantly reduced NSP5-mediated DDX3X ubiquitination. In conclusion, this study clarified the molecular mechanism by which NSP5 antagonizes DDX3X-mediated antiviral immune responses via the ubiquitination pathway, providing new insights into PEDV-host interactions and potential targets for antiviral intervention.IMPORTANCERecurrent outbreaks of porcine epidemic diarrhea (PED) have led to substantial economic losses in the global swine industry. To proactively control PED, it is crucial to investigate the pathogenic mechanisms of PEDV, particularly by exploring the interactions between viral proteins and host factors. In this study, we identified a significant phenomenon: PEDV infection activates DDX3X, enhancing the antiviral activity of the RLR pathway, while PEDV NSP5 recruits TRIM28 to target DDX3X for degradation, thus suppressing immune responses. These findings shed light on the complex regulatory interplay between PEDV proteins and host factors, deepening our understanding of the role and mechanisms of PEDV NSP5 in immune suppression.
authors: Zhang Y, Bai B, Tang Y, Wang C, Zhang Y, Li Y, Shi H, Li B, Yang B, Fu Y, Liu G.

title: Complete genome sequence of Rhizobium alamii strain MD26, isolated from a beach pea (Lathyrus japonicus) root nodule.
abstract: Rhizobium alamii is an exopolysaccharide-producing rhizosphere bacterium. We report the complete genome of strain MD26, isolated from beach pea (Lathyrus japonicus) root nodule tissue from a Massachusetts shoreline. The 7.55-Mb genome comprises five circular replicons, three without counterparts in the type strain, and encodes no known nodulation or nitrogen-fixation genes.
authors: Crosson S, Erickson L, Wald JW, Juliano A, Kahn A, Palka MV, Microbial Diversity Summer Course 2026, Spear JR, Dawson SC, Fiebig A.

title: The FOXA2-BNIP3 axis alleviates acute necrotizing pancreatitis by promoting mitophagy in pancreatic acinar cells to inhibit mtDNA-Mediated AIM2 inflammasome activation.
abstract: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis (ANP) is a severe inflammatory pancreatic disease characterized by pancreatic necrosis and systemic inflammation, with complex pathogenesis, rapid progression, and poor prognosis. Mitochondrial dysfunction in pancreatic acinar cells represents a pivotal early event in ANP; however, mitophagy, a central component of mitochondrial quality control, remains poorly characterized in terms of its role, regulatory networks, and therapeutic potential in ANP. In this study, we demonstrated that BNIP3 (BCL2 interacting protein 3) expression was significantly downregulated in patients with ANP and negatively correlated with inflammatory severity. Consistently, BNIP3-mediated mitophagy was impaired in the pancreatic tissue of ANP mouse models. Notably, restoration of BNIP3 expression using a novel adeno-associated virus targeting pancreatic tissue (AAV-PAN)-Bnip3 gene therapy vector alleviated pancreatic necrosis and systemic inflammatory injury, promoted mitophagy, and inhibited mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Mechanistically, BNIP3-dependent mitophagy facilitated the clearance of damaged mitochondria and prevented mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release into the cytosol, thereby suppressing AIM2 (absent in melanoma 2) inflammasome activation and subsequent acinar cell pyroptosis. Furthermore, we identified the transcription factor FOXA2 (forkhead box A2) as a direct upstream regulator that bound to the Bnip3 promoter and positively regulated its expression. FOXA2 was downregulated in ANP, whereas pancreas-specific FOXA2 overexpression activated BNIP3-mediated mitophagy and conferred protection against inflammatory injury. Together, these findings uncovered a previously unrecognized mechanism whereby the FOXA2-BNIP3-AIM2 axis mitigated pancreatic and systemic inflammatory injury in ANP by enhancing mitophagy to restrain mtDNA-dependent AIM2 inflammasome activation, highlighting the FOXA2-BNIP3-AIM2 axis as a promising target for gene therapy.
authors: Huang Z, Zhang L, Ma H, Wang Z, Li H, Hu X, Zhou M, He M, Wu J, Cheng L, Su T, Feng Y, Ma Y, Zhang W, Ji L, Wang G.

title: PHB2 connects mitochondrial membrane remodeling to selective autophagy.
abstract: PHB2 (prohibitin 2), a well-known inner mitochondrial membrane mitophagy receptor, has recently emerged as a potential sensor of intracellular bacteria. A recent study shows that increased exposure of the inner mitochondrial membrane protein PHB2 enables its interaction with bacterial surface proteins and the recruitment of the E3 ubiquitin ligases ARIH1 (ariadne RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase 1) or PRKN (parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase), thereby promoting xenophagy. This finding expands the role of damaged mitochondria from autophagic cargo to an active platform for antibacterial defense. It also raises broader questions regarding how an inner mitochondrial membrane protein becomes accessible to invading bacteria, why PHB2 can recognize bacterial proteins, and what determines whether exposed PHB2 promotes mitophagy, xenophagy, or co-degradation of both cargos. Here, we discuss PHB2 as a potential damage-unmasked bacterial sensor, the contribution of mitochondrial membrane remodeling to its exposure, and the evolutionary relationship between mitochondrial and bacterial recognition. We further consider whether impaired mitophagy may compromise xenophagic competence in aging and disease.
authors: Wu Y, Wu Q, Zhan ZJ, Guo Y, Wang C, Lu G.

title: Germline ATP2B2 Variant Associates With Central Nervous System Involvement in Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia.
abstract: BackgroundGenome-wide association studies (GWASs) can uncover inherited determinants of clinically relevant leukemia phenotypes, but their utility depends on precise phenotyping. Central nervous system (CNS) involvement in childhood B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL) is prognostically important, but its underlying biology remains poorly understood. We investigated inherited determinants using a sensitive, standardized definition of CNS involvement.ProcedureWe conducted a pooled observational cohort GWAS of CNS involvement at diagnosis among 674 patients with BCP-ALL from the Nordic Society of Pediatric Hematology and Oncology (NOPHO) ALL2008 and ALLTogether1 cohorts. CNS involvement was defined as ≥10 leukemic blasts detected in diagnostic cerebrospinal fluid by flow cytometry (FCM). Association testing used logistic regression adjusted for white blood cell count and genetic ancestry. Cox regression assessed variant associations with time to relapse. Findings were evaluated in an independent Associazione Italiana di Ematologia e Oncologia Pediatrica-Berlin-Frankfurt-Münster ALL 2000 protocol (AIEOP-BFM2000) cohort through targeted analysis.ResultsAmong 10,242,929 variants passing quality control, rs13059398, an intronic ATP2B2 variant, was associated with CNS involvement at genome-wide significance (p = 3.28 × 10-8; odds ratio [OR] = 6.07; 95% confidence interval, 3.2-11.5). The variant was carried by 21/113 (18.6%) CNS-positive and 29/559 (5.2%) CNS-negative patients. Although directionally consistent in the validation cohort, the association was not statistically significant. ATP2B2, predominantly expressed in CNS tissues, encodes the plasma membrane Ca2+ ATPase plasma membrane calcium ATPase 2 (PMCA2). There was no association with time to relapse.ConclusionsGermline variation at ATP2B2 was associated with FCM-defined CNS involvement in childhood BCP-ALL. These findings identify ATP2B2 as a candidate locus for further investigation of the biological mechanisms underlying leukemic CNS involvement.

title: Generation and multidimensional profiling of a rituximab-resistant ABC-type diffuse large B-cell lymphoma cell line.
abstract: BackgroundRituximab resistance remains a major issue in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), especially the ABC subtype. This study aimed to characterize the transcriptomic and DNA methylation alterations in rituximab‑resistant ABC-type DLBCL cell lines.Research design and methodsRituximab-resistant cell lines were generated from ABC (NU-DUL-1-R) and GCB (SU-DHL-6-R) subtypes using stepwise concentration escalation and were validated by flow cytometry-based complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) and antibody‑dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) assays, as well as CD20, CD55, and CD59 expression. Transcriptome sequencing and 850K methylation array analysis were performed on parental and resistant NU-DUL-1 cells. Differentially expressed genes and methylated positions were identified, followed by enrichment analyses and integrated analysis.ResultsBoth resistant cells showed significantly reduced CDC and CD20 downregulation. NU-DUL-1-R cells exhibited impaired ADCC, whereas SU-DHL-6-R cells retained ADCC, but upregulated CD55 and CD59. Integrated analysis identified eight genes (PLD4, MS4A7, FCRL5, PREX1, RASGRP3, ADAM28, RINL, TINAGL1) in NU-DUL-1-R cells with concordant changes in DNA methylation and mRNA expression. Enrichment analysis implicated cAMP, MAPK and PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathways in rituximab-resistance.ConclusionsThis study provides a preliminary characterization of rituximab-resistant ABC-DLBCL cell lines in vitro. The identified subtype-specific mechanisms and candidate genes support further exploration for personalized and epigenetic-targeted therapies.
authors: Wei T, Wang Y, Chang S, Gao G, Li Q.

title: Comparative and Sex-Specific Assessment of Proteomics, Clinical, and Genomic Data on Visceral Adipose Tissue Volume Using Machine Learning in UK Biobank: Advancing Precision Medicine.
abstract: BackgroundVisceral adiposity is a key driver of insulin resistance, which in turn is a strong risk factor for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.MethodsWe investigated the overall and sex-specific associations between plasma proteomics and visceral adipose tissue volume, and their intersection with clinical and genomic data to identify critical candidate proteins for visceral adiposity possibly linked to insulin resistance. We analyzed data from UK Biobank participants, using multistep machine learning to establish linear and nonlinear associations.ResultsThe combined model, integrating clinical, proteomic, and polygenic data, accounted for 67% of visceral adipose tissue variance. Our research revealed significant protein interactions with environmental factors and identified sex-specific proteins correlated with visceral adipose tissue variance in both males and females.ConclusionsThe findings suggest that a small number of plasma proteins explain a significant portion of the variance of visceral adipose tissue beyond nonproteomic measures, offering a potential single-source, personalized measurement of visceral adiposity that is easily accessible and may facilitate improved prediction and understanding of the biology of insulin resistance.
authors: Azizi Z, Gupte T, Kho PF, Zhou J, Nzenkue K, Guarischi-Sousa R, Panyard DJ, Chen ML, Abbasi F, Clarke SL, Knowles JW, Tsao PS, Assimes TL.

title: Triterpenoid saponins from the aerial parts of Phytolacca americana and their anti-influenza A virus activity.
abstract: Phytolacca americana L. (Phytolaccaceae), a perennial species native to North America, is rich in oleanane-type triterpenoid saponins. In this study, ultra-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC-QTOF-MS) profiling of the aerial-part extract revealed characteristic fragment ions of phytolaccagenin- and phytolaccagenic acid-type saponins with diverse glycosylation. MS-guided annotation enabled targeted isolation and structural elucidation of two previously undescribed compounds, one oleanane-type triterpenoid saponin (1) and one neolignan (3). Additionally, compound 2, which had been reported only based on mass spectrometric data, was isolated, and its structure was fully elucidated for the first time, together with those of 10 known oleanane-type triterpenoid saponins (4-13). Their structures were elucidated by comprehensive one-dimensional and two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopic analyses combined with UPLC-QTOF-MS data. Although P. americana extracts have been reported to inhibit influenza A virus infection in previous studies, the bioactive constituents responsible for this antiviral activity have not been identified. The crude extract and isolated saponins were evaluated using complementary in vitro assays. In H1N1-infected A549 cells, compound 11 (3-O-trisaccharide phytolaccagenic acid) reduced viral NS1 RNA levels at 6 and 24 hpi as determined by RT-qPCR. Antiviral activity was further confirmed by plaque reduction and immunoblot analyses, with a plaque-assay IC50 of 57.98 ± 0.26 µM.
authors: Tian S, Park J, Kim YJ, Li S, Im WR, Jeon SH, Na M.

title: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing as an adjunctive diagnostic tool for Clonorchis sinensis infection: a case report.
abstract: Clonorchis sinensis is a foodborne liver fluke. This case highlights acute cholangitis in a non-endemic area, where raw-fish history was initially absent and identified only after multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion. Conventional tests were negative. A 53-year-old female had fever, epigastric pain, leukopenia, elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and liver enzymes, and progressive eosinophilia (6.3% to 19.7%). Abdominal computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) showed cholangitis. Plasma and stool metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected C. sinensis (4 and 3375 reads), prompting stool microscopy that confirmed characteristic eggs. This complementary strategy enabled timely praziquantel, with resolution of fever and abdominal pain, declining eosinophilia, and improved liver function. She was discharged on day 16 and asymptomatic at 30-day follow-up. Clonorchiasis should be considered in eosinophilic cholangitis even in non-endemic areas; mNGS is a valuable complementary tool when conventional tests fail and presentations are atypical.
authors: Zhang L, Han D.

title: Chemoselective annulation of a tropolone linchpin enables divergent total syntheses of algicidal roseobacticides.
abstract: Roseobacticides are algicidal tropofuranones produced by the marine roseobacter Phaeobacter inhibens during interactions with the bloom-forming coccolithophore Gephyrocapsa huxleyi. We report a divergent synthesis based on chemoselective annulation of the multifunctional 2-methoxy-6-(methylthio)tropone with aryl- and indolylacetates, followed by subsequent oxidation or substitution at the C-7 sulfur functionality, enabling the first total syntheses of roseobacticides A, B, C and I and the proposed structure of L. Synthetic roseobacticides showed potent algicidal activity against G. huxleyi and Amphidinium carterae.
authors: Yang S, Aryal N, Stewart AWE, Burchill L, Quintana FM, Durham BP, Williams SJ.

title: DNA triangular prism-engineered multicolor chemiluminescence capsules for multiplexed visual detection of nucleic acid biomarkers.
abstract: Chemiluminescence (CL) capsules, featuring long-lasting emission and facile functionalization, hold great potential for multiplexed analysis of nucleic acid biomarkers. Herein, we report a strategy that utilizes DNA triangular prism (TP) scaffolds to spatially engineer trivalent catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) amplification on multicolor CL capsules for the multiplexed visual detection of avian influenza virus (AIV) DNA biomarkers. Three multicolor CL capsules are fabricated by co-encapsulating luminol alone, luminol with coumarin 6 (C6), and luminol with both C6 and Nile red (NR), denoted as LUM@TP-3H2, C6/LUM@TP-3H4, and NR/C6/LUM@TP-3H6. TP-3DNAzyme exhibits approximately 1.6-fold higher peroxidase-like activity than free DNAzyme in solution, and TP-functionalized capsules show stronger CL signals and higher CL amplification efficiency than capsules with directly anchored CHA hairpins. Upon target-triggered CHA reaction and H2O2 addition, these TP-functionalized capsules generate blue, green, and red light, respectively, through chemiluminescence resonance energy transfer (CRET), along with an intense and long-lasting CL emission over 1200 s. The capsule-based CL imaging assay is recorded with a common smartphone, exhibiting a linear range of 10-1000 pM and detection limits of 0.57 pM, 0.82 pM, and 1.97 pM for H1N1, H5N1, and H7N9, respectively, with recoveries of 97.41-104.87% in 100-fold diluted human serum. Altogether, this work provides a versatile CRET platform by using TP-engineered multicolor capsules with trivalent CHA amplification for smartphone-based multiplexed visual detection.

title: Influence of the lipid thioether modification and formulation method on lipoplex structure, stability and transfection efficiency in HEK293T cells.
abstract: Lipoplexes, formed by electrostatic interactions between nucleic acids and cationic lipids, must protect their cargo, enable cellular uptake and promote intracellular release for non-viral gene delivery. Although traditionally produced by bulk complexation, scalable microfluidic methods are now available. However, how lipid chemistry and formulation jointly influence physicochemical properties and biological performance remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we compared two structurally matched cationic lipids differing only in their hydrophobic chains: BSV107-S containing two thioether-functionalized chains, and BSV107, containing two mono-unsaturated chains. Each lipid was formulated either by complexing DNA with preformed liposomes obtained by thin-film hydration or by one-step DNA/lipid complexation through microfluidic assembly. We hypothesized that thioether incorporation would increase membrane fluidity and enhance intracellular plasmid release. Both lipids formed nanosized lipoplexes, with hydrodynamic diameters ranging 70-100 nm for microfluidic formulations and 100-140 nm for bulk-prepared lipoplexes at R ≥ 2. Cryo-TEM and SAXS revealed a multilamellar organization, with BSV107-S microfluidic lipoplexes showing larger interlamellar spacings than BSV107 or bulk-prepared systems. In HEK293T cells, transfection efficiency depended on the interplay between the lipid composition and formulation, with BSV107-S consistently outperforming BSV107 regardless of the formulation method. This improved performance correlated with increased membrane fluidity, measured by FRAP, supporting the role of thioether groups in modulating membrane dynamics. Together, these results establish structure-formulation-property relationships linking lipid chemical structure, formulation, physicochemical properties and biological performance, providing insights for the rational design of more efficient non-viral gene delivery systems.
authors: Rochedy M, Dechamboux L, Dupont A, Berchel M, Jaffrès PA, Chapel JP, Vives T, Leroyer P, Tranchimand S, Gauffre F, Nallet F, Schatz C, Loyer P, Bravo-Anaya LM.

title: Integrated single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics define tumour cell metaprograms and tumour microenvironment organisation in choroid plexus tumours.
abstract: BackgroundChoroid plexus tumours (CPTs) are rare intraventricular brain neoplasms derived from choroid plexus epithelium, predominantly affecting young children. They include benign choroid plexus papilloma (CPP), atypical CPP (aCPP), and malignant choroid plexus carcinoma (CPC) and segregate into three DNA-methylation subgroups: paediatric A (pedA), paediatric B (pedB), and adult.MethodsTo resolve subtype-specific biology, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing on 43 CPTs and integrated 12 non-neoplastic foetal, paediatric, and adult choroid plexus references, complemented by spatial transcriptomics in a subset of 16 tumour sections and 2 normal choroid plexus samples.ResultsTumour embeddings and correlation analyses demonstrated that CPTs cluster by methylation subtype rather than WHO grade, revealing epigenetically driven relationships despite divergent histology. We identified 10 tumour metaprograms spanning epithelial differentiation, ciliogenesis, proliferation, extra cellular matrix remodelling, and stress responses. PedA and adult tumours showed relatively homogeneous program distribution dominated by differentiation or ciliation states, whereas pedB tumours exhibited marked heterogeneity with selective enrichment of hypoxia, interferon signalling, early stress response, and TGF-β signalling. Spatial mapping revealed consistent anticorrelation of these programs with ciliogenesis and differentiation programs, suggesting stress-associated dedifferentiation. Elevated stress and hypoxia scores correlated with poorer survival. PedB tumours showed enrichment of interferon- and lipid-associated myeloid populations, that carried pro-angiogenic signatures. They were spatially co-localised with hypoxic and interferon I expressing tumour areas, that were predicted to interact with myeloid cells via immunosuppressive cues, shaping a pro-angiogenic, pro-tumour environment.ConclusionsThis study identifies stress- and hypoxia-associated dedifferentiation programs that are selectively enriched in pedB tumours, correlate with poor clinical outcome, and antagonise multiciliogenesis and epithelial differentiation. Their spatial co-localisation with immunosuppressive, pro-angiogenic macrophage populations links developmental arrest to microenvironmental remodelling and aggressive behaviour. These findings provide a biologically grounded framework for risk stratification and highlight hypoxia, angiogenesis and macrophage polarisation as candidate therapeutic targets in high-risk CPTs.
authors: Klötergens A, Inserte C, de Faria FW, Verma A, Schüftan E, Roy R, Banerjee V, Albert TK, Lu IN, Kordes U, Obrecht-Sturm D, Thomas C, Kerl K.

title: Chromosomally-Encoded Hok/Sok Toxin/Antitoxin Systems Inhibit Phage Infection
abstract: ABSTRACT  The primary physiological role of toxin/antitoxin (TA) systems is phage defense; they are also used to stabilize mobile genetic elements. In the initial publication in 1996, plasmid-encoded Hok/Sok, a type I TA system (protein toxin, RNA antitoxin that inhibits toxin mRNA), was shown to inhibit T4 phage infection in  Escherichia coli by reducing its efficiency of plating and burst size and by increasing the time for mature phage to form (latent period). This publication also identified that the mechanism of Hok/Sok inhibiting T4 was host transcription shutoff, arguably the most-general phage inhibition system since most phages impair host transcription. However, recently, the role of Hok/Sok in phage inhibition has been challenged. Therefore, here we investigated the role of four  E. coli chromosomally-expressed,  hok + /sok + loci and the one orphan  hok + locus and found that the Hok proteins inhibit the infection of  E. coli by BASEL phage 48, a Vequintavirus with myovirus morphology. Of the five Hok proteins, the greatest phage inhibition was by HokB, and infection by BASEL phages 34 and 39 were also inhibited by HokB. We also find BASEL phage 48 requires the WecB-generated receptor NGR for infection. Therefore, chromosomally-derived orphan Hok proteins, produced at physiological levels, are relevant for phage inhibition.
authors: Seo E, Cingle ME, Wood TK.

title: Targeted cancer ablation via programmable sensing of amplified oncogenic RNA
abstract: Selectively eliminating cancer cells based on their oncogenic drivers holds great promise but remains challenging for targeted cancer therapy. Here, we present ORCA (Oncogenic RNA-triggered Cancer Ablation), a programmable and modular platform that couples RADAR-based detection of oncogenic RNA with conditional expression of therapeutic payloads in cancer cells. We identify RADAR sensors targeting the transcripts of endogenously amplified oncogenes, including  MYC ,  FGFR2 and wild-type  KRAS in colorectal and gastric cancer cells. Focusing on colorectal cancer (CRC) driven by extrachromosomal DNA-amplified  MYC , we demonstrate targeted ablation of high-  MYC cancer cells using two orthogonal strategies: anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy and enzyme-prodrug therapy.  In vivo delivery of ORCA using adeno-associated virus (AAV) suppresses tumor growth in a subcutaneous xenograft model and prolongs survival in a CRC liver metastasis model. ORCA establishes oncogenic RNAs as actionable inputs for targeted cancer therapy via programmable RNA sensing, thus offering a strategy to target tumors through the transcripts of otherwise difficult-to-drug oncogenes such as  MYC .
authors: Zhang M, Hu Y, Yamada-Hunter SA, Sotillo E, Dai H, Call CC, Tousley AM, Kim SJ, Liu W, Winslow MM, Mackall CL, Gao XJ.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Longevity Research: From Molecular Clocks to Interventional Geroscience
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the scale, resolution, and modalities through which biological aging can be estimated, but evidence that these estimates are valid intervention targets or surrogate endpoints remains limited. We conducted a narrative review of PubMed-indexed literature identified through documented PubMed and Consensus searches in October 2026, plus a separate search of primary US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA) documents. No protocol was registered, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were not searched, and screening was by a single reviewer. We distinguish four biomarker properties: chronological-age estimation, prognostic association, responsiveness to intervention, and validated surrogacy. Deep-learning clocks across epigenomic, proteomic, retinal, electrocardiographic, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) modalities report low chronological-age error, and several show prognostic associations with mortality, but calibration was rarely reported in the records reviewed and head-to-head comparisons with mortality-trained clocks in the same cohort were uncommon. Randomized trials show that responsiveness is clock-specific: in the CALERIE trial, caloric restriction slowed DunedinPACE but did not significantly change PhenoAge or GrimAge, and effect sizes were small. Machine learning has accelerated senolytic and mTOR-pathway candidate nomination, and a generative-AI-designed TNIK inhibitor reached phase 2a in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, an age-related disease indication rather than an aging indication. Coverage of the twelve hallmarks of aging by AI studies is uneven: epigenetic alteration and cellular senescence are best represented, whereas autophagy, proteostasis, genomic instability, and telomere attrition are thinly represented. Constraints include reliability, tissue specificity, confounding by ancestry and social factors, the gap between prediction and causation, and the absence, in the primary documents consulted, of a pathway that accepts a biological-age measure as a surrogate endpoint. We propose an evidence ladder and a translational chain for appraising AI-derived aging biomarkers and set out priorities for 2026-2030.
authors: Borkowski AA.

title: FOS and SGK1 as Senescence-Associated Hub Genes in Osteoarthritis: A Bioinformatics and Experimental Validation Study.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a highly prevalent degenerative joint disease, and the molecular mechanisms underlying its development and progression remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify cellular senescence (CS)-associated hub genes and signaling pathways involved in OA and to evaluate their potential biological significance. Two Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets (GSE51588 and GSE236924) were analyzed to identify CS-associated differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses were performed, followed by construction of a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network. Hub genes were identified using the cytoHubba plugin in Cytoscape, and drug enrichment analysis was conducted to identify compounds targeting the selected hub genes. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the candidate genes. The bioinformatics findings were further evaluated using in vitro chondrocyte experiments and an anterior cruciate ligament transection (ACLT) rat model of OA. Six hub genes (FOS, SGK1, DDIT4, EIF4EBP1, SOD2, and NAMPT) were identified, with enrichment primarily in the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mechanistic target of rapamycin (PI3K/AKT/mTOR) signaling pathway. Western blotting and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analyses demonstrated increased expression of FOS and SGK1 under inflammatory conditions. LY294002, identified through drug enrichment analysis as a pan-PI3K inhibitor, was associated with reduced SGK1 expression and attenuation of OA-related pathological changes. These findings identify FOS and SGK1 as senescence-associated hub genes that are associated with chondrocyte senescence and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, providing candidate molecular targets for further investigation of OA pathogenesis.
authors: Huang C, Zhang H, Wang X, Tang Z, Hu Y, Song W, Wang R.

title: Metabolic Memory in Oral Inflammation.
abstract: The global rise in metabolic diseases has increased the severity and therapeutic complexity of oral inflammatory disorders. Persistent inflammation driven by metabolic memory presents a central pathological mechanism. Even after metabolic parameters are normalized, abnormal gene expression can persist, leading to prolonged disease progression and recurrent episodes. In the oral cavity, metabolic memory is most clearly evident in periodontitis and impaired wound healing, where sustained immune dysregulation and tissue destruction remain after hyperglycemia or hyperlipidemia has been corrected. Epigenetic reprogramming presents a key molecular mechanism of metabolic memory, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and expression of noncoding RNAs. The epigenetic alterations collectively reprogram immune cell function, driving the dysregulation of innate and adaptive immunity while influencing the fate of oral stromal cells and epithelial cells. Prolonged inflammation contributes to an altered host-microbiota interaction, reinforcing disease persistence and treatment resistance. Metabolic disorders induce coordinated epigenetic changes that can be grouped into permissive and repressive events affecting gene transcription. Permissive events include increased histone acetylation, enrichment of activating histone methylation marks (e.g., H3K4me3), and DNA demethylation at inflammatory gene loci. These modifications promote an open chromatin structure to enhance transcription factor access. Repressive events include increased DNA methylation and enrichment of repressive histone methylation marks (e.g., H3K9me3). DNA methylation typically occurs in promoter regions of genes, and repressive histone changes lead to the formation of compact chromatin, both of which reduce transcriptional activity. Noncoding RNAs generally decrease target messenger RNA stability or inhibit translation further, reinforcing a repressive effect. The combined effect of these modifications is a shift in protein expression that reinforces chronic inflammatory signaling in abnormal metabolic conditions. This review comprehensively summarizes the epigenetic mechanisms by which metabolic memory sustains oral inflammation at molecular, cellular, and tissue levels, as well as potential preventive and therapeutic interventions.
authors: Liu R, Cui A, Dong H, Graves DT, Wang Q.

title: From Pesticide Exposure to Persistent Molecular Damage: An Integrated Framework of Genomic Instability, Epigenetic Dysregulation, and Long-Term Toxicity.
abstract: Pesticide toxicity is increasingly recognized as a chronic and mechanistically complex process extending beyond acute tissue injury. Evidence concerning cellular stress, genotoxicity, epigenetic alterations, susceptibility, and mixture effects has often been evaluated separately, limiting unified interpretation of persistent biological consequences. This review integrates experimental, epidemiological, and mechanistic evidence using an adverse outcome pathway (AOP)-informed framework to organize pesticide-associated molecular initiating events (MIEs), key events (KEs), key event relationships (KERs), and adverse outcomes (AOs), while distinguishing established AOPs from mechanistically plausible AOP-informed modules. We examine interconnected oxidative, mitochondrial, calcium, endoplasmic reticulum, genomic, and epigenetic responses, with particular emphasis on bidirectional crosstalk between mitochondrial metabolism, redox signaling, and epigenetic regulation. Genetic susceptibility and combined pesticide exposure are also considered as modifiers of these relationships and of the persistence and biological significance of molecular changes. Particular attention is given to transient epigenetic responses, persistent epigenetic alterations, intergenerational effects, and true transgenerational inheritance, for which human evidence remains limited. Rather than assuming a single linear pathway, the review highlights convergent and branching relationships in which different pesticide classes may initiate distinct molecular events affecting overlapping downstream KEs. Molecular associations are not considered evidence of causal KERs without appropriate support from biological plausibility, temporal and dose-response concordance, mechanistic evidence, essentiality, and applicability. The review further considers how multi-omics approaches, including MOFA/MOFA+, mixOmics, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and relevant toxicology/data resources, together with exposure assessment, chemical grouping, read-across, and cumulative-risk approaches, can provide complementary evidence within an AOP-informed framework. The contribution of this review lies primarily in integrating and organizing existing evidence rather than proposing a new toxicological mechanism, AOP, or regulatory framework. Future toxicological strategies should integrate longitudinal evidence, susceptibility factors, exposure mixtures, and quantitative dose-response information to evaluate candidate KEs, their relationships, and relevance to AOs.
authors: Jalali A, Shahmohammadi S, Zolfaghary H.

title: Single-cell profiling reveals monocyte mitochondrial dysfunction in patients with cirrhosis progressing to acute-on-chronic liver failure.
abstract: Background & aimsPatients with acute decompensation (AD) of cirrhosis are at a high risk of developing acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF), a syndrome characterized by multi-organ failure and high short-term mortality. Prospective studies addressing the cellular mechanisms that drive the transition from AD to ACLF are lacking. In this study, we aimed to determine whether peripheral immune cell subsets at hospital admission predict the progression from AD to ACLF and to delineate underlying molecular mechanisms.MethodsWe prospectively enrolled 63 patients with AD and 15 healthy donors across five European centres, with a 90-day follow-up. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from 16 patients with distinct trajectories and 4 controls.ResultsProgression to ACLF was associated with expansion of classical monocytes, particularly subcluster "C2", which specifically displayed impaired energy metabolism with reduced oxidative phosphorylation (pConclusionsWe identified and validated a distinct monocyte subpopulation with defective energy metabolism in patients with AD with poor outcomes, supporting a link between monocyte bioenergetic dysfunction and ACLF development. Impact and Implications:The cellular mechanisms that drive progression from acute decompensation (AD) to acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) remain poorly understood, limiting the development of effective strategies for therapeutic intervention. By integrating prospective single-cell transcriptomics, functional bioenergetic analyses, and validation in independent multicentre cohorts, we identified a distinct monocyte subset characterized by impaired oxidative phosphorylation that is associated with subsequent ACLF development. These findings are relevant to clinicians and researchers because they suggest that immune-metabolic dysfunction emerges before overt ACLF and may contribute to disease progression. While further mechanistic and prospective validation studies are required, our results provide a framework for the investigation of monocyte bioenergetics as a potential therapeutic target in patients with decompensated cirrhosis.

title: A sequence-informed hybrid framework for predicting antibiotic minimum inhibitory concentrations in previously unseen Escherichia coli pathogens.
abstract: IntroductionWhen an Escherichia coli pathogen is newly encountered, antimicrobial susceptibility information may be incomplete or unavailable. We investigated whether minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) could be predicted for previously unseen pathogens by jointly using pathogen genomic sequence information, antibiotic characteristics, and observed pathogen-antibiotic MIC patterns.Hypothesis or gap statementThe predictive value of integrating pathogen genomic information, antibiotic characteristics, and observed pathogen-antibiotic MIC patterns within a hybrid collaborative-filtering framework for previously unseen E. coli pathogens remains unclear.AimTo develop and evaluate Model C for predicting MIC values in previously unseen, genomically characterised E. coli pathogens.MethodologyThe study used 9377 E. coli pathogens, 26 antibiotics, and 51,554 exact MIC measurements among 243,802 possible pathogen-antibiotic combinations. Model C combined observed MIC patterns, genomic features related to antimicrobial resistance (AMR), nucleotide-sequence comparisons across 265 AMR-related loci, and antibiotic characteristics. Five-fold pathogen-out validation excluded all MIC measurements from each test pathogen from training and model selection. The common validation cohort contained 9058 pathogens and 50,460 observed MIC values; Models 3B and 3 were evaluated as comparators.ResultsIn pathogen-out validation of the 50,460 observed MIC values, Model C achieved a mean absolute error of 0.5931 log₂ MIC units, root mean squared error of 0.8477, and Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9055. Model C performed best overall. A final model fitted to all 50,460 observed MICs predicted the remaining 185,048 unmeasured MICs.ConclusionModel C estimated MIC values for previously unseen E. coli pathogens using genomic, antibiotic, and observed interaction information. Independent external validation is required. Predictions may help prioritise confirmatory testing but should not replace antimicrobial susceptibility testing or be used alone to guide treatment.
authors: Mikawa YG.

title: Bovine-associated viruses at the human-animal interface: Zoonotic risks, spillover dynamics, and one health implications.
abstract: Cattle serve as critical ecological reservoirs and amplifying hosts for numerous zoonotic viruses, thereby playing a central role in their maintenance, evolution, and interspecies transmission. Here, we briefly evaluate six viral pathogens of significant public health relevance linked to cattle, namely cowpox virus, bovine coronavirus, influenza A virus (H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b), bovine rotavirus, bovine leukemia virus, and SARS-CoV-2. This review focuses on advances in viral characterization, host tropism, and the mechanisms that may facilitate spillover through routes such as direct contact, environmental exposure, and foodborne transmission. It further highlights the bidirectional nature of pathogen exchange at the human-animal interface, where cattle may act as a source of viral variants with potential public health implications, though the risk varies considerably among the viruses discussed. Moreover, we discuss the imperative for integrated surveillance and One Health interventions to mitigate these transmission risks, highlighting cattle as valuable sentinel species within global health security frameworks.
authors: Yu C, Xu Q, Xu D, Zhang Q, Li M, Zhang B.

title: Regulation of biofouling in quorum sensing membrane bioreactors: mechanistic analysis from the mixed liquor to the biofilm cake.
abstract: Membrane biofouling is a key factor limiting the long-term application of membrane bioreactors (MBR); it is complex in composition, comprising both inorganic and organic substances. Quorum sensing (QS)/quorum quenching (QQ) has been shown to regulate microbial behaviour in MBR by modulating the secretion of signalling molecules. Many high-quality publications show that QS offers a new perspective on biofouling in MBR. However, the specific mechanisms by which QS influences membrane biofouling have not been summarised. This review synthesises the existing literature to demonstrate the relevance of QS/QQ and to summarise the categories of QS signalling molecules and their functions. To clarify the role of quorum sensing in mixed liquor, this paper examines the complex mechanisms by which QS drives the evolution of activated sludge and the formation of membrane biofilms, and establishes the links between QS, mixed liquor, activated sludge, and membrane biofilms, elucidating its unique bridging role. The paper discusses behavioural changes in QS microorganisms in order to elucidate the microscopic origins of biofouling in membranes, thereby enabling effective control of biofouling.
authors: Yu S, Liu Z, Wang S, Wu J, Lin X, Yi K, Huang J, Li X.

title: Cellular membranes as contested territories in the virus-host conflict.
abstract: Cellular membranes emerge as contested territories in the virus-host conflict. Many viruses depend on host membrane systems throughout their life cycle for entry, replication, assembly, and egress. At the same time, innate immune sensing and interferon (IFN) signaling are themselves organized around membrane-associated platforms. Cellular membranes therefore function both as essential substrates for viral replication and as central sites of antiviral defense. In this review, we examine how IFN-induced responses reshape membrane biology through coordinated changes in lipid metabolism, membrane biophysics, intracellular trafficking, and organelle organization. These membrane-centered defenses restrict viral entry, alter endomembrane permissiveness, interfere with virion release, and disrupt the formation and function of virus-induced replication organelles. We further discuss how positive-strand RNA viruses counteract these pressures by reprogramming lipid metabolism and actively remodeling intracellular membranes to preserve replication-competent niches. Together, these observations support a unifying framework in which viruses and host defenses compete for control over membrane identity, organization, and accessibility. This membrane-centered perspective connects innate immune signaling, membrane homeostasis, and viral replication, and highlights membrane-associated processes as promising targets for broad-spectrum antiviral strategies.
authors: Zoladek J, Nisole S.

title: Folding Free Energy and Evolution Guided Rational Engineering of Arginine Deiminase Enables Enhanced Catalytic Efficiency, Structural Robustness, and Antitumor Efficacy.
abstract: Arginine deiminase (ADI) is a promising therapeutic enzyme for targeting arginine-auxotrophic cancers, but its clinical application is limited by insufficient catalytic efficiency and poor stability. In this study, we developed a rational protein engineering strategy integrating folding free energy (ΔΔG) prediction and evolutionary conservation analysis to optimize ADI from Pseudomonas mendocina. A comprehensive site-saturation mutational scan was performed using the Pythia framework, followed by ConSurf-based filtering to exclude highly conserved residues, thereby efficiently identifying candidate beneficial mutations. Experimental evaluation showed that several single mutations enhanced enzymatic activity, and combinatorial optimization further revealed synergistic effects. Notably, the triple mutant K91L/N95E/Y346E exhibited the most significant improvement, achieving a 2.7-fold increase in catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) compared to the wild type. In addition, this variant demonstrated enhanced thermal stability and improved plasma stability, with an extended half-life and higher residual activity. Importantly, in vitro cytotoxicity assays confirmed that the engineered mutant displayed superior antitumor activity against colorectal cancer cells. Overall, this study highlights the effectiveness of integrating thermodynamic and evolutionary constraints for enzyme engineering and provides a promising strategy for developing ADI-based anticancer therapeutics.
journal: European journal of pharmaceutical sciences : official journal of the European Federation for Pharmaceutical Sciences
authors: Zhang M, Liu M, Tang Y, Li J, Wang C, Zhao W, Cui Y.

title: PGRP-S2 contributes to Toll-1-dependent antiviral immunity and apoptosis-associated signaling during IAPV infection in honey bees.
abstract: The Toll pathway mediates antimicrobial peptide (AMP) synthesis and participates in antiviral innate immunity in insects. However, how Toll-dependent antiviral responses are regulated during viral infection and how AMPs mediate antiviral defense remain incompletely understood. Here, we found that the Toll pathway constitutes an important part of the transcriptional response to Israeli acute paralysis virus (IAPV) infection in honey bees. PGRP-S2 was markedly up-regulated upon infection and exhibited physical associations with the IAPV capsid protein VP3 and with Toll-1, as validated by complementary co-immunoprecipitation, pull-down, and immunofluorescence analyses. Silencing PGRP-S2 substantially elevated viral titers and diminished the expression of Toll-dependent AMPs, including defensin 1. Functional assays indicated that defensin 1 was associated with apoptosis-related responses and suppressing viral replication. Knockdown of defensin 1 correlated with reduced apoptosis-associated signaling and enhanced viral titers, whereas overexpression of defensin 1 in Sf9 cells was associated with cell death. Collectively, our findings support a contribution of PGRP-S2 to the Toll-1-dependent antiviral response and link defensin 1 to apoptosis-related responses during IAPV infection, providing new insights into antiviral immunity in honey bees.
authors: Zhuang J, Deng Y, Liu M, Yang D, Jin H, Jaffar G, Yang S, Yuan C, Qin X, Yang X, Zhao H, Ma M, Hou C.

title: Intracerebroventricular administration of research-grade AAV2/5 selectively transduces neonatal choroid plexus and limits ventriculomegaly at low doses.
abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) administration into cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) can mediate transduction of target cells to enable sustained delivery of proteins into CSF, offering promising avenues for both CNS therapies and mechanistic studies. Despite advantages of AAV tropism-based cellular selectivity, both preclinical studies and clinical trials report short- and long-term adverse effects, including inflammation. Considering the vulnerability of the developing CNS and importance of inflammation in pediatric hydrocephalus, side effects of CSF-directed AAV administration may be further exacerbated in neonatal models. In this study, we use standard neonatal preclinical models to address dose-dependent risks of CSF-delivered intracerebroventricular (ICV) injections of research-grade AAV2/5 to P0.5 mouse pups, with a focus on cellular tropism and ventriculomegaly. At a lower dose (1 μL of 1 × 1012 genome copy (GC)/mL), AAV2/5 tropism was limited to choroid plexus (ChP) epithelial cells, but was more permissive at a higher-doses (1 μL of 4 × 1012 GC/mL). Furthermore, ICV injections of AAV2/5 during both early and late neonatal stages induced dose-dependent ventriculomegaly. After higher-dose AAV2/5 ICV injections at P0.5, neonatal ventriculomegaly progressed rapidly. Importantly, neonatal ventriculomegaly, permissive tropism, and persistent CSF inflammation that was induced by a higher AAV dose were not fully resolvable in adulthood. In addition to neonatal effects, E13.5 embryos and adult animals were also susceptible to higher-dose ICV AAV2/5-induced ventriculomegaly and tropism breaching. Taken together, our data emphasize critical considerations for rigorous CSF-based AAV delivery, particularly during mouse brain development, highlighting the need for optimized dosages for perinatal ICV AAV research applications.
authors: Liu LL, Noguera A, Humphries R, Zhou B, Fame RM.

title: Ca<sup>2+</sup> is an intracellular danger signal promoting STING activation.
abstract: Calcium release in host cells is essential for viral infection and survival, and mutations disrupting calcium homeostasis are associated with chronic viral infections or autoimmune diseases in patients, yet the biological significance of calcium (Ca2+) signaling on stimulator of interferon genes (STING) activation remains unclear. Here, we show that cytosolic Ca2+ is sensed by host cells as an immediate-early danger signal. Viral infection-activated Rho GTPases and phospholipase C-β (PLCβ) induce ITPR-mediated endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ release, while STING translocation induces TRPV2-mediated ER Ca2+ release, both leading to store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE) through ORAI channels. Ca2+ influx activates calmodulin (CaM)-dependent protein kinases CaMKK and CaMK1D. Activated CaMK1D phosphorylates STING, allowing for TBK1 trans-autophosphorylation. Inhibiting Ca2+ signaling or mutating CaMK1D-phosphorylating STING sites impairs STING activation. Consistently, Ca2+ signaling is important for the host defense against DNA viruses in mice. These results support a two-signal mode for STING activation in which the Ca2+-CaM-CaMKK-Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase (CaMK) cascade is indispensable.
authors: Zhou N, Gao P, Zhao H, Liu Q, Wang X, Li Y, Wang F, Liu Y, Jiang Q, Fang R, Wang C, Lai L, Jiang Z.

title: The AMPK-ALDH7A1 axis drives metabolic reprogramming and anti-tumor immunity in hepatocellular carcinoma via KDM5C inhibition.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a feature of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet how respiratory suppression arises remains unclear. Here, we identify an evolutionarily conserved metabolic-epigenetic axis integrating metabolic regulation with tumor suppression and anti-tumor immunity. Through comparative studies in yeast, HCC cell lines, and orthotopic/autochthonous HCC mouse models, we demonstrate that AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/Snf1-mediated phosphorylation of aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH7A1/Ald6 promotes its nuclear translocation and local acetate production, leading to inhibition of histone lysine demethylase KDM5C/Jhd2. This results in H3K4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) accumulation at respiratory genes, activating their transcription and maintaining mitochondrial function. During HCC pathogenesis, loss of AMPK signaling disrupts this pathway, impairing ALDH7A1 nuclear translocation and enabling KDM5C-mediated respiratory suppression. Notably, AMPK-ALDH7A1-acetate-mediated KDM5C inhibition also potentiates cyclic guanosine monophosphate (GMP)-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling, driving CD8+ T cell infiltration and synergizing with immune checkpoint blockade. Our work defines the evolutionarily conserved AMPK-ALDH7A1-KDM5C axis and establishes acetate as a dual regulator of mitochondrial metabolism and anti-tumor immunity, offering therapeutic strategies for targeting metabolic vulnerabilities in HCC.
authors: Tong Y, Wang J, Ma R, Wang M, Zhang T, Dong H, Ge F, Ye C, Yin T, Yu X, Li S.

title: Disrupted glutathione homeostasis contributes to copper-induced oxidative stress and DNA damage in human granulosa cells.
abstract: Copper (Cu) is a widespread environmental heavy metal that plays an essential role as a trace element in organisms. However, growing evidence indicates that excessive Cu exposure has toxic effects on ovarian function. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanisms remain largely unknown. This study aimed to evaluate the toxic effects of Cu on human granulosa cells and explore the potential mechanisms. An exploratory transcriptomic analysis was performed on Cu-exposed cells to investigate identified candidate genes and pathways (based on nominal p < 0.05). Pathway enrichment analysis showed that these DEGs were significantly overrepresented in several pathways, including GSH metabolism, and DNA damage processes. Cu exposure caused a concentration-dependent increase in DNA damage within cells, with oxidative stress serving as the underlying mediator. Disturbed GSH homeostasis contributes to Cu-induced oxidative stress and DNA damage, as verified by pretreatment with GSH‑MEE and BSO. However, without measuring GSH synthesis flux or GSSG, alternative causes of GSH depletion cannot be excluded. The BSO experiment should be interpreted as evidence for GSH depletion and ROS, not as direct confirmation of DNA damage. In summary, these findings elucidate the mechanisms of Cu-induced DNA damage in granulosa cells, thereby providing new perspectives on the pathways underlying female reproductive disorders.
journal: Journal of trace elements in medicine and biology : organ of the Society for Minerals and Trace Elements (GMS)
authors: Pan G, Huang M, Liu S, Yang M.

title: Pathogenicity and zoonotic potential of a novel pdm09-lineage H1N2 swine influenza A virus spatiotemporally linked to transboundary pig trade.
abstract: International swine trade can disseminate influenza A viruses across borders, creating opportunities for reassortment with endemic swine viruses and the emergence of novel strains with zoonotic potential. Here, we characterize a novel H1N2 reassortant, A/swine/Korea/1030-3/2023 (1030-3), detected in South Korea and spatiotemporally associated with European swine lineages and international pig movement. 1030-3 harbors seven gene segments (PB2, PB1, PA, HA, NP, M and NS) closely related to a recent Danish zoonotic H1N1 virus of the 2009 pandemic (pdm09) lineage, and an N2 segment derived from an endemic Korean HxN2. In vitro assays demonstrated that 1030-3 preferentially bound human-type α2,6-linked sialic acid receptors and replicated efficiently in polarized human airway epithelial cells, although these properties were also observed in the endemic Korean H1N2 comparator 1027-1. In mice, 1030-3 caused moderate clinical signs and respiratory replication comparable to an early pdm09 reference strain NL09. In guinea pigs, 1030-3 transmitted to a subset of direct-contact animals but showed no detectable aerosol transmission under the conditions tested. In pigs, the natural host, 1030-3 replicated efficiently and transmitted to all direct-contact animals, with high respiratory shedding and a greater cumulative shedding burden in contact pigs than NL09. Contemporary human sera showed reduced neutralizing activity against 1030-3 relative to both human seasonal H1N1 and 1027-1, while antiserum against a recent H1N1 vaccine antigen also neutralized 1030-3 less efficiently. These findings identify a European-associated H1N2 swine influenza reassortant detected in South Korea that combines a distinct pdm09-derived genomic and antigenic background with efficient replication and transmission in pigs, α2,6-linked receptor preference, and reduced neutralization by human sera, underscoring the need for trade-aware surveillance of swIAVs and continued monitoring at the swine-human interface.
authors: Kim SC, Kim HJ, Kim B, Park GS, Seo BJ, Kim C, Jeong CG, Oem JK, Moon SH, Jung SK, Oh Y, Cho HS, Kim YK, Lee CY, Kim WI.

title: Modulation of riboflavin biosynthesis enzymes in non-typhoidal Salmonella isolates differentially impacts human MAIT cell activation.
abstract: Invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS) sequence type 313 (ST313) isolates have emerged in sub-Saharan Africa, with a high incidence of multidrug resistance, enhanced intracellular persistence, increased dissemination and immune evasion. ST313 isolate D23580 was shown to avoid activation of mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells compared with a genetically similar, non-invasive Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm) 4/74 strain, but the mechanism remains unclear. Here, we studied immune responses to infection with typhoidal strains and ST313 isolates using comparative transcriptomic profiling of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). MAIT cells responded to typhoidal strains but not to D23580. To uncover underlying mechanisms, we engineered an inducible CRISPRi system targeting riboflavin biosynthesis enzymes (rib), which process MAIT ligands, in D23580 and 4/74 strains. Several rib hypomorphs exhibited prolonged lag time in minimal media, which was more pronounced in D23580 than in 4/74. In PBMC infection, knockdown of lumazine synthase (RibH) and riboflavin synthase (RibE) resulted in contrasting MAIT cell activation phenotypes. RibH knockdown restored MAIT cell activation in D23580 but did not affect activation in 4/74. Conversely, RibE knockdown diminished MAIT cell activation by 4/74 but had no impact on MAIT cell activation by D23580. Metabolomic analysis revealed accumulation of the biosynthetic intermediate DMRL in RibE knockdown and a differential impact on riboflavin biosynthesis end products between D23580 and 4/74 RibH knockdown, suggesting altered pathway flux between the strains. Our results indicate RibH and RibE as pivotal nodes for strain-specific MAIT-activation during Salmonella infection of human PBMCs, illustrating teir central role in the complex interplay between bacterial metabolism and host immunity.
authors: Vainman L, Kulicke CA, Oketade N, Bossel Ben-Moshe N, Ciolli-Mattioli C, Solomon A, Hinton JCD, Dobos KM, Lewinsohn DM, Hen-Avivi S, Avraham R.

title: Geochemical signatures of magnetite are conserved in diverse populations of environmental magnetotactic bacteria.
abstract: Magnetotactic bacteria (MTB) synthesize intracellular magnetite nanoparticles in a genetically controlled manner. They may represent some of the earliest biomineralizing organisms on Earth, and a unique window into ancient life and the environments that hosted it. Yet, identification of their mineralogical remains in ancient rocks is highly challenging due to the lack of reliable and lasting proxies. Previous results obtained from laboratory cultures of single strains of MTB revealed trace element and Fe isotope patterns that are not shared by any other source of magnetite, which could be used as reliable proxies for the identification of ancient MTB. However, the environmental relevance of these previous findings for environmental and mixed population of MTB is unknown. We report the trace element and Fe isotope compositions of magnetite extracted from environmental MTB collected in the water column of Lake Pavin, France, and show that the most distinctive geochemical traits (enrichment in Mo, Se, Sn, and light Fe isotopes) of magnetite produced by MTB cultivated in the laboratory are conserved in environmental populations. They represent potential biological signatures that can be searched in ancient rocks and coupled with magnetic and mineralogical tracers to support the presence of MTB and reconstruct their emergence and evolution.
authors: Busigny V, Praharaj A, Amor M, Mathon FP, Monteil CL, Menguy N, Benzerara K, Mehta N, Jézéquel D, Viollier E, Lefèvre CT.

title: Neural Stem Cell Therapies for Central Nervous System Regeneration: Advances, Challenges, and Integrative Technologies.
abstract: Neural stem cells (NSCs) are promising candidates for central nervous system (CNS) regeneration because they self-renew and differentiate into neural lineages. Advances in genome engineering, extracellular vesicles (EVs), biomaterials, organoids, single-cell technologies, and precision medicine have expanded approaches for characterizing, engineering, delivering, and evaluating NSC-based therapies for neurological disorders. CRISPR/Cas9 and related platforms may enable more precise modification of NSC function, while NSC-derived EVs offer potential cell-free strategies. Engineered hydrogels and three-dimensional scaffolds may improve cell survival, engraftment, migration, and integration. Organoids and single-cell omics provide increasingly detailed models of cellular heterogeneity and lineage specification. However, clinical translation remains limited by immune compatibility, tumorigenic risk, manufacturing standardization, graft survival and integration, and regulatory requirements. Rigorous preclinical validation, standardized manufacturing, appropriately designed clinical trials, long-term safety monitoring, and harmonized regulatory frameworks are required before routine clinical application.
authors: Marei HE.

title: Therapeutic opportunities of marine-derived bioactive compounds against SARS-CoV-2 and other enveloped viruses.
abstract: Marine ecosystems are a vast, underexplored reservoir of bioactive compounds with unique structural diversity and potent biological activities. Enveloped viruses, including severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the causative agent of COVID-19, continue to pose significant global health threats, exacerbated by emerging variants, limited therapeutic options beyond vaccines, and challenges such as drug resistance and immune dysregulation. Compounds derived from marine organisms, including lectins (e.g., griffithsin from red algae Griffithsia sp.), sulfated polysaccharides (e.g., iota-carrageenan from red algae Chondrus crispus), polyphenols (e.g., dieckol from brown algae Ecklonia cava), and depsipeptides (e.g., plitidepsin from tunicates), have shown promising antiviral effects in preclinical studies. These molecules primarily act by inhibiting viral entry (via the spike glycoprotein or glycan binding), replication (targeting proteases such as the main protease [Mpro] and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase [RdRp]), or by modulating host immune responses (e.g., reducing cytokine storms or oxidative stress). In vitro, in vivo, and in silico evidence highlights their potential against SARS-CoV-2 and related enveloped viruses (e.g., HIV, HSV, influenza, HCMV), which share mechanistic similarities, including envelope-mediated fusion and RNA-based replication. This narrative review provides a cohesive overview of selected marine-derived bioactive compounds with reported activity against SARS-CoV-2 and other enveloped viruses. It examines their sources, structural features, mechanisms of action, key activity metrics (e.g., IC₅₀/EC₅₀ values), and translational prospects, and addresses challenges such as scalability, preclinical-to-clinical gaps, and sustainability aligned with the European Blue Economy. By integrating recent findings, this review aims to highlight promising leads and guide future research toward innovative, broad-spectrum antiviral therapies.
authors: Balasubramaniyam T, Rampogu S, Go Y, Nathan VK, Zdanowski R, Kubiak JZ.

title: Structure of MPXV DNA ligase complex reveals a virus-specific pocket for selective inhibition.
abstract: Mpox, caused by monkeypox virus (MPXV), remains a public health concern, yet the structural basis of poxvirus DNA ligase function has been poorly defined despite strong genetic and biochemical evidence supporting its essential role in viral DNA replication and repair. Here, we report the crystal structure of MPXV DNA ligase (MpxvLig) in complex with nicked DNA at 2.04 Å resolution. MpxvLig adopts the canonical three-domain architecture of ATP-dependent DNA ligases, comprising an N-terminal DNA-binding domain (DBD), a nucleotidyltransferase domain, and a C-terminal oligonucleotide-binding fold domain (OBD), which together form a clamp-like configuration that embraces nicked DNA for catalysis. The structure captures MpxvLig in an active catalytic state corresponding to the adenylylation step, in which Lys233 forms a covalent ligase-AMP intermediate. Comparative structural and biochemical analyses with the catalytic core of human DNA ligase III reveal substantial differences in domain arrangement and DNA engagement, consistent with the stronger DNA-binding capacity and higher ligation activity of MpxvLig in vitro. Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) further shows that apo-MpxvLig adopts an extended flashlight-like conformation in solution. Notably, we identify a virus-specific small-molecule-binding pocket within the DNA-binding domain. Mitoxantrone binds directly to this pocket and inhibits MpxvLig activity at micromolar concentrations, while exerting minimal effects on the human ligase. Mutations in pocket-defining residues markedly attenuate this inhibition, supporting an on-target mechanism. Together, these findings establish the structural basis of poxvirus DNA ligation and provide a framework for the rational development of selective antiviral inhibitors targeting MpxvLig.
authors: Chen A, Fang N, Ye M, Qiu Y, Zhang Y, Huang J, Ding J, Ji C, Li J.
