title: Optimizing Genetic Analyses for Movement Disorders: A Unified Panel Approach and Targeted Reanalysis of 4,046 Clinical Exomes.
abstract: BackgroundMolecular testing for genetic movement disorders (MDs) increasingly relies on exome- or genome-based virtual gene panels. In the absence of consensus guidelines, MD panel design remains heterogeneous across laboratories, with international variation in panel configuration and gene content.ObjectiveThe aim of this work was to develop a reproducible framework for a unified MD panel design, generate a comprehensive, curated gene-phenotype dataset, and evaluate clinical utility via targeted exome reanalysis.MethodsCandidate genes were extracted from multiple resources and assessed using predefined criteria for panel inclusion and gene-disease validity. Genes were tiered as Green, Amber, or Red based on evidence strength. Phenotypic spectrum and age at onset were assessed for Green genes based on published literature. Newly added Green and Amber genes were investigated in 4,046 exomes from previously undiagnosed MD cases.ResultsAmong 2,090 extracted genes, 640 were selected. The final panel included 537 Green, 36 Amber, and 67 Red genes, expanding the prior panel by 283 genes and removing 42. Across Green genes, only 17% were linked to a single MD feature, whereas the remainder associated up to eight. Age-at-onset data indicated both pediatric and adult presentations in 43% of genes. Targeted exome reanalysis using a 220-gene list identified 37 clinically relevant variants across 28 genes, resolving 16 cases and increasing diagnostic yield by 0.4%.ConclusionsThis study offers a systematic framework for designing a unified MD panel by integrating evidence from multiple sources and accounting for phenotypic and age heterogeneity. Targeted reanalysis yielded actionable diagnoses, confirming its benefit in routine clinical practice. © 2026 The Author(s). authors: Barbarii T, Smeekens SP, Pennings M, Astuti G, Vissers LELM, Yntema HG, Gilissen C, van de Warrenburg B, Kamsteeg EJ.

title: IDENTIFICATION OF CANDIDATE GENES UNDERLYING A NOVEL QTL FOR ROOT LENGTH AND DIAMETER IN BARLEY IN RESPONSE TO SALINITY
abstract: ABSTRACT  Salinity is a major agricultural problem that decreases growth and yield of crops and is expected to worsen with climate change. Improving salt tolerance through breeding could be facilitated by identification of genetic loci and candidate genes affecting root traits that enhance water and nutrient uptake while limiting accumulation of toxic ions. In this study, a Clipper x Sahara 3771 doubled haploid (DH) barley mapping population was screened for root growth responses to saline conditions in a controlled environment. Quantitative trait loci (QTLs) were mapped for root traits including seminal root length, root diameter and root potassium. Major QTLs affecting seminal root length and average root diameter were detected in the distal region of the short arm of chromosome 2H, indicating that this region is a key determinant of root architecture under both control and saline conditions. The linkage map was improved by using newly designed assays for SNPs on chromosome 2H and a 2.5-Mb interval was identified for investigation of candidate genes. Bulked segregant RNA sequencing (BSR-Seq) of contrasting salt-tolerant and salt-sensitive DH lines identified differentially expressed genes associated with root growth maintenance and ion homeostasis in root tips. These findings identify specific region on chromosome 2H as a major genomic region affecting barley root architecture, especially under saline conditions, and identify differentially expressed candidate genes in that region.
authors: Mather D, Situmorang A, Brien CJ, Shelden MC.

title: Spatial transcriptomics of pediatric tuberculosis lymph nodes reveals a conserved hypoxia–SPP1 niche
abstract: Pediatric tuberculosis (TB) often presents as primary disease involving the mediastinal lymph nodes; however, its granuloma microenvironment remains poorly characterized because these population patient tissues are rarely available for study. Here, we use spatial transcriptomics to profile 60 granulomas from four children aged 4 to 36 months. We identified nine recurrent transcriptional microenvironments shared across granulomas, despite their marked histological heterogeneity. One macrophage-rich microenvironment showed strong hypoxia-associated activity and  secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) enrichment. This microenvironment was present in both non-necrotic and necrotic lesions and overlapped with a Mtb-persistence macrophage signature previously identified in murine TB lymph nodes. Pathway analysis revealed the enrichment of both antimicrobial and regulatory programs within this microenvironment, suggesting partial immune control rather than uniform inflammatory or suppressive activity in this region. SPP1 expression was associated with regions enriched for both M1- and M2-like macrophages, suggesting a macrophage program that extends beyond conventional polarization classifications and may be influenced by the local granuloma microenvironment. We further observed a similar spatial association between hypoxia-associated activity and SPP1 expression in an independent adult TB dataset (pooled Spearman ρ=0.65) and validated this association at protein level by multiplex immunofluorescence in our pediatric TB granuloma sample. Overall, this study identified a hypoxia-associated  SPP1 -enriched microenvironment that may contribute to incomplete bacterial clearance and could provide a framework for evaluating host-directed strategies to enhance sterilizing immunity without exacerbating tissue damage.

title: Compost-associated microbiota modulates root transcriptional responses and enhances tomato drought resilience
abstract: Summary  Compost is a promising sustainable alternative to mineral fertilization because it supplies nutrients and organic matter while hosting diverse microbial communities. However, even if its application to plants has been proven to alleviate different biotic and abiotic stresses, it remains unclear whether its benefits arise from its physico-chemical properties, its associated microbiota, or both. In this study, we compared the impact of compost, sterile compost and an NPK treatment providing equivalent macronutrient inputs on tomato plants cv. Micro-Tom. After assessing physiological parameters of the leaves and molecular responses of the roots under optimal conditions, we performed a drought stress experiment under the three fertilization treatments, complementing the analysis with the investigation of substrate water-retention properties. Although all fertilized treatments improved plant performance relative to nutrient-poor soil, RNA sequencing revealed distinct root transcriptional profiles among compost, sterile compost and NPK, with the compost treatment upregulating several pathways related to plant growth and health, such as hormone signaling, nutrient metabolism, and stress responses. When subjected to severe water stress, compost-treated plants retained the highest photosynthetic efficiency and compost showed the highest available water content compared to the other treatments. These findings suggest that compost may enhance tomato drought resilience through combined effects of substrate water availability and compost-associated microbiota.
authors: Cipriani R, Strickler SR, Petruzzellis F, Ghirardello G, Greggio L, Zanardi W, Bonato T, Baldan B, Nigris S.

title: Molecular insights into the regulation of coenzyme selection in NADP-specific glutamate dehydrogenase from  Saccharomyces cerevisiae
abstract: Coenzyme specificity is one of the crucial aspects of the functional regulations in enzymes. Understanding the molecular basis of coenzyme specificity in glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is highly essential as this is the only enzyme that fulfils various physiological demands in terms of energy production and/or nitrogen assimilation via its strict functional regulation by connecting carbon and nitrogen metabolic cycles in every living organism. We have studied  S. cerevisiae GDH3 (ScGDH3), as a model system for NADP-specific fungal GDHs. K272R and S250E mutants of ScGDH3 exhibited remarkable alteration in coenzyme specificity, with 15-55-fold and 3-14-fold more preference towards non-specific coenzymes [NAD(H)], respectively. S250E exhibited higher NADH affinity (∼ 1.3-fold) than that of towards NADPH. K272R showed ∼ 10-fold increased coenzyme affinity (  1/K  M ) and binding affinity (  1/k  d ) towards NADH, compared to the wild type enzyme (ScGDH3-WT). We solved the crystal structure of ScGDH3-K272R complexed with NADP  + at 2.50 Å resolution with a unique oligomeric arrangement having two distinct subunit conformations (“open” and “super-closed”) and it is the first structure of a GDH from  S. cerevisiae . Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide insights into NADH binding and its increased affinity to ScGDH3-K272R. Further structure-based sequence analyses unravelled that a lysine and an arginine are naturally preferred residues for providing NADP(H) and NAD(H) specificity, respectively for various amino acid dehydrogenases. Taken together biochemical and structural data, our study successfully illustrates the evolutionary conserved mechanism of coenzyme related regulation in fungal and other GDHs; as well as amino acid dehydrogenases.
authors: Banerjee A, Roy A, Saha S, Godsora BKJ, Bhaumik P.

title: Establishing  de novo  microbial biosynthesis of anisole
abstract: ABSTRACT  Anisole is a valuable aromatic ether and promising green solvent whose industrial manufacture relies exclusively on petroleum-derived phenol and hazardous alkali-mediated methylation. Here, we establish the first  de novo microbial biosynthesis of anisole from glucose in  Pseudomonas putida KT2440 by integrating retrosynthetic pathway design with growth-coupled directed evolution. Using a selection platform in an engineered double auxotroph, in which growth depends on S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation, we evolved a promiscuous plant chavicol O-methyltransferase to yield phenol O-methyltransferase 1 (POMT1; bearing a key D264N substitution), which improved anisole production by 2.3-fold over the wild-type enzyme. To overcome product volatility, we integrated an  in situ two-phase extraction system using dodecane that achieved near-quantitative product recovery. Then, we compared two phenol routes from the shikimate pathway, selected the 4-hydroxybenzoate route, and raised precursor supply by deleting competing reactions and introducing feedback-resistant and reduced-flux variants in two shikimate pathway enzymes. The final strain produced up to 0.57 mM anisole (62 mg/L) from glucose.
authors: Bruinsma L, Rosas Gomez D, La Rocca C, Escrig Molina JE, Martins dos Santos VAP, Batianis C.

title: How to name dark fungal taxa outside the Code: The International Standard to Catalogue Dark Fungal Taxa (ISCDFT)
abstract: There is an exponential increase in the number of fungal OTUs being documented by environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding. Many of these, the so-called dark fungal taxa (DFT), are known only from eDNA data, with no associated physical specimen or derived culture. Of the millions of fungal species predicted to exist, only ~205,000 are currently described, making it likely that many of these unknown or undescribed fungi are represented only by eDNA data. For more than a decade mycologists have struggled with whether the  International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (the  Code ) should allow for formal description of fungal taxa from eDNA data alone, i.e. with a DNA sequence serving as a type. It is, however, unlikely that an amendment to the  Code with this provision will pass in the near future. It is therefore imperative to establish an informal yet structured naming system to allow unified communication about DFT. The system proposed herein applies most of the principles of the  Code to generate designations that, while nomenclatorially invalid, can nonetheless be integrated into fungal classifications and diversity assessments. We used the 2025 Westerdijk Spring Symposium "DNA Sequences as Type" to bring mycologists together to work out community consensus-driven conventions and standards for what we call the International Standard to Catalogue Dark Fungal Taxa (ISCDFT). The established guidelines principally refer to naming conventions, quality and standards for the underlying data, and standards regarding the underlying analysis leading to the detection of new DFT. The ISCDFT does not compete with the  Code but enables the community to catalogue DFT and integrate these into fungal classifications while adhering to broadly established principles. For ease of immediate implementation, we provide examples to illustrate these newly established guidelines, a checklist for publishing new DFTs under the ISCDFT, and convert some previously published fungal names based on eDNA sequences to ISCDFT-compliant names.

title: A multidimensional “omics” approach reveals biased signaling through flg22- and UDP-glucose-induced, AtRGS1-driven signaling circuits
abstract: Abstract  Different cellular inputs into a central signaling core elicit different outputs in a process called biased signaling. Often this occurs by imprinting the signaling core with a phosphorylation bar code, functionally analogous to a microprocessor. The bacterial peptide flg22 and UDP-glucose both utilize a heterologous G protein core that contains a 7-transmembrane RGS protein, AtRGS1, to mediate changes differentially in plant defense and growth. Both flg22 and UDP-glucose launch rapid endocytosis of AtRGS1 at the plasma membrane but the destination and route are signal specific. flg22 directs plasma membrane AtRGS1 to the nucleus followed by different gene expression profiles. UDP-glucose does not direct AtRGS1 to the nucleus and does not elicit transcriptional reprogramming. Instead, UDP-glucose causes a massive, time-dependent restructuring of the G protein complex that likely traffics to the endosomal compartment. Associated with these two outcomes are phosphorylation bar codes that correlate with different patterns of AtRGS1-associated partners over time.
authors: Walley J, Li Z, Simoni E, Yang J, Montes C, Jones A.

title: Critical regions for human brain development include SON and ITSN1 defined by a panel with chromosome 21 interstitial deletions.
abstract: Abstract    Aneuploidies of chromosome 21 (CHR21), including Down syndrome and partial monosomy 21, are major causes of mental retardation and provide unique opportunities to identify candidate genes regulating human brain development. We identified 10 individuals with partial CHR21 deletions and defined molecular breakpoints with high resolution genomic arrays, FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization) and quantitative Southern blots. Patient records and neuroimaging generated by the authors or by referring physicians were reviewed. We defined regions from proximal to distal on CHR21, a region consistent with a normal range of cognition, a region associated with microcephaly, and a third region associated with polymicrogyria and partial agenesis of the corpus callosum. Three individuals with severe cortical dysgenesis including polymicrogyria (PMG) with callosal hypoplasia or agenesis shared a ~649 kb minimal region at 21q22.11-22.2 whose distal border lies within  ITSN1  and contains SON. Seven individuals with large proximal deletions outside this interval, had mild cognitive deficits and did not share this phenotype. Comparison of the human phenotypes with those seen with loss-of function mutations in  SON  or  ITSN1  indicate that the 649kb deleted region disturbs vertebrate brain development with components likely attributable to ITSN1 and SON.
authors: Korenberg JR, Sarnat HB, Pulst S, Hattori M, Chen X.

title: Strigolactone analog GR24 modulates hyphal growth, mitochondrial activity, and superoxide accumulation in the ectomycorrhizal fungus Rhizopogon roseolus
abstract: Abstract    Plant hormone strigolactone (SL) is an important rhizosphere signal that mediate communication between plants and diverse soil organisms. However, the role of SL in ectomycorrhizal (ECM) fungi remains largely unexplored, despite ECM fungi representing a major group of plant symbiotic fungi. To address this knowledge gap, we examined the effects of widely used SL analog GR24 with different stereoisomers and concentrations on several ECM fungal species. Deeper investigation on cellular and transcriptional response to GR24 was conducted on  Rhizopogon roseolus  . The evaluated parameters include fungal growth and branching, mitochondrial activity, superoxide accumulation, Ca  2+  signaling, and gene expression. Our findings reveal that ECM fungal responses to GR24 depend on fungal species, as well as GR24 stereoisomers and concentration. Further analysis on  R. roseolus  suggested that GR24 enhanced mitochondrial activity and increased mitochondria-associated superoxide accumulation. Based on pharmacological approach, the response of  R. roseolus  to GR24 required extracellular Ca  2+  influx. Consistent with these morphological and cellular responses, GR24 induce transcriptional response in genes related to cell-wall biosynthesis, mitochondrial respiratory chain, superoxide detoxification, and Ca  2+  signaling. Together, these findings provide novel insight into SL responsiveness in ECM fungi by integrating morphological, cellular, and transcriptional analyses.
authors: Pratiwi MN, Nathawan K, Chollada S, Hiroyuki A, Aimi T, Shimomura N.

title: Turning Large Electron Microscopy Datasets into Quantitative Measurements with Model-Assisted Analysis
abstract: Abstract  Large electron microscopy datasets require extensive annotation and review before they can be converted into reliable measurements. ACORN is an open-source, locally executable application that offers image preparation, reviewed annotation, task-specific model training, batch inference, calibrated measurement, and statistical analysis in a single format. Users can create and correct annotations manually or with promptable segmentation and use the reviewed annotations to train models directly within ACORN. Its Cryo-EM Lab Utility (CLU) assistant also allows users to request any analysis or training operations in plain language. To show its use cases, we evaluated ACORN using low-dose cryogenic TEM images of polymeric nanoparticles and SEM images of bacterial spores. YOLO models trained in ACORN produced validation F1 scores of \(0.906\pm0.013\) and \(0.624\pm0.016\), respectively. Controlled simulations built in ACORN provided 25,983 exact object annotations for further model development and a controlled evaluation of software performance. On held-out simulation images, equivalent-circular-diameter mean absolute error was 3.60~nm (10.1\%) for TEM particles and 31.48~nm (3.7\%) for SEM spores among matched detections. The software logs every interaction, training step, and annotation in a sample history for provenance tracking. ACORN provides an environment where annotations, image calibration, model checkpoints, object measurements, and statistical records are easily accessible and traceable. This software provides a traceable path from electron microscopy images to quantitative results in multiple user-friendly formats.
authors: Williams AN, Harris CR, Oh J, Zachman MJ, Borisevich AY, Hoglund ER, Haque A, Harris SB, Toro-González M, Lasseter JC, Hochanadel LH, Vasileva DP, Morrell-Falvey JL, Michener JK, Davern SM, Sanders BC, Retterer ST.

title: Selection and validation of intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) alone beneficiaries among elderly patients with stage T1-2N1M0 nasopharyngeal carcinoma and ACE-27 scores < 2: a multi-center study
abstract: Abstract  Background  Elderly patients are underrepresented in clinical trials supporting concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) as the standard treatment for patients with stage T1-2N1M0 nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). This study aimed to develop and validate a prognostic nomogram in elderly patients (≥ 60 years) with stage T1-2N1M0 NPC to distinguish low-risk subgroup for whom intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) alone is sufficient. Methods  This multi-center study retrospectively analyzed 615 elderly patients with stage T1-2N1M0 NPC and Adult Comorbidity Evaluation-27 (ACE-27) scores
authors: Zhang Y, Yu H, Mo H, Cai H, Zhang L, Yang Q, Lin X, Tian Y, Chen X, Wen Y.

title: Ecological niche and plantation composition differentially shape bacterial community composition and assembly across the root-soil continuum in Populus simonii plantations
abstract: Abstract    Mixed plantations are widely established to restore degraded sandy landscapes, yet bacterial community patterns across roots and surrounding soils remain poorly understood. This study examined bacterial diversity, composition, inferred assembly patterns, environmental associations, and predicted functional potential in contrasting  Populus simonii  plantations. We analysed 60 composite samples from root (R), rhizosphere (RS), and non-rhizosphere soil (NRS) in four stands in the Kubuqi Desert, northern China. These comprised a  P. simonii  monoculture and mixtures with  Salix psammophila  ,  Caragana korshinskii  , and  Pinus sylvestris  var.  Mongolica  , with five plots sampled per stand. Root communities exhibited lower richness and diversity and distinct taxonomic composition compared with the two soil compartments. PERMANOVA confirmed significant effects of both ecological niche (  F   = 24.995,  p   = 0.001) than stand type (  F   = 2.649,  p   = 0.005) on community composition, with niche showing the stronger association. Null-model classifications varied among sample groups. Homogeneous selection was the most frequently assigned category in most groups, whereas dispersal limitation accounted for a larger proportion of comparisons in the sampled  P. simonii  and  C. korshinskii  mixture. Co-occurrence patterns also varied across ecological niches and plantation types, with the rhizosphere showing the highest connectivity and mixed plantations generally exhibiting greater connectivity than the monoculture. Soil water content was strongly associated with bacterial community variation (  r²  =0.815,  p   = 0.0005). Predicted KEGG and COG profiles varied among niche and plantation combinations, but no consistent functional response to mixed planting was observed. Together, these results reveal that bacterial taxonomic composition and community assembly responded to different ecological dimensions, ecological niche was more strongly associated with compositional differentiation, whereas assembly processes varied more clearly among the four sampled stands. This decoupling highlights the multidimensional organization of bacterial communities across the root-soil continuum in sandy plantations.
authors: Ren Y, Yang G, Su M, Guo X, Qiao S, Shang J.

title: Evaluating ANO6 as a Parkinson's disease candidate gene: A human genetic investigation of common and rare variant associations.
abstract: ANO6 (TMEM16F), a Ca2+-activated lipid scramblase and ion channel, has been implicated in α-synuclein secretion and propagation, a hallmark of Parkinson's disease (PD). To evaluate whether genetic variation in ANO6 contributes to PD risk, we analyzed common and rare variants across large-scale datasets. Relying on genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from 63,555 PD cases, 17,700 proxy cases, and 1.7 million controls, we identified seven noncoding common variants within ANO6 that reached genome-wide significance, but these signals were driven by linkage disequilibrium (LD) with the nearby LRRK2 p.G2019S variant. We further tested rare variant burden in 4879 PD cases and 65,279 controls. Rare variant burden analysis showed significant enrichment only when all rare variants were aggregated (meta-analysis PFDR = 0.02), with no signal detected in functional categories. Overall, human genetic data does not support an important role for ANO6 in PD.
authors: Parlar SC, Leonard H, Senkevich K, Liu L, Teferra M, Global Parkinson's Genetics Program (GP2). Electronic address: cornelis.blauwendraat@nih.gov, Gan-Or Z.

title: Identification and binding-site mapping of RNA-binding proteins interacting with microRNA precursors in Arabidopsis.
abstract: BackgroundMicroRNAs (miRNAs) play key roles in modulating gene expression. Upon transcription, primary miRNA transcripts (pri-miRNAs or MIRNAs) fold into stem-loop structures. Endonucleolytic cleavage releases a miRNA/miRNA* duplex from the stem, which is subsequently matured. In higher plants, the pri-miRNA hairpins vary widely in length and structure. Pri-miRNA processing is extensively regulated by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and the range of underlying mechanisms continues to expand.ResultsHere, we performed an unbiased screen to identify Arabidopisis thaliana candidate RBPs that interact with pri-miRNAs, using pri-miRNA159a and pri-miRNA398b as paradigms. Nucleoplasmic proteins were significantly enriched in pulldowns with bead-immobilized in vitro transcripts of the stem-loop regions of these pri-miRNAs compared with pulldowns using empty beads. The enriched proteins included several serine/arginine-rich (SR) splicing factors, notably RS31 and SR34a, extending previous findings that RS40 and RS41 bind pri-miRNAs and participate in miRNA biogenesis. Mutant analysis indicated that selected candidate interactors affect pri-miRNA and/or mature miRNA accumulation. To validate candidate interactions with pri-miRNAs in vivo, we performed individual-nucleotide resolution crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (iCLIP). Whereas our conventional plant iCLIP procedure detected only a few crosslink sites on pri-miRNAs, likely because of the low abundance of these transcripts, our improved plant iCLIP2 protocol enabled the identification of binding sites on numerous pri-miRNAs. RS31 and SR34a bound overlapping sets of pri-miRNAs and contacted both stem-loop regions and flanking regions upstream and downstream of the stem-loop. Binding-site mapping resolved overlapping and distinct contact regions and highlighted the importance of complete pri-miRNA annotations for interpreting interactions beyond annotated transcript boundaries.ConclusionIn vitro pulldowns of nucleoplasmic proteins identified candidate RBPs associated with pri-miRNA stem-loops, and the improved plant iCLIP2 protocol revealed in vivo binding of RS31 and SR34a to a subset of pri-miRNAs. Together, these findings expand the repertoire of candidate RBPs implicated in plant miRNA biogenesis and support a role for SR proteins as candidate regulators of miRNA abundance.
authors: Winkel AR, Bitterer VW, Lewinski M, Reichel M, Lüders J, Scheibe M, Kalyna M, Laloum T, Duque P, Staiger D, Butter F, Köster T.

title: Neoadjuvant botensilimab with or without balstilimab in pMMR and dMMR colon cancer: the phase 2 UNICORN trial.
abstract: Preoperative immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are active in patients with deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) colon cancer (CC), whereas proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) CC has been consistently considered resistant to first-generation ICIs. In the phase 2 UNICORN trial, we evaluated short-course preoperative botensilimab (BOT; multifunctional Fc-enhanced anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody) alone or in combination with the anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody balstilimab (BOT + BAL) in 56 patients with resectable, locally advanced CC. Twenty-eight patients with pMMR CC were sequentially enrolled in BOT (n = 14) and BOT + BAL (n = 14) cohorts. Twenty-eight patients with dMMR CC followed the same sequential allocation strategy. The primary endpoint of centrally assessed pathological major response (pMR) rate (≤10% of residual viable tumor) was met in all cohorts, except pMMR BOT. Specifically, the pMR rate was 0% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0-23.2%) in pMMR BOT, 36% (95% CI: 12.8-64.9%) in pMMR BOT + BAL, 36% (95% CI: 12.8-64.9%) in dMMR BOT and 100% (95% CI: 76.8-100%) in dMMR BOT + BAL. Secondary endpoints included safety, quality of life, describing treatment-induced transcriptional dynamics, peripheral blood mononuclear cell dynamics, radiomics and radiogenomics features, fecal microbiota composition and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) dynamics. Eight (29%) and 15 (54%) patients treated with BOT and BOT + BAL, respectively, experienced immune-related adverse events, most commonly flu-like syndrome and diarrhea. Single-cell spatial transcriptomic analysis of matched baseline and post-treatment samples highlighted high baseline PD-L1 stromal expression and low post-treatment regulatory T cell signatures in pMMR responders, whereas dMMR responders displayed high baseline FCGR2A and FCGR3A expression on intratumoral macrophages. Clearance of ctDNA before surgery correlated with pathological response and lack of recurrence at data cutoff. Preoperative BOT + BAL elicits pathological responses in patients with pMMR or dMMR CC, supporting the combination as a promising strategy to expand ICI benefits to the early-stage setting. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05845450 .

title: Pheno+: An Electronic Health Record-Integrated, Clinician-in-the-Loop Application for Efficient Phenotyping in Clinical Genomics
abstract: ABSTRACT  Objective  To evaluate the efficiency and diagnostic utility of Pheno+, an electronic health record (EHR)-integrated application that streamlines the generation of structured phenotypes for genomic testing and analysis. Materials and Methods  We developed Pheno+ as a Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies on Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (SMART on FHIR) application embedded within the University of Utah Health EHR. Pheno+ applies ClinPhen to clinician-selected clinical notes to identify candidate Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, which clinicians review and curate within the EHR. We conducted an eight-case crossover evaluation comparing workflow time between Pheno+ and a standard workflow that involved physician chart review and molecular geneticist-led HPO term selection. In a separate cohort of 17 patients with confirmed monogenic diagnoses, we assessed the diagnostic utility of Pheno+-derived HPO terms by evaluating Exomiser gene prioritization performance using these terms. Results  Pheno+ reduced mean total workflow time by 66%, from 31.1 to 10.5 minutes (p Discussion and Conclusion  Pheno+ reduced the time and personnel required to generate clinician-curated HPO term lists while producing phenotypes that improved causative gene prioritization. These findings support EHR-integrated, clinician-in-the-loop phenotyping as an efficient approach to generating diagnostically informative phenotype data for clinical genomic workflows.
authors: Lebleu EL, Cooperstein IB, Jenkins SM, Bayrak-Toydemir P, Mao R, Ward A, Di Sera T, Solorzano CM, Ellsworth T, Simek K, Taber P, Warner P, Kawamoto K, Marth GT, Tristani-Firouzi M.

title: Decoding adenomyosis: integrative insights from genetics, multiomics, and advanced computational analyses.
abstract: Adenomyosis is an oestrogen-driven, inflammatory uterine disorder characterised by endometrial glands and stroma in the myometrium resulting in abnormal bleeding, pain, and poor reproductive outcomes. Multiple contributors to its pathogenesis and pathophysiology have been identified over the years using a variety of experimental approaches and technologies, with gaps in integrating these approaches into a comprehensive paradigm of adenomyosis pathobiology. This review provides integrative insights from recent studies focused on genetics, multiomics, and advanced computational approaches. These demonstrate that select genes are causally linked to adenomyosis and that genomic and epigenetic mechanisms promote the enhanced oestrogen and diminished progesterone signalling and associated inflammation that are pathognomonic of the disorder, supported by orthogonal validation including novel 3D in vitro cell models. In addition, advanced computational tools, including AI-driven platforms that integrate multiomics data, reveal promising therapeutic candidates for mitigating disease progression and symptoms and improving fertility and pregnancy success.
authors: Liu B, Irwin JC, Giudice LC.

title: Cachexia defined by the Asian Working group for cachexia 2023 criteria and gut microbiota diversity in post-stroke patients capable of oral intake.
abstract: Background & aimsCachexia defined by the Asian Working Group for Cachexia (AWGC) 2023 criteria is associated with adverse outcomes in older adults, but its relationship with gut microbiota diversity remains unclear. This study aimed to examine the association between cachexia and gut microbiota diversity in stroke patients.MethodsThis cross-sectional study examined post-acute stroke patients capable of oral intake. Cachexia was assessed at admission using the AWGC 2023 criteria. Gut microbiota diversity was evaluated using the Shannon index, amplicon sequence variant (ASV) richness, and Faith's phylogenetic diversity (PD) based on 16 S rRNA gene sequencing of fecal samples. Multiple linear regression analyses were performed after adjustment for potential confounders.ResultsA total of 130 patients were included; the mean (SD) age was 78.4 (7.1) years, and 58% were men. Cachexia was diagnosed in 15% (19/130) of patients. After adjustment, cachexia was independently and negatively associated with the Shannon index (β = -0.282, p = 0.002), ASV richness (β = -0.279, p = 0.001), and Faith's PD (β = -0.264, p = 0.006). Among the AWGC 2023 components, underlying disease, low body mass index, decreased handgrip strength, and elevated C-reactive protein were independently associated with lower gut microbiota diversity.ConclusionsIn this cross-sectional study, cachexia was independently associated with lower gut microbiota diversity in post-acute stroke patients. These findings are associative rather than causal and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.
authors: Nagano F, Yoshimura Y, Wakabayashi H, Matsumoto A, Shimazu S, Bise T, Kido Y, Kuzuhara A, Yoneda K, Maeda K.

title: Treatment of viral retinitis after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with maribavir: A report of three cases and a review of the literature.
abstract: Viral retinitis subsequent to allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo - HSCT) is a severe post - transplant ocular complication. This study presents data on three patients who developed viral retinitis after allo - HSCT. All three patients received letermovir and acyclovir prophylaxis for cytomegalovirus (CMV) or other viral infections post - transplantation. They exhibited Epstein - Barr (EB) virus and/or CMV viremia and were associated with post - transplant lymphoproliferative disorders, which improved after rituximab therapy. Viral retinitis was diagnosed during immunosuppressive therapy (7-8 months post - transplantation), with negative peripheral blood viral DNA quantification at the time of diagnosis. Intravitreal injection of ganciclovir or foscarnet sodium demonstrated suboptimal efficacy, whereas visual improvement was achieved through combined oral antiviral therapy using maribavir. These findings imply that enhanced vigilance for viral retinitis and intensified fundus monitoring are necessary for patients with prior CMV or EB virus viremia during letermovir prophylaxis for CMV. Intravitreal injection combined with oral maribavir represents a novel therapeutic approach for patients with suboptimal responses to ganciclovir or foscarnet sodium.
authors: Shi Y, Wang X.

title: Biogenic gold nanoparticles in breast cancer nanomedicine: sustainable synthesis, multifunctional engineering, and the road to clinical translation.
abstract: The use of plant, algal, microbial or biomolecule based reducing and capping agents to synthesize gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) has paved the way for the use of these materials as versatile candidates for breast-cancer nanomedicine. In addition to being a more sustainable synthetic pathway, the biological elements attached to the surface of AuNP can have an impact on the formation process, the stability of AuNP in solution, the interaction with cells and the therapeutic activity of the particles. This review critically assesses the recent advances of biogenic AuNPs for application in breast cancer, ranging from direct phytogenic anticancer formulations, engineered drug delivery system, HER2 associated biosensing platform, photoresponsive therapies, and multimodal theranostic constructs. Preclinical reported mechanisms are increased cellular uptake, increased oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, increased DNA damage, cell-cycle arrest, and apoptosis. Additionally, Biogenic AuNPs offer flexible surfaces for the conjugation of chemotherapeutics, phytochemicals, nucleic acids, antibodies, photosensitizers and tumour-targeting ligands, thus providing opportunities for subtype-specific strategies for HER2-positive disease and triple-negative breast cancer. Currently however, in vitro studies dominate the evidence base, and many of these studies make use of limited models of cell lines. Although the bioinorganic nature of Biogenic AuNPs is scientifically interesting, their clinical applicability will rely on the development of reproducible synthesis procedures, characterization in biological environments, validation for the respective sub-type, quantitative biodistribution and clinically representative preclinical models.
authors: Singh UR, Mishra G, Leharwani M, Abourehab MAS, Gupta G, Wen Goh K, Kesharwani P.

title: Microplastic exposure and obesity-related metabolic dysfunction: A proposed gut microbiota-metabolite framework.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs), as emerging global contaminants, have infiltrated aquatic systems, soil, and food chains, raising concerns about their health risks, particularly their potential link to metabolic disorders like obesity. This review evaluates evidence that MP exposure may influence host energy metabolism and adipogenesis and examines the potential involvement of the gut microbiota and its metabolites. Dietary MP exposure can alter microbial communities and associated metabolic pathways. Such dysbiosis may impair intestinal barrier integrity, trigger chronic inflammation, and promote adipose dysfunction, thereby potentially contributing to obesity-related metabolic disturbances. We synthesize findings from animal studies, in vitro models, and multi-omics approaches, highlighting the roles of MP physicochemical properties, exposure dose, and duration in obesity-related metabolic effects. Current limitations include insufficient long-term assessments at environmentally relevant concentrations, uncertainties in cross-species extrapolation, and unclear interactions with co-pollutants. Future studies could combine organ-on-a-chip (OoC) models with microbial and host single-cell or spatial approaches to test microbiota-host crosstalk. Overall, this review synthesizes emerging evidence on the potential links between MP exposure and adipogenesis dysregulation and identifies priorities for future mechanistic research and risk assessment.
authors: Han T, Fang Y, Zhang Z, Liang B, Wang Y, Hao R, Li Y, Wang J.

title: Characterization of peritrophin-like protein PvPT-L1 from Penaeus Vannamei: Potential association with dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase DLD from Lactiplantibacillus plantarum Ep-M17 and implications for probiotic adhesion and immune modulation.
abstract: Probiotics are widely used to promote growth and health in Penaeus vannamei; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying their interaction with the host remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified a peritrophin-like factor, PvPT-L1, as a putative critical mediator of the probiotic effects of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum Ep-M17. Full-length cloning revealed that PvPT-L1 contains three typical chitin-binding domains and shares high homology with Penaeus japonicus PT-L1. PvPT-L1 was predominantly expressed in the midgut, with considerable transcript abundance in the hepatopancreas and foregut. In vitro binding assays confirmed that recombinant rPvPT-L1 may bind to chitin and associated with both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Notably, PvPT-L1 significantly enhanced the intestinal adherence of L. plantarum Ep-M17 in a HEK-293 T cell model. RNA interference (RNAi) against PvPT-L1 resulted in 466 differentially expressed genes, disrupting redox homeostasis, proteostasis, and transmembrane transport, suggesting its essential role in maintaining gut barrier integrity. Using His pull-down and LC-MS/MS, we identified dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (DLD) that may be associated with bacterial cells as a potential interacting partner of PvPT-L1; this interaction was further validated by molecular docking, dynamics simulations, and co-immunoprecipitation. Functionally, oral administration of recombinant rDLD appeared to mitigated intestinal epithelial apoptosis. Interestingly, although rDLD suppressed hemocyte phagocytic activity, it effectively reprogrammed immune effector transcription and alleviated pathogen-induced apoptosis, hinting at a shift from robust internalization toward balanced immunomodulation. Collectively, these findings provide insights into a potential DLD-PvPT-L1 axis that may link physical adhesion and immune calibration, offering new mechanistic clues into probiotic-host immune interactions in crustaceans.
authors: Du Y, Li B, Yang X, Chen J.

title: Polystyrene nanoplastics exacerbate hepatic insulin resistance and glycolipid metabolism disorders in high‑fat diet‑induced obese mice.
abstract: Nanoplastics are emerging environmental contaminants with potential metabolic health risks, yet their chronic effects on high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity‑related metabolic disorders remain poorly understood. This study investigated whether long‑term oral exposure to polystyrene nanoplastics (PS‑NPs) aggravates hepatic insulin resistance and glycolipid metabolism disorders in HFD‑induced obese mice, and elucidated the underlying molecular mechanisms. Male C57BL/6 J mice were fed a HFD for 32 weeks with concurrent oral gavage of PS‑NPs (10 mg/kg, every 3 days). PS‑NPs co‑exposure significantly exacerbated body weight gain, fasting hyperglycemia, glucose intolerance, and insulin resistance compared with HFD alone. Hepatic histopathology revealed aggravated steatosis, inflammatory infiltration, and glycogen depletion in PS‑NPs‑treated obese mice. Mechanistically, PS‑NPs further suppressed hepatic protein levels of phosphorylated AKT (Ser473), insulin receptor (INSR), and glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2), while upregulating mRNA expression of gluconeogenic regulators (FOXO1, PCK1) and lipogenic genes (SREBF1, ACACA). In vitro, using HepG2 cells with high‑concentration insulin‑induced insulin resistance, PS‑NPs reduced insulin‑stimulated AKT phosphorylation, decreased INSR and GLUT2 protein expression, upregulated G6PC1 and ACACA, and downregulated SLC2A2, suggesting a cell‑autonomous sensitization to metabolic stress. Gut microbiota analysis revealed that PS‑NPs co-exposure further reduced microbial diversity and increased the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio in HFD-fed mice. Collectively, these findings indicate that HFD-induced obesity creates a metabolically vulnerable state that amplifies nanoplastic-induced hepatic insulin resistance and glycolipid dysregulation via interference with insulin signaling and transcriptional reprogramming. This positions chronic nanoplastic exposure as an underappreciated environmental driver in the obesity-diabetes nexus, highlighting the need for future risk assessment that considers host metabolic vulnerability and diet-pollutant interactions.
authors: Tang Y, Li T, Kuang X, Wu J, Qin D, Luo M, Han Z, Zheng Y.

title: Protocol for isolating intracellular Salmonella RNA from primary murine macrophages.
abstract: Isolation of intracellular bacterial RNA from infected cells remains challenging, limiting studies of bacterial transcription during host cell infection. Here, we present a protocol for isolating intracellular Salmonella enterica RNA from primary murine macrophages for transcriptomic analysis. We describe steps for macrophage infection, selective host cell lysis, bacterial recovery, and RNA purification for sequencing. This protocol uses standard laboratory equipment, is completed in 3 days, and can be adapted to other bacteria that replicate within macrophages. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Massicotte et al.1.
authors: Massicotte MA, Coombes BK.

title: Cytomegalovirus and cancer stem cells: a hidden alliance in tumor progression and therapy resistance.
abstract: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a widely spread β-herpesvirus that can establish life-long latency in the human host and remains asymptomatic in healthy immunocompetent hosts. In immunocompromised populations, such as transplant recipients, HIV/AIDS patients, and cancer patients, CMV presents an opportunity to reactivate and influence disease progression. There is a growing, but still contested, body of evidence suggesting that while CMV is not a classical oncogenic virus, it may act as an oncomodulatory virus, exerting an indirect impact on tumor biology. CMV DNA, RNA, or proteins have been detected in tumors such as glioblastoma, breast, colorectal, and pancreatic cancers in several studies, although other studies using comparable or more sensitive assays have failed to detect the virus in the same tumor types, so this association should not be regarded as established. In addition, CMV presence in tumor tissues is associated with immune suppression, therapy resistance, angiogenesis, and inflammation-all indicators of hallmark cancer progression. Of particular interest related to CMV in the context of cancer is its potential relationship with cancer stem cells (CSCs), a rare cell subpopulation of tumor cells, although a potent subpopulation for self-renewal, metastasis, and resistance to conventional cancer therapies. CMV has been shown to modulate numerous signaling pathways (Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, Notch, and This review summarizes emerging connections between CMV infection and CSC biology, highlighting the ability of the virus to alter tumor behavior through effects on pluripotent transcription factors (i.e., Oct4, Sox2, Nanog), modulation of cytokine networks (i.e., IL-10, TGF-β), and inducing immune escape mechanisms. As we develop a better understanding of the CMV-CSC connection, this may inform new therapeutic strategies that utilize antiviral approaches to work alongside contemporary CSC-targeted therapies, providing relief in instances of drug resistance, relapse, and poor prognosis in CMV-positive tumors. We also critically appraise the strength and consistency of the underlying evidence, propose reasons for conflicting findings, and put forward a context-dependent, bidirectional model of CMV-CSC interaction together with testable predictions.
authors: Kumar S, Kumari P, Kumar R, Qamar Z, Dang S, Tripathi VM, Chandravanshi LP.

title: JAK1/2 Inhibition Restores Tissue Integrity by Rewiring Type 1/2 Immunity Toward Targetable IL-17 Responses
abstract: Effective immune responses require coordinated communication between immune and epithelial cells to eliminate pathogens while limiting tissue damage. Disruption of this balance drives chronic inflammation and progressive tissue destruction. The Janus kinase (JAK) pathway coordinates cytokine signaling across these compartments and has emerged as a therapeutic target in inflammatory diseases. However, the consequences of JAK inhibition within a complex inflammatory environment remain incompletely understood. Here, we dissect the molecular, cellular, immunological and phenotypical effects of topical JAK1/2 inhibition in a chronic model of tissue-destructive skin inflammation driven by barrier dysfunction and bacterial superinfection. Single-cell transcriptomics and functional profiling revealed that JAK1/2 blockade selectively suppressed pathogenic CD8⁺ T cells and their IFN-γ production while shifting Th2-polarized CD4⁺ T cells toward a Th17 phenotype, preserving type 3 immunity consisting of IL-17A-producing γδ-T cells and neutrophil responses. This immune rebalancing occurs rapidly and concomitantly with the restoration of epithelial barrier integrity through tight junction reinforcement, followed by recovery of antimicrobial defenses and reduced bacterial burden. Combination of JAK1/2 and IL-17A blockade further improved tissue homeostasis by targeting residual type 3-driven pathology. Thus, JAK1/2 inhibition acts as selective immunomodulator rather than a broad immunosuppressant, targeting pathogenic type 1/2 responses while preserving type-3-associated antimicrobial defense programs. These findings reveal how JAK1/2 inhibition coordinates immune rebalancing with epithelial repair and support its therapeutic potential in chronic type 1/2-driven inflammatory disease, while identifying residual IL-17A-mediated pathology as a target for combination therapy.
authors: Jin R, Strobl K, Artner-Gent L, Tuechler J, Gladkova M, Mann U, Farlik M, Barozzi I, Sibilia M, Bauer T.

title: Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analysis identifies BCHE and FOXM1 as oxidative-stress markers linked to prognosis and immune-microenvironment remodeling in nasopharyngeal carcinoma
abstract: Abstract  Background  Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), an Epstein–Barr virus–associated head-and-neck cancer, typically carries dense yet dysfunctional immune infiltrates. Oxidative stress shapes both tumor progression and immune escape; whether oxidative-stress genes (OSGs) carry prognostic and immunological information in NPC has not been examined at bulk and single-cell resolution. Methods  Three NPC microarray cohorts (GSE12452, GSE53819 and GSE64634) were integrated using robust rank aggregation and ComBat-corrected limma, and genes identified by both strategies were intersected with 1,398 OSGs from GeneCards. Candidate prognostic OSGs were tested in the RNA-seq cohort GSE102349 (n = 88) using univariate Cox, LASSO and multivariable Cox regression together with Kaplan–Meier analysis, time-dependent ROC curves and a nomogram. We further applied Hallmark gene-set enrichment, CIBERSORT, an immune-cell LASSO signature, checkpoint correlation, ssGSEA and drug-sensitivity prediction, and replicated the findings in three independent cohorts and a single-cell RNA-seq dataset (GSE150430), where in-silico knockout, transcription-factor regulon, trajectory and cell–cell communication analyses were also performed. Results  Of 722 consistent differentially expressed genes, 67 were NPC-specific OSGs. BCHE emerged as the consistently prognostic OSG (univariate HR = 1.85, P = 0.009; optimal-cutoff Kaplan–Meier P = 0.003, high-versus-low HR = 4.1; the sole LASSO-retained multivariable term). FOXM1 failed multivariable retention but still defined a high-risk subgroup by optimal-cutoff Kaplan–Meier (P = 0.012, HR = 4.4). Enrichment analysis tied FOXM1 to E2F/G2M/MYC proliferation programs and BCHE to epithelial–mesenchymal-transition and Wnt signaling; both genes were inversely related to interferon and complement pathways. A ten-cell immune signature and checkpoint correlations outlined an immune-suppressed compartment. At single-cell level, both genes localized to malignant cells within a shared early malignant state, and malignant–immune crosstalk was dominated by MIF- and galectin-mediated signaling. Conclusion  Convergent bulk and single-cell evidence supports BCHE as a prognostic OS marker for risk stratification and FOXM1 as a proliferation-linked marker of malignant state in NPC. Both track with immune-microenvironment remodeling and await experimental and prospective validation.
authors: Chen Z, Wu D, Sun B, Liu C, Zhao M, Tian Y, Kong X, Zhou C.

title: Staged sternal distraction for early thoracic expansion in Shwachman-Diamond syndrome.
abstract: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS) is a rare inherited multisystem disorder with variable skeletal involvement; severe neonatal thoracic dystrophy is uncommon but can cause thoracic insufficiency and mimic Jeune syndrome. We report staged sternal distraction in a 5-month-old infant with a severely constricted thorax, pulmonary hypoplasia, refractory pulmonary hypertension, tracheostomy-dependent respiratory failure and an iatrogenic posterior tracheal wall injury. Subsequent trio long-read genome sequencing identified compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in SBDS, c.183_184delinsCT (p.Lys62Ter), inherited paternally, and c.258+2T>C, inherited maternally, establishing a molecular diagnosis of SDS. At presentation, the chest circumference measured 36cm, compared with an age-expected value of 41cm. The patient underwent staged median sternotomy distraction followed by stabilisation with custom fibular allograft struts. At approximately 3 months, chest circumference had increased to 41cm, peak inspiratory pressures had decreased from 40-50cm H2O to the mid-20cm H2O range, pulmonary hypertension was no longer evident on echocardiography, and the tracheal injury had healed. At 6 months, he remained on home mechanical ventilation, with peak inspiratory pressures in the upper 20cm H2O range. To our knowledge, operative thoracic expansion specifically for SDS-associated thoracic insufficiency has not previously been described. In carefully selected infants with severe thoracic insufficiency who are not yet candidates for conventional thoracic reconstruction, staged sternal distraction may serve as an interim strategy to achieve meaningful thoracic expansion.
journal: Annals of the Royal College of Surgeons of England
authors: Jarrin Lopez A, Zhao A, Darawsheh R, Kephart D, Sebastian VA, Idowu O, Babbitt C, Kim S.

title: Differential transcriptomic responses of pmgA and ssr1600 single-knockout mutants to short-term and prolonged high-light exposure in the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803.
abstract: PmgA and Ssr1600, homologs of the anti-sigma factor and the anti-sigma antagonist of the bacterial partner-switching system, respectively, are involved in coordination of the repression of photosystem I content and chlorophyll biosynthesis under prolonged high-light (HL) conditions in the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803. To characterize the transcriptional responses associated with PmgA and Ssr1600 during HL acclimation, we compared global gene expression profiles of the wild-type (WT) and knockout strains of pmgA (ΔpmgA) and ssr1600 (Δ1600) under low-light conditions and at 15 min, 1 h and 12 h after the shift to HL. The knockout of pmgA or ssr1600 induced temporally distinct transcriptomic alterations between short-term and prolonged HL exposure. At 15 min, Δ1600, but not ΔpmgA, showed enhanced induction of stress-responsive genes, including sigB and heat-shock genes, together with derepression of pmgA. At 12 h, both mutants showed significant upregulation of genes related to chlorophyll biosynthesis, photosynthetic electron transport, nitrogen assimilation, and amino acid biosynthesis. Considering that Ssr1600 does not accumulate in ΔpmgA, these observations can be explained by a shift in the role of Ssr1600, from the suppressor of the amplification of the stress response by PmgA under short-term HL conditions to a factor mediating signal output from the PmgA-Ssr1600 module under prolonged HL conditions, although the contribution of secondary effects cannot be excluded. Our transcriptomic data do not support the hypothesis that PmgA acts as a canonical anti-sigma factor for any of the sigma factors examined in this study, SigB, SigD and SigE, under either condition.
authors: Nakamura R, Kawai S, Hirose Y, Hihara Y.

title: Collagen-stimulating activity of a pentapeptide conjugate and self-assembly into micelles.
abstract: We present a lipopeptide conjugate, farnesyl-mercapto(diethylene glycol)-KTTKS (FMdEG-KTTKS), designed to include the KTTKS collagen-stimulating sequence attached to a terpenoid branched lipid chain via a short hydrophilic spacer. This conjugate stimulates fibroblasts to produce greater than 200% more collagen per cell than conventional stimulants. This activity is observed at low concentration, well below a critical micelle concentration (CMC) determined by fluorescence probe measurements. Above the CMC, this molecule self-assembles into well-defined spherical micelles, as shown by cryogenic-transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM) and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS). The behaviour of this conjugate is contrasted with that of related lipopeptides: FMdEG-KTTKS forms micelles across a wide pH range, instead of nanotapes observed for C16-KTTKS (Matrixyl™). The molecule is shown to stimulate production of type I collagen (beneficial for anti-aging treatments) and promotes repopulation of fibroblasts in a cell monolayer after scratching, as a simple model for skin injury. FMdEG-KTTKS also has anti-inflammatory activity, reducing the production of nitrite in macrophages challenged with bacterial lipopolysaccharide.
authors: de Mello L, Castelletto V, Seitsonen J, Hamley IW.

title: Early Renal microRNA Signatures of Septic Acute Kidney Injury in Neonatal Pigs.
abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a major complication of neonatal sepsis, yet the early molecular events underlying sepsis-associated AKI (SA-AKI) in the maturing kidney remain poorly defined. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression that may contribute to the inflammatory, stress, and remodeling responses associated with SA-AKI. We profiled renal miRNA expression in neonatal pigs 12 h after cecal ligation and puncture (CLP)-induced polymicrobial sepsis. CLP increased plasma lactate, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin and was accompanied by evidence of kidney injury, including increased plasma creatinine, symmetric dimethylarginine, and urinary neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin. NanoString profiling of 803 endogenous miRNAs, followed by sequence-based porcine annotation, identified a distinct renal miRNA signature that separated CLP and sham kidneys by principal component analysis. Differential expression analysis identified 14 upregulated and 5 downregulated miRNAs in septic kidneys. Several differentially expressed miRNAs were associated with biomarkers of systemic inflammation and kidney injury. Integrating miRNA profiles with target-gene expression revealed inverse miRNA-mRNA relationships involving PTGS2, FOS, AKT1, KLF6, NF-κB1, and SMAD2, with ssc-miR-374b-5p showing the broadest inverse relationship with these upregulated targets. Pathway enrichment analysis further implicated HIF-1, TGF-β, FoxO, autophagy/mitophagy, cell-cycle regulation, focal adhesion, and cellular senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate rapid remodeling of the renal miRNA landscape during early polymicrobial sepsis and identify candidate miRNA-mRNA regulatory networks that may contribute to the early pathogenesis of neonatal SA-AKI.
authors: Adepoju AE, Fanous MS, Michael OS, Cruz JE, Mankuzhy PD, Adebiyi A.

title: Recent Developments in (Archaeal) Pyrrolysine and Selenocysteine Specification and Metabolism.
abstract: Although many naturally occurring modified amino acids have been identified in living organisms, only two, selenocysteine and pyrrolysine, are genetically encoded. Each amino acid is inserted cotranslationally into proteins imparting catalytic functionality. Both selenocysteine and pyrrolysine are encoded in genes by what are otherwise stop codons. The 2 aa contrast in how they are biosynthesized. Selenocysteine is synthesized on the dedicated tRNASec following serylation by seryl-tRNA synthetase. Pyrrolysine is made as a free amino acid and then used to aminoacylate its specific tRNAPyl by pyrrolysyl-tRNAPyl synthetase. The 2 aa further differ in how message context influences translation. Translation of UGA as selenocysteine relies heavily on the presence of a specific messenger RNA (mRNA) sequence found in the transcript. In contrast, local message context stimulates, but is not required for, relatively efficient translation of UAG as pyrrolysine.
journal: Cold Spring Harbor perspectives in biology
authors: Peiter N, Rother M, Krzycki JA.

title: Dengue Virus Pathogenesis: Innate Immune Signaling and Cell Death Receptor Pathways.
abstract: BackgroundThe infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV) involves a complicated interaction between viral replication and the body's immune responses. As the first line of defense, the innate immune response limits viral replication but can also lead to immunopathology if it is improperly regulated. The DENV activates several pattern-recognition receptor (PRR) pathways, such as the RIG-I-like receptor (RLR), the Toll-like receptor (TLR), and the cGAS-STING signaling pathway, all of which control interferon and inflammatory responses.ObjectivesThe purpose of this review is to outline the molecular mechanisms involved in the process of innate immune recognition and signaling when DENV infects cells, with a specific focus on the virus's immune-evasion tactics and the relationship between innate immune signaling and programmed cell death; it also examines the possible implications of these pathways for the development of a dengue vaccine and for antiviral approaches.DiscussionThe RNA of DENV is mainly detected by RNA-sensing pathways such as the RLRs and TLRs, while cGAS-STING signaling can be triggered indirectly as a result of virus-associated cellular stress and the presence of cytosolic DNA. DENV counteracts these antiviral responses by acting on key signaling molecules such as MAVS, STING, TBK1, IRF3, and STAT2, thus promoting viral persistence and replication. At the same time, death-receptor pathways involving tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR), Fas (CD95), and TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) receptors control caspase-8-dependent apoptosis and may play a role in the elimination of infected cells as well as in causing tissue injury and immunopathology. The interaction between innate immune signaling, inflammatory responses, and caspase-8-mediated cell death therefore serves as an important factor in determining the balance between antiviral protection and disease progression. If these mechanisms are understood, this could form the basis for developing strategies that boost antiviral immunity while reducing excessive inflammation and pathological cell death.ConclusionThe way in which dengue disease develops is due to the continuous interaction between the body's antiviral innate immune responses, the virus's ability to evade the immune system, and programmed cell death. It might be possible to enhance control of dengue disease by targeting these closely related pathways, whether by means of vaccine development, antiviral drugs, or therapies that act on the host. Yet any intervention focused on a specific pathway will need to take into account the stage of the disease, the cellular environment, and the possible risk of weakening the protective antiviral immunity.
authors: Islam F.

title: A Standalone Flavoprotein Monooxygenase Directs Divergent Tropolone Skeletal Editing through Baeyer-Villiger-Triggered Rearrangement.
abstract: Late-stage oxidative remodeling of tropolone cores underpins the remarkable scaffold diversity in fungal meroterpenoid biosynthesis. However, the mechanistic basis by which a single enzymatic catalyst diverts a common substrate toward carbon-excising ring contraction versus carbon-retentive skeletal rearrangement remains elusive. Here, via comparative transcriptomics and targeted gene deletion, we identified a standalone host-encoded class A flavoprotein monooxygenase, ANIA_01821 (AN1821), as indispensable for tropolone ring remodeling in Aspergillus nidulans. A functionally homologous enzyme, AO090103000276 (AO276), from Aspergillus oryzae was further characterized as a tractable biocatalyst for in vitro studies. Reconstitution assays using purified AO276 revealed that this single flavoprotein monooxygenase alone converts the bistropolone meroterpenoid eupenifeldin into both ring-contracted phenolic products and carbon-retentive bridged polycycles, establishing a unified enzymatic origin for two structurally distinct natural-product scaffolds. Structure-guided mutagenesis uncovered a precisely organized electrostatic network that is critical for flavin-dependent oxygenation. Complementary well-tempered metadynamics simulations and quantum-chemical calculations support a Baeyer-Villiger branching mechanism, wherein the AO276 active site may preferentially stabilize alternative migration-competent conformations of a putative Criegee intermediate. Each conformation aligns a distinct C-C bond in an antiperiplanar geometry relative to the O-O bond; restricted conformational interconversion within the active site could preserve the initial reactive geometry and bias divergent carbon migration. Collectively, our findings identify conformational preorganization as a plausible contributor to regiodivergent enzymatic Baeyer-Villiger catalysis, offering a rational strategy for steering oxidative skeletal remodeling in complex natural product molecules.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
authors: Chen Z, Liu J, Bai S, Wang X, Zhang C, Liu B, Qi X, Hu Y.

title: [A case of Mowat-Wilson syndrome due to a de novo c.3515del frameshift variant of ZEB2 gene].
abstract: ObjectiveTo explore the genetic etiology of a fetus with Mowat-Wilson syndrome (MWS) due to a novel de novo heterozygous frameshift variant of ZEB2 gene.MethodsA pedigree presenting at the Affiliated Women and Children's Hospital of Ningbo University in February 2024 was enrolled. Clinical data were retrospectively analyzed. Amniotic fluid samples of the fetus and peripheral blood samples of the couple were collected for trio-whole exome sequencing (Trio-WES). Candidate variant was verified by Sanger sequencing. The pathogenicity of the candidate variant was assessed based on guidelines from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). Postnatal follow-up was performed, and the pathogenicity of the variant was re-assessed by incorporating newly acquired phenotypic features. This study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of the hospital (Ethics No.: EC2023-094).ResultsPrenatal ultrasonography at 20+2 weeks of gestation identified ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta and polyhydramnios. Trio-WES revealed that the fetus has harbored a novel c.3515del (p.Met1172ArgfsTer69) heterozygous frameshift variant of the ZEB2 gene. Sanger sequencing confirmed that neither parent has carried the same variant. Based on the ACMG guidelines, the variant was initially classified as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS) based on PVS1_Moderate+PM2_Supporting+PS2_Supporting criteria. After birth, the infant exhibited typical MWS features including hypertelorism, low-hanging columella, neck hypotonia, cerebral hypoplasia, corpus callosum agenesis, and abnormal earlobe morphology. Growth delay, feeding difficulties, and motor delay were observed at 4-month follow-up. Combined with postnatal phenotypic data, the variant was re-classified as likely pathogenic (LP) based on PVS1_Moderate+PM2_Supporting+PS2_Moderate+PP4_Supporting criteria.ConclusionThe newly identified ZEB2 c.3515del represents a likely pathogenic variant, which expanded the mutational spectrum of the ZEB2 gene. Longitudinal prenatal-to-postnatal phenotypic integration is critical for re-assessing VUS in MWS patients and providing evidence-based references for prenatal genetic diagnosis and genetic counseling of similar cases.

title: Inhalation of Gardenia jasminoides flower essential oil attenuates stress-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities in mice.
abstract: BackgroundGardenia jasminoides Ellis is a traditional medicinal and aromatic plant, but the neurobehavioral potential of its flower-derived essential oil remains insufficiently understood.PurposeThis study aimed to evaluate whether G. jasminoides flower essential oil (GEO) inhalation attenuates chronic stress-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities and to characterize the accompanying hippocampal, metabolic, and gut microbial responses.MethodsGEO was chemically profiled by headspace solid-phase microextraction coupled with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and evaluated in a chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mouse model. Mice were exposed to GEO by inhalation during the final 2 weeks of the 6-week CUMS procedure. Behavioral performance was assessed using the open field test, elevated plus maze, tail suspension test, forced swim test, and sucrose preference test. Hippocampal morphology, inflammatory and oxidative stress-related indices, neurochemical markers, serum corticosterone, serum metabolomics, hippocampal transcriptomics, gut microbiota composition, and hippocampal neuroimmune/synaptic signaling markers were further analyzed.ResultsChemical profiling tentatively annotated 59 volatile constituents in GEO, with linalool and linalyl acetate identified as the predominant constituents. GEO inhalation attenuated CUMS-associated behavioral abnormalities, with significant changes observed most consistently in the GEO-20 group. GEO exposure was also associated with increased hippocampal dendritic spine density relative to the CUMS group, lower inflammatory and oxidative stress-related indices, higher hippocampal brain-derived neurotrophic factor, γ-aminobutyric acid, and 5-hydroxytryptamine levels, and lower serum corticosterone. Serum metabolomics identified GEO-20-associated changes in metabolic features and pathways involving nucleotide/purine metabolism, arachidonic acid-related lipid mediator pathways, bile acid-related metabolism, and neuroactive metabolic processes. Hippocampal transcriptomics identified GEO-20-associated changes in neuroimmune-, neuroactive ligand-receptor-, and γ-aminobutyric acid synapse-related transcriptional profiles. Gut microbiota analysis revealed GEO-20-associated changes in microbial richness, community composition, discriminatory taxa, and genus-level co-occurrence patterns. Targeted molecular assays showed lower hippocampal glial reactivity and inflammatory signaling-related markers after GEO exposure, whereas GEO-20 was associated with higher levels of mitochondrial regulatory and synaptic plasticity markers.ConclusionGEO inhalation attenuated chronic stress-associated neurobehavioral abnormalities in mice and was accompanied by changes in hippocampal neuroimmune and synaptic plasticity-related markers, together with broader systemic metabolic and microbial responses.
journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
authors: Bian X, Liu J, Zhao X, Zhang Y, Zhang T, Yang X, Sun X.

title: ME53 Modulates AcMNPV Proliferation via Interaction with GP64 and miR-34-5p-Targeted Synergistic Insecticidal Strategy against Spodoptera frugiperda.
abstract: This study developed a chemical engineering strategy to improve baculovirus biopesticides by engineering the Autographa californica multiple nucleopolyhedrovirus (AcMNPV) and regulating host metabolism in Spodoptera frugiperda. Overexpression of the me53 gene enhanced the viral replication, nucleocapsid assembly, and budding virus titers. ME53 interacted with GP64 via hydrogen bonds to promote the membrane fusion. Meanwhile, miR-34-5p negatively regulated AcMNPV proliferation, and inhibition of this miRNA upregulated me53 and GP64. In larvae, miR-34-5p disturbed the metabolism and impaired development. Combining the me53-overexpressing virus with miR-34-5p inhibition synergistically accelerated killing and increased mortality. Engineered viruses were stably produced and showed an improved virulence and safety. This work provides an efficient, eco-friendly biopesticide platform through genetic engineering and host metabolic regulation, supporting sustainable pest control.
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
authors: Wang C, Hou S, Fu Y.

title: Identification and Engineering of an l-Threonine Aldolase from Agrobacterium pusense for Efficient l-Serine Synthesis.
abstract: l-Serine is a high-value amino acid, but enzymatic production is limited by insufficient catalytic activity and limited formaldehyde tolerance. A metagenomic library derived from glufosinate-exposed soil was mined to identify an l-threonine aldolase from Agrobacterium pusense (ApLTA). The substrate tunnel and active pocket were engineered through tunnel analysis, structural comparison, consensus design, and residue plasticity-guided polarity scanning. The resulting quadruple mutant D88M/T202S/A57S/F234M (Mut4) exhibited 48.5-fold higher catalytic efficiency than wild-type ApLTA. At 1 M formaldehyde loading, Mut4 increased l-serine concentration from 23.0 to 87.3 g L-1, with a space-time yield of 21.8 g L-1 h-1, the highest reported for LTA-catalyzed l-serine synthesis. Mut4 also showed enhanced activity toward multiple aromatic aldehydes. Molecular dynamics simulations further revealed the molecular basis for its enhanced catalytic efficiency. This study provides the first demonstration of highly efficient l-serine synthesis using an engineered LTA and offers a new strategy for enzymatic l-serine production.
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
authors: Sun S, Guo M, Zhou Y, Deng F, Wang H, Wei D.

title: Lactate Metabolic Restriction Is Linked to Granulosa Cell Dysfunction and Early Atresia-Like Changes via H4K12la-Mediated Epigenetic Remodeling and p53 Signaling in Goats.
abstract: Lactate metabolism is a pivotal component of the follicular microenvironment, yet how altered lactate availability influences granulosa cell (GC) fate during early follicular atresia remains elusive. We found significantly lower lactate concentrations in the follicular fluid of atretic goat follicles compared to healthy counterparts. In vitro, pharmacological inhibition of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) depleted intracellular lactate, leading to suppressed GC proliferation and G0/G1 arrest without increasing apoptosis. Notably, these proliferative defects were significantly attenuated by exogenous sodium L-lactate supplementation, suggesting that lactate availability plays an important role in GC cell-cycle progression. Transcriptomic profiling further indicated a broad suppression of cell-cycle and DNA replication programs following LDH inhibition. At the epigenetic level, restricted lactate availability was associated with decreased global protein lactylation and specific reductions in histone H4 lysine 12 lactylation (H4K12la). Integrative analysis of CUT&Tag data identified the checkpoint regulator growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible alpha (GADD45A) as a candidate target associated with altered H4K12la occupancy. CUT& RUN-qPCR confirmed reduced H4K12la enrichment at the GADD45A promoter, while siRNA-mediated GADD45A knockdown partially alleviated the LDH inhibition-induced G1/S arrest. Furthermore, metabolic stress was accompanied by activation of p53-mediated signaling, characterized by elevated γH2AX, p53, p21, and p38 levels. Silencing TP53 attenuated GADD45A induction and partially restored proliferative markers. Collectively, our findings support a model in which restricted lactate metabolism is associated with impaired goat primary GC proliferation, potentially through a coordinated mechanism involving H4K12la-mediated epigenetic remodeling and p53-associated stress signaling, both converging on GADD45A and contributing to early follicular degeneration.
authors: Zhu M, Zhou Z, Li D, Yu W, Wang J, Wang L, Wan Y.

title: Protein Isoaspartate Repair in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: An Integrative Bioinformatic Analysis of the PCMT Gene Family.
abstract: Protein homeostasis is a fundamental determinant of neuronal survival, and its disruption contributes to the pathogenesis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Protein L-isoaspartate O-methyltransferases (PCMTs) are evolutionarily conserved proteins involved in the recognition and processing of damaged proteins through the repair of isoaspartyl residues and protein quality-control pathways; however, their potential involvement in ALS remains largely unexplored. Here, we performed a comprehensive in silico characterization of the PCMT family (PCMT1, PCMTD1, and PCMTD2) by integrating structural, transcriptomic, single-cell, genetic, and protein modeling analyses. Domain analysis demonstrated that all three proteins share a conserved PCMT domain, while predicted S-adenosylmethionine-binding motifs were identified in PCMT1 and PCMTD2 but not PCMTD1, indicating evolutionary conservation with functional divergence. Expression profiling revealed that PCMT family genes are expressed in ALS-relevant tissues and broadly distributed across neuronal, glial, vascular, and immune cell populations in both healthy and ALS-associated brain single-cell data sets. Analysis of multiple independent ALS transcriptomic cohorts identified consistent upregulation of PCMT family members, with PCMTD1 exhibiting the most reproducible disease-associated expression changes across nervous system tissues and peripheral blood. Gene set correlation analyses further revealed distinct relationships between PCMT expression and neuronal pathways, with PCMT1 showing positive associations with axonal transport and synaptic signaling, whereas PCMTD1 and PCMTD2 displayed largely inverse correlation patterns. Rare missense variants identified in ALS patients were predicted to impair protein function and decrease protein stability, while structural modeling suggested that several substitutions may disrupt conserved residues and the local protein architecture. Collectively, these findings identify the PCMT family as previously underexplored candidates associated with ALS and provide a comprehensive framework for future mechanistic studies investigating their roles in neuronal protein homeostasis and neurodegeneration.
authors: Yardimci BI, Zurel AG, Biterge B.
