title: GmRVE8a, a circadian clock-associated gene, negatively regulates flowering and maturity in soybean.
abstract: Precise regulation of flowering time and maturity is critical for achieving high and stable soybean yields, and the circadian clock plays a central role in coordinating these developmental transitions. Soybean is a typical short-day crop with a pronounced photoperiodic response; however, the molecular mechanisms linking circadian regulation to photoperiod-dependent flowering and maturity remain incompletely understood. Here, we integrated genome-wide association analysis with deep learning approaches using 257 soybean germplasm accessions spanning 14 maturity groups and identified GmRVE8a, a homolog of the Arabidopsis circadian clock gene REVEILLE, as a strong candidate locus associated with soybean maturity across two field environments. Haplotype analysis demonstrated that accessions carrying the GmRVE8aH1 haplotype consistently flowered and matured significantly later than those carrying GmRVE8aH2. Functional validation revealed that knockout of GmRVE8a markedly accelerated flowering and maturity, whereas overexpression of GmRVE8a significantly delayed both processes. qRT-PCR assays further suggested that GmRVE8a may repress flowering and delay maturity by promoting the expression of GmFT4, a flowering-inhibitory member of the FT family, and is unlikely to act by directly regulating E1 expression. Collectively, our findings suggest GmRVE8a as a circadian clock-associated negative regulator of soybean flowering and maturity, and highlight it as a promising candidate for molecular breeding aimed at improving adaptation to diverse photoperiodic environments.
journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology
authors: Sun S, Yang M, Wu T, Jiang B, Sun X, Jia H, Yao X, Sun Y, Li Q, Wang P, Jiang L, Qin C, Yuan S, Qi Z, Sun S, Li H, Han T, Sun B.

title: Single-cell transcriptomics revealed immunological and molecular profiling of pangolin viruses at the viral interface.
abstract: Pangolins have been identified as potential intermediate hosts for various viruses, including coronaviruses related to SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying their viral susceptibility remain poorly understood. Here, we establish the first comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic atlas for two pangolin species Manis pentadactyla and Manis javanica, generated through single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of 245 618 high-quality cells from 12 major tissues, combined with 123 bulk transcriptome datasets. This resource is integrated with cross-species data from Homo sapiens, Eptesicus fuscus, Sus scrofa, Mus musculus, and Panthera tigris. Our analysis reveals a myeloid-biased hematopoiesis in pangolin bone marrow, dominated by monocytes and T cells, which contrasts sharply with the lymphoid-skewed composition observed in H. sapiens and M. musculus. We also identify species-specific features, including thyroid-specific expression of FKBP5 in M. pentadactyla, and MIF-signaling-mediated cellular interactions in intestinal lymph. Furthermore, key viral receptors ( AXL, NRP1, DPP4, ACE2, SCARB1, and UVRAG) are broadly expressed in immune cells (e.g., B cells, T cells, and macrophages), fibroblasts, and endothelial cells across tissues, as confirmed by single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analyses. Cross-species comparisons reveal fundamental differences in splenic immune architecture, hematopoietic lineage distribution, and viral receptor expression. Together, these findings based on single-cell transcriptomic profiling establish a molecular and cellular framework for understanding pangolins as potential mixing vessels for viruses and provide a foundation for the targeted surveillance of emerging zoonotic pathogens.

title: Microbe Profile: Saccharopolyspora erythraea: antibiotic factory and biosynthetic model organism.
abstract: Saccharopolyspora erythraea is a filamentous actinomycete best known as the industrial source of erythromycin, a macrolide antibiotic that remains an important medicine and precursor for the semisynthetic drugs clarithromycin and azithromycin. Beyond its industrial importance, S. erythraea has had a profound influence on natural product bioscience. Studies of erythromycin biosynthesis led to the discovery of modular polyketide synthases and established the principles of assembly-line enzymatic logic that underpin modern understanding of microbial polyketide biosynthesis. Consequently, S. erythraea has served both as an antibiotic production platform and as a model organism for investigating and engineering complex biosynthetic pathways. Continued efforts to understand its metabolism, genetic changes during strain improvement, and the reprogramming of its polyketide synthase machinery are expected to support the development of next-generation antibiotics and biotechnological applications.
authors: Syvret EA, Wilkinson B.

title: A Multidimensional Framework for Integrated Toxicity Assessment and Prioritization of Naphthenic Acids in Marine Medaka (Oryzias melastigma): Neurotoxicity and Mechanistic Insights.
abstract: Petroleum pollution poses a major challenge to global environmental health. Petroleum-derived naphthenic acids (NAs) are frequently detected in marine environments, yet their multidimensional toxicity and mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we developed an integrated toxicity framework combining bioassays, toxicity screening, computational simulations, transcriptomics, and bioinformatics to characterize NAs toxicity in marine medaka (Oryzias melastigma). A concentration gradient spanning environmentally detected levels to higher-effect concentrations (0.015-30 mg/L) revealed developmental defects, cardiac suppression, behavioral disruption, and metabolic dysfunction. CRITIC-AHP-based prioritization identified neurotoxicity as the predominant toxicity dimension, with cyclopentylpropionic acid (CPPA) and cyclohexylpropionic acid (CHPA) identified as major contributors. Mechanistically, these compounds were associated with distinct candidate pathways involving CXCR3-CXCL10 neuroinflammatory responses and DPP10-Kv4.2 ion homeostasis disruption. Their divergent toxicity profiles may be associated with differences in hydrophobicity and molecular flexibility. Rescue experiments supported these pathways, restoring swimming velocity by 60.32% and 62.09%, respectively. Furthermore, NAs induced neurobehavioral alterations and transcriptional signatures overlapping with Alzheimer's disease-associated genes, with 14 and 12 candidate genes identified for CPPA and CHPA. Collectively, this study provides a cross-scale perspective linking physicochemical properties, toxicity pathways, and adverse outcomes of NAs, offering a conceptual approach for toxicity screening and mechanism elucidation of contaminants.
authors: Chu J, Cui S, Zhou Y, Kong Q, Wang Y, Xia Y, Zhang H.

title: Molecular Size Mediates Sunlight Effects on the Biodegradation of Aquatic Dissolved Organic Matter: Insights from the Reservoir Wetland and Incubation Experiment.
abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) in aquatic ecosystems is crucial to climate, water quality, and water sanitation. However, little is known about how photochemical and biological processes interact to regulate the cycling of DOM in water environments. Here, we investigate the photobiochemical processing of different molecular weight (MW) fractions of aquatic DOM by incubating them with microbes in the dark and light/dark cycling environments via microcosm experiments. Light exposure has distinct effects on the medium (MMW; 1-20 kDa) and low (LMW; <1 kDa) MW fractions and can enrich photoautotrophic bacteria and taxa that could benefit the utilization of aromatic compounds. The decay of the MMW fraction displays the highest light sensitivity, with light increasing the net depletion of tannin- and condensed aromatic-like molecules and production of labile substrates (e.g., protein-like) from photoautotrophic bacteria. In contrast, the net decomposition of the LMW fraction is the least promoted by light exposure, as light induces the net production of complex aromatic molecules that are more persistent. Our findings provide new insights into the photobiochemical and molecular mechanisms underlying the ecological impacts of aquatic DOM and their relevance for wider processes.
authors: Zhou P, Tian L, Song S, Siddique MS, Friese K, Herzsprung P, Tanentzap AJ, Graham N, Yu W.

title: Large Methane Emissions during Ice-Melt Periods in a Temperate Pond.
abstract: Large methane (CH4) emissions during ice-melt periods have been frequently reported in lakes, but whether similar processes occur in ponds remains largely unknown. Here, we conducted observations in a temperate pond across two consecutive ice seasons (2022-2024), with daily sampling during ice melt, to characterize ice-melt CH4 dynamics, reveal potential CH4 production pathways, and estimate the contribution of ice-melt emissions to the annual CH4 budget. CH4 concentrations increased sharply prior to ice melt, resulting in a diffusive pulse during the ice-melt periods (20.1 ± 14.1 mg m-2 h-1), approximately 11 times higher than that during observed ice-free periods (1.8 ± 2.5 mg m-2 h-1). In contrast, CH4 ebullition during ice melt remained low (0.21 ± 0.15 mg m-2 h-1). Despite the brief duration (∼7 days), ice-melt CH4 emissions accounted for 8.7% of annual total CH4 emissions (diffusion + ebullition) and 22.3% of annual diffusive CH4 emissions from June 2022 to May 2023. Variations in water chemistry and sediment microbial communities suggest that both anaerobic and aerobic CH4 production may have contributed to these emission pulses. Particularly, CH4 concentration increased concurrently with chlorophyll a and dissolved oxygen before ice melt, suggesting possible phytoplankton-derived CH4 production under oxic conditions. Given the ubiquity of seasonal freeze-melt cycles in temperate ponds, incorporating ice-melt CH4 fluxes is necessary to refine global CH4 budget estimates.
authors: Niu X, Yan Z, Hao L, Liu L, Li SL, Peacock M.

title: Randomization of the Damaged Base-Capping Loop Rewires Substrate Specificity in Formamidopyrimidine-DNA Glycosylase.
abstract: Formamidopyrimidine-DNA glycosylase (Fpg) is a bacterial base excision repair enzyme that removes 8-oxoguanine (8-oxoG) and some other oxidatively damaged nucleobases from DNA. Fpg hydrolyzes the N-glycosidic bond of the damaged nucleotide and nicks DNA at the resulting apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) site by β-elimination. Together with bacterial endonuclease VIII and eukaryotic homologues, more specific for damaged pyrimidines, Fpg belongs to a helix-two-turn-helix (H2TH) superfamily of DNA glycosylases. Crystal structures of Fpg reveal that the enzyme recognizes 8-oxoG by flipping it out of the DNA duplex and capping it with a flexible tetrapeptide loop. However, this loop is poorly conserved and contacts 8-oxoG only through the main-chain amides, raising questions about the enzyme specificity determinants. To clarify the mechanism of 8-oxoG recognition, we have produced and characterized five variants of Fpg from Lactococcus lactis with a randomized capping loop. All of these mutants were deficient in 8-oxoG repair, both in vitro and in the E. coli complementation assay, yet retained the ability to bind AP site-containing DNA, form a Schiff base covalent reaction intermediate, and catalyze β-elimination. The mutants were still active in the removal of 5-hydroxyuracil (OHU), an alternative Fpg substrate. All loop mutants showed relaxed opposite-base specificity, processing AP sites and OHU opposite either C or A. Thus, whereas the general architecture of the active site in H2TH DNA glycosylases is permissive for the excision of a wide range of oxidized bases, the capping loop endows Fpg with the specificity for its biologically relevant substrate, 8-oxoguanine.
authors: Bulgakov NA, Amanova MM, Endutkin AV, Makasheva KA, Coste F, Castaing B, Golyshev VM, Lomzov AA, Yudkina AV, Zharkov DO.

title: [Advances in the application of metal-organic framework materials for rapid detection of contaminants in aquatic products].
abstract: Aquatic products are rich in high-quality protein and essential nutrients such as minerals，fatty acids，and vitamins，offering significant nutritional value. However，during their production and processing，they are susceptible to contamination by hazardous substances including heavy metals，veterinary drug residues，illegal additives，and pathogenic microorganisms. Thus，rapid detection technologies serve as a critical means for the timely identification of such food safety issues. However，the complex matrix of aquatic products presents significant analytical challenges，making separation and enrichment steps generally essential prior to detection. Current rapid detection methods often lack compatible rapid sample pretreatment approaches，which can lead to issues such as false positives or missed detection. Among the novel materials，metal-organic frameworks （MOFs） have emerged as a potential class of porous materials for the separation and detection of contaminations in aquatic products owing to their exceptional properties. Firstly，the ultra-high specific surface areas provide abundant active sites. Secondly，the uniform and tunable pore sizes can be tailored for molecular sieving and selective adsorption. Moreover，they are easy to functionalize through pre-design or post-synthetic modification，allowing the introduction of specific binding sites，catalytic moieties，or functional molecules. Lastly，MOFs are constructed through the coordination-driven self-assembly of metal ions and organic linkers，endowing them with considerable structural diversity that can be tailored for diverse applications. These attributes make MOFs exceptionally promising as advanced materials for tackling complex analytical challenges in food safety. This review provides a comprehensive and systematic summary of the application advances of MOFs and their composite materials in the rapid detection of contaminants in aquatic products over the past decade. In sample pretreatment，MOFs and their composites serve as superior adsorbents in various sample preparation techniques such as solid-phase extraction，solid-phase microextraction，magnetic solid-phase extraction，stir bar sorptive extraction，and QuEChERS. For solid-phase microextraction （SPME），MOFs coated on fibers enhance the extraction efficiency of volatile or semi-volatile compounds. In magnetic solid-phase extraction （MSPE），magnetic MOF composites enable rapid separation from liquid samples using an external magnet，significantly simplifying and expediting the process. These applications significantly enhance the selectivity and enrichment efficiency of contaminants in aquatic products while simplifying the pretreatment process. In rapid detection，MOF composites are used to develop enhanced detection platforms by leveraging their unique optical，electrochemical，and catalytic properties. In electrochemical analysis，conductive MOFs or MOF-modified electrodes amplify the signals of targets. For fluorescence detection，luminescent MOFs serve as sensitive probes，often in ratiometric modes to improve accuracy. MOFs also act as excellent substrates or enhancers in surface-enhanced Raman scattering （SERS） platforms，boosting Raman signals for ultra-sensitive detection of molecules. In immunoassays，MOFs are used as label carriers or signal amplifiers，improving detection limits for targets. Additionally，when integrated with aptamer-based biosensors，the large surface area of MOFs allows high-density immobilization of aptamers，enabling highly specific and sensitive detection of targets in complex matrices. These methods offer high sensitivity，specificity，and potential portability，providing innovative solutions for detecting trace contaminants in the complex matrix of aquatic products. Furthermore，this review discusses the challenges and future prospects of MOFs for the analysis of aquatic products. The significant challenges include the limited hydrolytic stability or chemical stability of certain MOFs in complex media，potential matrix effects in real samples that can affect performance，and the need for scalable and cost-effective synthesis of functionalized MOFs. Future efforts should focus on designing more stable and target-specific functionalized MOFs，promoting the integration of sample pretreatment and detection processes，and incorporating artificial intelligence for data analysis to establish an intelligent rapid detection system for aquatic product safety，which is of great significance for safeguarding public health.

title: Monitoring-Network Composition and Analytical-Method History Shape Temporal Inference of Fecal-Coliform Exceedance in an Urban River-Lake Network, Taihu Basin, China.
abstract: Changing station composition and analytical methods can complicate microbial water-quality trends. We analyzed 2573 fecal-coliform (FC) observations from 64 reconciled sections in the Wuxi river-lake network, Taihu Basin, between December 2021 and August 2026. Records were available for 53 of 57 calendar months; four monthly files were irretrievably lost following a system error. Overall, 853 observations (33.15%) exceeded the common Class III FC benchmark of 10,000 counts L-1. A fixed panel of 21 sections contributed 1113 observations. Pooled and fixed-panel Sen slopes were 0.503 and 0.344 percentage points per month; their paired difference was 0.158 (section-bootstrap 95% interval 0.011-0.327). Binomial mixed models with calendar-month effects and section random intercepts gave annual odds ratios of 1.59 and 1.51, respectively. Adding an indicator for the reported October 2023 change from the rapid paper-strip method to the enzyme-substrate method reduced these estimates to 1.26 (section-clustered 95% interval 1.08-1.47) and 1.36 (1.02-1.81). Within the enzyme-substrate period alone, annual odds ratios were 1.17 (0.96-1.43) and 1.35 (0.93-1.98). Thus, the full-period association remained positive under seasonal and method-period adjustment, but the shorter, single-method record did not resolve a temporal association. Between-section heterogeneity and sensitivity to the monitoring population support reporting station coverage and analytical-method history alongside pooled trends. The method-period contrast cannot separate analytical effects from environmental changes occurring at the same time.
journal: Water environment research : a research publication of the Water Environment Federation
authors: Zhao Q, Shen R, Guo W, Lou M, Shen H, Li A, Shen Y.

title: Ramping up the heat: Induction of systemic and pulmonary immune responses and metabolic adaptations in mice.
abstract: Heatwaves are an increasing public health concern, yet most animal studies use sudden extreme heat exposure that poorly reflects real-world conditions. This study examined the effects of gradual exposure to extreme heat on mice. Adult male and female C57Bl/6 mice were randomly assigned to heat-exposed, control, or pair-fed experimental groups. Heat-exposed mice underwent a single 8-h temperature ramp from 20°C to 38°C; control and pair-fed mice remained at ambient temperature. Multi-omics analyses after heat exposure included cytokine profiling in serum and lung, cecal microbiome characterization, lung transcriptomics, and serum metabolomics. Heat exposure altered several serum and lung cytokines (IL-17α, MIP-1α, MIP-1β, IL-1α, IL-12(p40), and RANTES). Random forest analysis identified microbial taxa that distinguished experimental groups, with a reduction in Lactobacillus observed in males; however, these effects were not statistically significant. Lung transcriptomics revealed changes in immune-related gene expression, particularly in pathways associated with B-cell activation. Serum metabolomics indicated modest disruptions in amino acid and energy metabolism, with enrichment of the glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism pathway. Integrated analyses identified associations among cytokines, gene expression, and bile acid-related metabolites. These findings demonstrate that gradual exposure to extreme heat triggers systemic and pulmonary responses in mice.
authors: Dean LE, Adamcakova-Dodd A, Lehmler HJ.

title: Divergent dependence on host gene sigma-1 receptor shapes hepatitis C and orthoflavivirus infection.
abstract: The Flaviviridae family encompasses major human pathogens, such as hepatitis C virus (HCV) and dengue virus (DENV). Despite shared genome organization and replication strategies, these viruses differ in host interactions, tissue tropism and replication dynamics, leading to distinct disease outcomes. Sigma-1 receptor (SIGMAR1) encodes an endoplasmic reticulum-associated protein that regulates lipid transport, autophagy and proteostasis. We previously showed that SIGMAR1 silencing reduces early HCV infection efficiency without affecting unrelated viruses. Here, we demonstrate that SIGMAR1 is rate-limiting for the formation of normal double-membrane vesicles (DMVs), the putative HCV replication compartments. In contrast, DENV and West Nile virus (WNV) RNA replication remained efficient following SIGMAR1 depletion, indicating a selective requirement for SIGMAR1 in HCV DMV formation. Notably, SIGMAR1 knockdown markedly impaired secretion of infectious DENV and WNV particles without reducing intracellular progeny, suggesting a role for SIGMAR1 in orthoflavivirus virion release. SIGMAR1 silencing also disrupted Golgi architecture and altered cellular detergent-resistant membrane composition, consistent with defects in vesicular trafficking. These findings identify SIGMAR1 as a host factor with distinct functions in the replication cycles of hepaciviruses and orthoflaviviruses and highlight its broader role in maintaining membrane organization required for efficient infection by Flaviviridae.
authors: García-Crespo C, Venturini V, Calvo G, Díaz-Piñero E, Castro V, Gastaminza P.

title: Follistatin-like 1 Promotes Neutrophil-mediated Host Defense against  Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of pneumonia and highly burdensome etiology of antibiotic-resistant infections constituting an urgent public health threat. Follistatin-like 1 (FSTL-1) is implicated in many processes including lung development and homeostasis, tissue remodeling, and inflammation though its role in antibacterial immunity remains poorly defined. We have observed that FSTL-1 is elevated in the lungs of both humans and mice during bacterial pneumonia. Using an inducible  Fstl1 knockout mouse model, we demonstrate that FSTL-1 is required for pulmonary bacterial clearance and neutrophil recruitment during  K. pneumoniae infection. Recombinant FSTL-1 rescues  Fstl1 -deficient susceptibility and enhances clearance of  K. pneumoniae in wild-type mice. Mechanistically, FSTL-1-mediated protection was lost upon neutrophil depletion and in  Cd14 -deficient or  Nr4a1 deficient mice – components of a lung-specific neutrophil transcriptional program. These findings identify FSTL-1 as a lung-derived factor that licenses neutrophil-mediated antibacterial defense via a novel FSTL-1/CD14/NR4A1-dependent signaling pathway critical for protection against bacterial pneumonia.
authors: Sugitani N, Henkel M, Applegate A, Partyka J, Wu T, Froelich NW, Dewicki A, Campfield BT.

title: Siderophore-mediated inhibition of Legionella pneumophila by environmental Pseudomonas isolates
abstract: AbstractThe genus Legionella comprises opportunistic pathogenic bacteria commonly found in natural and engineered water systems, where they interact with environmental microbes and protozoa, primarily in biofilms. Legionella pneumophila is the main causative agent of Legionnaires’ disease and is transmitted through inhalation of contaminated aerosols. Iron availability is a critical factor for L. pneumophila growth, persistence, and virulence, yet iron is often limited in aquatic environments. To overcome iron scarcity, many bacteria produce siderophores, secondary metabolites that scavenge ferric iron. Because siderophores are chemically diverse and species specific, they play a key role in inter-species competition and can withhold iron from competitors. Here, we investigated the effects of iron depletion and siderophore-mediated competition on L. pneumophila using commercial pyoverdines and pyoverdine extracts from environmental Pseudomonas strains. Growth assays showed that L. pneumophila can grow under iron-limited conditions but with lag phases extended by more than 20 hours. Commercial pyoverdines inhibited growth in a concentration-dependent manner, primarily by increasing the time to mid-log phase (t_mid). Culture supernatants and crude pyoverdine extracts caused the strongest inhibition, including lag-phase extensions of up to 55 hours or complete growth arrest. These results demonstrate that siderophore-producing Pseudomonas competitors can suppress L. pneumophila by limiting iron availability.

title: HU promotes fidelity and leader-repeat integration during CRISPR adaptation in the type III-A system of Thermotoga profunda
abstract: AbstractCRISPR–Cas adaptive immunity relies on the acquisition of foreign DNA fragments as spacers within CRISPR arrays. Although spacer integration is generally catalysed by the conserved Cas1–Cas2 integrase complex, accurate integration frequently requires accessory factors. In the type I-E CRISPR–Cas system of Escherichia coli, the DNA-binding protein integration host factor (IHF) promotes leader-proximal spacer acquisition. The DNA bending properties of IHF exerted at the CRISPR locus are thought to form the mechanistic basis for the supportive function of IHF. However, many organisms lack IHF posing the questions how integration specificity is achieved in these organisms and whether analogous host factors contribute to adaptation in other CRISPR-Cas systems. Here, we investigated spacer integration in the type III-A CRISPR–Cas system of the hyperthermophilic bacterium Thermotoga profunda. Using reconstituted in vitro integration assays, we show that the TpCas1–TpCas2 complex alone exhibits limited integration fidelity and generates substantial off-target integration events. We identify the highly conserved histone-like protein HU (TpHU) as a critical cofactor for accurate spacer acquisition. Addition of TpHU strongly promotes integration at the leader-repeat junction while suppressing erroneous integration into non-canonical sites. TpHU therefore acts as a determinant of integration fidelity and target-site selection during adaptation.

title: Env-specific antibodies promote post-treatment control in SIV-infected macaques
abstract: Latency reversal, but not reservoir reduction, has been achieved by combining antiretroviral therapy, CD8α lymphocyte depletion and N-803 in SIV-infected rhesus macaques. In this study, after cessation of antiretroviral therapy, anti-SIV Env antibodies enabled post-treatment control with reduced rebound and enhanced expression of antiviral CD4+ T cell gene signatures.

title: Gene-level structure of prior knowledge and perturbation responses informs target-level predictability in prior-informed models
abstract: Background: Predictive models of transcriptional responses to unseen genetic perturbations increasingly incorporate biological prior knowledge. However, it remains unclear how well prior knowledge reflects each target's perturbation-response relationships and how closely prior-derived measures track target-level predictive performance. Here, we develop a gene-similarity framework to quantify agreement among eight sources of biological prior knowledge and between prior knowledge and co-function or co-regulation relationships derived from six Perturb-seq datasets. Results: In genome-wide and essential-gene screens, prior agreement accounted for 30-47% of the variance in co-function agreement and 35-43% in co-regulation agreement. Agreement with Perturb-seq responses was higher for essential genes, lower for transcription factor and signaling genes, and varied with gene expression characteristics and cellular context. We compared prior agreement and prior-derived train-test similarity with measures based on the observed test response in tracking target-level predictive performance. Across three prior-informed models, predictions were more accurate for targets whose observed perturbation-response relationships better matched prior knowledge and that were more similar to training perturbations. Notably, prior agreement and prior-derived train-test similarity, calculated without the test response, tracked relative differences in target-level predictive performance. The strength of these associations varied across models and datasets and, for train-test similarity, across prior sources. Conclusion: Our framework reveals gene- and context-level heterogeneity in how biological knowledge aligns with perturbation responses, and provides an a priori basis for assessing relative perturbation predictability before perturbation responses are measured.
authors: Park, J., Sim, H., Hwang, B.

title: Contig-Resolved Genetic Context of Antimicrobial Resistome in Sediments of Two Contrasting Wastewater-Impacted Rivers
abstract: River sediments harbor diverse antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants; however, gene abundance alone provides limited insight into their genomic context, mobility potential, and associated bacterial hosts. This study employed an assembly- and read-mapping metagenomic framework to surface-sediment metagenomes (40.78 Gb clean data) from two contrasting wastewater-impacted Indian rivers, Adyar (Chennai) and Musi (Hyderabad), retaining sample-, contig- and open reading frame level provenance. ARG-carrying contigs (ACCs; n = 2,402) were annotated for mobile genetic elements (MGEs), biocide/metal resistance genes (BMRGs), virulence factor genes (VFGs), nitrogen-cycling genes (NCycGs), and putative host taxonomy. The resistomes exhibited substantial diversity (264 ARG subtypes) and spatial heterogeneity, with subtype richness in the Adyar (up to 171 subtypes) than in the Musi, where richness progressively declined downstream. Rank IV determinants dominated ARG abundance (77.82%), whereas Rank I determinants accounted for only 9.89%. MGEs were detected on just 3.12% (75/2,402) of ACCs, predominantly comprising plasmid-like contigs and proximal ARG-MGE associations. Co-occurrence with BMRGs was observed on 386 ACCs, whereas VFGs were uncommon (26 ACCs) and primarily represented dual-annotated efflux and envelope-integrity determinants rather than independent virulence loci. NCyc annotations were sparse (12 ACCs), with no evidence of complete nitrification or denitrification pathways. Taxonomic classification resolved 217 ACCs to the species level, with no matches to curated human pathogenic bacteria. Only two Acinetobacter-assigned ACCs exhibited both genus-level pathogenicity and mobility evidence. These findings highlight the importance of integrating mobility and host-taxonomic information to distinguish baseline environmental resistance from potential priorities for AMR surveillance.
authors: Kashyap, A., Sonkar, V., Nambi, I. M., Thatikonda, S.

title: SigBridgeR: An R Toolkit for Standardized Identification and Benchmarking of Phenotype-Associated Cell Subpopulations in Single-Cell Transcriptomics
abstract: AbstractBackgroundSingle-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has revolutionized our understanding of cellular heterogeneity, yet linking specific cell subpopulations to clinically relevant phenotypes remains a major challenge. Although multiple computational methods have been developed to integrate bulk transcriptomic and single-cell data for phenotype-associated cell identification, differences in algorithmic strategies, parameter configurations, software implementations, and output formats make it difficult to compare methods fairly, reproduce analyses, and determine which approach is most suitable for a given biological question.ResultsHere, we present SigBridgeR, an extensible R framework that integrates eight representative phenotype-associated cell subpopulation identification algorithms within a unified workflow. Using paired bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq datasets from four cancer types under both binary and survival phenotypes, we performed a comprehensive benchmark combining positive and negative control experiments, accuracy evaluation, Hallmark pathway enrichment analysis, parameter sensitivity analysis, and computational performance profiling. The benchmark revealed substantial differences in algorithm robustness, biological consistency, computational efficiency, and parameter sensitivity. Across multiple evaluation criteria, Scissor and scAB consistently achieved the most balanced overall performance, whereas several methods exhibited important limitations, including poor scalability, high parameter sensitivity, or unstable phenotype detection.ConclusionsSigBridgeR provides standardized preprocessing, unified algorithm interfaces, and an extensible registry-based architecture for phenotype-associated cell subpopulation analysis. By integrating systematic benchmarking and optimized implementations into a single platform, SigBridgeR facilitates reliable evaluation of existing methods, simplifies multi-algorithm analyses, and supports the development of improved phenotype-guided single-cell analysis methods for precision medicine.

title: From Biopsy to Pathology: A Retrospective Cohort Study of Predictors of Gleason Score Upgrading in Grade Group 1 Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Background/aimThis study aimed to identify pre-treatment predictors of Gleason score (GS) upgrading in patients with biopsy-confirmed Grade Group 1 (GS 3+3) prostate cancer (PCa) - those typically considered candidates for active surveillance according to National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines - so as to refine risk stratification and avoid under-treatment.Patients and methodsA retrospective analysis was conducted on patients with biopsy-proven GS 3+3 PCa who underwent radical prostatectomy (RP) at a tertiary referral center between 2010 and 2023. Preoperative clinical, pathological, and biochemical data were collected, including prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, PSA density, prostate volume (PV). Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of GS upgrading. Collinearity among PSA, PV, and PSA density was assessed using variance inflation factors and correlation matrix analysis.ResultsAmong the 121 patients included in the study, 64.46% experienced GS upgrading at the final pathology. Patients with GS upgrading were older (median age 67.5 years), had higher PSA density (median 0.3 ng/ml/cm³ vs. 0.18 ng/ml/cm³, p=0.0033), and exhibited a smaller median PV (36.4 ml vs. 41 ml, p=0.0145) compared to those without upgrading. These findings highlight the limitations of biopsy-based grading in accurately assessing tumor aggressiveness.ConclusionGS upgrading is common in patients initially diagnosed with GS 3+3 PCa and is associated with pre-treatment clinical factors, including PSA density and smaller PV. Identifying these predictors preoperatively may improve risk stratification and guide personalized treatment strategies. Future research should focus on integrating genomic and molecular markers to increase the predictive accuracy and optimize patient management.
authors: Su HC, Su YC, Lee HY, Juan YS, Wu WJ, Lu K.

title: Crystallographic fragment screening in cancer and antiviral drug discovery: from electron density to translational outcomes.
abstract: IntroductionCrystallographic fragment screening (CFS) provides an experimental starting point for small-molecule discovery by defining a fragment's binding site, pose and routes for chemical elaboration. By establishing a structural hypothesis before major medicinal-chemistry investment, CFS reduces early uncertainty and the risk of pursuing a binding mode inferred from activity or modeling but not supported by experimental structural evidence.Areas coveredThis review examines how CFS advances fragments into lead series, preclinical candidates and clinical molecules. Oncology examples include kinase inhibitors, the PHIP2 bromodomain, the transcription factor brachyury and the metabolic enzyme PYCR1. Antiviral examples include viral proteases, polymerases, the influenza PA endonuclease and the SARS-CoV-2 immune-evasion protein Mac1. It also considers the practical requirements and limitations of CFS, criteria for hit validation and prioritization, and how high-throughput crystallography, reusable structural datasets and computational or machine-learning methods can support chemical elaboration and translational decision-making. Relevant literature was identified through targeted PubMed searches conducted from March to September 2026, supplemented by reference-list screening of relevant primary studies and reviews.Expert opinionCFS is most powerful when it provides an experimentally grounded binding hypothesis early in discovery. It converts weak binding into actionable geometry, reveals ligandable pockets and supplies credible design starting points. Computational and machine-learning methods can extend this information by exploring chemical space, ranking fragment elaborations and supporting multiparameter prioritization, but they do not replace experimental determination of binding modes or functional validation. Future progress will depend on reusable structure-affinity datasets and tighter structure-design-synthesis-test cycles that connect crystallographic evidence to biological decisions.
authors: Balıkçı E, Grimes JM.

title: EXPRESS: Feline granulocytic anaplasmosis in Europe: anamnesis, clinicopathological abnormalities, bacterial DNA load, treatment, and outcome.
abstract: Feline granulocytic anaplasmosis (FGA) is caused by Anaplasma (A.) phagocytophilum. Fever and thrombocytopenia are the most common clinicopathological abnormalities.ObjectivesThe aim was to investigate regionality, seasonality, clinicopathological parameters, treatment, and outcomes in cats with FGA.MethodsThe database of a commercial laboratory was retrospectively screened for A. phagocytophilum-polymerase chain (PCR)-results on EDTA-blood submitted by European veterinarians from 01/2022 to 12/2025. Hematological data and bacterial DNA loads quantified by digital droplet-PCR were analyzed. Questionnaires were sent to the veterinarians asking for underlying diseases, anamnesis, clinicopathological abnormalities, treatment, and outcome in cats with FGA.Results43/702 cats (6.1%) tested positive by A. phagocytophilum-PCR in Europe. Questionnaires were available for 29/43 cats (67.4%), all of which had outdoor access. Lethargy (23/29; 79.3%), anorexia (22/29, 75.9%), and fever (>39.5°C, 18/29, 62.0%) were the most reported findings. Thrombocytopenia was detected in 14/18 cats (77.8%) without concurrent diseases, anemia and leukopenia in 2/20 cats each (10.0%), eosinopenia in 10/17 (58.8%), and lymphopenia in 8/17 cats (47.1%). The bacterial DNA load was available for 27/43 cats (25 x 102-87 x 106, median 124 x 105/ml EDTA-blood), revealing no significant correlation with hematological parameters. 20/21 cats (95.2%) were treated with doxycycline and one (4.8%) with enrofloxacin. Uncomplicated course of disease was reported in 19/21 cats (90.5%). In one cat treated with doxycycline for 10 days, another positive PCR was recorded one month later. Clinical signs recurred immediately in another cat treated with doxycycline for five days only.Conclusions and relevanceFGA should be considered in cats with outdoor access, lethargy, inappetence, and most often mild thrombocytopenia and/or anemia, regardless of fever. Infected cats usually responded well to doxycycline with individual relapses if treated for 10 days or shorter. Treatment for 14 days to clear the infection, and PCR monitoring after finishing treatment are recommended.
journal: Journal of feline medicine and surgery
authors: Meyer L, Moritz A, Baneth G, Strube C, Jindal K, Müller E, Schäfer I.

title: Occult Hepatitis B Virus Infection Among HBsAg-Negative Maintenance Haemodialysis Patients in Malaysia: Association with Anti-HBs Serostatus
abstract: Abstract  Background  Occult Hepatitis B infection (OBI)—defined as the presence of replication-competent HBV DNA in HBsAg-negative individuals—poses a severe transmission and reactivation risk in haemodialysis units. This study aims to investigate the prevalence and clinical characteristics of detectable HBV DNA among HBsAg-negative maintenance haemodialysis patients, particularly those with anti-HBc positivity. Methods  A retrospective observational study was conducted involving 2,146 patients who attended the dialysis unit at Universiti Malaya Medical Centre (UMMC) from 1 January 2019 to 30 June 2024. Patients established on maintenance haemodialysis were included, while those with HBsAg positivity or missing data were excluded. Patient demographics, clinical variables, and biochemical information were extracted from the Electronic Medical Record (EMR). Data collection was conducted using REDCap version 14.3.13, and statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 29.0 and Python version 3.10.16. A Firth penalised multivariable binary logistic regression model was constructed utilising OBI status as the dependent variable to identify independent clinical predictors, addressing potential small-sample bias inherent in standard logistic regression. Results  Among 2,146 screened patients, 1,635 patients were included. Anti-HBc IgG positivity was identified in 23.5% (N = 384) of the cohort. HBV DNA testing was not performed in 146 patients under the testing practices prevailing during the study period. Within the tested core-positive subgroup (N = 238), overall OBI prevalence was 9.2% (N = 22). In patients with positive HBV DNA, 54.6% were concurrently Anti-HBs IgG positive (≥ 10 IU/L), and 18.2% possessed an Anti-HBs IgG level ≥ 100 IU/L. The multivariable Firth penalised logistic regression model revealed that while an Anti-HBs titre ≥ 10 IU/L was a significant negative predictor of OBI (OR 0.18, 95% CI 0.07–0.50, p = 0.001), it failed to exclude active viraemia entirely. Conclusion  Our study identified an overall OBI prevalence of 9.2% in a tested Malaysian ESKD cohort. Firth penalised logistic regression model utilising OBI status as the dependent variable confirmed that relying solely on Anti-HBs IgG to infer viral clearance is inadequate in this immunocompromised population, especially given that over half (54.6%) of OBI patients maintained Anti-HBs IgG positivity.
authors: Tan XYJ, Em JM, Ng ML, Lim SE, Abdullah A, Kun LS.

title: Integrated single-cell transcriptomics reveal E2F1-driven multidrug resistance in medulloblastoma and identify Palbociclib as a therapeutic candidate
abstract: Abstract    Purpose  Medulloblastoma (MB) is a malignant pediatric brain tumor where tumor recurrence driven by acquired multidrug resistance remains a paramount clinical challenge. Resolving the intratumoral heterogeneity underlying this resistance is urgently required to identify novel therapeutic targets. Methods  Single-cell RNA sequencing data and large-scale bulk transcriptomes were integrated and comprehensively analyzed. Multidrug-resistant subpopulations were identified by mapping ridge regression-based drug sensitivity predictions to single-cell profiles. Developmental trajectories and core regulatory networks were reconstructed, and essential transcription factors were functionally evaluated by computational vector field perturbations. The prognostic value of specific cellular states was assessed, and potential therapeutic antagonists were screened using computational databases and spatial molecular docking. Results  Two distinct multidrug-resistant reservoirs were identified, an  E2F1  -driven DNA repair state exhibiting cross-resistance to genotoxic agents, and a  ZIC5  -regulated neuronal differentiation state associated with Hedgehog signaling. Trajectory inference and in silico perturbations demonstrated that the continuous accumulation of  E2F1  is critical for maintaining the chemoresistant DNA repair phenotype. Clinical deconvolution revealed that elevated  E2F1  expression acts as a robust indicator of poor overall survival. Subsequently, computational pharmacogenomic screening and molecular docking identified palbociclib as a highly potent inhibitor capable of precisely binding and targeting the CDK4/6-E2F1 axis. Conclusion  An  E2F1  -driven DNA repair program and a  ZIC5  -associated differentiation state directly govern distinct multidrug resistance mechanisms in MB. Targeting the CDK4/6-E2F1 axis with palbociclib represents a promising precision therapeutic strategy to overcome chemoresistance in high-risk patients.
authors: Yao Y, Zhang J, Liang P, Ji H.

title: Long-term Glucocorticoid Exposure in Angiostrongylus cantonensis Meningoencephalitis Without Eosinophilic Response—Insights Into Treatment Withdrawal From a Medical- Humanities Perspective: A case report
abstract: Abstract    Background  Angiostrongylus cantonensis is the primary pathogen responsible for human eosinophilic meningitis. Atypical infection presentations lacking peripheral or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) eosinophilia occasionally occur under immune-modulated conditions. Long-term glucocorticoid use is a plausible contributor to blunted eosinophilic inflammatory responses. This case highlights that chronic steroid-induced immune alteration may lead to diagnostically challenging, eosinophil-negative neuroangiostrongyliasis, requiring heightened clinical vigilance.  Case presentation  A 48-year-old male with a 30-year history of psoriasis and chronic irregular oral dexamethasone use presented with generalized pain, fever, and altered mental status. Admission laboratory tests revealed neither peripheral nor cerebrospinal fluid eosinophilia. CSF metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) identified 1853 specific reads of  Angiostrongylus cantonensis  , confirming the diagnosis of neuroangiostrongyliasis. Given the patient’s critical neurological deterioration and family concerns regarding irreversible severe neurological sequelae, the family declined antiparasitic treatment; the standard albendazole-glucocorticoid regimen was not administered.  Conclusions  To our knowledge, this is a real-world case of molecularly confirmed  A. cantonensis  meningoencephalitis characterized by double-negative eosinophil results, strongly associated with decades-long irregular glucocorticoid exposure. Normal eosinophil counts cannot rule out parasitic neuroinfection in patients receiving chronic glucocorticoid therapy. CSF-mNGS successfully resolved this diagnostic deadlock, validating its role as a critical alternative diagnostic tool when conventional testing yields negative results. Family-initiated treatment withdrawal illustrates prevalent real-world challenges in prognostic expectation management, risk communication, and shared decision-making for severe neglected tropical central nervous system infections.
authors: Wang Z, Xue Z, Pu Q, Zhi D, Wang W, Yu A, Dong Z, Wang G, Liu A.

title: Transcriptomic Features Associated With Kinase Inhibitor Sensitivity in KMT2A-Rearranged AML.
abstract: Background/aimKMT2A-rearranged (KMT2A-r) acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has a transcriptional program, but its relationship to drug sensitivity remains incompletely characterized. This study investigated whether a KMT2A-r-like transcriptomic state is associated with ex vivo kinase inhibitor sensitivity.Materials and methodsTARGET-AML RNA-sequencing data with fusion and cytogenetic annotations were used to define a predefined, biology-informed, continuous KMT2A-r identity score based on KMT2A-rearrangement-associated genes. The score was applied to Beat AML primary samples with matched normalized expression, ex vivo drug-response area under the curve (AUC) values, malignant cell-type scores, and FLT3-internal tandem duplication status. Associations were assessed using Spearman correlation and covariate-adjusted linear regression.ResultsKMT2A-r AML exhibited increased expression of HOXA genes, MEIS1, PBX3, MEF2C, and FLT3 in TARGET-AML. The identity score differentiated KMT2A-r AML from other fusion groups in TARGET-AML; when applied to Beat AML, higher KMT2A-r identity scores were associated with lower AUC values for kinase inhibitors. After adjustment for malignant cell-type scores and FLT3-internal tandem duplication status, cabozantinib, sorafenib, and pelitinib retained significant negative associations with AUC. Further adjustment for FLT3 expression attenuated these associations, whereas an FLT3-excluded score preserved their direction.ConclusionA KMT2A-r-like transcriptomic state is associated with candidate kinase inhibitor sensitivity patterns in primary AML datasets and appears linked to, but not fully explained by, FLT3-related biology.
authors: Choi W, Lee S.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Graph Methods for Microbiome Research: A Systematic Review.
abstract: The complexity of high-throughput sequencing data in microbiome research necessitates advanced analytical methods to decipher microbial community structures and interactions. Graph-based methods, which model taxa as nodes and their relationships as edges, have emerged as a powerful framework for this purpose. However, the rapid evolution of these techniques, from classical network analysis to modern graph representation learning, has created a fragmented and complex methodological landscape. This systematic review provides a comprehensive synthesis and structured overview of the field. We systematically review the literature and propose a three-part classification to categorize the primary contribution of each study: (1) novel methods for microbial network representation, (2) applications of classical graph analysis, and (3) the emerging use of graph representation learning for predictive modeling. We summarize the most frequent applications within each class, including keystone species identification, community clustering, and graph-based disease classification. Furthermore, we identify critical cross-cutting challenges, such as the lack of standardized tools and the need for improved model interpretability. By structuring the current landscape of graph-based methods, this review serves as a crucial guide for researchers to select appropriate models and highlights key gaps to direct future research.
authors: Shum-Tim C, Islam P, Boyajian JL, Abosalha A, Kassab A, Santos M, Khan KA, Stern K, Emad A, Prakash S.

title: Bacterial effectors targeting the host ubiquitin system.
abstract: Intracellular bacteria are largely shielded from humoral immunity but remain vulnerable to cell-autonomous defense mechanisms, many of which depend on the ubiquitin system. To evade autophagy and lysosomal targeting, numerous bacteria have evolved secreted effectors that disrupt or manipulate the host ubiquitin machinery to their advantage. Bacterial deubiquitinases can protect bacterial surfaces or their enclosing vacuoles from ubiquitin coating and interfere with host inflammatory and cell death pathways. Conversely, bacterial ubiquitin ligases may induce the degradation of host proteins, engaging in an evolutionary arms race with host ligases. In addition, ubiquitin-modifying and ubiquitin-crosslinking effectors can disable major host defense signaling pathways. In the present overview, we summarize currently known ubiquitin-directed effectors, their targets, and their roles in bacteria-host interaction.
authors: Eschger P, Hermanns T, Hofmann K.

title: Rare and Novel Hepatitis C Virus Genotype Subtypes and Response to Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir in A5360 (MINMON) Clinical Trial.
abstract: The introduction of potent, well-tolerated direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) has transformed hepatitis C virus (HCV) therapy and spurred global elimination efforts. However, the extensive genetic diversity of HCV may affect antiviral efficacy, particularly in low and middle-income regions where limited data currently exist. Using samples from the ACTG A5360 (MINMON) trial, which evaluated a minimal-monitoring strategy with 12 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) across five countries, we characterized rare and novel HCV subtypes and assessed baseline resistance-associated substitutions (RASs) and treatment response. Genotype/subtype assignments were obtained by NS5B short-fragment sequencing and confirmed through next-generation and whole-genome sequencing. Among 399 participants, 389 (97.5%) were successfully genotyped; whole-genome sequencing in unresolved genotypes identified several provisional novel genotype 4 subtypes and a putative new genotype 7 subtype (7c). Despite the presence of baseline NS5A RASs, all participants with initially unsubtyped infections achieved sustained virologic response (SVR12). Reduced SVR was observed primarily among genotype 3b infections (78%), consistent with prior data linking A30K + L31M RASs to decreased NS5A inhibitor susceptibility. Overall, SOF/VEL achieved high SVR across genotypes, including rare and novel subtypes. These findings underscore both the increased recognition of global HCV genetic diversity and the robust performance of pangenotypic DAA regimens, supporting universal adoption of simplified treatment strategies, as proposed by the MINMON trial, towards HCV elimination. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03512210.
authors: Han WM, Solomon S, Wagner-Cardoso S, Li J, Parvangada A, Sulkowski M, Naggie S, Martin R, Mo H, Maiorova E, Wyles D, ACTG A5360 study team.

title: Modulation of the FAK-Src Signalling Axis by Oncoviruses: Molecular Mechanisms, Functional Consequences, and Therapeutic Opportunities.
abstract: Oncoviruses play a role in cellular transformation and cancer progression by manipulating host signalling pathways, such as the FAK-Src axis. Preclinical evidence suggests that viral proteins can modulate this axis through direct interactions, integrin signalling, tumour suppressor inactivation, transcriptional and kinase reprogramming, calcium/ROS signalling, regulation of phosphatases, and epigenetic modifications. Important examples include HPV E2 and E6/E7, EBV LMP1 and LMP2A, HBV HBx, HCV Core and E2, and KSHV proteins. FAK-Src disruption can activate pathways such as PI3K/AKT, Rho GTPase, AP-1, and NF-κB, thereby enhancing migration, invasion, survival, angiogenesis, and modulation of the immune response. In some infections, this axis may also be involved at different stages of the viral life cycle. This review examines the molecular mechanisms of FAK-Src regulation by oncoviruses and its functional and therapeutic implications. It also reviews FAK/Src targeting strategies, distinguishing experimental inhibitors, multitargeted agents, and compounds under clinical evaluation, emphasising the limited clinical evidence specific to each virus. Finally, pFAK and pSrc are reviewed as potential markers of pathway activation and pharmacodynamic interaction with the target; however, current evidence is insufficient for their use as valid diagnostic or predictive biomarkers. A better understanding of the virus-host-FAK/Src interaction could help develop mechanism-based therapeutic approaches and biomarker-based patient selection.
authors: Albalawi YA, Deebani AO, Almadani HM, Almessiry BK, Mohammedsaleh ZM, Kaabi AMH, Abdulfattah AM, Assiri RA.

title: Immune-Excluded Mucosal Melanoma: Spatial Mechanisms of Checkpoint Resistance and Biomarker-Guided Therapeutic Opportunities.
abstract: Mucosal melanoma is a rare, aggressive melanoma subtype arising from melanocytes within mucosal surfaces of the head and neck, anorectal, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts. Unlike ultraviolet-driven cutaneous melanoma, mucosal melanoma has lower tumor mutational burden, fewer BRAF V600 alterations, greater structural genomic complexity, and recurrent drivers including mutations in KIT, NRAS, NF1, SF3B1, and copy-number alterations. It is often diagnosed at advanced stages, recurs locally, disseminates early, and responds less favorably to immune checkpoint inhibition than cutaneous melanoma. Low neoantigen burden contributes to this resistance, but emerging evidence indicates that antitumor immunity is also shaped by spatially organized tumor-immune interactions, site-specific mucosal biology, suppressive myeloid and stromal programs, angiogenic signaling, and underexplored innate checkpoint pathways. Here, we review mucosal melanoma as a biologically distinct model of immune-excluded melanoma, summarizing its clinical behavior, genomic architecture, immunotherapy outcomes, and mechanisms of checkpoint resistance, with emphasis on restricted intratumoral CD8-positive T-cell infiltration, macrophage- and stroma-rich barriers, angiogenic remodeling, and candidate innate checkpoints including B7-H3, CD24-Siglec-10, CD47-SIRPα, and B7-H6/NKp30. We further discuss how spatial and circulating biomarkers may support response-adapted translational studies and define actionable immune states across mucosal melanoma sites.
authors: Truong-Balderas KM, Chang RC, Lasalle C, Rogers MC, Wang Y, Amber KT, Mansini AP.

title: Microeukaryotic Diversity and Habitat Structuring in a Desiccating Alkaline Maar Lake (Central Mexico).
abstract: Microeukaryotes are important components of microbial food webs in saline and alkaline lakes, yet their diversity and distribution across distinct microhabitats remain poorly understood. We characterized microeukaryotic communities associated with microbialites, microbial mats, hypersaline waters, and sediments in the desiccating maar lake Rincón de Parangueo (central Mexico) using 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. After quality filtering and rarefaction, 417 amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) belonging to 17 eukaryotic phyla were identified. Community composition differed among microhabitats, with mats harboring the highest number of exclusive genera and water containing the fewest. No genus was shared across all four microhabitats. The greatest taxonomic overlap occurred between mats and water, suggesting ecological connectivity between benthic and planktonic environments. Ordination analyses and environmental data indicated strong habitat filtering associated primarily with salinity and conductivity. Co-occurrence network analysis revealed a highly modular community structure (Q = 0.789), with distinct habitat-associated modules and limited connectivity among them. Chlorophyta dominated assemblages, particularly in microbialites and water, whereas Bacillariophyta, Amoebozoa, Discoba, Aphelidiomycota, and Rotifera were present. Recurrent taxa such as Dunaliella and Picocystis occupied central network positions. These results demonstrate strong microhabitat-scale structuring and highlight the importance of fine-scale environmental heterogeneity in shaping diversity within alkaline maar lakes.
authors: Moguel B, Cerca M, Sanchez-Sanchez J, Muñoz-Velasco I, Vega-González M, Olmedo-Álvarez G.

title: Diversity of Ascetosporeans Associated With Feather Hydroids in New Caledonia.
abstract: Ascetosporea is a group of parasitic protists within Endomyxa that primarily infect marine invertebrates and can cause serious damage to fishery resources such as oysters and prawns. Although approximately 50 species have been formally described, environmental DNA (eDNA) studies suggest that their diversity remains largely underestimated, with many lineages yet to be discovered. Their ecological roles and host ranges are also poorly understood, partly because no complete life cycle has been elucidated, likely due to the difficulty of maintaining live cells in laboratory conditions. In this study, we investigated feather hydroids as potential hosts of ascetosporeans in New Caledonia, where this group has not been previously examined. Using metabarcoding with ascetosporean-specific primers, we detected 46 operational taxonomic units (OTUs) from three hydroid individuals. Of these, 31 OTUs were affiliated with environmental clades ENDO-3a and ENDO-2, whereas two and four OTUs were assigned to Paradinida and Haplosporida, respectively. Notably, seven OTUs were consistently detected across all samples, suggesting that they may have been broadly associated with the feather hydroids in this environment. These findings indicate that ascetosporean diversity and host associations in marine ecosystems are substantially underestimated.
authors: Yabuki A, Yamazaki A, Yamakita T, Miwa T, Fukuba T, Olu K, Toyofuku T.

title: 6PPD-Quinone Promotes Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease through Immune-Inflammatory Disruption.
abstract: 6PPD-quinone (6PPDQ), a transformation product of the tire antioxidant 6PPD, is widely detected in environmental and human matrices, yet its relevance to metabolic liver disease remains unclear. We examined its potential contribution to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) by integrating disease-burden analysis, computational toxicology, human transcriptomics, and cross-model validation. The intersection of predicted 6PPDQ targets with MASLD transcriptomic signatures identified 103 candidate genes enriched predominantly in immune and inflammatory pathways. Three machine-learning algorithms prioritized six hub genes, ASPM, ERN1, GADD45B, GINS2, LDLR, and MYPOP, which discriminated MASLD from controls with a combined AUC of 0.997. Immune deconvolution and single-cell analyses were associated with this signature with hepatic immune remodeling and intercellular communication. Molecular docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations predicted stable interactions between 6PPDQ and several targets, particularly ERN1. Environmentally informed low-dose oral exposure produced hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and injury in mice, while LC-MS/MS confirmed internal exposure. Concordant transcriptional responses were reproduced in the hiPSC-derived liver organoids. Integration of these findings supported a provisional adverse outcome pathway linking 6PPDQ exposure to MASLD-related liver injuries. Collectively, these results implicate 6PPDQ as a plausible environmental hazard for metabolic liver injury and support expanding the risk assessment of tire-derived contaminants beyond that of aquatic ecotoxicity.
authors: Zuo X, Ma L, Hou X, Zhang C, Tan S, Zhang Y, Pu Y, Zhang J.

title: A semi-automated genetic screen using genome-wide association analysis identifies modulators of stress-induced sleep in Caenorhabditis elegans.
abstract: Animals sleep more when they are sick. In Caenorhabditis elegans, stress-induced sleep (SIS) follows cellular injury such as exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light. The genetic regulators of SIS remain incompletely defined. Using robotic automation, high-throughput imaging, and genome-wide association analysis, we performed a semi-automated screen of 940 whole-genome-sequenced Million Mutation Project (MMP) strains. We quantified behavioral activity and quiescence before and after ultraviolet (UV) radiation. We applied the Sequence Kernel Association Test (SKAT) to this behavioral data to prioritize a set of associated genes and observed significant enrichment of known SIS genetic regulators. Based on these results, we conducted a candidate validation screen for additional genes regulating SIS. We identified three genes (strd-1, cla-1, and egl-8), mutations in which reproducibly influence SIS. Further exploration of these genes holds potential for enhancing our understanding of the molecular basis of SIS. These findings establish a pipeline for automated behavioral phenotyping coupled with gene-based association to accelerate studies of C. elegans neurogenetics.
authors: Li ZJ, Honarpisheh H, Kutagulla S, LeCure KM, Liang J, Raizen DM, Fang-Yen C.

title: The 2027 BCPT Perspectives on Studies Involving Natural Products, Traditional Chinese Medicine and Systems Pharmacology.
abstract: Natural products, including isolated compounds, complex extracts, traditional medicinal preparations and marine, microbial, fungal and animal-derived materials, remain important sources of therapeutic agents and pharmacological discovery. However, variation in biological source materials, preparation methods, chemical composition and experimental design may compromise reproducibility and interpretation. This guideline presents the requirements of Basic & Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology for studies involving natural products and their semisynthetic or biotransformed derivatives. It provides recommendations for documenting scientific and ethnopharmacological rationale, taxonomy, authentication, provenance, sustainable and lawful sourcing, extraction, chemical characterisation, dosing, bioactivity, safety and data accessibility. Particular emphasis is placed on studying the preparation actually administered, using pharmacologically relevant concentrations and doses, controlling vehicle effects and assay interference and aligning mechanistic and therapeutic claims with the supporting evidence. Complex mixtures do not necessarily need to be reduced to a single active constituent; however, their composition must be adequately characterised, and claims concerning individual constituents, additivity, synergy or antagonism require experimental substantiation. Computational, network and systems-pharmacology analyses should be transparent and reproducible, with experimental validation of central predictions. These recommendations apply equivalent standards to natural products and other interventions while recognising the additional information required to define complex biological materials and improve overall translational relevance.
authors: Tveden-Nyborg P, Yang B, Albayrak G, Simonsen U, Lykkesfeldt J.

title: Alr2204-Alr2205 form a functional modular thioredoxin system that enhances oxidative stress tolerance in cyanobacteria.
abstract: The cysteine-mediated catalytic reactions are essential for redox homeostasis in photosynthetic organisms. In the genome of cyanobacterium Anabaena PCC 7120 (Anabaena), the genes encoding thioredoxin reductase (TR; alr2204) and the atypical thioredoxin (Trx; alr2205) are contiguously located, but whether these proteins function as a redox pair remains unknown. Interestingly, Alr2204 and Alr2205, respectively, show high homology to the TR and Trx domains of the chloroplast NADPH-thioredoxin reductase C (NTRC). To delve into its possible role, Alr2204 was overexpressed in Anabaena. The resulting strain displayed elevated TR activity and demonstrated enhanced resistance to oxidative stresses. Biochemical characterization showed Alr2204 to be a FAD-associated, predominantly alpha helical protein with NADPH-dependent TR activity. Notably, Alr2204 supported the function of Trx Alr2205, indicating that Alr2204-Alr2205 formed a cognate redox pair wherein Alr2204 donated electrons to Alr2205. When co-expressed in Anabaena, Alr2204 copurified with Alr2205, and together these proteins enhanced the cellular levels of the reduced form of 2-Cys-Prx, a physiologically vital antioxidant protein. Importantly, Alr2204-Alr2205 also sustained peroxidase activity of 2-Cys-Prx. This is the first study to show that Alr2204-Alr2205, though independently synthesized, are functionally analogous to the NTRC protein, and Trx systems can be modulated to enhance stress resistance in organisms.
authors: Waghamare N, Hurali DT, Patwardhan RS, Banerjee M, Ballal A.

title: Sphingosine-1-Phosphate Attenuates LPS-Induced Inflammatory Cardiac Injury in Association With RASGRP1-S100A9-NLRP3 Signaling.
abstract: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induces endotoxemia-associated inflammatory cardiac injury rather than classical viral or autoimmune myocarditis. Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) regulates cardiovascular and immune responses, predominantly through S1P receptors, but whether it also modulates macrophage-associated inflammatory signaling during LPS-induced cardiac injury remains incompletely understood. This study investigated the role of the RASGRP1-S100A9-NLRP3 signaling axis in the cardioprotective effects of S1P. Transcriptomic and single-cell RNA-sequencing analyses were used to identify inflammation-associated candidate genes and their cellular distribution. Male Sprague-Dawley rats received a single intraperitoneal injection of LPS (8 mg/kg) followed by S1P treatment for 6 weeks. Histopathology, echocardiography, serum cardiac-injury markers, oxidative-stress indices, inflammatory cytokines, Western blotting, and cellular metabolic-flux assays were evaluated. RAW264.7 macrophages were used for mechanistic cellular studies. RASGRP1 or NLRP3 overexpression and S100A9-R101Q mutation were used to assess functional contributions. Molecular docking and molecular-dynamics simulations were complemented by SPR, MST, CETSA, DARTS, and Co-IP assays to evaluate S1P-RASGRP1 target engagement and pathway-associated protein interactions. Bioinformatic analyses identified RASGRP1 as a macrophage-enriched, inflammation-associated hub gene. In LPS-treated rats, S1P reduced myocardial inflammatory injury and collagen deposition, improved ejection fraction and fractional shortening, and decreased cardiac-injury, oxidative-stress, and inflammatory markers. In RAW264.7 macrophages, S1P attenuated inflammatory and oxidative-stress responses, restored oxidative phosphorylation and glycolytic capacity, and reduced the abundance of RASGRP1, S100A9, NLRP3, and ASC. SPR and MST supported a concentration-dependent biophysical interaction between S1P and RASGRP1; CETSA and DARTS provided complementary target-stability evidence. The molecular-dynamics trajectory showed substantial rearrangement of S1P from the starting pose before reaching a plateau and therefore supports conformational sampling rather than preservation of the original docked pose. Co-IP supported protein associations within the proposed inflammatory network. RASGRP1 or NLRP3 overexpression attenuated several S1P-associated protective effects. The S100A9-R101Q mutation also weakened several S1P-associated protective responses. SPR indicated a lower apparent dissociation constant for R101Q than for WT S100A9 after model-specific fitting, which is consistent with stronger or more persistent NLRP3 binding rather than loss of the S100A9-NLRP3 interaction. S1P mitigates LPS-induced inflammatory cardiac injury in association with altered macrophage RASGRP1-S100A9-NLRP3 signaling. Biophysical and target-stability assays support direct engagement of RASGRP1 by S1P. However, these findings do not establish RASGRP1 as the sole mediator of S1P activity, exclude contributions from canonical S1P receptor signaling, or demonstrate a strictly linear RASGRP1-S100A9-NLRP3 signaling cascade. Because the LPS model primarily represents endotoxemia-associated inflammatory cardiac injury, extrapolation of these findings to classical viral or autoimmune myocarditis should be made with caution.
authors: Yue C, Li Q, Li C, Yang T, Huang X, Yue F, Long Q, Li R, Lei R, Ma Q, Hu C, Yang Q, Yan Y, Liu Y, Yan Q, Yang M.

title: Novel ex vivo models reveal segment-specific infection of the human efferent ducts and epididymis: implications for Zika virus persistence and shedding in semen.
abstract: Study questionCan human epididymis and efferent ducts (ED) support Zika virus (ZIKV) replication ex vivo and act as a source of prolonged viral shedding in semen of infected men?Summary answerOur novel ex vivo models demonstrate that ZIKV exhibits segment-specific tropism, with sustained replication in the ED epithelium and restricted infection of epididymal stromal macrophages, identifying these organs as distinct reservoirs for viral persistence in semen.What is known alreadyThe 2015-2017 ZIKV outbreak revealed that the virus persists in semen and can be sexually transmitted by men long after the acute phase of infection. While the human testis is an established reservoir, animal studies and longitudinal semen analyses suggest that additional organs within the male genital tract contribute to the prolonged excretion of infectious ZIKV. However, the specific roles of the human EDs and epididymis have remained unexplored due to the lack of physiologically relevant human models.Study design, size, durationOrganotypic cultures of human EDs and epididymis corpus (EC) were developed and characterized using post-mortem tissues obtained from 11 uninfected organ donors (age range 29-79 years, median age: 58 years). Using this innovative ex vivo platform, we investigated ZIKV replication kinetics, cellular tropism, and the resulting impact on tissue viability and innate immune responses over a 9-day culture period.Participants/materials, setting, methodsED and EC tissues were dissected and cultured on PET inserts at the air/medium interface. Tissue integrity was validated via histology, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) viability assays, and transcriptomic/protein marker expression, assessed by RT-qPCR and immunohistochemistry. Explants were exposed to ZIKV, with replication monitored via viral RNA (vRNA) quantification, as assessed by RT-qPCR, and plaque assays for infectious virion release. Cellular targets were identified using RNAscope combined with immunohistochemistry. To determine the impact of the infection, we analyzed the innate immune response by RT-qPCR and ELISA and cell viability by LDH assays and cleaved caspase 3 expression, as well as the transcriptional and protein expression of a selected panel of cell markers, assessed by RT-qPCR and immunohistochemistry.Main results and the role of chanceThe ex vivo models preserved global tissue architecture, viability, and the expression of epithelial, macrophage and smooth muscle markers throughout the study. ZIKV infected the ED epithelium, with replicative vRNA persisting from 3 days post-infection (dpi) until the end of culture (P = 0.01). Conversely, in the EC, infection was limited to stromal macrophages and smooth muscle cells, peaking at 3 dpi before diminishing (P = 0.002). Both segments exhibited robustly repeatable results across donors. Notably, both ED and EC exhibited limited antiviral responses and weak pro-inflammatory responses to ZIKV infection. ZIKV replication did not induce significant changes in morphology, viability or functional marker expression, suggesting a non-cytopathic infection mechanism.Limitations, reasons for cautionWhile these organotypic cultures preserved multi-lineage cell types for 9 days, epithelial morphology and organization were gradually impacted, and the expression of a subset of functional and hormone-responsive markers (e.g. AQP1, ESR1, AR) decreased. Furthermore, the ex vivo setup cannot replicate in vivo viral entry via systemic circulation or luminal flow from the testis, nor can it account for the influence of infiltrating systemic leukocytes and global inflammation.Wider implications of the findingsThese novel human ED and EC culture systems bridge a critical gap in reproductive research. Our findings reveal a dual cellular pathway for ZIKV shedding, epithelial in the ED and macrophage-mediated in the EC, offering a mechanistic explanation for the prolonged presence of ZIKV in human semen. Furthermore, this ex vivo platform provides a new tool for studying male reproductive tract-pathogen interactions, as well as the efficacy of antiviral drugs.FundingThis study received funding from the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under grant agreement no. 733176, ZikaPLAN (grant agreement no. 734584) and ZIKAlliance (grant agreement no. 734548), and was funded in part by Inserm and the University of Rennes.DisclosuresWe declare no conflict of interest.Trial registration numberN/A.
authors: da Silva J, Satie AP, Houzet L, Lista Brotos MJ, Mathieu R, Goepp A, Aubry F, Dejucq-Rainsford N.

title: Human airspace macrophage signatures are conserved during sterile lung injury and repair.
abstract: RationaleAirspace macrophages (AM) are implicated in both persistent inflammation and tissue repair following acute lung injury. Distinct subsets of AM are associated with lung pathology in humans, but whether unique AM signatures are specific to disease states or represent a conserved response to lung inflammation is unknown.ObjectivesWe sought to test the hypothesis that conserved subsets of inflammatory and reparative AM could be identified by transcriptional programming in a human model of self-resolving acute lung injury.MethodsA total of 15 participants underwent BAL before and at a pre-assigned time point after endobronchial exposure to bacterial endotoxin. Bronchoalveolar lavage cells were subjected to single cell RNA sequencing, and longitudinal assessment of AM programming during resolution of inflammation and lung repair was performed.Measurements and main resultsWe identify transcriptionally distinct subsets of tissue resident and recruited AM present at all time points, in all participants. Two recruited AM populations increase following inflammation: one that aligns with classical monocytes and one with interstitial macrophages (IAM). Airspace macrophage subsets display unique patterns of gene expression throughout the time course. Comparison of subset-specific markers to those identified in disease states reveals that IAM express many so-called pathogenic markers during normal lung repair.ConclusionsBy applying a uniform inflammatory stimulus to healthy adults and examining BAL cells obtained at precise time points thereafter, we construct a time-resolved kinetic of AM transcriptional programming during typical lung repair. Our data demonstrate that IAM share transcriptional similarity to AM identified in disease states and suggest they may reflect a conserved cellular response to tissue injury.
journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
authors: Moore CM, McManus SA, Wynn EA, McClendon JD, Janssen WJ, Mould KJ.
