title: Genetic mapping of fruit texture in American cranberry reveals multitrait QTL and a complex genetic architecture.
abstract: Fruit texture is a key quality trait in cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon Ait.), with a direct impact on processing efficiency and overall profitability for the industry. To elucidate the genetic basis of cranberry texture, we conducted the first QTL mapping study in this crop, implementing a fruit compression method with 10 mechanical texture traits in 2 biparental populations, CNJ02 (n = 168) and CNJ04 (n = 67), over 2 years. These 10 traits, associated with flesh hardness/stiffness and elasticity, showed similar phenotypic patterns of transgressive segregation and generally strong positive correlations. However, traits accounting for fruit size and shape effects (stress/strain-related traits and maximum contact pressure), together with slope-related parameters, exhibited consistently high heritability across populations, supporting their potential utility for breeding and genetic analyses. Genetic mapping revealed multiple consistently detected multitrait QTL distributed across chromosomes 1,2,3,4,5,8,9,10,11 and 12, suggesting a complex genetic architecture. These genomic regions explained, on average, 4.67% to 18.6% of the phenotypic variance in CNJ02 and 10.97% to 27.75% in CNJ04. Candidate genes identified within these regions point to cell wall dynamics, including pectin modification, cellulose biosynthesis, and hemicellulose metabolism, as potentially relevant processes underlying cranberry fruit texture. Our findings provide loci in association with texture traits in cranberry and insights for the genetic improvement of this essential trait, informing the design of genotyping platforms and the implementation of genomic-assisted breeding approaches. Furthermore, we anticipate that these results will guide future studies aimed at optimizing postharvest fruit handling and management practices.
authors: Lopez-Moreno H, Torres-Meraz MA, Ariza-Hernandez I, Kawash J, Rojas-Barros P, Maule AF, Atucha A, Neyhart JL, Sideli GM, Polashock J, Iorizzo M, Digman M, Zalapa J.

title: Integrative Analysis of Nucleotide Metabolism-Related Genes Reveals a Diagnostic Signature and In Silico Functional Disruption in Hypertrophic Scarring.
abstract: Hypertrophic scar (HTS) is a fibrotic skin disease characterized by excessive extracellular matrix accumulation and chronic inflammation. This study aimed to investigate cellular heterogeneity, immune alterations, and nucleotide metabolism-related biomarkers in HTS and to explore their potential mechanisms. Single-cell RNA sequencing data were analyzed using Seurat for cell clustering and annotation. Nucleotide metabolism activity was evaluated to identify key cell populations and candidate genes. Bulk transcriptomic datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were used for differential expression analysis, and machine learning algorithms were applied to develop a diagnostic model. Sixteen cell clusters were identified, with macrophages showing prominent activation of nucleotide metabolism pathways and immune-related signaling. The optimal Enet + svmLinear model achieved strong predictive performance (area under the curve = 0.934), and Shapley Additive exPlanations analysis identified NCF1 and GPR34 as key predictive genes. These genes were also associated with immune cell infiltration. In vitro validation using THP-1-derived M2 macrophages showed that NCF1 and GPR34 promoted transforming growth factor-β1 secretion and enhanced fibroblast activation, while their knockdown reduced α-smooth muscle actin and collagen I expression. Collectively, this study reveals the important role of macrophage-associated nucleotide metabolism in HTS and identifies NCF1 and GPR34 as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets.
journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
authors: Luo Q, Yang X, Shen J, Yan M, Wang X, Liang Y, Guan L.

title: Unveiling the antioxidant and antimicrobial potential of Astragalus tephrosoides methanol extract: Phytochemical screening, GC-MS profiling, computational and experimental approaches.
abstract: BackgroundPlant-derived bioactive compounds have significant pharmaceutical applications.ObjectivesThis study focused on the methanol extract of Astragalus tephrosoides (A. tephrosoides) to evaluate its phytochemical composition, biological activities and in-silico properties.MethodPhytochemical screening, GC-MS profiling, antioxidant (DPPH), antimicrobial and phytotoxic assays were performed. Molecular docking against bacterial proteins (DNA gyrase, lanosterol-14-α-demethylase, PBP2A and chitin synthase) and density functional theory (DFT) analyses were conducted for the bioactive compounds identified by GC-MS.ResultsPhytochemical analysis confirmed the presence of alkaloids, steroids, terpenoids, saponins, phenolics, volatile oils and coumarins in the extract. GC-MS analysis revealed the presence of 17 bioactive compounds. The extract exhibited notable antioxidant activity (IC50 = 0.66 mg/mL), comparable to that of ascorbic acid (IC50 = 0.58 mg/mL). Antibacterial effects were observed with net absorbance values of 0.860 (E. coli, P. aeruginosa), 0.770 (B. subtilis), 0.656 (S. aureus) and 0.550 (S. typhi) and MICs of 1.0-0.12 µg/mL. The extract exhibited antifungal activity comparable to that of miconazole and moderate phytotoxicity (66.6%) at 1000 μg/mL. Docking revealed moderate binding affinities, while DFT analysis revealed significant HOMO/LUMO gaps, indicating their thermodynamic stability.ConclusionA. tephrosoides contains bioactive compounds with promising antioxidant, antimicrobial and moderate phytotoxic activities, as supported by computational studies.
authors: Batool F, Wajid M, Alzahrani HA, Chohan TA, Mansour AA, Imran M, Khan A, Masroor D.

title: The Gain-of-Function GLP1R R131Q Variant Preserves β-Cell Function and Enhances Response to GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.
abstract: ObjectiveGenetic variation in the glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor (GLP1R) has been implicated in type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk and treatment response. We investigated whether GLP1R R131Q, which was previously reported as a T2D-protective variant in genome-wide association studies, alters receptor signaling, β-cell function, and response to glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs).Research design and methodsTrajectory of β-cell function was evaluated in a 20-year community-based prospective cohort in Korea (n = 6,373), where participants underwent biennial 2-h 75-g oral glucose tolerance tests, and disposition index was used as surrogate marker. Pharmacogenetic response to GLP-1RAs was assessed in a hospital-based T2D cohort in Korea (n = 177). Hyperglycemic clamp studies (n = 17), human islet experiments (n = 21), and in vitro assays were conducted to characterize GLP1R R131Q effects on receptor signaling and islet function.ResultsGLP1R R131Q was associated with slower decline in disposition index in individuals without T2D, with reductions from baseline of 30% in homozygous carriers, 35% in heterozygotes, and 37% in wild-type individuals. In people with T2D, each allele conferred an additional 0.53% or 5.8 mmol/mol reduction in HbA1c after 6 months of GLP-1RA treatment (P = 5.8 × 10-4). Hyperglycemic clamp and human islet experiments demonstrated allele-dependent enhancement of GLP-1RA-stimulated insulin secretion (P = 0.050 and P = 0.037, respectively). In vitro, GLP1R R131Q increased GLP-1RA-stimulated cAMP production with directional observations consistent with pathway bias.ConclusionsGLP1R R131Q is a gain-of-function variant associated with preservation of β-cell function and enhanced glycemic response to GLP-1RA treatment, supporting further investigation as a candidate pharmacogenetic marker for precision diabetes care.

title: Distinct Transcriptomic Profiles in ART-Treated People With HIV Are Associated With NF-κB-Regulated Gene Expression and Inflammatory Cytokine Signatures.
abstract: ObjectiveDespite effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), people with HIV (PWH) continue to experience elevated morbidity, potentially driven by persistent immune dysregulation. This study aimed to define transcriptomic heterogeneity in peripheral CD4 + T cells and identify immune signatures associated with clinical stratification in ART-treated PWH.DesignWe analyzed transcriptomic and immunologic (plasma cytokine) data from a well-characterized cohort of ART-suppressed PWH to identify biologically meaningful subgroups.MethodsBulk RNA sequencing was performed on peripheral CD4 + T cells from 154 ART-treated PWH. Plasma levels of immune mediators were also quantified. We applied Pairwise Controlled Manifold Approximation (PaCMAP), a novel dimensionality reduction technique, to identify transcriptomic clusters and assessed their associations with clinical and immunological parameters, including CD4:CD8 ratio and cell-associated HIV DNA/RNA.ResultsPaCMAP identified 3 distinct transcriptomic clusters among PWH. These clusters were enriched for differential expression of genes regulated by NF-κB, suggesting a role for chronic immune activation and inflammation. While clustering was not associated with HIV reservoir size, there was a modest association with CD4:CD8 ratio, a key marker of immune recovery. In addition, plasma levels of IL-1β, TNF-α, and G-CSF differed across clusters, supporting a link between plasma cytokines and CD4 + T-cell transcriptomic diversity.ConclusionsOur findings define transcriptomic subgroups in ART-treated PWH that are characterized by NF-κB-driven gene expression and distinct inflammatory cytokine profiles. These immune signatures may serve as biomarkers for immunological stratification and provide insights into persistent immune dysfunction despite viral suppression.
journal: Journal of acquired immune deficiency syndromes (1999)
authors: Wang Y, Gornalusse GG, Bhatt U, Siegel DA, Barbehenn A, Hoh R, Martin J, Hecht F, Pilcher C, Semenova L, Murdoch DM, Margolis DM, Levy CN, Jerome KR, Rudin CD, Hladik F, Deeks SG, Lee SA, Browne EP.

title: A C. elegans model for functional analysis of conserved ADPKD variants in cilia, extracellular vesicles, and sensory signaling.
abstract: Interpreting the pathogenic significance of missense variants in human disease gene candidates remains a major challenge in precision medicine. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), a common cause of kidney failure, results from mutations in PKD1 or PKD2, encoding polycystin-1 and polycystin-2. Here, we establish C. elegans as a platform for the functional classification of PC2 variants by characterizing PKD-2C180S, the C. elegans ortholog of the likely pathogenic human variant PC2C331S. Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing with dual-color fluorescent reporters and super-resolution imaging, we show that PKD-2C180S reduces cell-body protein levels, abolishes ciliary and extracellular vesicle (EV) localization, and eliminates sensory function, phenocopying a pkd-2 null allele. In heterozygous animals, PKD-2C180S is recessive and exerts no dominant-negative effect on wild-type PKD-2 trafficking, protein levels, or function, establishing that PKD-2 is haplosufficient in this model. PKD-2C180S also abolishes ciliary and EV localization of the PC1 homolog LOV-1 and reduces LOV-1 cell-body levels, phenocopying pkd-2 null animals, consistent with PC2 acting as a molecular chaperone for PC1 stability and trafficking. Genetic epistasis analysis shows that PKD-2C180S protein levels and ciliary trafficking defects are intrinsic to the mutant protein and independent of lov-1 and the ciliary kinesin-3 klp-6. Quantitative analysis reveals that LOV-1•PKD-2 is more abundant at the ciliary membrane and more efficiently packaged into EVs than PKD-2 alone in lov-1 mutants. We conclude that PC2C331S may perturb protein stability and/or polycystin complex formation prior to ciliary/EV trafficking. This work establishes a C. elegans pipeline for mechanistic classification of conserved ADPKD-associated missense variants.
authors: Wang J, Nava Cruz C, Walsh JD, desRanleau E, Nikonorova IA, Barr MM.

title: Optimization of RNA Sequencing Workflow in Brush Swabs of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is associated with poor survival due to challenges with timely diagnosis and surveillance. Noninvasive biopsy methods, such as brush swab biopsy, have emerged as a promising approach with several clinical advantages over surgical biopsies, which may help overcome challenges in diagnosis, prognostication, and surveillance. We aimed to evaluate a noninvasive brush swab method for nucleic acid collection suitable for RNA sequencing in patients with OSCC. Brush swabs were collected from tumor sites before surgery, followed by corresponding fresh-frozen tissue samples from the same sites during surgical resection. Thirty-nine patients were enrolled [median age, 65 years (IQR, 55-73)]. As expected, tissue samples yielded higher RNA concentration and integrity than swabs [456.3 ng/μL (IQR, 291.3-651.3) vs. 73.2 ng/μL (IQR, 34.9-106.3); DV200, 91.6% (IQR, 85.9-93) vs. 82% (IQR, 77.3-87.8); both P Prevention relevanceBrush swab sampling is a simple, minimally invasive method to assess molecular changes in oral cancer, yielding results comparable with tissue samples. Its low burden and repeatability support early detection, monitoring, and risk assessment. Its practicality in dental and community settings enables broader access to screening and preventive care.
authors: Luong BA, Dong MP, Nguyen-Le DM, Arambula M, Asam K, Thomas CM, Callahan NF, Walker PC, Nguyen KK, Chen Wongworawat Y, Ye Y, Xu K, Aouizerat BE, Viet CT.

title: Tumor Microbial Burden Drives Immune Responses through Regulation of Interferon Signaling.
abstract: Tumor microbes are increasingly recognized for modulating tumor behavior and therapy responses. Intratumoral microbial burden (ITMB) analysis across cancers revealed regulation of immune pathways and activated mast cells, mostly in colorectal and gastric cancers. High-ITMB colorectal cancer leads to interferon (IFN) regulation and is associated with improved outcomes in advanced disease. Single-cell sequencing revealed induction of IFN-related genes (IRG) within microbe-containing human colorectal cancer. Gastrointestinal-luminal mismatch repair-deficient (MMRd) tumors had higher ITMB than proficient tumors. In a rectal MMRd cohort with 100% remission after immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), tumor microbes and microbe-containing mast cells increased. In ICB-sensitive syngeneic murine MMRd tumor models, local tumor microbial depletion impaired ICB efficacy while downregulating IFN signaling. Forced upregulation of IRGs in ADAR1-deficient cancer cells restored immunotherapy responses during microbial ablation. These data highlight dynamic interplay among ITMB, host defense, and immunogenicity, which seems key to determine therapy responses.SignificanceThe ITMB is linked to transcriptional and immune functional changes that seem to determine tumor sensitivity to immunotherapy. These findings highlight the key role of tumor-resident microbes in shaping the tumor ecosystem, which could be targeted to modulate therapy responses.

title: A Highly Sensitive ERA-CRISPR/Cas13a Assay for Detection of Vibrio vulnificus.
abstract: BackgroundVibrio vulnificus is a halophilic marine bacterium widely distributed in coastal environments and seafood products and is responsible for severe human infections and foodborne disease outbreaks. Rapid and sensitive detection of V. vulnificus is therefore critical for clinical diagnosis and seafood safety monitoring.ObjectiveThe objective of this study was to develop and evaluate a rapid, sensitive, and specific nucleic acid detection method for V. vulnificus suitable for application in complex biological and food matrices.MethodsAn enzymatic recombinase amplification (ERA)-clustered regularly interspaced short panlindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 13a (Cas13a)-based nucleic acid detection assay was established by coupling ERA with Cas13a-mediated collateral cleavage of fluorescent RNA reporters. The analytical performance of the assay was systematically evaluated using V. vulnificus standard plasmids, artificially contaminated human serum samples, and spiked oyster homogenates.ResultsThe assay exhibited high specificity for V. vulnificus, with no cross-reactivity observed for other common Vibrio species. The LOD was 1 × 10-1 copies/μL for standard plasmid templates. In complex matrices, including human serum and oyster samples, the assay achieved an LOD of 1 × 101 CFU/mL. The entire detection process was completed under isothermal conditions within 45 min.ConclusionA sensitive and specific ERA-CRISPR/Cas13a-based assay for the detection of V. vulnificus was successfully developed and validated. The method demonstrates strong analytical performance in both biological and seafood matrices.HighlightsA rapid isothermal ERA-CRISPR/Cas13a assay for V. vulnificus detection was developed. High specificity was achieved without cross-reactivity to other Vibrio species. The assay enables sensitive detection in serum and oyster samples. The method shows potential for routine seafood safety surveillance and marine pathogen monitoring.
authors: Pan Y, Nie X, Lü P.

title: An interdisciplinary comparative framework for antimicrobial efficacy and environmental risk assessment of antibiotics integrating human and environmental health: A case study from patient to river.
abstract: Pharmaceutical residues in aquatic environments are a global concern. The "benign by design" concept seeks to reduce pharmaceutical pollution, among others, through the development of environmentally less persistent derivatives of active pharmaceutical ingredients on the market. Here, we go beyond persistence alone by applying an interdisciplinary framework for comparative environmental risk assessment (ERA) to evaluate a novel fluoroquinolone derivative, ciprofloxacin-hemi (CIP-hemi), versus its conventional counterpart, ciprofloxacin (CIP). The framework integrates antibiotic efficacy, human pharmacokinetics, environmental degradability, and ecotoxicity to nontarget organisms to evaluate the balance of human health needs and environmental protection, combining experimental data with in silico modeling. We show that CIP-hemi, despite its higher overall degradability than CIP, does not exhibit lower risk to aquatic ecosystems at comparable therapeutic efficiency, except in a few specific scenarios where clinically unrealistically high doses are administered to patients. While CIP-hemi has lower predicted environmental concentrations than CIP when the same dose is administered, due to its faster hydrolysis in urine, higher doses of CIP-hemi are required to match the therapeutic efficacy of CIP due to the higher minimum inhibitory concentrations for pathogenic bacteria that are commonly treated with CIP. Consequently, even though CIP-hemi has higher predicted no-effect concentrations for aquatic ecosystems (201 ng L-1) and antimicrobial resistance selection in aquatic environments (56,000 ng L-1) than CIP (22 and 79 ng L-1, respectively), the higher doses needed generally cause higher environmental risks. Ciprofloxacin-hemi could achieve lower risk than CIP for antimicrobial resistance selection in some scenarios but only when administered intravenously and at unrealistically high doses. On the basis of this comparative ERA, we conclude that focusing on higher degradability alone is insufficient in searching for "greener" derivatives of existing antibiotics. Rather, an interdisciplinary framework is needed that integrates degradability, therapeutic efficacy, human pharmacokinetics, and ERA to improve the development of environmentally safer pharmaceuticals.
authors: Zhang Q, De Sutter PJ, Amorim JF, Järvinen P, Moermond CTA, Suk M, Kümmerer K, Demeestere K, Sikanen TM, De Schamphelaere KAC.

title: Targeted Metagenomic Sequencing for the Rapid Diagnosis of Chlamydia Caviae Pneumonia in an Elderly Patient without Known Immunosuppression or Animal Exposure: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: BackgroundChlamydia caviae, a pathogen primarily causing conjunctivitis and respiratory diseases in guinea pigs, rarely infects humans. Previous human cases were mostly associated with direct contact with sick guinea pigs or occurred in immunocompromised individuals.Case presentationWe report a case of a 79-year-old female from Sichuan, China, without known immunosuppressive disease or therapy who presented with fever, fatigue, and left upper lobe consolidation, and was diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). She had no documented history of contact with guinea pigs or other pets. Empirical antibiotic therapy proved ineffective. Subsequently, probe capture-based targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS, specifically the MetaCAP™ panel) of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) rapidly identified C. caviae (sequence count: 1107, relative abundance: 54.50%) as the highly probable causative pathogen. Following targeted therapy with a doxycycline-moxifloxacin combination regimen, the patient's temperature rapidly normalized, achieving significant clinical and radiological improvement before discharge.ConclusionThis case demonstrates that pulmonary infection caused by C. caviae can occur in individuals without known immunosuppressive conditions and without direct animal contact, raising questions about potential alternative transmission routes and zoonotic reservoirs. The early application of targeted next-generation sequencing is of critical clinical value for the precise diagnosis and prompt management of rare and elusive respiratory pathogens.
authors: Li J, Li L, Wang J, Liu C, Rong X, Yang J, Si G.

title: Integrative transcriptomic, molecular dynamic simulation and in vitro analysis identify Evodiamine as a multi-target therapeutic agent against cisplatin-resistant non-small cell lung cancer.
abstract: An integrative transcriptomic, computational, and experimental approach was employed to identify molecular determinants of cisplatin resistance in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and to investigate the therapeutic potential of Evodiamine (Evo). Analysis of multiple Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets identified 100 overlapping differentially expressed genes, followed by protein-protein interaction network analysis that prioritized SPP1, GPX3, HBEGF, and KLF2 as key hub genes. Expression analysis demonstrated significantly increased SPP1 and reduced GPX3 and KLF2 expression in NSCLC tissues, while survival analysis revealed an association between elevated SPP1 expression and poor overall survival. Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment analyses indicated that the identified hub genes were predominantly associated with extracellular matrix organization, ErbB signaling, glutathione metabolism, and apelin signaling. Molecular docking analysis demonstrated favourable binding of Evo to the identified hub proteins, with SPP1, GPX3, HBEGF, and KLF2 showing docking scores of -9.1, -8.9, -8.9, and - 8.5 kcal/mol, respectively. Subsequently, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated stable SPP1-Evo interactions throughout the simulation period. In vitro validation further demonstrated that Evo significantly reduced cell viability (A549: IC50 = 4 ± 0.23 µM, A549CR: IC50 = 2 ± 0.31 µM), clonogenic growth, migration, and invasion in both cisplatin-sensitive and cisplatin-resistant NSCLC (A549, A549CR) cells. Interestingly, Evo showed better sensitivity towards A549CR cells than parental A549. Evo treatment also increased intracellular reactive oxygen species generation, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, DNA damage, and apoptotic cell death. Furthermore, Evo modulated the expression of the identified hub genes in NSCLC cells, supporting their potential involvement in its anticancer activity. Collectively, the integrated bioinformatics, molecular docking, molecular dynamics, and experimental findings identify SPP1, GPX3, HBEGF, and KLF2 as potential molecular regulators associated with cisplatin resistance and demonstrate the multi-target anticancer activity of Evo against cisplatin-sensitive and cisplatin-resistant NSCLC, supporting its potential as a therapeutic candidate for overcoming cisplatin resistance.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05107-0.
authors: Patra SK, Rajeshwari R, Barik K, Kumar A, Biswal BK.

title: AURKA, BIRC5 and AURKB as core signature genes associated with endocrine-disrupting chemical exposure in Hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: PurposeThis study aimed to systematically explore the molecular mechanisms of Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) induced by endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) and identify core signature genes with clinical utility.MethodsBioinformatics analysis, machine learning, and in vitro experiments were integrated. TCGA-LIHC (The Cancer Genome Atlas-Liver Hepatocellular carcinoma) and GSE76427 datasets were used for target screening and validation. Toxicological analysis, target prediction, functional enrichment, Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network, and three machine learning algorithms were applied to prioritize signature genes. In vitro experiments verified the effects of single EDC on HCC cells and gene dependence.ResultsAURKA (Aurora Kinase A), BIRC5 (Baculoviral IAP Repeat Containing 5) and AURKB (Aurora Kinase B) were identified as core signature genes, consistently upregulated in HCC with AUC (area under the curve) > 0.77. Their low expression correlated with better survival rate. EDCs (e.g., MBP) promoted HCC proliferation and invasion, which was dependent on AURKA. Signature genes negatively correlated with anti-tumor immune infiltration.ConclusionAURKA, BIRC5, and AURKB were identified as candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets potentially mediating EDC-induced HCC, providing insights into EDC-related hepatocarcinogenesis mechanisms.
authors: Liu Q, Zhu H, Gao H, Yang F, Zhang S, Wang X, Hao Y, Niu Z, Zhou X.

title: Metabolic cascades drive spatial prebiotic fermentation in a defined gut consortium
abstract: Dietary fiber deficiency shifts the gut microbiota to degrade host mucus, compromising intestinal homeostasis. Mechanistically linking in vitro metabolic dynamics of fiber degradation to in vivo outcomes remains challenging due to a lack of representative model systems. Introducing spatial mucin structures to a defined Oligo-Mouse-Microbiota (OMM12) in vitro consortium allowed us to recapitulate the spatio-temporal dynamics of xylooligosaccharide (XOS) processing in gnotobiotic mice. XOS supplementation rapidly established a stable community state in vitro and in vivo across compositional, metabolic and transcriptional levels. XOS supplementation established distinct functional guilds: Bifidobacterium animalis and Blautia coccoides partitioning xylose and arabinose catabolism, whilst profiting from XOS degradation by Bacteroides caecimuris. Along the colonic axis, a spatial XOS gradient exposes Bl. coccoides's substrate preference for xylose and drives longitudinal functional adaptations. Altogether, our predictive platform proves that regional microenvironments govern prebiotic efficacy, highlighting spatial cascades as essential parameters for targeted microbiome interventions.
authors: Berthold DL, Realini NR, Sichert A, Hausmann A, Sauer U.

title: Integrative multi-omics re-analysis of public sequencing and metabolomics repositories defines the mucosal immune and metabolic landscape of  Helicobacter pylori  infection and supports CagW as a rational mRNA-LNP vaccine antigen
abstract: Background  Helicobacter pylori colonises 40-45% of the global population, is a WHO Group I carcinogen, and is increasingly hard to eradicate amid rising resistance; no vaccine is licensed. CagW, a VirB6-family cagPAI component, has been advanced as a DNA-vaccine antigen that protects mice; a codon-optimised CagW-Fc mRNA in lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNP) is a candidate antigen design intended to engage humoral and cellular immunity. To define the infected gastric mucosal niche in which such a vaccine must operate, we mined public sequencing, single-cell and metabolomics repositories.  Methods  NCBI GEO, MetaboLights and NCBI Protein were interrogated. Bulk transcriptomes of  H. pylori -infected vs uninfected gastric epithelial cells (GSE295523; 24 libraries: HGC27, AGS, MKN45, GES-1) were re-analysed with a cell-line-blocked design; DEGs (BH-adjusted) were annotated via g:Profiler (GO, KEGG, Reactome) and 13 functional signatures scored. Single-cell composition was quantified from a mouse gastric scRNA-seq atlas (GSE224840; 16,434 cells) and sorted gastric CD8+ tissue-resident memory (TRM) vs splenic memory T cells (GSE216894). Targeted gastric metabolomics was re-analysed for epithelial ornithine decarboxylase (Odc) deletion (MTBLS3235) and cystathionine-gamma-lyase (Cth) deletion (MTBLS2851). CagW conservation was computed across 400 NCBI records (286 variants) with Kyte-Doolittle topology and four B cell epitope scales.  Results  Infection induced 326 up- and 115 down-regulated genes (FDR  1), dominated by TNF/NF-kappaB (KEGG hsa04668, P=5.5×10-11), integrated stress response (ATF4-CHAC1-DDIT3-TRIB3-ASNS) and Th17 chemokines (CXCL8 +3.43, CCL20 +1.32, CXCL1 +1.30, IL23A +1.02). MHC-I presentation rose (Delta-z +0.76; MHC-II unchanged); the arginine/polyamine module (SLC7A1 +1.19, ARG2 +1.33, SAT1 +1.50, ODC1 +0.58) was co-induced. scRNA-seq showed immune expansion in infected mucosa (39.8% vs 21.2% cells; OR 2.46; cell-level frequencies reported descriptively because cells are not independent; direction confirmed at sample level, n=4 vs 4), driven by plasmacytoid DCs (OR 8.9), neutrophils (OR 3.0), macrophages (OR 2.7) and cDCs (OR 2.1), with epithelial de-differentiation. Gastric CD8+ TRM cells showed a residency-effector program (Itgae +6.2, Cd69 +2.3, Gzmb +4.8, Ifng +5.3) with egress-gene loss (Sell -11.4, S1pr1 -9.7, Klf2 -5.2). Metabolomics confirmed both nodes: Odc deletion raised arginine (+3.08) and Cth deletion raised spermidine (+0.40) while lowering leukotriene B4 (-0.33). CagW was conserved across 286 variants (median 98.3% identity; 96.4% residues >=95% conserved), carried four transmembrane helices, and showed a surface-biased conserved epitope envelope at residues 505-530 and 63-79. Conclusions  Public multi-omics define an NF-kappaB/ATF4-driven, Th17-polarised, metabolically stressed niche where antigen-presenting cells expand, epithelium de-differentiates, and CD8+ TRM cells act locally. Here CagW is exceptional among cagPAI antigens: near-universal conservation plus an accessible, conserved surface. These findings provide a systems-level rationale for prioritising CagW as a conserved, epitope-accessible vaccine antigen and inform next-generation multi-antigen designs.
authors: Zhao Y, Cheng H, Zhou S, He L, Xiu C, Huang B, Lu X.

title: In vivo frataxin expression of a triplex purified minicircle.
abstract: Friedreich's ataxia (FRDA) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by (GAA•TTC)n repeat expansions in the Frataxin (FXN) gene, resulting in reduced expression of Frataxin, a mitochondrial protein essential for energy production and iron-sulfur cluster assembly. Minicircles (MCs) are non-viral DNA vectors offering improved safety and efficiency over conventional plasmids. We used a novel method to purify MCs using biotin-conjugated triplex-forming and strand-invading oligonucleotides (ONs). A 21 bp H-DNA-forming sequence was incorporated into the plasmids to enhance binding specificity of the ONs. The ON-plasmid complexes were removed using streptavidin magnetic beads. This approach yielded highly purified MCs. In FRDA patient-derived fibroblasts, the purified MCs expressed FXN mRNA and restored Frataxin protein levels to those observed in healthy cells, demonstrating the therapeutic potential of this approach. More interestingly, MC-FXN treatment of an FRDA mouse model using hydrodynamic tail vein injection resulted in an 18-fold and 3-fold increase of Frataxin in the mice livers and hearts, respectively, supporting the translational relevance of this modality.
authors: Mozafari N, Milagres S, Cuellar R, Lundin KE, Fredriks M, Ho TT, Azam MDG, Napierala JS, Napierala M, Wengel J, Smith CIE, Blomberg P, Zain R.

title: Analysis of antiviral effects of anti-EGFR DNA aptamers against African swine fever virus in Vero cells.
abstract: African swine fever virus (ASFV) causes high mortality in pigs and severe socio-economic losses worldwide. With no effective vaccines or antiviral drugs currently available, novel therapeutic strategies are urgently needed. Since ASFV exploits the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) for host cell entry, targeting EGFR could reduce viral uptake. We developed novel EGFR-specific DNA aptamers and investigated their anti-ASFV and virucidal activities using cytopathic effect (CPE)-based assays in Vero cells. Aptamer safety was evaluated by assessing cytotoxicity and genotoxicity using the MTT and comet assays, respectively. Aptamers showed no virucidal, cytotoxic, or genotoxic activity. Treatment of Vero cells with the dimeric anti-EGFR aptamer significantly reduced viral titers by 47% at 10 μM without cytotoxic or genotoxic effects. We also report, for the first time, that cetuximab (an anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody) at concentrations 0.017 and 0.034 μM reduced ASFV titers by 43-57% comparable to that of the dimeric aptamer. These findings identify the dimeric anti-EGFR aptamer as a promising compound for further analysis of antiviral effectiveness against ASFV in porcine macrophages in vitro and in vivo.
authors: Hakobyan A, Hovhannisyan G, Harutyunyan T, Sargsyan A, Igityan H, Zakaryan H, Nechaev A, Alieva R, Oleynikov I, Tashlitsky V, Aroutiounian R, Zavyalova E.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-directed engineering of Clostridium beijerinckii enhanced butanol production from whey permeate.
abstract: Whey permeate (WP), an abundant, lactose-rich byproduct of the dairy industry, constitutes an environmental and economic burden on the industry. Despite the high fermentable sugar content of WP, its bioconversion to biobutanol is limited by poor lactose-utilization culminating in low solvent productivity by native solventogenic microorganisms. In this study, we report CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome engineering of Clostridium beijerinckii NCIMB 8052 (hereafter, C. beijerinckii) to improve butanol production from lactose-rich WP. A native putative lactose transporter encoded by Cbei_4545 and an aldehyde reductase (mgR) from Clostridium pasteurianum were integrated into the chromosome of C. beijerinckii at the acetoacetate decarboxylase gene locus to improve lactose utilization and solvent production. The resulting recombinant strain was evaluated alongside the wildtype using lactose, untreated WP, and ion exchange (Amberlite™) resin-treated WP. Across all feedstocks tested, the recombinant strain consistently outperformed the wildtype, producing peak butanol titers of 7.9 g/L, 9.7 g/L, and 20.9 g/L on lactose, WP, and resin-treated WP, respectively, compared to 4.3 g/L, 7.1 g/L, and 11.3 g/L for the wildtype. These results demonstrate the utility of targeted CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering to substantially improve lactose utilization and butanol production in C. beijerinckii. In this work we constructed a strain of C. beijerinckii with strong potential for conversion of abundant and cost-effective WP to biobutanol.
authors: Okereke O, Duduyemi A, Ujor VC.

title: DNA-PK inhibition overcomes resistance to oncolytic virotherapy.
abstract: Oncolytic virotherapy is a promising therapeutic strategy that uses replication-competent viruses to selectively destroy malignancies. However, the therapeutic effect of certain oncolytic viruses (OVs) varies among cancer patients. Thus, it is necessary to overcome resistance to OVs through rationally designed combination strategies. Here, through an anticancer drug screening, we show that DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PK) inhibition sensitizes cancer cells to OV M1 and improves therapeutic effects in refractory cancer models in vivo and in patient tumour samples. Infection of M1 virus triggers the transcription of interferons (IFNs) and the activation of the antiviral response, which can be abolished by pretreatment of DNA-PK inhibitor (DNA-PKI), resulting in selectively enhanced replication of OV M1 within malignancies. Furthermore, DNA-PK inhibition promotes the DNA damage response induced by M1 virus, leading to increased tumour cell apoptosis. Together, our study identifies the combination of DNA-PKI and OV M1 as a potential treatment for cancers.
journal: Translational research : the journal of laboratory and clinical medicine
authors: Xiao X, Liang J, Huang C, Li K, Xing F, Zhu W, Lin Z, Xu W, Wu G, Zhang J, Lin X, Tan Y, Cai J, Hu J, Chen X, Huang Y, Qin Z, Qiu P, Su X, Chen L, Lin Y, Zhang H, Yan G.

title: cGAS-STING dependent immunity in insects: insights from Drosophila flies.
abstract: The cGAS-STING pathway constitutes an evolutionarily ancient antiviral defense mechanism, originating in bacteria. It is conserved in most animals, although with some differences. In insects, the model Drosophila melanogaster provides unique opportunities to decipher the function and regulation of this important pathway in hosts beyond mammals and shed light on its evolution. Here, we review recent advances in Drosophila that clarify the relationship between the cGAS-STING and IMD pathways, which both act through the NF-κB transcription factor Relish. We next consider the expansion of the cGLR family in Drosophila flies and the unexpected discovery of new cyclic dinucleotides (CDNs) besides cGAMP. We present the contribution of these CDNs in induction of systemic immunity and immune training in flies and discuss the conservation of these properties in other insects.
authors: Cai H, Wei Z, Huang J, Duan X, Imler JL.

title: Identifying phase separation modulators mediated by the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein using a structure-based drug discovery approach.
abstract: IntroductionAs severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to evolve through mutations and acquire resistance to existing antiviral agents, the persistence of post-pandemic infections remains a significant global health concern. To address these challenges, it is crucial to develop novel therapeutic agents that target previously unexplored viral or host mechanisms.ObjectivesThe nucleocapsid (N) protein of SARS-CoV-2 plays a critical role in viral RNA replication and genome packaging through its ability to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). Targeting the condensation of N-RNA complex could potentially serve as an effective therapeutic strategy against coronavirus infections. The present study provides a successful exemplification of antiviral agent discovery by targeting the viral N protein on the basis of its structural characteristics.MethodsA total of 23 virtual screening compounds and 16 hit derivatives were prepared. Their binding affinity and antiviral activities were evaluated using surface plasmon resonance and immunofluorescence assay, respectively. The impact of these compounds on condensate formation was verified through fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, as well as the inhibition of N condensate formation in cells.ResultsStructure-based virtual screening, target protein binding affinity quantification, and cell culture-based anti-SARS-CoV-2 assays enabled the identification a hit compound, D21. Subsequent structural optimization of series I and II yielded compound II8, which exhibits stronger binding affinity for the N protein and effectively inhibits the formation of N-RNA condensates, thereby demonstrating its potential to modulate LLPS, a mechanism underlying its antiviral activity. In vivo evaluation showed that II8 displays antiviral activity in a human ACE2-expressing mouse model when administered intranasally as a pre-incubated mixture with SARS-CoV-2. Due to the pharmacokinetic profile of compound II8, further structural modifications are still required.ConclusionOur findings suggest that compound II8 may serve as a localized prophylactic nasal spray, providing valuable insights for further development of LLPS modulators as next-generation antiviral agents.
authors: Du S, Jang Y, Hu X, Li P, Wang B, Ra HS, Kang D, Wang X, Wang N, Liu X, Kim M, Zhan P.

title: A zinc-sequestering polymer disrupts zinc homeostasis to suppress fungal viability and virulence.
abstract: Zinc is a central structural cofactor in fungi, supporting transcriptional control and mitochondrial function, and its tightly regulated homeostasis presents an underexploited antifungal intervention point. Targeting zinc-dependent architectures offers a mechanistically distinct alternative to conventional membrane- or cell wall-directed antifungals. Here we report a zinc- deprivation fungicide (ZDF) by grafting high-affinity bipyridine chelators onto ε-poly-l-lysine, enabling intracellular sequestration of labile zinc without overt membrane disruption. ZDF-induced zinc depletion disrupts zinc-dependent RNA processing, particularly mitochondrial tRNA modification, thereby collapsing mitochondrial translation, impairing oxidative phosphorylation, and inducing profound energetic failure. ZDF further remodels zinc-dependent regulatory networks, downregulating drug efflux to restore azole-resistant strains and suppressing biofilm maturation via zinc-responsive Zap1-Dpp1-farnesol axis. This strategy shows high selectivity over mammalian cells, and outperforms clinical azoles in murine cutaneous wound and rabbit keratitis models. By employing the unique role of zinc as an essential structural cofactor for fungal transcriptional regulators, this work defines intracellular zinc sequestration as a non-membrane-directed antifungal strategy that exploits a central regulatory dependency in fungi.
journal: Journal of controlled release : official journal of the Controlled Release Society
authors: Sun X, Rong S, Qiu Y, Yu Z, Shen F, Sun Y, Lin Z, Cheng Y, Hu J.

title: Integrating single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing with ML algorithms identified MYBL2 as a candidate transcriptomic biomarker for diagnosing laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC).
abstract: Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC) poses significant clinical challenges due to pronounced tumor heterogeneity. To identify robust, consistent biomarkers across cohorts, we integrated bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data from GSE127165 and GSE142083 and validated candidate biomarkers in the external cohort GSE13060. Candidate gene prioritization incorporated differentially expressed genes, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) results, and markers of malignant epithelial cells exhibiting high copy number variation (High-CNV) derived from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) (GSE206332). Additional analyses included functional enrichment, immune association (adjusted for tumor purity), quasi-temporal analysis, and CellChat inference to elucidate the biological roles of top genes. The integrated approach identified 254 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), comprising 86 upregulated and 168 downregulated genes. WGCNA revealed a tumor-associated module containing 870 genes. Intersecting these findings with high-CNV malignant epithelial markers reduced the candidate pool to 16 genes, and LASSO regression retained five key features: MYBL2, KRT17, UCHL1, PTHLH, and ODC1. Among these, MYBL2 demonstrated the strongest and most consistent performance. MYBL2 was further associated with proliferative programs, including E2F targets, the G2/M checkpoint, DNA repair, and MYC targets. Gene signatures from these subclusters were enriched in bulk tumors and positively correlated with MYBL2 expression in independent cohorts. The results also indicate that MYBL2-high malignant epithelial states are linked to distinct connectivity patterns within the tumor microenvironment.
authors: Mehrabi T, Isavi M, Gholami A, Hamidieh AA, Heidarzadeh-Pilehrood R.

title: Dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR delivery systems for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma.
abstract: Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy, and effective gene therapy remains limited by ocular barriers, tumor heterogeneity, and inefficient nucleic acid delivery. This review critically analyses the molecular rationale, engineering principles, emerging nanoarchitectures, biological validation, and translational prospects of dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR delivery systems for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma. The manuscript also highlights key challenges and future strategies for clinical implementation. Current evidence indicates that dual-vector platforms enable independent optimization of mRNA and CRISPR cargos while maintaining coordinated spatiotemporal therapeutic activity. We conducted a literature search in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for relevant studies published from January 2015 to September 2026. Functional cargo partitioning, vector modularity, programmable intracellular trafficking, and ocular-targeted nanoengineering improve delivery precision and reduce biological compromise associated with co-encapsulation. Lipid, polymeric, hybrid, biomimetic, and viral-nonviral architectures each provide distinct engineering advantages depending on therapeutic objectives. Preclinical studies support enhanced genome editing, transient protein restoration, improved tumor suppression, and reduced off-target effects. Nevertheless, manufacturing scalability, regulatory standardization, long-term safety, and clinical validation remain major barriers to translation. Dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR systems represent a promising next-generation platform for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma by enabling coordinated and programmable therapeutic delivery. Continued advances in modular nanoengineering, personalized cargo selection, and clinically scalable manufacturing will be essential for successful translation into precision ocular oncology.
authors: Thakur SK, Malviya R, Chandra P, Sridhar SB, Shareef J, Wadhwa T.

title: Systematic assessment of transcriptomic and phenotypic biological profiling for mechanism-based hazard assessment using target-annotated reference chemicals in renal proximal tubular epithelial cells.
abstract: Integrating high-throughput in vitro data into next-generation risk assessment (NGRA) workflows requires screening strategies that yield quantitative potency estimates and mechanistically interpretable biological signals. Transcriptomic and morphological profiling are increasingly adopted for early-stage hazard identification by enabling triage of substances for resource-intensive follow-up and prioritizing candidates most likely to present meaningful risk. In this study, we aimed to characterize biological concordance and uncertainty by quantifying how well high-throughput transcriptomics (HTTr) and Cell Painting PLUS (CPP) bioactivity profiles recover target-relevant biological signals in immortalized human renal proximal tubule epithelial RPTEC/TERT1 cells using 313 reference chemicals with high-confidence target annotations. Through quality control procedures and biological activity filters we yielded 142 reference chemicals spanning 66 different targets, which were systematically evaluated for biological concentration-responses by HTTr and CPP. HTTr was evaluated using TXG-MAPr-based qualitative and quantitative gene network activity analysis. HTTr showed the most prominent activity for targets that were highest expressed in RPTEC/TERT1 cells. Active chemical-pairs showed strong gene network activity correlation albeit with different potencies. Similarly, the highest transcriptomic concordance was observed for reference chemicals acting in the same pathway, such as EGFR/MEK or PI3K/AKT/mTOR. CPP often showed high sensitivity primarily at the organelle level providing limited mechanistic insight for chemical grouping. Collectively, the results support HTTr and CPP as complementary early-tier assays within an in vitro weight-of-evidence safety testing framework. Although CPP is suitable as a cost-effective screening modality, HTTr offers higher mechanistic resolution for mode-of-action inference in high-throughput bioactivity screening and therefore remains necessary for high-confidence mechanistic interpretation.
authors: van Kessel HW, Wedler M, Helmke PS, Žīgure D, Ferguson SS, Harrill J, Ecker G, Liu S, Oelgeschläger M, Callegaro G, van de Water B.

title: JrTTG2 confers drought tolerance in walnut via the JrGSTU8-mediated antioxidant pathway and interaction with JrEPSIN1.
abstract: Drought significantly limits the productivity and quality of Juglans regia, yet the regulatory mechanisms governing drought tolerance in this economically vital nut tree remain largely elusive. Here, we report that the WRKY transcription factor JrTTG2 acts as a central hub in the walnut drought response by integrating transcriptional and protein-interaction networks. We identified JrTTG2 as a hypersensitive early-response gene, exhibiting a robust 333-fold induction in walnut roots under drought stress. Ectopic expression of JrTTG2 in Arabidopsis and poplar significantly enhanced drought tolerance, primarily by maintaining root architecture, increasing biomass, and reducing oxidative damage. Conversely, RNAi-mediated silencing of PagTTG2 in poplar led to stunted root systems and compromised antioxidant defense under water deficit. Transcriptomic and molecular analyses revealed that JrTTG2 directly binds to the W-box in the promoter of the JrGSTU8 gene to activate its transcription, thereby facilitating ROS scavenging. Furthermore, yeast two-hybrid and BiFC assays demonstrated that JrTTG2 physically interacts with the vesicle trafficking protein JrEPSIN1. Both JrGSTU8 and JrEPSIN1 showed highly synchronized induction with JrTTG2 in walnut roots during drought. Taken together, this study provides a novel dimension to the molecular mechanisms of woody plant adaptation and offers a promising candidate gene for breeding drought-tolerant walnut varieties.
authors: Li D, Peng S, Lu Y, Xie M, Wang T, Chen S, Xu ZF, Yang G.

title: Multimodal profiling and intersectional genetics reveal CA1 border inhibitory neuron diversity and postnatal emergence of retrosplenial connectivity
abstract: ABSTRACT  Inhibitory neurons (INs) at the stratum radiatum/stratum lacunosum-moleculare border of hippocampal CA1 comprise diverse populations, including long-range-projecting neurons that innervate the retrosplenial cortex (RSCtx). However, their molecular organization and developmental connectivity remain poorly understood. Here, we combine multimodal transcriptomic profiling, intersectional genetics, and retrograde tracing to characterize CA1 border INs. We identified two major caudal ganglionic eminence-derived,  Cxcl14 -enriched populations distinguished by  Syt6/Cck -related and  Ntng1 -expressing transcriptional profiles. We then generated a  Cxcl14 -Cre mouse line that, when combined with an IN-specific viral enhancer, provides genetic access to CA1 border INs. Retrograde labeling established that CA1 INs projecting to the RSCtx belong to the  Ntng1 -expressing population, and that this long-range projection emerges during postnatal mouse development, between postnatal days 3 and 5. Finally, analysis of genes encoding cell-surface proteins, key regulators of connectivity, revealed distinct expression profiles in RSCtx-projecting and SYT6-positive INs. Together, these findings establish a molecular and developmental framework for CA1 border IN diversity and provide a genetic strategy for investigating the assembly and function of these inhibitory circuits.
authors: Martínez Vizcaíno N, Thrupp N, Lorente-Echeverría B, Daaboul D, Alabi M, Milián Alastruey C, Linaro D, Fourne Y, Vandenbempt J, Lukacsovich D, Földy C, Lamote J, Wojno M, Poovathingal S, Fiers M, Wierda K, Lim L, Calafate S, de Wit J.

title: APOSTART1 and APOSTART2 role in female gametophyte progression in Arabidopsis thaliana.
abstract: Main conclusionAtAPOSTART1 and AtAPOSTART2 contribute to female gametophyte development in Arabidopsis thaliana, with their mutation affecting megaspore degeneration and female gametophyte progression. Apomixis is a form of asexual seed reproduction that allows clonal plant propagation. Because it does not naturally occur in major crop species, its introduction could enable the fixation of elite hybrid genomes, leading to consistent high-quality yields of grains, fruits, and vegetables. Despite its significance, many aspects of apomictic reproduction remain poorly understood. PpAPOSTART6 was previously identified as a promising candidate gene associated with apomixis in Poa pratensis, a species exhibiting aposporic apomixis. PpAPOSTART6 is expressed in sexual Poa pratensis ovules throughout development, whereas in apomictic accessions, its expression is delayed at later stages of -ovule development. To gain further insight into PpAPOSTART6 function, we have studied the expression and function of its closest orthologs in Arabidopsis thaliana, AtAPO1 and AtAPO2 (formerly EDR2). Analysis of atapo1 atapo2 double mutant revealed defects in spore degeneration and in the proper differentiation of the functional megaspore and subsequent female gametophyte development, supporting a role for AtAPO1 and AtAPO2 in the degeneration of non-functional megaspores. Together with subcellular localization analyses and genetic evidences, our results support a role for AtAPO1 and AtAPO2 in megaspore degeneration, potentially involving programmed cell death and mitochondrial function. These findings provide a functional framework for further investigating PpAPOSTART6 association in apomixis regulation.
authors: Petrella R, Gabrieli F, Cavalleri A, Marconi G, Cucinotta M, Albertini E, Colombo L.

title: cAMP receptor proteins in mycobacteria.
abstract: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling is a major regulatory system in mycobacteria, and the cAMP receptor protein (CRP) serves as its principal transcriptional effector. In Mycobacterium tuberculosis, CRP controls a broad regulon associated with metabolic adaptation, respiration, cell envelope-associated processes, dormancy-related resuscitation, and virulence. Structural and biophysical studies have demonstrated that mycobacterial CRPs differ from the classical Escherichia coli paradigm: apo-CRP adopts restrained or asymmetric conformations, whereas cAMP binding promotes a more symmetric, DNA-binding-competent state and enhances the specificity of CRP-DNA interactions. In Mycobacterium smegmatis, the major paralog Crp1 (MSMEG_6189) regulates metabolic and respiratory adaptation, oxidative stress defense, and isoniazid susceptibility, whereas Crp2 (MSMEG_0539) appears to play a more limited or subsidiary role. Recent findings further reveal that CRP activity is modulated by lysine acetylation, cooperative promoter recruitment with the virulence-associated response regulator PhoP, and respiratory inhibition-induced increases in intracellular cAMP, thereby linking metabolic and respiratory status to adaptive and virulence-associated gene regulation. This review summarizes the structure, allosteric regulation, regulon, and physiological functions of mycobacterial CRPs, highlighting their role as central integrators of cAMP signaling, respiratory and metabolic state, persistence-associated physiology, and antibiotic susceptibility.
authors: Oh JI, Oh Y, Hwang Y.

title: SerRS2 Identifies an Inflamed-Exhausted Hepatocellular Carcinoma Phenotype with Enhanced DNA-Sensing and Increased Anti-PD-1 Responsiveness.
abstract: BackgroundSeryl-tRNA synthetase 2 (SerRS2, encoded by SARS2) is a mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase essential for mitochondrial protein translation and homeostasis. Its clinical and immunological significance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains unclear.MethodsTranscriptomic and clinical data from 371 TCGA-LIHC patients were analyzed to evaluate SerRS2 expression, prognosis, immune infiltration, T-cell exhaustion, and DNA-sensing-related features. Four single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets were analyzed to characterize the cellular distribution of SerRS2. Public immunotherapy cohorts were evaluated for associations between SerRS2 expression and immune checkpoint blockade outcomes, and an independent HCC cohort was used for qPCR validation. Group comparisons were performed using Student's t-test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test, correlations using Pearson or Spearman analyses, and survival outcomes using Kaplan-Meier analysis with the Log rank test, as appropriate.ResultsSerRS2 was significantly upregulated in HCC and associated with advanced pathological stage and poorer survival. Elevated SerRS2 expression was consistently associated with increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration and exhausted T-cell abundance and positively correlated with PDCD1, TOX, LAG3, HAVCR2, and CTLA4. SerRS2 was also positively associated with cGAS (MB21D1) and DDX41, but not STING1, and SerRS2-high tumors exhibited increased exhaustion and DNA-sensing scores. Collectively, these findings support a SerRS2-associated inflamed-exhausted immune phenotype characterized by increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration, T-cell exhaustion-related features, and enrichment of DNA-sensing-related transcriptional programs. Single-cell analyses revealed heterogeneous SerRS2 expression across multiple cellular compartments, supporting its interpretation as a tissue-level rather than tumor-cell-specific signal. In public cross-tumor immunotherapy cohorts, elevated SerRS2 expression was associated with improved outcomes following PD-1 blockade, whereas comparable associations were not consistently observed for PD-L1 or CTLA-4 blockade, suggesting potential relevance of the SerRS2-associated immune phenotype to PD-1 blockade. These immune associations were further supported by qPCR validation in an independent HCC cohort.ConclusionSerRS2 is associated with an inflamed-exhausted immune phenotype in HCC and may represent a candidate tissue-level biomarker for immune stratification. Its potential relevance to PD-1 blockade warrants prospective validation in HCC-specific immunotherapy cohorts.
authors: Li P, Zhu G, Li D, Liang M, Zhang L, Li J, Jia Y, Zou B.

title: Targeting Skin Hyperpigmentation with Nature-Derived Tyrosinase Inhibitors: Sources, Mechanisms, and Translational Challenges.
abstract: Skin hyperpigmentation represents a highly prevalent dermatological issue that severely affects skin appearance and quality of life. Tyrosinase is well recognized as the critical rate-limiting enzyme in the melanin biosynthesis pathway, making it a prime target for skin-lightening interventions. Although synthetic depigmenting agents are widely used in cosmetics, their clinical applications are severely restricted by safety concerns, skin irritation, and chemical instability. In recent years, natural tyrosinase inhibitors originating from plants, fungi, marine organisms, and microbial metabolites have attracted extensive attention due to their promising efficacy, structural diversity, and multi-target activities, although long-term clinical and systemic safety data remain limited. This review comprehensively summarizes the molecular mechanisms underlying melanogenesis inhibition by natural compounds, their major biological sources, and representative active components, as well as key evidence from in vitro enzymatic assays, cellular models, and human clinical trials. We further discuss critical challenges in formulation development, including chemical instability, insufficient skin permeability, and safety considerations for long-term topical use. Finally, future research directions and translational opportunities are explored. By integrating recent advances and unresolved bottlenecks, this review aims to provide a scientific basis and rational guidance for the design and development of safe and effective natural-based skin-lightening products.
authors: Sun Z, Li Y, Wang X, Wang R, Ma W.

title: MicroRNA-26 Family in Human Diseases: Context-Dependent Regulation, Biomarker Potential, and Preclinical Nano-Delivery Strategies.
abstract: PurposeThis review aims to summarize the expression patterns, molecular mechanisms, and preclinical nanodelivery strategies of microRNA-26 (miR-26) family members, and to critically evaluate their potential as biomarker candidates and preclinical therapeutic targets in human diseases, including cancers, cardiovascular diseases, metabolic disorders, and neurodegenerative conditions.MethodsA structured narrative review was performed in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar from database inception to August 2026. Peer-reviewed original articles and reviews in English were included. Data on miR-26 isoform expression, target genes, signaling pathways, therapeutic modulators, and nanocarrier systems were extracted and narratively synthesized. A four-tier evidence classification system (Levels I-IV) was applied to distinguish well-established findings from speculative or inferred associations.ResultsmiR-26 family members-predominantly miR-26a-5p and miR-26b-5p-are highly conserved small non-coding RNAs that post-transcriptionally regulate proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, metabolism, and immunity in an isoform-specific and context-dependent manner. In most solid tumors, miR-26a-5p and miR-26b-5p are downregulated and function as tumor suppressors, although context-dependent oncogenic roles exist. Circulating and tissue miR-26 isoform levels show statistically significant associations with diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment response in several cancers, supporting their utility as biomarker candidates. However, direct miR-26 mimics or inhibitors remain exclusively preclinical, with no human clinical trials initiated to date. Lipid-, polymer-, and inorganic-based nanocarriers are being explored in preclinical models, but their precision, safety, and biodistribution require systematic validation. Clinical-stage agents targeting downstream effectors of miR-26-regulated pathways do not constitute direct miR-26 modulation and should not be presented as miR-26 therapeutics.ConclusionmiR-26 family members serve as versatile regulatory hubs and biologically plausible biomarker and preclinical therapeutic target candidates. At present, miR-26 should be viewed primarily as a validated biomarker associate and a promising preclinical target-not as an established therapeutic modality. CRISPRa, microbiome-miR-26 interactions, and AI-assisted nanorobots remain future hypotheses rather than established translational strategies.
authors: Wang R, Ge R, Li Z, He Z, Pan Y, Zhao X.

title: Dietary caffeic acid phenethyl ester alleviates copper-induced hepatointestinal damage by modulating lipid metabolism, intestinal microbiota, and oxidative-inflammatory responses in yellow catfish (Pelteobagrus fulvidraco).
abstract: The widespread application of copper (Cu) in aquaculture poses severe hepatointestinal toxicity risks to teleosts. This study investigated the ameliorative effects of dietary caffeic acid phenethyl ester (CAPE) on Cu-induced hepatointestinal damage in yellow catfish (Pelteobagrus fulvidraco). Following a four-week feeding trial with graded CAPE (0, 200 (LCAPE), and 1000 mg/kg (HCAPE)) intervention and a subsequent 7-day Cu challenge (0.8 mg/L), Cu-exposed fish exhibited elevated mortality, growth retardation, hepatic steatosis, and systemic oxidative stress. Concurrently, Cu toxicity disrupted the intestinal microecology by depleting commensal taxa potentially associated with host homeostasis (e.g., Phyllobacterium and Methylobacterium) and favouring stress-associated or potentially opportunistic taxa (e.g., Sediminibacterium and Bradyrhizobium). Conversely, CAPE intervention, particularly the HCAPE group, effectively improved survival rate, fortified intestinal physical barriers (increased goblet cell number and zo1 expression), and alleviated hepatic triglyceride accumulation. CAPE intervention enhanced intestinal and hepatic antioxidative capacity and alleviated Cu-induced lipid dysmetabolism and tissue lesions, which might be associated with the potential regulation of the SIRT1/FXR signalling axis and the PKC/p38MAPK/NF-κB inflammatory pathway. However, the LCAPE group did not resolve transcriptional inflammation, exhibiting elevated hepatic nfκb and il1β as well as increased intestinal il1β and reduced zo1 expression relative to the Cu group. Furthermore, CAPE induced a dose-dependent modulation of the intestinal microbiota composition; the LCAPE group significantly restructured the taxonomic composition, enriching commensal genera such as Variovorax while reducing the relative abundance of potentially opportunistic genera including Sediminibacterium and Staphylococcus. In contrast, the HCAPE group exhibited negligible genus-level differences compared to the Cu group. In conclusion, dietary CAPE alleviates Cu-induced hepatointestinal injury in yellow catfish, an effect associated with improved lipid metabolic parameters, altered intestinal microbial composition, and enhanced antioxidative and anti-inflammatory defences, highlighting its protective application in fish under Cu exposure.
journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part D, Genomics & proteomics
authors: Wang L, Xue X, Li Y, Cao J, Wang S, Li J, Liu S, Chu L.

title: Microplastics amplify Cr(VI)-mediated RP4 plasmid conjugative transfer through coupled interfacial, oxidative, and metabolic regulation.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) can accumulate heavy metals and influence plasmid-mediated antibiotic resistance gene (ARGs) transfer, yet the regulatory mechanisms under metal-associated MP exposure remain poorly understood. Here, a polystyrene microplastic-Cr(VI) composite (PSMPs@Cr) was established to investigate RP4 plasmid conjugative transfer by integrating physicochemical characterization, physiological measurements, transcriptomic analysis, and multivariable modeling. PSMPs@Cr exhibited a non-monotonic effect on conjugative transfer, with the highest conjugative transfer frequency (9.4 × 10-2) observed at 20 ppm Cr loading, representing a 4.75-fold increase compared with the control. Cr adsorption reconstructed the MP interface by modifying surface charge, wettability, morphology, and colloidal stability, which was accompanied by altered bacterial adhesion behavior. Meanwhile, PSMPs@Cr exposure induced coordinated changes in ROS accumulation, antioxidant responses, ATP production, membrane-associated functions, and energy metabolism. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed treatment-dependent regulation of oxidative stress, membrane transport, cellular communication, and metabolic pathways. Random forest-SHAP analysis identified zeta potential, CAT activity, ATP, and ROS as relatively important variables associated with CTF variation. Overall, PSMPs@Cr-associated ARGs transfer was linked to coupled interfacial, redox, and energetic processes rather than a single regulatory pathway, providing new insights into how microplastic-metal interactions influence plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer under complex contaminant exposure scenarios.
authors: Zhang L, Zhang J, Pan H, Li H, Guo H, Wang T.

title: Environmental determinants of large vessel vasculitis onset: a scoping review with complementary narrative synthesis of genetic susceptibility.
abstract: ObjectivesLarge vessel vasculitis (LVV), including giant cell arteritis (GCA) and Takayasu arteritis (TAK), are rare immune-mediated disorders characterized by inflammation of large arteries. Epidemiological patterns, marked geographic gradients, age and sex differences, and temporal clustering, suggest that environmental factors contribute to disease onset in genetically susceptible individuals, yet no systematic mapping of this evidence exists. The study sought to systematically map current evidence on environmental exposures investigated in relation to LVV onset, identify methodological gaps, and characterize research priorities. Genetic susceptibility data were additionally synthesized to contextualize gene-environment interactions.MethodsWe conducted a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed and Embase were searched from inception to August 2026. Studies were eligible if they assessed environmental exposures in relation to GCA or TAK onset using an epidemiological design with a comparator group, Mendelian randomization, or mechanistic approach with direct relevance to human susceptibility. Genetic susceptibility was synthesized through a complementary narrative review.ResultsOf 3,596 records identified, 2,137 were screened after deduplication, and 44 studies were included in the narrative synthesis, of which 34 with established temporality and epidemiological design were summarized in a structured evidence table. Air pollution, infections, antibiotic use, hormonal exposures, and cardiometabolic factors emerge as candidate environmental modulators of LVV onset, although causal links remain uncertain. Genetic susceptibility implicates antigen presentation, immune regulation, innate immune activation, and vascular remodeling pathways, which likely modulate individual responsiveness to environmental triggers.ConclusionsThis review identifies multiple candidate environmental exposures in LVV and highlights critical methodological gaps regarding exposure timing and genomic integration. Integrative exposomic-genomic approaches represent the critical next step toward identifying modifiable risk factors and preventive strategies.
authors: Pacoureau L, Barde F, Yates M, Pagnoux C, Nguyen Y, Seror R.

title: A MultiOmics time-resolved systems map of gene regulation in  Toxoplasma gondii
abstract: Understanding how  T. gondii builds an invasion-competent cell has been limited by its rapid, asynchronous division cycle, incomplete gene function annotation, and studies that have examined one regulator or complex at a time. Here, we placed acute perturbation of 21 transcriptional and epigenetic factors, promoter occupancy, chromatin accessibility, and molecular validation on a common single-cell clock. The resulting consensus map links the lytic-cycle programs to candidate activating and repressive inputs, organizes genes into 108 co-regulated communities, and nominates regulatory partnerships that would not have emerged from any single data type. The work bridges three longstanding gaps: it resolves perturbation responses in cell-cycle time, distinguishes promoter occupancy from perturbation-linked regulation, and turns a large multidimensional dataset into an experimentally navigable map. We indeed confirmed known factor interactions such as MORC/HDAC3, and recovered combinations such as the Cdc5/SNIP1 and DMAP1/EPL1 as coregulatory nodes (that in other systems have been described to cooperate). Furthermore, we discovered a novel apicomplexan specific combination of AAF1/AP2XI-5 that provides mechanistic insights of the unique AP2 transcription factor family.
authors: Wu Y, Arriojas AA, Shankar N, Aggarwal S, Lou J, Prathap P, Dua S, Diffendall GM, Li J, Pamunuwa P, Oppong P, Graia O, Izhaki-Tavor LS, Weerapana E, Léger-Abraham M, Duraisingh MT, Zarringhalam K, Gubbels M.

title: Fe-N Bonded g-C<sub>3</sub>N<sub>4</sub>/LaFeO<sub>3</sub> S-Scheme Heterojunction Nanosheets as a Sunlight-Driven Photocatalytic Antimicrobial Platform for Marine Antifouling.
abstract: Marine biofouling poses significant challenges to maritime industries and threatens environmental sustainability and ecological security. Photocatalytic antimicrobial platform has emerged as promising antifouling strategy in marine applications. In this study, an S-scheme heterostructure of g-C3N4/LaFeO3 nanosheets with Fe─N bonding is constructed to serve as a highly efficient and stable photocatalytic antimicrobial platform for marine use. The material demonstrates excellent antifouling performance, achieving 99.9% eradication of E. coli and 100% degradation efficiency of methylene blue. Through combined experimental characterization and density functional theory calculations, a unique photochemical-physical synergistic reinforcement mechanism is proposed. The S-scheme heterojunction, featuring a built-in electric field and Fe─N electron transfer channels, not only facilitates charge transfer and separation but also lowers the reaction energy barrier of key intermediates and accelerates surface photocatalytic kinetics, thereby promoting continuous reactive oxygen species generation. Furthermore, the nanosheet structures exhibit strong electrostatic attraction toward bacterial cell membranes, leading to physical insertion and membrane damage. This synergistic mechanism contributes to outstanding antibacterial and biofilm inhibition performance. Notably, the exceptional antifouling efficacy is maintained for approximately 180 d in real marine environments. These results underscore the practical potential and feasibility of the developed platform for real-world applications in shallow sea settings.
authors: Ran L, Zhang Y, Tang Q, Leung MKH, Ran B.

title: Creation and evaluation of induced allotetraploids from wild Arachis species expands the genetic reservoir for peanut early leaf spot resistance.
abstract: Early leaf spot (ELS), caused by Passalora arachidicola, remains one of the most economically important foliar diseases of peanut (Arachis hypogaea), and resistance within the cultivated germplasm is limited. Fungicide applications are commonly used to manage this disease, but this practice increases production costs, the risk of fungicide resistance, and environmental concerns. Wild Arachis species harbor diverse resistance alleles, but their direct use in breeding is constrained by ploidy barriers. In this study, eight induced allotetraploids derived from nine wild Arachis species were produced. Along with their diploid parents, they were evaluated for ELS resistance using in vitro detached leaf bioassays. Disease resistance was quantified using multiple components, including incubation period, lesion number, sporulation, and diseased leaf area. Several allotetraploids-particularly MagDio1, MagKuhl1, MagHoeh1, and ValMicro1-exhibited significantly reduced lesion development, limited sporulation, and slower disease progression compared with cultivated controls. In all cases, induced allotetraploids displayed resistance levels equal to or greater than those of both diploid parents, indicating enhanced resistance following allotetraploidization. Notably, Arachis hoehnei and its derived allotetraploid consistently exhibited strong resistance across disease components, identifying this phylogenetically distinct species as a novel resistance source. These results demonstrate that induced allotetraploids represent peanut-compatible reservoirs of diverse ELS resistance alleles and provide practical resources for breeding programs aimed at developing cultivars with more durable and diversified resistance to early leaf spot.
authors: Dong A, Hopkins M, Bertioli D, Leal-Bertioli S.

title: Recurrent Neurodevelopmental Disorder Associated With a Dominant-Negative TOP2B H63Y Variant.
abstract: We describe a 7 year-old boy with severe neurodevelopmental disorder, medically-refractory epileptic encephalopathy, hyperkinetic movement disorder, hypotonia, cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and hypomyelination who was found to have a heterozygous de novo TOP2B NM_001330700.2:c.187C>T, p.(His63Tyr) variant. This is the third individual reported with the H63Y variant and severe neurodevelopmental disorder. The phenotype associated with the H63Y variant differs greatly from the TOP2B-related Immunodeficiency and Congenital Anomalies Spectrum (TICAS) syndrome that has been reported with heterozygous loss-of-function variants affecting the TOPRIM domain and adjacent regions of TOP2B. DNA topoisomerase II beta (TOP2B) is an essential enzyme that resolves DNA supercoils and knots to facilitate transcription and replication. To investigate the functional impact of this variant, we studied the homologous yeast variant, top2 H20Y (H20Y). Homozygous H20Y strains exhibited reduced viability, while heterozygous H20Y acted as a loss-of-function allele incapable of supporting growth. Overexpression of the chimeric human H63Y variant in yeast was lethal. Despite its dysfunction, H63Y retains partial enzymatic activity and appears to function as a dominant negative variant that induces DNA damage. Thus, this work establishes a novel gene-disease association between TOP2B-H63Y and a neurodevelopmental disorder we propose to name TOP2B-related neurodevelopmental disorder. Further studies should elucidate the pathogenic mechanisms underlying H63Y-associated phenotypes.
journal: American journal of medical genetics. Part A
authors: Ha ZY, Dinatto L, Meagher K, Guimond C, Friedman JM, Stirling PC, Patel MS.

title: Phosphorylation of RpoD upregulates suilysin and enhances Streptococcus suis virulence.
abstract: Streptococcus suis (S. suis) is a prevalent zoonotic pathogen that severely threatens the swine industry and human public health. Suilysin (SLY), a major pore-forming toxin of S. suis, is indispensable for bacterial hemolytic activity and systemic pathogenicity, yet the upstream regulatory mechanism controlling SLY production remains unclear. Serine/threonine kinase (STK) has been characterized to modulate bacterial physiology and virulence by phosphorylating multiple substrate proteins. Our previous phosphoproteomics analysis indicated that the housekeeping sigma factor RpoD was a potential STK substrate. In vitro phosphorylation assays combined with mass spectrometry, co-immunoprecipitation and site-directed mutagenesis confirmed that STK directly phosphorylated RpoD at Thr-208 residue. Phenotypic tests revealed that RpoD phosphorylation had no obvious impact on bacterial growth and biofilm formation but specifically promoted the thermotolerance and hemolytic activity of S. suis. Notably, the rpoD overexpression mutant strain SC19-rpoD significantly upregulated the transcription and protein production of SLY, whereas the phosphorylation-deficient mutant SC19-rpoD T208A abolished this promotion effect, indicating that Thr-208 phosphorylation is required for sly upregulation, although the underlying molecular mechanism remains to be fully defined. Furthermore, mouse infection models demonstrated that the SC19-rpoD T208A mutant exhibited alleviated splenic pathological injury, reduced bacterial loads in multiple organs, and significantly improved host survival, indicating that the loss of RpoD phosphorylation impairs S. suis virulence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that STK-mediated phosphorylation of RpoD at Thr-208 is required for sly upregulation and contributes to the S. suis pathogenesis.
authors: Tian Y, Zhao Z, Yin H, Liu X, Fu J, Gao L, Li Y, Fang R, Peng L.
