title: The ecological adaptability of pinewood nematode populations: survival strategies, mechanisms and co-evolution.
abstract: BackgroundBursaphelenchus xylophilus (pinewood nematode, PWN) is the causal agent of pine wilt disease and ranks among the most destructive invasive pests threatening global forest ecosystems. Since its introduction to China, this nematode has triggered massive ecological and economic losses, while its distribution range continues to expand northward. The association between the widespread dispersal of B. xylophilus in invaded areas and the ecological adaptability of its populations has drawn considerable attention.ResultsThis review systematically synthesizes recent research advances regarding the ecological adaptability of PWN populations, elaborating on molecular mechanisms and ecological strategies that enable the nematode to colonize novel environments. In terms of thermal adaptation, differentially expressed genes, small heat shock protein families and the accumulation of key metabolites collectively shape adaptive pathways to resist extreme high and low temperature stress. For host adaptation, PWN displays polyphagous feeding habits and relies on diverse arboreal fungi as nutritional resources when pines were weakened or died. Detoxification enzyme cascades and effector proteins enable the nematode to counteract host defensive metabolites. Specifically, effectors suppress host peroxidase activity, thereby quenching reactive oxygen species bursts and disrupting plant hormone regulatory pathways to attenuate pine immune responses. Co-evolutionary interactions between PWN and vector beetles manifest across multiple dimensions, including synchronized life cycles, specialized dispersal-stage juveniles, and infochemical-mediated interspecies communication. PWN also forms intricate interaction networks with associated fungi and bacteria, which exert vital functions in nutrient acquisition, pathogenicity enhancement and terpenoid degradation. Notably, ascaroside pheromones serve as central signaling molecules that modulate interspecific competition and reproductive phenotypic plasticity. Population genetic analyses have uncovered shifts in genetic diversity, regulatory pathways governing population structure and reproductive efficiency, as well as synergistic evolutionary correlations between invasive population genetics and pathogenicity. Multi-omics analytical frameworks provide novel perspectives for dissecting the adaptive evolution of PWN.ConclusionThe invasive success and widespread dispersal of B. xylophilus are fundamentally driven by its strong population ecological adaptability. Finally, this review summarizes the existing research gaps and proposes future research priorities alongside targeted pest management strategies. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: Ying CX, Wen TY, Ding XL, Wu XQ.

title: Detectability of Melissococcus plutonius and Paenibacillus larvae DNA in beeswax following thermal processing.
abstract: Commercial beeswax recycling commonly relies on thermal processing (121 °C) to eliminate honeybee pathogens. However, residual DNA from inactivated pathogens can persist, causing highly sensitive qPCR assays to detect non-viable targets and complicate molecular surveillance. This study evaluated the post-treatment detectability of Paenibacillus larvae (American foulbrood, AFB) and Melissococcus plutonius (European foulbrood, EFB) DNA in apiary-derived wax samples and cultured bacteria before and after a simulated industrial autoclave treatment. Autoclaving profoundly reduced DNA amplifiability across all targets. In wax samples, all baseline-positive AFB samples became undetectable (Cq > 40). Conversely, M. plutonius DNA remained detectable in 5 out of 12 baseline-positive wax samples (post-treatment Cq range: 23.40 to 38.91). In matrix-free bacterial suspensions, both pathogens remained detectable after autoclaving, though P. larvae exhibited a smaller thermal amplification delay (+4.59 cycles) than M. plutonius (+9.66 cycles). In conclusion, standard high-pressure steam sterilization significantly degrades, but does not eliminate, M. plutonius DNA within beeswax from clinically diseased apiaries, allowing target fragments to remain detectable via sensitive qPCR assays. While P. larvae DNA is rendered completely undetectable in apiary-derived wax matrices, M. plutonius DNA can variably persist post-treatment. This contrasts with matrix-free bacterial suspensions, where DNA from both pathogens remains detectable across initial dilution gradients. Consequently, utilizing wax from these infected apiaries for foundation manufacturing can introduce historical DNA signatures that remain amplifiable, potentially confounding downstream molecular surveillance for identification of healthy carrier hives that are at risk of developing, or spreading, disease.
authors: Rutkowski K, Sørum H, Dahle B, Robertson L.

title: Differential Fe<sup>2+</sup> distribution and iron metabolism-related features in hemocyte populations of the blood clam Anadara granosa.
abstract: In vertebrates, macrophage-mediated erythrocyte clearance is central to iron recycling, but how comparable iron-handling functions are partitioned among hemocyte populations in red-blooded bivalves typified by the blood clam Anadara granosa remains unclear. In this study, erythrocytes and non-erythrocytic hemocytes were separated to characterize differences in the distribution of detectable ferrous iron (Fe2+) and iron metabolism-related transcriptional features and to identify candidate molecules associated with iron handling. Fe2+ assays showed higher assay-detectable Fe2+ in non-erythrocytic hemocytes than in erythrocytes. Localized enhancement of Fe2+ signals was further observed in phagocytosis-like regions, suggesting a possible association between erythrocyte-associated cellular interactions and localized Fe2+ enrichment. Comparative transcriptomic analysis revealed the upregulation of iron metabolism-related genes in non-erythrocytic hemocytes, together with functional annotations involving metal ion transport and intracellular processing, including phagosome, endocytosis, and lysosome. Among these genes, the DMT1/SLC11A2 homolog from A. granosa (AgDMT1) was more highly expressed in non-erythrocytic hemocytes and retained conserved features of the DMT1/SLC11A2 family. Together, these findings indicate a functional differentiation in iron metabolism between hemocyte populations, suggest a potential association between phagocytosis-related cellular processing and localized Fe2+ enrichment, and support AgDMT1 as a candidate Fe2+ transporter in non-erythrocytic hemocytes.
authors: Zhu J, Li L, Shi S, Zhang M, Liu H, Bao Y.

title: Clinical characteristics and maternal whole-exome sequencing findings in patients with recurrent oocyte, zygote, and early embryo maturation arrest: a single-center experience.
abstract: ObjectiveTo characterize the clinical phenotype, cumulative assisted reproductive technology (ART) experience, and maternal whole-exome sequencing (WES) findings in patients with recurrent Oocyte, Zygote, and Early Embryo Maturation Arrest (OZEMA), and to assess the contribution of phenotype-guided genomic evaluation in this clinically challenging population.DesignRetrospective cohort study conducted in a fertility clinic within a general private hospital equipped with an in‑house genetic laboratory.SubjectsA total of 115 females with a history of OZEMA were included, all of whom presented to the ART clinic.Main outcome measuresThe distribution of pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants in established OZEMA-associated genes, variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in established genes, monoallelic variants in established autosomal recessive genes, and exploratory candidate-gene findings. ART outcomes were described according to whether a prioritized WES finding was reported.ResultsThe mean female age was 33.47 +/- 4.37 years, with a median infertility duration of 6.0 years (range, 1.0-21.0). Patients had experienced recurrent OZEMA across multiple ART cycles (median, 4; range, 1-16). Parental consanguinity was observed in 37 of 115 cases (32.2 %). Prioritized maternal WES findings were identified in 64 of 115 patients (55.7 %): 12 patients (10.4 %) had P/LP variants in established genes with genotypes consistent with the reported inheritance pattern, 17 (14.8 %) had VUS in established genes, 15 (13.0 %) had monoallelic variants in established autosomal recessive genes without a second relevant allele, and 20 (17.4 %) had exploratory candidate-gene findings. No prioritized WES finding was identified in 51 patients (44.3 %).ConclusionsPhenotype-guided maternal WES identified established P/LP findings with inheritance-consistent support in a clinically meaningful subset of patients with recurrent OZEMA and revealed a broader spectrum of additional genomic findings. These results support genomic evaluation, while the clinical interpretation of VUS, monoallelic findings in recessive genes, and exploratory candidate-gene findings should remain evidence-based.
authors: Kahraman S, Cetinkaya M, Cetinkaya CP, Madjunkova S, Kara B, Ayaz A, Aktoz F.

title: Threshold dynamics and intervention strategy optimization in a maize-vector delayed system for streak virus disease.
abstract: Maize streak virus disease (MSVD), primarily transmitted by leafhoppers, is an important viral disease of maize. The delay involved in vector-mediated transmission may affect the disease epidemic patterns and control timing. In this study, a delayed transmission model coupling the interaction of maize and vector interaction is formulated, aiming to reveal the mechanism of delay on disease epidemic patterns and optimal control strategies. Theoretical analysis shows that delay does not alter the stability threshold of disease-free equilibrium. However, under suitable spectral and transversality conditions, increasing the delay will induce Hopf bifurcation at an endemic equilibrium, and the system will transform from steady-state convergence to periodic oscillation. Upon this foundation, an optimal control model with three measures with the numerical scenarios considered, including preventive control through weeding, removal of infected maize plants, and chemical control through pesticide spraying, are investigated. Numerical simulations indicate that increasing the delay postpones the action window and reduces peak intensity of three control measures, whereas its influences depend on the initial infection status of vector leafhoppers. When infected leafhoppers are absent initially, an increase in delay inhibits the evolution of MSVD. In contrast, when infected leafhoppers are already present, it promotes the spread of MSVD among maize. Under optimal control, the three measures exhibit a temporal structure of removal first, spraying second, and weeding last under optimal control, which provides a possible phased guidance for phased prevention and control under limited resources. These results reveal that the interplay between transmission delay and initial vector infection fundamentally shapes the effectiveness of each control measure, implying that the optimal timing and priority of removal, spraying, and weeding must be dynamically aligned with the specific phase of disease progression.
authors: Liu L, Gao Z, Tang S, Li Y.

title: Locus-specific endogenous retroviral transcriptional modulation in viral hepatitis-driven hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs) are remnants of ancient infections integrated into the primate germ line. HERV transcriptional reactivation has been observed in several diseases, including cancer, where it may reflect epigenetic deregulation, cellular stress, inflammation, and infections. Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most diffuse and deadly cancers worldwide, with chronic hepatitis infections as major etiological factors. In this context, the activation of specific HERV loci in HCC and their relationship with the broader tumor-associated transcriptional landscape remain poorly defined. Here, we characterized the expression of ∼3300 HERVs in a public RNA-seq dataset comprising HCC samples, predominantly of viral etiology, and non-HCC liver controls. We identified 185 differentially expressed HERVs, predominantly upregulated in HCC (n = 145): comparisons with GTEx healthy liver transcriptomes, inflammatory gene profiling, and covariate-adjusted analyses supported the consistency of this HCC-associated transcriptional signature. Aggregate expression scores of upregulated and downregulated HERVs showed significant associations with histological grade, with opposite trends across G1-G3 tumors. 16 HERV loci were consistently upregulated in all tumor tissues, and their aggregate expression increased significantly with histological grade, supporting their prioritization as a candidate HCC-associated signature. HERV-correlated pathway analyses revealed grade-associated patterns involving metabolic, inflammatory, interferon-related, and proliferative transcriptional programs. De novo transcript reconstruction identified candidate HERV-derived transcripts requiring experimental validation. Overall, the study provides a comprehensive characterization of HERV modulation in a predominantly viral-associated HCC cohort and identifies conserved HERV signatures embedded within the broader transcriptomic remodeling, for future independent and functional studies of their potential relevance to liver cancer biology.
authors: Grandi N, Soddu E, Chabukswar S, Scognamiglio S, Yen Y, Liu CH, Lin LT, Tramontano E.

title: Microplastics and antibiotic toxicity in aquatic organisms: Exposure, interactions and mechanisms.
abstract: Micro- and nanoplastics co-occur with antibiotic residues in aquatic environments, but whether particles increase antibiotic hazard remains unresolved. We conducted a structured qualitative synthesis of original aquatic co-exposure studies identified through Europe PMC searches to 25 September 2026, a complementary OpenAlex search and citation chasing. Experiments were compared by organism, particle properties, both contaminant concentrations, exposure route, comparator design and endpoint. Reported outcomes include amplification, attenuation and dose- or endpoint-dependent reversals. Marine bivalve and other invertebrate studies extend this evidence to low antibiotic concentrations, but low antibiotic exposure does not by itself establish realistic particle exposure. Microbiome shifts were distinguished from host injury and fitness impairment. A mixture response exceeding either single treatment does not establish synergy, and increased tissue accumulation does not alone establish particle-mediated delivery. Our study-level appraisal separates conditional co-exposure findings from designs capable of identifying an interaction and from evidence supporting a specific mechanism. The five-level hierarchy is proposed as a framework for evaluating current claims and designing future research; its highest levels are evidentiary targets, not a claim that the existing literature has already established causal pathways at environmentally realistic exposures.
journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Toxicology & pharmacology : CBP
authors: Wang K.

title: Persistent Hepatocyte Plasticity and Lipid Metabolic Reprogramming After Hepatitis C Virus Cure.
abstract: Background and aimsChronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection disrupts hepatocyte polarity and promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), contributing to liver disease progression. Although direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) eradicate HCV infection in most patients, the risk of fibrosis progression and hepatocellular carcinoma persists after viral clearance. Whether antiviral cure fully restores hepatocyte differentiation, polarity, and epithelial identity programs remains unclear. We investigated whether HCV-induced EMT and lipid metabolism alterations are fully reversible following DAA treatment.MethodsHuh7 hepatoma cells and Huh7 cells stably expressing a full-length HCV replicon were cultured in three-dimensional Matrigel to assess morphogenesis, polarity-associated features, and EMT. Spheroid morphology, canalicular-like organization, EMT markers, and transcriptomic signatures were analyzed using microscopy, immunofluorescence, RT-qPCR, and microarray analysis. The effects of DAA treatment (sofosbuvir with or without velpatasvir) were evaluated in vitro. Publicly available transcriptomic data from liver biopsies collected before therapy and within five days after its completion, were analyzed.ResultsHCV replicon expression altered canalicular-like organization and induced actin-rich protrusions in 90% of Huh7-R spheroids. DAA treatment efficiently suppressed HCV replicon expression and partially restored epithelial morphology, reducing protrusions to 25%, without normalizing them to the control level (2.5%). EMT-associated changes, including reduced E-cadherin and increased N-cadherin expression, were only partially corrected by DAA treatment. Transcriptomic EMT scoring showed persistent mesenchymal features in DAA-treated cells and in patient biopsies collected at the end of treatment. In parallel, genes involved in lipid metabolism and hepatocyte differentiation remained dysregulated.ConclusionsThese findings show incomplete restoration of epithelial organization after suppression of HCV replicon expression in vitro and incomplete normalization of selected transcriptional signatures at the end of DAA treatment in patient liver samples. They suggest that cellular plasticity and metabolic reprogramming may persist after treatment and contribute to long-term liver disease risk.
journal: Cellular and molecular gastroenterology and hepatology
authors: Agnetti J, Cherief S, Desterke C, Bou-Malham V, Benzoubir N, Tan TZ, Thiery JP, Samuel D, Gassama-Diagne A.

title: Interactions between Hexokinase 2 and host proteins and their involvement in tissue tropism upon Hepatospora eriocheir infection in Eriocheir sinensis.
abstract: Hepatospora eriocheir is the causative pathogen of hepatopancreatic necrosis disease (HPND) in Eriocheir sinensis, and this microsporidian parasite specifically colonizes crab hepatopancreatic tissue. The molecular mechanisms underlying such tissue-specific infection remain largely unclear. Microsporidian parasites generally undergo extensive genomic degeneration, accompanied by the loss of oxidative phosphorylation pathways and most glycolysis-related genes. Nevertheless, H. eriocheir retains two paralogous hexokinase genes. Among them, HeHK2 exhibits relatively high sequence conservation but lacks detectable catalytic activity, indicating that this protein exerts non-enzymatic functions during pathogen infection. Immunofluorescence assays verified that H. eriocheir mainly resides in hepatopancreatic epithelial cells of crabs. Immunoprecipitation-Mass Spectrometry (IP- LC-MS/MS) was adopted to screen potential host proteins interacting with HeHK2. Three candidate proteins, including mitochondrial amidoxime reducing component (mARC), alpha-amylase 2-like protein and C-type lectin, were selected for subsequent co-immunoprecipitation validation based on their biological functions associated with host energy metabolism and innate immune regulation. Histological and ultrastructural observation further revealed mitochondrial aggregation and abnormal morphological changes in infected hepatopancreatic tissues. These interactions suggest a working model in which HeHK2 may contribute to hepatopancreas-specific infection by modulating mitochondria-associated host metabolism and innate immunity; however, direct functional evidence for this model requires further investigation.
authors: Ding Z, Wu Y, Wu Q, Xu Y, Shen Y, Zhang X.

title: Ebola Virus VP40 C-terminal Lysine Residue Mediates Lipid Interactions and Dimer-Dimer Interactions.
abstract: The Ebola virus (EBOV) matrix protein VP40 is the main driver of viral assembly and budding, processes which depend on its ability to oligomerize at the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane (PM). VP40 forms dimers in the cytoplasm that traffic to the membrane and assemble into higher-order oligomers, but the specific molecular determinants governing the stability of these oligomeric interfaces are not fully understood. Here, we investigate the role of the C-terminal lysine residue, Lys326, in mediating VP40-lipid and VP40-VP40 interactions. Using a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and computational site-saturation mutagenesis, we predicted that while Lys326 has a minimal role in the stability of the isolated VP40 dimer, it is a critical determinant in stabilizing the interfaces of higher-order structures like tetramers and hexamers. Experimentally, mutation of this residue to alanine or aspartic acid (K326A or K326D) impaired VP40 PM localization, oligomerization, and in a charge-dependent manner, virus-like particle production. Our results indicate that a cationic residue is crucial not only for interactions with anionic phospholipids in the PM but, more importantly, for forming stabilizing networks across VP40 dimer-dimer interfaces. Together, these findings identify Lys326 as a keystone residue that couples membrane binding to the stabilization of essential higher-order oligomers, revealing a critical interface for EBOV assembly that could be exploited for future antiviral strategies.
authors: Woods HM, Narkhede YB, Karki U, Norris MJ, Chapagain PP, Wiest O, Stahelin RV.

title: Whole-Exome Sequencing Identifies a Rare CSRP3 Variant Associated With Familial Brugada Syndrome in a Lebanese Family.
abstract: IntroductionBrugada syndrome (BrS) is an inherited arrhythmia associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death. Although traditionally regarded as a primary cardiac channelopathy, pathogenic variants in SCN5A account for only 20%-30% of clinically diagnosed cases, leaving most patients genetically unresolved. Emerging evidence suggests that structural cardiac genes may also contribute to BrS susceptibility. We investigated the genetic basis of BrS in a consanguineous Lebanese family with three affected brothers.Methods and resultsWhole-exome sequencing was performed in all affected individuals, followed by variant calling, annotation, and phenotype-driven prioritization using Franklin (Genoox). Candidate variants were evaluated according to allele frequency, inheritance model, segregation, and ACMG/AMP classification. Evolutionary conservation, AlphaMissense prediction, protein domain annotation, and structural modeling were performed to assess the potential functional impact of the prioritized variant. Whole-exome sequencing identified a rare homozygous CSRP3 missense variant (NM_003476.5:c.56 A > G; p.His19Arg) shared by all three affected siblings. Following exome-wide filtering under a recessive inheritance model, CSRP3 represented the only rare homozygous coding variant, while no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were identified in established Brugada syndrome-associated genes. The variant was absent from public population databases and an internal cohort of Lebanese exomes. His19 was highly conserved across vertebrate species, AlphaMissense classified the variant as likely pathogenic (score = 0.942), and structural modeling predicted alterations within the N-terminal LIM domain that may affect protein stability and local residue interactions.ConclusionsOur findings nominate CSRP3 as a candidate susceptibility gene for Brugada syndrome and support the emerging role of structural cardiac genes in inherited arrhythmia syndromes. Although functional validation is required to establish causality, this study highlights the value of whole-exome sequencing in consanguineous and underrepresented populations for identifying rare candidate variants contributing to BrS susceptibility.
authors: Bashir Z, Kadhi A, Ballout J, Samara B, Khoury M, Nemer G, Refaat M.

title: Label-Free Nucleic Acid Amplification in a Self-regulated All-Fiber Photothermal Microcavity.
abstract: Nucleic acid amplification commonly relies on fluorescent labels and electrically driven thermal control, limiting simplicity, scalability, and remote deployment. Here, we establish a label-free optical strategy based on amplification-associated refractive-index (RI) evolution within a confined optothermal microcavity. During amplification, the accumulation of nucleic acid products alters the composition and molecular polarizability of the reaction medium, contributing to a progressive increase in its effective RI. This bulk RI change is converted into interferometric phase accumulation under thermally stabilized conditions, enabling real-time optical readout without labels. We implement this strategy in a 0.94 nL fiber Fabry-Perot microcavity that integrates localized optothermal regulation and phase-sensitive interrogation within a single optical pathway. The confined geometry enables rapid optothermal heating, reaching a 1 °C temperature rise in 15 ms, nearly three orders of magnitude faster than conventional electrical heating. Using hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA as a model target, we achieve a detection limit of 5.24 copies/nL and quantitative agreement with fluorescence-based assays, while isothermal amplification reduces the total assay time by approximately 50% relative to commercial qPCR. Frequency-division multiplexing enables parallel multi-target analysis, while stable transmission is maintained over 20 km fiber links. Our results establish amplification-associated RI evolution as a promising label-free transduction mechanism for fiber-integrated molecular diagnostics.
authors: Yan M, Cheng G, Zhou X, Zhang YN, Zhao Y, Warren-Smith SC, Nguyen LV, Qin X, Li X.

title: Cd47 deficiency in mouse brain under excitotoxic stress.
abstract: CD47, a transmembrane protein with well-established immune and neurodevelopmental roles, was recently identified as an abundant presynaptic protein in humans, non-human primates, and mice. To investigate how Cd47 influences neuronal stress and injury, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing of hippocampi from wild-type (WT) and Cd47 knockout (KO) mice exposed to kainic acid (KA) at convulsive (KA25; 25 mg/kg) or subconvulsive (KA3; 3 mg/kg) doses. Integrating cell-type annotations with Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) revealed distinct neuronal and glial gene modules whose co-expression structure differed by genotype and by KA exposure. Notably, certain modules showed KA-associated changes in co-expression structure only in Cd47-deficient cells. Enrichment analyses of these modules highlighted translational, bioenergetic, and synaptic gene sets. Comparing transcriptome-wide distributions using Wasserstein distance demonstrated that vehicle-treated KO cells most closely resembled WT cells exposed to KA3, of all fifteen pairwise comparisons. These findings suggest that Cd47 loss shifts the hippocampal transcriptome toward a state resembling mild excitotoxic stress, implicating Cd47 as a candidate regulator of neuronal stress adaptation and providing a hypothesis for testing that role.
authors: Kiamari M, Perna A, Santoro M, El Ariss A, Berson E, Zhao J, Gajera CR, Fox EJ, Montine KS, Aghaeepour N, Montine TJ.

title: Viral disease outcomes are indistinguishable between experimentally infected bats and rodents.
abstract: A common explanation for bats being a conspicuous source of zoonotic viruses is their purported ability to coexist with viruses without suffering overt disease. Widespread acceptance of the idea that bats have unusual antiviral traits has catalyzed the discovery of unique features of bat immune systems which may have translational value as broad-spectrum antivirals, particularly if they evolved as a byproduct of bats' unique life history rather than through conventional co-evolutionary processes. Surprisingly, whether bats compared to other host groups suffer less disease from co-evolved viruses or from viruses generally has not been formally assessed. Here, synthesizing 86 years of experimental infections, involving 54 viruses, 85 host species, and over 5,600 animals, we document disease in bats following inoculation by taxonomically diverse viruses, including ones that are relatively benign in humans. The occurrence of overt disease, the likelihood of mortality, and the severity of disease in bats were indistinguishable from those experienced by rodents, another group associated with many zoonotic viruses. These patterns were consistent when considering only bat-associated viruses inoculated into bats and rodent-associated viruses inoculated into rodents and among inoculations which lacked shared co-evolutionary history. Instead, disease outcomes following infection were shaped by experimental design, viral host range, and evolutionary context. Unexceptional disease in bats from novel or co-evolved infections suggests that order-level host life history traits such as flight have inconsistent consequences for antiviral immunity and highlights the need to evaluate the functional properties of putatively unique features of bat immunity in vivo. While these results do not exclude the possibility of developing broader-acting or more potent antivirals from bat immune systems or diminish the potential value of mechanistic insights into bat immunity, they suggest that bat immune systems were shaped by conventional co-evolutionary processes rather than through unique circumstances that endow exceptional antiviral defenses.
authors: Farrell MJ, Tucker SK, Mollentze N, Streicker DG.

title: In situ functionalized bacterial cellulose for functional and smart nanomaterials: an expanded biochemical, biophysical, and industrial biotechnology review.
abstract: In situ functionalization of bacterial cellulose (BC) enables the incorporation of compatible functional components during biosynthesis, in contrast to post-synthetic and hybrid modification approaches. BC is produced extracellularly by Komagataeibacter species and has high purity, water-holding capacity, and crystallinity, while its mechanical and biological properties are influenced by production and processing conditions. This narrative review evaluates 78 primary and review articles published between 2005 and 2025. Building on earlier reviews of BC modification, it provides an integrative biochemical, biophysical, and industrial biotechnology perspective on in situ functionalization strategies linking bacterial metabolism and cellulose synthase activity to the incorporation of carbon nanomaterials, conductive polymers, and nanoparticles within the BC matrix. These functionalized nanocomposites often exhibit improved mechanical, thermal, electrical, antimicrobial, and bioactive properties, although additive incorporation may reduce crystallinity depending on concentration, dispersion, and interaction mechanisms. The roles of c-di-GMP signaling, carbon flux regulation, cellulose synthase-directed extrusion, and enzyme-assisted co-assembly in governing material architecture and structure-property relationships are discussed. Key limitations include additive dispersion, bacterial viability, protocol reproducibility, product biocompatibility, and process scale-up. Functionalized BC offers exciting potential as a customizable biofabrication platform for advanced nanomaterials useful in bioelectronics, tissue engineering, wound healing, packaging, and sustainable industrial applications.
authors: Bertelli M, Tchuenbou-Magaia F, Imran M, Radecka I.

title: A symbiogenic merger enabled by oxygen initiated the evolution of eukaryotes.
abstract: Recently, extensive genetic information about archaeal hosts at the basis of eukaryogenesis has come to light. Characterization of these first eukaryotic common ancestor (FECA) related organisms allows improved understanding of the enigmatic FECA to last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) transition. However, these gene-centered discoveries have the unfortunate side effect of entrenching erroneous ideas about early eukaryotic evolution. This is apparent in the two-Domain vision of life, with eukaryotes seen as specialized Asgard archaea, while underestimating the contribution of the endosymbiont to eukaryogenesis. Establishment of the alpha-proteobacterium as the future mitochondrion is treated as one of many such endosymbiotic occurrences, ignoring its unique evolutionary position. I will marshal evidence for symbiogenic mechanisms involved in the FECA to LECA transition, with a key role for the endosymbiont's electron transport chain and its acceptor molecular oxygen, especially in the incarnation of reactive oxygen species occurring in the host cytoplasm. We should overcome overestimating gene determinism, while not sufficiently allowing for effects of biological hierarchies, emergent properties, and chance. Many eukaryotic properties are best understood by envisaging the crucial uptake of the future mitochondrion as a merger instead of an acquisition. This merger is characterized by a new kind of elaborate cellular entity emerging as a result of rapid coevolution, replacing a scenario in which already complex pre-eukaryotes acquired endosymbionts, accompanied by important, but limited, changes. Successful mergers are rare because they are intrinsically more difficult, but synergistically open up completely new areas of possibilities, as illustrated by incredible eukaryotic success.
authors: Speijer D.

title: Heterologous expression of soy leghemoglobin LBC2 in engineered Tremella fuciformis yeast-like cells and associated pigmentation responses.
abstract: The development of microbial platforms for producing soy leghemoglobin is of interest for potential applications in alternative meat products. In this study, Tremella fuciformis yeast-like cells (YLCs) were evaluated as a host for heterologous expression of soy leghemoglobin C2 (LBC2). Recombinant vectors pGEH-P4-LBC and pGEH-gpd-LBC were introduced into YLCs via Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation. Transformants were screened by PCR, quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), and fluorescence microscope, and construct maintenance was assessed over five generations. LBC2 transcript levels in the gpd- and P4-driven transformants reached approximately 15-fold and 50-fold those of the wild-type strain, respectively. SDS-PAGE revealed a protein band with an apparent molecular mass of approximately 15 kDa, consistent with the predicted molecular mass of LBC2 (15.52 kDa). Combined BCA and densitometric analyses yielded preliminary estimates of 99.5 and 194.1 mg/L associated with this band in the gpd- and P4-driven transformants, respectively, with greater band intensity observed in the P4-driven strain. Supplementation with 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) induced pigmentation changes in both liquid and solid cultures. RGB-based image analysis showed that the highest image-derived response occurred at 1.6 mmol/L ALA in liquid culture and 2.4 mmol/L in solid culture. Pigmentation also varied with ALA concentration and culture conditions. Overall, these findings provide preliminary evidence supporting heterologous LBC2 expression in T. fuciformis YLCs and establish a basis for further optimization of recombinant protein accumulation and investigation of associated pigmentation changes.
authors: Hao M, Huang X, Wang Y, Li R, Wei X, Ma A.

title: Marine-derived quorum sensing inhibition as an anti-virulence strategy against biofilm formation and antibiotic tolerance in Aeromonas hydrophila.
abstract: BackgroundBiofilm formation by Aeromonas hydrophila complicates infection control and is associated with reduced antibiotic susceptibility. Seaweed metabolites may interfere with quorum sensing, offering potential antivirulence approaches. This study compared three seaweed extracts for antibacterial, antibiofilm, and quorum sensing inhibitory activities.Methods and resultsRepresentative compounds reported from Ecklonia cava, Codium fragile, and Grateloupia elliptica were docked against AhyR. Biological assays assessed environmental effects on biofilm formation, antibiotic susceptibility, and extract effects on biofilms and swarming in A. hydrophila, alongside violacein inhibition in Chromobacterium violaceum. Biofilm biomass was quantified by crystal violet staining. Gene expression was examined by quantitative real-time PCR after seven days of repeated exposure to extracts at half the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Sub-inhibitory florfenicol exposure enhanced biofilm formation, particularly at 35 °C; biofilm biomass peaked at 1% NaCl in salinity assays. Florfenicol and amoxicillin MICs were 128-fold and eightfold higher in biofilm-derived cells than in planktonic cells, respectively. Docking predicted possible AhyR interactions. E. cava showed the strongest antibacterial and antibiofilm activities and swarming inhibition. G. elliptica produced the largest violacein inhibition zone at half MIC (14.13 ± 1.30 mm) and reduced luxS, hcp, recA, rpoS, ompA, and acrB expression after repeated exposure.ConclusionsThe extracts showed distinct activity profiles, with E. cava exhibiting the strongest antibiofilm effects and G. elliptica the strongest quorum sensing inhibition. G. elliptica warrants further investigation as an antivirulence candidate. Its active constituents and direct effects on AhyR require validation.

title: Adjunctive recombinant human thymosin β4 therapy improves antibacterial outcomes against Staphylococcus aureus.
abstract: Thymosin β4 (Tβ4) is an endogenous multifunctional protein with growing therapeutic applications, including infectious diseases; however, its intrinsic antibacterial activity remains unclear. Previous research with the peptide and related shellfish homologs has suggested broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties, including activity against Staphylococcus aureus. Here, we evaluated the antibacterial activity of recombinant human Tβ4 (rhTβ4) alone and in combination with antibiotics against S. aureus strain 8325-4 and two clinical isolates. Direct antibacterial activity of rhTβ4 (15.625-16,000 µg/mL) was assessed by broth microdilution and colony-forming unit enumeration. Interactions between rhTβ4 and antibiotics were evaluated using checkerboard assays examining total, planktonic, and biofilm-associated bacterial populations. Biofilms were further analyzed using crystal violet staining and SYTO9/PI labeling to assess biomass and membrane integrity, respectively. Moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin, oxacillin, and vancomycin were evaluated. rhTβ4 alone exhibited modest growth-modulating effects but lacked substantial direct antibacterial activity. In contrast, rhTβ4 demonstrated synergistic interactions with multiple antibiotics, resulting in reduced bacterial growth primarily within total and planktonic populations. Limited effects were observed against established biofilms, as rhTβ4 did not significantly reduce biofilm biomass or membrane integrity, and combination treatments produced antibiotic-dependent biofilm responses. Collectively, these findings indicate that rhTβ4 possesses little intrinsic antibacterial activity against S. aureus but can synergistically augment the effects of select antibiotics in vitro, supporting its utility as an adjunctive therapeutic strategy.IMPORTANCEStaphylococcus aureus remains a leading cause of severe infections worldwide, and the rise in antibiotic resistance emphasizes the need for new therapeutic strategies. Thymosin β4 (Tβ4), a naturally occurring human peptide already known to promote tissue repair, may also enhance bacterial clearance. This study demonstrates that recombinant human Tβ4 exhibits direct growth-modulating activity against S. aureus and, more importantly, synergizes with multiple antibiotics to reduce bacterial growth. These findings suggest that Tβ4 could serve as an adjunctive therapy, improving the efficacy of conventional antibiotics while leveraging its immunomodulatory and wound-healing properties. By uncovering a potential antimicrobial dimension to a well-characterized endogenous peptide, this work broadens the therapeutic scope of Tβ4 and supports its further development as a novel strategy for treating antibiotic-resistant or biofilm-associated infections.
authors: Banga L, Patel D, Shawky M, Carabulea A, Ebrahim AS, Liu L, Berger E.

title: Light-induced phyB-NPR1 interaction activates systemic acquired resistance.
abstract: Light perception by phytochromes controls different aspects of plant-environment interactions including plant immunity; however, the underpinning molecular mechanisms are less well-understood. Upon localized attack on leaves by avirulent pathogens, the systemic accumulation of salicylic acid (SA) is required for the establishment of systemic acquired resistance (SAR) throughout the plant to curtail pathogen spread. We demonstrate that light-mediated Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier 1 (SUMO) conjugation to phytochrome B (phyB) is critical for increasing cellular SA levels to orchestrate SAR upon avirulent bacterial infection. SA promotes SUMOylation of phyB, which enables it to interact with the SA receptor, Nonexpressor of Pathogenesis-Related 1 (NPR1) via its SUMO1-interacting motif. SUMOylation of phyB is enhanced by the accumulation of SUMO-Conjugating Enzyme (E2) (SCE1) and the degradation of SUMO protease Overly Tolerant to Salt 1 (OTS1) in SAR-induced systemic tissues. Using confocal imaging, we show that SUMOylated phyB undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation together with NPR1 in nuclear bodies. We further validated through immunoprecipitation, ChIP and RNA-seq analysis that SUMOylated phyB associates with NPR1 and TGA transcription factors in nuclear photobodies to induce the expression of PR1 gene. We reveal a post-translational modification mechanism in which light-induced SUMOylation of photoreceptors promotes SAR by regulating NPR1 function.
authors: Ghosh S, Ghosh S, Long X, Mansi M, Clark L, Srivastava AK, Kakkunnath S, Orosa B, Bhagat PK, Bailey M, Gough C, Zhang C, de Lucas M, Sadanandom A.

title: Genetic Variants in Ciliary Body Development Genes and Their Association with Myopia: A Systematic Review.
abstract: PurposeNumerous genetic variants have been implicated in myopia pathogenesis, yet their biological mechanisms remain unclear. One proposed mechanism is that variants in genes involved in ciliary body development may influence ciliary muscle structure and accommodative function, thereby influencing individual variation in myopia risk. The aim was to systematically evaluate published evidence linking myopia with genetic variants in genes implicated in ciliary body developmental pathways and identify candidate variants for comparison with ciliary muscle properties to validate this mechanistic pathway.MethodsA comprehensive search of existing literature was conducted across PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, ProQuest, and Scopus on July 2 2025 and February 25 2026. References and citations of papers considered eligible for inclusion were examined to identify additional papers. Studies were included if they examined the association between myopia and single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within 1 kb of notch receptor 2 (NOTCH2), catenin beta 1 (CTNNB1), transforming growth factor beta 2 (TGFB2), paired box 6 (PAX6), and bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4). Covidence was used to identify and conduct a narrative synthesis of findings from eligible studies. Quality assessment was performed using adapted versions of the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.ResultsTwenty-two studies-12 observational studies, five genome-wide association studies (GWAS), and five GWAS meta-analyses-were identified. Observational studies only examined SNPs within 1 kb of TGFB2 and PAX6, with rs7550232 (TGFB2) providing the strongest evidence for an association with myopia. GWAS and GWAS meta-analyses examined SNPs related to all five genes, with rs2953 (CTNNB1) and rs17563 (BMP4) having the most compelling evidence of an association with myopia.ConclusionGenetic variants identified in observational studies were distinct from those identified in GWAS and GWAS meta-analyses, which frequently examined overlapping cohorts. Further studies are required to validate these associations and clarify whether these variants influence myopia risk through an underlying mechanism involving ciliary muscle physiology.
authors: Lee J, Breed R, Voisey J, Schmid KL.

title: Harnessing Wastewater-Based Epidemiology for One Health surveillance of enteric viruses.
abstract: Wastewater-Based Epidemiology (WBE) is an approach that is widely used to monitor the occurrence and distribution of pathogens shed by human populations through wastewater. This review critically evaluates the application of WBE of enteric viruses within a One Health paradigm. It highlights how enteric viruses from human and animal sources end up in wastewater and aquatic environments, and how their presence can be used to predict the occurrence of diseases in human and animal populations. The review highlights the untapped potential for the application of WBE beyond human populations to a more holistic One Health approach. This study further highlights the challenges in implementation of WBE and proposes the integration of anthropogenic and socioeconomic determinants in contextualising WBE. Overall, this study proposes a holistic framework for improving the understanding of enteric viral epidemiology in wastewater environments and advancing predictive, evidence-driven public health interventions.
authors: Chibwe M, Bux F.

title: Longitudinal changes in gut microbial evenness and dominance during anti-CD20-containing chemoimmunotherapy with concurrent trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis in patients with B-cell lymphoma.
abstract: Reduced gut microbial diversity is associated with adverse outcomes in hematological malignancies. However, longitudinal studies during lymphoma chemoimmunotherapy rarely distinguish richness from evenness. We investigated whether microbial diversity shifts during anti-CD20-containing chemoimmunotherapy reflect loss of detected taxa or redistribution of relative abundances. In this prospective, single-center exploratory study, 40 patients with B-cell lymphoma provided pretreatment stool samples and 18 paired post-treatment samples. All 18 participants received trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) prophylaxis from treatment initiation through post-treatment sampling, without additional systemic antibacterial exposure between collections or during the 3 months preceding baseline. Following 16S rRNA gene V3-V4 sequencing, Pielou's evenness (q = 0.0077) and Shannon diversity (q = 0.0208) decreased post-treatment, whereas observed features and Faith's phylogenetic diversity did not change significantly (q = 0.4923 and 0.7660, respectively). Dominance significantly increased (Simpson, q = 0.0154; Berger-Parker, q = 0.0237). Beta diversity showed no detectable compositional shift, no genus-level taxon met differential-abundance criteria, and newly dominant taxa varied across individuals. These changes accompanied the combined treatment exposure in a cohort that may overrepresent clinically stable patients; the chemoimmunotherapy and TMP-SMX contributions were inseparable. These alterations appear modest and predominantly structural, with the clearest changes in evenness and dominance, and substantial uncertainty about richness.
authors: Ito S, Otake S, Nakagawa M, Takahashi H, Miura K, Nakamura H, Komine-Aizawa S.

title: Fungal volatiles affect lateral root formation and increase plant tolerance to osmotic stress
abstract: Symbiotic fungi communicate with plants via volatile organic compounds (VOCs), even before physical contact. While fungal VOCs are known to promote plant development under control conditions, their effects under abiotic stress remain poorly characterized. Here, we exposed  Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings to VOCs from the ectomycorrhizal fungi  Laccaria bicolor and  Hebeloma cylindrosporum , and the endophyte  Serendipita indica , under osmotic stress. Time-course transcriptional analysis revealed a rapid, transient induction of auxin transport genes within 3 days of VOC exposure, with minimal early cytokinin modulation. Using auxin-(  aux1-7, axr1-3 ) and cytokinin-resistant (  cre1, arr1-4 ) mutants, we show that this early response bypasses classic auxin/cytokinin antagonism, promoting lateral root proliferation by day 10 under both control and stress conditions. Transcriptomic profiling indicated that fungal VOCs modulate glucosinolate and leucine metabolism and regulate potassium (  HAK5 ) and iron (  IRT1 ) transporters. Genetic and phenotypic analyses of  hak5-2 and  akt1-2 mutants, together with nitric oxide signaling components, revealed that potassium transport and nitric oxide-dependent IRT1 regulation are essential for translating VOC perception into developmental responses. These findings underscore the multifaceted mechanisms by which fungal VOCs coordinate plant development and abiotic stress tolerance.  Highlight  Fungal volatile organic compounds reprogram auxin and cytokinin signaling, ion transporters, and defense metabolism to enhance root development and osmotic stress tolerance in Arabidopsis seedlings.
authors: Miñambres E, Fermoso-Domínguez J, Rodríguez-Sufuentes S, Marco-Montori P, Lorenzo Ó, Calvo-Polanco M.

title: Carboxymethyl Dextran Coated Iron Oxide Magnetic Nanoparticles as Vehicles for CRISPR Ribonucleoproteins
abstract: The efficient and safe intracellular delivery of CRISPR ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) remains a major challenge for the development of genome editing strategies. Magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (MNPs) offer an attractive and biocompatible delivery platform. However, their use for the delivery of functional CRISPR RNPs remains comparatively underexplored. Here, we developed carboxymethyl dextran (CMD)-coated MNPs as non-viral carriers for Cas9 and Cas12a RNPs. Nanocomplexes were formed through electrostatic interactions, without the need for chemical coupling reagents or additional surface functionalization. Both RNPs efficiently associated with MNPs, and the resulting nanocomplexes exhibited stable physicochemical properties and retained their cargo in serum-supplemented culture medium for up to 24 hours. Cellular uptake was confirmed by microscopy, while biocompatibility assays revealed no overt cytotoxicity. Functional genome editing was demonstrated at reporter and endogenous gene loci in HEK-293T cells, as well as in primary human dermal fibroblasts. Finally, we explored the therapeutic potential of this platform for recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (RDEB) by targeting COL7A1 exon 80, with the aim of removing the prevalent c.6527insC mutation while preserving the reading frame. Cas9 RNP nanocomplexes enabled exon 80 deletion. These findings establish CMD-coated MNPs as a versatile platform for the delivery of Cas9 and Cas12a RNPs and support further investigation of magnetic nanoparticle-mediated genome editing for inherited skin disorders.

title: A novel metalloprotease family discovered through a tardigrade
abstract: Tardigrades possess numerous proteins with poorly understood functions, including candidates proposed to have been acquired through horizontal gene transfer. Here, we characterized RvY_14254 from  Ramazzottius varieornatus , previously designated ATPM5, whose homologs are widely distributed across bacteria and eukaryotes but remain largely uncharacterized. We determined the crystal structure of the protein, hereafter termed  Rv Peti, at 1.35 Å resolution.  Rv Peti adopts a compact, C-shaped architecture with no close structural homologs in the Protein Data Bank and contains a conserved His-Asp-Asp (HDD) metal-binding motif within a deep surface pocket. Structural comparison revealed partial similarity of the active-site architecture to that of metalloproteases, including pseudoalterin. Anomalous diffraction analyses demonstrated that the HDD site can accommodate Zn² and Mn² . Biochemical assays showed that  Rv Peti exhibits Zn² -dependent proteolytic activity, which was strongly reduced by a metal chelating reagent and by alanine substitutions of the metal-coordinating residues. In contrast, only weak esterase activity was detected, with the substrates tested. These results identify  Rv Peti as a founding member of a previously uncharacterized family of metalloproteases and provide a structural framework for investigating the physiological and evolutionary roles of this widespread protein family.  statement  Tardigrades, organisms capable of surviving extreme environment stress, possess numerous poorly characterized proteins. We determined the crystal structure of one such protein and found that it adopts a novel fold containing a metal-binding site. Biochemical analyses confirmed zinc-dependent proteolytic activity that was lost upon mutation of the metal-binding residues. These findings define a previously unrecognized metalloprotease family conserved across bacteria and eukaryotes, providing a structural framework for future function studies.
authors: Higashi T, Fukuda Y, Inoue T.

title: Targeted Gene Sequencing for Head and Neck Cancer Candidate Genes in the Nepal case-control study
abstract: Head and Neck cancer (HNC) remains a major global cancer burden, with high incidence and mortality in low- and middle-income countries. Although several genetic variants associated with HNC risk have been identified, cancer predisposition genes in underrepresented populations remain poorly understood. We conducted a hospital-based case-control study at B.P. Koirala Memorial Cancer Hospital in Nepal with 315 HNC cases and 323 controls. Demographic, lifestyle, and clinical data were collected through in-person interviews. Targeted gene sequencing of 493 candidate HNC risk genes were performed, followed by gene- and pathway-based association analyses, and clinical annotation of the identified variants. Consistent with prior findings, HNC incidence increased significantly with alcohol and cigarette use, lower education, and lower socio-economic status. Gene-based analyses identified several genes with suggestive associations prior to multiple-testing adjustment, including  HSPG2 ,  KRT6B ,  SLC4A2 , and  FREM1 . Similarly, no pathways remained statistically significant after adjustment. However, it identified potential biological processes, including extracellular matrix organization, epithelial differentiation, and transcription regulation. Analysis of six cancer predisposition genes (  APC ,  BAP1 ,  BRCA1 ,  BRCA2 ,  RAD51B , and  MUTYH ) identified pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants with clinical relevance, although no significant enrichment was observed between cases and controls. This study provides the first targeted sequencing analysis combined with epidemiological data for HNC in the Nepalese population, an underrepresented high-risk group. While no significant genetic associations were identified, clinically relevant rare variants were detected. Larger studies in South Asian populations are needed to improve the detection of rare variants and to inform risk assessment.  Novelty and Impact  This study presents the first integrated targeted sequencing and epidemiological analysis of head and neck cancer in the Nepalese population, an underrepresented and understudied high-risk group. Using a validated 493-gene panel, we sequenced 315 HNC cases and 323 controls. We identified clinically relevant pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants in known susceptibility genes, including  BRCA1 ,  BRCA2 ,  RAD51B , and  MUTYH . This study also confirmed the strong associations of tobacco, alcohol, and chewing habits with HNC risk, emphasizing the need to study cancer risk in different populations and cultural settings.
authors: Thapa I, Chang CE, Snow AK, Rosenthal J, Bell R, Wood A, Siwakoti B, Gautam DK, Sapkota A, Tavtigian SV, Feng B, Hashibe M.

title: Pho92 direct interaction with Not1 recruits the CCR4-NOT complex to m  6  A containing mRNAs to modulate meiosis in  S. cerevisiae
abstract: N  6 -methyladenosine (m  6 A) is the most abundant internal modification in eukaryotic mRNAs. In  S. cerevisiae , m  6 A is exclusively deposited during meiosis, where it plays an essential role in meiotic progression. In this context, the absence of Pho92, the sole known m  6 A-binding protein in budding yeast, leads to the abnormal persistence of m  6 A-containing mRNAs, ultimately resulting in delayed meiosis. Here, we investigate how m  6 A recognition by Pho92 regulates gene expression. Using complementary  in vivo and  in vitro approaches, we identify direct interactions between Pho92 and Not1, the scaffold subunit of the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex. Structural analyses reveal that a short evolutionarily conserved motif in Pho92 adopts an α-helical conformation that docks onto specific regions of Not1. Functionally, these interactions are required for efficient meiotic progression. Altogether, our findings demonstrate that Pho92 couples m  6 A recognition to the main deadenylase to shape the meiotic transcriptome. More broadly, our work provides mechanistic insights into how epitranscriptomic signals interface with the core mRNA decay machinery to regulate gene expression during cellular differentiation. title: Persistent Malignant Stem Cells Drive Relapse After Transplantation in the Myelodysplastic Neoplasms
abstract: The myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS) are initiated in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Allogeneic transplantation is the only curative treatment, but relapse remains common. To detect rare MDS HSCs, we developed an ultra-low-input DNA sequencing assay and applied it to a multicenter post-transplant cohort. HSC mutation detection preceded relapse by a mean of 98 days and strongly predicted relapse (95.7% vs. 30.3%; hazard ratio, 8.8; P=1.5e-7). Mutations detected only in unfractionated marrow did not predict relapse. We developed methods to measure donor-host HSC chimerism, improving relapse prediction sensitivity. Single-cell protein, DNA, and RNA analyses with mitochondrial lineage tracing confirmed MDS cell enrichment within immunophenotypically- and transcriptionally-defined HSCs, identifying shared ribosomal gene downregulation and candidate mechanisms of venetoclax sensitivity. Venetoclax/azacytidine depleted detectable MDS HSCs in longitudinally evaluated patients. These findings establish that HSC mutation detection predicts post-transplant relapse, provide a rationale for preemptive intervention, and define shared biological features of transplant-resistant MDS HSCs.

title: Nasal Epigenome-Wide Association Study of Respiratory and Allergic Biomarkers in Mexican American Young Adults
abstract: ABSTRACT  Background  Mexican Americans have low asthma prevalence, but they experience a disproportionate clinical asthma burden. Nasal DNA methylation (DNAm) is a biomarker of airway diseases, but its relevance in young adult Mexican Americans and links to air pollution are underexplored. Objective  To identify nasal DNAm markers associated with asthma, allergic sensitization, fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), and lung function and evaluate associations with air pollution. Methods  We tested associations between nasal DNAm at 804,220 CpGs (EPICv2) and respiratory outcomes in 354 young adults from CHAMACOS (age 22) and evaluated replication in 540 adolescents from Project Viva (age 13). Epigenome-wide association studies were adjusted for confounders, and significance was declared at a false discovery rate (FDR)Results  We identified 49 CpGs associated with FeNO and 557 DMRs across multiple respiratory outcomes (FDRConclusions  We identified nasal DNAm markers implicated in airway epithelial integrity and immune response, predominantly associated with FeNO.
authors: Perez-Garcia J, Gunier RB, Eskenazi B, Balmes J, Kogut K, Guo W, Rifas-Shiman SL, Hivert M, Oken E, Gold DR, Holm S, Holland N, Cardenas A.

title: Implementation and Evaluation of Marker Rescue and qPCR Assays for Detection of Replication-Competent Retrovirus in Gene Therapy Products
abstract: Quality control of retroviral gene therapy vectors requires reliable detection of replication- competent retrovirus (RCR) particles. Cell-based assays remain the standard for detecting RCR, while PCR-based assays serve as rapid, complementary methods. Despite their widespread use, few studies provide comprehensive protocols and performance data to guide assay setup. Here we provide a detailed description and performance assessment of a cell-based firefly luciferase marker rescue assay for RCR testing. Additionally, we describe the setup and assessment of a qPCR-based RCR assay targeting retroviral  pol gene sequence. Different viral copy numbers of MuLV were used to determine the final sensitivity of the marker rescue assay with and without initial amplification. Different q-PCR strategies were investigated for RCR testing using different types of primers, including env and pol genes. The marker rescue assay detected 73.2 RCR genome particles without amplification, while the amplification phase enabled detection of functional RCR particles and increased sensitivity, with the amplification step increasing viral particles by up to 5.23 × 10³ fold. The PCR-based RCR assay using retroviral  pol gene could detect approximately 7.32 × 10  3 viral particles. This study offers a resource for establishing RCR testing procedures for clinical-grade retroviral vector products.
authors: Ebrahimiyan H, Sayadmanesh A, Baharvand H, Basiri M.

title: Genome-wide association study in Arabidopsis reveals IAN genes regulate pollen heatwave tolerance
abstract: Abstract    Pollen development is highly sensitive to heatwave conditions in many plant species. Oftentimes, heatwave-induced pollen abortion leads to reduced yield, which is detrimental to crop cultivation and ultimately food security. Though genetic studies have identified loci that affect the level of pollen heatwave tolerance in a few species, no causal genes have been identified, yet. Exploring natural variation for pollen heatwave tolerance is key to finding novel genetic elements involved in protection against damage. In this study, we developed a novel pollen phenotyping protocol, combining MTT-staining with automated image analysis for machine-learning-based pollen classification in Arabidopsis. This assay was employed to screen an Arabidopsis diversity panel consisting of 208 accessions originating from the Iberian Peninsula and Morocco exposed to a controlled long-term, heatwave-like temperature regime. Using GWAS, we identified a QTL encompassing a cluster of immune-associated nucleotide-binding protein (IAN) genes (  IAN2  to  IAN5  ). The  ian2 ian3 ian4 ian5  quadruple mutant was more tolerant to heatwave-like conditions, indicating that these genes repress pollen viability under these conditions. These findings validate our novel phenotyping assay and, together with previous reports that IAN genes repress pollen tolerance to more severe heat, identify the IAN genes as candidate breeding targets for adaptation of crops to a warmer climate.
authors: Frencken M, Brink DMvd, Hurk Jvd, Krabben Lvd, Serin EA, Rieu I.

title: StCCR6-Mediated Lignin Biosynthesis Enhances Potato Resistance Against Ralstonia solanacearum
abstract: Abstract    Background  Bacterial wilt, caused by Ralstonia solanacearum, is one of the most destructive soil-borne diseases worldwide and severely threatens global potato (Solanum tuberosum) production. Lignin deposition in the cell wall constitutes a critical physical barrier for plant defense; however, the regulatory mechanisms governing lignin-mediated resistance in potato remain incompletely understood. Results  Based on previously published temporal transcriptome and metabolome datasets of potato tubers treated with a low dose of deoxynivalenol (DON) across four time points (0, 4, 12, and 48 h), we dissected the defense response. Multi-omics screening revealed that the phenylpropanoid biosynthetic pathway (ko00940) was significantly enriched at 12 h, and  StCCR6  (CCR2), a cinnamoyl-CoA reductase gene, was identified as the most strongly DON-responsive node. Metabolomic profiling further showed that DON treatment drove the accumulation of the lignin monomers coniferyl alcohol and sinapyl alcohol. Functional validation using transgenic lines demonstrated that StCCR6 overexpression thickened cell walls via accelerated lignin deposition and elevated the activities of ROS-scavenging enzymes (SOD, POD, and CAT), thereby enhancing resistance to R. solanacearum in a detached-leaf assay. Conversely, StCCR6 knockout lines exhibited reduced lignin content, elevated reactive oxygen species and oxidative damage, and increased pathogen susceptibility. Conclusion  These results establish StCCR6 as an essential regulator that couples lignin-based physical defense with enzymatic antioxidant scavenging under low-dose DON induction, providing a valuable genetic target for engineering broad-spectrum disease resistance in crops.
authors: Han Y, Liu Y, Sun P, Du C, He F, Wang J, Wang L, Zhang X, Wang Y, Li F.

title: A miRNA-mediated gene regulatory network supports seasonal plasticity in the temperate coral Astrangia poculata.
abstract: Phenotypic plasticity is critical for sessile marine invertebrates facing intensifying climate change. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) - small non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression - are compelling candidates for mediating such plasticity, but their role in coral biology remains poorly characterized. We used the temperate coral Astrangia poculata, which endures annual temperature ranges exceeding 25°C, to investigate miRNA-mediated plasticity across seasonal and thermal contexts. Adult aposymbiotic colonies were exposed to ambient seasonal temperatures (∼5-22°C) and a chronic +3°C warming treatment from February to August 2021. Monthly physiological sampling showed that seasonal temperature variation drove significant shifts in photosynthesis, respiration and soluble protein, whereas the +3°C treatment had minimal physiological effect. RNA-seq across three time points (February, June and August) revealed that seasonal temperature variation also drove the strongest molecular response. Transcriptional functional enrichment shifted from winter protein homeostasis and cellular integrity to summer immunity, metabolism and reproduction. We also identified 51 A. poculata miRNAs (46 novel), providing the first characterization of the miRNA repertoire in this species. Target prediction and co-expression analyses revealed that although mRNA-miRNA networks appear to maintain a stable infrastructure across seasons and treatments, specific interactions may be rewired to drive seasonal biology. This dynamic regulation is associated with putative suppression of energy-intensive cell division and morphogenesis during winter quiescence, while shifting to regulate tissue remodeling and reproduction genes during the summer. These results establish miRNAs as seasonal gene regulators in a temperate coral and suggest that the molecular infrastructure underlying its plasticity may also confer resilience to moderate thermal stress.
authors: Ashey J, Gilligan C, Putnam HM.

title: Comparison of the Effects of Potato Vine-Kill Methods on the Preharvest DNA Levels of Soilborne Fungal Pathogens, Incidence of Potato Virus Y in Progeny Tubers, and Yield in the San Luis Valley, Colorado.
abstract: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is susceptible to several fungal pathogens, including Alternaria solani, Alternaria alternata, Rhizoctonia solani, and Colletotrichum coccodes, which can significantly reduce yield and tuber quality. Vine-kill is commonly used by potato producers to facilitate harvest, enhance tuber maturation and skin set, and manage tuber size. This study evaluated how different vine-kill methods affect soil DNA levels of these four fungal pathogens, potato virus Y (PVY) incidence in progeny tubers, and tuber yield and size distribution in the San Luis Valley, Colorado. Treatments included pulling, flailing, and chemical desiccation with Reglone (diquat dibromide) combined with either Aim EC (carfentrazone-ethyl) or Super Tin 4L (triphenyltin hydroxide). Vine-kill methods did not significantly affect yield, size profile, or PVY incidence. However, soil pathogen DNA levels measured as DNA copy number by quantitative PCR varied among treatments and year. In 2022, pulling resulted in the lowest levels of A. solani, A. alternata, and R. solani and the second-lowest level of C. coccodes. In 2023, pulling provided no significant benefit, but in 2025, it reduced soil levels of all four pathogens relative to desiccation and natural senescence, whereas flailing resulted in the lowest soil pathogen DNA levels in 2025 for both R. solani and C. coccodes. Between the two commonly used practices, flailing generally resulted in lower detected fungal pathogen DNA levels than chemical desiccation. Overall, pulling and flailing reduced soil fungal pathogen DNA levels, suggesting that vine-kill practices might influence disease management in potato production systems.
authors: Chikh-Ali M, Zeng Y, Daniel J, Usman Aslam HM, Charkowski AO.

title: ATP-free fatty aldehyde biosynthesis enables an autonomous lux-based bioluminescence system.
abstract: Autonomous bioluminescence systems enable continuous light emission in engineered organisms by genetically encoding both luciferase enzymes and their substrate biosynthetic pathways, offering a powerful platform for non-invasive and long-term monitoring of biological processes. However, bioluminescence output is highly sensitive to substrate availability and host metabolic state, often leading to signal instability under energy-limited conditions. Here, we report an alternative luciferin biosynthetic strategy for the bacterial Lux bioluminescence system in which the adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-dependent LuxEC complex is replaced by α-dioxygenase (αDOX), an enzyme that directly converts fatty acids into fatty aldehydes without consuming ATP. Using machine learning-guided directed evolution, we engineered αDOX variants that markedly enhanced bioluminescence intensity when coupled with bacterial luciferase. The resulting ATP-free Lux bioluminescence system enabled single-cell-level bioluminescence imaging and showed a smaller reduction in light emission than the native LuxCDABE system under several antibiotic treatments, although these experiments do not establish ATP availability as the causal mechanism.
authors: Kusuma SH, Nagai T.

title: Tire-derived 6PPD-quinone promotes conjugative gene transfer through respiratory bioenergetic perturbation.
abstract: Tire-derived N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N'-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine quinone (6PPD-Q) is transported by roadway runoff into urban waters, yet its sublethal effects on microbial gene exchange remain poorly resolved. Here, 5 μg/L 6PPD-Q increased the transconjugant fraction from 0.25% to 0.65% in a lake-water enriched biofilm community and enhanced plasmid transfer in a defined donor-recipient system. Relative to its parent compound 6PPD, 6PPD-Q more strongly altered oxidative phosphorylation, ATP/ADP ratios, and NAD+/NADH balance. Molecular simulations indicated membrane partitioning and predicted quinone-site interactions resembling those of ubiquinone analogues, while cyclic voltammetry and partial growth rescue of a ubiB-deficient strain supported quinone-associated redox activity. 6PPD-Q also increased succinate dehydrogenase activity, oxygen consumption, membrane potential, and ATP/ADP ratios. Respiratory-chain and bioenergetic inhibitors attenuated both these responses and the transfer enhancement, linking the phenotype to cellular energy metabolism. Extracellular filament-like structures, migration responses, and appendage-related transcription changed concurrently, although the structures could not be assigned to a specific pilus system. These results support respiratory bioenergetic perturbation as an upstream contributor to 6PPD-Q-enhanced conjugation and identify microbial gene exchange as a water-quality endpoint relevant to tire-contaminated runoff and receiving waters.
authors: Yang B, Tan C, Peng Y, Zhang Q.

title: Serum [-2]proPSA as a Candidate Phenotypic Correlate of Molecular Alterations and Prognostic Marker in Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer.
abstract: BackgroundSerum biomarkers that complement molecular profiling and provide prognostic information are of interest in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC).MethodsWe performed a single-centre retrospective exploratory analysis of 31 patients with mCRPC receiving systemic therapy. Baseline serum total PSA, free PSA, [-2]proPSA (p2PSA) and prostate health index (PHI) were evaluated together with tumour somatic molecular alterations and overall survival (OS). Baseline p2PSA was analysed both continuously after log2 transformation and using an exploratory 300 pg/mL threshold. On-treatment p2PSA change was reanalysed as a time-dependent covariate because follow-up sampling occurred at variable times.ResultsMedian age was 75.1 years (range 60.2-83.2). Median follow-up was 38.3 months (95% CI 22.5-42.8). Each doubling of baseline p2PSA was associated with shorter OS (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.16-1.96; p = 0.0019). Patients with p2PSA > 300 pg/mL (n = 8; 6 deaths) had shorter OS than those with p2PSA ≤ 300 pg/mL (n = 23; 8 deaths; HR 4.61, 95% CI 1.46-14.56; log-rank p = 0.0043). Total PSA, free PSA and PHI were also associated with OS, and adding p2PSA to total PSA did not significantly improve model fit (likelihood-ratio p = 0.156). Baseline p2PSA was higher in patients with a pathogenic/likely pathogenic somatic alteration detected (n = 9) than in those with no pathogenic alteration detected (n = 22; Mann-Whitney p = 0.0348; Cliff's delta 0.49), but this association attenuated after exclusion of extreme values. On-treatment p2PSA change was not associated with OS after time-dependent modelling (failure to achieve ≥ 50% decline: HR 1.44, 95% CI 0.42-4.90; p = 0.557).ConclusionsIn this small hypothesis-generating mCRPC cohort, higher baseline p2PSA was associated with poorer OS and with the presence of pathogenic/likely pathogenic somatic tumour alterations. These findings support prospective validation of p2PSA as an exploratory prognostic marker and candidate phenotypic correlate, rather than a surrogate for tumour genomics.
authors: Conteduca V, Garofoli M, Bruno G, Landriscina M, Fiorenza M, Polito C, Sirica R, Terracciano D.

title: A Multi-Tissue Transcriptomic Resource for the Brahminy Blindsnake Indotyphlops braminus (Squamata: Typhlopidae).
abstract: The Brahminy blindsnake (Indotyphlops braminus), an all-female, parthenogenetic, and triploid snake, is an informative species for studying polyploidy and asexual reproduction in vertebrates. In this study, we analyzed tissue expression patterns in I. braminus using a PacBio-derived transcript reference and Illumina RNA-seq. Differential expression and annotation over-representation analyses were used to characterize tissue-associated expression differences and over-represented annotations across ovary, heart, liver, and skin from the same three individuals. The three overlapping eye-spot pools were described at the library level. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was used only as an exploratory analysis of the 12 four-tissue libraries. A total of 835,353,682 clean read pairs were retained, and gene expression profiles showed broad differences among the four formally analyzed tissues. Of 30,224 tested genes, 13,849 showed a tissue effect, and 4228 candidate tissue-enriched genes were identified by requiring higher expression in all three relevant pairwise comparisons. Six representative annotation terms remained significant in the sensitivity analysis, and 3 of 11 non-gray co-expression modules passed the prespecified stability rule across nine alternative networks. This study provides an additional multi-tissue transcriptomic resource for I. braminus, with candidate sets that can guide future functional and comparative tests of hypotheses concerning parthenogenesis, triploidy, fossoriality, and visual reduction.
authors: Sun K, Ji X, Lu J, Lu A, Wang Y, Zhu F.

title: Identification and prognostic value of non-hotspot POLE exonuclease domain mutations in endometrial cancer.
abstract: BackgroundEndometrial cancer with somatic POLE exonuclease domain mutations (EDMs) has a highly favorable prognosis; however, the clinical implications of non-hotspot EDMs in POLE remain unclear.Materials and methodsIn 793 patients with endometrial cancer enrolled at the National Cancer Center and Juntendo University Hospitals, 25 prespecified variants were screened using the Luminex assay. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was carried out to evaluate 54 patients with hotspot and non-hotspot EDMs. In patients with endometrial cancer (n = 4864) registered in Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (GENIE), those harboring hotspot EDMs were matched with randomly sampled patients without EDMs, and a polymerase epsilon (POLE) score for gene panel testing was developed.ResultsIn our cohort, POLE-EDMs, including hotspot (n = 91) and non-hotspot (n = 12) EDMs, were identified in 103 (12.9%) of 793 patients. The prevalence of grade 3 and advanced-stage endometrial cancer was higher in patients with non-hotspot EDMs than in those with hotspot EDMs. WES analysis of 54 patients revealed no significant differences in genomic mutations between the groups, and four non-hotspot EDMs were identified. A POLE-specific mutational signature was observed in tumors with EDM. In addition, the POLE score criteria were developed based on hotspot EDMs using the GENIE cohort, achieving a detection sensitivity of 0.94. Using the established POLE score, we identified nine non-hotspot EDMs.ConclusionsWe identified 13 novel candidate non-hotspot EDMs using a newly established POLE score for gene panels and demonstrated an association between non-hotspot EDMs and favorable prognosis. The identification of additional non-hotspot EDMs will facilitate precise molecular classification of endometrial cancer.
