title: Identification of a stable major locus and candidate genes for drought tolerance during wheat germination.
abstract: Key messageWe identified QRSH.scwl-4B as a pleiotropic QTL for basal shoot growth and drought-stress response at the wheat germination stage, predicted its putative candidate genes, and confirmed it as a promising locus for drought-tolerance and limited yield loss. Drought stress during germination severely reduces the wheat germination rate and seedling establishment, leading to significant yield losses. Understanding the genetic control of this trait is important for breeding drought-tolerant and high-yielding wheat varieties. Here, we detected 21 quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for maximum root length (MRL), root number (RN) and shoot height (SH) under control (CK) and drought treatment (DT) at the germination stage using a recombinant inbred line (RIL) population. Among them, QSH.scwl-CK-4B, QSH.scwl-DT-4B and QRSH.scwl-4B were co-localized to a common region on chromosome arm 4BS, which exhibited pleiotropic effects on both basal shoot growth and the drought-stress response. QRSH.scwl-4B was also identified by bulked segregant analysis sequencing (BSA-Seq), mapped to a 2.09 Mb interval on 4BS, and explained 24.32%-30.89% of the phenotypic variation (PVE). Through RNA-seq, BSA-Seq and parental genome sequencing, TraesCS4B03G0104700 and TraesCS4B03G0102800 were identified as the putative candidate genes. KEGG enrichment analysis suggested that TraesCS4B03G0104700 may regulate drought tolerance during germination via jasmonic acid (JA) biosynthesis. Moreover, the positive allele of QRSH.scwl-4B increased productive tiller number (PTN) by 13.37%, while showing only limited adverse effects on other yield-related traits. This suggests that QRSH.scwl-4B is a promising locus for improving wheat drought tolerance, with potentially minimal negative impact on yield. Collectively, these findings provide a foundation for cloning QRSH.scwl-4B and for improving drought tolerance in wheat through molecular breeding.
journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
authors: Liu J, Wang D, Zhou Q, Qin N, Liu J, Liu X, Li Y, Peng H, Ma J.

title: Integrative machine learning for identifying transcriptomic signatures of neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy response in locally advanced rectal cancer.
abstract: BackgroundPredicting tumour response to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) in locally advanced rectal cancer remains an unresolved clinical problem. The substantial inter-patient variability in pathological response means that molecular biomarkers capable of prospective patient stratification are urgently needed. However, transcriptomic biomarker studies in this setting are prone to methodological limitations -  particularly data leakage -  that produce irreproducible performance estimates and hinder translation.ObjectiveThis study aimed to identify a biologically interpretable transcriptomic signature of nCRT response in rectal cancer through an integrative machine learning framework designed with strict attention to leakage prevention and methodological transparency.MethodsGene expression microarray profiles from 46 rectal cancer patients (24 responders, 22 non-responders; GEO: GSE35452; 22,189 gene features) were analysed. Phenotype was defined by the Mandard tumour regression grade (TRG) [1]: responders = TRG 1-2 (complete or near-complete pathological response); non-responders = TRG 3-5. All patients received fluoropyrimidine-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery. A preliminary variance filter -  applied to the complete dataset because variance is a class-label-free operation -  retained the 1000 most variable genes; sensitivity analyses at 500, 2000, and 5000 genes are reported in Supplementary Note S1. A label-leakage-controlled sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline was constructed in which all preprocessing -  including standardisation and feature selection -  was performed independently within each training fold. Four feature selection algorithms were applied per fold (ANOVA F-statistic, mutual information, L1-penalised logistic regression, and Random Forest importance), and a fold-specific consensus gene set was constructed at each outer iteration (Algorithm ??). Eight classifiers were evaluated as an exploratory multi-algorithm comparison.ResultsThe pooled out-of-fold AUC across the five outer folds was 0.987 for Gaussian Naïve Bayes (95% percentile bootstrap CI: 0.949-1.000), with a mean fold-wise AUC of 0.990 ± 0.020. Based on the pooled out-of-fold predictions, specificity was 87.0%, and balanced accuracy was 91.5%. A 109-gene consensus candidate panel was identified across the fold-specific feature-selection analyses. Within this panel, six genes showed statistically significant differential expression between responders and non-responders: WBP1L, CEBPB, ATE1, and BAG2 showed lower expression in non-responders, whereas BSG and ZFAND2B showed higher expression. Functional enrichment analysis of the 109-gene candidate panel, using the 1000 variance-filtered genes as the background universe, identified biological processes related to DNA damage response, signal transduction, apoptotic signalling, protein regulation, and immune-related processes. The results are exploratory and require validation in independent cohorts. FAM175A was selected by feature importance but showed non-significant DE ( p=0.393 ) within the discovery cohort. Functional enrichment analysis of the consensus candidate set (clusterProfiler; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR  ConclusionThis discovery study demonstrates that an integrative, label-leakage-controlled machine learning framework can identify biologically coherent transcriptomic candidates for nCRT response prediction in rectal cancer. Given the single retrospective cohort of 46 patients and absence of independent external validation, all findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. External validation in independent prospective cohorts is required before any clinical or translational inference can be drawn.
authors: Mirghayed MMR, Soror AA, Rezaei A, Sardouei AHM, Hajipour M, Behtaji S, Shoar MR, Yavuz M, Fadaei Y.

title: Valorization of prawn shell waste-derived chitosan into hydrazone functionalized Schiff base for colorimetric ion sensing, solid-state fluorescence, antimicrobial, antifungal, and antioxidant applications.
abstract: In this study, we converted prawn shell waste-derived chitosan into a hydrazone-functionalized Schiff base containing 2-hydroxy-1-naphthaldehyde moieties through sequential chemical modifications. We characterized the synthesized chitosan-based Schiff base using FTIR, UV-visible spectroscopy, 1H NMR, 13C NMR, HR-MS, and HPLC. The hydrazone Schiff-base formation was confirmed by characteristic CN stretching in the FTIR spectrum and azomethine (CHN) proton signals in the 1H NMR spectrum, consistent with hydrazide condensation with 2-hydroxy-1-naphthaldehyde. The material exhibited colorimetric sensing, solid-state fluorescence, antimicrobial, antifungal, and antioxidant properties. Naked-eye color changes were observed in the presence of Fe2+, Fe3+, Pb2+, OH-, CN-, and CO32- ions, while fluorescence changes occurred with Al3+ and Ag + ions. The detection limits for Al3+, Ag+, Fe3+, Fe2+, and Pb2+ were 3, 5, 9, 10, and 12 ppm, respectively, while those for OH-, CN-, and CO32- were 8, 4, and 3 ppm, respectively. The compound also exhibited strong yellow-green solid-state fluorescence under UV irradiation. Furthermore, the compound showed antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, antifungal activity against Candida albicans, and 76.11% DPPH radical-scavenging activity. Molecular docking studies using a representative oligomeric model of the material indicated predicted binding affinities of -6.8, -6.5, and -8.7 kcal/mol for C. albicans CYP51, E. coli DNA gyrase B, and S. aureus Sortase A, respectively. Overall, this work demonstrates an eco-friendly, sustainable approach to valorizing prawn shell waste into advanced, multifunctional bio-based materials with promising environmental, analytical, and biomedical applications.
authors: Thakur MS, Naik VA, Gaikwad KR.

title: Dietary Rosa roxburghii Tratt polysaccharides improve intestinal health and alleviate deoxynivalenol-induced oxidative stress and immune imbalance in broilers.
abstract: Deoxynivalenol (DON) is a common mycotoxin contaminating poultry feed, which can induce oxidative stress, immune disorders and barrier damage in the intestinal tract of broilers, seriously affecting performance and feed safety. Rosa roxburghii Tratt polysaccharides (RRTPs), a characteristic wild plant resource, have been reported to have antioxidant and immunomodulatory activities. However, whether RRTPs can effectively combat DON induced intestinal disorders in broilers has not been systematically studied. In this study, one-day-old male broilers were acclimated for 3 days and then subjected to dietary supplementation with RRTPs (100, 200, and 400 mg/kg diet) under normal conditions or combined with DON exposure (4 mg/kg diet) for 42 days to evaluate the protective effects of RRTPs against DON-associated intestinal injury. The results showed that under normal physiological conditions, RRTPs could improve body weight gain and feed efficiency, up-regulate the expression of tight junction proteins, modulate jejunal microbiota composition without significantly altering microbial diversity, and enhance mucosal innate immune defense. Under DON exposure, RRTPs significantly reduced the contents of intestinal reactive oxygen species and malondialdehyde, restored the total antioxidant capacity and mitochondrial DNA content, inhibited cGAS-STING-related signaling responses, and regulated the expression of markers associated with M1/M2 macrophages. In summary, RRTPs supplementation alleviated DON-associated intestinal injury by improving redox status and immune-related responses, providing insights into the potential application of Rosa roxburghii Tratt polysaccharides in mycotoxin risk mitigation.
authors: Wang X, Liu Y, Ge J, Liu P, Cai G, Song R, Zou H, Gu J, Yuan Y, Liu X, Liu Z, Bian J.

title: Deciphering interfacial photoelectron transfer in a Thiobacillus denitrificans-CdS Biohybrid for efficient vanadate bioreduction.
abstract: Vanadium (V) is a re-emerging environmental hazard currently. Microbial vanadate [V(V)] reduction is a key process for its detoxification, which is commonly driven by electron-donor provided chemical energy. The contribution of ubiquitous solar energy for V(V) bioreduction remains largely unknown. This study investigated V(V) removal in an artificial photosynthetic biohybrid system for promising utilization of solar energy. The synthesized Thiobacillus denitrificans-CdS biohybrid under light achieved a V(V) removal efficiency of 96.3 ± 2.7% within 4 days, along with biomass growth. Characterizations including XANES and EXAFS verified that V(V) was reduced to insoluble tetravalent V [V(IV)] oxide precipitates containing V=O and V-O on the biohybrid interface. Crucially, the in situ precipitated V(IV) narrowed the semiconductor bandgap and suppressed carrier recombination, continuously boosting the photocurrent density for enhanced V(V) removal. Biochemical quantification and inhibitor tests confirmed the involvement of cellular compounds, especially cytochrome c in electron transfer, eventually contributing to V(V) reduction. Transcriptomic analysis and gene transcription quantification suggested that genes such as narG and norB were also potentially associated with V(V) reduction. This study employed solar energy to sustainably power non-photosynthetic microorganism to reduce V(V), providing previously unrecognized understanding of V geochemistry and promising novel strategy for V remediation.
authors: Wang L, Xu Y, Li B, Zhang B.

title: Nocardia terpenica bacteremia confirmed by blood culture in a patient with granulocytopenia and Aspergillus fumigatus coinfection: a first case report.
abstract: BackgroundNocardia terpenica is a rare environmental actinomycete without prior report of human bloodstream infection. In immunocompromised hosts, it often causes mixed infections, complicating diagnosis and treatment.Case presentationWe report the first bacteremia case of N. terpenica in an adult with severe granulocytopenia after B-ALL induction chemotherapy. Blood culture (positive at 5.9 days) revealed branched Gram-positive rods; species was confirmed by MALDI‑TOF and whole‑genome sequencing (WGS). Plasma mNGS also detected Aspergillus fumigatus, and chest CT showed halo/air‑crescent signs, establishing concurrent invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. The patient cleared infection after combined antibiotics (trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, voriconazole, imipenem/cilastatin, vancomycin) and completed subsequent chemotherapy.ConclusionWe report the first case of N. terpenica bacteremia, highlighting that this species can cause bloodstream infection in severely immunocompromised hosts. Prolonged culture incubation and molecular diagnostics (WGS and mNGS) are essential for timely diagnosis and optimal management.
authors: He X, Zhou J, Long S, Liu H, Zou G, Song G.

title: AMV063 of Betaentomopoxvirus amoorei encodes a functional Caspase-2 essential for virus-mediated apoptosis.
abstract: The genome of Betaentomopoxvirus amoorei (AMEV) is approximately 232 kb in size and encodes around 256 predicted open reading frames (ORFs), many of which are associated with host interaction and apoptosis modulation. A comprehensive functional characterization of the AMV063 ORF was conducted in this study. The AMV063 protein was heterologously expressed using a baculovirus-based expression system. In parallel, gene silencing of the AMV063 ORF was achieved by deleting the corresponding sequence and generating a recombinant AmΔ063/gfp virus through homologous recombination. To investigate functional outcomes, apoptosis-sensitive CF-70-B2 cells were either treated with purified AMV063 protein, infected with the recombinant AmΔ063/gfp virus, or both. After treatment, the caspase-2 enzymatic activity was measured, apoptotic responses were assessed using TUNEL staining, and cell viability was measured via the trypan blue exclusion test. Exposure to AMV063 protein resulted in a marked increase in caspase-2 activity, and a corresponding elevation in TUNEL-positive cell death. Conversely, in cells infected with the AmΔ063/gfp virus, caspase-2 activity, TUNEL positivity, and overall cell death were significantly reduced compared with those infected with the control AmΔsph/gfp virus. These findings indicate that the AMV063 ORF sequence encodes a protein associated with caspase-2-like activity and that the recombinant AMV063 protein is capable of inducing apoptotic responses in host cells. This study represents the first functional characterization of the AMV063 ORF, demonstrating that it is a functional caspase-2-like gene.
authors: Bilgili-Tetikoğlu F, Demirbağ Z, Muratoğlu H.

title: Alignment-free discovery of conserved RNA structures in the human genome
abstract: Many functional RNAs were first found as conserved RNA structures, and their roles in gene regulation were identified later. In humans and other vertebrates, imperfect genome alignments have hindered the discovery of such structures. Here we present RLMHelix, which selects candidate conserved RNA structures from single sequences before any alignment by scoring helices supported by language-model dependencies and thermodynamics. Through distillation, RLMHelix rapidly scans the transcribed human genome and ranks known RNAs higher than conventional thermodynamic scanning. Two-thirds of 15,821 candidates are new to four earlier genome-wide screens, yet agree with in-cell probing, and over half retain structural signal in homologues. In eCLIP data and in exploratory pull-downs, higher RLMHelix scores were associated with more binding by double-stranded RNA-binding proteins. By linking candidates to their binding proteins, RLMHe-lix yields testable functional hypotheses and illuminates a path from unrecognized human RNA structures to RNA biology and therapeutic targets.
authors: Sumi S, Makino K, Onoguchi M, Adachi S, Saito H, Hamada M.

title: Green synthesis of Brassica rapa-mediated magnesium oxide nanoparticles MgO NPs with ROS-driven antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacteria.
abstract: The ability of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria to develop antibiotic-resistant biofilms enables their ongoing survival in various environments. In this study, MgO NPs were synthesized using an environmentally sustainable green method mediated by Brassica rapa. The antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of the synthesized MgO nanoparticles were evaluated against clinical isolates of A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae, and E. coli. These nanoparticles were checked for their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities by broth microdilution assay and microtiter plate assay. The biogenic MgO NPs exhibited strong antibacterial activity with an MIC of 125-250 µg/ml and bactericidal effects at 500-1000 µg /ml. Planktonic growth inhibition exceeded 90% at 50 µg/ml after 48 h and reached 99% at 100 µg/ml after 72 h. Biofilm formation was suppressed by 60-90% at 50 µg/ml while pre-established biofilms were reduced by 97-99% following prolonged exposure. Mechanistic studies demonstrated substantial destruction of extracellular polymeric substances. Specifically, proteins decreased by 68%, carbohydrates by 55%, and extracellular DNA by 33%, while intracellular reactive oxygen species simultaneously increased by 2-3 times. The results demonstrate that Brassica rapa-derived MgO NPs function as effective, sustainable nanomaterial that prevents biofilm formation by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens.
journal: International microbiology : the official journal of the Spanish Society for Microbiology
authors: Muzammil S, Khalid MH, Siddique MH, Ijaz MU, Taj Z, Nisar MA, Hayat S, Hashem A, Alarjani KM, Alharbi MG, Abd Allah EF.

title: Cardiomyocyte-targeted HSP60 modulates myocardial remodeling pathways and peripheral blood mononuclear cell mitochondrial membrane potential in hypertensive diabetic rats.
abstract: Arterial hypertension and diabetes mellitus frequently coexist and synergistically accelerate adverse left ventricular remodeling through mitochondrial dysfunction, sterile inflammation, and extracellular matrix disorganization. Heat shock protein 60 (HSP60) is a mitochondrial chaperone involved in proteostasis and stress adaptation, but it remains unclear whether cardiomyocyte-restricted augmentation of HSP60 can modulate myocardial remodeling and influence systemic immune-cell bioenergetics. Male spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) and normotensive Wistar-Kyoto (WKY) rats were studied with or without streptozotocin-induced diabetes. Animals were assigned to WKY, SHR, WKY+HSP60, SHR+HSP60, WKY + DM+HSP60, and SHR + DM+HSP60 groups. HSP60 was delivered using an adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (AAV9) vector under the cardiac troponin T promoter. Myocardial remodeling was assessed by histomorphometry and Masson's trichrome staining, myocardial signaling by immunohistochemistry and RT-qPCR, and peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) mitochondrial membrane potential by JC-1 flow cytometry. Cardiac HSP60 delivery showed a context-dependent pattern. In hypertensive diabetic rats, this pattern included altered NLRP3 subcellular localization, modulation of mitochondrial regulatory and inflammatory-fibrotic transcripts, and increased PBMC mitochondrial membrane potential. PBMC polarization inversely correlated with myocardial fibrosis. Normotensive and single-pathology groups did not show a comparable integrated response profile. These findings indicate that cardiomyocyte-targeted HSP60 overexpression is associated with remodeling-related changes in myocardium and peripheral immune-cell bioenergetics under combined hypertensive and diabetic stress. PBMC mitochondrial membrane potential may represent a candidate peripheral indicator of myocardial state in this preclinical setting.

title: ZmHY5L synergistically affects endosperm starch quality and grain morphology through G-box-mediated transcriptional regulation of the maize waxy gene.
abstract: Key messageThis study confirms that ZmHY5L positively regulates the transcription ofwaxy gene through specifically binding to G-box elements on its promoter, and can simultaneously affect starch quality and grain morphology of maize endosperm. The waxy gene in maize encodes granule-bound starch synthase (GBSSI) protein, which controls the synthesis of amylose and is one of the key genes affecting grain quality and yield, but its regulatory mechanism remains not fully understood. Taking two characteristic Yunnan waxy maize landraces as materials, this study through DNA pull-down combined with mass spectrometry screened the upstream regulatory factor of waxy gene, and identified ZmHY5L, a basic leucine zipper (bZIP) family transcription factor that is one of the homologous genes of Arabidopsis HY5. Numerous previous studies have shown that HY5 is a core transcription factor in the light signaling pathway‌. This study subcellular localization verified that ZmHY5L protein is localized in the nucleus; EMSA and yeast one-hybrid assays further confirmed the direct interaction between ZmHY5L and the regulatory region of waxy gene. By constructing ZMHY5L gene editing mutants for phenotype comparison, it was found that the mutation of ZmHY5L gene significantly reduced the GBSSI protein content in maize kernels, while the amylopectin proportion, grain volume, hundred-grain weight of the mutants were remarkably increased, the gelatinization characteristics of starch also changed obviously, without altering the total starch content of kernels. This study confirms that ZmHY5L positively regulates the transcription of waxy gene through specifically binding to G-box elements on its promoter, and can simultaneously affect starch quality and grain morphology of maize endosperm.
journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
authors: Du J, Ye Y, Chen X, Li F, Yin G, Wu X.

title: Ecophysiological assessment of aquatic plants in a Southern Türkiye Lake: heavy metal bioconcentration, phytochemicals, and biological activities.
abstract: In the present study, the aquatic macrophytes of Golbasi Lake, located in Hatay Province, the southern part of Türkiye, were investigated for heavy metal pollution. The investigation focused on commonly found macrophytes, such as Ceratophyllum demersum, Lemna minor, and Salvinia natans, to assess cadmium, cobalt, copper, chromium, iron, lead, manganese, nickel, and zinc using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry. Nickel and lead concentrations exceeded the prescribed threshold values. Cadmium, lead, nickel, and zinc concentrations were higher, with copper and iron exceeding the critical values. Among the three species, L. minor showed the greatest accumulation of Cd, Cu, Pb, and Zn, with Cd concentrations approximately 2911% and 300% higher than those in C. demersum and S. natans, respectively. L. minor exhibited the highest total phenolic and flavonoid contents, which were approximately 24.9% and 34.2% higher, respectively, than those of C. demersum. In contrast, S. natans showed the highest DPPH radical-scavenging activity, approximately 14.4% higher than C. demersum. All the extracts showed antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus; the highest antibacterial activity was observed for L. minor. The present study thus shows the impact of agricultural, industrial, mining, and drainage activities on the Golbasi Lake ecosystem, highlighting the role of aquatic plants as bioindicators for heavy metal detection. The results emphasize the need to remove heavy metals before discharging them into Golbasi Lake and to implement effective environmental management strategies to maintain the balance of nature and the eco-sustainability of the Golbasi Lake ecosystem.
authors: Yalcin IE.

title: Epigenetic aging in people with HIV across the life course: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Epigenetic aging algorithms are emerging tools for understanding the biological effects of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). A growing body of literature has applied DNA methylation-based epigenetic clocks in people living with HIV (PWH) across the life course, examining epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) in relation to HIV infection, antiretroviral therapy (ART), comorbidities, and clinical biomarkers (e.g., viral load, CD4 T-cell counts). This systematic review (Prospero: CRD420251126874) summarizes and synthesizes the current evidence on epigenetic aging in PWH across the life course and identifies critical knowledge gaps for future research. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Medline through June 26, 2026. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and assessed studies for risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. We created a narrative synthesis of results and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA. Fifty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. More than half (n = 33) examined EAA in PWH compared to an uninfected control population. We identified heterogeneity in study populations and design, biospecimens profiled, platforms used for DNA methylation analysis, and epigenetic clocks employed. Only 6 studies included participants younger than 18 years and no studies focused exclusively on individuals over 65 years. Only 10 studies examined longitudinal changes in EAA. Thirty-seven papers evaluated associations between EAA and comorbidities. A meta-analysis of HorvathAge EAA across 14 studies found a mean difference of 3.41 years (95%CI 2.22, 4.60) in PWH relative to controls. Current evidence supports accelerated EAA among PWH but highlights substantial methodological heterogeneity and important knowledge gaps. Longitudinal studies of EAA in PWH are needed in populations under 18 and over 65, to clarify the effects of ART, clinical biomarkers, and age-related comorbidities, and determine the clinical utility of epigenetic aging biomarkers.
journal: The journals of gerontology. Series A, Biological sciences and medical sciences
authors: Kinkade C, Wimbish A, Senthilkumar A, Coker MO, Luo L, Yin MT, Kuhn L, Corley MJ, Shiau S.

title: Heavy metal stress mitigation in plants by metal-resistant fungi: molecular and biotechnological insights.
abstract: Heavy Metals (HMs) are persistent, non-biodegradable metallic elements that accumulate into soils due to weathering processes and anthropogenic activities, such as mining, smelting and industrial discharges. They can be classified as essential (Cu, Zn, Ni, Fe, Mn), which are toxic in excessive amounts, and non-essential (Cd, Pb, As, Hg), which are dangerous even in small amounts. HMs affect plant metabolism causing production of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS), growth inhibition and nutrient deficiency, Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings germination was lowered to 55% and 21% at concentrations of 50 and 100 mg L⁻1 CdCl₂. Phytochelatins, metallothioneins and vacuole sequestration protect plants, but become ineffective at high concentrations of HMs. Metal-resistant fungi help to cope with stress conditions using mechanisms of biosorption, bioaccumulation, biomineralization, bioleaching and biotransformation, adapted Aspergillus niger managed to leach 78.5% Ni and 82.3% Mo during 30 days, while Penicillium chrysogenum eliminated 63% Cd in soil. Partners of fungi, such as Trichoderma and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, regulate production of ROS, activation of MAPKs and ABA/JA/SA/ethylene/auxin signaling pathway and expression of MT, PCS, GST, ABC, NRAMP and HMA genes under control of WRKY, MYB, NAC and bZIP transcription factors.
authors: Choudhary S, Singh K, Sharma A, Mehta A, Gupta S, Juneja G.

title: Affinity and Conformations of Ca  2+  -Calmodulin Bound to Peptides Containing the Calmodulin-Binding Motif of HIV-1 Matrix Protein
abstract: Background  Protein–protein interactions enable viruses to adapt and replicate by modifying host factors. Thermodynamic characterization of viral–host complexes can reveal viral mechanisms, broader principles of protein interactions, and properties relevant to anti-HIV-1 inhibitor development. Here, we examine the binding of the HIV-1 matrix (MA) protein to host calmodulin (CaM). MA, the N-terminal domain of Gag (group-specific antigen), directs Gag to the plasma membrane for viral assembly and maturation and may recruit CaM to facilitate this trafficking. However, the MA–CaM interaction remains poorly characterized. MA contains a noncanonical N-terminal CaM-binding motif with hydrophobic regions that may mediate CaM binding and a central, positively charged KKK cluster. Objective  We aimed to determine the binding affinities of MA to calcium-bound CaM (Ca  2+ -CaM), elucidate protein regions that are critical to the heterocomplex formation, and monitor the conformational alterations in Ca  2+ -CaM upon binding to MA.  Methods  We studied Ca  2+ -CaM binding to synthetic MA peptides representing full-length wild type (FL WT), a C-terminal truncation lacking the KKK cluster, and an FL K→N/K→H/K→Q triple mutant of the MA CaM-binding motif. The peptides were C-terminally labeled with Cy3, and FL CaM S39C with Cy5. Binding affinity was measured by ensemble Förster resonance energy transfer (eFRET) using 100 nM Cy3-MA and increasing Cy5-Ca  2+ -CaM concentrations in the range of 50 nM to 2.5 µM. Conformational changes in doubly spin-labeled Ca  2+ -CaM upon MA binding were probed by double electron-electron resonance (DEER) spectroscopy.  Results  Cy3 quenching and FRET analyses of complexes with Cy5-Ca  2+ -CaM yielded dissociation constants of ∼80 nM for FL WT MA, ∼65 nM for the truncation, and ∼250 nM for the triple mutant, with corresponding binding free energies of ∼−9.8 to ∼−9 kcal/mol. These values indicate stable, specific complexes and show that the KKK cluster contributes little to MA–Ca  2+ -CaM binding. DEER measurements of Ca  2+ -CaM labeled at S39C and A103C showed that FL WT MA binding shifted the ∼5.3 nm interspin distance of extended Ca  2+ -CaM to a broader ∼1.8–3 nm distribution, indicating a major CaM restructuring.  Conclusion  These findings define key energetic and structural features of MA-Ca  2+ -CaM interactions and clarify how HIV-1 proteins exploit CaM.
authors: Saffarian Delkhosh A, Ogunbowale A, Hadadianpour E, Mahmud KM, Borbat PP, Georgieva ER.

title: Integrative Multi-Omics Identifies a Causal Immune Gene Panel for Sepsis Diagnosis and Targeted Therapy.
abstract: IntroductionSepsis diagnosis remains challenging due to the lack of specific biomarkers that reflect immune dysregulation, as conventional markers lack immune specificity and causal grounding.MethodsWe performed a two-sample Mendelian randomization meta-analysis to identify immune phenotypes causally linked to sepsis, with associated genes mapped via multi- -omics annotation. Integrating three GEO datasets (n = 1,039), we constructed a diagnostic panel using six machine learning models, validated its cell-type specificity via singlecell RNA-seq, confirmed protein-level expression using public proteomic datasets, and predicted potential therapeutic compounds targeting the panel genes.ResultsWe characterized protective and risk immune phenotypes in sepsis, identifying 119 genes enriched in immune-metabolic pathways. Machine learning refined these to a six-gene panel (LY9, CD244, OLFML2B, TMEM59, TBC1D2, and FCER1G), with NNET achieving an AUC of 0.973 (95% CI: 0.951-0.996). Single-cell transcriptomics revealed cell-type-restricted expression, while proteomic data corroborated differential expression of key genes in sepsis-related contexts. Drug repurposing analysis prioritized candidates, highlighting its translational potential.DiscussionThis six-gene panel links immune-based diagnosis directly to therapeutic intervention. The identified genes not only serve as diagnostic biomarkers but also point to repurposable compounds. By connecting causal immune genes to existing drugs, the panel provides a clinical pathway from biomarker detection to targeted sepsis therapy.ConclusionThis study establishes a causally grounded, diagnostically robust six-gene immune panel for sepsis with demonstrated therapeutic potential, offering a translational framework for biomarker-guided diagnosis and targeted immunotherapy.
authors: Li J, Tan W, Zhu Z, Wu F, Yan J.

title: Colonic Epithelial Differentiation-associated Remodeling and Gut Barrier Damage are Associated with Depressive-like Behaviors Under Chronic Stress.
abstract: IntroductionMajor depressive disorder and gastrointestinal dysfunction are frequently comorbid in clinical populations, but the colonic epithelial programs that accompany stress-associated behavioral changes remain incompletely defined. The cellular heterogeneity of the intestinal epithelium further limits high-resolution dissection of stress-induced colonic dysfunction. We therefore profiled crypt-enriched colonic epithelium from a Chronic Social Defeat Stress (CSDS) model in male mice at single-cell resolution.MethodsWe assessed behavior, colonic histology, permeability, and crypt-enriched single-cell transcriptomes during CSDS. Separate intervention experiments used systemic DAPT, a γ-secretase inhibitor, or intramucosal AAV-mediated Occludin expression; an antibiotic-depletion experiment was also performed.ResultsEarly CSDS was accompanied by social avoidance and detectable colonic inflammation, crypt injury, and barrier dysfunction, before the broader multidomain behavioral phenotype observed at day 10. Stress was associated with expansion of cycling colonic stem and transit-amplifying cells, impaired secretory-lineage maturation, disrupted tight-junction-associated programs, mucus-barrier impairment, bacterial encroachment, and enrichment of a Reg3b-high epithelial state. In the specific interventions used here, systemic pharmacological Notch inhibition or local AAV-mediated Occludin expression was accompanied by improvement in selected barrier-related readouts and stress-associated behavioral phenotypes.DiscussionThese findings identify temporally coordinated colonic epithelial remodeling and barrier damage in male mice exposed to CSDS and support an association between epithelial homeostasis and depressive-like behaviors. This crypt-enriched dataset should therefore be interpreted as a cell-state-resolved resource that generates hypotheses for future epithelial-specific, lineage-tracing, and mechanistic studies.ConclusionColonic epithelial remodeling and barrier damage are associated with CSDS-associated depressive-like behaviors in male mice.
authors: Gao J, Xiao S, Gao Z, Yang A, Cheng J, Wen J, Zhou H, Wang G, Aa J, Zhang Y.

title: Microbial dynamics across commercial spaceflights of varying duration.
abstract: Spaceflight introduces environmental stressors that can alter human microbiomes and immune responses. We analyzed 259 and 17 biospecimens for microbiome and single-cell studies from n = 6 astronauts across two commercial International Space Station (ISS) missions: Axiom 2 (10-day mission) and Axiom 3 (21-day mission). Samples included saliva, stool, urine, and body swabs from 10 anatomical sites, profiled via 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene amplicon sequencing. Gut and oral microbiomes remained stable, while skin-associated communities exhibited transient diversity shifts post-flight. Taxonomic analysis revealed individual and site-specific patterns, as well as from the spaceflight/ISS environment. Cytokine profiling from single-cell data indicated immune activation, with IL-32 and IL-16 transcripts elevated in Axiom 2 and Axiom 3. Microbiome and interleukin correlation analyses found 14 significant associations in Axiom 2 data. These findings provide an integrated view of microbiome individuality. Our study represents a descriptive comparison of two missions, informing strategies for crew health on future long-duration missions.

title: Rapid visual and direct detection of Acinetobacter baumannii and carbapenem resistance by oligoDNA-gold nanoparticles biosensor in clinical samples.
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a major nosocomial pathogen responsible for extensively drug-resistant (XDR) infections in healthcare settings and is ranked as a critical priority one pathogen on World Health Organisation list. However, clinical diagnosis generally is given as (Acinetobacter calcoaceticus-baumannii) ACB complex, including A. baumannii, A. calcoaceticus, A. nosocomialis, and A. pittii, and among these, A. baumannii is the most clinically significant species. Further the conventional diagnostic methods take 4-48 h and many of them require sophisticated infrastructure, highlighting the urgent need for rapid and economical detection methods both for A. baumannii and its carbapenem resistance determinants. Among the carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii, blaOXA-23 and blaNDM are the predominant β-lactamase genes, with New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) conferring broad-spectrum carbapenem resistance and severely limiting the therapeutic options. In the present study, oligoDNA-gold nanoparticle (AuNP)-based biosensors were developed for the direct, rapid and visual detection of A. baumannii, blaOXA-23 and blaNDM in clinical respiratory samples without the need for DNA purification or amplification. The biosensor for the detection of A. baumannii targeted a conserved region of the Outer Membrane Nuclease encoding nucAb gene, enabling its accurate identification. blaOXA-23 biosensor detected blaOXA-23 gene, which is the highly prevalent carbapenem resistance gene in A. baumannii while the other biosensor, based on the conserved region of blaNDM gene, detected blaNDM-1 not only in A. baumannii but also its variants in Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. These biosensors produced visual results within 30 min, with a detection limit of 0.5 ng/µL DNA or 10³ CFU/mL to support early clinical decision-making for optimised therapy and antimicrobial resistance surveillance.
authors: Chalana A, Gupta V, Sharma P, Capalash N.

title: Myristic acid promotes cell-to-cell spread of Marek's disease virus by inhibiting STING-mediated IFN-β production and reprograming metabolic profiles.
abstract: Myristic acid (MA), which is typically synthesized by various cellular processes as a physiological metabolite, has recently emerged as an endogenous immune regulator through N-myristoylation. This post-translational modification (PTM) has been shown to suppress STING-mediated production of type I interferon (IFN-I), leading to inhibition of antiviral innate immunity in mammals. Although a variety of mammalian viruses manipulate N-myristoylation for efficient replication and immune evasion, little is known about whether avian viruses also exploit MA-induced PTM for their benefits. For this purpose, our present study used primary chicken embryo fibroblasts (CEFs) as a model to analyze the effects of MA on the IFN-I production induced by the STING signaling pathway, and evaluated whether MA facilitates replication of Marek's disease virus (MDV) in vitro. In the context of cGAMP stimulation, the mRNA levels of both TBK1 and IRF7 were decreased by MA treatment, leading to suppression of IFN-β synthesis. Interestingly, the presence of MA significantly dampened the expression of IRF7 and IFN-β transcripts at 72 h post-infection with MDV. This inhibitory effect can be reversed by the N-myristoyltransferase inhibitor DDD85646. Noticeably, MA treatment significantly elevated the expression of MDV glycoprotein gC and led to larger viral plaques, indicating enhanced cell-to-cell spread; however, MDV replication was not improved in the presence of MA. Moreover, metabolomic analysis revealed that MDV infection caused significant alterations in multiple metabolic pathways, including glycerophospholipid metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, and cofactor biosynthesis. In MDV-infected CEFs, MA exacerbated abnormalities of lipid metabolism and specifically activated inflammation-related pathways such as arachidonic acid metabolism and α-linolenic acid metabolism. Taken together, the present study provides a novel understanding on how MDV manipulates N-myristoylation to establish a favorable metabolic program for efficient cell-to-cell spread.

title: Multi-omics insights into the effects of selenium yeast-enriched water on the hepatic responses of hybrid (Megalobrama amblycephala ♀ × Ancherythroculter nigrocauda ♂).
abstract: The health-promoting effects of selenium (Se) in fish have been well established; however, current research mainly focuses on dietary Se supplementation. Waterborne Se exposure serves as a complementary approach, yet the regulatory effects and underlying molecular mechanisms of farming fish in Se yeast-enriched water on hepatic function remain unclear. This study used the hybrid fish "Xianfeng No. 2" (Megalobrama amblycephala ♀ × Ancherythroculter nigrocauda ♂) as the experimental animal model. After three weeks of culture in Se yeast-enriched water at a target total Se concentration of 0.07 mg L-1, integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses were conducted to explore the hepatic responses to organic Se. Firstly, metabolomic analysis identified 399 metabolites, among which 16 high-confidence characteristic markers potentially closely associated with flesh quality were screened out, including nutritionally valuable metabolites such as docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), clupanodonic acid (DPA), and leucinic acid. Differential metabolites were significantly enriched in pathways pertaining to amino acid metabolism, substance transport and biosynthesis. Secondly, transcriptomic analysis revealed that multiple redox-and immune-related genes were significantly up-regulated in the Se-treated group, including selenoproteins (SELENON, GPX2, and TXNRD3), the complement system (CFB, CFH, and C3), and antioxidant-regulatory genes (GFER and FOXO3), pointing to potential molecular signatures of altered hepatic immune function and antioxidant defense. Thirdly, integrated multi-omics analysis preliminarily identified coordinated changes in retinol and vitamin B6 metabolic pathways. Elevated expression of CYP26A1 and PDXP was associated with the accumulation of vitamin A and pyridoxamine, which may provide a molecular basis for alterations in hepatic antioxidant defense. This study preliminarily reveals potential regulatory mechanisms underlying Se biofortification and quality improvement in fish reared in Se yeast-enriched water at the molecular and metabolic levels, providing a theoretical basis and candidate targets for Se-enriched fish culture and molecular breeding.
journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part D, Genomics & proteomics
authors: Fang Y, Lan M, Qin Q, Wang G, Yu Y, Li Q, Bai Q, Song Z, Ye L, Ji W, Sun Y, Zhang L.

title: Thymic single-cell RNA sequencing reveals the immunosuppressive microenvironment in chicken model simulating vertical transmission of recombinant ALV.
abstract: Avian leukosis virus (ALV) induces immunosuppression and tumorigenesis. In this study, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was used to analyze the transcriptional dynamics of thymic immune cells in specific-pathogen-free (SPF) chickens, which were intra-embryonic infected with the naturally recombinant ALV-FJ15TH0, at 1-day-old (d), 28d, and 56d post-hatch. Using subgroup-specific marker genes and cell state analysis, we identified six T-cell clusters, two B-cell clusters, and a macrophage cell cluster. Differential gene analysis revealed that ALV infection resulted in a significant enrichment of downregulated genes across all immune cell subsets at 28d. Functional enrichment analysis indicated that ALV infection activated the FoxO immunosuppressive pathway, PI3K pathway, MAPK pathway (CD4+CD8+ T cells and M2 macrophages at 1d), multicellular synergistic regulation of the cancer pathway (CD4+CD8+ T cells, M2 macrophages, and Cytotoxic T cells at 28d), and ErbB signaling pathway, Notch signaling pathway (CD4+CD8+ T cells and M2 macrophages at 56d). Cell-cell communication analysis revealed that ALV infection induced the strongest predicted communication via the PPIA-BSG axis at 28 d. Analysis further inferred that CD147 (BSG) was associated with multiple signaling pathways, including MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT, which may contribute to the immunosuppressive microenvironment. BCL11B, SP3, and EP300 were identified as potential regulatory components with subset-specific associations with JUN, BRAF, and MYB, potentially involving the MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and FoxO signaling pathways. This study reveals the dynamic evolution of the thymic immune microenvironment following ALV-FJ15TH0 infection, providing a resource for understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying ALV-induced immunosuppression and offering a foundation for future investigation of its potential relationship with tumorigenesis.
authors: Zhang D, Pan Y, Zhong Z, Gu Q, Qiu W, Chen N, Meng K, Gong Z, Zeng Y, Zhao J, Liu P, Wu Y, Wu X.

title: Genomic characterization and selection signals in Italian black Atriana chickens using high-density SNP array.
abstract: The black Atriana (ATRI) is a local Italian chicken breed of historical and cultural importance. This study evaluated its genetic diversity and population structure and identified putative signatures of selection using runs of homozygosity (ROH) and the integrated haplotype score (iHS). Nineteen ATRI birds and 494 birds from 24 Mediterranean local breeds were genotyped with the Affymetrix Axiom 600 K Chicken Genotyping Array. After quality control, 505 birds and 495,454 autosomal SNPs were retained. In ATRI, observed heterozygosity, expected heterozygosity, and minor allele frequency averaged 0.345, 0.358, and 0.270, respectively. The inbreeding coefficients based on observed versus expected homozygosity and on ROH were 0.037 and 0.222, respectively. Principal component, NeighborNet, and ADMIXTURE analyses supported a distinguishable ATRI genomic profile while indicating affinities with several Mediterranean breeds. ROH and iHS analyses identified six candidate regions each, including two overlapping regions on chromosomes 2 and 14. These regions contained genes previously associated with growth, production, and environmental-response traits, including PTP4A3, TSNARE1, NDUFB6, WFIKKN1, and IFT140. Given the limited ATRI sample size, these candidate signals should be interpreted as exploratory and validated in larger independent populations. The findings provide baseline genomic information to support genetic monitoring and conservation planning for ATRI.
authors: Saleh MS, Perini F, Camarda A, Bettini S, Mugnai C, Landi V, Lasagna E.

title: Psl exopolysaccharide regulates biofilm formation and environmental adaptation in Pseudomonas fluorescens PF07.
abstract: Pseudomonas fluorescens PF07, a prevalent psychrotrophic spoilage bacterium, relies heavily on robust biofilm formation to persist in food environments and exert spoilage effects. Nevertheless, the distinct contributions of exopolysaccharides to its biofilm maturation and stress adaptation remain unclear. Herein, we systematically characterized the genetic determinants and biological functions of three exopolysaccharides (Psl, alginate and PNAG) in modulating PF07 biofilm development and resistance to food-processing-associated stressors. Single, double, and triple deletion mutants targeting the pslB, alg8, and pgaC genes were constructed to evaluate the contributions of these biosynthetic systems, and transcriptomic analysis was performed to explore the underlying responses. Deletion of pslB markedly impaired biofilm formation, pellicle development, and extracellular matrix production, whereas deficiency of alg8 or pgaC caused only minor phenotypic changes compared with the wild-type strain, indicating that Psl is the primary structural determinant of the PF07 biofilm matrix. Furthermore, double- and triple-mutants lacking pslB exhibited more severe reductions in biofilm biomass and thickness, suggesting that alginate and PNAG make supplementary but secondary contributions to the Psl-dominated biofilm matrix. In addition, ΔpslB exhibited substantially reduced biofilm formation under low temperature and ionic stress and decreased tolerance to sodium hypochlorite and benzalkonium chloride, in contrast with limited alterations for the Δalg8 and ΔpgaC mutants. Consistently, catalase and superoxide dismutase activities were significantly weakened in the ΔpslB mutant but largely unaltered in the Δalg8 mutant, indicating that Psl deficiency was associated with reduced antioxidant enzyme activities and suggesting a potential role of Psl in the antioxidant response of PF07. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed significant changes in genes associated with stress adaptation and metabolism, including the upregulation of aqpZ, the downregulation of osmY, and alterations in multiple metabolism-related genes. Thus, these findings demonstrate that Psl is a pivotal structural polysaccharide in the biofilm matrix of P. fluorescens PF07 and plays critical roles in biofilm structure and tolerance to cold, ionic, and oxidative stresses, providing new insights into potential strategies for controlling P. fluorescens biofilms in food-processing environments.
authors: Lu Z, Zhou Z, Feng L, Zhu J.

title: Immune profile dysregulation of high grade- compared to low grade-pseudomyxomas.
abstract: BackgroundPseudomyxoma peritonei is a rare and poorly understood cancer. The histological characteristics that classify pseudomyxoma as either low-grade or high-grade are major prognostic factors. The present study aimed to identify differentially expressed genes in low-grade and high-grade pseudomyxomas using transcriptomic analysis, in order to improve our understanding of their pathophysiology.MethodsTwo cohorts of pseudomyxoma peritonei FFPE samples composed by 13 low grade and 11 high grade tumours respectively were selected. The expression of several biomarkers (CK7, CK20, MUC2, MUC5AC, Ki67) were analysed by immunohistochemistry. Gene expression profiles were studied using Nanostring™ technology and included the tumour signalling 360™ panel (760 tumour signalling related genes and 20 internal reference controls) and the inflammation v2 panel (249 inflammation-related human genes and 6 internal reference controls).ResultsThe study revealed distinct transcriptomic profiles of the immune response in low grade and high grade, indicating dysregulation of immune cell migration and/or chemotaxis, as well as modulation of cellular metabolic activities and cell signalling. In addition, in high grade pseudomyxoma peritonei, there are genes and signalling pathways linked to the response to lipopolysaccharides and bacterial molecules were also downregulated. Our results strengthen both the role of immune response and the role of bacterial involvement in pseudomyxoma peritonei pathophysiology.
authors: Bourgin C, Golias M, Ollivier E, Levergeois R, Cochonneau D, Thibaudeau E, Dumont F, Vignaud T, Heymann MF, Heymann D.

title: Ancestral Quadruplication of Protein Kinase R in Tarsiers Hints Towards Novel Primate-Virus Innovations
abstract: Tarsiers, an elusive family of primates found in Indonesia and the Philippines, sit at an essential point in primate evolution, with their divergence between that of Strepsirrhini (lemurs) and Simiiformes (monkeys and apes). Through homology searches, we have discovered that tarsiers carry the first known case in primates of a gene expansion of protein kinase R (PKR), a kinase involved in the response to viral infection. PKR was quadruplicated in the ancestor of tarsiers and has been maintained since then in all sequenced tarsier species. The extra copies lack the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) binding domains necessary for detecting viral infection yet largely maintain the residues necessary for the kinase function that carries out PKR’s antiviral function. We show that three of the four PKR copies indeed maintain kinase activity, one of which appears to be resistant to the viral PKR antagonist K3 from vaccinia virus. Our analyses of site and branch-site positive selection reveal that the tarsier PKRs are under positive selection. We propose that these extra copies could serve as a diversification strategy to bypass viral inhibitors that bind PKR’s kinase domain, or they could alternatively serve as decoys that shield the canonical PKR from viral inhibition. This is the first instance of mammal PKR duplicates lacking dsRNA-binding domains and may highlight an innovation in an ancient, long-standing molecular arms race between viruses and a close relative of humans.
authors: Heneghan PG, Grieve TR, Sadhu MJ.

title: A Review of Rhizosphere Processes, Plant Performance and Production Trade‑Offs in Soil Versus Solid‑Substrate Cultivation of Greenhouse Strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa)
abstract: Strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) is an economically important berry crop in protected horticulture, mainly produced through soil‑based and solid‑substrate soilless systems. Soil cultivation possesses strong physicochemical buffering and abundant indigenous microbial resources, but suffers from continuous cropping obstacles including soil degradation and soil‑borne pathogen accumulation. Solid‑substrate cultivation can isolate soil‑borne pathogens and enables precise rhizosphere manipulation; however, it is constrained by low buffering capacity, unstable microbial assembly, peat‑related ecological costs, and waste‑substrate disposal risks. This review builds a unified analytical framework centered on the cascade "medium physicochemical properties – microbial community – extracellular enzymes – root physiology – yield‑quality performance" and clarifies the conceptual boundaries among soil cultivation, solid‑substrate cultivation, and hydroponics. We analyze the sources of heterogeneity across published results, including cultivar genotype, medium properties, water‑fertilizer management, growth stage, and analytical methodology. Most existing evidence is correlational, whereas rigorous causal manipulation experiments remain scarce, which explains why no universal consensus has been reached on the relative superiority of the two production modes. Key research gaps include fragmented rhizospheric mechanism research, lack of cross‑study standardized experimental conditions, insufficient normalization of enzyme and microbiome datasets, and a shortage of long‑term multi‑objective field assessments. We highlight that microbial–functional decoupling frequently occurs in both soil and solid‑substrate systems, indicating that microbial community composition alone cannot represent real rhizosphere biogeochemical processes. Based on evidence synthesis, differentiated optimization strategies are proposed: soil systems should prioritize soil‑health restoration, whereas solid‑substrate systems need peat‑substitute development, microbial–habitat compatible inoculation, and substrate circular regeneration. Shared future directions cover in‑situ rhizosphere sensing, causal validation experiments, and multi‑objective evaluation balancing yield, fruit quality, resource cost, and environmental footprints. This review provides theoretical references for sustainable protected strawberry production.
authors: Zha Y, Hu S, Liu A, Li C, Lai W, Li X, Wang J, Yu H, Xiao W.

title: Hydrogels in Pharmacy and Medicine: An Illustrated Review of Preparation Methods, Process Control and Drug Delivery Applications
abstract: Hydrogels, three-dimensional hydrophilic polymer networks that can imbibe large volumes of water or biological fluids without dissolving, have become one of the most versatile platforms in pharmaceutical and biomaterial science. Their high water content, soft tissue-like mechanics, biocompatibility and tunable network architecture allow them to be engineered as topical, ophthalmic, mucosal, oral and injectable dosage forms and as scaffolds for regenerative medicine. This illustrated review provides a critical, practice-oriented account of the field, with particular emphasis on how hydrogel dosage forms are prepared. Physical cross-linking methods (ionic gelation, polyelectrolyte complexation, thermoresponsive gelation, freeze–thaw cycling and supramolecular assembly) and chemical cross-linking methods (free-radical and photo-initiated polymerization, small-molecule cross-linkers, click and dynamic covalent chemistries, and enzyme-mediated and radiation cross-linking) are examined in terms of their mechanisms, typical materials and conditions, critical process parameters, advantages and limitations. The preparation of conventional pharmaceutical gels based on carbomers, cellulose ethers, poloxamers and polysaccharides is described step by step, together with drug-loading strategies, processing into beads, micro- and nanogels, films, sponges, microneedles and printed constructs, and a troubleshooting guide for the most frequent formulation failures. Advanced architectures that overcome the intrinsic weakness of conventional networks, including hybrid, interpenetrating, nanocomposite, double-network and Tetra-PEG hydrogels, are then discussed, followed by the characterization and quality-control methods needed to establish critical quality attributes such as gel fraction, swelling and mesh size, rheology, morphology, release kinetics, stability, microbiological quality and biocompatibility. The review subsequently analyzes drug release mechanisms, route-specific delivery strategies, stimuli-responsive and hierarchical systems, the selection of drug candidates with reference to physicochemical properties and the Biopharmaceutics Classification System, and applications in tissue engineering and wound care. Finally, clinically approved products and the main translational barriers, namely mechanical fragility, burst release, residual reagents, sterilization, batch-to-batch variability and regulatory classification, are critically evaluated to identify realistic routes towards next-generation, clinically useful hydrogel dosage forms.
authors: Ramesh KA, Mawazi SM.

title: Modulating DNA Methylation in Mature Hair Cells to Mitigate Cisplatin-Induced Hearing Loss: A Review
abstract: Cisplatin-induced hearing loss (CIHL) is a debilitating side effect in cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy. So far, epigenetic studies in the inner ear have largely focused on developmental biology to regenerate hair cells. In post-mitotic hair cells, on the other hand, DNA methylation regulates transcriptomic response to external stimuli. Adult mammalian hair cells are locked in the G0 phase, and passive demethylation via DNA replication does not occur under normal physiological conditions. However, external stimuli such as cisplatin can aberrantly upregulate DNMT methyltransferases (DNMTs), resulting in promoter methylation and silencing protective genes. From this angle, DNMTs modulation is an attractive therapeutic strategy to protect hearing during chemotherapy. Recent studies suggest that non-nucleoside inhibitors such as RG108 and natural polyphenolic compounds downregulate DNMTs, and at the same time, protect auditory cells. These compounds function via the inhibition of the DNMT catalytic site but can also act through downregulating DNMT1 and DNMT3A/B at mRNA and protein levels. Polyphenols are also antioxidants, decreasing reactive oxygen species, thereby increasing cell survival. Furthermore, it is suggested that upregulating TET-mediated active demethylation can be another angle to modify DNA methylation in cancer and CIHL models. However, functional DNA methylation should be distinguished from non-functional, passenger DNA methylation to elucidate the compounds’ otoprotective effects. In addition, the candidate compounds should not interfere with cisplatin’s antitumor effect. In this review, we investigate the relationship between DNA methylation and CIHL in the post-mitotic inner ear and evaluate the therapeutic potential of candidate DNMT inhibitors.
authors: Koo C, Fuentes R, Tan X.

title: Investigation of the molecular mechanisms of action of sophorolipids in MCF-7 cells: therapeutic potential against breast cancer.
abstract: A mixture of lactonic and acidic sophorolipids exerted concentration-dependent cytotoxicity against human breast ductal adenocarcinoma (MCF-7) cells, with an IC₅₀ of 82.54 µg/mL as determined by resazurin assay. Phase-contrast microscopy revealed morphological alterations including cell swelling, loss of adhesion, and impaired membrane integrity. Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated cell cycle arrest in the S phase, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, and a predominance of necrosis-like cell death at higher concentrations. Transcriptional profiling by RT-qPCR identified overexpression of CDKN1A, GADD45A, ERN1, and BBC3, alongside repression of ACTB and GAPDH, indicating activation of DNA damage and stress-response pathways, endoplasmic reticulum stress, structural collapse, and metabolic dysfunction. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that sophorolipids induce mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum stress, culminating in homeostatic failure and cell death in MCF-7 cells, positioning these biosurfactants as promising candidates for the development of natural antiproliferative therapies.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05096-0.
authors: Martins LHS, de Lima LVA, da Silva MF, da Silva NG, de Assis MCT, Carvalho ICO, Fuzzinato IM, Silva BB, da Costa DA, de Azevedo Silva MP, Celligoi MAPC, Mantovani MS.

title: Investigation of Polyethylene (PE) Exposure in Labeo rohita (Hamilton, 1822): Accumulation, Stress Responses and In Vitro Biodegradation of PE by a Gut-Associated Bacterium.
abstract: The aquatic biome is exposed to a significant threat of persistent contamination by polyethylene (PE) in the ecosystem. A critical research gap exists in PE-induced tissue-specific bioaccumulation, associated immune and stress responses in fish, followed by potential bioremediation solutions. The present study investigated the bioaccumulation of PE particles and subsequent oxidative stress in Labeo rohita induced by two different doses (0.1 and 0.5 mg/L) over 2 weeks. Additionally, the biodegradation potential of gut-associated microbial isolates was also evaluated. We found that PE accumulation was highest in the intestine (33.0 ± 2.5 particles/g), followed by gills (20.5 ± 1.9 particles/g) and liver (8.0 ± 1.4 particles/g), indicating a significant, dose- and time-dependent increase. Substantially, it triggered a tissue-wise oxidative stress response of antioxidant (SOD, CAT, GPx) and stress marker (Hsp70) genes, showing significant upregulation in gill, liver, and intestine. Furthermore, this work identified a gut-associated bacterium, Proteus vulgaris KG-SD-15807, demonstrating significant PE biodegradation capability. Quantitative analysis revealed achievement of 3.00% ± 0.16% weight loss over 30 days of incubation. Qualitative characterization through FT-IR, FE-SEM, and GC-MS analyses indicated polymer oxidation, surface erosion, and formation of distinct metabolic degradation intermediates. The present findings reveal the significant bioaccumulation and stress response due to PE in a commercially important fish, Labeo rohita. Moreover, the identified bacterium acted as a PE biodegradation agent. This research has significant implications for future explorations focused on the long-term impacts of PE in aquatic animals and the optimization of biodegradation efficiency of Proteus vulgaris for applied bioremediation.
authors: Dey S, Rout AK, Ghosh K, Kumar V, Saha A, Das BK, Behera BK.

title: Comprehensive regulatory network construction highlights lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA-TF interactions and key molecular drivers in rheumatoid arthritis.
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent inflammation and progressive joint damage. Although numerous molecular contributors have been reported, the integrated regulatory architecture linking coding and non-coding transcripts remains incompletely defined. This study aimed to construct a multilayer lncRNA-miRNA-mRNA-transcription factor (TF) network to prioritize candidate regulators associated with RA. Publicly available RNA-sequencing datasets from RA and control samples were retrieved from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive. Differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2. High-confidence miRNA-mRNA interactions were obtained from miRDip, miRNA-lncRNA associations from miRNet, and TF annotations from AnimalTFDB. Functional enrichment analyses were conducted to identify overrepresented biological themes. Network topology and module structure were evaluated in Cytoscape using CytoHubba and MCODE. Integration of interaction datasets identified 179 mRNAs targeted by 93 miRNAs, of which 90 miRNAs were connected to 404 annotated lncRNAs. Twenty-five TFs were incorporated into the regulatory framework. Degree-based analysis highlighted QKI, hsa-miR-497-5p, and KCNQ1OT1 as the most connected nodes within their respective categories. Module detection revealed five densely interconnected sub-networks, indicating coordinated regulatory organization. Several prioritized elements have previously been implicated in immune or inflammatory regulation, supporting the biological relevance of the network. This integrative analysis delineates a comprehensive regulatory landscape of RA and provides a ranked set of candidate molecules for future experimental validation. Among these, CCDC6 was identified as a downregulated gene positioned within a highly connected module and linked to multiple hub miRNAs and lncRNAs, suggesting potential functional importance in RA pathobiology.
journal: Mammalian genome : official journal of the International Mammalian Genome Society
authors: Selvaranganathan R, Murugesan G, Nagendran P, Natarajan J.

title: Microbiome interactions in renal cell carcinoma: evidence, challenges and opportunities.
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is a heterogeneous malignancy with limited predictive biomarkers to guide treatment. Emerging evidence suggests that the microbiome might influence systemic immunity, therapeutic response and clinical outcomes. In metastatic RCC, the gut microbiome has been linked to the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors, whereas the existence of a tumour microbiome remains a topic of debate. Circulating microbial DNA in blood has been proposed as a minimally invasive window into systemic immune status, offering a potential tool for monitoring treatment response, but its role in RCC is largely unexplored. Evidence from mechanistic studies, primarily from other solid cancer types, suggests that microbiome-immune crosstalk, microbial metabolites and functionally redundant pathways across taxa could modulate tumour biology. However, progress in RCC microbiome research remains limited by small cohorts, methodological variability and challenges in working with samples with a low microbial biomass, which are highly prone to contamination. Emerging spatial and multi-omics technologies now enable high-resolution mapping of these complex interactions, offering the potential to transform our understanding of the cancer microbiome. A structured roadmap is required to overcome technical and analytical challenges in RCC microbiome studies, enabling the identification of clinically relevant microbial signatures and their role in shaping tumour immunity.
authors: Lindgaard C, Hvidt AK, Keller AK, Thingholm L, Kristensen SS, Lyskjær I.

title: Pobacilamides A and B, two linear depsipeptides from a marine-derived Bacillus sp. ROA-056.
abstract: Through the intensive investigation of the chemical components for the culture broth of marine-derived Bacillus sp. ROA-056, two new linear peptides, namely, pobacilamides A (1) and B (2), have been discovered. Their planar structures were elucidated through mass spectrometry, and 1D and 2D NMR analyses. Both peptides were composed of valine (Val), 2-hydroxyisovaleric acid (HIVA), and 2-hydroxyisocaproic acid (HICA), while pobacilamide A (1) contained leucine (Leu). The absolute configurations of Val and Leu were defined by acid hydrolysis and advanced Marfey's method, while those of HIVA and HICA were established by GC-MS analysis of O-trifluoroacetylated (S)-(+)-3-methyl-2-butyl ester. Compounds 1 and 2 displayed selective antibacterial activity against Gram-positive bacteria, including Bacillus subtilis and Kocuria rhizophila, with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) values from 0.25 μg/mL to 4 μg/mL. Pobacilamide B (2) showed the strongest activity against K. rhizophila with an MIC of 0.25 μg/mL. No antibacterial activity was observed against Gram-negative strains. These results suggested that compounds 1 and 2 have considerable potential as targeted antibacterial agents for Gram-positive pathogens.
authors: Lee EY, Kim DA, Lee JY, Lee J, Choi B, Paik MJ, Kim H, Lee S, Lim KM, Nam SJ.

title: Mapping human genetic associations to drug targets in valvular heart disease: an integrative evidence synthesis.
abstract: BackgroundValvular heart disease (VHD) lacks disease-modifying pharmacological therapies. Drug repurposing guided by human genetics may help identify therapeutic opportunities. We aimed to integrate human genetic associations, drug-target information, and clinical evidence to identify repurposing opportunities and prioritise potentially druggable targets across the VHD spectrum.MethodsWe retrieved VHD-associated genetic variants from the NHGRI-EBI Genome-Wide Association Studies Catalogue and Ensembl, interrogated annotated genes in the Open Targets Platform, and evaluated linked drugs through structured searches of MEDLINE and ClinicalTrials.gov. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251071741).FindingsWe identified 1464 genetic associations corresponding to 844 unique variants and 582 candidate genes. Of these genes, 431 had tractability information and 51 had linked compounds, comprising 388 distinct pharmacological agents, 273 in phase 3 or 4 of clinical development. Drug-linked targets were concentrated in aortic stenosis. Clinical evidence supported therapeutic potential for 14 drugs, with preclinical or mechanistic cardiovascular support for eight additional drugs and adverse cardiovascular signals for four. An exploratory evidence-weighted framework prioritised targets according to genetic-functional evidence, tissue and mechanistic context, and translational tractability.InterpretationThis genetics-informed evidence synthesis identifies drug-repurposing opportunities and a substantial gap between genetically supported targets and available therapies. The findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework for mechanistic validation and future valve-focused studies.FundingLimburg Clinical Research Centre of UHasselt, Jessa and ZOL; British Heart Foundation; National Institute for Health and Care Research; UK Research and Innovation; European Research Council; Horizon Europe.
authors: Moura-Ferreira S, Ustunkaya T, Siddiqui M, Kukendrarajah K, Schmidt F, Ahmed R, Khanji M, Chahal A, Verwerft J, Providencia R.

title: First evidence of measles virus detected from exhaled breath in humans.
abstract: ObjectivesMeasles is among the most transmissible human infections, yet direct capture of measles virus from an infected person's exhaled breath has not been described. We assessed whether measles virus RNA can be detected from exhaled breath using facemask sampling (FMS).MethodsWe studied a 23-year-old unvaccinated woman with laboratory-confirmed measles (throat-swab RT-qPCR positive on day 5 post symptom onset). From day 10 post symptom onset, longitudinal sampling was performed for six consecutive days with duplicate specimens collected at each timepoint from the throat, face, cutaneous lesions and exhaled breath using a surgical mask fitted with polyvinyl alcohol sampling strips (FMS). Dissolved mask strips and swab eluates underwent RNA extraction followed by RT-qPCR targeting measles nucleoprotein and haemagglutinin genes, with human RNase P as a sample adequacy control. Quantification was derived from nucleoprotein-gene standards and normalised per strip or per 100 μL of swab eluate.ResultsMeasles virus RNA was consistently detected in exhaled breath captured by FMS and remained >10ˆ4 genome copies per sampling strip despite sampling beginning 10 days after symptom onset. During FMS collection, the participant reported no respiratory symptoms and did not vocalise. RNA kinetics differed by sampling site: throat and facial swabs increased even after complete rash resolution, whereas cutaneous-lesion swabs yielded comparatively low RNA levels. FMS kinetics diverged from throat swabs over time, suggesting distinct patterns of virus emission across compartments.ConclusionsThis study provides the first empirical evidence that measles virus RNA can be captured directly from the exhaled breath of an individual with measles. Although RNA detection does not confirm infectious virus, persistent high-level exhaled RNA supports FMS as a practical, non-invasive tool to study measles respiratory emission and may inform understanding of transmission and the duration of potential contagiousness. Empirical sampling of different respiratory compartments may help refine infection-prevention guidance during resurgent outbreaks.
journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
authors: Pan D, Fletcher E, Decker J, Williams C, Martin CA, Nazareth J, Choi JS, Toovey OTR, White HA, Bell D, Nguyen Van-Tam JS, Pareek M, Barer MR.

title: Particle size-dependent developmental and neurotoxic effects of epoxiconazole nanoformulations and its active ingredient in zebrafish larvae.
abstract: Epoxiconazole (EPO), a widely used triazole fungicide that can enter aquatic ecosystems through agricultural runoff, poses potential risks to non-target aquatic organisms. Although nano-enabled pesticide formulations can control release and reduce application rates, their toxicological evaluation remains insufficient, particularly with respect to size-dependent biological effects. Here, zebrafish larvae were exposed to free EPO and EPO-loaded mesoporous silica nanoparticles (EPO@MSNs) with particle sizes of 30, 150 and 450 nm to investigate size-associated differences in developmental toxicity and their underlying mechanisms. Overall, EPO exposure induced developmental and neurovascular abnormalities, neurobehavioral impairment, and neurotransmitter imbalance, accompanied by oxidative stress, innate immune activation, inflammation, and apoptosis. Nanoencapsulation reshaped the toxicological profile of EPO, with the overall toxicity, as integrated by PCA, following the order EPO@MSNs-30 < EPO@MSNs-150 < EPO@MSNs-450 < free EPO. Transcriptomic analyses further demonstrated that nanoformulation shifted the dominant molecular responses from metabolism- and detoxification-related processes in free EPO toward nanoparticle-associated intracellular processing in EPO@MSNs-30 and broader extracellular matrix, vascular, and inflammatory responses in EPO@MSNs-450. These findings demonstrate that particle size is associated with both the overall toxicological profile and the molecular response patterns of MSN-based pesticide formulations, providing mechanistic insights for the biosafety assessment and rational design of nano-enabled pesticide formulations.
authors: Zhang Y, Li Y, Jasper CS, Zhang S, Liu Z, Qian Q, Wang Z, Wang H, Meng Z, Yan J.

title: A nuclease-associated short pAgo system from Pleomorphomonas koreensis with dual DNA and RNA collateral activity.
abstract: Argonaute (Ago) proteins play pivotal roles in nucleic acid targeting across eukaryotes and prokaryotes. While eukaryotic Ago (eAgo) proteins utilize RNA guides to cleave complementary RNA, prokaryotic Ago (pAgo) proteins often employ DNA guides for DNA targeting. This study focuses on the short pAgo system from Pleomorphomonas koreensis (Pko-SPARDA), which consists of a DUF4365-APAZ protein (PkoRE) and an Ago protein (PkoAgo). Upon RNA-guided target DNA recognition, Pko-SPARDA exhibits nonspecific cleavage activity toward ssDNA, dsDNA, and RNA, demonstrating potential for nucleic acid detection. Biochemical characterization revealed that Pko-SPARDA prefers Mn2+ or Mg2+ as cofactors, operates optimally at 40-45 °C, and is sensitive to mismatches in the central and 3'-supplementary regions of the guide RNA. Notably, the system accommodates a range of guide lengths (14-40 nt) and shows higher activity with 5'-phosphorylated guides. Additionally, guide RNA 5'-phosphorylation universally enhances Pko-SPARDA trans-cleavage activity, and this principle extends to microRNA-guided activation, advancing the understanding of short pAgos and highlighting Pko-SPARDA's utility in molecular diagnostics by bridging a gap left by CRISPR systems due to its lack of sequence constraints like PAM motifs.
authors: Chen Z, Yu N, Yu X, Li W, Wang L, Ma L.
