title: Active components alignment of Gegen Qinlian Decoction for inflammatory bowel disease: exploring the possible role of the SphK1/S1P/NF-κB pathway.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceGegenqinlian Decoction (GQD) has been used as a folk remedy for gastrointestinal diseases in China over thousands of years, and demonstrates significant efficacy against inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We previously showed that the active components alignment of GQD inhibits nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) p65 signal transduction and plays a key role in preventing and treating IBD. With growing insights into the gut microbiota and its metabolites, the molecular mechanisms underlying therapeutic effects of GQD against IBD require further elucidation. This is particularly relevant given the previously reported relationship between the host NF-κB pathway and the gut microbiota.Aim of the studyTo explore the therapeutic mechanisms of GQD and its aligned active components against IBD, with a focus on microbiota-involved regulation of the host sphingosine kinase 1 (SphK1)/sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P)/NF-κB signaling pathway, using both 2,4,6-Trinitrobenzenesulfonic acid (TNBS)-induced rat colitis and dextran sulfate sodium salt (DSS)-induced mouse colitis models and cultured cells.Material and methodsIn this research, the therapeutic effect of GQD on TNBS-induced colitis rats was evaluated through the measurement of body weight, colorectal length, disease activity index (DAI), colon length and hematoxylin-eosin staining. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomic analyses were performed to evaluate the restoration of gut microbial and metabolic homeostasis by GQD. Network pharmacology and molecular docking were then utilized to explore the potential relationships between specific targets and the active components alignment (ACA) of GQD on IBD treatment. To further validate the in vivo effects of the ACA, a dextran sulfate sodium salt (DSS)-induced mouse colitis model was established, and body weight, DAI, colorectum length, histopathology, S1P levels, and SphK1/S1PR1 expression were assessed. Experimental validation in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages and NCM460 colonic epithelial cells was subsequently conducted to determine whether this active components alignment suppressed the SphK1/S1P/NF-κB pathway via molecular and cellular assays, including cell metabolomics, ELISA, Western blot, and immunofluorescence staining.ResultsGQD significantly relieved symptoms, colonic inflammation, and intestinal damage in TNBS-induced colitis rats. It partially reversed gut microbiota dysbiosis, modulated sphingolipid metabolic pathways, and downregulated the expression of sphingolipid-related Sphk1 and S1PR1 proteins, as well as S1P levels, in colon tissues (p ConclusionGQD restored gut microecological homeostasis and rectified sphingolipid metabolic disturbances. Its active components alignment afforded anti-inflammatory and colitis-protective effects, partially via modulation of the SphK1/S1P/NF-κB signaling pathway. The consistent therapeutic and mechanistic effects observed in both TNBS-induced rat colitis and DSS-induced mouse colitis support that the eight-component alignment largely recapitulates the key effects of the complete GQD formulation. These findings provide novel mechanistic insights and a scientific rationale for the clinical application of GQD in the management of IBD.
authors: Liu S, Zhang D, Zong Z, Hu Y, Bai J, Li J, Sun W, Yang X, Chen Y, Yang B, Wang H, Wang J, Wu D, Li W, Liu J, Xu B.

title: Therapeutic advances in chronic hepatitis B and Delta: where are we now and where are we headed?
abstract: Chronic hepatitis B (HBV) and delta (HDV) infections remain major global health challenges. Nucleos(t)ide analogues (NUCs) and bulevirtide, a recently approved entry inhibitor, effectively suppress HBV and HDV replication, respectively, thereby reducing the risk of liver-related complications. However, they rarely induce functional cure, defined as sustained HBsAg loss, and generally require long-term administration. This limitation is primarily driven by the persistence of covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) and integrated HBV DNA, which are not targeted by existing treatments. A broad range of novel therapeutic strategies is currently under investigation. Virus-directing agents, including small interfering RNAs, antisense oligonucleotides, nucleic acid polymers, and capsid assembly modulators, have shown promising antiviral activity. However, their efficacy as monotherapy remains modest, with HBsAg loss observed at moderate rates and mainly among patients with a favorable baseline profile. Combination strategies integrating direct antivirals with immune modulation (therapeutic vaccines, toll-like receptor agonists or monoclonal antibodies) may represent a promising pathway to increase the rates of functional cure. In HDV infection, emerging phase 3 combination strategies are also showing promising results, supporting a shift toward more effective, multi-targeted treatment approaches. Building on these advances, the convergence of novel antivirals and immune-modulating strategies, together with precision biomarkers, makes functional cure a realistic long-term objective in HBV and HDV infection.
authors: Pocurull A, Battistella S, Forns X, Lens S.

title: Recombinant spinach ribosome-inactivating protein induces cytotoxicity and alters gene expression associated with PTEN/AKT/mTOR signaling, apoptosis, and stemness in HT29 cells.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major therapeutic challenge, highlighting the need for novel anticancer strategies. These challenges have increased interest in bioactive natural molecules with anticancer potential. In this study, we investigated the antitumor activity of a recombinant spinach (Spinacia oleracea) type I ribosome-inactivating protein (SoRIP) in HT29 colorectal cancer cells and evaluated its effects on cellular survival, apoptosis, and stemness-associated pathways. The SoRIP coding sequence was cloned, heterologously expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3), and purified by Ni-affinity chromatography, yielding a recombinant protein of approximately 22 kDa. Recombinant SoRIP reduced HT29 cell viability in a concentration-dependent manner after 48 h of treatment, with an IC50 of 48 μg/mL and cell viability of 51.3 ± 2.5% at this concentration. Annexin V-FITC/PI flow cytometry demonstrated a concentration-dependent increase in total apoptotic cells, reaching approximately 15%, 58%, and 79% following exposure to 12, 48, and 180 μg/mL SoRIP, respectively. At the transcriptional level, SoRIP increased CASP3 expression by up to 3.8-fold and PTEN expression by up to 4.3-fold, while reducing AKT and mTOR expression to 0.60- and 0.70-fold, respectively, at 48 μg/mL. BCL2 and CD44 expression were also reduced to approximately 0.65- and 0.70-fold, respectively. These findings indicate that recombinant SoRIP is associated with reduced cell viability, enhanced apoptosis, and coordinated transcriptional modulation of PTEN/AKT/mTOR-related, apoptosis-associated, and stemness-associated genes in HT29 cells. Collectively, these results support SoRIP as a candidate for further investigation in the HT29 colorectal cancer model.
authors: Ranjbar M, Maghsodiyan S, Khakdan F, Bayram M.

title: The clinical relevance of multiple sclerosis genetics: from susceptibility to disease severity and progression.
abstract: Large-scale genome-wide association studies have identified hundreds of multiple sclerosis risk loci, most of which implicate immune pathways and establish multiple sclerosis as a highly polygenic, immune-mediated disease. These findings help explain why immune-modifying therapies suppress relapses and new lesion formation. However, susceptibility genetics does not adequately explain disability accumulation, variation in disease course, or treatment response. Evidence from rare-variant studies, genetic studies of disease severity and disability progression, epigenetic analyses, gene-environment studies, and Epstein-Barr virus research is beginning to extend this genetic framework from susceptibility to disease expression. Still, the direct clinical relevance of this research remains constrained by modest individual-level predictive value, underpowered studies of genetic determinants of disease severity and disability progression, complex regulatory mechanisms linking variants to function, and restricted generalisability across populations. At present, multiple sclerosis genetics is most useful for interpreting mechanisms, prioritising therapeutic targets, supporting causal inference, informing biomarker discovery, and enriching research cohorts. Future clinical value will likely depend on integrating genetic architecture with longitudinal clinical, imaging, biomarker, and multi-omic data to identify the contexts in which prevention or treatment is most likely to succeed.
authors: Jensen LT, Gold R, McVean G, Attfield KE, Fugger L.

title: Biomarker tests for invasive Candida infection in critically ill patients in the UK (A-Stop): a multicentre diagnostic test accuracy study.
abstract: BackgroundThe current practice of empirical antifungal treatment for suspected invasive Candida infection in the intensive care unit (ICU) leads to overtreatment. Biomarkers might better target treatment; however, their diagnostic accuracy in this patient group is uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate whether a biomarker or a combination of biomarkers has sufficiently high negative predictive value (NPV) to enable early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in patients in ICUs.MethodsIn this prospective, multicentre, diagnostic test accuracy study, we recruited patients who had been started on empirical antifungal treatment for suspected candidiasis and had blood cultures drawn within 24 h of starting treatment from 43 UK ICUs. We tested a research blood sample, collected within 24 h of the standard-of-care care blood culture (ie, within 48 h of starting empirical antifungal treatment), with three DNA detection tests (Fungiplex, T2Candida, and CandID) and one (1,3)-β-D-glucan test (Fungitell). We assessed the accuracy of these tests against an international consensus definition of proven invasive Candida infection and a constructed reference standard for proven or probable infection. The primary outcome was NPV for exclusion of proven Candida infection; we also reported sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios.FindingsAmong 4005 patients screened, 1251 were enrolled. A total of 1225 participants, recruited between April, 2018 and Feb, 2023, were evaluable, among whom 54 (4·4%) had proven invasive Candida infection. The median duration of antifungal treatment was 9 days (IQR 5-15), and survival at 28 days was 76·8%. The index tests had similar NPVs: 96·6% (95·3-97·6) for Fungiplex, 97·1% (94·7-98·6) for T2Candida, 96·7% (95·4-97·8) for CandID, and 97·2% (95·5-98·4) for Fungitell; however, sensitivity varied widely among the tests, from 27·5% to 68·6%. The optimal test combination was Fungitell and CandID, which had an NPV of 97·5% (95·7-98·7) and a sensitivity of 75·0%. Combining these biomarkers with standard-of-care blood culture testing further increased the NPV to 98·6% (97·0-99·4), with a sensitivity of 85·1%.InterpretationNo single biomarker had sufficiently high sensitivity to justify stopping empirical antifungal treatment. Combining Fungitell and CandID with standard-of-care blood culture testing could provide a sufficiently high NPV to allow early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in this patient group, thereby reducing overtreatment, although this gain in sensitivity is accompanied by a reduction in specificity. Randomised trials are needed to confirm the clinical and cost-effectiveness of this diagnostic strategy before it is adopted in practice.FundingUK National Institute for Health and Care Research Health Technology Assessment Programme and the Research Charitable Trust Fund of the Belfast Health & Social Care Trust.
authors: McMullan R, Loughlin L, Toase S, Campbell C, Clarke M, Curran T, Dark P, Guiney M, Harrison DA, Lindsay J, Mills C, Morris KP, Perkins GD, Simpson AJ, Stevenson M, Walsh T, White PL, McAuley DF, A-Stop Study Investigators.

title: NF-κB phosphorylation controls enhancer selection to shape the inflammatory gene program.
abstract: Inflammatory transcriptional responses mediated by NF-κB are diverse despite similar upstream activation signals. Because phosphorylation of the NF-κB subunit RelA/p65 promotes interaction with co-activators CREB-binding protein/E1A binding protein p300 (CBP/p300) and selectively affects gene expression, we asked whether this modification distinguishes regulatory architectures underlying distinct immune functions. In macrophages carrying a Rela Ser276Ala mutation, p65 phosphorylation at serine 276 (S276) was dispensable for NF-κB binding to primed enhancers but essential for recruitment to nucleosome-occluded regions lacking pre-bound transcription factors (TFs) and activating histone marks. Such latent enhancers required phosphorylated NF-κB to recruit CBP/p300, promote histone acetylation, and open chromatin. Genes linked to these enhancers, including inflammatory mediators, were selectively impaired in S276A macrophages. Although antiviral responses remained intact, Rela Ser276Ala mice resisted endotoxin shock but were susceptible to bacterial infection. Thus, NF-κB responses are functionally partitioned by enhancer architecture: phosphorylation-sensitive sites define a latent enhancer compartment with NF-κB-dominated regulatory architecture, whereas primed sites are embedded in broader networks of lineage-determining and inducible TFs, yielding distinct biological outputs.

title: In silico conservation and HLA-binding profiles of HMPV F and G protein epitopes: implications for universal vaccine development.
abstract: BackgroundHuman metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a significant cause of respiratory infection, yet no licensed vaccine exists. Variability across viral subgroups, particularly in the attachment (G) protein, can complicate universal design. We assessed the immunogenetic regions in the fusion (F) and G proteins to identify stable vaccine targets.MethodsWe analyzed N = 324 Pittsburgh and N = 655 global HMPV genomes (2017-2022) for genome diversity per viral subgroup. Previously identified epitope sequences were obtained from the Immune Epitope DataBase (IEDB) for F and G proteins and sequence similarity was determined. Using NetMHCpan-4.1, we identified and computed inferred human leukocyte antigen (HLA) binding affinities for 15 epitope variants (1 or 2 substitutions) against universally common human alleles.ResultsThe F protein was highly conserved across all subgroups (>96% amino acid sequence identity). In the G protein, we identified a conserved epitope cluster (G3-G7) where epitope G7 was present in 91% of A2 genomes. Functional modeling of the G-protein epitope variants revealed that the majority of HLA alleles maintained or gained binding affinity, a subset exhibited diminished binding (escape), suggesting these regions are subject to ongoing antigenic drift. B-genotypes showed fewer retained binders and were notably underrepresented in the current epitope databases.ConclusionThe conserved F protein remains an optimal target for neutralization, while the G3-G7 cluster provides a robust secondary target for T-cell mediated immunity. A bivalent vaccine strategy could pair the stable F protein with these high-frequency G-protein epitopes to elicit an immune response. This approach addresses the A2 subgroup, and incorporating B-genotypes through ongoing surveillance and epitope mapping will be essential to achieve comprehensive, multi-antigen coverage across circulating HMPV strains.
authors: Pless LL, Griffith MP, Waggle KD, Coyle H, Spratt A, Beatty AB, Johnson M, Heffelfinger EM, D'Agostino HEA, Susick M, Alicea G, Balasubramani GK, Zimmerman RK, Nowalk MP, Williams J, Harrison LH.

title: Towards forecasting antimicrobial resistance evolution: concordance of  in vitro  and  in vivo  studies
abstract: Summary  Antimicrobial resistance is a major global health concern, and current measures to address the problem are new drugs, prudent use and rapid diagnostics. Recently, the idea of forecasting resistance evolution experimentally to prevent resistance  a priori has gained attention. But how well do experimental data on antimicrobial resistance evolution reflect resistance in strains from patients?  We conducted a systematic review and analysis to compare  in vitro and  in vivo data. We collected and analysed literature on experimental resistance evolution published between 1977 and 2024 available on PubMed for ESKAPE pathogens plus  E .  coli (ESKAPEE). We catalogued the magnitude of resistance evolution via minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) changes across antimicrobial classes. We then focussed on  P. aeruginosa and  E. coli under ciprofloxacin (CIP) selection, as these were most frequent bacterial species used in experimental evolution. CIP-selected gene mutations and amino acid substitutions, as well as the associated MICs in experimentally evolved  P. aeruginosa and  E. coli isolates, were compared with corresponding  in vivo data.  In vitro and  in vivo isolates of  E. coli showed high concordance in the selected gene mutations and the specific amino-acid changes. Similar results were found for  P. aeruginosa Evolved MIC values differed significantly depending on the respective gene mutation and the total number of mutations, but not due to the origin of the strains –  in vitro or  in vivo . Our findings clearly show that experimental resistance evolution  in vitro could predict the emergence of antimicrobial resistance evolution  in vivo .  This study supports the idea that experimental data can be used to forecast the risks of resistance emergence and therefore contribute to antimicrobial stewardship. It will be important to investigate how generalizable these findings are for other bacteria-antimicrobial combinations.
authors: Herzog M, Murphy RA, Rolff J.

title: COGNITIVE HETEROGENEITY AND AGING: AN AGE-INDEPENDENT CILIARY GENE PROGRAM TRACKS COGNITIVE RESILIENCE IN MICE
abstract: ABSTRACT  Cognitive decline with age is often viewed as inevitable, yet older animals show striking heterogeneity in functional trajectories, with many preserving cognitive integrity despite physiological decline. The biological basis of this resilience remains poorly understood, partly due to insensitive behavioral testing paradigms. Using an automated home-cage platform and hippocampal RNA sequencing, we integrated behavioral phenotyping with transcriptomic profiling to disentangle molecular programs linked to cognitive performance from chronological age. Behavioral data from 906 C57BL/6 mice across 129 standardized studies, trajectory-based modeling, variance-partitioned correlation, and stability-driven gene prioritization identified a transcriptional signature (271 genes) linked to cognitive state independent of age. Preserved cognition was associated with higher expression of genes governing ciliary structure and motility, neurite organization, and synaptic architecture, while impairment was associated with neuroimmune and metabolic-stress programs. A 38-gene cilia structural module score remained associated with resilience after controlling for age (partial rho = −0.81), with consistent effects across leave-one-out resampling. Because the constituent genes were selected on this same outcome, the module-level magnitude is not an unbiased effect-size estimate; recalibration against a null that reapplies the full selection procedure gave an empirical p of 0.026. This divergence emerged among genetically identical mice, indicating non-genetic, discrete hippocampal molecular signatures underlying individual differences. Cell-type attribution against the Allen Brain Cell Atlas localized the module predominantly to ependymal cells, with 27 of 38 genes ependymal-restricted (median detection 90.2% in ependymal cells versus 1.1% in CA1 glutamatergic neurons) and three genes (Dnah9, Dnai4, Kif9) also detected in CA1. The association was not attributable to ependymal tissue content: the module score was unrelated to Foxj1 expression (rho = −0.016) and the partial correlation was unchanged after adjustment for ependymal and choroid plexus marker panels, indicating that the module reflects how strongly the ciliary program is expressed rather than how many ependymal cells each sample contained. These findings support a conceptual shift: cognitive trajectories appear shaped by intrinsic molecular set points rather than by chronological age, with expression of a motile ciliary program at the cerebrospinal fluid interface, rather than the abundance of the cells carrying it, emerging as a candidate correlate of resilience. This approach offers a generalizable strategy for dissecting functional heterogeneity from aging and identifying pathways for hypothesis-driven tests of resilience across the lifespan.
authors: Logan S, Unnikrishnan A, Baier M, Kurup K, Drevets D, Diaz-Garcia C, Jung W, Oh T, Ding K, Sonntag W.

title: Daphnia magna bioconverts eicosapentaenoic acid continuously and independently of dietary supply.
abstract: Freshwater food webs are increasingly exposed to eutrophication and warming, which can shift phytoplankton community composition and reduce the availability of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids to higher trophic levels. We investigated whether the model freshwater crustacean Daphnia magna can compensate for a dietary lack of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) through endogenous EPA synthesis from its precursors, and whether this response depends on food quality, temperature, and genetic background. Two D. magna strains, isolated from contrasting temperate regions, were exposed to four diets ranging from edible cyanobacteria-dominated to cryptophyte-enriched communities at 15, 20, and 25 °C. Using deuterium labelling, compound-specific hydrogen isotope analysis, fatty acid quantification and fitness measurements, we assessed EPA bioconversion and its consequences for consumer performance. Cyanobacteria-rich food reduced biomass accrual, delayed reproduction, decreased body size, and lowered offspring production. Despite these pronounced fitness effects, endogenous EPA production remained stable across all dietary treatments. Instead, bioconversion was primarily governed by water temperature, reaching a maximum at approximately 20 °C, and was slightly higher in the cold-adapted strain, consistent with underlying biochemical constraints on metabolic processes. Slight differences between the two strains suggest an important contribution of genetic background in determining EPA biosynthesis. These results indicate that endogenous EPA synthesis in D. magna was not actively regulated but was constantly active and potentially buffered against low dietary EPA levels, but did not fully compensate for poor food quality.
journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part B, Biochemistry & molecular biology
authors: Pilecky M, Kesti P, Amorim C, Fuchs I, Ruiz T, Taipale SJ, Kouba A, Wassenaar LI, Jardine T, Guo F, Kainz MJ.

title: Sequence-programmed peptide nanozyme hydrogel with microenvironment-responsive dual catalytic activity for infected wound healing.
abstract: Natural enzymes orchestrate complex biological processes through highly coordinated and multifunctional catalysis, yet their practical translation is limited by poor stability and environmental sensitivity. Here, we report a peptide-engineered nanozyme hydrogel that enables programmable, microenvironment-responsive catalytic switching in response to the wound microenvironment for active regulation of wound healing. Inspired by the catalytic motifs of natural hydrolases and oxidases, an amphiphilic peptide (C16-GAVFFAHHGGEE) was rationally designed to coordinate Cu2+ and self-assemble into a β-sheet-rich nanofibrous hydrogel. The resulting system exhibits pH-dependent catalytic switching, functioning as an oxidase (OXD)-like nanozyme under acidic conditions to generate bactericidal reactive oxygen species for localized antibacterial activity (Km = 32.45 mM, vmax = 0.61 µM s-1), while transitioning to hydrolases (HYD)-like activity under alkaline conditions to hydrolyze prodrugs and modulate inflammatory responses (Km = 888.15 mM, vmax = 3.55 mM s-1). Distinct from conventional nanozyme-based wound dressings that provide isolated or static functionalities, this system dynamically links catalytic activity with the evolving wound microenvironment, thereby enabling coordinated intervention in bacterial infection, redox imbalance, and inflammation. In vitro studies demonstrate high cytocompatibility and broad-spectrum antibacterial activity. In a diabetic infected wound model, the hydrogel achieved almost complete wound closure within 12 days, accompanied by enhanced re-epithelialization, reduced inflammation, collagen deposition, and angiogenesis. This work establishes a strategy for integrating environment-responsive, dual enzyme-mimetic catalytic switching within a single peptide-based material, offering a programmable platform for actively modulating complex wound healing processes. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Chronic infected wounds require biomaterials capable of dynamically adapting to complex and evolving pathological microenvironments; however, most existing nanozyme systems exhibit static or single-function catalytic behavior. Here, we report a sequence-programmed peptide nanozyme hydrogel that integrates switchable multienzyme-mimetic catalysis within a single self-assembled peptide sequence. By coordinating Cu2+ within a β-sheet nanofibrous network, the hydrogel achieves microenvironment-responsive catalytic switching between antibacterial oxidase-like activity under acidic conditions and anti-inflammatory hydrolase-like activity under alkaline conditions. This work establishes a direct structure-function relationship between peptide molecular design, supramolecular assembly, and adaptive therapeutic performance. The study provides a structurally simple yet multifunctional biomaterial platform for active microenvironment modulation and offers new insights into the design of peptide-based catalytic biomaterials for wound healing and other biomedical applications.
authors: Sun Y, Shen Y, Ge H, Wang K, Liang Y, Xu X, Wang Z, Zhang C, Yuan W, Chen Z, Du W, Wang Y, Su R, Qi W, Wang Y.

title: Time-fractional modeling framework for Microcystis blooms and microcystin dynamics.
abstract: Microcystin risk in cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms cannot be inferred reliably from total biomass alone because toxin concentrations depend on toxigenic biomass, toxin synthesis, intracellular retention, extracellular release, removal, and transport. This study developed a toxin-explicit, spatiotemporal time-fractional advection-dispersion-reaction (TF-ADR) framework for coupled cyanobacterial biomass and microcystin dynamics, using Lake Pontchartrain Estuary as a case-study implementation. The model resolves four transported state variables: toxigenic Microcystis biomass, non-toxigenic Microcystis biomass, intracellular microcystin, and extracellular microcystin. Environmental forcing fields, hydrodynamic velocities, and field observations from July-December 2021 were used to evaluate biomass structure, toxin partitioning, biomass-toxin decoupling, and process-level source-sink controls. Results showed that biomass-growth and toxin-synthesis favorability were related but not identical, reflecting different environmental controls on biomass accumulation and toxin production. The biomass module reproduced broad bloom structure, while the toxin simulation showed that microcystin was dominated by the intracellular pool, with median modeled intracellular and extracellular fractions of 0.978 and 0.022, respectively. Estuary-wide diagnostics showed that upper-tail total microcystin peaked before upper-tail total biomass, despite strong temporal association between the two signals. Pooled station-node analysis also showed a monotonic but non-linear biomass-toxin relationship, with total microcystin more strongly associated with toxigenic biomass than with total biomass. Process diagnostics indicated that toxin behavior reflected intracellular synthesis, release to the extracellular pool, dissolved-phase removal, and hydrodynamic redistribution. These findings demonstrate that separating toxigenic biomass, non-toxigenic biomass, intracellular toxin, and extracellular toxin provides a process-based modeling framework for interpreting microcystin risk in spatially heterogeneous estuarine systems, allowing government agencies to take proactive measures for protecting seafood and human health.
authors: Hofioni SO, Deng Z, Bargu S.

title: Frequency-dependent fitness effects are ubiquitous in rapidly adapting microbial populations.
abstract: In simple microbial populations, the fitness effects of selected mutations are typically assumed to be constant, regardless of mutant frequency. This assumption underpins predictions about evolutionary dynamics, epistasis, and the maintenance of genetic diversity. Here, we systematically test this assumption using beneficial mutations from early generations of the Escherichia coli long-term evolution experiment (LTEE). Using flow cytometry-based competition assays, we find that frequency-dependent fitness effects are the norm rather than the exception, occurring in ∼80% of strain pairs tested. Most competitions exhibit negative frequency dependence, where fitness advantages decline as mutant frequency increases. We demonstrate that the strength of frequency dependence is predictable from invasion fitness measurements, which explain approximately half of the biological variation in frequency-dependent slopes. We also observe violations of fitness transitivity in several strain combinations, indicating that competitive outcomes cannot always be predicted from fitness measured against a single reference strain. High-resolution measurements reveal that frequency dependence changes substantially within the growth cycle, with the net per-cycle effect reflecting the balance of opposing dynamics at different growth phases. Our results demonstrate that, even in a model system designed to minimize ecological complexity, subtle interactions between closely related genotypes create frequency-dependent selection that can fundamentally alter evolutionary trajectories.
authors: Ascensao JA, Abedi KD, Prasad AN, Hallatschek O.

title: HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection of macrophages escapes restriction by the BST-2 host cell factor independently of the Vpu counteracting viral protein.
abstract: As HIV-1 target cells, macrophages can be infected by cell-to-cell virus transfer from infected T cells through cell-cell fusion leading to the formation of virus-productive multinucleated giant cells (MGCs). We recently demonstrated that this route of infection escaped host cell restriction acting on the early steps of the viral life cycle. Here, we investigated whether restriction factors acting on late steps of HIV-1 replication were also bypassed in virus cell-to-cell infection of macrophages. We focused on the impact of the interferon(IFN)-induced factor BST-2/tetherin acting on virus release, a process counteracted by the Vpu viral protein. We show that deletion of Vpu did not significantly affect HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection of IFN-stimulated macrophages, and virus assembly in virus containing compartments was not affected in MGCs. Accordingly, depletion of BST-2 in IFN-stimulated macrophages had no impact on virus cell-to-cell transfer, formation of MGCs and virus production. However, cell-to-cell infection of macrophages was still sensitive to the nelfinavir protease inhibitor, whereas we previously showed that this route of infection was resistant to antiviral drugs acting on early steps of virus replication. Our results show that HIV-1 cell-to-cell infection of macrophages escapes restriction factors acting on both early and late steps of the virus life cycle, but displays resistance to antiviral drugs specifically acting on the early steps of virus replication.
authors: Yan S, Durringer A, Woottum M, Benichou S.

title: Selective Cognitive and Affective Benefits of 3D-Printed Bacteriophage T4 Models in High School Molecular Biology Instruction: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
abstract: Teaching abstract molecular concepts poses persistent challenges in high school biology education. This study evaluated a custom-developed three-dimensional (3D) bacteriophage T4 model for teaching the Hershey-Chase experiment in a Grade 11 classroom. Using a quasi-experimental design, 92 students were assigned to either model-based instruction (n = 46) incorporating hands-on assembly of a disassemblable 3D-printed phage model, or conventional instruction (n = 46). Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires assessed conceptual understanding and affective outcomes. ANCOVA revealed no significant overall cognitive difference between groups, F(1, 89) = 1.42, p = 0.237. However, item-level analysis showed the model group significantly outperformed on structural component identification (52.2% vs 26.1%, p = 0.018, ϕ = 0.27). Affective outcomes significantly favored the model condition, including lesson enjoyment (p = 0.038), model construction interest (p = 0.028), perceived knowledge mastery (p = 0.033), perceived instructional utility (p = 0.028), and modeling skill need (p = 0.049). These findings suggest that curriculum-aligned 3D model-based instruction selectively enhances representational competence for spatially complex concepts and improves situational affective engagement.
authors: Xu L, Li Y, Wang L, Yang C.

title: Combined toxicity of cyanotoxins and anthropogenic contaminants on Chlorella vulgaris: insights from single and binary mixture exposures.
abstract: Aquatic organisms in eutrophic brackish and freshwater systems are chronically exposed to natural and anthropogenic contaminants, including cyanotoxins, metals and pesticides, mainly driven by cyanobacterial blooms and human activities. However, the environmental risks posed by their combinations to the aquatic environment remain poorly understood. This study investigated the growth response of Chlorella vulgaris exposed to four single-chemical compounds (microcystin-LR, cylindrospermopsin, terbuthylazine, and cadmium) and five binary mixtures for 7 days. In single-chemical exposures, terbuthylazine was the most toxic to C. vulgaris, followed by cadmium, cylindrospermopsin and microcystin-LR. The obtained growth data were compared with concentration addition predictions based on individual toxicities using the MIXTOX tool, testing deviations for synergistic/antagonistic interactions, dose ratio and dose level dependencies. Mixture effects varied with composition and exposure time. Antagonism was the prevailing type of interaction between the chemical compounds after 4 days of exposure, while dose level dependency was the only deviation observed after 7 days. Regarding dose level dependency, synergism was observed at low doses of each chemical in three of the five tested binary mixtures. Time was an important factor in the change in the toxicity pattern. This synergistic effect poses a significant risk to aquatic organisms exposed simultaneously to cyanotoxins and anthropogenic contaminants in the environment.
authors: Pinheiro C, Azevedo J, Campos A, Silva PV, Vasconcelos V, Loureiro S.

title: Identical consensus genomes of bovine coronavirus in respiratory and enteric specimens from a single cow and sequence variation after cell culture passage.
abstract: Bovine coronavirus (BCoV) causes respiratory and enteric diseases in cattle, but the relationship between viral genetic variation and anatomical distribution remains unclear. We compared BCoV genomes detected in a tracheal swab and diarrheic intestinal content from the same adult cow. The two clinical specimens had identical 31,015-nt consensus genomes. After five passages in HRT-18 cells, the recovered tracheal isolate differed at three consensus-level amino acid positions (HE N104D, S Q179K, and S E965D) and showed marked within-sample heterogeneity. These findings highlight the importance of direct sequencing of clinical specimens because cell-culture passage can alter viral population composition.
authors: Nakagawa K, Yoshida A, Kuwata K, Kitamura Y.

title: CaSNF1 interacts with and phosphorylates CaHD-ZIP to enhance cold tolerance in pepper.
abstract: Cold stress severely restricts pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) growth and productivity by disrupting cellular homeostasis and inducing oxidative damage. Although HD-ZIP transcription factors play important roles in plant abiotic stress responses, the molecular mechanisms regulating their function during cold stress remain largely unknown. Here, we characterized the pepper HD-ZIP transcription factor CaHD-ZIP and demonstrated that it is a nuclear-localized, cold-responsive protein that positively contributes to cold stress tolerance. To further investigate the regulatory mechanism underlying CaHD-ZIP function, a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) screen identified the sucrose non-fermenting 1-related protein kinase CaSNF1 as a previously unrecognized interacting partner of CaHD-ZIP. Their interaction was confirmed by yeast two-hybrid, luciferase complementation imaging, and bimolecular fluorescence complementation assays, with BiFC indicating that the interaction occurs predominantly in the nucleus. In vitro phosphorylation analysis further demonstrated that CaSNF1 directly phosphorylates CaHD-ZIP, providing biochemical evidence for a functional regulatory relationship between these proteins. Complementary loss- and gain-of-function analyses, including virus-induced gene silencing and transient overexpression in pepper together with stable overexpression in Arabidopsis, demonstrated that CaSNF1 positively regulates cold tolerance. Silencing of CaSNF1 increased oxidative damage, impaired antioxidant enzyme activities, and suppressed the expression of antioxidant and cold-responsive genes, whereas overexpression produced the opposite effects and significantly enhanced cold tolerance. Together, these findings identify CaSNF1 as a CaHD-ZIP-interacting kinase and reveal a potential CaSNF1-CaHD-ZIP regulatory module involved in pepper cold stress adaptation. This study advances our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying pepper cold tolerance and provides potential genetic targets for improving cold resilience in pepper and other Solanaceae crops.
journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
authors: Ullah I, Pei Y, Wang M, Hussain A, Guo J, Zhang H, Chen R.

title: Revisiting porcine circovirus infections in Uruguay: first evidence of PCV3 circulation and PCV2d as the sole genotype detected.
abstract: Porcine circoviruses (PCVs) are widespread among pig populations, and porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2) is a major pathogen affecting swine health and productivity worldwide. Although PCV2 genetic diversity was previously characterized in Uruguay, updated information has been lacking for more than a decade, and porcine circovirus type 3 (PCV3) has not been reported. This study aimed to characterize recent PCV2 clinical cases and retrospectively investigate PCV3 circulation in archived samples previously analysed for PCV2. Complete PCV2 genomes obtained from clinical cases detected between 2017 and 2020 belonged to PCV2d. PCV3 was detected in archived samples from 2010 to 2014, including domestic pigs and wild boars, providing the first evidence of PCV3 circulation in Uruguay. All characterized PCV3 strains clustered within PCV3a, and PCV2/PCV3 coinfection was observed in several PCV3-positive samples. These findings indicate that PCV2d predominated among the investigated clinical cases from non-vaccinated farms and confirm PCV3 circulation in Uruguay, making it the fifth South American country to report the virus. Continued molecular surveillance is warranted to monitor PCV2 and PCV3 diversity and better understand the epidemiology of PCVs in Uruguay and across South America.
authors: Ramos N, Galiano A, Betancour G, de Oliveira LGS, Buroni F, Boabaid F, Arbiza J.

title: The Sensitivity of  13  C-Metabolic Flux Analysis to Biomass Composition Underscores the Need for Accurate Biomass Formulation in  Escherichia coli
abstract: Quantifying intracellular fluxes through  13 C-metabolic flux analysis (  13 C-MFA) provides a detailed view of cellular metabolism. While model formulation, including biomass synthesis reactions, is known to influence flux estimations, the degree to which biomass composition affects  13 C-MFA outcomes in  Escherichia coli remains debated. Here, we reconstructed a genome-scale  13 C-MFA model of  E. coli incorporating explicit nucleotide biosynthesis and a modular biomass formulation that separates protein, RNA, and other components. Using isotopic labeling experiments and systematic perturbations of biomass composition, we demonstrate that  13 C-MFA can robustly differentiate subtle shifts in the protein/RNA ratio, with deviations as small as 2–3% producing statistically significant but biologically interpretable changes in model fit. Reaction-level analyses revealed consistent flux adjustments across amino acid and nucleotide biosynthesis, while pathways in one-carbon metabolism, particularly serine, glycine, and threonine interconversions, exhibited the strongest responses. Collectively, these results highlight the robustness and discriminative power of  13 C-MFA and also demonstrate the importance of accurate biomass composition measurement in  E. coli 13 C-MFA, given the method’s intrinsic sensitivity to macromolecular stoichiometry.
authors: Cai Y, Antoniewicz MR.

title: CST–Polα/primase, backed up by Rif1, protects telomeric ss-dsDNA junctions from damage recognition and resection
abstract: The yeast Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 (CST) complex is critical for telomere length regulation and telomere protection. Recent studies further implicate Polα/primase (PP) as an essential partner of CST in executing these functions, but the mechanistic bases remain poorly understood. Using the pathogenic yeast  Nakaseomyces glabratus , a model amenable to mechanistic dissection of CST-PP, we analyzed the protection mechanisms of CST-PP by combining mutations that disrupt individual subunits or complex assembly with mutations in DNA damage response (DDR) and DNA repair factors. The complete loss of Cdc13 – which eliminates the CST-PP assembly – results in telomere damage recognition involving Rad9, Rad24 and Mec3, as well as aberrant resection mediated by Exo1 and Sgs1. In contrast, disrupting the interaction between CST and PP leads to proliferation defects triggered primarily by Exo1, implying a more selective protection function for PP. The involvement of the DDR clamp loader and clamp together with Exo1 points to ss-dsDNA junctions with recessed 5’ ends as a crucial lesion in the absence of Cdc13. Further analysis implicates RNase H1 and H2 in promoting DNA damage, possibly by exposing such junctions. Based on similarities between Cdc13 and POT1, a telomere protein previously implicated in junctional protection, we modeled Cdc13 binding to a ss-dsDNA junction and showed that point mutations at the proposed interaction site impaired telomere protection and altered the distribution of the telomere C-strand 5’ ends  in vivo . We further demonstrate that Rif1, another telomere protein with junctional binding activity, supports the protection function of CST-PP. Together, our findings illuminate the molecular basis of telomere DNA damage and of CST-PP mediated telomere protection.
authors: Yu EY, Calugaru K, Younten T, Huang S, Lue NF.

title: Cap-specific N6-adenosine methyltransferases and applications in m6A Cap-1 mRNA synthesis
abstract: In addition to the 5’ Cap-1 structure, the initiating adenosine of mammalian mRNA can be further modified by PCIF1 (Phosphorylated C-terminal domain-interacting factor 1) to form 2’-O,N6-dimethyladenosine (m6A Cap-1). While the biological role is still under investigation, the implications of m6A Cap-1 in mRNA metabolism and viral-host interactions have spurred interest in PCIF1 and m6A Cap-1 as biomarkers, drug targets, and research tools. Here, we identify and characterize two PCIF1-like cap-specific N6-adenosine methyltransferases, PC04 and PC05 and evaluate their applicability in m6A Cap-1 mRNA synthesis  in vitro. We found that both enzymes are highly specific to the m7G cap structure and highly active on Cap-1 RNA oligonucleotides and trinucleotide Cap-1 analogs at nanomolar concentrations. We demonstrate that PC04 or PC05 methylation reactions can be incorporated into established post-transcriptional capping and cap analog-based co-transcriptional  in vitro transcription (IVT) workflows to produce m6A Cap-1 RNAs. Finally, we show that PC05 can be combined with a previously reported FCE::T7 RNA polymerase fusion to synthesize m6A Cap-1 mRNA from DNA templates in a single step, co-transcriptional manner. The robustness of the PCIF1-like cap N6-adenosine methyltransferases can accelerate research into the biological roles of cap m6A modification and development of highly effective mRNA-based therapeutics. authors: Kneller DW, Dai N, Chan SH.

title: Root gene regulatory network analysis reveals roles for defense hormones and secondary metabolites in establishment of disease-suppressive soil
abstract: Summary  Plants recruit beneficial microbiota in their rhizosphere to alleviate stresses. In  Arabidopsis thaliana , foliar infection by  Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (  Hpa ) has been shown to establish a disease-suppressive microbiome that promotes protection against  Hpa infection of the subsequent plant generation grown in this conditioned soil - a phenomenon known as soil-borne legacy (SBL). The root responses involved in SBL establishment have remained largely unclear.  In this study, time-series RNA-seq of roots from  Hpa -infected plants grown in natural soil was conducted over seven days post-inoculation. A gene regulatory network of the responding roots was constructed. The role of predicted key components was verified in follow-up assays.  Root transcriptional reprogramming started within one day after foliar infection. Genes associated with salicylic acid (SA)-mediated defense were upregulated, while those linked to secondary metabolism and jasmonic acid (JA) responsiveness were downregulated. SA accumulation increased at 1 dpi, and JA decreased by 3 dpi. Transcriptional regulation occurred primarily in the tips of the roots. Mutant analyses confirmed that SA, JA, indole glucosinolates, camalexin, and flavonoids contribute to SBL establishment. Our findings reveal rapid systemic transcriptional reprogramming in roots upon foliar pathogen attack, uncovering novel roles of hormone signaling and secondary metabolism in shaping a disease-suppressive soil beyond their known defense functions.
authors: Qi R, Glavincheska I, Spooren J, Liu X, Van Laatum M, Verstappen F, Kappers IF, Berendsen RL, Pieterse CM, Van Wees SC.

title: NAD metabolism mediates a sex-specific protection against early life infections
abstract: Sex influences early-life immunity and infection outcomes, yet how metabolic mechanisms regulate these effects remain unclear. As nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) can support mitochondrial metabolism and immune function, here we explore how NAD metabolism contributes to sex-specific protection against infections in early life. First, in two independent cohorts of 700 and 386 children, we found that females at birth had higher blood NAD levels than males, and strikingly higher birth NAD levels were associated with reduced infection burdens during the first 3 years of life in females, but with tendency of increased burdens in males. At 18 months, plasma nicotinamide associated with sex-specific cytokine responses to antigen challenges and showed a stronger positive association with tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) activity in females. Next, we verified the causal effects of NAD metabolism on infection protection by testing the supplementation of NAD precursor nicotinamide riboside (NR) in infected newborn piglets, used as a translational model of infection-sensitive infants. NR treatment improved survival, bacterial clearance, and disease tolerance only in females, but not in males. Mechanistically, NR increased levels of hepatic TCA cycle metabolites fumarate and malate, and enhanced hepatic inflammatory, hormonal, and mitochondrial-associated transcriptional programs, again only in females. Finally, the sex-specific immune functions mediated by NR were also validated in blood and immune cells  in vitro . Collectively, we identified NAD metabolism as a sex-dependent immunometabolic mediator in early-life infection. Our findings suggest the potential of sex-stratified nutritional interventions in infection-sensitive infants.
authors: Klabunde B, Olsen KA, Spiegelhauer M, Kellezi ED, Memushaj A, Thysen AH, Long NP, Brix S, Pedersen C, Bønnelykke K, Chawes B, Treebak J, Bæk O, Nguyen DN.

title: Drp1 deficiency enhances macrophage efferocytosis and partially restores gut microbial dysbiosis in colitis
abstract: Abstract    Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) is a key regulator of mitochondrial fission, but its role in intestinal macrophages and gut microbial homeostasis during colitis remains unclear. Herein, Drp1 expression was increased in intestinal macrophages from patients with ulcerative colitis and mice with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, as demonstrated by transcriptomic, single-cell, and immunofluorescence analyses. To determine its functional role, colitis was induced in conditional Drp1 knockout mice and littermate controls. Macrophage Drp1 deficiency reduced disease activity, colon shortening, histopathological injury, and mucus barrier disruption. Colonic transcriptomic profiling further revealed reduced inflammatory signaling and enrichment of pathways related to macrophage differentiation, apoptotic-cell clearance, and efferocytosis. Consistently, Drp1-deficient macrophages exhibited enhanced apoptotic-cell uptake  in vitro  . Furthermore, 16S rRNA sequencing showed that Drp1 deficiency partially reversed colitis-associated alterations in gut microbial community structure, without significantly affecting overall alpha diversity. This microbial remodeling was characterized by increased  Akkermansia  and  Muribaculaceae  , while reduced  Escherichia-Shigella  and  Enterococcus  . Collectively, these findings indicate that Drp1 deficiency attenuates acute colitis by reshaping macrophage functional states and enhancing efferocytosis, while being associated with improved mucosal integrity and partial restoration of gut microbial dysbiosis.
authors: Huang C, Liao Y, Zhang Y, Guo X, Xiang L, Zhang L, Ye Z, Zhao Y, Li Y, Zhou Y, Zhou Y.

title: Development and Laboratory Evaluation of a Standardized Procedure for Environmental Sampling and Molecular Detection of Human Papillomavirus
abstract: Abstract  Background  Environmental surveillance of infectious pathogens is increasingly important for disease prevention and control; however, heterogeneity in sampling, preservation, and transport procedures can substantially affect molecular detection results. Methods  Human papillomavirus (HPV) was used as a non-enveloped DNA virus model to evaluate six determinants of surface sampling performance: swab type, surface material, sampling interval, swab pre-moistening, ambient temperature, and preservation medium. An HPV-positive inoculum was prepared by pooling approximately 150 anonymized male urethral swab specimens, followed by saline elution, genotype confirmation, and quantitative testing. HPV DNA was quantified by real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR). Outcomes were the positive detection rate and a prespecified log-scale recovery index. Results  Polyester and sponge swabs achieved the highest positive detection rates (both 98.04% ± 3.40%), whereas polyester swabs had the highest mean log-scale recovery index. HPV DNA was more readily recovered from smooth, non-porous, non-absorbent surfaces (ceramic tile and polypropylene) than from wood or woven fabric. Dry polyester swabbing yielded a higher positive detection rate than PBS-pre-moistened swabbing (88.75% ± 2.80% vs 80.00% ± 5.23%; P = 0.032), although the log-scale recovery index did not differ significantly. Sampling from 1 to 24 h after inoculation did not significantly affect either outcome. Exposure to 35°C reduced both the positive detection rate and the log-scale recovery index compared with 15°C and 25°C. Dedicated viral transport media maintained HPV DNA detectability throughout 28 days of storage at 2–8°C. PBS first fell below the prespecified 70% detection threshold on day 7, whereas normal saline remained at or above the threshold through 3 h and fell below it at 6 h. Conclusions  Under the tested laboratory conditions, dry polyester swabs combined with dedicated viral transport media provided the most practical overall approach for molecular recovery of HPV from environmental surfaces. Surface properties and ambient temperature were the principal determinants of HPV DNA detectability. These findings support protocol standardization but do not establish viral infectivity or fomite transmission.
authors: Duan X, Yang M, Xie Y, Wang X, Xu L, Tao Z.

title: Evidence that the perinatal maternal microbiome mediates metabolite signaling programs that drive sex-specific microglial metabolic alterations and Alzheimer’s disease susceptibility
abstract: Abstract  Maternal microbiome-dependent programming of neuroimmune and metabolic pathways during early development may critically shape sex-specific susceptibility to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) later in life. We have documented that in mouse models of Aβ deposition, broad-spectrum antibiotic (ABX)-mediated perturbations of the gut microbiome postnatally (P14-P21) selectively reduces Aβ pathology only in male, but not in female animals. Here, we shift the developmental window upstream to test whether perinatal maternal microbiome perturbations shapes the pathological trajectories of offspring. Dams were treated with the broad-spectrum ABX from preconception through gestation, without direct exposure of the offspring. Strikingly, maternal microbiome disruption selectively reduced cortical Aβ burden in female offspring, with no effect in males, effectively reversing the sex bias observed following postnatal ABX manipulations. To explore the mechanisms underlying this effect, we now report that female offspring exhibited coordinated shifts in microbial composition and amino acid metabolism, that are coupled to cortical transcriptional programs enriched for GPCR signaling and Rho GTPase pathways. As many microbial metabolites and amino acid-derived ligands signal through GPCRs that are expressed by microglia, these transcriptional changes suggest enhanced GPCR-mediated nutrient sensing in microglia of female animals. These systems level changes in microglia drive a metabolically engaged amyloid clearing phenotype, providing a mechanistic link between maternal microbiome disruption and enhanced Aβ clearance in females. Together, these findings demonstrate that maternal microbial inheritance and developmental timing critically shape sex specific AD susceptibility and position temporal microbiome modulation as a potential precision strategy for disease prevention.
authors: Saha P, Slimmon N, Nadgauda A, Patel P, Mishra D, Poli PB, Inukai A, Fernandez A, Weigle I, Zhang X, Sisodia SS.

title: Co-circulation of H5N1 and H5N6 high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses in migratory birds at a coastal wintering site in China.
abstract: Since 2020, H5Nx high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs) belonging to hemagglutinin (HA) clade 2.3.4.4b have undergone widespread dispersal in wild birds, posing substantial threats to global poultry populations and mammals worldwide. In this study, we report the co-circulation of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 and H5N6 HPAIVs associated with mortality events in Anseriformes and Charadriiformes at a coastal wintering site in Fujian Province, China. H5N1 and H5N6 viruses were identified in four species of waterfowl (Bean Goose, Eastern Spot-billed Duck, Eurasian Wigeon, and Eurasian Curlew). Phylogenetic analysis indicated that these H5N1 and H5N6 isolates were clade 2.3.4.4b strains circulating within Eurasia and lacked known mammalian adaptation markers in key proteins. The infected birds exhibited severe systemic multi-organ pathology, with the most pronounced damage observed in the lungs. H5N6 and H5N1 viruses caused lethal injury in BALB/c mice, with H5N1 leading to systemic infection. Environmental sampling also revealed the presence of H5N1 HPAIVs alongside low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (LPAIVs) such as H3N1 and H6N1. Our findings highlight the complex and dynamic transmission patterns of H5 HPAIV in wild bird populations and the substantial threat they pose to mammals, underscoring the critical importance of sustained surveillance for high pathogenicity avian influenza in wild birds.
authors: Hu X, Xiang H, Wang W, Kong Y, Liang H, Li M, Miao Y, Han H, Sun Z, Yu M, Peng P, Gao J, Zhang G, Xu Y, Li Y, Gao Y.

title: The Virome of Rhubarb Consists of Diverse Viruses Belonging to at Least Four Families.
abstract: Culinary rhubarb (Rheum spp.) comprises herbaceous perennials that are primarily clonally propagated. Like other asexually reproduced crops, rhubarb is vulnerable to virus transmission, but its virome remains poorly characterized. In April 2024, foliar virus-like symptoms, including chlorotic and necrotic leaf spots, chlorosis, and stunting, were observed on cultivar 'Kerwin' in the rhubarb collection at Cornell AgriTech in Geneva, NY. Symptomatic leaf tissue tested positive for tomato ringspot virus (ToRSV) in a double-antibody sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay using specific antibodies. Subsequently, the virome of 40 rhubarb entries was determined using high-throughput sequencing (HTS) and bioinformatic analyses. Sequence information suggested the presence of ToRSV (genus Nepovirus, family Secoviridae), cherry leafroll virus (genus Nepovirus, family Secoviridae), Arabis mosaic virus (genus Nepovirus, family Secoviridae), broad-leafed dock virus A (BLDVA, genus Macluravirus, family Potyviridae), tobacco streak virus (TSV, genus Ilarvirus, family Bromoviridae), and beet curly top virus (BCTV, genus Curtovirus, family Geminiviridae) in composite leaf samples. The occurrence of these RNA and DNA viruses was confirmed in composite and individual samples after deconvolution by RT-PCR or PCR, respectively, using one or two primer pairs, in combination with bidirectional Sanger sequencing of the amplicons. The symptoms of cultivar 'Kerwin' could not be definitively assigned to ToRSV due to co-infection with BLDVA. This is the first characterization of the rhubarb virome by HTS and the first report of ToRSV, BLDVA, TSV, and BCTV in culinary rhubarb. These findings have implications for the propagation of clean material, distribution of germplasm, and future breeding efforts in rhubarb. [Formula: see text] Copyright © 2026 The Author(s). title: SDHC Gene is a Potential Player in the Pathogenesis of Congenital Heart Disease and Neurodevelopmental Disorder by Promoting eNOS Signaling, Suppressing Inflammation and Improving Angiogenic Endothelial Function.
abstract: IntroductionCongenital Heart Disease (CHD) and Neurodevelopmental Disorders (NDD) frequently co-occur due to shared genetic defects in embryonic angiogenesis and mitochondrial metabolism; however, the regulatory mechanisms linking these pathways remain poorly understood.ObjectiveTo identify pathogenic genes underlying CHD-NDD co-development and investigate the regulatory role of Succinate Dehydrogenase Complex Subunit C (SDHC) in endothelial angiogenesis.MethodsBlood samples from 70 children (13 CHD+NDD, 33 CHD, 24 NDD) were analyzed by Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) and Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS). Candidate genes were identified through bidirectional deduplication, multi-library comparison, PPI network analysis, and functional enrichment analysis. SDHC expression was examined by immunofluorescence in the developing mouse heart and brain. In Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) with SDHC overexpression or knockdown, eNOS and TNF-α protein levels were measured by Western blot. Cell migration and tube formation were quantified by scratch and Matrigel assays.ResultsWES identified high-frequency SDHC mutations, including T→TTA (Chr1:161293485, 33.33%) and C→CT (Chr1:161332091, 55.56%) in CHD+NDD. Bioinformatics suggested SDHC involvement in cardiac and neural development. In mice, cardiac SDHC increased age-dependently by 71.83% (P DiscussionThese findings suggest SDHC dysregulation may affect CHD-NDD comorbidity through eNOS modulation and inflammatory responses in HUVECs. The presence of SDHC variants in 7 of 13 patients (53.8%) and functional data indicate SDHC may serve as a candidate angiogenesis regulator linking cardiovascular and neurodevelopmental abnormalities. However, the small cohort (n = 13 CHD + NDD), absence of healthy controls, and lack of patient-derived variant validation limit definitive conclusions. The biological consequences of the identified variants remain unknown because variant-specific functional analyses were not performed. Future studies require expanded cohorts and in vivo SDHC- specific models to investigate potential associations.ConclusionSDHC may play potential roles in eNOS signaling, inflammation suppression, and endothelial angiogenic function. These findings suggest SDHC as a candidate gene associated with CHD-NDD comorbidity.
authors: Deng X, Zhao Y, Deng W, Wang Z, Zhou K, Xu Q, Li X, Qin X, Guo L, Tan Y, Qian Y, Xiao Y, Jiang ZS.

title: Three new species of Hohenbuehelia (Agaricales, Basidiomycota) from China based on morphological and multi-locus phylogenetic evidence.
abstract: The genus Hohenbuehelia, widely distributed in temperate and tropical regions, plays an important role in forest ecosystems. However, the species diversity of Hohenbuehelia in China has been underestimated. This study presents the morphological and molecular characterization of three novel Hohenbuehelia species from China, enhancing the understanding of this genus in the region. Hohenbuehelia albomarginata is characterized by small, gray-brown to brown basidiomata with a frosted, concolorous tomentum on the pileus, often white at the margin, and elongate basidiospores. Hohenbuehelia striata differs in having brown, glabrous basidiomata that are laterally or dorsally attached, lacking a stipe or pseudostipe, with a very faintly translucent-striate pileus margin and ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid basidiospores. Hohenbuehelia guizhouensis has a gray-brown to brown pileus covered with white tomentum, lamellae radiating from the point of attachment, and elongate, ellipsoid to subreniform basidiospores. Phylogenetic analyses based on multigene sequence data further support their taxonomic distinctiveness. All species are comprehensively described, illustrated, and compared with closely related and morphologically similar taxa. This study expands the known diversity of Hohenbuehelia and highlights the need for further exploration of fungal diversity in China.
authors: Luo T, Che NJ, Feng WC, Cui YY, Li J.

title: Graphene family nanomaterials - atrazine - extracellular polymeric substances: a triangular interplay during short- and long-term exposure of marine microalgae Chlorella sp.
abstract: The co-occurrence of graphene family nanomaterials (GFNs) and organic pollutants in aquatic environments raises concerns regarding their individual as well as combined effects on marine primary producers. The present research investigates the toxicity of graphene, graphene oxide (GO), and reduced graphene oxide (rGO), both individually and in combination with atrazine (ATZ), in the marine microalga Chlorella sp. over short-term (72 h) and long-term (360 h) exposure periods, with a particular focus on the protective role of algal extracellular polymeric substances (EPS). For the determination of toxicity, growth, photosynthesis, reactive oxygen species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), and antioxidant enzyme activities were studied. The results show that GFNs in various combinations with ATZ can inhibit growth, hinder photosynthesis, induce oxidative stress and accelerate lipid peroxidation. Among the three GFNs studied, rGO was the most toxic, followed by GO and graphene. Exposure to binary mixtures of GFNs and ATZ resulted in different responses compared to the individual pollutants, indicating the effect of the combination of GFNs and ATZ, as well as the exposure duration. Importantly, EPS markedly alleviated the adverse effects of ATZ, GFNs and their combination by reducing oxidative stresses and improving photosynthesis and biochemical responses. The uptake study revealed decreased accumulation of ATZ in cells in the presence of EPS. Finally, the current work concludes that algal EPS is an important natural defence system that regulates the bioavailability and toxicity of GFNs and other organic contaminants such as ATZ, even when they co-occur in the environment for a long duration.
authors: Debroy A, Pulimi M, Mukherjee A.

title: A planthopper-secreted miRNA facilitates viral infection by disrupting plant growth-defense balance in rice.
abstract: Insect vectors can enhance the pathogenicity of plant arboviruses, yet the molecular mechanisms driving this cross-kingdom manipulation remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that white-backed planthoppers secrete a specific microRNA, miR-133, into rice to facilitate southern rice black-streaked dwarf virus (SRBSDV) infection. Mechanistically, insect-derived miR-133 functions via cross-kingdom RNA interference to directly repress the GOLDEN2-LIKE transcription factor 31 (OsGLK31). OsGLK31 acts as a dual regulator that promotes growth via OsYUCCA-mediated auxin biosynthesis and confers antiviral immunity through OsLOX11-mediated jasmonic acid (JA) biosynthesis. In the absence of infection, the plant repressor OsJAZ10 binds to OsGLK31 to specifically inhibit its immune function, thereby prioritizing growth. However, insect infestation disrupts this balance: insect-secreted miR-133 represses OsGLK31 expression, while OsJAZ10 blocks the transcriptional activity of residual OsGLK31 protein on OsLOX11. This coordinated blockade suppresses both auxin and JA biosynthesis, causing severe dwarfism and dampened viral resistance. Our findings reveal miR-133 as a cross-kingdom effector that disrupts the host plant growth-defense balance to pave the way for viral invasion, offering potential targets for antiviral crop improvement.
authors: Zhang B, Jia S, Zhu Y, Gao Q, Ding W, He H, Gao H, Jing D, Li Y, Qiu L.

title: The Influence of Nitrogen on Alnus glutinosa Susceptibility to Phytophthora × alni.
abstract: Riparian forest ecosystems face multiple anthropogenic pressures, including chronic nitrogen (N) pollution and invasive pathogens. However, the putative synergies among them are poorly understood. In the case of the keystone N-fixing tree Alnus glutinosa attacked by the exotic pathogen Phytophthora × alni, such pressures may act synergistically. N can indirectly promote susceptibility to the pathogen by affecting native soil microbiome composition and disrupting alder's symbiotic partnership with actinobacteria of the genus Frankia. In a greenhouse experiment that involved the manipulation of N through fertilization and Frankia nodulation through soil sterilization, we examined the interactive effects of nodulation, soil microbiota, and P. × alni infection on alder performance. We found that alder survival after infection was strongly influenced by the origin of the substrate in which the plants were grown. Under N-fertilization, mortality due to Phytophthora was higher in plants grown without alder soil amendments. In contrast, in soils amended with alder soil, N-fertilization did not increase alder susceptibility to the pathogen, although it significantly reduced Frankia nodulation. Nodulation was lowest in plants carrying the highest pathogen loads, showing that P. × alni infection not only kills alders but also undermines N-fixation. Our findings show that N-fertilization and P. × alni suppress nodulation and therefore can simultaneously contribute negatively to the N-fixing central function of alders in river ecosystems. Our results also seem to discard any protective role of soil microbiome or Frankia nodulation against P. × alni on alder.
authors: Vieites-Blanco C, Caballol M, Oliva J.

title: Two-component system VraSR senses host defense peptide PMAP-36 to promote Streptococcus suis pathogenicity through regulating accD expression.
abstract: Streptococcus suis (S. suis) is an important zoonotic pathogen that causes severe infections in humans and animals worldwide. Upon infection, the host innate immune system produces host defense peptides (HDPs) to resist S. suis invasion. PMAP-36, a porcine-derived HDP, has been shown to fail to kill S. suis, suggesting that this pathogen has evolved strategies to evade PMAP-36-mediated immune defense. However, the exact mechanism by which S. suis responds to PMAP-36 remains unclear. Here we showed that PMAP-36 significantly enhanced S. suis adhesion, cytotoxicity, and virulence gene expression. The two-component system (TCS) VraSR was essential for PMAP-36 to promote S. suis pathogenicity. We demonstrated that PMAP-36 directly bound to the sensor kinase VraS. Further transcriptomic analysis revealed that VraSR sensed PMAP-36 to regulate fatty acid biosynthesis, in which a key gene accD expression was significantly downregulated in both PMAP-36-treated ΔvraS and ΔvraR mutant strains. Deletion of accD attenuates S. suis in vivo pathogenicity, including reduced bacterial loads, alleviated organ damage, and decreased inflammatory response. Additionally, VraSR-mediated accD expression was critical for S. suis-induced cytotoxicity and inflammatory response, as deletion of vraS or vraR fails to reduce inflammatory cytokines production due to sustained high accD expression. This study reveals VraSR-mediated virulence regulatory mechanism in response to HDP activation, which provides new insight into the development of novel strategies to combat S. suis infection.
authors: Pan Y, Lu Y, Zhang T, Hu Z, Liu H, Su B, Lei R, Zhang T, Zhang Y, Cao X, Li Z, Fang R, Peng L.

title: Meeting Report of the 6th edition of metabolism and cancer symposium.
abstract: The 6th International Meeting "Metabolism and Cancer" was held at the Convention Center in La Grande Motte, France, on October 8-10, 2025. The three-day conference brought together 240 participants from eleven countries and featured 29 scientific presentations, including 15 invited lectures delivered by leading investigators in the field of oncometabolism. The program was structured into four thematic sessions: (i) diet, cachexia, microbiome, and microenvironment; (ii) stem cells and metabolic plasticity; (iii) epigenetics, epitranscriptomics, and metabolism; and (iv) metabolic control of drug resistance, therapy, and biomarkers. This meeting report highlights key conceptual advances and emerging directions discussed during the conference. Future progress in cancer metabolism will depend on elucidating the cross-talk between tumors and peripheral tissues, as organism-level metabolic regulation is likely to critically influence tumor growth, plasticity, and treatment sensitivity. Moving forward, a systems-level integration of metabolic, genomic, and spatial data is poised to redefine cancer metabolism from a descriptive field into a source of actionable vulnerabilities for precision oncology.
authors: B Sant'Anna-Silva AC, Del Bove C, Efthymiou G, Henry E, Henry L, Kundnani J, Rossignol R, Zimmermann S.

title: First Report of Tenacibaculum maritimum Infection in Grouper (Epinephelus spp.) Aquaculture in Taiwan.
abstract: Between April 2024 and 2025, six independent outbreaks of ulcerative skin disease occurred in cultured groupers (Epinephelus spp.) across southern Taiwan and Penghu County during winter-to-spring seasonal transitions at water temperatures ranging from 19°C to 24°C. Affected fish presented with extensive epidermal erosion and deep dermal ulceration on the operculum, lateral trunk and caudal peduncle regions. Histopathology revealed marked integumentary breakdown characterised by epithelial sloughing, deep dermal necrosis and dense basophilic mats of filamentous bacteria tracking along necrotic subcutaneous myofibres. Wet-mount microscopy and Gram-stained lesion smears consistently revealed sheets of long, slender, Gram-negative rods across all cases (n = 18). Eighteen representative isolates exhibiting pale-yellow, flat, adherent colonies with irregular margins were recovered on Marine Agar formulated with natural seawater (salinity 30‰-35‰). Species-specific PCR and near-full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing (1505 bp; > 99.5% identity to the type strain NCIMB 2154T) confirmed the aetiology to be Tenacibaculum maritimum. Physiological profiling revealed a narrow salinity tolerance window (30‰-45‰), in contrast to the broader range of classic temperate strains (10‰-35‰). This study represents the first definitive isolation and molecular/physiological characterisation of T. maritimum in farmed groupers in Taiwan, expanding its host spectrum and geographical range into subtropical mariculture zones.
authors: Wu ST, Hsieh CY.

title: Substitutions in the yeast Nrd1 RNA-binding domain have distinct effects on NNS terminator recognition.
abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) regulate gene expression through combinatorial interactions with RNAs and proteins. The essential S. cerevisiae nuclear RBP Nrd1 serves as a model to investigate the effects of RBPs on transcription and RNA processing. Nrd1 binding to short, noncoding RNAs elicits termination of their synthesis by RNA polymerase (RNAP) II, promotes polyadenylation by the TRAMP complex, and enables 3'-trimming by the nuclear exosome. How Nrd1 discriminates its substrate RNAs and coordinates these processes is not well understood. Here, we made deletions and substitutions in Nrd1 to assess the contributions of different domains to its function. We confirmed the contribution of known protein interaction domains in NNS terminator recognition and identified a region C-terminal to the RNA-binding domain (RBD) required for efficient termination in vivo. We also characterized three RBD substitutions, two of which were obtained in a screen for spindle pole body assembly defects and one of which increases RNAP II terminator recognition by S. pombe Seb1, a Nrd1 ortholog. All three caused NNS terminator readthrough in vivo and decreased RNA-binding affinity of the RBD in vitro. Surprisingly, the substitution with the most severe in vitro RNA-binding defect, G344D, exhibited readthrough of only a minority of snoRNA terminators affected by the original nrd1-5 substitution (V368G), which had the least severe RNA-binding defect. Transcriptome analysis showed that Nrd1-G344D caused dysregulation of mRNAs largely distinct from those affected by Nrd1-5 and identified a role for Nrd1-dependent termination in phosphate regulation similar to that of Seb1 in S. pombe. We conclude that the G344D and V368G substitutions in the RNA recognition motif distinguish between some of the diverse substrates of Nrd1.
authors: Zawisza KA, Goguen EC, Brow DA.

title: A yeast surface display platform for oral delivery of a SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain dimer inducing mucosal and systemic immunity.
abstract: The development of scalable and stable antigen delivery systems remains a central challenge in vaccine biotechnology, particularly for oral immunization targeting mucosal immunity. Here, we report a yeast surface display (YSD)-based platform for the oral delivery of a SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD) dimer. A head-to-tail tandem RBD was genetically fused to the Aga2p subunit and anchored to the cell wall of Saccharomyces cerevisiae via the Aga1p-Aga2p system, generating the YSD-RBD-dimer construct. Flow cytometry confirmed clear surface expression, with 51.1% dual-positive cells recognizing both HA-tag and RBD epitopes. Under simulated gastric conditions (pH 1.2), the antibody-binding signal associated with surface-displayed RBD-dimer showed 97.57% retention after 2 h, indicating preservation of antibody-accessible RBD-associated epitopes. In vivo fluorescence tracking revealed gastrointestinal transit with signals peaking in Peyer's patches at 6 h and mesenteric lymph nodes at 12 h. Oral immunization elicited both systemic and mucosal immune responses, characterized by elevated serum anti-RBD IgG and fecal secretory IgA. Notably, vaccine-induced sera substantially inhibited RBD-ACE2 binding in a cell-based assay, with an inhibition rate of 81.6% ± 6.4%. Antigen-specific lymphocyte proliferation and transcriptional analysis revealed a mixed Th1- and Th2-associated response, with greater induction of IFN-γ and T-bet than of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and GATA-3. No apparent systemic toxicity or histopathological abnormalities were observed, supporting the preliminary safety of the platform. Collectively, this study supports the feasibility of a scalable yeast surface display-based platform for oral delivery of protein antigens and induction of coordinated systemic and mucosal immune responses.
authors: Zhi X, Zhang Y, Guo Z, Xu W, Shi X, Liu R.
