title: Predictors of HIV reservoir size and decay dynamics in early-treated paediatric infection: a prospective, multicentre longitudinal cohort study.
abstract: BackgroundEarly antiretroviral therapy (ART) after perinatal HIV infection can restrict reservoir size and diversity, offering potential for remission. We evaluated HIV-1 DNA dynamics up to four years of age and predictors of reservoir size in early-treated African children.MethodsIn this prospective, multicentre cohort study, infants with perinatal HIV from South Africa, Mozambique, and Mali who initiated ART before 6 months of age and within 3 months of diagnosis were enrolled. Children were followed at 2, 6, 12, and 24 weeks, then biannually for 4 years. Total HIV-1 DNA in PBMCs was quantified longitudinally by droplet digital PCR in 207 children. The main outcomes were HIV-1 DNA reservoir size at year 3 (log10 copies/million PBMC) and longitudinal HIV-1 DNA decay. Multivariable models were developed to identify predictors of reservoir size using generalised additive regression models, and decay dynamics were evaluated using mixed-effects Poisson models including random intercepts and viral load slopes.FindingsOf 207 children, 155 (75%) had >12 months of follow-up. HIV was diagnosed at a median age of 31 days (IQR: 0, 47) and ART started at 33 days (IQR: 23.5, 69.5). Nineteen of 155 (12.3%) had undetectable HIV-1 DNA at year 4. Median decay rate was -0.020 log10 copies/million cells/month (-0.212/year). Smaller reservoirs at year 3 were associated with lower pre-ART viral load (β = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.09, 0.43) and faster first-year HIV-1 DNA decay rate (β = 1.09, 95% CI: 0.02, 2.19), with trends toward smaller reservoirs among females (β = -0.41, 95% CI: -0.87, 0.04) and larger reservoirs among children whose mothers reported social challenges (β = 0.42, 95% CI: -0.04, 0.87). Faster decay correlated with longer time on ART, lower serial viral loads, sustained viral suppression >12 months, earlier ART initiation, and region (Mali). Maternal health issues correlated with slower decay. Eleven "excellent controllers" maintained durable viral suppression, immunological control, and undetectable total HIV-1 DNA at last follow-up.InterpretationEarly virological parameters may help identify children likely to develop smaller HIV reservoirs. Early ART is key to faster reservoir reduction. Maternal health issues influence reservoir decay, reflecting a parental legacy effect. Sex differences should be further explored to understand mechanisms of reservoir control. Children with sustained virological suppression, preserved immune status, and undetectable total HIV-1 DNA may represent candidates with favourable characteristics for HIV remission strategies, as these factors have been associated with a reduced burden of persistent HIV infection and have been observed in rare cases of post-treatment control.FundingEPIICAL consortium through ViiV Healthcare and Penta Foundation.

title: Reservoir or Island? Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana) as a Host of 'Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni'-Related Strains.
abstract: Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana L.) is a native shrub that is widely found across North America and is a host of 'Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni' associated with X-disease of stone fruits. This pathogen is of major concern to U.S. cherry and peach growers, with the most recent and ongoing outbreak in the Pacific Northwest causing major economic harm. To investigate the role of chokecherry as a potential reservoir and source of orchard-associated strains, we surveyed wild chokecherry trees across 12 U.S. states and compared the strains present with those in commercially cultivated Prunus species. Approximately 47% of chokecherry sampled tested positive for a 'Ca. P. pruni'-related strain and phylogenetic analysis revealed high strain diversity, including six distinct clades and four newly identified lineages. In contrast, 'Ca. P. pruni' strains isolated from cultivated cherry and peach trees exhibited lower diversity and were infected by known disease outbreak-associated strains such as Northwestern-X. These data suggest limited transmission between wild and cultivated hosts in the western United States, with patterns indicating spillover from orchards into nearby chokecherry populations rather than the reverse. However, in states east of the Rocky Mountains, chokecherry likely functions as a reservoir for orchard infections.
authors: Hoskins M, Shires M, Thompson A, Molnar C, Cowell S, Harper S.

title: Reduction of aflatoxin contamination in maize kernels mediated by host-induced gene silencing.
abstract: Aflatoxins produced by some species of Aspergillus pose a significant threat to global food safety, because they contaminate a variety of crops including maize. In this study, we used host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) to reduce aflatoxin accumulation in maize upon infection with Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus. Two RNAi constructs were designed and introduced into maize, one targeting two essential fungal genes involved in ergosterol biosynthesis (CYP51A and CYP51B) and the other targeting three aflatoxin biosynthesis genes (AflC, AflD, and AflR). The presence of RNAi transgenes was confirmed in 17 and 14 independent lines possessing the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi construct and the AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi construct, respectively. Most transgenic lines had single-locus integrations and one or two copies of the transgene. Transgene expression varied considerably among the lines. Small RNA sequencing confirmed the production of siRNAs from the HIGS trigger sequences. Levels of CYP51A, AflC, AflD, and AflR transcripts in Aspergillus spp. were successfully decreased upon infection of transgenic maize. However, significant reduction in the level of CYP51B transcripts was not achieved and the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi transgene had no discernible effect on fungal growth in infected maize. In contrast, we observed significant reductions in aflatoxin accumulation in four AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi transgenic lines infected with A. flavus and in two transgenic lines infected with A. parasiticus. Notably, one AflC/AflD/AflR transgenic line exhibited minimal aflatoxin contamination upon kernel infection with A. parasiticus. These results demonstrate the potential of HIGS to reduce aflatoxin production in mature corn kernels.
authors: Ahmed A, Cavanaugh K, Baldrich P, Stergiopoulos I, Michelmore R.

title: Virus transmission required for maintenance and host adaptation mirrors neurophysiological differences in rabies-derived peptides.
abstract: Pathogen adaptations to new hosts are central to the disease ecology of cross-species transmission and host switching of viruses. The rabies virus is a model for adaptations to different hosts as it induces behavioral changes that facilitate transmission, while being maintained in distinct species-specific cycles of infection. Here, we demonstrate that the rabies virus requires distinct transmission dynamics in two hosts with different ecologies to establish maintenance, using agent-based modeling, analyses of virus glycoprotein-mediated manipulation of neuroreceptor function, and phylogenetic analysis. Epidemiological models suggest that rabies virus variants adapted to arctic foxes, which sustain rabies virus at very low host densities, require a higher probability of transmission than viruses adapted to raccoons. Using in vitro electrophysiology, we demonstrate that the rabies glycoprotein-derived peptides from arctic fox rabies variants are more potent antagonists of alpha7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. These findings suggest a possible functional basis for the behavioral modifications that drive enzootic rabies transmission in the context of host ecology. In addition, a large proportion of residues that may drive rabies virus adaptation to raccoons and arctic foxes are found within this neurotoxin-like region. Furthermore, a residue in the neurotoxin-like region of the mature rabies virus glycoprotein (residue 183) has been associated with pathogenicity, host switching, and disease ecology in previous studies. We propose the hypothesis that rabies virus transmission dynamics adapt to the ecology and physiology of novel hosts through the selection of glycoproteins that elicit specific degrees of behavioral modification and transmission probability.
authors: Remal A, Acheson ES, Leighton PA, Rees EE, Rhodes J, O'Brien BCV, Weltzin MM, Hueffer K.

title: Characterization of Chromone Biosynthetic Pathway Reveals a Noncanonical Mode of Fungal Polyketide Cyclization.
abstract: Fungal nonreducing polyketide synthases (NRPKSs) produce therapeutically and ecologically important aromatic polyketides. The product template (PT) domain of fungal NRPKSs catalyzes the regioselective aldol cyclization of the reactive poly-β-ketone chain during polyketide maturation and is essential for product fidelity of the NRPKSs. Herein, we discovered the fungal NRPKS MecA of which the polyketide cyclization steps do not involve a functional PT domain. MecA is encoded in the biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) responsible for the formation of 5-hydroxy-7-methoxy-2,3-dimethylchromone (1) from the biocontrol fungus Trichoderma afroharzianum T22. Heterologous expression and in vitro enzymatic assays fully established a biosynthetic pathway of 1 that involves three enzymes: MecA, dehydratase MecB, and methyltransferase MecC. The PT domain of MecA does not contain the conserved catalytic histidine that is essential for aldol cyclization activity. Consistent with the predicted inactive PT domain, MecA was demonstrated to catalyze a C1-C6 Claisen condensation as the first cyclization step of the pentaketide precursor, instead of the canonical aldol cyclization. Reconstitution of dissected MecA domains further demonstrated that the activity of MecA was not affected when the PT domain was removed. A Claisen Cyclase (CLC) domain that typically catalyzes Claisen cyclization in NRPKSs is also absent in MecA, implying the observed C1-C6 cyclization step is catalyzed by the remaining domains. This work contributes to the diversity of NRPKS cyclization chemistry and enables further genome mining and engineering of NRPKSs that may lead to biosynthesis of new aromatic polyketides.
authors: Choi S, Wong B, Sun Z, Tang Y.

title: From discovery to clinical implementation: a bibliometric analysis of DNA methylation biomarkers in non-small cell lung cancer, 1999-2025.
abstract: BackgroundDNA methylation alterations are stable, biologically informative, and detectable in tissue and circulating DNA, making them promising biomarkers for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, few methylation biomarkers have entered routine clinical practice. We aimed to characterize the evolution and translational challenges of this field.MethodsPublications on NSCLC, DNA methylation, and biomarker applications were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection through 31 December 2025. After PRISMA-based screening, bibliometric and knowledge-map analyses were performed.ResultsA total of 1,910 publications were included. Annual output increased after 2010 and peaked in 2022. Lung Cancer was the most productive journal, whereas Cancer Research had the highest citation impact. China contributed the largest publication volume, while the United States had the highest citation impact. Foundational studies focused on promoter hypermethylation, methylation-specific PCR, and methylated DNA detection in accessible biospecimens. Research priorities shifted from candidate-gene studies toward methylation signatures, liquid biopsy, multi-omics integration, immunotherapy-related applications, and computational modeling.ConclusionNSCLC methylation biomarker research has evolved toward integrated translational frameworks. Future progress requires multicenter validation, standardized platforms, clinically defined methylation panels, and AI-assisted integration.Protocol registrationwww.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero identifier is CRD420261426546.
authors: Li Y, Wu F, Liu W, He X, Chen C.

title: Human astroviruses: molecular virology.
abstract: SUMMARYHuman astroviruses (HAstVs) are important etiologic agents of pediatric gastroenteritis and are increasingly recognized as pathogens associated with extraintestinal disease, including encephalitis and meningitis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Despite their clinical relevance, widespread prevalence, and expanding genetic diversity, no approved vaccines or antiviral therapies are available. Progress toward effective interventions requires a comprehensive understanding of HAstV molecular biology, including mechanisms of cell entry, viral replication, and immune recognition. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of HAstV epidemiology, clinical manifestations, evolution, and taxonomy, emphasizing recent advances in molecular and structural virology. We examine the HAstV replication cycle, including emerging insights into receptor usage, double-membrane vesicle biogenesis, protease-driven maturation, the capsid's membrane-lytic activity, and virion uncoating. Recent advances in determining high-resolution structures of the capsid core and spike of classical and non-classical HAstVs are highlighted, providing a framework for understanding virion assembly, maturation, and antibody neutralization. These molecular and structural insights highlight conserved and clade-specific vulnerabilities, refine current models of HAstV biology, and identify key molecular determinants that may serve as targets for antiviral development and vaccine design. We also outline critical unresolved questions that define priorities for future research.
authors: Lentz A, López T, Ykema M, Tao YJ, DuBois RM, Arias CF.

title: Genomic sequencing of recent rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus 2 strains from diseased European rabbits supports a novel incursion into Washington State, USA.
abstract: Five feral European rabbits found dead in Washington state tested positive for rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus 2 (RHDV2) by qPCR. Genomic sequencing revealed a nearly identical RHDV2 strain present in the rabbits. The RHDV2 strain was determined to be divergent from previous United States detections, suggesting a novel RHDV2 incursion.
authors: Torrevillas BK, Jenckel M, Falghoush AM, Neely NE, Oliveira R, Itle A, Smith B, Snekvik KR, Waltzek TB.

title: Inhibition of Horizontal Gene Transfers under Antibiotic Stress Switches Multi-Drug Resistance to Multi-Drug Hyper-susceptibility in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
abstract: AimsTo study the effect of spatial distancing between bacteria on horizontal gene transfers, and on the evolution of multi-drug resistance and multi-drug susceptibility to antibiotics.Methods and resultsWe controlled the plating density of bacteria on agar, and showed that, by repeatedly stressing P. aeruginosa with aztreonam, spatial distancing lowers the rate of minimum inhibitory concentration increase and the number of resistant strains. More importantly, resistant PAO1 that evolved without horizontal gene transfers exhibited 2- to 64-fold increases in susceptibility as that of the wild-type PAO1 to multiple unrelated antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin, imipenem, and tetracycline, with which the bacteria were not treated a priori. While biofilm formation by the wild-type PAO1 is generally promoted by antibiotics, biofilm formation by the hypersusceptible PAO1 was inhibited by the sub-minimum inhibitory concentration of antibiotics.ConclusionsBy spatial distancing, stressing PAO1 with aztreonam caused bacteria to become multi-drug hyper-susceptible rather than the reported multi-drug resistant. The biofilm formation by the hyper-susceptible strain was inhibited, rather than promoted, by sub-lethal concentrations of multiple antibiotics.
authors: Iradukunda AM, Sauve NJ, Neogi N, Bender JB, Hall MA, Hess HT, Horzempa J, Luk YY.

title: First confirmed outbreak of mud crab reovirus (MCRV) causing mass mortality in orange mud crab Scylla olivacea in India.
abstract: Mud crab reovirus (MCRV) has emerged as a major challenge in mud crab farming, often leading to sudden mortality and severe economic losses. This study documents an outbreak of MCRV in a Scylla olivacea fattening facility at Bideipur, Odisha, India. Crabs in poor health condition were collected for analysis. The affected animals were sluggish, showed a grey and unhealthy hepatopancreas with autotomy. Histological examination revealed basophilic inclusion bodies together with necrotic changes in the hepatopancreas, gills, and muscle. Transmission electron microscopy confirmed the presence of non-enveloped, icosahedral viral particles arranged in crystalline arrays predominantly within the cytoplasm, together with nuclear alterations including chromatin condensation and nucleolar displacement. Reverse transcription (RT)-PCR produced a distinct amplification at ~433 bp, verifying MCRV infection. Experimental challenges using oral exposure, waterborne transmission, and cohabitation all resulted in complete mortality, demonstrating both the virulence of the virus and its ease of transmission. This study provides the first evidence of MCRV infecting S. olivacea in India. This outbreak underlines the need for consistent health screening, the use of virus-free seed, and strict biosecurity protocols if mud crab aquaculture is to remain sustainable.
authors: Kundu A, Ganesan K, Gopalakrishnan A, Luricson L, Chandrakanthan S, Prabhu NM.

title: Biosynthesis, enzymatic basis, and transcriptional regulation of benzylisoquinoline alkaloids in medicinal plants.
abstract: Benzylisoquinoline alkaloids (BIAs) are a class of structurally diverse secondary metabolites, with over 2,500 identified variants classified into seven major categories based on their core skeletons. These compounds exhibit significant pharmacological activities - including antitumor, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory effects - and serve as important sources of clinical drugs such as morphine, berberine, and magnoflorine. Currently, BIAs are primarily obtained through plant cultivation and extraction. However, factors such as low in-planta content, seasonal constraints, and environmental variability contribute to vulnerabilities in the supply chain. In light of these challenges, microbial biosynthesis using engineered strains (e.g., yeast) has emerged as a promising alternative, though it requires complete elucidation and functional expression of all pathway enzymes. Enhancing BIAs production in crops through transcriptional regulation - targeting key enzymes, transcription factors (such as WRKY, bHLH, and AP2/ERF families), and phytohormone signaling - represents a feasible interim strategy. Advanced approaches, including coexpression of enzyme genes and transcription factors, hold promise for accelerating the development of industrial-scale alkaloid-producing cell factories and crop improvement, thereby enabling sustainable drug supply.
journal: Zeitschrift fur Naturforschung. C, Journal of biosciences
authors: Zhao Y, Zhang M, Peng Y, Zheng Y, Tan R, Jiang H.

title: Spatial modeling of risk factors for human exposure to West Nile virus in rural Madagascar
abstract: Background  West Nile virus (WNV) is an emerging disease transmitted from bird hosts to humans by Culex mosquitoes. Thousands of human cases of WNV infection are reported each year in the United States and Europe, and circulation has been confirmed in Africa and the Indian Ocean, including Madagascar. However, little is known about the current riskscape for people in Madagascar, and what determines its local distribution and human exposure across the population. The goal of this study was to assess WNV seroprevalence and identify associated socio-ecological risk factors in rural Madagascar. Methodology and principal findings  A cross-sectional serological survey was conducted in Ifanadiana District in 2021, nested within a representative longitudinal cohort. We evaluated serological responses to WNV in 3,948 individuals using a multiplex bead assay. We estimated WNV seroprevalence using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and characterized environmental, socioeconomic, and demographic factors that could be associated with exposure to WNV using various data sources, including optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite images, climate variables, and household survey data. Overall seroprevalence was 43%, and populations living in geographically isolated areas and those engaged in agricultural activities were at higher risk, while proximity to dense forests and residential areas were protective against WNV exposure. Conclusions  This study found high rates and local heterogeneity in WNV exposure in a rural district of Madagascar. In addition, environmental, climatic, and socio-demographic data were determinants of WNV transmission, providing a valuable tool for surveillance and decision-making in arbovirus prevention and control. Extending this approach to other orthoflaviviruses could improve understanding of local viral co-circulation and promote the development of more precise and context-specific prevention strategies.
authors: Randriamihaja M, Rasoloharimanana LT, Veeragandham S, Miller AC, Finnegan KE, Bos S, Razafinjato B, Mitsinjoniala E, Kotchofa JA, Garneret P, Razanadranaivo HL, Ihantamalala FA, Rakotonanahary RJ, Chevalier V, Bonds MH, Schoenhals M, Evans MV, Popper SJ, Garchitorena A.

title: Elevated environmental CO  2  stimulates photosynthesis and induces differential oxidative responses in two Caribbean reef-building coral species
abstract: Reef-building corals maintain intracellular photosymbiosis with dinoflagellate algae, allowing them to use photosynthetic products as metabolic fuel. Carbon dioxide (CO  2 ) is a key substrate for photosynthesis, but its rapid increase in the global ocean due to anthropogenic emissions (known as “ocean acidification”) may disrupt coral symbiosis. We examined the effects of elevated CO  2 on photosynthetic O  2 production, oxidative damage, and antioxidant systems in the Caribbean reef-building corals  Porites astreoides and  Orbicella franksi . Coral colonies collected at 3m depth in Bocas del Toro (Panama) were exposed to control (∼390 μatm CO  2 , pH ∼8.00) or elevated CO  2 (∼1,060 μatm CO  2 , pH ∼7.70) conditions in outdoor flow-through aquaria for 10 days. Flowing seawater had higher O  2 concentrations in elevated CO  2 tanks, with the largest differences at higher irradiance. Microsensor measurements confirmed that acute and chronic exposure to elevated CO  2 significantly stimulated photosynthetic O  2 production in both species. Despite increased O  2 production. neither species showed significant changes in lipid peroxidation, reduced glutathione, or superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione-S- transferase activities. Protein oxidation was unchanged in  O. franksi but significantly decreased in  P. astreoides . These results are consistent with partial relief of carbon limitation in  P. astreoides symbionts under elevated CO  2 , potentially improving photosynthetic efficiency and decreasing reactive oxygen species production. These findings support the resilience of  P. astreoides to OA and suggest that elevated CO  2 may increase daytime O  2 levels on future reefs, with implications for the aerobic metabolism of reef organisms.
authors: Tresguerres M, Sabatini S, Linsmayer L, Galindo-Martínez C, Thies A, Hamilton T, Kline DI.

title: Two decades of changing Enterococcus epidemiology and antimicrobial susceptibility in a Brazilian tertiary university hospital, 2002–2023
abstract: Abstract    Background  Enterococcus  spp. are major opportunistic hospital pathogens characterised by remarkable environmental persistence, genomic plasticity, and the ability to acquire antimicrobial resistance determinants. This study aimed to evaluate the occurrence, temporal dynamics, clinical distribution, and phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility trends of  Enterococcus  spp. clinical isolates in a tertiary teaching hospital in southern Brazil over a 22-year period (2002–2023). Methods  A retrospective, observational study based on positive clinical cultures from hospitalised patients. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, unique isolates were analysed for species, clinical specimens, hospital ward, hospital outcome, and antimicrobial resistance. The study was divided into two periods: January 2002 through March 2019, and April 2019 through December 2023. Results  A total of 6,283 isolates were included, comprising 4,881 (77.7%)  E. faecalis  and 1,286 (20.5%)  E. faecium  . Urine was the primary clinical specimen for both species. An increase in the frequency of isolates was observed in recent years, peaking in 2021 for  E. faecalis  and in 2022 for  E. faecium  .  E. faecium  maintained high resistance rates, whereas in  E. faecalis  , vancomycin resistance increased from 6.6% to 25.2% between the analysed periods. Linezolid resistance remained low in both species. Conclusions  Although  E. faecalis  predominated throughout the period,  E. faecium  was disproportionately associated with bloodstream infections, Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admissions, deaths, and antimicrobial resistance. The significant increase in antimicrobial resistance among both species underscores the importance of continuous microbiological surveillance and species-specific analysis, as well as the need to strengthen infections prevention and control measures.
authors: Cardim SL, Olak APS, Aurora DMLdO, Junior ERdO, Aragon-Alegro LC, Cardim ST, Jorge MA, de Santana EHW, Vespero EC, Ogatta SFY, Perugini MRE.

title: TSOpt: Fast and robust training-set design for genomic selection and sparse testing
abstract: Abstract  Which candidates are phenotyped largely decides the accuracy of genomic prediction, yet few programmes design training sets formally. Existing tools evaluate the design criterion, the mean generalised coefficient of determination (CDmean), in a reduced marker space or repeatedly inside stochastic searches, optimise for one assumed heritability, and offer little built-in support for multi-environment trials or historical records. TSOpt removes these limits. It updates the exact CDmean by rank-one steps, so a design for several hundred lines takes about 0.1 s, averages the criterion over the unknown heritability, and uses one engine for line × environment and line × trait units, lines already phenotyped, hybrids, plot costs and major genes. We tested it on 328 elite lines from eight seasons of the International Rice Research Institute’s irrigated breeding programme. Twenty-five TSOpt lines predicted untested lines as accurately as 76–167 random lines. TSOpt raised predictive ability over random sampling by 0.097 (95% confidence interval 0.045–0.150), was ahead of STPGA on average, and ran at least 900 times faster. With a quarter of line × season combinations tested over four seasons, its sparse-testing allocations predicted untested combinations better than balanced random allocation, even when scored with correlations unseen by the design; with half tested, it did not. Forward in time, all design methods gained little and the full history remained the best training set. On six public panels TSOpt matched STPGA, TSDFGS and published TrainSel designs, much faster. Lines with the highest mean relationship to the targets never beat random choice.
authors: Hussain W.

title: Optimization of AAV9 Dose and Fluorescein Concentration for Vagus Nerve Injection in Rats
abstract: Background:  /Objectives: Direct intraneural delivery of adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (AAV9) via peripheral nerves remains largely unexplored. This study evaluated the feasibility of AAV9 delivery into the vagus nerve, identified an optimal dose, and determined an optimal fluorescein dye concentration for tracking injection fidelity. Methods: Rats received left vagus nerve injections of 5 µL AAV9/GFP at doses of 2.5 × 10⁹, 2.5 × 10¹⁰, 7.6 × 10¹⁰, 2.5 × 10¹¹, or 6.5 × 10¹¹ vector genomes (vg)/rat, mixed with 1% luxol fast blue dye. Controls received vehicle with dye. Transduction in the nodose ganglia of the vagus nerve and medulla was assessed. Fluorescein compatibility was evaluated in CHO Lec2 cells using concentrations of 0%, 0.0001%, 0.004%, and 0.01% at high and low multiplicities of infection. In vivo compatibility was subsequently confirmed using 2.5 × 10¹¹ vg/rat with 0.001%, 0.002%, 0.004%, or 0.008% fluorescein. Results: Transduction of critical autonomic nervous system sites increased with dose. The two highest doses (2.5 × 10¹¹ and 6.5 × 10¹¹ vg/rat) produced abundant, comparable transduction in the nodose ganglia and medulla, identifying 2.5 × 10¹¹ vg/rat as the optimal dose. Fluorescein did not inhibit AAV9 transduction in CHO Lec2 cells at the concentrations tested. In vivo, 0.004% fluorescein provided clear visualization during vagus nerve injection. Conclusions: Direct intraneural administration of AAV9/GFP at 2.5 × 10¹¹ vg/rat with 0.004% fluorescein offers an effective formulation for vagus nerve delivery in rats. Further validation and dose-scaling studies are suggested to establish feasibility for translation to larger animals and humans.
authors: Regmi NL, Armao D, Chen X, Hu Y, Bailey RM, Gray SJ.

title: Diversity and Fungicide Sensitivity of Colletotrichum Species Causing Glomerella Leaf Spot and Apple Bitter Rot in Northern China.
abstract: Glomerella leaf spot (GLS) and apple bitter rot (ABR), collectively associated with over 20 Colletotrichum species, are two distinct diseases that cause substantial losses in apple production. In this study, phylogenetic analysis of 177 isolates collected across five provinces in northern China identified four species within the Colletotrichum gloeosporioides species complex, namely C. aenigma, C. fructicola, C. gloeosporioides, and C. siamense. C. siamense was the dominant agent of ABR (68.8%), whereas C. aenigma was the primary cause of GLS (76.9%), a pattern distinct from pathogen populations in the American continents. Fungicide profiling of the 177 isolates revealed that 41.2% of isolates showed high-level resistance to the quinone outside inhibitor (QoI) fungicide pyraclostrobin, largely attributable to the G143A mutation in the cytb gene. In contrast, sensitivity to the DMI fungicide difenoconazole remained largely unaltered. Inter- and intraspecific variation in fungicide tolerance was evident, with C. aenigma exhibiting significantly greater tolerance to both pyraclostrobin and difenoconazole compared with C. siamense. Further screening of nine additional fungicides identified prochloraz, fluazinam, penthiopyrad, and cyprodinil as highly effective against pyraclostrobin-resistant isolates. This study reveals the diversity of Colletotrichum pathogens of apple in northern China, highlights a critical need for fungicide resistance surveillance in production, and provides useful information for mitigating QoI fungicide resistance based on rational fungicide rotation.
authors: Chen W, Wu C, Ma H, Wu R, Zheng Y, Qiao Z, Qaisar MH, Zhang R, Sun G, Zhu M, Liang X.

title: Layer-number-controlled Fe-tea polyphenol metal-phenolic network-coated PLCL/gelatin electrospun membranes for active preservation of yellow sweet cherries.
abstract: To address postharvest fruit spoilage from microbial contamination and oxidation, biodegradable PLCL/gelatin electrospun membranes were functionalized with layer-number-controlled Fe-tea polyphenol (Fe-TP) networks via layer-by-layer assembly. Fe-TP deposition increased fiber diameter, improved hydrophilicity, and enhanced mechanical strength while maintaining flexibility. Increasing the number of assembly cycles enhanced TP release and antioxidant activity, delayed degradation, and improved antibacterial activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Cytocompatibility and hemolysis assays indicated favorable biosafety. SEM and leakage assays suggested membrane disruption and intracellular leakage as possible antibacterial mechanisms. In yellow sweet cherry preservation, the Fe-TP effectively delayed decay. Although Fe-TP/PLCL-Gel 8 exhibited stronger antibacterial and hydrophilic performance, the Fe-TP/PLCL-Gel 4 achieved the best overall balance of mechanical properties, release, safety, and preservation efficacy, with a day-7 decay rate of only 1.85% ± 3.21%, versus 50.00% ± 5.56% for PE control. This layer-optimized multifunctional electrospun membrane offers a highly effective, promising material for fruit preservation.
authors: Liu J, Yan T, Wang Q, Bao J, Li Y, Piao J, Chai H, Zhou G.

title: Computational prioritization and molecular dynamics analysis of FOXA2 missense variants with potential relevance to colorectal cancer.
abstract: The pioneer transcription factor FOXA2 controls developmental gene programmes, metabolic homeostasis and epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity, and its expression dysregulation is a recognized feature of colorectal cancer. The structural and thermodynamic consequences of FOXA2 missense variants remain poorly defined. We interrogated 659 missense SNPs across the human FOXA2 locus within an integrated multi-algorithm framework. Sequential filtering with SIFT, PolyPhen-2, PhD-SNP and SNPs&GO converged on three high-confidence deleterious variants (M190I, R197Q and L402P), which were profiled further with ConSurf, I-Mutant 2.0, MUpro, MutPred2 and DynaMut2. Conservation and structural mapping placed M190I (ConSurf-8) and R197Q (ConSurf-9) in the winged-helix DNA-binding domain (PF00250) and L402P (ConSurf-5) in the HNF_C domain (PF09354). R197Q is solvent-exposed and predicted to perturb promoter DNA contacts, whereas the buried M190I and L402P substitutions are predicted to act through local destabilization at the substitution site. In three independent 50-ns molecular dynamics replicates per system, all variants deviated from wild-type backbone behavior. M190I converged prematurely into a displaced conformational state, whereas R197Q and L402P continued to drift late in the trajectories. Backbone fluctuations increased non-locally, clustering in flexible regulatory segments (~290-316) and the C-terminal transactivation domain 2 (452-456). Principal component analysis indicated a more concentrated collective-mode structure in the mutants, and dynamic cross-correlation analysis weakened residue coupling, consistent with disrupted long-range communication. Of twelve trajectory-level comparisons, only the R197Q hydrogen-bond reduction reached nominal significance (p = 0.025, Hedges' g = -2.28), indicating a large reduction in average hydrogen-bond count relative to wild-type; the remaining eleven comparisons showed non-significant moderate-to-large effects. Expression enrichment was highest in colorectal cancer cell lines, providing expression-level context for FOXA2 in CRC biology. These findings computationally prioritize M190I, R197Q and L402P as candidates for experimental validation.
authors: Mia MS, Talukder MEK, Tanmoy MSI, Raisa IJ, Datta BK, Shadhin MST, Tahsin N, Imon RR, Aktaruzzaman M, Zargar S, Wani TA.

title: USF2 deficiency enhances intracellular clearance of Salmonella Typhimurium via xenophagy and LC3-associated phagocytosis.
abstract: The upstream stimulatory factor 2 (USF2) is a transcription factor known as a transcriptional activator that binds to E-box motifs in gene promoters. Recently, we reported that USF2 is also a transcriptional repressor of the genes that encode lysosomes and autophagy machinery, and that its deficiency results in the elevation of autophagy. The present study was designed to determine whether the absence of USF2 is responsible for more effective protection of the host cells from bacterial infection and intracellular bacterial growth. In this context, we employed Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (S. Typhimurium) as a model pathogen and monitored the changes in intracellular bacterial burden observed in the wild-type (WT) cells and USF2-deficient cells over the time course of infection. The number of intracellular bacteria increased after infection in WT cells but remained similar or decreased in USF2-deficient cells. This phenomenon was observed in various cell types, including mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), RAW264.7 macrophage-like cells, and primary bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs). The phagocytosis levels were the same in WT and USF2-deficient macrophages, but the latter had a higher basal autophagy, increased lysosome abundance, and increased expression of lysosomal genes. In addition, the components of LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP), such as LC3B and RUBICON, together with reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, were elevated in USF2-deficient macrophages. Our results demonstrated that the enhanced autophagy in non-phagocytic cells and the elevated autophagy and LAP in phagocytes both contribute to the improved clearance of intracellular pathogens in USF2-deficient cells.
authors: Kwon J, Jeon J, Kim JW, Bae H, Kim J, Yu YS, Baek SH, Kim KI.

title: Antimicrobial susceptibility and virulence phenotypes of Escherichia coli isolated from bovine milk and feces in Brazil.
abstract: Escherichia coli is a versatile pathogen that causes bovine mastitis and acts as a reservoir of virulence and antimicrobial resistance genes, causing risks to both animal and public health. This study characterized 83 E. coli isolates from milk samples of cows with clinical (n = 19) or subclinical mastitis (n = 33) and fecal samples from lactating cows (n = 31) in Brazil. The isolates were evaluated for phylogenetic group, antimicrobial susceptibility, extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL), plasmid-mediated colistin resistance (mcr), O157 genotype, and biofilm formation. Phylogenetic classification revealed predominance of phylogroups A and B1. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed resistance to phenicols (38.6%), β-lactams (27.7%), polymyxins (20.5%), and tetracyclines (20.5%), with multidrug resistance (MDR) observed in 20.5% of isolates, most frequently among clinical mastitis and fecal strains. ESBL production was detected in 47.4% of the isolates evaluated, often concomitant with MDR. All isolates tested negative for the mcr genes, despite 20.5% being colistin-resistant, and were also negative for the O157 antigen. Biofilm formation was widespread, observed in 79.5% of the isolates. These results demonstrated the circulation of diverse antimicrobial-resistant profiles of E. coli strains in Brazilian dairy farms. Taken together, the coexistence of multidrug resistance, ESBL production, and biofilm-forming ability among isolates from mastitic milk and bovine feces indicates that antimicrobial-resistant E. coli strains are present in both clinical and intestinal reservoirs within dairy herds. Furthermore, the detection of colistin-resistant isolates lacking the investigated mcr genes suggests the involvement of alternative resistance mechanisms that warrant further investigation.
journal: Comparative immunology, microbiology and infectious diseases
authors: Moreira JLF, Gonçalves MS, Custódio DADC, Andrade RS, da Costa GM, de Sá Guimarães A, Pereira CR, Dorneles EMS.

title: Aircraft and Airport Wastewater Surveillance for Public Health Preparedness Demands an Integrated and Sustainable Approach.
abstract: As domestic and international travel has expanded, the risk of the cross-border dissemination of infectious pathogens has increased, as clearly evidenced during the COVID-19 pandemic. Aircraft- and airport-based wastewater surveillance can provide timely, aggregate evidence of pathogen circulation among mobile populations and may complement clinical, genomic, and syndromic surveillance at points of entry. The strongest evidence for this approach comes from SARS-CoV-2 RNA detection and variant monitoring in aircraft lavatory wastewater, airport terminal wastewater, and airport-associated wastewater systems. However, aviation wastewater signals require cautious interpretation because detectability depends on pathogen shedding dynamics, passenger lavatory use, flight duration, sampling matrix, sample volume, assay sensitivity, sequencing depth, and the availability of epidemiological metadata. This structured narrative review synthesizes current evidence on aircraft and airport wastewater surveillance and examines the scientific determinants that influence surveillance validity and interpretation. Key methodological considerations include sampling design, sample preservation, nucleic acid extraction, molecular detection, sequencing, bioinformatics, inhibition assessment, recovery controls, assay sensitivity, and quality assurance. The review emphasizes that wastewater signals are aggregate and matrix-dependent and should not be interpreted as individual-level diagnosis, direct evidence of transmission, or definitive attribution to a specific flight, route, country, or population. Although SARS-CoV-2 surveillance is comparatively well-documented, multi-pathogen surveillance for enteric viruses, respiratory viruses, vaccine-preventable infections, emerging pathogens, and antimicrobial resistance markers requires pathogen-specific validation and clearer interpretation criteria. Aircraft and airport wastewater surveillance is therefore best viewed as an early-warning and situational-awareness approach whose value depends on converting technical signals into scientifically interpretable evidence.
authors: Vaidya SR, Pandey PG, Giri S, Pati S.

title: Nelfinavir Synergizes with Cisplatin and Promotes GSDME-Associated Lytic Cell Death in Platinum-Resistant Ovarian Cancer Cells.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Platinum resistance limits the efficacy of ovarian cancer treatment and arises through multiple mechanisms, including enhanced DNA repair, activation of stress responses, and increased survival signaling. Nelfinavir (NFV), an HIV protease inhibitor with reported anti-tumor activity, is a candidate for drug repurposing, but its interaction with cisplatin (CDDP) in ovarian cancer has not been established. Here, we investigated whether NFV enhances CDDP cytotoxicity in platinum (Pt)-resistant ovarian cancer cells and characterized the associated cell death response. Methods: Drug interaction was assessed using cell vitality and viability assays and Loewe additivity modeling together with Bliss and ZIP analyses. Cell death was characterized by Annexin V/7-AAD staining, mitochondrial membrane potential analysis, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release, immunoblotting, pharmacological caspase inhibition, and bulk mRNA sequencing with differential expression and gene set enrichment analyses. Results: NFV synergistically enhanced CDDP cytotoxicity across three Pt-resistant ovarian cancer cell lines, reducing CDDP IC50 values by 4.2-5.8-fold and producing mean Loewe synergy scores of approximately 25-30. Combination treatment increased LDH release and was accompanied by caspase-8, caspase-3, PARP, and the pore-forming death effector gasdermin E (GSDME) cleavage. Caspase inhibition attenuated viability loss and GSDME processing. Transcriptomic analysis identified enrichment of stress- and death-associated programs, including the unfolded protein response (UPR), apoptosis, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-associated signaling, and TNF/NF-κB signaling. Conclusions: Together, these findings demonstrate a reproducible synergistic interaction between CDDP and NFV in Pt-resistant ovarian cancer cells and characterize an associated lytic cell death phenotype involving apoptotic signaling and accompanied by GSDME processing. These findings support further investigation of NFV as a repurposed combination partner to enhance CDDP cytotoxicity in Pt-resistant ovarian cancer.
authors: Forgie BN, Prakash R, Marno D, Abdalbari FH, Zorychta E, Noman ASM, Goyeneche AA, Gilbert L, Burnier JV, Telleria CM.

title: Yield and Yield Components in Soybean Using Genome-Wide Association Studies, GWAS: Current Status, Challenges, and Breeding Prospects.
abstract: Molecular-genetic analysis of soybean yield and yield components under drought is a crucial element for the development of effective breeding strategies and sustainable agricultural production. The aim of this review is to critically analyse current data from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and identified genetic loci, SNP markers, and candidate genes associated with yield components in soybean in dry conditions with limited water supply and adequate watering (controls). In the results, 346 genetic associations, and 229 candidate genes with KEGG-based potential functions were sufficiently described in published papers and selected for the current study. Three statistically significant metabolic pathways were identified with isoflavonoid biosynthesis, glycosaminoglycan degradation and cysteine and methionine metabolism. The main limitation of the presented analysis was found in the low level of heritability for the studied traits, together with human factors such as carrying out and interpreting GWAS affecting the results presented in the current study. Additionally, complex multigenic controls were reported for the studied traits in soybean and a high level of genotype × environment interactions. Nevertheless, the presented data provide a basis for developing molecular strategies to improve soybean yield in conjunction with better potential drought tolerance.
authors: Amangeldiyeva A, Didorenko S, Maikotov B, Jenisbayeva A, Shavrukov Y, Yerzhebayeva R.

title: Shenqi Granules Ameliorate Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury by Regulating Glucocerebrosidase and Uridine Metabolism in Microglia.
abstract: Objective: Shenqi Granules is a traditional Chinese medicine formula derived from the classic prescription Shenqi Formula (SQF), composed of Astragali Radix (Huangqi) and Codonopsis Radix (Dangshen). SQF shows neuroprotection in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI), but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Methods: The rat model of middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) was established using the suture method to evaluate the neuroprotective effect of SQF. Blood-absorbed components were identified via UHPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS, and potential targets and pathways were predicted through network pharmacology. Non-targeted metabolomics of serum and feces was performed using UHPLC-Orbitrap MS, and core metabolic pathways were selected based on regulation magnitude (RM). Gut microbiota structure was analyzed by 16S rRNA sequencing, with associations between microbiota and metabolites assessed via the Mantel test and redundancy analysis (RDA). Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to screen core Hub genes for ischemic stroke (IS). Based on single-cell RNA data, a uridine transport/metabolism-associated transcriptional signature score (Uridine_Score) was constructed, and cell type-specific coupling between glucocerebrosidase (GBA) and this transcriptional signature was analyzed. Microglial temporal trajectory analysis was conducted using Monocle3. Molecular docking between core components and GBA was verified by AutoDock, and GBA mRNA expression was confirmed by RT-qPCR. Results: High-dose SQF reduced infarct volume and neuronal damage and improved behavior. A total of 28 absorbed components and 31 shared IS targets were identified. Metabolomics revealed nucleotide metabolism as a core pathway common to both serum and fecal samples. SQF restored gut-blood uridine balance (serum uridine 0.41× Sham → 0.85× post-SQF), reduced fecal dTMP and hypoxanthine. 16S rRNA sequencing demonstrated that the overall correlation between microbial community structure and nucleotide metabolites was statistically significant (Mantel r = 0.307-0.321, p p Conclusions: SQF reprograms nucleotide metabolism via the gut-blood axis and enhances microglial GBA-uridine transport/metabolism-associated transcriptional coupling.
authors: Liu HX, Li YC, Liu CX, Yang MK, Zhou SY, Dong AA, Pei K, Wen SY.

title: Expression Profile of Transfer RNA-Derived Fragments in Chinese Mitten Crab (Eriocheir sinensis) After Challenge with Aeromonas hydrophila.
abstract: The Chinese mitten crab (Eriocheir sinensis) is an important cultured crab in China; however, its aquaculture productivity is severely limited by bacterial pathogens, including Aeromonas hydrophila. Transfer RNA-derived fragments (tRFs) are an emerging class of functional small non-coding RNAs that have been implicated in host-pathogen interactions and immune regulation; yet, their roles in the antibacterial defense of crustaceans remain poorly understood. To investigate the immune response of the Chinese mitten crab to A. hydrophila infection, we employed high-throughput sequencing to characterize the expression profiles and functional features of tRFs in crab hemocytes following a bacterial challenge. The results revealed that tRFs exhibited a conserved length distribution (15-20 nt) and subtype composition, with 5'-tRFs representing the dominant subtype in both control and infected groups. Notably, infection specifically induced the abundance of tRF fragments of 35-nt tRF fragments and slightly altered the proportion of tRF subtypes. Differential expression analysis identified 415 significantly upregulated and 3 downregulated tRFs upon A. hydrophila infection, suggesting widespread changes in tRF abundance during infection. Target prediction and functional enrichment analyses were performed for the top 30 differentially expressed tRFs; the predicted targets were significantly associated with VEGF signaling pathway, DNA replication proteins, FoxO signaling pathway, and NF-kappa B signaling pathway. The reliability of the sequencing data was confirmed by stem-loop RT-qPCR validation. Collectively, our findings advance the understanding of tRF expression in crustacean immunity and suggest that tRFs may be associated with the immune response of crabs against bacterial infection, pending functional validation.
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
authors: Kong T, Liu L, Liu H, Tran NT.

title: An Evidence-Tiered Developmental Framework for Congenital Vertebral Malformations: Spatiotemporal Thresholds in Genotype-Phenotype Interpretation.
abstract: Congenital vertebral malformations (CVMs) encompass formation, segmentation and mixed defects, with or without scoliosis. This narrative review relates human genetic findings to paraxial mesoderm specification, somitogenesis, sclerotome differentiation and vertebral morphogenesis. An author-defined evidence hierarchy distinguishes established disease relationships, emerging susceptibility mechanisms and hypothesis-generating observations; it is not a formal ClinGen classification. Replicated TBX6 dosage mechanisms and disease-specific segmentation disorders provide stronger etiological evidence than candidate-gene burden signals, regulatory hypotheses or accessible-tissue methylation associations. Evidence is assigned to a defined gene-disease or mechanism-phenotype relationship, not to a gene or pathway universally. Building on previous developmental and gene-environment models, we outline a conceptual spatiotemporal threshold framework in which dosage, developmental stage, tissue distribution and modifiers may influence vertebral anatomy. No numerical human threshold has been established. Explicit appraisal criteria, relationship-specific evidence summaries and proposed experimental tests separate demonstrated findings from extrapolation. Standardized vertebral and rib phenotyping, associated anomalies and inheritance remain essential for genomic interpretation. Molecular diagnosis may inform counseling and syndrome-specific evaluation but does not independently establish prognosis or surgical indications.
authors: Wang X, Zhang Q, Ji E, Sui Y, Zhu Q, Li K, Xue X.

title: Optimization and Comparative Evaluation of DNA Extraction Protocols for Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi in Coffee Roots.
abstract: Molecular studies of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) in coffee root require DNA extracts that are sufficiently pure for PCR amplification. Coffea arabica roots remains challenging because of the abundance of phenolic compounds, polysaccharides, and other inhibitors. This study compared four DNA extraction protocols, including two CTAB-based phenol-chloroform methods, a commercial extraction kit, and a modified commercial kit incorporating mechanical disruption, proteinase K predigestion, and β-mercaptoethanol treatment. Quality of total DNA extracts was assessed using NanoDrop spectrophotometry (A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios), agarose gel electrophoresis, and PCR amplification of the AMF SSU (18S rDNA) region using AMV4.5NF/AMDGR primers. Conventional phenol-chloroform methods yielded high DNA concentrations but poor purity, indicating substantial co-extraction of inhibitory compounds. The commercial kit without predigestion yielded lower spectrophotometric purity but still produced successful AMF-targeted PCR amplification. In contrast, the modified protocol yielded the highest spectrophotometric purity ratios while retaining successful amplification across all samples. These results indicate that incorporation of the predigestion step was associated with higher post-extraction spectrophotometric ratios without compromising successful AMF-targeted PCR amplification. The optimized protocol provides a reproducible method for obtaining PCR-quality DNA from coffee roots and represents a methodological contribution to molecular studies of the diversity of AMF and other root-associated microorganisms in coffee agroecosystems.
authors: Gómez-Godínez LJ, Ortiz-Gasca A, Aguirre-Noyola JL, Ruvalcaba-Gómez JM, De Los Santos-Villalobos S, Arteaga-Garibay RI.

title: The Role of the OBSCN Gene in Cardiomyopathy: A Review of Molecular Mechanisms and Clinical Significance.
abstract: Cardiomyopathies are genetically heterogeneous myocardial diseases that can lead to heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. OBSCN encodes obscurin, a giant sarcomere-associated protein involved in sarcomere organization, cytoskeletal coupling, calcium handling, and cell-cell adhesion signaling. This review synthesizes current evidence on OBSCN variants in cardiomyopathy, focusing on their spectrum, phenotypic associations, and potential pathogenic mechanisms. Curated variants were systematically interpreted according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) and the Association for Molecular Pathology (AMP) guidelines. Putative truncating variants predominated among variants of uncertain significance, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was the most frequently reported phenotype. Co-occurring variants in established or candidate cardiomyopathy-associated genes were reported for some OBSCN variants, particularly missense variants. However, co-occurrence alone does not establish an independent pathogenic contribution, oligogenic inheritance, or a genetic modifier effect. Potential mechanisms include obscurin insufficiency, destabilization of sarcomeric scaffolding, impaired sarcoplasmic reticulum coupling, dysregulated calcium homeostasis, altered mechanotransduction, and defective intercellular adhesion. Overall, OBSCN is an emerging but incompletely characterized cardiomyopathy-associated gene, and truncating variants warrant further clinical and mechanistic investigation.
journal: Journal of cardiovascular development and disease
authors: Chen J, Sun X, Wu S, Hu J, Zou Y, Hong K, Shen Y.

title: Dissecting the Radioresponse Heterogeneity of Lung Adenocarcinoma Cells From the Perspective of Transcriptional and Regulatory Landscape.
abstract: Radioresistance severely compromises radiotherapy efficacy for lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), yet the intrinsic heterogeneity of cellular radioresponses among isogenic tumor cells remains poorly characterized. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing (scATAC-seq) to dissect the transcriptional and regulatory landscape underlying heterogeneous radioresponses in single-cell-derived LUAD cells following 6 Gy γ-ray irradiation. We found that isogenic LUAD cells harbored intrinsic molecular determinants for divergent radiosensitivity and displayed heterogeneous radioresponsiveness upon irradiation. A radiation-associated transcriptional cell state, coupled with DNA damage repair, apoptosis, and cell cycle regulation, emerged at 6 h post-irradiation. Inhibition of lysine demethylase 4B (KDM4B) enhanced LUAD radiosensitivity by intensifying DNA damage, whereas reduced expression of cyclin B1 (CCNB1) and DNA topoisomerase IIα (TOP2A) potentially contributed to radiation-triggered G2/M arrest. Notably, the radiation-associated regulatory cell state emerged earlier than radiation-induced transcriptional cell state. RNA polymerase II subunit A (POLR2A) functioned as a core regulator in high-responsive LUAD cells. Based on these findings, we proposed a hypothesis for the radiosensitization of LUAD cells. Collectively, this study provides multilayer mechanistic insights into LUAD radioresponse heterogeneity and yields actionable molecular candidates for developing improved radiosensitization strategies to advance precise radiotherapy for LUAD.

title: Long-term Effectiveness, Treatment Persistence, and Timing of Virological Failure With Long-Acting Cabotegravir Plus Rilpivirine in Real-World HIV Care: RELATIVITY Cohort.
abstract: BackgroundLong-acting injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine (CAB + RPV LA) is an established maintenance option for virologically suppressed people with human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1), but long-term real-world persistence and virological failure (VF) data remain limited.MethodsRELATIVITY is an ongoing nationwide ambispective multicenter cohort of adults with HIV who switched from suppressive oral antiretroviral therapy to CAB + RPV LA in routine care in Spain. Data through 1 March 2026 were analyzed. The outcomes were virological suppression, treatment persistence, protocol-defined VF, and time to discontinuation-related events. Virological failure was defined as 2 consecutive HIV-1 RNA values ≥200 copies/mL or 1 value ≥500 copies/mL prompting discontinuation.ResultsAmong 3349 participants, 3343 had valid follow-up dates; the median follow-up was 25.1 months (19.3-30.8). Virological suppression was documented in 3197/3349 (95.5%) overall and 3197/3309 (96.6%) with an evaluable closest viral load; 40 (1.2%) lacked an evaluable value. Injection adherence was ≥90% in 3257/3280 (99.3%) evaluable participants. Overall, 2979/3349 (89.0%) remained on CAB + RPV LA. Virological failure occurred in 28/3349 (0.8%); 20/28 (71.4%) occurred within the first 12 months after switching. Emergent integrase strand transfer inhibitor and/or nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor resistance was detected in 19/28 VF cases, and 24/28 achieved virological suppression after switching to oral therapy. Treatment-limiting injection-site reactions and systemic adverse events occurred in 2.4% and 1.6%, respectively.ConclusionsLong-acting injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine showed high virological suppression and persistence beyond 2 years in routine care. Virological failure was uncommon and clustered mainly within 12 months, supporting early virological monitoring and prompt resistance-guided management.

title: Astragali Radix-Curcumae Rhizoma synergistically potentiates 5-fluorouracil antitumor efficacy in colorectal cancer by disrupting DNA repair-cell cycle coordination.
abstract: BackgroundAstragali Radix (HQ) and Curcumae Rhizoma (EZ), collectively termed AC, are commonly used as an herb pair in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) for colorectal cancer (CRC). Although AC has been used as an adjuvant to chemotherapy, the molecular basis by which it enhances the efficacy of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) remains incompletely defined.MethodsThe antitumor effect of AC alone and in combination with 5-FU was evaluated in a HCT116 xenograft mouse model and in CRC cell lines with different genetic backgrounds. Potential systemic toxicity was assessed using serum biochemical markers. Transcriptomic changes induced by AC were analyzed by RNA sequencing and integrated with network pharmacology and The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) (GSE17536, GSE17537, GSE41258, GSE20916). Key targets were validated by Western blotting and immunofluorescence. Cell viability, drug interaction, apoptosis, cell-cycle distribution and DNA damage were assessed using CCK-8 assays, Synergy Finder analysis, flow cytometry, and γ-H2AX staining. Bioavailable AC-derived constituents were characterized by UPLC-QTOF-MS, and candidate active compounds were further evaluated by molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, cellular thermal shift assay, and functional validation.ResultsAC potentiated the antitumor efficacy of 5-FU in vivo and did not exacerbate 5-FU-associated hepatic or renal biochemical toxicity under the tested conditions. In vitro, AC-containing serum extracts inhibited CRC cell viability, induced reversible G2/M-phase arrest, and enhanced 5-FU sensitivity in HCT116, CT26, and HCT15 cells. AC treatment caused limited early apoptosis, whereas delayed apoptosis was observed after prolonged exposure, suggesting that cell-cycle arrest represents the primary early response. RNA-seq and integrative analyses showed that AC suppressed pathways associated with DNA replication, mismatch repair, ribosome biogenesis, and cell-cycle progression. AC downregulated key regulators involved in cell-cycle control, DNA repair, and stress-survival signaling, including PLK1, CDK1, CCNB1, CDC25A, c-JUN, MSH2, BRCA1, and p-AKT. Combination treatment further increased γ-H2AX accumulation and reduced cell-cycle regulatory proteins. Functional validation indicated that c-JUN overexpression partially attenuated AC-mediated 5-FU sensitization, whereas pharmacological AKT inhibition partially mimicked the sensitizing effect of AC. Among the serum-exposed constituents, Demethoxycurcumin and Kumatakenin were identified as bioavailable active compounds that partially recapitulated the effects of AC by inducing G2/M-phase arrest and enhancing the antiproliferative activity of 5-FU. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and CETSA supported their target engagement with cell-cycle regulators, particularly CCNB1 and CDK1.ConclusionAC enhances the therapeutic efficacy of 5-FU in CRC by weakening DNA repair-cell-cycle coordination and stress-survival signaling, thereby increasing 5-FU-induced DNA damage and promoting cell-cycle arrest. Demethoxycurcumin and Kumatakenin may represent important bioavailable contributors to this chemosensitizing effect, although the complete AC extract likely acts through multi-component and multi-target mechanisms. These findings provide mechanistic support for the use of AC as an adjunctive strategy to improve 5-FU-based chemotherapy in CRC.
authors: Wang S, Huang K, Cheng Y, Sun C, Wang K, He Q, Yin G, Tang D, Zhang Y, Tan X.

title: Genome-wide analyses identify 60 loci associated with liver triglyceride content.
abstract: We performed a large-scale genome-wide association study meta-analysis of magnetic resonance imaging-derived liver triglyceride content across 71,488 European-ancestry participants from the UK Biobank, approximately doubling the sample size of previous genome-wide association studies1. We identified 60 independent loci, including 31 not previously reported, and estimated the single nucleotide polymorphism-based heritability of liver triglyceride content at 25%. Integrative fine-mapping and gene-prioritization analyses nominated candidate effector genes for 48 loci. Of the 31 newly identified variants, 14 were validated in meta-analyses of clinically diagnosed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (42,163 cases and 1,646,254 controls). People in the highest versus lowest decile of a polygenic risk score for liver triglyceride content had 2.71-fold higher odds of cirrhosis and 7.47-fold higher odds of hepatocellular carcinoma. Plasma proteins associated with the liver triglyceride polygenic risk score were enriched for metabolic remodeling and inflammatory pathways, with liver-enriched protein signatures increasing and visceral adipose signatures decreasing with higher genetic risk. Together, these findings refine the genetic architecture of liver triglyceride content, linking polygenic susceptibility to downstream metabolic and inflammatory pathways and providing insights into the genetic basis of steatotic liver disease.
authors: Jamialahmadi O, Mowlaei S, Gelev KZ, Mancina RM, Flagiello V, Kozlitina J, Pajukanta P, Valenti L, Romeo S.

title: Pseudouridylation landscape across 42 nuclear-encoded S. cerevisiae tRNAs.
abstract: Pseudouridine is the most abundant RNA base modification due to its prevalence in tRNA and rRNA, where it serves as a key modulator of structure and function. Yet, in the widely used model organism, the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, tRNA pseudouridine sites have not been comprehensively annotated. Here, we performed two high-throughput methods established for detecting tRNA pseudouridylation positions: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) and 2-bromoacrylamide-assisted cyclization sequencing (BACS). Using DRS, we sequenced cytosolic tRNA from seven pseudouridine synthase (PUS) knockout S. cerevisiae strains, including deletion strains of Pus1, Pus3, and Pus7. Analysis of these data verified thirty-two existing pseudouridine annotations and predicted an additional ten previously unannotated pseudouridine sites. Our analysis also revealed DRS signal changes at several non-uridine sites with the loss of a PUS, including apparent changes in modification abundances at position 37 upon deletion of Pus3. Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and primer extension assays, however, indicated no change in the abundance of these modifications with the loss of Pus3, underscoring the need for caution in interpreting DRS-based signal changes. Using BACS, we confirmed the ten DRS-predicted novel sites, while further detecting eleven additional previously unannotated pseudouridine sites. Combining existing modification annotations from the Modomics database with our DRS and BACS datasets, we created a map of all detected pseudouridines-totaling 126 sites, including 21 novel sites-and the enzymes responsible for their catalysis, across the forty-two nuclear-encoded S. cerevisiae tRNA isoacceptors.
authors: Barry ML, Abu-Shumays RL, Barnes LE, Shaw EA, Reinsch JL, Basham ZD, Jain M, Koutmou KS, Garcia DM.

title: Impact of nationwide parvovirus B19 DNA screening and identification of transfusion-transmitted infections.
abstract: Background and objectivesParvovirus B19 (B19V) testing is often not required to release blood components. However, the European Pharmacopoeia requires that plasma pools for fractionation contain no more than 104 IU/mL of B19V DNA. In France, pool B19 nucleic acid testing (NAT) screening was performed by Établissement Français du Sang since 2015. Since June 2024, positive pools are broken down into individual testing, allowing for the identification and management of infected blood donations.Materials and methodsB19V NAT is performed in pools of 96 donations (P96) with the DPX Parvo/hepatitis A virus assay (Roche). A P96 with a viral load >104 IU/mL B19V DNA is considered positive. All individual donations (IDs) testing reactive for B19V by ID-NAT are excluded from plasma-based medicinal products production, and the corresponding blood components are destroyed if not yet transfused.ResultsFrom June 2024 to June 2025, 99 of 2,627,678 donations (3.7/100,000) were B19V DNA positive. All blood components related to 90 donations were discarded. Of the remaining nine donations, 13 blood components (9 platelet concentrates [PCs] that had undergone pathogen reduction (PR) and four red blood cell [RBC] concentrates) were transfused before NAT results were obtained. Two B19V transmissions were reported in recipients (0.078/100,000 transfusions) after transfusion of 1 PR-PC and 1 RBC unit.ConclusionB19V DNA testing for plasma intended for fractionation performed in blood services helps in avoiding transmissions by the related blood components, provided positive donations are detected prior to their transfusion. Delayed availability of results may result in transfusion-transmitted B19V infection, which cannot prevented by current PR technology.

title: Analytical validation of MethyLiverDx-Sigma, a plasma cfDNA methylation assay for hepatocellular carcinoma detection.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance relies on ultrasonography and alpha-fetoprotein, both limited in sensitivity for early-stage disease; aberrant methylation of circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) offers a promising blood-based approach. Reported here is the analytical validation of MethyLiverDx-Sigma (MLDx-s), an assay that detects methylated RNF135 and DNMT3A in bisulfite-converted plasma cfDNA by methylation-specific PCR with high-resolution melting (HRM), with GAPDH as an endogenous control. Performance was evaluated following CLSI EP05-A3, EP07, EP12-A2, and EP37. Precision of quantification cycle (Cq) and melting peak temperature (Tm) was assessed by variance-component analysis within one site and across two sites and two operators. Because precision studies used bulk bisulfite-converted reference DNA, the reported coefficients of variation (CVs) primarily characterize the PCR-HRM detection module; end-to-end variability in clinical plasma specimens may be higher. Interference and cross-reactivity were evaluated in low-positive and contrived-negative samples against reproducibility-derived limits, with dose-response testing of reactive substances. Detection was 100% at both levels, and every run met control-validity criteria. Cq repeatability CVs ranged from 0.53% to 1.68%, and total reproducibility CVs ranged from 1.10% to 2.37%; all Tm CVs were ≤0.20%. All 18 interferents and 16 microbial cross-reactants evaluated in low-positive samples met the predefined acceptance criteria. In negative samples, hemoglobin, SARS-CoV-2, and measles virus produced concentration-dependent non-specific amplification, and dose-response testing established their respective no-effect concentrations. These findings characterize the analytical precision and multisite reproducibility of the PCR-HRM detection module and the analytical specificity of MLDx-s, complementing its previously reported clinical performance for plasma-based HCC detection.
authors: Kim SC, Choi H, Chung J, Lee ST, Kim YJ.

title: Emergence of bimodal First Passage Time distributions from Transcription Translation Coupling.
abstract: Transcription and translation are fundamentally stochastic processes that drive significant variability in mRNA and protein levels within living cells. In certain cellular environments, these processes occur simultaneously, motivating the Transcription-Translation Coupled (TTC) model. We present a simple model of stochastic gene regulation incorporating TTC that yields bimodality in protein synthesis dynamics. By casting the estimation of protein synthesis times as a first-passage time (FPT) problem, we demonstrate that TTC generates robust bimodal FPT statistics with possible implications for bacterial survival strategies.
authors: Saha A, Ghosh A.

title: Functional analysis of SmCSN5 in salt stress tolerance of Salvia miltiorrhiza.
abstract: Salt stress limits plant growth, but the contribution of COP9 signalosome subunit 5 (CSN5) to salt tolerance in Salvia miltiorrhiza remains unclear. Here, we combined heterologous overexpression in Arabidopsis thaliana with overexpression and RNA interference in S. miltiorrhiza hairy roots. SmCSN5 transcript abundance increased with NaCl concentration and showed a transient response to 150 mM NaCl, peaking at 6 h among the sampled times. SmCSN5 overexpression improved germination and growth under salt stress and was associated with higher proline accumulation and antioxidant enzyme activities. Overexpressing Arabidopsis also maintained higher relative water content and chlorophyll content, with lower electrolyte leakage, malondialdehyde content, and ROS-associated staining. Separate ion measurements showed lower Na⁺ content, higher K⁺ content, and lower Na⁺/K⁺ ratios in overexpressing Arabidopsis and hairy roots. SmCSN5 RNA interference produced opposite physiological and ion-accumulation responses in hairy roots. Yeast two-hybrid and luciferase complementation assays identified SmCBL3 as a candidate SmCSN5-interacting protein. Collectively, these findings support a positive role for SmCSN5 in salt tolerance, accompanied by improved antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, and ion homeostasis. Whether these responses improve medicinal metabolite production under salinity remains unresolved.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Shao S, Wang M, Zhu W, Ma P.

title: The conserved function of bHLH121 and overexpression of N-terminal bHLH121 fragment suppresses iron deficiency response in Arabidopsis.
abstract: Iron (Fe) homeostasis is fundamental to plant growth and development and is centrally regulated by a well-conserved network of basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors. In Arabidopsis thaliana, bHLH121 regulates the expression of FER-like iron deficiency-induced transcription factor (FIT) and clade Ib bHLH38/39/100/101 genes, among others. However, its functional conservation remains unexplored, and some contradictory results have been reported regarding the effects of bHLH121 overexpression. Here, we investigated the evolutionary conservation of bHLH121 through complementary tests in the Arabidopsis bhlh121 mutant created by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. We also investigated the effects of ectopically expressing full-length, N-terminal, and C-terminal fragments of bHLH121 on plant responses to Fe deficiency in Arabidopsis. Transgenic plants overexpressing the full-length bHLH121 driven by the cauliflower mosaic virus 35S promoter (bHLH121 ox) resulted in shorter roots and more severe leaf chlorosis compared to wild-type plants under Fe-limiting conditions. Moreover, overexpression of the N-terminal fragment (N121 ox) rendered plants highly sensitive to Fe deficiency, whereas overexpression of the C-terminal fragment (C121 ox) did not. Consistent with the phenotypic observations, N121 ox plants accumulated lower Fe content, and the ferric chelate reductase activity was significantly reduced. In N121 ox plants, the induction of key Fe regulatory genes, especially FIT, was significantly inhibited under Fe deficiency. Confocal imaging showed that both N121-GFP and C121-GFP fusion proteins could localize to the nucleus. Electrophoretic mobility shift assay showed that both full-length bHLH121 and N121 could effectively bind the probes derived from the promoter of FIT. The present work reveals a conserved function of bHLH121 in Fe homeostasis across several dicot species and demonstrates that overexpression of N121 potently suppresses Fe deficiency responses in Arabidopsis.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Zhou P, Liu C, Pan Y, Fei Y, Shen R, Wang R, Lan P.

title: Integrative single-cell and computational pathology analyses reveal a C11orf24-associated stem-like epithelial population linked to tumor microenvironment remodeling and immune evasion in bladder cancer.
abstract: BackgroundCancer stem-like cells drive tumor progression and therapeutic resistance, yet the epithelial stemness hierarchy in bladder cancer (BLCA) remains poorly defined. We aimed to characterize stemness-associated epithelial populations and their clinical significance.MethodsWe analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from 92,218 cells across 13 treatment-naïve BLCA samples to characterize epithelial stemness and tumor-microenvironment interactions. Spatial transcriptomics and independent bulk cohorts were used for orthogonal and clinical validation. An HStem-associated histopathology-based prognostic model was developed by integrating quantitative image features with deep-learning representations, followed by functional validation of the candidate gene C11orf24.ResultsWe identified a highly stem-like epithelial population (HStem) at the apex of the differentiation hierarchy, exhibiting MYC activation, oxidative phosphorylation, and DNA repair enrichment, with preferential presence in advanced-stage tumors. HStem cells were inferred to serve as major communication hubs within the TME, interacting extensively with fibroblasts and endothelial cells via MIF-CD74/CXCR4 and MIF-CD74/CD44 axes. An 86-gene HStem signature enabled development of a robust image-based prognostic model. High-risk tumors showed immune exclusion, immunosuppressive enrichment, T-cell dysfunction, and predicted checkpoint blockade resistance. C11orf24 emerged as a candidate stemness-associated regulator; C11orf24-positive cells displayed enhanced stemness and stromal interactions. Functional experiments demonstrated that C11orf24 perturbation altered clonogenic growth, migration, and invasion in BLCA cells. Pharmacogenomic analyses identified predicted therapeutic vulnerabilities that warrant experimental validation.ConclusionsWe identify an HStem population associated with BLCA progression, microenvironmental remodeling, and immune evasion. Integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics with computational pathology, we establish a clinically relevant stemness framework and identify C11orf24 as a potential therapeutic target, offering opportunities for stemness-directed precision oncology.
authors: Wang Y, Zhang S, Luo X, Wang Z, Wang Y, Li N, Liu Y, Gao J, Zhang R, Jia Z, Shi R, Zhang L.
