title: Plant-Based Virus-like Particle (VLP) Vaccines Against Influenza and Hepatitis Viruses.
abstract: The rapid evolution of pathogens, particularly viruses, poses a continuous threat to global public health, necessitating the development of highly scalable and cost-effective vaccine platforms. Plant-based virus-like particles (VLPs) have emerged as a transformative approach in vaccinology, leveraging the innate capacity of plant systems to produce highly immunogenic, non-infectious, and structurally authentic viral mimics. VLP-based recombinant antigens contained within the plant tissues (particularly in seeds) show better stability and can be transported and stored at ambient temperatures, without the requirement of a cold chain framework, and edible vaccines offer needle-free vaccine administration. Plant-based expression systems use natural cellular structures such as plant cell walls and seed endosperms to encase antigens, functioning as a natural shield against digestion and thermal degradation. Grain host plants are inimitably adapted for prolonged storage owing to natural seed desiccation wherein recombinant antigens accumulate within vacuoles or intracellular protein bodies segregated from active degradation. By simply cultivating more plants, vaccine production can be scaled up while transient plant expression systems speed up production within a few weeks, which is critical for quick responses to emerging new disease outbreaks. By genetic modification, plants can be used to express several antigens, facilitating the development of multi-component vaccines against many diseases at a single shot. Recently, plant-derived VLP vaccines, principally targeting influenza and hepatitis viruses, have been shown to elicit robust immune responses through the expression of their surface antigens in plants such as lettuce, potato, and tobacco (Nicotiana benthamiana). Despite their potential, significant challenges persist, including the achievement of consistent dosing, the attainment of high and reproducible expression levels, and the navigation of complex regulatory frameworks for plant-derived pharmaceuticals which remain unsolved. The current review focuses on recent developments in the production of plant-based influenza and hepatitis vaccines and explores the advantages, challenges, and application of such vaccines in combating these infections.
authors: Shahgolzari M, Hefferon K, Yavari A, Gaobotse G, Masisi K, Faija M, Makhzoum A, Venkataraman S.

title: Ecological Mechanisms Underlying the Persistence of Yersinia pestis in the Natural Plague Foci of Kazakhstan: An Integrated Ecological Framework.
abstract: Plague remains a significant natural-focal infection, yet the mechanisms underlying the long-term persistence of Yersinia pestis during inter-epizootic periods remain incompletely understood. This study integrated published evidence with epizootiological monitoring data from Kazakhstan (1990-2025) and detailed field and laboratory investigations conducted during 2021-2023 to develop an integrated ecological framework of plague persistence. Abiotic and biotic niches, reservoir hosts, flea vectors, and adaptive states of Y. pestis were evaluated according to the strength and type of supporting evidence. Long-term surveillance identified spatially recurrent enzootic cores and documented the continued presence of the great gerbil (Rhombomys opimus)-flea host-vector system across major desert plague territories. Field investigations covered approximately 120,000 km2 and included 4586 environmental and biological samples. Bacteriological examination yielded 24 viable Y. pestis isolates belonging to the Medievalis biovar, whereas real-time PCR detected Y. pestis-specific DNA in 88 of 4586 samples (1.92%), with the highest positivity observed in ectoparasite suspensions (66/868; 7.60%). Laboratory evidence was concentrated in five investigated foci containing recurrent enzootic core areas, while no positive findings were obtained in three comparison foci. These findings support an evidence-weighted ecological framework in which established host-vector transmission operates within spatially structured reservoir populations and heterogeneous environments, while additional environmental and bacterial persistence mechanisms remain plausible but require further experimental validation.
authors: Abdel Z, Meka-Mechenko T, Zhumadilova Z, Mussagalieva R, Abdirassilova A, Baitursyn B, Zarkymanova A, Abdeliyev B, Shaki N, Issaeva S.

title: Tissue-Specific miRNA Responses to Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus Strains in Mice.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Tick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV) is a vector-borne flavivirus that targets the CNS and causes severe encephalitis with long-term neurological sequelae. As the geographic range of its vectors expands and climate conditions shift, the incidence of tick-borne encephalitis continues to rise, yet no specific antiviral therapy has been developed to date. Understanding the molecular mechanisms of tissue-specific immune responses during TBEV infection is essential for identifying novel therapeutic targets and biomarkers. Methods: In this study, quantitative reverse transcription PCR with stem-loop primers was used to examine changes in the levels of seven immunoregulatory miRNAs (let-7i, miR-9-5p, miR-21a-5p, miR-30a-5p, miR-146b-5p, miR-181a-5p, miR-486-5p) in blood plasma, peripheral organs (spleen, liver), and four central nervous system structures (olfactory bulb, cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, spinal cord) of BALB/c mice. Three experimental groups were compared: (1) infection with the Aina strain (Siberian subtype), (2) infection with the Sofyin strain (Far Eastern subtype), and (3) vaccination with the vaccine "Tick-E-Vak". Results: It was shown that both infection and vaccination induce pronounced tissue-specific changes in the miRNA profile. MiR-181a-5p is a negative regulator of TLR4/NF-κB signaling. Its downregulation was the most reproducible change observed across all compartments and in all three groups, suggesting a possible universal mechanism for derepression of the proinflammatory cascade. Two miRNAs (miR-30a-5p and miR-146b-5p) were altered in all examined tissues and may be considered candidate markers of antigenic stimulation. Conclusions: The direction of their changes in plasma and tissues was frequently opposite, suggesting redistribution of miRNAs between the tissue and circulating pools, which is important for the interpretation of plasma biomarkers. Infection-specific changes were identified for let-7i and miR-9-5p in the CNS. The most pronounced changes were observed in the structures most affected by neuroinvasion (olfactory bulb, spinal cord), making them candidate markers associated with TBEV infection and CNS involvement. Infection with the Aina strain induced more pronounced miRNA changes in peripheral organs and the CNS than the Sofyin strain, despite the higher epidemiological lethality of the latter. This suggests that the pathogenicity of individual strains in the mouse model may not always correspond to the subtype-based lethality classification in humans and is determined by strain-specific features of tropism and infection kinetics.
authors: Mikheeva EV, Chicherina GS, Aulova KS, Nevinsky GA, Timofeeva AM.

title: Single-Cell Transcriptomics Reveals Rora-Associated Aberrant Granulosa Cell Differentiation in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome.
abstract: IntroductionPolycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is characterized by follicular developmental arrest, yet the molecular basis underlying impaired granulosa cell (GC) differentiation remains incompletely understood.MethodsWe constructed a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of ovaries from DHEA-induced PCOS-like mice and matched vehicle controls, and leveraged spatial transcriptomics as an orthogonal reference for major cell-type annotation, followed by in-depth profiling of GC heterogeneity. Pseudotime inference, co-expression networks, and regulon activity analysis were integrated, and findings were validated in independent human GC datasets. In silico Rora perturbation, cell-cell communication analysis, and drug repositioning were additionally performed.ResultsWe identified a subset of luteinized mural GCs with robust Rora regulon activation, termed Rora-regulon-active GCs. This subset was markedly enriched in PCOS and was reproducibly observed in independent human GC datasets. Rora-regulon-active GCs exhibited an incomplete luteinization phenotype coupled with lipid-metabolic reprogramming. In silico Rora knockdown partially reconfigured GC differentiation trajectories and shifted the PCOS-skewed subset composition toward control, with concordant changes in metabolic transcriptional programs. Cell-cell communication analyses implicated stromal-derived Mdk-Sdc1 signaling and suggested additional crosstalk with macrophages potentially mediated by ligands such as Vegfa. In silico drug repositioning prioritized betaine hydrochloride and bempedoic acid as candidate therapeutics.DiscussionOur study delineates a Rora-associated aberrant GC differentiation program linked to PCOS, nominating this aberrant program as a potential cellular basis of PCOS-associated follicular arrest and providing mechanistic and translational leads for precision-targeted therapy.
authors: Ji P, Sun S, Xu X, Chen S.

title: Heparinization of anodized aluminum oxide (AAO) membranes for affinity separations of biocolloids.
abstract: Affinity membranes are developed by the immobilization of heparin onto anodized aluminum oxide (AAO) supports via amine grafting followed by amide coupling. Optimized procedures give heparinized AAO (HEP-AAO) membranes with a stable layer of 0.832-1.33 mg heparin per m2 pore area in 224 nm diameter pores. Following the heparinization of the membrane, the bioavailability of heparin is demonstrated through the capture and release of fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2), a protein for which heparin acts as a ligand. The capping of unreacted amines using citraconic anhydride reduces nonspecific protein binding without loss of heparin activity. The pore accessibility of colloidal particles is confirmed through the electrostatically-driven binding and release of 20 nm fluorescent amine-grafted silica nanoparticles, which are used as a model system to investigate the capture and release of biocolloids. Application of heparinized AAO membranes for the affinity capture and release of adeno associated virus 2 (AAV-2) is demonstrated in tangential flow filtration. Preliminary results for the affinity capture of AAV-2 pre-filtered culture medium capture significant AAV2 with negligible retention of host protein and DNA, paving a path for further optimization of viral vector purification.
authors: Daugherty KE, Martin LD, Leach-Baughman M, Edmonds KL, Dutch RE, Chwatko M, Rankin SE, Knutson BL.

title: SlMYB21 and SlMYB24 cooperatively regulate petal coloration and movement in  Solanum lycopersicum
abstract: In seed plants, reproductive success depends on the precise coordination of floral organ development. Here, we identify and characterize the  Solanum lycopersicum transcription factor (TF) SlMYB24 as a member of the R2R3-MYB subgroup 19. While  Slmyb24 mutants exhibited no obvious phenotypic alterations, the previously characterized  Slmyb21 mutant displayed defects in floral development that were further exacerbated in the  Slmyb21 Slmyb24 double mutant, resulting in a severe phenotype characterized by female sterility and whitish petals that failed to open. Petals of  Slmyb21 Slmyb24 exhibited reduced xanthophyll content and elevated abscisic acid (ABA) levels, accompanied by reduced water content and decreased levels of primary sugars. Integration of transcriptome (RNA-sequencing) and cistrome (DNA affinity purification sequencing, DAP-seq) data identified genes involved in carotenoid and ABA biosynthesis and water transport as candidate regulatory targets of SlMYB21 and SlMYB24. These TFs activated the promoters of  PHYTOENE SYNTHASE2 (  PSY2 ),  LYCOPENE β-CYCLASE (LCY-B ) and the petal-expressed aquaporin  TONOPLAST INTRINSIC PROTEIN1.1 (  TIP1.1 ), whereas they repressed  9- cis  -EPOXYCAROTENOID DIOXYGENASE1 (  NCED1 ) promoter activity. In addition, SlMYB21 bound to the  SlMYB24 promoter and activated its expression. Promoter studies and electrophoretic mobility shift assays revealed that  SlMYB21 and  SlMYB24 bind the AC-rich DNA-binding motif ‘GTTAGGT’, which is to be found in the respective promoters and is consistent with the extensive overlap in their binding profiles. Together, these results reveal that the functions of SlMYB21 and SlMYB24 extend beyond fertility to coordinate petal pigmentation and opening.
authors: Friesch M, Zhang C, Smits H, Decker-Hibbel J, Harborth L, Weinmar S, Bühler I, Santiago A, Echeverría J, Syrowatka F, Matus JT, Hause B.

title: Structural basis of self-loading by replicative helicases
abstract: DNA replication is conserved in all forms of life on earth, from subcellular structures such as viruses to human cells. Here we study a group of virus parasites whose replication is initiated by helicases like those found in simian viruses and eukaryotic cells. The process by which these viral helicases initiate the replication of the DNA remains poorly understood. Here, we show how the helicase binds the parasite’s origin of replication with its carboxy terminal domains (CTDs) adopting flexible and different conformations. The CTD’s flexibility moves the DNA towards the inside of the helicase’s ring and bends the DNA at three discrete positions curving it. Our cryo-EM snapshots show that the helicase deforms the DNA while self-loading onto it as the first stage of the initiation of DNA replication, suggesting that initial melting and self-loading are coupled processes in this type of virus parasites.
authors: Qiao C, Qiao C, Mir-Sanchis I.

title: Pharmacologic inhibition of OLIG2 by CT-179 disrupts mitotic progression and enhances standard-of-care chemoradiotherapy in glioblastoma
abstract: Background  Glioblastoma (GBM) remains uniformly fatal. The basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor OLIG2 is universally expressed in diffuse glioma, sustains the tumor-propagating stem-like fraction, and opposes p53-mediated genotoxic responses, but has historically been considered undruggable. We characterized CT-179, a brain-penetrant small-molecule OLIG2 inhibitor, as a candidate therapeutic for GBM. Methods  Target engagement was assessed by cellular thermal shift assay, differential scanning fluorimetry, crosslinking, and electrophoretic mobility shift assay. Anti-tumor activity was evaluated across eleven patient-derived GBM cell lines, in zebrafish oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-derived tumors, and orthotopic and subcutaneous GBM models, including combinations with radiotherapy plus temozolomide and with selective Bcl-2 family inhibitors.  Results: : CT-179 engaged OLIG2 and altered the conformation of dimerized OLIG2 on chromatin without preventing dimerization or fully displacing OLIG2 from DNA. CT-179 reduced OLIG2-positive OPC’s and OPC-derived tumors in zebrafish and inhibited proliferation across all eleven GBM lines (IC50 Conclusions  CT-179 is a brain-penetrant inhibitor of an established GBM driver with single-agent and combination activity across several orthotopic models, supporting clinical development for GBM and translational evaluation in other OLIG2-dependent CNS malignancies. Key Points  CT-179 is the first brain-penetrant small-molecule inhibitor of OLIG2 with potent activity across patient-derived glioblastoma models. CT-179 induces apoptosis through mitotic catastrophe and slippage rather than collapse of receptor tyrosine kinase signaling. Oral CT-179 combined with radiotherapy and temozolomide eliminates the great majority of subcutaneous patient-derived GBM xenografts without overt toxicity. Oral CT-179 extends single-agent survival across two independent adult orthotopic patient-derived backgrounds (GBM8 and G06); intraperitoneal CT-179 is associated with reduced intratumoral OLIG2 and Ki-67 staining in GBM8 tumors. Intraperitoneal CT-179 plus radiotherapy significantly extends survival in an MGMT-unmethylated GBM6 orthotopic model where temozolomide contributes minimally and supports the rationale for further evaluation in MGMT-unmethylated GBM. Importance of the Study  Glioblastoma is uniformly fatal, and durable disease-modifying therapies that disable the lineage transcription factor programs sustaining the GBM stem-like state have remained elusive. OLIG2 is universally expressed in diffuse glioma and is a central driver of stemness, lineage-restricted RTK signaling, and resistance to genotoxic therapy, yet has historically been considered undruggable. This study reports the foundational preclinical characterization of CT-179, a brain-penetrant small molecule that engages OLIG2 directly and induces glioblastoma cell death through disrupted mitotic progression. Oral CT-179 crosses the blood-brain barrier, prolongs survival in orthotopic patient-derived xenografts, and substantially enhances the efficacy of standard-of-care radiotherapy and temozolomide. Activity in an MGMT-unmethylated orthotopic patient-derived GBM model in combination with radiotherapy is of particular translational interest, since this is the patient population for which temozolomide contributes minimally and the unmet need is greatest. These data establish proof of concept for direct pharmacologic inhibition of OLIG2 in GBM and provide a translational rationale, including an MGMT-stratified combination strategy, for combining CT-179 with current standard-of-care chemoradiotherapy. Lay Summary  Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive brain cancer in adults, and almost all patients die of their disease. One reason is a protein called OLIG2, which keeps tumor cells in an immature, treatment-resistant state and has long been considered impossible to target with drugs. We studied CT-179, a small molecule that enters the brain and blocks OLIG2. In glioblastoma cells and in mice, CT-179 forced dividing tumor cells into a faulty, lethal division, extended survival on its own, and strengthened the effect of standard radiation and chemotherapy. These results support testing CT-179 in people with glioblastoma.

title: Planktonic Growth and Biofilm Formation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa under Combined Treatment with Rifampicin and Moringa oleifera Leaf Ethanolic Extract
abstract: Biofilm formation by Pseudomonas aeruginosa complicates antimicrobial treatment, particularly in persistent infections, and motivates the assessment of plant-derived antibiotic adjuncts. The influence of Moringa oleifera leaf ethanolic extract on rifampicin responses across planktonic growth and biofilm formation requires concentration-resolved evaluation. Three independent experiments assessed planktonic growth and crystal violet-stained biofilm biomass across ethanolic extract–rifampicin concentration matrices. Conventional PCR screened selected biofilm-associated genes. The ethanolic extract alone yielded 99.33–119.33% planktonic growth relative to controls at 1–64 µg/mL. Rifampicin alone reduced growth to 58.67 ± 1.15% and 6.67 ± 0.58% at 16 and 32 µg/mL, respectively. Adding 16 µg/mL ethanol fraction to 16 µg/mL rifampicin yielded 44.67 ± 30.99% growth, compared with 58.67 ± 1.15% for rifampicin alone. At 32 µg/mL rifampicin, the same fraction addition yielded 16.00 ± 13.00% growth, compared with 6.67 ± 0.58% for rifampicin alone. Biofilm biomass at 16 µg/mL rifampicin was 55.67 ± 67.00%, reaching 70.00 ± 86.88% with ethanol fraction addition. All 49 paired comparisons per assay yielded false-discovery-rate-adjusted q-values above 0.05. PCR detected pelA, pslA, pslD, pqsA, lasR, and ndvB. The concentration matrices revealed distinct planktonic growth and biofilm biomass responses. These findings position complementary planktonic and biofilm measurements as essential criteria for assessing plant–antibiotic combinations, providing concentration-specific evidence to guide formulation screening and antimicrobial candidate prioritization.

title: Small RNA sequencing revealed microRNAs involved in growth and development of the oyster mushroom Pleurotus ostreatus.
abstract: Although microRNAs are essential regulators of development in complex eukaryotes, little is known about their functions in fungi. With its clear genetic system and ease of cultivation, Pleurotus ostreatus presents a model mushroom for this research. Nevertheless, the role of milRNAs in the growth and development of P. ostreatus is not yet critically understood. This study characterized milRNAs in three developmental stages of the P. ostreatus by combining small RNA sequencing, genomic alignment, and FungiSNC database. The differentially expressed milRNAs showed a dynamic expression pattern, suggesting that they may be involved in developmental regulation. The interaction diagram of milRNA-mRNA showed that there might be a synergistic relationship between milRNAs, and they may target the genes of same family related to growth and development. Four representative milRNAs were selected for qRT-PCR verification, and their expression trends were consistent with the sequencing results. In addition, the dual luciferase reporter assay showed that Po-milR-1 had targeting relationships with the hydrophobin and 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase. It is speculated that Po-milR-1 may participate in the growth and development of P. ostreatus by targeting these genes. This study provides new insights into the regulatory mechanism of milRNAs in P. ostreatus, and lays the foundation for further research on the molecular function of milRNAs in edible fungi.
authors: Li Y, Yan B, Xu D, Ma A.

title: Yupingfeng alleviates allergic rhinitis by modulating gut microbiota and succinate to inhibit mTOR/S6K signaling.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceYupingfeng granules (YPF), derived from the classic traditional Chinese medicine prescription Yupingfeng powder, have been recommended in clinical practice guidelines for the management of allergic rhinitis (AR), and their clinical efficacy is widely recognized. However, the underlying pharmacological mechanisms have not been thoroughly investigated.Aim of the studyThis study aimed to investigate whether YPF protects the nasal epithelial barrier and alleviates AR by modulating the gut microbiota and pathways related to its metabolites.Materials and methodsAn OVA-induced AR mouse model was established and phenotypically evaluated. The dependence of YPF efficacy on gut microbiota was assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing, antibiotic depletion, and fecal microbiota transplantation. 1H-NMR metabolomics was used to identify key metabolites, followed by exogenous supplementation for validation. Nasal mucosal transcriptome sequencing was performed to explore downstream pathways, and functional validation was conducted in OVA-induced HNEpCs through metabolite intervention, YPF co-treatment, mTOR knockdown, and MHY1485 treatment.ResultsYPF dose-dependently reduced nasal rubbing and sneezing, attenuated IgE-mediated type 2 inflammation, and ameliorated nasal epithelial barrier injury in OVA-induced AR mice. YPF remodeled the gut microbiota and increased microbial diversity. Gut microbiota depletion attenuated the protective effects of YPF, whereas FMT from YPF donors reproduced them. Metabolomic analysis identified succinate as a key YPF-responsive metabolite, and exogenous succinate aggravated nasal epithelial barrier injury. Transcriptomic analysis suggested that succinate-induced nasal mucosal injury may involve mTOR signaling activation. In vitro, succinate aggravated OVA-induced barrier injury in HNEpCs, with disrupted Occludin distribution and enhanced mTOR/S6K phosphorylation, whereas YPF co-treatment reversed these changes. mTOR knockdown mimicked the protective effects of YPF, whereas MHY1485 attenuated them.ConclusionYPF alleviates OVA-induced AR by remodeling the gut microbiota, reducing succinate accumulation, and suppressing mTOR/S6K signaling to preserve nasal epithelial barrier integrity.
authors: Zuo Y, Li Y, Huang Z, Zeng H, Liu Q, Zhou Y, Chen X, Chen W, Wang K, Chen Q.

title: Efficient fucoxanthin production by fed-batch photo-fermentation cultivation of genetically engineered heterotrophic-growth Phaeodactylum tricornutum.
abstract: The marine diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum is considered a promising platform for commercial fucoxanthin production due to its naturally high fucoxanthin content. However, its industrial application remains limited by low biomass productivity and high production costs associated with conventional photoautotrophic cultivation. To address these challenges, metabolic engineering was employed to convert the obligate photoautotrophic strain into a glucose-utilizing strain capable of heterotrophic growth, thereby enabling high-density cultivation. In this study, the wild-type P. tricornutum Pt1 was genetically engineered, and the transformant Glut1-45 was identified as the superior strain based on its enhanced growth performance compared with other transformants. Subsequently, an efficient photo-fermentation process was developed through systematic optimization of cultivation conditions for Glut1-45. The results demonstrated that light supplementation, together with a mixed nitrogen source containing inorganic sodium nitrate and organic tryptone, markedly enhanced glucose utilization and cell growth. Moreover, Glut1-45 exhibited no significant growth inhibition at glucose concentrations below 10 g L-1, whereas concentrations exceeding 20 g L-1 significantly inhibited cell proliferation. By maintaining glucose concentrations below 5 g L-1 during fed-batch photo-fermentation, high-cell-density cultivation and enhanced fucoxanthin production were successfully achieved. The maximum biomass concentration reached 10.05 g L-1, while the maximum fucoxanthin content reached 14.87 mg g-1 dry cell weight, yielding the highest fucoxanthin titer of 146.58 mg L-1. These results demonstrate the potential of integrating metabolic engineering for glucose utilization with fed-batch photo-fermentation to achieve high-cell-density cultivation and enhanced volumetric fucoxanthin production, providing a feasible strategy for efficient P. tricornutum-based fucoxanthin biomanufacturing.
authors: Jin H, Hu Z, Hao X, Li C, Pan Y, Hu H.

title: Excess IL-18 drives fatal mousepox cytokine storm via NK cell immunodeficiency and nonspecific T-cell hyperactivation.
abstract: Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a hyperinflammatory syndrome with multiple contributors, often including an infectious trigger. The Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS) subtype is linked to marked IL-18 excess, cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CTL) activation, and natural killer (NK) cell abnormalities. We asked how excess IL-18 shapes NK and CTL responses to viral challenge. Mice with chronic IL-18 overproduction (Il18tg), showed baseline NK-cytopenia and CTL activation resembling MAS-susceptible patients. NK transcriptomes reflected IL-18/IFNg-axis activation and cell cycle upregulation. LCMV infection of Il18tg mice causes HLH/MAS without affecting viral control, but is not a significant NK challenge. Early after infection with NK-dependent mousepox, Il18tg NKs failed to activate appropriately, but CTLs quickly hyperactivated and mousepox control remained intact. Mousepox-infected Il18tg mice then developed signs of HLH/MAS including hepatosplenic necrosis. Their viral control was impaired, possibly because they failed to expand mousepox-specific CTLs. Il18bpKO mice, despite more normal resting lymphocytes, succumbed similarly to viremic HLH/MAS. Transfer of pre-activated NKs into Il18tg mice partially rescued virus-specific CTL responses, viral control, and survival. Thus, excess IL-18 contributes to HLH/MAS via disparate effects on CTL and NK cells, demonstrating a novel, context-specific NK immunodeficiency and highlighting how subtle host-pathogen interactions can affect the mechanisms and treatment rationale of life-threatening HLH/MAS.
authors: Varghese JA, Huang L, Carro SD, Landy EE, Frank-Kamenetskii A, Klinghoffer H, Morrissette JA, Dang V, Eisenlohr LC, Canna SW.

title: Clinical characteristics and prognosis of central nervous system Klebsiella pneumoniae infection: a focus on hypervirulent and classical strains.
abstract: ObjectiveTo investigate the clinical characteristics, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of 20 cases of central nervous system (CNS) Klebsiella pneumoniae infection diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), and to compare the differences between classical Klebsiella pneumoniae (cKP) and hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKP) in central nervous system infections.MethodsRetrospective single-center study of 20 mNGS-diagnosed CNS K. pneumoniae infections (January 2022 - March 2026). Univariate analysis compared hvKP and cKP groups.ResultsAmong 20 patients, 19 were diagnosed by CSF mNGS and 1 by abscess fluid mNGS. The cKP group had a higher proportion of tumor history (P = 0.029) and a marginally higher rate of neurosurgery history (P = 0.082). Type 2 diabetes was common in both groups (66.7% vs. 62.5%). The hvKP group had higher rates of focal neurological deficits (77.8% vs. 12.5%, P = 0.015) and bacteremia/sepsis (66.7% vs. 37.5%, P = 0.009), while the cKP group had more delirium (62.5% vs. 11.1%, P = 0.050). CSF mNGS positivity (95%) surpassed culture (23.5%, P ConclusionhvKP and cKP CNS infections differ significantly. hvKP is associated with community-onset severe disease (multiple brain abscesses, pyoventricle, focal deficits) and high mortality, while cKP links to nosocomial factors and better outcomes. mNGS is key for diagnosis, offering high CSF positivity and concurrent virulence/resistance profiling. Potential prognostic factors identified include high CSF mNGS reads, resistance genes, early liver abscess drainage, timely intravitreal injection, and combination therapy.

title: Pest resistance function of BtACO8 gene from Balsas teosinte.
abstract: The peach aphid (Myzus persicae) is a major agricultural pest that causes significant yield losses and transmits numerous plant viruses. We profiled BtACO8 expression in Balsas teosinte and found that aphid infestation induced its transcripts 12.6-fold at 12 h post-infestation relative to non-infested controls. We therefore cloned BtACO8, encoding 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate oxidase, and investigated its role in aphid resistance by heterologous overexpression in Arabidopsis thaliana. Three homozygous BtACO8-OE lines were obtained and used for functional characterization. Compared with wild-type plants, OE lines showed higher trichome density and greater callose deposition, and supported over 50% fewer aphids, with reduced nymph hatching and reproductive capacity. Although ethylene content did not differ significantly between OE and wild-type plants, AtEIN2, a key component of ethylene signaling, was significantly upregulated in OE lines after aphid infestation. These results suggest that BtACO8 enhances aphid resistance through physical barriers and enhanced ethylene signaling, rather than through increased ethylene production. BtACO8 from Balsas teosinte is therefore a promising candidate gene for improving aphid resistance in crops.
authors: Xu R, Shan J, Bian L, Chen X, Cao J, Yang L.

title: A transcriptional repressor co-regulatory network integrates iron homeostasis and mycobacterial stress tolerance to oxidative stress.
abstract: A hallmark of Mycobacterium tuberculosis survival and proliferation within the host is attributable to the effective stress response of the pathogen against hostile environmental conditions. Although controlled iron (Fe) uptake and maintenance of Fe homeostasis are closely associated with intracellular survival of mycobacteria, the underlying mechanism that accounts for the interdependence of mycobacterial Fe regulation and oxidative stress response remains unknown. In this study, we discovered that Fe accumulation connects intra-bacterial redox environment via the phoP locus. Gene expression analyses coupled with genetic, biochemical, and transcriptomic studies uncover a distinct mechanism that utilizes Lsr2 and the virulence regulator PhoP to modulate transcriptional control of the major Fe storage protein-encoding gene bfrB. Remarkably, regulated expression of bfrB determines bacterial tolerance to oxidative stress and its intracellular survival. Although both regulators could independently influence bfrB expression, the most fundamental insights are derived from the inhibition of Lsr2 binding at the bfrB regulatory region of the phoP-KO mutant strain owing to Lsr2-PhoP protein-protein interactions. Building on these results, we proposed a model suggesting how Lsr2-PhoP interaction, or lack thereof, contributes to stress-specific regulation of bfrB expression. Collectively, these results uncover a key mechanism integrating Fe accumulation to oxidative stress response, an essential pathogenic determinant of M. tuberculosis.IMPORTANCEWhile the availability of Fe remains essential for Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and replication of the pathogen in human macrophages, Fe may be harmful as it catalyzes the generation of toxic reactive oxygen species from products of aerobic respiration to induce oxidative stress. Although interdependence of mycobacterial Fe regulation and oxidative stress response has been reported, the mechanism connecting Fe acquisition and oxidative stress response is yet to be fully understood. Results reported in this study identify and elaborate on a new mechanism of regulation of expression of the major mycobacterial Fe storage protein, which determines bacterial tolerance to oxidative stress and impacts intracellular survival of the pathogen. We demonstrate that the virulence-associated phoP locus controls Fe accumulation and contributes to the intra-bacterial redox environment. The results uncover a distinctly different transcriptional control mechanism of the major Fe storage protein requiring a co-repressor-dependent regulatory circuit, including nucleoid-associated protein Lsr2 and the virulence regulator PhoP. Together, these results unveil a unique mechanism of stress-specific gene expression, which integrates Fe homeostasis to oxidative stress response, an essential pathogenic determinant of M. tuberculosis.
authors: Mehta K, Kajal, Goar H, Bamniya B, Sarkar D.

title: Microglial Ring1 enhances post-phagocytic myelin debris processing: Attenuation of cognitive dysfunction after hemorrhagic shock and reperfusion.
abstract: AbstractCerebral ischemia-reperfusion induces myelin injury, resulting in cognitive impairment. Efficient clearance of myelin debris is important for neural repair. The E3 ubiquitin ligase Ring1 (RING finger protein 1) participates in ubiquitin signaling and gene expression regulation, However, whether Ring1 ameliorates cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury-induced cognitive impairment by promoting microglial post-phagocytic myelin debris processing remains unknown. In this study, we employed a hemorrhagic shock and reperfusion model, a hippocampal myelin debris injection model, and an in vitro microglia-myelin debris co-culture model to simulate cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, and combined these models with proteomic and transcriptomic analyses and Ring1 gain- and loss-of-function approaches. Hemorrhagic shock and reperfusion induced hippocampal myelin injury and cognitive dysfunction, while hippocampal administration of myelin debris further impaired cognition. Transcriptomic analysis identified Ring1 as a candidate regulator associated with postphagocytic myelin debris processing. Ring1 overexpression alleviated cognitive deficits and hippocampal myelin injury and restored mitochondrial DNA-encoded gene expression and adenosine triphosphate levels after hemorrhagic shock and reperfusion. In contrast, Ring1 knockdown in the microglia-myelin debris co-culture model reduced mitochondrial DNAencoded gene expression and adenosine triphosphate levels and delayed post-phagocytic myelin debris processing. Mechanistically, Ring1 interacted with mitochondrial transcription factor B2, with K27-linked ubiquitin signals detected in Ring1- and mitochondrial transcription factor B2-containing immunocomplexes. Ring1 depletion reduced mitochondrial transcription factor B2-associated K27-linked ubiquitin signaling, mitochondrial DNA-encoded gene expression, adenosine triphosphate levels, and post-phagocytic myelin debris processing. Collectively, our findings suggest that Ring1 attenuates hemorrhagic shock and reperfusion-related cognitive impairment by promoting microglial post-phagocytic myelin debris processing through mitochondrial transcription factor B2-associated K27-linked ubiquitin signaling and mitochondrial regulation.
authors: Lu W, Huang W, Ding R, Fu H, Mao S, Hu S, Zhang G, Gao X, Nie J, Chen X, Zhang Y, Tang Y, Zhang J, Liu Q, Hu X.

title: Schaftoside, a functional flavonoid from fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum L.), alleviates depression and cognitive deficits via the microbiome-gut-brain axis in stressed mice.
abstract: Depression involves dysregulation of central and peripheral networks, with gut microbiota alterations increasingly implicated in pathogenesis. Trigonella foenum-graecum L. (fenugreek), a functional food and medicinal herb, has been used traditionally for neurological disorders, yet its specific neuroprotective constituents remain poorly characterized. This study evaluated the antidepressant potential of schaftoside, the predominant flavonoid of fenugreek seed flavonoids, and explored its mechanisms involving the microbiome-gut-brain axis in a chronic restraint stress (CRS) mouse model. Male Kunming mice were subjected to CRS and orally administered schaftoside (20, 50, and 125 mg kg-1) or fluoxetine (10 mg kg-1) for 28 days. Behavioral assessments (tail suspension, forced swim, novel object recognition, and Y-maze) demonstrated that schaftoside dose-dependently ameliorated depressive-like behaviors and cognitive impairments. It attenuated hippocampal neuronal damage and neuroinflammation, restoring hippocampal 5-HT, NE, and ACh levels. Intestinal barrier integrity was improved, evidenced by enhanced tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) and mucin (MUC2) expression, alongside reduced colonic pro-inflammatory cytokines and elevated IL-10. 16S rRNA profiling revealed that schaftoside reshaped gut microbiota composition, notably suppressing stress-enriched Bacteroides and promoting butyrate-producing Butyricicoccus. Untargeted metabolomics identified restoration of tryptophan and α-linolenic acid metabolism pathways. Spearman correlation analysis revealed significant associations between specific gut genera, fecal metabolites, and host inflammatory/neurochemical markers. Hippocampal transcriptomics indicated enrichment of cAMP signaling, dopaminergic, and serotonergic synapse pathways. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from schaftoside-treated donors partially recapitulated the behavioral, anti-inflammatory, and intestinal barrier-protective effects in antibiotic-pretreated recipient mice, accompanied by restoration of the gut microbiota and metabolite profiles. These findings demonstrate that schaftoside, the major flavonoid of fenugreek seeds, exhibits promising antidepressant-like potential through modulation of the microbiome-gut-brain axis, supporting the functional food application of fenugreek-derived flavonoids for stress-related mood disorders.
authors: Dai Y, Song P, Cheng C, Cheng L, Dai C, Lu W.

title: Combinatorial mosaics dissect the residue level basis of ACE2 binding divergence between SARS-CoV-2 and RaTG13
abstract: The spike proteins of SARS-CoV-2 and the closely related bat coronavirus RaTG13 differ in their binding affinity of human ACE2. This is due to differences in the receptor binding domain (RBD), the region primarily responsible for ACE2 binding, which are only 89% identical on the amino acid level, compared to 96% for the remainder of their genomes. Here, we constructed a combinatorial library of RBD mosaics containing combinations of 18 amino acid differences between SARS-CoV-2 and RaTG13 and measured human ACE2 binding using yeast surface display and fluorescence-activated cell sorting. The mosaics revealed a broad range of binding phenotypes. The effects on ACE2 binding were concentrated at eight positions, including all six variable positions that directly contact ACE2. Although the SARS-CoV-2 spike binds human ACE2 stronger than RaTG13 spike, the SARS-CoV-2 residues Q493 and Q498 each reduced ACE2 binding relative to RaTG13’s tyrosines. By measuring the effects of these residues across many combinations of other sequence differences, we identified sequence context dependence for residues 493 and 498, finding that the deleterious effects of Q493 and Q498 were attenuated by the SARS-CoV-2 residues at positions 483, 484, and 494. Together, these results provide a residue-level account of the sequence differences underlying the difference in ACE2 binding by SARS-CoV-2 and RaTG13 RBDs, including which differences have the largest effect and which depend on sequence context. This work demonstrates that mosaic libraries provide a robust approach for resolving the contributions of sequence differences across diverse backgrounds. Significance Statement  Closely related proteins can differ greatly in function. Identifying which sequence differences underlie the difference in phenotype can be difficult. We built a large library of receptor binding domains that independently combined 18 differences between SARS-CoV-2 and the related bat coronavirus RaTG13 and measured their relative binding to human ACE2. Most of the difference in binding was concentrated to eight positions, and the effects of two of these positions, 493 and 498, changed depending on nearby amino acids. These results show that combinatorial mosaic libraries can resolve functional differences between homologous proteins at the residue level while also revealing context dependent effects.
authors: Giovanetti SM, Sadhu MJ.

title: Pathogenicity Validation of  Parastagonospora pseudonodorum  on Wheat and Barley
abstract: Parastagonospora pseudonodorum , previously known as  Phaeosphaeria avenaria f. sp.  tritici (Pat1), is a fungal species within the Septoria blotch complex that causes yield losses in cereal crops worldwide. First reported in Canada in 1942 under an earlier taxonomic name. However, successive taxonomic changes in addition to its close resemblance to  Parastagonospora nodorum , the causal agent of Septoria nodorum blotch have complicated its identification and its role in pathogenicity. Recent molecular identification of  P. pseudonodorum in Western Canadian wheat samples necessitated the re-evaluation of its pathogenicity and raised concerns about potential misidentification with the closely-related species  P. nodorum. These two species secrete combinations of various necrotic effectors (NEs) that contribute to their virulence. In this study, we examined the pathogenicity of  P. pseudonodorum following Koch’s postulates. Our results confirmed the ability of  P. pseudonodorum to infect the leaves and spikes of both hosts, but the symptoms was weaker on the leaves of both hosts and wheat spikes, whereas more evident damage was observed on barley spikes. While a limited number of genotypes was tested as a proof of concept, but the observed differences in symptom severity suggest host and tissue associated variation in susceptibility. These results highlight the need to expand our monitoring of the leaf spot complex to include this species and to further explore its host range and genomic characterization. Awareness of this pathogen is essential, particularly given its association with cereal spikes and its quarantine status in some countries which could impacts the export of Canadian grains overseas.

title: Spatial Patterns of White Matter Hyperintensities and Cognitive Function in Older Adults: A Community-Based Study
abstract: Objectives  White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are associated with cognitive decline in older adults. We examined whether anatomically defined spatial WMH patterns are associated with cognitive performance and subsequent decline in a large community-based cohort with approximately six years of follow-up. Methods  We analyzed 1,667 participants (mean age 76 years) from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study. WMH were segmented from FLAIR images and mapped to 112 white matter regions using deep-learning-based parcellation. Principal component analysis identified dominant WMH distribution patterns; candidate components were selected by Horn’s parallel analysis and retained if stable across resampled split samples. Linear mixed-effects models examined associations between WMH patterns and cognitive performance at baseline and follow-up, adjusting for demographic, genomic, and vascular risk factors. Robustness was assessed using analyses accounting for total WMH burden, study center, and selective attrition. Results  Of 14 candidate principal components (PCs) identified by parallel analysis, eight met the resampling stability criterion and were retained, together explaining 42% of the variance. Three components were associated with cross-sectional or future cognition. PC3, characterized by deep white matter burden in the corpus callosum and anterior corona radiata with relative preservation of superficial white matter, showed no cross-sectional association at baseline but was associated with accelerated decline across multiple domains. Interpretation  A deep spatial pattern of WMH loading on the corpus callosum and anterior corona radiata was associated with subsequent cognitive decline in the absence of a cross-sectional association at baseline, independent of total lesion burden.
authors: Chen X, Nishimaki K, Tomoshige S, Chotiyanonta JS, Uchida Y, Wasserman BA, Gottesman RF, Guallar E, Windham BG, Oishi K.

title: Paper-Based Microfluidic Continuous-Flow Electroporation (µCEP) for Bacterial Transformation through Pore-Scale Electric-Field Enhancement
abstract: Electroporation (EP) is an established method for introducing biomolecules such as DNA into bacterial cells. Commercially available cuvette-based EP systems are expensive to use and limited to small sample volumes making them impractical for high-throughput applications. Furthermore, high electric fields are required in these systems which can promote electrolysis and Joule heating, thereby reducing cell viability. Herein, we report a scalable, low-cost technique called Microfluidic Continuous-Flow Electroporation in Paper (µCEP) which takes advantage of the insulating nature of glass fiber paper and its micron-sized pores to amplify the electric field strength experienced by cells. The µCEP device is fabricated by sealing glass fibers between PDMS membranes using a combination of corona plasma treatment and heat-pressing. Our results demonstrate that the µCEP technique enables transformation of  E. coli at lower applied electric field strengths with transformation efficiencies comparable to or higher than those of cuvette-based EP under the tested conditions. The continuous-flow format and lower required applied field provides a low-cost approach to bacterial electroporation while maintaining cell viability comparable to that of conventional cuvette-based EP.
authors: Jaiswal B, Islam MN, Gagnon ZR.

title: Phylogenetic harmonization of cross-cohort vaginal microbiome data for machine-learning prediction of preterm birth

title: ASCC1 Promotes Malignant Progression of Pancreatic Cancer by Regulating the NF-κB Signaling Pathway
abstract: Abstract  Background  Pancreatic cancer is a highly aggressive malignancy with an extremely low five-year survival rate, underscoring an urgent need to identify novel molecular targets. ASCC1, a key component of the ASC-1 complex, plays a critical role in transcriptional regulation and DNA repair. Recent studies have suggested that ASCC1 might be involved in tumorigenesis; however, its function in pancreatic cancer remains largely undefined. Methods  In this study, we utilized the TCGA-PAAD dataset to screen for prognostically relevant genes using Cox regression and LASSO regression analyses, which identified ASCC1 as a candidate marker. The expression of ASCC1 in pancreatic cancer tissues was subsequently validated by immunohistochemistry and Western blot analyses. ASCC1 knockdown cell lines were established to assess cellular proliferation, migration, and invasion via CCK-8, Transwell, and wound healing assays, respectively. Changes in NF-κB and EMT-related protein expression were evaluated by Western blot. In vivo, a subcutaneous xenograft model in nude mice was employed to validate the functional impact of ASCC1 knockdown. Additionally, GSEA and ssGSEA were applied to explore the involvement of related signaling pathways and immune characteristics. Results  ASCC1 was significantly overexpressed in pancreatic cancer and correlated with poor clinical outcomes. Knockdown of ASCC1 markedly inhibited cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, accompanied by reduced expression levels of phosphorylated p65 and phosphorylated IκBα, and suppression of the EMT process. In the nude mouse xenograft model, ASCC1 knockdown significantly retarded tumor growth. Furthermore, GSEA revealed enrichment of the NF-κB signaling pathway, while immune analyses indicated that high ASCC1 expression was associated with increased infiltration of various immune cell subsets and a positive correlation with immune checkpoint molecules. Conclusions  The findings indicate that high ASCC1 expression in pancreatic cancer is associated with adverse prognosis and may promote tumor progression by activating the NF-κB pathway, inducing EMT, and modulating the tumor immune microenvironment. ASCC1 may thus serve as a promising prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target for pancreatic cancer.
authors: Wang N, feng R, Zhou H, Li C, Cui J, Wang F, Wang F, Cui Y, Chen Y.

title: Influence of Biotic and Abiotic Factors on the Gut Microbiome of the Western Honey Bee
abstract: Abstract    The gut microbiome of the honey bee plays key roles in digestion, growth and immunity. While there is some evidence that pathogens, such as  Nosema  , modulate the composition of honey bee gut microbiota, field-based studies assessing other environmental cofactors, are lacking. This knowledge gap constrains both disease management strategies and policy development for honey bee protection. This study examined the effects of  Nosema  , arable land use, seasonality and latitude on honey bee gut microbiota under natural conditions across Great Britain. Using worker bees collected via a citizen science beekeeper network, we extracted DNA from digestive tissues. This was analysed using qPCR to detect  Nosema ceranae  and  Nosema apis  , alongside 16S rRNA metabarcoding to characterise microbiome composition. Approximately 40% of colonies contained the parasite  N. ceranae  , while  N. apis  was not detected. Increases in the amount of arable land cover surrounding hives significantly reduced  N. ceranae  gene copy number. Although  N. ceranae  caused significant shifts in microbiome diversity indices, environmental fitting (envfit) permutation tests revealed this was not a significant factor in influencing the gut composition in comparison to other factors such as seasonal variation. Both seasonality and latitude indicated that climate and honey bee diet shapes the honey bee gut microbiome. Multivariate analyses identified shifts in both core and low-abundance taxa in arable landscapes, highlighting the influence of dietary differences and increased pesticide exposure upon the gut microbiota. Collectively, these findings improve our understanding of factors associated with declining honey bee health and colony collapse.
authors: Bennett MJR, Woodcock BA, Busi SB, Pywell R, Savage J, Gweon HS, Suresh M, Newbold LK.

title: Cross-Omics Identification of Core Epithelial Genes Associated with Folate Metabolism in Cervical Cancer and Prediction of an IL1RN/VEGFA Diagnostic Model and Candidate Drugs
abstract: Abstract  This study integrated single-cell transcriptomics, bulk transcriptomics, GWAS, spatial transcriptomics, and drug-gene data to identify core epithelial genes associated with folate metabolism in cervical cancer. scPagwas revealed the strongest association between epithelial cells and genetic risk for the disease; hdWGCNA and WGCNA, combined with differential expression and folate metabolism gene sets, identified IL1RN and VEGFA. In the CESC cohort, IL1RN expression was downregulated and VEGFA was upregulated; external validation confirmed this trend, and the AUC of the two-gene diagnostic model was 0.771 (95% CI: 0.685–0.848). Enrichment analysis indicated that both genes are involved in DNA repair, the cell cycle, the VEGF/mTOR pathway, and the folate one-carbon pathway, and are associated with immune infiltration. Single-cell localization analysis showed that both IL1RN and VEGFA are expressed in epithelial cells; pseudo-time-series, virtual knockout, and spatial transcriptomics analyses revealed their dynamic expression, regulatory networks, and spatial heterogeneity. Molecular docking analysis demonstrated that beclomethasone can simultaneously target both IL1RN and VEGFA. In summary, IL1RN/VEGFA may serve as potential diagnostic biomarkers for cervical cancer, and beclomethasone is a candidate therapeutic agent.
authors: Yan Z, Gao G, Tang S, Yang Z, Xin J, Lin H, Pan L, Chen S, Teng S, Zhang L, Chen J.

title: Nickel(II) coordination compounds of 4'-chloro-fenamic acid: characterization and biological activity.
abstract: With the aim of investigating whether the coordination of fenamates to Ni(II) affects the biological profile, a chloro-derivative of fenamic acid (4'-chloro-fenamic acid) was synthesized and used as a ligand for the synthesis of seven nickel(II) complexes in the absence or presence of the nitrogen-donors pyridine, β-picoline, 1H-imidazole, 1,10-phenanthroline, 2,9-dimethyl-1,10-phenanthroline, and 2,2'-bipyridylamine. The characterization of the resultant Ni(II) complexes was performed with diverse techniques (elemental analysis, molar conductivity measurements, mass spectrometry, IR and UV-vis spectroscopy, and single-crystal X-ray crystallography). The compounds were evaluated for their in vitro biological activity in terms of the antioxidant activity via free radical scavenging and H2O2 reduction, the antimicrobial activity against two Gram-positive and two Gram-negative bacterial strains, the interaction with calf-thymus DNA, the cleavage of supercoiled pBR322 plasmid DNA (pDNA) in the dark or under UVB/UVA/visible light irradiation, and the binding affinity toward bovine and human serum albumins. The antioxidant activity of the compounds is noteworthy against 2,2'-azinobis-(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) radicals and H2O2, and comparable with that of the reference compounds. The complexes exhibit notable antimicrobial activity against the strains tested. The compounds interact with calf-thymus DNA via intercalation with binding constants of 105-106 M-1 magnitude. The pDNA-cleavage ability of the compounds is significantly enhanced under irradiation. All the compounds can bind tightly and reversibly to both albumins tested.
authors: Galina AA, Malis G, Damala AZ, Fylaktakidou KC, Hatzidimitriou AG, Kalogiannis S, Psomas G.

title: Structural programming of inorganic materials using DNA frameworks.
abstract: Supramolecular assembly through non-covalent interactions is an attractive strategy for building ordered functional systems. DNA exhibits precise programmability at the nanoscale and self-assembles via Watson-Crick pairing. These properties make it an ideal candidate for large-scale supramolecular templates. Since the emergence of DNA nanotechnology, DNA supramolecular frameworks have become powerful tools to regulate inorganic material structures, enabling direct functional design at the molecular level. Inorganic materials offer excellent mechanical and chemical properties. DNA framework structure programming exploits geometric constraints and site specificity to precisely control nucleation, growth, and alignment, enabling the formation of well-defined morphologies. This review summarizes progress in the structural programming of inorganic materials using DNA framework structures. It first traces the development of DNA nanotechnology and highlights its advantages in templating. Then, methods for constructing DNA framework structures, interaction mechanisms guiding programmatic inorganic growth, and characterization techniques are explored. Key strategies including metallization, silicification, calcification, and nanocluster assembly are examined, with a focus on their development, optimization, and performance metrics. Application prospects in nanoelectronic devices, medicine, and chemical catalysis are outlined. Finally, key issues and challenges in DNA-guided synthesis are discussed, along with an outlook on future development. The review aims to provide a systematic reference for controlled structural formation of inorganic materials via DNA framework structures and promote high-quality inorganic material design.
authors: Yu F, Li B, Jia S, Liu X, Lin Y.

title: Cotton Cultivar Effects on DNA-Based Quantification of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum Race 4 in Soil.
abstract: The soilborne fungal pathogen Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum race 4 (FOV4) poses a risk to U.S. cotton (Gossypium spp.) following detection in California, Texas, and New Mexico. This study evaluated the influence of cotton cultivar resistance on relative variation in soil FOV4 DNA quantity, a proxy for inoculum density, in a naturally infested field over 2 years. Field trials included Upland (G. hirsutum) and Pima (G. barbadense) cotton cultivars and measured plant mortality, root necrosis, and lint yield. Bulk soil FOV4 DNA was quantified by qPCR at three timepoints each year: planting, midseason (first flower), and late season (crop maturity). Susceptible Pima cultivars exhibited the highest mortality, most severe necrosis, and lowest yields, whereas resistant Pima and Upland cultivars had lower necrosis with variable mortality and yield. Commercial Upland cultivars with differing degrees of susceptibility showed intermediate mortality and necrosis yet high yields. Midseason soil FOV4 DNA levels varied among cultivars in both years (P = 0.011, 0.028), with elevated levels in a subset of susceptible cultivars. Late season DNA levels varied among cultivars in 2021 (P = 0.017) but not in 2020 (P = 0.080) and did not correspond to resistance designations. Within cultivars, mortality correlated with FOV4 DNA levels at planting (P R2 [R2MF] = 0.810) and late season (P R2MF = 0.802), necrosis with late season DNA levels (P R2 = 0.849), and yield showed no correlation with FOV4 DNA at any timepoint. These findings relate host response to DNA-based soil pathogen quantification and emphasize resistance variation as a determinant of FOV4 disease ecology and management success.
authors: Chagoya JC, Monclova-Santana C, Chappell T, Wheeler TA, Ulloa M.

title: Enhancing Aquatic Persistence Assessments: Effects of Photosensitizers and Surfactants on Photochemical Degradation in the Environment.
abstract: Photochemical processes substantially influence the environmental fate of chemicals, yet current persistence assessments rarely account for indirect photochemistry or interfacial effects. Here, we systematically investigated the photodegradation of the fungicide carbendazim, which is classified as persistent in aquatic environments according to current regulations. Experiments were conducted in aqueous systems in presence of key environmental photosensitizers (nitrate, chromophoric dissolved organic matter [CDOM], iron) and representative non-ionic surfactants, with a particular focus on the role of the air-water interface. Across 36 controlled irradiation experiments, carbendazim degradation was strongly enhanced by nitrate, CDOM, and Fe-CDOM interactions. Additionally, surfactants induced accelerated degradation after a pronounced lag phase, highlighting the importance of processes at the air/water interface. In contrast to the persistence classification of carbendazim, first-order degradation rates of up to 9.68 × 10-2 d-1 were observed, corresponding to extrapolated environmental half-lives of 75 days even under the low-light conditions of southern Sweden, and of ∼46 days at the sunniest European location defined by the Forum for the Co-ordination of Pesticide Fate Models and their Use (FOCUS). Dedicated experiments indicated that interfacial enrichment of carbendazim, surfactant, and CDOM are a prerequisite for efficient photosensitized transformations. Bulk-phase experiments showed that increasing bicarbonate concentrations inhibited carbendazim degradation, confirming hydroxyl radicals as the dominant oxidants under these conditions. A case study with two natural waters further indicated significant photodegradation in the aquatic environment (environmental half-lives, DT50, of 5.8-106 days for low-light conditions). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that interfacial processes and indirect photochemistry can dominate the environmental transformation of recalcitrant chemicals such as carbendazim. Persistence assessments that rely solely on degradation in the dark may therefore underestimate degradation rates in sunlit surface waters. Incorporating representative irradiation, photosensitizers, and interfacial processes into regulatory higher-tier assessments will enable more realistic evaluations of chemical persistence in aquatic environments.
authors: Brüggemann M, Rey B, Meunier L, George C.

title: From epigenetic marks to biomarker qualification in fetal alcohol spectrum disorder: a critical review of DNA methylation, chromatin and regulatory RNA.
abstract: IntroductionFetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is a preventable cause of neurodevelopmental disability, yet diagnosis remains multidisciplinary and affected people may be identified late. Epigenetic research has expanded since the 2017-2018 primer series.Areas coveredThis critical narrative review evaluates DNA methylation, chromatin and regulatory RNA by tissue, developmental window, intended use and evidence maturity. An author-generated, unvalidated four-gate heuristic separates discovery, analytical validation, clinical validation and clinical utility. A fetal alcohol syndrome blood methylation classifier has promising development-stage evidence, while maternal extracellular-vesicle-associated microRNA remains a proof-of-concept prenatal candidate. Acetyl-CoA synthetase 2 (ACSS2) provides one experimentally supported metabolism-chromatin link in mice alongside other plausible mechanisms. Small cohorts, tissue differences, ancestry, parental exposure histories and limited independent validation constrain interpretation.Expert opinionNo epigenetic assay reviewed here is suitable for stand-alone FASD diagnosis. Clinical utility discussions describe future research, not demonstrated benefit. Progress requires reproducible assays, independent evaluation in the intended population, and evidence that testing improves care without increasing stigma or inequity.
authors: Mandal C, Jung KH, Chai YG.

title: TurboID proximity labeling combined with structure prediction identifies C3H61/AtTZF5 as a tail-binding protein of Arabidopsis class VIII myosin ATM1.
abstract: Higher plants possess two classes of myosin molecular motors, class XI and class VIII, both unique to the plant lineage. The diverse cellular functions of class XI myosins, including organelle transport and nuclear positioning, have been elucidated largely through systematic identification of cargo adaptor proteins that bind to their globular tail domains (GTDs). In contrast, no proteome-wide screen for class VIII myosin tail-binding proteins has been reported; the few known interacting proteins were each discovered through studies focused on the binding partner rather than on the myosin itself, leaving the full repertoire of class VIII myosin-associated proteins largely unknown. Here, we employed TurboID-based proximity labeling to systematically identify proteins associated with the GTD of the class VIII myosin ATM1 in Arabidopsis thaliana, as this approach covalently biotinylates neighboring proteins in vivo, enabling their identification even after proteolytic degradation during cell lysis. We identified 233 non-redundant candidate ATM1-proximal proteins. Candidates were prioritized by AlphaFold3-based protein complex structure prediction and evaluated experimentally. By integrating AlphaFold3 prediction, co-immunoprecipitation, subcellular co-localization in living cells under stress, and structure-guided interface mutagenesis, we identified C3H61/AtTZF5 as an ATM1 tail-binding protein. C3H61/AtTZF5, a tandem CCCH zinc finger protein whose family members have been implicated in mRNA turnover, co-localized with the ATM1 tail in eIF4A2-positive granules under heat stress, and targeted substitutions at the AlphaFold3-predicted interface completely abolished the interaction. These findings strongly support a direct association between ATM1 and C3H61/AtTZF5, suggesting a possible link between this class VIII myosin and post-transcriptional gene regulation during stress responses.

title: Biomass to bioenergy transition through sustainable bioconversion and circular bioeconomy strategies.
abstract: Access to modern electricity and clean cooking technologies remains uneven across much of Africa, despite the continent's abundant biomass resources, which have the potential to enhance energy security while supporting the transition toward a circular bioeconomy. However, a substantial proportion of agricultural, forestry, municipal, and marine organic residues is still treated as waste rather than valorized within the formal energy sector. Morocco exemplifies this disconnect. Although the country has achieved near-universal rural electrification, biomass derived from agricultural and marine resources contributes less than 2% of the modern energy mix, highlighting that the principal challenge lies not in resource availability but in the development of efficient conversion pathways and integrated deployment strategies. This review examines recent advances in biomass-to-bioenergy technologies, with particular emphasis on sustainable bioconversion processes, including enzymatic hydrolysis, microbial fermentation, anaerobic digestion, and microbial fuel cells. Beyond evaluating technological progress, we assess research trends, innovation dynamics, and technology transfer through bibliometric and patent analyses to identify leading research areas, emerging technologies, and geographical disparities across Africa. We further discuss the role of life cycle assessment in evaluating the environmental sustainability of biomass conversion pathways and demonstrate its importance in identifying low-carbon alternatives capable of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. We conclude that Africa's energy sovereignty depends on moving away from generic policies toward integrated, country-specific deployment strategies that prioritize locally available biomass within circular bioeconomy frameworks.
authors: Niya B, Mahmud A, Ou-Douaou A, Boutafda A, Benhida R, Danouche M.

title: Integrative miRNA-multi-omics analysis of brain-metastasis predisposition in non-small cell lung cancer prioritizes HDAC inhibitors and anti-miR-330-3p as hypothesis-generating therapeutic candidates.
abstract: Brain metastasis (BM) is the leading cause of death in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet its molecular drivers remain poorly targeted. Here we present an integrative in-silico pipeline that moves from miRNA discovery to therapeutic hypothesis generation. Reprocessing the GSE23019 miRNA microarray cohort (7 BM+ versus 5 BM- primary tumors) recovered the published BM-associated miRNAs miR-328 and miR-330-3p and, through validated miRNA-target interactions, yielded a signature of 828 up-regulated and 177 down-regulated genes enriched for extracellular-matrix and vasculature programs. Resampling analyses show this discovery-cohort signal is directionally reproducible but statistically fragile (no probe passes FDR control; permutation P = 0.29), so we carry it forward only as a seed for independent testing. In 519 TCGA lung adenocarcinomas, multi-omics factor analysis linked the signature to a latent stromal factor whose association with worse overall survival persisted after adjustment for stage, age, sex and smoking (adjusted HR 1.26 per SD, 95% CI 1.07-1.48), and miRNA-target anti-correlation nominated miR-330-3p-> VEGFA as the strongest effector axis (Spearman rho = -0.37). Connectivity mapping against ~ 693,000 LINCS L1000 signatures identified histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibition as the only enriched reversal mechanism (odds ratio 30.7, FDR = 0.0019). Blood-brain-barrier and lipophilicity machine-learning models ranked panobinostat first among 30 candidates, and anti-miR-330-3p is the prioritized miRNA therapeutic. Single-cell analysis of 208,506 lung-cancer transcriptomes and spatial co-localization across 13 NSCLC pucks mapped the program to cancer-associated fibroblasts, indicating the bulk signature tracks stromal composition. Knowledge-graph propagation recovered HDAC1 and HDAC2 among top-ranked genes, though sensitivity analyses show this convergence partly reflects hub structure. All nominations are hypothesis-generating and require experimental validation.
authors: Shah FH, Cho JS, Konishi H, Lee SH, Jo YR, Huh SJ, Jung J, Jeong NY, Chung HJ.

title: CLEC1B and RAC1 in peripheral immune remodeling associated with sleep disturbance: an exploratory integrative study.
abstract: BackgroundSleep disturbance is closely linked to immune dysfunction, but the molecular features of associated peripheral immune remodeling remain incompletely defined.ResultsIn this exploratory study, we integrated blood eQTL data and GWAS summary statistics with mouse PBMC single-cell data, a human PBMC transcriptome cohort, and mouse PBMC measurements. The single-cell dataset comprised one control, one 24-hour sleep-deprivation, and one 48-hour sleep-deprivation library. Descriptive single-cell patterns showed contraction of the B-cell compartment and expansion of granulocytes. Mendelian randomization nominally prioritized RAC1 and CLEC1B, with limited co-localization support. Both genes showed lower expression in the human cohort and were associated with altered B-cell communication and metabolic states. In mouse PBMCs (n = 3 per group), Clec1b qPCR showed a downward trend (P = 0.072), whereas Rac1 qPCR expression was lower after sleep deprivation (P = 0.017). Lane-level western blot analysis also showed lower CLEC1B (P = 0.0056) and RAC1 (P = 0.0016) protein abundance.ConclusionsThese exploratory integrative analyses nominate CLEC1B and RAC1 as candidate genes associated with peripheral B-cell remodeling in a sleep-disturbance context. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant targeted functional studies of their roles in sleep-related immune remodeling.
authors: Li Y, Liu C, Zheng H, Lin J.

title: Harnessing catalytic knowledge to guide enzyme discovery and evolution with AlphaEnzyme
abstract: Retrieving an enzyme for a target reaction provides a starting point for evolution, but predicting how to improve it remains difficult. This requires connecting evolutionary information with the structural and chemical context of catalysis. Here we present AlphaEnzyme, an enzyme foundation model built on a structure-grounded representation of an enzyme paired with its reaction, from which catalytic compatibility, kinetics and mutational response are read out together. On a time-separated benchmark, AlphaEnzyme achieves a top-1 catalyst retrieval success rate of 30.1%, against 17.2% for the strongest baseline. Michaelis constant predictions achieve the highest rank correlations among the compared methods, reaching 0.64 for enzymes sharing at most 40% identity with the kinetic training set. The model also enriches high-fitness TrpB variants at a budget of 16 candidates without target-specific fitness training. In prospective transaminase engineering, several prioritized variants exceed the parent, with the best design yielding a 30.4-fold increase in product signal in a lysate-based assay while retaining (R)-selectivity. Together, AlphaEnzyme provides a common molecular basis for selecting starting enzymes and prioritizing sequence changes for their improvement.
authors: Liu Y, Zheng S.

title: Metformin lowers HMGA1a and RBM3 protein in breast cancer cells, and its effect on ESR1 splicing depends on cell density and exposure time
abstract: The ESR1 gene produces ERα46, an N-terminally truncated isoform generated by skipping of exon 1, which is reduced in tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer cells. We have reported that metformin moves the ratio of full-length ERα to ERα46 in opposite directions in MCF-7 cells and their tamoxifen-resistant subline TAMR1, and that metformin reduces TAMR1 xenograft growth (Harada et al., Am J Pharm Health Res 2022;10(11)). That report leaves two questions open: whether the effect is dosedependent and stable across culture conditions, and what splicing factor might carry it. Here we report the experiments that bear on both. Across a full dose range from 0.25 to 5 mM at high seeding density, metformin produced no consistent change in the full-length share of ESR1 transcript in either line: densitometry of the gel gave 42%, 43%, 42%, 43%, 45% and 48% in MCF-7 cells and 55%, 44%, 52%, 47%, 68% and 43% in TAMR1 cells. The reported shift therefore depends on the seeding density used, and the comparison that produced it is not reproduced at high density. At low density the MCF-7 response persisted to 48 h (52%, 62% and 68% at 0, 2.5 and 5 mM). Metformin lowered HMGA1a protein in MCF-7 cells and showed the same tendency in TAMR1 cells, at both seeding densities, and lowered RBM3 protein in TAMR1 cells at 24 and 48 h. HMGA1a is the factor we previously showed to generate ERα46 by trapping U1 snRNP at an upstream pseudo-5′ splice site, so a fall in HMGA1a predicts less ERα46, the opposite of what was seen in TAMR1 cells at low density. The fall in RBM3, the protein through which metformin alters splicing in myotonic dystrophy, is the more plausible candidate. RT-PCR of the xenograft tumours from the earlier study detected full-length ESR1 transcript in the untreated and tamoxifen-plus-metformin groups but not in the singleagent groups, with amplification failing in several lanes; these panels do not separate the treatments. Taken together, the direction of the metformin effect on ESR1 splicing is conditional on culture density and does not survive a dose-response test at high density, and HMGA1a is unlikely to be the factor that carries it.
authors: Harada Y, Tanaka T, Hamaguchi Y, Horita Y, Harada H, Mori M, Murata Y, Ohe K.

title: FeatureMAP enables network-guided interpretation of untargeted metabolomics
abstract: Untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics generates thousands of features, but incomplete metabolite annotation and reliance on predefined pathways limit their biological interpretation. Here we present FeatureMAP, an LC-MS feature-centric computational framework that integrates multi-evidence metabolite annotation, network-guided refinement, metabolic module discovery, and structured large language model-based functional interpretation. Across ten public datasets, FeatureMAP improved MS1-based metabolite candidate prioritization while reducing annotation redundancy. In semi-synthetic benchmarks, FeatureMAP recovered coordinated metabolic perturbations, achieving 92% recovery of a simulated perturbation, and distinguished concurrent metabolic processes. Controlled benchmarks further evaluated functional interpretation under competing metabolite-level signals. Based on FeatureMAP, we additionally developed PhenoMAP, a phenotype-aware knowledge graph comprising 12,929 dysregulated metabolic modules from 501 human metabolomics studies spanning 326 phenotypes. Module-level comparisons revealed reproducible metabolic similarities across independent studies and biologically supported relationships among phenotypes. Application to Alzheimer's disease cerebrospinal fluid and cellular datasets identified convergent membrane-lipid alterations and implicated galactose-linked glycosphingolipid remodeling. Together, FeatureMAP and PhenoMAP enable network-grounded interpretation of incompletely annotated LC-MS metabolomics data and systematic investigation of metabolic dysregulation across biological conditions.
authors: Wang Y, Zhang F, Peng G, Qiu L, Zeng L, Liu Y, Kinchagawat J, Yang X, Liu C, Johnson C, Su Q, Wang C, Shen X.

title: Beneath functional traits: material organization in postgenomic ecology and evolution
abstract: Ecology has progressed from describing species diversity through taxonomic indices to explaining ecological processes using functional traits. Yet traits such as growth, body size, reproduction, and resource-use efficiency are compressed representations of biological systems whose functions emerge from complex material organization. Here, I develop trait compression as the many-to-one relationship through which distinct biochemical and material states generate similar conventional ecological traits. Drawing on the view of organisms as open, far-from-equilibrium multielement systems, I argue that elemental inventories and log compositional coordinates (LCCs) offer tractable descriptions of material organization without requiring exhaustive molecular reconstruction. Environmental geochemical heterogeneity in natural rock pools and ionomic variation among laboratory-maintained isolates of the zooplankter, Daphnia, illustrate the diversity of material conditions and organismal states. Observations of experimentally evolved populations of the bacterium, Serratia marcescens, demonstrate that similar growth rates can accompany distinct multielement compositions. Reanalysis of recombinant Daphnia pulicaria clones further reveals substantial variation in body phosphorus (P) content among clones exhibiting overlapping growth rates, but little improvement in predicting growth across phosphorus environments when body P is included alongside initial growth. Together, these observations illustrate trait compression while distinguishing material heterogeneity from its predictive consequences. I propose that material-state differences become ecologically consequential when they predict distinct responses among organisms exhibiting similar initial traits. Trait compression thus identifies a testable limitation of conventional trait-based approaches and provides a framework for connecting biochemical organization to ecological prediction and evolutionary outcomes.
authors: Jeyasingh P.
