title: When, Where, and How Experience Becomes Structure: Mechanisms for Recursive Self-Improvement in LLM Agents
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) studies how AI systems modify themselves and carry those changes into the generation of subsequent improvements. LLM agents can pursue this process by using interaction experience to revise Prompt, Memory, Skill, and Harness in some cases while keeping the task-execution model’s weights fixed. However, execution feedback does not directly specify which component should change, and a locally successful revision may not remain useful across tasks or subsequent improvement cycles. Understanding how experience becomes persistent agent structure therefore requires examining when evidence justifies a change, where that change should act, and how it is constructed, verified, and retained. This survey connects four components--Prompt, Memory, Skill, and Harness--with seven analytical functions: Collect, Evaluate, Diagnose, Abstract, Update, Verify, and Consolidate. The resulting framework supports comparisons of instruction revision, memory management, skill construction and maintenance, and Harness evolution through their update loops. These comparisons examine how mechanisms use observations to construct candidate changes, distinguishing feedback that triggers revision from evidence that supports retention. The analysis further addresses coordinated updates across components and the revision or retirement of retained components as tasks, tools, and models change. Finally, we identify cross-component attribution, long-term effectiveness, and independent validation as key challenges, and outline controlled and longitudinal evaluations of task-performance gains, the contribution of inherited state, and the effectiveness of subsequent updates.
authors: Dai S, Ruan J, Zhang B, Xu Z, Cheng L, Zeng K, Su Z, Hong F, Jia N, Shi W, Li D, Luo C, Chen Y, Ma Z, Yan X, Li Y, Xing M, Mao H, Dai B, Zeng Z, Fan G.

title: Oxygen fugacity, temperature, and pressure of Siberian eclogitic diamonds: Implications for the Archaean convecting mantle redox state.
abstract: Kimberlite-borne eclogite xenoliths ultimately derive from ancient subducted oceanic crust. Some specimens still record the chemical and redox conditions of their igneous protoliths, allowing a view into contemporaneous convecting mantle sources. However, accurate reconstructions are limited because eclogites have been exposed to metasomatism in the subcontinental mantle for billions of years. Here, we investigated garnet and clinopyroxene inclusions, both touching and nontouching pairs, in 19 eclogitic diamonds from the Siberian craton, hence shielded from post-entrapment overprint. Inclusion compositions indicate average sampling depths of 180 to 280 km, temperatures of 1030° to 1540°C (±60°C), and redox conditions, for most of the samples, oxidized enough for diamonds to have originated from water(carbonate)-rich fluids. The reconstructed bulk composition points to basaltic oceanic crust formed from an Archaean convecting mantle region that was more oxygen-depleted than today, providing compelling evidence of redox heterogeneities in the source rocks of ancient oceanic crust.
authors: Marras G, Mikhailenko D, McCammon CA, Aulbach S, Lu Y, Tao R, Logvinova A, Zedgenizov D, Stagno V.

title: Local translational program at the muscle-tendon junction endows domain identity in muscle syncytia.
abstract: How cells establish specialized subdomains is a fundamental question in cell and tissue biology. Skeletal muscle fibers, among the largest cells in the body, are multinucleated and form distinct regions such as the neuromuscular and myotendinous junctions (MTJs), the latter forming a critical interface between muscle and tendon that transmits contractile force. While transcriptional heterogeneity among myonuclei has been described, whether local translation contributes to domain identity remains unknown, largely due to the lack of tools for domain-specific manipulation. Here, we introduce MTJ-AAV, a viral system that enables selective genetic targeting of MTJ myonuclei. This approach allowed MTJ-specific ribosome tagging and revealed extensive translational regulation underlying MTJ biology and its remodeling during exercise. Untranslated regions of these transcripts were sufficient to control regionalized translation. Notably, the Krüpper-like factor-family transcription factors emerged as translationally up-regulated targets at the MTJ, where they drive local gene expression. Our findings establish local translation as a key layer of subcellular specialization and provide a versatile toolkit for dissecting spatial molecular regulation within muscle syncytia.
authors: El Khazen N, de Carvalho Neves J, Franke V, Smith C, Mankhong S, Jauliac E, Yedigaryan L, Lefebvre E, Akalin A, Maire P, Kim M.

title: Iron sourcing strategies and adaptive protein responses to iron deprivation in the intraerythrocytic parasite Babesia divergens.
abstract: Iron is indispensable for the survival and pathogenicity of Babesia parasites, yet the mechanisms underlying its acquisition remain largely unresolved. In contrast to other apicomplexan parasites, tick-borne Babesia species rapidly lose the parasitophorous vacuole following erythrocyte invasion and do not form hemozoin, suggesting the evolution of distinct strategies for iron metabolism. Here, we demonstrate that Babesia divergens utilizes a sequential, multi-route iron acquisition system to meet its metabolic demands within host erythrocytes. Kinetic uptake analyses reveal a pronounced preference for ferrous iron (Fe2+), which is imported through an active, energy-dependent process supported by extracellular ferric reductase activity that converts host-derived ferric iron (Fe3+) into a bioavailable form prior to uptake. Using immunogold transmission electron microscopy, we provide evidence for the active internalization of host transferrin and show that parasite proliferation is dose-dependently inhibited by apo-transferrin, establishing iron as a limiting factor for parasite growth. Quantitative proteomic profiling revealed a limited, stage-specific response to deferoxamine-induced iron deprivation. Three proteins showed statistically significant changes in abundance in free merozoites: the conserved multipass membrane protein Bdiv_019230 increased, whereas the hypothetical protein Bdiv_002300 and the putative serine hydroxymethyltransferase Bdiv_027330 decreased. No proteins reached the statistical significance threshold in intraerythrocytic parasites. These results identify a small set of statistically supported candidates for investigating the response of extracellular B. divergens merozoites to iron-restricted conditions.
authors: Levytska V, Mach J, Robbertse L, Goulding CW, Malych R, Jalovecka M, Sutak R, Sojka D.

title: Integrative analysis reveals shared biomarkers and pathways in osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis using machine learning and single-cell sequencing.
abstract: BackgroundOsteoporosis (OP) and Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) are prevalent chronic diseases characterized by bone loss and immune dysregulation. Evidence suggests that patients with RA are at increased risk of developing OP; however, the shared molecular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely understood.MethodsPublicly available bulk transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets for OP and RA were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to identify shared gene modules associated with both diseases. Functional enrichment and protein-protein interaction analyses were performed to characterize common biological pathways. Machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest (RF) and Support Vector Machine (SVM), were used to identify and validate shared hub genes and to construct diagnostic models. Immune cell infiltration was evaluated using CIBERSORT, and the cellular localization of hub genes was further validated using scRNA-seq analysis.ResultsWGCNA identified 329 genes shared between OP- and RA-associated modules, which were significantly enriched in muscle-related processes, cytokine signaling, and immune-inflammatory pathways. RF analysis identified three shared candidate genes: ANO5, IL27RA, and CNTN3. Among these, ANO5 and IL27RA demonstrated consistent expression evidence and literature support, whereas CNTN3 emerged as a computationally nominated candidate requiring cautious interpretation and experimental validation. An SVM-based model incorporating these genes demonstrated robust predictive accuracy in both OP and RA validation cohorts. Immune infiltration analysis revealed distinct yet coordinated immune landscapes, with hub genes showing significant correlations with T cells, macrophages, B cells, and plasma cells. ScRNA-seq analysis revealed that ANO5 was predominantly expressed in macrophages and fibroblasts, IL27RA was mainly enriched in T cells, whereas CNTN3 showed minimal enrichment at the single-cell level in both OP bone and RA synovial tissues.ConclusionThis integrative bioinformatics and machine learning study identifies shared molecular signatures and immune-related mechanisms underlying OP and RA. ANO5 and IL27RA emerge as robust candidate regulators linking immune dysregulation and bone remodeling, whereas CNTN3-although identified by machine learning-requires cautious interpretation and further investigation due to limited supporting evidence. These findings provide novel insights into the pathogenesis of RA-associated OP and highlight potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets for their comorbidity.
authors: Zhao J, Chen Y, Yang F, Tian C, Luo W, Su Z, Yang B, Liu W, Yang H.

title: In vivo Nupr1 regulates oxidative stress-endoplasmic reticulum stress crosstalk and mitochondria-dependent apoptosis in varicocele-related testicular injury.
abstract: Varicocele (VCL) is a major cause of male infertility and is closely associated with oxidative stress (OS)-induced testicular injury. Increasing evidence suggests that endoplasmic reticulum stress (ERS) interacts with OS and mitochondrial dysfunction in the pathogenesis of spermatogenic impairment, but the molecular regulators linking these processes remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated the role of Nupr1 in VCL-related testicular stress responses. Re-analysis of transcriptomic data from VCL rat testes identified Nupr1 as a candidate gene associated with OS, ERS, and apoptosis. Nupr1 expression was significantly increased in VCL testes and was similarly upregulated in GC-2 and TM4 cells under H2O2-induced OS or tunicamycin-induced ERS. Stable knockdown of Nupr1 in GC-2 cells reduced viability under oxidative challenge, increased intracellular ROS accumulation, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, and enhanced apoptosis, accompanied by increased cleaved caspase-3 expression and an elevated Bax/Bcl-2 ratio. Notably, Nupr1 deficiency attenuated the adaptive ERS response, as shown by reduced expression of GRP78, IRE1/p-IRE1, PERK/p-PERK, and ATF6. Pharmacological induction of ERS with tunicamycin further worsened cell injury in Nupr1-deficient cells, whereas 4-PBA failed to restore cell viability or GRP78 expression. Collectively, these findings indicate that Nupr1 is involved in the cellular stress response relevant to VCL and may help maintain adaptive UPR signaling and mitochondrial homeostasis in spermatogenic cells under oxidative stress.
authors: Jiang X, Tang L, Ma Z, Wu X, Zhang Z, Nian W, Li T, Liao Y.

title: Integrated Single-Step Duplex CRISPR-Based System for Point-of-Care Detection of Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Treponema pallidum Directly from Whole Blood.
abstract: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and syphilis are two major sexually transmitted diseases that pose serious threats to public health, underscoring the urgent need for fast and sensitive diagnosis for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and Treponema pallidum (TP). Here, we developed a single-step duplex CRISPR assay that integrated reverse transcription, recombinase polymerase amplification, in vitro transcription, and CRISPR/Cas12a and Cas13a detection for simultaneous HIV and TP nucleic acid testing. We further engineered a fully integrated, low-cost microfluidic chip that consolidated whole-blood sample processing, nucleic acid release, and single-step duplex CRISPR detection. The chip featured a rapid plasma separator with a press-actuated design that removed inhibitors and extracted plasma within minutes without external equipment. The entire process was coupled with a homemade smartphone-based portable device that provided thermal incubation, dual-channel fluorescence excitation, and automated image analysis via a dedicated mobile application. This integrated system enables "sample-to-answer" detection within 30 min directly from whole blood, achieving a limit of detection of 2.5 copies/μL of both HIV and TP and demonstrating 100% sensitivity and specificity concordant with the real-time PCR in 51 cases of clinical samples. This work demonstrates a transformative point-of-care diagnostic platform that combines minimal user steps, equipment independence, and robust multiplex detection for decentralized pathogen testing.
authors: Xu Z, Wang Y, Wei M, Miao P, Zhang H, Li M, Wang S, Rong Z, He K.

title: A DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein-Arp complex-CAPZA3 scaffold is essential for perinuclear theca assembly and fertilization.
abstract: Fertilization is a fundamental biological process that enables the fusion of a spermatozoon with an oocyte to initiate embryonic development. However, the underlying mechanisms leading to fertilization failure remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrated that the actin-related protein (Arp) family members ACTRT2 and ACTRT3 are essential for fertilization in both humans and mice, whereas ACTL10 is dispensable for fertility and the human-specific ACTL8 may play a role in early spermatogenesis. Ultrastructural and immunofluorescence analyses revealed that, during spermatogenesis, ACTRT2 or ACTRT3 deficiency disrupts the assembly of subacrosomal layer of the perinuclear theca (SAL-PT), leading to acrosome detachment and subsequent manchette abnormalities, which in turn impairs the formation of the postacrosomal sheath of the PT. These structural defects were accompanied by reduced abundance of the candidate sperm-borne oocyte-activating factors PAWP and PLCζ. Moreover, knockout of Actrt2 or Actrt3 severely impaired spermatozoa's ability to penetrate the zona pellucida during in vitro fertilization. Mechanistically, ACTRT2, ACTRT3, ACTL7A, ACTL7B, and ACTL9 form a testis-enriched Arp complex in the SAL-PT and maintain the stability of one another. This complex interacts with the PT protein CAPZA3, which subsequently binds and stabilizes PLCζ. Additionally, the Arp complex interacts with DPY19L2/FAM209-associated proteins to mediate acrosome anchoring to the nuclear envelope. Therefore, these findings established a sequential DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein-Arp complex-CAPZA3 scaffold extending from the nuclear envelope to the acrosome that is indispensable for fertilization. Collectively, we defined a previously unidentified structural and molecular framework for fertilization and provided insights into the diagnosis and treatment of fertilization failure.
authors: Ruan T, Shen G, Zhuo L, Zhang Y, Wang X, Tian E, Tian Y, Tang X, Chen D, Jiang C, Yang X, Ma J, Zhao S, Zhao C, Cui X, Jiang X, Yang Y, Wang Y, Shen Y.

title: Osteoclastogenesis associated gene signatures in postmenopausal low bone mineral density: cross-dataset transcriptomics and whole-blood validation.
abstract: BackgroundOsteoporosis is characterized by reduced bone mass and increased fracture risk, yet minimally invasive molecular correlates of postmenopausal low bone mineral density remain limited.MethodsWe independently reanalysed two human osteoclastogenesis RNA-seq datasets, GSE225974 and GSE246769, using differential-expression, Gene Ontology, KEGG, Hallmark gene set enrichment, and cross-dataset concordance analyses. Six candidate genes, LGALSL, FAXDC2, DHCR7, MYL9, RHOC, and ITGB5, were subsequently evaluated by RT-qPCR in whole blood from 100 postmenopausal women with normal bone mineral density (n=30), osteopenia (n=30), or osteoporosis (n=40).ResultsAcross the two RNA-seq datasets, 1,782 differentially expressed genes were shared, including 1,240 concordantly upregulated and 385 concordantly downregulated genes, with strong cross-dataset effect-size correlation (r=0.74). GO and KEGG analyses identified replicated sterol/lipid, skeletal-development, adhesion/integrin, and actin-cytoskeletal programs, while Hallmark GSEA identified 22 concordantly enriched gene sets, including oxidative phosphorylation, fatty-acid metabolism, and cholesterol homeostasis. BMD was positively correlated with calcium intake and physical activity. Conversely, deteriorating bone health was positively associated with high cholesterol, low BMI, early menopause. All six candidate genes were significantly and concordantly upregulated during osteoclastogenesis in both datasets. Whole-blood RT-qPCR analysis demonstrated progressively higher relative expression across normal-BMD, osteopenia, and osteoporosis groups for all six candidates. Expression analysis from the serum validated LGALSL, RHOC, MYL9 and ITGB5 elevated expression in osteoporosis cases.ConclusionThese findings identify reproducible osteoclastogenesis-associated transcriptional programs and support the six candidate genes as candidate signature correlating with the postmenopausal BMD status.
authors: Anbreen N, Iqbal MJ, Wahab H, Manzoor S, Tariq A, Aruge S, Menotta M.

title: Quinalphos-induced chromosomal instability, DNA damage, and Bax/Bcl-2 dysregulation in mouse bone marrow: protective effects of piperine.
abstract: Quinalphos (QNP), an organophosphate insecticide, is known to induce genotoxic and cytotoxic effects in non-target organisms. This study evaluated the impact of subacute QNP exposure on chromosomal stability, DNA integrity, and apoptosis-related gene expression in bone marrow cells of male Swiss albino mice, and assessed the genoprotective potential of piperine (PIP), a bioactive compound from Piper nigrum. Mice were allocated into six groups: control (2% gum acacia), QNP I (0.375 mg/kg b.w.), QNP II (0.75 mg/kg b.w.), PIP alone (10 mg/kg b.w.), QNP I + PIP, and QNP II + PIP. All treatments were administered orally for 28 days. Genotoxicity was evaluated using micronucleus, chromosomal aberration, and alkaline comet assays. The expression of Bax and Bcl-2 was assessed by quantitative real-time PCR. QNP exposure produced a dose-dependent increase in micronucleated erythrocytes, chromosomal aberrations, and DNA damage, as indicated by increases in comet assay parameters. QNP upregulated pro-apoptotic Bax and downregulated anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 mRNA expression, consistent with activation of apoptosis-related signalling. Co-administration of PIP reduced several QNP-induced genotoxic alterations, although the magnitude of attenuation varied among endpoints, and did not fully restore Bax/Bcl-2 expression balance. Overall, PIP reduced QNP-induced genotoxic and apoptosis-related changes, although its protective effects were endpoint-specific. These findings suggest that PIP may have potential as a natural candidate for mitigating QNP-associated genetic damage. Clinical trial number: Not applicable.
authors: Singh P, Kumar V, Bagri P, Batra K, Lather D.

title: Dual-mode biosensing featuring fluorescence and electrochemiluminescence for regional resolution of single-nucleotide variants.
abstract: Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) are a critical molecular basis for antibiotic resistance in pathogenic bacteria. However, precise detection of mutant targets remains challenging because they may exist at low abundance and often coexist with wild-type sequences in complex biological matrices. Herein, we report a target-triggered strand displacement reaction that releases two functional DNA strands: one activates the trans-cleavage activity of CRISPR/Cas12a to generate a fluorescent signal, while the other competitively displaces cadmium sulfide quantum dots pre-modified on a gold electrode surface, decreasing the electrochemiluminescence (ECL) signal. The two functional strands hybridize to distinct regions of the probe, enabling the two signaling channels to respond differentially to single-base mismatches at different locations. Taking the response to wild-type targets as a reference, synchronized changes in both signals reflect target concentration. A significant decrease in the fluorescence signal alone, with the ECL signal unchanged, indicates that the mismatch occurs within the fluorescence recognition region, whereupon the unaffected ECL channel may serve for quantification. Conversely, when the ECL signal decreases while the fluorescence signal remains stable, the fluorescence channel may serve for quantification. This design enables a single probe to discriminate between wild-type and mutant targets based on the differential responses of the two signaling channels. Our strategy thus provides a new avenue for single-base nucleic acid detection.
authors: Yang H, Lai T, Zhang H, Zhan M, Chen S, Zhang X, Chen L, Hu S.

title: Development and evaluation of non-target analysis methods for characterization of cyanobacterial secondary metabolites.
abstract: Cyanobacteria are of global concern, impacting ecosystems and posing a public health risk from production of bioactive secondary metabolites, including several classes of potent mammalian toxins. Because of the thousands of possible metabolites, non-target analysis (NTA) using high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) is of increasing interest for studying cyanobacteria. However, performance evaluation of these NTA methods is rarely considered, potentially raising concerns over the quality and validity of results. Here, a NTA workflow was developed for cyanobacterial metabolite profiling using data-dependent LC-HRMS/MS acquisition and semi-automated data processing, including product ion, mass list, and spectral library searching using metabolomics software. Rigorous method optimization and performance evaluation at each step were carried out based on detection of cyanotoxins in a multiclass cyanobacterial matrix reference material. Deeper profiling of this material further extended its utility for evaluation of NTA performance for metabolite classes beyond traditional cyanotoxins in the future. The workflow was applied to a set of environmental benthic cyanobacterial biofilm samples associated with recent animal deaths. This led to the detection of 116 secondary metabolites from microcystin, anatoxin, cyanopeptolin, anabaenopeptin, aeruginosin, and cyanobactin classes, greatly increasing reported compound diversity for benthic cyanobacteria, which have been poorly characterized compared to planktonic bloom-forming species. Because of the association of anatoxins in these samples with animal deaths, additional structural elucidation of two newly detected analogues was carried out via analytical scale semi-synthesis. The approaches presented are broadly applicable to class-based NTA in other fields where improved confidence in detection results is increasingly important.
authors: Zamlynny L, Wright EJ, Jamieson RC, Beach DG.

title: YAP coordinates lipid and cholesterol metabolism in papillary thyroid cancer through a glucose-AMPK-gated TEAD1-SREBP1/2 axis.
abstract: To determine whether Yes-associated protein (YAP), a transcriptional coactivator frequently activated in cancer, coordinates lipid and cholesterol metabolism in papillary thyroid cancer (PTC), YAP was overexpressed or silenced in BCPAP and TPC-1 cells, and transcriptomic, biochemical and functional analyses were performed. Glucose deprivation and the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activator metformin suppressed YAP nuclear localization and lipogenic programs, whereas AMPK inhibition by Compound C or YAP overexpression (OE) restored them. Mechanistically, YAP associated with TEA domain family member 1 (TEAD1), occupied canonical TEAD-binding motifs in the SREBF1 and SREBF2 promoters, and activated their transcription in a TEAD1-dependent manner: TEAD1 knockdown abolished YAP-induced SREBF promoter activity, while eight-group genetic epistasis experiments showed that TEAD1 or SREBP1/2 depletion was required for YAP-driven proliferation, clonogenic growth, neutral-lipid and cholesterol accumulation, and expression of FASN, SCD, HMGCR and HMGCS1. Pharmacological SREBP blockade by fatostatin or AMPK activation by metformin reversed YAP-driven phenotypes in vitro and restrained xenograft growth in vivo, with comparable tumor-weight inhibition between the two treatments and no effect on body weight.Clinically, YAP1 expression correlated with lipogenic genes and with shorter disease-free survival in the TCGA-THCA cohort and with SREBP expression in 200 paired PTC specimens. These findings support a model in which glucose-AMPK signaling gates a YAP-TEAD1-SREBP1/2 axis that promotes lipid and cholesterol metabolism and PTC growth, and suggest metformin and SREBP-targeting strategies as candidate therapeutic approaches.
authors: Chen H, Wang J, Zhu Y, Song H, Qiu Z, Luo Q, Shen C.

title: Zinc promotes osteogenesis through enhanced preosteoblast proliferation, osteogenic differentiation, and bone-related transcriptomic remodeling.
abstract: Zinc (Zn) is an essential trace element that contributes to skeletal development, bone remodeling, and mineral homeostasis, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its effects on osteoblast differentiation remain incompletely defined. This study investigated the effects of Zn ions on preosteoblast growth and osteogenic differentiation and characterized Zn-responsive transcriptomic changes. Under osteogenic conditions, Zn increased alkaline phosphatase activity, mineralized matrix formation, and expression of osteogenic markers, including alkaline phosphatase (ALP), osteocalcin, procollagen I, and Runx2. RNA sequencing identified over a thousand differentially expressed genes following Zn²⁺ treatment. Functional enrichment analysis revealed modulation of bone-related pathways, including Wnt, TGF-β/BMP, Hippo, and PI3K-Akt signaling, as well as extracellular matrix (ECM)-receptor interaction, focal adhesion, and osteoclast differentiation. Transcriptomic analysis highlighted osteogenesis-associated candidate genes, including Wnt16, Lrp6, Bmp6, and Tnfrsf11b. Together, these findings associate Zn-enhanced osteogenic responses with changes in bone-related gene expression and identify candidate signaling relationships for future functional investigation.
authors: Zhou J, Sha A, Dickerson J, Wang J, Zhu D.

title: Novel 3D-printed microfluidic chip for automated real-time multi-route in vivo nanoplastics toxicity testing.
abstract: Plastics are one of the most pervasive pollutants in marine environments, with smaller-sized plastics, such as nanoplastics (NPLs), posing significant but understudied threats to marine organisms. Traditional bulk and end-point testing methods offer limited capability for real-time, in situ assessment of nanotoxicity. In this study, we present a fully 3D-printed, automated microfluidic chip designed for multi-route in vivo nanotoxicity testing, which addresses the limitations of conventional methods by offering automated and dynamic exposure conditions alongside real-time monitoring through fluorescence imaging and oxygen sensing. Additionally, this platform simplifies the fabrication process, avoiding the time-consuming soft-lithography typically used for microfluidic chips and increasing accessibility to users without specialized expertise. As a proof of concept, the chip was used to assess nanotoxicity in model marine organisms across different trophic levels: Artemia franciscana (instar II and III stages) and a mixture of five microalgae. Polystyrene nanoplastics, one of the most prevalent plastics in marine environments, were used as the model NPLs and tested in two exposure routes: waterborne and foodborne. The results revealed distinct uptake dynamics; in Artemia, NPL-associated fluorescence initially increased and subsequently declined during waterborne exposure, whereas it continued to increase over the measured period during foodborne exposure. Oxygen-consumption responses varied by organism and exposure route: waterborne exposure produced a higher trend in Artemia and a significant increase in algae, whereas foodborne exposure produced a response comparable to its control. Together, continuous oxygen sensing and fluorescence imaging demonstrated the capability of the chip to monitor complementary physiological and NPL-uptake responses under multiple exposure routes in real time.
authors: Dey P, Bradley TM, Boymelgreen A.

title: Overcoming platinum resistance by the disulfiram metabolite CuET in novel preclinical models of human carcinomas.
abstract: Overcoming resistance to standard-of-care chemotherapy represents an unmet need in oncology. To help address this challenge, here we established and characterized a panel of human cisplatin-resistant lung and breast cancer cell lines and patient-derived organoids from high-grade serous ovarian carcinomas (HGSOC), and show that platinum resistance can be overcome by treatment with diethyldithiocarbamate-copper (CuET), a metabolite of the alcohol-aversion drug disulfiram. All platinum-resistant models remained sensitive to CuET, consistent with distinct cytotoxicity mechanisms: proteotoxic stress for CuET and DNA damage for cisplatin, respectively. Platinum adduct and DNA damage response analyses suggested diverse mechanisms of cisplatin resistance among our models. Considering potential CuET-based therapies, our gene knock-down and functional assays in preclinical models, complemented with immunohistochemical analysis of tissue samples from cohorts of triple-negative breast cancer and HGSOC patients indicate that levels of metallothioneins, rather than NPL4 (the molecular target of CuET) warrant further evaluation as candidate biomarkers of CuET sensitivity. This dataset provides a resource of platinum-resistant models of common carcinomas, identifies CuET as a compound overcoming such resistance and provides leads for predictive biomarker discovery, with potential clinical implications in oncology.
authors: Arampatzis S, Buchtová T, Bartkova J, Bay ML, Halvorsen CL, Machacova Z, Skrott Z, Mistrik M, Dulina E, Andujar-Sanchez M, Høgdall E, Schnack TH, Høgdall C, Mosgaard BJ, Boennelycke M, Laursen JB, Jensen A, Kjær SK, Kallunki T, Strauss R, Bartek J.

title: Evaluation of the plant glucoside monoterpene indole alkaloid brachycerine for potential protection of human skin against ultraviolet damage.
abstract: Sunlight ultraviolet radiation A and B (UV-A and UV-B) affect human skin and may be a cause of cancer. Damage to skin nerve fibers and cell DNA is often observed following excessive unprotected exposure. Plants produce numerous specialized metabolites involved in stress mitigation. Brachycerine, a major leaf glucoside alkaloid from the tree Psychotria brachyceras, absorbs in the UV range and is a powerful antioxidant protecting the photosynthetic machinery against this radiation. Herein, the protective effects of new skincare formulations containing brachycerine or foliar extract were tested on ex vivo human skin exposed to UV. Nerve fibers were identified by immunofluorescence, and UV damage or neuroprotection effects were assessed by image analysis. DNA integrity of UV-B treated samples was evaluated by comet assays. UV-A and UV-B significantly reduced (circa 50%) the measured nerve endings density in the untreated or placebo-treated samples. Pre-treatment with tested skincare formulations completely blocked the effects of UV on nerve endings. UV-B-induced DNA damage was abolished by both the alkaloid and the extract. Cytotoxicity assays showed that brachycerine was not toxic to mammalian cells. Formulations with brachycerine or leaf extract effectively protected ex vivo human skin exposed to UV, indicating that these phytochemicals are potential candidate components of new broad spectrum natural sunscreens.
authors: do Nascimento NC, Fonseca BL, Bonorino C, Bauer ME, Matsuura HN, Ceravolo IP, Moura DJ, Saffi J, Fett JP, Fett-Neto AG.

title: Immunomodulatory and Antioxidant Biomimetic Hydrogel Coloaded with Glycyrrhizic Acid and Copper Gallate for Synergistic Cartilage Regeneration.
abstract: Articular cartilage lesions are persistently restrained by three interwoven pathological drivers: chronic inflammatory response, sustained oxidative stress, and progressive extracellular matrix (ECM) catabolism. Coupled with the inherently weak self-repair capacity of hyaline cartilage, effective therapeutic interventions for such injuries remain an unmet clinical demand owing to the inherently poor self-repair capacity of hyaline cartilage, effective therapeutic interventions remain an unmet clinical demand. Herein, we engineered a biomimetic composite hydrogel designated ECM/HAMA/GA@Cu-GA, which integrates decellularized cartilage extracellular matrix, methacrylated hyaluronic acid (HAMA), glycyrrhizic acid (GA), and copper gallate (Cu-GA). This integrated hydrogel platform simultaneously endows biomimetic mechanical support, potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidative bioactivities, as well as robust chondrogenic induction capacity. In vitro cellular evaluations verified the outstanding biocompatibility of the composite hydrogel. The biomaterial efficiently polarizes macrophages toward the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, suppresses the secretion of pro-inflammatory mediators and matrix-degrading proteases, and facilitates the migration and chondrogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs). Transcriptomic profiling suggested that its underlying molecular mechanisms may involve activation of the PI3K/Akt signaling cascade and blockade of the NF-κB-mediated inflammatory pathway. In vivo assessments using rat articular cartilage defect models demonstrated that the ECM/HAMA/GA@Cu-GA hydrogel achieves satisfactory synchronous regeneration of hyaline cartilage and subchondral bone at 4 and 8 weeks post-implantation, with superior regenerative performance relative to all control groups. Collectively, this multifunctional hydrogel enables comprehensive remodeling of the pathological joint microenvironment with favorable biosafety profiles, representing a translatable candidate strategy for clinical management of cartilage degenerative disorders.
authors: Luo D, Shen S, Li Y, Li Y, Wang Z, Xu Y, Li Y, Zhuo N.

title: Rethinking Pathogenesis of Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis.
abstract: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease characterized by progressive fibroinflammatory injury of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts that may lead to cirrhosis, hepatobiliary malignancy, and death, with liver transplantation representing the only effective intervention in end-stage disease. Rather than a single dominant pathomechanism, the data support a model in which four axes-bile acid metabolism, the intestinal microbiome and gut barrier, biliary epithelial dysfunction, and Th17-skewed immune dysregulation-are reciprocally coupled and converge on a shared periductal fibrogenic output dominated by TGF-β signaling. This review summarizes key mechanistic advances from genetic, epigenomic, single-cell, spatial transcriptomic, and microbiome studies. These investigations implicate antigen presentation pathways, Th17-skewed immune responses, cholangiocyte senescence and profibrotic signaling, and disrupted gut-liver communication as central drivers of chronic biliary injury. Emerging spatial and multi-omics approaches further reveal complex cellular crosstalk among cholangiocytes, immune cells, macrophages, and mesenchymal populations within portal inflammatory niches. We discuss evolving biomarkers and recent clinical trial data targeting bile acid metabolism, fibrosis, the microbiome, and immune pathways. In conclusion, research data suggest viewing PSC as a network disease, which provides a unifying framework for disease pathogenesis and may enable biomarker-guided patient stratification and mechanism-based therapy development targeting distinct pathogenic pathways.
authors: Demir M, Weglage J, Sigal M.

title: Synthesis and self-assembly of new quinuclidinolium-based surfactants: enhanced activity of cytochrome c and efficient antimicrobial activity.
abstract: Bio-based surfactants are a great alternative to conventional surfactants owing to their low toxicity and minimal environmental impact. Herein, four new 3-quinuclidinol-based surfactants, namely, [C16Qui][Br], [C12Qui][Br], [C12AQui][Br] and [C8Qui][Br], have been synthesized and characterized for the first time. The thermal stability of all the surfactants at higher than 250 °C makes them suitable for high-temperature applications. The self-assembly behavior of these surfactants is thoroughly characterized using various techniques. The interactions between relatively hydrophobic bulky head groups, along with other hydrophobic interactions, drive micelle formation. Small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) measurements provide insights into the micellar structures of all surfactants: [C16Qui][Br] assembles into spherical micelles, [C12Qui][Br] and [C12AQui][Br] form prolate ellipsoidal structures, and [C8Qui][Br] arranges into loosely packed, random polymer-like micelles. The micellar structure of short-chain surfactants is solely driven by interactions between head groups, while more compact micellar structures are observed for long-chain surfactants. The presence of an amide functionality near the quinuclidinolium head group further governs the characteristics and properties of the micelles. The interlocking of head groups in the self-assembled structure and distinct structural arrangement of surfactant ions are studied through 1H-NMR spectroscopy and 2D 1H-1H correlation and nuclear Overhauser effect spectroscopies (COSY and NOESY). The aqueous solutions of these surfactants are employed as a catalytic reactor to enhance the enzymatic activity of cytochrome c. The synergistic effect of hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions enhances the enzymatic activity in both monomeric and micellar forms. Interestingly, these surfactants exhibit good microbial inhibition depending upon their structural features and net charge. The present study provides additional understanding of the synthesis of bio-based surfactants and their utilization in diverse biocatalytic and medical applications.
authors: Kondal M, Kaur R, Sharma K, Singh M, Kaur N, Pati PK, Kumar S, Aswal VK, Kang TS.

title: Intergenic Spacer 1 Haplotype Genotyping Enables Efficient Dissection of Population Diversity of the Wheat Stripe Rust Fungus (Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici).
abstract: Wheat stripe rust caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici (Pst) is a destructive disease affecting wheat production because of its capacity for long-distance dispersal. This pathogen exhibits high genetic diversity, yet the low resolving power of currently used molecular markers has restricted in-depth understanding of its migration routes. We previously detected variations among isolates in the ribosomal intergenic spacer 1 (IGS1) region of Pst. In the current study, Pst IGS1 fragments were amplified directly from DNA extracted from wheat rust lesions each bearing a single uredinium, and the intraspecific variation pattern of IGS1 was comprehensively analyzed. Thirty polymorphic loci characterized by variations in repeat units and subunits were detected, with up to 12 polymorphic loci identified within single isolates. Among the 3,050 field samples examined, 506 distinct haplotypes were identified based on combinations of these polymorphic loci, demonstrating that the IGS1 haplotypes can be effective markers for revealing genetic diversity of Pst. Furthermore, IGS1 haplotypes allowed dissection of genetic structure and gene flow among different Pst populations. The IGS1 haplotype genotyping system features several advantages: it requires no fungal isolation or culturing, relies on only one pair of specific primers, and supports high-throughput sample processing. It therefore represents a powerful tool for elucidating the gene flow and genotype flow among populations as well as for tracking long-distance dispersal of Pst both on regional and continental scales.
authors: Chen Y, Liang X, Zhu M, Dang H, Hao B, Ju L, Jin S, Zhan G, Yue H, Wang M, Hsiang T, Zhang R, Cai L, Kang Z, Sun G.

title: Honeybee (Apis mellifera) venom and its bioactive peptides tertiapin and apamin modulate the proteome of SARS-CoV-2-infected cells.
abstract: The continuing emergence of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) variants highlights the need for host-directed antiviral strategies with specific molecular mechanisms. Honeybee (Apis mellifera) venom (HBV) contains bioactive peptides with immunomodulatory and membrane-active properties, yet their effects on SARS-CoV-2 infection remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we investigated the antiviral activity and proteomic impact of whole HBV and two venom-derived peptides, apamin (APA) and tertiapin (TERT), in human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2-expressing HEK293 cells infected with SARS-CoV-2 spike-pseudotyped lentiviral particles. Cell viability and membrane integrity assays showed that HBV, APA, and TERT exerted limited cytotoxicity at the tested concentrations. In pseudovirus infectivity assays, HBV displayed the strongest inhibitory effect, reducing viral infectivity to 61.3% at 2 μg/mL, whereas APA reduced it to 73.3% at 0.5 μg/mL, and TERT showed weaker inhibitory activity. Comparative nano-liquid chromatography matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization tandem mass spectrometry revealed treatment-associated remodelling of the host-cell proteome. A shared signature of 215 proteins across HBV-, APA-, and TERT-treated infected cells was enriched in binding and catalytic activity, translational proteins, metabolite interconversion enzymes, cytoskeletal proteins, and pathways linked to integrin, Wnt, interferon, and Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription signalling. Protein-protein interaction analysis highlighted functional clusters associated with cytoplasmic translation, viral mRNA translation, and the Sec61 translocon complex, with EFTUD2, EPRS1, and HSPA4 emerging as central hubs. HBV treatment additionally promoted immune-related and interferon-stimulated gene products, including factors involved in innate antiviral defence, cytoskeletal organization, ion transport, and membrane structural reinforcement. These findings suggest that HBV reduces SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus infectivity through a multifactorial host-directed mechanism involving antiviral signalling, cellular architecture, and proteostasis, supporting further investigation of bee venom-derived compounds as antiviral agents.
authors: Matuszewska-Mach E, Konieczny I, Matysiak J, Rzetecka-Mańka N, Warowicka A.

title: Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics reveals selective organization of α-synuclein inclusions
abstract: α-Synuclein inclusions, the lesions typical of Parkinson’s disease, have been interpreted as protective deposits, toxic species or failed degradation products, each predicting a different composition and correlating that enrichment with neuron dysfunction and eventual degeneration. Distinguishing them requires measuring what an inclusion concentrates relative to the cell that built it. Here we developed Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics, which uses ultrasensitive mass spectrometry to profile laser-microdissected inclusions against the remainder of the same cell or a matched host. In HEK293 cells, iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons and post-mortem patient brain, each inclusion concentrated a selective subset of its cell’s proteome, independent of abundance and dominated by membrane, in neurons largely presynaptic. Inclusions took up whole assemblies, with subunits moving together in 421 of 438 complexes, and the V-ATPase alone was enriched in all three systems. Degradation cargo stayed with the receptors that route it, consistent with sequestration and failed degradation acting together. Neuritic and somatic inclusions differed, the former rich in UBQLN2 and the latter in intermediate filaments. In the cell line, phosphorylated α-synuclein was tenfold higher in the inclusion than in the rest of the cell, with about one third of the rise already present before an inclusion was visible. Measured against its host, the composition of an inclusion becomes a readout of how it formed and a source of candidate markers and therapeutic targets.

title: Defining nutrient dependencies of intestinal  Klebsiella pneumoniae  guides rational probiotic engineering
abstract: Summary  Klebsiella pneumoniae is a major cause of antibiotic-resistant infections, yet the ecological determinants enabling its intestinal expansion remain poorly defined. Here, we combined  in vivo transcriptomics and metabolomics to identify carbon sources exploited by  K. pneumoniae during colonization of the antibiotic-disrupted gut across strains and dietary contexts. Despite its metabolic breadth,  K. pneumoniae consistently exploited a restricted set of substrates, including arabinose, raffinose, oligogalacturonate, arabitol, xylose, and gluconate, that contributed to intestinal fitness, with related metabolic signatures also observed in antibiotic-treated human samples. Guided by these findings, we engineered  Escherichia coli Nissle to enhance consumption of these nutrients and assembled a defined consortium, NICHE, designed to reinforce colonization resistance through nutrient competition. NICHE restricted intestinal expansion of multidrug-resistant and hypervirulent  K. pneumoniae in preventive and therapeutic settings, with efficacy influenced by dietary nutrient availability. Together, this work defines exploitable  K. pneumoniae nutrient dependencies and a framework for rational probiotic engineering.
authors: Zhou Y, David C, Kulkarni G, Long T, Garzón MJ, Prados J, Kloehn J, Rohr OV, Meister I, Xavier KB, Ubeda C, Yu F, Chen L, Becattini S.

title: GSET: Gene Signals from Embedding Trajectories select compact contexts for mechanistic GRN inference
abstract: Mechanistic inference of gene regulatory networks from temporal transcriptomic data can become computationally prohibitive at transcriptome scale, making gene selection an important determinant of which regulatory relationships can be recovered. However, gene selection for GRN inference commonly relies on static expression or co-expression structure, rather than prioritizing dynamically informative genes whose temporal patterns capture how transcriptional programs change and relate to one another. We introduce GSET (Gene Signals from Embedding Trajectories), an upstream retrieval framework that extracts dynamic information from temporal gene embeddings using two complementary signals: an optimal transport residual, which captures gene-specific deviations from global embedding movement, and a KL divergence, which detects changes in local co-expression neighborhoods. Temporal gene-embedding similarity identifies static transcriptional programs, whereas vectorial GSET signals represent coordinated temporal changes among genes, complementing this static structure. Lagged comparisons of these signals further prioritize temporal relationships between programs and candidate bridge genes associated with their transitions. Integrated with CardamomOT, GSET combines static program cores with dynamically retrieved bridge genes into compact, program-informed gene sets for mechanistic GRN inference. In synthetic benchmarks, at equal gene budget these sets recover more of the regulatory links between programs than static selections of the same size, and inference on the edges within the set is comparable to that of the full-gene model on the same gene pairs. On a time course of mouse fibroblasts reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells, GSET traces the transition from the fibroblast program to the cell-cycle program. By providing a dynamic retrieval layer upstream of GRN inference, GSET nominates bridge genes as candidate regulators of cell-state transitions, which, once refined by a mechanistic model such as CardamomOT and confirmed by perturbation experiments, could open the way to controlling these transitions.
authors: Weizmann Z, Ventre E.

title: Resolving how genetic perturbations act through gene regulatory paths
abstract: Perturb-seq measures transcriptional responses to thousands of genetic perturbations, but each gene’s response mixes the contributions of many regulatory paths, so how a perturbation acts cannot be resolved from expression alone, however large the model. Here we present REGA-perturb, which supplies this missing information rather than adding model complexity: reference epigenomes define a scaffold of possible transcription factor (TF)–regulatory element–gene paths, and perturbation responses, pooled through shared latent programs, determine how each path is used, requiring only RNA measurements. Across three CRISPR interference screens totaling 2.4 million cells, REGA-perturb inferred TF–target relationships that agreed with ChIP-seq binding with a gain over random more than four times that of the best existing method, separated candidate direct from indirect targets, and predicted targets of TFs withheld from training. It also inferred perturbation-induced changes in TF activity not reflected in TF transcript levels, and resolved perturbation-specific regulatory rewiring in which opposing regulatory changes cancel at the expression level.
authors: Ren L, Duren Z.

title: Integrative hdWGCNA and Machine-Learning Analysis Identifies Gastric Cancer Candidate Genes and Supports a Functional Role for KRT18.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is a frequently detected malignancy worldwide. This study aimed to identify epithelial cell-associated candidate genes in GC by integrating single-cell and bulk transcriptomic data and to explore their biological relevance using computational analyses, with in vitro functional assessment limited to KRT18. Multi-omics data were integrated to investigate the molecular mechanisms of GC. The single-cell data were processed using Seurat. Subsequently, CellChat was employed to analyze cell communication. The co-expression network of epithelial cells was constructed using high-dimensional WGCNA (hdWGCNA), and module hub genes were identified. Differential expression analysis was performed with Limma, and candidate genes were screened using LASSO and SVR-RFE. Compounds were computationally prioritized using Enrichr and DSigDB; molecular docking was not used as validation. Lastly, the biological function of KRT18 was examined in GC cells. Five candidate genes were identified: GPRC5A, KRT18, EPCAM, CLDN7, and CLDN4. These genes were associated with E2F TARGETS, GLYCOLYSIS, and OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION and correlated with multiple inferred immune-cell fractions. Drug-set enrichment nominated genistein as a computational candidate but did not establish direct binding or therapeutic efficacy. In vitro assays showed that KRT18 knockdown reduced the viability, migration, and invasion of GC cells. These findings nominate exploratory epithelial cell-associated candidate genes in GC and provide functional evidence for KRT18; further external validation is required before clinical application.
authors: Ran Y, He Y, Huang Y, Li T.

title: Identification and Validation of Autophagy- and Inflammatory-Related Genes in Childhood Asthma via Integrated Bioinformatics and Clinical Samples.
abstract: Childhood asthma (CA) is a prevalent chronic airway disease, yet the roles of autophagy and inflammation in its pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Transcriptomic datasets were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Inflammation- and autophagy-related genes were identified using weighted gene co-expression network analysis and consensus clustering and intersected with differentially expressed genes (DEGs) to identify candidate genes. Subsequently, 101 machine learning algorithm combinations were evaluated to select key genes for diagnostic model construction. Functional characterization involved immune infiltration analysis, gene set enrichment analysis, and transcription factor network construction. Mendelian randomization (MR) was used to assess potential causal relationships between key genes and CA, and gene expression was validated by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) in clinical blood samples. The analysis identified 39 candidate genes associated with autophagy and inflammation. Machine learning identified 10 key genes, and the resulting diagnostic model achieved areas under the curve of 0.768, 0.751, and 0.710 in the training, test, and validation sets, respectively. Pathway and immune infiltration analyses revealed enrichment in signaling, metabolic, and immune-regulatory functions and significant correlations with immune cell infiltration. MR analysis suggested a potential causal association between genetically predicted STYXL1 expression and CA risk. qPCR analysis in five CA patients and five healthy controls showed expression patterns consistent with the transcriptomic findings. However, the small clinical validation cohort limits the generalizability of these results. This study identifies a 10-gene peripheral blood diagnostic signature associated with CA and highlights STYXL1 as a potential causal risk gene supported by genetic evidence. Larger clinical cohorts and functional studies are required to validate these findings.
authors: Huang M, Wu J, Xu D.

title: Network Pharmacology Identifies Stigmasterol as an Anti-Gastric Cancer Agent Targeting HSP90AA1 for Ubiquitin-Mediated Degradation.
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major cause of cancer mortality. We combined network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, public database analyses, and cell-based assays to investigate stigmasterol and heat shock protein 90 alpha family class A member 1 (HSP90AA1). Computational screening prioritized HSP90AA1 as a candidate target. In AGS and MKN-45 cells, stigmasterol treatment reduced cell viability and DNA synthesis, increased the proportion of Annexin V-positive cells, and decreased HSP90AA1 protein abundance. No statistically significant change in HSP90AA1 mRNA abundance was detected under the conditions tested. Increased ubiquitin signal in HSP90AA1 immunoprecipitates and attenuation of protein loss by MG-132 were consistent with proteasome involvement. Public database analyses showed higher HSP90AA1 expression in GC tissues and an association with clinical stage. These findings link stigmasterol treatment to HSP90AA1 downregulation in GC cells. Direct binding, the contribution of HSP90AA1 loss to the cellular effects, and in vivo efficacy remain to be established.
authors: Zhang H, Zhang Y, Ling Y, Jiang G, Wu J, Shi X, Zhao Y.

title: First principles study of chalcogen vacancy effect on the optoelectronic and photocatalytic properties of transition metal dichalcogenides monolayers.
abstract: In working conditions, chalcogen vacancies spontaneously occur in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) monolayers, affecting their optoelectronic and photocatalytic properties. To study how chalcogen vacancies affect such properties, we use quantum mechanical calculations considering prototypical MX2 (M = Mo, W, X = S and Se) TMDCs monolayers. Band structure calculations reveal that the introduction of vacancies produce electronic states about the Fermi level, hence resulting in the reduction of the band gap. Work function and electrostatic potential calculations show that the introduction of vacancies induce an asymmetry in the electrostatic potential, which may facilitate the charge separation; such feature is absent in a pristine monolayer. All the considered defective structures are capable of performing hydrogen evolution reaction, while co-catalyst is required to perform oxygen evolution reaction when used for water splitting. WS2 and WSe2 defective monolayers can serve as promising candidates for reducing CO2 into useful chemical products. The presented results show that vacancy-containing TMDCs monolayers own photocatalytic capabilities compared to the pristine counterparts, thus showing that defective TMD monolayers have prospective applications and should not be regarded as flawed products to be discarded. Finally, the results might constitute guidelines for the experimental synthesis of vacancy-engineered MX2 monolayers for optoelectronic devices and photocatalytic applications.
authors: Wahab T, Cammarata A, Polcar T.

title: Gut-Induced Synuclein Propagation: A New Mechanism in Neurodegenerative Disease.
abstract: Gut-induced synuclein propagation has emerged as a potential mechanism linking gastrointestinal disturbances with the development and progression of Parkinson disease and related synucleinopathies. These disorders are characterized by progressive accumulation and spreading of misfolded α-synuclein (α-Syn), leading to selective neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Although traditionally considered brain-centered diseases, increasing evidence indicates that gastrointestinal abnormalities, peripheral α-Syn pathology, and gut-associated immune alterations may precede neurological manifestations, suggesting that peripheral processes can influence disease evolution. Here, we review clinical, pathological, and experimental evidence supporting the role of intestinal environmental stress, microbial dysregulation, barrier dysfunction, and immune activation in promoting α-Syn misfolding, aggregation, and transmission through interconnected pathways. However, peripheral α-Syn abnormalities alone are unlikely to be sufficient to initiate neurodegeneration, indicating the presence of additional biological constraints. We propose a cumulative-threshold and biological-gates framework in which α-Syn induction, seed formation, propagation efficiency, anatomical connectivity, and neuronal vulnerability collectively determine whether gut-associated pathology progresses into a self-sustaining neurodegenerative cascade. Understanding the determinants that enable gut-induced synuclein propagation may provide new insights into disease heterogeneity and guide biomarker development and mechanism-based therapeutic strategies for synucleinopathies.
journal: The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
authors: Sun Y, Li B, Ye K.

title: The Tartary Buckwheat FtMYB15 Coordinates Cadmium Uptake and Detoxification by Regulating FtZIP3 and FtGSTU19 Expression.
abstract: Tartary buckwheat (Fagopyrum tataricum) is a crop of significant value, yet its cultivation in cadmium (Cd)-contaminated soils poses risks to food safety. Understanding the molecular mechanisms of Cd uptake is crucial for developing strategies to minimize its accumulation. Here, we demonstrate that the Tartary buckwheat transcription factor FtMYB15 promotes Cd2+ influx and enhances Cd accumulation in transgenic hairy roots. Yeast one-hybrid (Y1H) and electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) results indicate that FtMYB15 binds to the MYB-binding sites (MBS) of the FtZIP3 promoter, thereby upregulating the expression of FtZIP3, which encodes a zinc/iron-regulated transporter-like protein. Overexpression of FtZIP3 similarly enhances Cd2+ influx and Cd accumulation in buckwheat hairy roots. Further analysis reveals that FtMYB15 binds to the MBS in the promoter of the tau glutathione S-transferase gene FtGSTU19 and upregulates its expression in buckwheat hairy roots both before and after Cd exposure. Overexpression of FtGSTU19 in buckwheat hairy roots enhances Cd detoxification capacity via its glutathione transferase activity, thereby alleviating Cd-induced oxidative stress. Heterologous expression of FtGSTU19 increases Cd tolerance in Arabidopsis. Expression of FtMYB15, FtZIP3, and FtGSTU19 is induced by Cd stress. Together, these findings demonstrate that FtMYB15 directly regulates the expression of FtZIP3 and FtGSTU19, thereby coordinating Cd uptake and detoxification in plants.
authors: Zhang X, Wei J, Tang X, Wang A, Zhou Y, Mai S, Liu Y, Yang Y, Li X, Wang J.

title: Pediatric suprasellar primary CNS lymphoma with cavernous sinus invasion and ischemic stroke: a case report and systematic review.
abstract: BackgroundPrimary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) is an exceptionally rare pediatric malignancy, accounting for less than 1% of childhood central nervous system tumors. Suprasellar involvement is particularly uncommon and frequently mimics more prevalent lesions, including germinoma and Langerhans cell histiocytosis, often resulting in delayed diagnosis.Case presentationWe report the case of a 12-year-old immunocompetent girl with a history of Epstein-Barr virus infection and a previously resected atypical smooth muscle tumor of the ileum who presented with high-grade fever, severe headache, and diplopia. She rapidly deteriorated neurologically, and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a rim-enhancing sellar-suprasellar lesion invading the cavernous sinus, causing critical internal carotid artery stenosis with bilateral watershed cerebral infarctions. Emergency endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal decompression was performed. Histopathological examination confirmed anaplastic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the non-germinal center B-cell subtype. Despite prompt surgical intervention and initiation of systemic chemotherapy, the patient developed central diabetes insipidus, severe hemodynamic instability, and ultimately died within few months.MethodsA systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Ovid, and Scopus were searched from database inception to 31 May 2026 to identify published cases of pediatric suprasellar primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL).ResultsFive studies comprising seven previously reported pediatric patients met the inclusion criteria. Six of seven historical patients (85.7%) achieved complete radiological remission, Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) or large-cell B-cell lymphoma was reported in four of seven patients (57.1%). Most patients achieved complete remission following intensive CNS-directed chemotherapy, although persistent endocrine dysfunction remained common. In contrast to previously reported cases, our patient presented with fulminant cavernous sinus invasion, critical internal carotid artery stenosis, and ischemic watershed cerebral infarctions, representing an exceptionally aggressive clinical phenotype.ConclusionPediatric suprasellar PCNSL is a rare but highly aggressive disease that should be considered in children presenting with diabetes insipidus, pituitary stalk lesions, or rapidly progressive suprasellar masses. Progressive radiologic evolution or atypical vascular complications should prompt early histopathological confirmation to facilitate timely diagnosis and initiation of treatment.
journal: Child's nervous system : ChNS : official journal of the International Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery
authors: AlShakhs FA, Alruwaili AA, Namer TS, Alsaiari SA, Almomen A, Algarni AA.

title: TERRA: an induced responder to telomere dysfunction.
abstract: Telomeric repeat-containing RNA (TERRA) has long been viewed as a constitutive component of telomeres. However, accumulating experimental evidence suggests that TERRA is instead a stress-responsive signal produced specifically at dysfunctional telomeres. Across yeasts and mammals, TERRA abundance changes as telomeres shorten or become damaged, engaging the appropriate maintenance pathway through interactions with shelterin, chromatin regulators and DNA repair factors, and through the controlled formation of RNA:DNA hybrids (R-loops). In telomerase-negative cells, transient accumulation of TERRA and R-loops promotes homology-directed telomere elongation. In telomerase-positive cells, TERRA appears to direct telomerase activity selectively toward short telomeres. When telomere damage remains unresolved, sustained TERRA expression and persistent R-loops drive cells toward senescence, inflammatory signaling and crisis-associated cell death. We propose here that TERRA functions as a molecular rheostat at damaged telomeres: transient and spatially controlled induction restores chromosome-end integrity, whereas persistent accumulation results in the removal of compromised cells from the proliferative pool. Defining how cells set these switch points will be essential for elucidating how TERRA shapes ageing and disease and for harnessing its therapeutic potential.
authors: Bento F, Andolfato M, Luke B, Azzalin CM.

title: Ca<sup>2+</sup> signature gates responsiveness to exogenous auxin in Arabidopsis roots.
abstract: Plants must continually balance growth with arrest, especially under stress. Auxin signaling acts as a central regulatory hub in this process, yet the mechanisms that dynamically tune auxin signaling in real time remain unknown. Here, we use the light-gated, Ca2+-permeable Channelrhodopsin 2 variant XXM2.0 to optogenetically impose defined Ca2+ signatures on Arabidopsis root cells. Repetitive light activation triggers cytosolic Ca2+ signals that in turn suppress membrane depolarization and Ca2+ transients triggered by exogenous auxin. Moreover, prolonged optogenetic Ca2+ stimulation affects auxin-responsive transcriptional reprogramming. As phenotypic output, reversible inhibition of root growth by suppressing cell division and elongation is observed. We further identify a candidate CaM7-CNGC14 module that likely mediates Ca2+-dependent gating of responsiveness to exogenous auxin as well as Ca2+-dependent root growth inhibition. Our study thus introduces a synthetic biology approach to decompose calcium-auxin crosstalk in plant cells, and demonstrates that optogenetically imposed cytosolic Ca2+ signals act as dynamic regulators of auxin susceptibility in roots.

title: SUMOylated DDX3 Promotes HBV Replication and Tumor Growth of Hepatocellular Carcinoma via TRIM28-DDX3-KLF4α Signaling Axis.
abstract: DDX3 has dual biological functions of regulating cell proliferation and antiviral effects. Herein, we focus on SUMOylation-mediated DDX3 in the interplay from hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection to HBV-associated hepatocellular carcinoma (HBV-HCC) progression. We identified dynamic regulation of SUMOylation and DeSUMOylation of DDX3 at four key lysine (K) residues (K81/K208/K215/K564) in response to HBV infection. During the early stage of HBV acute infection, SENP1 interacts with DDX3 to keep DDX3 deSUMOylation for inhibiting HBV replication. During persistent HBV replication, as SENP1 downregulation and HBV polymerase accumulation, DDX3 disassociates with SENP1 to bind with TRIM28, which induces DDX3 SUMOylation. Meanwhile, SUMOylated DDX3 enhances alternative splicing of KLF4 mRNAs to generate KLF4α isoform that involves in Cyclin D1-mediated cell cycle progression, weakens tumor suppressor function of DDX3 and promotes HBV-HCC. Moreover, DDX3 expression is positively correlated with KLF4 mRNA, and high DDX3 level with low TRIM28 expression indicates a better overall survival for HBV-HCC patients. Our findings reveal the dynamic regulation between SUMOylation and deSUMOylation of DDX3, including mediating HBV gene transcription, virus antigen secretion, and cell proliferation. Furthermore, the TRIM28-DDX3-KLF4 axis as a novel therapeutic target for HBV-HCC, exhibiting the dual ability to inhibit tumor progression and disrupt the HBV-host interaction.
authors: Yang Y, Kong T, Wang B, Jin X, Huang L, Zhang N, Tang S, Syed SE, Liang S.

title: CA1-associated epithelial-state remodeling in colon cancer cells exposed to polystyrene nanoplastics: Integrated multi-omics and In vitro analyses.
abstract: Polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPs) directly encounter the gastrointestinal epithelium after ingestion, yet the epithelial molecular states linking exposure to colon cancer cell behavior remain unclear. We integrated bulk transcriptomics, interpretable machine learning, WGCNA, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, structural analyses, and in vitro experiments to investigate CA1-associated epithelial responses. Intersecting 2139 colon cancer differentially expressed genes with 766 styrene-associated genes yielded 159 candidates. Among 45 classification models, LASSO + GBM ranked highest in an exploratory cross-cohort comparison, with an apparent training AUC of 1.000 and comparison-cohort AUCs of 0.999 and 0.925. CA1 had the highest SHAP importance and was located in the WGCNA module most strongly associated with tumor/normal status. Single-cell and organoid analyses showed attenuation of epithelial CA1/CA2 and carbonic anhydrase-bicarbonate-related programs, with concordant spatial trends; TCGA-COAD and Human Protein Atlas data further supported reduced CA1 expression. Low CA1 was associated with reduced metabolic and bicarbonate-related programs and enhanced inflammatory signaling. Docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics showed only weak, dynamic styrene-CA1 contacts. In HCT116 cells, PS-NPs decreased CA1, CA2, and Occludin expression, altered stress-, inflammation-, and apoptosis-related molecules, and increased scratch closure, with generally stronger changes at higher doses and after Tioxolone co-treatment. Collectively, these findings identify a CA1/CA2-low epithelial state associated with PS-NP exposure and suggest that CA1-associated epithelial-state remodeling may be part of the cellular response to PS-NPs.
journal: Food and chemical toxicology : an international journal published for the British Industrial Biological Research Association
authors: Guo B, Song Y, Qin J, Wu X, Chen Z, Guo J, Sun J, Pei L.

title: Rethinking inflammaging: Spatiotemporal decoupling and the failure of inflammatory regulation.
abstract: Chronic low-grade inflammation (inflammaging) is a central feature of aging, yet its magnitude and trajectory vary substantially among individuals and tissues. This variability is not fully explained by chronological age or cumulative inflammatory exposure. We therefore examine inflammaging through a spatiotemporal framework focused on how inflammatory responses are initiated, contained, resolved, and distributed across tissues. The framework integrates established mechanisms-including defective resolution, epigenetic drift, cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), cytosolic DNA sensing, inflammasome activation, cytokine dysregulation, and loss of immunometabolic flexibility. We use the term spatiotemporal decoupling to describe the observable divergence between chronological age and inflammatory state across time, tissues, and individuals. The term does not denote a newly discovered molecular pathway; its value lies in organizing existing evidence around failures of regulatory closure and in generating testable predictions about inflammatory persistence and tissue heterogeneity. This perspective suggests that systemic inflammatory markers alone are unlikely to identify the mechanism sustaining inflammation in a given patient or tissue. Therapeutic strategies should therefore be matched to the dominant process and disease context, with attention to tissue delivery, host defense, repair, and other consequences of pathway inhibition. Candidate approaches include restoration of resolution, modulation of senescent-cell burden or SASP, selective control of innate immune sensing and cytokine signaling, and improvement of metabolic flexibility. Overall, the review distinguishes established components of inflammaging from their proposed integration in a spatiotemporal model and identifies the evidence needed to test its translational relevance.
authors: Deng X, Wang L, Luo M, Wu J.

title: Ethnopharmacological basis of Huangqin Tang in colorectal cancer: Repurposing a classical formula to overcome PD-1 resistance via lactylation blockade.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceHuangqin Tang (HQT), documented in the Shanghan Lun, is traditionally prescribed for "dysenteric disorders" (Li Ji). Modern clinical studies confirm its efficacy against ulcerative colitis and colorectal cancer-associated inflammation, providing a verified traditional basis for investigating its immunomodulatory effects in colorectal malignancy. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.Aim of the studyThis study aimed to investigate the regulatory role of lactate-induced protein lactylation in MIF-driven PD-1 resistance and to determine if HQT can reverse this phenotype through metabolic reprogramming.Materials and methodsCT26-bearing BALB/c mice were administered HQT intragastrically combined with intraperitoneal anti-PD-1 antibodies. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes were profiled by flow cytometry. Integrative transcriptomics and network pharmacology were utilized to screen candidate targets. LC-MS/MS-based lactylomic profiling identified specific modification sites. Lactate modulation assays, and site-directed mutagenesis (NF-κB1 K249R) coupled with rescue experiments were performed in vitro to validate the molecular cascade mechanistically.ResultsHQT synergized with anti-PD-1 to suppress tumor growth and prolong survival. This combination remodeled the immune microenvironment, increasing CD8+ T cells and M1-like macrophages while reducing M2 macrophages and MDSCs. Mechanistically, HQT inhibited tumor glycolysis and lactate production. Lactylomic analysis revealed that lactate induced NF-κB1 lysine 249 (K249) lactylation in CD4+ Tregs, driving MIF transcription. Introducing the K249R mutation abolished lactate-induced MIF expression and reversed immunosuppression. HQT effectively reduced NF-κB1 K249 lactylation, disrupting the MIF-driven feedback loop.ConclusionNF-κB1 K249 lactylation acts as a critical post-translational switch linking tumor glycolysis to Treg-mediated immunosuppression. HQT overcomes PD-1 resistance by suppressing this axis. These findings support combining metabolic intervention with immunotherapy and highlight K249 lactylation as a potential biomarker for treatment response.
authors: Song L, Zhang X, Liu A, Li X, Chen P, Liu X, Zeng A.

title: Cycloastragenol suppresses LPS-induced macrophage inflammation and promotes M2 polarization via TLR4/NF-κB signaling and SIRT1-related regulation.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceAstragalus has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine for tonifying qi and supporting defensive functions. Cycloastragenol (CAG), a characteristic triterpenoid aglycone derived from Astragalus saponins, has emerging pharmacological relevance in immune and inflammatory regulation, but its role in macrophage inflammatory regulation and phenotypic remodeling remains insufficiently defined.Aim of the studyTo investigate the effects of CAG on lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced macrophage inflammation and phenotypic remodeling, focusing on Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling and the involvement of sirtuin 1 (SIRT1).Materials and methodsRAW 264.7 macrophages were pretreated with CAG before LPS stimulation. Cytokine secretion, phenotype markers, and inflammatory signaling were evaluated by ELISA, immunofluorescence, reverse transcription quantitative PCR, and Western blotting. SIRT1-targeting small interfering RNA was used for functional evaluation. Network pharmacology prioritized candidate targets, while two acute inflammatory tissue transcriptomes and a normal human immune atlas provided expression context. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations explored candidate CAG-protein interactions.ResultsCompared with LPS alone, CAG at 20 μmol/L reduced TNF-α from 56.15 ± 2.17 to 25.80 ± 1.87 pg/mL and IL-1β from 93.55 ± 2.66 to 44.49 ± 2.85 pg/mL (mean ± standard deviation; both Tukey-adjusted P ConclusionsCAG attenuated LPS-induced macrophage inflammation and favored M2-associated phenotypic remodeling, with SIRT1 contributing to these effects. These findings support CAG as a promising Astragalus-derived immunomodulatory candidate and provide a basis for further exploration of its clinical translational potential.
authors: Zhou X, Qin S, Guo Y, Niu W, Chang X, Wang S, Wang J, Xu C.

title: Pharmacological characterization of clinical candidate CORT118335 (miricorilant), a selective glucocorticoid receptor modulator, in short-term preclinical models for MASLD.
abstract: CORT118335 (miricorilant) is a selective glucocorticoid receptor (GR) modulator (SGRM) that is currently being evaluated in clinical trials for the treatment of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), based on strong efficacy in mouse models. We reveal gene-specific GR modulation by CORT118335 in the mouse liver. In cell-based models, we evaluated the biological activity of CORT118335 metabolites. Metabolite CORT118335-P9a showed potent GR agonism, while metabolite CORT118335-P9b was largely inactive. CORT118335-P9a concentrations in the mouse liver were very low, and therefore neither metabolite is likely to contribute to the beneficial effects of CORT118335 in vivo. We investigated various aspects of CORT118335 activity in reducing lipid levels in the mouse liver using a model of short-term high-fat diet feeding. Daily administration of CORT118335 appeared to lower hepatic triglyceride rapidly within several days after treatment initiation, specifically in male mice, and these effects were reversed after 7 days of treatment discontinuation. No synergy was observed between the lipid-lowering effects of CORT118335 and the TRβ agonist VK2809 or the PPARγ agonist pioglitazone. At a dose of 6 mg/kg/day, CORT118335 induced evident transcriptional effects with modest lowering of hepatic triglyceride levels, while higher doses induced a more pronounced lipid lowering but less ongoing transcriptional activity for hepatic lipid metabolism genes. Altogether we substantiate the potential of selective GR modulation using CORT118335 as a lipid-lowering strategy in MASLD and highlight the complexity of SGRM-mediated hepatic lipid lowering.
authors: Moll TJA, Gentenaar M, Viho EM, Hoekstra AT, Afkir S, Deurloo JN, Laman PV, Schonk AW, Henst MW, Hunt HJ, Meijer OC, Kroon J.
