title: Global Trends and Burden of HIV Coinfection With Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis From 1990 to 2021: The Global Burden of Disease Study 2021.
abstract: BackgroundTuberculosis (TB) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) remain global health threats. Extensively drug-resistant TB with HIV co-infection is associated with substantial mortality worldwide. This study aimed to estimate the global burden and temporal trends of extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis and human immunodeficiency virus co-infection (HIV/XDR-TB) from 1990 to 2021.MethodsWe used the Global Burden of Diseases Study 2021 data to estimate the global burden of HIV/XDR-TB from 1990 to 2021. We employed a Disease Modeling-Meta-Regression model to estimate incidence, prevalence, mortality, and disability-adjusted life years. Mortality was calculated using population attributable fraction methods, accounting for HIV/XDR-TB overlap. Results were stratified by Socio-demographic Index (SDI) and reported with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs).ResultsIn 2021, global HIV/XDR-TB incidence was 1,606.42 cases (95% UI, 1,163.94-2,182.83), with an age-standardized incidence rate of 1.94 per 10 million and a -15.59% change (95% UI, -36.38 to +10.26) since 2010. Mortality estimates indicated 840 deaths (95% UI, 385.44-1,491.72) in 2021, with an age-standardized death rate of 1.01 per 10 million (95% UI, 0.47-1.80), representing a 35.85% decline from 2010 (95% UI, -50.45% to -17.75%). The burden was highest among those aged 35-39 and consistently higher in males. Regionally, Eastern Europe and Southern Sub-Saharan Africa showed the highest burden, while Oceania had the greatest increase. Substantial heterogeneity was observed across regions and SDI levels.ConclusionDespite declines in HIV/XDR-TB burden, significant regional and demographic disparities persist, highlighting the need for targeted public health strategies in high-burden regions.
authors: Lee EH, Kim YS, Kim MS, Ravindran R, Yon DK, Kang YA, Shin JI, Smith L.

title: A molecular networking-guided strategy for identifying anti-osteoporotic sterols from the soft coral Sclerophytum humesi.
abstract: Marine soft corals represent a rich source of structurally diverse secondary metabolites; however, their potential effects on bone metabolism remain poorly explored. In this study, an integrated molecular networking- and bioactivity-guided strategy was employed to identify potential anti-osteoporotic constituents from the soft coral Sclerophytum humesi. LC-MS/MS-based molecular networking was integrated with biological activity data to prioritize bioactivity-associated molecular families for targeted isolation. In a glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis zebrafish model, fraction SH-E3 exhibited a pronounced ability to restore impaired skeletal mineralization and was therefore prioritized for further chemical investigation. Targeted isolation of SH-E3 afforded one previously undescribed compound (1) together with eight known metabolites (3-10), including six sterols: ergosta-5,24(28)-dien-3-ol (5), ergosta-5,22-dien-3-ol (6), cholesterol (7), gorgosterol (8), (3β)-33-norgorgost-5-en-3-ol (9), and ergost-5-en-3-ol (10). Parallel investigation of SH-E7 yielded a second previously undescribed compound (2), structurally related to 1. Evaluation of compounds 1-10 in MG-63 cells revealed that sterols 5-10 enhanced alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity to varying degrees, whereas compounds 1-4 exhibited relatively weak or negligible effects. These findings indicate that the osteogenic activity of SH-E3 is primarily associated with its sterol-enriched chemical profile. Collectively, this study demonstrates the utility of integrating molecular networking with biological activity for the efficient prioritization of bioactive constituents from chemically complex marine extracts and highlights soft-coral-derived sterols as promising candidates for further investigation of their potential roles in glucocorticoid-induced bone loss.
authors: Peng BR, Chen YS, Wang TM, Luu PV, Pham QV, Lai GY, Wang HW, Chen LY, Su JH, Lai KH, Le HG, Pham NT, Tran TN, Lee MH.

title: Multi-target network modulation of Traditional Chinese Medicine in radiation enteropathy: mechanistic insights and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Radiation enteropathy (RE) is a common and clinically significant complication of abdominal and pelvic radiotherapy, characterized by multifactorial pathological processes including oxidative DNA damage, epithelial barrier disruption, immune-inflammatory dysregulation, vascular injury, fibrosis, and gut microbiota dysbiosis. Despite its clinical burden, effective disease-modifying therapies remain limited. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), widely used in the management of gastrointestinal disorders, has attracted increasing attention as a complementary approach for radiation-induced intestinal injury. Accumulating experimental evidence indicates that TCM formulas, herbal extracts, and bioactive phytochemicals may exert protective effects through coordinated regulation of interconnected pathological processes. Reported protective effects involve several interconnected pathological processes, but the supporting evidence remains uneven. Most studies use acute, single-dose animal models, and many mechanistic conclusions rely on pathway-marker changes rather than functional perturbation. This review therefore evaluates TCM interventions according to disease stage, intestinal site, irradiation design, and the strength of mechanistic support. Multi-target regulation is treated as an interpretive framework rather than a mechanism established for every intervention. Clinical evidence remains limited by small samples, heterogeneous preparations, inconsistent endpoints, and inadequate follow-up. Translation will require standardized products, clinically relevant fractionated and tumor-bearing models, exposure-relevant mechanistic validation, and rigorous trials that assess intestinal benefit without compromising tumor control.
authors: Tan B, Chen X, Shao G, Su H, Ma X, Ni X, Lu L, Lin Z, Ji G, Xu H.

title: Adaptive Laboratory Evolution of Simplified Microbial Consortia: Mechanisms, Experimental Frameworks and Applications.
abstract: Microbial bioprocesses based on monocultures can be constrained by the substrate range, metabolic burden and stress tolerance of individual strains. Simplified microbial consortia, composed of a limited number of characterised members, can distribute metabolic tasks and enable interactions such as cross-feeding and division of labour. This review examines adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) in these systems, with emphasis on co-evolutionary, modular and hybrid experimental frameworks. We distinguish evidence obtained with defined multispecies consortia from adjacent evidence derived from enrichment communities, ALE-like selection systems and intraspecific multi-lineage populations. Across these systems, ALE can alter genetic, regulatory and ecological processes that influence resource partitioning, stress tolerance and community performance, although direct mechanistic evidence remains limited and taxonomically narrow. We critically assess applications in pollutant degradation, lignocellulosic biomass and lignin conversion, high-value compound biosynthesis and waste valorisation, considering their degree of technological validation. Finally, we discuss how longitudinal multi-omics, metabolic modelling and automated experimentation may improve the predictability, reproducibility and industrial relevance of consortium ALE.
authors: Mercado B, Martínez-Montañés F, Pascual J.

title: Comprehensive proteomic profiling reveals mRNA splicing suppression during human oocyte aging.
abstract: Reproductive aging impairs female fertility, and oocyte aging is considered a major driver of this phenotype, which manifests with increased aneuploidy and miscarriage risk, while no effective treatments have been widely implemented to date. Here, we report comprehensive protein expression profiling of oocytes during human aging, comparing fully grown germinal vesicle oocytes (FGO) and metaphase II (MII) oocytes; we describe the effect of aging on the maturation profiles across multiple age groups, including 25, 30, 35, and 40 years old. This analysis uncovered differential protein dynamics upon aging, with FGOs displaying protein expression alterations as early as 30 years, whereas these changes were delayed until the age of 35 or 40 in MII oocytes, particularly in proteins associated with mRNA splicing, translation, and chromosome segregation. Integration with transcriptomic data revealed suppression of splicing machineries as a potential initiating factor driving oocyte aging, characterized by deficiencies in mitochondrial function and chromosome segregation. This was validated by splicing inhibition, which suppressed mitochondrial function and ROS levels in mouse and human oocytes. Further, splicing factor DHX15 was identified as a candidate regulator of stage-specific oocyte aging. Together, our work systematically delineates the dynamic protein landscapes of human oocytes across multiple age groups, providing molecular targets and potential therapeutic strategies for clinical intervention.
authors: Yin C, Hou Z, Zhao R, Wang M, Ling S, Zhang C, Feng X, Zhao S, Chen ZJ, Wu K, Zhang H, Guo X, Zhao H.

title: Interferon-activated neutrophils characterize coronary microvascular dysfunction in women with ANOCA
abstract: Background  Coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) is a common cause of ischemic symptoms in patients with angina and non-obstructive coronary arteries (ANOCA), predominantly women. Neutrophils may contribute to CMD via vascular inflammation and endothelial injury. We therefore investigated neutrophil and coronary endothelial cells in women with ANOCA. Methods  In this cross-sectional study, we collected blood samples from ANOCA patients (n=123, 84% women) undergoing coronary function testing. Complete blood counts (CELL-DYN, n=123) and neutrophil activation (AQUIOS, n=76) were assessed. Isolated neutrophils were profiled using single-cell RNA-seq (n=11). Guidewire-derived coronary endothelial cells (n=7) isolated during coronary function testing were cultured to passage 2 for bulk RNA-seq. Results  Of 103 women with ANOCA, 23 (22%) were diagnosed with CMD (CFRConclusion  Reduced CFR in women with ANOCA is associated with neutrophil activation, expansion of an IFN-activated neutrophil population, and altered immature neutrophil transcriptional programs. Neutrophil activation is accompanied by distinct endothelial signatures. These findings implicate neutrophil–endothelial interactions in CMD and identify IFN-associated neutrophil states as targets for mechanistic investigation. Clinical Perspective  What is new?  This study provides the first characterization of circulating neutrophils in coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD), identifying an increased proportion of interferon (IFN)-activated neutrophils and an IFN-enriched immature neutrophil phenotype Reduced neutrophil surface CD62L expression was associated with altered endothelial gene expression and increased endothelial proliferative and metabolic activity, suggesting a potential neutrophil-endothelial interaction in CMD What are the clinical implications?  Neutrophil activation and IFN signaling emerge as candidate pathways for further investigation into the mechanisms underlying CMD and as potential targets for future therapeutic research The association between lower CFR in women and an increased IFN-activated neutrophil population supports further investigation of sex-specific immune mechanisms in CMD.
authors: de Jong E, Kapteijn DM, Daniels MA, Zweers B, Peeters DA, Vrisekoop N, Civelek M, Haitjema S, Mokry M, Damman P, van de Hoef TP, Benavente ED, den Ruijter HM.

title: Prefrontal cortex transcriptomes distinguish Alzheimer’s disease from asymptomatic amyloid pathology, neuropeptide loss, immune-complement activation and glial remodelling
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is now defined biologically by cortical amyloid-β (A) and tau (T) pathology, yet the transcriptional programmes that separate symptomatic AD (A+T+) from amyloid-positive, tau-negative pathology ageing (A+T−) and from pathology-free controls (A−T−) remain incompletely resolved in the association cortex. We re-analysed bulk RNA-sequencing data from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) of 15 donors (BioProject PRJNA1017546; 87 sequencing runs aggregated to donor level): Normal (n = 2), pathology ageing (n = 5) and AD (n = 8). Differential expression was tested with DESeq2 (adjusted P  1), and up- and down-regulated gene sets were analysed separately by Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG over-representation. APOE and TREM2 p.Arg47His contrasts were treated as exploratory. AD versus Normal yielded 341 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; 223 up, 118 down) and AD versus pathology ageing yielded 496 (358 up, 138 down), whereas pathology ageing versus Normal yielded only six. Genes reduced in AD were dominated by neuropeptide and hormone signalling (  VGF ,  VIP ,  CRH ,  GRP ,  TAC1 ,  PENK ; neuroactive ligand–receptor interaction, adjusted P = 8.8 × 10; neuropeptide hormone activity, adjusted P = 6.3 × 10), most of which also differed from pathology ageing. Genes increased in AD were enriched for interferon-γ response, myeloid activation, adaptive immunity and classical complement (  C1QA ,  C1QB ,  C1QC ). Relative to pathology ageing, AD additionally showed induction of gliogenesis, oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination programmes (gliogenesis, 21 genes, adjusted P = 2.6 × 10;  SOX10 ,  MYRF ) and of the microglial purinergic receptor gene  P2RX7 (log FC = 1.46, adjusted P = 1.5 × 10). All six pathology-ageing DEGs, including the myeloid genes  VSIG4 and  CD163 , were also DEGs in AD, and 50 DEGs shared by the two AD contrasts moved in the same direction. Genotype-stratified analyses were underpowered or confounded with diagnosis. In the DLPFC, AD is therefore characterised by a graded loss of neuropeptidergic signalling, myeloid–complement activation that begins at the pathology-ageing stage, and an AD-specific glial/oligodendrocyte response. These signatures nominate candidate biomarkers and mechanisms for early intervention, but the small cohort demands replication in larger, covariate-annotated datasets.
authors: Aliyu YM, Sagir U, Sajjad F, Khurshid S, Tarique F, Maikudi IS.

title: Spatial Transcriptomic Profiling Reveals Niche-Governed Efferocytosis-Related Gene Signatures and Degradation-Phase Dysregulation in Myocardial Infarction
abstract: Clearing dying cardiomyocytes by efferocytosis is required for inflammation resolution and cardiac repair after myocardial infarction (MI). Whether the three functional stages of efferocytosis (recognition, engulfment and degradation) are coordinated by the local cellular neighborhood in the human infarcted myocardium is unknown. We analyzed 24 human cardiac Visium spatial transcriptomic samples (20 MI, 4 control; 94,029 spots; 19 independent donors) from a published multi-omic map of human MI[4]. Multiview interaction-based spatial transcriptomics (MISTy) identified 12 gene programs with spot-level neighborhood dependency; donor-level aggregation showed positive neighborhood gains for 22 of 23 programs after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (FDR < 0.05), including all three efferocytosis stages[5]. Efferocytosis module activity tracked macrophage proportions (Spearman rho = 0.41-0.44). Controlling for macrophage abundance removed the engulfment-related association but left a degradation-related association with endothelial and fibroblast proportions, indicating niche-dependent regulation of the degradation stage. Distance-stratified analysis showed neighborhood effects beyond direct cell-cell contact, without simple short-range dominance. Mendelian randomization linked NR1H3, STAU1, CTSS and ITGAV expression to MI risk (FDR < 0.05)[14], and connectivity-map analysis nominated niclosamide as a candidate for reversing the efferocytosis-degradation program[15]. Model-based in silico perturbation attributed the neighborhood dependency to vascular-stromal neighbors; virtual knockout of NR1H3 predicted coordinated downregulation of efferocytosis genes. Efferocytosis subprograms are thus spatially decoupled in the human infarcted myocardium, with degradation as a niche-regulated step, providing spatial and genetic leads for targeting infarct repair.
authors: Zhou Y, Wen J, Cao J, Liao J, Li G, Mao Y.

title: Metal Complexes of Platinum, Palladium, and Ruthenium: From Chemical Design to Medical Applications
abstract: Metal-based compounds have emerged as promising candidates for anticancer therapy, offering structural diversity and mechanisms of action beyond those of conventional chemotherapeutic agents. This review examines palladium-, platinum-, and rutheni-um-based compounds, focusing on their coordination chemistry, structure–activity rela-tionships, anticancer mechanisms, and therapeutic potential. Platinum-based agents re-main established components of cancer treatment, although their clinical use is limited by toxicity and drug resistance. Palladium complexes have demonstrated diverse biological effects, including DNA interactions, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis, while ruthenium compounds exhibit distinct pharmacological properties in-fluenced by ligand structure, biological transformations, and interactions with cellular targets. Recent developments, including Pt(IV) prodrugs and multifunctional plati-num-based nanomedicines, highlight strategies to improve drug delivery and therapeutic performance. Despite encouraging preclinical findings, challenges involving selectivity, stability, mechanistic understanding, and clinical translation remain. Further research integrating rational molecular design, comprehensive biological evaluation, and clinically relevant models is essential to advance the development of safer and more effective met-al-based anticancer therapies.

title: Dynamic epigenetic changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy in major depressive disorder.
abstract: Although antidepressants remain the main pharmacological treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), therapeutic response varies, highlighting the need for molecular markers that predict treatment response, as well as insights into the biological processes underlying antidepressant efficacy. Candidate-gene and cross-sectional epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have reported DNA methylation signatures associated with antidepressant response; however, findings remain inconsistent. To date, no longitudinal EWAS has examined methylation trajectories across multiple time points during antidepressant treatment in MDD. Within the Early Medication Change trial, DNA methylation data was generated for 162 patients with MDD (81 responders, 81 non-responders) and 48 matched healthy controls. Patients were assessed at four times across eight-weeks of standardized antidepressant treatment, while controls were assessed twice. Differentially methylated positions (DMPs) and regions (DMRs) were identified using longitudinal EWAS models and the comb-p algorithm. Baseline methylation levels were associated with depressive symptom severity at day 28 and day 56 through two and six DMRs, respectively (e.g., TNRC6C, CAT), whereas no single DMP reached significance. Longitudinal analyses identified one DMP associated with improvement in depressive symptoms (YLMP1) and three DMRs showing methylation changes over time (e.g., GPR126, PM20D1). Combined patient-control analyses revealed additional DMPs and DMRs associated with diagnosis and temporal effects. This study provides first longitudinal evidence of regionally coordinated DNA methylation changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy, revealing alterations in genes involved in neuroplasticity and inflammatory processes that are associated with clinical response. Replication and functional validation will be essential to determine their relevance for personalized antidepressant treatment.
authors: Müller S, Frank J, Zillich E, Streit F, Koch VN, Schiele MA, Domschke K, Tadic A, Herzog DP, Wagner S, Müller MB, Treccani G, Gassen NC, Rietschel M, Witt SH, Lieb K, Engelmann J, Zillich L.

title: A traffic-informed screening framework for prioritizing tire and road wear particle monitoring and mitigation in the Delaware River Basin.
abstract: Tire and road wear particles (TRWPs) are traffic-derived contaminants generated continuously on road surfaces and delivered to streams episodically by stormwater runoff. Direct TRWP measurements remain too sparse in most river basins to calibrate predictive concentration models, yet managers must decide where to monitor, when to sample, and where mitigation is likely to be effective. This study presents a distributed hydrologic particle-transport screening framework for TRWP/TWP prioritization in the Delaware River Basin. The framework combines Annual Average Daily Traffic (AADT), road-network connectivity, 90 m hydrologic routing, and 3-h particle-transport simulations for water years 2011-2018. Because published source factors depend strongly on whether they represent total tread mass, an airborne particle fraction, or a specific vehicle class, model output is interpreted as a source-scenario and relative-priority indicator rather than a validated estimate of absolute in-stream concentration. The reference scenario uses a 51.1 mg vehicle-km-1 passenger-car total-wear factor and identifies the lower-basin urban corridor near Philadelphia and Wilmington as the strongest source-connectivity convergence zone. In the WY2018 reference scenario, modeled indicators at the Lower Delaware outlet are one to two orders of magnitude larger than those at the Upper Delaware outlet. A representative October 2017 event illustrates how dry-weather buildup followed by runoff-generating rainfall can create candidate storm-recession sampling windows. Multi-year monthly patterns identify fall and late-winter to early-spring as candidate monitoring periods, while turbidity records indicate that conventional sediment indicators should not be used as standalone TRWP proxies. The framework translates sparse traffic, hydrologic, and water-quality information into testable monitoring and mitigation priorities.
authors: Li Z, Huang Y, Sun N, Duan Z, Wigmosta M, Yang Z, Maurer B.

title: Psychosocial correlates of dementia screening intention among chinese community-dwelling older adults in the Yangtze River Delta region of China: A machine learning and network analysis study.
abstract: ObjectivesScreening plays a pivotal role in preventing and managing dementia. However, screening intention remains insufficient among some older adults, particularly in developing countries. This study aimed to identify key sociodemographic and psychosocial factors associated with intention to screen for dementia among community-dwelling older adults in China and to examine their interrelationships.MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted between April and October 2025 among 10,797 community-dwelling older adults in the Yangtze River Delta region of China, recruited from Shanghai municipality and Jiangsu, Zhejiang, and Anhui provinces. We collected sociodemographic information and psychosocial measures, including dementia screening-related health literacy, stigma, perceived benefits, approval from significant others, and perceived burden on family. Multiple machine-learning models were developed and compared, and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) were used to rank the relative contribution of candidate variables. Network analysis was then applied to the top-ranked variables to characterize their interrelationships and centrality.ResultsAmong the models examined, XGBoost demonstrated comparatively strong overall performance and generalisability. SHAP analysis suggested that stigma was the factor most associated with dementia screening intention, followed by perceived benefits. Network analysis further identified perceived benefits as a central node, with positive connections to screening-related health literacy and approval from significant others, and a negative connection to stigma. Perceived family burden was positively associated with stigma.ConclusionsStigma was the strongest factor negatively associated with screening intention, while perceived benefits served as a central hub. Future interventions to promote screening intention among older adults may benefit from reducing stigma and enhancing perceived benefits.
authors: Luo D, Yang B, Yin T, Wang Z, Qi X, Wang R, Gu J, Sun F, Ji H, Mi Z, Yin H, Liu H, Song Y, Bai Y.

title: Circulating Tumor DNA and Cell-Free DNA as Candidate Biomarkers After Image-Guided Locoregional Therapy in Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Colorectal Liver Metastases: A Systematic Review.
abstract: PurposeTo review ctDNA and cfDNA as biomarkers after locoregional therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and colorectal liver metastases (CRLM).Materials and methodsPubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched (July 2026) for ctDNA/cfDNA studies in HCC or CRLM patients undergoing TACE, Y90, or ablation; Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessed risk of bias.ResultsEleven studies were included (eight HCC, three CRLM; n≈820). Pre-treatment ctDNA mutations predicted survival after TACE (CTNNB1: HR 5.3, 95% CI 1.4-20.6; TP53: HR 5.3, 95% CI 1.4-10.1; KEAP1: HR 22.0, 95% CI 2.2-221.0). A cfDNA/ctDNA score stratified progression-free survival after TACE (1.3 vs 10.3 months; p=0.002). ctDNA predicted death after ablation in HCC (HR 2.6, 95% CI 1.5-4.7; p=0.001) and recurrence in CRLM (HR 2.97, 95% CI 1.47-6.03; P=0.003). Y90 evidence was limited.ConclusionCtDNA and cfDNA correlated with treatment outcomes after locoregional therapy; evidence is heterogeneous and biomarker-driven trials are required before clinical implementation.
journal: Journal of vascular and interventional radiology : JVIR
authors: O'Sullivan NJ, Temperley HC, Mac Curtain BM, Kelly ME, Solomon SB, Hui JZ, Moriarty JM.

title: Integrated Assessment of Cyanobacterial Blooms, Pesticides, and Reproductive Toxicity in a Eutrophic Reservoir.
abstract: The Barra Bonita Reservoir (São Paulo, Brazil) is a eutrophic system subject to intense anthropogenic pressures, including nutrient enrichment and contamination by emerging pollutants. This study evaluated the seasonal dynamics of water quality, cyanobacteria, cyanotoxins, and pesticides, and assessed their biological effects through in vivo exposure experiments using zebrafish (Danio rerio). Water samples were collected in summer, autumn, winter, and spring of 2024 for limnological, chemical, and toxicological analyses. Results revealed pronounced seasonal variability, with eutrophic conditions persisting throughout the year, characterized by high nutrient concentrations and continuous cyanobacterial dominance. Cyanobacterial densities exceeded regulatory limits in all seasons, with a marked bloom in spring, accompanied by peak microcystin concentrations (27.83 ± 5.56 μg/L). Pesticide occurrence also varied seasonally, with greater chemical diversity in summer and maximum concentrations of fipronil (11.4 ng/L) and hexazinone (1.9 ng/L) in spring. In vivo assays demonstrated that exposure to reservoir water induced significant modulation of genes related to the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, steroidogenesis, and germ cell development, indicating modulation of endocrine related transcriptional pathways. Additionally, all exposure groups showed reduced spermatozoa production compared to controls, while androgen (11-ketotestosterone) plasma levels were normal in most seasons but significantly increased in spring. These findings highlight seasonal associations between eutrophic conditions, contaminant occurrence, and molecular and reproductive responses. This study underscores the importance of integrated monitoring and management strategies to mitigate risks associated with cyanobacterial blooms and pesticides in tropical reservoirs.
authors: Moraes ACN, Souza BM, Ribeiro AO, Nogueira MG, Vilar MCP, Azevedo SMFO, Montagner CC, Nobrega RH.

title: Beyond classification accuracy: Building trustworthy artificial intelligence for clinical electroencephalography.
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) remains important in clinical neuroscience because it records brain activity as a time-resolved physiological process. It offers millisecond temporal resolution, can be used at the bedside and supports prolonged monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded EEG analysis through automated pattern recognition, representation learning, large-scale screening and decision support in epilepsy, sleep medicine, cognitive disorders, psychiatric conditions, intensive care, disorders of consciousness and anaesthesia monitoring. High classification accuracy in a research dataset, however, is not clinical readiness. EEG signals are shaped by physiological state, artefacts, acquisition systems, preprocessing choices and clinical context. Labels may come from expert annotations, diagnostic categories, behavioural scales, treatment responses or long-term outcomes, and these sources do not always define the same biological target. This review argues that EEG-AI translation should be judged by the strength of its evidence, not by technical performance alone. We examine why EEG is valuable yet hard to standardize, how EEG features can serve as candidate biomarkers, and why translational maturity differs across clinical scenarios. We then discuss the evidence gaps behind high-performing models, focusing on target validity, data leakage, confounding, external validation and clinically aligned metrics. Finally, we argue for clinical understandability rather than model interpretability alone, and for human-machine workflows rather than isolated classifiers. Future EEG-AI systems should be assessed by whether their outputs are biologically plausible, externally generalizable, understandable to clinicians and safe in real-world care.
authors: Hu S, Huang Y, Zhang J.

title: Investigating the toxicological effects of 3-Phenoxybenzoic acid exposure on sarcopenia via integrated network toxicology, machine learning, bioinformatics, and in vitro validation.
abstract: 3-Phenoxybenzoic acid (3-PBA), a widespread degradation product of pyrethroid insecticides, poses potential health risks, but its mechanistic role in sarcopenia remains unclear. We integrated network toxicology, machine learning using LASSO, Elastic Net, random forest, and SVM-RFE, SHAP analysis, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and in vitro validation to investigate its underlying effects. A total of 119 candidate genes were prioritized, and five candidate hub genes (GOT2, HDAC4, NDUFS3, ORAI1, and PLIN3) were identified. Enrichment analyses indicated associations with energy metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, muscle contraction, oxidative stress-related processes, and mitochondrial function. Molecular docking and MD simulations supported the plausibility of interactions between 3-PBA and selected hub proteins, while revealing distinct dynamic behaviors among the simulated complexes. In differentiating C2C12 cells, 3-PBA suppressed cell viability, increased Atrogin-1 and MuRF1 expression, decreased Myog mRNA expression, and altered the transcript levels of the five candidate hub genes. Further functional assays and MYOM3 immunofluorescence analysis showed decreased intracellular ATP levels, increased intracellular Ca2+ levels, enhanced lipid peroxidation, and an overall reduction in MYOM3-positive fluorescence and MYOM3-positive myotube-like structures following 3-PBA exposure. These findings suggest that 3-PBA exposure is associated with disturbances in cellular energy status and Ca2+ homeostasis, oxidative injury, and altered myogenic structural characteristics, providing experimental support for its potential adverse effects on skeletal muscle cells and its possible relationship with sarcopenia.
authors: Zhao P, Lu Y, Ma Z, Zhang Y, Yang X, Li Y, Liu X.

title: Network Medicine Identifies a FOSL1/SNAI1-CCND1/CXCR4 Network Associated with N-Methyl-N'-nitro-N-nitrosoguanidine-Related Gastric Precancerous Lesions and Modulated by Apigenin.
abstract: N-Methyl-N'-nitro-N-nitrosoguanidine (MNNG) is a direct-acting alkylating carcinogen. We investigated how MNNG-associated gene networks relate to gastric precancerous lesions (GPL) and gastric cancer (GC), and whether apigenin modulates selected network components. Public stage-resolved transcriptomes were integrated with co-expression analysis, protein-interaction topology, toxicant-associated gene mapping, network proximity, and machine-learning feature selection. Public expression and survival resources informed prioritization; clinical gastric-tissue transcriptomics and MNNG-exposed GES-1 cell transcriptomics/proteomics provided separate expression evidence. Intervention experiments used 10 μM MNNG for 48 h with 10 or 20 μM apigenin in cells, and 200 mg/L MNNG for 20 weeks with 15 or 30 mg/kg/day apigenin during weeks 9-20 in rats. The analyses identified an expression-associated network involving GDF15, TGFB1, FOSL1, SNAI1, CCND1, CXCR4 and PLAU, with inflammatory, proliferative and matrix-remodeling programs. Clinical and cellular evidence varied by cohort and assay. Apigenin was prioritized using its negative proximity Z-score (-2.166), short network distance (1.069), and biological plausibility. It counter-regulated selected MNNG-associated expression changes, particularly involving FOSL1, SNAI1, CCND1 and CXCR4. Docking and 50-ns molecular dynamics simulations provided supportive computational evidence for candidate structural hypotheses. Together, the findings nominate an apigenin-responsive network associated with MNNG-related gastric molecular alterations and prioritize its components for subsequent functional investigation.
authors: Ou J, Li Z, Ma G, Ma L, Deng A, Wu S, Cui Y, Situ J, Yang J, Fang J, Fang S, Zhang K, Xiang Y, Chen X, Li H, Li J, Pan H.

title: Regulation of ketone body metabolism: biochemical mechanisms controlling ketogenesis and ketolysis.
abstract: Traditionally considered as alternative energy substrates, ketone bodies (KBs), notably β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB) and acetoacetate, are now recognized as key metabolic intermediates whose circulating levels must be tightly controlled to ensure energy homeostasis. KBs are mostly hepatically produced, via ketogenesis, and catabolized by extrahepatic tissues during fasting or carbohydrate restriction. The regulation of KBs metabolism relies on a coordinated network of hormonal, enzymatic and transcriptional mechanisms that control KBs synthesis and degradation. KBs anabolic and catabolic rates are controlled by the rate-limiting enzymes 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA-synthase 2 (HMGCS2), governing ketogenesis, and succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid-CoA transferase (SCOT), driving ketolysis. Their activity and expression are finely orchestrated, especially by the insulin/glucagon ratio, to adapt to the organism's fluctuating energy demands. Transcriptionally, ketogenesis is regulated through peroxisome-proliferator-activated-receptor-alpha (PPARα) and the transcription factor forkhead-box-A2 (FOXA2), which respond to nutrient availability and hormonal cues. In parallel, ketolysis is tightly controlled through the regulation of SCOT expression, notably via PPARα-dependent mechanisms, as well as through post-translational modifications (PTMs) affecting enzyme activity. Together, these regulatory mechanisms ensure a precise balance between KBs production and utilization. Emerging evidence also suggests that additional modulators, such as the gut microbiota, indirectly influence KBs metabolism by affecting substrate availability and metabolic signaling pathways, although its quantitative contribution remains to be established. Here, we provide a mechanistic overview of the pathways governing KBs metabolism, with focus on the regulation of ketogenesis and ketolysis. We discuss how these processes are integrated at multiple levels to maintain systemic energy homeostasis and consider their implications for metabolic disease.
authors: Nasser S, Balcerczyk A, Pirola L.

title: Comparative proteomics of the venomous barb and epidermal mucus from the Atlantic stingray (Hypanus sabinus): Discovery of novel toxin candidates.
abstract: When deployed, the venomous barb of the stingray causes immediate tissue damage with intense pain that is sometimes followed by significant tissue necrosis. The venom toxins that mediate these responses are currently not well understood. We report here for the Atlantic stingray (Hypanus sabinus), a bottom-up proteomic analysis comparing the venomous barb proteome (both ventral and dorsal tissues) with the proteome of the pectoral fin epidermal mucus (control). Using this comparative approach, a novel set of putative venom proteins were identified as both abundant and enriched within the heterogenous barb tissue extracts that exhibited distinct bioactivities. Additionally, exocyst complex proteins that tether and traffic secretory vesicles to cell membrane were identified within the ventral barb proteome, providing evidence for a distinct secretory apparatus. Among the identified venom toxin candidates, SE-cephalotoxin (CTX)-like isoforms were discovered as the most abundant in the venomous barb. From phylogenic analysis, the SE-CTX-like proteins belong to a novel rapunzel-like (Rpzl) gene family found in cartilaginous fish that is closely related to the rapunzel (Rpz) gene family exclusive to bony fish. The function of these proteins is currently unknown, however structural modelling indicates Rpzl monomers may form oligomeric pore-forming complexes. Several other abundant proteins enriched in the barb with homology to known venom toxins were identified and include Lgals12, Hyal6, Glipr2, Capg, Kng1, Ctsd, Halt1, and St14a. Collectively, the venom proteins described here are expected to be responsible for causing intense pain and tissue necrosis that provides the Atlantic stingray with an effective means of predation defense.
journal: Toxicon : official journal of the International Society on Toxinology
authors: Doupnik CA, Chaput D, Guedouar EG, Margres MJ, Walsh CJ, Luer CA.

title: P2Y6R is associated with adipose inflammation and muscle wasting in pancreatic cancer cachexia.
abstract: BackgroundPancreatic cancer has one of the highest incidences of cancer-associated cachexia, a multi-organ wasting syndrome driven by complex tumor-host interactions. Although adipose tissue functions as an active endocrine organ contributing to systemic inflammation, the mechanisms linking adipose inflammation to skeletal muscle wasting remain incompletely understood.MethodsAn orthotopic pancreatic tumor mouse model was combined with pharmacological P2Y6R inhibition using MRS2578. Cachexia-associated targets were identified by transcriptomic analysis of mouse datasets, and P2Y6R function was examined in vitro cancer-associated adipocyte (CAA) and C2C12 myotube models.ResultsTranscriptomic analysis identified P2Y6R as a cachexia-associated gene, with expression selectively upregulated in visceral adipose tissue and CAAs under pancreatic cancer conditions. In contrast, P2Y6R expression was minimal in skeletal muscle and comparatively low in tumor tissue. In the orthotopic model, pharmacological inhibition of P2Y6R with MRS2578, initiated before overt weight loss, attenuated body weight loss. This was accompanied by reduced serum IL-6 and IL-1β levels (IL-1β at 3 mg/kg only) and decreased expression of the atrogenes mRNA expression in skeletal muscle. In vitro, conditioned medium from CAAs suppressed myotube differentiation, whereas P2ry6 knockdown in adipocytes attenuated this effect. Mechanistically, the P2Y6R-dependent secretome of cancer-associated adipocytes was associated with increased atrogene expression and altered FOXO3 phosphorylation in myotubes.ConclusionsOur findings indicate that P2Y6R is associated with adipose inflammation and muscle wasting in pancreatic cancer cachexia, and that pharmacological P2Y6R inhibition attenuates cachexia progression in a preventive setting. These results suggest a potential contribution of adipocyte P2Y6R to adipose-muscle crosstalk and highlight P2Y6R as a candidate therapeutic target for cancer-associated muscle loss.
authors: Kim J, Chae J, Choi J.

title: Mechanical stress accelerates intervertebral disc degeneration through PIEZO1-YAP1/TEAD1-mediated NEDD4 activation and NFS1 ubiquitination-dependent mitochondrial dysfunction.
abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IDD) is a major cause of chronic low back pain, and excessive mechanical stress is considered an important driver of nucleus pulposus cell (NPC) dysfunction. However, the molecular mechanisms linking mechanotransduction to mitochondrial injury and protein homeostasis remain incompletely understood. In this study, we established a 100 kPa static compression model in primary mouse NPCs and combined transcriptomic and proteomic profiling with cross-layer comparative analysis to identify candidate regulators associated with mechanical stress-induced degeneration. NFS1 was identified as a key protective molecule whose protein abundance decreased under mechanical compression without a statistically significant decrease in its corresponding transcript abundance. NFS1 depletion impaired mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production, increased reactive oxygen species accumulation, and promoted NPC senescence, apoptosis, and ferroptosis-associated molecular changes, whereas NFS1 overexpression alleviated these degenerative phenotypes. Mechanistically, the E3 ubiquitin ligase NEDD4 interacted with NFS1 and was involved in regulating NFS1 ubiquitination and proteasomal stability under mechanical stress. Upstream, mechanical compression activated PIEZO1-dependent Ca2+ signaling, promoted YAP1 dephosphorylation and nuclear accumulation, and enhanced NEDD4 transcription through YAP1- and TEAD1-dependent transcriptional regulation. Pharmacological inhibition or genetic knockdown of PIEZO1 attenuated these signaling changes, while NEDD4 knockdown or NFS1 restoration mitigated PIEZO1 activation-induced oxidative stress, apoptosis, and matrix degeneration. In vivo, AAV-mediated NEDD4 knockdown or NFS1 overexpression alleviated structural and histological degeneration in a mouse tail compression model. Collectively, these findings identify a mechanosensitive PIEZO1-YAP1/TEAD1-NEDD4-NFS1 regulatory axis that links abnormal mechanical loading to impaired mitochondrial homeostasis and NPC degeneration, providing a potential therapeutic framework for mechanically driven IDD.
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease
authors: Chen F, Chen S, Peng F, Zhang H, Lv C, Sun C, Du Y, Li T, Xi Y.

title: The thioredoxin system in cellular senescence and ageing: From redox homeostasis to therapeutic targeting.
abstract: The major characteristics of cellular senescence are stable cell-cycle arrest, accumulation of DNA damage responses, mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic remodeling, and the release of pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors. Redox imbalance plays a significant role in the initiation and maintenance of senescence, and the mammalian thioredoxin system-comprising cytosolic Trx-1, mitochondrial Trx-2, thioredoxin reductases (TrxR1, TrxR2), and the inhibitor TXNIP-is at a key juncture between oxidative stress, cellular ageing, and age-related diseases. Evidence was identified through a structured literature search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception to July 2026 using predefined search terms and eligibility criteria. Primary experimental studies in mammalian cells, tissues, or animal models that directly measured senescence markers were prioritised. Reviews, non-mammalian studies, and studies reporting only general oxidative-stress endpoints were included only when they provided essential mechanistic context and are clearly labelled as such. This review focuses primarily on mammalian mechanisms linking the thioredoxin system to senescence initiation, senescence maintenance, inflammaging, tissue dysfunction, and translational geroscience. We distinguish isoform-specific and context-dependent effects of Trx-1, Trx-2, TrxR, and TXNIP. We also discuss therapeutic strategies targeting the thioredoxin system, including redox modulation, isoform-selective inhibitors, senomorphic approaches, and disease-specific interventions. Overall, the thioredoxin system is a significant molecular link between redox homeostasis, cellular senescence, ageing biology, and age-related pathology, and a candidate target for future geroscience interventions, although direct evidence in aged mammals remains limited.
authors: Yu Y, Bai Y, Wan T, Tang X.

title: Short‑chain fatty acid-related metabolism may be an important factor affecting intramuscular fat deposition in the longissimus dorsi muscle of Min pigs: evidence from integrated multi‑omics analysis.
abstract: ObjectiveIntramuscular fat (IMF) deposition is an important determinant of pork quality. Although Northeast Min (Min) pigs are characterized by high IMF content, its molecular basis remains unclear. This study investigated the molecular basis of differential IMF deposition between Min and Duroc × Landrace × Yorkshire (DLY) pigs through integrated multi-omics analysis of longissimus dorsi muscle.MethodsSix Min and six DLY pigs raised under identical conditions were compared at a similar body weight (~100 kg). Longissimus dorsi samples were used for IMF determination and untargeted metabolomics, and four pigs per group were randomly selected for matched transcriptomic and proteomic analyses.ResultsMin pigs had significantly higher IMF content than DLY pigs (p ConclusionEfficient IMF deposition in Min pigs may be associated with altered SCFA-related metabolic processes, providing insights into pork fat trait improvement and differential fat deposition.

title: Integrative single cell and machine learning analysis identifies fibroblast centric hub genes and therapeutic candidates in lung adenocarcinoma and ischemic cardiomyopathy.
abstract: BackgroundIschemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) are distinct diseases but may share fibroblast mediated mechanisms involving tissue remodeling and inflammation. However, their common molecular features at single cell resolution remain insufficiently defined.MethodsWe integrated single cell RNA sequencing datasets from ICM and LUAD with bulk transcriptomic profiles from TCGA LUAD, GSE18842, and GSE48166. Differential expression analysis identified 36 shared core genes. A total of 127 combinations of machine learning algorithms and feature selection methods were benchmarked to identify six hub genes: KRTCAP3, RUNX2, DBF4B, C11orf80, COL3A1, and ZFP64. UCell, scMetabolism, SCISSOR, Monocle 3, CellChat, scTenifoldNet/scTenifoldKnk, virtual drug screening, and molecular docking were used for functional characterization.ResultsFibroblasts were the dominant cellular source of the six hub genes in both ICM and LUAD. COL3A1 progressively increased along fibroblast pseudotime trajectories. Virtual overexpression and knockout analyses showed convergence on extracellular matrix organization, inflammatory response, and immune regulation. Cell communication analysis identified fibroblasts as major senders of COLLAGEN signaling, with recipient cells shifting from inflammatory monocytes under normal conditions to proliferating macrophages in ICM and tumor cells in LUAD. Molecular docking nominated Digoxin, Ergotamine, and Ledipasvir as candidate RUNX2-binding compounds with favorable predicted docking scores.ConclusionsThis study provides a single cell framework linking ICM and LUAD through fibroblast driven extracellular matrix remodeling and inflammation, and identifies potential molecular targets and therapeutic candidates for further validation.
authors: Pu Z, Liu Z, Zhang H, Han Y.

title: Unveiling the nitro-oxidative dimension of copper toxicity in Phytophthora infestans.
abstract: Copper (Cu) is an essential heavy metal widely used as a component of fungicides against pathogens, including Phytophthora infestans (Mont.) de Bary, the main cause of late blight disease. Despite the widespread use of Cu-based pesticides, data on their accumulation and long-term effects on economically important plant pathogens remain scarce. Therefore, this study assessed Cu-dependent alterations in nitro-oxidative homeostasis within P. infestans structures, as imbalances in reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS) may disrupt pathogen development and host interaction. Biochemical and molecular methods were used to analyze two P. infestans genotypes with contrasting virulence toward potato cv. Bzura. Our results idicate that exposition of Avr/vr P. infestans to Cu stress reduced pathogen viability and increased the formation of ROS (superoxide radical anion, hydrogen peroxide) and RNS (nitric oxide, peroxynitrite, nitroxyl) within the pathogen structures. In the Avr genotype, Cu enhanced overall ROS production, whereas in the vr genotype only hydrogen peroxide was increased. Furthermore, Cu treatment induced genotype-specific nitro-oxidative DNA/RNA modifications: the Avr genotype showed elevated apurinic/apyrimidinic sites in DNA along with increased 8-OHG and 8-NG levels in RNA, while the vr genotype exhibited only higher 8-NG levels in DNA. To assess the impact of Cu exposure on P. infestans pathogenicity, disease index and molecular analyses of disease progression were conducted, revealing Cu-dependent acceleration of pathogen growth and host colonization. Overall, Cu-induced responses varied according to the pathogen's virulence profile, indicating distinct heavy-metal stress adaptation strategies among P. infestans genotypes and offering a potential explanation for the inconsistent effectiveness of Cu-based disease management strategies.
authors: Gajewska J, Suarez SA, Wesołowski MS, Sobieszczuk-Nowicka E, Floryszak-Wieczorek J, Arasimowicz-Jelonek M.

title: Integrative network toxicology and machine learning reveal the potential role of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural in exacerbating pulmonary fibrosis.
abstract: Background5-Hydroxymethylfurfural (5-HMF), a ubiquitous furan derivative formed during the thermal processing of carbohydrate-rich foods, represents a widespread dietary exposure. However, its potential contribution to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) remains unclear. This study investigated the molecular links between 5-HMF and IPF using an integrated computational and experimental approach.MethodsIPF-related genes were identified through transcriptomic analysis combining differential expression analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis. Candidate targets were obtained by intersecting IPF-associated genes with predicted 5-HMF targets. Functional enrichment analysis, ensemble machine learning, and SHAP interpretation were performed to prioritize candidate targets, while molecular docking was used to explore potential 5-HMF-target interactions. A bleomycin-induced mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis was further used to evaluate the effects of 5-HMF on fibrotic lung injury and the transcriptional expression of prioritized candidate genes.ResultsA total of 1,776 IPF-associated genes and 143 predicted 5-HMF targets were identified, yielding 12 overlapping candidate targets. Enrichment analysis implicated these genes in fibrosis-related pathways, including chemical carcinogenesis-receptor activation and estrogen signaling. Machine learning analysis prioritized seven core targets (CA2, CA4, ESR2, F10, HSP90AA1, PLA2G1B, and PTPRB), all of which accommodated 5-HMF in their orthosteric pockets in blind docking, albeit with weak, non-selective Vina scores (-4.5 to -5.4 kcal/mol). In vivo, 5-HMF significantly exacerbated bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, as demonstrated by aggravated lung injury, increased collagen deposition, and elevated expression of Hsp90aa1, Pla2g1b, Ca4, F10, Acta2, and Col1a1.ConclusionOur findings suggest that 5-HMF may exacerbate fibrotic lung injury through multiple fibrosis-related molecular targets and pathways. These findings provide preliminary evidence for a potential association between 5-HMF exposure and the aggravation of pulmonary fibrosis, while further studies are required to determine whether 5-HMF can independently initiate fibrotic pathology.

title: Biomedical properties and emerging translational potential of bovine milk extracellular vesicles.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles have garnered significant attention in the biomedical field due to their potential as therapeutic agents and diagnostic tools. Bovine milk extracellular vesicles (BMEVs), in particular, have emerged as a promising tool in biomedical research due to their unique biocompatibility, stability, and ease of isolation. As an alternative to extracellular vesicles sourced from human cells, such as stem cells or blood, these naturally occurring nanovesicles are increasingly recognized for their dual role as potential therapeutic carriers and diagnostic candidates. To map the evolution and knowledge structure of the field, we conducted a CiteSpace analysis that reveals how BMEVs research has expanded beyond nutritional science to emerge as a versatile biomedical platform with rapidly broadening applications. Also, this review systematically examines the biogenesis, isolation techniques, and structural features of BMEVs, while highlighting their applications in drug delivery, disease therapy, and diagnostics. Current preclinical studies provide preclinical evidence supporting potential therapeutic applications. However, clinical safety, therapeutic efficacy, reproducibility, dosing, biodistribution, immunogenicity, large-scale manufacturing, and regulatory acceptance remain to be established. Future research should focus on optimizing drug-loading strategies, enhancing targeted delivery, and exploring novel biomedical applications.
authors: Guan X, Hou X, Meng W, Guo HD.

title: Palmitoylation-related gene signature analysis links ENPP6 to potential protection of renal tubule against ischemia-reperfusion injury.
abstract: BackgroundAcute kidney injury (AKI), particularly ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), lacks effective targeted therapies. Protein S-palmitoylation is a reversible lipid modification involved in cellular stress responses, but its role in AKI remains unclear. We aimed to identify palmitoylation-related genes in AKI and explore their potential functions.MethodsPublic transcriptome datasets of AKI kidney tissues were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Palmitoylation-related common hub genes were screened by integrating DEG analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data and online clinical databases were used to determine cellular localization and clinical relevance. ENPP6 was further validated in a mouse renal IRI model and hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R)-treated renal tubule cells.ResultsSix candidate common hub genes were identified: EDN1, VMP1, ENPP6, MYC, CXCR4, and EFNA1. Among them, ENPP6 was enriched in renal tubular cells and showed the strongest association with indices of renal function. ENPP6 expression was significantly reduced in the renal tubules of IRI mice at both the mRNA and protein levels. In renal tubule cells, ENPP6 overexpression was accompanied by increased overall protein S-palmitoylation. Functionally, ENPP6 overexpression improved cell viability and alleviated H/R-induced injury.ConclusionsENPP6 expression was reduced in renal IRI and was positively associated with renal function. In renal tubular cells, ENPP6 overexpression was accompanied by increased global protein S-palmitoylation and reduced H/R-induced injury. These findings identify ENPP6 as a potential protective factor and a candidate for further mechanistic investigation in ischemic AKI.
authors: Cao S, Hou Y, Wang Y, Lin S, Zhu Y, Zhang L, Xu J, Chen J, Xia J.

title: Cross-regulatory sRNA networks shape adaptive stress responses in  Staphylococcus aureus  : RsaC and RsaOI regulate galactose metabolism and cell wall homeostasis
abstract: A  bstract   Staphylococcus aureus is a major human pathogen whose adaptability relies on network of regulators, including two-component systems, transcription factors and small regulatory RNAs. Yet most of these regulators are dispensable for growth, suggesting cooperation or redundancy between them. To explore this hypothesis, we performed a yeast one-hybrid screen of 43 TFs against the promoters of seven sRNAs, which identified 27 novel TF-sRNA promoter interactions. We then focused on three sRNAs. We showed that  srn_9342 is repressed by VraR and MntR, which also control  rsaOI and  rsaC , respectively. We found that  rsaC , like  rsaOI , is induced by acidic pH and vancomycin exposure, whereas  srn_9342 expression remained unchanged. We also demonstrated  in vitro that Srn_9342 interacts with both RsaOI and RsaC. Its role toward these two sRNAs remains unknown, but this interaction raises the possibility that it modulates their availability or activity. RsaOI and RsaC both act on the tagatose pathway for galactose utilization, through different genes:  lacD for RsaOI, as previously reported, and  lacC for RsaC, newly identified here. We showed that both sRNAs are required for surface charge remodeling and for growth under subinhibitory vancomycin. They also modulate the virulence factors PSMα and protein A. Both sRNAs reduce PSMα production, whereas protein A is decreased by RsaOI, likely through Rot, and increased by RsaC through an unknown, probably indirect mechanism. Together, our results suggest that a single cell wall stress can engage several regulators that could cooperate on shared targets or pathways, which may explain why individual regulators are dispensable.
authors: Robin H, Germain M, Silard C, Dreano S, Augagneur Y, Chabelskaya S, Rouillon A.

title: Tripartite toxin-antitoxin system regulates the production and release of pneumolysin by  Streptococcus pneumoniae
abstract: The production of toxins is critical to the success of bacteria, with their targets and outcomes varying widely. Pneumolysin (Ply), produced by the major human pathogen  Streptococcus pneumoniae, is a cytolytic pore forming toxin that plays many diverse roles including inducing tissue damage and inflammation, evasion of many aspects of the human immune system, invasion of the bacteria into deeper tissue, and transmission to new hosts. Despite its importance, many aspects of the biology of this toxin have to date remained unknown, in particular, what role of the three other genes that form part of the  ply operon play in Ply production. Here we demonstrate that these genes encode a complex regulatory system, that includes a putative membrane destabilising protein (PlyA) and a MazEF-like toxin-antitoxin system (PlyB and PlyC), the toxin of which (PlyC) destabilises the Ply transcript. We propose a tripartite model whereby when the operon reaches relatively high levels of expression PlyA destabilises the  S. pneumoniae membrane creating a stress that triggers a necessary negative feedback loop which results in the degradation of the PlyB antitoxin, release of the PlyC toxin and degradation of the  ply transcript, thereby providing a means by which Ply production can be tightly regulated. Given the importance of Ply to the ability of  S. pneumoniae to cause infection, identifying the factors that result in the shutdown of Ply production and release by the bacteria would seem promising target for future therapeutic strategies.
authors: Bonini D, Woodall C, Takebayashi Y, Boura M, Richards C, Baltazar M, Khan I, Granneman S, Wilkinson OJ, Dillingham MS, Kadioglu A, Massey RC.

title: Genetic and Epigenetic Landscape of Self-Identified Hispanics/Latino in All Of Us
abstract: Human genetic studies still underrepresent many populations, limiting discovery and interpretation of medically relevant variation. Extensive admixture in self-identified Hispanic/Latino populations increases the need for representative reference data and ancestry-aware interpretation of medically relevant variation. We used long-read sequencing to analyze genetic variation, ancestry, and DNA methylation in 1,490 self-identified Hispanic/Latino participants from the All of Us Research Program. We identified 10 million novel variants and more than 100 candidate phenotype associations, with fine-mapping prioritizing structural variants over nearby single-nucleotide variants in more than half. We linked 3,329 tandem repeats to DNA methylation, resolved widespread allele-specific methylation, and identified ancestry-linked regulation across paralogous genes. These results reveal previously inaccessible genetic and regulatory variation and show the value of long-read sequencing for diverse populations.
authors: English AC, Fu Y, Paulin LF, Izydorczyk MB, Behera S, Li Q, Zheng X, Zhu Y, Paschall J, Tietz GE, Honorato-Mauer J, Morina LB, Griffith S, Pisupati A, Wang S, Dugan-Perez S, Shen H, Weissenberger GM, Vee V, Gearhart J, Kokosinski M, Han Y, Myers B, Sanchez AM, Mawhinney MZ, Craig BD, Marosy BA, Mehta HH, Garimella KV, Khan ZM, Venner E, Atkinson EG, Gibbs RA, Eichler EE, Talkowski ME, Doheny KF, Muzny D, Schatz MC, Metcalf GA, Timp W, All of Us Research Program Long-Read Working Group, Sedlazeck FJ.

title: Transcriptome analysis provides insights into candidate genetic regulators of birch response to salt stress
abstract: Background  Soil salinization is a worldwide matter of concern and can result in a series of agricultural and ecological problems. Previous transcriptome data have shown genetic regulatory mechanisms of salt stress response in  a salt-tolerant species of Betula halophila and a salt-sensitive species of B. platyphylla , but comparative analysis of transcriptional changes in the the two species remains limited.  Aims  We compared gene expression in leaves of  B. halophila and leaves and roots of  B. platyphylla .  Methods  Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified after 24 h of salt stress, followed by Gene Ontology enrichment and gene regulatory network (GRN) construction. Selected DEGs were examined by quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR). Results  Compared with 0 h, 956 DEGs were found in  B. halophila leaves (BHLeaf), 2,955 in  B. platyphylla leaves (BPLeaf), and 3,827 in  B. platyphylla roots (BPRoot). BHLeaf DEG expression patterns were similar to those of BPRoot. DEGs from BHLeaf and BPRoot were enriched in cell wall organization or biogenesis, whereas hormone biosynthesis and signaling genes were altered mainly in  B. platyphylla . RT-qPCR showed that selected DEGs were induced by 200 mM NaCl for 24 h in  B. platyphylla .  Conclusions  Our work uncovered genetic mechanisms of salt stress response commonly and uniquely occurring in two birch species and provides resources for breeding salt-tolerant birch. Highlights  Salt stress altered the expression of 956, 2,955 and 3,827 genes in the two birch species. BHLeaf expression patterns were similar to those of BPRoot. The expression changes of nine selected DEGs were examined by RT-qPCR in  B. platyphylla .

title: LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy alters Schwann cell calcium homeostasis and increases peripheral nerve inflammation
abstract: LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy (LAMA2-RD) affects skeletal muscle and peripheral nerves, yet the consequences of LAMA2 deficiency on peripheral nerve integrity beyond early postnatal development remain incompletely understood. We investigated sciatic nerve architecture and molecular alterations across postnatal life in hypomorphic  Lama2  dy2J/dy2J mice. LAMA2 localizes around the abaxonal surface of myelinating Schwann cells in control nerves. LAMA2-deficient nerves exhibited patchy regions lacking myelinated axons from early postnatal stages into adulthood, including expanded Remak bundles along with axons completely lacking normal Schwann cell ensheathment. In adult nerves, myelin infolding and reduced myelin circularity revealed abnormalities in the architecture of myelin that had formed. Bulk sciatic nerve RNA sequencing identified altered calcium-signaling and immune-related transcriptional signatures. Complementary Fura Red measurements in primary nerve-derived Schwann cell cultures demonstrated decreased intracellular calcium in LAMA2-deficient samples, while ATP-evoked responses were preserved. Older LAMA2-deficient nerves also exhibited increased CD45  + CD11b  + myeloid-cell infiltration. Together, these observations extend the characterization of LAMA2-associated neuropathy into adulthood and identify calcium homeostasis and neuroimmune responses as candidate processes relevant to persistent peripheral nerve pathology.
authors: Wang J, Khati M, Heron M, Munir A, Akinyele O, Johnson MA, Vockley G, Pandey UB, Kemaladewi DU.

title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya and related parahenipaviruses
abstract: Langya virus is a zoonotic parahenipavirus with pandemic potential that causes acute febrile illness in people. We identified endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) as an entry receptor for Langya, Wenzhou, and Mojiang parahenipaviruses. A 3.1 Å cryo-electron microscopy structure reveals that Langya attachment glycoprotein engages EPCR through a site distinct from that of Nipah’s ephrin binding site. This binding mode resembles those of protein C and a malarial adhesin, demonstrating convergent evolution. Interface substitutions abolish entry, whereas natural variation explains differential human EPCR use and predicts receptor compatibility across 26 animal species. These findings establish EPCR as a receptor for the Langya clade and provide a structural framework for understanding cross-species transmission and human infection potential.

title: A decade of open biodiversity data in the Azores: closing knowledge gaps and building a foundation for long-term monitoring
abstract: Ten years of dedicated biodiversity research and coordinated open-data publication have built an extensive, reusable knowledge base for the Azores. We synthesize this collective achievement through the AZORES BIOTA and BioMonI-Plot collections, evaluating its contribution to addressing the Wallacean and Prestonian shortfalls and identifying priorities for future research and monitoring. Focusing on the nine islands of this North Atlantic archipelago, we review publications issued between 2016 and May 2026, encompassing terrestrial and marine organisms across six kingdoms. We combine curated publication and dataset metadata with Darwin Core occurrenceID-linked species and subspecies records to assess spatial, taxonomic, temporal and methodological coverage, species accumulation by colonization status, and island species–area relationships. Across 91 publications, the collections document 931 animal, 1,185 plant and 742 fungal species and subspecies, alongside taxa from three additional kingdoms, and identify 598 additions to the Azorean Biodiversity Portal reference list. This sustained effort has substantially expanded accessible knowledge of species distributions, contributing to reducing the Wallacean shortfall. Arthropod abundance datasets and repeated standardized surveys also alleviate the Prestonian shortfall by enabling assessments of population and community change. Together, these resources establish valuable baselines for biodiversity assessment, invasion surveillance and conservation planning. The synthesis also reveals uneven coverage among islands, taxa and habitats, with spatial differences in research effort complicating interpretation of species–area relationships. The Azorean experience demonstrates the substantial scientific value of sustained regional expertise, collaboration and standardized open-data publication for understanding island biodiversity. By consolidating achievements and making remaining gaps explicit, this synthesis provides a foundation for targeted investment in underrepresented biota, spatially balanced surveys and sustained abundance monitoring, strengthening the evidence base for future biodiversity research and conservation.

title: A randomized dose-escalation phase I clinical trial of a nucleoprotein-based genetic vaccine against Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever
abstract: Abstract    Crimean–Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is an emerging tick-borne virus transmitted primarily by Hyalomma ticks, whose geographic distribution is expanding. CCHFV infection is associated with high case-fatality rates, and there are currently no widely approved vaccines available globally. We were the first to demonstrate that a genetic DNA vaccine (CCHF-N-pVAX1) targeting the nucleoprotein (N) of CCHFV can confer robust protection against lethal disease in mice and attenuate clinical symptoms in non-human primates (NHPs), providing proof-of-concept for a previously underexplored vaccine strategy through activation of NP-specific T cells and antibodies. The CCHF-N-pVAX1 vaccine was tested in a phase I clinical trial in 15 healthy volunteers (HVs) with three dose groups (0.45 mg, 0.90 mg, and 1.80 mg). Five HVs per group received vaccinations at day 0, 28, and 84 given intramuscularly using  in vivo  electroporation (EP; IGEA Medical), followed by 3 months of follow-up. The protocol-defined completed study reports the primary safety evaluation and secondary immunogenicity assessments through day 169. No power calculations were performed. All patients experienced temporary pain in close proximity to the vaccination/EP procedure. The vaccine was safe, and no serious adverse event (SAE) occurred. 139 other Adverse Events (AEs) occurred; 69 reactogenicity and 70 other. The AEs were mostly of mild grade (n = 123); 10 AEs were of moderate intensity, and 6 AEs were of severe intensity (diarrhea (n = 1), headache (n = 1), and fatigue (n = 4)). Most AEs (114/139) were likely or possibly related to the vaccine/EP. CCHFV N-specific antibodies and T cells appeared after the 2nd dose, and mean levels peaked after the 3rd dose at 1207 ± 2747 (endpoint titres) and 621 ± 561 (IFN-g spotforming cells), respectively. The T cell responses remained high during the 3-month follow-up. The data was consistent with our previous studies in NHPs. In conclusion, we show for the first time that a genetic nucleoprotein-based vaccine against CCHF is safe and immunogenic in humans, inducing strong T- and B-cell responses in most vaccine recipients, and suggesting a potential to confer protection against severe disease in humans. EU clinical trial number 2023-508556-18-00/IN, ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT06684431.

title: Comparative Evaluation and Uncertainty Analysis of Depth–Damage Functions for Flood Loss Estimation Using 2D Hydraulic Modelling
abstract: Abstract  Flood-induced economic losses in data-scarce regions are difficult to quantify reliably because hydraulic modelling, depth–damage relationships, and building-exposure data are rarely combined within a single, locally calibrated framework. This study developed an integrated methodology for estimating residential flood damage in the Poldokhtar urban floodplain on the Kashkan River, western Iran, a reach that experienced severe inundation in 2016 and 2019. The two-dimensional CCHE2D model was calibrated and validated against surveyed cross-sections and 30 field control points, achieving a velocity RMSE of 0.075 m s⁻¹ and no statistically significant difference between simulated and observed flood depths (paired t-test, p = 0.718). Four candidate depth–damage functions — two exponential forms, a piecewise linear function, and a cubic polynomial — were fitted to locally observed damage data; the exponential function S2 (Y = 1 − exp(− 0.94x)) provided the best performance (RMSE = 11.05%, MAE = 8.41%, CC = 0.96). Three approaches for converting relative damage into monetary loss were compared, showing that spatially disaggregated building information (Approach A2) reduced the relative error to 6.4%, compared with 31.1% and 41.3% for approaches based on generalized building values, and that a fixed regional recovery coefficient performed adequately only at shallow depths. A McNemar test further revealed a statistically significant asymmetry between simulated and satellite-derived flood extents (χ² = 14.02, p = 0.00018). The results demonstrate that coupling calibrated hydraulic simulation with locally derived depth–damage functions and spatially explicit exposure data substantially improves flood-loss estimation accuracy, offering a transferable framework for flood-risk assessment in other data-scarce Iranian floodplains.
authors: Salehi H, Tahmasebipour N, Zeinivand H.

title: Glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B overexpression-a marker of resistance to cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 inhibitors.
abstract: BackgroundResistance to cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 inhibitors remains a major clinical challenge in treating estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, with no reliable predictive biomarkers currently available for patient selection.MethodsTo investigate resistance mechanisms, we generated drug-tolerant persisters to abemaciclib and palbociclib in a panel of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer cell lines. Clariom D human transcriptomic profiling was performed to identify differentially expressed genes, and the data were compared with published data from the PEARL (Phase III study of palbociclib plus endocrine therapy versus capecitabine in patients with HR-positive/HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer resistant to aromatase inhibitors) clinical trial to verify the clinical relevance. The impact of stable glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B overexpression in sensitive cells was studied in in vitro and in vivo xenograft models.ResultsCyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) 4 and 6 inhibitor-resistant drug-tolerant persisters exhibited G1 arrest and demonstrated increased senescence. Transcriptomic profiling of drug-tolerant persister models identified 154 genes consistently associated with resistance across cell lines. In the comparison with published resistance-associated genes from the phase III PEARL trial, glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B was a strongly upregulated candidate in both datasets. Glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B overexpression in sensitive cells conferred resistance to CDK 4 and 6 inhibition, enhanced migratory capacity, and accelerated tumor progression, abrogating the growth-inhibitory effects of abemaciclib observed in control tumors. Across all treatment arms, glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B overexpression tumors failed to respond to CDK 4 and 6 blockade. Glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B overexpression increased the expression of integrins, including integrin beta 1 (ITGB1) and integrin alpha 5 (ITGA5), and activated protein kinase B (AKT) and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) signaling, as evidenced by elevated phospho-AKT (Ser473) and phospho-ERK 1 and 2 (Thr202/204). Treatment of glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B overexpression cells with the antibody-drug conjugate glembatumumab vedotin, as a single agent, potently decreased cell viability. Additionally, strong synergy with abemaciclib was observed.ConclusionsGlycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma protein B is a potential biomarker and therapeutic target that may help identify patients unlikely to benefit from CDK 4 and 6 inhibition.
journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
authors: Gu Y, Ruan L, Hou Y, Gilbert-Ross M, Johnson S, Brown T, Kalinsky K, Badve SS, Gökmen-Polar Y.

title: Obesity-associated transcriptomic remodelling in hidradenitis suppurativa and treatment response.
abstract: Obesity is characterized by chronic low-grade inflammation and metabolic dysfunction. It is a major risk factor for hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), where it is associated with increased disease severity and metabolic comorbidity. Obesity promotes a pro-inflammatory, immunometabolic state marked by adipokine imbalance and alters the local skin environment through mechanical stress, occlusion and microbiome disruption. Mechanistic transcriptomic analyses further suggest that obesity induces tissue-specific changes in HS skin, including metabolic signalling in lesions and early barrier dysfunction in perilesional skin. In practice, obesity is associated with more severe and treatment-refractory disease but remains a modifiable risk factor. Weight loss, bariatric surgery and metabolism-directed therapies show potential to reduce disease burden, although controlled studies are limited. Overall, obesity acts as both a systemic and local modifier of HS, supporting its classification as an immunometabolic disorder.
journal: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
authors: Kapur S, Solone XK, Mi R, Sidhu KS, Gershater M, Cruz J, Hamzavi I, Adrianto I, Zhou L, Mi QS.

title: Underlying Mechanisms of Helicobacter pylori in Caries Progression and the Corresponding Dual-Responsive Hydrogel-Based Intervention.
abstract: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infects nearly half of the global population. Given that H. pylori is considered poorly adapted to the oral environment, previous studies have mainly focused on gastric infection. By contrast, how H. pylori persists in the oral cavity and relates to oral diseases remains unclear. This study investigates the role of H. pylori in caries progression. The results show that H. pylori is retained within Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans) biofilms, and its presence is associated with transcriptional remodeling in S. mutans, alongside increased overall cariogenic potential of the mixed biofilm. In a rat caries model, H. pylori co-colonization aggravates caries progression and oral microbiota dysbiosis. To address this pathological niche, a multifunctional hydrogel, termed GPAM, is designed by integrating a Cu2O@Pt heterojunction (MCP) with amorphous calcium phosphate (ACP). Under activation by yellow light and ultrasound, MCP generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) to disrupt S. mutans-H. pylori mixed biofilms. Meanwhile, released Cu2+ reduces H. pylori urease activity, and ACP promotes tooth remineralization. GPAM also shows microbiota-modulating potential. Together, these findings provide insight into H. pylori-associated caries progression and support GPAM as a multifunctional therapeutic strategy for mixed biofilms and caries-related damage.
authors: Lan Z, Shen X, Zhong T, Zhang W, Zhang S, Wang M, Zhu Y, Zhou Z, Gao N, Che H, Weng X, Dai X, Xu Y, Wang X.
