title: Functional Conservation Amid Extreme Divergence in Freshwater SAR11 Hypervariable Region 2
abstract: The Ca. Pelagibacterales order (SAR11) is a ubiquitous bacterioplankton in aquatic ecosystems. The genomes of SAR11 bacteria contain hypervariable region 2 (HVR2), the largest HVR with extreme diversity. Previous studies collectively indicated the enrichment of cell-surface modification genes on HVR2, which have been hypothesized to facilitate phage evasion. However, characterisation of HVR2 has primarily targeted marine clades and been limited for freshwater SAR11 (aka. Fontibacterium). Here, we employed single-cell genomics and recovered 176 Fontibacterium HVR2 sequences from Lake Biwa (Japan) and Lake Zurich (Switzerland), across multiple sampling years for Lake Biwa. Comparative sequence analyses revealed that freshwater HVR2 showed high intra-population diversity and appears to evolve independently of the rest of the genome, mirroring patterns observed in marine counterparts. Nevertheless, highly conserved HVR2 sequence pairs were observed for distinct Fontibacterium species from the two intercontinental habitats, suggesting horizontal transfers of HVR2 with conserved functional configurations across divergent lineages and large spatial scales. Further comparison with 145 marine HVR2 sequences revealed HVR2 sequences displaying synteny between Fontibacterium and marine SAR11, and 209 gene families conserved across habitats, including three near-universally conserved families. All examined freshwater HVR2s contained initiator methionine tRNA genes concentrated near the boundaries of the 5S region, suggesting a tDNA-anchored integration mechanism. These results suggest the functional equivalence of HVR2 across marine and freshwater SAR11 clades, and the existence of a shared pool of HVR2 sequences that evolve reticulately through mutual genetic exchange, independent of the vertical inheritance of the rest of the genome.
authors: Daniel, S., Andrei, A.-S., Nishikawa, Y., Takeyama, H., Ogata, H., Okazaki, Y.

title: A dual-mode chromogenic and fluorescent in situ hybridization approach for bacterial 16S rRNA detection in oral formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples.
abstract: The combined use of fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and chromogenic in situ hybridization (CISH) targeting bacterial 16S rRNA might facilitate the discrimination of bacterial signals from background noise, supporting the interpretation of bacterial spatial localization in tissues. In this study, we applied a fluorescein isothiocyanate-labeled universal 16S rRNA probe to both FISH and CISH to enable direct comparison of these methods using oral formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples. FISH and CISH were performed on saliva-derived and tongue FFPE samples. Because formalin fixation can reduce hybridization efficiency, the effect of the duration of fixation on 16S rRNA detection was evaluated using FFPE samples prepared from cultured bacteria. Both FISH and CISH generated clear positive signals with comparable staining patterns in saliva-derived FFPE samples, accompanied by a strong positive correlation between their signal area ratios. 16S rRNA detectability was maintained after formalin fixation for up to 72 h, and both methods visualized the bacterial localization in human tongue FFPE samples. Thus, this approach permits comparison of FISH and CISH staining patterns and enables complementary chromogenic evaluation of bacterial localization findings obtained by FISH, as CISH is not affected by tissue autofluorescence. The preservation of 16S rRNA detectability after formalin fixation for up to 72 h suggests that this approach may be applicable to clinical FFPE samples fixed for similar durations. In addition, inexpensive oligonucleotide probes and the ability of CISH to produce permanent slides using routine pathology equipment enhance its practical applicability. This method might represent a useful platform for evaluating the spatial localization of bacteria in oral FFPE samples.
authors: Sano H, Okabe R, Imai M, Sato T, Okada Y.

title: Genome sequence of Microbacterium sp., an endophyte isolated from Zea mays in South Africa.
abstract: Microbacterium species are plant-associated actinobacteria with plant growth-promoting potential. Here, the 3.42 Mb circular genome of strain ARC56GC isolated from maize leaves in South Africa is reported. Comparative genomics identified Microbacterium testaceum as its closest relative, while average nucleotide identity (ANI) analyses suggest that ARC56GC represents a genomically distinct lineage within the M. testaceum species complex.

title: Transcriptome and 16S rRNA analysis reveal the regulatory mechanisms underlying the differences in fat deposition between distinct broiler breeds.
abstract: IntroductionBaicheng oil chicken (BC) is a local Chinese breed renowned for its high intramuscular fat (IMF) content and excellent flavor.ObjectivesThis study compared BC with yellow-feathered broilers (YF) to investigate the mechanisms underlying significant differences in fat deposition.MethodsEight YF and eight BC samples were selected from 80 YF and 80 BC individuals of similar body weight, respectively, followed by transcriptomics and 16S rRNA gene sequencing accordingly.ResultsThe results showed that compared to YF, BC of the same weight had significantly less abdominal and hepatic fat deposition but a markedly higher breast muscle IMF level. Serum TG and LDL-C levels were significantly higher in the YF group than in the BC group, whereas HDL-C levels were notable lower. 16S rRNA analysis revealed an enrichment of f_Streptococcaceae and g_Lactobacillus in the YF and BC groups, respectively. Analysis of differentially expressed genes found in both liver and ileum tissues indicated enrichment primarily in the hepatic PPARG/FABP1 and intestinal PPARA/FABP1 pathways, which also influence the gut microbiota. The BC group exhibited significantly higher expression of genes related to fatty acid uptake, synthesis, and storage in breast muscle tissue (CD36 and FABP3, ACACA and FASN, and TMEM68, DGAT2, and PLIN2), while gene expression related to fatty acid oxidation was significantly lower (CPT1A and PPARA) compared to the YF group. Concurrently, the expression of lipoprotein receptors (LDLR and SCARB1) was significantly higher in the BC group than in the YF group. Spearman correlation analysis showed that the gut microbiota was influenced by the hepatic PPARG/FABP1 and intestinal PPARA/FABP1 pathways, confirming that the gut-liver axis jointly contributed to the distinct fat deposition patterns observed in the two broiler chicken breeds.ConclusionsThese findings have significant implications for improving chicken meat quality.
authors: Wang F, Jing W, Xue Y, Nan S, Liang J, Nie C.

title: Association Between Gut Microbiota Dysbiosis and Synovial Inflammation in Carpal Osteoarthritis of Ili Racehorses: A Preliminary Study Integrating Imaging, Synovial Fluid Analysis, and Fecal 16S rRNA Sequencing.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a leading cause of lameness and premature retirement in racehorses. Gut microbiota may contribute to OA pathogenesis through the gut-joint axis, but this relationship remains unclear in racehorses. This study focused on six OA-affected Ili racehorses and six healthy Ili racehorses from the same region; the Ili horse originated from Yili, Xinjiang, China. OA severity was assessed by clinical examination, lameness grading, radiography, arthroscopy, synovial fluid biomarker analysis, and fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Associations between differential gut microbiota and synovial inflammatory markers were evaluated by Spearman correlation analysis. OA horses exhibited higher lameness scores and typical radiographic findings. Compared with healthy controls, OA horses exhibited significantly higher synovial concentrations of IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, total protein, COMP, and MMP-3. Gut microbiota analysis revealed reduced microbial diversity and significant compositional alterations in OA horses. Spearman correlation analysis demonstrated significant associations between these microbial changes and synovial inflammatory mediators as well as cartilage degradation markers. Overall, gut microbiota dysbiosis in Ili racehorses with carpal OA may be associated with synovial inflammation and abnormal cartilage metabolism via the gut-joint axis. However, the experimental scale and the number of animals will be increased as needed for further validation.

title: Integrated LC-MS/MS Metabolomics and 16S rRNA Gene Sequencing to Identify Associated Molecular Signatures of Physalis Calyx seu Fructus Against Acute Pharyngitis.
abstract: This study aimed to characterize the metabolic and microbial alterations associated with Physalis Calyx seu Fructus (PCF) treatment in a rat model of acute pharyngitis (AP). The therapeutic effects of PCF on AP were evaluated by assessing physiological characteristics, analyzing pharyngeal pathological changes and quantifying serum inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α using ELISA. Untargeted metabolomics based on HRLC-MS/MS was applied to plasma and cecal contents, while 16S rRNA gene sequencing served to characterize the gut microbiota within the cecal contents. Spearman correlation and correlation network analysis were applied to explore associations between gut microbiota and metabolites. As expected, PCF intervention significantly alleviated AP-related clinical symptoms, reduced serum pro-inflammatory cytokines, and attenuated pharyngeal histopathological lesions. Metabolomics analysis revealed that PCF suppressed elevated plasma lysophosphatidylcholine levels, reversed the excessive accumulation of oxidized lipids in cecal contents, and elevated multiple bile acids. These metabolic alterations were predominantly enriched in the glycerophospholipid metabolism and primary bile acid biosynthesis pathways. Microbiota profiling revealed that PCF selectively enriched Akkermansia, which may contribute to re-establishing microecological homeostasis. In summary, PCF exerts therapeutic efficacy against AP, potentially linked to the modulation of systemic metabolic profiles, enrichment of beneficial intestinal bacteria, and restoration of intestinal microecological balance.
authors: Zhang C, Chen Y, Lu Y, Deng F, Yang L, Guo D.

title: A New Higher-Level Taxonomy of Monothalamous Foraminifera.
abstract: Monothalamous foraminifera are a highly diverse, paraphyletic assemblage of single-chambered lineages characterized by an organic or agglutinated test or lacking any external covering. Traditional morphology-based taxonomy divides them into the organic-walled Allogromiida and agglutinated Astrorhizida. Molecular systematics showed that this division is not justified as different wall types occur within the same lineages. Twenty years ago, based on molecular phylogenetic data, the monothalamids were classified into 13 lineages, called clades. Since then, the diversity of monothalamids from different habitats and regions has been extensively studied both genetically and morphologically, and many new species and genera have been described. Here, we analyzed 70 sequences of the 18S rRNA gene, representing 66 described species. We also analyzed 23 sequences of the COI gene for selected taxa. Based on molecular phylogenetic analyses and available morphological data, we establish a new formal higher-level taxonomy of monothalamous foraminifera. We introduce 5 new orders and distinguish 1 suborder and 34 families, of which 20 families are new. Our classification establishes a new taxonomic system that we hope will provide the foundation for organizing the vast diversity of monothalamous foraminifera revealed by recent studies.

title: No Trace of Blastocystis Parasite in Bats Caught in the Western and Southwestern Regions of Iran.
abstract: BackgroundBlastocystis is a common parasite found in the human intestine, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloating, and diarrhoea. Bats are potential hosts for this parasite, but little is known about their infection with Blastocystis.ObjectiveGiven the diversity of bat species in Iran, this study aimed to investigate Blastocystis infection in bats caught in the southwestern and western regions of the country.MethodsFaecal samples were collected from 115 bats from five caves located in Fars, Kurdistan, and Kermanshah provinces. DNA was extracted, using the phenol-chloroform method, and PCR was performed to identify the Blastocystis 18S rRNA gene. Information on bat species was analysed descriptively.ResultsThe four main bat species caught were Miniopterus pallidus (40%, n = 46), Myotis blythii (40%, n = 46), Rhinopoma microphyllum (12.18%, n = 14), and Rhinolophus euryale (7.82%, n = 9). However, none of the 115 stool samples examined showed evidence of Blastocystis infection by the molecular PCR method.ConclusionThis study found no evidence of Blastocystis infection in the bat species examined. The unique lifestyle and diet of bats, such as living on cave walls and roofs, may explain this absence. Further studies are needed to clarify the role of bats in the epidemiology of Blastocystis in other regions of Iran.
authors: Mosayebi MA, Pouryousef A, Omidian M, Shahabi S, Sarkari B.

title: SARS-CoV-2 variant-dependent alterations in nasopharyngeal microbiota and host inflammatory response.
abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic saw multiple outbreaks occur over short periods. This was linked to the virus's high infectivity and rapid mutation rate, which hindered the development of effective treatments and a comprehensive understanding of COVID-19 pathophysiology. The nasopharyngeal tract, the main entry site of SARS-CoV-2, interacts with angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptors via the viral spike glycoprotein, triggering pro-inflammatory responses that affect both tissue integrity and the resident microbiota. Viral infection induces dysbiosis by modulating microbiome diversity. Although distinct variants produce independent symptoms and viral loads, their impact on the nasopharyngeal microbiota and host inflammatory profile remains poorly understood. To address this, we analyzed nasopharyngeal samples from Chilean individuals collected during different phases of the pandemic. The microbiota was characterized by 16S rRNA gene sequencing (V3-V4 region), and cytokine expression was quantified by RT-qPCR. Finally, applied rigorous data processing and machine-learning models, Random Forest and K-Nearest Neighbors, to identify associations between SARS-CoV-2 variants, inflammatory markers, and opportunistic bacterial genera. Our results reveal that SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with distinct immunomicrobial signatures marked by increased TNF-α expression and the expansion of opportunistic taxa. These variant-dependent alterations indicate that host inflammatory responses and microbial dysbiosis are closely intertwined in the nasopharyngeal environment. This study provides a comprehensive framework integrating microbial and host factors to better understand the mechanisms underlying COVID-19 pathogenesis and highlights the potential of combining microbiome and cytokine profiling with machine-learning approaches to differentiate infection outcomes across viral variants.IMPORTANCEUnderstanding how SARS-CoV-2 infection alters the upper respiratory microbiota and host immune responses is essential to uncover the mechanisms underlying COVID-19 severity. In this study, we integrate bacterial 16S rRNA sequencing, inflammatory markers, and machine learning to identify key descriptors of infection such as TNF-α, Acinetobacter, Prevotella, and Staphylococcus. These markers define a conserved immunomicrobial signature across viral variants, linking inflammatory activation with microbial dysbiosis in the nasopharyngeal environment. Our findings highlight the value of the correct and robust application of machine learning models and nested cross-validation strategies in high-dimensional (wide) data sets to improve variant discrimination, reveal host-microbe interactions, and support the development of therapeutic strategies for respiratory viral infections.
authors: Maulen M, Pezoa-Soto I, León D, Dominguez EM, Martin AJM, Díaz-Vásquez WA.

title: Genetic Diversity and Genealogical Relationships of Anolis nebulosus and Anolis microlepidotus
abstract: Clouded Anole (Anolis nebulosus) and Guerreran Oak Anole (Anolis microlepidotus), there are two endemic species of Mexico. They can be found in tropical deciduous forest, semi-evergreen forest, xeric scrub, and pine-oak forests. It has been reported that Anolis species present a rapid adaptation to their habitat, which occurs in a few generations, and episodes of natural selection that lead to evolution on a contemporary time scale have also been observed. The aim of this study was to evaluate the genetic diversity and the genealogical relationships of groups of A. nebulosus and A. microlepidotus individuals. The study was carried out on specimens collected from locations in central Mexico, through the markers of 16S ribosomal RNA (16S rRNA). Both species showed a high haplotype and nucleotide diversity, suggesting a large and stable population with an ancient history. However, low haplotype and nucleotide diversity were observed in both species, alongside high genetic differentiation among groups of individuals from different localities; this suggest low vagility and supports the proposal to consider multiple phylogeographic lineages as evolutionarily significant units.

title: Molecular diagnosis of a case of Dibothriocephalus nihonkaiensis infection in Suzu City, Ishikawa Prefecture, Japan.
abstract: In this study, we intended to report a case of Dibothriocephalus nihonkaiensis infection diagnosed in Suzu City, Ishikawa Prefecture, Japan. A 23-year-old man from Aichi Prefecture moved to Suzu City, one of the most severely destroyed areas by the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake, to engage in reconstructive works. He visited the internal medicine department of Suzu General Hospital by the passage of long slender worm in his stool. Numerous operculated helminth eggs were detected from his stool samples, and a tapeworm strobila with the scolex was found after the treatment of praziquantel (10 mg/kg). Magnesium citrate was administered before and after praziquantel treatment, and stool samples were collected from the patient. The expelled tapeworm measured approximately 1.7 m in length. Morphological examination revealed a relatively small scolex with 2 suckling grooves, suggesting an immature adult specimen. Phylogenetic analysis of the mitochondrial 16S rRNA and cox1 genes identified the parasite as Dibothriocephalus nihonkaiensis. This case highlights the importance of integrating morphological and molecular approaches for accurate species identification in cases with complex epidemiological backgrounds.
authors: Kawabata K, Shimosaki R, Ikku R, Saito H, Mizuhara K, Dejima A, Mochizuki K, Murakami M.

title: Strain-level proteotyping and expression of specific toxins in patients with recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection.
abstract: ObjectivesRecurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) remains a major clinical challenge, and routine diagnostics that detect toxin genes rarely confirm toxin expression or resolve strain relatedness. We assessed whether combining whole-genome sequencing (WGS) with mass spectrometry proteotyping could resolve recurrence mechanisms and confirm toxin production.MethodsWGS, protein-level toxin typing and liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) proteotyping were combined. Of 33 isolates, 31 were collected at discrete time points from 14 patients and two lacked patient attribution. Datasets comprised 32 genomes and 29 proteomes (28 matched). Average nucleotide identity (ANI) and core-SNP distances were assessed.ResultsMost serial isolates in the high-molecular-weight (HMW)-selected cohort shared ANI groups (>99% ANI), including persistence over 353 days, consistent with relapse; one patient showed two ANI groups compatible with reinfection. Six isolates from three patients formed a divergent lineage uniquely carrying cdtA/cdtB, an A3/B5 toxin background, and the only reported acquired resistance-gene hits. LC-MS/MS detected TcdA- and TcdB-derived peptides in all 29 profiled isolates, spanning conserved and subtype-discriminating regions.ConclusionsLC-MS/MS proteotyping provides an expression-level layer concordant with genotype and, integrated with WGS, distinguishes relapse from reinfection and links divergent lineages to specific toxin and resistance profiles, complementing genomic and immunoassay-based CDI characterisation.
authors: Seguí G, Piñeiro-Iglesias B, Jacobsson G, Waller JE, Karlsson R.

title: Molecular detection of pulmonary tuberculosis and Candida albicans co-infection in people living with HIV/AIDS in Nigeria.
abstract: ObjectivesConcurrent pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) and antifungal-resistant candidiasis pose significant clinical and public challenges in resource-limited settings. This study determined the prevalence of PTB and antifungal-resistant Candida albicans co-infection among people living with HIV/AIDS (PLWHA) in Gombe State, Nigeria.MethodsSputum samples from 348 PLWHA were processed and tested for Mycobacterium tuberculosis using GeneXpert equipment. Moreover, C. albicans was isolated and identified using CHROMagar, germ tube test, and 18S rRNA-ITS-PCR sequencing, and its antifungal susceptibility patterns were determined by the disc diffusion method.ResultsThe prevalence values for C. albicans, PTB, and C. albicans-PTB co-infections were 9.2%, 9.2%, and 6.3%, respectively. All Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains were rifampicin-susceptible but were significantly associated with age (P = .0033) and biological sex (P = .03). About 40.6%, 31.3%, and 28.1% of the C. albicans strains were resistant to fluconazole, voriconazole, and amphotericin-B, respectively. PLWHA aged >60 years had significantly higher odds of C. albicans infection (OR = 54.6, P = .0156). History of antibiotic use, pet ownership, and presence of PTB were significantly associated with C. albicans (P ConclusionThe levels of PTB and C. albicans mono- or co-infections among PLWHA were moderate, with a high frequency of fluconazole-resistant C. albicans. This study provided updated local surveillance data on pulmonary infections among PLWHA.

title: Gut microbiome differences in youth with perinatally acquired HIV and fatty liver disease: a multicentre study
abstract: Abstract    Background  Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) is increasingly prevalent in youth with perinatally acquired HIV (YPHIV). Gut dysbiosis has been proposed as a potential contributor to MAFLD, but its role in YPHIV remains poorly understood.  Methods  In this prospective multicentre study, 86 participants (34 YPHIV, 52 uninfected controls), with and without overweight-associated MAFLD underwent ultrasound liver steatosis assessment and stool 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Multivariable models evaluated microbial diversity, taxonomic abundance, and predicted functions..  Results  HIV infection was associated with reduced microbial diversity, distinct compositional shifts, and altered functional pathways, whereas MAFLD showed no significant overall microbiome signature. Within YPHIV, MAFLD correlated with decreased Parabacteroides abundance and subtle functional differences despite preserved diversity.  Conclusions  HIV infection predominantly influences gut microbiome composition in youth, with MAFLD-related microbial alterations being modest. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for HIV-associated dysbiosis in studies of liver disease and suggest potential microbial targets for further investigation in YPHIV with MAFLD.
authors: Vallejo G, Elena M, Montes ML, Oliveira A, Mercadal M, Busca C, Escosa L, Díez C, Navarro ML, Carrasco I, Talavera A, Serrano-Villar S, Sainz T.

title: Single Nucleotide Variant Calling in Polyploid Plant Genomes From Illumina Short Reads: A Practical Workflow Illustrated With Coffea arabica L.
abstract: The detection of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) from DNA sequencing data is an essential approach for mutation discovery, enabling the identification of genetic variations that influence key traits, such as stress tolerance, productivity, and quality in crop species. A practical, step-by-step guide is presented for analyzing Illumina short reads for SNV calling in polyploid plant genomes using the command line in a Linux environment. As a worked example, the sequences used in this workflow were obtained from Coffea arabica L., a tetraploid species, whose leaves were subjected to chemical mutagenesis with ethyl methanesulfonate or sodium azide, inducing mutations that can be analyzed for genetic variation. The analysis begins with preprocessing raw sequencing data, including quality control and trimming, followed by read alignment to a reference genome. Key bioinformatics tools within the Linux environment are employed, such as FastQC for quality assessment, Trim Galore for optional adapter and low-quality sequence removal, and BWA for sequence alignment. Variant calling is performed using the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK), with a focus on identifying SNVs resulting from mutagenic treatments. Further steps include filtering strategies to eliminate false positives and ensure high-confidence variant calls, followed by functional annotation with SnpEff. Given the tetraploid nature of C. arabica, special considerations in SNV calling and data interpretation (i.e., ploidy setting, allele balance) are required to account for its complex genome structure. Common challenges encountered during the analysis are addressed, along with strategies for troubleshooting. By following this workflow, users gain foundational experience in bioinformatics, particularly in next-generation sequencing data analysis, and the same framework can be transferred to other polyploid plant species. A workflow script with placeholders for all file names, a conda environment, and a container image are provided to automate the analysis. The workflow also contributes to research on genetic variation in C. arabica L. © 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC. Basic Protocol: SNV calling from Illumina reads in polyploid plant genomes using tetraploid C. arabica L. as a case study.
authors: Solano-González S, Muñoz-Flores C, Gatica-Arias AM.

title: PHANES: an integrated resource of protein features for the human proteome
abstract: Protein analysis and machine-learning workflows increasingly rely on large-scale numerical representations of proteins. While protein language models provide powerful embeddings, their limited interpretability and high computational cost hinder their use in many biological applications. We present PHANES, a human proteome database and web server providing a comprehensive, biologically interpretable set of features for 20335 proteins. PHANES integrates sequence-derived physicochemical descriptors, structure-based and graph-theoretical features computed from AlphaFold predictions, thermostability indices, and tissue expression specificity. In addition to precomputed features for the human proteome, an integrated web server enables on-demand feature calculation for user-provided protein structures. PHANES supports data export, visualization and comparative analysis at the level of individual proteins and protein groups, bridging the gap between complex numerical representations and biological interpretation while providing an interpretable foundation for exploratory analyses and downstream machine-learning applications. PHANES is freely available at  https://tools.tartaglialab.com/phanes .
authors: Miltiadis-Vrachnos D, Armaos A, Broglia L, Monti M, Fiorentino J, Tartaglia GG.

title: MitImpact 4: a genome-wide resource for the interpretation of coding and non-coding mitochondrial DNA variants.
abstract: Mitochondrial DNA variants are a frequent cause of inherited disease, yet their computational interpretation has focused almost exclusively on the 13 protein-coding genes. Variants in tRNA and rRNA genes, which carry a disproportionate share of the known pathogenic alleles, have remained a diagnostic blind spot, because their effect depends on RNA structure rather than on protein sequence and few dedicated predictors exist. MitImpact 4 removes this asymmetry. The database now covers all 49 704 single-nucleotide variants that can occur in the mitochondrial genome and reports their functional consequence, phylogenetic conservation, local mutational constraint, and population frequency in gnomAD, HelixMTdb, and ToMMo. Missense variants are annotated with APOGEE 2 and with newly added predictors, including AlphaMissense, ESM1b, VARITY, and LIST-S2, while tRNA and rRNA variants receive predictions from nAPOGEE, our RNA-specific model, alongside MitoTIP and PON-mt-tRNA. For both classes, scores are accompanied by posterior probabilities of pathogenicity that can be used within the ACMG/AMP framework for mitochondrial DNA. Clinical annotation from ClinVar and MITOMAP, including ClinGen expert-panel classifications, is integrated in a redesigned interface that also annotates user-submitted VCF files. MitImpact 4 is freely available at https://mitimpact.mcb2lab.org.
authors: Giovannetti A, Napoli A, Liorni N, Petrizzelli F, Biagini T, Gasbarrini A, Caputo V, Mazza T.

title: BILBO: a self-hosted platform for large-scale RNA-Seq analysis with a functional annotation clustering framework.
abstract: RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) has become a central approach for transcriptomic studies, but its practical application still requires the coordination of multiple computational steps and often produces large gene expression outputs whose integrative biological interpretation remains challenging. Here, we present BILBO (Bioinformatics Integration for Large-scale Biological Operations), a self-hosted and fully containerized platform designed to support reproducible, end-to-end RNA-Seq analyses, from data acquisition to integrative functional interpretation. BILBO consolidates widely adopted open-source tools into standardized workflows, enabling automated retrieval of public or private RNA-Seq data, quality control, alignment, quantification, normalization, differential expression analysis, and generation of publication-ready outputs within a unified environment. Beyond workflow integration, BILBO introduces a novel functional annotation clustering framework that organizes genes using Gene Ontology (GO)-based semantic similarity. The approach separates genes by regulatory direction and ontology, computes Wang semantic similarity among GO annotations, applies complete-linkage hierarchical clustering, refines assignments through silhouette-based pruning, and selects representative genes as semantic medoids. To further enhance biological interpretability, BILBO integrates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation strategy that links representative genes and functional clusters to curated scientific literature through hybrid retrieval and DOI-linked evidence chunks. In a controlled SEQC/MAQC-III benchmark against nf-core/rnaseq, BILBO preserved differential-expression effect sizes (cross-workflow Spearman ≥ 0.994) and the expected behavior of the reference mixtures, whereas BILBO required 68% less peak temporary disk space but 25% more wall time. In the SEQC dataset, the resulting clusters showed strong coherence with independent MSigDB pathways, comparable to a GOSemSim-based reference workflow, and remained stable under moderate parameter changes. Together, these features position BILBO as an integrative and scalable solution that bridges the gap between large-scale RNA-Seq data processing and higher-level functional insight, promoting reproducibility, interpretability, and accessibility in transcriptomic research.
authors: da Silva VLC, Alvarenga JVR, Linhares-Neto MV, Noman M, Chalfun-Junior A.

title: Characterizing the fragmentation of AlphaFold predictions.
abstract: MotivationThe Nobel Prize-winning program AlphaFold2 computes plausible structures of (well) folded proteins. The main quality assessment is based on the predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT), a per-amino acid confidence score.ResultsTo enhance quality assessment, we provide novel quantitative measures to identify coherent amino acid (a.a.) stretches along the sequence in terms of pLDDT values. These constructions, grounded in standard techniques from topological data analysis and combinatorics, provide a canonical framework for identifying regions along the protein backbone and analyzing their properties, such as their propensity for disorder and their consistency with a null model. The outcome of our analysis can readily be used to select reliable regions/domains within proteins whose pLDDT values span the entire pLDDT range.ResultsAvailability and implementation: The software acompanying this work is available in the package Alphafold_analysis of the Structural Bioinformatics Library.
authors: Cazals F, Sarti E.

title: PED in 2027: integrating experimental and predicted protein conformational ensembles at scale.
abstract: The Protein Ensemble Database (PED; https://proteinensemble.org) is the primary deposition resource for structural ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). PED 2027 (released in September 2026) substantially expands its scope by integrating ensembles determined or refined using experimental data with clearly identified collections of computational predictions. The release introduces a multi-method collection targeting 3319 DisProt proteins and 2452 manually curated disordered regions, together with AlphaFlex ensembles for 10 022 human proteins containing IDRs. Alternative predictions for the same sequence are retained as independent records with method-specific provenance, enabling comparison across ensemble-generation approaches. A scalable deposition workflow accommodates individual experimental studies and proteome-scale collections while preserving quality control and curator oversight. The PED controlled vocabulary standardizes experimental data acquisition, computational generation, selection, and refinement. Precomputed IDPEnsembleTools and CIDER analyses provide structural and sequence-derived descriptors directly on ensemble pages. A redesigned interface and extended REST API support discovery, visualization, download and programmatic access. Interoperability with UniProt, DisProt, MobiDB, and experimental-data repositories connects ensembles with sequences, annotations, and supporting measurements. PED 2027 therefore provides an interoperable, analysis-ready platform for studying IDP/IDR conformational behaviour.

title: Chromosome-level genome assembly and annotation of the transverse lady beetle Coccinella transversoguttata.
abstract: The transverse lady beetle Coccinella transversoguttata Faldermann, 1835 is an ecologically important aphid predator and a declining native biocontrol agent in parts of its range. To provide a genomic resource for evolutionary, ecological, and applied research, we generated a chromosome-level genome assembly using PacBio HiFi long reads, Illumina whole-genome short reads, Hi-C chromatin conformation capture, and full-length transcriptome sequencing. The final assembly spans 376.3 Mb and comprises 58 scaffolds ≥1 kb, of which 363.4 Mb (96.6%) was anchored onto 10 chromosome-scale pseudomolecules. Assembly contiguity was high (contig N50 = 41.6 Mb; scaffold N50 = 41.6 Mb), and completeness was supported by 98.4% complete arthropod BUSCOs. Repetitive sequences constituted 58.2% of the genome, and 13,808 protein-coding genes were annotated with strong transcriptomic and homology-based support. Comparative analysis with a recently published conspecific genome revealed strong chromosome-scale collinearity but notable differences in total assembly size, repeat content, and local structural variation, suggesting either population-level genomic divergence or methodological differences in repeat resolution. Cross-species synteny with Coccinella septempunctata Linnaeus, 1758 further demonstrated substantial conservation of chromosome architecture across the genus. This resource provides a high-quality reference genome with broad utility for comparative genomics, predator ecology, biological control, and genome evolution studies in Coccinellidae.
authors: Wu XL, Jin PF, Liu HL, Chen ZT, Liu S, Li MY, Pu DQ.

title: OSCAR: an omics atlas of paired single-cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq for decoding cell-specific gene regulation.
abstract: Paired single-cell chromatin accessibility and transcriptome profiles provide a powerful framework for dissecting cell-specific regulatory programs underlying diverse biological processes and human diseases. The rapid accumulation of paired single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (scATAC-seq) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data has led to an urgent need to comprehensively integrate these data to illustrate the regulatory landscape at single-cell resolution. To address this need, we developed OSCAR (an Omics atlas of paired Single-Cell ATAC and RNA-seq, https://bio.liclab.net/OSCAR/) to curate large-scale paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data and to provide comprehensive regulatory annotations and analyses. The current version of OSCAR catalogs 7749 898 human cells from 1136 samples across 30 tissue types. Importantly, OSCAR integrates paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq profiles for joint cell clustering and peak-to-gene linkage identification, and provides detailed (epi)genetic annotations for marker peaks and regulatory elements of marker genes, including super-enhancers, enhancers, enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), common and risk single nucleotide polymorphisms, expression quantitative trait loci, transcription factor binding sites, transcription factor/transcription co-factor binding peaks, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 target sites, DNase I hypersensitivity sites, chromatin accessibility regions, DNA methylation sites, chromatin interaction regions, and topologically associating domains. Furthermore, OSCAR provides three online analysis tools, including cell type enrichment analysis, sequence-based peak regulatory analysis, and peak-to-gene linkage analysis. Hence, OSCAR is a useful platform to query, browse, analyze, and visualize cell-specific regulatory programs across diverse human tissues and diseases.
authors: Song C, Zhou Y, Feng C, Dai X, Xiao J, Fan X, Wang K, Xiao P, Zheng Y, Luo W, Li C, Wang Q.

title: The Pathomycosphere: A Spatially Defined Framework in Pathogen Ecology.
abstract: Fungal pathogens have historically been studied as autonomous agents, as self-contained units independent of their associated microbiota, with disease outcomes attributed to fungal virulence factors acting on susceptible hosts. However, many pathogenic fungi harbor bacterial associates that influence their ecology, persistence and virulence. The pathobiome concept addressed this limitation by framing disease as an outcome of multi-kingdom interactions. Yet most pathobiome studies rely on correlative analyses of microbial abundances with pathogens, lacking spatial resolution to identify which microorganisms physically interact with pathogenic structures. Conversely, the hyphosphere provides micrometer-scale spatial resolution but has been investigated predominantly in non-pathogenic fungi. Here, we propose the pathomycosphere as a spatially defined and experimentally tractable subset of the pathobiome: a hypha-associated microbial assemblage in which physical association with the pathogenic member, prolonged or transient has a consequence for the pathogen's biology, with pathogenicity residing in the fungus, an associated microorganism or their interaction. This framework bridges the pathobiome and hyphosphere concepts by anchoring disease-associated microbial interactions to hyphal interface, where mechanistic investigation becomes feasible. Pathomycosphere provides operational tractability to explore microbial partnerships contributing to pathogenesis, and positions fungal-associated bacterial consortia as important components of pathogen biology with relevance to disease ecology beyond agricultural systems.
authors: Abeysinghe G, Antony-Babu S.

title: Women's health outreach using a rapid and fieldable Nanopore-based microbiome profiling workflow.
abstract: Background In recent years, scientific interest in the vaginal microbiome has increased due to its impact on women's health. Colonization of the Lactobacillus species in the vagina may contribute to protection against vaginal infectious diseases. In order to create public awareness regarding vaginal health and to provide insights into the vaginal microbiome, a rapid field microbiome analysis using Nanopore sequencing was evaluated at Lowlands, a three-day music festival in the Netherlands. This study aimed not only to evaluate a rapid sequencing workflow, but also to explore citizen science as a tool for health promotion and public engagement in women's health. Methods The workflow at Lowlands contained the following steps; (i) Dialogue concerning vaginal health, with invitation to participate. (ii) Informed consent and questionnaire to investigate knowledge on vaginal health, life-style and contraceptive usage; (iii) self-collection of a vaginal swab; (iv) DNA isolation using QuickExtract DNA extraction solution; (v) Ultrafast amplification of the 16S rRNA gene using NextGenPCR thermal cycling using 16S Barcoding kit 24 V14; (vi) Library preparation and sequencing was performed according to the manufacturers protocol using R10 chemistry; (vii) For data-analysis, MABA16S was used, with slight modifications. This workflow was established within 4 hours and results were communicated with interested participants.

title: LIGR-Nue for the global mapping of the bacterial sRNA targetome in vivo
abstract: Interactions between regulatory small RNAs (sRNAs) and their target transcripts are central for post-transcriptional regulation in bacteria. Based on RNA-seq analysis, we determined the relative abundance of several sRNAs in the photosynthetic cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 under photoautotrophic growth conditions and after transfer to darkness. We observed an increase in the abundance of the sRNAs DsiR1 to 58.6% and of CsiR1 to 19% of the sRNA transcriptome after transfer to darkness. We then developed a duplex-directed, transcriptome-wide mapping strategy of RNA-RNA interactions in vivo, called LIGR-Nue, which involves aminomethyltrioxsalen-mediated UV cross-linking, proximity ligation, crosslink reversal, reverse transcription and sequencing. The data were analysed using the RNANUE pipeline for the detection of chimeric reads and mapping, and benchmarked against known targetome data for the sRNAs PsrR1 and NsiR4. Using this methodology, we identified RNA-RNA interactions, such as PsrR1 as a regulator of carbon assimilation, and DsiR1 as a global silencing factor of photosynthesis-associated mRNAs in the dark. This data enables the comprehensive analysis of sRNA functions in post-transcriptional gene regulation. LIGR-Nue is broadly applicable to map RNA-RNA interactions in bacteria.
authors: Mandal, M., Adelmann, C., Georg, J., Kurukuti, S., Voss, B., Hess, W. R., Prakash, J. S. S.

title: Photosynthetic community restructuring along a desalination brine-discharge gradient in northern Chile.
abstract: Rapid expansion of seawater desalination in arid coastal regions has increased the need for sensitive biological tools to assess brine-discharge effects. This study evaluated marine photosynthetic communities along a discharge gradient in Flamenco Bay (northern Chile) using physicochemical profiling, pigment measurements, 18S rRNA metabarcoding, and diversity metrics. The discharge point showed a strong near-field salinity anomaly (41.75±3.36 versus 33.71 ± 0.44 PSU at the reference station), whereas differences in the photosynthetic assemblage extended over a broader area. Genus richness was stable across stations (9-11 genera), but Shannon diversity was reduced at impacted stations (1.06-1.09) relative to the reference (1.87). Near-field stations were dominated by Myzozoa (especially Karlodinium), whereas the reference supported a more balanced assemblage of Ochrophyta, Myzozoa, Chlorophyta, Cryptophyta, and Haptophyta. Bray-Curtis dissimilarity showed that differences among stations were driven mainly by shifts in relative sequence abundance rather than taxonomic replacement. PERMANOVA confirmed significant differences in community composition among stations (pseudo-F = 1.99, p = 0.018), and ordination (PCoA) showed discharge-influenced stations clustering separately from the reference site. The Integrated Response Index identified the discharge point as showing the strongest deviation and biological differences at 500 m despite low physicochemical deviation. Community-level differences may remain detectable where salinity and related variables approach reference conditions, so physicochemical monitoring alone may not fully capture spatial variation in community structure around desalination outfalls. Future studies integrating high-resolution hydrodynamics with replicated temporal sampling would distinguish brine-driven effects from natural spatial variability, strengthening the bioindicator value of these community-level metrics.
authors: Cruces E, Rojas-Lillo Y, Oses R, Bonnail E.

title: Fecal microbiome-based clustering identifies distinct disease subtypes with differing metabolomic profiles and treatment outcomes in canine chronic enteropathy.
abstract: Canine chronic enteropathy (CE) is a heterogeneous disorder with variable clinical outcomes. We aimed to identify fecal microbiome and metabolomic signatures associated with CE severity and treatment outcomes. Fecal samples from dogs with CE (n = 56), acute diarrhea (n = 8), and healthy controls (n = 126) were analyzed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing and GC-MS-based untargeted metabolomics. CE dogs exhibited significantly reduced microbial diversity compared with the other groups, and unsupervised Partitioning Around Medoids clustering identified two microbiome clusters within the CE cohort. Cluster 2 was characterized by dysbiosis, with enrichment of Streptococcus, Enterococcus, and Klebsiella, and depletion of short-chain fatty acid producers, including Fusobacterium and Blautia. Among dogs with baseline Canine Chronic Enteropathy Clinical Activity Index (CCECAI) > 3, 10 of 12 Cluster 1 dogs (83.3%) achieved remission (CCECAI ≤ 3) after treatment, compared with 7 of 18 Cluster 2 dogs (38.9%; p = 0.0256). CCECAI scores decreased significantly after treatment in Cluster 1 (p = 0.0005) but not in Cluster 2 (p = 0.077). Fecal propanoic acid and kynurenic acid levels also differed between clusters. These findings suggest that gut microbiota and associated metabolites may contribute to differences in CE severity and treatment outcomes.
authors: Li J, Aoki T, Miyata S, Fukaya A, Hayashi Y, Hirao H, Yoshimoto S, Nagaoka K.

title: Gut microbiome-mediated associations between dietary intake and type 2 diabetes in a Korean population.
abstract: AimsType 2 diabetes (T2D) is influenced by multiple risk factors, including dietary intake, which may affect disease risk through interactions with the gut microbiome. This study sought to identify microbial features that mediate these associations in a Korean population.MethodsData from 1,347 participants aged 30-64 years were analyzed. Dietary intake was assessed using a food frequency questionnaire, and gut microbiome profiles were generated by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing of the V3-V4 region. MaAsLin2 and mediation analyses were then performed.ResultsForty-eight amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were associated with T2D. Lachnospira ASV054, Romboutsia B ASV190, and Clostridium T ASV104 were inversely associated with T2D and statistically mediated the associations of bread, starchy food, and kimchi intake with T2D, respectively (q ConclusionsSeveral gut microbial features inversely associated with T2D partially mediated diet-T2D associations and exhibited suppressive effects for rice cake and UPF intake. These findings suggest that the gut microbiome may play an important role in mediating associations between dietary intake and T2D.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Transcriptomic Data Analysis and Visualization: Multi-Model Workflow Evaluation
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive benchmarking evaluation of large language models(LLMs) and agentic coding systems for automated analysis and visualization workflows for transcriptomic data, in particular human responses to COVID-19 infection. Multiple models, including ChatGPT 5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1, and Llama4-Scout, were assessed across a series of scientific prompts designed to test their ability to reproduce workflow components such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, outlier detection, reproducibility, and code generation. The benchmark protocol involved varying prompt specificity and examined both quantitative metrics such as clustering scores and outlier counts as well as qualitative aspects such as code quality and reproducibility. Results indicate that prompt specificity improves code structure and methodological correctness, but quantitative performance depends heavily on preprocessing choices and execution environment. While some models produced strong code and reproducible outputs, alignment with scientific targets like label-based clustering was inconsistent. The findings highlight the promise and limitations of current LLMs for automating scientific data analysis and visualization and suggest directions for future benchmarking and workflow standardization.
authors: Iyer A, Subedi A, Butler KS, Krishnakumar R.

title: Ultrafast Workflow for Accurate Full-Length ABO Genotyping Using Nanopore Sequencing.
abstract: Rapid ABO discrepancy resolution is critical for transfusion safety. However, current short-read sequencing cannot resolve phase across the 21.9-kb ABO gene. Here, the aim is to develop a nanopore-based workflow for full-length ABO genotyping. A workflow combining a long-range PCR amplicon spanning the ABO gene was generated from genomic DNA from 63 serologically discrepant donors and sequenced using the Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) Platform. PacBio HiFi sequencing was used as an orthogonal reference standard. Variant calling and haplotype reconstruction were performed using a unified bioinformatics pipeline. The workflow was further evaluated with another nanopore sequencing platform, PolySeq, where the sequencing accuracy is lower than that of ONT R10.4 chemistry. In this study, 63 discrepant samples of 280,712 donors yielded 126 full-length haplotypes. The nanopore workflow delivered results within 6 hours versus >46 hours for PacBio. ONT showed 100% concordance with PacBio HiFi outside homopolymer regions. Causal variants were resolved in 92.06% of samples. Homopolymer errors were confined to intron 1 without phenotypic impact. PolySeq platform also produced PacBio-comparable consensus accuracy after applying deep learning-based error correction, with superior chimerism sensitivity, confirming the robustness of the workflow. In conclusion, this ultrafast nanopore workflow enables same-day, full-length ABO haplotype resolution, which provided a rapid, cost-effective genotyping solution of complex variants for precision transfusion and aided global haplotype database development.
journal: The Journal of molecular diagnostics : JMD
authors: Liang S, Yao Y, Wu F, Liu T, Sun L, Peng L, Ning L, Tang X, Zhu F, Cui D.

title: Bluues2: An enhanced web server for fast and accurate electrostatic analysis of proteins and protein complexes.
abstract: Electrostatic interactions play a crucial role in protein structure, stability, and function. We present Bluues2, a significantly enhanced web server for calculating electrostatic properties of proteins using the Generalized Born model. The new version features improved accuracy through refined GB radius calculations using NanoShaper for molecular surface generation, extended functionality for analyzing protein-protein and protein-ligand complexes including calculation of binding free energies and electrostatic complementarity, enhanced interface with integrated Mol* structure viewer, and compatibility with the DRMAAtic framework for efficient job management. Bluues2 provides comprehensive electrostatic analyses including pKa predictions, surface potentials, solvation free energies, and complex interface properties in a user-friendly format accessible to both experts and non-specialists.
journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
authors: Piovesan D, Rasekh N, Soler MA, Rocchia W, Esposito G, Fogolari F, Tosatto SCE.

title: Automated reconstruction of reproducible protein databases with RepDBmaker.
abstract: RepDBmaker is a reproducible Snakemake pipeline designed for the automated construction of large-scale protein sequence databases. It enables the seamless downloading of sequences from different public databases and the integration of user-specified proteomes. The pipeline also performs standardized taxonomic annotations to all compiled sequences and contamination screening in eukaryotic proteomes. In addition, RepDBmaker generates queryable database files for Basic Local Alignment Search Tool Program (BLASTP), DIAMOND, and MMseqs2, with the option of taxonomy-aware sequence clustering to produce less redundant datasets. To showcase its utility, we used RepDBmaker to build a Tree-of-Life-scale database comprising 482 million protein sequences from 160,045 publicly available genomes and transcriptomes. RepDBmaker offers an off-the-shelf but customizable solution for researchers undertaking large-scale evolutionary projects that require extensive, well-annotated protein databases. The pipeline is available at https://github.com/Gabaldonlab/RepDBmaker.
journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
authors: Mutti G, Gabaldón T.

title: Digital Kennison: a bioinformatics pipeline for rapid mapping of sequences to the Drosophila melanogaster Y chromosome.
abstract: The Drosophila melanogaster Y chromosome is currently known to contain 13 single-copy protein-coding genes, 6 of which are essential for male fertility, as well as several noncoding genes and abundant repetitive DNA. Localization of Y-linked sequences has traditionally relied on labor-intensive crosses using Kennison's translocation strains, which map Y-linked loci by generating flies deficient for each of the 6 Y chromosome fertility regions (ks-1, ks-2, kl-1, kl-2, kl-3, and kl-5). Here, we present Digital Kennison, a computational pipeline that recasts this classical mapping strategy as a sequence-based analysis. The pipeline queries 8 genomic databases derived from Kennison's strains using BLAST and read coverage, assigning sequences to fertility regions or the centromeric region with a calibrated confidence score. We benchmarked the method on 60 Y-linked sequences spanning all 7 regions, including single-copy protein-coding genes, Mst77Y family members, noncoding RNAs, and the centromere. Digital Kennison achieved 97% precision while resolving challenging cases, including boundary-spanning genes (PRY and Ppr-Y), fragmented Mst77Y copies, and FDY, which has a closely related autosomal paralog. Beyond validating known localizations, the pipeline localized the unmapped gene CG41561 to the kl-1region and reassigned the transcript CR40629-RC from the kl-2 region to kl-5. It also localized 7 of 16 recently transferred Y-linked sequences, including 4 with high confidence. Applied to 904 R6 scaffolds, Digital Kennison assigned 75% to fertility regions, including 5 currently annotated as autosomal-pericentromeric. Digital Kennison reduces sequence localization from weeks of genetic crosses to minutes of computation while preserving the power of classical translocation mapping.

title: Protein co-scientist aided simulations of the structural and functional impact of O-GlcNAc Transferase TPR domain deletions and amino acid substitutions associated with X-Linked Intellectual Disability
abstract: O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) is an essential glycosyltransferase that regulates cellular processes through the addition of O-linked β-N-acetyglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) to target proteins. Substrate recognition and protein-protein interactions are mediated by the tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain, yet the contributions of individual TPR repeats to structural stability and function remain poorly understood. Here, we employed an integrated computational framework combining an AI protein co-scientist, Speak to a Protein, which incorporates Boltz-2 for structure prediction and rDock for ligand binding evaluation, with external tools including AlphaFold3 for more advanced structure prediction and the HDOCK server for protein-protein docking. This framework was used to investigate how deletions of TPR domains and disease-associated amino acid substitutions within the TPR domain affect OGT structure and function. Five synthetic truncation OGT isoforms, thirteen single-TPR deletion variants, and five X-linked intellectual disability (XLID)-associated amino acid substitutions were modeled and aligned to wild-type OGT for comparison. Structural perturbations were quantified using backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD), while functional effects were assessed through docking analyses with UDP-GlcNAc, Host Cell Factor 1 (HCF1), and Tet methylcytosine dioxygenase 1 (TET1). Variation in TPR length altered global protein structure and induced long-range conformational changes within the catalytic domain despite no sequence modifications in that region. Single TPR deletions showed that individual repeats contribute unequally to structural stability, with deletions in mid-to-late TPR domains producing the largest structural disruptions. Disease-associated amino acid substitutions also generated conformational changes and reduced predicted ligand binding, consistent with known reductions in enzymatic activity in XLID. Protein-protein docking analyses demonstrated substrate-specific effects, as domain deletion and amino acid substitution variants of OGT had different interactions with TET1 and HCF1. Collectively, these findings identify the TPR domain as a regulatory domain that governs structure, ligand recognition, and protein interactions. More broadly, this work demonstrates how the integration of a protein co-scientist with protein structure modeling tools can be used to predict the structural and functional consequences of domain deletions or natural amino acid variants.
authors: Barth S, Bechard A, Krafft A, Yip C, Aboagye C, Fehl C, Siwo GH.

title: A python-based automated pipeline for phylogenetic tree construction, visualization, and comparative statistical evaluation.
abstract: Phylogenetic analysis is a fundamental concept in computational biology, which helps in understanding evolutionary relationships, species divergence, and functional conservation based on biological sequence data. In general, phylogenetic analysis involves a number of sequential steps, such as sequence collection, multiple sequence alignment, model selection, phylogenetic tree construction, and statistical validation, which are usually carried out using different software tools with heterogeneous workflows. In this work, we propose a Python-based phylogenetic analysis pipeline, which integrates a number of important steps in phylogenetic analysis into a unified framework. The proposed system incorporates a number of popular sequence alignment algorithms, such as Multiple Alignment using Fast Fourier Transform (MAFFT), Multiple Sequence Comparison by Log-Expectation (MUSCLE), and ClustalW, as well as different phylogenetic tree reconstruction approaches, such as Neighbor-Joining (NJ), Unweighted Pair Group Method with Arithmetic Mean (UPGMA), Maximum Likelihood (ML), and Maximum Parsimony (MP). In addition, tree visualization, as well as comparative assessment using topological distance measures and statistical hypothesis tests, is performed in the proposed system, which includes Robinson-Foulds (RF), Approximately Unbiased (AU), Kishino-Hasegawa (KH), and Shimodaira-Hasegawa (SH). The results obtained from the analysis of the datasets demonstrate that the combination of the MAFFT-based alignment methods with the ML tree reconstruction strategy results in the generation of trees with high statistical support according to the tests used for the analysis.

title: Chloroplast Genome Assembly and Genetic Structure Analysis of Coffea arabica L. Based on Maternal Inheritance Markers.
abstract: Background: Codon usage bias has been analyzed in the Coffea arabica L. nuclear genome, yet comprehensive genomic resources for this species remain limited. The chloroplast genome, characterized by its maternal inheritance and high conservation, represents a valuable resource for investigating plant phylogeny, crop domestication, and maternal lineage evolution. Results: We assembled complete chloroplast genomes for 52 C. arabica accessions, encompassing four cultivars (Geisha, Catimor, Bourbon, and Caturra), four improved breeding lines within the Geisha group (Yunka No. 3, Yunka No. 4, G02, and G13), two Catimor breeding lines (CCCA25 and T5175), and four accessions of unknown cultivar origin. Comparative genomics, unrooted phylogenetic reconstruction (neighbor-joining and maximum likelihood), haplotype inference, and exploratory principal component analysis (PCA) were integrated to characterize the genetic architecture of these chloroplast genomes. These genomes ranged from 155,133 bp to 155,192 bp in length, displayed the typical quadripartite architecture, and exhibited GC contents of 37.43-37.44%. Gene annotation identified 131 genes, comprising 86 protein-coding genes, 37 tRNAs, and 8 rRNAs. Codon usage analysis revealed a pronounced bias toward A or U at the third codon position. We detected 194 SSR loci per plastome, among which mononucleotide A/T repeats predominated. Neighbor-joining and maximum-likelihood phylogenies, PCA, and haplotype network reconstruction consistently resolved the 52 accessions into three genetic clusters (C1-C3; C1 represented by a single divergent accession) and five distinct haplotypes. SNP and InDel profiling further showed that intergenic spacer (IGS) regions harbored the highest density of genetic variation. Conclusions: These genomes provide resources for germplasm characterization, phylogenetic studies, and marker-assisted breeding in coffee. They also establish a chloroplast-genome framework that, when integrated with nuclear genomics and expanded sampling, will help fully resolve the maternal history, domestication, and allopolyploid origin of Coffea arabica.
authors: Wu Y, Gu X, Li Y, Liu D, Bi X, Hu F.

title: A human gut-associated picobirnavirus establishes the Picobirnaviridae as the third clade of RNA bacteriophages.
abstract: Picobirnaviruses (PBVs) are commonly detected RNA viruses in human and animal guts and are associated with multiple human diseases. Although PBVs have been assumed to infect vertebrate hosts, there is neither direct evidence for this nor any culture system to propagate PBVs. Here we demonstrate that a PBV infects bacteria and is therefore an RNA phage. Two different PBVs from human faeces were propagated in germ-free mice after faecal microbiota transplantation, establishing a mouse model for PBV. One PBV could be cultured in vitro, in a community of anaerobic gut bacteria, and its growth could be inhibited by multiple antibiotics. RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization revealed PBV RNA within bacterial cells, and enrichment and sequencing of PBV RNA-containing cells identified a previously unidentified 'Candidatus Anaerotignum faecalis' as its host. Our findings define the family Picobirnaviridae as only the third clade of RNA phages in addition to leviviruses and cystoviruses.

title: MobiDB in 2027: machine-actionable access to intrinsic protein disorder knowledge
abstract: AbstractMobiDB (https://mobidb.org) integrates structural and functional annotations for intrinsically disordered proteins and regions across UniProtKB. The 2027 release strengthens semantic consistency, programmatic access, and reproducible reuse. A refined controlled vocabulary groups features in a hierarchical way and distinguishes evidence classes and types annotation sources as providers, methods, or aggregation rules. A new versioned REST API, along with a developed MCP server, enables scripts, workflows, and tool-using artificial intelligence systems to retrieve and combine evidence-bearing records through documented operations. The redesigned website applies the same vocabulary to protein entries, documentation, and cross-proteome statistics. Additional developments include standardized Nextflow production workflows, updated RING Protein Data Bank interaction processing, integration of Motif Map of the Proteome and Linear Motif mediated Protein–Protein Interaction Database annotations, and a release-aware catalogue of static datasets for large-scale analysis. Following the recent increase in reference proteomes in UniProtKB, MobiDB now provides a more representative estimate of long-disorder with a median residue coverage of 12.3% in eukaryotes, 1.9% in archaea, 1.7% in bacteria, and 3.4% in viruses; and protein prevalence of 48.7%, 11.9%, 11.2%, and 25.0%, respectively. Together, these developments make disorder knowledge easier to discover, relate to function, and reuse with explicit provenance.

title: MethMarkerDB 2.0: an expanded and functionally annotated database for cancer DNA methylation biomarkers
abstract: AbstractCancer-associated differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are promising biomarkers for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic response, but their biological significance and potential applications remain to be systematically explored across datasets. To support this, we released MethMarkerDB 2.0 (https://methmarkerdb.hzau.edu.cn/v2), which provides several improvements over the previous version: (i) Expands the data resource from 13 to 21 cancer types and from 658 to 1236 whole-genome methylome samples, comprising ∼5.6 million candidate DMRs and 6411 literature-curated biomarker records.(ii) Integrates 450K DNA methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Epigenome-Wide Association Study Atlas and transcript annotations into the “MethMarker Gene Search” module. These data provide complementary evidence from independent datasets and platforms and allow users to examine CpG-level information for individual DMRs. Additionally, cell-type-resolved reference methylation data allow users to check cellular-background methylation. (iii) Introduces four analysis modules to characterize DMR methylation patterns across age groups and spatial ecotypes, and connect DMRs with transcription factor binding evidence and cancer cell-line drug responses. Moreover, the “Methylation-Cas Designer” supports guide RNA design for methylation-sensitive restriction enzyme–Cas assays and targeted epigenome editing. In summary, MethMarkerDB 2.0 provides expanded resources, diverse functional analyses, and experimental design tools, facilitating the interpretation and application of cancer-associated DMRs.

title: oRNAment V2: an expanded database of putative RNA binding protein target sites in the transcriptomes of diverse model species
abstract: AbstractRNA binding proteins (RBPs) modulate the expression, form, and fate of RNA transcripts throughout their lifecycle, thereby serving as essential regulators of gene expression. Despite impactful high-throughput experimental advances that have enabled in vitro and in vivo identification of RBP binding sites, few resources provide a comprehensive catalog of potential RBP binding sites transcriptome-wide. To address this limitation, we previously developed oRNAment, a database of putative RBP binding sites across coding and non-coding transcriptome regions in human and four model species. Here, we present oRNAment V2, a significantly enhanced resource, with an expanded collection of RBPs, motifs, species, and the addition of intronic sequences. The updated oRNAment resource now predicts a total of 3 808 264 959 putative RBP binding sites across the transcriptomes of human and 14 species. Novel features of oRNAment include predictions of binding site evolutionary age, annotations of CLIP support, and visualizations with UCSC track hubs for all putative RBP binding sites. On the front end, oRNAment’s web interface enhances functionality and usability by providing improved search and filtering functions, download options, and visualizations. With its expansion, oRNAment V2 continues to provide an important resource to support research by the RNA community. oRNAment V2 is available at https://rnabiology.ircm.qc.ca/oRNAmentv2.

title: Long-read metagenomic characterization of the resistome and mobilome in heavy-metal-contaminated soils
abstract: IntroductionHeavy-metal contamination is widely proposed to co-select for antibiotic resistance by placing metal- and antibiotic-resistance genes on the same mobile elements, yet the evidence for this rests largely on short-read co-occurrence rather than on direct observation of physical linkage.MethodsWe applied Nanopore long-read metagenomics to four soils from the Ridder polymetallic mining and metallurgical district of East Kazakhstan, where zinc, cadmium and lead exceed a single local reference site by up to two orders of magnitude. Physical linkage between antibiotic- and metal-resistance genes was tested at the contig, read, genome and community levels against chance expectation.ResultsEnsemble binning of two complementary assemblies produced 261 metagenome-assembled genomes, 97% of them lacking a GTDB species assignment and dominated by Actinomycetota, together with 73 closed circular elements including complete phages and plasmids. Screening this catalogue recovered 991 antibiotic-resistance and 395 metal-resistance loci. In these metal-enriched soils, the two classes were rarely physically linked. Only four contigs carried both, against 28.9 expected under a degree-preserving null model, a 0.14-fold depletion that was robust to catalogue thresholds; co-carriage on single reads was likewise rare. At the genome level the classes were independent, and in 22 of 24 dual-carrier genomes they occupied different contigs. The mobilome nonetheless carried metal resistance preferentially: contigs called as plasmids were enriched for metal genes relative to the catalogue base rate, and a 142-kb plasmid predicted to be conjugative encoded copper, cadmium/zinc, mercury and silver efflux systems, a complete type-IV secretion system and a CBASS anti-phage defense system, but no antibiotic-resistance gene. No genome belonged to an ESKAPE or WHO-priority pathogen genus.DiscussionThese soils are therefore a large environmental resistance reservoir, but no direct clinical-risk linkage was demonstrated in the present dataset. Community co-occurrence should not be read as evidence of physical linkage. Co-selection through cross-resistance or co-regulation was not excluded.

title: Genomic characterization and early macrophage inflammatory responses to an emerging Mycobacterium wolinskyi isolate
abstract: Mycobacterium wolinskyi is an emerging rapidly growing nontuberculous mycobacterium increasingly recognized as a cause of skin, soft-tissue, and device-associated infections, including infections in immunocompetent individuals. However, its genomic characteristics and interactions with host immune cells remain poorly understood. In this study, we characterized a clinical M. wolinskyi isolate, designated QL01, recovered from a facial skin infection in an 11-year-old child, by combining antimicrobial susceptibility testing, whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomic analysis, and macrophage infection assays with transcriptomic profiling. QL01 was resistant to clarithromycin, imipenem, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, while remaining susceptible to amikacin, linezolid, moxifloxacin, minocycline, and doxycycline. Whole-genome sequencing generated a complete circular chromosome and identified antimicrobial resistance-associated homologs and host interaction-associated homologs. Comparative analysis revealed variable conservation of type VII secretion system (T7SS)- and Mce-associated loci among representative rapidly growing mycobacteria. Following uptake by mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages, viable intracellular QL01 remained recoverable after 24 h. RNA sequencing revealed an early innate immune and pro-inflammatory transcriptional response, with enrichment of TNF, NF-κB, Toll-like receptor, and C-type lectin receptor signaling pathways. RT-qPCR further confirmed increased expression of Ccl2, Tnf, Il1b, Tlr2, Clec4e, and Tnfaip3. ELISA confirmed increased secretion of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IFN-β. Inhibition of IKK/NF-κB signaling attenuated QL01-induced phosphorylation of p65 and IκBα and reduced inflammatory cytokine secretion. These findings characterize the genomic features of a clinical M. wolinskyi isolate and describe the early macrophage response to this emerging nontuberculous mycobacterial species.

title: Distinct associations of rhizoid-sphere and endophytic bacteria with dominant moss traits along an elevational gradient on Segrila Mountain
abstract: Microbial communities associated with alpine mosses remain poorly characterized in southeastern Tibet, particularly the distinction between bacteria at the rhizoid-soil interface and those inside moss tissues. We used 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to characterize 36 rhizoid-sphere and 12 endophytic samples from three dominant mosses (Actinothuidium hookeri, Ptilium crista-castrensis, and Dicranum fuscescens) across four elevations (3,700–4,300 m) on Segrila Mountain. We combined community analysis, SPIEC-EASI networks, random forests, and path modeling to examine how habitat, elevation, soil properties, and bacterial community attributes were related to moss traits. The endophytic network showed higher clustering (0.665) and modularity (0.84) and a larger proportion of positive partial correlations (94.71%) than rhizoid-sphere’s (0.305, 0.79, and 83.48%). Elevation uniquely explained 25.9% of the variation in rhizoid-sphere bacterial composition (p = 0.0001), compared with 7.9% for moss species (p = 0.0093), while neither factor significantly explained endophytic composition (both p > 0.05). Soil properties explained rhizoid-sphere community variation (adjusted R2 = 0.199, p = 0.001), whereas the endophytic model was nonsignificant (adjusted R2 = 0.029, p = 0.239). Random-forest models most strongly predicted moss tissue K (LOOCV R2 = 0.58) and N (LOOCV R2 = 0.48). In path modeling, rhizoid-sphere Shannon diversity was positively associated with morphology (β = 0.500, p = 0.0005) and negatively associated with nutrient (β = −0.263, p = 0.0036). These findings highlight the rhizoid-sphere as an interface linking elevation, soil conditions, bacterial community variation, and moss traits.

title: Lineage-aware evaluation of machine learning for observed cross-genus occurrence of IncC plasmids in public databases
abstract: IntroductionIncC plasmids contribute to the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance across bacterial hosts. We developed an IncC-specific model to classify plasmids belonging to highly similar cross-genus pairs observed in public databases and evaluated its performance when related lineages were kept together during validation.MethodsThe development cohort comprised 988 PLSDB plasmids (266 label-positive), and a separately sourced RefSeq cohort contained 250 plasmids. The operational label denotes occurrence in databases rather than experimentally measured transfer. Among five standalone learners, LightGBM with 100 foldwise-selected 4-mers (LightGBM-100) was retained, with a fixed threshold of 0.306 derived via nested random-CV Youden-index selection.ResultsUnder random five-fold cross-validation, pooled out-of-fold AUROC and average precision (AP) were 0.960 and 0.928, respectively, but fell to 0.742 and 0.498 with primary Mash-component blocking and to 0.712 and 0.412 with more permissive blocking. At the random-CV-derived threshold, blocked sensitivity was 0.259 and 0.162, respectively. In RefSeq, LightGBM-100 achieved an AUROC of 0.937 and an AP of 0.894, although 81 of 84 positives lay within Mash distance d < 0.00124 of the development cohort and the labels partly relied on pair evidence from both databases. Biological features did not reproducibly improve the 4-mer model after lineage blocking, and family- and order-crossing outcomes showed similar limitations.DiscussionThis study establishes an IncC-specific, lineage-aware benchmark for predicting database-observed cross-genus occurrence and demonstrates how lineage relatedness and database representation shape predictive performance. The model may help prioritize plasmids within represented sequence backgrounds for follow-up, while the integrated biological analyses provide a basis for targeted experimental investigation.
