title: Subtype-Resolved Secretome and Surface-Marker Remapping of Lung Fibroblasts in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
abstract: Single-cell atlases have resolved the fibroblast compartment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) into discrete subtypes [1], but subtype-resolved secretory output and surface-marker logic for prospective isolation remain incompletely defined. We re-analyzed the Habermann et al. single-cell atlas of fibrotic lung (GSE135893; 114,396 cells, including 3,605 fibroblast-lineage cells, of which 2,653 IPF/control cells entered the main contrasts) [1], quantifying detection rates and mean expression of 72 secreted genes and 16 candidate surface markers across four curated subtypes, validated by full-transcriptome re-clustering. Inflammatory chemokine production was concentrated in HAS1-high fibroblasts (CXCL2 in 70.4% of cells, CXCL8 in 46.9%), whereas PLIN2+ fibroblasts carried an angiogenic bias (VEGFA 65.6%). CSF1 was silenced upon myofibroblast differentiation irrespective of diagnosis (fibroblasts 34.2–48.6% versus myofibroblasts 8.7–14.8%), a differentiation-linked rather than disease-specific switch, and the interferon-γ–inducible chemokines CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11 were detected in only 0.0–2.6% of cells across subtypes (maximum 2.6% = CXCL9, 5/196 control myofibroblasts). A CD34-low/PDPN-high/CD73-high/FAP+ panel resolved all four subtypes at the marginal transcript level (pending joint, antibody-level validation), whereas CD90 lost discriminatory value in disease. CD10 (MME) marked a control-enriched, putatively resolving myofibroblast state that contracted from 23.0% to 5.4% in IPF; its interleukin-4 induction was tested across cohorts and remains unresolved. Key findings replicated in two independent cohorts (GSE136831; GSE122960) and were spatially corroborated by GeoMx profiling (GSE255174), while CSF1 and compartment-level chemokine effects varied across cohorts. Fibroblast subsets thus carry distinct, isolable secretory identities in IPF, providing a transcriptome-resolved resource for protein-level and spatial validation of fibroblast functions in fibrotic lung.
authors: Shen C, Li D, Chen H.

title: bZIP-Mediated Activation of a Late Embryogenesis Abundant Protein MsLEA2 Enhances Aluminium Tolerance in Medicago sativa.
abstract: The phytohormone abscisic acid (ABA) is rapidly induced in roots exposed to aluminium (Al) stress, yet the mechanisms by which it modulates Al-detoxification genes remain elusive. Here we uncover a hierarchical ABA-responsive regulatory network that orchestrates a Late Embryogenesis Abundant (LEA)_2 protein MsLEA2, which modulates Al tolerance in alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.). Using yeast one-hybrid (Y1H) assays, luciferase complementation imaging (LCI), mutagenesis, and electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), we show that three antagonistic bZIP transcription factors-MsABF2 (activator), MsDPBF3 (hyper-activator) and MsGBF1 (repressor)-dynamically regulate MsLEA2 expression through spatially distinct ABRE motifs, enabling precise transcriptional control. Functional analyses reveal that MsLEA2 acts as a multifunctional hub, that promotes (i) oxalate exudation via interactions with aquaporins (MsPIP2;1, MsPIP2;2, MsTIP1;1), (ii) reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging, and (iii) cell wall remodelling through binding to UDP-xylose synthase (MsUXS1). Golgi-targeted MsLEA2 facilitates apoplastic Al exclusion, a mechanism distinct from its cytoplasmic homologue AtLEA14, underscoring the importance of subcellular compartmentalisation in Al detoxification. Our findings establish LEA_2 proteins as pivotal components of secretory-pathway-mediated Al tolerance and provide actionable targets for engineering crops resilient to acidic soils.
authors: Sun L, Mo X, Lv A, Liu X, Zhao E, Zhang Y, Hu W, Zhang Y, Xing Q, An Y, Zhou P.

title: Uterus Transplant Living Donor Evaluation and Selection: An Approach to Optimizing Donor and Recipient Outcomes.
abstract: BackgroundSince the first live birth from uterus transplantation (UTx) in 2014, there has been an ever-growing interest in the technique from patients and transplant programs worldwide. The Dallas UTx program first reported a live birth in the United States in 2017 and has subsequently completed 40 transplants with a living-donor-predominant approach. To date, the published scientific literature has focused on recipient and newborn outcomes, with relatively limited discussion surrounding living donor evaluation.MethodsThe aim of this study was to describe the methodology, evolution, and outcomes from living donor evaluation at the Dallas UTx program.ResultsOver a 9-y period, 1329 women volunteered for living donation evaluation. A total of 72 women proceeded to full evaluation, with 38 deemed eligible (37 nondirected donation, 97%). Six women withdrew following evaluation, and 28 were deemed ineligible. Thirteen were declined for vasculature concerns (the main reason for exclusion), and 8 because of other abnormalities found on imaging. Two potential candidates were deemed ineligible because of medical comorbidities, and a further 3 on psychological evaluation. An additional 2 candidates were ineligible following committee review. Twenty-seven (68%) recipients have delivered a child, 4 have delivered 2 children, and 6 are currently pregnant.ConclusionsSuccessful living donor UTx requires thorough donor evaluation. Favorable donor, recipient, and newborn outcomes were observed within the context of this comprehensive donor evaluation and selection process.
authors: Jacques A, Fischbach C, Warren AM, Testa G, Johannesson L.

title: Prognostic value of cell differentiation-related genes in follicular lymphoma based on integrated single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing.
abstract: Follicular lymphoma (FL) is the most common indolent B-cell lymphoma and follows a heterogeneous clinical course; however, reliable molecular markers for risk stratification are still lacking. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE182434) with bulk transcriptomic data from three GEO cohorts (GSE66166, GSE119214, GSE16131) and applied pseudotime trajectory analysis, consensus clustering, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and LASSO Cox regression to derive a cell differentiation-related gene signature (CDRGS) and a prognostic risk model. Model performance was evaluated by time-dependent ROC analysis, the concordance index, calibration curves, decision-curve analysis, and multivariable Cox regression, and the expression of the signature genes was examined by RT-qPCR, western blot, and immunohistochemistry in lymphoma cell lines, in a SU-DHL-4 xenograft model, and in an independent cohort of patients with FL. Pseudotime analysis resolved three differentiation states, and consensus clustering based on the CDRGS stratified patients into three molecular subtypes with different overall survival. A three-gene model comprising SIRPG, FLT3LG, and LAG3 separated high- and low-risk patients in the training cohort and in the GSE119214 validation cohort, with separation in the same direction but not reaching significance in GSE16131, and remained associated with overall survival after adjustment for M7-FLIPI in the two cohorts in which that index was available. All three genes were expressed at higher mRNA and protein levels in lymphoma cell lines than in a non-malignant B lymphoblastoid line, indicating that the malignant cells themselves express them. In an independent patient cohort, the expression of the three-gene panel varied with risk score and with established clinical indices in the directions predicted by the model coefficients. We constructed a cell differentiation-related prognostic model for FL and found that SIRPG, FLT3LG, and LAG3 provide candidate biomarkers of the immune microenvironment that carry prognostic information beyond M7-FLIPI and merit prospective validation.
authors: Xiang X, Deng W.

title: Ginsenoside Rg6 ameliorates COPD by targeting RAGE to suppress MAPK/NF-κB signaling, thereby preserving alveolar barrier integrity and attenuating EMT.
abstract: BackgroundChronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is pathologically characterized by progressive alveolar epithelial barrier disruption, a pathological process primarily driven by chronic cigarette smoke exposure. While Ginsenoside Rg6 (Rg6) has shown therapeutic promise in pulmonary injury models, its direct molecular targets and the precise mechanisms by which it preserves barrier integrity remain unclear.PurposeThis study investigates whether Rg6 mitigates COPD by directly targeting the RAGE receptor, thereby suppressing the downstream signaling axes concurrently preserve alveolar barrier integrity and attenuate epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT).MethodsThe therapeutic efficacy of Rg6 was evaluated in CSE-challenged MLE-12 alveolar epithelial cells and an LPS/CS-driven mouse COPD model. Transcriptomic profiling was utilized to identify upstream regulatory nodes. Direct Rg6-RAGE engagement was rigorously validated via molecular docking, MD simulations, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), DARTS, and CETSA. The functional dependency of Rg6's protective effects on RAGE was dissected using siRNA knockdown in vitro and AAV-shRAGE delivery in vivo.ResultsOral Rg6 significantly ameliorated pulmonary function decline, emphysema, and the inflammatory microenvironment in COPD mice, achieving efficacy comparable to dexamethasone. Crucially, Rg6 effectively preserved alveolar barrier integrity, restored tight junctions, and attenuated EMT-associated phenotypic shifts. Transcriptomic profiling identified the AGE-RAGE axis as the central upstream hub governing this structural protection. Comprehensive biophysical assays confirmed that Rg6 directly binds to and thermodynamically stabilizes the RAGE protein pocket. Mechanistically, Rg6 suppressed RAGE-mediated hyperactivation of the MAPK (p38, JNK) and NF-κB (p65) cascades, which serve as the central drivers for tight junction disassembly and EMT in epithelial cells. Furthermore, RAGE ablation in vitro and in vivo demonstrated that Rg6's capacity to preserve epithelial architecture is primarily RAGE-dependent.ConclusionsRg6 directly targets alveolar RAGE to inhibit the RAGE-MAPK/NF-κB signaling cascade. By suppressing this axis, Rg6 concurrently preserves alveolar barrier integrity and attenuates EMT-like transitions, actively restoring alveolar structural homeostasis and positioning it as a promising therapeutic candidate for COPD.
journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
authors: Wu J, Wang Q, Gao P, Geng X, Wang N, Bu Y, Wang C, Wang F, Tan L, Liu J.

title: Mechanism-Driven Nanomedicine for Radiation Injury and Protection: Redox Homeostasis, the DNA Damage Response, and Microbiome-Based Strategies.
abstract: Radiotherapy is a cornerstone of cancer treatment but is limited by injury to normal tissues. Radiation-induced ROS, DNA double-strand breaks, mitochondrial dysfunction, dysregulated DNA damage responses (DDR), and persistent inflammation drive acute and chronic toxicity. Radioprotective strategies must protect normal tissues without weakening tumor control. This review examines nanomedicine strategies for normal-tissue radioprotection through three mechanisms: (1) redox regulation by nanozymes, radical scavengers, and antioxidant delivery systems; (2) modulation of DDR pathways and cell fate; and (3) microbiome and metabolite regulation. We discuss how these strategies affect molecular damage, inflammation, and tissue repair and assess whether they preserve normal tissues without compromising antitumor immunity or radiotherapy efficacy.
authors: Li H, Du X, Zhou C, Wang Y, Su K, Li S.

title: Integrative Analysis of Epidermal Barrier Dysfunction Regulators in Psoriasis.
abstract: IntroductionPsoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by keratinocyte hyperproliferation and compromised epidermal barrier function. Although tight junction disruption is a key pathological hallmark, the upstream transcriptional mechanisms driving the downregulation of core barrier proteins such as claudin-1 (CLDN1) remain insufficiently characterized.MethodsWe implemented an integrative multi-omics framework combining weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and machine-learning algorithms to prioritize core diagnostic features in psoriasis. Upstream transcription factors regulating CLDN1 were computationally predicted using the JASPAR, hTFtarget, and KnockTF databases. The regulatory effect of E74-like ETS transcription factor 3 (ELF3) on the CLDN1 promoter was evaluated using dual-luciferase reporter assays, and the inflammatory response of the axis was examined in TNF-α-stimulated HaCaT keratinocytes via quantitative real-time PCR.ResultsMachine-learning prioritization identified CLDN1 as a robust diagnostic feature that is significantly downregulated in psoriatic lesions. Multi-database integration converged on ELF3 as a candidate negative regulator of CLDN1. Dual-luciferase reporter assays demonstrated that ELF3 overexpression significantly suppressed wild-type CLDN1 promoter activity, whereas mutation of the predicted binding site abolished this repression. In TNF-α-stimulated HaCaT cells, ELF3 was markedly upregulated with a concurrent downregulation of CLDN1.Discussion These findings suggest that ELF3 functions as a candidate transcriptional repressor of CLDN1 promoter activity and provide preliminary in vitro and computational insights into the transcriptional alterations associated with epidermal barrier disruption in psoriasis, highlighting potential avenues for restoring structural barrier integrity.
authors: Liu Y, Wang Y, Zhu H, Liu Y, Wang J, Li F, Zhang Y, Peng Z, Wang W.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Analyses Identify Shared Inflammation-Related Candidate Genes in Psoriasis and Acute Myocardial Infarction.
abstract: BackgroundPsoriasis and acute myocardial infarction (AMI) are both closely associated with immune-inflammatory dysregulation; however, the shared molecular features of psoriasis-AMI comorbidity remain incompletely characterized. To address this gap, this study aimed to identify novel shared inflammation-related candidate genes between psoriasis and AMI and to characterize their cellular expression patterns using public transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing data. The main finding was the identification of shared inflammation-related candidate genes and their cell-type-specific expression patterns in psoriasis-AMI comorbidity.MethodsTranscriptomic datasets related to psoriasis and AMI were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. GSE30999 and GSE66360 were used as discovery cohorts. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using limma with adjusted P value ResultsA total of 57 shared DEGs were identified in the psoriasis and AMI discovery cohorts, including 51 commonly upregulated and 6 commonly downregulated genes. Enrichment analysis showed that these genes were mainly involved in processes related to cellular response to lipopolysaccharide, chemotaxis, cytokine activity and chemokine activity, and were significantly enriched in the IL-17, NF-κB, TNF and chemokine signaling pathways, as well as lipid and atherosclerosis-related pathways. PPI network and cytoHubba analyses identified 9 consensus hub genes. External validation and ROC analyses showed that S100A9, S100A12 and CXCL1 were significantly upregulated in both psoriasis and AMI validation datasets and showed moderate discriminatory performance between groups. Single-cell analysis showed that S100A9 and S100A12 exhibited prominent myeloid inflammation-related expression profiles in psoriatic lesions and AMI peripheral immune cells, whereas CXCL1 expression was relatively restricted, suggesting that it may primarily reflect chemokine-mediated inflammatory cell recruitment.ConclusionThis study identified S100A9, S100A12 and CXCL1 as candidate genes potentially associated with shared inflammatory features of psoriasis-AMI comorbidity. These findings suggest that myeloid cell activation and chemokine-mediated recruitment of inflammatory cells may contribute to the molecular link between the two diseases; however, further clinical and experimental validation is required.
authors: Fang RN, Shen Y, Li JH, Zhu BC, Jia N, Chen Y, Feng HS, Zhang WT.

title: Identification of Five Candidate Genes and Development of an Exploratory Diagnostic Nomogram for COPD Using Integrative Single-Cell and Bulk Transcriptomic Analyses.
abstract: BackgroundIntegrative transcriptomic analyses can prioritize genes associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), but expression associations require experimental assessment.MethodsSingle-cell GSE173896 and bulk GSE57148 data were analyzed using clustering, co-expression networks, CellChat, differential expression, immune deconvolution, pseudotime, and virtual knockout analysis. A five-gene logistic nomogram was developed in GSE57148. Clinical RT-qPCR included 30 participants with COPD and 30 without COPD. Two independent IL6-targeting siRNAs were examined in HBEC3-KT and BEAS-2B cells using epithelial-macrophage co-culture, cytokine measurements, and wound-healing assays.ResultsNHSL2, CDKL5, CRIP1, TNNI2, and IL6 were prioritized as candidate genes. Clinical RT-qPCR supported higher CDKL5, IL6, and NHSL2 expression and lower CRIP1 and TNNI2 expression in COPD. IL6 knockdown reduced epithelial IL6 expression and attenuated several macrophage-associated transcriptional responses in co-culture after epithelial cigarette smoke extract exposure. Secretory responses varied by cell line and siRNA; co-culture IL-10 reductions were significant in the HBEC3-KT system but not in the BEAS-2B system. IL6 knockdown also reduced epithelial wound closure. The nomogram was evaluated within its development cohort and lacked independent external validation.ConclusionThe study identifies five COPD-associated candidate genes and provides experimental evidence linking epithelial IL6 perturbation to selected co-culture responses and wound closure. These findings do not establish a COPD-specific mechanism or therapeutic benefit. The nomogram remains exploratory and requires independent validation.
journal: International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
authors: Wang J, Zhang H, Mu Q, Li X, Sun D.

title: A preliminary investigation of DNA methylation-based multiplex system for semen identification and age estimation.
abstract: The identification and age estimation of body fluid stains found at crime scenes provide crucial information for reconstructing events and narrowing down the potential suspect pool. In this study, we developed a multiplex methylation SNaPshot system containing seven age-related CpGs (AR-CpGs) and two semen-specific CpGs that enables simultaneous acquisition of information on donor age and sample type from a single reaction. Four candidate AR-CpGs derived from previous in-house screening (cg17791346, cg06880412, cg25093603, and cg06966678) were incorporated into system and showed Pearson correlation coefficients (R) ranging from 0.527 to 0.717 with chronological age. The performance of the multiplex system was evaluated using 40 semen samples and 19 non-semen samples for semen identification and age estimation. The system showed high specificity for semen identification within the evaluated sample set and remained effective with 50 ng DNA input. Five types of machine learning models were developed using a non-overlapping historical dataset of 136 semen samples and were independently evaluated using 34 semen samples with complete 7 CpG methylation profiles from the present test cohort, with performance evaluated using Mean Absolute Deviation (MAD) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). The best-performing linear kernel Support Vector Machine (SVM) model achieved a MAD of 4.648 years based on valid semen age prediction profiles. In addition, 20 simulated semen-containing mixture samples were analyzed to evaluate the performance of the system in semen-containing mixtures. Based on the established semen detection criteria, 12 mixtures were classified as semen detected, whereas 8 were classified as semen not detected. Age estimation was performed using evaluable mixture samples, achieving a MAD of 8.865 years. This study presents an integrated approach for semen detection and donor age estimation, offering a more efficient and practical tool for forensic casework involving suspected semen samples.
authors: Huang Y, Xu J, Xiao Y, Yang H, Deng B, Lv M, Jian H, Qu S, Liang W.

title: Metal-organic frameworks for antibiotic removal from water and wastewater.
abstract: The persistence of antibiotics in aquatic environments has emerged as a critical environmental challenge due to their extensive use, incomplete metabolism, and continuous release from municipal, hospital, and industrial sources. Their accumulation in water and wastewater systems fosters antimicrobial resistance, disrupts ecosystems, and poses severe risks to public health. Conventional adsorbents such as activated carbon and zeolites often fall short in terms of selectivity, regeneration, and adsorption capacity, necessitating innovative alternatives. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), with their tunable porosity, high surface areas, adjustable chemical functionalities, and structural diversity, have attracted significant attention as next-generation adsorbents for antibiotic removal. This review provides a comprehensive discussion of the occurrence and impacts of antibiotics in aquatic systems, followed by a critical evaluation of the adsorption performance of pristine MOFs, MOF derivatives, and MOF-based composites. Emphasis is placed on synthetic methodologies, purification/activation strategies, and mechanistic insights underlying antibiotic-MOF interactions. Furthermore, the study highlights the regeneration potential of MOFs for sustainable applications, compares their performance with conventional adsorbents, and identifies the persisting challenges in stability, scalability, and selectivity. Finally, knowledge gaps and future directions are outlined, focusing on defect engineering, hybrid frameworks, and other critical factors governing efficient application in real wastewater treatment to accelerate the translation of laboratory studies into practical deployment. By consolidating advances and challenges, this work positions MOFs as promising candidates for addressing the global threat of antibiotic pollution in water and wastewater.
authors: Adegoke KA, Babarinde CO, Adegoke OR, Oladeji OS, Oyebamiji AK, Bamisaye A, Adesina AA, Bello OS, Said MA.

title: Gastric Cancer: Epidemiology, Risk Factors, Pathogenesis, Clinical Features, Diagnosis, and Management.
abstract: Gastric cancer is a multifactorial disease shaped by diverse risk factors and a complex pathogenesis spanning from chronic atrophic gastritis to invasive malignancy. Its global incidence shows marked geographic disparities, and advances in understanding its pathogenic mechanisms have improved diagnosis and treatment. Although the relationship between gastric cancer and macrophages has been extensively investigated, a systematic review integrating the entire clinical and biological continuum of gastric cancer, from epidemiology to management, with a focus on macrophages remains lacking. This review summarizes the epidemiology and multidimensional risk factors for gastric cancer, including infectious, dietary, genetic, microbiome, and metabolite-related factors. We describe the evolution of precancerous conditions, molecular alterations such as miRNA expression, and the bidirectional interactions between gastric cancer cells and macrophages that drive tumor progression within the tumor microenvironment. We also review clinical features, diagnostic approaches based on screening and endoscopy, and current management strategies, including surgery, systemic therapies, targeted therapies, immunotherapy, macrophage-targeted therapies, macrophage metabolic reprogramming, and recent preclinical and clinical advances. Overall, this review integrates evidence from epidemiology, molecular biology, immunology, and pathology to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding gastric cancer pathogenesis and current as well as emerging therapeutic strategies.
authors: Xin Y, Wang X, Wu Y, Liu Q, Ren Q, Wang H, Zhai J.

title: Co-transcriptomic network analysis of host-parasite interactions reveals genes underpinning parasite fitness
abstract: Interactions between parasites and their host organisms generate continuous variation in infection outcomes. Although dual transcriptome studies have demonstrated extensive molecular dialogues between interacting species, it is still unclear how natural variation in host and parasite gene regulatory networks and coordination between them contribute to diverse disease phenotypes. Here, we re-contextualized co-transcriptomes from recombinant inbred lines of the plant-parasitic root-knot nematode  Meloidogyne hapla infecting  Medicago truncatula host plants with relative measures of ‘infection intensity’ as a proxy for parasite load. We used infection intensity to estimate interaction gradients on gene expression by calculating its covariance with transcript levels. Quantitative analyses of interaction gradients for host and parasite transcriptomes identified major differences in development-related transcriptional programs along the infection continuum. In addition, integrated network analyses connected host cell wall remodeling with parasite protein production and secretion. Silencing of candidate root-knot nematode genes reduced host galling and parasite reproductive fitness, providing experimental support for our network-derived predictions. Together, our findings present an integrated systems genetics framework connecting naturally occurring genetic variation to quantitative disease phenotypes.
authors: Inskeep TR, Celis E, Nguyen A, Groen SC.

title: Charged-Fermion Mass Phenomenology and the Pati–Salam Mass Plane: Sp(18) Normalization and a USp(6) Mass Construction
abstract: The pattern of charged-fermion masses suggests a connection between the shapes of quark and lepton spectra. This revised and expanded study examines the resulting Pati–Salam mass plane in complementary $\mathrm{Sp}(18)$ and $\mathrm{USp}(6)$ constructions. It relates the logarithmic plane to a specified source geometry and develops an economical $N=1$ supersymmetric $\mathrm{USp}(6)$ realization. In a common-profile embedding, a single route-odd normalization coefficient controls the component normal to the plane. Exact finite matrix identities show how the relation is modified by noncommuting kinetic terms and by the middle singular value. Three candidate composite operators $P_0A^jL_0$, $j=0,1,2$, have charges compatible with the restricted family-source texture; one active right-handed ten-plet pair then yields a charged-mass determinant relation.In a local radiative example, heavy-threshold gauge transport, full-matrix Standard-Model evolution below 10 TeV, and the retained gluino, bino and colorless-Higgsino mass and kinetic corrections give $m_s(M_Z)=53.12642$ MeV for the finite boundary $c_{K6}=3/4$. The other eight charged masses and CKM mixing, including its CP invariant, are reproduced using the existing down-soft sector. The same canonical tree messenger block gives $H_\ell/H_d=1.540962$ and a squared-splitting ratio of $2.375000$. The choice of $c_{K6}$ was informed by the known strange-mass range. Taking that mass as a ninth input instead calibrates $c_{K6}=0.727266026$; neither procedure derives the coefficient from strong dynamics.The $\mathrm{Sp}(18)$ analysis retains conditional current–scalar matching identities and local vacuum tests for its own specified action. An analytic bound below $0.018\%$ controls the family-direction dependence of a separate canonical $\mathrm{USp}(6)$ flavon kernel, while a reduced high-scale charged-source system provides independently checked evolution and matching identities. Local vacuum and selected flavor tests are available in specified reference configurations; the complete pole spectrum and baryon amplitudes require further matching. These results define a concrete effective mass benchmark, conditional heavy-mass tests and a source-normalization target for a microscopic completion.
authors: Krivenko-Emetov YD.

title: Mechanical and Structural Evolution of Drill Bit Metal Under Compressive Load in Smart Mining Systems
abstract: In this work, we investigate the atomic-scale mechanical behavior of key metals (Al, Au, Cu, and Ni) used in drilling alloy and structural components for smart mining systems. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed to explore their stress-strain behavior under uniaxial compression from 300 K to 1000 K. The results display a linear decrease in uniaxial compressive strength (UCS) and Young’s modulus with increasing temperature due to lattice expansion and weakened interatomic potential derived from the Embedded Atom Method (EAM) formalism. Among all the metal studied, Ni exhibits the highest mechanical performance, maintaining a compressive strength of 7.40 GPa at 1000 K, which makes it a promising candidate for high-performance drilling alloys operating in severe thermal environments. Cu shows moderate thermal stability with a UCS of 5.54 GPa at 1000 K, whereas Au demonstrates the lowest thermal resistance and the greatest softening tendency, reaching only 2.21 GPa at the same temperature. Common neighbor analysis (CNA) and Radial Distribution Function (RDF) reveal that Ni preserves stronger atomic ordering because of its higher cohesive energy, while structural degradation is associated with the reduction of perfect Face Centered Cubic (FCC) configurations and the formation of defects and dislocations under compression. In comparison, Al shows stable defect recovery on heating, giving better resistance to thermal fatigue in automated mining sensor housings. These atomistic results that are temperature dependent are valuable input parameters for predictive algorithms and digital twins in advanced mining engineering.
authors: Mes-adi H, Amharech A, AlShuaibi A, Touti E, Maaider K.

title: DTX3 Suppresses the NPM3-RUVBL1 Axis to Inhibit Homologous Recombination Repair and Abrogate Tumor Radioresistance.
abstract: Aberrant remodeling of DNA damage repair pathways after radiotherapy constitutes a primary driver of tumor radioresistance and compromised therapeutic efficacy. Ubiquitination has been reported as a critical post-translational modification governing the DNA damage response and repair cascade. However, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying ubiquitination-mediated radioresistance remain poorly characterized. The E3 ubiquitin ligase Deltex 3 (DTX3) is validated as a negative regulator of tumor radioresistance that improves radiotherapy efficacy in vitro and in vivo models. Mechanistically, DTX3 physically interacts with nucleophosmin 3 (NPM3), catalyzes K27-linked polyubiquitination of NPM3 at the Lys102 residue, and consequently triggers proteasomal degradation of NPM3. Loss of NPM3 further destabilizes the RUVBL1-TIP60 complex, diminishes H4K16 acetylation, and impairs homologous recombination repair. Consistently, elevated NPM3 expression counteracts DTX3-mediated radiosensitization. Clinically, low DTX3 levels are correlated with inferior overall survival and elevated post-radiotherapy recurrence across multiple human malignancies. The study reveals DTX3 as a potent suppressor of homologous recombination repair and a promising therapeutic candidate to overcome tumor radioresistance.
authors: Xiao JH, Xie CJ, Chen YH, Cheng H, Li SH, Li W, Bin YW, He RM, Li YQ, Feng P.

title: Caffeic acid mitigates myocardial fibrosis via suppressing MAPKs/CREB-mediated inflammation in myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury mice.
abstract: BackgroundMyocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury (MIRI) represents a major form of secondary damage during reperfusion therapy, in which inflammation and myocardial fibrosis are key pathological features. Caffeic acid (CA), a natural phenolic compound abundant in dietary sources, has been implicated in cardiovascular protection; however, the mechanisms by which CA modulates post-MIRI inflammation and fibrosis remain insufficiently defined.ObjectiveTo clarify the molecular target(s) and signaling mechanism(s) through which CA attenuates inflammation-associated myocardial fibrosis after MIRI.MethodsA LAD ligation-based murine MIRI model was used to evaluate the anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic efficacy of CA. A co-culture system using cardiac fibroblasts and RAW 264.7 macrophages, along with adoptive cell transfer, was applied to interrogate macrophage-fibroblast crosstalk. Transcriptomic profiling (RNA-seq) was performed to identify candidate pathways involved in CA-mediated protection. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assay, CETSA, immunofluorescence, and western blotting were used to assess MAPKs/CREB signaling as a putative intervention axis, and pharmacological activation of MAPKs (anisomycin) or CREB (forskolin), or MAPK14 ablation, was employed to probe pathway involvement.ResultsCA improved cardiac function and alleviated inflammatory and fibrotic pathology in MIRI mice, accompanied by suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Conditioned medium from LPS-stimulated RAW 264.7 cells promoted fibroblast activation, and adoptively transferred macrophages within the myocardium promoted fibrotic protein expression; both effects were attenuated by CA. RNA-seq implicated MAPK signaling in the protective mechanism of CA, and downstream analyses supported inhibition of the MAPKs/CREB axis. Notably, CA achieved effects comparable to those of MAPK14 ablation, whereas anisomycin or forskolin partially blunted the anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects of CA, consistent with functional involvement of MAPKs/CREB signaling in CA-mediated protection during MIRI.ConclusionCA mitigates MIRI-associated myocardial fibrosis by suppressing MAPKs/CREB-mediated inflammatory signaling, supporting its potential to improve long-term post-MIRI remodeling.
authors: Xiang M, Ouyang X, Song S, Yang M, Sarapultsev A, Luo S, Dong Y, Hu D.

title: Antisense Oligonucleotides with 5'-decoy technology triggers nonsense-mediated decay of SCN9A to elicit long-lasting analgesia.
abstract: The voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.7 (SCN9A) is a genetically validated target for pain therapy, but achieving therapeutic isoform selectivity remains a formidable challenge for small-molecule inhibitors. Here, we overcome this bottleneck through a highly selective RNA-targeted strategy that dictates SCN9A alternative splicing. We first identified ASO50 as the most potent baseline candidate antisense oligonucleotide (ASO). Subsequent 5'-decoy (5D) sequence screening yielded an upgraded candidate, L9C-ASO50, which is engineered to competitively intercept U1 snRNA, achieving a cooperative spatial hindrance that robustly suppresses exon 5 recognition. This targeted exon exclusion introduces a frameshift that triggers robust, obligate transcript clearance via the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway, ensuring complete functional silencing without cross-reacting with homologous NaV channels. Mechanistically, we define the underlying cis-trans regulatory architecture, revealing a homeostatic tug-of-war where the RNA-binding protein ELAVL2 enforces exon inclusion, paradoxically antagonized by the canonical SR protein family. Crucially, CNS-restricted delivery of L9C-ASO50 produces profound and sustained mechanical and thermal analgesia. These findings establish splice-modulated transcript degradation as a viable therapeutic paradigm for chronic pain and provide a broadly applicable blueprint for engineering targeted RNA therapeutics.
authors: Meng S, Yang X, Liu X, Li S, Ma Y, Wang X, Zhang H, Chen R, Azhar Z, Guo Y, Fu Q.

title: Banxia Xiexin decoction attenuates ethanol-induced acute gastric mucosal injury and gastric dysmotility: an integrated pharmacological and transcriptomic study.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceBanxia Xiexin Decoction (BXD), a classical formula for gastric dysmotility. Ethanol-induced acute gastric injury causes mucosal damage and dysmotility; whether BXD improves this is unclear.Aim of the studyTo investigate whether BXD alleviates gastric dysmotility in ethanol-induced acute gastric mucosal injury and its possible link to interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC) autophagy and PI3K/AKT/mTOR.Materials and methodsAn ethanol-induced acute gastric mucosal injury rat model was established. We assessed gastric injury grossly and histologically and measured gastric emptying by the phenol red method. ICC integrity, autophagic markers, and PI3K/AKT/mTOR proteins were assessed by immunofluorescence, Western blot, and transmission electron microscopy. Network pharmacology and transcriptomics predicted pathways; we validated LY294002 in vitro.ResultsBXD dose-dependently attenuated ethanol-induced gastric mucosal injury; high and medium doses improved gastric emptying and preserved ICC network integrity. Ethanol induced autophagic substrate and vacuole accumulation in ICC, which BXD reduced, although a serum contribution cannot be excluded. These effects may involve PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. Network pharmacology and transcriptomics suggested this axis as a candidate pathway; LY294002 partially attenuated BXD-induced mTOR phosphorylation in vitro, suggesting a contributory but not causal role of PI3K activity in reducing autophagic substrate accumulation.ConclusionBXD reduced gastric mucosal injury and improved gastric motility, with preserved ICC network integrity and reduced autophagic substrate accumulation in ICC. However, causality between ICC preservation and improved gastric emptying was not established, and ICC pacemaker function was not assessed. Direct ICC protection by BXD serum and a causal role of PI3K/AKT/mTOR remain to be confirmed.
authors: Zhang F, Gu J, Li Y, Zhang Y, Ge F, Zhang D, Zhang D, Chen M.

title: Integrative network pharmacology, machine learning, and experimental validation identify the TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3 axis as a potential mechanism underlying the therapeutic effects of Lingguizhugan decoction in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceLingguizhugan decoction, a traditional formula originating from Zhang Zhongjing's Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases, has shown cognitive benefits in APP/PS1 mice in our earlier study, partly through restoration of meningeal lymphatic drainage and enhancement of amyloid-β (Aβ) removal. Whether other molecular events contribute to its therapeutic action in Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains to be clarified.Aim of the studyThis work was designed to clarify additional potential mechanisms by which LGZG may act against AD.Methods and materialsThe chemical constituents of LGZG were profiled by UPLC-Q-TOF-MS. Candidate targets and pathways were screened by integrating public databases, transcriptomic analysis, network pharmacology, and enrichment analysis. Eight machine learning models and SHAP analysis were subsequently used to prioritize candidate regulators. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were performed to evaluate the potential interactions between representative LGZG constituents and TLR4. APP/PS1 mice and BV2 microglial cells were used for experimental validation. Spatial learning and memory, hippocampal pathological alterations, Aβ deposition, inflammatory cytokines, microglial inflammatory phenotype-associated markers, and TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3 signaling were evaluated using behavioral testing, histological staining, ELISA, immunofluorescence, qRT-PCR, and Western blotting. TAK-242 inhibition and TLR4 overexpression were further used to assess the involvement of TLR4 signaling.ResultsTwenty-three candidate constituents were retained following chemical profiling and in silico screening of LGZG. Integrated analysis of network pharmacology, AD-related genes, and transcriptomic data identified 46 candidate LGZG-AD-DEG targets. Machine learning and SHAP analyses further prioritized several inflammation-related regulators, including RELA and NFKBIA, supporting inflammation-related signaling as a major direction for subsequent validation. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations suggested potential interactions between representative LGZG constituents and the TLR4 receptor. In APP/PS1 mice, LGZG improved spatial learning and memory, attenuated hippocampal neuronal injury, reduced Aβ deposition, and decreased IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α levels. LGZG also reduced hippocampal TLR4, P-IκBα, P-NF-κB, and NLRP3 expression and decreased TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3-related signals in Iba1-positive microglia. In LPS-stimulated BV2 cells, LGZG shifted inflammatory phenotype-associated markers toward a less pro-inflammatory profile and suppressed TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3 signaling. TAK-242 treatment and TLR4 overexpression experiments further supported the involvement of TLR4 signaling in these effects.ConclusionLGZG alleviated cognitive impairment, hippocampal pathological alterations, Aβ deposition, and neuroinflammatory responses in APP/PS1 mice. Integrated bioinformatic analyses and experimental validation suggest that regulation of TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3 signaling contributes to the anti-neuroinflammatory effects of LGZG in AD.
authors: Hu D, Li D, He L, Mao S, Zhu YA, Chen X, Zhang J, Zhou C, Zhou X.

title: Inhibition of neutrophil extracellular trap formation ameliorates astrocyte pyroptosis via CUL7-dependent NLRP3 ubiquitination in mice with sepsis-associated encephalopathy.
abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) encompasses acute brain dysfunction during sepsis and may be followed by persistent cognitive impairment among survivors. Although neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) have been implicated in sepsis-related organ injury, their role in astrocyte fate determination and neuroinflammation during SAE remains poorly defined. Here, using a cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) model, we demonstrate that NETs accumulate in both the circulation and hippocampus following sepsis. Pharmacological inhibition or degradation of NETs markedly alleviated blood-brain barrier disruption, neuroinflammation, neuronal death, and acute neurobehavioral abnormalities. Mechanistically, NET accumulation was associated with enhanced astrocyte pyroptosis via activation of the NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3)-caspase-1-gasdermin D (GSDMD) pathway. Activation of NLRP3 abolished the neuroprotective effects conferred by NET inhibition. Transcriptomic analysis of human hippocampal tissues identified cullin 7 (CUL7) as a sepsis-associated candidate, and subsequent experiments showed that its expression was restored following NET inhibition. CUL7 physically interacted with NLRP3, enhanced its ubiquitination, and reduced its protein stability, thereby restraining astrocyte pyroptosis. Notably, CUL7 overexpression improved acute neurobehavioral outcomes, preserved blood-brain barrier integrity, and attenuated neuroinflammation in septic mice. Collectively, our findings identify a previously unrecognized NETs-CUL7-NLRP3 axis that governs astrocyte pyroptosis and contributes to the pathogenesis of SAE, highlighting CUL7 as a potential therapeutic target.
authors: Sun Y, Cheng J, Chen X, Wu H, Xiao Z.

title: Asynchronous functional recovery and structural reconfiguration of water-sediment networks in an actively restored lake.
abstract: Internal nutrient loading often constrain the recovery of shallow eutrophic urban lakes. While temporal lags between water and sediment recovery are recognized, how active restoration reshapes their structural relationships remains poorly understood. We conducted a one-year in situ restoration experiment in Nanhu Lake (Wuhan, China) using 6 ha-scale ecological enclosures (two replicate enclosures per treatment) to evaluate a gradient of restoration treatments: a baseline ecological restoration (ER; submerged macrophytes (Vallisneria natans), microbial flocculants, and algaecides), phosphorus retention treatment (PR; ER + lanthanum-modified bentonite), and nitrogen-phosphorus reduction treatment (NPR; PR + high-efficiency nitrogen removal materials). Compared with the same season before restoration, water-column conditions changed rapidly across all treatments, with significantly higher dissolved oxygen and lower total phosphorus and chemical oxygen demand, although chlorophyll a and NH4+-N also increased. In contrast, sediment responses lagged behind those of the water column. While most sediment physicochemical parameters remained unchanged after one year, sediment phosphorus-binding capacity increased, whereas total nitrogen and the potential DNRA rate decreased. No significant overall differences among the three restoration treatments were detected across the full sampling period. Furthermore, ecological network analysis identified fewer cross-compartment associations after restoration, suggesting reduced coordination between water-column and sediment dynamics, while water-column total nitrogen retained the highest closeness centrality in both periods. These findings highlight asynchronous water-sediment responses during the first year of restoration and support a phased management perspective that accounts for rapid water-column responses alongside slower sediment adjustment.
authors: Shi W, Zhou Z, Wei J, Zhang J, Lin G, Chen X, Yuan S, Zhao B, Zhang Q.

title: A new risk to food security: Co-transport, accumulation, and deterioration of nutritional quality mediated by surface charge of nanoplastics and flame retardants in the soil-crop system.
abstract: The pervasive coexistence of nanoplastics (NPs) and organophosphorus flame retardants (OPFRs) in agro-ecosystems poses direct threats to food security and environmental sustainability, yet the underlying synergistic toxicities remain largely unknown. This study explores how surface-charge properties may mediate the combined toxicity of carboxylated (PS-COOH) and aminated (PS-NH2) polystyrene NPs with the OPFR triethyl phosphate (TEP) in rye. Through integrated short-term hydroponics and full-life-cycle soil cultivation coupled with multi-dimensional analyses, we demonstrate that positively charged PS-NH2 exerts significantly greater toxicity than PS-COOH. Mechanistically, our results suggest that TEP may promote the formation of NP-containing complexes via van der Waals-type interactions, potentially serving as a carrier to enhance root uptake and translocation of PS-NH2 into grains. This synergistic-like response triggered severe oxidative stress (H2O2 levels 10-fold higher than control), disrupted metabolic homeostasis, and altered the rhizosphere microbiome, with elevated relative abundances of taxa such as Comamonadaceae under TEP-containing treatments. Transcriptomics revealed specific activation of phenylpropanoid biosynthesis and repression of ion transport and energy metabolism pathways. Consequently, the PS-NH2 + TEP co-exposure delayed heading by 22 days, reduced 1000-grain weight by 28.89%, slashed grain crude fat by 55.58%, and increased indigestible fiber by 62.67%. These findings underscore that NP surface charge is a critical determinant of phytotoxicity. The resultant cascade of physiological disruptions may compromise crop yield and nutritional integrity, creating plausible entry points for contaminants into the food chain and ultimately raising concerns for global food security and ecosystem resilience.
authors: Hu J, Xing N, Bao G, Yuan Y, Bao L, Sana S.

title: Hyperoside promotes ferroptosis in prostate cancer by modulation of tryptophan metabolism via flotillin-2 reduction.
abstract: BackgroundHyperoside (HYP), a flavonoid derived from Hypericum perforatum, has been demonstrated to effectively inhibit prostate cancer (PCa) both in vitro and in vivo. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying this effect remain to be elucidated.AimTo investigate the specific mechanisms by which HYP exerts its anti-PCa effects.MethodsWe identified HYP targets using small-molecule target prediction and molecular docking, validated by Western blotting, the cellular thermal shift assay and Microscale thermophoresis (MST). Downstream signaling was explored via RNA sequencing, Western blotting, and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). Tryptophan (TRP) metabolism was assessed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and Western blotting, whereas ferroptosis was evaluated by gene set enrichment analysis, biochemical assays, reactive oxygen species (ROS) measurement, and Western blotting. Rescue experiments using RO8191 and kynurenine (KYN), together with in vivo xenograft models, were used for validation.ResultsHYP interacted with flotillin-2 (FLOT2), downregulating its expression, thereby inhibiting Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) and Indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) expression, blocking the conversion of TRP to KYN, and weakening KYN-aryl hydrocarbon receptor feedback. HYP upregulated ACSL4 and downregulated glutathione peroxidase 4 and SLC7A11, resulting in lipid peroxidation, ROS accumulation, iron overload, and glutathione depletion. RO8191 or KYN reversed these effects. In vivo, HYP suppressed tumor growth, disrupted TRP metabolism, and induced ferroptosis.ConclusionBy interacting with FLOT2 and suppressing the STAT3/IDO1/TRP metabolism axis, HYP induces ferroptosis in PCa, thereby identifying a novel therapeutic axis for PCa and supporting the potential of HYP as a promising natural therapeutic candidate.
authors: Pan C, Gao Y, Jin Y, Wang X, Yin D, Yao L, Tan S.

title: Prevalence and spectrum of skin diseases in adults in China: a nationwide cross-sectional study.
abstract: BackgroundSkin diseases have been identified as a public health priority at the 78th World Health Assembly, with a call for strengthened national surveillance and evidence-based responses. However, in China, comprehensive national epidemiological data on the prevalence of skin diseases have been lacking. We aimed to bridge this data gap by conducting the China Skin Health study, a large-scale, population-based, cross-sectional study.MethodsIn this study, we used a multistage stratified cluster random sampling design to obtain a nationally representative sample of adults aged 18 years or older from diverse geographical regions of China. We collaborated with provincial centres for disease control and prevention to establish a survey team comprising public health workers and ten to 12 certified dermatologists in each of the five provinces selected for the study. Residents' committees disseminated study information through posters and WeChat groups to recruit participants, and data were collected at local community health centres. Standardised electronic questionnaires were administered by trained interviewers to collect information on demographic and other characteristics. Certified dermatologists examined sun-exposed areas (eg, scalp, face, neck, and extremities) in all participants, as well as unexposed areas reported as concerns by respondents, for common skin diseases spanning 12 categories and more than 60 specific conditions. Clinical diagnoses were made on the basis of observed skin manifestations. The total number of skin conditions was recorded for each participant, and the mean number of skin conditions was calculated. Point prevalence of skin diseases was defined as the proportion of participants with a dermatologist-confirmed diagnosis of any listed condition at the time of the survey. Sampling weights derived from the study sampling framework and the 2020 National Population Census were applied when calculating prevalence and conducting logistic regression analyses. The absolute number of dermatological cases nationwide was estimated by applying prevalence estimates to the 2020 Chinese census data.FindingsFrom July 1, 2022, to June 27, 2024, 153 593 participants completed the survey and were included in the analysis. The study population had a mean age of 48·5 years (SD 16·8), with 75 512 (49·2%) men and 78 081 (50·8%) women; 98 926 (64·4%) participants resided in urban areas. The age-standardised prevalence of skin diseases was 55·6% (95% CI 51·2-59·9), corresponding to an estimated 618 million (95% CI 567-666) affected adults in China, with a mean of 0·98 (SD 1·22) skin diseases per person. Prevalence increased with age, from 42·0% (95% CI 35·3-48·6) in those aged 18-29 years to 79·5% (75·8-83·1) in those aged 80 years or older (pInterpretationSkin diseases could affect more than half of Chinese adults. These findings highlight a substantial unmet need and should inform national priorities.FundingNational Key R&D Program of China, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences Innovation Fund for Medical Sciences, National Natural Science Foundation of China, and Non-profit Central Research Institute Fund of Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences.
authors: Li J, Jin H, Zhang Y, Zhou P, Hu Y, Zhang L, Jin G, Ding Y, Fu H, Wang Y, Wang G, Lv C, Jin D, Chen T, Nie J, Chen Y, Peng Q, Yang Y, Yu M, Wang H, Lu Y, Shan G, Lu Q.

title: Design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of diosgenin derivatives containing arylsulfonamide moieties as anti-osteosarcoma agents through modulation of the Hippo pathway.
abstract: Forty-two novel diosgenin derivatives were designed and synthesized, and their anti-osteosarcoma activities were systematically evaluated in vitro. Some of the compounds suppressed the proliferation of osteosarcoma cell lines MG-63, U-2 OS, and 143B in vitro. Among them, compound 5a displayed potent inhibitory activity against U-2 OS and 143B cells, with IC50 values of 2.32 μM and 2.38 μM, respectively. Further in vitro studies revealed that compound 5a could inhibit cell migration, suppress colony formation, and induce apoptosis in U-2 OS and 143B cells. Mechanistic studies indicated that compound 5a modulated the Hippo-YAP/TAZ signaling axis, as evidenced by increased YAP/TAZ phosphorylation, reduced nuclear accumulation of YAP/TAZ, decreased expression of downstream target genes, and suppressed TEAD transcriptional activity. YAP/TAZ overexpression further supported the involvement of the YAP/TAZ-TEAD axis in the action of compound 5a. Notably, pharmacokinetic characterization showed a plasma half-life of 5.53 h after intravenous administration, and compound 5a exhibited anti-osteosarcoma activity in murine models without obvious toxicity-related changes under the tested conditions. Importantly, compound 5a suppressed pulmonary metastasis in a mouse model, which represents a major clinical challenge in osteosarcoma treatment. These findings suggest that compound 5a is a promising candidate for further development in the treatment of osteosarcoma.
authors: Si XJ, Yan BH, Zhan XC, Chang JL, Sun XY, Lin GQ, Wang YJ, Yang YP, Feng CG.

title: Difenoconazole-based fungicide formulations interfere with the embryogenesis of the two aquatic vertebrate organisms Xenopus laevis and Danio rerio.
abstract: Amphibians are among the most threatened vertebrate groups worldwide, with more than 40% of amphibian species currently at risk. Besides habitat loss, pesticide exposure is considered a major driver of this decline. While herbicides such as glyphosate have been widely studied, the effects of fungicides - particularly triazoles - remain underexplored. Difenoconazole (DFZ) is one of the most commonly used triazole fungicides, characterized by environmental persistence. However, its impact on amphibian and fish embryonic development has not been systematically investigated. This study examined lethal and sublethal effects of two DFZ-containing formulations - Difcor® (Difcor; professional use) and COMPO® Duaxo Universal Pilz-frei (Compo; non-professional use) - on Xenopus laevis embryos. Embryos were exposed to environmentally relevant (0.01-1 mg a.i./L) and higher concentrations (10-100 mg a.i./L) for 14 days. Endpoints included mortality, morphology, cardiac and neural development, oxidative stress, gene expression, cell proliferation, and apoptosis. Both formulations caused concentration-dependent mortality with LC50 values of 12.34 mg a.i./L (Difcor) and 16.28 mg a.i./L (Compo). Sublethal effects occurred from 0.01 mg a.i./L, including reduced body length, smaller head and eye areas, pericardial edema, and altered heart rate and mobility. Difcor additionally impaired neural and cardiac development, reduced mhcα expression, and increased proliferation and apoptosis. Complementary analyses with the formulation Difcor in Danio rerio embryos confirmed concentration-dependent mortality and revealed sublethal morphological changes such as peracardial edema. Overall, DFZ-containing formulations exert pronounced lethal and sublethal effects in amphibian and fish embryos, highlighting the need to include amphibians and fish more systematically in the environmental risk assessment of triazole fungicides.
authors: Flach H, Kaminski F, Dietmann P, Köhler J, Weidinger G, Kühl SJ.

title: Myeloid integrin α9β1 deficiency protects alveolar bone by remodeling the immune microenvironment of periodontitis.
abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease initiated by microbial infection that can lead to periodontal tissue damage and alveolar bone resorption. Macrophages contribute to the regulation of periodontal inflammation and local tissue homeostasis, but the role of integrin α9β1 in these processes remains unclear. Here, we combined analysis of human gingival single-cell transcriptomic data, a mouse model of myeloid cell-specific conditional Itga9 deletion, in vitro experiments with bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMMs), and conditioned-medium experiments in gingival fibroblasts to investigate how α9β1 affects the immune microenvironment and bone destruction in periodontitis. ITGA9 was highly expressed in human gingival macrophages and was further upregulated in periodontitis. Itga9 deletion altered the basal transcriptional state of BMMs and their response to Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg), with reduced TNF production, downregulation of inflammation-related gene sets, and lower AKT and S6 phosphorylation following Pg stimulation. In vivo, myeloid Itga9 deletion reduced periodontal tissue damage and alveolar bone loss and was accompanied by changes in local immune cell composition and fibroblast-associated communication networks. Gene sets related to skeletal development, ossification, and extracellular matrix (ECM)-receptor interactions were positively enriched in fibroblasts. Further in vitro experiments showed that conditioned medium from Pg-stimulated KO BMMs was less inhibitory to gingival fibroblast mineralization than that from Pg-stimulated Het BMMs, as reflected by higher expression of mineralization-related genes, greater alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, and increased mineralized nodule formation. These findings suggest that myeloid integrin α9β1 contributes to the regulation of immune and stromal cell functions in periodontitis and that targeting this receptor may help reduce inflammation-associated bone destruction and support the mineralization potential of gingival fibroblasts.
authors: Xu S, Li W, Bai Z, Yang S, Zhu W, Li J, Xia J.

title: The dynamics of large biomolecular assemblies.
abstract: With recent advances in cryo-electron microscopy/cryo-electron tomography (cryoEM/cryoET), computational capabilities and machine learning, there has been an incredible increase in the speed of structure determination for large biomolecular assemblies. In order to connect these static descriptions with biological function, one needs reliable and accurate approaches to quantify the factors that regulate dynamics. For this, models that employ simplified energetics and/or coarse-grained representations have become indispensable tools for integrating structural insights, biochemical analyses and physical principles. Here we discuss examples where molecular simulations have provided a framework for understanding dynamics in assemblies of increasing size and complexity. We focus on three classes for which there have been notable advances in recent years: ribosomes, viral capsids and nuclear pore complexes. Each possesses unique physical attributes that have required distinct theoretical and computational strategies. Together, these studies provide a rich conceptual and technical foundation that can help shape our perspective on the machinery of the cell.
authors: Wanes G, Ding E, Onuchic JN, Whitford PC.

title: Evaluation of the DPPH<sup>⋅</sup> free radical scavenging activity of 236 marine microbial metabolites.
abstract: A total of 236 marine microbial metabolites were evaluated for their DPPH⋅ (1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazyl) radical scavenging activity. Initial assay showed that 27 compounds at 100 µM had radical scavenging activity in different degrees with RSA% values of 53.93-99.00%. Further testing revealed that 13 compounds had potent activity with IC50 values of 4.94-18.64 µM, including peniciphenalenin F (53), asperindopiperazine A (82), asperindopiperazine C (83), 2-deisoprenyl-neoechinulin A (84), dipodazine (85), 20 R,25S-preshamixanthone (100), phthalimidinic acid A (104), 2-hydroxyemodic acid (105), asperthecin (106), talamin A (120), 2-aminobenzamide (146), isodihydroauroglaucin (231), and flavoglaucin (232). Asperindopiperazine C (83), dipodazine (85), 2-hydroxyemodic acid (105), talamin A (120), isodihydroauroglaucin (231), and flavoglaucin (232) were six most active compounds with IC50 values of 4.94-9.86 µM, which were stronger than or equivalent to that of the control ascorbic acid (IC50: 9.56 µM). These identified compounds show promising in vitro radical-scavenging activity and warrant further investigation using complementary antioxidant assays and appropriate cellular or biological models.
authors: Liu Y, Liu S, Liu X, Sun C, Ha Y, Yi W, Qin L, Yong K, Chen M, Ma M, Song T, Kaleem S, Li Q, Zhang X, Lian XY, Zhang Z.

title: Type III CI factors from wAlbB induce cytoplasmic incompatibility via a Host Modification mechanism.
abstract: The widespread prevalence of the endosymbiotic bacterium Wolbachia among insect species relies on its ability to invade and manipulate host reproduction via several ways, among which cytoplasmic incompatibility (CI) is most studied. Two non-mutually exclusive models, the Host-Modification (HM) and the Toxin-Antidote (TA), have been proposed to explain the molecular basis of CI. Here, we investigate the CI-inducing activity of the Type III CI factors (cifs) from wAlbB, a strain currently being deployed to combat mosquito-borne diseases. This set of Cifs displays conserved subcellular localization dynamics in various insect cells. Both cifA and cifB are required for the induction of DNA damage in cultured cells, and transgenic Drosophila. Moreover, these cifs induce CI in Drosophila through the two-by-one manner, meaning cifA and cifB act together during spermatogenesis to induce CI, and maternal cifA can reverse the effect. Mechanistically, genetic, biochemical, cellular, and proteomic analyses reveal that this pair of cifs acts during the early stage of spermatogenesis but is dispensable in late-stage germline cells for CI induction. Collectively, our findings support the notion that wAlbB Type III cifs induce CI via a HM-based mechanism. Additional analyses suggest that different Wolbachia strains may employ distinct molecular mechanisms to induce CI.
authors: Hou X, Goh FG, Liu S, Liu Y, Yong XE, Lin Q, Cai Y.

title: Transcriptomic age acceleration is associated with plasmablast-related immune remodeling in IgG4-related disease.
abstract: Biological aging profoundly influences immune function, yet its role in shaping immune remodeling within chronically inflamed tissues remains unclear. We investigated whether transcriptomic age identifies a plasmablast-associated immune aging pattern in IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD). To address this question, bulk RNA sequencing was performed on submandibular gland lesions from 49 patients with IgG4-RD and 3 controls. Transcriptomic age (tAge) was estimated using a transcriptome-based aging model, and age acceleration was calculated as the residual from chronological age. Associations between age acceleration, immune transcriptional modules, and clinical characteristics were evaluated using Spearman correlation analyses. Transcriptomic age correlated with chronological age (ρ = 0.473, P< 0.001), whereas age acceleration was associated with serum IgG4 concentrations (ρ = 0.446, P = 0.001). Among immune transcriptional modules, the plasmablast signature showed the strongest positive association with age acceleration (ρ = 0.312, nominal P = 0.029), although this association did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons (FDR-adjusted P = 0.304). Germinal center B-cell and activated B-cell programs showed inverse trends. The plasmablast module also correlated with serum IgG4 levels. Together, these exploratory findings suggest a coordinated pattern linking transcriptomic age acceleration, plasmablast enrichment, and enhanced IgG4 responses. Rather than establishing a mechanistic pathway, these findings identify a candidate plasmablast-associated immune aging pattern that warrants validation in independent cohorts.
authors: Yamamoto M, Kamekura R, Uehara M, Ichii Y, Takano K.

title: Navigating the phase-dependent m⁶A landscape in chronic wounds: engineering biomaterials for stage-matched intervention and durable repair.
abstract: Durable healing of chronic wounds requires coordinated control of inflammation, vascular repair, and matrix remodeling. N⁶-methyladenosine (m⁶A) RNA methylation is a candidate layer of post-transcriptional regulation in these processes, but its effects are cell-, target-, phase-, and disease-context dependent. The current direct evidence is concentrated in diabetic wound models, where distinct m⁶A-associated mechanisms have been reported in keratinocytes, endothelial cells, macrophages, and fibroblasts. These findings do not support a uniform systemic intervention. Instead, they motivate the testable question of whether local, time-limited delivery can achieve target engagement without disrupting repair in other cell compartments. This review synthesizes the evidence by wound phase and etiology, distinguishes direct wound studies from biological analogies, and evaluates biomaterial functions required for local exposure, controlled release, and durable-repair assessment. We emphasize the remaining gaps in human-relevant validation, pharmacokinetics, manufacturing, and long-term safety.
authors: Yin X, Liu J, Li H, Zhang C, Fan L, Wang K, Sun S.

title: Environmental monitoring of the Lagoon of Lake Patria in South Tyrrhenian sea, Italy.
abstract: The ecosystem health state of one of the most important lagoons in south Italy, Lake Patria, on the Tyrrhenian Sea was studied. Thirty-one superficial sediment sites were monitored and analyzed for bathymetric conditions, granulometry, morphoscopy, total organic carbon, benthic foraminifera, ostracod and macrofauna assemblages, microbiology and eco-toxicological features, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon loads. The survey revealed that lagoon depth was quite variable with a range from -1 to over -20 m and sediment were classified as medium sand seaward, very coarse sand in the northern sector, and fine or very fine gravel. Fecal coliform and Fecal Enterococci were absent, whereas sulfite reducing Clostridia levels were minimally detected and only at discrete locations, likely due to chemical pollution. Meiobenthic abundance and diversity indices highlighted oligotypic conditions with dominance of species tolerant to salinity and anoxic fluctuations and no substantial biodiversity difference respect to historical data. Macrobenthos survey showed a substantial decreasing of taxa respect to historic survey with only dead bivalves or presence of just one living gastropod species, Ecrobia ventrosa, likely due to anoxia and/or pollution conditions. Significant hot spots of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons surpassing the legal limits up to threefold were determined near wastewater delivering canals.

title: CauYL, encoding a magnesium chelatase H subunit, is required for chlorophyll accumulation and normal leaf coloration in cauliflower.
abstract: Key messageFine mapping and CRISPR/Cas9 validation identified CauYL(BOB03G201420), encoding the H subunit of magnesium chelatase, as the causal gene for the yellow-green leaf phenotype in cauliflower. As the primary photosynthetic pigment in plants, chlorophyll captures light energy to drive photosynthesis and regulate plant growth. In addition, it confers green coloration to plants by absorbing blue and red light wavelengths. Despite the important role of chlorophyll in vegetables, the genetic regulation of chlorophyll accumulation in cauliflower remains largely unknown. In this study, we identified a cauliflower mutant "K-6" from an ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) mutagenized population, that displayed a stable yellow-green phenotype. The mutant showed much lower chlorophyll contents and decreased photosynthetic rate compared with the WT plants. Genetic inheritance analysis revealed that this yellow-green trait was controlled by a recessive gene. The target gene, designated CauYL, was mapped to an approximately 103.07 kb region on chromosome 3, based on BSA-seq and traditional linkage analyses. We identified a candidate gene BOB03G201420 encoding the H subunit of magnesium chelatase. Sequence analysis revealed a non-synonymous single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) within the coding sequence, resulting in an alanine-to-threonine substitution at a highly conserved residue. We employed CRISPR/Cas9 to knockout the CauYL gene in the WT background, and successfully generated CauYL mutants, which showed a yellow-green trait resembling that of the K-6 mutant. Transcriptome analysis showed that differentially expressed genes between K-6 and WT were significantly enriched in photosynthesis, riboflavin metabolism, and related pathways. Collectively, our results demonstrate that the CauYL gene is essential for maintaining the green coloration and photosynthetic competence of cauliflower, providing a valuable genetic target for improving photosynthetic efficiency and leaf color traits in cauliflower breeding.
journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
authors: Huang W, Cui J, Wen Z, Wu Y, Shan X, Sun D, Han F, Zhang X.

title: Does pre-treatment with doxycycline improve the efficacy of combination minocycline and metronidazole for macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma genitalium infections?
abstract: Antimicrobial options for Mycoplasma genitalium are limited. Our prior study found a 14-day regimen of minocycline and metronidazole (minocycline + metronidazole) achieved microbial cure in 76.7% (n = 56/73, 95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 65.4%-85.8%) of macrolide-resistant infections, with an efficacy of 90.3% (n = 28/31, 95% CI: 74.2%-98.0%) if preceded by 7 days of doxycycline. We aimed to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of sequential doxycycline and 14 days of minocycline + metronidazole in a larger cohort. Microbial cure was defined as a negative test-of-cure using transcription-mediated amplification 14-90 days after completing minocycline + metronidazole. The proportion cured and 95% CIs were calculated, and univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to examine factors associated with cure. Adverse effect data were collated. Overall, microbial cure following minocycline + metronidazole was 80.9% (n = 212/262, 95% CI: 75.6%-85.5%). Microbial cure was similar among 181 patients who received doxycycline pre-treatment (82.3%, 95% CI: 76.0%-87.6%) compared with 81 patients without pre-treatment (77.8%, 95% CI: 67.1%-86.3%, P = 0.387); individuals who had failed prior regimens were more likely to experience cure with doxycycline pre-treatment. A higher proportion of cervicovaginal infections were cured following minocycline + metronidazole compared to urethral infections. Gastrointestinal and central nervous system adverse effects were not significantly increased with the addition of doxycycline. In this larger data set, doxycycline pre-treatment did not significantly enhance the efficacy of minocycline + metronidazole. In our setting, cure following minocycline + metronidazole was comparable to cure following moxifloxacin, but this generic regimen is more widely accessible and cures 80% of M. genitalium infections with dual-class resistance. The regimen's higher efficacy for cervicovaginal infections may reflect a sex-effect and/or its additional influence on vaginal dysbiosis.
authors: Htaik K, Vodstrcil LA, Plummer EL, Matthews LG, Aguirre I, Kong FYS, Bradshaw CS.

title: Comparison of self-sampling versus clinician-sampling HPV DNA cervical cancer screening in South African women living with and without HIV.
abstract: IntroductionHuman papilloma virus (HPV) testing is the preferred primary screening method for cervical cancer, and HPV self-sampling has the potential to improve screening uptake. We compared the test performance and agreement of self- and clinician-sampling HPV in women living with HIV (WLWH) and HIV-negative women in Gauteng and Western Cape Province, South Africa.MethodsCervical cancer screening was performed in previously unscreened women using cytology, self- and clinician-collected HPV (Hybrid Capture 2 assay). Screen-positive participants underwent colposcopy and biopsy, and a random sample of negative screens had punch biopsy regardless of colposcopy findings. Performances of screening tests were evaluated against histology results adjusted for verification bias. The kappa statistic for HPV concordance between self- and clinician-collected HPV was also calculated.ResultsIncluded for analysis were 903 women with a mean age of 41.5 years, of which 43.3% were WLWH. In WLWH/HIV-negative women, the sensitivity of self-sampling HPV was 74.7%/67.4% and of clinician-sampling HPV was 77.1%/59.2% to detect cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade3+, whereas the specificity for clinician-sampling HPV was 75.0%/86.8% compared with 70.3%/79.8% for self-sampling HPV to detect CIN2+. In both HIV groups, Cohen's kappa agreement between the two sampling methods was good (0.63 and 0.62, respectively).ConclusionSelf-collected HPV sampling is an acceptable and viable option for primary cervical cancer screening in all women given the superior sensitivity to cytology. The statistically significant difference in HPV test performance among HIV-negative women according to sampling method confirms the benefit of a further triage test when self-sampling is used for HPV-base cervical screening, especially in HIV-negative women.
journal: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
authors: Snyman LC, Visser C, Dreyer GJ, Lukhwareni A, van der Merwe FH, Botha MH, Richter K, Dreyer G.

title: Bictegravir/Lenacapavir: A 2-Drug Regimen for the Treatment of HIV-1 Infection.
abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the efficacy and safety of bictegravir/lenacapavir for the treatment of HIV-1 infection.Data sourcesA literature search was conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar (January 2016-August 2026) using the search terms bictegravir and lenacapavir. Other data sources included abstracts presented at recent conferences and the prescribing information.Study selection and data extractionAll English-language studies assessing the efficacy and safety of bictegravir/lenacapavir for the treatment of HIV-1 infection were considered for inclusion.Data synthesisBictegravir is an established second-generation integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), whereas lenacapavir is a novel capsid inhibitor. Both antiretrovirals are highly active against HIV-1. Bictegravir/lenacapavir 75 mg/50 mg was shown to be safe and effective in two phase 3 clinical trials after switching from complex antiretroviral therapy (ART) or bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. The Food and Drug Administration approved this combination for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults who are virologically suppressed on stable ART with no resistance to the individual components. It is available as a single-tablet regimen (STR) taken orally once daily.Relevance to Patient Care and Clinical Practice in Comparison With Existing Drugs:Bictegravir/lenacapvir is the first INSTI-capsid inhibitor 2-drug STR indicated for the treatment of HIV-1 infection. The combination could be useful for patients who want to simplify their regimen and/or those who cannot use a nucleos(t)ide or a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor. It is not active against hepatitis B virus coinfection.ConclusionsBictegravir/lenacapvir is safe and efficacious as a 2-drug regimen for the treatment of adults with HIV-1 infection.
authors: Chahine EB, Faragon JJ, Patel N, Sherman EM.

title: The Microbiome-Arginine-Immune Axis in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Metabolic Competition and Therapeutic Opportunities.
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is strongly influenced by metabolic and immune dysregulation. Recent evidence highlights the role of L-arginine metabolism and arginase isoforms (ARG1/ARG2) in tumour progression, immune suppression, and metabolic reprogramming. This narrative review integrates published evidence with an independent bioinformatic reanalysis of publicly available transcriptomic and immune infiltration datasets to examine arginase signalling in oral squamous cell carcinoma and to explore how oral dysbiosis may contribute to extracellular arginine depletion and tumour-promoting immune dysfunction. These findings support the microbiome-arginine-immune axis as a promising framework for future biomarker development and metabolism-based therapeutic strategies in OSCC.
authors: Ramachandran P, Gopalakrishnan R, Gunasekaran R, Kannan K, Ganapathy D, Pitchiah S.
