title: Orange-pigmented Paracoccus marcusii, symbiotic with the coral Favites sp., shows antibacterial properties against multidrug-resistant (MDR) clinical samples.
abstract: The increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria presents a critical challenge in clinical settings, prompting the search for novel antibacterial agents. Orange-pigmented marine bacteria, strain NOE18, were isolated from coral Favites sp. on Kartini Beach, Jepara, Central Java, Indonesia, and cultured in the laboratory. The aim of this research includes molecular identification of strain NOE18, extracting orange pigment from strain NOE18, and investigating the antibacterial efficacy of orange-pigmented NOE18 against MDR clinical isolates. Strain NOE18 was identified as Paracoccus marcusii based on 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis. Its orange pigment was extracted using methanol and methanol:acetone (7:3), characterised by LC-HRMS, and evaluated for antibacterial activity against multidrug-resistant (MDR) clinical isolates using the microdilution method. The pigment exhibited antibacterial activity against all tested MDR isolates, with minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) values of ≥25 mg/mL and ≥50 mg/mL, respectively. LC-HRMS analysis identified canthaxanthin, adonirubin, and 3-hydroxy-3'-oxo-β,ε-carotene as the dominant carotenoids, which are likely responsible for the observed antibacterial activity. The findings suggest that Paracoccus marcusii, as a symbiont of Favites sp., possesses notable antibacterial properties against MDR pathogens. This underscores the potential of marine-derived bacteria as sources for developing new antimicrobial agents. Further investigation is needed to evaluate the mechanisms of action of specific compounds.
authors: Evy Prastiyanto M, Khairunnisa A, Wathon MH, Kusmita L, Sabdaningsih A, Rukmana RM, Putri WA.

title: The TBK1-OTUB2-IRF3 signalling complex promotes neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.
abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway-mediated chronic inflammation drives neurodegeneration in natural aging and various neurodegenerative diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Here, we identify Otubain-2 (OTUB2) as a pivotal regulator that orchestrates the STING signalosome to amplify inflammatory responses. The function of OTUB2 in neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration was investigated through genetic deletion and pharmacological inhibition of OTUB2 in hTARDBP transgenic mice​, adeno-associated virus-mediated TDP43 overexpression mice, and aged mice. Biochemical assays were performed to dissect underlying molecular mechanisms. OTUB2 inhibited K63 ubiquitination of TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), thereby suppressing TBK1 kinase activity and promoting cell death mediated by hyperactivated receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1). Additionally, OTUB2 functioned as a scaffold facilitating assembly of the TBK1-interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) signalling complex, a prerequisite for IRF3 phosphorylation, and enhanced IRF3 dimerization by reducing its K11 ubiquitination. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of OTUB2 significantly ameliorated neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration in both ALS and aged mouse models. This study establishes OTUB2 as a critical regulator of cGAS-STING signalling and a potential therapeutic target for neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.
authors: Zhang J, Wang D, Chen J, Lu Y, Deng D, Xu B, Xu Y, Jin K, Xu J, Liu B, Ruan J, Wang X.

title: Integrative drug discovery for Parkinson’s disease with DIMER
abstract: Translating Parkinson’s disease (PD) genetics into therapeutic candidates requires approaches that account for interconnected disease mechanisms and their cellular context. Here we present DIMER (  D irect and  I ndirect  M odule  E valuation for  R epurposing and screening), a framework that connects network-based drug repurposing and target-directed virtual screening through shared disease-associated gene sets. Applying DIMER to PD, we integrated genetic risk and mechanism-associated gene sets with drug-target interactions, disease transcriptomes, and single nucleus expression profiles. Network analysis identified 423 repurposing candidates, with 71% of qualifying drug-gene set associations arising through targets outside the corresponding disease gene set. Transcriptional reversal analysis and cell type-resolved networks further distinguished candidates by their predicted effects on disease-associated expression and their cellular context, while target-set separation nominated potentially complementary drug combinations. For target-directed virtual screening, DIMER adapted a pretrained compound-protein interaction model to screening library chemistry and incorporated known-ligand similarity into compound ranking. Library adaptation improved compound-target pair classification performance, whereas ligand-informed ranking increased early enrichment of known active compounds. Consensus screening of 1.82 million compounds against seven PD-associated proteins yielded a shortlist of 22 compounds supported by at least five ranking runs. In a complementary experimental evaluation, four repurposing candidates (polydatin, fedratinib, sorafenib and venlafaxine) attenuated the loss of dopamine neuron marker signals in human midbrain organoids exposed to 6-hydroxydopamine. Together, these findings establish DIMER as a framework for translating disease-associated genes into pharmacological hypotheses and prioritizing candidates for experimental testing.
authors: Guo S, Yang X, Dong Y, Yu L, Sangjizhuoma A, Sie KL, Zhu K, Zhang Y, Zhao X, Kerman E, Li R, He J.

title: Keratin 17 Defines an Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition-Associated Migratory Cell State in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by early invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance that contribute substantially to its poor clinical outcome. Keratin 17 (K17) is a recognized marker of the aggressive basal-like subtype of PDAC and an independent predictor of adverse prognosis; however, the biological basis for this association remains incompletely understood. To define K17-associated cellular programs, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from 42 patients, Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) proteomic data from 140 tumors, MACSima multiplex spatial imaging of 63 patients, dual-plex immunohistochemistry of 60 cases, and three-dimensional spheroid migration assays. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis demonstrated significant enrichment of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-associated gene programs among K17-positive malignant epithelial cells. Consistent with this finding, K17-positive tumors in the CPTAC cohort exhibited enrichment of the Hallmark EMT pathway at the protein level. Among six candidate markers identified through transcriptomic analyses, laminin subunit gamma-2 (LAMC2) was the only candidate associated with K17 at every validation step. Tumors positive for both K17 and LAMC2 had significantly worse overall survival than double-negative tumors (adjusted hazard ratio = 2.53). Multiplex spatial imaging localized K17-positive cells predominantly to poorly differentiated tumor regions and demonstrated frequent single-cell co-expression with LAMC2. Whole-slide dual-plex immunohistochemistry further confirmed the association between K17 and LAMC2 and showed progressive enrichment of K17/LAMC2-positive tumor cells with increasing intratumoral histologic grade. Functionally, gain- and loss-of-function studies in three-dimensional PDAC spheroids demonstrated that K17 promotes migratory outgrowth, and differences in proliferation did not account for this effect. Collectively, these findings identify K17 as a marker of a poorly differentiated, EMT-associated migratory cell state in PDAC and provide functional evidence that K17 contributes to tumor-cell migration.
authors: Sarkar S, Ghosh M, Delgado-Coka L, Powers S, Sathian R, Davuluri R, Gong X, Mak M, Villar J, Qi X, Babu S, Marchenko N, Shroyer KR.

title: Activated ADAM10-targeting antibody 1H5 suppresses NOTCH-driven glioma progenitors
abstract: ABSTRACT  Background  High-grade gliomas (HGGs) remain associated with high morbidity, mortality, and invariable recurrence after neurosurgical resection and chemoradiation. A major contributor to treatment failure is a population of stem-like glioma progenitor cells (GPCs) that depend on NOTCH-signaling for self-renewal and survival; clinical attempts to inhibit NOTCH with γ-secretase inhibitors failed due to systemic toxicity. Methods  Here, we investigate the anti-HGG therapeutic potential of a fully-human monoclonal antibody, 1H5, that selectively targets activated-ADAM10, an α-secretase required for NOTCH receptor processing, with high tumor specificity. We show that ADAM10 is markedly overexpressed and highly activated in primary and recurrent HGGs, using patient tissue, RNA-sequencing data, and early-passage HGG cell lines. Results  Across a panel of patient-derived HGG lines, sensitivity to 1H5 correlates with the cell-surface levels of activated-ADAM10, and shRNA-mediated ADAM10 knockdown recapitulates the growth-inhibitory effects of 1H5. ADAM10 inhibition suppresses NOTCH-pathway components and target genes, reduces expression of GPC markers, and impairs neurosphere formation while depleting Sox2- and Ki67-positive cells. We further find that 1H5 induces HGG cell death predominantly via necroptosis, characterized by survivin loss and increased phosphorylated MLKL and by transcriptional changes in necroptosis-related genes. In three-dimensional explants derived from primary HGG, 1H5 reduces growth and GPC marker expression while increasing TUNEL staining. Finally, convection-enhanced delivery of 1H5 in orthotopic xenograft models achieves high local intracranial concentrations, slows tumor growth, and prolongs survival, with regional pharmacodynamic effects consistent with NOTCH pathway suppression and necroptosis. Conclusions  These data support ADAM10-targeting 1H5 as a candidate for further preclinical development in HGG.
authors: Tosi U, Ghita G, Saha N, Mrad ZA, Giantini-Larsen A, Yu K, Jungverdorben J, Nikolov DB, Tabar V, Yang Y.

title: Vault Packaging Dynamics: Cargo Loading Stabilizes MVP Conformation for High-Payload Cytokine Delivery in Cancer Therapy
abstract: Summary  Recombinant vaults are dynamic protein cages with a large interior volume that can encapsulate therapeutic cargo. Using integrative cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM), cryogenic electron tomography (cryoET) and charge-detection mass spectrometry (CDMS), we characterized recombinant empty and interleukin-2 (IL-2)–packaged human vaults produced in yeast to define assembly, packaging heterogeneity and conformational dynamics relevant to optimized cancer and immune therapeutics. CryoEM maps at 2.79 Å (packaged) and 3.16 Å (empty) reveal a D39-symmetric barrel built from 78 major vault protein (MVP) subunits each with an interaction domain (INT) that anchors a cargo on the inner surface at MVP repeats R3– R4. CDMS deconvolution of empty versus packaged particles yields two IL-2–INT vault populations centered near 100 and 400 molecules per vault, with a maximum of ∼660 copies/vault (i.e., many more copies than the 78 available INT anchors), matching cryoET estimates of ∼150–600. Both methods show that highly packaged vaults are enlarged and distorted. Empty particles are conformationally flexible, which promotes initial cargo entry; loading then stabilizes the barrel and condenses cargo, producing vaults that each contain many hundreds of IL-2 molecules. These data establish the structural basis of vault encapsulation and a quantitative framework for engineering vault-based delivery vehicles.

title: Transcriptomic similarity guides source selection beyond tissue lineage
abstract: Perturbational and pharmacogenomic maps remain incomplete across cellular contexts, leaving a practical source-selection question before response prediction: which measured context should inform an unmeasured target? We tested whether baseline transcriptomic similarity ranks candidate sources for held-out targets, separating source ranking from aggregation and transfer-uncertainty decisions. Similarity tracked matched-response concordance in LINCS and GSE306429; selected-source utility exceeded random expectation in GSE306429 (ΔU = 0.034; P = 0.002) and in exact-time-matched MIX-Seq tasks (ΔU = 0.046). In the full GDSC2 analysis, the drug-balanced ranking effect was 0.359 (95% CI, 0.337–0.383). In a lineage-restricted analysis of the same eligible subset, within-tissue ranking remained positive at 0.130 (95% CI, 0.119–0.141), retaining 35.8% of the same-subset global effect (0.363; 95% CI, 0.342–0.386). Global transcriptomic top-1 selection exceeded tissue-matched random selection by 0.154 (95% CI, 0.143–0.164). Thus, baseline similarity adds source-ranking information after tissue matching in the evaluated setting, while ranking alone does not resolve whether to aggregate sources or how to quantify transfer uncertainty.
authors: Jiang L, Pang J, Luo B, Wu X, Li X, Zhang H.

title: Efficient translation of chaperones by eIF5A safeguards proteostasis under heat stress
abstract: ABSTRACT  The increase in global temperature poses a major threat to cells and organisms because it disrupts cellular proteostasis. We discovered that the evolutionarily conserved and essential translation elongation factor eIF5A is necessary for a rapid response to heat-stress in yeast cells. Lack of eIF5A results in ribosome stalling on heat-stress-induced mRNAs, reducing the synthesis of chaperones, primarily impacting those that undergo robust synthesis via high codon optimality, such as Hsp70 Ssa1 and Hsp12 chaperones. This new eIF5A role in translation appears to be direct, as eIF5A binds preferentially to induced mRNAs with high codon optimality and its polysome association increases under heat-shock. Low levels of Hsp70 in eIF5A mutants delay Hsf1 feedback inhibition during stress adaptation and cause the accumulation of protein aggregates, resulting in low cellular viability to heat-stress. Overall, our results show that eIF5A is crucial for heat-stress resistance by facilitating rapid and efficient translation of high codon-optimal chaperones. Therefore, eIF5A emerges as a key regulator of cellular proteostasis, providing a novel perspective on its significant involvement in neurodegenerative diseases and aging.
authors: Bernal V, Chi L, Prieto-Diez S, Segui J, Barba-Aliaga M, Alepuz P.

title: A five-gene risk model based on carnitine-related genes for predicting prognosis in ovarian cancer
abstract: Abstract    Background:  Ovarian cancer (OV) remains a highly lethal gynecological malignancy and is associated with unfavorable long-term outcomes. Carnitine participates in metabolic adaptation of tumor cells by modulating fatty acid oxidation and redox balance. This study sought to identify carnitine-associated prognostic biomarkers in OV and to characterize the molecular features linked to these markers.  Methods:  Publicly available datasets were used throughout the study. Candidate biomarkers were progressively selected through weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), differential-expression analysis, regression-based screening, and machine-learning procedures. The selected genes were incorporated into a prognostic risk model, after which patients with OV were assigned to a high-risk group (HRG) or low-risk group (LRG) according to their calculated risk scores. Functional enrichment, immune-infiltration, and drug-sensitivity analyses were subsequently conducted to characterize biological differences associated with risk status. Biomarker expression was further examined using single-cell transcriptomic data to prioritize relevant cell populations.  Results:  The multistage selection procedure yielded five biomarkers: ALPL, RAB38, SLC4A8, ZMAT4, and IGLON5. Using these genes, the risk model separated patients into the HRG and LRG, with inferior survival observed in the HRG. Across the five biomarkers, 14 shared signaling pathways were identified, among them "Apoptosis", "Hedgehog signaling pathway", and "Ribosome". Scores for 21 immune-cell populations also differed significantly between the two risk categories. Drug-response prediction identified significant between-group differences in the half-maximal inhibitory concentration values of 73 compounds; several agents, including GSK1904529A and ML323, had lower predicted IC₅₀ values in the HRG. Single-cell analysis resolved five cell types and prioritized epithelial cells as the candidate key population.  Conclusion:  The five genes ALPL, RAB38, SLC4A8, ZMAT4, and IGLON5 were identified as candidate prognostic biomarkers for OV. Their expression was linked to carnitine-associated metabolic characteristics and immune features, supporting further experimental investigation and prospective evaluation of their prognostic value.
authors: Liu L, Liu X, Luo P, Fu X, Ding Y, Li F, Wu Y, Zhang Y.

title: Multi-Objective Thermo-Mechanical Topology Optimization of Lightweight Structures for Structural Stiffness, Thermal Performance, and Dynamic Characteristics
abstract: Abstract    This study presents a multi-objective topology optimization framework for lightweight thermo-mechanical structures subjected to simultaneous mechanical, thermal, and dynamic requirements. A two-dimensional simply supported structure is modeled using a structured quadrilateral finite element mesh comprising 4,800 Q4 elements and 4,961 nodes. The material distribution is parameterized using the Solid Isotropic Material with Penalization (SIMP) approach with a penalization factor of 3.0 and a prescribed volume fraction of 40%. Three coupled performance criteria are considered: structural compliance, total heat transfer, and fundamental natural frequency. Thermal, structural, and modal finite element analyses are sequentially performed for each candidate topology within a multi-objective evolutionary optimization procedure. The optimized configuration preserves the prescribed material volume and total mass of 31.20 kg while redistributing material toward mechanically and dynamically efficient regions. The results show a reduction in structural compliance from 8.70646×10  − 2  to 8.65559×10  − 2  , corresponding to a 0.584% improvement. The fundamental natural frequency increases from 145.63 to 148.24 Hz, representing a 1.793% improvement, while the second and third natural frequencies reach 295.03 and 555.69 Hz, respectively. Total heat transfer changes only marginally from 43.2021 to 43.2368 W, corresponding to a 0.0804% increase. The final optimized structure exhibits a maximum displacement of 4.6663×10  − 4  m, maximum von Mises stress of 1.0372×10  5  Pa, mean von Mises stress of 1.3848×10  4  Pa, and maximum heat flux of 421.08 W/m². The results demonstrate that coupled topology optimization can improve structural stiffness and dynamic performance while maintaining a fixed material budget and nearly unchanged thermal behavior. The proposed framework provides a computationally efficient basis for the design of lightweight structures requiring simultaneous mechanical, thermal, and vibration performance.
authors: Idan MF.

title: Alpha- and Gamma-Synuclein Proteins Define Complementary Metabolic and Invasive Programs in Melanoma Development, Progression, and Prognosis
abstract: Abstract  Melanoma, a highly aggressive skin cancer, remains a major clinical challenge due to its metastatic capacity and resistance to therapy. Synuclein proteins — alpha-synuclein (αS) and gamma-synuclein (γS), traditionally studied in neurodegeneration — are increasingly recognized as contributors to melanoma progression, yet whether they define distinct tumor cell states or act through shared mechanisms remains unclear. Here, we show that SNCA and SNCG are robustly anti-correlated across independent transcriptomic and proteomic cohorts and at single-cell resolution, marking two complementary malignant cell states. Both synucleins support melanoma proliferation, migration, and invasion, and are internalized by melanoma cells in a prion-like manner that enhances tumor growth in vitro and in vivo. Functionally, however, αS and γS diverge along distinct axes. αS is transcriptionally coupled to a MITF-linked mitochondrial program and functionally sensitizes complex I: its silencing improves mitochondrial bioenergetics and blunts the response to a second respiratory challenge, while exogenous fibrils impair it, alongside a corresponding shift in pigmentation. γS instead sustains an integrin-FAK-Rac1-MAPK signaling axis and β-catenin regulation that drives invasive behavior; its silencing reduces MAPK output and confers cross-resistance to three mechanistically distinct therapeutic agents — cisplatin, vemurafenib, and paclitaxel. These opposing programs converge on a shared differentiation axis: SNCG-high cells define a dedifferentiated, MITF-low, invasive malignant subpopulation that is independently associated with shorter progression-free interval in stage IIC melanoma. Collectively, these findings establish αS and γS as functionally distinct, mechanistically convergent regulators of a metabolic-versus-invasive cell-state dichotomy in melanoma, nominate SNCG as a candidate prognostic biomarker, and identify complex I sensitization and FAK/MAPK signaling as candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities.
authors: Marquez MM, Malizia F, Zanotti L, Mian M, Ponce PM, Mamberto M, Avila A, Laluce NC, Farré C, Binolfi A, Bustelo X, Anselmino L.

title: COVID-19 and male infertility - A review
abstract: Abstract  Background:  Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), caused by SARS-CoV-2, is a systemic illness capable of influencing the male reproductive system through fever, inflammation, oxidative stress, vascular injury and endocrine disturbance. Because spermatogenesis is temperature-sensitive and spermatozoa are vulnerable to oxidative damage, semen quality may be altered during acute infection and early recovery. Objective: This systematic review evaluates the association between COVID-19 and male reproductive function, with a focus on conventional semen parameters, sperm DNA fragmentation and oxidative stress, reproductive hormones, SARS-CoV-2 detection in semen, and the time course of recovery. Methods: Published human studies of confirmed or previous SARS-CoV-2 infection were identified through structured searches of electronic literature sources. Eligible observational studies reported at least one male reproductive outcome, including semen quality, sperm functional integrity, reproductive hormones, or viral detection in semen/testicular material. Findings were synthesised qualitatively in accordance with PRISMA 2020 reporting principles (Page et al., 2021). Results: Across the available evidence, the clearest pattern is a short-term reduction in sperm concentration, total sperm count and motility after infection, although individual studies differ in magnitude and not all report persistent abnormalities. Longitudinal and pre/post-infection studies indicate improvement over subsequent months in many men (Guo et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2025). Sperm DNA fragmentation and seminal oxidative/inflammatory markers may also increase after COVID-19 (Hajizadeh Maleki and Tartibian, 2021; Yuan et al., 2025). Endocrine studies report transient reductions in testosterone or altered gonadotrophin relationships, particularly during symptomatic disease (Ma et al., 2021; Majzoub et al., 2024). SARS-CoV-2 RNA is rarely detected in semen; one early study reported positive samples, whereas most subsequent cohorts did not (Li et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2021). Conclusion: COVID-19 can act as a temporary reproductive stressor in men, particularly after symptomatic or febrile illness. Current evidence supports predominantly indirect mechanisms such as fever, inflammation, oxidative stress and endocrine disturbance, rather than persistent seminal infection. The evidence is insufficient to conclude that COVID-19 commonly causes permanent infertility. When semen results are abnormal soon after infection, repeat assessment after approximately one spermatogenic cycle may help distinguish transient suppression from persistent dysfunction.
authors: Suresh R, Kumar R.

title: PIN1-p53 bifurcation dictates opposite cell fate decisions in Alzheimer’s disease and glioblastoma via distinct energy landscape topologies
abstract: Abstract  Although Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and glioblastoma (GBM) share common aging-related risk factors, they lead to opposite cellular fates—neurodegeneration versus uncontrolled proliferation. The system-level mechanisms driving this striking divergence remain elusive. Here, we integrated single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic data from AD (84 donors) and GBM (18 samples) to comparatively map the energy landscape of cell fate decisions in these two diseases. By computing a PIN1-p53 Bifurcation Index and CellEnergy landscape, we reveal that AD and GBM diverge at a critical Bifurcation Point. AD cells descend from a Health Peak into a deep AD Valley, characterized by a senescent profile with PIN1 downregulation and p53 activation. In contrast, GBM cells settle on a flat, low-energy GBM Plateau, exhibiting a proliferative profile driven by PIN1 overexpression and p53 suppression. We further identified pioneer gene candidates at the Bifurcation Point, with MDM2 and PIN1 upregulated in AD, and BBC3 in GBM. Interpreted within the Hyper Solution Landscape (HSL) framework, these findings provide a biological explanation for the path-dependent nature of cell fate decisions and provide a mechanistic framework linking the PIN1-p53 axis to the inverse comorbidity between AD and cancer, suggesting that the PIN1-p53 axis acts as a critical decision node.
authors: Lyu J.

title: PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1 switch PlABI5-PlCesA6 function to regulate seed dormancy and germination in Paeonia lactiflora.
abstract: Seed dormancy is a key strategy for plants to adapt to fluctuating environments and ensure population propagation. Paeonia lactiflora seeds exhibit typical double dormancy, characterized by a prolonged germination cycle and low emergence rate that severely restrict their large-scale propagation. Although ABI5, the core transcription factor (TF) in the abscisic acid (ABA) signaling pathway, acts as a critical hub in maintaining seed dormancy, its upstream dynamic regulatory mechanism and downstream cell-wall-related target genes remain largely unknown. In this study, two upstream regulators of PlABI5, PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1, were identified via yeast one-hybrid screening, and their regulatory mechanism was characterized. The results showed that both PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1 belonged to the R2R3-MYB family. When acting alone, they directly bound to and activated the PlABI5 promoter, inhibiting seed germination. Upon forming a protein complex in the nucleus, their regulatory function was reversed and they repressed PlABI5 transcription to promote germination, supporting a proposed monomer activation-complex inhibition switch model. Furthermore, PlABI5 specifically targeted the PlCesA6 promoter and inhibited its expression without affecting the homolog PlCesA3. PlCesA6 positively regulated seed germination by promoting hypocotyl cell elongation, and its overexpression rescued the inhibition caused by PlMYB51/PlMYB1R1 overexpression. Collectively, this study proposes a working model for the PlMYB51/PlMYB1R1-PlABI5-PlCesA6 cascade in controlling seed dormancy and germination, and identifies a putative functional switching mode of MYB TFs mediated by protein-protein interactions. These findings provide key gene resources and a theoretical basis for artificial dormancy breaking and molecular breeding in P. lactiflora.
authors: Xin R, Zhou X, Guan S, Kang X, Song W, Wang Y, Wang S, Sun X.

title: MASLD Liver Transplant: Evolution of Frequency, Age Trends, and Factors Associated With Outcomes.
abstract: BackgroundMetabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has rapidly emerged as a leading indication for liver transplantation (LT) in the United States. There remains a need to understand the evolution of transplant volumes and recipient profiles and outcomes. In this study, we aim to analyze current MASLD LT trends to aid in identifying opportunities for this patient population.MethodsWe analyzed UNOS data for primary liver transplants (2010-2024), identifying MASLD by diagnosis codes and stratifying transplants into three eras (2010-2014, 2015-2019, and 2020-2024). Analyses included annual MASLD transplant counts and proportions, era-specific annual percent change, comparisons of donor, operative, and recipient characteristics, Kaplan-Meier curves, multivariable Cox regression for overall post-LT mortality, and competing-risk regression for waitlist outcomes.ResultsIn total, 18 153 MASLD LT recipients were included (Era 1: 2734; Era 2: 6127; Era 3: 9292). Annual MASLD LT volume increased from 461 in 2010 to 2090 in 2024. Annual percent change was +10.6% (Era 1), +20.1% (Era 2), and +5.9% (Era 3). In Era 3, recipients were as young as 8 y. Era 3 waitlist candidates had significantly higher likelihood of transplant (sHR 1.52; 95% CI, 1.46-1.58) and lower risk of waitlist mortality (sHR 0.44; 95% CI, 0.40-0.48). Recipient survival increased from 97.0% to 98.3% at 30 d, and 90.5% to 92.6% at 1 y (both P ConclusionsFrom 2010 to 2024, MASLD LT rose markedly but relative growth plateaued. Increasing age diversity, including pediatric recipients, highlights the need for earlier recognition and optimized management.

title: [Evolution of surgical strategies for secondary hyperparathyroidism].
abstract: Secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT) is an important component of chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD). It may be accompanied by bone pain, pruritus, abnormalities in bone metabolism, and vascular and soft-tissue calcifications, thereby increasing the disease burden in patients with end-stage kidney disease. Historically, surgical management of SHPT was mainly based on persistently elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels and patients' responses to medical therapy, gradually establishing a management strategy centered on PTH control. This strategy has played an important role in selecting candidates for surgery and facilitating multidisciplinary communication. With the evolution of the CKD-MBD concept and accumulating evidence on clinical outcomes, the goals of surgical treatment have gradually expanded from merely lowering PTH levels to improving bone metabolism, relieving symptoms, controlling CKD-MBD-related target-organ damage, and improving long-term outcomes. Based on current guidelines, expert consensus, and clinical studies, this review discusses the historical basis and limitations of PTH threshold-based strategies and examines the evolution of surgical management for SHPT, with particular emphasis on the timing of surgical evaluation, surgical indications, choice of surgical procedure, perioperative management, postoperative follow-up, and future directions for optimization.
journal: Zhonghua wai ke za zhi [Chinese journal of surgery]
authors: Zheng X, Zhou L, Ou XH, Wang Q, Shi YY, Li ZH.

title: Chaihu-Shugan-San attenuates depression by downregulating liver LCN2 to suppress LHb GluN2B-associated glutamatergic signaling.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceThe liver-brain axis has emerged as a critical pathway in depression pathogenesis, yet the molecular basis of this crosstalk remains largely unexplored. Chaihu-Shugan-San (CSS), a classic Traditional Chinese Medicine formula for "soothing the liver and relieving depression" has shown both hepatoprotective and antidepressant effects, but whether these actions are linked via the liver-brain axis and through what molecular mechanism remains unknown.Aim of the studyThis study aimed to determine whether CSS exerts antidepressant effects via the liver-brain axis and to elucidate the mediating role of liver lipocalin 2 (LCN2) and its receptor SLC22A17 in regulating lateral habenula (LHb) function.Materials and methodsA chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mouse model was established. CSS (2, 4, 8 g/kg) or fluoxetine (10 mg/kg) was orally administered. Depressive-like behaviors were assessed by sucrose preference, open field, and forced swim tests. Hepatic injury was evaluated by serum ALT/AST and H&E staining. Liver transcriptomics and LHb single-cell RNA sequencing were performed to identify key molecules, followed by qRT-PCR, Western blot, ELISA, and immunofluorescence for validation. The causal role of LCN2 was tested via liver-specific AAV-mediated overexpression.ResultsCSS ameliorated CUMS-induced depressive-like behaviors and liver injury. Transcriptomics and PPI network analysis identified Lcn2 as a hub gene. CSS reversed CUMS-induced elevation of LCN2 in the liver, serum, and LHb, as well as the upregulation of its receptor SLC22A17 in the LHb. LHb single-cell sequencing revealed that CSS restored CUMS-induced changes in astrocyte subcluster ASC6, including downregulation of AQP4 and SLC38A1 and impaired intercellular communication. Consequently, CSS reduced the elevated expression of c-FOS and GluN2B and restored AQP4 and SLC38A1 in the LHb. Importantly, liver-specific Lcn2 overexpression recapitulated CUMS-like depressive phenotypes and LHb abnormalities, including elevated SLC22A17 and GluN2B, and largely abolished the antidepressant effects of CSS.ConclusionCSS ameliorates depressive-like behaviors in association with downregulation of hepatic LCN2 and its candidate receptor SLC22A17 in the LHb, restoring ASC6-mediated glutamate homeostasis, and suppressing GluN2B-related Glutamatergic Signaling. These findings are consistent with a model in which LHb function may be modulated via the liver-brain axis through hepatic LCN2 and its candidate receptor SLC22A17, although the direct source of LHb LCN2 remains to be determined, offering experimental support for the scientific basis of CSS in "soothing the liver and relieving depression."
authors: You X, Song C, Chen W, Zheng Y, Wang R, Liu W, Wei Y.

title: Directed Evolution of the Cbx1 Chromodomain Generates a High-Affinity Trimethyllysine-Binding Variant.
abstract: Directed evolution is a powerful and versatile strategy for engineering proteins with enhanced affinity and tailored molecular recognition properties. Here, we applied phage display-guided directed evolution to enhance the binding of the wild-type Cbx1 chromodomain (Cbx1-CD) to an H3K9me3-containing peptide. Screening a soft-randomized library targeting residues surrounding the aromatic cage yielded C29, which bound the H3K9me3 peptide with a KD of 57 nM and exhibited an approximately 14-fold lower dissociation rate constant than Cbx1-CD. Across an H3K9me3-derived alanine-scanning series and a peptide panel, C29 showed stronger binding signals than Cbx1-CD for multiple peptides containing trimethyllysine (Kme3), suggesting lower flanking-sequence dependence for C29 than for Cbx1-CD. An AlphaFold3 model of the C29-H3K9me3 complex suggested local changes in the hydrophobic and electrostatic environment surrounding the Kme3-binding pocket, providing a mechanistic hypothesis for C29's enhanced affinity and reduced flanking-sequence dependence. When two Kme3-containing peptides were spiked into a 100-fold molar excess of unmodified background peptides, C29-conjugated beads effectively enriched both Kme3 peptides relative to the unmodified background. These findings define C29 as a high-affinity Kme3-binding Cbx1 chromodomain variant and support its further evaluation as an affinity reagent for Kme3-containing peptide enrichment.
authors: Li S, Wang D, Yang B, Dong G, Liu H, Wang B, Li L.

title: Experimental evidence that dietary antioxidants induce an antiviral transcriptomic signature in a wild seabird.
abstract: Infectious disease emergence in natural systems is driven by complex host-pathogen-environment interactions. Nutritional factors, particularly dietary antioxidants, can modulate physiological states by enhancing immune function and mitigating oxidative damage, but the underlying molecular mechanisms in wildlife remain poorly understood. To bridge this gap, we conducted a transcriptomic analysis of blood samples from both healthy and clinically affected magnificent frigatebirds Fregata magnificens chicks treated with either resveratrol (a plant-derived polyphenol with known antiviral and antioxidant properties) or a placebo. Resveratrol supplementation induced significant gene expression changes, particularly in diseased individuals, where we identified the upregulation of ten key genes in treated sick chicks, including the interferon-stimulated genes (IFI6, OASL2) and immune regulators (SOCS1, PLAC8); two additional transcripts were unannotated. Furthermore, resveratrol treatment was associated with increased expression of DDX60, a potent antiviral factor, and CYGB1, which supports cytoprotection. In contrast, healthy chicks showed fewer differentially expressed genes, primarily associated with metabolism and cellular organization. Collectively, our results reveal a transcriptional signature consistent with dietary antioxidants such as resveratrol acting as active molecular modulators of host defense, rather than simple passive antioxidants, although direct evidence of enhanced antiviral protection (e.g. reduced viral load) remains to be established. This study highlights the utility of transcriptomic approaches to link nutritional ecology with disease dynamics, offering a framework for understanding how dietary quality shapes host defense strategies and population resilience under increasing pathogen pressure.
authors: Sebastiano M, Eens M, Chastel O, Maigné L, Costantini D.

title: Recent advances in platinum-based single-atom photocatalysts from atomic engineering to sustainable solar utilization.
abstract: The development of efficient, low-cost photocatalysts is crucial for advancing photocatalysis, a promising technology that uses solar energy to mitigate environmental pollution and produce renewable fuels and chemicals. Among various candidates, single-atom catalysts (SACs) have garnered increasing attention due to their maximized atomic utilization efficiency and highly tunable electronic structures. In particular, Pt-based SACs exhibit exceptional promise, leveraging the high activity, structural stability, and low toxicity of Pt species in photocatalytic processes. In this paper, advanced characterization techniques for identifying and investigating the atomic structure of Pt SACs are emphasized. Subsequently, the types of supports used for anchoring Pt single atoms (SAs) are classified to elucidate their formation mechanisms and coordination environments. Furthermore, the recent advances in Pt-based SACs for photocatalytic applications are comprehensively summarized, including photocatalytic hydrogen evolution, CO2 reduction, and environmental remediation. Finally, the challenges and prospects of Pt-based SACs in practical applications are expounded from multiple perspectives. This review advances the core mechanistic understanding of single-atom photocatalyst rational design, holding great promise for breakthroughs in fundamental catalytic research and theoretical innovations in sustainable catalysis.
authors: Xia B, Xiao FJ, Wen R, Lu KQ, Zhang ZS.

title: CXCL9 Knockdown Inhibits Tumor Progression and Angiogenesis in Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma via JAK-STAT3 Signaling Pathway.
abstract: Background: Advanced clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) has a poor prognosis and frequent targeted therapy resistance, which urgently requires novel prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This study aimed to screen hub genes from our previously constructed ccRCC prognostic gene signature and clarify the oncogenic function and molecular mechanism of CXCL9 in ccRCC progression. Methods: Bioinformatic PPI network analysis was performed to screen candidate hub genes; qRT-PCR and IHC verified CXCL9 expression in clinical tissues and cell lines. Lentiviral shRNA was used to stably knock down CXCL9, followed by cell proliferation, apoptosis, migration, invasion and tube formation assays. Rescue experiments, transcriptomic and metabolomic sequencing, as well as subcutaneous xenograft mouse models were applied to validate molecular mechanisms and in vivo tumor phenotypes. TCGA-KIRC dataset was analyzed to evaluate correlations between CXCL9 expression, clinical parameters, sunitinib sensitivity and overall survival. Results: CXCL9 was determined as a hub gene and substantially upregulated in ccRCC. High CXCL9 expression correlated with distant metastasis, advanced pathological stage, shorter overall survival, and improved sunitinib sensitivity. CXCL9 knockdown suppressed ccRCC malignant phenotypes and angiogenesis, while inducing cell apoptosis. Mechanistically, CXCL9 bound CXCR3 to activate JAK-STAT3, EMT, and inflammatory pathways, which was further validated by multi-omics and rescue assays. In vivo assays further confirmed that CXCL9 silencing markedly restrained xenograft tumor growth. Conclusions: The CXCL9/CXCR3/JAK-STAT3 cascade serves as a core driver of ccRCC progression. CXCL9 can act as a novel prognostic biomarker and promising therapeutic target for ccRCC.
authors: Zong S, Wang K, Wang Y.

title: Combined Expression of FOXO and Tribbles Proteins Predicts Survival of Glioma Patients.
abstract: Background: High-grade gliomas remain therapeutically challenging and are associated with poor survival outcomes. Current biomarkers inadequately stratify patients for therapy selection and fail to support early detection of disease progression. The FOXO transcription factors and Tribbles pseudokinases are key regulators of the PI3K/AKT pathway and have been implicated in cancer progression, however, their prognostic value in gliomas remains unclear. This study aimed to determine whether transcriptional profiles of FOXO and Tribbles family members predict survival in glioma patients. Methods: Using RNA-seq data from TCGA and CGGA, along with microarray datasets REMBRANDT and Gravendeel, we analyzed the association of FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4, FOXO6 and TRIB1, TRIB2, TRIB3 mRNA levels with overall survival and WHO classification. We also experimentally validated the functional role of FOXO1 and TRIB3 in glioblastoma cells through gene depletion assays. Results: Using the TCGA RNA-seq cohort, we identified a FOXO/Tribbles transcriptional signature characterized by ↑FOXO1, ↓FOXO3/4 and ↑TRIB1/2/3, which was subsequently evaluated in independent microarray cohorts that confirmed the prognostic relevance of coordinated FOXO/Tribbles family dysregulation despite cohort-specific differences in the optimal gene combinations. Grade 4 tumors exhibited elevated FOXO1 and TRIB1/TRIB2/TRIB3, but reduced FOXO3/FOXO4 levels compared to lower-grade gliomas. Experimental validation supported a potential role of FOXO1 and TRIB3 in promoting glioblastoma cell viability. Conclusion: The combined FOXO/Tribbles expression signature (↑FOXO1/↓FOXO3/FOXO4/↑TRIB1/TRIB2/TRIB3) may represent a candidate prognostic biomarker requiring further validation before clinical application, particularly involving emerging agents directed against TRIB2, TRIB3, and FOXO1, as well as small-molecule activators of FOXO3.
authors: Santos BF, Maia AT, Grenho I, Besouro-Duarte A, Sepúlveda-Sánchez JM, Ferreira BI, Link W.

title: Biochanin A Induces Cuproptosis and Inhibits Lung Metastasis in triple-negative Breast Cancer.
abstract: Background: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) constitutes an invasive breast tumor subtype, marked by scarce available therapies and unfavorable patient prognosis. Natural products have attracted increasing attention as potential anticancer agents due to their multitarget activities and relatively low toxicity. This study aimed to investigate the antitumor effects of Biochanin A (BCA) in TNBC and to explore its underlying molecular mechanisms. Methods: The effects of BCA on TNBC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion were evaluated in vitro. Transcriptomic profiling, network pharmacology analysis, and mechanistic experiments were conducted to investigate the potential involvement of cuproptosis. The antimetastatic effects of BCA were further assessed in vivo using a mouse model. Results: BCA significantly inhibited the proliferative, migratory, and invasive capacities of TNBC cells. Integrative bioinformatics analyses identified cuproptosis as a potential mechanism underlying its antitumor activity. Mechanistic investigations suggested that BCA induces cuproptosis, accompanied by dysregulation of copper homeostasis, increased oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and altered expression of cuproptosis-related proteins. Bioinformatics analysis further suggested that LIPT1 may be involved in this process. In vivo experiments demonstrated that BCA markedly suppressed lung metastasis in TNBC mouse models. Conclusions: BCA exhibits potent antitumor and antimetastatic activities against TNBC, potentially through the induction of cuproptosis, with LIPT1 possibly involved in this process. These findings provide experimental evidence supporting further investigation of BCA as a promising therapeutic candidate for TNBC.

title: Single-Cell and Spatial Insights into Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Towards Cell-State-Targeted Immunotherapy.
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, and only a subset of patients derive durable benefit from immune-checkpoint blockade. Single-cell and spatial approaches reveal cellular states and tissue organization that bulk profiling cannot resolve. These findings suggest that therapeutic responses may depend on both cellular function and the local interactions that sustain it. This narrative review integrates single-cell transcriptomic, spatial, functional and clinical studies of the OSCC microenvironment. We distinguish OSCC-specific findings from broader head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and pan-cancer evidence. Computational inference, tissue association, experimental perturbation and clinical validation are considered separately. Malignant, myeloid, fibroblast, vascular and lymphoid states form spatially organized niches whose composition varies across anatomical sites and treatment settings. We examine their relevance to immune escape and chemotherapy resistance and assess strategies directed at specific cell states and intercellular circuits. Although selected circuits have functional support in experimental models, many spatial signatures remain observational and lack clinical validation. Clinical translation will require reproducible tissue assays, causal testing of candidate interactions and independent biomarker validation. Practical considerations include marker-panel selection, spatial scoring, tissue availability and the feasibility of sampling primary tumors and metastatic sites before, during and after treatment. Prospective studies must also determine whether biomarker-guided treatment improves outcomes, rather than assuming that a spatial association predicts therapeutic benefit. This review aims to critically synthesize current evidence, identify key knowledge gaps and define requirements for translating cell-state and spatial-niche insights into selective immunotherapeutic strategies for OSCC.
authors: Chen Y, Hou L.

title: Multi-Omics Machine Learning Framework Identifies CAPS, NUBPL, and RRBP1 as Hubs Linking Neuroinflammation and Mitophagy in Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: IntroductionAlzheimer's Disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline and the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau protein. The role of mitophagy in AD pathogenesis is not well understood. This study explores how mitophagy-related genes affect AD progression through transcriptomic analysis, machine learning, and immune profiling.Materials and methodsPost-mortem transcriptomic data from the middle temporal gyrus (training dataset GSE132903, 97 AD cases and 98 controls) were analyzed. A total of 552 Differentially Expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using stringent criteria (unadjusted p-value  0.5). Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) was performed to identify gene modules associated with mitophagy.ResultsThree diagnostic biomarkers were identified and validated using LASSO, Random Forest, and XGBoost: CAPS (AUC = 0.83), NUBPL (AUC = 0.756), and RRBP1 (AUC = 0.78). CIBERSORT analysis revealed a distinct neuroinflammatory profile in AD, characterized by M1 macrophage polarization and CD4+ T cell depletion. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) showed that these biomarkers were associated with metabolic pathways, suggesting a role for metabolicepigenetic interactions in AD progression.DiscussionThe integration of differential expression analysis, WGCNA, and three machine learning algorithms consistently identified CAPS, NUBPL, and RRBP1 as robust diagnostic candidates, which were independently validated in an external cohort. These findings suggest that mitophagyrelated genes may contribute to AD through mechanisms involving neuroinflammation and metabolic pathways. Nevertheless, the generalizability of these biomarkers across demographics necessitates validation in larger, more diverse cohorts.ConclusionOur findings indicate that these mitophagy-related genes may serve as biomarkers for AD. A nomogram model incorporating these biomarkers showed promising diagnostic performance (training AUC = 0.834; validation with GSE29378: AUC = 0.716). In summary, our research suggests that mitophagy-related genes play a role in AD through immune and metabolic pathways. Understanding these mechanisms could lead to new approaches for the diagnosis and treatment of AD.
authors: An X, Cao M, Yi Z, Wang Y, Yu W, Ren Z.

title: Atractylenolide III alleviates MASLD by inhibiting lipid synthesis and apoptosis via PTEN.
abstract: BackgroundMetabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has emerged as a major global health issue. This study aims to investigate the ameliorative effects of atractylenolide III (ATL III) on MASLD and its underlying molecular mechanisms, thereby providing theoretical basis and experimental support for the development of therapeutic drugs for MASLD.MethodsA high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mouse model and a combination of oleic acid and palmitic acid (PO)-induced lipid deposition model in AML-12 hepatocytes were established. The therapeutic effects of ATL III on hepatic lipid accumulation, injury, and inflammation were evaluated using biochemical assays, histopathological staining, immunofluorescence, Western blot (WB), and quantitative real-time PCR. Transcriptome sequencing was performed to screen for key targets, and molecular docking together with cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) were used to validate the potential binding between ATL III and the target protein. The findings were further verified using a liver-specific Pten knockdown mouse model.ResultsIn vivo experiments showed that ATL III significantly ameliorated hepatic lipid accumulation, injury, and inflammatory response in HFD feeding mice. In vitro experiments demonstrated that ATL III effectively reduced lipid accumulation in PO-induced AML-12 cells without affecting cell viability. Transcriptome sequencing and KEGG enrichment analysis revealed that the differentially expressed genes regulated by ATL III were enriched in the phosphatidylinositol 3‑kinase (PI3K)/serine/threonine protein kinase B (AKT), fatty acid metabolism, and apoptosis pathways. Further studies showed that ATL III engaged PTEN in a cellular context and upregulated its expression, thereby inhibiting excessive AKT activation. WB analysis confirmed that ATL III regulated lipid synthesis and apoptosis-related proteins via the PTEN/AKT axis. Notably, liver‑specific knockdown of Pten significantly attenuated the ameliorative effects of ATL III on the expression of the above molecules, as well as on liver injury and lipid accumulation.ConclusionsATL III ameliorates hepatic steatosis, injury, and inflammation in HFD-induced MASLD mice. Mechanistically, ATL III upregulates PTEN expression and suppresses excessive AKT activation, thereby reducing hepatic lipid synthesis and hepatocyte apoptosis. Liver-specific knockdown of Pten attenuates the protective effects of ATL III, confirming that PTEN is functionally required for its beneficial actions. These findings suggest that ATL III represents a potential therapeutic candidate for MASLD by acting through the PTEN/AKT pathway.
journal: Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology
authors: Shen X, Chen L, Lian Y, Zhang Y, Mei H, Qiu J, Lu D, Jiang Y, Dou X.

title: Dual-response whole-cell microalgae biosensor based on ALP-associated electrochemical sensing of heavy metal cations in freshwater.
abstract: The increasing contamination of freshwater with heavy metal cations has accelerated the development of eco-friendly microalgae-based biosensors due to their high sensitivity and sustainability. However, most existing systems rely solely on inhibitory (turn-off) responses, limiting their analytical capabilities. In this study, a chronoamperometric biosensor was developed using living Scenedesmus sp. MN738556 immobilized on a glassy carbon electrode within a bovine serum albumin-glutaraldehyde matrix. The biosensor demonstrated distinct ALP-associated electrochemical responses for different heavy metal cations. An ultralow detection limit of 0.1 μg/L was achieved for Cd2+ through enzyme inhibition (turn-off). In contrast, Zn2+ and Ni2+ exhibited concentration-dependent biphasic responses, including enzyme activation (turn-on) below critical concentrations (5 mg/L for Zn2+ and 300 μg/L for Ni2+) and inhibition at higher levels. The biosensor also showed good selectivity in binary mixtures with minimal interference below threshold concentrations. This biphasic response system supports a promising strategy for cation-dependent modulation of electrochemical biosensing of heavy metal cations in freshwater environments.
authors: Iravani S, Ahmadzadeh H, Sajjadizadeh HS, Rounaghi G.

title: Transcriptome analysis of mRNA and long non-coding RNA profiles in the brains of CVA10-infected suckling mice.
abstract: Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) caused by Coxsackievirus A10 (CVA10) remains an important public health concern. Although most infections are self-limiting, severe cases may develop neurological complications, including acute flaccid paralysis and aseptic meningitis. However, host transcriptional responses to CVA10 infection within the central nervous system (CNS) remain poorly understood. Here, we established a CVA10-infected ICR suckling mouse model and performed transcriptomic profiling of brain tissues using RNA-seq, followed by RT-qPCR validation. A total of 243 differentially expressed mRNAs and 776 differentially expressed lncRNAs were identified in the brains of CVA10-infected mice. Interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) such as Ifit1 exhibited significant dysregulation in CVA10-infected brain tissue. Integrated GO and KEGG functional enrichment analyses revealed that these genes were significantly associated with innate immune and inflammatory responses, particularly interferon-related signaling pathways. Protein-protein interaction network analysis identified ten immune-related hub genes, including Irf7, Rsad2, Isg15, Stat1, Ifih1, Ifit1, Ifit3, Oasl2, Rtp4 and Usp18. RT-qPCR validation showed overall agreement with RNA-seq findings, supporting the reliability of the transcriptomic analysis. Long non coding RNAs can extensively regulate these immune-related genes in both directions. These results offer a foundation for further investigation of the molecular basis of CVA10-related neurological disease, and for exploring candidate biomarkers and molecular targets.
authors: Cao M, Wang M, Li L, Xing W, Liu P, Li J.

title: Structure-activity relationship and target identification of marine anthranilamides as anti-inflammatory agents.
abstract: Pro-inflammatory cytokines mediate intestinal inflammation and tissue lesions, making their inhibition a promising therapeutic approach for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). In this work, a series of anthranilamide derivatives were rationally designed and synthesized via multi-site structural optimization based on marine natural product (MNP) 3. Among all the derivatives, compound 17 displayed potent inhibitory activity against pro-inflammatory cytokines at 10 μM in vitro, with inhibition rates of 104% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) and 93% for interleukin-1β (IL-1β). Mechanistic studies revealed that compound 17 acts as a selective histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor with IC50 values of 395 nM and 6.7 μM against HDAC6 and HDAC1, respectively. Molecular docking simulations were conducted to predict its detailed binding mode with HDAC6. Notably, compound 17 exerted remarkable therapeutic efficacy in a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis mouse model, effectively ameliorating colonic pathological damage. Collectively, these results establish compound 17 as a selective HDAC6 inhibitor with favorable anti-IBD activity, supporting its further development as a promising lead candidate.
authors: Zhou Y, Ji G, Chen Y, Li L, Wang X, Naseer A, Xue X, Yang J, Lu T, Wang L, Liu Z, Wang P, Wang CY.

title: Nodal T Follicular Helper Cell Lymphoma With Epstein-Barr Virus-Positive Neoplastic T Cells Derived From Clonal Hematopoiesis.
abstract: IntroductionNodal T follicular helper cell lymphoma (nTFHL) with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-positive neoplastic T cells is rare.MethodsWe report a woman with nTFHL and analyzed EBV-infected cells using an immunobead-based method and assessed somatic mutations in lymphoma and lymphoma-uninvolved bone marrow by targeted sequencing.ResultsEBV DNA was enriched in the CD4-positive fraction containing neoplastic T cells. Shared TET2 mutation was identified in both lymphoma and bone marrow, whereas additional TET2 and RHOA G17V mutations were restricted to the lymphoma.ConclusionThese findings support a stepwise model of EBV-positive nTFHL arising from TET2-mutated clonal hematopoiesis with subsequent acquisition of a RHOA mutation.Trial registrationThe authors have confirmed clinical trial registration is not needed for this submission.
authors: Kishi D, Hiramoto N, Yamashita D, Maruoka H, Shiroishi Y, Nishikubo M, Shimomura Y, Yamamoto R, Nagai Y, Torii Y, Kimura H, Nannya Y, Ogawa S, Kondo T.

title: A review of ring-type rotational MEMS traveling-wave ultrasonic micromotors: design, detection, control, and application validation.
abstract: The ring-type rotational microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) traveling-wave ultrasonic micromotor has emerged as an important candidate for micro- and small-scale precision rotary actuation because of its thin-film structure, low driving voltage, less electromagnetic interference, and strong potential for system-level integration. In recent years, continuous advances in MEMS wafer processing, lead zirconate titanate (PZT) thin-film deposition and etching, and multi-layer interconnect packaging have driven substantial progress in micro-stator design, output performance, online sensing, motion control, and application validation of ring-type rotational MEMS traveling-wave ultrasonic micromotors (R-MTWUMs). Centered on the framework of design, detection, control, and application, this review systematically summarizes the development of R-MTWUMs. It first outlines their operating principles and representative fabrication processes, and then critically reviews the evolution of micro-stator configurations from substrate supported structures to nodal circle anchored and flexibly supported structures, and further to stator teeth and ball-amplified structures. Key performance metrics, including quality factor, driving voltage, torque, and rotation speed, are comparatively analyzed. On this basis, the review further summarizes the main detection methods used for R-MTWUMs, discusses recent progress in angular position sensing, driving and control, feedback electrode-based mode monitoring, and closed-loop control, and assesses their application potential through the application validation. Finally, this review summarizes major development trends, discusses the remaining challenges in fabrication, mechanism, evaluation, on-chip sensing, and closed-loop control, and outlines future research directions to accelerate the transition of R-MTWUMs from laboratory prototypes to practical engineering systems.
authors: Xie J, Wang C, Dong L, Zhang Z, Zhou H, Zhang Y, Sun Y, Sun Y, Zhou T, Song C.

title: Myocardial inflammatory activity and structural injury are discordant in connective tissue disease compared with acute suspected viral myocarditis: a CMR study.
abstract: Background and aimIn connective tissue diseases (CTD), myocardial T2 elevation is a frequent CMR finding, yet whether it translates into myocardial injury remains uncertain. We compared T2 and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) between CTD-associated myocardial involvement and acute suspected viral myocarditis, a clinical model in which inflammatory activity and structural injury commonly co-occur in the acute phase, to assess whether the association between myocardial inflammatory activity and structural injury differs between disease contexts.MethodsPatients from two prospective institutional registries were included. Active myocardial inflammation was defined using a study-specific CMR definition based on the T2 component of the updated Lake Louise Criteria, requiring T2 elevation ≥ 40 ms, applied identically in both groups. Inflammatory activity was quantified by myocardial T2 mapping and structural injury by LGE.ResultsA total of 181 patients were included (CTD n = 44; viral myocarditis n = 137). CTD patients were predominantly female (75% vs. 44%; p ConclusionMyocardial T2 elevation in CTD may not be invariably associated with LGE-defined myocardial injury and may carry different implications than in acute suspected viral myocarditis. Disease-specific contextualization of CMR inflammatory markers is warranted.
journal: Clinical research in cardiology : official journal of the German Cardiac Society
authors: Treiber JM, Wilhelmi T, Binz C, Backhaus SJ, Wolter S, Rieth A, Rademann M, Kriechbaum S, Müller-Ladner U, Sossalla S, Klemm P, Rolf A.

title: Capture of long-missing heme oxygenases that degrade both heme b and heme c.
abstract: Heme serves as a crucial cofactor for hemoproteins and as an iron reservoir; yet, its accumulation is toxic, necessitating efficient degradation pathways. While the catabolism of free heme b is well characterized, the enzymes that disrupt its counterpart covalently tethered to a peptide (heme c) have remained elusive. Here, through a pipeline of multiple in silico analyses, we predict a distinct Core-only type of heme oxygenases (HOs) within the HugZ superfamily to have the potential to degrade both heme b and peptide-tethered heme c. Biochemical and physiological characterization confirms that representative Core-only-type HOs confer balanced dual-substrate specificity. In contrast, the C-extension and N-fusion-type HOs degrade heme b, but not heme c, because the entry of heme c into the active pocket is blocked by their extra domains. Moreover, we show that the degradation of heme c by the Core-only-type HOs requires proteolytic digestion of heme c-carrying proteins by a protease such as DegQ, which occurs in the periplasm. Overall, this work provides an integrated evolutionary, structural, biochemical, and physiological framework that defines a novel strategy for heme recycling and adaptive metabolic flexibility in bacteria.
authors: Hou J, Dong W, Yang H, Liang Y, Gao H.

title: N1 neuraminidase monoclonal antibodies 2H08 and 3H03 have decreased binding and inhibition properties against H1N1 influenza viruses circulating after 2018
abstract: Influenza viruses are global public health problem. Vaccines are available but have to be updated annually due to antigenic drift of the main vaccine component, the surface glycoprotein hemagglutinin (HA). The second surface glycoprotein of the virus, neuraminidase (NA), has recently moved into the spotlight of vaccine development. However, its antigenic evolution is understudied. We found that two broadly protective N1 NA antibodies, which had previously been shown to bind and inhibit most N1 NA, lost activity to recent N1s from seasonal H1N1 viruses. Here, we show that this drop in activity can mostly be attributed to a change in electrostatic surface potential from neutral to positively charged. This effect was not observed when historic human plasma samples were tested, suggesting that the drop of activity is specific to the two tested mAbs but does not broadly impact the polyclonal human response. Finally, we confirmed that the tested mAbs were fully active against recently emerged panzootic clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 NA. Importance  The influenza virus NA has become an important target for vaccine development. The characterization of antigenic changes described in this manuscript contributes to our understanding of conservation of epitopes in NA.
authors: Bhavsar D, Hermann E, Monahan B, Nardulli J, Gleason C, Simon V, Krammer F.

title: Self-Evolving Recommender Systems: A Survey and an Evaluation Audit
abstract: In 2026 a new kind of recommender research appeared: large language model (LLM) agents that propose changes to a recommender's configuration or source code, train the changed model, and keep what the evaluation says is better. Within nine months about thirty such systems were reported, from open-source research harnesses to production loops at Google, Meta, Amazon, Alibaba, Kuaishou, Tencent and NetEase. We organise them, together with search-space AutoML and the agentic recommenders that update their own memory or weights, by what the loop changes, who proposes the change, and which chain of signals decides whether it survives, and we synthesise their recurring designs and the changes they keep. Because a self-evolving system is only as good as the signal it selects on, we then audit how 27 configuration-, code- and component-level loops are evaluated, coding each paper's full text against eight criteria with released evidence. Of the 16 loops that select candidates offline, three of the ten that report ranking metrics rank the full catalogue, eight do not say which data keep or reject candidates, four select on the data they report, and two state that the test set was used once; none reports its headline result with the spread over repeated evolution sessions, and three compare against a non-LLM search at equal budget. Of the 19 loops that run online experiments, none corrects for the many rounds it tests and one confirms its final candidate in a fresh experiment. Where transfer to held-out data is checked, some selected gains survive and some do not. Four loops report that their agent inflated the metric or leaked the target; where the paper says what caught it, it was people or the agent's own diagnosis, not the acceptance rule. We distil these findings into a two-tier reporting standard mapped to the audit criteria.

title: Four Null Microscopic Spacetime Theory
abstract: This paper proposes that spacetime has a microscopic causal structure beneath the smooth geometry of general relativity. The basic microscopic object is a spacetime cell generated by four future directed lightlike (null) directions. These directions form a local causal frame. Although each generator is individually null, the four generators and their six mutual pairings \(G_{ab}=q_a\cdot q_b\) reconstruct the spacetime metric exactly,\[ g^{\mu\nu}=\left(G^{-1}\right)^{ab}q_a^{\mu}q_b^{\nu}. \]The smooth metric of general relativity is the large scale description of this cell structure. At this microscopic level gravity is organized differently. The two physical gravitational wave polarizations are carried by the shear of the null geometry and propagate from cell to cell by a discrete Huygens law. The scalar and vector parts of gravity do not become additional waves; they remain constrained by the null Raychaudhuri and Damour equations. Each cell also determines its own local clock, a timelike direction fixed directly by its four null generators, so no independent preferred frame field is introduced. The radiative law contains one finite cell coefficient, fixed exactly by the specified four null two shell construction:\[ a_4=\frac{51491}{600000}, \]and reduces at long wavelengths to the massless gravitational wave equation of general relativity. The free theory has two degenerate polarizations, no birefringence, positive residue, causal propagation across the tested band, and positive discrete energy. Variational integrability tests reproduce the Einstein interaction at leading order and select, within the complete tensor basis tested, a unique \(O(L_c^2)\) completion with\[ x=8a_4; \]these nonlinear coefficients are supported by strong numerical certificates rather than a closed analytic proof. The same four null cell also supports electromagnetism. Potentials live on generator links and field strengths on the six bivector channels, whose exact Hodge structure splits them into electric and magnetic sectors. The resulting Maxwell construction satisfies the expected gauge constraints and Einstein--Maxwell curvature coupling. More generally, the cell carries a \((1,4,6,4,1)\) hierarchy of geometric objects connected by the boundary relation\[ \partial^2=0, \]linking its one through four dimensional structures within a single causal framework. The proposal therefore provides a candidate microscopic spacetime structure with an Einstein--Maxwell infrared limit and definite finite cell corrections. General three dimensional nonlinear constraint preservation, evolution through caustics, microscopic selection of the shell separation, and full quantum consistency remain open.
authors: Dolu G.

title: Dihydroartemisinin Engages NQO1 and Promotes Ferroptosis-Related Oxidative Stress in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Dihydroartemisinin (DHA), a bioactive derivative of Artemisia annua L. (AAL), has shown antitumor activity in several malignancies, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, the molecular determinants linking DHA exposure to ferroptosis in NSCLC remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify functionally relevant targets of DHA-associated ferroptotic stress and to investigate the role of NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (NQO1) in this process. An integrated network pharmacology and transcriptomic approach was used to identify ferroptosis-related candidate targets of A. annua. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were used for target prioritization, followed by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) to evaluate the interaction between DHA and NQO1. The effects of DHA on ferroptosis-related phenotypes and redox homeostasis were examined in A549 and PC9 cells. NQO1 overexpression, NQO1 knockdown, and GPX4 rescue experiments were performed to assess pathway involvement. Antitumor activity and NQO1-associated effects were further evaluated in mouse tumor models. Network pharmacology identified 15 active components of AAL and 61 NSCLC-associated therapeutic targets enriched in ROS-related and ferroptosis-associated pathways. Among 10 ferroptosis-related core targets, NQO1 was prioritized based on disease relevance, predicted DHA interaction, selective protein suppression, and complementary computational and experimental evidence. DHA was selected for mechanistic validation based on its pharmacological relevance and anti-NSCLC activity. SPR supported direct DHA-NQO1 binding (KD = 7.61 × 10-6 M). Mechanistically, DHA suppressed NQO1 expression through transcriptional inhibition and enhanced protein degradation. DHA induced ferroptosis hallmarks, including ROS burst, LPO and Fe2+ accumulation, GSH/GSSG depletion, MDA elevation, and GPX4 inactivation, in A549 and PC9 cells. NQO1 overexpression partially reversed these effects, whereas NQO1 knockdown phenocopied DHA-induced ferroptotic responses. GPX4 overexpression partially rescued the ferroptotic phenotype induced by NQO1 depletion, supporting a functional link between NQO1 and the GPX4 antioxidant axis. In vivo, DHA suppressed tumor growth, an effect partially reversed by NQO1 overexpression. DHA triggers ferroptosis in the NSCLC models examined, particularly in LUAD-derived cell models, in part through NQO1-mediated ROS burst and impairment of the GSH/GPX4 antioxidant defense. These findings identify NQO1 as a critical mediator of DHA-induced ferroptosis in these models and provide a mechanistic rationale for further investigation of DHA and related artemisinin derivatives in NSCLC.
authors: Guo X, Tao G, Zhang M, Han L, Yan S, Wang C, Zhang J, Guo X, Hu K, Gong Y, Wu Q, Xie C.

title: A single-molecule spin-photon interface.
abstract: Optical interfaces that connect long-lived spin qubits to photons are a central requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum information processing. At present, solid-state atomic defects are leading candidates because of their inherent spin and optical coherence1,2. Building on these advancements, synthetically tailored molecular systems represent a fundamental change in the field, using precise atomic control and consistent bottom-up assembly3,4. However, a molecular platform that concurrently satisfies the demands of a robust spin-photon interface-namely, the combination of bright fluorescence, high spectral stability and long ground-state spin lifetimes-has yet to be realized at the single-molecule level. Here we show that a triplet ground-state carbene molecule, embedded within a structurally matched host crystal, functions as a robust spin-photon interface with single-molecule addressability. The system exhibits narrow ZPLs, spectral stability over more than an hour, spin-selective optical transitions and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent control yields millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at a temperature of 4.5 K. These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics5,6 while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design7 and processable materials8-10.
authors: Roggors S, Unden T, Aubele A, Mentzel P, Bayer G, Salhov A, Scharpf J, Plenio MB, Retzker A, Jelezko F, Eichhorn TR, Schaub TA, Pfender M, Neumann P, Schwartz I.

title: Interpreting antiretroviral exposure and drug-drug interactions in pregnancy: A clinically anchored framework for HIV pharmacology.
abstract: In pregnancy, antiretroviral drug-drug interactions must be interpreted against dynamic changes in gastrointestinal physiology, plasma-protein binding, renal elimination, hepatic enzyme activity and membrane transporter expression. Interaction studies quantify geometric mean exposure ratios relative to nonpregnant adults, but these measures describe relative pharmacokinetic change rather than whether effective exposure is preserved. For HIV treatment, validated exposure-response targets remain reasonable starting anchors when pregnancy-specific targets are unavailable. No evidence indicates that gestational immune adaptation alone requires a different intrinsic antiviral target. Pregnancy alters target attainment by altering drug disposition and variability, and it can modify the pharmacokinetics of both the victim antiretroviral and the perpetrator drug. For long-acting injectable PrEP, protective exposure, dosing interval and pharmacokinetic tail require separate consideration from treatment targets. This review evaluates candidate evidentiary anchors, including protein-adjusted in vitro inhibitory concentrations, exposure-response relationships, therapeutic drug-monitoring targets and model-informed probability of target attainment. Evidence from integrase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, tenofovir formulations and long-acting agents demonstrates that similar proportional reductions in exposure can have different clinical implications depending on therapeutic margin, resistance barrier, interaction mechanism, formulation and pharmacologically relevant matrix. A newly proposed six-domain framework integrates clinical context, active analyte, exposure metric, evidentiary anchor, distributional target attainment and clinical outcomes. Physiologically based and population pharmacokinetic models provide evidence when pregnancy-specific data are unavailable, but their use should reflect model verification and uncertainty. The central objective is therefore not to define a universal pregnancy threshold but to determine whether pharmacologically effective exposure is maintained in the setting of gestational physiology and concomitant medicines.
authors: Eke AC.

title: Ciguatera poisoning associated with cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum syndrome (CLOCCS): Clinical case description and literature review.
abstract: Ciguatera poisoning (CP) is a marine foodborne illness caused by the ingestion of fish and marine invertebrates contaminated with neurotoxins known as ciguatoxins, produced by benthic microalgae from Gambierdiscus and Fukuyoa genera. Although the classical triad of digestive, cardiovascular, and peripheral neurological manifestations that characterizes this poisoning is now well recognized and extensively described in the literature, central neurological involvement remains poorly documented and understood. The present paper describes, to our knowledge, the fifth reported case worldwide of cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum syndrome (CLOCCS) occurring in the context of CP. A review of the previously reported cases was also undertaken to improve understanding of the pathophysiology of this syndrome, its clinical manifestations, imaging features, and prognosis, given the rarity of such presentations in CP.
authors: Oehler E, Molina B, Pradier M, Hemmer M, Picard B, Gatti Howell C, Guéry R.
