title: SAMHD1 regulation, dNTP metabolism, and lentiviral transduction in human primary alveolar macrophages.
abstract: Host dNTPase SAMHD1 kinetically restricts HIV-1 replication in nondividing cells, including myeloid cells and resting CD4+ T cells, by depleting cellular dNTP pools required for viral reverse transcription. In contrast, some SIVs and HIV-2 encode a viral accessory protein, Vpx, which promotes SAMHD1 protein degradation, thereby elevating cellular dNTP pools and enhancing viral replication kinetics in nondividing target cells. Here, we investigated the regulation dynamics of SAMHD1 and dNTP pools in human primary alveolar macrophages (AMs). We found that SAMHD1 in AMs was predominantly unphosphorylated and that CDK1 expression was limited, whereas early differentiated MDMs expressed CDK1 and phosphorylated SAMHD1. In contrast, human primary monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) transiently expressed CDK1 and phosphorylated SAMHD1 during early differentiation. Additionally, AMs displayed a distinct nucleotide-metabolism enzyme profile, with undetectable RRM2 and minimal TK1 expression but detectable RRM1, RRM2B/p53R2, DCK, and NDPK. Indeed, quantification of cellular dNTPs revealed substantially lower basal dNTP levels in AMs than in MDMs. Although Vpx treatment increased dNTP levels in AMs, the nucleotide pools were lower than those in MDMs treated with Vpx. In AMs, HIV-1 vector transduction kinetics is delayed; however, Vpx treatment accelerates the vector transduction. Furthermore, Vpx-deficient SIV vector exhibited minimal transduction in AMs, highlighting the critical role of Vpx in overcoming SIV restriction by SAMHD1 in AMs. Collectively, these findings identify a SAMHD1-mediated dNTP metabolic barrier that limits lentiviral transduction in tissue-resident macrophages such as AMs.
authors: Taki S, Tao S, Alvarez NN, Tan T, Auld SC, Flenaugh E, Javia V, Abdelfattah M, Riddick T, Ibegbu C, Schinazi RF, Staitieh BS, Rengarajan J, Kim B.

title: A High-Resolution Mass Spectrometry Workflow for Xenobiotic Metabolite Discovery and Toxicity Prioritization: Disperse Orange 61 as a Case Study.
abstract: Extensive characterization of xenobiotic metabolites remains a major challenge in mass spectrometry-based exposomics, as untargeted high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) can detect extensive chemical diversity but often lacks sufficient structural annotation and prioritization strategies for unknown metabolites. Here, we developed a built-for-purpose HRMS-based workflow combining untargeted metabolomics, in silico metabolite prediction, structural annotation, and toxicity prioritization to characterize xenobiotic biotransformation products using Disperse Orange 61 (DO61) as a case study. Sprague-Dawley rats were exposed to DO61 via oral gavage, and liver, plasma, and urine samples were analyzed by ultra-high performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC) coupled to HRMS in positive and negative ionization modes. Statistically significant features were prioritized and screened against a BioTransformer-generated suspect library containing predicted Phase I, Phase II, reductive, and microbial transformations. HRMS-based annotation, supported by bromine isotope pattern analysis and MS/MS fragmentation, identified putative DO61 metabolites, while SIRIUS-derived molecular formula predictions provided additional confidence through fragmentation-based structural evaluation. The workflow experimentally confirmed reductive azo cleavage as an early DO61 transformation, producing two aromatic amine products, and revealed extensive downstream metabolism of the parent compound and both cleavage products. Computational toxicity prediction further prioritized confirmed and putatively annotated metabolites with potential mutagenic relevance for a future evaluation. This workflow demonstrates how integrating untargeted HRMS with computational approaches can facilitate metabolite discovery, improve structural annotation confidence, and prioritize metabolites for toxicological evaluation, providing a hypothesis discovery strategy for characterizing xenobiotic metabolism and supporting exposure and hazard assessment within the field of exposomics research.
journal: Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry
authors: Overdahl KE, Roberts G, Gentry EC, Waidyanatha S, Dunnick J, Jarmusch AK.

title: Imidazopyridines as anticancer chemotypes: Structure-activity relationships, molecular targets, and lead optimization opportunities.
abstract: Cancer is multifactorial in nature and has been regarded as a leading cause of death worldwide. Imidazopyridine has emerged as a privileged scaffold for expanding the chemical space toward the generation of novel anticancer lead molecules with improved physicochemical and drug-like properties. This review highlights the recent advancements over the past four years in the rational design and development of imidazopyridine scaffold-based derivatives for the generation of potential anticancer agents. Emphasis has been placed on comparative structure-activity relationships (SAR), recurring structural features across different molecular targets, molecular docking analysis, and the determination of IC50 values. Imidazopyridine-based derivatives have exhibited significant anticancer activity by targeting various biomarkers and signaling pathways, including the inhibition of protein kinases, disruption of tubulin polymerization, inhibition of DNA topoisomerases and estrogen receptor alpha, modulation of histone deacetylases, interference with the DNA replication machinery, induction of apoptosis, and arrest of cell-cycle progression. ADMET and physicochemical profiling revealed that compounds 41, 107, 111, 116, and 122 possessed desirable predicted physicochemical and favorable ADMET properties. Further structural optimization and experimental validation of compounds 41, 107, 111, 116, and 122, which exhibited favorable predicted physicochemical and ADMET profiles, may help determine their potential as anticancer candidates against their respective molecular targets.
authors: Sofi FA, Khatun S, Wanjari PJ.

title: Integrative Multiomics Mendelian Randomization Prioritizes Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress-Related Genes Associated With Gastric Cancer Risk.
abstract: BackgroundEmerging research indicates connections between endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and gastric cancer (GC), but related genetic factors remain unclear. This study is aimed at prioritizing ER stress-related genes associated with GC risk using multiomics data.MethodsWe integrated GC GWAS data from FinnGen (discovery) and United Kingdom Biobank (replication) cohorts with QTL datasets, including mQTLs, eQTLs, and pQTLs. Summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) and colocalization analyses were performed to prioritize candidate genes, followed by characterization using transcriptomic profiling (GSE118916), methylation-expression correlation analysis (TCGA-STAD), and single-cell RNA-seq analysis (GSE270680).ResultsSMR analyses identified 83 mQTL, 10 eQTL, and 2 pQTL signals associated with GC risk. Among these, colocalization evidence was observed for 47 mQTL, 5 eQTL, and 2 pQTL signals. Transcriptomic analysis showed that PCSK6, YOD1, and RNF5 exhibited expression changes directionally consistent with their SMR associations with GC risk, whereas CTNNBIP1 showed an inconsistent expression pattern. PCSK6 was supported by mQTL, eQTL, and mQTL-eQTL evidence but lacked colocalization. YOD1, identified through pQTL-SMR, showed strong colocalization evidence (PPH4 = 0.95). RNF5 was highlighted via eQTL-SMR but lacked colocalization support. CTNNBIP1 was supported by mQTL, eQTL, and mQTL-eQTL evidence and colocalization, with a significant methylation-expression correlation observed in TCGA-STAD. Single-cell RNA-seq revealed that PCSK6 was predominantly expressed in fibroblasts, YOD1 in epithelial cells and mast cells, and RNF5 broadly across fibroblasts, epithelial cells, and selected immune cells.ConclusionsThis multiomics study prioritized PCSK6, YOD1, and RNF5 as ER stress-related candidate genes showing genetic associations with GC risk and directionally consistent expression patterns, with single-cell analysis indicating distinct cell-type-specific expression patterns. These findings offer useful context for future functional and mechanistic investigations of the prioritized candidate genes.
authors: Yang D, Liu Y, Meng X, Wang C, Yu Z, Zhang T.

title: “Every New Day Is a Gift”: Heart Transplantation Beyond 70 Years—From Chronological Age to Biological Reserve and the Patient Perspective
abstract: Heart transplantation has evolved from an experimental procedure performed mainly in younger patients into an established treatment for selected individuals with advanced heart failure. One important change has been the declining role of chronological age as an isolated criterion for transplant candidacy. Historical experience, together with advances in immunosuppression, surgical techniques, perioperative care, and patient selection, has shown that carefully selected patients in their seventh decade can achieve favorable outcomes after transplantation. Contemporary guidelines recommend a multidimensional assessment that considers comorbidities, functional status, frailty, organ function, nutritional status, cognitive and psychosocial factors, and the potential for postoperative recovery and rehabilitation. Recent registry data indicate that heart transplantation is increasingly being performed in patients aged ≥70 years and can be associated with favorable outcomes, although these recipients remain a highly selected population. This narrative review summarizes the historical evolution of age criteria in heart transplantation, the evidence concerning recipients aged ≥70 years, and the growing importance of biological and functional reserve in transplant evaluation. Particular attention is paid to frailty as a multidimensional geriatric condition rather than simply a consequence of chronological age. The review is complemented by the perspective of Umberto, a 72-year-old man who recently underwent heart transplantation. His experience illustrates the emotional, functional, and social dimensions of transplantation in later life and provides a patient-centered perspective on the geriatric principle that chronological age should be interpreted in the context of biological reserve, resilience, and individual potential for recovery.
authors: Ferrara N.

title: Mechanisms of Radioresistance Involving the cGAS-STING Pathway in Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Novel Solutions to Enhance Radioimmunotherapy
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a major cause of cancer-related deaths, and cases are on the rise due to increased prevalence of metabolic syndromes and alcohol consumption. HCC has a poor prognosis and is challenging to treat due to the immune-tolerant nature of the liver and resulting immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Radiotherapy has emerged as an effective HCC treatment that is able to remodel the TME of HCC tumors by inducing dsDNA breaks that activate the cGAS-STING pathway and downstream anti-tumor immune response. However, numerous mechanisms of radioresistance can limit radiotherapy efficacy, including suppression of radiation-induced cGAS-STING activation and, paradoxically, the immunosuppressive effects that can arise from sustained or context-dependent cGAS-STING signaling. In this review, we will first examine how underlying conditions such as liver matrix stiffness, gut bacteria dysbiosis, and tumor mutations can impair STING activation and how novel STING agonists and DNA damage response (DDR) inhibitors can promote radiosensitivity by enhancing STING activation. We will further discuss how immunotherapy can synergize with radiotherapy by mitigating the immunosuppressive effects of STING activation as well as how artificial intelligence can be integrated to improve HCC patient outcomes.
authors: Subramanian S, Dokic L, Pandita RK, Ramose KS, Pandita S, Gregoire V, Krishnan S, Rogers S, Pandita TK.

title: Neuroprotectant development from small molecule inhibitors of CHOP/ATF4 expression.
abstract: Glaucoma is a neurodegenerative disease that is in urgent need of neuroprotective therapies. We previously revealed the critical role of neuronal endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress induced by optic nerve injury in glaucomatous neurodegeneration. We also demonstrated that modulation of the ATF4-CHOP branch of ER stress provides significant neuroprotection. Here, we present multiple new chemical series identified by high-throughput screening that inhibit ER stress-induced C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) expression. We perform a structure-activity relationship analysis of one "hit" compound and establish two analogs with potent activities on inhibiting the expression of CHOP and activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4). We further demonstrate their neuroprotective efficacy in two optic neuropathy models; in both models, they increase survival of retinal ganglion cell somata and axons and preserve visual function. Together, this proof-of-concept evidence establishes the new ER stress modulators as promising candidates for further drug development to provide neuroprotective therapy for glaucoma and other optic neuropathies, and potentially for diverse CNS axonopathies.
authors: Li M, Yan X, Yang H, Liu L, Feng X, Bian F, Huang H, Dalal R, Solow-Cordero DE, Schow S, Liu D, Hu Y.

title: Species-specific gene programs define divergent antiviral responses in Marburg virus reservoir bats and humans.
abstract: Bats tolerate viruses that cause severe disease in humans. Egyptian rousette bats, the natural reservoirs of Marburg virus (MARV), sustain asymptomatic infection, whereas humans develop severe and fatal disease. To define the basis of this divergence, we establish a comparative framework using primary and immortalized Egyptian rousette and human cells exposed to double-stranded RNA and interferon (IFN). Bat cells upregulate antiviral effectors while limiting inflammatory amplifiers, a pattern further supported by analysis of independent in vivo MARV infection datasets. In contrast, human cells activate antiviral programs and immune hyperactivation in response to MARV. Integrating transcriptomic and proteomic analyses, we identify species-specific immune programs encompassing differential IFN-stimulated gene regulation, apoptotic control, and cytokine signaling. Our findings establish an integrative framework for understanding species-specific antiviral responses associated with MARV reservoir biology, identify pathways linked to immunopathogenesis in humans, and provide a foundation for future studies of host responses to filovirus infection.
authors: Pastor AF, Shirsathe S, Vidal-Freire S, Ferressini-Gerpe NM, Guito J, Somavarapu R, Patiño-Galindo JA, Giannetti E, Tagliavia M, Pan H, Worwa G, García-Sastre A, Towner JS, Johnson JR, Kuhn JH, Sanchez-Lockhart M, Palacios G.

title: Building virtual cell dynamics that evolve with biological measurements
abstract: Virtual cell models built from single-cell measurements need to predict how cells change over time, but new biological measurements often reveal dynamical relationships that existing models cannot express. Translating such measurements into dynamics therefore requires deciding what biological relation should be modeled, where it should enter the formulation and how its recovery should be validated. Here we present CellCompass, an agentic AI system that couples a scientific agent with an extensible dynamical engine for modeling state transitions and population change, along with fate and molecular readout. CellCompass reuses existing formulations when sufficient and designs, implements and refines new ones when experimental measurements introduce additional constraints. To assess this capability, we developed DynBench100, a benchmark of 100 simulated single-cell time-course scenarios with hidden dynamical ground truth. CellCompass achieved the highest aggregate performance among the tested general-purpose and biomedical agents across six dynamical tasks. Across four real single-cell studies, it retained an existing velocity-growth model to reconstruct context-dependent epithelial-mesenchymal transition and developed three new dynamical formulations for distinct experimental measurements. In drug-response data, incorporating metabolic RNA labeling reduced pulse-control identifiability error by 31.1%, revealing staged response programs and generating testable predictions for perturbing a candidate adaptive program. In hematopoietic lineage tracing, incorporating clonal barcodes improved clone-fate agreement by 54% over the strongest dynamical baseline, identifying early lineage priming among transcriptionally similar progenitors. Finally, in time-resolved CITE-seq data, CellCompass reduced future surface-protein distribution error by 13.2% for RNA-initialized trajectories, uncovering lineage-specific temporal offsets between transcriptional and protein programs. Together, CellCompass provides a framework in which virtual-cell dynamics can expand with the biological measurements used to constrain them.
authors: Zhang Z, Wang Z, Tian Q, Zhou B, Zhou T, Nie Q, Zhou P.

title: Bibliometric Analysis of Traditional Chinese Medicine-Derived Bioactive Constituents in Macrophage Polarization Regulation.
abstract: Macrophage polarization contributes to inflammatory regulation, tumor immunity, tissue repair, and fibrosis. However, the knowledge structure, research evolution, and emerging pharmacological directions concerning the regulation of macrophage polarization by traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-derived bioactive constituents have not been systematically characterized at the field level. English-language articles and reviews published between 1 January 2000 and 31 March 2026 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. After screening, 478 records were analyzed using VOSviewer 1.6.20 and CiteSpace 6.3.R1 to characterize publication trends, contributors, collaboration networks, co-citation relationships, keyword clusters, and citation bursts. Publication output increased markedly after 2019 and accelerated from 2022. China contributed the largest number of publications, with TCM-focused universities and institutes forming the principal institutional network. Major research themes included M1/M2 polarization, inflammatory signaling, tumor-associated macrophages, inflammatory bowel disease, gut microbiota, fibrosis, wound healing, and network pharmacology. Flavonoids, polyphenols, saponins, polysaccharides, and alkaloids were the main constituent classes identified. Recent research increasingly links macrophage regulation with immunometabolism, disease-specific microenvironments, microbiota-metabolite interactions, and direct target validation. The findings map the development and pharmacological directions of this research field and highlight the need for chemical profiling, multi-omics, single-cell technologies, and experimental target validation to clarify the material basis, molecular mechanisms, and disease-context-dependent effects of representative constituents.
authors: Guo W, Zheng H, Han N, Liu L, Cheng Z, Jin P, Li Y, Jia Z.

title: Substrate recognition and stage-dependent transformation of aflatoxin B1 by mediator-free Bacillus laccase frL103.
abstract: Enzyme-based mitigation of aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is commonly evaluated by parent-toxin depletion. This study characterized the stage-dependent, mediator-free transformation of AFB1 by recombinant Bacillus laccase frL103 and assessed chemical, biological, and structural outcomes. UHPLC-HRMS profiling at 0, 30, and 60 h yielded 2846 filtered features and showed that the AFB1 response decreased to 23.8% and 14.8% of the initial value at 30 and 60 h, respectively. A feature at m/z 329.0660 increased at 30 h and declined to 17.7% of that response at 60 h; accurate mass and MS/MS fragmentation supported its putative identification as AFQ1. A lower-abundance feature at m/z 327.0504 was putatively assigned as Dehydro-AFQ1, a proposed dehydrogenated AFQ1-related product. The 60 h reaction mixture produced higher viability than intact AFB1 in HepG2 and 293T cells, structure-based predictions retained endpoint-dependent hazard signals for the proposed products. In molecular dynamics simulations, AFB1 and its proposed products differed in hydration, distance distributions relative to the T1 copper center and binding-pocket retention. These findings establish a stage-resolved, product-centered framework for evaluating enzymatic AFB1 transformation. This approach links bioprocess performance with product evolution, cytotoxicity attenuation, and substrate recognition, while identifying the need for product confirmation, quantitative mass balance.
authors: Bian L, Wang T, Pan F, Cai J, Li X, Zhang C.

title: Exogenous 6-benzylaminopurine application delays leaf yellowing in pak choi (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis) during storage by regulating endogenous N<sup>6</sup>-benzyladenine metabolism and chlorophyll catabolism.
abstract: BackgroundPostharvest yellowing of pak choi is a critical issue affecting its commercial quality. This study investigated the mechanism by which 6-benzylaminopurine (6-BA), a synthetic form of the cytokinin benzyladenine (BA), regulates endogenous cytokinin (CK) metabolism and the signal transduction involved in the yellowing of pak choi during storage at 20 °C.ResultsTreatment with 6-BA inhibited the expression of the key chlorophyll catabolic genes BcCLH1 and BcSGR1, retarded chlorophyll breakdown, and eventually mitigated leaf yellowing. The treatment also maintained a high level of BA (the predominant CK in pak choi), enhanced the activity of cytokinin oxidase/dehydrogenase (CKX) and increased the transcript abundance of the associated genes BcCKX3/6/7, and upregulated the expression of the N-glycosylation-related UDP glycosyltransferase (UGT) genes BcUGT75D1/76C2/89A2. These changes accelerated BA degradation and inactivation, contributing to the maintenance of BA homeostasis. This relationship was also associated with the maintenance of greater expression of genes involved in CK transport (BcPUP1/5/9/13 and BcENT3) and signal transduction (BcAHK2/4, BcAHP3, and type A and B Arabidopsis response regulators (ARRs) BcARR4/6/7/9/15 and BcARR11/12/14/18, respectively) in 6-BA-treated pak choi.ConclusionThese findings suggest that the protective effects of 6-BA treatment against chlorophyll degradation may be attributed to elevated BA levels, enhanced signal transduction capacity, accelerated BA degradation and inactivation, and feedback regulation between type A and B BcARRs. The findings identify a candidate regulatory pathway and key regulatory genes involved in the CK-mediated delay of pak choi leaf yellowing. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
journal: Journal of the science of food and agriculture
authors: Song L, Hu W, Tang J, Li R, Zhang M, Cao M, Liu R, Ke T, Wang S, Luo H.

title: Nitrogen response differences at the flowering stage of maize (Zea mays L.) affect nitrogen use efficiency: a physiological and pathway analysis of nitrogen uptake, photosynthetic characteristics, and carbohydrate synthesis.
abstract: BackgroundReducing nitrogen (N) inputs while maintaining crop yield aligns with sustainable development goals. It is therefore important to elucidate the physiological mechanisms underlying maize N use efficiency (NUE). The physiological traits and transcriptional profiles of two maize cultivars, 'Qiangsheng 101' (QS) (a low N-sensitive cultivar) and 'Zhengdan 958' (ZD) (a low N-tolerant cultivar), were analyzed at two N application rates: 150 kg ha-1 (low N, LN) and 300 kg ha-1 (normal N level, NN).ResultsCompared with LN-ZD, LN-QS showed reductions of 11.22% to 14.29% in grain yield (GY), 11.73% to 23.53% in NUE, and 13.11% to 15.97% in radiation use efficiency (RUE). Relative to LN-ZD, LN-QS showed a 17.14% to 17.60% reduction in the relative chlorophyll content (SPAD) value and a 14.29% to 19.23% reduction in the net photosynthetic rate (Pn). Soluble sugar content decreased and starch content increased in LN-QS relative to LN-ZD (P ConclusionUnder low N conditions, the reduction in N uptake and metabolic capacity in QS led to diminished photosynthetic performance, which subsequently constrained carbon assimilation, ultimately reducing NUE and GY, while ZD remained stable. These results provide valuable insights for the optimization of N management strategies and the improvement of maize productivity. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
journal: Journal of the science of food and agriculture
authors: Jin F, Zhang Y, Shao Y, Ma Y, Li R, Liu D, Ding R, Su W, Han Q.

title: Sublethal and transgenerational effects of fenoxycarb and novaluron on Asian citrus psyllid, Diaphorina citri (Kuwayama) (Hemiptera: Psyllidae).
abstract: BackgroundThe Asian citrus psyllid, Diaphorina citri Kuwayama, is the primary vector of 'Candidatus Liberibacter' species causing citrus Huanglongbing. Sublethal effects of the insect growth regulators fenoxycarb and novaluron on this pest remain poorly characterized. We evaluated their sublethal and transgenerational effects on D. citri by integrating toxicity bioassays, age-stage, two-sex life tables and transcriptome sequencing.ResultsToxicity to nymphs was stage- and application-method-dependent: fenoxycarb was more toxic than novaluron to fifth-instar nymphs under spray treatment but not under topical application, and younger instars were more susceptible than older instars. Sublethal doses (LD₁₀ and LD₃₀) stimulated reproduction in surviving F₀ adults (higher R₀ and longer T) but reduced the intrinsic (r) and finite (λ) rates of increase because the prolongation of T outweighed the gain in R₀. In the F₁ generation, fecundity and R₀ decreased under fenoxycarb (with a smaller, non-significant reduction under novaluron), whereas r and λ increased owing to shortened generation time. Thus, population parameters changed in different directions rather than showing uniform inhibition. LD₃₀ prolonged F₁ nymphal development, with the direction of the dose-response differing between the two insecticides. Transcriptome analysis identified 745 and 2484 differentially expressed genes under fenoxycarb and novaluron treatments, respectively; changes in the expression of hormone-signaling, chitin-metabolism and reproduction-related genes represent transcriptional associations rather than validated mechanisms.ConclusionFenoxycarb and novaluron exert transgenerational sublethal effects on D. citri. With the divergent transcriptional responses, these laboratory-based findings provide a basis for designing application and resistance-management strategies for D. citri, pending field or semi-field validation. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: Liu T, Zhang Q, Yuan C, Pan D, Lu Z, Wang J, Dou W.

title: Prevalence of occult hepatitis B infection among blood donors from 2015 to 2025: A meta-analysis based on testing modalities and temporal trends.
abstract: Background and objectivesOccult hepatitis B infection (OBI) remains an important concern for global blood safety. Published studies have reported inconsistent OBI prevalence among blood donors, and the influencing factors remain unclear. This meta-analysis aimed to estimate the pooled OBI prevalence and explore potential sources of heterogeneity.Materials and methodsWe retrieved eligible studies published from 2015 to 2026. Pooled prevalence was calculated using a random-effects model. Subgroup analyses were conducted by testing method, study period, sample size, region, and national hepatitis B virus (HBV) screening conditions. Publication bias and result robustness were assessed via multiple statistical approaches.ResultsSignificant between-study heterogeneity was identified. All subgroup analyses produced statistically significant interaction results (p for interaction ≤ 0.015). The prevalence of OBI varied remarkably across subgroups stratified by HBV-DNA testing method, research period, sample size, geographic region, national HBV endemicity, and blood screening level. The pooled OBI prevalence was higher in the 2023-2024 subgroup, although this likely reflects geographic confounding rather than a genuine temporal increase. No substantial publication bias was detected, and the overall pooled estimate was stable. High residual heterogeneity still persisted in all stratified subgroups.ConclusionOBI is prevalent among global blood donors and affected by detection techniques, study period, sample size, region, and local screening capacity. Standardized molecular testing and long-term surveillance are recommended to reduce transfusion-transmitted HBV risks and ensure blood safety.
authors: Chen H, Jiang Y, Li L, Wang Y, Wang J, Wu S, Zhang M, Bai X.

title: MicroRNAs profiles reveal potential epigenetic biomarkers of chronic occupational pesticide exposure.
abstract: Occupational exposure to pesticides has been increasingly associated with adverse health outcomes, potentially mediated by post-transcriptional mechanisms such as microRNA (miRNA) regulation. However, data on miRNA profiles in healthy exposed populations remain limited, particularly with respect to exposure duration. This study aimed to analyze miRNA expression profiles in occupationally exposed individuals according to exposure time and to elucidate underlying mechanisms and potential biomarkers. We conducted a cross-sectional study of occupationally exposed (n = 32) and non-exposed (n = 16) individuals. Differential expression analysis identified 14 miRNAs altered between groups (p 30 years). Additionally, machine learning algorithms were applied to identify robust biomarker candidates. By intersecting multiple linear regression and machine learning outputs, we consistently identified miR-1255b-5p (AUC 0.861-0.768) and miR-433-5p (AUC 0.744-0.611) as potential biomarkers of overall exposure. Additionally, miR-620 (AUC 0.938-0.785) was associated with shorter exposure periods, while miR-1269a (AUC 1.000-0.820) and miR-519d-3p (AUC 0.812-0.719) were selected for long-term exposure. Significant correlations were found between specific miRNAs and quantified pesticide residues, notably a negative correlation between miR-1269a and imidacloprid metabolite (r = -0.53, p = 0.03) and positive correlations with carbofuran (r = 0.57, p = 0.02) and desdimethyldiuron (r = 0.57, p = 0.02). Our findings provide new evidence that occupational pesticide exposure is associated with specific alterations in circulating miRNA profiles. miRNA profiling has emerged as a promising tool for risk assessment, though longitudinal studies with larger cohorts are warranted to validate these biomarkers.
authors: Lima IB, Francisco LFV, Birolli WG, Dos Santos Neto ÁJ, Marques MMC, Silveira HCS.

title: Cellular Responses of Microcystis aeruginosa to Environmentally Relevant PFBA Concentrations under Different Nutrient Conditions.
abstract: Perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA), a short-chain alternative to perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), has been increasingly detected in aquatic environments due to its widespread applications. However, its ecological effects on aquatic organisms under environmentally relevant exposure levels and different nutrient conditions remain poorly understood. In this study, Microcystis aeruginosa was exposed to PFBA concentrations of 0.2 and 200 μg/L under different nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) availability, resulting in a 7 × 3 nutrient condition × PFBA concentration experimental design including the PFBA-free controls. The acute toxicity test showed that PFBA inhibited algal growth in a concentration-dependent manner, with a 72-h half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) of 24.83 mg/L, indicating that the concentrations used in this study were far below acute toxic levels. On Day 3, 200 μg/L PFBA significantly inhibited algal growth under N-limited conditions, with inhibition rates of 29.80% and 23.13% in the LN (1 mg/L N, 7.1 mg/L P) and LNP (1 mg/L N, 0.05 mg/L P) groups, respectively. In contrast, 0.2 μg/L PFBA showed a slight growth-promoting effect under moderate nutrient conditions. However, after 10 days of exposure, PFBA did not significantly affect algal density in most treatment groups, and the effects of PFBA observed during the early exposure stage were attenuated over prolonged cultivation. Nutrient limitation significantly reduced algal growth, chlorophyll a content, and intracellular microcystin-LR levels, while promoting oxidative stress responses and extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) secretion. Under the experimental conditions, N limitation exerted stronger inhibitory effects on algal growth than P limitation and induced more pronounced oxidative stress responses. Although PFBA did not significantly alter the final algal density, it still was associated with changes in several physiological and molecular responses under specific nutrient conditions, including changes in reactive oxygen species accumulation, antioxidant enzyme activities, extracellular polymeric substances secretion, and the expression of photosynthesis-related genes (psaB, psbD, and rbcL). This study provides insights into the toxicological effects of PFBA on microalgae in aquatic environments.
authors: Wang J, Yu G, Zhang M, Wang Z, Zheng Z.

title: Divergent morphological responses accompany the warming-induced competitive shift from Planktothrix (maladaptive plasticity) to Microcystis (functionally beneficial morphological stability).
abstract: Cyanobacterial blooms, particularly those dominated by Microcystis and Planktothrix, are becoming more frequent in eutrophic freshwaters worldwide. Although these two species often exhibit seasonal succession linked to rising temperatures, the role of morphological responses in shaping their temperature-dependent competitive dynamics remains largely unexplored. In this study, we conducted controlled laboratory experiments to examine how temperature (20, 26, and 32 °C) modulates the competitive interaction between Planktothrix agardhii and Microcystis aeruginosa under both mono-culture and co-culture conditions. Population growth and morphological traits of both species were tracked throughout the experiment. Key findings include: (1) At 20 °C, the two species coexisted with only weak mutual inhibition; at 32 °C, M. aeruginosa nearly outcompeted P. agardhii, and competitive displacement rates increased markedly along the temperature gradient. (2) P. agardhii showed strong morphological plasticity in response to competition, characterized by shortened filaments, increased cell width, and a reduced surface area to volume ratio, with the most severe morphological degradation coinciding with the strongest competitive suppression at 32 °C, a pattern consistent with a maladaptive stress response rather than beneficial acclimation; (3) M. aeruginosa maintained stable morphology across all temperatures when competing against P. agardhii. These results indicate that temperature, morphological strategy, and competitive outcome are closely associated, and that opposing morphological responses, maladaptive plasticity in P. agardhii versus a stable and functionally beneficial morphology in M. aeruginosa, accompany the temperature-driven shift in bloom composition. Notably, filament fragmentation in Planktothrix populations may serve as an early indicator of an impending transition toward Microcystis-dominated toxic blooms under climate warming.
authors: Wang Z, Liu Y, Chen S, Ye L, Xiao P, Zuo J, Yang S, Li R, Zhang H.

title: Transcriptomics-informed phenotypic screening of Rhodiola sachalinensis identifies herbacetin as a cardioprotective candidate against adverse cardiac remodeling.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceRhodiola sachalinensis Boriss. (Crassulaceae) is a traditional Chinese medicinal plant whose roots and rhizomes are used to invigorate qi and promote blood circulation and have been documented for the management of qi deficiency and blood stasis, chest pain, and angina. Consistent with these traditional uses, modern pharmacological studies have reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cardiovascular protective activities of R. sachalinensis. However, owing to its complex chemical composition, the bioactive constituents contributing to its cardioprotective effects remain poorly defined.Aim of the studyThis study aimed to identify cardioprotective constituents of Rhodiola sachalinensis oral solution (RS) through an integrated transcriptomics-informed phenotypic screening strategy and to elucidate the potential mechanisms underlying their effects on cardiac remodeling.Materials and methodsThe protective effects of RS were evaluated in an isoproterenol (ISO)-induced cardiac remodeling model, followed by cardiac transcriptomic profiling. Transcriptomic signatures were then integrated with complementary phenotypic assays of phenylephrine-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and transforming growth factor-β1-induced cardiac fibroblast activation to screen a library of 101 candidate constituents. The prioritized compound was further evaluated in ISO-induced cardiac remodeling and myocardial infarction (MI) models.ResultsTranscriptomic profiling of RS-treated hearts identified disease-associated signatures that informed the selection of complementary phenotypic assays for cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and fibroblast activation. Screening of 101 candidate constituents prioritized herbacetin (HBT), a flavonoid showing dual activity in both assays. In vivo, HBT attenuated ISO-induced cardiac dysfunction, cardiomyocyte enlargement, and myocardial fibrosis. These effects were associated with improved mitochondrial ultrastructure, preservation of mitochondrial network integrity, and restoration of ISO-suppressed OPA1 expression. In a complementary MI model, HBT improved cardiac function and reduced adverse remodeling. Mass cytometry (CyTOF) and immunofluorescence analyses further showed that HBT treatment was associated with reduced CCR2-positive inflammatory macrophage features and increased MRC1-positive reparative macrophage features during the early post-MI response.ConclusionsThis study establishes a transcriptomics-informed phenotypic screening strategy for identifying bioactive constituents of RS and identifies HBT as a cardioprotective flavonoid constituent. HBT exhibited protective effects across complementary models of cardiac remodeling, with additional evidence of mitochondrial preservation and altered post-infarction macrophage-associated features in the respective experimental settings. These findings expand the cardiovascular pharmacological understanding of R. sachalinensis and provide a framework for discovering bioactive constituents from complex medicinal plants.
authors: Wang Y, Situ Q, Hou X, Hua S, Wang Y, Zhang S.

title: Desoxo-narchinol A and water extract of Nardostachys jatamansi ameliorate house dust mite-induced atopic dermatitis by regulating Nrf2/HO-1 signaling.
abstract: Nardostachys jatamansi has traditionally been used to treat gastrointestinal disorders. Although it was recently reported to have anti-inflammatory properties, the pharmacological potential of water extract of Nardostachys jatamansi (WENJ) against atopic dermatitis (AD)-like skin inflammation remains unclear. We investigated the effects of WENJ on a house dust mite-induced AD-like mouse model by assessing phenotypic severity, histopathological changes, and cytokine expression. Transcriptomic analysis of murine skin tissues was performed to identify gene expression signatures and key transcription factors contributing to the efficacy of WENJ. In addition, the role of the primary bioactive component of WENJ, desoxo-narchinol A, was examined in interleukin (IL)-4/IL-13-stimulated human keratinocytes, with a focus on nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2)/heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) signaling. In the AD-like mouse model, oral administration of WENJ markedly alleviated AD-like symptoms, reduced immune cell infiltration and inflammatory mediator expression, and restored the expression of skin barrier proteins such as filaggrin. The Nrf2/HO-1 pathway was identified as a key molecular pathway underlying the effects of WENJ on AD-like skin inflammation. Moreover, desoxo-narchinol A significantly increased Nrf2/HO-1 expression in keratinocytes, and exhibited the ability to bind Keap1 in molecular docking analysis. These findings demonstrate that WENJ and its active constituent desoxo-narchinol A exert anti-inflammatory and skin-protective effects through activation of the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway, highlighting their potential as promising therapeutic candidates for AD and related inflammatory skin conditions.
authors: Shim KS, Kim HJ, Baek SJ, Gu DR, Kim YJ, Kim SC, Chae S, Kim T, Kim KM.

title: PsWRKY7 enhances anthocyanin accumulation via transcriptional activation of PsDFR2 in tree peony petals.
abstract: Anthocyanin biosynthesis dominates tree peony petal pigmentation, yet WRKY-mediated transcriptional regulation remains poorly understood. Three cultivars with gradient petal colors, white-flowered 'Fengdan', pink-flowered 'Shinkajishi', red-flowered 'Hongxialanman', were used to explore this mechanism. Anthocyanin content gradually increased across three flower developmental stages (S1-S3) in the order of 'Fengdan', 'Shinkajishi' and 'Hongxialanman'. Three PsDFR homologs were identified; all contained the conserved PLN02650 domain identical to AtDFR. PsDFR1 and PsDFR2 expression rose in parallel with anthocyanin levels, whereas PsDFR3 was barely detectable. Cis-element analysis revealed no W-box motif in the PsDFR1 promoter, while two W-box cis-elements were found on the PsDFR2 promoter. Yeast one-hybrid screening identified six PsWRKY proteins binding the PsDFR2 promoter. Among them, only PsWRKY7 maintained a sustained positive correlation with anthocyanin accumulation across all stages. Y1H, EMSA and dual-luciferase assays confirmed PsWRKY7 specifically binds the W-box2 cis-element of PsDFR2 promoter and activates its transcription. Spatiotemporal profiling showed the cultivar-dependent expression pattern of PsWRKY7 was consistent across petals, leaves and stems at S1-S3. Transient overexpression in petunia showed PsWRKY7 increased anthocyanin content and activated multiple biosynthetic genes including PhDFR. Our findings demonstrate PsWRKY7 promotes anthocyanin accumulation by activating PsDFR2, providing a valuable gene resource for tree peony color breeding.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Lan L, Wang J, Cao L, Wang X, Wang H, Li Y, Wang L, Gao J, Yuan X, Fu Z, Zhang H.

title: Spatial transcriptomic profiling reveals candidate genes associated with male gametophyte development in CMS-D8 cotton F1 hybrids.
abstract: Gossypium trilobum cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS-D8) is characterized as being of the gametophytic type. Meiosis in F1 hybrids leads to the production of both fertile and sterile male gametophytes, making them a suitable material for studying the development of male gametophytes. Paraffin section analysis indicated that stage 8 represents a critical developmental period associated with male gametophyte abortion. Spatial transcriptomic analysis of 4.5-5 mm F1 buds revealed distinct spatial expression patterns, including enrichment of genes related to energy production and conversion in a putative meiotic-cell-associated spatial cluster. Cell-level analysis further resolved two transcriptionally distinct male gametophyte populations, between which genes associated with mitochondrial structure and cellular metabolic processes were differentially expressed. GhAAT showed differential expression between these two male gametophyte populations. Furthermore, phenotypic analysis of the Arabidopsis aat mutant revealed reduced pollen viability and a lower proportion of fully developed seeds, providing cross-species evidence consistent with a possible involvement of AAT in male reproductive development. In summary, this study provides a spatial transcriptomic profile of D8F1 buds and identifies GhAAT as a candidate gene associated with CMS-D8 pollen formation. These findings provide candidate genes and spatial information for further investigation of male gametophyte development in CMS-D8 cotton.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Feng J, Han J, Zhang H, Zhang X, Zhang M, Tang H, Qi T, Guo L, Xing C, Wu J.

title: Lactylation at the crossroads: a metabolic-epigenetic-immune integrator in intestinal homeostasis and disease.
abstract: Lysine lactylation (Kla) is a metabolite-sensitive post-translational modification implicated in DNA repair, tumorigenesis, chemoresistance, and innate immunity. Recent studies also implicate Kla in intestinal disorders. This review synthesizes current evidence on protein lactylation in intestinal inflammation, inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer, irritable bowel syndrome, intestinal fibrosis, radiation-induced injury, and enteric infection. We distinguish lactate-mediated receptor signaling and metabolic effects from covalent Kla, compare evidence across cell types and disease stages, and assess preclinical strategies targeting the lactate-lactylation axis. We also discuss microbiota-host metabolic crosstalk and mucus-penetrating nanodelivery, including the cross-border emulsification effect, an oil-in-water double-emulsion concept that describes traversal of the mucus barrier rather than a biochemical form of lactylation. Collectively, the available evidence supports a metabolism-epigenetics-immunity framework for gut pathophysiology, while highlighting unresolved questions concerning stereochemistry, site specificity, causality, safety, and prospective clinical validation.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps drive immunoinflammatory remodeling in abdominal aortic aneurysm: from inflammatory amplification to precision therapy.
abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a chronic vascular disorder characterized by progressive aortic wall dilation, extracellular matrix degradation, and an increased risk of catastrophic rupture. Currently, no effective pharmacological therapy is available to prevent or slow AAA progression. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) have emerged as a critical pathological platform linking dysregulated innate immunity to vascular structural deterioration. In the AAA microenvironment, local inflammation, oxidative stress, metabolic disturbances, altered mechanical forces, and platelet activation collectively contribute to the induction of NETosis. Persistent NET formation promotes immunoinflammatory remodeling of the aortic wall by activating inflammatory sensing pathways, including TLR9, cGAS-STING, and NLRP3, modulating macrophage responses, inducing vascular smooth muscle cell ferroptosis and phenotypic switching, and exacerbating proteolytic degradation, oxidative injury, and immunothrombotic responses. During disease progression, NETs may transition from early drivers of inflammatory amplification to sustained regulators of vascular remodeling, while in advanced AAA they may synergize with intraluminal thrombus formation and structural destabilization to accelerate disease progression. Circulating NET-associated biomarkers represent promising candidates for complementing conventional imaging-based risk assessment; however, their specificity and predictive value require further validation. Therapeutic strategies targeting PAD4-mediated NET formation, the oxidative metabolic environment, NET-associated effector molecules, DNase I-mediated NET degradation, and nucleic acid sensing pathways have demonstrated potential in preclinical studies. This review systematically summarizes the emerging roles of NETs in AAA pathogenesis and discusses future precision strategies integrating biomarkers, multi-omics profiling, and imaging-based risk stratification with stage-specific therapeutic interventions.
journal: Translational research : the journal of laboratory and clinical medicine
authors: Wang L, Zhu J, Li Y, Zhu Z.

title: Cognitive flexibility and cortical transcriptomic correlates of individual differences in mice following prolonged voluntary ethanol drinking.
abstract: Prolonged alcohol consumption is associated with cognitive dysfunction, but behavioral outcomes vary across individuals. We combined prolonged voluntary alcohol drinking, a cross-modal rule-switching task, and cortical RNA sequencing in male C57BL/6 J mice to examine behavioral and molecular heterogeneity. Alcohol-drinking mice showed heterogeneous learning outcomes: most reached criterion with performance broadly comparable to controls, whereas a subset failed, without a clear association with drinking level. Within the alcohol-drinking group, transcriptome-wide analyses revealed cortical expression differences between learner and nonlearner pools. Associations with overall trial burden largely paralleled these differences, while learner-only analyses identified additional associations with learning performance. We also examined eight prespecified inhibitory-signaling candidate genes across frontal, parietal, and temporal cortex. Of 264 gene-behavior associations, 22 reached nominal permutation significance in the full cohort and 11 in learner-only pools; none survived multiple-testing correction. Excluding nonlearners altered the pattern of nominal associations, with some retaining their direction, others reversing, and additional associations emerging among learners. Nominal associations predominantly involved SST/SST-receptor- and VIP/VIPr-related genes. These findings highlight heterogeneous learning outcomes during prolonged voluntary alcohol drinking, accompanied by cortical transcriptomic variation associated with learning performance, and identify exploratory molecular associations warranting further investigation.
authors: Wen Y, Hu S, Tian J, Liu YU, Zuo Y.

title: Tetrandrine attenuates diabetic kidney disease by suppressing the TLR4-NF-κB-NLRP3 inflammatory signaling pathway in proximal tubular cells.
abstract: BackgroundDiabetic kidney disease (DKD) involves persistent tubular inflammation. Tetrandrine (Tet), a bioactive alkaloid from Stephania tetrandra S. Moore, has renoprotective potential, but its effects on TLR4-associated inflammatory signaling remain incompletely understood.MethodsMale KK-Ay mice received Tet (10, 20, or 40 mg/kg/day) for 12 weeks. Biochemical parameters, urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio, renal histopathology, and single-nucleus transcriptomes were assessed. Pathway-associated changes were examined in kidney tissues and palmitic acid (PA)-stimulated HK-2 cells. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation, and siRNA-mediated TLR4 silencing were used to investigate the mechanism.ResultsTet improved metabolic and renal injury indices and alleviated renal histopathological damage in KK-Ay mice. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing revealed bidirectional transcriptional remodeling in proximal tubular cells, including reduced expression of selected inflammation- and injury-associated genes. Structural analyses supported a plausible Tet-TLR4 interaction, while CETSA showed increased TLR4 thermal stability. Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation supported reduced TLR4-MyD88 association after normalization to the respective immunoprecipitated proteins. Tet reduced TLR4 expression, NF-κB p65 activation, and NLRP3-associated inflammatory signaling, with lower mature IL-1β levels in PA-stimulated HK-2 cells. TLR4 silencing reduced MyD88 abundance, the p-p65/total p65 ratio, and mature IL-1β and IL-6 levels compared with negative-control siRNA.ConclusionTet ameliorates experimental diabetic kidney injury, improves metabolic parameters, and attenuates proximal tubular inflammatory responses. The findings support TLR4 as a candidate cellular target and link Tet treatment to reduced TLR4-MyD88 association and attenuation of NF-κB/NLRP3-associated inflammatory signaling.
authors: Yan Y, Wang W, Chen H, Chen Y, Liu P, Liu C, Wang G, Yu R, Zhao H.

title: Evaluation of Andes virus vaccine-derived human antibody for protection in Syrian hamsters: a passive transfer study using phase 1 trial sera.
abstract: BackgroundAndes virus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and is uniquely capable of person-to-person transmission, with no licenced vaccines or therapeutics available. A Phase 1 trial (NCT03682107) demonstrated that an ANDV DNA vaccine targeting Gn/Gc envelope proteins elicits neutralising antibodies in humans. We evaluated whether these human antibodies protect against lethal disease in an animal model.MethodsDay 197 sera from vaccinated human subjects were pooled, purified, and passively transferred to female Syrian hamsters one day prior to lethal ANDV challenge across two independent experiments. Controls included normal human IgG, PBS (negative controls), and SAB-400 (positive control). Neutralising antibody levels were quantified using pseudovirion neutralisation assays (PsVNA) and plaque reduction neutralisation tests (PRNT) to determine exploratory cutoff titres predicting survival.FindingsHuman antibodies from DNA-vaccinated subjects-unlike normal IgG-conferred significant protection against lethal ANDV challenge in both experiments. The exploratory cutoff titres predicting protection were determined to be 31-184 for PsVNA50 and 20-80 for PRNT50, depending on the analysis population and model parameters.InterpretationVaccine-induced human antibodies are sufficient to protect against lethal ANDV infection in an established animal model. If confirmed, these results indicate that neutralising antibody titres could serve as a surrogate endpoint and correlate of protection for future hantavirus Gn/Gc-targeted vaccines.FundingDefense Health Program and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
authors: Hooper JW, Lesko S, Principe L, Josleyn M, Kwilas S, Norris S, Tomashek KM, Paulsen G.

title: PCB-118 increases PDE4D abundance and thermal stability in bladder cancer cells: An integrative toxicogenomic and cellular study.
abstract: Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are persistent environmental contaminants with potential carcinogenic effects, but their molecular associations with bladder cancer remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated toxicogenomic, transcriptomic, single-cell, structural, and cellular analyses to identify candidate proteins responsive to PCB-118 in bladder cancer. Differentially expressed genes and weighted gene co-expression network modules derived from GSE13507 were integrated with curated PCB-associated genes, followed by random forest and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator analyses. PDE4D, SH2D3C, and NRG1 were consistently prioritized and showed concordant expression patterns in an independent cohort. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses revealed distinct expression distributions across tumor-associated stromal, endothelial, epithelial, and immune cell populations. Molecular docking predicted favorable interactions between PCB-118 and all three candidate proteins, with PDE4D showing the lowest binding energy. During 100-ns molecular dynamics simulations, the PCB-118-PDE4D complex exhibited the most stable and compact structural behavior. In T24 bladder cancer cells, exposure to PCB-118 at 5-20 nM increased PDE4D protein abundance. An exploratory cellular thermal shift assay showed an apparent increase in PDE4D thermal stability following PCB-118 treatment, providing preliminary support for a possible interaction at the cellular level. These findings identify PDE4D as a candidate PCB-118-responsive protein in bladder cancer cells and provide a basis for investigating its functional contribution to PCB-associated cellular effects.
authors: Wang H, Wang B, Liu H, Wu J.

title: Bisphenol A induces ACSL4-associated ferro-aging-like urothelial injury: Implications for Hunner-type interstitial cystitis.
abstract: Hunner-type interstitial cystitis (HIC) is an inflammatory subtype of interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome marked by persistent urothelial injury and bladder dysfunction. Bisphenol A (BPA) can disturb redox and inflammatory homeostasis, but its relevance to HIC-associated urothelial vulnerability remains unclear. This study examined whether acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) contributes to BPA-associated ferro-aging-like urothelial injury. Among non-pregnant adult women, higher creatinine-corrected urinary BPA was associated with a phenotype predominantly characterized by urgency urinary incontinence (UUI), and the primary Mendelian randomization analysis suggested higher interstitial cystitis (IC) risk with genetically proxied BPA exposure. Integrated transcriptomic, BPA-target, and machine-learning analyses prioritized ACSL4 as a consistent HIC-associated candidate. HIC tissues showed higher ferro-aging-like transcriptional scores and ACSL4 expression; single-cell analyses further identified disease-associated urothelial cell-state remodeling, with higher ACSL4 expression and SenePy scores in HIC urothelial cells. Structure-based modeling suggested a plausible BPA-ACSL4 interaction, while cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) indicated BPA-associated thermal stabilization of ACSL4. In primary human urothelial cells, BPA increased ACSL4 mRNA and protein expression, lipid peroxidation, iron accumulation, p21 expression, senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-Gal) positivity, inflammatory signaling, and barrier impairment, together with reduced Lamin B1 and ZO-1 expression and transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER). ACSL4 silencing and vitamin C attenuated these changes. In mice, PRGL493 and vitamin C each attenuated multiple BPA-induced bladder abnormalities. Together, these findings support an ACSL4-associated ferro-aging-like urothelial injury phenotype involving iron-lipid stress, senescence-associated changes, inflammation, and barrier impairment, with relevance to selected features of HIC.
authors: Wu W, Xu Y, Lu Z, Zhang Y, Cai L, Gao F, Niu Z, Zong D, Wang H, Xue P.

title: Mechanistic insights into ENO2-driven glycolysis and tumor progression in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Background and aimsNeuron-specific enolase 2 (ENO2) has been implicated in tumor metabolism, but its biological role in hepatocellular carcinoma remains incompletely defined. This study aimed to investigate the expression, prognostic relevance, and functional role of ENO2 in HCC.MethodsPublic transcriptomic datasets, RNA sequencing, WGCNA, survival analyses, and pathway enrichment analyses were integrated to identify HCC-associated genes. ENO2 expression was validated in HCC cell lines and paired clinical tissues.Gain- and loss-of-function, catalytic-rescue, glycolytic-inhibition, and pyruvate-rescue experiments were performed to evaluate glycolytic activity, proliferation, colony formation, migration, invasion, and tumor growth.ResultsENO2 was upregulated in HCC and was associated with advanced tumor stage and unfavorable survival outcomes in public datasets. ENO2 overexpression increased glycolytic activity and malignant phenotypes, whereas ENO2 depletion produced opposite effects. In ENO2-depleted cells, re-expression of shRNA-resistant ENO2 wild type restored the impaired glycolytic and malignant phenotypes, whereas the catalytic-deficient ENO2 mutant failed to restore them. Moreover, 2-deoxy-D-glucose attenuated ENO2 overexpression-associated phenotypes, while pyruvate partially rescued phenotypes associated with ENO2 depletion. ENO2 expression was also associated with altered PI3K and AKT phosphorylation.ConclusionsENO2 may contribute to HCC progression by enhancing glycolytic metabolism and malignant phenotypes, partly in association with PI3K/AKT signaling. ENO2 is a candidate metabolic and prognostic biomarker that requires validation in larger independent clinical cohorts and warrants further investigation as a therapeutic candidate.
authors: Liu Y, Zhang XR, Dai L, Li HL, Jin XR, Qi HB, Tang K, Li Q.

title: Isolation and structure elucidation of pyridinium-type metabolites from the sponge Agelas nakamurai.
abstract: Chemical investigation of the Formosan marine sponge Agelas nakamurai led to the isolation of four pyridinium compounds (1-4). The structures were elucidated through comprehensive spectroscopic analysis, including 1D and 2D NMR and HRESIMS. Among these, agelapyridinium A (1) is a naturally undescribed 2,4-dimethyl-1-phenylethylpyridinium, while pyridinebetaine C (2) is a new 2,4-dimethylated sulfonate-containing pyridinium betaine. Additionally, the known metabolites pyridinebetaine A (3) and pyridinebetaine B (4) were identified for the first time from this organism. All isolated compounds were shown to be inactive in inhibiting the growth of the few tested cancer cell lines and bacteria in the conducted bioassays. The putative biosynthetic pathways for the isolated pyridinium compounds were also proposed herein.
authors: Fu CW, Chiang L, Chao CH, Chiou SF, Wang HC, Yu MC, Sheu JH.

title: On the limits of marginal protein folding stability: methodological goals and drawbacks.
abstract: ContextWhy do proteins remain at the edge of stability rather than evolving toward maximal thermodynamic robustness? Can we trust the computational methods that inform about when and how stability falls off that edge? Marginal stability, the confinement of protein folding free energies to a window of approximately 5-15 kcal/mol, is broadly observed in biophysics, and its mechanistic causes, involving evolutionary and biophysical properties, remain under debate and require accurate predictions. In this regard, protein folding stability is currently predicted using both traditional structure-based homology-modeling methods and modern sequence-based deep-learning methods. However, comparisons among these methodologies remain scarce.MethodsUsing four viral proteins of biomedical interest and considering that rapidly evolving viral proteins provide a useful system for understanding thermodynamic tolerance under the competing demands of structural integrity and adaptive flexibility, we compared predicted protein stability from both approaches across independent random mutational trajectories and naturally occurring sequence variants available in public databases. The results showed a general methodological impasse. As random mutations accumulated, structure-based methods predicted a progressive decline in stability toward collapse, a pattern driven by the enforced conservation of protein structure. In contrast, sequence-based methods failed as sequences moved into uncharted regions of parameter space. Together, protein stability landscapes predicted using current computational approaches are inherently shaped by technical limitations, leading to uncertainty in the evaluation of marginal stability and stability changes associated with biological processes.
authors: Ferreiro D, Zoni V, Arenas M.

title: Expression associated polymorphisms and 6-mercaptopurine hematologic toxicity in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia patients.
abstract: Aim6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) is a key agent in chemotherapy of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Although variants in TPMT and NUDT15 are used to guide dosing, they explain only part of the variability in 6-MP toxicity. Our study aims to identify novel genetic determinants of 6-MP tolerance through expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) analysis.Materials and methodsWe used transcriptomic data from patients treated according to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute protocols to identify novel variants that may contribute to interindividual variability in 6-MP tolerance. We identified 17 white blood cells specific eQTLs in genes showing at least four-fold higher expression in patients with severe neutropenia. Association analyses of these variants with 6-MP dose intensity and neutropenia frequency were subsequently performed in 280 ALL patients.  .ResultsIn these exploratory analyses, homozygotes for minor allele of the rs2012694 variant in the L1TD1 gene was associated with increased neutropenia and reduced 6-MP dose intensity. Conversely, three variants in the CPE gene, rs12509669, rs3775317, and rs35411578, demonstrated protective effect against neutropenia and improved 6-MP tolerance.ConclusionThese findings highlight CPE and L1TD1 as candidate loci influencing 6-MP tolerance and provide new insights for the personalization of 6-MP therapy in children with ALL.
authors: Sabirova Z, Fuchs C, Meskaoui A, Ouelaa R, Frémond X, Oukaour A, Ahmed Yahia K, Gagné V, Théorêt Y, Nava T, Leclerc JM, Laverdière C, Sinnett D, Tran TH, Krajinovic M.

title: The RNA m6A reader YTHDF2 depletion phenocopies high glucose induced-cellular stress response in diabetic kidney disease
abstract: RNA modification, especially the m6A RNA methylation, has been increasingly associated with several physiological and pathophysiological processes. The proteins that help in establishment of the modification and its removal along with the reader proteins that facilitate the functional outcome, together play an important regulatory role in disease manifestation. Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is one such example, which is categorized as a multifactorial disorder that involves complex metabolic, oxidative, inflammatory, and fibrotic alterations, mediated through genetic, epigenetic and signalling cascades. However, the contribution of m6A-associated RNA regulators in DKD manifestation is relatively less explored. In this study, using HFD+STZ-induced diabetic mice and high glucose-treated renal cell models, we identified the m6A reader protein, Ythdf2 as a consistently downregulated candidate. YTHDF2 depletion in the renal cell line altered cellular viability, proliferation and increased oxidative stress under high-glucose conditions. Click-IT EU labeling further revealed altered RNA processing effects following YTHDF2 depletion and glucose stress. In corroboration with the above observations in animal and cell line models, independent human DKD transcriptomic datasets demonstrated conserved inflammatory and fibrotic signatures as well as reduced YTHDF2 expression in DKD glomeruli. The YTHDF2 downregulation was found to be inversely correlated with several disease-associated inflammatory and fibrotic genes. Together, these findings identify YTHDF2 dysregulation as a potential post-transcriptional mechanism associated with cellular stress and disease-associated molecular programs in DKD.
authors: Sankar S H H, Puranik A, Tripathy K, Singh N, Kesharwani A, Parihar VK, Bharathavikru RS.

title: Exploring the antimicrobial potential of streptococcal fratricins
abstract: Many streptococci are competent for natural transformation, during which they express a murein hydrolase that lyses and kills closely related species, thereby making homologous DNA available for uptake by competent cells. This process, termed fratricide, is mediated by enzymes known as fratricins. The most extensively studied fratricin, CbpD from  Streptococcus pneumoniae , is highly specific, efficient, and rapid in its killing, highlighting the potential of fratricins as targeted antimicrobial agents. Here, we screened nine putative fratricins to evaluate their antimicrobial activity. Of these, Zoocin A from  Streptococcus agalactiae , ScrM from  Streptococcus dysgalactiae , and CbpD from  Streptococcus vestibularis were successfully purified. Zoocin A exhibited the broadest target range, whereas ScrM and CbpD-ves showed somewhat narrower activity. All three enzymes predominantly targeted streptococci. Notably, Zoocin A was active against  Streptococcus mutans and  Streptococcus sobrinus , species associated with dental caries. The enzymes were also active against  S. agalactiae ,  S. dysgalactiae , and  S. pyogenes , which are associated with severe infections in humans and animals. We characterised the activity and stability of Zoocin A and ScrM and found that both retained activity under physiologically relevant conditions of pH, temperature, and ionic strength. ScrM activity was independent of divalent cations, whereas Zoocin A activity required cations and was observed with both Ca  2+ and Mn  2+ . For both enzymes, peptidoglycan cleavage was localised to the septal region of dividing cells. Zoocin A shows promise as an antimicrobial agent against  S. mutans , but its efficacy against biofilms would likely benefit from further optimisation or combination with biofilm-disrupting agents.  Importance  Streptococci are major pathogens of humans and animals, causing infections ranging from common mucosal and dental diseases to severe invasive and systemic infections. The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance among clinically important streptococci is a major challenge to healthcare systems who are running out of treatment options. It is therefore necessary to develop new approaches to prevent and treat streptococcal infections. Fratricins are streptococcal peptidoglycan hydrolases that mediate killing of closely related bacteria during natural competence, suggesting that they could be harnessed as targeted antimicrobials against pathogenic streptococci. However, the diversity and antimicrobial potential of fratricins remain poorly explored. By identifying and characterising putative fratricins, this work contributes to expanding the repertoire of antimicrobials and provides a foundation for developing fratricin-based approaches to combat streptococcal infections.
authors: Moe R, Kjos M, Straume D.

title: Epigenetic clocks and nonlinear aging in  Odocoileus  deer
abstract: Population age structure has important consequences for population dynamics and is a key parameter for wildlife demography and management. Epigenetic clocks have emerged as accurate molecular tools for estimating chronological age. Ungulates are among the most intensively managed wildlife worldwide, yet epigenetic clocks have been developed for only two cervid species. Here, we develop a novel epigenetic clock for mule deer (  Odocoileus hemionus ) and a multi-species clock for the  Odocoileus genus, and use them to investigate variation in age-associated DNA methylation across the mule deer lifespan. The mule deer clock achieved accuracy comparable to recently developed mammalian epigenetic clocks (r ≈ 0.9; MAE ≈ 5% of species lifespan). The multi-species  Odocoileus clock showed lower predictive performance (r = 0.72; MA = 0.782 years), but its broader taxonomic applicability may be particularly valuable where  Odocoileus species occur sympatrically and hybridize. Cross-sectional epigenetic age estimates supported nonlinear age-associated methylation dynamics across the mule deer lifespan, whereas longitudinal changes in epigenetic age indicated that clocks optimized for cross-sectional age estimation may lack sufficient resolution to quantify short-term within-individual changes. Overall, our results highlight the value of integrating clock-level, CpG-level, and longitudinal analyses to investigate aging in wild populations. We also identify strongly age-associated loci that provide candidates for developing targeted, scalable, and lower-cost assays.
authors: Montana L, Stewart C, Hall LE, Shafer ABA.

title: Lost and found:  beer belly  is a novel, ancient regulator of animal development
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) can provide new insights into the regulation of developmental processes by revealing unknown or overlooked genes. We identified a novel gene called  beer belly (  bebe ) as a marker of a segment addition zone (SAZ) associated cell cluster in a single-cell atlas of the spider  Parasteatoda tepidariorum . Here we show that  bebe is an ancient toolkit gene encoding a previously uncharacterised protein predicted to be secreted, which likely plays an important role in the development of most animal phyla. However, we could not identify a  bebe ortholog in any mammal or holometabolous insect, suggesting it has been lost in these lineages and explaining why it has been overlooked to date. Knock-down of  bebe expression in  P. tepidariorum demonstrates that it regulates SAZ size and consequently segment size by interacting with  Wnt8 . Our findings also suggest that  bebe may regulate segmentation in other invertebrates and play additional developmental roles in bilaterian and non-bilaterian animals, and likely ancestrally, through modulation of Wnt signalling. This study emphasises the promise of applying single-cell sequencing across a diverse range of species to better understand the regulation of development beyond candidate genes from traditional models, allowing us to better characterise the animal developmental toolkit and its evolution.
authors: Schultz ZX, Blakeley G, Aase-Remedios ME, Grillmayer DV, Leite DJ, Frankish T, Sutton G, Genikhovich G, Scholpp S, Pechmann M, Martín-Durán JM, Turetzek N, Janssen R, McGregor AP.

title: BLOOM: Biologically Informed Flow Matching for Transcriptomic Virtual Embryo Modeling
abstract: Constructing a virtual embryo requires a generative representation of how heterogeneous cell populations change across developmental time. Here we introduce BLOOM, a biologically informed framework for conditional generation of developmental cell populations. BLOOM integrates temporal population context with developmental and regulatory priors through conditional flow matching to generate cell-expression distributions at queried stages in either temporal direction. Evaluation spans three mouse single-cell atlases covering prenatal development, visual-cortex maturation and multi-organ endothelial specialization. In comparisons with 22 time-series forecasting baselines, BLOOM ranks first for gene- and cell-expression correlations across all three datasets. Measured-stage evaluations support recovery of developmental expression patterns, population organization and marker-specific temporal relationships. Biological analyses connect these predictions to cell-state identities, gene programmes and regulatory associations. At unmeasured stages, interpolation and autoregressive history and future rollouts extend simulated expression dynamics between and beyond measured timepoints. Analyses of marker genes and temporal descriptors identify candidate differences in the timing of muscle-associated, neural and vascular-specialization programmes. Input-based gene perturbations further probe predicted responses of edited genes and associated molecular programmes across time. Together, BLOOM supports transcriptomic virtual embryo modeling by bridging temporal sampling gaps, exploring extended developmental trajectories and prioritizing gene-dependent hypotheses for experimental investigation.
authors: Liang Z, Li S, Li B, Huang Y, Yu L.

title: Long-term experimental evolution of seasonal influenza A/H3N2 virus reveals diverse evolutionary potential
abstract: The repeatability of evolutionary outcomes is a fundamental question with implications for predicting the evolution pathogens like influenza viruses. Here, we tested whether seasonal A/H3N2 influenza virus evolution follows reproducible paths in a simplified setting where the natural cellular environment is maintained but adaptive immune selection is removed. We serially passaged replicate populations of an A/H3N2 virus for 1,200 generations across 12 independent differentiated human airway epithelium culture lines (three replicates of four donors) and performed deep sequencing to reconstruct the evolutionary dynamics. Rates of variant accumulation differed significantly among lines but not among donors, and parallel evolution was minimal. Populations generated polymorphisms not observed in the global human population, reversions to historical sequences, and changes at positions held near-invariant globally since 1968. These findings suggest A/H3N2 evolutionary trajectories are shaped less by intrinsic functional constraint than by selective context and help explain why predicting influenza virus evolution remains difficult.
authors: de Rooij AJH, Hulme KD, van Leeuwen S, de Haan K, van Groeningen LE, van Hoesel M, Félix Garza ZC, Eggink D, de Jong SPJ, Han AX, Russell CA.

title: Divide and conquer: a viral bifunctional RNA utilizes both RNA and protein to modulate pro-tumourigenic pathways
abstract: ABSTRACT  Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is an oncogenic herpesvirus that causes the endothelial cell neoplasm Kaposi’s sarcoma (KS) and other B-cell malignancies. The viral transcript  kaposin is largely composed of GC-rich direct repeats (DRs) and is expressed during all phases of KSHV replication.  Kaposin is polycistronic, encoding for at least 3 kaposin (Kap) proteins; of these, KapB is the most abundant and well-studied. Recent work from our lab discovered that  kaposin is found in nuclear speckles (NSs) and that DRs are required for NS retention. During latency,  kaposin is predominantly in NSs and is not exported or translated into KapB. During viral reactivation, abundant  kaposin correlates with  kaposin escape from NSs and KapB protein production. Thus, although  kaposin is a latent transcript, KapB protein production occurs only during lytic reactivation. The spatiotemporal regulation of  kaposin translation by NS retention during KSHV latency likewise suggests that these two biomolecules may have distinct functions. Because historically  kaposin was viewed as a protein-coding mRNA, overexpression studies attributed any function to KapB even though both  kaposin and KapB were produced in these systems. Armed with the knowledge that  kaposin is a bifunctional RNA which derives function from both the transcript and the protein(s) it encodes, it remains unclear whether prior phenotypes should be attributed to  kaposin or KapB. In this study, we developed a reductionist overexpression system to uncouple the effects of these biomolecules. To mimic  kaposin during viral latency, we used a construct capable of forming  kaposin NSs that does not translate reported Kap proteins (ΔStarts). To mimic late lytic reactivation, we used a recoded construct, AltB, that does not form  kaposin NSs, is readily exported from the nucleus, and translates abundant KapB. We found that KapB protein induced actin stress fibre formation, cell enlargement, increased total levels of Yes-associated protein (YAP) and increased YAP-target gene transcription including pro-growth and pro-inflammatory transcripts. Conversely,  kaposin RNA induced cell autonomous p-body disassembly with an overall reduction in pro-growth and pro-inflammatory transcripts, suggesting  kaposin might sustain cell survival while dampening immune signalling. Taken together, we demonstrate that  kaposin RNA and KapB protein have distinct and sometimes opposing effects on cellular growth and inflammatory signalling pathways, highlighting the ability of a viral bifunctional RNA to use both its RNA and protein products to mediate viral tumourigenesis.
authors: Bui-Marinos MP, Corcoran JA.
