title: Modulation of planarian seizure-like activity via antiseizure medications
abstract: Acute chemical exposure to organophosphorus compounds (OPs) arising from terrorist attacks or accidental poisonings pose a serious threat to human health. Acetylcholinesterase inhibition due to acute OP exposure causes a cholinergic crisis, manifested as increased secretions, respiratory distress, loss of consciousness, seizures, and ultimately death if left untreated. Benzodiazepines, such as midazolam, are currently used to stop OP-induced seizures, but must be administered within minutes after exposure to be effective. This makes midazolam impractical for large-scale civilian emergencies. Thus, there is a need to identify novel antiseizure medications (ASMs) that are equally effective even when administered later. It has been challenging to identify such compounds with traditional mammalian testing; high throughput screening assays that can quickly and cost-effectively evaluate many candidates for their potential as an ASM are needed. Planarians are aquatic invertebrates that are suitable organismal models for OP neurotoxicity studies due to the conservation of OP targets and their ability to metabolize OPs. Here, we built on our prior work that introduced a computational image analysis pipeline to quantify planarian seizure-like activity (pSLA) in two planarian species (  Dugesia japonica and Girardia dorotocephala) . We previously used this approach to characterize pSLA following acute exposure (up to 30 minutes) to seizurogenic compounds. In the present study, we asked whether pSLA induced by the OP pesticide parathion, pentylenetetrazole, or NMDA could be rescued by co-exposure to four ASMs: midazolam, topiramate, MK-801, and carbamazepine. All tested ASMs were effective at reducing parathion-induced pSLA in one planarian species. However, ASM responses varied substantially across proconvulsants and planarian species. Defining the molecular mechanisms underlying pSLA will be essential for establishing planarians as a reliable model for ASM discovery.
authors: Ireland D, Bormann E, Coffinas E, Rabeler C, Collins ES.

title: Integrative Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Explainable AI for Disease Mechanism and Biomarker Discovery in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
abstract: ABSTRACT  Invasion is an early step in the metastatic spread of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet cells within a single tumour or cell line differ in their capacity to invade, and it is unclear which transcriptional features distinguish cells that invade from those that do not. We re-analysed the public single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset GSE329526, in which ClonMapper-barcoded MDA-MB-231 cells were separated in a transwell assay into invasive (five samples, 6,289 cells) and non-invasive (five samples, 5,983 cells) fractions and compared with the parental population (one sample, 3,022 cells). An initial cell-level analysis combined Wilcoxon differential expression, an XGBoost classifier with a random cell split, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Enrichr over-representation analysis. Because cells from the same sample are not independent, we then repeated the analysis at the sample level, using differential expression on sample means (five versus five), XGBoost with cross-validation that held out whole samples, a quality-control-metric baseline model, SHAP on held-out samples and rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA). At the sample level, 6,651 of 11,727 tested genes differed between invasive and non-invasive samples (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05), including the ten top-ranked cell-level genes such as  PHLDA2 ,  ANTXR2 ,  VIM and  HMGA1 (FDR 0.0007–0.0022) and the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) regulators  TGFBR2 ,  JAG1 ,  SDCBP and  WWTR1 . With whole samples held out, XGBoost distinguished invasive from non-invasive cells with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.92 (range across folds 0.89–0.95); removing ribosomal and mitochondrial genes did not change performance (AUC 0.92), whereas a model using only four quality-control metrics reached 0.63, and every held-out invasive sample received a higher mean predicted probability of invasion (0.74–0.79) than every non-invasive sample (0.20–0.28). On held-out samples, SHAP ranked inflammatory and stress-response genes highest (  CCL2 ,  LGALS12 ,  DUSP1 ,  CXCL3 ,  KYNU ,  CXCL2 ), and GSEA showed higher KRAS signalling (normalised enrichment score [NES] 2.30, FDR 0.001) and E2F targets (NES 1.62, FDR 0.038) and lower interferon-α and -γ responses (NES −1.97 and −1.65; FDR 0.001 and 0.019) in invasive samples. The ribosomal genes that dominated the original SHAP ranking were absent from the held-out ranking. Invasive MDA-MB-231 cells therefore carry a transcriptional state that is reproducible across independent transwell samples and involves EMT-related, inflammatory and proliferative programmes. Limitations include a single cell line, sequencing of the invasive and non-invasive populations in separate libraries and the absence of external validation; the candidate genes reported here are hypotheses that require confirmation in independent experiments and patient material.
authors: Huda T, Biswas S.

title: Rainfall increases similarity in plant species composition between grazed and ungrazed sites in a tropical semi-arid grassland
abstract: 1. In peninsular India, semi-arid grasslands support marginal farmers and rich endemic biodiversity, yet are commonly designated as wastelands, and fragmentation has caused heavy grazing by domestic and wild mammals. The impacts of unmanaged grazing and increasingly variable monsoon rainfall on the plant community are unknown. 2. We studied an ancient tropical semi-arid grassland in a drought year and a subsequent wet year. In replicated grazed and long-term ungrazed sites, we assessed plant community composition, richness, biomass, traits and functional groups, as well as invertebrate herbivory, fungal infection, soil and plant nutrient stoichiometry. 3. We found that grasses dominated over forbs and legumes. The species richness rose from 35 in the dry year to 84 in the wet year, reflecting the grassland's long evolutionary history of high variation of annual rainfall. However, community composition differed greatly between grazed and ungrazed sites, especially in the dry year. Grass Heteropogon contortus was abundant in the wet year, while Chrysopogon fulvus dominated ungrazed sites in the dry year. H. contortus may persist under heavy grazing owing to its low palatability, whereas fast-growing C. fulvus may outcompete it given sufficient rain and no grazing. Specific leaf area was unrelated to grazing, but increased in the wet year, probably reflecting more acquisitive species. 4. Most plants had insect damage, which was 10% lower in the wet year despite high community-level plant nitrogen, perhaps because high plant density reduced per capita herbivory. Fungal disease incidence was high in the wet year, possibly due to rapid pathogen growth in the humid microclimate. Plant and soil C:N ratios were low in the wet year, when greater legume cover may have increased N availability. 5. Synthesis. Both grazing and rainfall shaped the plant community. Grazing affected species composition, whereas rainfall affected species richness, herbivory and disease incidence. As climate change makes the Indian monsoon more extreme and land use confines grazers to smaller areas, plant species diversity is likely to decline, even among plants adapted to both aridity and grazing.
authors: V. R S, van Nouhuys S.

title: Amniotic Fluid Stem Cell-Derived Secretome MRG1061 Improves Alveolarisation and Reduces Lung Inflammation in Experimental Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia
abstract: Abstract    Background  Mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC)-derived secretomes are emerging as scalable, cell-free candidates for regenerative and immunomodulatory therapy, but their mechanistic cargo signatures and translational potential remain incompletely defined. We developed MRG1061, a clinically translatable, amniotic fluid-derived stem cell (AFSC)-derived secretome produced using the proprietary Secretomix® platform, and sought to define its protein cargo, predict key inflammatory and regenerative pathways, and functionally validate these predictions in human  in vitro  systems and an  in vivo  model of lung injury. Methods  Proteomic profiling of MRG1061 was performed across multiple batches and analysed using pathway enrichment and disease-annotation tools to identify inflammation- and repair-relevant signatures, including blinded enrichment for bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) and related chronic inflammatory conditions. Predicted anti-inflammatory and regenerative activities were then tested in human  in vitro  assays using lipopolysaccharide-stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells, an NF-κB reporter lung adenocarcinoma cell line, primary human alveolar epithelial cells, and human lung fibroblasts. To assess  in vivo  relevance, MRG1061 was evaluated in a neonatal hyperoxia-induced lung injury model, with quantitative analyses of lung structure and inflammatory gene expression. A separate study in healthy mice assessed systemic safety by repeated dosing and serum biochemistry. Results  MRG1061 contained extracellular vesicles and a complex protein cargo enriched for pathways linked to innate and adaptive immune regulation, NF-κB signalling, redox homeostasis, apoptosis, and disease annotations that included BPD. Consistent with these predictions, MRG1061 reduced inflammatory gene and protein expression and NF-κB activity in human immune and lung epithelial assays, modulated disturbed proliferation of primary human alveolar epithelial cells, and decreased stress-induced senescence in lung fibroblasts. In neonatal hyperoxia-exposed mice, MRG1061 improved lung architecture and attenuated expression of key inflammatory cytokines and inflammasome components. Repeated administration to healthy mice revealed no adverse effects on survival or standard serum biochemical parameters. Conclusions  MRG1061 exhibits a cargo-defined, multi-modal anti-inflammatory and regenerative profile that translates into measurable effects in human  in vitro  systems and  in vivo  lung injury, while maintaining a favourable safety signal in healthy animals. These data support further development of MRG1061 as a stem cell-free biologic for inflammatory and degenerative lung disease.
authors: Doktor F, Parnell A, Antounians L, Feist D, Mellows B, Figueira RL, Fortuna V, Khalaj K, Asadpour A, Lo E, Rai A, Ray S, Stasiewicz K, Widera D, Zani A, Patel K, Mitchell R.

title: Mediator Selection in Linear and Nonlinear Mediation Analysis via Adaptive Measurement Errors Infusion
abstract: Abstract    Background:  Mediation analysis investigates intermediate mechanisms through which an exposure influences an outcome. When there are multiple candidate mediators, mediator selection should precede the estimation of mediation effects but remains challenging when pathway signals are weak or imbalanced, when mediator-outcome relationships are nonlinear, and when there are mediator-exposure and/or mediator-mediator interactions. Most existing methods rely on coefficient-based regularization under linear outcome models. We propose a multiple-mediator selection framework based on the measurement error model-ing (MEM) principle, which quantifies a mediator’s importance by how much the fit of the exposure–mediator and mediator–outcome pathways degrades when the mediator is deliberately perturbed by a controlled infusion of artificial measurement error.  Results:  For linear mediation systems, the proposed adaptive MEM procedure distributes a constrained measurement-error precision budget across mediators under a joint Gaussian working criterion, then selects exposure–mediator and mediator–outcome pathways separately, and lastly retains a mediator only if it is selected in both pathways. For nonlinear mediator-outcome relationships, an adaptive kernel MEM extension retains linear exposure–mediator models and replaces the error precisions for the mediators in the outcome model with coordinate-specific inverse bandwidths. In simulations, linear MEM was competitive with established methods designed for linear mediation systems, with a modest advantage when mediator residuals were correlated. Kernel MEM substantially improved the selection of mediators entering the outcome model through quadratic or interaction terms relative to the linear methods and outper-formed a generic kernel-ridge importance benchmark in most simulation settings. Applied to a DNA methylation study of childhood trauma and adult cortisol stress reactivity, the linear and kernel MEM methods selected eight and three loci, respectively, several of which had been reported in previous analyses of the same data.  Conclusions:  The proposed MEM framework provides a practical approach to multiple mediator selection under linear and nonlinear mediator-outcome relationships, yielding candidate mediators supported by evidence from both pathways.
authors: Liang C, Zhou W, Liu M.

title: The ACVR1C-GAS6 Antagonistic Axis Drives Metabolic Decompensation and Liver Fibrosis in MASLD: Mechanistic Insights from Multi-omics Analyses
abstract: Abstract    Background  Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most prevalent chronic liver disease worldwide, and liver fibrosis stage is the strongest determinant of long-term morbidity and mortality in affected patients. However, the molecular switches driving the transition from compensated steatosis to progressive fibrogenesis remain poorly characterized, limiting the development of early diagnostic biomarkers and targeted therapeutic interventions.  Methods  We integrated machine learning-based bulk transcriptome screening, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomic validation, and transcriptional regulatory network analysis to systematically dissect the functional roles and interplay of ACVR1C and GAS6 during MASLD progression.  Results  We identified the ACVR1C-GAS6 antagonistic axis as a central regulatory hub governing hepatocyte metabolic homeostasis and macrophage functional polarization. ACVR1C exerts a previously unrecognized homeostatic gatekeeper role in sustaining hepatocyte detoxification pathways, whereas GAS6 is progressively upregulated across fibrosis stages with a distinct expression threshold marking fibrogenesis onset. Mechanistically, GAS6 drives polarization of heme-related macrophages via the MERTK-STAT3 cascade, which synergizes with direct hepatic stellate cell activation to promote liver fibrosis through a dual pathway. Spatial transcriptomic analysis in a mouse MASLD model further confirmed enhanced in situ co-localization of Gas6 and Mertk in diseased liver tissue.  Conclusions  The ACVR1C-GAS6 axis provides a novel molecular framework for understanding MASLD progression, and represents promising candidate biomarkers for disease risk stratification and therapeutic targets for clinical translation.
authors: Chen S, Zeng Z, Zhang M, Liu X.

title: Investigating the environmental response mechanisms of urban basin to reclaimed water system: A case study in Northeast China
abstract: Abstract  Reclaimed water (RW) replenishment is an effective approach to addressing regional water scarcity in river basins; however, such artificial interventions significantly influence the basin environment. This study investigates the environmental response mechanisms in the Hejiagou (RHJ) River Basin in Harbin, a typical water-scarce city in Northeast China, under RW replenishment. Through in-situ monitoring from 2021 to 2024, MIKE21 modeling simulations, and statistical analysis, this study explores the basin's environmental response mechanisms under RW replenishment. The results indicate that RW recharge increased channel storage capacity by 34.62%. During non-frozen periods and when water shutdown conditions were not present, flow rates stabilized at 2 ~ 3m³/s, with velocities exceeding 2.5 m/s. Fluctuations in discharge water quality emerged as the primary factor influencing downstream river segments, with seasonal and spatial variations determining differential quality levels across different reaches. The physical, chemical, and biological properties of sediments and microorganisms downstream of the discharge point were highly correlated with water quality. Long-term discharge and scouring elevated the downstream riverbed by 0.5 ~ 1.0m, with an average scour depth of 0.9m/a. Hydrodynamic simulations revealed substantial impacts of the discharge point on all river segments. Recommendations for strategies, such as wastewater treatment plant upgrades and dredging, provide scientifically grounded guidance for mitigating similar environmental issues in catchment areas.
authors: Ge Q, Zhang g, Zhu c, Huang X, Zhao S, Feng G.

title: Identification and Functional Characterization of a Cardosin B Homolog in Physcomitrium patens with Milk-Clotting Activity
abstract: Abstract    Plant aspartic proteases are promising alternatives to animal-derived milk-clotting enzymes, although their potential in bryophytes remains largely unexplored. In this study, we investigated endogenous homologs of Cardosin B from  Cynara cardunculus  in the moss  Physcomitrium patens  and evaluated their potential milk-clotting activity. A BLASTp search against the  P. patens  proteome identified 16 candidate proteins, of which three exhibited high sequence similarity to Cardosin B (55–56%) and conserved structural features, including two catalytic aspartate residues and saposin-like domains. The closest homolog,  PpAP1  (PpV7_05g0093900-5), was selected for functional characterization. Stable transgenic  P. patens  lines overexpressing PpAP1 were generated, and increased  PpAP1  transcript accumulation was confirmed by quantitative RT-PCR. Milk-clotting assays revealed coagulation exclusively in protein extracts from PpAP1-overexpressing plants, whereas wild-type extracts showed no detectable activity. Notably, coagulation was completely abolished in the presence of aspartic protease inhibitors, supporting the involvement of aspartic protease activity. These findings provide functional evidence linking PpAP1 overexpression to milk-clotting activity and identify this moss-derived protease as a promising candidate for further biochemical characterization and potential applications in dairy biotechnology.
authors: Baroffio A, Panario AV, Villadóniga C, Pérez-Díaz L, Ruibal C.

title: Automatic Assessment and Grading of Chinese Grammar Knowledge for International Chinese Education Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Abstract  Accurate assessment of Chinese grammar in international Chinese education requires more than detecting a malformed sentence: a system must identify the linguistic construction being tested, distinguish acceptable variants from true violations, assign a rubric-consistent grade, and justify feedback using inspectable pedagogical evidence. While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides access to external grammar resources, conventional retrieve-then-generate architectures do not guarantee that retrieved rules license individual diagnostic or grading decisions. We formulate grammar assessment as proof-carrying constrained inference, and propose PC$^2$G (Proof-Carrying Counterfactual Grading), a model in which rule retrieval, error-span inference, minimal repair, ordinal scoring, and uncertainty-aware feedback are coupled by a shared latent evidence graph. Candidate evaluations must carry rule-level support certificates and satisfy counterfactual necessity, paraphrase consistency, rubric monotonicity, and abstention constraints. A variational objective combines evidence posterior learning with structured prediction and a distributionally robust counterfactual term; a conformal audit layer is designed for deployment-time risk control when calibration assumptions hold. We detail an evaluation protocol using publicly released Chinese learner and native-speaker grammatical error corpora, clarify which tasks their gold annotations actually support, and propose a separate human-grade annotation extension. The evaluation compares retrieval-assisted baselines on Chinese grammatical error corpora, and analyzes graded proxy agreement, evidence faithfulness, retrieval noise, counterfactual stability, and selective prediction.
authors: Wang Y, Lou R, Ke L, Duo Q.

title: PALR-DNA: A Probability-Aware Latent Recovery Framework for Error-Resilient Image Storage in DNA
abstract: Abstract  In DNA-based image storage, base errors inevitably degrade image reconstruction quality. Existing deep-learning methods are effective in correcting base errors while often overlooking uncertainty encoded in low-probability predictions, thereby limiting reconstruction quality. To address this issue, PALR-DNA, a probability-aware latent recovery framework for error-resilient image storage in DNA, is proposed in this study. It represents images as spatially indexed latent vectors and exploits byte-level probability distributions for recovery from noisy DNA sequences. Specifically, a DNA-to-latent recovery transformer is developed to map variable length noisy sequences directly to byte probability distributions. Top-K candidate beam search is employed to explore high-probability candidates and select sequences with valid spatial indices passing cyclic redundancy checks. Bytewise maximum-probability estimation approximates unresolved latent vectors from the remaining probability information. Reconstruction results for 543 images demonstrate that PALR-DNA outperforms the baseline methods across 1–5% error rates, with larger gains at higher rates. At 5%, it achieves a latent-vector recovery accuracy of 93.61%, peak signal-to-noise ratio of 27.45 dB, and multiscale structural similarity index measure of 0.918, while remaining stable across error compositions. Overall, PALR-DNA provides a new approach to error-resilient image reconstruction in DNA storage by retaining byte-level probability information.
authors: Chen S, Zhao R, Wu T, Huang T, Huang X, Sun Q.

title: Single-cell-informed machine learning reveals prognostic and immune features of multiple myeloma
abstract: Abstract    Background  Multiple myeloma (MM) is clinically heterogeneous, and the International Staging System (ISS) captures this heterogeneity only in part. We aimed to build a transcriptomic risk model anchored in single-cell and stage-associated gene expression, and to explore its immune context and therapeutic implications. Methods  Bone marrow single-cell RNA sequencing data from 18 MM and 18 control samples were integrated with ISS stage-stratified RNA sequencing data from the MMRF CoMMpass cohort (n = 764). Candidate genes were filtered by univariate Cox regression, and 101 combinations of 10 machine learning algorithms were benchmarked. The model was validated in three independent cohorts (GSE136337, GSE2658 and GSE4581) and examined with T cell subclustering, immune deconvolution, drug sensitivity prediction, genetic dependency data and molecular docking. Results  Integration yielded eight candidate genes, five of which (  DLGAP5  ,  CENPF  ,  PFDN2  ,  HNRNPF  and  MAP2K1  ) were associated with overall survival. A random survival forest plus supervised principal components model achieved a C-index of 0.69 in training and 0.62 to 0.63 in validation, outperformed 16 published MM signatures and remained independently prognostic after adjustment for age, sex and ISS stage (HR 2.02, 95% CI 1.70 to 2.41). High-risk patients had lower immune and stromal scores, higher TIDE scores and fewer predicted immunotherapy responders. Docking supported binding of risk-associated compounds to  MAP2K1  . Conclusion  This five-gene signature refines risk stratification beyond ISS, marks an immune-depleted high-risk phenotype and nominates  MAP2K1  as a candidate therapeutic target in MM.
authors: Li Q, Dai J, Liu H, Sharma A, Schmidt-Wolf IG, Pu J.

title: Secondary Analysis of Clinical Bulk RNA-Sequencing Samples from Dengue Virus-Infected Patients Reveals EGFR, mTOR, and VEGF-A as Potential Therapeutic Targets
abstract: Almost half of the human population lives in areas where dengue virus (DENV) is endemic and are at risk of infection. The aim of the current study was to analyze 65 publicly available bulk RNA-sequencing samples from the GEO NCBI database. We hypothesized that investigating gene expression in patients with DENV infection compared to healthy controls could identify potential therapeutic targets and augment our understanding of the intracellular transcriptomic response to DENV infection. We report various genes with significant differential expression and multiple predicted drug targets that could be repurposed to reduce the signs and symptoms associated with DENV infection.
authors: Eldredge AK, Pickett BE, Walker ND.

title: Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy for food safety analysis: sample presentation, data interpretation, and application readiness.
abstract: Food-safety decisions require rapid screening of adulteration, origin fraud, elemental contamination and freshness loss. Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) provides direct multi-element fingerprints with short acquisition times and little reagent consumption. Its performance in foods, however, depends on a coupled analytical chain: sample presentation controls laser coupling and mass removal; plasma evolution and acquisition govern emission; calibration and modelling determine interpretation; and validation establishes reliability beyond the development dataset. This critical review uses that chain to assess food-related LIBS workflows. It examines powders, moist tissues, fatty materials, liquids and spatially heterogeneous samples, then considers plasma-aware acquisition, preprocessing, chemometrics, deep learning and multimodal fusion. Task-specific comparisons with ICP-based methods, near-infrared spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy and hyperspectral imaging clarify where LIBS adds value. Pelletization provides a reproducible baseline for many powders, whereas moist, fatty and liquid matrices often require flattening, phase control, immobilization or enrichment. Readiness is strongest for selected mineral-related authenticity screens and elemental warning at concentrations clearly above a decision threshold, provided that independent validation and quality control are available. Closed-set provenance and portable sorting are generally less mature, while regulatory trace confirmation, cross-instrument transfer and realistic microbial analysis require stronger evidence. Progress depends on end-to-end timing, threshold-focused validation, interpretable models, drift monitoring and selective confirmation with complementary techniques.
authors: Hou Y, Li Z, Lian J.

title: Plant Polyphenol-Polysaccharide Complexes for Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Molecular Interactions, Nano-Delivery Design, and Translational Evidence.
abstract: ContextPlant polyphenol-polysaccharide complexes (PPCs) combine polyphenol bioactivity with the protective, mucoadhesive, and microbiota-accessible properties of polysaccharides. However, the literature often groups chemically distinct polyphenols together, extrapolates structure-function relationships across nonequivalent carriers, and interprets concurrent microbiota or short-chain fatty acid changes as causal mechanisms.ObjectiveThis review critically evaluated how molecular interactions and measurable structural attributes of PPCs influence gastrointestinal stability, colon-oriented release, biological effects relevant to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and translational readiness.Data sourcesTargeted searches of PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were completed through July 20, 2026. Peer-reviewed original studies and relevant reviews published in English were considered.Data extractionEvidence was classified as direct PPC evidence, PPC-relevant formulation evidence, or non-PPC mechanistic and engineering evidence. Information on carrier chemistry, payload, structural attributes, release behavior, biological outcomes, and translational considerations was extracted.Data analysisQuantitative findings were compared only when carrier chemistry, payload, test conditions, and outcomes were sufficiently aligned; heterogeneous data were not pooled. Non-covalent assembly and covalent conjugation can alter molecular organization, physicochemical stability, and release, but no universal relationship between degree of substitution and release is supported. Epigallocatechin-3-gallate, quercetin, and anthocyanins require compound-specific carrier selection. PPC and PPC-relevant interventions are associated with changes in NF-κB-related signaling, epithelial-barrier markers, microbiota composition, and individual short-chain fatty acids, whereas receptor- or microbiota-mediated causality remains largely unverified. Responsive platforms also differ in stability, release control, scale-up burden, and clinical readiness.ConclusionsPPC-based nano-delivery is a promising preclinical approach, but translation requires matched studies linking structure, properties, and release, mediator-level mechanistic validation, standardized characterization, reproducible manufacturing, formulation-specific safety assessment, and comparison with established IBD therapies.
authors: Mu J, Ma F, Zheng X, Fan Y, Fu J.

title: IL-6 Blockade with Clazakizumab is Associated with Low Myeloid Cell Activation and Increased Type 2 Immune Responses in Non-survivors of COVID-19.
abstract: BackgroundIL-6 inhibitors have been associated with reduced mortality in severe COVID-19 in randomized clinical trials, but the comprehensive immunological impact of IL-6 blockade in the setting of an acute viral infection is poorly understood.MethodsTo gain insight into the systemic immune response to IL-6 inhibition in COVID-19, we utilized samples from patients who participated in a randomized placebo-controlled trial of clazakizumab, a direct anti-IL-6 monoclonal antibody, in severe COVID-19 in the pre-vaccine era. We applied multidimensional measurements of cytokines, chemokines, whole blood transcriptomes, and high-dimensional immune-metabolic flow cytometry to samples before and after treatment to study the changes in immune signatures after IL-6 blockade and to identify pathways associated with positive clinical outcomes.ResultsClazakizumab was associated with a distinct myeloid activation signature and type 2 (T2) cytokine response. Non-survivors who received clazakizumab demonstrated a decoupling of these two clazakizumab-associated phenotypes, exhibiting the most pronounced T2 response coupled with less myeloid activation. Furthermore, elevated baseline levels of the emergency myelopoiesis related cytokine, IL-27, were strongly associated with non-survival after receipt of clazakizumab.ConclusionsThese findings suggest that specific biomarkers may identify patients most likely to benefit from IL-6 blockade and could lead to more personalized applications in COVID-19 and other inflammatory conditions in which IL-6 targeted therapies are in use.
authors: Stoddart L, Johnston TS, Zhou W, El-Diwany R, Leung S, Alachkar N, Wesson RN, Thompson EA, Cox AL, Karaba AH.

title: Nutritional optimization of hydroponic green fodder using dairy farm wastewater.
abstract: This study evaluates the reuse of dairy farm wastewater (DFW) as an alternative irrigation and fertigation source for winter hydroponic green fodder (barley and oats), with a focus on nutritional optimization. The wastewater was characterized (pH, TS/TFS/TVS, TN, TP, K, COD, turbidity, and coliforms/E. coli) and disinfected using hydrogen peroxide (H2O2; 0.05, 0.2, and 0.4 M; 10, 30, and 60 min), with and without UV radiation (254 nm). A factorial experiment compared fresh water, commercial fertilizer (Triple 18), and five DFW dilution levels (0, 25, 50, 75, and 100%) in terms of biomass production, plant height, root development, dry matter, ash content, crude protein, fiber fractions, and microbial safety. Hydroponic green fodder irrigated with disinfected DFW showed no detectable coliforms or E. coli after growth, confirming the effectiveness of the disinfection process. Productivity indicators were comparable to conventional treatments at intermediate dilution levels. However, the use of DFW significantly influenced the nutritional composition of the fodder, with distinct responses between barley and oats. Intermediate dilutions (DFW-25 to DFW-75) consistently provided the most favorable balance between crude protein and structural fiber fractions, whereas full-strength effluent (DFW-100) tended to reduce yield or increase fiber content, depending on the species. These findings demonstrate that diluted dairy farm wastewater can be effectively integrated into hydroponic systems as a partial substitute for freshwater and synthetic fertilizers. This approach enhances resource use efficiency and supports the development of circular and sustainable livestock production systems, particularly in regions facing water scarcity and limited arable land.
authors: Oliveira GA, Santana Á, Mérida LGR, Rodriguez CB, Padrón RAR.

title: Glutathione at the Interface of Specialized Sulfur Metabolism and Sulfur Homeostasis.
abstract: Glutathione (GSH) is a central component of plant sulfur metabolism, best known for its roles in redox homeostasis, detoxification, and stress protection. Increasing evidence indicates that GSH also functions at the interface between primary and specialized sulfur metabolism. In plants, the best-characterized examples are concentrated in a limited number of lineages, particularly Brassicaceae and Allium species, where GSH is recruited into glucosinolate, camalexin, and S-alk(en)ylcysteine sulfoxide biosynthesis. Emerging observations further highlight the contribution of GSH degradation enzymes to sulfur transfer during specialized metabolite formation, linking GSH turnover to broader sulfur allocation networks. Beyond biosynthesis, GSH conjugation plays critical roles during specialized metabolite degradation by reducing the reactivity of intermediates, shaping immune-related metabolic outcomes, and enabling sulfur recycling through coordinated pathways of GSH degradation and resynthesis. Comparable GSH-dependent strategies in microbes and animals underscore the evolutionary conservation of GSH as a versatile metabolic scaffold. Collectively, these findings support a revised view in which specialized metabolism is embedded within dynamic GSH-dependent sulfur fluxes rather than functioning as an isolated sulfur sink. This review aims to integrate recent advances that highlight the role of GSH in connecting primary and specialized sulfur metabolism in response to environmental and developmental cues.
authors: Sugiyama R, Ito T, Ohkama-Ohtsu N, Hirai MY.

title: O-GlcNAcylation of GSDMD promotes mitochondrial dysfunction and hepatocyte injury in MASLD.
abstract: Background/aimsCell-membrane gasdermin D (GSDMD) plays a key role as a pyroptosis executor of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). However, the mitochondrial translocation of GSDMD occurs even during the metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver (MASL) phase, which involves mainly hepatic steatosis without tremendous inflammatory responses or sustainable hepatic cell death; the underlying mechanism is unknown. We investigated the role of GSDMD in the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).MethodsLiver tissues from patients with MASLD and control subjects were obtained to evaluate GSDMD expression and distribution. GSDMD△hep mice and their floxed littermate controls, GSDMDfl/fl mice, were fed a high-fat, high-cholesterol diet (HFHCD) for 4 and 12 weeks to develop MASL or MASH, respectively. Additionally, GSDMD△hep mice were administered an adeno-associated virus 8 (AAV8) vector expressing wild-type GSDMD (GSDMD-WT) or GSDMD O-GlcNAcylation site mutants (GSDMD-T174/S178A) and were provided with an HFHCD or a methionine-choline-deficient diet.ResultsGSDMD expression and mitochondrial translocation were increased in patients and experimental mice with MASLD. The translocation of GSDMD-NT to mitochondria impaired the mitochondrial membrane potential and promoted the leakage of cytochrome c and mitochondrial DNA, thus inducing early hepatocyte apoptosis, and was required for pyroptosis in MASLD. O-GlcNAcylation at T173/T175 (in humans) or T174/S178 (in mice) of GSDMD was responsible for GSDMD mitochondrial translocation and mitochondrial dysfunction. Targeting O-GlcNAcylation with Celecoxib suppressed GSDMD mitochondrial translocation and the development of MASLD.ConclusionsTargeting mitochondrial GSDMD-mediated programed cell death (PCD) pathways may provide new insights into the potential theoretical basis for MASLD interventions.
authors: Wang X, Jiang M, Xie N, Chen X, Wang W, Yang S, Zhao T, Chen Q, Zhang F, Wang L, Liang J, Zhang Z, Zhuge Y, Xu B.

title: Investigating emerging contaminants in dams from the Vhembe District in Limpopo and, for the first time, in the Orlando Dam, Gauteng Province, South Africa.
abstract: Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), including certain organophosphate pesticides, herbicides, fungicides, and metals, as well as pharmaceuticals such as antiretroviral drugs (ARVs), are contaminants of increasing concern in freshwater sources in South Africa (SA). One surface water sample from each site was collected from dams in an urban area, Gauteng Province, and from a rural area, the Vhembe District in the Limpopo Province in SA. The water was tested for dolutegravir, nevirapine, tenofovir disoproxil, lamivudine, and efavirenz, human and veterinary pharmaceuticals, insecticides, herbicides, fungicides, and metals. Analytical methods included gas chromatography coupled to time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC-TOF), liquid chromatography-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LC-TOF) screening, and liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS/MS). The metals were determined by a semi-quantitative inductively coupled plasma (ICP)-scan. The Orlando Dam screened positive for the five ARVs and two antibiotics, sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, and fourteen pesticides were present in the Orlando Dam, two at the Nandoni Dam, one at the TateVondo Dam, three at the Albasini Dam, and two at the Xikundu Weir from the rural area. From 68 metals measured, aluminium (Al), manganese (Mn), and (Zn) were above water quality guidelines. This is the first report of selected ARVs, organochlorine pesticides as EDCs, organophosphate pesticides, herbicides, fungicides, and metals in the Orlando Dam, Gauteng Province, SA.
journal: Environmental science and pollution research international
authors: Seshoka MF, van Dyk J, Barnhoorn IJ.

title: Novel insights into the versatility of the metallothionein NmtA in a filamentous cyanobacterium.
abstract: Metallothioneins (MTs) are low molecular weight, intracellular, metal sequestering proteins that are unusually rich in cysteine content. Although physiologically comparable to well defined eukaryotic MTs, studies on the roles of prokaryotic MTs are limited. We had previously characterized unannotated prokaryotic MT, namely nmtA in the diazotrophic filamentous cyanobacterium, Anabaena PCC 7120. In the present study, by modulation of the in vivo levels of NmtA, we identified its role in metal homeostasis and detoxification and antioxidant protection in Anabaena 7120. While overexpression of NmtA in Anabaena (AnnmtA+) resulted in enhanced accumulation of Zn2+ and resistance to Cd2+, downregulation of NmtA (AnASnmtA) caused increased Cd2+ sensitivity and lesser accumulation of Zn2+. Probing into metal dependent expression of nmtA, we identified metal sensing motifs in α5 helix of AzuR, the negative regulator of NmtA by site directed mutagenesis. Transcriptome analysis of recombinant Anabaena overexpressing AzuR (AnazuR+) recognized differential gene expression that regulated Zn2+ metabolism. The protective role under oxidative stress of NmtA was affirmed by free radical scavenging ability via oxidative stress-induced Zn2+ mobilization by NmtA and enhanced sensitivity of AnASnmtA to H2O2 stress. The metal binding potential of NmtA prompted us to immobilize NmtA onto citrate functionalized magnetic nanoparticles (CMNP-NmtA) that demonstrated ~ 51% Cd2+ removal from industrial wastewater supplemented with 10 µg/mL Cd in presence of other heavy metals. Overall, this study established the multifaceted functions of metallothionein from diazotrophic, filamentous cyanobacterium advancing information on the otherwise less explored prokaryotic MT diversity.
journal: Biometals : an international journal on the role of metal ions in biology, biochemistry, and medicine
authors: Divya TV, Pimple MV, Acharya C.

title: Decoding the molecular landscape of radiation-induced oral mucositis: Integrated molecular networks and therapeutic targets.
abstract: ObjectiveThis narrative, mechanism-oriented review aimed to provide an integrated overview of the molecular mechanisms underlying radiation-induced oral mucositis (RIOM) and identify potential therapeutic targets with translational and clinical relevance.DesignTargeted literature searches were conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar from inception to September 3, 2026. Relevant literature was selected and synthesized to examine RIOM molecular mechanisms, regulatory networks, and potential therapeutic targets, with a clear distinction between direct RIOM evidence and mechanistic insights extrapolated from other diseases or experimental models. Therapeutic approaches were discussed in relation to their stage of development, clinical relevance, and limitations to clinical translation.ResultsCurrent evidence indicates that RIOM is driven by a complex and interconnected molecular network involving radiation-induced DNA damage and oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling amplification, diverse cell death modalities, immune and stromal dysregulation, epithelial barrier disruption, microbiota imbalance, and impaired tissue repair. By integrating these processes into a unified pathogenic framework, this review highlights the dynamic interplay between tissue injury, inflammation, and repair failure that underlies disease progression. Furthermore, emerging molecular targets involved in these pathways are mapped across the course of RIOM development.ConclusionsThis review summarizes the key molecular mechanisms that govern the initiation and progression of RIOM and, on this basis, delineates molecular drug targets with potential translational and clinical relevance. These insights provide a conceptual framework to enhance our understanding of RIOM pathobiology and may develop more effective prevention and treatment strategies.
authors: Xu T, Liu Z, Li J, Gao K, Pei Y, Wei Z, Min Y, Peng X.

title: A compact generative language model learns the compositional grammar of phase-separating proteins.
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of intrinsically disordered proteins drives the formation of biomolecular condensates, yet the sequence-level grammar that promotes condensation remains difficult to specify from first principles. Existing protein language models are typically trained on large, folded-protein-rich sequence corpora and may not optimally capture the compositional biases of LLPS-prone disordered proteins. Here, we show that a compact generative language model, with an architecture and size (∼17 M parameters) selected via systematic hyperparameter optimization and cross-validation, trained from scratch on a small set of phase-separating protein sequences, can learn sequence features associated with condensate formation. The model generates thousands of sequences that reproduce length-dependent trends in disorder, charge decoration, hydropathy patterning, and sequence entropy, with training and generative behavior stable across independent seeds. Homology analysis indicates that generated sequences are not full-length copies of known proteins, but instead combine short segments matching natural proteins with a novel, model-generated sequence. Descriptor-based screening of short generated sequences yielded a pool of disordered candidates, from which five synthetically feasible peptides were selected for experimental testing. Four of them show condensate-like signatures under near-physiological conditions, including droplet-like assemblies and increased turbidity. Coarse-grained phase-coexistence simulations of a subset of generated sequences with longer lengths show a broad range of phase-separation tendencies, with 12 of 89 sequences comparable to the strongly phase-separating hnRNPA1 low-complexity domain. These results suggest that compact, task-specific generative models can learn information-rich sequence grammars from small curated datasets and propose experimentally testable condensate-forming peptides.
authors: Wasim A, Pramanik U, Das A, Latua P, Rudra JS, Mondal J.

title: Feeder-free expansion and early cardiomyogenic commitment of a human umbilical cord blood-derived cell population with very small embryonic-like stem cell (VSEL)-Like features.
abstract: BackgroundHeart failure following myocardial infarction remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Very small embryonic-like stem cells (VSELs) derived from human umbilical cord blood (hUCB) represent a promising candidate cell source for cardiac regenerative applications; however, their cardiomyogenic potential has not been systematically investigated.MethodsA small, non-hematopoietic, cord blood-derived cell population previously characterized by our group as VSEL-like was isolated via sequential centrifugation and expanded ex vivo for 7 days under serum-free cytokine-supplemented conditions. Pluripotency-associated marker expression was assessed by RT-qPCR and baseline transcriptional profiles were compared with Wharton's jelly-derived mesenchymal stem cells (WJ-MSCs) across thirteen genes. Cardiomyogenic differentiation was induced using sequential 5-AZA and TGFβ1, with molecular and morphological assessment at Day 10 of differentiation.ResultsPooling of two UCB units yielded an approximately 4-fold ex vivo expansion (p < 0.001). Following expansion, OCT4 expression increased, whereas NANOG, SOX2 and CXCR4 decreased, indicating culture-associated remodeling of the pluripotency-associated transcriptional profile. Baseline transcriptional profiling revealed significantly higher expression of cardiac/mesoderm-associated markers (GATA4, NKX2.5, BRACHYURY, MESP1, TBX5) in VSEL-like cells compared with WJ-MSCs, consistent with mesodermal/cardiac lineage priming. Following induction, significant upregulation of GATA4, NKX2.5, cTnI (TNNI3) and cTnT (TNNT2) alongside MESP1 downregulation at Differentiation Day 10 was consistent with early cardiac lineage commitment. Embryoid body-like formation and cardiomyocyte-like morphology further supported changes consistent with early cardiomyogenic commitment. These findings support early cardiomyogenic commitment of hUCB-VSEL-like cells under feeder-free, chemically defined 5-AZA/TGFβ1 conditions and provide a foundation for further functional validation in cardiac regenerative medicine research.
authors: Iliadou A, Gounari E, Papameletiou E, Aivaliotis M, Bikiaris DN, Koliakos G.

title: Transcriptome dissection of the Zeb2-associated network reveals a role for  NRPS15  in zearalenone biosynthesis in  Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fungal secondary metabolites, including mycotoxins, play important roles in fungal biology and represent major concerns for food and feed safety. Zearalenone (ZEA) is an estrogenic polyketide mycotoxin produced by several  Fusarium species, yet the genetic network governing its production remains poorly characterized. Here, we investigated genes associated with ZEA production in  Fusarium graminearum using two complementary transcriptomic approaches. Time-resolved transcriptome analysis revealed transcriptional changes preceding detectable ZEA accumulation. Temporal clustering further revealed coordinated changes in primary metabolism, transcriptional regulation, carbohydrate utilization, and stress- and transport-associated pathways during ZEA-inducing cultivation. Genotype-based transcriptome analysis of  ZEB2 deletion and overexpression strains subsequently identified Zeb2-responsive genes. Functional screening identified  NRPS15 , encoding a previously uncharacterized nonribosomal peptide synthetase-like protein adjacent to the ZEA biosynthetic cluster, as an important contributor to ZEA production. Deletion of  NRPS15 markedly reduced ZEA production and expression of  PKS4 ,  PKS13 ,  ZEB1 , and  ZEB2 .  NRPS15 expression did not restore ZEA production in the absence of Zeb2.  NRPS15 orthologs were conserved in several ZEA-producing  Fusarium species, and deletion of  NRPS15 substantially reduced ZEA production in  Fusarium culmorum . These findings expand the functional genetic context of ZEA production beyond the canonical four-gene biosynthetic cluster.
authors: Lee N, Han JW, Kim J, Shin J, Park AR, Lee Y, Kim H, Park J, Son H.

title: Exposure to polyethylene terephthalate nanoplastics elicits renal injury with limited compensation and associated intestinal alterations: A time-resolved multi-omics study.
abstract: Polyethylene terephthalate nanoplastics (PET-NPs) are emerging contaminants of toxicological concern. However, the temporal progression of PET-NPs-induced renal injury during repeated oral exposure remains poorly understood. Male C57BL/6 J mice received PET-NPs at 50 mg/kg/day by oral gavage for 14, 28, or 56 days to characterize time-dependent nephrotoxicity and intestinal alterations. Fluorescence imaging detected gastrointestinal signals at all time points and a time-dependent increase in renal fluorescence following administration of Nile red-labeled PET-NPs. PET-NPs exposure was associated with impaired intestinal barrier integrity and altered gut microbial composition. Renal assessments revealed functional impairment, tubular injury, inflammatory activation, oxidative stress, and lipid peroxidation. Integrated renal transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses identified alterations in inflammatory signaling, redox homeostasis, oxidative phosphorylation, and lipid metabolism. Mean TUNEL positivity was numerically highest at 28 days and remained elevated relative to controls at 56 days. At 56 days, tubular injury, renal dysfunction, and inflammation persisted alongside increased Ki-67 positivity. Although the renal Nrf2/HO-1/GPX4 antioxidant axis was activated, glutathione depletion, lipid peroxidation, and renal injury indicated insufficient antioxidant compensation. Repeated oral PET-NPs exposure elicited time-dependent nephrotoxicity characterized by inflammatory-redox-lipid metabolic remodeling and constrained antioxidant compensation. These findings provide a time-resolved multi-omics framework for assessing PET-NPs-associated renal hazards following repeated oral exposure.
authors: Cui M, Wang X, Li T, Ma H, Li S, Sang R, Zhang X.

title: Fine-mapping of microbeam radiation therapy-induced DNA damage in 2D cell and 3D epidermis models.
abstract: BackgroundMicrobeam radiation therapy (MRT) delivers spatially fractionated, high-dose radiation in parallel beam arrays, creating spatial fractionation by alternating peak and valley dose regions. While this approach offers significant potential for tumor control with reduced normal tissue toxicity, the precise biological dose and damage distribution, particularly the relative contributions of direct and non-targeted (bystander) effects, remain incompletely understood.MethodsWe employed complementary biodosimetric approaches to quantify DNA damage responses in two-dimensional CHO-K1 cell monolayers and three-dimensional epidermis tissue models following MRT. Biological dosimetry in CHO-K1 monolayers was performed using the cytokinesis-block micronucleus (CBMN) assay for micronuclei (MN) and nucleoplasmic bridges (NPB). In epidermis models, DNA double-strand break (DSB) damage was analyzed by immunofluorescence (IF) with γH2AX+53BP1 DSB markers. Spatial and temporal mapping of damage in tissue sections was performed across microbeam peak and valley regions and compared with physical dosimetry and broadbeam irradiation.ResultsIn 2D CHO-K1 cells, MN- and NPB-based biological dosimetry closely matched physical dose measurements, with accurate dose reconstruction in valleys but substantial underestimation in peaks due to extensive cell death and loss of scorable nuclei. In 3D epidermis models, MRT induced distinct spatial patterns of DNA damage with pan-γH2AX-positive cells indicating excessive DSB formation at peak regions at early time points, whereas 53BP1 DSB foci predominated in dose valleys. Over 24 h, pan-γH2AX signals declined to sham levels, while 53BP1 foci persisted, particularly in peak regions, indicating DNA damage regions refractory to repair. Comparative analyses revealed that valley cells exposed to 1 Gy MRT radiation exhibited in average significantly more 53BP1 foci at 0.5 h than after uniform 1 Gy broadbeam irradiation, suggesting a bystander contribution from adjacent high-dose peaks. By 24 h, however, damage levels converged between MRT valleys and broadbeam, indicating that bystander-associated excess damage was transient.ConclusionCBMN-based biological dosimetry reliably quantifies absorbed dose in MRT valleys but is limited in peak regions. 3D epidermis models enable spatial and temporal mapping of DNA damage, revealing persistent complex damage in peak-region cells and provide evidence for transient bystander effects in valley regions. Extending previously established biodosimetric and DNA damage mapping approaches to X-ray MRT, these findings, obtained in one cell line and one tissue model, contribute to the understanding of DSB induction, repair dynamics, and non-targeted effects in MRT.
authors: Nguyen M, Dombrowsky AC, Treibel F, Müller J, Raulefs S, Bartzsch S, Combs SE, Eder S, Schmid TE, Scherthan H.

title: An injectable ROS-responsive natural drug self-delivery hydrogel relieves neuropathic pain by remodeling DRG macrophage-mediated neuroinflammation.
abstract: Neuropathic pain remains a major clinical challenge owing to complex neuroimmune mechanisms and limited disease-modifying therapies. Neuroinflammation within the dorsal root ganglion (DRG), particularly macrophage infiltration and pro-inflammatory polarization, is a key driver of sensory neuronal sensitization and pain persistence. Here, we report an injectable reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive natural drug self-delivery hydrogel for localized and sustained treatment of neuropathic pain. Single-cell transcriptomic reanalysis revealed marked macrophage accumulation in injured DRGs, accompanied by M1-like polarization and aberrant phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)-Akt activation. Mechanism-guided virtual screening identified glycyrrhizic acid (GA), a bioactive natural product, as a promising PI3K-targeting candidate. To improve local bioavailability, GA was engineered into a 1,4-phenylenediboronic acid (1,4-PBA)-functionalized self-assembled hydrogel, termed GA-PBA-GA (GPG), through dynamic boronate ester bonds and non-covalent interactions. The GPG hydrogel exhibited injectability, self-healing, biodegradability, biocompatibility, and inflammation-associated ROS-triggered GA release. In vitro, GPG suppressed PI3K-Akt signaling, reduced pro-inflammatory macrophage activation, and promoted M1-to-M2 repolarization. In a rat model of L5 spinal nerve ligation-induced neuropathic pain, peri-DRG administration alleviated mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity, improved gait and electrophysiological function, reduced DRG macrophage-mediated neuroinflammation, and attenuated spinal microglial activation. This ROS-responsive natural drug self-delivery hydrogel provides a minimally invasive strategy for remodeling DRG neuroinflammation and achieving sustained relief of neuropathic pain through localized drug delivery.
authors: Xing X, Yang G, Liu P, Chen C, Gao H, Li J, Yu H, Feng Y, Jiang G, Wang L, Li P, Zhou L.

title: Single-cell multi-omics reveals archetypal regulatory programs shared across T cell subsets.
abstract: T cells differentiate into functionally distinct subsets in response to pathogens, yet essential immune functions such as self-renewal, expansion, cytokine production, and cytotoxicity are common to multiple subsets and therefore must be programmed via shared regulatory mechanisms. To uncover these "archetypal" epigenomic programs, we integrated a single-cell multiomic (scATAC+RNA-seq) dataset of CD4 and CD8 T cells responding to acute and chronic viral infection with a comprehensive bulk ATAC-seq compendium. Our analysis reveals a modular architecture governing T cell identity, implicating distinct transcription factors in reusing regulatory programs across subsets and lineages. Notably, translationally important progenitor CD8 T cells, critical for sustained immunity and present in both acute and chronic infection, exhibit a composite regulatory state, combining a CD8 exhaustion program with a follicular helper CD4 T cell program. In sum, this resource and generalizable computational framework will aid the mechanistic dissection of adaptive immunity and immunotherapy design.
authors: Walker SK, van der Veeken J, Rudensky AY, Pritykin Y.

title: SPARK: Bayesian Structure Learning of Enhancer-based Gene Regulatory Networks from Single-cell Multiomics Data and Prior Knowledge
abstract: Enhancer-based gene regulatory networks (eGRNs) linking enhancers with recruited transcription factors (TFs) and downstream target genes can help decipher complex regulatory mechanisms, such as the function of GWAS variants at enhancers. Molecular assays that profile gene expression and chromatin state jointly from the same cells (such as 10x Multiome) are a rich source of input data for eGRN reconstruction. However, these assays lack mechanistic evidence for enhancer-gene and TF-enhancer links, which can be contributed by prior knowledge from other assays and analyses. Here, we present SPARK, an eGRN reconstruction framework that formally combines single-cell multiome data with mechanistic prior knowledge. SPARK represents eGRNs as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and learns them using Bayesian inference, with a prior on the network structure constructed from heterogeneous sources of evidence. In a simulation study, we show that SPARK benefits from prior knowledge and outperforms existing DAG-based and regression-based algorithms. Finally, we use SPARK to study the regulatory circuitry of enhancers harboring immune disease GWAS variants in human primary monocytes, revealing known and novel regulatory links as candidates for experimental validation.
authors: Masaki N, Acharya S, Malysheva V, Koturan S, Bottolo L, Spivakov M.

title: Longwall Top-Coal Caving: A Review of Geomechanics, Recovery, Operational Control, and Technology
abstract: Longwall top-coal caving (LTCC) combines the mechanical extraction of the lower seam with caving and drawing of the coal above the cutting horizon. Its performance depends on linked geomechanical, strata-support, granular-flow, operational, and control processes: caving does not by itself ensure selective recovery. This global critical review synthesises research on stress redistribution, fracture-controlled cavability, roof rupture and weighting, drawbody and coal–gangue boundary evolution, drawing interval and sequence, support interaction, hazards, modelling, monitoring, and automation. It distinguishes recurring mechanisms from mine-specific numerical settings and appraises the evidence by study type, represented variables, and degree of field validation. The review's central contribution is a mechanism-to-control assurance framework that connects potential failure states to candidate indicators, mine-approved responses, and verification measures. It treats drawing initiation, sequence, adjustment, and termination as safety-critical decisions within a multi-objective goal of clean-coal recovery, dilution control, ground stability, and hazard management. The evidence remains dominated by simulations and mine-specific cases, with few end-to-end field-validated control demonstrations. The proposed framework is a synthesis for testing, not a validated universal controller; indicators and operating limits require site-specific calibration and field verification.
authors: Balasubrahmanyam N.

title: Evolutionary Mismatch During the Menopausal Transition in Gen X Women: A Clinical Framework for Midlife Management
abstract: Chronic stress, circadian disruption, sedentary behaviour, industrialised diets and disturbances in the gut microbiome have created an evolutionary mismatch between ancestral physiology and the modern environment. When midlife women enter the menopausal transition, cumulative exposure to lifestyle and environmental factors may exacerbate the hormonal changes associated with menopause. As a result, midlife women can present with a mixture of vasomotor, somatic, urogenital, psychological and cognitive symptoms that are often poorly diagnosed and treated in isolation. Our previous review described how evolutionary mismatch in Generation X (Gen X) women disrupts perimenopausal physiology through converging endocrine, psychosocial stress and immunometabolic mechanisms, amplifying symptoms and cardiometabolic risk. This included a detailed discussion of the endocrine changes that underpin the menopausal transition, how chronic psychosocial stress overwhelms whole-body stress response systems, and the impact of converging immunometabolism mechanisms such as chronic inflammation and insulin resistance on whole-body energy homeostasis. In the current review, we extend this model by proposing a Gen X clinical phenotype and an evolutionary realignment framework that translates it into an integrated approach to clinical management. The proposed framework addresses circadian alignment, metabolic flexibility, nutritional and lifestyle factors, allostatic load, environmental exposures, cerebral and mitochondrial health, musculoskeletal function, gut–hormone–microbiome signalling and menopausal hormone therapy, offering practitioners a systems-based approach to midlife care that addresses underlying physiological drivers rather than isolated symptoms.
authors: Hitch V, O'Brien CL, Parker J.

title: Controllable Molecular Delivery from Maternal Cells: A Mechanistic Hypothesis for Selective Chromosome Dosage Compensation in Trisomy 21
abstract: Background:  Expression imbalance in trisomy 21 involves multiple genes and cell types. Establishing XIST expression on a selected chromosome 21 has enabled chromosome-wide silencing and improved some functional outcomes in cultured cells and differentiation models. Extending this capability to patient cells without prior engineering remains constrained by homolog recognition, intact cargo delivery, nuclear localization, and persistence of action. Maternal cells can be investigated as a production platform, but cannot be assumed to possess an innate ability to recognize or repair an additional chromosome in their offspring.Hypothesis. Following identification of a target haplotype and assessment of the functional suitability of the two homologs to be retained, a controllably delivered engineered molecular system might establish single-homolog, chromosome-wide repression in the patient’s own trisomy 21 cells and bring prespecified cellular functions closer to a matched disomic reference. XIST-mediated cis silencing is the principal mechanism considered; physical chromosome elimination is a separate comparative branch. Maternal cell–derived extracellular vesicles are a candidate delivery vehicle, and mother–offspring matching is a platform subhypothesis. IFNAR1 and IFNAR2 modulation serves only to validate local tool activity and function, not as a substitute for chromosome-wide dosage compensation.Discriminating tests. Haplotype recognition, cargo release and nuclear availability, single-homolog action, chromosome-wide expression changes, protection of disomic cells, and functional benefit must be tested separately. Direct-delivery benchmarks, unloaded products, nontargeting cargo, cross-family comparisons, and single-cell analyses distinguish effector activity, delivery performance, source advantages, and cell-population selection. Stopping production, stopping XIST transcription, and reversing established silencing are distinct endpoints.Significance. This framework focuses on chromosome dosage compensation in the patient’s own cells and generates conditional predictions for steps that have not yet been connected experimentally. It reports no original experimental data, presents no complete therapeutic cargo system, and does not claim novelty solely from combining existing modules.
authors: Zhang W.

title: xNNPCD identifies regulators of programmed cell death by integrating perturbation transcriptomes with cancer dependency profiles.
abstract: Programmed cell death (PCD) encompasses regulated processes whose dysregulation shapes cancer fitness, yet computational studies use known PCD genes for prognosis rather than discovering regulators. We developed xNNPCD, an interpretable neural-network framework that links CRISPR-Cas9 perturbation signatures from CMap to gene dependency profiles from DepMap. The model constrains hidden neurons to five PCD pathways and iteratively refines a prior gene-PCD pathway mask matrix derived from GO, KEGG, and Reactome using pathway-neuron ablation. This converts binary gene-pathway relationships into continuous-valued associations and improves dependency prediction over random forests, fully connected multi-layer perceptrons, and its own non-iterative variant. The learned mask matrix recovers annotated death regulators and nominates candidate regulators, including RPL23A, HSPA5, SNRPA1, SLC6A2, and ASAH1; combined with dependency scores, it separates pathway coupling from regulatory direction. Transferring the refined mask matrix and learned weights to compound-induced perturbation data enables in silico drug screening, identifying BRD-K19103580 and decitabine as therapeutic agents for apoptosis and ferroptosis, respectively. The pathway-resolved drug profiles can facilitate the design of combination therapies targeting complementary PCD pathways to overcome single-pathway resistance. Overall, xNNPCD offers a pan-cancer, interpretable approach that generalizes across perturbation modalities for mapping the regulatory landscape and elucidating the molecular processes of PCD in cancer.
authors: Yin Q, Chen L.

title: Postdeployment Performance of a Commercial Artificial Intelligence System for Pulmonary Nodule Detection at Chest CT: Examination-Level Agreement, Clinical Indication, and Image-Based Review Across 13,536 Examinations.
abstract: Postdeployment performance of pulmonary nodule detection AI is rarely measured. This retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of prospectively collected routine data evaluated a commercial detection system (ClearRead CT; Riverain Technologies), deployed with a candidate-size threshold of greater than 3 mm, across 13,536 consecutive chest CT examinations at one academic center (January 2025-January 2026). Final reports, classified by natural language processing (NLP; validated against manual review of 896 reports: sensitivity 99.5%, specificity 99.6%, κ 0.99), served as the examination-level comparator; randomly selected discordant examinations were reviewed on images. Because radiologists viewed AI output before reporting, report-referenced results are presented as agreement; accuracy estimates are given only after image review. AI was positive in 9142 examinations (67.5%) and reports documented a nodule in 3919 (29.0%). Positive percent agreement was 80.6% (95% CI 79.4, 81.8), negative percent agreement 37.8%, and report-referenced positive predictive value 34.6%; 5982 examinations (44.2%) were AI positive/report negative, and Cohen κ was 0.13 (maximum attainable, 0.33). Agreement was 98.6% for screening, 38.3% for oncologic, and 32.6% for inpatient/emergency examinations, which contributed 76.1% of discordance. On image review, 291 of 298 (97.7%) AI-positive/report-negative examinations contained only non-nodule structures, and 196 of 198 (99.0%) AI-negative/report-positive examinations contained an unmarked nodule larger than 3 mm, 45 of them (23.0%) larger than 6 mm. Review-adjusted examination-level sensitivity was 81.2%, specificity 38.2%, and positive predictive value 35.4%. These findings describe one configuration at one institution; performance should be measured locally, by indication, and against image review.
journal: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
authors: Zhang JMF, Patel P, Junior MM, See KB, Mancano AD, Gaultier T, Hochhegger B.

title: A biomimetic nanoparticle coordinates antibacterial and immunomodulatory functions to promote periodontal regeneration.
abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder driven by pathogenic microbial communities and an imbalanced host immune response, finally leading to progressive breakdown of periodontal soft and hard tissues. Current treatments primarily target infection but often fail to resolve inflammation or support subsequent tissue repair. Hence, we developed NMm@MINO, a biomimetic nanoparticle constructed by coating minocycline-loaded gelatin nanoparticles with a hybrid neutrophil-macrophage membrane. NMm@MINO formed a stable core-shell structure with a hydrodynamic diameter of (261.53 ± 11.59) nm and a membrane shell thickness of ~21 nm, maintaining colloidal stability for 30 days. Minocycline release was protease-responsive, with ~50% payload released within 2 h under gelatinase exposure and reaching equilibrium at ~8 h. In vitro, NMm@MINO achieved > 99% killing efficiency against Porphyromonas gingivalis and Staphylococcus aureus. Simultaneously, NMm@MINO reprogrammed polarization by downregulating M1-associated transcripts (Nos2, Tnf, Il1b, and Cd86) and upregulating M2-associated markers (Mrc1, Arg1, and Tgfb1), corroborated by decreased iNOS and increased CD206 immunofluorescence. NMm@MINO further enhanced osteogenesis (upregulating Alpl, Spp1, Runx2), suppressed RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis (reduced TRAP staining and downregulated Acp5, Tnfrsf11a, Ctsk, Fos, and Mmp9; decreased c-Fos immunofluorescence), and promoted fibroblast migration with increased Collagen I immunofluorescence. In a ligature-induced rat periodontitis model (days 3, 7, and 14), local NMm@MINO reduced inflammation (IL-6/CRP IHC; decreased Il6, Crp, and Il1b), improved collagen remodeling (H&E/Masson; increased Col1a1), and mitigated alveolar bone loss (micro-CT: CEJ-ABC, BV/TV, Tb.N, Tb.Th, and Tb.Sp) while modulating osteoclast/osteogenic markers (TRAP, RANKL/OPG IHC; Acp5, Tnfsf11, Tnfrsf11b, and Runx2). Collectively, NMm@MINO coordinates antibacterial, immunomodulatory, and pro-regenerative actions for periodontitis therapy.
authors: Tang Y, Xu J, Zheng F, Xue Q, Cheung SW, Sun M, Zhou S, He Y, Xiang L.

title: Temporal multi-omics reveals regulatory transitions and renoprotective candidates in cisplatin-induced kidney injury.
abstract: Cisplatin is a classic first-line platinum drug extensively used in chemotherapy for solid tumors, yet its clinical applications are limited by dose-dependent nephrotoxicity. The dynamic molecular mechanisms underlying cisplatin-induced kidney injury and regeneration remain incompletely understood. Here, we established two complementary mouse models, a single high-dose cisplatin (SHDC) model and a repeated low-dose cisplatin (RLDC) model, to recapitulate acute and progressive/persistent patterns of renal injury, respectively. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses reveal temporal transcript-protein discordance and persistent molecular remodeling. Temporal analysis of protein regulatory dynamics suggests that progression from acute to persistent kidney injury involves a shift from metabolic and xenobiotic-handling responses toward sustained stress and inflammatory programs. Multi-omics factor analysis and random forest modeling prioritize six candidate regulatory genes (NFKB2, JUNB, TNFAIP3, PROS1, NFKBIA, and S100A11) with discriminative value in human AKI cohorts. Upstream transcriptional factor analysis identifies TP53 and STAT1 as critical regulatory nodes. Transcriptome signature-based drug prioritization identifies candidate compounds capable of reversing the molecular signature associated with cisplatin injury, and we validated the renoprotective effects of CGP60474 and A-443654 in both in vitro and in vivo settings. Lastly, we constructed a publicly accessible, interactive Mouse Cisplatin Nephrotoxicity Omics Database (MCNOD) to facilitate data mining and exploration. Collectively, these findings provide critical insights into the dynamic regulatory mechanisms underlying cisplatin nephrotoxicity and contribute to the development of targeted renoprotective strategies.
authors: Gan Z, Zhou H, Liang H, Ding L, Wu Q, Shen J, Huang J, Wang X, Hu N, Ma H, Shao W, Dai L.

title: From loci to mechanisms: wheat autoimmunity as a window into plant immune activation.
abstract: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is a major staple crop, and developing broad-spectrum resistance to multiple fungal pathogens is essential for sustainable production. Wheat autoimmunity (WAI) mutants represent genetic resources that spontaneously activate immune responses under non-stress conditions, exhibiting lesion-mimic or leaf-tip necrosis phenotypes and enhanced resistance to multiple foliar diseases, including powdery mildew and rusts. Increasing evidence indicates that WAI arises from dysregulation of immune homeostasis across multiple regulatory levels, involving receptor activation, cellular homeostasis, and membrane transport processes, ultimately converging on evolutionarily conserved defense outputs such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, activation of defense-related genes, ion fluxes, and programmed cell death (PCD). Recent advances have identified key WAI-associated loci, including nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich-repeat receptors (NLRs), membrane proteins, regulatory components, and transporters, revealing mechanistically distinct pathways underlying constitutive immunity and its trade-off with growth. This review summarizes recent progress in the genetics and molecular mechanisms of WAI, critically assesses its roles in broad-spectrum, multi-disease resistance, and discusses strategies to minimize the growth and fitness costs. Furthermore, we propose that structure-guided allele optimization combined with spatiotemporal regulation of gene expression holds promise for the rational engineering of WAI alleles that confer durable disease resistance while minimizing associated fitness costs.
journal: Journal of genetics and genomics = Yi chuan xue bao
authors: Li W, He M, Xiong F, Wu Q, Jia H, Liu Z.

title: Identification and experimental validation of phospholipase D family member 6 (PLD6) as a mitochondria-related candidate gene in knee osteoarthritis.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to cartilage degeneration in knee osteoarthritis (KOA), but the role of phospholipase D family member 6 (PLD6), a mitochondrial outer membrane phospholipase, remains unclear. This study combined transcriptomic analyses and functional experiments to investigate PLD6 in KOA. Integrated analysis of three human cartilage transcriptomic datasets identified eight mitochondria-related candidate genes through differential expression and weighted gene co-expression network analyses. Machine learning, external human validation, and cross-species evaluation prioritized PLD6 for further investigation. PLD6 expression was reduced in damaged cartilage compared with paired macroscopically intact cartilage from patients with KOA, in cartilage from mice subjected to destabilization of the medial meniscus, and in interleukin-1β (IL-1β)-treated primary murine chondrocytes. In primary murine chondrocytes, PLD6 knockdown reduced type II collagen expression, mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitochondrial respiration, while increasing matrix metalloproteinase 13 (MMP13) expression, the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, and reactive oxygen species levels. PLD6 overexpression under IL-1β stimulation reduced MMP13 expression and the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio and partially restored mitochondrial respiration. These findings suggest that PLD6 downregulation may contribute to chondrocyte mitochondrial dysfunction and cartilage degeneration, supporting PLD6 as a candidate target for further investigation in KOA.
authors: Zhang J, Wang Q, Zhou J, Wei J, Zhang X, Li B, Liu L.

title: A piperamide natural compound is compatible with an inactive DFG-out conformation of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2: In silico and in vitro model study.
abstract: Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2 (VEGFR2) is a well-known key regulator of angiogenic cancers. In a structure-based virtual screening of Indonesian natural compounds, dehydropipernonaline (DPN), a piperamide from Piper species, emerged as a promising VEGFR2-binding candidate. However, its inhibitory activity against VEGFR2 has not been experimentally validated. This study combined molecular simulations and cellular assays to investigate the potential interaction between DPN and VEGFR2. Molecular docking predicted that DPN occupies the regulatory domain pocket (RDP) spanning the catalytic and juxtamembrane (JM) domains, overlapping the binding region of the type II inhibitor tivozanib. All-atom simulations revealed that DPN remains stably associated with the DFG loop. Free-energy surface analysis identified two dominant minima corresponding to a DFG-out/JM-out conformation resembling the inactive, tivozanib-bound VEGFR2 structure rather than the active DFG-in state. Binding free-energy calculations further supported favourable, predominantly hydrophobic stabilization of the DPN-VEGFR2 complex. Experiments in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) were consistent with these predictions. At 10 μM, DPN reduced VEGFR2, PLCG1 (phospholipase C gamma 1) and PRKCE (protein kinase C epsilon) transcripts, total and phosphorylated VEGFR2 (Tyr1054/1059), and VEGF-induced proliferation, but this concentration also reduced cell viability by ~24%, so non-specific cytotoxicity cannot be excluded. At 1 μM, which did not significantly reduce viability, DPN reduced proliferation relative to VEGF-stimulated cells but had no significant effect on the molecular readouts. Collectively, these findings indicate that DPN is compatible with, and remains stably bound within, an inactive type II-like DFG-out conformation of VEGFR2, consistent with (though not proof of) a stabilizing effect on this state; this is accompanied by reduced VEGFR2 signalling readouts at a partially cytotoxic concentration. DPN is therefore highlighted as a candidate natural lead compound for further evaluation in anti-angiogenic drug development.
authors: Setyawati I, Shaleh I, Septaningsih DA, Sari RK, Setiawan AG, Christy M, Batubara I, Park TS.
