title: From off-target to on-demand: Precision engineering and translational evaluation of next-generation base editors.
abstract: Due to the increasing demand for clinical gene therapy and the limitations of current treatment methods, there is an urgent need to develop gene-editing tools that are safer, more precise, and more clinically implementable. Deaminase-based base editors have emerged as gene-editing platforms with significant therapeutic potential because they can achieve precise single-base substitutions without inducing DNA double-strand breaks. However, the challenges of applying base editing in clinical practice extend beyond whether the intended edit can be achieved. The critical question is whether the editing system can reliably provide predictable, controllable, and verifiable outcomes across complex sequence contexts, diverse cell environments, and actual delivery conditions. This review focuses on the engineering optimization and clinical translation of base editors. We first systematically analyze the major factors affecting the clinical translation of base editors across four dimensions: editing efficiency, editing precision, safety, and delivery, together with the corresponding optimization strategies. We then summarize the applications of artificial intelligence and computational approaches in base editor design, screening, and risk assessment. We further discuss the ex vivo and in vivo pathways for clinical translation, including their respective requirements for product quality and safety evaluation. Finally, based on representative clinical programs, we discuss how editing performance, safety, and delivery factors influence development decisions for candidate base-editing systems across different therapeutic contexts, and propose minimum reporting recommendations to improve the consistency of key data and cross-study comparability.
authors: Wang W, Song J, Du Y, Zhou C, Zuo X, You G, Luo C, Huang Y, Jiang Z, Li X, Wang Q.

title: Candidate bioactive flavonoids and an optimized combination from Abelmoschus manihot (L.) flower with effects on high-glucose-associated and renal injury phenotypes in zebrafish.
abstract: Abelmoschus manihot (L.) Medik. (AM) is traditionally used for kidney-related disorders, with its flower listed as the medicinal part in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia. However, the pharmacological basis underlying the preferential use of the flower in conditions involving glucose dysregulation and renal injury remains unclear. In this study, different AM parts and solvent extracts were evaluated in independent zebrafish models of high-glucose-associated metabolic disturbance and renal injury. HPLC fingerprinting, spectrum-effect analysis, independent pharmacological evaluation, uniform design, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and qRT-PCR were integrated to identify candidate bioactive constituents, optimize their combination, and explore potential mechanisms. Among the tested parts, AM flowers (AMF) showed the most pronounced and consistent effects on high-glucose-associated and renal injury phenotypes, with the 95% ethanol extract of AMF (AMF-95) being the most effective preparation. AMF-95 enhanced 2-NBDG uptake, reduced glucose, creatinine, and kidney injury molecule-1 levels, relieved renal edema, and improved renal histopathology. Spectrum-effect analysis revealed strong associations between eight major flavonoids, and the measured pharmacological effects, and independent pharmacological evaluation supported their bioactivity, supporting their selection as a candidate bioactive flavonoid group. An optimized constituent combination, designated combination No. 6, showed the best performance and effects comparable to those of AMF-95 under the tested experimental conditions. Network pharmacology and molecular docking predicted potential involvement of inflammation, insulin resistance, AGE-RAGE, and MAPK-related processes, with preliminary transcriptional support from whole-larvae qRT-PCR. These findings support AMF as the preferential medicinal part for high-glucose-associated and renal injury phenotypes and provide candidate flavonoids and an optimized combination for further investigation.
authors: Yue GY, Zhang MY, Xu WL, Li F.

title: mRNA encoding norovirus VP1 produces antigenically functional virus-like particles in vitro.
abstract: Human norovirus is a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis worldwide across all age groups, yet no licensed vaccine is available. The major capsid protein, VP1, self-assembles into highly immunogenic virus-like particles (VLPs) that have shown promise in clinical studies. Recently, mRNA has emerged as a compelling platform for norovirus vaccination. However, whether VP1-encoding mRNA can drive authentic VLP formation in human cells relevant to the vaccination environment has remained unknown. In this study, we used multiple human cell lines, including THP-1-derived macrophage-like cells, to model the post-vaccination environment. Transfection with norovirus GII.4 VP1 mRNA or lipid nanoparticle-formulated VP1 mRNA induced both intracellular and extracellular VP1 expression. Sucrose gradient purification and electron microscopy confirmed VLP assembly. These particles retained key antigenic and functional properties, including recognition by norovirus-specific antibodies in human serum and binding to histo-blood group antigens. Collectively, our findings provide direct evidence that VP1-encoding mRNA can generate structurally and functionally relevant norovirus VLPs in physiologically relevant human cell systems. These results strengthen the mechanistic rationale for mRNA-based norovirus vaccines and support their continued development.
authors: Reyes Ballista JM, David C, Pirrone A, Gonzalez-Fernandez E, Wei J, Wen Z.

title: New molecular and historical evidence on ancient Egyptian embalming.
abstract: Mumia vera aegyptiaca was a mummy-derived medicinal substance widely used in medieval and early modern medicine, yet its material composition and biological activity remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate Egyptological and pharmaceutical-historical analysis of 41 textual sources with LC-MS/MS-based metabolomics, molecular networking, machine-learning-assisted annotation, and bioactivity testing to investigate ancient Egyptian embalming materials and historical Mumia vera samples. We analyzed 24 objects from university and pharmacy museum collections, including historical Mumia vera products, mummified body parts, embalming residues, bandages, and two mummified skulls. Comparative metabolomics revealed substantial heterogeneity among materials labeled as Mumia vera, but also recurrent molecular signatures consistent with aged conifer resins, including oxidized abietane-type diterpenoids. Several samples contained Aloe-associated metabolites, including aloeresin A/D- and aloin-related compounds. These data reveal Aloe-associated metabolites in ancient Egyptian embalming-related materials and support the presence of Aloe spp.-derived exudates in selected samples. The convergence of molecular and textual evidence further raises the possibility that a previously unresolved Egyptian term from the 2nd millennium BC may refer to Aloe sp. or an Aloe-derived product. Comparative metabolomics also linked an inconspicuous powder sample to a specific mummified head, although their curatorial association had not been securely documented. Finally, a historical Mumia vera aegyptiaca extract modestly protected MDCK cells from influenza virus-induced cytopathic effects, whereas the isolated major compound 7-oxodehydroabietic acid was inactive on its own. Together, these findings show how integrating textual scholarship, pharmaceutical history, and molecular analysis can refine the interpretation of ancient Egyptian embalming practices, museum objects, and historical medicines.
authors: Berger T, Naimi A, Hardes K, Sachße C, Gericke R, Marner M, Mühlemeyer F, Pommerening T, Reher R.

title: Hydrophobic remodeling of the SARS-CoV-2 RBD large loop attenuates ACE2 engagement and viral fitness.
abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 Omicron subvariant JN.4 harbors a unique A475V substitution within the receptor binding domain (RBD) but exhibits limited expansion compared to its parallel descendant JN.1. Here, we investigate how hydrophobic remodeling within RBD large loop (residues 475-490) modulates receptor engagement and spike function. Cryo-electron microscopy reveals that A475V induces local remodeling of the receptor-binding motif (RBM) and alters the RBD-ACE2 interaction geometry. Local refinement revealed that the bulky valine substitution disrupts the local interaction network surrounding residue 475, resulting in a 3.5-fold reduction in ACE2-binding affinity compared with BA.2.86. In contrast to the L455S substitution in JN.1, which primarily alters the receptor-binding interface, A475V within the flexible large loop influences both local loop conformation and global spike conformational properties. Systematic mutagenesis identifies A475 and F486 as functionally constrained hydrophobic residues that preserve the structural framework of ACE2 engagement despite extensive sequence variation within the surrounding loop. Together with molecular dynamics simulations and functional assays, our findings establish the RBD 475-490 large loop as a structurally plastic yet functionally constrained element that balances receptor recognition, conformational stability, and antigenic diversification. These results provide a mechanistic framework for understanding region-specific evolutionary constraints that shape SARS-CoV-2 RBD adaptation.
authors: Wang A, Guo H, Yang H, Chen H, Imojara A, Ju B, Zhang Z, Yan R.

title: The Trichomonas vaginalis pseudocyst is a viable cell stage with a distinct transcriptome and an intact membrane.
abstract: Trichomonas vaginalis is the causative agent of trichomoniasis, the most common non-viral sexually transmitted infection (STI). Despite its prevalence, low levels of public knowledge and research funding and the absence of T. vaginalis screening or control programs have led to its categorization as a "neglected" STI. Unlike other STIs in the USA, prevalence increases with age, peaking among individuals in their 40s. Both a motile trophozoite stage and a non-motile pseudocyst state have been described for the parasite, although it was long debated whether the latter is a quiescent stage or a degenerate form on its way to cell death. Here we characterize the T. vaginalis pseudocyst by flow cytometry, membrane integrity assays, transcriptomics, and reversion studies. Pseudocysts were induced by culturing trophozoites in acidic media or in iron depleted media, with a variety of resulting survival rates. Flow cytometry studies showed that pseudocysts have intact cell membranes and express phosphatidylserine on their cell surface. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting studies also identified distinct sub-populations of parasites, revealing the importance of using pure live pseudocyst cultures in reversion studies. Pseudocysts were transcriptionally active for several days and had consistent subsets of genes with increased expression compared to trophozoites, although decreased transcription of genes involved in metabolism. Comparative transcriptomics of pseudocysts and trophozoites of two T. vaginalis strains revealed distinct cell states. Combined, our results provide evidence that the pseudocyst cell state is a stress-induced stage of T. vaginalis that can remain viable for days, with implications for a role in persistent infections.
authors: Shiratori M, Callejas-Hernández F, Orosco JC, Sullivan SA, Carmona Fontaine C, Carlton JM.

title: Role of Leu and Val synthesis in sensing mitochondrial nutrient and energy availability.
abstract: How cells integrate nutrient availability to coordinate metabolism and growth remains poorly understood. Here, we identify branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) synthesis as a metabolic sensing system linking mitochondrial activity to translational and transcriptional control. Yeast limits Leu and Val import and instead relies on their synthesis, allowing BCAA production to reflect mitochondrial anabolic capacity. Reduced Val synthesis activates Gcn2, whereas reduced Leu synthesis inhibits TORC1, together decreasing translation efficiency and restricting growth. This response lowers levels of the transcriptional repressor Mig1, suppressing the Warburg/Crabtree effect and promoting alternative carbon source utilization. Remarkably, pharmacological inhibition of Leu/Val synthesis induces this metabolic reprogramming even in nutrient-rich medium, indicating that mitochondrial BCAA synthesis can partially override other nutrient-sensing pathways. Thus, BCAA synthesis couples mitochondrial anabolic capacity to Gcn2 and TORC1 activity and, through translational control of transcription factor abundance, shapes cellular metabolism.
authors: Phan J, Gay L, Dokládal L, De Virgilio C, Salcedo L, Tha S, Wandvik C, Babst M.

title: AnchorSED: A Segmentation Enhanced Detection Framework Based on Sparse Anchor for Multi-View 3D Object Detection.
abstract: Existing 3D detection methods typically exploit 2D image information through region-level feature extraction and auxiliary semantic supervision. However, these strategies do not explicitly establish a correspondence between 3D candidates and corresponding 2D instance-level representations, which limits the ability to handle objects with complex shapes or severe occlusions. To address this limitation, we propose an anchorbased framework that establishes an anchor-conditioned 2D-3D interaction for jointly exploiting 2D and 3D annotations. Specifically, each 3D anchor and its sampled points are projected onto multiple image planes to identify anchor-associated regions of interest (ROIs), from which view-specific instance segmentation masks are predicted. These 2D representations are subsequently mapped back to their corresponding 3D anchors and aggregated through geometry-aware cross-modal feature alignment. Our approach extends conventional sparse detectors by introducing three components: (1) multi-view ROIs prediction, which maps 3D anchors and sampled points onto multi-view image planes to predict regions of interest (ROIs); (2) multi-view instance segmentation, generating pixel-accurate masks corresponding to predicted ROIs; and (3) cross-modal feature alignment, which fuses geometrically consistent 2D segmentation features with their associated 3D anchors. Furthermore, to bridge the geometric discrepancy between 2D images and 3D objects, we distill multi-scale visual knowledge from a pretrained large-scale self-supervised vision model into our detector, enhancing geometric consistency. Evaluated on the nuScenes benchmark, our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining computational efficiency. The code and auxiliary supervision data are available at https://github.com/HuiAuto/AnchorSED.
journal: IEEE transactions on image processing : a publication of the IEEE Signal Processing Society
authors: Cheng S, Zhang L, Ding X, Liu J.

title: Integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomics with virtual knockout analysis identifies FOS as an epithelial-associated candidate gene in chronic atrophic gastritis.
abstract: Chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) is a precancerous lesion characterized by epithelial injury, glandular atrophy, and impaired gastric function. Molecular targets linking epithelial alterations with potential traditional Chinese medicine-derived compounds remain unclear. GEO bulk transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs), which were intersected with CAG-related genes for enrichment analysis. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis and reverse network pharmacology were used to identify key targets and construct a drug-component-target network. Single-cell RNA sequencing, virtual knockout, molecular docking, CCK-8 assay, and RT-qPCR in 1‑Methyl‑3‑nitro‑1‑nitrosoguanidine (MNNG)-treated GES-1 cells were then integrated to prioritize and evaluate FOS. A total of 502 DEGs and 54 intersected CAG-related genes were identified, with enrichment in wound healing, epithelial junction organization, tight junctions, cAMP signaling, gastric cancer, and digestive or secretory pathways. Five key genes-APOA1, CFTR, FOS, HMOX1, and VIM-were identified, all with AUCs above 0.80. Among 21,679 single cells, FOS was the only key gene predominantly enriched in gastric epithelial cells. Virtual knockout predicted associations between FOS-network perturbation and five genes involved in hormone processing and gastric secretory pathways. Docking generated candidate fisetin-FOS and kaempferol-FOS poses for preliminary compound prioritization. MNNG reduced GES-1 cell viability and significantly increased FOS mRNA expression. Integrated computational analyses highlighted FOS as an epithelial-associated candidate gene in CAG and suggested exploratory associations with gastric secretory pathways. These findings support further functional and compound-intervention studies of the FOS/AP-1 axis.
authors: Li S, Duan H, Liu X, Shan M, Shen Z, Wu M, Wang P, Yao Q, Fu W.

title: The Historical Evolution of Head and Neck Tumor Pathology in WHO Classifications: From Morphology to Molecular Taxonomy.
abstract: PurposeThe WHO classification of head and neck tumors over the past five decades were reviewed, highlighting the major conceptual and taxonomic changes that have shaped contemporary head and neck pathology.MethodsMajor WHO classifications of head and neck tumors were reviewed, with a focus on changes in diagnostic concepts and taxonomic principles rather than individual additions or removals of tumor entities.ResultsWHO classifications have evolved from morphology-based, site-specific systems to an integrated clinicopathological and molecular taxonomy. Early editions emphasized histomorphology and presumed tissue of origin. Subsequent classifications, however, increasingly incorporated immunophenotypic and molecular findings. The recognition of virus-associated neoplasms and recurrent molecular alterations has contributed to defining new entities and refining existing categories. The fifth edition further standardized tumor taxonomy by introducing essential and desirable diagnostic criteria, reflecting a biology-driven approach to classification.ConclusionThe evolution of WHO classifications reflects major advances in tumor biology and has substantially influenced diagnostic practice and clinical interpretation. Future classifications will likely incorporate increasingly sophisticated molecular, digital, and computational approaches while maintaining standardized, reproducible, and clinically meaningful diagnostic criteria.
authors: Mariano FV, Lavareze L, Antolini-Tavares A, Franchi A, Nadal A, Simpson R, Leivo I, Bradová M, Skálová A, de Lima-Souza RA, Ferlito A.

title: Systems toxicology and multi-omics prioritize an MTBC-related computational signature in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Computational prioritization can nominate candidate constituents from complex exposures, but it does not establish exposure or causality. We integrated an areca-constituent library with archived ADMET predictions and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) transcriptomic data to evaluate 2-methyl-1,2,3,4-tetrahydro-beta-carboline (MTBC) as a candidate for further study. Replacing GTEx salivary controls with 44 TCGA-HNSC adjacent normals reduced the OSCC Judge Gene Set from 2,108 to 773 genes and yielded an 11-gene MTBC-related computational signature. In bulk data, this signature was not more tumour-discriminatory than expression-matched random Judge Gene Sets. Patient-level single-cell analysis did not support the previously reported positive association with epithelial state, whereas a cross-tissue cutaneous SCC analysis showed spatial alignment with TLS scores but did not validate an oral or areca-specific effect. A leakage-safe penalized classifier distinguished 51 oral tumours from 44 adjacent normals in internal evaluation (development nested-CV AUC 0.964, 95% CI 0.916-0.997), but no external or screening claim is made. These results define a reproducible computational prioritization framework and an exploratory MTBC-related expression signature that requires direct exposure measurement and experimental validation.
authors: Qiu Y, Zhao C, Wang H, Zhang J, Guo J, Zhao J, Jin L, Cheng Y.

title: The stability explanation for lncRNA discovery bias is not testable with current half-life coverage.
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are nominated as candidate disease regulators from steady-state RNA-seq differential-expression (DE) catalogs, and short-lived lncRNAs have been proposed to be systematically missed because rapid decay lowers steady-state abundance. We asked how much of that bias it can account for, using 18 half-life strata drawn from 16 metabolic-labeling datasets across 13 human cell lines and 17 uniformly processed disease cohorts (16 TCGA tumor-versus-normal contrasts, one non-alcoholic fatty liver cohort; recount3), matching the half-life cell line to the tumor tissue where possible. Under the pre-filter used here the abundance floor leaves only 24% of annotated lncRNAs testable, and downsampling BRCA recovers just 18% of its full-cohort DE lncRNAs at n = 5 per group. Its upstream driver is not resolved. Across six tissue-matched half-life datasets - four cell lines - the median half-life-abundance correlation is ρ = 0.195 (cluster-bootstrap range - 0.003 to 0.293, descriptive rather than a formal interval at so few clusters); dropping the weakest match gives 0.143. Among the lncRNAs carrying a half-life we find no excess exclusion of the short-lived relative to the long-lived; but half-lives are measurable only where a transcript is expressed, and only in cell lines, so that comparison is confined to a subset selected on the quantity at issue. The limiting factor is coverage: only 10.0% of annotated lncRNAs, and 4.4% of those below the filter, have any measured half-life - under 1% counting tissue-matched cell lines only. We provide SIEVE, open-source code producing these detectability figures for a given design, and specify the data the hypothesis needs.
authors: Tani H.

title: An exploratory analysis of circulating cytokine profiles, pain-associated transcripts and autoantibody responses associated with treatment response in knee osteoarthritis
abstract: Background  Pain response to treatment in knee osteoarthritis (OA) varies substantially between individuals, but the biological factors underlying this heterogeneity remain poorly understood. We investigated whether circulating protein, transcriptional and autoantibody features were associated with variation in pain response to lifestyle interventions in people with knee OA. Methods  We performed an exploratory multi-modal analysis using participants from the INSPIRE randomised controlled trial and, for proteomic analyses, an independent WebEx cohort. Circulating inflammatory proteins were measured using Olink proximity extension assay at baseline and 6 weeks. Associations between baseline protein concentrations, longitudinal protein changes and pain response were assessed using multivariable regression, with multivariate protein patterns examined using supervised and sparse partial least squares approaches. Whole-blood transcriptomic data from INSPIRE were analysed using limma, restricted a priori to pain-associated genes represented in the Human Pain Genetics Database (HPGDB), with a responder-by-visit interaction used to assess differential longitudinal expression. Finally, exploratory IgG binding to murine satellite glial cells (SGCs) was assessed in selected INSPIRE participants with contrasting clinical responses to exercise. Results  No circulating protein or transcriptomic association remained significant after correction for multiple testing. Several nominal associations were observed in the proteomic analyses, including baseline IL-10RA and CST5 in INSPIRE and OSM and TNFSF14 in WebEx. Longitudinal changes in IL-17A and TSLP were nominally associated with improvement in pain in INSPIRE, with a similar nominal association between IL-17A and pain improvement observed in WebEx. In the transcriptomic analysis, MMP9 showed the strongest nominal association with differential longitudinal expression according to pain response under both the ΔNRS ≤ −1 (log2 fold change = 0.91, p = 0.008) and ΔNRS ≤ −2 (log2 fold change = 1.02, p = 0.004) definitions; neither association remained significant following FDR correction. Exploratory SGC-binding analysis identified markedly increased baseline IgG binding in one participant with worsening pain, but this pattern was not consistently observed among other participants with poor clinical responses. Paired analyses provided no evidence of a consistent increase in SGC-binding IgG following exercise. Conclusions  This exploratory multi-modal analysis found no robust molecular signature of the pain response that survived correction for multiple testing. Nominal associations involving several circulating proteins, including IL-10RA, IL-17A and MMP9 provide potential leads for future investigation, but these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the multiple comparisons and limited sample sizes. Exploratory autoantibody analyses likewise provided no evidence of a consistent SGC-binding signature. Larger, independently powered studies are required to determine whether these candidate molecular features are reproducibly associated with treatment-related variation in pain response.
authors: Franks S, Kouraki A, Kelly T, Berwick R, Neiland H, Goebel A, Valdes AM.

title: Affinity Maturation Enables Dual Targeting of Cancer-Associated MUC1-Tn/STn and Drives Potent Tumor Control
abstract: A major challenge in solid tumor immunotherapy is identifying tumor-restricted antigens while overcoming intratumoral antigen heterogeneity. The truncated O-glycans Tn (GalNAcα-O-Ser/Thr) and STn (Neu5Acα2-6GalNAcα-O-Ser/Thr) are aberrantly displayed on the transmembrane glycoprotein MUC1 across a broad spectrum of epithelial malignancies, making MUC1-Tn/STn an attractive shared tumor-associated antigen class. However, heterogeneous intratumoral Tn/STn expression renders single-glycoform-specific antibodies vulnerable to antigen-driven escape. To address this challenge, we used structure-guided directed evolution and yeast surface display to affinity-mature the anti-MUC1-Tn antibody 5E5, generating variants with high-affinity dual recognition of MUC1-Tn and MUC1-STn. Co-crystal structures revealed that heavy-chain CDR loops cooperatively engage the GalNAc moiety primarily through hydrogen-bonding networks, in which HCDR3 residue 98 fine-tunes glycoform preference: Tyr98 favors MUC1-Tn recognition, whereas His98 enhances MUC1-STn engagement, while both support high-affinity recognition of both glycoforms. When reformatted as bispecific T-cell engagers, the affinity-matured variants mediated potent and durable cytolytic activity against cancer cells with heterogeneous glycan profiles, suppressed mixed Tn/STn tumors in vivo where the parental antibody failed, and showed enhanced activity in patient-derived tumor-like clusters. Together, these findings establish functional glycoform coverage as a design principle for antibody engineering, whereby a single paratope is optimized to recognize a defined spectrum of tumor-associated glycoforms while preserving antigen specificity, providing a strategy to overcome glycan heterogeneity in solid tumor immunotherapy. Highlights  Directed evolution of antibody 5E5 generates variants with high-affinity dual recognition of MUC1-Tn and MUC1-STn. HCDR3 98 acts as a fine-tuning mechanism for glycoform preference, Tyr98 preferentially favors the recognition of MUC1-Tn, His98 shifts this preference toward MUC1-STn, whilst both residues support high-affinity binding to both glycoforms. A broadly transferable W27d substitution enhances glycopeptide recognition across structurally distinct anti-MUC1-Tn/STn antibody scaffolds. Engineered bispecific T-cell engagers overcome intratumoral glycan heterogeneity, suppressing tumor growth where the parental antibody fails.
authors: Ye J, Zhu X, Lu H, Coppola J, Zhang D, Tian Y, Yang Z, Chung S, Cui L, Zhi J, Wen L, Xi JJ, Wilson IA, Jardine J, Wu P.

title: Prediction transfer does not imply reliability transfer in single-cell foundation models
abstract: Single-cell foundation models are increasingly transferred across tissues, diseases, perturbation screens, and experimental platforms. Although substantial effort has focused on prediction transfer, it remains unclear whether a model’s assessment of its own reliability transfers similarly across biological contexts. Here we define reliability transfer as the ability to transfer an accurate assessment of when model predictions are likely to be correct or incorrect and investigate its behavior across ten perturbation-prediction systems spanning multiple datasets, models, and evaluation settings. We find that reliability transfer varies substantially across source-target pairs and cannot be inferred from predictive performance alone, indicating that prediction transfer and reliability transfer constitute distinct forms of generalization. Analyses of biological annotations, network connectivity, target exposure, and contextual factors reveal that prediction reliability is associated with both shared and context-dependent signals, with their relative importance differing across systems. To characterize this variability, we introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints, context-level signatures derived from strictly cross-fitted SHAP explanations that summarize how reliability estimators combine biological and contextual information when assigning confidence. Across systems, contexts with similar attribution-magnitude fingerprints tended to transfer reliability more successfully, and fingerprint similarity identified transfer sources achieving higher reliability-transfer performance within the observed candidate set. However, these relationships weakened under stricter cross-family transfer settings, indicating that transferable reliability structure remains partly dependent on shared contextual information. Finally, transferred reliability estimators produced different perturbation rankings despite identical perturbation predictions, illustrating a practical consequence of reliability transfer for downstream prioritization. Together, these results establish reliability transfer as a distinct aspect of foundation-model generalization and introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints as a framework for characterizing transferable reliability structure across biological contexts.
authors: Sriram A, Luo T, Zhang L, Kim S, Park HJ.

title: Verteporfin Suppresses Vascular Smooth Muscle Cell Growth-Associated Responses and Modulates YAP Nuclear Localization-Related Signaling
abstract: Abstract  Intimal hyperplasia and restenosis following vascular interventions are major clinical challenges, with vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) proliferation playing a critical role in their development. Yes-associated protein (YAP), a key effector of the Hippo signaling pathway, regulates VSMC phenotypic modulation and proliferation, and its activity is closely associated with nucleocytoplasmic localization. Although verteporfin (VP) has been reported to inhibit YAP-associated signaling, its effects on VSMCs and the potential involvement of YAP nuclear localization remain incompletely understood. In this study, primary rat VSMCs were stimulated with platelet-derived growth factor-BB (PDGF-BB) to induce a proliferative phenotype. The effects of VP on cellular metabolic activity and YAP-associated signaling were investigated using CCK-8 assays, Western blotting, immunofluorescence, subcellular protein fractionation, and quantitative real-time PCR.PDGF-BB stimulation increased YAP expression and was accompanied by changes in VSMC phenotypic markers. VP treatment reduced CCK-8 signals in a concentration-dependent manner, and 3 μM VP was selected for subsequent experiments. VP decreased YAP protein expression and altered the expression and subcellular distribution of several YAP-associated regulatory proteins, including angiomotin (AMOT), protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 14 (PTPN14), α-catenin, and zonula occludens-2 (ZO-2). Furthermore, VP reduced the mRNA expression of the YAP-associated transcriptional targets CTGF and CYR61. These effects differed in several respects from those observed with the structurally related compound protoporphyrin IX (PPIX).Collectively, these findings suggest that VP attenuates growth-associated responses in PDGF-BB-stimulated VSMCs and modulates YAP-associated signaling, potentially involving regulatory processes related to YAP nucleocytoplasmic localization. This study provides preliminary evidence supporting further investigation of VP as a potential therapeutic candidate for vascular proliferative diseases.
authors: Su Z, Liu S, Wu Q, Li J, Fan Z, Guo S, Zhu R, Wu W.

title: Decision-Dependent Adversarial Planning for Cyber-Resilient Solar-Rich Power Grids
abstract: Abstract  The rapid expansion of solar photovoltaic (PV) capacity has exposed the grid to escalating cyber threats that exploit the growing digital footprint of renewable infrastructure. Existing joint planning methods for PV and battery energy storage systems (BESSs) largely optimize techno-economic performance without capturing how deployment decisions reshape cyber threats. Temporal aggregation can obscure seasonal operations and storage-state evolution, while plan-dependent attacks create a costly mixed-integer search. To bridge the gap, we develop a simulation-driven Decision-Dependent Adversarial Bayesian Optimization (DD-ABO) framework that combines hourly full-year simulations preserving seasonal operations and BESS trajectories, candidate-specific adversarial PV-curtailment evaluation, and a random-forest surrogate with expected improvement for sample-efficient PV-BESS planning. Experiments using 2025 New England load and solar data mapped to the IEEE 39-bus system show that approximately half of the selected worst-case attacks begin at the upper neck of the duck curve, and meanwhile the resulting plans exhibit cross-zone and vendor diversification under the modeled dependencies. Relative to attack-agnostic Bayesian optimization, DD-ABO reduces the mean worst-case attack-induced operational penalty and mean expected energy not served within the evaluated scenarios by 80.2\% and 85.0\%, respectively, with only a marginal increase in base-case operational cost and no statistically significant increase in annualized investment or fixed maintenance costs. These results demonstrate that, in this case study, decision-dependent adversarial planning can improve cyber resilience through deployment structure rather than capital or maintenance over-provisioning.
authors: Liu Y, Xu B, Ma W, Zhao S, Liu M, Deng R, Cheng P, Chen J.

title: AI-Driven miRNA Target Identification Combined with Nanocarrier-Based Therapy Enhances Amastigote Clearance in Canine Visceral Leishmaniasis: An Integrated In Silico and Ex Vivo Study
abstract: Abstract  Study rationale and knowledge gap:  Canine visceral leishmaniasis is a major zoonotic disease in which intracellular Leishmania infantum persists within macrophages, while treatment limitations and emerging resistance highlight the need for improved therapeutic strategies. MicroRNA-mediated regulation of host immune responses and nanoparticle-based drug delivery offer complementary approaches, but their integration with artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted target identification has not been adequately investigated in canine visceral leishmaniasis. This study addressed this knowledge gap by integrating computational miRNA–gene prioritization with nanoparticle-mediated drug delivery and ex vivo validation in primary canine macrophages. Methods  Publicly available transcriptomic datasets and experimentally supported miRNA–gene interactions were analysed using machine-learning approaches to prioritize candidate regulatory miRNAs. The selected candidates were evaluated in primary macrophages obtained from 16 dogs using miltefosine-loaded PLGA nanoparticles, miRNA modulation and combination treatment. Parasite burden, cell viability, cytokine responses and expression of selected immune-related genes were assessed during the experimental period. Results  The computational framework identified miR-155 and miR-146a among the principal candidates for experimental investigation. The selected machine-learning model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.89 during cross-validation and 0.84 during transfer to the canine dataset. Experimentally, the combination of PLGA-miltefosine nanoparticles with miR-155 modulation produced the greatest reduction in intracellular parasite burden, reaching a 78% reduction in infection index at 48 h compared with infected untreated controls. The combination was also associated with increased TNF-α, IL-12 and iNOS expression and reduced IL-10, together with a favourable cytotoxicity profile under the conditions tested. Key findings:  These findings provide ex vivo proof-of-concept evidence that AI-assisted miRNA prioritization can be integrated with nanoparticle-based miltefosine delivery and host-directed miRNA modulation to enhance intracellular L. infantum suppression in primary canine macrophages. The computationally predicted miRNA–gene interactions remain hypothesis-generating and require direct functional validation. Further studies incorporating target-level validation, nanoparticle uptake, broader immune profiling and in vivo evaluation are needed to determine the therapeutic relevance of this combined approach.
authors: Spyridonis A, Lefkaditis M, Pappas I, Lialiaris T, Perakis P.

title: Upregulation of chitinase and β-1,3-glucanase enzymes and modulation of biochemical defense response by fungal endophytes against Rhizoctonia solani in cotton
abstract: Abstract    Rhizoctonia solani  is an important soil-borne pathogen of cotton, causing damping-off, root infection, and poor seedling establishment. The use of beneficial fungal endophytes as seed biopriming agents offers a promising approach for enhancing host defense and reducing dependence on use. In this study, selected fungal endophytes were evaluated to induce biochemical and molecular defense responses against  R. solani  in cotton. Seed biopriming with  Diaporthe longicolla  ,  Trichoderma sulphureum  , and  Daldinia eschscholtzii  substantially strengthened the defense status of cotton against  R. solani  . Among these,  D. eschscholtzii  produced the most pronounced accumulation of soluble proteins, sugars, reducing sugars, phenolics and total antioxidants, together with enhanced catalase activity at both 15 and 30 DAS.  T. sulphureum  was particularly effective in activating phenylalanine ammonia-lyase, while its peroxidase activity was highest at 30 days. At the molecular level, early defense activation was evident from strong induction of chitinase and β-1,3-glucanase transcripts. Chitinase expression increased approximately 8.5-, 16-, and 26-fold following treatment with  D. longicolla  ,  T. sulphureum  , and  D. eschscholtzii  , respectively, at 15 days after sowing, whereas β-1,3-glucanase reached approximately 9-fold induction with  D. eschscholtzii  . Transcript accumulation generally declined at 30 days, indicating a stronger early molecular response. Overall,  D. eschscholtzii  consistently elicited the broadest biochemical and molecular defense response, while  T. sulphureum  showed notable activation of phenylpropanoid- and peroxidase-associated defenses. Seed biopriming with fungal endophytes enhanced cotton defense against  R. solani  through coordinated modulation of biochemical defense mechanisms and pathogenesis-related gene expression.
authors: Vennela BS, Hiremani NS, Verma P, Das J, Nagrale DT, Gawande SP, Thube SH, Kumar SS, Meshram MD, Behere GT.

title: Urinary Untargeted Metabolomic Profiling in First-Episode Drug-Naïve Patients with Major Depressive Disorder: A Case-Control Study
abstract: Abstract    Objective  To investigate the urinary metabolomic profiling of first-episode drug-naïve patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-TOF-MS) untargeted metabolomics, so as to identify potential differential metabolites and functional pathways, and provide experimental evidence for the research on objective diagnostic biomarkers of depression. Methods  A case-control study was performed. A total of 55 first-episode drug-naïve MDD patients and 35 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were enrolled. Fasting early-morning urine samples were collected for UHPLC-Q-TOF-MS untargeted metabolomic detection. The k-nearest-neighbor (KNN) algorithm was applied for missing-value imputation. The Mann-Whitney U test combined with Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) multiple-testing correction was used to screen differential metabolites. Principal component analysis (PCA) and orthogonal projections to latent structures-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were adopted to explore the overall separation trend of metabolic profiles between the two groups. Chemical and functional classification of metabolites was conducted based on the ClassyFire system, and binomial tests were performed to evaluate the enrichment rate of differential metabolites for each category. Post-hoc statistical power analysis was also carried out. Results  In total, 5932 metabolites were identified. The relative standard deviation (RSD) of peak areas for all metabolites in quality-control samples was below 30%, indicating satisfactory data quality. Univariate analysis showed that 179 metabolites had raw  P   no metabolite reached the statistical significance threshold of adjusted Pₐdⱼ   *. PCA revealed substantial overlap of urinary metabolomic profiles between the two groups without obvious group separation. The OPLS-DA model yielded a cross-validated predictive Q² value of − 1.185, suggesting model over-fitting and lack of genuine discriminative power. Sixty-six candidate exploratory differential metabolites (39 up-regulated and 27 down-regulated) were obtained according to exploratory screening criteria; among them, 18.2% represented drug-like compounds with false-positive annotations and 3.0% were smoking-related confounding metabolites. Functional classification via ClassyFire showed relatively higher differential rates for phenylpropanoids and polyketides, benzenoids, and organic acids and derivatives. Nevertheless, binomial tests demonstrated that none of the chemical categories exceeded the 5% random expectation level. Power analysis indicated that the present sample size only provided 1.61% statistical power for detecting a medium effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.5), and a total sample size of at least 473 subjects would be required to detect such a medium effect. Significant inter-group differences in smoking rate, alcohol-drinking rate and education level were observed between patients and controls, which served as important confounding factors. Conclusion  No robust urinary differential metabolites survived multiple-testing correction in this cohort of strictly medication-naïve first-episode MDD patients, and multivariate models failed to effectively discriminate cases from controls. High inter-individual variability of the urinary metabolome, insufficient statistical power, false-positive metabolite annotations, and confounders such as smoking jointly limited the findings of this study. Alterations in phenylpropanoid, benzenoid and organic-acid metabolic pathways suggested by exploratory analyses can only serve as hypothesis-generating clues for future research, which need further validation by large-scale, multi-center targeted metabolomic studies with rigorous confounder control. This study provides important negative evidence for urinary metabolomic biomarker research in depression, and highlights the necessity of rigorous statistical correction, model validation, metabolite annotation quality control and adequate sample size in metabolomic biomarker investigations.
authors: Cheng X, Zhang X, Chen L, Wang A, Pan M.

title: Reframing Leishmania 360° in the MISEV2023 Era: A Translational Framework for Extracellular Vesicle Biomarkers and One Health Implementation
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) mediate communication between Leishmania parasites and their hosts through the transfer of proteins, lipids and nucleic acids that influence immune responses, parasite persistence and disease progression. Despite more than a decade of investigation, translation of EV-associated discoveries into clinical, veterinary and public-health applications remains limited. Methodological heterogeneity, inconsistent reporting practices and insufficient validation continue to impede the development of clinically actionable biomarkers. Concurrently, the evolution from MISEV2018 to MISEV2023 reflects the broader maturation of extracellular-vesicle science, shifting the field from descriptive characterisation towards greater emphasis on reproducibility, functional validation and translational relevance. Here, we revisit the Leishmania 360° concept through the complementary lenses of MISEV2023, translational medicine and One Health. We argue that the principal challenge is no longer the identification of vesicular cargo, but the establishment of evidence-based frameworks capable of determining whether EV-associated signals are sufficiently validated to support clinical, veterinary or public-health decision-making. A central conceptual advance is the Dual-Compartment Liquid Biopsy Paradigm, whereby parasite-derived and host-response EVs are interpreted as complementary indicators of pathogen biology and host pathophysiology, providing a multidimensional framework for diagnosis, prognosis, treatment monitoring and surveillance. Building upon this concept, we introduce LEV-MISEV, a claim-to-evidence framework that extends MISEV2023 principles beyond methodological reporting by linking biological, clinical and public-health claims to proportional evidentiary requirements. We further propose a staged translational framework comprising the Translational Readiness Level for Extracellular Vesicles (TRL-EV) and the Leishmania 360° Translational Evidence Matrix. Whereas TRL-EV evaluates biomarker maturity along the pathway from discovery to implementation, the Translational Evidence Matrix assesses the overall strength of evidence across biological, analytical, clinical, operational and One Health domains. Together, these complementary frameworks identify translational bottlenecks, prioritise validation efforts and support evidence-based implementation planning. Finally, we position EV signatures as a molecular intelligence layer within climate-informed One Health surveillance systems integrating human, canine, vector and environmental data. Application of these frameworks indicates that no EV-based application in leishmaniasis has yet progressed beyond the stage of clinically associated biomarker candidates. We therefore propose a translational roadmap that integrates biological plausibility, analytical validity, clinical validity, implementation readiness and One Health utility. Collectively, these concepts reposition EVs not merely as sources of candidate biomarkers, but as components of a translational platform capable of supporting precision diagnostics, therapeutic monitoring, risk assessment and integrated surveillance. More broadly, the proposed framework may provide a transferable model for evidence-based biomarker development across infectious, parasitic and vector-borne diseases beyond leishmaniasis.
authors: Gabriel ÁM, Galué-Parra A, Pereira WLA, Pedersen KW, Silva EOd.

title: Effects of hydrological changes on the sources and optical properties of dissolved organic matter in wetlands of the middle reaches of the Yellow River.
abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) in riverine wetlands is the core carrier of the carbon cycle. However, the dynamics of DOM in large riverine wetlands subject to anthropogenic hydrological regulation remain poorly understood, and the differences in DOM composition and sources among hydrological periods are still unclear. In this study, water samples were collected from the riparian wetland in the Wuzhi section of the middle reaches of the Yellow River during the dry season (DS), normal season (NS), water-sediment regulation scheme (WSRS), and wet season (WS). Ultraviolet-visible (UV-vis) absorption spectroscopy and excitation-emission matrix (EEM) spectroscopy, combined with parallel factor analysis (PARAFAC), were used to characterize the composition and sources of DOM across hydrological periods. Two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy (2D-COS) was applied to reveal the ordered pattern of DOM fluorescent components along the flow direction. The results showed that DOM content, composition, and sources differed among periods. DOC concentration was highest during the WSRS, followed by that during the WS, and was lower during the DS and NS. Three components were identified. Humic-like components C1 and C3 peaked in the WS, whereas the protein-like component C2 peaked in the DS. Within the same season, the water-sediment regulation event caused a significant change in the fluorescence intensity of C2. Spectral parameters indicated that DOM in the WS may have been influenced by terrestrial and autochthonous sources, while autochthonous contributions appeared to be stronger in the other periods. 2D-COS analysis revealed an ordered pattern of DOM fluorescent components along the flow direction, following the sequence protein-like → microbial humic-like → terrestrial humic-like components. This pattern may be influenced by multiple processes including tributary input, agricultural runoff, and sediment release. This study helps to address the limited understanding of DOM dynamics in wetlands under hydrological disturbance and provides baseline data for interpreting the compositional changes and along flow variation patterns of DOM in riparian wetlands across hydrological periods.
authors: Wu L, Wan Y, Zhang M, Zhao T, Xiao Y.

title: Nutrimental Determinants of Chronological Aging and Competitiveness in the snf1Δ Warburg Model.
abstract: Cancer, one of the world's leading causes of death, is characterized by a complex metabolic reprogramming that features the Warburg effect as one of its hallmarks. The Warburg effect involves increased glucose and amino acid metabolism, which promotes tumor proliferation and progression. Although cancer has historically been attributed to genetic mutations, recent studies suggest a possible metabolic origin. However, a key characteristic of cancer cells is their greater adaptability than normal cells, as evidenced by their resistance to chemotherapy, which stems from their high mutability. This underscores the need to examine the relationship between metabolic reprogramming and cancer development from both metabolic and evolutionary perspectives. In this context, Saccharomyces cerevisiae snf1∆ strain has emerged as an ideal cellular model for studying the Warburg effect. This study aimed to determine whether deletion of the SNF1 gene in S. cerevisiae affects its chronological aging and competitiveness in a glucose and amino acid-dependent manner. Herein, we provide evidence that the snf1∆ strain changes the chronological aging depending on nutrimental condition, under low-nutrient levels shortens (0.1% glucose + 0.1× amino acids), and increases under high-nutrient levels (5% glucose + 3× amino acids). Competitiveness of the snf1∆ strain in cocultivation with wild-type was also improved in 5% glucose + 3× amino acids, by approximately two orders of magnitude. These results indicate that snf1∆ strain aging and competitiveness are also sensitive to nutrimental status, as was observed in cancer cells.
authors: Correa-Olivares A, Champagne ACL, Bertadillo-Jilote AD, Leon KIL, Garcia-Gutierrez DG, Nava GM, Sanchez-Quezada V, Madrigal-Perez LA.

title: SMARTFlexDB: a paired apo-holo RNA structure database and analysis platform for RNA conformational flexibility and small-molecule recognition.
abstract: RNA structures can undergo substantial conformational changes upon small-molecule binding, yet existing structural resources provide only static RNA-ligand snapshots without connecting ligand-bound (holo) RNA structures to corresponding ligand-free (apo) conformations. SMARTFlexDB is a curated database and analysis platform that uses paired apo-holo RNA structures to characterize conformational differences and RNA-small molecule recognition. Candidate pairs were identified from the Protein Data Bank by matching RNA chains with at least 90% sequence identity and coverage, and fully conserved binding pocket nucleotides. The current release contains 434 binding pockets from 266 holo structures, linked to 186 apo structures to yield 1187 pocket-level apo-holo pairs organized into 734 database entries, spanning 150 small molecules and 23 RNA functional classes. Each entry integrates RNA sequence and secondary-structure annotations, apo and holo three-dimensional structures, RNA-ligand atomic interactions, and quantitative descriptors of global and local conformational changes. An interactive web interface enables users to explore sequence alignments and structural overlays, compare secondary structures and RNA motifs, and upload paired apo-holo structures for customized analysis. By linking ligand-bound and ligand-free RNA structures, SMARTFlexDB provides a robust foundation for investigating RNA structural flexibility and supporting RNA-targeted small-molecule drug discovery. The database and analysis platform are available at https://aidd.rc.ufl.edu/app/smartflexdb/.
authors: Jiang S, Wei J, Taghavi A, Seabra G, Childs-Disney JL, Li C, Disney MD, Li Y.

title: Salivary <sup>1</sup>H NMR metabolic profiling of diabetic patients with and without periodontitis: an exploratory pilot study.
abstract: BackgroundPeriodontitis is a widespread chronic inflammatory condition that frequently coexists with diabetes mellitus (DM). Identifying non-invasive biomarkers is essential for early detection, targeted therapy, and better understanding of the bidirectional relationship between these two diseases. This study aimed to investigate salivary metabolomic profiles in diabetic individuals with and without periodontitis to identify candidate metabolites associated with periodontitis in patients with diabetes.MethodsThis pilot study compared salivary 1H NMR metabolomic profiles of patients with diabetes with and without periodontitis (n = 13 per group). Unstimulated whole saliva was collected from both groups. Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) was applied to differentiate between the groups. Spectral variables with VIP > 1 were selected for metabolite annotation, followed by metabolite set enrichment analysis (MSEA) to identify dysregulated metabolic pathways.ResultsUsing the PLS-DA model, a total of 78 discriminating variables were identified, leading to the annotation of ten key metabolites: glycolic acid, thymidine, tyramine, deoxyguanosine, cytidine, uridine, NADPH, ADP, serotonin, and nicotinate. MSEA revealed significant pathway disturbances, with pyrimidine metabolism emerging as a notably enriched pathway.ConclusionThe metabolomics study of saliva using 1H NMR showed distinct metabolic disturbances, particularly in pyrimidine metabolism, in diabetic periodontitis. Although these altered metabolites could serve as potential candidates for non-invasive biomarkers, independent validation from a large cohort is still required before they can be translated into clinical diagnostic use.
authors: Vaziri-Amjad S, Zalei B, Rabienejad N, Golshaian A, Taherkhani A.

title: Adenovirus early proteins E1A and E3-19K reveal separable regulatory states of the ER stress sensor IRE1a.
abstract: The unfolded protein response (UPR) controls cellular homeostasis and viral infections. It is canonically initiated by dissociation of ER chaperone BiP/GRP78 from lumenal domains of transmembrane sensor proteins, including the central UPR sensor inositol-requiring enzyme 1 alpha (IRE1a). This results in IRE1a activation and splicing of X-box binding protein 1 (XBP1) mRNA, leading to transcriptional activation of XBP1 for cellular adaptation and sustained infection. Human adenovirus (AdV) preferentially activates the IRE1a-XBP1 pathway through the viral membrane protein E3-19K, yet the mechanisms underlying this selective activation remain unclear. Here, we show that AdV uses two distinct early proteins to dissociate BiP from IRE1a and activate IRE1a-mediated XBP1 splicing. The immediate early protein E1A forms a complex with the cytoplasmic domain of IRE1a, sufficient to dissociate BiP from IRE1a without inducing XBP1 splicing or UPR activation. In contrast, E3-19K is expressed downstream of E1A, associates with the lumenal domain of IRE1a, and induces XBP1 splicing without promoting BiP dissociation from IRE1a. Both proteins were detected in IRE1a-containing complexes, consistent with stepwise viral regulation. Together, our findings show that canonical IRE1a activation hallmarks can be mechanistically separated during viral infection, revealing distinct AdV-regulated IRE1a activation states with discrete upstream and downstream signaling outputs.
authors: Sengupta D, Srivastava S, Bezrukov F, Hemmi S, Greber UF, Prasad V.

title: Fluoxastrobin Targets NAD[P]H:Quinone Oxidoreductase to Disrupt Membrane Redox Balance and Suppress Lasiodiplodia theobromae, an Emerging Tea Pathogen.
abstract: Tea diseases caused by Lasiodiplodia theobromae are prevalent in many tea-producing countries, substantially affecting both the yield and quality of tea. In this study, fluoxastrobin, a strobilurin fungicide, exhibited a half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) of 143.44 μg/ml for inhibiting mycelial growth in vitro. At a dose of 800.0 μg/ml, it demonstrated 42.00% antifungal activity against leaf spot on detached tea twigs. Micromorphological observations revealed that fluoxastrobin induced hyphal abnormalities, including surface roughness, deformation, and swelling. Integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and bioinformatic analyses indicated that fluoxastrobin significantly modulated the expression and abundance of genes, proteins, and metabolites associated with energy metabolism pathways. Fluoxastrobin notably reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, thereby inhibiting electron transport and impairing energy production. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations suggested that fluoxastrobin binds to NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase (NQO), with a binding free energy of -10.1 kcal/mol. A microscale thermophoresis assay revealed a dissociation constant (Kd) of 0.121 μM for fluoxastrobin binding to NQO, which is significantly lower than that of azoxystrobin (0.319 μM). A surface plasmon resonance assay further confirmed the stronger binding affinity of fluoxastrobin to NQO, with a Kd value of 7.098 × 10-5 M. To enhance disease control efficacy, the combination of fluoxastrobin with pyrrolnitrin or osthole at a ratio of 1:2 was screened, yielding EC50 values of 0.0036 and 15.25 μg/ml and synergistic ratio values of 1.29 and 4.00, respectively. Collectively, these findings suggest that fluoxastrobin targets quinone oxidoreductase to disrupt membrane redox balance and suppress L. theobromae, supporting its potential application in the management of tea diseases.
authors: Hamza MA, Li D, Chen Z, Ni H, Bu X, Chen Z.

title: Immune function in burn patients: Pathophysiology, monitoring, and emerging therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Severe burn injury causes extensive local tissue damage and systemic immune alterations that affect infection risk, wound healing, organ function, and survival. The immune response is characterized by rapid activation of innate immune cells, including neutrophils and monocytes, with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL‑6, TNF‑α, IL‑1β) and complement activity. Simultaneously, adaptive immunity is often impaired, with reduced T and B lymphocyte function, while diminished dendritic cell activity may further compromise antigen presentation and adaptive immune responses. This combined hyperinflammatory and immunosuppressive state, known as burn-induced immune dysfunction, contributes to delayed wound healing, increased susceptibility to secondary infections, sepsis, and multiple organ dysfunction. Monitoring immune function is essential but challenging. Routine markers, including white blood cell count (WBC) and C-reactive protein (CRP), provide limited insight, whereas procalcitonin (PCT), pancreatic stone protein (PSP), and cytokine panels (IL‑6, IL‑8, IL‑10) improve early detection of infection and immune classification. Flow cytometry allows characterization of immune cell populations and functional markers such as monocyte HLA‑DR and T cell PD‑1, while functional assays assess neutrophil, monocyte, and lymphocyte responsiveness. High-resolution molecular approaches, including transcriptomics, proteomics, and single-cell profiling, reveal persistent alterations not captured by conventional assays. Therapeutic strategies to restore immune balance include targeted cytokine modulation, immune checkpoint inhibition, hemoadsorption, metabolic and nutritional interventions, and novel approaches such as nanotechnology or microbiome modulation. Early surgical excision and topical treatments, including cerium-nitrate with silver sulfadiazine, may also attenuate systemic inflammation. However, robust clinical evaluation of these interventions is limited, and their timing, dosing, and patient selection remain under investigation. This review integrates mechanistic, translational, and clinical evidence to provide a framework for understanding burn-induced immune dysfunction. Future research should aim for standardized immune phenotyping, longitudinal multi-omics integration, AI-assisted monitoring, and evaluation of mechanism-based immunomodulatory strategies to improve patient outcomes.
journal: Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries
authors: Korkmaz HI, Boer DP, van der Ven F, Meeder M, Papendorp S, Pijpe A, Vries AM, Bosma E, van Zuijlen PPM.

title: Enhanced wound healing potential of a carboxymethyl cellulose/gelatin-based hydrogel containing decellularized amniotic membrane and Matricaria chamomilla extract: A multifunctional composite dressing.
abstract: BackgroundChronic wound healing remains a complex biological process influenced by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, microbial invasion, and insufficient tissue regeneration. Therefore, the design of multifunctional biomaterials that integrate structural support with biological regulation has emerged as a promising strategy in advanced wound care. This study sought to develop a composite hydrogel incorporating decellularized amniotic membrane (dAM)-derived extracellular matrix components alongside Matricaria chamomilla extract, with the goal of achieving enhanced regenerative and therapeutic outcomes.MethodsA CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM hydrogel was prepared using decellularized dAM and subsequently evaluated in terms of its physicochemical and biological characteristics. The effectiveness of the decellularization process and preservation of ECM components were first examined, followed by characterization of hydrogel morphology, rheological properties, swelling and degradation behavior, and pH stability. Its biological performance was further assessed through hemocompatibility, cytocompatibility, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial assays, as well as a full-thickness wound model.ResultsIncorporation of dAM and chamomile extract resulted in a stable hydrogel with favorable physicochemical and biological characteristics. The decellularization procedure removed 97.9% of the DNA. The resulting composite hydrogel exhibited an average pore size of 78.3 ± 9.8 µm, and all hydrogel formulations showed hemolysis rates below the 5% threshold accepted for blood-contacting biomaterials, with values ranging from 3.8% to 4.5%. The composite hydrogel also supported enhanced fibroblast viability (109.6 ± 11.3%) and demonstrated antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial activities against wound-associated pathogens. In vivo, treatment with CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM accelerated wound closure (85.7 ± 6.3% at day 14) and supported tissue regeneration, outperforming both the dAM-containing hydrogel (78.9 ± 9.9%) and the commercial DuoDERM dressing (58.9 ± 4.5%), as evidenced by improved re-epithelialization, collagen deposition, angiogenesis, and early signs of tissue remodeling.ConclusionThe CMC/GEL-Chamomilla-dAM hydrogel combines a dAM-containing extracellular matrix scaffold with chamomile-derived bioactive compounds, creating a favorable microenvironment for tissue repair. The addition of chamomile extract to the dAM-containing scaffold was associated with improved wound closure and tissue regeneration. While the present study design does not permit a definitive assessment of synergy between dAM and chamomile, these findings support the potential of this formulation as a multifunctional biomaterial platform for advanced wound healing applications.
authors: Zamani S, Ghorbani M, Molzemi S, Farahani MK, Raei M.

title: A parallel SEC Column configuration strategy for comprehensive characterization of HPV type 16 virus-like particles.
abstract: Characterisation of human papillomavirus-like particles (HPV VLPs) is challenging due to their large size and inherent structural heterogeneity. Monitoring oligomerisation of L1 proteins during VLP assembly is particularly difficult, as conventional large-pore-size exclusion chromatography (SEC) columns lack the resolving power to distinguish between L1 monomers and higher-order oligomers. This study presents an analytical approach utilizing two SEC columns with distinct pore sizes arranged in parallel, facilitating the separation of a wide range of molecular species within a single workflow. Hyphenation with multi-angle light scattering (MALS) provides the absolute molecular weight of the resolved species. Using the proposed parallel SEC column configuration, five distinct peaks were successfully resolved, compared to only two peaks with the 2000 Å column and three peaks with the 300 Å column, highlighting the enhanced separation capability for VLP species in 30 min, reducing both analysis time and sample consumption by up to 50% compared with performing two separate single-column analyses. This approach also simplifies the analytical workflow and lowers operational costs relative to more complex platforms such as 2D-LC systems. The proposed method was employed to characterise aggregates, monomeric VLPs, partially assembled VLPs and free L1 proteins in crude, purified and reassembled VLP samples. The proposed approach was validated using commercially available Gardasil HPV-VLP. Overall, the workflow enhances resolution across the size spectrum, provides accurate quantification of intact VLPs, reduces runtime and improves overall analytical throughput for VLP characterisation.
authors: Peruri V, Kumar S, Rathore AS.

title: Capillary-confined photonic crystal sensor for dual-mode monitoring of PFOA.
abstract: Herein, we report a capillary-confined, high-concentration self-assembly strategy that overcomes the persistent limitations of conventional photonic crystals, including mechanical fragility, slow assembly, and angle dependence. Specifically, the robust capillary housing protects the photonic crystal from mechanical damage, the high-concentration assembly process reduces fabrication time, and only self-compensating optical shift (-13.7 nm) over all viewing angles enables viewing-less angle-dependent readout. This process also yields a distinctive FCC/SC hybrid lattice, providing new insight into confined colloidal crystallization. For Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) detection, the sensor produces a stable colourimetric response that from yellow to red under 0.1 mg·L-1 within 10 min. Furthermore, integration of an aggregation-induced emission (AIE) fluorophore affords a dual-mode probe. Inspired by the adaptive signaling of bioluminescent fungi, the probe operates through a surface-tension-driven capillary transport and PFOA-mediated interfacial hydrophobisation mechanism. This design enables an highly sensitive fluorescence turn-on response from 0.0005 to 0.25 mg·L-1, observed as an expanded and intensified emission zone, followed by a sequential "turn-off" response from 0.5 to 5 mg·L-1, manifested as a receding emission zone with reduced intensity. The resulting detection limit reaches 0.11 μg·L-1. Practical utility was confirmed by spike-recovery experiments in environmental water samples, with excellent recoveries (94-102% at 0.5 mg·L-1 for CCPC and ~ 98% at 0.005 mg·L-1 for AIE-CCPC), in agreement with LC-MS/MS. Overall, this work delivers a rapid, robust, and sensitive sensor for PFOA monitoring. This integrative design offers a practical platform for field-deployable environmental sensing.
journal: Journal of colloid and interface science
authors: Liu Y, Wu D, Guo J, Xu Z, Qiu L, Geng J, Wang Y, Meng Z.

title: Superoxide dismutase 3 (SOD3) suppresses periostin to attenuate IL-4/IL-13-driven epithelial inflammation.
abstract: Superoxide dismutase 3 (SOD3) is an extracellular antioxidant enzyme with an emerging role in the regulation of inflammatory responses; however, its involvement in type 2 cytokine interleukin-4 (IL-4)/interleukin-13 (IL-13)-associated inflammation remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the effects of SOD3 on IL-4/IL-13-induced inflammatory responses in human keratinocytes (HaCaT) and bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B). SOD3 significantly suppressed IL-4/IL-13-induced periostin expression at both the mRNA and protein levels in both cell types. Mechanistically, SOD3 interacted with the IL-4 receptor α (IL-4Rα) and attenuated activation of the downstream Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (JAK/STAT6) pathway, resulting in reduced periostin expression. Periostin knockdown and recombinant periostin add-back experiments further demonstrated that SOD3 reduced the phosphorylation of nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB), p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), largely through suppression of periostin. Consistent with these findings, SOD3 decreased the expression of periostin-associated mediators, including vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP), transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), and attenuated periostin-induced production of the pro-inflammatory cytokines tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Collectively, these findings suggest that SOD3 attenuates IL-4/IL-13-driven epithelial inflammation, at least in part, through modulation of the IL-4Rα/JAK/STAT6/periostin axis and downstream NF-κB/MAPK signalling pathways, and suggest its potential as a therapeutic candidate for type 2 inflammatory diseases.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05112-3.
authors: Tran GB, Nguyen NH, Kim TY, Nguyen CT.

title: Cathodic protection mitigates D. vulgaris corrosion of welded X80 steel in acidic soil.
abstract: Microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC) of welded pipeline steel in acidic soils is a critical safety concern, yet the role of cathodic protection (CP) in such inoculated environments remains largely unexplored. This work systematically evaluates CP potentials (-850, -950, and - 1050 mV vs. SCE) on the corrosion behavior of welded X80 steel in both sterile and Desulfovibrio vulgaris (D. vulgaris) - inoculated acidic soil solution. We demonstrate that while CP effectively reduces general corrosion, D. vulgaris colonization lowers the charge-transfer resistance by an order of magnitude, indicating severe MIC persists even under protection. A counterintuitive finding is that CP induces localized alkalization and hydrogen evolution, which suppress D. vulgaris metabolic activity, resulting in shallower but far more numerous corrosion pits in inoculated solutions than in sterile ones-revealing an altered pitting propagation mechanism. Among the tested potentials, -850 mV offers the optimal balance between corrosion mitigation and hydrogen-related risks, as supported by the highest polarization resistance. These findings provide new mechanistic insights into electrochemical-biological interactions under CP and offer practical criteria for optimizing CP strategies to combat MIC in acidic soil environments.
authors: Qin T, Liu L, Wang J, Peng B, Cao X, Huang Y, Wei B, Wu T.

title: Selection of a high-affinity DNA aptamer for puerarin and its application in fluorescence sensing.
abstract: Puerarin (Pue), a naturally occurring isoflavone, is an important quality marker of Pueraria lobata, a widely used traditional Chinese medicinal material. Reliable determination of Pue is therefore relevant to both pharmaceutical quality control and studies of its biological activity. Here, a library-immobilized capture-SELEX protocol was used to isolate DNA sequences that recognize Pue. The predominant candidate, Pue-1, displayed an apparent dissociation constant (Kd) of 738 nM in a thioflavin T (ThT) fluorescence assay. An independent microscale thermophoresis (MST) measurement yielded a Kd of 111 nM. Pue-1 showed substantially weaker responses to the structurally related flavonoids tested, supporting its preferential recognition of Pue. A target-induced strand-displacement design was subsequently used to construct a turn-on fluorescent aptasensor, which exhibited preferential responses to Pue over the tested interferents. In 200-fold-diluted Pueraria root extract, the assay achieved a limit of detection of 29.5 nM, with spike recoveries ranging from 93.2% to 96.2%. These results demonstrate the suitability of Pue-1 as a recognition element for constructing a fluorescent sensing platform for Pue.
authors: Qu Z, Zou L.

title: Phosphate-Engineered DNA Reporters Boost CRISPR-Cas12a Trans-Cleavage for Rapid and Sensitive Nucleic Acid Detection.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas12a molecular diagnostics rely on target-activated collateral cleavage of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) reporters to generate fluorescence signals, yet the mechanisms governing reporter substrate processing remain poorly understood. Here we show that Cas12a trans-cleavage involves both endonucleolytic cleavage and exonucleolytic trimming. We further demonstrate that terminal phosphate modification of ssDNA substrates accelerates substrate cleavage activity and modulates trans-cleavage kinetics, thereby enhancing fluorescence output. Guided by this mechanistic insight, we engineered fluorophore-quencher ssDNA reporters bearing terminal phosphate modifications and identified a 3'-phosphate-engineered reporter that enables faster signal generation and higher fluorescence intensity. Incorporation of the engineered reporter into the CRISPR-Cas12a system enabled the development of Phos-CRISPR (Phosphate-engineered DNA reporters boost CRISPR), a rapid, sensitive, and specific nucleic acid detection platform that achieves results within 20 min, approximately threefold faster than conventional CRISPR assays. Applied to herpes simplex virus 1 detection, the Phos-CRISPR combined with recombinase polymerase amplification achieved a limit of detection of 20 aM and accurately identified clinical swab samples. These findings provide a general framework for understanding Cas12a trans-cleavage activity and establish a mechanistically informed strategy for enhancing next-generation CRISPR diagnostics.
authors: Yang R, Guo C, Pei M, Zhang J, Guan X, Zhang S, Liu X, Schalper KT, Avery L, LaSala R, Banach D, Liu C.

title: A single-nucleus multiome profiling reveals the regulatory programs driving plant nematode-induced syncytium.
abstract: Plant-parasitic cyst nematodes induce the formation of specialized feeding structures, known as syncytia, within host roots by orchestrating extensive transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming. Here, we generated parallel single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq libraries from fully developed Heterodera schachtii-induced syncytia on Arabidopsis roots. We analyzed high-quality transcriptome and chromatin profiles independently and in an integrated framework. We identified multiple transcriptomic cell states, several of which were highly syncytium-enriched and spanned vascular and cortical identities. Differential expression analysis identified hundreds of syncytium-enriched genes, and pseudotime trajectory inference points to potential compartmentalization or functional heterogeneity of syncytium nuclei, consistent with the possibility of distinct transcriptional programs within or between mature syncytia. Joint clustering of snATAC-seq with snRNA-seq delineated syncytium-unique chromatin accessibility landscapes, with several cell states exhibiting extensive open chromatin linked to upregulated genes. Motif enrichment across these accessible regions highlighted cis-regulatory elements mainly for AP2, bZIP, bHLH, MYB, and TCP transcription factors and identified functionally validated members of these families as candidate regulators of syncytium identity. Our study establishes a multiome atlas of syncytial cells and uncovers the regulatory programs driving nematode feeding site maintenance, as well as transcriptionally distinct nuclear states that may reflect functional specialization within or between the syncytia.
authors: Hewezi T, Zadegan SB, Li P, Öztürk C, Rice JH, Krishnan HB.
