title: From cell factories to photobiocatalysts: reengineering cyanobacteria for solar-driven chemical manufacturing.
abstract: To achieve more sustainable, light-powered chemical manufacturing, cyanobacterial engineering is expanding from conventional carbon-accumulating "cell factories" toward the complementary use of cyanobacteria as "whole-cell photobiocatalysts." This review critically examines this conceptual extension. By shifting the engineering focus from carbon-centric biosynthesis to electron- and energy-coupled catalysis, this emerging approach partially decouples target-product formation from the de novo assembly of CO2-derived carbon skeletons. Instead, it exploits photosynthetically generated reducing equivalents and ATP to support redox and energy-dependent enzymatic transformations, thereby reducing dependence on external cofactor- or energy-regeneration systems. We outline a multidimensional engineering framework that integrates carbon-flux redirection ("push"), coupling to photosynthetically generated reducing equivalents and ATP ("drive"), and product-removal-driven "pull" through secretion, volatilization, or in situ extraction. We further highlight advances in light-tolerant and stress-robust cyanobacterial chassis, together with emerging process strategies based on attached-growth and biofilm photobioreactors. We also critically consider genetic instability, variable enzyme-coupling efficiency, and scale-dependent light and mass-transfer limitations. Finally, we discuss the biophysical and energetic limits of light-to-chemical conversion, competition for reducing power, the largely conceptual potential of temporally decoupled light harvesting and dark-phase catalysis, and the need to select economically viable target products using rigorous techno-economic and life-cycle analyses. Collectively, this review provides conceptual and practical guidance for developing sustainable photosynthetic biomanufacturing platforms.
authors: Pan K, Liu D, Chen L, Sun T, Zhang W.

title: Elevated GANAB fuels PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint-mediated immune escape by maintaining PD-L1 stability in bladder cancer.
abstract: BackgroundBladder cancer (BCa) is one of the most common malignancies of the urinary system, with limited treatment options and extremely poor prognosis in advanced stages. Although immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis have been approved for clinical use, the objective response rate remains low (15%-25%), and acquired resistance frequently develops. The molecular mechanisms underlying PD-L1-mediated immune evasion in bladder cancer remain incompletely understood. Post-translational modification of PD-L1, particularly N-glycosylation, stabilizes the protein and enhances its immunosuppressive function; however, the specific enzymes regulating this process have not been systematically identified in BCa.MethodsWe analyzed single-cell sequencing data from public databases to identify malignant epithelial subpopulations and constructed prognostic models using high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA), LASSO regression, and machine learning. Crucially, we performed extensive experimental validation beyond bioinformatics prediction: Ganab was stably knocked down in MB49 bladder cancer cells using lentivirus-mediated shRNA, and the effects on cell proliferation and migration were assessed by CCK-8 and wound healing assays. An orthotopic bladder cancer model was established in C57BL/6 mice by intravesical inoculation of MB49-luciferase cells, with tumor growth monitored by live bioluminescence imaging. Tumor tissues were subjected to single-cell RNA sequencing to dissect the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) at single-cell resolution. Mechanistically, Western blotting, PNGase F deglycosylation, immunofluorescence, and bidirectional co-immunoprecipitation were employed to elucidate how GANAB regulates PD-L1 glycosylation. Flow cytometry and CellChat analysis were used to evaluate T-cell subset remodeling and PD-L1/PD-1 signaling attenuation.ResultsWe identified a malignant epithelial subpopulation (Epi_3) characterized by high tumor stemness scores and extensive copy number variations. A 15-gene prognostic signature was successfully constructed, in which GANAB exhibited the highest predictive weight. GANAB protein expression progressively increased along the pseudotime trajectory of tumor progression. Experimentally, inhibition of Ganab significantly suppressed MB49 cell proliferation and migration in vitro, and markedly inhibited orthotopic tumor growth in vivo. Mechanistically, GANAB regulated PD-L1 N-glycosylation, yielding two distinct PD-L1 bands: a 45 kDa glycosylated form (Gly-PD-L1) and a 33 kDa non-glycosylated form (Non-gly-PD-L1). Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed that GANAB specifically interacted with non-glycosylated PD-L1 (33 kDa) but not with glycosylated PD-L1 (45 kDa), indicating that GANAB interacts with non-glycosylated PD-L1 and may facilitate its entry into the ER glycosylation pathway. Single-cell analysis of shGanab tumor tissues revealed profound remodeling of the TIME: exhausted T cells (Tex) were reduced, effector memory T cells (Tem) were increased, and PD-L1/PD-1 signaling between tumor cells and T-cell subsets was attenuated. SCENIC analysis identified Stat1 as a key upstream transcription factor, and IMvigor210 cohort analysis confirmed positive correlations among GANAB, STAT1, PD-L1, and CD8A expression. Patients with high GANAB expression exhibited poorer immunotherapeutic responses and worse prognosis.ConclusionsOur findings establish a robust prognostic model for BCa patients through integrated single-cell and bulk transcriptome analysis. More importantly, we demonstrate through both in vitro and in vivo experiments that the core gene GANAB promotes bladder cancer progression and immune evasion by regulating PD-L1 N-glycosylation along the PD-1/PD-L1 axis, thereby remodeling the tumor immune microenvironment. In the TCGA cohort, GANAB expression correlated strongly with the T-cell-inflamed gene expression profile (TEP; Spearman R = 0.85, P < 2.2e-16), indicating that GANAB-high tumors represent an inflamed yet immunotherapy-resistant phenotype. We acknowledge that the relationship between GANAB and other established biomarkers, including tumor mutation burden and PD-L1 combined positive score, as well as its expression profile across normal tissues, remains to be characterized. Furthermore, specific GANAB inhibitors are currently unavailable, and the ubiquitous expression of GANAB as a housekeeping endoplasmic reticulum enzyme raises potential on-target safety concerns that preclude immediate therapeutic targeting. Therefore, rather than advocating direct GANAB inhibition, we propose that GANAB serves as a candidate stratification biomarker and mechanistic node for glycosylation-mediated checkpoint resistance. Its clinical utility should be evaluated alongside emerging modalities such as ferroptosis-targeted nanomedicines and antibody-drug conjugates, with future efforts focused on biomarker validation and the development of tumor-specific delivery strategies before any therapeutic application can be considered.
authors: Jin X, Xu Y, Ling K, Li H, Wang J, Liu J, Yang X, Mu H.

title: Diacylglycerol-mediated casein aggregation in yogurt: Insights into coagulation kinetics and protein network assembly.
abstract: As a functional structural lipid, diacylglycerol (DAG) is reported to strengthen the gel structure of the fermented dairy. However, whether DAG accelerates the coagulation process, how it affects gel network structure, and the mechanisms underlying above effects remain unknown. In this study, soybean diacylglycerol (SDAG)-fortified yogurt was prepared and the mechanisms of DAG-mediated casein aggregation were investigated through the coagulation kinetics and protein network assembly. The results showed that SDAG group completed coagulation 1 h earlier than control groups and exhibited an 18.6% increase in gel strength. Mechanistically, it was proposed that DAG may promote the proliferation of lactic acid bacteria, enhance lactose utilization and lactic acid production, and accelerate the destabilization and coagulation of casein micelles to shorten the coagulation process. DAG increased the proteolytic activity by 1.86 times and was associated with reduced α-casein and β-casein band intensities (by 2.4% and 3.95%, respectively), which may expose hydrophobic regions and thiol sites, thereby forming a compact network. The proportion of intermolecular β-sheet increased from 16% (CK) to 28% (SDAG group), while β-turn decreased from 20% to 17%, indicating a conformational transition from disordered to ordered structures. Molecular docking suggested that free hydroxyl groups of DAG may serve as molecular bridges to crosslink caseins via hydrogen bonds, potentially promoting coagulation. DAG accelerated acid production, facilitated structural ordering, and may enhance protein cross-linking, thereby shortening coagulation time and facilitating a compact gel network, although the esterase-glycerol pathway remained to be confirmed. This study provides mechanistic support for developing functional dairy products.
authors: Lu Y, Zhao J, Meng X.

title: Direction-aware graph attention modeling and co-expression integration reveal novel core regulators of shared drought and salinity stress responses in rice leaves.
abstract: Although differential expression analysis has identified numerous drought- and salinity-responsive genes in rice, it cannot resolve the directional, transcription factor (TF)-driven regulatory architecture underlying responses across independent drought and salinity datasets. To address this, we applied TF-Anchored Directed SiGaResNet, a signed, direction-aware graph attention residual network with a TF-anchored edge-retention rule and permutation-based validation, to RNA-seq profiles from 92 rice leaf samples (51 stress, 41 control) derived from independent drought and salinity studies. Unlike conventional correlation- or co-expression-based approaches, the framework constrains regulatory inference around TF nodes while learning directed, signed relationships through supervised graph representation learning. Differential expression analysis identified 719 genes (405 upregulated, 314 downregulated), with induced transcripts enriched in stress-response and hormone-signaling processes and repressed transcripts dominated by photosynthesis- and secondary-metabolism-related processes. The framework showed strong cross-validated classification performance (MCC = 0.78 ± 0.17; AUC = 0.95 ± 0.05). The resulting directed gene regulatory network comprised 137 nodes and 163 edges and exhibited a sparse, modular architecture (modularity = 0.77; 15 communities), with TFs significantly enriched among regulatory source nodes (P < 0.001). Hub regulators were distributed across multiple TF families, predominantly bZIP, MYB-related, and NAC. Eighteen of thirty-two prioritized TF-encoding genes were independently corroborated within stress-associated WGCNA modules, and four comparatively uncharacterized candidates (Os07g0176200, Os05g0569300, Os03g0231000, and Os02g0187700) received convergent computational support from promoter cis-element enrichment, protein functional-association topology, and leave-one-out cross-validation classification. Quantitative real-time PCR further confirmed stress-responsive expression of all four candidates under separate drought and salinity treatments, supporting their prioritization as putative candidate regulators. These findings indicate that direction- and sign-aware graph attention modeling can integrate transcriptomic information from independent drought and salinity studies to identify biologically coherent, TF-centered regulatory patterns and prioritize candidate regulators for further functional investigation, without establishing causal regulatory mechanisms.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Safarzadeh M, Tohidfar M.

title: Temporal trends and compartment-specific behaviour of <sup>137</sup>Cs across five decades of environmental monitoring in tropical Malaysia.
abstract: Long-term environmental surveillance of radiocesium (137Cs) in tropical regions provides important baseline data for assessing radionuclide behaviour under low-background conditions, yet multi-compartment synthesis studies from Southeast Asia remain scarce. This study presents a retrospective analysis of 137Cs activity concentrations across five environmental compartments: seawater (n = 609), soil (n = 483), sediment (n = 474), biota (n = 114), and airborne particulates (n = 20 seasonal records), in Malaysian environments spanning 1972-2024. Censored observations below analytical detection limits were treated using Regression on Order Statistics (ROS), with Limit of Detection (LOD) substitution sensitivity assessed under three scenarios (Xi = 0, LOD/2, LOD). A complementary statistical framework combining Mann-Kendall (MK) trend analysis, Pettitt change-point detection, cumulative sum (CUSUM) diagnostics, relative detectability metrics (SNR), and segmented regression was applied to characterise temporal structure and compartment-specific behaviour. A statistically significant monotonic decline was identified in seawater only (τ = -0.547, p = 0.002), however, a candidate change-point at 1995 (p = 0.026) was excluded from primary inference owing to a 9-year sampling gap (1987-1994; Table S3). Soil and biota exhibited declining tendencies (τ = -0.167 and -0.500, respectively) that did not reach statistical significance (p > 0.05). Sediment results were excluded from trend inference as the direction of the apparent trend reversed between LOD substitution scenarios, indicating that the result is driven by the high proportion of censored values (74.7%) rather than the quantified data. Airborne observations (85% non-detect) were reported descriptively only. Indicative effective half-lives of 137Cs were estimated across all four compartments under a sensitivity analysis spanning five historically motivated starting years (Table S2). Seawater yields T½ (eff) = 27.7-30.8 yr across the primary fits, bracketing the physical half-life (30.17 yr), while biota yields T½ (eff) ≈ 12-19 yr, consistent with biological turnover superimposed on radioactive decay. Soil and sediment estimates are sensitive to starting year and are considered indicative only. Signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) were below 1 for soil (0.455), sediment (0.060), and biota (0.260); seawater showed marginal detectability (SNR = 1.35, consistent across all LOD substitution scenarios), reflecting the long-term declining trend rather than a post-2011 enrichment signal. Statistical inference is subject to inherent limitations of the analytical framework: the MK test has reduced power for episodic signals and censored-data-rich series; the Pettitt test assumes a single dominant change-point; and CUSUM results are treated as exploratory given irregular sampling intervals and high censoring rates in several compartments. The results document baseline temporal trajectories of 137Cs in a tropical low-background environment and highlight compartment-specific differences in temporal sensitivity, data sufficiency, and inferential reliability as central challenges for long-term radionuclide surveillance in tropical radioecology.
authors: Sanusi MSM, Gin KYH, Hashim S, Idris HN, Taha RM.

title: Potent antimicrobial pyridyl-imine derivatives: experimental and computational insights into their biological activity.
abstract: Dermatophytic infections remain a persistent therapeutic challenge, particularly due to the increasing resistance to conventional antifungal agents. In search of alternative antifungal scaffolds, a series of 2-pyridyl-imine derivatives (PYE1-PYE11) was synthesized and evaluated for antimicrobial, cytotoxic, and biomolecular interaction properties. All compounds exhibited antimicrobial activity, with the ortho-vanillin derivative PYE10 showing the highest potency, including remarkable activity against Proteus mirabilis (MIC = 0.01 mg/mL) and Trichophyton mentagrophytes (MIC = 0.05 mg/mL). Fluorescence displacement assays provided evidence for PYE10-DNA interactions involving both intercalative and minor-groove-associated binding modes, while human serum albumin binding studies revealed 1:1 complex formation, indicating appreciable interaction with HSA. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations identified favorable and stable binding of the most active compounds within the CYP51B active site, supporting the experimentally observed antifungal activity. Computational thermodynamic analysis indicated that Fe2⁺ chelation is protonation-dependent under physiological conditions. Structure-activity relationship analysis revealed that antimicrobial activity is influenced by the electronic nature of substituents, aromatic planarity, molecular flexibility, and the ability to establish multiple intermolecular interactions. In silico ADMET evaluation demonstrated favorable drug-likeness and pharmacokinetic profiles, highlighting these pyridyl-imine derivatives as promising candidates for further antimicrobial development.
authors: Dragojević JS, Milanović Ž, Milisavljević K, Petrović N, Kosanić M, Arsenijević D, Gabričević M, Kostić MD, Divac VM.

title: PSMB7 is associated with DNA damage repair and immune microenvironment features and serves as a prognostic biomarker.
abstract: BackgroundThe clinical significance and biological roles of PSMB7 in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to comprehensively characterize PSMB7 expression, prognostic value, epigenetic regulation, immune associations, and in vitro functions in LUAD.MethodsPSMB7 expression, clinicopathological associations, prognostic value, epigenetic regulation, co-expression networks, functional pathways, and relationships with the tumor immune microenvironment were systematically evaluated across multiple datasets. External validation was performed in the GSE31210 cohort. Prognostic nomogram performance was additionally evaluated using Harrell's concordance index (C-index) and time-dependent decision curve analysis (DCA). In vitro experiments, including Western blotting, CCK-8 assays, and flow cytometry, were conducted to assess the effects of PSMB7 on cell proliferation and irradiation-induced apoptosis in LUAD cell lines.ResultsPSMB7 was significantly upregulated in LUAD and was associated with advanced pathological T and N stages and overall clinical stage. ROC analysis indicated that PSMB7 showed potential discriminatory ability between LUAD and normal lung tissues. High PSMB7 expression independently predicted unfavorable outcomes across multiple prognostic endpoints. Nomogram evaluation using calibration, C-index, and DCA provided complementary evidence for prognostic performance. PSMB7 hypomethylation was associated with poorer survival. PSMB7 expression was positively correlated with DNA mismatch repair genes, RNA modification regulators, and malignant tumor phenotypes. GSEA showed significant enrichment of oncogenic, cell-cycle, metabolic, DNA-repair, and stress-response pathways. In addition, PSMB7 expression was strongly associated with immune scores, immune-cell infiltration, and the expression of immune modulators, MHC molecules, chemokines, and chemokine receptors in LUAD. In vitro, PSMB7 knockdown suppressed cell proliferation and enhanced irradiation-induced apoptosis, whereas PSMB7 overexpression promoted proliferation and reduced apoptosis after irradiation.ConclusionPSMB7 is a candidate independent prognostic biomarker in LUAD and is associated with malignant progression, immune microenvironment features, and cellular responses to irradiation consistent with a potential role in radioresistance. These findings support PSMB7 as a potential therapeutic target in LUAD.
authors: Shen Y, Wan Y, Ren B, Wu L, Jin L, Zhu Y, Huan J, Peng Q.

title: Identification and experimental validation of candidate biomarkers for Parkinson's Disease through integrated bioinformatics, Mendelian randomization, and machine learning.
abstract: BackgroundIdentifying reliable biomarkers and therapeutic targets is important for improving the early diagnosis and treatment of Parkinson's disease (PD). This study aimed to identify PD-related core genes, validate their expression, and explore potential therapeutic drugs.MethodsPD transcriptomic datasets were analyzed using differential expression analysis, Mendelian randomization, and machine learning. Candidate genes were validated using quantitative PCR (qPCR) in an MPTP-induced PD mouse model. Potential drugs were screened using the DSigDB database, followed by molecular docking and 100-ns molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate protein-ligand binding and stability.ResultsSeven potential core genes-AMIGO2, ATG7, CDK2AP2, CYP27A1, MT1X, NIPSNAP1, and TTC19-were identified. AMIGO2, ATG7, NIPSNAP1, and TTC19 were downregulated, whereas CDK2AP2, CYP27A1, and MT1X were upregulated. The results of animal experiments validated the abnormal expression of ATG7, NIPSNAP1, TTC19, CYP27A1, and MT1X. Drug screening identified 239 candidate compounds, five of which met the screening criteria. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations provided computational support for relatively stable interactions between the top three drug-target complexes.ConclusionThis study identified several PD-related core genes and experimentally validated the expression of selected genes in an MPTP-induced PD mouse model. In addition, several potential therapeutic compounds were identified through computational analyses, providing candidates for further experimental investigation.
authors: Guan X, Yu W.

title: Targeting the epigenetic landscape of ECFCs: a new opportunity to enhance vascular repair.
abstract: Endothelial colony-forming cells (ECFCs) are endothelial progenitor cells characterized by robust proliferative and vasculogenic capacities, making them promising candidates for therapeutic tissue revascularization. However, the clinical application of ECFCs is hindered by their functional impairment under pathological conditions, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Accumulating evidence indicates that aberrant epigenetic modifications, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNA-mediated regulation, have been implicated in disease-associated ECFC dysfunction. In this review, we summarize current insights into the epigenetic regulation of ECFCs in pathological contexts, discuss epigenetic intervention strategies aimed at restoring ECFC function, and further highlight the therapeutic potential of ECFC-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) as carriers of epigenetic cargo that promotes vascular repair. Collectively, a deeper understanding of the epigenetic landscape of ECFCs and ECFC-derived EVs may facilitate the development of novel therapeutic approaches for vascular regeneration and accelerate the clinical translation of ECFC- and EV-based therapies.
authors: Liu Y, Lyons CJ, Lagonda CA, Luo Y, Cheng L, Fang Z.

title: Conserved Brain-Associated CD8  +  T Cell Programs and Their Regulation by the Brain Microenvironment
abstract: CD8  + T cells are increasingly recognized as components of the healthy brain, yet whether their specialized functional characteristics are conserved across species and how the brain microenvironment regulates their effector programs remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized brain-associated CD8  + T cells in the common marmoset and investigated their regulation by brain-derived signals. Flow cytometric analysis revealed a substantial population of CD8  + T cells in the healthy marmoset brain parenchyma that exhibited high IFN-γ competence but minimal granzyme B (GzmB) expression, resembling the functional phenotype previously identified in mice. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of mouse and marmoset CD8  + T cells revealed tissue-associated transcriptional heterogeneity and distinct differentiation- and effector-associated programs. To investigate how the brain microenvironment shapes these characteristics, we exposed activated mouse CD8  + T cells to brain lysate and performed targeted CRISPR interference screening of 107 cell-surface receptor genes coupled with single-cell RNA sequencing. Brain lysate selectively reduced  Gzmb and  Ifng expression while increasing  Tnf and  Xcl1 , indicating differential regulation of cytotoxic and inflammatory effector programs. Receptor perturbations revealed heterogeneous transcriptional responses and identified candidate pathways potentially involved in sensing brain-derived signals. Together, these findings identify shared functional characteristics of brain-associated CD8  + T cells across rodents and nonhuman primates and establish a framework for understanding how the neural microenvironment shapes adaptive immune function.
authors: Park K, Sanchez T, Jeon S, Schade PF, Hildebrand DGC, Yim YS.

title: WTAP-mediated m6A methylation stabilizes pIgR mRNA and attenuates smoke-induced epithelial inflammation and apoptosis.
abstract: Smoke inhalation injury (SII) dramatically elevates burn patient mortality. Although N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation is emerging as a central epitranscriptomic regulator of lung inflammation and injury, its specific involvement in SII remains unknown. Using an in vivo mouse SII model and smoke extract-treated MLE-12 cells, we show that smoke exposure downregulates the m6A writer-complex component WTAP and reduces global m6A methylation. WTAP knockdown attenuates epithelial inflammation, apoptosis, and STAT3 activation. Integrating transcriptomics with weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and MeRIP-qPCR, we identify pIgR as a downstream target: WTAP modifies m6A methylation within the 756/772 region of pIgR mRNA, and its knockdown prolongs pIgR mRNA half-life and elevates pIgR expression. pIgR silencing reverses the protection conferred by WTAP knockdown. These findings define a WTAP/m6A/pIgR axis that shapes the early epithelial response to smoke inhalation and identifies WTAP as a candidate therapeutic target for SII.
authors: Li J, Huang S, Guo G.

title: Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyzes reveal hepatic regulatory mechanisms of residual feed intake during the late growth stage of slow-growing yellow-feathered broilers.
abstract: This study aimed to characterize hepatic molecular features associated with residual feed intake (RFI) during the late growth stage of slow-growing yellow-feathered broilers through integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyzes. RFI was measured in 478 individually caged male Langya chickens from 96 to 133 days of age. After the feeding trial, the chickens were ranked in ascending order of RFI and classified into low-RFI (LRFI) and high-RFI (HRFI) subpopulations using the population mean RFI as the cutoff. Eight healthy chickens were then randomly selected from each subpopulation to form the LRFI and HRFI groups (n = 8 per group). Following slaughter and tissue collection at 133 days of age, hepatic transcriptomic and LC-MS-based untargeted metabolomic analyzes were conducted. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and differentially abundant metabolites (DAMs) were subsequently subjected to enrichment and correlation analyzes. Compared with HRFI chickens, LRFI chickens had lower feed intake (FI) and higher eviscerated carcass yield and breast muscle yield. They also had lower abdominal fat percentage and muscle fat width, whereas BWG and metabolic body weight were similar between groups. Liver profiling identified 850 DEGs and 282 DAMs. Integrated KEGG analysis identified 15 pathways significantly enriched in both datasets. The amino acid metabolism-related pathways among these shared pathways collectively pointed to aromatic amino acid (AAA)-related metabolism, including biosynthesis of amino acids, phenylalanine metabolism, phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan biosynthesis, and tryptophan metabolism. A total of 16 DEGs and 29 DAMs were mapped to these pathways and showed widespread significant correlations. Among them, IL4I1, AFMID, ASS1, PHGDH, MAOB, IDO2, HAAO, and PAH were identified as candidate genes associated with RFI. These results characterized hepatic molecular features associated with RFI during the late growth stage of slow-growing yellow-feathered broilers. These findings indicate that hepatic AAA-related metabolism may play a potential role in RFI divergence during the late growth stage in slow-growing yellow-feathered broilers. The identified AAA metabolism-related pathways provide a focused set of candidate genes, metabolites, and pathways for further investigation of their roles in RFI and feed efficiency, and provide a theoretical basis for molecular breeding and breed conservation of slow-growing broilers.
authors: Chen Z, Sun Y, Wang J, Li F, Zhao X, Liu W, Han H, Lei Q, Zhou Y, Cao D, Liu J.

title: CTRP3 disruption promotes a tendon-like matrix signature in tenogenically induced canine adipose-derived stem cells.
abstract: IntroductionTendon injuries heal through disorganized extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition rather than the restoration of native collagen architecture, thus resulting in suboptimal functional recovery. Although adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) are attractive for tendon regeneration because of their accessibility and expandability, their tenogenic differentiation efficiency is lower than that of tendon-derived stem cells (TDSCs). C1q/TNF-related protein 3 (CTRP3) is an adipokine implicated in ECM remodeling and fibrosis; however, its role in tendon lineage regulation is unknown.ObjectiveCTRP3 (C1q/TNF-related protein 3) contributes to extracellular-matrix remodeling and, in tendon, is associated with a pathological fibrotic matrix signature; we therefore reasoned that reducing CTRP3 would favor a more mature tendon-like matrix. Using a loss-of-function approach based on clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), we investigated whether CTRP3 disruption alters tenogenic marker expression, at both the transcript and protein levels, and the tendon-associated ECM marker profile of canine ADSCs relative to wild-type ADSCs and native TDSCs.MethodsCRISPR/Cas9-mediated CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs were generated and validated using sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, and Western blotting. Wild-type ADSCs, CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs, and TDSCs were subjected to tenogenic induction for 0-3 weeks. Tenogenic transcriptional and ECM markers were analyzed at mRNA and protein levels.ResultsCTRP3-disrupted ADSCs showed increased collagen type I and tenomodulin (TNMD) expression during tenogenic induction compared with wild-type ADSCs. COL III expression showed a transient increase followed by a decline, with lower expression in CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs than in WT cADSCs at week 2. CTRP3 disruption increased early Mkx and Scx expression at the earliest time points but did not consistently alter the early transcriptional program, which rose comparably across all groups. CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs showed partial, marker- and time-point-dependent overlap with native cTDSCs, mainly for selected late ECM markers rather than across the overall transcript and protein profiles.ConclusionCTRP3 disruption shifted the tendon-associated ECM marker profile during the tenogenic differentiation of ADSCs, with reduced COL III accumulation, rather than uniformly enhancing tenogenic differentiation. Although early transcriptional changes were observed, the more consistent differences were found in late tendon-associated ECM markers. The modulation of CTRP3 may represent a candidate strategy worth further investigation for stem cell-based tendon regeneration in veterinary medicine.
authors: Kim S, Lee JH, Jang G, Kang BJ.

title: Mapping the Intellectual Architecture of Inflammation-Centered Macrophage Research in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Dual-Database Bibliometric and Scientometric Analysis, 2005-2025.
abstract: BackgroundChronic liver inflammation provides a major biological context for hepatocarcinogenesis, and macrophages link innate immune sensing, fibrogenesis, immune suppression and therapeutic resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), Kupffer cells and inflammation-associated myeloid populations have been extensively investigated in HCC; however, the intellectual structure and thematic connectivity of this inflammation-centered research field remain incompletely defined.ObjectiveThis study aimed to map the intellectual architecture, evolutionary trajectory and inter-module connectivity of inflammation-centered macrophage research in HCC using bibliometric and scientometric methods.MethodsA total of 9218 English-language articles and reviews on macrophage-related HCC from 2005 to 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus after systematic deduplication. CiteSpace, VOSviewer and bibliometrix were used to perform co-citation clustering, reference historiographic mapping, keyword co-occurrence analysis, publication-volume-adjusted keyword correlation analysis, citation burst detection, journal dual-map overlay and multi-level collaboration profiling.ResultsAnnual publication output increased from 84 articles in 2005 to 1129 in 2025. Co-citation analysis resolved 13 well-defined clusters (modularity Q = 0.744; mean silhouette S = 0.884), and historiographic mapping identified four sequential stages: foundational inflammation and hepatocarcinogenesis, mechanistic expansion of TAM function, immune-regulatory convergence and spatial immunology. Keyword dynamics showed a transition from viral hepatitis, innate immunity, Kupffer cells and fibroinflammatory terminology toward TAM-mediated immune suppression, immunotherapy, single-cell analysis, SPP1-positive macrophage-associated spatial immune barriers and computational precision oncology. After annual publication-volume adjustment, the foundational viral-innate module and the contemporary computational-precision oncology module showed a negative inter-module Pearson correlation (mean r = -0.383), lower than expected under label-permutation and temporal-succession null models (both p ConclusionMacrophage-related HCC research has evolved from inflammation-centered hepatocarcinogenesis toward spatially resolved and computationally assisted immunology. The low-connectivity interfaces identified in this study should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating bibliometric signals rather than as evidence of biological or clinical disconnection or as stand-alone research priorities derived from network structure alone. Their potential translational relevance should be considered alongside published mechanistic and clinical evidence and requires future mechanistic, spatial and prospective clinical validation.
authors: Chai K, Chen C, Wu K, Zhao X.

title: Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis Identifies GPX3 and CSF3R as Candidate Markers of Diabetes-Associated Myocardial Injury.
abstract: PurposeThe clinical relationship between diabetes mellitus (DM) and myocardial injury (MI) is well established, yet the antioxidant protection mechanisms involving glutathione peroxidase that link DM to MI remain insufficiently characterized. Here, across multiple organs and tissues, we explored the relationship between extracellular antioxidant defense and inflammatory signaling in DM-induced MI.MethodsThe analyses integrated six single-cell RNA-seq datasets (21 diabetic samples; 122,801 cells) with the bulk transcriptomic dataset GSE184050 (113 samples); LASSO regression yielded a cross-validated area under the curve (AUC) of 0.701, and GPX3 and CSF3R were further validated in a T2DM-AS mouse model (n = 3 per group for histological and Western blot analyses).ResultsWe identified glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3) and colony-stimulating factor 3 receptor (CSF3R) as candidate markers associated with DM-induced MI. CSF3R was enriched in injury- and inflammation-related pathways including PI3K-Akt signaling, whereas GPX3 was enriched in antioxidant and defense-related pathways. CSF3R enrichment was also associated with reduced activity of the cardioprotective cGMP-PKG pathway. Endothelial dysfunction and collagen remodeling, potentially involving monocyte-endothelial crosstalk, are proposed as candidate intermediates in this cascade. Histological examination confirmed extensive MI in DM mice, characterized by disordered cardiomyocyte arrangement and widespread myofiber rupture. Western blot analysis showed that myocardial GPX3 expression was significantly downregulated in DM mice compared with non-diabetic controls, whereas CSF3R was markedly upregulated, changes that were specific to the diabetic milieu and not observed in atherosclerosis alone.ConclusionGPX3 and CSF3R were identified as candidate markers associated with diabetes-related cardiac injury and warrant validation in independent human cardiac datasets and mechanistic experiments.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
authors: Song J, Long Y, Zhang W, Liu L.

title: Association of Plasma CCDC88A Expression Combined with Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate with Rheumatoid Arthritis Disease Activity: A Cross-Sectional Exploratory Study.
abstract: BackgroundRheumatoid arthritis (RA) disease activity is assessed using composite clinical indices that combine examination findings, patient and physician‒reported assessments, and laboratory markers. Circulating RNA may provide complementary molecular information, but evidence for plasma RNA markers of current RA activity remains limited.PurposeTo identify plasma RNA transcripts associated with cross-sectional RA disease activity and to explore whether plasma RNAs concentration provides complementary discriminatory information when combined with hematological parameters.Patients and methodsThis cross-sectional, two-stage study used targeted RNA sequencing to screen plasma from 25 patients with established RA and 14 healthy controls (HCs). Patients with RA were categorized as having high disease activity (HDA; DAS28-ESR >5.1, n=13) or low disease activity/remission (LDA/remission; DAS28-ESR ≤3.2, n=12). The expression of the leading candidate, CCDC88A, was assessed by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) in 108 plasma samples, including 78 patients with RA and 30 HCs.ResultsPlasma CCDC88A expression was lower in patients with RA than in HCs (median [interquartile range], 0.55 [0.29-0.81] vs 0.94 [0.59-1.12]; p=0.003). For cross-sectional discrimination between moderate activity and LDA/remission, the area under the curve (AUC) was 0.659 for CCDC88A, 0.746 for erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and 0.785 for their combination.ConclusionMolecular markers, when combined with peripheral blood-derived parameters, such as ESR, may potentially serve as supporting indicators of RA disease activity.
authors: Cieśla M, Wołkow P, Darmochwał-Kolarz D, Podgórska D, Kolarz B.

title: PROMISE-Surv: Proteomics-guided survival representation transfer for deployable transcriptomic cancer modeling.
abstract: BackgroundDeep proteomic and phosphoproteomic profiling captures functional tumor signaling, but these assays are unavailable in most large survival cohorts. Existing multi-omics approaches often require complete molecular profiles or reconstruction of missing modalities, leaving unclear whether survival-relevant protein-layer information can be transferred directly to routinely available data. We therefore investigated whether proteomics-informed survival structure could be transferred to an RNA-plus-clinical model without reconstructing missing protein measurements.MethodsPROMISE-Surv was developed as a teacher-student framework using complete-case CPTAC/PDC tumors from lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC), and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) as the multimodal discovery cohort (n = 314). The student model was then deployed in matched TCGA cohorts from the same cancer types (n = 1571), with independent GEO cohorts used as endpoint-specific external stress tests.ResultsAcross ten repeated held-out splits, the blended student achieved a mean C-index of 0.687 (95% CI, 0.638-0.730); matched discovery scores preserved teacher-derived risk ordering across all three cancers (Spearman ρ=0.981-0.989). In TCGA, transferred risk stratified survival in KIRC and LUAD and recovered cancer-specific RNA programs linked to adverse tumor biology, with concordant pathway-level support from RPPA. Cross-cancer analysis identified eight directionally conserved RNA-risk markers, while enrichment of the broader candidate ranking implicated RNA processing and ribosome biogenesis. These findings support biological coherence of the transferred risk representation.ConclusionsPROMISE-Surv provides a biological-transfer framework for extending proteomics-informed survival structure to RNA-plus-clinical cohorts without protein-layer measurements.
authors: Nguyen DPQ, Ho NT, Ta HDK.

title: The Tango of cGAS-STING and Phagocytosis in Disease: From Molecular Mechanisms to Pharmacological Targeting.
abstract: The cGAS-STING pathway is a central cytosolic DNA sensor that orchestrates innate immune responses beyond type I interferons, including autophagy, senescence, metabolism, and cell death. Phagocytosis-essential for clearing pathogens, debris, and apoptotic bodies-critically bridges innate and adaptive immunity. This review examines the bidirectional, context-dependent interplay between these fundamental processes and highlights how nanotechnology is uniquely positioned to exploit this crosstalk for therapeutic gain. We delineate four paradigms: STING activation upstream induces phagocytosis in lung inflammation, sepsis, spinal cord injury, cancer, and viral infection; phagocytosis initiates STING by delivering immunogenic cargo; positive feedback loops amplify antitumor immunity; and STING can suppress phagocytosis in obesity-driven adipose inflammation. Importantly, this axis exerts opposing regulatory effects across disease settings, being protective or pathogenic, synergistic or antagonistic, depending on cell type, stimulus, and pathological context. We further synthesize advanced nanoplatforms-biomimetic nanoparticles, hybrid membrane vesicles, DNA nanodevices, lymph node-targeted nanovaccines, and "Trojan horse" nanocapsules-engineered to co-deliver STING agonists, phagocytosis checkpoint inhibitors, and immunogenic cargo. These nanotherapies enhance antitumor and antimicrobial defense, resolve inflammation, and overcome barriers such as the blood-brain barrier. By integrating mechanism with nanobiotechnology, this review provides a conceptual framework for the cGAS -STING-phagocytosis network and a roadmap for next-generation nanomedicines treating cancer, infection, neurodegeneration, and inflammatory disorders.
authors: Wang H, Chen J, Wang Z, Wu F.

title: Comparative multi-omics reveals distinct transcriptomic and metabolomic profiles during fruit development in highbush and rabbiteye blueberries.
abstract: Blueberry fruit quality is shaped by coordinated changes in gene expression and metabolite composition during development, but how these processes differ between cultivated blueberry species (highbush and rabbiteye) across developmental stages (green, pink and ripe) remains unclear. We integrated texture analysis, transcriptomics and metabolomics, to determine the contributions of developmental stage (green, pink, and ripe) and species differentiation to variation in transcriptomic and metabolomic profiles and fruit texture. Both factors influenced gene expression and metabolite accumulation. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses revealed strong species-associated variation, whereas developmental stage defined a conserved ripening trajectory. Across species, ripening was characterized by coordinated downregulation of photosynthesis pathways and increased accumulation of anthocyanins, flavonoids, phenolic acids, terpenoids, and carbohydrates. Species-associated differences remained across developmental stages: rabbiteye fruit exhibited higher expression of genes involved in stress responses, metabolite transport, and specialized metabolism, together with greater accumulation of phenylpropanoid derivatives and organic acids. In contrast, highbush fruit showed higher expression of genes associated with primary metabolism, nutrient transport, intracellular trafficking, and cell wall-related processes, accompanied by increased accumulation of flavonol glycosides, sphingolipids, and structural metabolites. Integrated multi-omics analyses identified key genes and metabolites for ripening and species, and their association with texture parameters. Candidate genes were prioritized through integration with previously reported genes involved in cell wall and lignin and flavonoid biosynthesis, providing potential targets for future functional characterization and marker -assisted breeding. Overall, developmental stage governs conserved ripening processes, whereas species-associated differences shape the transcriptomic and metabolomic landscape associated with fruit quality traits.
authors: Mengist MF, Taghavi T, Iorizzo M.

title: Cancer-selective cytotoxicity of a semi-synthetic derivative of oleuropein via proteostasis network impairment.
abstract: Cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide, driving continued research for innovative therapies with enhanced specificity and efficacy. Natural products have long been recognised as a valuable source of anticancer agents due to their structural diversity and unique biological activities. Building on the anticancer potential of oleuropein, a major olive tree (Olea europaea) metabolite, we evaluated a newly synthesised semi-synthetic analogue, GS32, for its cytotoxic activity in vitro. Cytotoxicity assays revealed that GS32 exhibited broad-spectrum activity against various cancer cell lines, while also displaying differential toxicity between normal and cancerous cells. Through transcriptomic analysis, we discovered that GS32 differentially disrupts key cellular pathways involved in stress response. Importantly, targeted phosphoproteomic profiling uncovered context-dependent modulation of key signalling pathways, including the AKT/mTOR and NF-κB axes, as well as stress-response regulators. Further experiments confirmed that GS32 disrupts the proteostasis network, leading to excessive proteotoxic stress, mainly in malignant cells. This study provides new mechanistic insight into the cellular effects of GS32 and identifies the compound as a candidate that merits further preclinical investigation.
authors: Gianniou DD, Kontos CK, Gkogkou E, Sarikaki G, Karousi P, Skaltsounis AL, Scorilas A, Kostakis IK, Trougakos IP.

title: Dioscin attenuates aniline-induced liver injury by targeting the ACOT2-mediated ROS-JAK2/STAT3-CLN5 axis and restoring mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation and lysosomal lipophagy.
abstract: Chronic aniline exposure causes prominent hepatotoxicity accompanied by hepatic lipid metabolic disorders and cellular senescence, yet the molecular cascade underlying aniline-triggered liver injury remains unclear. Here, a 90-day chronic aniline intoxication mouse model and an AML12 murine hepatocyte model were established to systematically dissect toxic mechanisms and identify candidate hepatoprotective agents. Adverse outcome pathway analysis revealed lipid metabolic disturbance and cellular senescence as core toxic events, with lipid metabolic disturbance acting as an upstream driver of aniline-induced hepatocyte senescence and injury. Integrated multi-omics analysis showed that acyl-CoA thioesterase 2 (ACOT2), a key rate-limiting enzyme in fatty acid β-oxidation, was markedly downregulated in aniline-damaged livers. Hepatic ACOT2 overexpression restored mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation capacity, alleviated lipid overload, excessive ROS accumulation and hepatic dysfunction, and reduced bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP) accumulation by suppressing neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis protein 5 (CLN5) expression. Mechanistically, ACOT2 deficiency caused ROS overproduction and activated JAK2/STAT3 signaling. Phosphorylated STAT3 translocated into the nucleus and directly bound the Cln5 promoter, enhancing its transcription. Elevated CLN5 disrupted lysosomal structural integrity and acidification, thereby blocking lipid degradation during lipophagy. Conversely, Cln5 silencing restored lysosomal homeostasis and autophagic flux and reduced hepatic lipid deposition. Virtual screening identified dioscin as a natural small molecule that directly interacts with ACOT2, as confirmed by molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation and surface plasmon resonance assays. PPARα-dependent transcriptional regulation contributed to ACOT2 suppression across multiple liver injury models, whereas dioscin restored ACOT2-dependent fatty acid oxidation and conferred broad hepatoprotection against aniline-, CCl4-, and APAP-induced liver injury. Collectively, this study reveals, in male mice and murine hepatocyte models, a previously unreported ACOT2-regulated ROS-JAK2/STAT3-CLN5 axis linking impaired mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, lysosomal dysfunction and defective lipid clearance during aniline hepatotoxicity. These findings further support dioscin as a promising hepatoprotective candidate drug that directly targets ACOT2.
authors: Xing Y, Zhang B, Chen Y, Wang H, Yu S, Chen L, Wang Y.

title: AIM2 as a therapeutic target in autoimmunity: balancing inflammasome inhibition with immune homeostasis.
abstract: Absent in melanoma 2 (AIM2) is a cytosolic pattern recognition receptor that functions as a critical sensor of double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) of microbial or host origin. Upon DNA recognition, AIM2 assembles into a multiprotein inflammasome complex that drives pyroptotic cell death and maturation of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18. Beyond its canonical role in host defense, aberrant AIM2 activation by self-DNA has been increasingly implicated in the pathogenesis of various inflammatory autoimmune diseases. This comprehensive review synthesizes current understanding of AIM2 biology. We examine the role of AIM2 in different immune cell populations, its effects on multiple downstream signaling pathways, and its complex association with autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and multiple sclerosis. Finally, we discussed therapeutic prospects and remaining challenges in targeting AIM2 for the treatment of autoimmunity.
authors: Xu WD, Liu Z, Su LC, Huang AF.

title: Heterologous expression of LbbHLH36 from Lycium barbarum enhances carotenoid accumulation in tomato fruits via synergistic activation of biosynthesis and suppression of degradation.
abstract: Carotenoids are critical determinants of nutritional quality in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) fruits, and their biosynthesis is tightly regulated by the bHLH transcription factor family. In this study, we investigated the heterologous regulatory function of LbbHLH36, a gene isolated from Lycium barbarum L., in carotenoid accumulation and its responsiveness to abiotic stresses in tomato. The LbbHLH36 coding sequence was cloned into the pNULPGE700 vector and introduced into the model tomato cultivar 'Micro Tom' via Agrobacterium-mediated leaf disc transformation. Quantitative real-time PCR revealed that LbbHLH36 transcript levels peaked in mature fruits of transgenic lines and were associated with significant upregulation of key early biosynthetic genes, including SlPSY1, SlPSY2, SlPDS, and SlZDS. Enzymatic assays further demonstrated increased activities of the rate-limiting enzymes phytoene synthase (PSY) and phytoene desaturase (PDS), alongside a marked suppression of carotenoid cleavage dioxygenase 4 (CCD4) activity in transgenic plants. Metabolomic analyses confirmed that overexpression of LbbHLH36 substantially elevated total carotenoid, lycopene, and β-carotene contents in tomato fruits. Furthermore, LbbHLH36 expression was strongly induced by high temperature, low temperature, drought, and salt stress, suggesting its potential involvement in crosstalk between stress responses and primary metabolism. Collectively, our findings reveal that LbbHLH36 acts as a positive regulator of carotenoid accumulation in tomato through a dual mechanism that concurrently regulate biosynthetic flux and attenuates catabolic degradation, highlighting its value as a candidate gene for nutritional quality improvement in Lycium barbarum, tomato, and other Solanaceous crops.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Liu S, She P, Hu S, Yue S, Zhao J, Liu Y, Zheng R.

title: Comparative analysis of KMT2A fusions in human models of acute myeloid leukemia.
abstract: Pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (AML) frequently involves chromosomal rearrangements, particularly KMT2A (MLL) gene fusions, with the KMT2A-MLLT4 (KM4-AML) fusion being highly aggressive and associated with poor prognosis. This study presents a comparative analysis of transcriptomic and epigenetic profiles between human leukemia models harboring KM4-AML and KMT2A-MLLT3 (KM3-AML) fusions. Transcriptomic signatures of KM4-AML models closely resembled those of patient samples, underscoring the model's clinical relevance. Epigenetic analysis revealed distinct chromatin accessibility and methylation patterns between KM4-AML and KM3-AML, particularly in enhancer regions linked to aggressive leukemia phenotypes. PROM1 was identified as a potential biomarker for KM4-AML, with its overexpression correlating with poor prognosis. Furthermore, high-throughput drug screening identified dopamine receptor antagonists (DRAs) as promising therapeutic candidates showing selective response for KM4-AML models. Docking simulations and NMR assays confirmed favorable binding interactions between DRAs and S100A8, S100A9 and ANXA6. These findings provide insights into the molecular mechanisms driving KM4-AML and offer potential therapeutic avenues for treatment.
authors: Safa-Tahar-Henni S, Milan T, DesCôteaux T, Roques É, Bonnet-Magnaval F, Osborne MJ, Bresson E, Mathien S, Chazin WJ, Hébert J, Borden KLB, Najmanovich R, Cellot S, Barabé F, Wilhelm BT.

title: A saturation-normalized thermal conductivity framework for municipal solid waste with composition-related differences in unsaturated response.
abstract: Thermal conductivity is important for landfill temperature evolution and thermal safety assessment. Moisture is generally regarded as the main factor controlling thermal conductivity in municipal solid waste (MSW), but the role of composition in shifting conductivity bounds and shaping unsaturated response remains unclear. In this study, thermal conductivity was measured at 20-23 °C using a transient thermal probe for four aged MSW samples with approximate landfill ages of 5, 10, 15, and 20 years and one fresh MSW sample based on typical Wuhan MSW composition. Specimens were prepared at target dry densities of 400-700 kg·m-3 under dry, saturated, and unsaturated conditions. Unsaturated specimens had volumetric water contents of 25.86-62.14% and saturation of 0.328-0.957. Dry-state thermal conductivity ranged from 0.0304 to 0.0616 W·m-1·K-1, while saturated values from 0.4735 to 0.7211 W·m-1·K-1. Under unsaturated conditions, thermal conductivity generally increased with moisture level, with sample-dependent variations. Saturation showed a slightly stronger association with thermal conductivity than volumetric water content. Among three candidate Ke-Sr formulations, the Côté & Konrad model performed best, with grouped fitting outperforming full-data fitting. Waste components were regrouped as rigid mineral skeleton, flexible low-thermal-conductivity barrier, and hydrophilic/biodegradable bridging components to interpret sample differences. The results suggest that skeleton-dominated components are more closely related to sustained heat transfer at medium to high saturation, whereas hydrophilic/biodegradable components mainly affect the early heat-transfer development at low saturation. The saturation-normalized framework supports estimating MSW thermal conductivity and interpreting composition-related differences in unsaturated response.
authors: Li R, Liu L, Chen Z, Hu Y, Li D.

title: Amelioration of early pathological changes in the 3xTg-AD mouse model: Mechanism of action of the Chinese herbal formula Tianqi Granules.
abstract: AbstractAlzheimer's disease is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline. This study investigated the effects of the Chinese herbal formula Tianqi Granules on early pathological progression in the 3xTg-AD mouse models and investigated the underlying mechanisms. After 31 days of Tianqi Granule treatment initiated at 5 months of age, Tianqi Granules-treated mice showed improved performance in the open-field test, novel object recognition test, and Morris water maze test. Amyloid deposition and glial activation were attenuated, and immunoreactivity for interleukin-1β and LC3 was reduced. Hippocampal transcriptome sequencing at multiple time points showed that, in untreated mice, early pathological progression occurred in three successive phases, with the dominant processes shifting from compensatory programs to failing homeostasis and subsequently to degenerative changes. Tianqi Granule treatment was associated with a three-phase response centered on the restoration of homeostasis and involving proteostasis, nuclear processes, lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, and redox-related pathways. Multiple biological domains were engaged rather than a single target. In males, an interferon-related program associated with Irf7 was induced early and shifted in the opposite direction under Tianqi Granule treatment during the same time window. Network pharmacology identified OPRK1 as the only candidate target shared by both sexes, making it a potential target for future investigation. These findings suggest that Tianqi Granule modulates the pathology of Alzheimer's disease through coordinated actions on multiple targets and may influence systemic metabolic homeostasis, providing experimental support for early therapeutic intervention in Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Zhang T, Xu L, Huang W, Chen Z, Miao J, Zhang Y, Zhu Y, Yuan Y, Gu X.

title: Divergent Immunometabolic Regulatory Networks Mediated by FOXO3 During Musculoskeletal Aging: Implications for Tissue-Adapted Precision Therapeutics.
abstract: Musculoskeletal aging exhibits prominent tissue heterogeneity. Forkhead box O3 (FOXO3) acts as a master transcription factor orchestrating aging, metabolism and immune homeostasis. Existing mechanistic investigations are largely restricted to single tissues, and a head-to-head comparison of FOXO3-governed immunometabolic regulatory networks between knee osteoarthritis (KOA) synovium and aged skeletal muscle remains absent. A retrospective multi-cohort transcriptomic analysis was performed using datasets retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Two KOA synovial cohorts (GSE55235 and GSE55457, n = 40) and two aged skeletal muscle cohorts (GSE28422 and GSE25941, n = 146) were enrolled, covering a total of 186 tissue samples. We integrated differential expression analysis, random-effects meta-analysis, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) performance evaluation, single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA), and partial correlation analysis adjusted for disease confounding effects. A bootstrap-scoring system was further established to prioritize candidate therapeutic strategies. FOXO3 exhibited opposing expression patterns: it was downregulated in KOA synovium yet upregulated in aged skeletal muscle. The coupling profiles between FOXO3 and immune or metabolic pathways displayed striking tissue-specific divergence. In KOA synovium, FOXO3 expression was positively correlated with mitochondrial energy metabolism and macrophage infiltration, accompanied by selective inflammatory immune infiltration. By contrast, aged skeletal muscle resided in an immune-quiescent microenvironment, where elevated FOXO3 was strongly negatively coupled to oxidative metabolic pathways. Distinct intervention strategies were derived from these divergent network signatures: combined FOXO3 activation and metabolic modulation was recommended for KOA, whereas supplementation with nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) precursors constituted the primary intervention for aged skeletal muscle. Opposite FOXO3 expression levels correspond to fundamentally distinct immunometabolic network landscapes during musculoskeletal aging. The functional output of FOXO3 is dictated by the tissue microenvironment rather than its transcriptional abundance alone. This study supports stratified precision geriatric interventions via tissue-specific modulation of the FOXO3 pathway across divergent musculoskeletal aging contexts.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.
authors: Zhang P, Wang X, Shi X, Yuan Y, Wang P, Zhao R, Xie D, Tan H, Cao G.

title: Limb-localized induction of regeneration reshapes brain and amputation-site transcriptional states in adult  Xenopus laevis
abstract: Limb regeneration requires coordinated tissue reconstruction and nervous system reintegration, yet whether regenerative induction alters brain responses to limb loss remains unclear. We analyzed transcriptomics from the paired brains and amputation sites of adult  Xenopus laevis after hindlimb amputation with or without a 24-hour exposure to localized, pro-regenerative multi-drug treatment (MDT) delivered through a wearable bioreactor device. At 24 hours post treatment (24 HPT), MDT brains showed increased vascular and basement membrane transcripts and enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation and mTORC1 programs. In the limb, an exploratory integrated stress response (ISR) score increased at 11 and 24 HPT and returned to control levels by 7 days post treatment (7 DPT), coinciding with induction of growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15), a cytokine responsive to mitochondrial stress. No corresponding increase in brain ISR score was detected. At 7 DPT, MDT brains showed enrichment of immune, heme metabolism and biosynthetic programs, reduced synaptic transmission gene expression and increased  gdf15.L . Relative to an external uninjured reference, MDT and amputation-only brains showed concordant changes, with treatment modifying selected programs. Cross-species comparative analyses identified partial overlap with an axolotl regenerative glutamatergic signature and separation from selected mammalian injury profiles. These findings reveal cross-tissue responses to regenerative induction, identifying candidate mechanisms of brain–body communication in biomedically engineered vertebrate limb regeneration.
authors: Russell SJ, Miller KA, Kaplan DL, Levin M, Murugan NJ.

title: Dosage-dependent disruption of corticofugal neuron development by Fezf2 loss
abstract: Background  Fezf2 (Forebrain Embryonic Zinc Finger 2) is a dosage-sensitive transcription factor required for the specification of corticofugal projection neurons, and rare predicted-deleterious Fezf2 variants are associated with human neurodevelopmental disorders. The cell-type-specific and temporal manner in which Fezf2 dosage shapes cortical development remains incompletely resolved at single-cell resolution. This study aims to quantify the temporal and cell-type-specific transcriptional response to progressive Fezf2 loss by re-analyzing a public single-cell atlas of mouse cortical development. Methods  We re-analyzed 20 single-cell RNA-seq samples spanning embryonic day (E) 10 to postnatal day (P) 4 across wild-type (WT), Fezf2-heterozygous (Het), and Fezf2-knockout (KO) genotypes, together with 3 wild-type single-cell ATAC-seq samples, from Di Bella et al. (2021) (GSE153164). After quality control, consensus doublet removal, and batch integration with two complementary methods (Harmony and scVI), we annotated cell types and quantified genotype effects. Because the source design includes a single library per genotype at most stages, we report effect sizes with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals and calibrate candidate dysregulation against a biological-noise null estimated from the two WT replicates at P1, rather than reporting formal inferential p-values. Results  We recovered 121,889 high-quality cells and 20,982 genes, resolving 17 transcriptionally distinct cell types. The most prominent genotype effect was a dosage-dependent depletion of subcerebral projection neurons (SCPNs) at P1 — the only timepoint at which all three genotypes were sampled: SCPNs comprised 2.21% of WT cells (mean of two replicates) but 0.18% of Het and 0.15% of KO cells, an approximately 13–15-fold reduction. Using the WT-replicate null (99th percentile |log2 fold-change| = 0.34), we identified 947, 1,119, and 838 genes exceeding this threshold in Maturing, Corticothalamic, and Callosal projection neurons, respectively. Genes downregulated in KO projection neurons were convergently enriched for cytoplasmic translation and ribosome biogenesis (adjusted P ≈ 8.8×10  −30 in Corticothalamic Neurons). Regulon-activity analysis nominated Six4, Atf5, and Myt1 as increased and Hdac7, Rest, and Kdm5a as decreased in KO cells.  Conclusions  Progressive Fezf2 loss is associated with a dosage-dependent, cell-type-specific disruption of cortical development, most notably near-elimination of the SCPN compartment by birth and a convergent downregulation of translational/maturation-associated genes across projection neurons. These associations nominate candidate downstream programs for experimental follow-up; they do not by themselves establish a mechanism.
authors: Hossain MJ, Abhi SNI, Islam MM, Shahjahan M, Tasnim UM, Das S.

title: CDKL5 deficiency alters cell subtype-specific molecular programmes and intercellular signalling in the mouse hippocampus
abstract: CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD) is a severe neurodevelopmental condition characterised by epilepsy, intellectual disability, and motor dysfunction. Loss of CDKL5 leads to altered synapse development, excitatory-inhibitory imbalances and glial changes, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood, particularly at the level of individual brain cell subtypes. Here, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on the hippocampus of 12 weeks old heterozygous female  Cdkl5 exon 6 deletion (  Cdkl5  tm1.1Joez/J ) and wild-type mice to characterise cell-subtype-specific transcriptional alterations associated with CDKL5 deficiency.  Analysis of 11,791 high-quality nuclei revealed cell-subtype-specific transcriptional changes across neuronal and non-neuronal populations. Differential expression was most prominent in intratelencephalic and extratelencephalic (IT–ET) glutamatergic neurons, which showed altered expression of genes involved in neuronal signalling and activity-dependent transcription, and in dentate gyrus (DG) neurons, which exhibited coordinated upregulation of multiple ribosomal protein genes. Gene set enrichment analysis revealed broader molecular alterations, with neuronal populations showing recurrent changes in pathways associated with synaptic organisation, neuronal development, axonal and dendritic processes, and neurotransmission. Altered gene expression was also evident among non-neuronal populations, although these displayed fewer changes. CellChat analysis inferred changes in predicted intercellular communication across excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations, particularly  Sema3c signalling, suggesting reorganization of hippocampal neuronal subtypes.  These findings provide a single-nucleus transcriptional atlas of the hippocampus in a CDD mouse model. In our dataset, CDKL5 deficiency was associated with cell-subtype-specific alterations in gene expression, including enrichment of gene pathways related to cellular metabolism, neuronal development and synaptic organisation, alongside alteration in predicted intercellular signalling. This dataset provides a resource for investigating the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying CDD and for prioritising candidate pathways for future therapeutic investigation.
authors: Villegas-Salmerón J, Egan S, Sanfeliu A, Higgins J, Heiland M, El-Mansoury B, Connolly NM, Henshall DC, Mamad O.

title: Sequence-only antigen context improves modeling of antibody hypervariable regions
abstract: The complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) of antibodies govern antigen specificity; consequently, CDR design should be performed conditional on the target antigen. Most published approaches depend on the availability of the antigen’s three-dimensional (3D) structure, which is often difficult to obtain experimentally. In contrast, sequence-only models circumvent this requirement but are typically trained on antibodies without incorporating antigen context; exposure to antigen sequences alone does not necessarily entail learning the underlying interaction determinants. Here, we introduce LangAAI, a masked language model that conditions exclusively on antibody and antigen primary sequences and therefore does not require 3D structures, docking poses, or epitope annotations. To assess whether the model exhibits genuine antigen conditioning, we replace the cognate antigen with a non-binding decoy. Whereas antigen-agnostic models are largely insensitive to this substitution, LangAAI shows a marked reduction in sequence recovery that is specifically concentrated in the hypervariable CDR3 loop. Across benchmarks, LangAAI improves amino-acid recovery relative to existing antibody language models, matches the performance of structure-based methods when evaluated under their respective protocols, and ranks experimentally measured variants by affinity comparably to inverse-folding models that use backbone coordinates. Collectively, these results support LangAAI as a structure-independent approach for antigen-aware antibody optimization, enabling prioritization of candidate variants for targets lacking solved antigen–antibody complexes.
authors: Bin Ashraf F, Lonardi S.

title: Factors Influencing Timely Utilization of HIV Viral Load Test Results in HIV Care: A Qualitative Study at Kisenyi Health Centre IV, Kampala
abstract: Structured Abstract  Timely utilization of HIV viral load (VL) test results is critical for effective monitoring of antiretroviral therapy (ART) and achieving viral suppression among people living with HIV. However, delays in utilizing VL results remain a challenge in many resource-limited settings. This study explored the factors influencing timely utilization of VL test results at Kisenyi Health Centre IV in Kampala, Uganda. A qualitative study design was employed using key informant interviews and structured facility observations. Eighteen healthcare workers involved in HIV care and viral load management participated in the study, including clinicians, laboratory personnel, data clerks, counsellors, and facility management staff. Data were collected using semi-structured interview guides and observation checklists. Interview transcripts were analysed using thematic analysis guided by the Performance of Routine Information System Management (PRISM) Framework. Three major themes emerged: technical, behavioral, and organizational factors. Technical barriers included unstable digital systems, limited computer access, unreliable internet connectivity, and fragmented health information platforms that delayed result retrieval. Behavioral factors included workload pressures, training gaps, and varying levels of staff motivation and accountability. Organizational challenges included staffing shortages, weak supervision, inconsistent feedback mechanisms, and occasional stock-outs of printing materials. Observational findings confirmed that manual printing and re-entry of VL results into electronic systems contributed to delays in clinical decision-making. Timely utilization of viral load results is influenced by a combination of technical, behavioral, and organizational factors. Strengthening digital system integration, improving health worker capacity, and enhancing facility-level management support could significantly improve VL result utilization and HIV treatment outcomes.
authors: Nabukenya M, Ssenyonga I, Alege JB.

title: Integrated Computational Pharmacology and Experimental Validation Identify the PLK2-TFEB Axis as a Therapeutic Mechanism of Kunkui Baoshen Decoction in Diabetic Kidney Disease.
abstract: IntroductionMetabolic stress and lipid homeostasis imbalance in proximal tubular cells (PTC) are increasingly recognized as critical contributors to diabetic kidney disease (DKD) progression, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. Kunkui Baoshen Decoction (KKBS) has shown clinical benefits in DKD, but its molecular basis remains unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the therapeutic targets and regulatory mechanisms of KKBS in DKD-associated proximal tubular injury.MethodsAn integrated multi-omics strategy combining network pharmacology, transcriptomic analysis, machine learning, and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was applied to identify candidate therapeutic targets of KKBS in DKD. Then, the protective effects of KKBS were further evaluated in db/db mice and high-glucose and high-lipid (HGHL)-induced HK-2 cells by assessing renal function, lipid metabolism, autophagic flux, transcription factor EB (TFEB) nuclear translocation, and fibrosis-related markers.ResultsKKBS effectively reduced urinary protein excretion, corrected aberrant lipid metabolism, and mitigated renal fibrotic lesions in db/db mice. Integrated multi-omics profiling highlighted polo-like kinase 2 (PLK2) as a potential therapeutic target, and scRNA-seq analysis demonstrated its progressive upregulation in PTC during DKD progression. Mechanistically, KKBS treatment reduced PLK2 expression, restored TFEB nuclear translocation, improved autophagic flux, and decreased lipid droplet accumulation. Similar effects were reproduced by PLK2 inhibition in HGHL-induced HK-2 cells.DiscussionThese findings support the PLK2-TFEB axis as a potential therapeutic target in DKD.ConclusionKKBS may alleviate lipid accumulation and fibrotic alterations in DKD by suppressing PLK2 expression, facilitating TFEB nuclear translocation, and restoring autophagy-lysosome-related function.
authors: Ni J, Zhang L, Zhu H, Yang Y, Yu J.

title: Polyphenol-starch complex regulates the butyric acid-NXPH4-PDX1 pathway and alters pancreatic α- and β-cell marker expression profiles via the gut microbiota to stabilize postprandial blood glucose levels in mice with type 2 diabetes.
abstract: Postprandial hyperglycemia is a major driver of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), yet whether food-derived starch-polyphenol complexes improve glycemic control through gut microbiota-dependent changes in pancreatic islet cell marker expression profiles remains unclear. Here, we show that a high-hydrostatic-pressure-treated complex of Lonicera caerulea berry polyphenols and wheat starch (LCBP-WS) forms resistant starch with an A + V crystalline structure and ameliorates postprandial hyperglycemia and insulin resistance in male T2DM mice. LCBP-WS increased intestinal butyrate and GLP-1 levels, reduced glucagon, improved glucose tolerance and pancreatic pathology, and altered pancreatic α-to-β-cell marker expression profiles, accompanied by increased INS, NKX6.1, NXPH4 and PDX1 expression. Antibiotic depletion of the gut microbiota largely abolished these benefits, increasing the glucose excursion area under the curve by 52.8% and suppressing the H3K27ac-NXPH4-PDX1 axis. In αTC1.6 cells, butyrate reversed high-glucose-induced endocrine dysfunction and induced changes in α-and βcell marker expression profiles. Mechanistically, butyrate enhanced H3K27ac enrichment at the NXPH4 locus, upregulated NXPH4 transcription, and stabilized PDX1 by limiting its proteasomal degradation. Genetic silencing of NXPH4 attenuated the effects of butyrate, whereas PDX1 overexpression partially restored them. Together, these suggest identify a gut microbiota-butyrate-H3K27ac-NXPH4-PDX1 pathway linking a food-derived resistant starch complex to changes in pancreatic islet cell marker expression and glycemic control, and suggest starch-polyphenol complexes as a potential dietary strategy for T2DM.
authors: Liu S, He M, Wang X, Chen Y, Zheng Y, Meng F, Chang X, Dong L.

title: A multi-omics computational framework identifies cell-type-specific therapeutic targets and active compounds of Tripterygium wilfordii Hook.f. against diabetic kidney disease.
abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a leading cause of chronic and end-stage kidney disease, and current therapies leave patients at high risk. Tripterygium wilfordii Hook.f. (TWHF), a traditional Chinese medicine, reduces proteinuria in DKD, but the compounds and molecular targets responsible remain poorly defined. We hypothesized that specific bioactive compounds of TWHF ameliorate DKD through interactions with cell-type-specific molecular targets, thereby modulating inflammatory, immune, and tissue-remodeling pathways involved in disease progression. By integrating transcriptomic analysis, immune-infiltration profiling, single-cell RNA sequencing, virtual gene knockout analysis, and molecular docking, this study developed a comprehensive computational framework to investigate the cell-type-specific and multi-target mechanisms of TWHF in DKD. Using the GEO study GSE30529 (with 22 microdissected human kidney samples), we intersected predicted TWHF targets with DKD-associated and differentially expressed genes from human kidney tubules, and identified four key genes (CCR2, MMP7, PLK2, and PSMB9) that were upregulated in DKD and negatively correlated with glomerular filtration rate. The immune microenvironment in diseased kidneys was found to be remodelled based on an immune-infiltration analysis. Single-cell analysis localized MMP7 to loop-of-Henle epithelial cells, CCR2 to leukocyte, and PLK2 and PSMB9 to endothelial cells, and these genes were implicated in epithelial remodeling and endothelial dysfunction based on virtual gene knockout analysis. Furthermore, molecular docking predicted interactions between the four key proteins and three hub TWHF compounds, with triptolide showing the strongest predicted affinity. In an independent triptolide-response dataset generated from A549 cells, triptolide produced a dose- and time-dependent reduction in PLK2 expression. Collectively, CCR2, MMP7, PLK2, and PSMB9 were identified to be candidate therapeutic targets and Triptolide as a leading active compound, with the potential triptolide-PLK2 regulatory relationship should be further investigated. These results support our hypothesis that TWHF acts through direct, multi-compound engagement of multiple cell-type-specific targets, pointing to a multi-target, multi-pathway mechanism for TWHF in DKD and providing a mechanistic framework for subsequent experimental validation.
authors: Wu R, Wu R, Gandotra S, Lv L, Lee B, He Y.
