title: Functional analysis and breeding application of the ZmDLE1 for maize plant height.
abstract: Plant height (PH) and ear height (EH) are critical agronomic traits in maize breeding, directly affecting lodging resistance, mechanical harvesting and yield potential. In this study, we identified a stable dwarf and low ear mutant, zmdle1-1, from an EMS-mutagenized population of the inbred line LY8405. Genetic mapping and allelism tests, together with a single nucleotide variant mutant (zmdle1-2) and a CRISPR-Cas9 knockout mutant (zmdle1-3), confirmed that the candidate gene ZmDLE1 (Zm00001d033231), which encodes Expansin-B4, is responsible for the reduced PH and EH. Compared with wild-type plants, zmdle1 mutants showed 35% lower PH and 63% lower EH, primarily due to a decreased number of internodes below the ear and shortened internode length. Transcriptome analysis revealed differential expression of hormone responsive genes, and exogenous hormone treatments demonstrated that GA₃, IAA and BR could promote PH in the mutants. Endogenous hormone measurements showed significantly reduced GA₁ and GA₃ levels in the mutants, suggesting that ZmDLE1 may regulate PH through GA biosynthesis or signaling. Importantly, when zmdle1-1 was crossed with five elite inbred lines, the resulting hybrids consistently exhibited markedly reduced PH and EH without compromising ear morphology or yield-related traits. Collectively, our findings establish ZmDLE1 as a key regulator of maize plant architecture and provide a valuable dwarfing resource for breeding high-density tolerant and mechanically harvestable maize hybrids.
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
authors: Zhou W, Liu J, Li Y, He H, Lian X, Dong X, Ma Z, Huang K, Li P, Zhou X, Zhou Y.

title: Thymoquinone exerts anti-inflammatory effects in multiple disease models by regulating immune-inflammatory homeostasis.
abstract: Thymoquinone (TQ), an abundant phytochemical identified from Nigella sativa seeds of the Ranunculaceae family, is recognized for its multifaceted biological effects involving inflammatory regulation, oxidative stress control, and immune modulation. This review summarizes the anti-inflammatory effects of TQ across inflammation-related diseases and integrates bibliometric analysis, network pharmacology, and molecular docking approaches to explore its potential cross-disease immunoregulatory mechanisms. Accumulating evidence suggests that TQ may exert immunoregulatory effects through modulation of key inflammatory and antioxidant pathways, including nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB), mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT), the NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2/heme oxygenase-1 (Nrf2/HO-1), and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ), accompanied by changes in pro-inflammatory mediator production, immune cell functions, and tissue responses in various inflammation-related disease models. Cross-disease mechanistic integrative network pharmacology analysis identified recurrent candidate nodes such as AKT1, TNF, and IL6 across different disease-related networks, suggesting that the broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory effects of TQ may involve coordinated modulation of partially shared immune-inflammatory networks, rather than targeting a single pathogenic pathway. Therefore, this review attempts to break away from the conventional summary model organized by individual diseases or single signaling pathways, and instead adopts the perspective of "immune-inflammatory homeostasis regulation" to comprehensively analyze the anti-inflammatory mechanisms of TQ across various diseases. This approach may facilitate a deeper understanding of its broad-spectrum immunomodulatory effects and potentially provide new theoretical insights for the translation of natural active products into precision immunotherapeutic strategies.
authors: Wang S, Wang H, Zhao Y, Liu Y, Zhou Y, Zhu N.

title: SATB2 as a novel messenger of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway drives CUMS-induced depression via gut-brain axis.
abstract: The microbiota-gut-brain axis is involved in the pathogenesis of depression; however, whether the cGAS-STING signaling pathway contributes to onset and progression of depression via gut microbiota dysbiosis remains unknown. This study aims to investigate the role of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway in chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced depressive-like behaviors. Additionally, it aimed to identify novel downstream signaling factors of this pathway. A comprehensive mechanistic investigation was conducted using CUMS rats, HT22 cells, and cGAS+/- mice, with behavioral tests to assess depressive-like behaviors. Changes in the gut-brain axis and the underlying molecular mechanisms were systematically evaluated by histopathological staining, transmission electron microscopy, immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, Western blotting, co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), transcriptomics, metabolomics, and 16S rRNA sequencing. The results showed that in rats, CUMS induced hippocampal and intestinal damage, inflammation, cGAS-STING activation, and SATB2 upregulation, accompanied by intestinal tight junction impairment. Co-IP assays suggested an interaction between SATB2 and STING/IRF3. Additionally, CUMS rats exhibited altered gut microbiota (decreased beneficial genera, increased opportunistic pathogens) and elevated tobramycin, acarbose, and inosine levels. SATB2 was identified as a potential novel downstream molecule of the cGAS-STING axis, potentially associated with depressive-like behaviors via CUMS-induced gut-brain axis dysregulation. This finding provides a basis for antidepressant intervention strategies targeting this pathway.
authors: Yan X, Gai L, Yang J, Li W, Zhu X, Huang H, Zhao Y, Huang Y, Chen Y, Li Q, Zhao J, Xu Z.

title: GM2A links keratinocyte metabolism to inflammation in psoriasis: Integrated transcriptomic and functional analyses.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis driven by abnormal keratinocyte proliferation and extensive immune cell infiltration. Emerging evidence links its pathogenesis to lipid metabolic dysregulation, yet the specific molecules bridging lipid remodeling to immune activation remain largely unknown. In this study, we integrated transcriptomic datasets through weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), differential expression analysis, and ensemble machine learning (random forest [RF] and support vector machine recursive feature elimination [SVM-RFE]), identifying ganglioside GM2 activator (GM2A) as a top lipid metabolism-related hub gene. Multi-cohort validation confirmed its robust upregulation in psoriatic lesions and its responsiveness to anti-psoriatic therapies. Furthermore, GM2A expression positively correlated with PASI scores and demonstrated strong diagnostic power in a nomogram-based model, reinforcing its candidacy as a diagnostic biomarker. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis revealed that GM2A is specifically elevated in spinous keratinocytes, where it drives ganglio-series glycosphingolipid reprogramming. Intercellular communication analysis demonstrated that spinous keratinocytes promote inflammatory infiltration primarily through the macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF)-CD74 signaling axis, targeting T cells and myeloid cells. In an imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasis-like mouse model, GM2A was significantly upregulated and predominantly localized to the thickened spinous layer, accompanied by elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines. In M5-induced HaCaT cells, GM2A knockdown reduced the mRNA levels of IL-17 A, TNF, IL-6, and IL-1β, attenuated p65 phosphorylation, and decreased MIF release into the supernatant. Additionally, molecular docking identified cyclosporine A as a potential direct binder of GM2A with high affinity. Collectively, our study delineates a novel GM2A-driven metabolic-immune axis in psoriasis, positioning GM2A as a potential diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target.
authors: Wan YW, Li G, Wu S, Ding S, Wang X, Jin X, Lu W, Tao X, Huang Y, Ying Z.

title: Prioritization of contaminants of emerging concern in European surface waters using occurrence, exposure, prediction, and regulatory status perspectives.
abstract: Contaminants of emerging concern (CECs) are increasingly detected in European aquatic environments, yet heterogeneous monitoring data, scarce toxicity information, and evolving regulatory frameworks limit their prioritization. This study developed an evidence-integrated multicriteria framework to prioritize CECs in European surface waters by combining occurrence, reported ecological risk, regulatory recognition, and QSAR-derived hazard & fate endpoints. From an initial list of 259 literature-relevant candidate contaminants, 45 CECs were retained after QSAR reliability filtering. Criteria were weighted using a hybrid AHP-CRITIC approach and ranked with PROMETHEE II. In the baseline model, risk quotient and detection frequency received the highest weights, indicating the strong influence of empirical risk and occurrence. Diuron, 17β-estradiol, tributyl phosphate, 4-n-octylphenol and 4-tert-octylphenol were the five highest-priority contaminants due to convergence of reported ecological risk with strong intrinsic hazard, particularly aquatic toxicity and bioaccumulation potential. Scenario-based sensitivity analysis showed that diuron, 17β-estradiol, 4-n-octylphenol, 4-tert-octylphenol and fluoranthene formed a consistent core priority group, while triclosan, butylated hydroxytoluene and propiconazole gained relevance under hazard-oriented configurations. None of the final 45 contaminants were included in Directive 2024/3019 relative to wastewater treatment plants due to lack of reliable toxicity data in the QSAR model, suggesting that the framework provides a complementary perspective to current European regulatory priorities. This approach supports transparent screening, monitoring design and anticipatory management of CECs in European surface waters.
authors: Gómez FS, Coz A, Llano T.

title: Live-cell, single-molecule imaging resolves the dual nature of mRNA silencing by SARS-CoV-2 Nsp1
abstract: SARS-CoV-2 nonstructural protein 1 (Nsp1) is a conserved viral factor that potently silences host transcripts by binding ribosomes. Yet how it acts at the level of individual mRNAs remains unclear, with competing models arguing that Nsp1 blocks translation initiation, stalls ribosome elongation, cleaves mRNA, or does all three. Here, we use Nascent Chain Tracking to quantify in living cells how Nsp1 reshapes mRNA abundance and translation dynamics with single-molecule resolution. Using reporter transcripts that vary in UTR architecture, initiation mode, and open reading frame length, we find that Nsp1 mainly silences our reporter transcripts by reducing their numbers rather than inhibiting initiation. Two routes to Nsp1-mediated mRNA loss are identified, both requiring cap-dependent initiation: an early route acting during or shortly after initiation and a later route associated with downstream translation that depends in part on ZNF598. Together, these two mechanisms make Nsp1 an efficient and robust suppressor of host gene expression. We further find that reporters containing the SARS-CoV-2 UTRs remain susceptible to Nsp1-mediated mRNA loss, but the 5’ and 3’ UTRs cooperate to increase translation output. Neither viral UTR alone increased translation beyond the host reporter, whereas combining both UTRs substantially enhanced translation in the absence of Nsp1. Together, our results reveal that Nsp1 uses dual, cap-dependent routes to promote mRNA loss across the translation cycle, while the SARS-CoV-2 UTRs provide a cooperative translational advantage rather than robust protection from Nsp1.
authors: Koch A, Wiggan O, Burns E, Geiss B, Snow CD, Morisaki T, Stasevich TJ.

title: Investigating the evolutionary plasticity of influenza virus splicing using influenza A virus segment 7 as a model system
abstract: Influenza viruses A, C and D (IAV, ICV, IDV respectively) utilise mRNA splicing to produce two proteins from their matrix gene segment; the matrix (M1) protein and an ion channel (M2). In IAV, the M1 and M2 open reading frames (ORFs) partially overlap and splice donor (SD) and splice acceptor (SA) sites in the M1 gene are used to produce an M2 polypeptide with an N-terminal sequence shared with M1. In ICV and IDV, the M1 and M2 ORFs are concatenated and splice sites downstream of the M1 coding region are used to produce a matrix protein from the spliced mRNA. To probe how these different splicing strategies might have evolved, we used reverse genetics to test the ‘evolutionary’ flexibility of IAV SD and SA sites. We found that relatively small numbers of mutations were sufficient to activate a variety of alternative SD and SA sites in a mini-replicon system, several of which led to the production of ion channel isoforms with variant ectodomains, as well as one that produced an M1 variant. Furthermore, several of the viruses with altered splicing patterns were viable, including five with both SD and SA sites changed. Three of these ‘rewired’ viruses had only modest fitness penalties, despite up to 3 nonsynonymous changes in M1 and a 34 amino acid insertion in M2. These results suggest that IAV segment 7 splicing strategies are evolutionarily flexible and have implications for how IAV, ICV and IDV matrix segments might have diversified from a common ancestor.
authors: Zhou S, Sharp CP, Gaunt ER, Pinto RM, Digard P.

title: Pharmacological basis of Suhexiang Wan in ischemic stroke: identification and functional characterization of piperlongumine as a brain-distributed bioactive constituent associated with STAT3-mediated blood-brain barrier protection.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceSuhexiang Wan (SHXW) is a classical traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formula that has been traditionally used for stroke-related disorders, including sudden loss of consciousness, neurological dysfunction, and hemiplegia. Although modern pharmacological studies have suggested its neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory properties, the brain-distributed constituents potentially associated with its therapeutic effects in ischemic stroke (IS) and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear.Aim of the studyThis study aimed to elucidate the pharmacological basis of SHXW in IS by identifying brain-distributed constituents and investigating a candidate constituent potentially associated with its protective effects against cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury (CIRI), with particular emphasis on blood-brain barrier (BBB) protection.Materials and methodsSHXW-derived constituents detected in brain tissue under middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) conditions were characterized using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). Integrated network pharmacology analysis was performed to predict potential therapeutic targets and signaling pathways. Piperlongumine (PIP) was further confirmed and quantified in SHXW and brain tissue using an authentic standard-based LC-MS/MS approach. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, biophysical binding assays, and cellular target-engagement experiments were used to investigate the interaction between PIP and signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3). The protective effects and associated mechanisms were evaluated in a mouse MCAO/R model and an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R)-induced brain microvascular endothelial cell injury model.ResultsAmong 1991 putatively annotated constituents of SHXW, 55 SHXW-derived constituents were detected in brain tissue under MCAO/R conditions. In the MCAO/R mouse model, SHXW significantly improved neurological deficits, reduced infarct volume and brain edema, decreased BBB permeability, and restored tight junction protein expression. Among the brain-detected constituents, PIP, a natural alkaloid derived from Piper longum L., was selected for further investigation based on its detection in brain tissue, network topology characteristics, predicted association with STAT3, and reported pharmacological relevance to ischemic injury. Authentic standard-based LC-MS/MS confirmed PIP in SHXW and brain tissue, with a PIP content of 48.21 ± 1.10 μg/g in SHXW and a brain concentration of 159.67 ± 8.37 ng/g at 2 h after SHXW administration. Biophysical and cellular target-engagement assays supported the interaction between PIP and STAT3. PIP partially recapitulated the protective effects of SHXW by alleviating neurological deficits, preserving BBB integrity, restoring endothelial barrier function, and suppressing STAT3-associated inflammatory responses. STAT3 knockdown partially phenocopied the endothelial protective effects of PIP, whereas restoration of STAT3 expression in STAT3-knockdown cells reversed the protective phenotype. PIP treatment attenuated the injury-associated changes following STAT3 restoration, supporting the functional involvement of STAT3-associated signaling in PIP-mediated BBB protection.ConclusionsThis study provides new insights into the pharmacological basis of SHXW in IS by integrating chemical profiling, brain distribution analysis, and pharmacological validation. SHXW exerted protective effects against CIRI and preserved BBB integrity. Among the SHXW-derived constituents detected in brain tissue, PIP was identified and functionally characterized as a bioactive candidate associated with BBB protection. The findings support the involvement of PIP-STAT3 interaction and STAT3-associated inflammatory signaling in PIP-mediated BBB protection. These results provide pharmacological evidence linking the traditional application of SHXW with its modern molecular mechanisms while highlighting brain-distribution-guided approaches for investigating the therapeutic basis of complex TCM formulas.
authors: Wang J, Ma S, Yu D, Wang Y, Ma C, Ma D, Chang X, Yang Y, Jin M, Wang Z, Wu W.

title: Long-term study on spatiotemporal prevalence, distribution, and diversity of clinically relevant and environmental Acinetobacter species in Canadian agricultural watersheds.
abstract: This study, conducted between 2018 and 2024, expands upon prior research through a culture-based investigation of the spatiotemporal prevalence, distribution, and diversity of Acinetobacter species across nine sites in an agriculturally-dominated watershed in eastern Ontario, Canada. Spatial analyses revealed, compared to medium to large stream order sites and forested reference site, agricultural drainage ditches consistently displayed higher Acinetobacter prevalence, cell concentrations, and diversity, likely due to direct proximity to livestock farms. Summer exhibited the highest Acinetobacter abundance and diversity, a pattern potentially linked to elevated temperatures, water stagnation, and seasonal runoff. Species-level identification revealed the widespread and persistent detection of several human health-associated species, including A. baumannii and A. pittii. The association of Acinetobacter species with upstream urban and agricultural land uses suggests that anthropogenically influenced waters may serve as critical sources for the environmental dissemination of pathogenic Acinetobacter and antimicrobial resistance genes. Furthermore, environmental Acinetobacter species, such as A. calcoaceticus, A. guillouiae, A. johnsonii, and A. soli, may play underappreciated roles in gene transfer and infection risk. This first in-depth analysis of Acinetobacter species within an agricultural aquatic ecosystem, offering a foundation for future research into environmental reservoirs of potential human pathogens and the spatiotemporal factors shaping microbial populations.
authors: Tang Y, Duckworth C, Schneiderman D, Craiovan E, Kumar A, Lapen DR, Khan I.

title: Nodule Cysteine-Rich (NCR) Peptides as Next-Generation Antimicrobials: A Computational Perspective on Structure, Mechanism, and Drug Design.
abstract: The rapid escalation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has rendered conventional antibiotics increasingly ineffective, necessitating the exploration of alternative therapeutic strategies. Nodule-specific cysteine-rich (NCR) peptides, a diverse class of plant-derived antimicrobial peptides produced by legumes, have emerged as promising candidates due to their potent and multifaceted biological activity. Unlike traditional antibiotics that target a single cellular pathway, NCR peptides exhibit pleiotropic mechanisms, including membrane disruption, transporter-mediated internalization, intracellular targeting of essential regulatory proteins, and metabolic interference. Recent advances have revealed that their activity is governed not only by primary sequence but also by complex structural determinants such as disulfide bond topology and intrinsically disordered functional domains. Furthermore, their broad-spectrum efficacy, including activity against biofilms and cross-kingdom pathogens, highlights their therapeutic potential in combating multidrug-resistant infections. Computational approaches - molecular dynamics simulations, flexible docking algorithms, and artificial intelligence-based design frameworks - are increasingly proposed as a route to optimizing peptide structure, stability, and target specificity. These individual tools have each been validated in other peptide contexts and, in a small number of cases, directly on NCR peptides; their assembly into a single, discovery-to-validation pipeline for NCR engineering, however, is a synthesis proposed by this review rather than a workflow that has itself been experimentally validated end-to-end. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the structural features, multimodal mechanisms, and computational strategies associated with NCR peptides, explicitly distinguishing experimentally established findings from the proposed in silico pipeline and its current, largely untested assumptions. It also examines current challenges, including instability, unpredictable toxicity, assay-dependent variability, and the still-preliminary evidence for reduced resistance development, and outlines a moderated set of future directions for AI-driven peptide engineering. On present, largely preclinical evidence, NCR peptides represent a promising - but not yet clinically validated - platform warranting further mechanistic and computational investigation as part of the broader antimicrobial pipeline.
authors: Pawar Y, Bidvi S, Choure R.

title: Identification and validation of stable reference genes for RT-qPCR analysis in blood samples from golden Syrian hamsters under different immunological conditions.
abstract: BackgroundThe golden Syrian hamster is the main experimental model for leptospirosis. However, there are no validated reference genes for reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis of blood samples.Methods and resultsThe expression stability of 11 candidate reference genes was evaluated in hamster blood under distinct immunological conditions, including Leptospira interrogans infection and different immunization strategies. Stability was assessed using BestKeeper, geNorm, NormFinder, and the comparative ΔCt method, with the consensus ranking calculated using the RefFinder approach implemented in the RefSeeker R package. The most stable reference gene was ppia, followed by gapdh and ppib, whereas actb was the least stable gene in the ranking. Normalization of tnf-α expression using actb resulted in an approximately 10-fold overestimation compared with ppia, demonstrating the impact of reference gene choice on data interpretation.ConclusionsThese findings support ppia as a reliable reference gene for RT-qPCR normalization in hamster blood under both infection and vaccination conditions.
authors: Nogueira JD, Bunde TT, Maia MAC, de Oliveira NR, Dellagostin OA, Bohn TLO.

title: Proofing the concept of a segmented biophotovoltaic process to produce electricity from marine cyanobacteria: an indoor and outdoor approach.
abstract: This study presents an innovative biophotovoltaic (BPV) process with three components: a cyanobacteria reservoir that serves as the biological engine; an electron-capture reactor that redirects transmembrane electrons; and a radiation-harvesting tower designed to maximize energy input and enhance system scalability. For the indoor (LED) and outdoor (solar radiation) tests, the most suitable resistances to yield the maximum current density were 164 Ω and 220 Ω, respectively. Indoor electricity generation peaked at 227 mW m- 2, with an average of 175 ± 47 mW m- 2, while outdoor tests peaked at 215 mW m- 2, with an average of 166 ± 26 mW m- 2, indicating similar efficiency under both conditions. To explain these efficiencies, the 5% loss in performance is most likely related to the increase in temperature from 20 °C to 32 °C and the resistivity of electrode materials. To confirm this, complementary experiments (in triplicate) demonstrated that an increase in incubator temperature to 32 °C also resulted in lower electricity generation (125 ± 25 mW m- 2). The heat conduction to the cyanobacteria medium led to harsher environmental conditions for Synechocystis pevalekii, and the increased resistivity caused voltage drops. Overall, the proof of concept of our BPV process demonstrated that it is technically possible to run in the system in an external laboratory environment using the segmentation approach and the radiation-harvesting tower.
authors: Castro GEO, Saldanha-Correa FMP, Peixoto G.

title: APV-Sankey: a k-mer persistence visualization tool for HT-SELEX data analysis to identify aptamer candidates.
abstract: APV-Sankey is a novel visualization and analysis tool for High-Throughput Systematic Evolution of Ligands by Exponential Enrichment (HT-SELEX) data. By tracking k-mer persistence and concatenation across SELEX rounds via Sankey diagrams, APV-Sankey provides a complementary framework for identifying aptamer candidates, assessing SELEX progression, and facilitating the interpretation of HT-SELEX data. We demonstrate that k-mer persistence analysis captures biologically relevant patterns in SELEX evolution, complementing existing approaches based on sequence abundance. We benchmark APV-Sankey against standard metrics including final-round abundance, fold enrichment, and k-mer frequency, showing that persistence provides an orthogonal ranking dimension (Spearman ρ = - 0.192 with abundance) with 90% of top-200 persistent k-mers unique to the persistence ranking. APV-Sankey generates structured, round-annotated k-mer datasets suitable for downstream deep learning applications in aptamer binding prediction, positioning it as a data analysis platform for in silico aptamer research.
authors: Zhang Y, Wang Y, Gao Y, Hu K, Gong H, Jia H, Zhang X, Lou X.

title: Information contracts determine what inverse perturbation benchmarks measure
abstract: Inverse perturbation benchmarks rank interventions toward a desired cellular state, but high accuracy can answer a different question from biological prioritization. We present InverseBench, which makes candidate information and endpoint construction explicit, and FSTN, a linear pipeline evaluated under it. With identical inputs, candidates and validation, nested ridge reaches Spearman 0.959 for a transcriptional principal-component proxy but 0.445 for independently measured K562 growth fitness across 7,354 genes. Controlled response-entry availability across seven tasks gives heterogeneous gains, 0.442 for CD4 activation and 0.116 for external fitness. Yet predefined shortlist comparisons show no primary-cutoff penalty in K562 or a melanoma co-culture screen, and secondary cutoffs reverse the K562 ordering. FSTN’s nonnegative set selector recovers 0.840 of measured two-gene constituents in three picks, against 0.771 for an unconstrained greedy. The framework separates proxy reconstruction, response-informed prioritization and unseen-intervention ranking: an endpoint-dependent accuracy gap does not by itself mean worse biological decisions.
authors: Li J, Huang LF, Song W, Li Y, Jakub JW, Qin H, Luo Y, Tao C.

title: Pat1 globally activates deadenylation-dependent decapping to clear inefficiently translated oligo(A)-tailed transcripts
abstract: In eukaryotes, mRNA turnover occurs mainly through the 5’ - 3’ mRNA decay pathway and involves deadenylation, decapping, and exonucleolytic mRNA body digestion. While the conserved protein Pat1 has initially been described as an activator of decapping for some deadenylated mRNAs, the role of deadenylation-dependent decapping has recently been questioned. Hence, Pat1 has alternatively been suggested to regulate specific mRNA decay pathways, given its modest impact on overall transcriptome composition. Here, we combine multi-omic and genetic approaches to characterize a  PAT1 deletion mutant in  Saccharomyces cerevisiae . Although transcriptome and proteome analyses confirm that only a limited subset of genes is affected by Pat1 inactivation, poly(A)-tail sizing demonstrates that Pat1 loss leads to transcriptome-wide accumulation of capped oligo(A)-tailed mRNAs. Together with the observation that oligo(A)-tailed mRNAs are bound by Pat1  in vivo in wild-type cells, this indicates that Pat1 is a general activator of deadenylation-dependent decapping. We further show that oligo-adenylated mRNAs are translated in  Δpat1 cells, albeit inefficiently. Altogether, our data indicate that Pat1 mediates the clearance of oligo(A)-tailed mRNAs protecting cells from the ensuing inefficient translation, without inducing major changes in overall transcript distribution.
authors: Labeauvie L, Peter J, Zuber H, Séraphin B.

title: Genetic dissection of terminal heat-stress tolerance in wheat revealed by QTL mapping
abstract: Abstract  Terminal heat stress adversely affects wheat development and productivity, but its genetic basis is strongly influenced by environmental variation. A doubled haploid population derived from KSG1222 × KSG1203 was evaluated for 17 phenological, morphological, spike, and yield-related traits under timely, late, and very late sowing across two years. Delayed sowing progressively reduced most traits, with biological yield, flag leaf area, peduncle length, and grain yield showing substantial reductions under severe heat stress. Biological yield, harvest index, thousand-grain weight, and spikelets per spike showed consistent positive associations with grain yield across environments. Genotyping-by-sequencing generated 122,112 polymorphic SNPs, of which 12,297 were used to construct a 2,737.84 cM linkage map. Combined individual- and multi-environment QTL analysis identified 179 QTLs, including loci with relatively stable additive effects and others strongly influenced by QTL × environment interactions. Multi-trait co-localization identified regions on chromosomes 4A and 7D affecting yield-related and developmental traits. Within the QTL intervals, 2,727 putative genes were annotated, of which 286 showed heat responsive expression based on in-silico expression profiling, and 170 were further prioritized based on their functional and biological relevance. These candidates implicated heat signalling, transcriptional regulation, proteostasis, redox homeostasis, photosynthesis, and carbohydrate metabolism in terminal heat-stress adaptation.  Key message Stable and environment responsive QTLs and heat responsive candidate genes highlight the complex genetic architecture of terminal heat stress adaptation and provide targets for improving wheat resilience.
authors: Parihar P, Jaiswal JP, Tewari M, Kumar S, Singh NK, Pandey D, Gill KS.

title: Polysaccharide from Phormidium persicinum (Reinke) Gom. promotes neuronal differentiation and mitigates hypoxia-induced neuronal disruptions in vitro
abstract: Abstract    Hypoxia is an important pathogenic factor affecting cellular metabolism and neurogenesis in neurological disorders. Neuronal stem cells (NSCs) are particularly sensitive to oxygen deprivation because they depend on tightly regulated metabolic programs during differentiation. Microalgal polysaccharides have recently gained interest due to their cytoprotective, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant properties, but their potential to prevent hypoxia-induced metabolic stress in neural lineage commitment is poorly understood. Therefore, the present study evaluates the potential of crude polysaccharide derived from an indigenous marine microalga to attenuate metabolic perturbations in differentiating NSCs exposed to chemical hypoxia. The crude polysaccharide was extracted from  Phormidium persicinum  (Reinke) Gom. and characterized for its biochemical components. The compositional analysis revealed the presence of 24.35% sulphate, 16.69% carbohydrates, 12.66% uronic acids, and 3.77% protein along with monosaccharides like rhamnose, xylose, galactose, and fucose. Also, the impact of polysaccharide on the outcomes of neuronal differentiation was investigated  in vitro  on human neuronal stem cells (SH-SY5Y) under cobalt chloride induced hypoxia stress. The treatment with polysaccharide at a concentration of 50 µg mL  − 1  supplemented with retinoic acid in the ratio of 80:20 induced a sustained formation of neurite outgrowth accompanied by metabolic stabilizations after differentiation. Furthermore, treatment with polysaccharide under hypoxic conditions promotes a more favourable metabolic profile, as reported by optimal levels of dopamine, epinephrine, serotonin, acetylcholinesterase, and adenosine triphosphatase. The study underscores the promising nature of novel algal polysaccharide for the treatment of neurodegenerative disorders and suggests further investigations to purify and pinpoint its bioactive components.
authors: Satpute S, Nadar T, Kannaujiya K, Bagwe A, Deodhar M, Sharma B.

title: Blue Carbon in Bangladesh: A Review of Mangrove Conservation, Carbon Sequestration, Coastal Resilience and Management Challenges
abstract: Abstract  Blue carbon ecosystems mangroves, salt marshes, and seagrasses are examples of ecosystems that capture and store carbon in coastal and marine environments, aiding with climate change mitigation. Because of the deltaic topography and coastline’s fragility, Bangladesh faces an overwhelming socioeconomic paradox which can be attempted to be overcome using blue carbon capture technologies. This paper examines the role that blue carbon ecosystems play in fostering climate resilience and biodiversity in the country and concurrently supporting emission reduction obligations nationally and globally. The article describes the existing ecological scenario and the carbon capture potential within the scope of anthropogenic pressures and climate stressors and vulnerabilities. Moreover, the research evaluates the current policies and proposes more dynamic integrated frameworks aimed at enhancing the coastal ecosystems’ capacity for long-term carbon storage. With the possibility of acting as a blueprint for climate resilience adaptability, Bangladesh’s coastal low-lying regions positioned them as prime candidates for blue carbon initiatives.
authors: Riday MSY.

title: Multi-Member-District System with Single Non-Transferable Voting
abstract: Abstract    The decomposition method of α-divergence developed by Wada and Kamahara (2024,  Public Choice  ) is applied to local-assembly elections in 20 ordinance-designated cities in Japan that employ the multi-member district system with single non-transferable voting (MMD-SNTV) in order to evaluate its proportionality. The disproportionality observed in single non-transferable voting (SNTV) and single transferable voting (STV), collectively referred to as S(N)TV, is largely attributable to disproportionality within single-candidate parties (independents). When only disproportionality within multi-candidate parties is considered, S(N)TV is comparable in proportionality to list proportional representation (PR) even under the D’Hondt (Jefferson) criterion. Under the Sainte-Laguë (Webster) criterion, S(N)TV is more proportional than list PR. One might therefore argue that S(N)TV achieves “superproportionality” (Cox 1994,  American Political Science Review  ), surpassing the D’Hondt standard. Wasted votes generated in individual electoral districts are largely offset by intra-party unequal representation, reducing the degree of disproportionality. Wasted votes in Ireland under STV are substantially higher than those in Japanese ordinance-designated cities that use SNTV. Under STV, substantially more candidates contest elections than under SNTV. Consequently, the dispersed distribution of first-preference votes before transfers creates a divergence between these initial preferences and the subsequent seat allocation. Although SNTV does not capture voters’ nuanced preferences through transfers, it achieves vote effectiveness through candidates’ rational behavior rather than through the mechanical operation of the electoral system; thus, MMD-SNTV could arguably be considered a quasi-PR electoral system.
authors: Wada J, Kamahara Y, Nakajima Y.

title: Pore architecture governs tannic acid release from porous Poria cocos polysaccharide beads for headspace antioxidant preservation of fruit.
abstract: Postharvest fungal decay and water loss waste substantial fruit, while sulfur dioxide pads leave sulfite residues and perform unevenly across commodities. Herein, tannic acid (TA) was loaded into Poria cocos polysaccharide (PCP) hydrogel beads via hydrogen-bond assembly; salt porogen leaching with gradient annealing created interconnected, PCP-tuned pore channels. Pore sizes of 24.9-36.4 μm shifted release from Fickian to anomalous transport, and medium-porosity PTB-2 was selected for balanced release, high moisture sorption, and bead quality. PTB-2 achieved 97.4% cumulative TA release (n = 0.55, R2 = 0.998), and with headspace DPPH scavenging reaching 66.9% at 48 h, linearly correlated with released TA (R2 = 0.982). Over 14 days, PTB-2 reduced grape decay to 19.2% (vs 76.7% control; UVASYS 14.2%) and cherry tomato decay to 21.3% (vs 58.6% control; UVASYS 53.1%), retaining anthocyanin and lycopene. This pore-tuned polyphenol platform offers a natural, broad-spectrum route to residue-minimized active fruit packaging.
authors: Qiao X, Zou J, Zhang Y, Zhou C, Qian R, Tan X, Wu S, Li C, Wu Y, Xiong H, Zhou Z.

title: Physiological, biochemical and transcriptomic insights into heterosis in a Penaeus vannamei hybrid population under combined hypoxia and high ammonia-N stress.
abstract: Hypoxia and high ammonia-N frequently co-occur in intensive shrimp culture and can severely impair physiological homeostasis and survival. This study investigated the physiological, biochemical, histopathological, and transcriptomic responses of an intraspecific Penaeus vannamei hybrid population (HY; Xinghai No. 1 ♀ × Blue Genetics ♂) and its parental populations (XH and BG) under combined hypoxia (2 mg/L dissolved oxygen) and high ammonia-N (35 mg/L) stress. HY showed the highest 48-h cumulative survival and positive survival heterosis, with mid-parent heterosis (MPH) of 28.42% and better-parent heterosis (BPH) of 19.61%. Histopathological changes in the gill and hepatopancreas of HY appeared less pronounced than those in the parental populations after 48 h. HY maintained relatively high SOD and GSH-Px activities and consistently lower ROS levels during stress, showed an early increase in GS activity, and accumulated less hemolymph ammonia-N than BG at 48 h. Transcriptomic comparisons revealed stage-dependent differences between HY and the parental populations. At 24 h, differentially expressed genes were mainly associated with protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum, amino acid and lipid metabolism, and redox-related processes, whereas at 48 h, enrichment shifted toward phagosome- and lysosome-related pathways and processes associated with intracellular clearance and extracellular remodelling. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified six modules significantly associated with stress-related physiological traits and ten candidate hub genes, including sod2, glrx3, tusc3, and prrc2a. These findings indicate that the enhanced stress tolerance of HY was associated with coordinated antioxidant, immune, nitrogen-metabolic, protein-homeostasis, and intracellular-clearance responses. The results provide physiological and molecular evidence for evaluating this specific hybrid combination under combined hypoxia and high ammonia-N stress and identify candidate genes for future functional validation.
journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part D, Genomics & proteomics
authors: Liu K, Huang C, Lu Z, Xia H, Liu J.

title: The effects of small ruminant lentiviruses infections on health, welfare and hematological parameters in dairy sheep.
abstract: The broader impact of small ruminant lentiviruses (SRLV) infections on overall sheep health remains insufficiently characterized, despite their recognized clinical importance. Τhis prospective longitudinal study evaluated the impact of SRLV infections on clinical health indicators and hematological profiles in 407 Chios and Lacaune dairy ewes from four intensive farms. Blood samples collected at pre-mating and pre-lambing over two consecutive lactation periods were tested for SRLV antibodies using ELISA and for viral DNA using real-time PCR. Individual health and welfare indicators were recorded including body condition score, foot and respiratory disorders, body abscesses, udder lesions and deformities, and wool quality. Hematological analyses quantified white blood cell, red blood cell and platelet counts and associated parameters. Mixed-effects binary and linear regression models were used to assess the associations of serological status, infection status (ELISA and PCR), and temporal infection and serological patterns with clinical and hematological outcomes. Ewes classified as PCR-positive but seronegative exhibited higher likelihood of lameness, arthritis, enlarged supramammary lymph nodes, udder skin and wart-like lesions. Also, infected animals demonstrated significantly lower white blood cell, lymphocyte, granulocyte, and monocyte counts, while the infected seronegative ewes had higher hemoglobin concentrations and reduced platelet distribution width, white blood cell, lymphocyte, and monocyte counts. These findings underscore the value of a prospective study design and the combined use of ELISA and PCR for elucidating the broader health consequences of SRLV infections. Further research is needed to explore the diagnostic utility of hematological profiles for the detection, staging, and monitoring of SRLV infections in dairy sheep.
authors: Kalogianni AI, Tsimpouri E, Goniotaki I, Katsiani M, Strogylou E, Gelasakis AI.

title: Herpes Simplex Virus Perinatal Management.
abstract: AimHerpes Simplex Virus (HSV) is a double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) virus with 2 serotypes, HSV-1 and HSV-2. Neonatal HSV infection is uncommon due to evidence-based interventions for pregnancy, delivery and the newborn. The study assessed whether pregnant women with a history of genital HSV and their infants were managed according to best practice recommendations.MethodsA retrospective analysis of pregnancies between January 2018 and December 2021. Included were women with documented HSV - either diagnosed, treated, or with positive laboratory testing.Results234 women with 261 pregnancies were identified. Mean maternal age was 32 (SD =/- 5.2). 110 (42%) pregnancies had visible lesions. 2 (0.07%) cases of primary HSV occurred within 6 weeks of delivery. 11 (4.2%) had lesions at labour onset - all were recurrences. Prophylaxis was prescribed in 178 (68%) pregnancies. 14 (5%) infants required evaluation, with only one yielding a positive swab requiring full acyclovir treatment.DiscussionGenital HSV prevalence in this population was 0.07% (2 cases), with incidence of 0.003% (1 case) of infant requiring treatment throughout this timeframe. Primary infection within 6 weeks of delivery was rare, with no cases at labour onset. Recurrent lesions were reported in under 50% (110 pregnancies). Requirement for infant evaluation was low (5%, 14 infants).
authors: Carey R, McCallion N, Eogan M, Lambert JS, Ferguson W.

title: ResearchOS: Research Compilation for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly support literature analysis, research ideation, experimen-tation, and scientific writing. Their collaboration depends on how source findings become research directions, how selected directions become experimental commitments, and how returned observations support manuscript claims. We introduce ResearchOS, an open-source multi-agent research system organized through research compilation, which gives these transitions explicit research artifacts and acceptance conditions. Source-linked reading and cross-paper synthesis establish a reusable research space. Within this space, a multi-agent evolutionary search develops structured study candidates using independent assessment, diagnosis-guided mutation, compatibility-aware crossover, and quality-diverse selection. Researcher-selected candidates undergo contribution review and study formalization before the approved plan is compiled into a contract for external execution. Returned records are checked against the study and connected to manuscript claims through evidence alignment and audit. An artifact-first runtime retains provenance, versions, researcher decisions, and recoverable state across the process. We present the architecture, evolutionary mechanism, execution interfaces, and representative system traces, illustrating how ResearchOS connects scientific exploration to executable investigations and evidence-supported reporting.
authors: Liang M, Xu C, Zhu T, Liu G, Wu J.

title: Flavor Modulation Strategies for Sodium Reduction in Processed Foods: A Review
abstract: Sodium chloride occupies a functional position in processed foods that a simple subtraction cannot easily replace: it is simultaneously a tastant, a preservative, a texture modifier, and — less obviously — a modulator of other flavors, suppressing bitterness and amplifying sweetness and umami. Population-level sodium intake nonetheless remains roughly double recommended levels in most industrialized countries, and processed and away-from-home foods account for the large majority of that intake, which has made flavor-preserving sodium reduction one of the more persistent problems in food product development. This review synthesizes recent literature on strategies that address the flavor consequence of sodium removal specifically, organized around five mechanistic categories: taste-receptor-level substitution (potassium and mineral salts, plant- and marine-derived alternatives), chemosensory flavor enhancement (umami compounds, yeast-derived and fermentation-derived salty/umami peptides, bitter blockers), cross-modal and multisensory perception strategies (odor-induced saltiness enhancement, herb and spice seasoning, taste-taste and taste-texture interactions), physical and structural engineering of salt and food matrices (crystal morphology, particle size reduction, inhomogeneous spatial distribution, encapsulation), and processing-assisted approaches (high-pressure processing, ultrasound). Across food categories — meat, bread and bakery, cheese, and snacks — the evidence indicates that no single strategy reliably sustains more than a 20–30% sodium reduction without a perceptible flavor penalty, but combinations of mechanistically distinct strategies (e.g., a potassium-based substitute plus a bitterness-masking polysaccharide plus a savory aroma) can compound their effects to reach 50% or more. The review also considers the industrial and regulatory context shaping which of these strategies actually reach the shelf, since global sodium reduction remains off-track against the World Health Organization's 2025 target despite two decades of reformulation research. It closes by identifying where the evidence base is thin — chiefly the durability of consumer acceptance over repeated exposure, and the scalability of some promising laboratory-stage technologies — and where near-term industrial opportunity is greatest.
authors: S G.

title: Identification and characterization of shared transcriptomic signatures in BRCA2-mutated metastatic breast cancer and lung adenocarcinoma: An integrative bioinformatics approach.
abstract: Breast cancer and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) are most prevalent forms of malignancies worldwide and are associated with BRCA2 variants. While BRCA2 pathogenic variants are well established in breast cancer, their transcriptional consequences in lung adenocarcinoma remain poorly characterized, and no study has directly compared the shared differentially expressed gene (DEG) signature between BRCA2-variant metastatic breast cancer and BRCA2-variant LUAD. In this study, we used an integrative bioinformatics approach to identify and characterize this shared transcriptomic profile using publicly available TCGA and GEO datasets accessed via cBioPortal. Top dysregulated genes were subjected to protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis using STRING and Cytoscape (CytoHubba, MCC algorithm), functional enrichment through Metascape and survival analysis through UALCAN, with disease associations validated against the DISEASES database. SERPINA1, PIGR, FGG and FCGBP were identified as candidate hub genes, common in both types of malignancies. The breast cancer gene set was associated with impaired BRCA2-RAD51-mediated homologous recombination, and the lung dataset had strong signatures of alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells and signatures specific to lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). SERPINA1 and PIGR were significant markers in breast cancer and FGG was significant marker in LUAD. The findings identify a partially overlapping epithelial transcriptional profile associated with BRCA2-variant breast and lung tumor datasets. However, these observations represent associations within BRCA2-altered cohorts and do not establish that BRCA2 dysfunction directly drives the identified transcriptional changes. SERPINA1, PIGR, FGG, and FCGBP therefore represent candidate tissue-dependent biomarkers requiring independent validation.
authors: Abid E, Bilal S, Shahid M, Farooq SMY.

title: CCR5, CD163, CSF1R, and FCGR3A as Candidate Biomarkers Associated With Mitophagy in Atherosclerosis.
abstract: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease, and the role of mitophagy in its pathogenesis remains unclear. To address this, this study integrated atherosclerosis-related transcriptome data and single-cell sequencing data from the GEO database, obtained mitophagy-related genes from MSigDB, and assessed mitophagy activity via GSEA and ssGSEA; WGCNA was used to screen disease- and mitophagy-associated module genes, and their intersection with differentially expressed genes yielded 286 candidate genes. A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network and cytoHubba algorithms were subsequently used to prioritize key genes, and dual machine learning algorithms (LASSO regression and SVM-RFE) to screen potential biomarkers, which were designated as CCR5, CD163, CSF1R, and FCGR3A. The expression patterns of all four candidates were further assessed in the independent GSE43292 dataset and were concordant with those observed in the discovery dataset. GSEA of samples stratified by candidate-gene expression identified enrichment of gene sets related to myogenesis, allograft rejection, and inflammatory responses; candidate drug-target associations were predicted using DSigDB, and exploratory AutoDock analysis suggested a feasible interaction between sunitinib and CSF1R. Additionally, exploratory single-cell analysis of three atherosclerosis patients identified seven major cell populations, with CD163, CSF1R, and FCGR3A showing macrophage-enriched expression within this dataset. Collectively, this study provides hypothesis-generating evidence for an association between mitophagy-related transcriptional patterns and atherosclerosis. Four candidate biomarkers (CCR5, CD163, CSF1R, and FCGR3A) were prioritized, and a potential CSF1R-sunitinib interaction was proposed for future experimental validation.
authors: Fu J, Dong Y.

title: Green-Synthesized Nanomaterials for Electrochemical Cyanotoxin Biosensing: Analytical Performance, Environmental Validation, and Sustainability Challenges.
abstract: Cyanobacterial blooms pose a persistent threat to aquatic ecosystems and public health through the production of diverse cyanotoxins, including microcystins, saxitoxins, cylindrospermopsin, and anatoxin-a. Electrochemical biosensors offer promising solutions for rapid, portable cyanotoxin monitoring; however, the environmental sustainability of nanomaterials and their synthesis requires critical evaluation. This review examines electrochemical cyanotoxin biosensors incorporating demonstrably green-synthesized or biomass-derived nanomaterials reported between 2013 and 2026. Particular emphasis is placed on biomass-derived carbon materials, their influence on bioreceptor immobilization, interfacial charge transfer, signal generation, and analytical performance. Confirmed green-synthesis approaches are distinguished from conventional nanomaterials and studies involving partially green processing or broader sustainability claims. Analytical performance is assessed through linear range, detection limit, selectivity, reproducibility, stability, and validation in environmental matrices. The available evidence reveals that genuinely green nanomaterial-based electrochemical cyanotoxin biosensing remains limited, with microcystin-LR dominating the qualifying studies. Key challenges include inconsistent material characterization, insufficient assessment of energy and resource consumption, limited life-cycle information, batch-to-batch variability, and inadequate validation using untreated environmental samples. Future research should prioritize reproducible and scalable sensing platforms while demonstrating sustainability through transparent reporting of synthesis conditions, resource requirements, environmental impacts, and end-of-life considerations, rather than relying solely on low detection limits or green-synthesis claims.
authors: Imane B, Helim R, F A Youssef A, Alahmad W, El-Raheem HA.

title: Functional characterization of the ecdysone receptor (EcR) in egg diapause termination and embryonic development in Calliptamus italicus (orthoptera: Acrididae).
abstract: BackgroundCalliptamus italicus is a dominant pest in the grasslands of Xinjiang and overwinters as diapausing eggs. Ecdysone (Ecd) is a key hormone for diapause termination in C. italicus eggs, but the function of its receptor EcR in this process remains largely unexplored. Here, whole-mount in situ hybridization (WISH) and RNA interference (RNAi) were used to characterize its function.ResultsWISH revealed that EcR was stably expressed in the mandibles, maxillae, thorax and legs from embryonic Stage II and subsequently expanded to the prothoracic glands, compound eyes, wings, ventral nerve cord and leg segments, with signals localized in the epidermis. RNAi-mediated silencing [2 μg μL-1 dsEcR; 71.3% efficiency at 48 h post-treatment (hpt)] resulted in disappearance of EcR signals from prothoracic glands and ventral nerve cord, and reduced signals in appendages. At the transcriptional level, silencing of EcR significantly reduced the expression of downstream genes E75 (88.2% at 12 hpt), FTZ-F1 (72.4% at 48 hpt) and Vg (75.6% at 48 hpt). By contrast, HR3 expression was significantly increased at 24-48 hpt. Phenotypically, EcR silencing delayed diapause termination, abnormal yolk absorption and a smaller head compared with the control group.ConclusionsEcR exhibited tissue-specific expression during embryonic development. EcR silencing was associated with altered expression of 20E signaling-related genes, and with delayed diapause termination and abnormal embryonic development. These findings provide candidate molecular evidence for EcR participation in endocrine regulation of diapause-associated processes, and may represent a candidate target for RNAi-based pest management strategies. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: He W, Ye X, Leng C, Yuan L, Hu H, Ji R, Yang K.

title: Cytotoxic activity of selinexor in BRAF<sup>V600E</sup>-driven pediatric low-grade glioma 3D cultures.
abstract: Pediatric low-grade gliomas (pLGGs) are the most common primary brain tumors in children and frequently harbor activating RAS/MAPK pathway alterations, including BRAFV600E. Although MEK inhibitors (MEKi) show clinical activity, responses are often incomplete and tumors commonly regrow after treatment discontinuation, highlighting the need for therapies that induce sustained regression. To systematically identify cytotoxic treatments, we initially screened 87 clinically relevant drugs in BRAFV600E-mutant BT40 3D multicellular aggregates and subsequently evaluated the prioritized XPO1-targeting strategy in BRAFV600E-mutant DKFZ-BT314 spheroids in proliferative (ON) and senescent (OFF) states and in fresh pLGG tissue cultures. High-content imaging with machine-learning-based analysis identified XPO1 inhibition as a vulnerability across models. The FDA-approved selective XPO1 inhibitor selinexor was active alone and in combination with MEKi. MEK-XPO1 co-inhibition reduced viable 3D culture area by more than 30% and suppressed regrowth for at least 10 d, even after medium change. DRAQ7 positivity and caspase-3/7 activation demonstrated cell death in the 3D cultures, while complementary 2D analyses showed PARP cleavage, nuclear fragmentation, and caspase activation. Transcriptomic analyses of pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma patient samples and BRAFV600E-induced senescence models revealed upregulation of MAPK, TGFβ, TP53, and FOXO pathway genes and anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members, including MCL-1. XPO1 inhibition reduced MCL-1 protein levels, consistent with disruption of anti-apoptotic signaling. Ex vivo drug sensitivity profiling of fresh tumor tissue from 20 patients from the LOGGIC Core BioClinical Data Bank demonstrated sensitivity to XPO1 inhibition at clinically achievable concentrations. In an exploratory BT40 zebrafish embryo xenograft experiment, 48 h of combination treatment numerically attenuated tumor growth compared with solvent treatment, although the difference was not statistically significant. Overall, our findings support XPO1 inhibition, alone or combined with MEK inhibition, as a candidate therapeutic strategy for BRAFV600E-driven pLGG that warrants further preclinical evaluation.

title: Hidden potential for mixotrophy in soil protists.
abstract: Mixotrophy, the ability of a single protist to combine phototrophy and phagotrophy, is widely recognized as an important functional strategy in aquatic ecosystems, where it shapes food-web structure and carbon cycling. In soil, however, mixotrophy remains largely overlooked despite increasing evidence for trophic flexibility among protists. Here, we argue that this neglect may reflect conceptual and methodological limitations rather than ecological absence. We highlight inconsistencies in trait-based classifications, delineate feeding traits that enable certain forms of mixotrophy, and evaluate soil microhabitats that support mixotrophic activity. Recognizing mixotrophy in soil challenges traditional views of distinct trophic categories and reveals its potential contributions to soil carbon fluxes. Incorporating mixotrophy into soil ecology is therefore essential for developing mechanistic and predictive models of terrestrial ecosystem functioning.
authors: Andersen JE, Sapkota R, Hansen PJ, Winding A.

title: A novel anti-PD-1/VEGF bispecific fusion protein with enhanced VEGF binding capacity and developability for synergistic immunotherapy.
abstract: Combination therapy targeting PD-1 and VEGF has demonstrated significant clinical benefits in multiple cancers. However, developing a single-molecule bispecific agent capable of simultaneously blocking both pathways with enhanced VEGF-binding capacity remains challenging. Here, we indicate the design, production, and comprehensive characterization of PKVBP, a novel anti-PD-1/VEGF bispecific fusion protein. PKVBP features a novel design that represents the first report of a bispecific fusion protein incorporating tandem VEGFR1 D2 domains at the C-terminus of an Fc-silenced human IgG4 backbone, enabling tetravalent VEGF engagement. Through systematic optimization of mammalian cell expression and a robust purification process, high-purity PKVBP was obtained with excellent recovery. Structural analysis confirmed proper assembly, domain integrity, and favorable thermal stability. Functional assays demonstrated simultaneous binding to PD-1 and VEGF, with substantially enhanced VEGF affinity and binding capacity compared to bevacizumab. Preliminary stability studies revealed that PKVBP maintains remarkable physicochemical and functional integrity under both long-term storage and stress conditions, with minimal oxidation and sustained target engagement. These findings highlight PKVBP as a promising bispecific candidate with superior VEGF-blocking capability and favorable developability, supporting its further investigation for synergistic cancer immunotherapy.
authors: Mao D, Xu J, Zhang D, Hang T, Zheng C, Xu M, Chen Q, Zhang X, Wu G, Huang K, Liu T, Guo Q, Ji L, Qian W, Hou S, Li J, Zhang X, Han F, Wang X, Li J, Wang H, Guo Y, Guo H, Sun Z.

title: N-(3-Trifluoromethylphenyl)sulfonyl-indole-3-carbaldehyde thiosemicarbazones induce apoptosis and modulate p53-associated signaling in prostate cancer: integrated experimental and computational studies.
abstract: Prostate cancer continues to be an important therapeutic challenge that demands the development of new apoptosis-inducing agents. In the present study, a series of N-(3-trifluoromethylphenyl)sulfonyl-indole-3-carbaldehyde thiosemicarbazone derivatives (5a-s) was synthesized and evaluated for their biological activity against the LNCaP prostate cancer cell line. Among the synthesized compounds, 5a and 5g showed strong antiproliferative activity and favorable selectivity toward non-malignant HEK293 cells, with IC50 values of 7.56 and 5.81 μM, respectively. Compound 5g increased the expression of TP53, CDKN1A, BBC3, and BAX, whereas compound 5a significantly reduced the expression of the anti-apoptotic BCL2 gene. Both compounds also modulated the expression of cancer- and DNA damage response-related genes, including c-MYC, KRAS, PTEN, ATM, and ATR. Molecular docking studies predicted favorable interactions of compound 5g with MDM2 (IFD score = -7.951 kcal/mol; ΔG_bind = -56.75 kcal/mol) and compound 5a with BCL-2 (IFD score = -8.636 kcal/mol; ΔG_bind = -59.55 kcal/mol). 500-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations further supported the dynamic stability and persistence of the proposed ligand-protein interactions. ADME and DFT analyses further indicated favorable pharmacokinetic and electronic properties of the lead compounds. Overall, the integrated experimental and computational findings identify compounds 5a and 5g as promising lead candidates for further investigation as apoptosis-inducing agents against prostate cancer.
authors: Kubra KT, Acar ÖÖ, Şenol AM, Şen A, Şenol H, Batool K, Albekairi NA, Rasool A, Shafiq Z, Alshammari A.

title: Single-cell and multi-algorithm profiling identifies SNRPG as a Claudin-1-associated regulator of malignant progression in triple-negative breast cancer.
abstract: BackgroundThe epithelial-cell states and molecular drivers underlying breast cancer (BC) metastasis remain incompletely defined. This study aimed to identify and validate core molecules associated with metastatic progression.MethodsSingle-cell transcriptomics, high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis, machine learning, and public cohort analyses were integrated to nominate progression-associated candidate genes. The functional relevance of SNRPG and its association with Claudin-1 expression were evaluated using clinical specimens, in vitro functional assays, dual-luciferase reporter assays, a subcutaneous xenograft model, and a tail-vein experimental lung metastasis model.ResultsSingle-cell analysis revealed a lymph node-enriched epithelial subpopulation with elevated copy-number variation burden and stemness-related features. Multi-algorithm screening prioritized SNRPG as a recurrent candidate feature associated with adverse tumor progression. SNRPG was upregulated in breast cancer and showed high expression in triple-negative breast cancer. Higher SNRPG expression was associated with poorer outcomes in exploratory microarray-based survival analyses. SNRPG knockdown reduced malignant phenotypes in vitro, restrained subcutaneous tumor growth, and decreased thoracic bioluminescence in a tail-vein experimental lung metastasis model. In TNBC cells, SNRPG knockdown increased Claudin-1 expression and CLDN1 promoter activity, whereas concomitant Claudin-1 knockdown counteracted several phenotypic effects of SNRPG depletion in vitro and in vivo.ConclusionsSNRPG is associated with lymph node-enriched epithelial-cell states and supports malignant phenotypes in the TNBC models examined. Increased CLDN1 expression contributes to the phenotypic effects of SNRPG depletion, although the mechanism linking SNRPG to CLDN1 remains unresolved.
journal: Biochimica et biophysica acta. Molecular basis of disease
authors: Ye Z, Mou J, Su H, Luo J, Cheng Y, Liu K, Yang Z, Qian D, Tang H, Xu M, Mu Y, Tang Y, Gui W, Pan Y, Chen Y, Meng X, Zheng Q.

title: Structural analyses of a heterodimeric SusCD complex captures intermediate states of maltooligosaccharide transport.
abstract: Bacteroides are abundant gut bacteria with diverse polysaccharide metabolizing capabilities encoded by co-transcribed polysaccharide utilization loci (PULs). The starch utilization system (Sus) is required for starch and α-glucan metabolism in Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron and has served as a model for PUL studies. However, the mechanism of maltooligosaccharide (MOS) transport and the architecture of the SusCD complex remain incompletely understood. Here, we used cryo-electron microscopy to capture multiple transport-relevant conformations of the SusD lipoprotein and the TonB-dependent transporter SusC in both unliganded and ligand-bound states. In the absence of ligand, SusCD adopts three conformations including an open state in which SusD is displaced from SusC, a state containing the SusC plug, and a state lacking density for the SusC plug. Three-dimensional variability analysis of the structure where SusD is displaced from SusC reveals continuous SusD mobility coupled to movement of the SusC N-terminus. The maltoheptaose-bound SusCD structure reveals two binding sites, one at the SusD-SusC interface and a second within SusC, indicating how MOS stabilizes a closed SusCD assembly. Notably, all structures show that SusCD is a heterodimer, unlike other Sus-like transporters that assemble into SusCD heterotetramers. Native mass spectrometry confirms this heterodimeric stoichiometry, and comparisons with other SusCD-like complexes suggest a structural basis for this distinct assembly of SusCD. Together, these data define substrate binding and intermediate transport states in a canonical PUL system and reveal architectural divergence among Sus-like carbohydrate transport complexes in Bacteroides.
authors: Cadigan MC, Fuentes NR, Salmen W, Roberts JR, Ruotolo B, Ohi MD, Koropatkin NM.

title: From individual-based models to macroscopic dynamics of antimicrobial resistance.
abstract: We introduce and discuss a kinetic framework describing the time evolution of the statistical distributions of a population divided into the compartments of susceptible, infectious, recovered, and resistant in the presence of a microbial infection driven by susceptible-infectious interactions. Our main objective is to quantify the impact of excessive and inappropriate antimicrobial use, which accelerates the spread of resistance by enabling a fraction of infectious individuals to transition into the resistant compartment. The model consists of a system of Boltzmann-type equations capturing binary interactions between susceptible and infectious individuals, complemented by linear redistribution operators that represent recovery, the development of resistance, and reinfection processes. In the grazing-collision limit, we show that this Boltzmann system is well approximated by a system of coupled Fokker-Planck equations. This limiting description allows for a more tractable analysis of the dynamics, including the characterization of the long-time behavior of the population densities. Our analysis highlights how interaction terms drive the system toward a stable equilibrium and quantifies the effects of inappropriate antimicrobial use on the distribution of resistant individuals. Overall, the results offer a multi-scale perspective that bridges kinetic theory with classical epidemic modeling.
authors: Menale M, Toscani G, Zanella M.

title: Lipid nanoparticles for precision nucleic acid delivery: linking cellular engineering to organ-specific targeting.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) represent clinically validated non-viral platforms for nucleic acid delivery, yet expanding their application toward precision gene therapy demands more than efficient particle formulation or tissue accumulation. Functional delivery requires navigating a sequential biological cascade: establishing biological access to target tissues, undergoing cell-specific uptake, escaping endosomal entrapment, and releasing intact cargo into the cytosol. Because each stage presents a distinct rate-limiting barrier, success at one step does not guarantee downstream therapeutic activity. This review provides a multiscale evaluation of LNP-mediated delivery, bridging ex vivo cellular engineering and organ-specific in vivo targeting. We first analyze how lipid composition, physicochemical properties, and cargo architecture dictate self-assembly and intracellular fate. For ex vivo applications-highlighting hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells and natural killer cells-we address the balance between high transfection efficiency and the preservation of cell viability, phenotype, and cytotoxic function. For in vivo platforms, we examine how administration routes, physiological barriers, and cellular accessibility govern delivery to the liver, spleen, pancreas, lung, kidney, and brain, emphasizing that bulk organ accumulation often masks poor intracellular bioavailability-particularly given that only 1-4% of internalized cargo reaches the cytosol. Finally, we organize these insights into a route-barrier-cell framework that evaluates biological access, cellular uptake, endosomal escape, and cytosolic activity as interconnected yet distinct performance metrics. Overcoming current translational hurdles-including species-dependent tropism, biological variability, repeated-dose immunogenicity, and manufacturing scalability-will be essential to transition LNPs from broad nucleic acid carriers into precision targeted therapeutics.
authors: Shin Y, Lee S, Trần NÁN, Chung M.

title: Celastrol induces lipid-associated stress and apoptosis in EBV-positive extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma with NCOR2-HDAC3 perturbation.
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-positive extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL) remains difficult to treat after relapse or refractory progression. We investigated celastrol-associated chromatin, lipid-metabolic, and stress responses in ENKTL cell-line models. Celastrol reduced SNK6 and SNT8 cell viability, increased apoptotic protein processing, and suppressed short-term SNK6 xenograft growth with increased histological markers of apoptosis. Chemical proteomics identified nuclear receptor corepressor 2 (NCOR2) and nuclear receptor corepressor 1 (NCOR1) among celastrol-associated proteins, and pull-down immunoblotting confirmed NCOR2 recovery. Probe recovery mapped to an NCOR2 region containing the deacetylase activation domain. Celastrol altered NCOR2 thermal stability, reduced its co-immunoprecipitation with histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3), and inhibited recombinant HDAC3/NCOR2 activity. Histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac) profiling at 2 h and RNA sequencing at 24 h revealed chromatin redistribution and associated stress-response and lipid-metabolic transcriptional changes. Selected apoptotic, lipid-metabolic, and stress-response protein changes were reproduced in SNT8 cells. In SNK6 cells, the HDAC3 inhibitor RGFP966 partially phenocopied selected celastrol-associated changes. NCOR2 depletion reduced lipid-metabolic enzyme expression and enhanced apoptotic-marker accumulation during celastrol treatment, whereas oleic acid conjugated to bovine serum albumin partially attenuated stress and apoptotic responses. Bulk RNA sequencing showed no coordinated induction of the examined EBV lytic-associated transcripts. These findings identify NCOR2-HDAC3-associated perturbation and lipid-associated stress as components of the celastrol response in EBV-positive ENKTL models.
authors: Huang X, Chen W, Fu Y, Liu T, Liu J, Shen J, Xie G.

title: A self-assembled and covalently stabilized FcRn-binding albumin fragment-payload assembly.
abstract: The short in vivo half-life of protein therapeutics remains a major limitation in their clinical translation, driving the development of human serum albumin (HSA)-based carrier systems capable of prolonged circulation through FcRn-mediated recycling. Previously, we reported an engineered HSA variant (AlbuC) that enables modular assembly with protein payloads via α-helical coiled-coil interactions; however, the reversibility of these interactions limited complex stability under diluted conditions. Here, we developed a second-generation AlbuC system by integrating heterodimeric coiled-coil motifs containing strategically positioned cysteine residues. Co-expression of the engineered AlbuC variant and a model payload in the oxidative cytoplasm of Escherichia coli SHuffle facilitated efficient in-cell heterodimerization and the formation of disulfide-stabilized AlbuC-payload complexes. Comparative biochemical analyses demonstrated that coiled-coil selection critically influenced intracellular AlbuC-payload assembly, with selected motifs yielding disulfide-linked complexes exhibiting enhanced structural stability and resistance to dilution. Importantly, the assembled complexes retained pH-dependent FcRn binding, a key feature for FcRn-mediated recycling. Furthermore, functional validation using a death receptor 5-targeting nanobody showed that a therapeutically relevant payload can be incorporated into AlbuC variants while preserving biological activity. Collectively, this study demonstrates a modular intracellular assembly strategy for generating disulfide-stabilized AlbuC-payload complexes that retain pH-dependent FcRn-binding capability and payload functionality.
authors: Cho YJ, Lee GJ, Park JH, Lim S, Shin SM, An YJ, Shin SO, Lim SI.

title: Defining early human developmental identity: A curated, cross-platform marker framework.
abstract: Early human development involves dynamic cell-state transitions, complicating distinction between transient transcriptional changes and stable lineage commitment in human pluripotent stem cell models. To address this challenge, we establish a curated, cross-platform marker framework for pluripotency and early germ-layer identity. Starting from an unbiased RNA-seq discovery set, we validated candidates by qPCR and evaluated the panel across independent bulk RNA-seq and embryonic single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets. This yielded 67 validated markers, of which 66 were retained for downstream transcriptomic analyses. Our framework identified early developmental states across heterogeneous datasets and showed lineage-associated enrichment in human and macaque embryonic references despite substantial transcriptional variability. Protein-level concordance was observed for detectable targets in KOLF2.1J proteomic data. To enable broad application, we introduce DeepDiff, a web-based resource integrating the marker framework and enabling automated fate classification. Together, this work provides a transferable framework for assessing early developmental identity across experimental contexts.
authors: Dobner J, Prigione A, Rossi A.

title: Interfacial assembly of PBAs/ZIF-8 composites for ultrahigh-capacity and selective thallium capture with exceptional alkaline tolerance.
abstract: Effective Tl+ elimination under extreme alkaline pH remains challenging, as alkali triggers decomposition of Prussian blue analogs (PBAs), lowering adsorption efficiency and generating secondary pollutants. Furthermore, conventional PBAs nanocrystals (+ adsorption capacity of 629.03 mg/g and a removal efficiency of 97.78%, significantly surpassing most reported adsorbents, with over 90% removal within 10 min. The micron-sized particles enable convenient separation by simple filtration, while the ZIF-8 shell confers stable Tl+ removal across pH 2-12, a tolerance unattainable by bare PBAs, through a complementary protection mechanism. In actual industrial leachate and in the presence of competing ions, the material reduces residual Tl+ to below 5 μg/L with a distribution coefficient Kd > 104 mL/g. Mechanistic studies confirm a near-equimolar K+/Tl+ ion-exchange pathway. This work offers a promising stabilization strategy for structurally vulnerable adsorbents and a viable candidate for deep Tl+ removal from hazardous wastewater.
authors: Sun H, Li K, Xiang F, Li S, Ma R.
