title: Exploring the impact of intraspecific interaction between sibling colonies of  Bacillus cereus  MSM-S1 in the absence and presence of antibiotics
abstract: Bacillus cereus is a spore-forming pathogen and food contaminant that can survive in hostile environments through different survival strategies. As part of survival,  B. cereus may also engage in intra- or interspecific interactions that shape its community structure and stress responses, enabling its persistence under unfavourable conditions. The present study explored intraspecific interactions, at the cell and molecular levels, between two sibling colonies of  Bacillus cereus MSM-S1 grown through swarming adjacently on nutrient agar in the absence and presence of gentamicin. While growing alone, gentamicin altered the symmetrical colony morphology of  B. cereus MSM-S1, which was associated with cell elongation, decreased flagellation and increased expression of the toxin gene  nheA . During interaction, both in the absence and presence of gentamicin, the motility of sibling colonies towards each other was restricted, forming a distinct line/zone of demarcation between the colonies. Microscopic analysis at different time points (day 3, 5 and 7) revealed progressive changes in the swirling arrangement of cells at the interaction zone. In the absence of gentamicin, cells became jammed at the interacting front by day 7, whereas this effect was not observed in the presence of gentamicin on day 7. Cells at the interacting zone underwent gradual sporulation; notably, sporulation was less in the presence of gentamicin. Further analysis suggested that nutrient limitation was the major contributory factor for the formation of the zone of no growth between the interacting colonies. Moreover, the expression of quorum-sensing genes was down-regulated in cells at the interacting zone without gentamicin, but notably, upregulated in the presence of gentamicin. The expression of chemotaxis regulator gene, cheY, was also upregulated in interacting zone cells both in the absence and presence of gentamicin. In addition, increased expression of the global transcriptional regulator codY in the interacting zone under both conditions suggested its involvement in metabolic regulation during sibling colony interaction. The findings highlight modulated quorum sensing and sporulation as adaptive mechanisms in  Bacillus cereus MSM-S1 to cope with external stress imposed by nutrient limitations caused by the growth of sibling colonies, whereas, cell elongation and toxin production together is a preferred survival strategy for a growing MSM-S1 colony when stress is imposed by gentamicin as antibiotic but sufficient nutrient is available.
authors: Prasad K, Chakraborty B, Saha SK, Sengupta TK.

title: NED-Net: an annotation–training loop for rodent EEG event detection
abstract: Long-term EEG monitoring is central to rodent epilepsy research, and manual review is laborious because recordings span hundreds to tens of thousands of animal-hours. Published automated detectors perform well on their development datasets but are typically fixed models that may not adapt to another laboratory’s electrodes, animals, or noise conditions. We introduce NED-Net, open-source software for training and maintaining seizure detectors. It uses reviewed candidate events as training labels, runs detection live during recording, and retrains as annotations accumulate. A detector trained on one mouse cohort (867 annotated seizures) achieved 93.6% precision in human review of 171 detections. Applied unchanged to a second cohort on the same acquisition system, its detections were mostly seizures (12 of 13 reviewed), but per-animal recall varied substantially (median 10%), with no convulsive reference seizure detected in four of 11 animals. Retraining with annotations from the second cohort raised convulsive recall from 15% to 64%, with at least one reference seizure detected in every animal. On recordings withheld from training, 75% of detections were seizures and 14 of 22 reference seizures were detected, whereas the source model and a model trained without these animals detected none. NED-Net supports evaluating and adapting detectors to local recordings.
authors: Mir MY, Ledri M.

title: Glycoconjugates tune the viscoelastic signature of mammary tumor progression
abstract: Breast cancer progression involves extensive remodeling of the tumor extracellular matrix (ECM), resulting in changes in mechanical properties. Tumors are viscoelastic, exhibiting both an initial elastic response to loading and a time-dependent viscous response. While it is well established that tumor elasticity or stiffness is elevated, changes in tissue viscoelasticity during breast cancer progression remain poorly characterized. Here, using a mouse model that recapitulates stages of human breast cancer progression (mouse mammary tumor virus-polyoma middle T antigen, MMTV-PyMT), we show that tumors from both early and late disease time points were significantly more viscoelastic than normal mammary glands. Spatial microindentation revealed that while local stiffness and viscoelasticity are strongly coupled in soft regions of normal tissue, this relationship weakens in late carcinoma. Compared to normal glands, carcinoma tissues also exhibited marked upregulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) and glycoproteins. Selective enzymatic degradation of sulfated GAGs, mucins, or O/N-linked glycans reduced viscoelasticity without altering stiffness, establishing glycoconjugates as major contributors to tumor viscoelasticity. In vitro, increasing matrix viscoelasticity drove non-transformed mammary epithelial cells (MCF10A) toward a malignant phenotype through focal adhesion kinase mechanosignaling. Our work establishes increased viscoelasticity as a defining mechanical feature of breast cancer progression, driven in part by the accumulation of glycoconjugates. These findings provide a fuller picture of tumor mechanical evolution and a benchmark for recapitulating matrix viscoelasticity in engineered models of breast cancer.
authors: Sharma A, Baude JA, Papez M, Gionet-Gonzales MA, Stowers RS.

title: Multi-omics framework prioritizes RNA Methylation Modification Genes in Alzheimer's Disease and Functional Validation of ZFP36 in Regulating Neuroinflammation
abstract: Abstract  Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, in which epitranscriptomic modifications, especially RNA methylation, may exert crucial regulatory effects. This study integrated bulk transcriptomics, single‑cell sequencing and machine learning to screen RNA methylation‑related genes in AD and explore the functional role of zinc finger protein 36 (ZFP36). We screened RNA methylation-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs) by overlapping AD-associated DEGs with RNA methylation-related genes using the GSE84422 dataset. Six hub genes (C3, ZFP36, S100A9, GADD45A, PHGDH, FBXW7) were screened via PPI centrality analysis, LASSO regression and random forest algorithms and validated in GSE122063. ssGSEA immune infiltration analysis showed ZFP36 had the strongest positive correlation with effector memory CD8+ T cell enrichment score. Single‑cell RNA‑seq of human prefrontal cortex samples revealed high ZFP36 expression in microglia, T cells and astrocytes. Consistent with the bioinformatic findings, in vivo experiments in 9‑month‑old 5xFAD mice verified that ZFP36 overexpression in the hippocampus improved spatial learning and memory. Cell experiments showed that ZFP36 overexpression alleviated LPS-induced inflammatory responses in microglia. Subsequent virtual screening identified the compound MCULE‑4171537037 with moderate binding affinity for ZFP36. These findings associate ZFP36 with AD-related neuroinflammatory features and support further evaluation of its potential as a candidate biomarker and therapeutic target.
authors: He D, Liu R, Tian Z, Xiong Z, Zhang K, Zheng X, Luo Z, Li X, Xiao P, Zhang Y.

title: Uncovering Physiological Responses of Idesia polycarpa 'Yuji' Under Alkali Stress via Transcriptomics
abstract: Abstract    This study aimed to investigate the growth, physiological, and molecular responses of  Idesia polycarpa  ‘Yuji’ under different intensities of alkali stress, thereby providing a theoretical basis for its wider cultivation and application in saline-alkali areas. Two-year-old  I. polycarpa  ‘Yuji’ seedlings were used in a pot experiment. A mixed alkali stress solution of NaHCO₃:Na₂CO₃ = 9:1 molar ratio was applied at three concentration gradients: J1, 60 mmol·L  − 1  ; J2, 90 mmol·L  − 1  ; and J3, 120 mmol·L  − 1  . Deionized water was used as the control treatment (CK). Our integrated analysis revealed that  I. polycarpa  ‘Yuji’ exhibited heightened sensitivity during the later stages of alkali stress, which progressively inhibited growth, damaged the microstructure of leaves and root tips, and severely impaired photosynthetic function, as evidenced by reduced pigment content and decreased net photosynthetic and transpiration rates. Physiological analysis revealed that as stress intensity and duration increased, soluble sugars (SS), soluble proteins (SP), proline (Pro) accumulated significantly, while malondialdehyde (MDA) content rose continuously, indicating severe oxidative damage to the cell membrane system. Peroxidase (POD) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activities showing distinct activation patterns. Hormonal analysis revealed that under J1 to J2 stress, abscisic acid (ABA) levels fluctuated, while indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), zeatin riboside (ZR), and gibberellic acid-3 (GA₃) levels increased, whereas under J3 stress they were suppressed. A total of 9,995 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified in the transcriptome sequencing of the control group (CK) and the J3 group. KEGG enrichment analysis revealed that DEGs were significantly enriched in pathways such as photosynthesis-antenna proteins. Transcriptome analysis identified 9 995 DEGs. KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that photosynthesis-antenna proteins, photosynthesis, and the plant MAPK signaling pathway played key roles in the response to alkali stress. In addition, hormone signal transduction-related genes, including  ARR  ,  ABF  ,  PYR  /  PYL  , and  AHP  , were significantly DEGs. This study clarified the physiological and molecular mechanisms underlying alkali tolerance in  I. polycarpa  ‘Yuji’ and identified candidate genes and key metabolic pathways associated with alkali stress resistance. These findings provide a theoretical foundation and genetic resources for stress-resistance improvement, efficient utilization of saline-alkali land, and the large-scale cultivation of this tree species.
authors: Chen C, Liu C, Dang Q, Shi Z, Wang Y, Li Z, Cai Q, Geng X, Zhang M, Dai L, Zhen L.

title: Single-cell transcriptomic inference of lactylation-related programs identifies PRDX1 as a candidate metabolic regulator in hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Abstract  Background  Lactate-derived lysine lactylation has emerged as a link between tumor metabolism and gene regulation. In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), however, the cellular distribution of lactylation-related transcriptional programs and their relationship to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely defined. Methods  We integrated 24 single-cell RNA-sequencing samples (16 HCC and 8 normal liver samples) with TCGA-LIHC bulk RNA-sequencing data. Lactylation-related gene-set activity was estimated using AUCell, UCell, singscore, ssGSEA, and AddModuleScore. Malignant hepatocytes were inferred by copy-number variation analysis, and high-score programs were examined by differential expression, hdWGCNA, CellChat, and CytoTRACE. Bulk transcriptomic feature selection was performed with Boruta, random forest, LASSO, and XGBoost. PRDX1 was then tested in HepG2 and Huh-7 cells by siRNA knockdown assays. Results  Lactylation-related scores were higher in HCC than in normal tissue and were associated with poorer overall survival in TCGA-LIHC. At single-cell resolution, the highest scores were observed in hepatocytes and myeloid dendritic cells, whereas B cells and plasma cells showed lower scores. High-score malignant hepatocytes displayed increased CytoTRACE scores and distinct ligand-receptor communication patterns. Intersecting high-score differentially expressed genes with hdWGCNA modules yielded 178 candidate genes. Machine-learning prioritization nominated BSG, ERGIC3, PPM1G, and PRDX1, whose higher expression was associated with poorer survival. PRDX1 knockdown reduced HCC-cell proliferation, colony formation, migration, invasion, and intracellular lactate production. Conclusions  This study defines a transcriptomic lactylation-related program in HCC and nominates PRDX1 as a candidate link between malignant behavior and lactate metabolism. Direct proteomic and clinical validation will be required to establish PRDX1-dependent lactylation mechanisms.
authors: Niu H, Zheng X, Li W, Niu Y, Liang J, Cao W, Ma S, Gao Y, Bao X, Luo J.

title: Mapping of early blight (Alternaria solani) disease tolerance in Tomato (Solanum Lycopersicum L.) through QTL-Seq and expression analysis of defense-related genes
abstract: Abstract    Early blight disease, caused by the necrotrophic fungi  Alternaria solani  ,is one of the most common and destructive foliar diseases affecting tomatoes. It initially appears as small, dark brown lesions with concentric rings on the lower leaves, which eventually yellow and die, leading to severe defoliation and reduced yield. In the present study, an F  2  segregating population derived from contrasting parents was used to identify major quantitative trait loci (QTLs) governing early blight tolerance using QTL-Seq, a bulked segregant analysis method. The analysis was based on bulked DNA pools of susceptible and resistant F  2  populations derived from a cross between the Punjab Chhuharah, a susceptible parent, and IIHR-2891, a resistant parent. Based on the sliding window analysis for SNP-index, ∆SNP-index plots, five novel QTLs across two chromosomes specifically chromosome numbers 2 and 6 were identified for early blight tolerance. Four QTL regions (  eb2.1, eb2.2 eb2.  3, and  eb2.4  ) were located on chromosome 2, and another QTL region (  eb6.1  ) was identified on chromosome 6. The identification and expression analysis of defense-related genes located in QTL regions like  NBS-LRR, DRG, RPG, ZFT, S1WRKY1  and  PROIHIN  during disease progression in contrasting parents suggests that these genes play a major role in early blight tolerance.
authors: M A, Satish D, Sriram S, T SA, S SK, Chittapur R, Ravishankar KV.

title: Integrated Metabolomic and Gut Microbiome Analyses Reveal the Therapeutic Effects of Xuanfei Heji in Rats With Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease.
abstract: BackgroundChronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a leading cause of death, underscoring the need for improved therapies. Xuanfei Heji (XFHJ), a hospital-prepared herbal formula, has been used clinically in the treatment of COPD. However, its mechanisms remain unclear.MethodsXFHJ constituents were profiled using UHPLC-HRMS. COPD was induced in rats by intratracheal lipopolysaccharide instillation and cigarette smoke exposure. Treatment effects were assessed using pulmonary function, lung histopathology, and proinflammatory cytokines. Untargeted serum metabolomics and fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing were performed; associations among differential metabolites, microbial taxa, and inflammatory markers were evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation analysis.ResultsChemical profiling tentatively identified 374 constituents. XFHJ improved pulmonary function and attenuated lung histopathological injury and inflammation. Tryptophan and glycerophospholipid metabolism were the principal treatment-associated pathways. XFHJ also altered gut microbial diversity and composition, with enrichment of potentially beneficial taxa such as Bifidobacterium, Roseburia, and several Clostridia-related taxa. Treatment-responsive taxa correlated positively with indole-related metabolites, which correlated inversely with pulmonary inflammatory markers.ConclusionsXFHJ exhibited significant therapeutic effects on COPD rats, and its mechanism may be correlated with regulating the intestinal microbiota structure and metabolic profiles of COPD rats, thereby attenuating lung histopathological injury and pulmonary inflammation.

title: Lead-aggravated duodenal barrier injury accompanied by fecal microbiota alterations in 5xFAD mice.
abstract: Lead (Pb) is a persistent environmental toxicant, yet its effects on intestinal homeostasis in the 5xFAD background remain poorly characterized. Six-month-old 5xFAD mice were exposed to 200 μg/L Pb in drinking water for 8 weeks, with age-matched wild-type and unexposed 5xFAD mice serving as reference groups. We integrated duodenal metal profiling, mucosal architecture assessment, proteomic analysis, and fecal 16S rRNA sequencing to characterize the Pb-associated intestinal responses. Pb exposure increased duodenal Pb burden and reduced Ca, Cu, and Mg concentrations relative to unexposed 5xFAD mice. These elemental changes were accompanied by more pronounced villus shortening, crypt deepening, a lower villus height-to-crypt depth ratio, and loss of AB-PAS-positive goblet cells, suggesting impaired mucosal architecture and mucus-associated protection. Duodenal proteomic screening identified Pb-associated patterns involving epithelial junction organization, cell adhesion, calcium signaling, mineral absorption, complement activation, and mucosal immune pathways. In parallel, Pb-exposed 5xFAD mice showed lower fecal microbial richness and diversity than the unexposed 5xFAD mice, together with reduced abundances of Lachnospiraceae-related commensals and compositional shifts involving taxa associated with inflammatory or barrier-stress responses. Chronic Pb exposure in 5xFAD mice was associated with concurrent changes in duodenal metal homeostasis, mucosal structure, pathway-level proteomic profiles, and distal fecal microbial ecology. The duodenal findings highlight the proximal small intestine as a relevant peripheral site of Pb toxicity.

title: Temporal dynamics of bacterial communities in Spodoptera exigua during Heliothis virescens ascovirus 3 h infection.
abstract: Ascoviruses are insect viruses that cause chronic disease in infected hosts. The infection results in the partition of infected cells into multiple virion-containing vesicles, where viral replication continues for weeks before mortality. The vesicles accumulate in the hemolymph (equivalent to blood). The interaction among the virus, the host, and the microbiome during infection is poorly understood. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the temporal dynamics of whole-body bacterial communities in Spodoptera exigua larvae infected with Heliothis virescens ascovirus 3 h (HvAV-3 h) during early (12 hpi), late (48 hpi), and very late (96 hpi) viral replication stages. The 16S rRNA gene sequencing approach revealed that the HvAV-3 h-infected larvae encountered a decrease in the relative abundance of family Leuconostocaceae and genus Weissella and an increase in the relative abundance of family Acetobacteraceae and genus Acetobacter, when compared to the mock larvae. Moreover, the qPCR quantification demonstrated statistically significant decreases in the bacterial load during the late and very late stages of infection relative to the mock-infected larvae. In contrast, we detected statistically significant increases in the viral load with infection progress. We confirmed the presence of some of the identified bacterial genera, such as Bacillus sp. and Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB), in uninfected S. exigua whole-body samples using a culture-based approach. Further research will be needed to identify the specific roles of the identified bacterial communities and to clarify the mechanisms that contribute to controlling the host bacterial load. Future studies should consider examining different host tissue microbial communities in this system given the HvAV-3 h wide tissue tropism.
authors: Zaghloul HAH, Xiao Z, Huang GH.

title: Time-resolved profiling reveals nonlinear dose-time trajectories of gut microbiota in PM<sub>2.5</sub> and PFOS exposure models.
abstract: The gut microbiota is a dynamic ecological system, yet environmental microbiome studies often provide only limited temporal resolution. We characterized gut microbial responses across multiple exposure levels and sampling stages in two independent but complementary mouse models of PM2.5 inhalation and perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) drinking-water exposure. Time-resolved 16S rRNA gene sequencing, ecological analyses, PICRUSt2-based functional inference, and generalized additive models (GAMs) were integrated to examine temporal succession and nonlinear dose-time relationships. Under unexposed conditions, temporal microbial succession was evident in both models, highlighting the importance of accounting for background community dynamics. Within the PM2.5 model, community restructuring was most apparent during early-to-intermediate exposure stages, with prominent nonlinear trajectories in Lactobacillus, Prevotella, and the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio. In the PFOS model, microbial restructuring extended across a longer observation period and involved taxa including Akkermansia, Allobaculum, and UBA7173. PICRUSt2 suggested temporal and dose-associated variation in predicted pathways related to nitrogen metabolism, carbohydrate utilization, and fermentation, although these functions were not directly measured. GAMs identified stage-specific nonlinear response windows in both models. These findings highlight the importance of jointly considering dose and time in environmental microbiome studies and demonstrate the value of time-resolved modeling for detecting microbial response patterns that may be missed by endpoint analyses.
authors: Ruan C, He Y, Ran N, Wang Z.

title: Indole-3-acetic acid attenuates experimental colitis and epithelial lipid droplet accumulation in association with PPAR-γ signaling.
abstract: Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), a tryptophan-associated metabolite, has been implicated in intestinal homeostasis. This study evaluated IAA protection in experimental colitis and examined possible peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPAR-γ)-associated responses. Fecal 16S rRNA sequencing compared control and dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-treated mice. Male C57BL/6 J mice received 3% DSS for 7 days with oral IAA (20 mg/kg/day). Complementary experiments used interleukin-1β (IL-1β)-stimulated HT29 cells, exploratory molecular docking, and wild-type or mutant peroxisome proliferator response element (PPRE) reporters. Subsequent pharmacological experiments combined IAA with GW9662 or rosiglitazone. DSS exposure was associated with altered microbial composition, including Lactobacillus-associated taxa. IAA attenuated weight loss, disease activity, colon shortening, histological injury, and TUNEL-positive cells, and partially restored tight junction proteins while lowering inflammatory cytokines. Similar epithelial protein and cytokine improvements occurred in HT29 cells. Docking provided a candidate pose within the PPAR-γ/RXR-α structural framework, and IAA partially restored PPRE reporter activity. GW9662 co-treatment produced less favorable profiles, whereas rosiglitazone showed no significant additional benefit in annotated comparisons with IAA alone. Protection accompanied higher PPAR-γ, lower perilipin 2 and epithelial lipid accumulation, and partial recovery of whole-colon Arg1/CD206 proteins. These findings support IAA protection and possible PPAR-associated signaling without establishing microbial causality, macrophage polarization, receptor necessity, or direct IAA-PPAR-γ binding.
authors: Lin Y, Cheng CS, Li WH, Chen CW, Zhao YL.

title: Dietary fibre responses emerge through host-dietary regime interplay: Apple pectin modulates immune reactivity in adult zebrafish
abstract: Dietary fibres are rarely consumed independently. Instead, they form part of an overall diet that includes dietary fibres from different sources, in varying amounts and consumed under different feeding patterns. Here, we tested how dietary regimes containing apple pectin, oat β-glucan, or cellulose shaped the host. We analysed gut microbiome composition by 16S rRNA sequencing, measured brain and intestinal SCFA profiles by targeted metabolomics, and assessed immunomodulation by measuring gene expression systemically in the blood and locally in the spleen, as well as intestinal enzyme activity. The dietary intervention was conducted for 12 weeks on adult female and male zebrafish (  Danio rerio ). Our results show that the gut microbial composition can be relatively stable across different dietary fibre exposure patterns yet still vary significantly between the sexes. Additionally, the effect of sex on the gut microbiome may become more evident when dietary fibres are administered at high dosages, but intermittently. Dietary fibre regimes can alter intestinal short-chain fatty acid profiles more readily than brain profiles, which show a stronger sexually dimorphic response. Interestingly, apple pectin modulated the zebrafish immune response through interactions dependent on the overall regime, tissue, sex, and host immune status. Notably, tissue  il1b gene expression differed depending on how apple pectin was administered and the host's physiological state. Collectively, our study emphasises the highly context-specific effects of dietary fibres, shaped by the dynamic interplay between the overall dietary regime and intertwined host factors.

title: A One Health Molecular Investigation and Exploratory Epidemiological Analysis of Cryptosporidium spp. in A Shared Human-Animal Ecosystem.
abstract: IntroductionCryptosporidium spp. are enteric protozoan parasites of public health importance, particularly in low-resource settings where humans, animals and environmental water sources frequently interact. This study investigated the prevalence, molecular diversity and environmental exposure-related variables in relation to Cryptosporidium infection in a rural community.MethodsA cross-sectional study was conducted using 180 faecal samples collected from humans, cattle, chickens, fish, cats, dogs, and ducks. Speciation and subtyping were determined through PCR amplification and sequencing of the 18S rRNA and gp60 genes. Epidemiological and environmental data were collected, and univariable analyses were conducted. An exploratory multivariable logistic regression model was subsequently performed for the human subset.ResultsThe overall prevalence of Cryptosporidium infection was 9.40%, with the highest rates observed in humans (14.8%) and cattle (13.5%). Molecular characterisation identified C. hominis, C. parvum, C. bovis and C. felis. Among humans, C. hominis was the predominant, whereas C. parvum was also detected, including mixed infections. gp60 analysis identified multiple subtype families, including Ia, Ib, IIa, IIc and IId. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated close genetic relationships between Bangladeshi isolates and previously reported reference strains from South Asia and the Middle East. Higher odds of Cryptosporidium infection were observed among individuals reporting river bathing and consumption of untreated water, whereas lower odds were observed among those reporting regular handwashing. No statistically significant associations were identified between evaluated environmental variables and infection among non-human hosts.ConclusionThe study demonstrated the circulation of multiple Cryptosporidium species and subtype families within a shared human-animal ecosystem. The contaminated surface water and inadequate hygiene practices may represent important environmental exposure interfaces for Cryptosporidium infection in the study area. However, given the cross-sectional design and limited number of positive cases, the epidemiological findings should be interpreted as exploratory associations rather than definitive transmission pathways. Further longitudinal One Health investigations are needed.
authors: Wakid MH, Aryal D, Sharifuzzaman, Hossain SS, Amin ARMB, Islam MS, Shahiduzzaman M.

title: Oral mycobiome composition and fungi-bacteria associations in children and young adults with type 1 diabetes.
abstract: BackgroundOral mycobiome in children and young adults with type 1 diabetes (T1D) remains poorly characterized.ObjectiveWe investigated oral fungal community structure and its associations with bacterial communities and immune mediators in individuals with established T1D compared with healthy controls (HC).DesignOral fungal and bacterial communities were characterized in 68 participants with T1D and 69 HC by ITS and 16S rRNA gene sequencing, alongside multiplex assessment of soluble immune factors. Sequencing data were processed with QIIME 2, immune factors with BioPlex Manager and statistical analyzes with R v.4.3.3.ResultsFungal alpha and beta diversity did not differ significantly between groups. However, several taxa were differentially abundant or prevalent in T1D, including Fusarium, Hanseniaspora, Meyerozyma, Cyberlindnera jadinii, Candida albicans, C. dubliniensis and Malassezia globosa. No significant differences emerged by HbA1c category (vs. ≥7%) within T1D. Notably, Cystobasidium/C. slooffiae and Trichoderma, detected exclusively in T1D, showed stronger positive associations with MCP-1/MCAF and IP-10, respectively, than in HC, while several fungal genera were inversely associated with distinct bacterial taxa.ConclusionsThese findings indicate that T1D is associated with selective, taxon-specific oral mycobiome alterations rather than generalized dysbiosis. The observed fungal-immune and fungal--bacterial links suggest biological relevance, warranting longitudinal and functional investigation.
authors: Campisciano G, Aldegheri L, Zanotta N, Catamo E, Robino A, Mione F, Cadenaro M, Navarra C, Tornese G, Comar M.

title: Pharmacogenomic Markers of Disease Susceptibility and Glucocorticoid Responsiveness in Pemphigus Vulgaris.
abstract: BackgroundResponse to glucocorticoid (GC) therapy in pemphigus vulgaris (PV) is variable and may be influenced by pharmacogenomic factors. This study aimed to evaluate the association between glutathione S-transferases (GST) gene polymorphisms and Multidrug resistance protein 1 (MDR1) or ATP-binding cassette sub-family B member 1 (ABCB1) variations with steroid responsiveness in PV patients and evaluate their role in conferring susceptibility to PV.Patients and methodsEighty participants were included: Group A: GC responders (n = 20), Group B: GC nonresponders (n = 20), Group A+B: Combined PV cases (n = 40), and Group C: healthy controls (n = 40). Disease severity was assessed using the Pemphigus Disease Area Index and Dermatology Life Quality Index. Glutathione S-transferase (GST) genotypes, GSTM1, GSTT1, and GSTP1, were analyzed by multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR); MDR1 2677G>A/T single nucleotide polymorphism was evaluated by amplification refractory mutation system PCR. MDR1 gene mRNA expression was quantified by reverse transcription-PCR using 18S rRNA as a housekeeping gene.ResultsAmong the 40 PV patients (mean age: 41.3 ± 13 years; male:female = 21:19), GSTM1 heterozygosity was significantly more frequent (45%) than in controls (28%) (P = 0.01; odds ratio = 4.636), suggesting its role as a risk factor. GSTT1 heterozygosity was more prevalent in controls (Group C; 58%) than in cases (Group A+B) (32%; P = 0.04), indicating a potential protective role. Among PV patients, nonresponders (Group B) had higher (though statistically non-significant) GSTT1 heterozygosity and combined variant genotypes, and GSTM1 heterozygosity was more frequent in responders (Group A). MDR1 genotype distribution (2677G>A/T) did not differ significantly between groups (A and B); however, downregulated MDR1 mRNA expression was evident in Group A and Group B compared to Group C.LimitationsSmall sample size, technical variability in mRNA quantification, and single-population analysis.ConclusionHeterozygosity in GSTM1 and GSTT1 may influence PV susceptibility and steroid responsiveness. MDR1 expression may correlate with treatment response but requires validation using stable reference genes.
authors: Pandhi D, Kar R, Aggarwal B, Chawla D.

title: Lactic Acid Bacteria and Lemon Peel Powder Enriched Boza, a Fermented Cereal-Based Beverage, Enhances Butyrate Production and Modulates Fecal Microbiota during In Vitro Fermentation.
abstract: Grain-based fermented products have gained increasing attention due to their nutritional and health-promoting properties. In this study, various formulations of boza, a traditional fermented cereal-based beverage, with and without lemon peel powder supplementation and probiotic cultures (Levilactobacillus brevis, Limosilactobacillus reuteri) were produced. The samples were tested for microbiological characteristics, pH and titratable acidity, bioactive properties, color parameters, sensory attributes, and their effects on the fecal microbiota. All fortified boza samples exhibited higher lactic acid bacteria and total mesophilic aerobic bacteria counts than control samples, accompanied by lower pH values. Boza supplemented solely with lemon peel powder were higher in total phenolic content, while samples containing lemon peel powder and probiotic cultures (synbiotic boza) exhibited higher antioxidant profile in FRAP assays. Furthermore, synbiotic boza products received higher sensory acceptability scores than controls. In vitro fecal fermentation analysis in which microbial short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and microbial compositional changes were assessed using gas chromatography and 16S rRNA sequencing, respectively showed that synbiotic boza products promoted the formation of SCFAs, particularly butyrate, at a level similar to those observed with inulin, a well-established fast-fermenting prebiotic. The increase in butyrate level was accompanied by an enrichment of butyrate- (i.e. Roseburia) and lactate-producing (i.e. Bifidobacterium) taxa. Overall, these findings demonstrate that the incorporation of lemon peel powder and probiotic cultures into boza can yield a synbiotic beverage with preserved technological quality and improved potential to modulate gut microbiota composition and function toward a healthier profile.
authors: Alkay Z, Buzrul S, Dertli E, Lindemann SR, Tunçil YE.

title: Integrated Volatile Metabolomics and Bacterial Community Profiling Identify Potential Quality Markers for Geographical Discrimination of Microcos paniculata L. Herbal Tea.
abstract: Microcos paniculata L. (ML) is an edible herbal tea plant with regional differences in flavor and bioactive quality. However, the chemical and microbial factors associated with these differences remain unclear. This study integrated HS-GC-Orbitrap-MS/MS, 16S rRNA sequencing, sensory evaluation, color analysis, and antioxidant assays to characterize ML samples from Guangdong, Guangxi, and Yunnan, China. Guangdong samples were characterized by the highest total phenolic and flavonoid contents and superior antioxidant capacity, whereas Yunnan samples showed the best sensory performance, particularly for aroma and taste attributes. A total of 133 volatile constituents were tentatively identified, mainly comprising olefins and cycloolefins, aromatic compounds, terpenes, alcohols, and ketones. Chemometric analysis revealed clear origin-dependent separation and identified 12 differential volatile compounds, including p-cymene, L-limonene, α-phellandrene, dimethyl sulfide, and ethylbenzene. Bacterial community analysis showed distinct origin-associated patterns, and several bacterial taxa were correlated with characteristic volatile compounds and quality traits. Functional prediction and multivariate correlation analysis suggested potential associations among environmental factors, bacterial communities, volatile metabolites, and antioxidant properties. These findings provide a foodomics-based framework for understanding geographical quality variation in ML and offer potential markers for origin traceability and quality evaluation of edible herbal tea resources.
authors: He Y, Xu P, Zhou J, Zheng J, Yuchi R, Wang X, Wei B, Cang S.

title: An Exploratory Longitudinal Analysis of Salivary Host, Bacterial and Fungal Extracellular Vesicles Following 6-Month Non-Surgical Periodontal Therapy in Periodontitis.
abstract: AimTo evaluate the longitudinal changes in salivary host and non-host extracellular vesicles (EVs) following non-surgical periodontal therapy (NSPT).Materials and methodsUnstimulated saliva and plaque (from a deep pocket) were collected from 25 Stage III/IV periodontitis patients at baseline and at 3 and 6 months post NSPT. Host salivary EVs and non-host EVs were isolated using immunoaffinity, and size-exclusion chromatography, respectively. Host EV cytokines were assessed by multiplex flow cytometry, and non-host EVs, saliva and plaque were profiled by 16S rRNA and fungal internal transcribed spacer (ITS) sequencing.ResultsPeriodontal parameters significantly decreased at 3 and 6 months post NSPT (vs. baseline), accompanied by increased host-EVs associated cytokines interleukin-4 (IL-4), IL-12 and IL-9 (not whole saliva). At both timepoints, bacterial EVs also declined, including the genera Filifactor, Parvimonas and Lentimicrobium and the species Fusobacterium nucleatum, Filifactor alocis, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola, Porphyromonas gingivalis, P. endodontalis, P. micra and Lachnospiraceae bacterium; similar reductions were observed in plaque and saliva taxa, including Treponema, Tannerella, Parvimonas, T. forsythia, T. socranskii and P. micra. At 6 months, fungal EVs from Malassezia arunalokei were decreased and the fungal Candida parapsilosis EVs were increased.ConclusionsNSPT led to changes in salivary host and non-host EV cargoes, suggesting that they may serve as a non-invasive tool for disease treatment monitoring in periodontitis.

title: Evaluating the use of blood pressure and oral microbiome screening in primary care dental clinics
abstract: Abstract  Blood pressure and oral microbiome screening are gaining popularity in non-medical settings, the hypotheses communicated to hypertensive patients being that: altering the abundance of certain bacterial species via oral hygiene could be beneficial for cardiovascular health, especially nitrate reducing species that lower blood pressure. title: Occurrence and antimicrobial resistance of Acinetobacter baumannii in cats, veterinary hospital environments and medical wastes in Bangladesh.
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii presence in veterinary hospitals and companion animals is still poorly investigated despite its significance. The present study aimed to investigate the prevalence, antimicrobial resistance patterns, and resistance genes of A. baumannii in cats, veterinary hospital environments, and veterinary medical wastes in Bangladesh. Samples were collected from oral, rectal, and wound swabs of cats (n = 100) attending ten veterinary hospitals, as well as from environmental surfaces (n = 111) and wastes (n = 61) generated within these facilities. Isolates were identified by PCR targeting 16S rRNA (genus) and blaOXA-51-like (species) genes; antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed by disk diffusion and broth microdilution following CLSI standards, and resistance genes (blaOXA-23-like, blaNDM-1) were screened by PCR. A high prevalence of A. baumannii was observed in cats (37%), while 26.1% in environmental samples and 21.3% in waste samples. Apparently sick cats had significantly higher prevalence (p = 0.049) than apparently healthy cats. All isolates were imipenem resistant, consistent with carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB). High resistance was also observed against cefotaxime and ceftriaxone. Multidrug resistance (MDR) was detected in 26.7%, 37.9%, and 30.8% of isolates from cats, environmental, and waste sources, respectively. The blaOXA-23-like gene was detected in only two cat isolates, whereas blaNDM was identified in one cat isolate and one environmental isolate. In conclusion, these findings identify cats, which live in close proximity to humans, as a possible CRAB reservoir, and veterinary hospital environments and waste as potential sources of persistence and dissemination, raising concern for zoonotic spread and underscoring occupational and public health risk.

title: Microbiota Changes During Chemotherapy in Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: A Comparative Assessment with Il-17 and Il-12 Levels
abstract: Objective:  This study aimed to investigate changes in gut microbiota composition during chemotherapy in patients with Hodgkin lymphoma (HL), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), and healthy controls, and to evaluate their potential impact on treatment outcomes. Additionally, changes in IL-12 and IL-17 levels during chemotherapy were assessed. Materials and Methods: Fifteen samples from patients with HL were collected after 2–3 cycles of therapy, whereas 15 samples from patients with NHL were collected after 3–4 cycles of therapy. Samples were also collected from healthy controls (n = 33). Microbial alpha diversity and microbiota composition were assessed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and an operational taxonomic unit (OTU) table generated through R/RStudio. The expression levels of IL-12 and IL-17 were quantified by real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Results: In HL patients, genera such as Agathobacter, Romboutsia, and Veillonella were predominantly identified in pre-treatment samples, whereas Dorea, Lactobacillus, and Weissella were enriched post-treatment. Actinobacteriota and Verrucomicrobiota were slightly more abundant before treatment. In NHL patients, Alistipes, Phascolarctobacterium, and Roseburia were characteristic of pre-treatment samples, while Lachnoclostridium, Parabacteroides, and UBA1819 were enriched post-treatment. Actinobacteriota levels increased modestly after chemotherapy. KEGG pathway analysis revealed distinct alterations in HL and NHL, and IL-12 levels differed significantly between NHL patients and healthy controls post-chemotherapy. Conclusions: Baseline gut microbiota profiling may help develop personalized strategies to mitigate chemotherapy-induced dysbiosis and enhance treatment efficacy. Microbiome modulation represents a promising adjunctive approach in lymphoma management.

title: Effects of C/N ratio and carbon-source composition on nutrient removal in a dual-sludge membrane bioreactor system (A<sub>2</sub>N-MBR).
abstract: Microbial competition that is driven by substrates plays an essential role in the stable denitrifying phosphorus removal (DPR) of low carbon wastewater treatment. This paper used a dual-sludge membrane bioreactor (A2N-MBR) to evaluate C/N ratios of 3-6 using acetate, followed by a comparison of acetate, propionate and their mixture at C/N = 5. Stoichiometric analysis estimated substrate allocations among denitrifying polyphosphate-accumulating organisms (DPAOs), denitrifying glycogen-accumulating organisms (DGAOs) and denitrifying ordinary heterotrophic organisms (DOHOs), while 16S rRNA gene sequencing and Pearson correlation analysis characterised community composition and its associations with nutrient removal. At C/N = 5, stoichiometric estimates assigned 53% of anaerobic COD consumption and 82% of anoxic nitrate reduction to DPAOs, with nitrate and phosphate removal efficiencies of 76.93% and 77.00%, respectively. At C/N = 6, the estimated substrate allocations shifted towards DGAOs and DOHOs pathways. Phosphorus removal was not as consistent as nitrate removal. In the subsequent carbon source comparison at C/N = 5, the acetate propionate mixture improved reactor performance. As a result, the maximum nitrate and phosphate removal efficiencies were 91.72% and 88.50%, respectively. Correlation analysis indicated that Thauera and Zoogloea were associated with NO3--N and PO43--P removal. Conversely, Nitrospira relative abundance was negatively associated with nitrate removal. All in all, these findings link substrate conditions with community composition and DPR performance within the respective C/N and carbon source comparisons.

title: Hidradenitis suppurativa skin microbiome: In-depth analysis and modulation by systemic therapies.
abstract: BackgroundHidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease with a multifactorial pathogenesis involving genetic, lifestyle and microbial factors. While cutaneous microbiome shifts have been reported for this disease, the impact of systemic immunomodulators and antibiotics on HS microbiome remains poorly defined.ObjectiveTo characterize species-level cutaneous dysbiosis in HS and evaluate the effects of three standard-of-care systemic therapies, clindamycin/rifampicin (ATB), adalimumab (ADA) and secukinumab (SEC) on skin microbial composition.MethodsWe performed 16S rRNA sequencing on 251 skin swabs from lesional and non-lesional sites of 52 HS patients and 31 healthy matched controls. In a sub-cohort of 28 patients, microbial shifts were evaluated following 12 weeks of therapy with ATB (n = 8), ADA (n = 12) and SEC (n = 8).ResultsHS skin exhibited profound dysbiosis defined by the depletion of homeostatic commensals (Cutibacterium acnes, Staphylococcus hominis, S. epidermidis) and a synergistic expansion of anaerobic pathogens, primarily Gram-positive anaerobic cocci (GPAC; Finegoldia magna, Peptoniphilus grossensis and Fenollaria massiliensis), Lawsonella clevelandensis and Campylobacter ureolyticus. A 13-taxa microbial signature accurately discriminated the HS phenotype (AUC = 0.92). Following 12 weeks of treatment, ATB markedly attenuated dysbiosis by reducing pathogen loads and significantly increasing microbial richness. In contrast, ADA and SEC did not alter pathogen abundance and were associated with a slight decline in protective commensals.ConclusionsSystemic antibiotics partially restore cutaneous microbiome homeostasis in HS by targeting anaerobic pathogens while preserving beneficial commensals, an effect not observed with the tested biologics. These findings highlight the need for microbiome-directed adjuvant therapies to complement immunomodulation in HS management.

title: Redescription of the Argasidae subfamilies, Argasinae and Ornithodorinae: Reflections on the genera Alveonasus and Otobius.
abstract: The Argasidae (soft tick) family has historically been classified into two subfamilies, the Argasinae and Ornithodorinae. The classic morphological definition of the subfamilies is based on a flattened body margin with a sutural line demarcated by cells or striations in the Argasinae, and a rounded body margin with no sutural line in the Ornithodorinae. Cladistic and molecular analysis also indicate two clades corresponding to two subfamilies, but the definitions of the subfamilies became invalid due to placement of Alveonasus and Proknekalia in the Argasinae and Carios and Chiropterargas in the Ornithodorinae. As such, no morphological definition to differentiate these new subfamilies exists. The current study updated descriptions congruent with cladistic and molecular analysis for the subfamilies based on the presence of a tracheal system, seta pd1 present on the palp femur, at least 4 setae on the proximal two-thirds of the palpal tibiotarsus and setae dm absent on tarsi II-III in Argasinae larvae. These characters are, respectively, absent, present or different in the Ornithodorinae. However, the grouping of Otobius lagophilus (for which a tracheal system is absent) in the Argasinae by molecular analysis invalidates this new definition of the subfamilies. We recognized that this may be a means to test the new classification hypothesis by predicting that the mitochondrial genome sequences belonging to O. lagophilus (ON756085, ON800860, ON800861) were erroneously assigned to this species. Sequencing of a 16S rRNA fragment from a O. lagophilus museum specimen showed grouping as sister to Otobius megnini within the Ornithodorinae, with no sister relationship to ON756085, ON800860, ON800861. We therefore conclude that these latter sequences were erroneously assigned to O. lagophilus. We additionally report mitochondrial genome sequences for Alveonasus cooleyi and Alveonasus eboris and data analysis suggests that the specimens misidentified as O. lagophilus probably represent a new Alveonasus species from Texas. The data supports the new definitions of the subfamilies, providing stable morphological characters allowing placement of species in subfamilies without the need for exclusive use of molecular data to differentiate the subfamilies. It also suggests that the subfamilies and their respective genera are indeed separate monophyletic natural lineages.

title: Longitudinal Gut Microbiota Changes in Mouse Models of Chronic Colitis, Colitis-Associated Cancer, and Chemotherapy-Induced Diarrhea.
abstract: BackgroundGut microbiota contributes to intestinal pathologies, but microbial and metabolic differences distinguishing inflammation-associated tumorigenesis from chronic colitis remain unclear. This study mapped stage-dependent microbiota dynamics and metabolic perturbations across three independent mouse models: chronic ulcerative colitis (CUC), AOM/DSS-induced colitis-associated cancer (CAC), and chemotherapy-induced diarrhea (CID).MethodsCUC, CAC, and CID were induced by cyclic DSS, AOM/DSS, and CPT-11, respectively. Disease progression was monitored via endoscopy, histopathology, and Disease Activity Index. Gut microbiota was profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing across three stages (R01-R03); metabolic and inflammatory changes were assessed by RT-qPCR and metabolite assays. Mediation analysis was used to explore whether the associations between microbial abundance and host metabolic/inflammatory markers were statistically consistent with an indirect pathway.ResultsCID showed distinct acute transient injury and a unique microbiota structure separate from CUC/CAC. In CUC and CAC, microbiota restructured stage-dependently: beneficial genera (Akkermansia) declined, while pathobionts (norank_o_Clostridia_UCG-014) increased. CAC showed upregulation of glycolysis genes (HK2, PKM2, LDHA, Glut1) together with elevated colonic lactate concentrations, and elevated colonic concentrations of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-17A and IL-22, indicating distinct colonic metabolic and inflammatory changes associated with gut dysbiosis. Mediation analysis showed that norank_o__Clostridia_UCG-014 showed consistently positive indirect effects, irrespective of the glycolytic enzyme and lactate enantiomer examined; and Allobaculum had a consistently positive indirect effect on both IL-17A and IL-22.ConclusionThese findings reveal distinct stage-specific microbial and metabolic signatures distinguishing AOM/DSS tumor-bearing mice from nonneoplastic chronic colitis and acute chemotherapy intestinal injury.

title: Baicalin and levofloxacin exert divergent modulation on gut microbiota and metabolome crosstalk in DSS-triggered ulcerative colitis.
abstract: Baicalin (BA), a bioactive flavonoid, and levofloxacin hydrochloride (LH), a fluoroquinolone antibiotic, both hold potential for ulcerative colitis (UC) treatment, yet the mechanistic differences in their regulation of gut microbiota and metabolome remain elusive. This study aimed to systematically compare their therapeutic efficacy and underlying mechanisms in a dextran sulfate sodium-induced murine colitis model, with a focus on gut microbial and metabolic modulation. Mice were randomized into Control, model, BA-treated, and LH-treated groups. Disease severity was assessed via body weight changes, disease activity index, colon length, and histopathological analysis. Western blot and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay were employed to detect NF-κB pathway activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, while 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomics profiled gut microbiota and metabolites. Both agents markedly ameliorated colitis symptoms, suppressed NF-κB activation, and cytokine expression, with BA showing superior cytokine inhibition. BA enriched beneficial Lactobacillus, regulating isoflavone/alkaloid synthesis; LH elevated Akkermansia abundance and modulated amino acid metabolism. These findings reveal distinct therapeutic mechanisms of BA and LH, laying a foundation for personalized UC therapy and validating BA's traditional medicinal utility.IMPORTANCEUlcerative colitis remains a prevalent inflammatory bowel disease with limited microbiota-targeted therapies. Baicalin and levofloxacin both alleviate dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis, yet their gut microbiome and metabolome regulatory mechanisms have not been directly compared. This study demonstrates that baicalin and levofloxacin exert anti-colitis effects via divergent microbiota-metabolite axes: baicalin enriches Lactobacillus and modulates isoflavone/alkaloid metabolism, while levofloxacin increases Akkermansia and reshapes amino acid metabolism. These distinct mechanisms provide new evidence for developing microbiota-based personalized strategies for ulcerative colitis treatment.
authors: Wang C, Wu W, Cui M, Zhang S, Wang C.

title: Taxonogenomic Investigation of Yoonia aquicola sp. nov., Isolated from Coastal Seawater.
abstract: An alphaproteobacterium, KMU-150T, was isolated from a coastal seawater sample collected in the Republic of Korea and investigated using a taxonogenomic approach. Cells were light beige in color, oval- to short rod-shaped, Gram-stain-negative, strictly aerobic, and non-motile. It was able to grow at 0-7.0% NaCl concentrations (w/v), pH 5.5-9.0, and 20-37 °C. A phylogenetic tree based on 16S rRNA gene sequences showed that strain KMU-150ᵀ clustered with the genus Yoonia within the class Alphaproteobacteria and was closely related to Yoonia litorea DPG-5ᵀ, with a sequence similarity of 98.4%. The sole respiratory quinone was Q-10, and the polar lipids consisted of phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylglycerol, two unidentified aminolipids, and an unidentified phospholipid. C18:1 ω7c was identified as a major (> 10%) fatty acid. Strain KMU-150T had a genome size of 3.4 Mb and a DNA G + C content of 63.0%. Phylogenomic trees robustly placed strain KMU-150ᵀ within the genus Yoonia. The ANI values between strain KMU-150ᵀ and species of the genus Yoonia ranged from 71.6 to 75.1%, and the dDDH value with Y. litorea DPG-5ᵀ was 19.5%, indicating that strain KMU-150ᵀ represents a novel species of the genus. The genome of strain KMU-150ᵀ was predicted to harbor five putative biosynthetic gene clusters, suggesting a possible capacity for secondary metabolite biosynthesis. Moreover, several genes associated with the degradation of biological molecules were identified in the genome of strain KMU-150T, indicating substantial potential for the synthesis of enzymes with valuable industrial applications. The taxonogenomic data obtained in this study support the conclusion that strain KMU-150ᵀ represents a novel species of the genus Yoonia, for which the name Yoonia aquicola sp. nov. is proposed. The type strain is KMU-150ᵀ (= KCCM 90340ᵀ = NBRC 117445ᵀ).

title: Gut microbial and SCFA profiling identifies a distinct Dorea-Megasphaera-Valeric acid axis associated with Pakistani beta thalassemia cohorts
abstract: Abstract      Background    : β-thalassemiais the most prevalent inherited blood disorder in Pakistan, driven by a high rate of consanguineous marriages. It has led to high rate of childhood morbidity that require lifelong blood transfusions casing toxic iron overload. Exploring the associated gut microbiome and metabolite shifts in this population can reveal how iron toxicity disrupts crucial bacterial pathways, offering a foundation for targeted nutritional therapies. This study investigates the gut microbial structural and functional alteration in three cohorts, namely healthy, Thalassemia Minor, and transfusion-dependent Thalassemia Major. A comprehensive multi-omic approach integrating 16S rRNA sequencing, metabolic pathway analysis via MetaCyc, and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) profiling using the Multiblock Sparse Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis, DIABLO framework, was employed to identify disease-specific microbial signatures.    Results    :  A strong decrease in abundance of  Alistipes  and  Bacteroides,  was observed with the disease progression. The Thalassemia Minor group exhibited an abundance of  Prevotella  and  Eubacterium  , whereas Thalassemia Major showed an increase in abundance of iron-tolerant species, including  Megasphaera, Sarcina,  and  Akkermansia  . On the functional side, a significant upregulation of pro-inflammatory lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis pathways was observed in the thalassemia cohorts as opposed to the healthy cohort. The healthy cohort maintained essential Mevalonate and Flavin biosynthetic pathways. Furthermore, a distinct metabolic signature of the  Dorea-Megasphaera-  Valeric acid axis was identified in the Thalassemia Major cohort.    Conclusion    :  Beta-thalassemia leads to shift from a balanced butyrate-rich environment towards an endotoxin-loaded pro-inflammatory state mainly due to iron overload-induced selective pressure. These findings support incorporation of iron-stable probiotics (e.g.,  Bifidobacterium  ) and postbiotic valeric acid along with standard chelation therapy, to rejuvenate the gut integrity and reduce systemic inflammation.

title: C. butyricum Combined With Resmetirom Provides Therapeutic Benefits in MASH Associated With Gut-Liver-Brain Axis Modulation.
abstract: Background and aimsResmetirom has emerged as a major advance in MASH pharmacotherapy as the first approved liver-targeted THR-β agonist; however, variable therapeutic efficacy and adverse responses may limit its clinical benefits. This study investigated whether C. butyricum could provide additional therapeutic benefits when combined with resmetirom and attenuate nausea/vomiting-like responses in association with changes across the gut-liver-brain axis.MethodsIn this study, we established a high-fat diet-induced MASH mouse model and administered C. butyricum, resmetirom, or their combination. Comprehensive biochemical, histological, molecular, 16S rRNA sequencing-based microbiome profiling, and gut-brain axis-related analyses were performed to evaluate the effects of combination therapy on hepatic metabolism, inflammation, fibrosis, intestinal barrier integrity, gut microbiota remodelling, microbial metabolites, and resmetirom-associated adverse responses.ResultsCombined treatment with C. butyricum and resmetirom produced additional therapeutic benefits compared with either monotherapy, markedly improving hepatic steatosis, lipid accumulation, insulin resistance, inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis in MASH mice. At the molecular level, combination treatment was associated with increased hepatic THR-β expression and coordinated changes in AMPK-related lipid metabolism, NRF2/HO-1 antioxidant, and TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB inflammatory markers. Furthermore, combination therapy restored intestinal barrier integrity, alleviated MASH-associated gut microbial dysbiosis, increased beneficial bacterial taxa, and increased faecal butyrate levels. Notably, C. butyricum attenuated resmetirom-induced nausea/vomiting-like responses, accompanied by reduced colonic and cerebral 5-HT/SP signalling, decreased brain Htr3a and Tacr1 mRNA expression, and suppressed neuronal FOS activation. Faecal butyrate levels were inversely associated with hepatic lipid burden and brain 5-HT/SP levels.ConclusionsC. butyricum combined with resmetirom provides additional therapeutic benefits and attenuates nausea/vomiting-like responses in MASH, accompanied by coordinated changes across the gut-liver-brain axis. This combination strategy provides a potential microbiota-based adjunctive approach for optimizing the therapeutic benefits of resmetirom in MASH.

title: SaeRS Gene Expression Following Exposure to Olive Leaf-Mediated Zinc Oxide Nanoparticles in Multidrug-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
abstract: AimThis pilot study assessed the transcriptional responses of saeR and saeS to green-synthesized zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) prepared using Olea europaea leaf extract in four multidrug-resistant clinical isolates of Staphylococcus aureus. Antimicrobial susceptibility profiles and the prevalence of pvl, agrI, agrII, and agrIII were also determined.Methods and resultsAntimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed on 40 clinical isolates. Four multidrug-resistant isolates were exposed to ZnO NPs at a subinhibitory concentration (1/2 MIC), and saeR and saeS expression was quantified by RT-qPCR using 16S rRNA for normalization and paired comparative Ct calculations. Untreated and exposed ΔCt values from the same isolate were compared using exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Resistance was highest to oxacillin (85.0%), fusidic acid (82.5%), ceftaroline (72.5%), and rifampin (70.0%), whereas gentamicin, doxycycline, tigecycline, and linezolid showed 97.5% susceptibility. The pvl gene was detected in 27.5% of isolates; agrI, agrII, and agrIII were detected in 17.5%, 20.0%, and 15.0%, respectively. saeR expression decreased numerically in all four isolates, but the paired comparison was not statistically significant (p = 0.125). saeS expression decreased in three isolates and increased in one isolate; this paired comparison was also not significant (p = 0.250).Conclusions significance and impactThe findings provide descriptive, isolate-specific evidence of transcriptional responses of saeR and saeS to sub-MIC ZnO-NP exposure in the four MDR S. aureus isolates examined and should not be generalized across S. aureus lineages. They do not establish direct SaeRS inhibition or reduction of virulence-associated phenotypes because only four isolates were assessed and no extract-only, Zn2+, chemically synthesized ZnO-NP, downstream virulence, protein-level, or functional controls were included. Larger controlled studies are required before biological or therapeutic implications can be drawn.

title: Human Gut Microbiota of Healthy Individuals Show Resilience to Acute Aflatoxin B1 Exposure Despite Solvent-Driven Community Shifts
abstract: Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is a potent mycotoxin linked to severe systemic health issues and gut microbiome disruption in in vivo models. However, it remains unclear whether AFB1 directly impairs human gut microbial composition and function or if observed dysbiosis is host-mediated. The objective of this work was to investigate the direct impact of acute AFB1 exposure on human gut microbiota from healthy individuals using anaerobic batch bioreactors. Fecal inoculum from 17 healthy adults was exposed to AFB1 concentrations ranging from 1,000 to 5,000 ppb, delivered in two solvents (ethanol and corn oil) under conditions simulating the large intestine. Metabolic activity was assessed via short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) and gas production measurements, while community structure was assessed using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. AFB1 concentrations remained stable throughout the incubations, indicating no significant microbial degradation of AFB1. Results showed that AFB1 did not significantly alter microbial SCFA output or community composition compared to solvent-only controls. Observed shifts in microbial profiles were primarily driven by the solvents used to bring AFB1 into solution rather than by the toxin. These findings demonstrate that healthy human gut microbial communities are resilient to direct, acute AFB1 exposure even at concentrations exceeding typical dietary levels. This suggests that microbiome disruption reported in vivo may be an indirect consequence of host-mediated factors, such as reactive metabolites or systemic immune responses, rather than direct toxicity by the parent compound. Importance  Aflatoxin B1 is a major global health threat, particularly in regions with high dietary exposure, where it is associated with liver cancer and childhood growth stunting. While research has linked aflatoxin exposure to changes in the gut microbiome, the mechanisms driving this “dysbiosis” are not known. This work provides evidence that the parent aflatoxin molecule does not directly affect healthy human gut microbes, even at very high concentrations. The observed resilience of these microbial communities suggests that the damage reported in living organisms is likely caused by host-specific responses to the toxin or by toxic byproducts created during liver detoxification. Furthermore, microbially driven detoxification of the parent aflatoxin molecule was not observed. Distinguishing between direct and indirect toxicity is essential for developing effective strategies and medical interventions to mitigate the health impacts of aflatoxin exposure worldwide.

title: Establishment and preliminary application of the Mo RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a rapid detection method.
abstract: Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae (Mo) is a common pathogen prevalent worldwide that causes pneumonia and leads to significant economic losses in sheep farming. Early testing of nasal swabs from diseased sheep in Xinjiang yielded a 51.5% positivity rate, indicating severe infection within the sheep population. Existing detection methods are time-consuming and rely on large-scale equipment, making them unsuitable for frontline clinical testing. Rapid, accurate, and on-site pathogen detection is essential for the early prevention and control of infectious diseases. Conventional nucleic acid detection methods are limited by long reaction duration, sophisticated instruments, and strict operating requirements, which restrict their application in grassroots rapid diagnosis scenarios. Herein, we established a combined Mo-RPA integrated CRISPR/Cas12a detection assay, which realized constant-temperature nucleic acid detection without large-scale laboratory equipment. The entire detection workflow was completed within 30 min under a constant temperature of 37°C. The optimized assay achieved a limit of detection of 10° copies/μL, with 100% analytical specificity against non-target pathogen strains. In clinical sample verification, the detection consistency between the established method and standard real-time PCR assay reached 100%. The established constant-temperature detection system integrates rapid nucleic acid amplification and CRISPR fluorescent signal output and provides a quantifiable on-site detection scheme for grassroots epidemic surveillance.ImportanceIn this study, we demonstrated a novel RPA-CRISPR-Cas12a-based diagnostic method for Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae (Mo) infection with high sensitivity and specificity. The detection rate reached 51.5% (85/165). Subsequently, an RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a rapid test targeting the 16S rRNA gene of Mo was developed, achieving a detection time of 30 min, 100% specificity, and a sensitivity of 100 copies/μL-10⁶ times more sensitive than PCR. During preliminary application, the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a method detected Mo in 84/102 samples (82.35%), representing 1.7 times the detection rate of PCR. Consequently, RPA-Cas12a testing has demonstrated significant potential for routine Mo screening and offers high accessibility for population screening or molecular diagnostics in resource-limited settings.

title: Gut microbiota-associated metabolic alterations contribute to 6PPD-Q-induced intestinal barrier dysfunction in mice.
abstract: N-(1,3-Dimethylbutyl)-N'-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine quinone (6PPD-Q), a ubiquitous tire-derived contaminant detected in environmental matrices and human samples, poses potential intestinal health risks to mammals. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. C57BL/6 mice were orally exposed to 6PPD-Q (4 mg/kg, once every 3 days for 28 days) with or without broad-spectrum antibiotic pretreatment to deplete gut microbiota. 16S rRNA sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, immunofluorescence, and periodic acid-Schiff staining were performed to characterize microbial, metabolic, and intestinal barrier alterations. 6PPD-Q exposure induced gut dysbiosis characterized by enrichment of Lachnospiraceae and depletion of Akkermansiaceae and Bacteroidaceae accompanied by alterations in tryptophan and nicotinate-nicotinamide metabolism, including reduced fecal serotonin and indole-3-propionic acid levels. Furthermore, 6PPD-Q exposure impaired intestinal barrier integrity, as evidenced by altered expression of tight junction proteins (ZO-1 and claudin-1), reduced goblet cell density, and decreased MUC2 expression. Notably, antibiotic-mediated microbiota depletion attenuated 6PPD-Q-associated microbial, metabolic, and intestinal barrier alterations, suggesting that gut microbiota contribute to 6PPD-Q-associated intestinal responses. Collectively, this study provides mechanistic insights into microbiota-associated mechanisms underlying 6PPD-Q-induced intestinal barrier alterations and advances understanding of potential health implications of tire-derived emerging contaminants.Importance6PPD-Q, a primary oxidation product of the rubber antioxidant 6PPD, is an emerging environmental pollutant widely detected in human blood and urine. While its systemic toxicity has been recognized, the role of the gut microbiota in mediating 6PPD-Q-induced intestinal barrier disruption remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that gut microbiota plays an important modulatory role in 6PPD-Q-induced intestinal barrier impairment using antibiotic depletion and mouse models. Multi-omics analyses revealed that 6PPD-Q altered the composition of gut commensals and disrupted metabolic homeostasis, while functional validation confirmed its impact on epithelial integrity. Our findings identify the gut microbiota as a key modulator of 6PPD-Q toxicity and provide novel mechanistic insights into the environmental health risks of tire-derived pollutants.
authors: Zhang Z, Zhang X, Liu W, Wang L, Wei M, Zhang C, Wang M, Zhu J, Yao Y.

title: Siwu Paste alleviates blood deficiency syndrome induced by cyclophosphamide and acetylphenylhydrazine in association with gut microbiota remodeling and improved splenic metabolic homeostasis.
abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevanceSiwu Paste (SWP), derived from the classical blood-tonifying formula Siwu Decoction, has long been used for blood deficiency-related disorders and has a well-established traditional basis and ethnopharmacological value. Blood deficiency syndrome (BDS) is a common syndrome in traditional Chinese medicine and is associated with impaired blood generation and hematopoietic dysfunction. However, the modern pharmacological mechanisms underlying the beneficial effects of SWP on BDS remain incompletely understood.Aim of the studyThis study aims to evaluate the therapeutic effects of SWP on cyclophosphamide and acetylphenylhydrazine induced BDS and to investigate the potential mechanisms underlying its improvement of hematopoietic function.MethodsThe chemical constituents of SWP were characterized by ultra-performance liquid chromatography-quadrupole-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC-Q-TOF-MS), and its potential mechanisms were predicted using network pharmacology. An acetylphenylhydrazine (APH)/cyclophosphamide (CTX)-induced BDS rat model was used to evaluate SWP efficacy through flow cytometry, histology, Western blotting, qPCR, 16S rRNA sequencing, and untargeted metabolomics. Broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), and exogenous adenosine diphosphate (ADP) supplementation experiments were performed to evaluate the contribution of the gut microbiota and the involvement of splenic ADP-related metabolic alterations.ResultsSWP significantly improved hematopoietic dysfunction, alleviated systemic inflammation, restored intestinal barrier integrity, reversed the Treg/Th17 imbalance, and reduced apoptosis within the CD45+CD34+ bone marrow cell population in BDS rats. Multi-omics analysis revealed that SWP significantly regulated gut microbiota composition and metabolic profiles; specifically, SWP treatment was associated with a significant increase in the relative abundance of Allobaculum and an upward trend in Lactobacillus, accompanied by a significant reduction in the relative abundance of total ADP in spleen tissue compared with the BDS group. FMT experiments partially transferred the hematopoietic and immunomodulatory effects associated with SWP treatment. Broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment and exogenous ADP supplementation attenuated several SWP-induced improvements in bone-marrow hematopoietic function and Treg/Th17 balance, consistent with the involvement of the gut microbiota-splenic metabolic axis in the therapeutic effects of SWP.ConclusionSWP alleviates bone marrow hematopoietic dysfunction in BDS rats, with these effects accompanied by gut microbiota remodeling, restoration of intestinal barrier integrity, suppression of inflammation, and improved metabolic homeostasis. These findings provide modern pharmacological evidence supporting the traditional TCM concept of "treating the marrow via the gut" in blood deficiency-related disorders.
authors: Wan D, Feng X, Xu S, Du Q, Yue W, Zhang S.

title: Morinda Officinalis Oligosaccharides Alleviate Post-Stroke Depression-Like Behaviors Alongside Increased Gut Microbial Diversity and Butyrate Levels and Reduced Hippocampal Pla2g4a Expression.
abstract: Background and purposePost-stroke depression (PSD) represents a common and debilitating complication after cerebral ischemia, yet mechanism-based therapies remain an urgent unmet need. The microbiota-gut-brain axis has been implicated in PSD pathophysiology, but the precise molecular pathways are largely elusive. Morinda officinalis oligosaccharides (MOO), a clinically approved antidepressant in China, exhibit poor oral absorption, raising the possibility of a gut-dependent mechanism.Experimental approachMale C57BL/6J mice were subjected to transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) followed by 21 days of chronic restraint stress (CRS) to establish a PSD model. MOO (50 mg/kg/day) was administered via gavage from Day 7 to 27. Depression-like behaviors, 16S rRNA-based gut microbiota profiling, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) quantification, intestinal and blood-brain barrier integrity assessments, and hippocampal proteomics were performed. The transferability of MOO-associated fecal effects was assessed using a donor-controlled fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) design. The butyrate-Pla2g4a relationship was further examined by sodium butyrate supplementation and AAV-mediated hippocampal Pla2g4a overexpression.Key resultsMOO administration altered gut microbial composition, increased the abundance of probiotics and decreased the abundance of harmful bacteria, and was accompanied by increased fecal butyrate levels. The donor-controlled FMT experiment provided preliminary evidence that fecally transferable factors from MOO-treated PSD donors may contribute to behavioral improvements in PSD recipients. MOO and sodium butyrate treatment were associated with improved indices of intestinal and blood-brain barrier integrity. Hippocampal proteomics identified Pla2g4a, a phospholipase linked to neuroinflammation, as a candidate molecule related to the observed effects. Both MOO and sodium butyrate treatment were associated with reduced hippocampal Pla2g4a expression, and Pla2g4a expression was inversely correlated with butyrate levels. Hippocampal Pla2g4a overexpression attenuated the behavioral improvements associated with sodium butyrate treatment, supporting the functional involvement of Pla2g4a in the response to sodium butyrate.Conclusions and implicationsMOO treatment was associated with improved depression-like behaviors in PSD mice, accompanied by gut microbial alterations, increased fecal butyrate, improved barrier integrity, and reduced hippocampal Pla2g4a expression. FMT findings provided preliminary evidence that fecally transferable factors from MOO-treated donors may contribute to behavioral improvements, while Pla2g4a overexpression attenuated the behavioral effects of sodium butyrate. These findings highlight a potential association among MOO, gut-derived butyrate, barrier integrity, and hippocampal Pla2g4a in PSD.
authors: Ma H, Chen Y, Deng X, Fang X, Xiao W, Long Q, Du L, Du F, Chen H, Wang Y, Gao B, Qiao X.

title: Stacked enviromic-genomic models improve prediction of genotype performance in new environments.
abstract: Genotype-by-environment interaction is a major challenge for breeding programs, limiting the predictive ability of genomic selection in untested environments. We propose a Stacked Generalization framework that integrates linear mixed models (factor analytic and genomic best linear unbiased prediction), enviromic reaction norms, and machine learning (Extreme Gradient Boosting) to predict phenotypic plasticity. The framework was evaluated on large multi-environment trials of maize and rice, under scenarios that simulate new environments and seasons. The genetic covariance structures differed between crops, requiring a factor analytic model of order k = 6 for continental maize and order k = 2 for the local rice network. Across all scenarios, the Stacking ensemble improved on the genomic baseline (M1), with gains in predictive ability from 10% (r=0.45 vs. 0.41 for M1) to 27.5% (r=0.51 vs. 0.40), and reduced the root mean squared error by 30% to 43% relative to the Enviromic Reaction Norm (M2) when ensembles were selected to minimize error. These gains relied on careful feature engineering. Latent variables from genomic and environmental dimensionality reduction (principal component analysis and PaCMAP) and their interactions were the most important features for the machine learning models, and the first genomic PaCMAP component ranked first for both crops. These results indicate that non-linear dimensionality reduction is a promising tool for genomic and enviromic prediction. By combining the stability of mixed models with the flexibility of machine learning, the framework improves robustness, reduces dependence on any single model, and enhances prediction in new environments, supporting cultivation zone expansion and recommending superior genotypes.
authors: Antonio de Godoy Filho M, Araújo MDS, Chagas JTB, Pinheiro JB.
