title: Top2All: Benchmarking sparse-to-transcriptome reconstruction from high-expression profiles across sex- and sex-steroid-defined conditions
abstract: Transcriptome-wide profiling at single-cell resolution is limited by sparse detection of gene expression, raising the question of how much transcriptomic information can be recovered from a small set of highly expressed genes. We developed Top2All, a Mouse-Geneformer-based framework for reconstructing transcriptome-wide expression from sample-specific sparse inputs. Using 24 cell-number-normalized RNA-seq profiles of mouse adrenal zona fasciculata cells across eight experimental conditions defined by sex and sex-steroid milieu, we evaluated condition-aware and no-condition models under replicate-wise out-of-fold and leave-one-condition-out validation. Top2All achieved near-unity sample-wise correlation with measured expression, but similarly high correlations were obtained using simple reference profiles, whereas gene-wise evaluation revealed substantially greater differences among methods. Explicit condition information did not consistently improve reconstruction, indicating that sex- and sex-steroid-associated condition information was already strongly encoded in the sparse expression profiles. Nearest-neighbor retrieval provided a stronger baseline than learned reconstruction, and input-depth analysis showed that increasing the number of input genes did not monotonically improve performance. These findings show that a relatively small set of highly expressed genes contains substantial information about transcriptomic state, while accurate reconstruction of gene-specific biological variation remains challenging. Sparse-to-transcriptome models should therefore be evaluated using gene-wise metrics, strong reference baselines, and tests of generalization beyond conditions represented during training.
authors: Nishio Y, Yamashita T, Baba T.

title: From microbial dysbiosis to immune evasion: evidence and emerging mechanisms of gut microbiota-mediated modulation of PD-1/PD-L1 efficacy in genitourinary malignancies
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis have transformed the treatment landscape for genitourinary malignancies, yet primary and acquired resistance remains a substantial clinical obstacle. The gut microbiome has emerged as a critical determinant of immunotherapy efficacy, with dysbiosis driving immune evasion through disruption of metabolite-mediated signaling, impairment of intestinal barrier function, and systemic immunosuppression. This review synthesizes current mechanistic understanding of how gut microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan catabolites, and bile acids, modulate PD-1/PD-L1 expression via epigenetic reprogramming, aryl hydrocarbon receptor activation, and T cell functional modulation. Specific bacterial taxa such as Akkermansia muciniphila and Blautia coccoides enhance antitumor immunity through distinct molecular pathways, while the genitourinary microbiome exerts local immunomodulatory effects. Clinical evidence supporting microbiome-based candidate biomarkers associated with ICIs outcomes and emerging therapeutic strategies including fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics, and dietary interventions are critically evaluated. This review distinguishes direct genitourinary-specific evidence from cross-cancer mechanistic evidence and provides a unified framework for understanding the microbiome-immunity axis and its translational potential in genitourinary oncology.

title: Cistanche deserticola exosome-like nanoparticles alleviate constipation through PINK1-dependent mitophagy and gut microbiota remodeling
abstract: IntroductionConstipation is a prevalent gastrointestinal disorder with limited long-term treatment options. This study investigates the therapeutic potential and mechanisms of Cistanche deserticola exosome-like nanoparticles (CELNs) in alleviating constipation, focusing on mitochondrial quality control and gut microbiota regulation.MethodsCELNs were isolated and characterized using ultracentrifugation, transmission electron microscopy, and nanoparticle tracking analysis. Using a loperamide-induced mouse model, constipation parameters, histopathology, inflammation, and gut microbiota were assessed after CELNs treatment. The role of PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1) was investigated with knockout mice, and mechanisms were analyzed via molecular and sequencing approaches.ResultsCELNs treatment significantly improved defecation, moisture content, and intestinal transit in constipated mice, reduced colonic inflammation, and restored gut morphology. Transcriptomic analysis revealed CELNs enriched pathways related to mitophagy and apoptosis. Crucially, CELNs activated PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, enhanced mitochondrial function, and inhibited apoptosis of interstitial cells of Cajal. These benefits were abolished in PINK1−/− mice. Furthermore, CELNs reversed constipation-associated gut microbiota dysbiosis, specifically enriching genera like Alistipes and Bacteroides. This microbial restoration was also PINK1-dependent.DiscussionIn summary, this study demonstrates that CELNs effectively alleviate constipation through a dual-pathway mechanism centered on PINK1. CELNs activate PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy to clear damaged mitochondria, thereby restoring energy homeostasis and suppressing ICC apoptosis. Simultaneously, CELNs remodel the gut microbiota in a PINK1-dependent manner, which may reinforce mitophagy activation. These findings elucidate a novel exosome-PINK1-mitophagy axis essential for restoring intestinal motility and highlight CELNs as a promising multi-target therapeutic strategy for functional gastrointestinal disorders.

title: Therapeutic effects of a potential probiotic product (Ogi-Pro) on gut microbiota and diarrhea alleviation: a preliminary in vivo evaluation in a murine model
abstract: BackgroundProbiotics have shown promise in improving gut health and alleviating diarrheal diseases; however, evidence supporting non-dairy probiotic formulations remains limited. This study evaluated the safety, gastrointestinal persistence, immunomodulatory activity, and anti-diarrheal efficacy of Ogi-Pro, a cereal-based probiotic formulation containing indigenous Lactiplantibacillus pentosus 15ST2 and Lacticaseibacillus casei KN3, in a castor oil-induced murine model of acute diarrhoea.MethodsSwiss albino mice received Ogi-Pro (1 × 109 CFU/mouse/day) by oral gavage for 14 days before induction of diarrhoea. Safety was assessed through general health observations, bacterial translocation, and histopathology. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated by fecal bacterial enumeration, diarrhoea frequency, intestinal histology, and cytokine expression using RT-qPCR and ELISA.ResultsOgi-Pro was well tolerated, with no evidence of bacterial translocation or treatment-related toxicity. Probiotic administration increased intestinal lactobacilli while suppressing coliform populations and reduced diarrhoea severity to a level comparable with the commercial probiotic control. Total lactobacilli count (TLC) in both groups were higher than total coliform counts (TCC) by 3 log cfu/mL, only the standard control group showed competitive growth between TLC and TCC. Histopathological examination showed preservation of intestinal architecture with only mild inflammatory changes as compared to the standard group. The expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10, in the treatment group was significantly (p < 0.05) elevated; while modulating IL-8 and TNF-α responses, indicating an immunomodulatory effect associated with improved intestinal homeostasis.ConclusionThese findings demonstrated that Ogi-Pro is a safe cereal-based probiotic formulation with promising anti-diarrheal and immunomodulatory properties in a murine model. The study supported the potential of traditional fermented cereal foods as non-dairy probiotic delivery systems while highlighting the need for mechanistic investigations and well-designed human clinical trials to establish clinical efficacy.

title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo models
abstract:
by Theresa M. Pauli, Theresa von Heyl, Beate Rieblinger, Sabrina Teresa Schleibinger, Wei Liang, Antonia Schmauser, Mithuoshni Arullmoli, Paul Derrer, Anika Eckstein, Sirradu Jagana, Camila Gatti Corrêa, Krzysztof Flisikowski, Tatiana Flisikowska, Benjamin Schusser

Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human–animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo. Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro, ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.

title: NON-NUCLEOSIDE REVERSE TRANSCRIPTASE INHIBITORS BLOCK THE INCORPORATION OF VIRAL GLYCOPROTEINS INTO HIV-1 VIRIONS
abstract: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) are a key component of antiretroviral therapy that block reverse transcription in newly infected cells. NNRTIs have also been reported to induce premature activation of the HIV-1 protease in virus-producing cells, an activity that has been optimized in a class of NNRTIs known as targeted activators of cell kill (TACK). In this study, we used the TACK compound Pyr01 to investigate how NNRTI-induced premature protease activation affects virion composition and infectivity. We found that Pyr01 treatment markedly reduces the incorporation of the HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycoprotein into virus particles in an Env cytoplasmic tail-independent manner. Pyr01 treatment also disrupts the virion incorporation of foreign viral glycoproteins and causes a substantial loss of the viral enzymes from virions. Virions produced from NNRTI-treated cells exhibit reduced membrane order. The defect in viral glycoprotein incorporation requires an active protease, implicating premature protease-mediated disruption of the Gag lattice and resulting changes in membrane properties as the primary mechanism underlying these effects. These findings reveal that NNRTI-induced premature protease activation during virus assembly fundamentally changes the protein composition and membrane order of HIV-1 virions to markedly reduce particle infectivity. These results have implications for the use of TACK compounds therapeutically and provide basic insights into the properties of the viral membrane that promote viral glycoprotein incorporation.
authors: Waheed, A. A., Ibrahim, H., Raghunath, G., Vijayan, R., Melikyan, G. B., Freed, E. O.

title: Sphingolipid Hydroxylation Governs Fungal Pathogenicity and Drug Susceptibility: Scs7 as a Druggable Target in Candida albicans
abstract: Sphingolipids are essential structural components of the fungal plasma membrane and key signaling hubs that orchestrate pathogenicity. While both fungi and mammals perform sphingolipid hydroxylation, they rely on evolutionarily divergent enzymatic systems, establishing a biochemical divergence exploitable for selective targeting. Here, through a screening of sphingolipid metabolic genes, we identify the sphingolipid -hydroxylase Scs7 as a central regulator of membrane homeostasis, virulence, and caspofungin susceptibility in Candida albicans. Genetic ablation of SCS7 depletes hydroxylated sphingolipids, disrupts memberane organization, and compromises cell wall integrity, which collectively impair hyphal morphogenesis, biofilm formation, and stress tolerance through blockade of the cAMP-PKA signaling axis. In a murine cutaneous infection model, SCS7 deletion markedly attenuates fungal burden, hyperinflammation, and epidermal barrier disruption, underscoring its non-redundant role in host-pathogen interaction. Leveraging the fungus-specific architecture of Scs7, we performed virtual screening and identified resveratrol as a natural Scs7 inhibitor. Resveratrol recapitulates the lipidomic and phenotypic defects of SCS7 deletion and synergizes with caspofungin to enhance fungal killing. Our study establishes sphingolipid -hydroxylation as a master determinant of fungal membrane fitness and validates Scs7 as a promising, fungus-specific antifungal target with dual anti-virulence and chemosensitizing activities.
authors: Mo, S., Chen, X., Yu, B., Peng, J., Zhan, M., Zhao, Q., Deng, Z., Zeng, L., Huang, X., Duan, J.

title: Evolutionarily distinct dengue virus type 2 with a unique type-specific neutralization determinant
abstract: Dengue viruses 1-4 (DENV1-4) mostly circulate in endemic cycles involving humans and Aedes mosquitoes. However, rare dengue outbreaks originate from non-human primates. These spillovers are caused by sylvatic virus genotypes that are closely related to endemic strains of the same serotype, but some are caused by strains that fall between the four canonical serotypes on phylogenetic trees. It is not clear whether these genotypic differences are reflected in corresponding antigenic differences. Here, we characterized the antigenic features of QML-22, a divergent strain most closely related to DENV2. On an antigenic map, QML-22 clustered with other globally representative DENV2 strains. QML-22 was not as well neutralized by antisera raised against endemic DENV2 and was better neutralized by antisera from DENV1, 3, and 4 infections than other strains of DENV2. QML-22 had a cluster of distinct amino acid residues in domain I of the envelope (E) protein, with only scattered point mutations elsewhere in the envelope. A potently neutralizing anti-DENV2 antibody that targets this site in domain I of the E protein, 3F9, had >1000-fold lower neutralization of QML-22 than other endemic DENV2 strains, whereas other cross-reactive and DENV2-specific antibodies neutralized QML-22 and endemic strains to similar titers. When antisera from non-human primates infected with QML-22 or DENV2 reference strain S16803 were depleted with the heterologous virions, homologous neutralization was unaffected but heterologous neutralization was reduced, suggesting homologous neutralization was due to distinct epitopes. Evolutionary analyses showed the 3F9 epitope was under relaxed selection pressure compared to other neutralizing epitopes and that QML-22 had unique amino acids in this epitope relative to the likely common ancestor of all DENV2. These findings provide insight into the antigenic diversification of DENV and the possible evolution of new serotypes.

title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of the endangered northern dragonhead sap beetle, Thymogethes norvegicus (Easton, 1959)
abstract: The northern dragonhead sap beetle (Thymogethes norvegicus) is believed to be endemic to Norway and is classified as endangered. Its life cycle is closely tied to the host plant northern dragonhead (Dracocephalum ruyschiana), itself classified as vulnerable in Norway. Here, we present a chromosome-level genome assembly of a male T. norvegicus. The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes, hap1 and hap2, of 1,142 and 1,109 Mb, with 96.3% and 96.8% scaffolded into chromosomes, respectively. Hap1 contains 8 autosomes and the X chromosome, while hap2 contains 8 autosomes. Assembly quality was high, with conserved single-copy ortholog completeness scores of 96.6% and 90.7% and combined k-mer completeness of 98.1%. A total of 13,484 and 12,550 protein-coding genes were annotated in hap1 and hap2, respectively. This assembly provides a valuable genomic resource for the conservation of this endangered endemic species totally dependent on the vulnerable plant, the northern dragonhead.
authors: Strand, M. A., Toerresen, O. K., Skage, M., Ferrari, G., Tooming-Klunderud, A., Elven, H., Jakobsen, K. S.

title: Prevalent Integration of both Xenotropic and Ecotropic Murine Leukemia Virus in the Human Genome of Xenografts
abstract: Humanized mouse models are widely used in medical research to represent human conditions (1, 2), but their fidelity could be compromised by mouse-originated infections. However, their susceptibility to mouse pathogens are rarely questioned (3). Here we screened 1,619 publicly available genomic sequencing runs from patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models for the integration of murine leukemia virus (MLV), a rodent retrovirus exists in the mouse genome as an endogenous retrovirus (4), within the human genome. We discovered substantial enrichment of human-MLV chimeric DNA in approximately 25% of them. Analyzing the human-MLV junctions, we found about 90% of them bearing the unmistakable hallmarks of retroviral integration, including the canonical MLV boundaries and the distinctive 4-bp target site duplications (5, 6). It was also assumed that mouse strains without the highly infectious Bxv1 provirus are safe from MLV contamination in xenografts (7, 8). However, we found many PDX models derived from Bxv1- strains, including the widely used NSG strain, are also contaminated by the supposedly rodent-specific ecotropic MLV (E-MLV). We further confirmed a complete E-MLV integrated into the human genome by both HiFi and sanger sequencing. Our discovery raises concerns that mouse-to-human retroviral transmission and integration is more common and less restrictive than previously appreciated. They support examination of MLV integration as a feature of humanized mouse models with implications on the fidelity of these models in recapitulating human cells and tissues. Our discovery also has underscored the importance of comprehensively inactivation of porcine endogenous retroviruses for the clinical application of xenotransplatation (9, 10).
authors: Zhuo, X., Basri, N. L., Saintilnord, W. N., Xing, X., Wang, T.

title: Avian reovirus triggered ferroptosis, modulated lipid metabolism, and induced lipid droplet formation in infected cells, which was mediated in part by the p10/FAST protein
abstract: In this study, we evaluated how avian reovirus (ARV) affected lipid metabolism and lipid droplets (LDs) in cell culture. ARV infection of chicken LMH cells significantly increased the size and number of LDs, however, LDs did not co-localize with virus factories, and neither overexpression by treatment with fatty acids (FAs), nor inhibition by treatment with TOFA or DGAT inhibitors significantly affected ARV replication. Lipidomic analysis revealed that following infection, total cellular lipid content increased approximately 25-fold, phosphatidylcholine (PC) content increased from 23.5 to 57.9%, and the polyunsaturated FA:monounsaturated FA ratio (PUFA:MUFA) decreased in membrane phospholipids but increased in triglycerides. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that there was also a reduction in the expression of genes involved in PUFA synthesis. As membrane PUFAs are susceptible to peroxidation, we investigated whether ARV induced ferroptosis. Consistent with this, ARV led to an increase in oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation that was partially iron dependent, and we found evidence that ferroptosis was proviral. Moreover, as ARV is known to form syncytia, we hypothesized that our observations were also the result of plasma membrane remodeling. Consistent with this, cells transfected with the ARV fusogenic p10/FAST protein formed syncytia, had a significantly upregulated number of LDs, and displayed hallmarks of ferroptosis. Taken together, we hypothesize that ARV induces syncytium formation and ferroptosis to facilitate viral spread to neighboring cells, but to prevent premature cell death due to these processes, lipid metabolism is modulated by infection, leading to an increase in LDs.
authors: Liu, M., Kehlbeck, D., Egana-Labrin, S., Brodrick, A., Sun, L., Jones, J., Sunny, N., Broadbent, A. J.

title: Hepadnavirus tropism determined by diversified NTCP functionality in Feline species
abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) exhibits a narrow host range, largely determined by sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptides (NTCP), a hepatic bile acid transporter acting as the HBV receptor. NTCP among animals appears to have evolved following trade-off mutations to lose its viral receptor activity while preserving its transporter function. Here, through profiling of the NTCP homologs from 23 mammalian species, we uncover unexpected functional heterogeneity of feline NTCPs. NTCPs derived from cat, tiger, and leopard supported viral preS1 binding and HBV infection, whereas lion-NTCP was deficient for preS1 binding and, notably, exhibited markedly reduced bile acid transport. Cat-NTCP was further demonstrated to have viral receptor function by productive infection in primary cat hepatocytes. Experimental mutagenesis identified double substitution at positions 191 and 268 as key determinants: introducing lion-type substitutions into cat-NTCP (G191R and T268A) abolished preS1 binding, whereas reciprocal substitutions in lion-NTCP restored receptor function. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that lion-NTCP adopts conformation in which a transmembrane helix bending enlarges the whole bile acid tunnel and disrupts preS1 compatibility. Such differences also determined host susceptibility to another feline-infected domestic cat HBV. These findings reveal diversified NTCP functionality with evolutionary plasticity that acquires resistance to hepadnavirus infection at the expense of physiological transporter function.
authors: Mifune, J., Ekimoto, T., Takeuchi, J. S., Kobayashi, C., Kurata, M., Shionoya, K., Kawano, M. X., Saito, A., Sureau, C., Ikeguchi, M., Watashi, K.

title: Desiccation stress enhances virulence potential of group B Streptococcus
abstract: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus, GBS) asymptomatically inhabits the gastrointestinal and female reproductive tracts but can also cause invasive diseases in susceptible individuals. Despite its clinical importance, relatively little is known about its ability to survive outside the host and whether environmental persistence contributes to transmission and infection. Here we investigate the GBS survival under nutrient starvation and desiccation, characterizing phenotypic and genomic adaptations associated with environmental persistence. GBS remained viable for 30 days during starvation at room temperature and for more than 80 days under desiccated conditions, with GBS grown to stationary-phase bacteria exhibiting greater survival than actively growing bacteria. Survival under desiccation was conserved among several clinically relevant GBS serotypes. Following rehydration desiccated GBS exhibited enhanced biofilm formation compared to control non-desiccated strains. Whole-genome sequencing identified mutations in genes involved in capsule biosynthesis, cell-envelope homeostasis, nutrient transport, and carbohydrate metabolism, suggesting that multiple adaptive pathways may contribute to environmental persistence. Importantly, desiccated GBS retained the capacity to colonize the vaginal mucosa and displayed increased invasion of reproductive tissues in a murine vaginal colonization model. In a systemic infection model, desiccated GBS exhibited enhanced virulence compared to control non-desiccated GBS, demonstrating that environmental survival does not diminish pathogenic potential. This environmental persistence may represent an underappreciated factor contributing to GBS transmission and the epidemiology of late-onset neonatal disease.
authors: Jafar, T., da Conceicao Mendonca, J., Boland, N., Burcham, L. R.

title: A ribosome-dependent small-ORF switch controls flagellar gene expression and virulence
abstract: RNA structures are active regulators of bacterial translation. Here, we identified a naturally occurring translation-enhancing small open reading frame (tesORF) that controls the expression of the flagellar operon fliFGHIJK in Salmonella enterica and other motile Enterobacterales. Nucleotide-resolution ribosome profiling revealed this previously unannotated 54-nucleotide ORF immediately upstream of fliF. Genetic, transcriptomic, and biochemical analyses support a model in which tesORF translation counteracts an inhibitory RNA structure, exposing the fliF ribosome-binding site and promoting translation initiation independently of the encoded peptide sequence. Disruption of tesORF translation reduced expression of the downstream operon and impaired motility and virulence-associated phenotypes in Escherichia coli, Salmonella, and Yersinia. Together, our findings reveal how translation of a conserved small ORF regulates an entire flagellar operon through RNA structural remodelling, with consequences expending to the wider flagellar regulon, linking RNA structural dynamics to bacterial motility and virulence.
authors: Lastovka, F., Bryant, O. J., Meggers, D., Alexeeva, E., Knorr, M., Narberhaus, F., Chung, B. Y.

title: Peptide Sequence Determines the Efficacy of Single-Dose AAV-Vectorized GLP-1R Agonists in Diet-Induced Obese Mice
abstract: Background:  Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists such as semaglutide produce substantial weight loss and glycemic improvement, but their long-term efficacy depends on sustained adherence to chronic dosing. Adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapy could, in principle, provide durable GLP-1R agonist (GLP-1RA) exposure from a single administration, but the degree of peptide engineering required for a vectorized GLP-1RA transgene to be efficacious in vivo is unknown. Methods: We generated four self-complementary AAV (scAAV) constructs encoding: native human GLP-1(7-36) (GLP-1), a DPP-IV-resistant Gly8-GLP-1(7-36) variant (Gly8), Exendin-4 (Ex4), or an Exendin-4 human IgG4 Fc fusion protein (Ex4-Fc). All four constructs were validated to secrete functional GLP-1R agonists in vitro using a conditioned-media potency assay. Subsequently, these constructs were packaged into PHP.eB capsids and administered as a single intravenous dose (5x1012 vg/kg) to diet-induced obese (DIO) mice alongside a vehicle control. Body weight, body composition, food intake, fasting plasma insulin, and oral glucose tolerance were assessed over a 3-week period. At the end of the study, tissues were harvested for assessments of plasma/liver lipids, tissue transgene transcript and peptide levels. Results: HEK293 cells transfected with the four AAV constructs all secreted active peptides/proteins as assessed by a cell-based GLP-1R activation assay, although the effective concentration of the GLP-1 constructs in the media spanned nearly four orders of magnitude 72 hours after transfection. In diet-induced obese (DIO) mice, Ex4 and Ex4-Fc vectors, but not GLP-1 or Gly8 vectors, produced significant reductions in body weight of up to 22.6% of starting body weight out to 21 days after a single dose. In addition, reductions in food intake, fat mass, and fasting insulin relative to vehicle were also observed for Ex4 and Ex4-Fc. Furthermore, Ex4-Fc improved oral glucose tolerance while reducing plasma cholesterol and liver triglycerides relative to vehicle. Although transcript levels did not differ appreciably among the four constructs in either brain or liver, measurable peptide product in plasma and brain lysate tracked the rank order of the in vitro supernatant screen, with GLP-1 and Gly8 groups indistinguishable from endogenous background. Conclusions: PHP.eB scAAV Ex4 and Ex4-Fc showed robust efficacy on multiple metabolic endpoints including weight loss and glucose tolerance. In contrast, vectorized GLP-1 and Gly8 showed no in vivo efficacy despite comparable levels of viral transcript in the brain and the liver. Vectorized GLP-1 and Gly8 also performed poorly compared to exendin-4-based constructs in vitro, suggesting that conditioned-media potency screening is a valid early filter for construct selection in vectorized-peptide AAV development. Engineering peptides to improve translation and secretion efficiency, in addition to circulating plasma stability, could further optimize vectorized GLP-1RA therapeutics.
authors: Lee D, Bokvist K, Nachtrab G, Mezo A, Brust T, Trefts E, Brusilovsky J, Suk J, Luczak V, Edwards L, Benedetto B, Onyia J, Woldbye D.

title: A Novel Immunosuppressive Effector Functions as a Bio-Adjuvant to Enhance the Activity of Bacillus Thuringiensis and Chemical Insecticides.
abstract: Host innate immunity is a major barrier to microbial infection and often limits the efficacy of biological and chemical pest-control agents. While microbial immunosuppressive effectors have been described, whether quorum-sensing systems coordinate virulence and immune suppression during host infection remains largely unknown. We demonstrated that the PlcR-PapR quorum-sensing system acts as a master regulator that promotes both processes (virulence and immune suppression) to enhance Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) pathogenicity. During infection, PlcR-PapR signaling induces production of the heptapeptide PapR7, which activates expression of patatin-like protein PisP, a previously uncharacterized and widely conserved protein. PisP suppresses host immunity by inhibiting nuclear translocation of the transcription factor DAF-16, thereby attenuating the expression of antimicrobial defense genes. Consistent with this mechanism, Bt strains overexpressing pisP display enhanced virulence against both nematodes and insect hosts. Importantly, exogenous PisP markedly potentiates the activity of Bt Cry5Ba toxin and several commercial chemical insecticides, enabling effective pest control at reduced doses. Together, these findings reveal a quorum-sensing-controlled mechanism that links virulence regulation to immune suppression during Bt infection and identify PisP as a conserved Bt-encoded immunosuppressive effector with strong potential as a bio-adjuvant for improving the efficacy and sustainability of biological and chemical pest-management strategies.
authors: Liu Z, Chen F, Wan L, Chen L, Zhang B, Li F, Luo H, Li L, Bravo A, Soberón M, Dai D, Zheng J, Sun M, Wang K, Peng D.

title: A Homozygous FOXA1 Variant Links Choreoathetosis, Bronchiectasis, and Anorectal-Axial Anomalies.
abstract: BackgroundFOXA1 encodes a forkhead-box pioneer transcription factor involved in chromatin accessibility, epithelial and endodermal lineage specification, pulmonary epithelial differentiation, and selected neurodevelopmental programs. Although somatic FOXA1 alterations are well recognized in cancer, a germline FOXA1-associated Mendelian disorder has not been defined.ObjectivesTo delineate the clinical and genetic features of a syndromic neuropulmonary phenotype associated with a homozygous FOXA1 variant.MethodsWe evaluated three affected individuals from an extended consanguineous Turkish family with childhood-onset action-induced hyperkinetic/choreoathetoid movement disorder, bronchiectatic lung disease, anorectal abnormalities, axial skeletal defects, and neurobehavioral features. Whole-exome sequencing with copy-number variant analysis, homozygosity mapping, and segregation analysis were performed.ResultsExome-based analysis did not identify diagnostic variants in known disease genes relevant to the combined neurological, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and skeletal phenotype. Homozygosity mapping identified a 16.8-Mb shared homozygous interval on chromosome 14 encompassing FOXA1. All three affected individuals carried the same homozygous FOXA1 c.623G>C, p.(Arg208Pro) variant, which segregated with the phenotype under an autosomal recessive model. The variant affects a conserved residue within the DNA-binding forkhead domain and was absent in the homozygous state from population databases. The clinical pattern partially overlaps with NKX2-1-related brain-lung disease but appears distinct, with preserved thyroid function and prominent bronchiectatic airway, anorectal, and axial skeletal involvement.ConclusionThese findings support FOXA1 as a plausible candidate disease gene for an emerging autosomal recessive syndromic neuropulmonary disorder with anorectal and axial skeletal involvement. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
authors: Üçtepe E, Hangül M, Uçar HK, Koç AS, Özkaya M, Dağdelen EÇ, Esen FN, Topçu V, Yeşilyurt A.

title: Transcription factor CaMYB73 mediates greenhouse whitefly-induced suppression of pepper defences.
abstract: BackgroundAlthough the herbivore manipulation of plant defences has been extensively studied, the molecular mechanisms by which the greenhouse whitefly Trialeurodes vaporariorum suppresses induced resistance in pepper and alters host-selection behaviour remain largely unclear. Here, we integrated behavioural, molecular, and biochemical analyses to elucidate how this pest manipulates pepper defence responses.ResultsIn host-choice assays, whiteflies preferred to settle and oviposit on previously infested pepper plants rather than uninfested controls. Consistent with this behavioural preference, greenhouse whitefly infestation significantly down-regulated key genes involved in phenylpropanoid metabolism, particularly those associated with flavonoid pathways, and significantly reduced the accumulation of total phenolics and flavonoids. Using yeast one-hybrid, electrophoretic mobility shift, and dual-luciferase reporter assays, we identified the R2R3-MYB transcription factor CaMYB73 as a negative regulator of CaPAL expression, which encodes the rate-limiting enzyme in phenylpropanoid metabolism. Mechanistically, CaMYB73 directly binds to a specific MYB-binding cis-element in the CaPAL promoter and represses CaPAL expression. Whitefly infestation strongly induced CaMYB73 expression, enabling the pest to attenuate phenylpropanoid defences through CaMYB73-mediated repression of CaPAL. Virus-induced silencing of CaMYB73 attenuated this suppression, restored the accumulation of total phenolics and flavonoids on whitefly attack, and significantly reduced whitefly settlement and oviposition.ConclusionThese findings reveal a novel mechanism by which greenhouse whiteflies exploit the CaMYB73-CaPAL regulatory module to compromise phenylpropanoid-mediated defences, thereby increasing host suitability for subsequent whitefly colonisation. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
authors: Guo H, Yang S, Hu J, Li C, Chang X, Jiao X.

title: Subcutaneous abscessation: An atypical presentation of Rhodococcus equi infection in a group of foals.
abstract: BackgroundIntegumentary manifestations of Rhodococcus equi infection in foals are infrequently reported in the literature. Subcutaneous abscessation as the primary clinical presentation in temporally clustered cases of foal rhodococcosis in an equine farm has not, to the authors' knowledge, been previously described.ObjectivesTo describe an outbreak of R. equi infection where foals presented with subcutaneous abscessation as the primary clinical sign.Study designClinical case series.Clinical summaryThree Thoroughbred foals aged 6-11 weeks developed subcutaneous abscesses over a 3-week period in July 2024, out of a cohort of 11 foals. Thoracic ultrasound examination was performed on all foals on the farm, and 6/11 (54%) had evidence of subclinical pneumonia. No foals other than the three cases with subcutaneous abscesses were clinically affected. Purulent aspirates from abscesses in two foals were subjected to microbiological diagnosis and yielded a pure culture of R. equi. Two of the three clinically affected foals received 4 weeks of systemic antimicrobial treatment, and all abscesses resolved. Whole-genome sequencing of one isolate demonstrated near identity to a previous UK isolate associated with pulmonary rhodococcosis, and did not reveal genetic features that could explain the atypical presentation.Main limitationsFinancial constraints on the farm precluded microbiological confirmation of diagnosis in the third foal. Sequencing of a single isolate precluded assessment of strain relatedness within the outbreak.ConclusionsR. equi infection should be considered in foals presenting with subcutaneous abscesses, even in the absence of overt respiratory signs. Exposure-related factors likely contributed to this presentation, and the possibility of a transcutaneous route of entry should be considered.
authors: Mellin J, Val-Calvo J, Floyd E, Scortti M, Vázquez-Boland JA, Cullen E.

title: Diffusion integrity testing of small-area sterilizing-grade membrane filters in single-use assemblies.
abstract: Sterile filtration represents the final critical step in biomanufacturing, where a sterilizing-grade membrane filter removes microbial contamination from the drug product - making filter integrity verification essential. While bubble point and gas-liquid diffusion tests are established non-destructive methods for hydrophilic membranes, diffusion testing offers high sensitivity to small defects and operates at lower test pressures. However, applying diffusion testing to small-area filters integrated into closed single-use assemblies remains challenging because pressure changes measured by automated integrity testers can arise not only from membrane diffusion, but also from assembly-related effects such as gas-permeable tubing, upstream volume and thermal equilibration. For low-area devices, these background contributions can become comparable to or greater than the membrane signal, reducing test sensitivity and complicating interpretation. This work presents a practical method for implementing diffusion-based integrity testing of small-format sterilizing-grade filters in final sealed single-use assemblies. The approach quantifies assembly-specific background contribution and incorporates it into an adjusted diffusion specification, allowing membrane-specific diffusion to be resolved without altering the assembled system. By accounting for system-derived measurement noise, the method enables reliable end-user integrity assessment of closed assemblies that cannot be reconfigured to reduce upstream volume or replace high-permeability tubing materials.
authors: Alembath A, Hersey J.

title: Multi-omics analyses of HFpEF progression and regression reveals multi-organ-specific metabolic dysregulation and impaired inflammation resolution.
abstract: BackgroundHeart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a complex cardiometabolic syndrome with limited effective therapies. Given its heterogeneity, whether withdrawal of cardiometabolic stress reverses HFpEF-associated inflammatory, metabolic, and molecular remodeling remains unclear.ObjectivesTo characterize multi-organ metabolic, molecular, and bioactive-lipid remodeling in an obesity-hypertension HFpEF model and determine the extent of recovery during an 8-week combined high-fat diet withdrawal and L-NAME cessation protocol using parallel multi-omics profiling.MethodsHFpEF was induced in C57BL/6 mice using a high-fat diet plus nitric oxide synthase inhibition(H + L). A regression cohort(R-H + L) underwent simultaneous return to standard chow and L-NAME cessation for 8 weeks. Multi-omics profiling included targeted and untargeted lipidomics, cardiac transcriptomics, metabolomics, fecal microbiome, and plasma short-chain fatty acid analyses, with detailed assessment of the left ventricle.ResultsH + L mice developed an obesity-hypertension HFpEF phenotype characterized by predominant diastolic dysfunction, concentric remodeling, hypertension, and increased fat mass. The combined regression of H + L protocol attenuated these phenotypic abnormalities but did not restore all measures to control levels. H + L was associated with multi-organ remodeling marked by altered arachidonic acid-derived oxylipid pathways, depletion of triacylglycerols and phospholipids, and enrichment of diacylglycerols and lysophospholipids, consistent with altered resolution-related lipid signaling. Cardiac transcriptomics revealed changes in immune, circadian, vascular, and mitochondrial gene programs, whereas metabolomics revealed altered energy, arginine, and redox metabolism. H + L was also associated with reduced microbial diversity and altered short-chain fatty acids, particularly acetate and propionate. Within the 8-week recovery window, partial reprogramming occurred, but differences remained in lipid signaling, metabolic stress responses, and microbiome-associated measures.ConclusionsThe HFD/L-NAME model is accompanied by extensive multi-organ metabolic and molecular remodeling. Combined withdrawal of HFD/L-NAME attenuates the HFpEF phenotype however did not fully normalize molecular profiles within the 8-week recovery period. Persistent lipid-remodeling and metabolic dysregulation may represent potential therapeutic targets thus warrants pathway specific investigation.
authors: Kain V, Upadhyay G, Suraksha K, Li S, Sundaraswamy PM, Jayaprakash J, Gowda D, Chainani N, Krishna N, Ghobrial M, Fouad A, Hui SP, Mishra SP, Hall N, Tan Z, Soto NH, Liu R, Jain S, Gowda SGB, Yadav H, Halade GV.

title: Multi-omics analysis reveals new mechanistic insights underlying the osteoanabolic effects of short chain fructooligosaccharide.
abstract: Despite evidence that short chain fructooligosaccharide (FOS) improves bone mass and intestinal mineral absorption, the mechanism driving these effects remains uncertain. This study investigated how FOS modulates molecular and cellular pathways in bone through alterations in the gut microbiota and metabolome. Eight-week-old C57BL/6 female mice were fed a control or FOS-supplemented diet (10%) for 4 weeks. Bone histomorphometry, femur and bone marrow transcriptomics, cecal content 16S rRNA sequencing, and serum untargeted metabolomics were performed. Mice fed the FOS diet exhibited greater femoral trabecular bone volume and cortical bone thickness and area. FOS increased trabecular and cortical bone formation (i.e., periosteal and endocortical surface), and enhanced mineralization on the trabecular and endocortical surfaces. These changes coincided with increased osteoblasts and osteocytes, while osteoclasts were unchanged. Transcriptomics on the flushed femur revealed enrichment of pathways involving calcium ion homeostasis, PPAR signaling and adipogenesis, while in the bone marrow pathways associated with T-cell modulation and extracellular matrix organization were enriched. FOS altered the gut microbiota, increasing the abundance of taxa associated with fermentation and aromatic compound degradation, and increased serum metabolites (e.g., indole, mevalonate, polyphenol, and fatty acid intermediates). These findings reveal new insights into gut microbial and serum metabolite shifts induced with short-term FOS supplementation accompanying a rapid increase in osteocytes as well as bone formation and mineralization.
authors: Adedigba P, Grez-Capdeville M, Knotts TA, Peng G, Cooper B, O'Connell TM, Prideaux M, Lucas EA, Smith BJ.

title: CD154 Blockade Improves Polyfunctionality of T Cells Specific for a Murine Homolog of Epstein-Barr Virus.
abstract: Anti-CD154 is a promising therapeutic for solid organ transplantation with ongoing clinical trials, but its impact on the immune response to EBV is unknown. Here, B6 animals were infected with a murine homolog of EBV (MHV68) and treated with anti-CD154 costimulation blockade. Results indicate that the ratio of virus-specific CD8+ T cells to MHV68-infected cells was not significantly reduced following in vivo anti-CD154. Interestingly, frequencies of multi-cytokine producing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were increased following treatment with anti-CD154 compared to either CTLA4-Ig or tacrolimus. This increased polyfunctionality was mechanistically underpinned by an increase in the frequency of CD8+ T cells expressing the memory/stem-like transcription factors TCF-1 and Eomes in the anti-CD154 group compared to CTLA-4Ig, tacrolimus, or untreated controls. Moreover, anti-CD154-treated mice exhibited smaller spleens with a significant decrease in the number of MHV68-YFP+ germinal center B cells compared to untreated mice. These data demonstrate that CD154 blockade does not significantly decrease the ratio of virus-specific T cells to infected cells and increases the quality of MHV68-specific CD8+ T cells in a mouse model. Overall, these findings suggest that an anti-CD154 costimulation blockade-based immunosuppression regimen may be beneficial regarding its ability to preserve protective anti-viral immunity during transplantation.
journal: American journal of transplantation : official journal of the American Society of Transplantation and the American Society of Transplant Surgeons
authors: Alexander KL, Ford ML.

title: A CONSTANS-like transcriptional co-activator couples ethylene signaling to jasmonate biosynthesis and is targeted by a fungal effector.
abstract: Ethylene and jasmonate synergistically regulate immunity against necrotrophic pathogens, but how ethylene signaling promotes jasmonate biosynthesis remains unclear. Here, we show that the apple CONSTANS-like (COL) protein MdCOL4 functions as a transcriptional co-activator that couples ethylene signaling to jasmonate biosynthesis during disease resistance. The ethylene-responsive transcription factor MdERF098 directly activates the jasmonate biosynthetic genes MdOPR2 and MdOPR3. MdCOL4 physically associates with MdERF098 and enhances its DNA-binding activity, thereby promoting MdOPR2/3 transcription, jasmonate accumulation, and resistance to apple Valsa canker, a destructive trunk disease caused by Valsa mali, a necrotrophic fungal pathogen. We further identify a fungal effector from V. mali, Vm11039, that translocates into the host nucleus and binds MdCOL4 with higher affinity than MdERF098, competitively disrupting the MdCOL4-MdERF098 complex. This interference attenuates jasmonate biosynthesis and promotes pathogen infection. Together, our findings uncover a transcriptional co-activation mechanism that couples ethylene signaling to jasmonate biosynthesis and establish transcriptional co-activator complexes as vulnerable regulatory hubs targeted by pathogen effectors to suppress hormone-mediated immunity, thereby providing a potential target for engineering resistance against necrotrophic diseases.
authors: Meng Y, Yuan W, Li J, Li L, Xu L, Huang L.

title: Functional diversification within the CYP81E subfamily involved in isoflavone biosynthesis in Glycyrrhiza glabra.
abstract: Leguminous plants produce structurally diverse isoflavonoids, whose biological activities are influenced by regioselective hydroxylation pattern catalyzed by cytochrome P450 enzymes. Members of the CYP81E subfamily function primarily as isoflavone 2'-hydroxylases and, less frequently, isoflavone 3'-hydroxylases (I3'H), but their functional diversity remains unclear. We performed a comprehensive functional characterization of CYP81E-like genes in Glycyrrhiza glabra. Transcriptome analysis and heterologous expression in Saccharomyces cerevisiae identified CYP81E106 as an I3'H active toward multiple isoflavones, whereas CYP81E105 oxidized prenylated isoflavones and other flavonoids. MS/MS analysis indicated oxidation within the prenyl moiety rather than the flavonoid backbone. Comparative in vitro enzyme and yeast bioconversion assays revealed differences in substrate preference and conversion efficiency, highlighting the influence of cellular context on catalytic performance. These findings demonstrate the functional diversification within the G. glabra CYP81E subfamily, expanding its catalytic repertoire beyond canonical B-ring hydroxylation to prenyl-group oxidation and providing insights into isoflavonoid structural diversification in legumes.
authors: Kubomura A, Nakamura K, Yasuno N, Munakata R, Arai T, Kobayashi O, Mamiya K, Wasano N, Yazaki K, Ohara K.

title: Characterizing clinical heterogeneity by whole-genome sequencing of 591 patients with Hemoglobin H disease.
abstract: Hemoglobin H (Hb H) disease, caused by the functional loss in three of the four α-globin genes, exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity that is not fully explained by primary α-globin genotypes. The genetic modifiers contributing to this phenotypic variability remain incompletely understood. Here, we present the largest whole-genome sequencing (WGS) study of Hb H disease to date, including 591 well-characterized patients and 1,246 ancestry matched controls from Southern China. Case-control GWAS identified two independent variants at the α-globin cluster, rs199594877 and rs34583256, with higher alternative allele frequencies in patients than in controls; rs199594877 was particularly enriched in patients with Hb Constant Spring (HCS). Case-only GWAS across 50 quantitative clinical traits identified six loci associated with hematological and iron metabolism phenotypes. At the HBS1L-MYB (HMIP) locus, rs11759553 was associated with increased Hb Bart's (γ4) levels (P = 3.66 × 10⁻¹⁴). In contrast to its beneficial effects in β-hemoglobinopathies, this association suggests that HMIP variation may have distinct biological consequences in Hb H disease. Together, these findings expand our understanding of the genetic architecture of phenotypic heterogeneity in Hb H disease and establish a comprehensive phenome-genome resource for α-thalassemia, providing candidate loci for further functional and clinical investigation.

title: Host infection selects for sRNA variants that drive bacterial social cheating.
abstract: Single-nucleotide mutations in regulatory small RNAs (sRNAs) represent a largely unexplored route to social cheating during bacterial infection. Here we show that arcZ, encoding a conserved Hfq-dependent sRNA in the plant pathogen Dickeya solani, undergoes recurrent single-nucleotide mutations during potato tuber infection. Five distinct arcZ alleles define a graded series of ArcZ functional impairment in which antifungal and protease activities are progressively reduced while virulence is compromised only in a subset of alleles. All five variants gain a fitness advantage exclusively during coinfection with wild-type arcZ1 cells. This advantage is strongest when variants are rare and declines as cheater frequency increases, ultimately correlating with reduced total bacterial productivity, the canonical signature of social cheating and a tragedy of the commons. No fitness benefit is detected in vitro. Transcriptomic profiling of five arcZ variants identifies a conserved core of 186 downregulated genes enriched in secreted and diffusible functions. Systematic genetic dissection, supported by quantitative proteomics, establishes BudAB-dependent limitation of tissue acidification as the dominant cooperative public good exploited during infection. Wild-type arcZ1 cells divert pyruvate flux toward acetoin via the BudAB pathway, maintaining a less acidic tissue environment that sustains disease progression; arcZ variants, which show reduced expression of this pathway, benefit from the less acidic environment maintained by wild-type cells without contributing to it. These results establish pleiotropic regulatory sRNAs as a previously unrecognized class of mutational targets for the emergence of social cheaters during host infection.
authors: Dubois Q, Brual T, Sprenger M, Utzinger V, Mercier R, Cigna J, Rodrigue A, Papenfort K, Attaiech L, Gueguen E.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated PD-L1 knockout reshapes temporal transcriptomic responses to PRRSV infection in porcine alveolar macrophages.
abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) suppresses innate antiviral immunity in porcine alveolar macrophages, and the PD-1/PD-L1 axis is thought to contribute to this immune dysregulation. This study investigated how PD-L1 knockout (KO) alters the host transcriptional response to PRRSV infection compared to wild-type (WT) immortalized porcine alveolar macrophages (iPAMs). PD-L1 KO iPAMs were generated by CRISPR/Cas9 targeting exon 2 of porcine CD274 locus, and knockout was confirmed in clone #35. After PRRSV-2 infection, KO#35 cells exhibited approximately 5-fold reduced viral RNA accumulation at 48 h post-infection compared with WT cells. Time-course RNA sequencing at 0, 6, and 48 h post-infection was then performed to characterize the transcriptional consequences of PD-L1 KO during acute PRRSV-2 infection. PD-L1 KO iPAMs exhibited downregulation of immune checkpoint and exhaustion-related genes (LAG3, PDCD1, TIGIT, TOX family) and NF-κB inhibitors (SOCS4, NFKBIA), alongside upregulation of antigen presentation (MHC I/II genes like SLA-2, SLA-5, B2M, SLA-DMA, SLA-DMB, HLA-DRA) and co-stimulatory molecules (CD80, CD86, CD40). Cytokine profiling indicated a reprogrammed response favoring antiviral signaling, including sustained elevation of CXCL10/11, ISGs (MX1/2, ISG15, IFIT1-3), and select interleukins (IL15, IL6), while suppressing pro-inflammatory TNF and CXCL8 across time points. Pathway enrichment analysis revealed significant enrichment of the cytokine-receptor interaction pathway. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) further identified a key co-expression module containing 1,763 DEGs that was associated with innate immune activation. Moreover, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis detected PXDN as a key hub gene connected to the PI3K-Akt signaling and natural killer cytotoxicity pathways. These findings provide transcriptomic insight into the association between PD-L1 deficiency and altered macrophage transcriptional responses to PRRSV infection in an in-vitro iPAM model and provide a basis for future mechanistic investigation of PD-L1 in PRRSV pathogenesis.
authors: Sheet S, Kim HJ, Kim WI, Kim S, Lee P, Cho A, Kim D.

title: Temperature-dependent Pathogenicity and Host-associated Dominance Patterns of Colletotrichum spp. Causing Apple Bitter Rot in Korea.
abstract: Apple bitter rot has intensified across Korea, yet the ecological processes shaping Colletotrichum populations in orchard landscapes remain unclear. We surveyed symptomatic apple fruits from four major production provinces during 2020-2023 and characterized 783 Colletotrichum isolates using ITS-GAPDH screening, morphology, and multilocus phylogenetics of 24 representative isolates. Multilocus analysis confirmed seven Colletotrichum species, while ITS-GAPDH sequence groups corresponding to C. siamense and C. fructicola predominated among apple-derived isolates and five additional groups occurred at lower frequencies. Surveys of orchard-adjacent black locust and walnut yielded 40 isolates from each host and revealed distinct host-associated patterns. Temperature assays were designed to evaluate fungal performance under favorable and supra-optimal conditions (20-40°C), rather than the complete thermal response curve. Responses were generally high at 20-30°C and declined at higher temperatures. Upper thermal 50% reduction temperatures (UT50) ranged from 29.66 to 36.58°C depending on species and trait, and no measurable mycelial growth occurred at 40°C. Fruit inoculation assays showed isolate- and cultivar-dependent variation in aggressiveness, with lesion development greatest at 20-30°C, reduced at 35°C, and absent at 40°C. Cross-infection tests with 27 isolates demonstrated bidirectional pathogenicity among apple, walnut, and black locust. Together, these results link host-associated community structure with species- and trait-specific upper thermal responses and highlight the potential contribution of surrounding woody hosts to bitter rot epidemiology.
authors: Kim J, Kim S, Kim H, Kang D, Choi HW, Hong SB, Jeon Y.

title: Dsg2 truncation causes a severe intestinal epithelial barrier breakdown and alters microbiome and immune response.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) including Crohn's disease (CD) are characterized by impaired intestinal epithelial barrier (IEB) function. Alterations in the desmosomal cadherin desmoglein 2 (Dsg2) have been linked to loss of IEB and intestinal inflammation in IBD. We investigated the pathogenic impact of a cytoplasmatic-truncating mutation in the desmosomal cadherin desmoglein 2 gene (DSG2) in an IBD patient. Genetic analysis of a CD patient revealed a likely pathogenic DSG2 mutation leading to a truncated protein lacking part of the intracellular domain. Generation of an enterocyte-specific mouse model to recapitulate the human mutation resulted in a lethal intestinal barrier defect which was evident in homozygous but not in heterozygous mice. In vitro, barrier defects correlated with changes in Dsg2 mobility and upregulation of pore-forming tight junction protein claudin-2. Organoids derived from heterozygous Dsg2 truncated mice exhibited increased epithelial susceptibility to proinflammatory cytokines. Bulk RNAseq followed by gene ontology analysis in homozygous mice revealed a skewed IL17/IL23 response overlapping with transcriptional changes in patients with CD. Furthermore, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed alterations in microbiome composition in animals that carried the Dsg2 truncation. In summary, a patient-derived mutation in the DSG2 gene causing cytoplasmic truncation in homozygous state induced a lethal intestinal barrier breakdown in mice paralleled by altered gut microbiota and intestinal immune response.

title: Lactobacillus-Based Therapy for Ulcerative Colitis: From Strain Heterogeneity and TCM-Mediated Modulation to Engineered Delivery and Precision Translation.
abstract: Although Lactobacillus sensu lato is widely considered a promising microecological intervention for ulcerative colitis, its clinical translation remains severely constrained by strain-specific efficacy, host microenvironmental dependency, and the risk of opportunistic systemic translocation across a compromised intestinal barrier. The historical assumption of genus-level therapeutic uniformity is increasingly inadequate, as even closely related strains can exhibit divergent or occasionally adverse clinical outcomes. This functional heterogeneity is rooted in distinct genomic architectures encoding carbohydrate-active enzymes, bile salt hydrolases, and surface adhesins, which collectively govern the metabolic and colonization behavior of live biotherapeutics. Furthermore, selectively expanding target strains within a competitive, exclusionary gut microbiota represents a major clinical bottleneck. To address these barriers, this review synthesizes the common protective networks of lactobacilli and the taxonomic heterogeneity that defines their efficacy and safety boundaries. We review how traditional Chinese medicine constituents may selectively modulate target strains through the potential substrate-enzyme compatibility and summarize advanced bioengineering platforms, including postbiotics (inactivated-cell preparations) and cell-free effector components, and responsive biomaterials, designed to protect these metabolic pathways. By deconstructing the molecular logic of functional divergence and pharmacological targeting, we argue that a promising direction for precision microecological therapy may involve moving beyond broad taxonomic classification toward quantitative matching of strain-specific functional and enzymatic fingerprints. This paradigm shift demands rigorous causal validation, context-responsive delivery systems, and a regulatory transition toward quality control standards incorporating biochemical effector activity units alongside, rather than instead of, viable-cell enumeration.
authors: Zhang T, Lei H, Zhao X, Wang H, Chen X, Zhai Y, Xu Z, Yin X, Li J, Liu H, Mamattohti M, Zhao C, Wu J.

title: Single nucleotide polymorphisms in PDCD1 (PD-1), CD274 (PD-L1), and PDCD1LG2 (PD-L2): current evidence and clinical significance in cancer immunotherapy.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) have transformed cancer treatment, but durable benefit and immune-related adverse events (irAEs) remain difficult to predict. Germline single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in PDCD1, CD274, and PDCD1LG2 may influence checkpoint expression and immune-cell function. This narrative review integrates clinical association studies with available mechanistic evidence and evaluates effect estimates, endpoint definitions, replication, ancestry, and functional support. The leading candidates are PDCD1 rs7421861 for survival outcomes, PDCD1 rs10204525 for irAEs, CD274 rs822336 for response and survival, and CD274 rs822339 and rs1411262 for survival. However, most cohorts are small and retrospective, allele coding is not always harmonized, and genotype-by-treatment interaction analyses are uncommon. No variant has therefore been validated for routine clinical use. Future studies should use prespecified endpoints and genetic models, adjusted estimates with 95% confidence intervals, appropriate multiple-testing correction, standardized allele and genome-build reporting, and independent multi-ancestry validation. Prospective biomarker-stratified trials should determine whether these variants improve prediction beyond PD-L1 immunohistochemistry, tumor mutational burden, microsatellite instability or mismatch-repair status, and established clinical factors. Multicenter consortia and individual participant data meta-analyses will be required to establish whether these germline markers can contribute to treatment selection or toxicity monitoring.
authors: Dimitrakopoulos FI, Loukopoulou M, Kottorou A, Kalofonos H, Koutras A.

title: Bacterial extracellular vesicles as carriers of genetic and regulatory messages.
abstract: Although bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) are increasingly recognized as mediators of communication, the contribution of their nucleic acid cargo remains poorly understood. Providing an overview of BEV-nucleic acid content and their roles, this review first examines their true significance. In particular, it highlights why they should not be treated as bulk cargo, given that DNA and RNA contents exhibit various sub-vesicular localizations that may define their ecological roles. We propose that this heterogeneity allows viewing BEVs as distinct subpopulations. Furthermore, recent studies increasingly propose the involvement of DNA associated with BEVs in horizontal gene transfer between bacteria and that of vesicular small RNA (sRNA) during host-bacteria interactions. Overall, this review offers insights into considering BEVs in an ecological context based on notable recent studies.
authors: Kubler L, Vial L, Nazaret F.

title: A conserved CusR-dependent regulatory pathway couples copper homeostasis with oxidative stress resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae.
abstract: Host-derived copper toxicity is a central antimicrobial strategy that restricts bacterial survival during infection, yet how pathogens integrate copper detoxification with oxidative stress resistance remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify the response regulator CusR as a pivotal coordinator of copper homeostasis and oxidative stress defense in Klebsiella pneumoniae. Loss of cusR results in profound defects in copper tolerance, marked intracellular copper accumulation, and hypersensitivity to hydrogen peroxide, accompanied by elevated intracellular reactive oxygen species. Mechanistically, CusR directly activates the cusCFBA copper efflux operon through promoter binding, whereas regulation of the copA transporter occurs independently of CusR. Importantly, a conserved aspartate residue (D56) within CusR is essential for its activity; both plasmid-based and chromosomal substitution of this residue abolish copper efflux regulation, disrupt copper homeostasis, and exacerbate oxidative stress susceptibility. Comparative sequence analysis further demonstrates that this residue is highly conserved across diverse bacterial species, underscoring its evolutionary importance in copper-responsive signaling. Collectively, our findings reveal a conserved Asp-dependent CusR-CusCFBA regulatory axis that couples copper detoxification to oxidative stress resistance, enabling bacterial adaptation to host-imposed copper stress.IMPORTANCECopper intoxication is an important host-mediated antimicrobial strategy that challenges bacterial pathogens during infection. Although copper resistance systems have been extensively studied, how bacteria coordinate copper detoxification with protection against oxidative stress remains poorly understood. In this study, we identify the response regulator CusR as a key factor linking copper homeostasis and oxidative stress resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae. We demonstrate that CusR directly controls the cusCFBA copper efflux system through promoter binding and that a conserved aspartate residue is essential for this regulatory function. Loss of CusR disrupts copper balance, increases reactive oxygen species accumulation, and reduces bacterial resistance to oxidative stress. These findings reveal a conserved regulatory mechanism that integrates metal stress adaptation with oxidative stress defense, providing new insights into how bacterial pathogens survive under host-imposed environmental pressures.
authors: Yang X, Cui X, Li M, Yao R, Li B, Peng W.

title: Pathogenic mechanisms of Echovirus 18-induced encephalitis in a novel hFcRn transgenic mouse model.
abstract: Echovirus 18 (E18) poses an escalating neurological threat in children, with its complex pathogenesis impeded by the absence of robust animal models for comprehensive mechanistic investigation. This study establishes an E18-induced viral encephalitis (VE) model in 7-day-old human neonatal Fc receptor (hFcRn) transgenic mice. After intracranial inoculation with 4.0  ×  106  PFU of E18, mice developed marked signs of infection, characterized by progressive weight loss, motor impairment, elevated viral loads in the brain, and histopathological evidence of VE, ultimately resulting in approximately 75% mortality. The E18-infected mouse brains were accompanied by lymphocytic and granulocytic infiltration, neuronal shrinkage, and focal hemorrhage, with magnetic resonance imaging revealing prominent signal abnormalities in the subarachnoid space and periventricular regions. Interestingly, although all cell types of the brain can serve as carriers of the virus at the single-cell level, E18 exhibits distinct cellular tropism by preferentially targeting astrocytes and microglia rather than neurons and neurofilaments. Additionally, E18 infection orchestrates a complex and adaptive immune response, with dynamic changes among astrocytic subtypes reflecting the evolution of this immune response. Overall, this study successfully establishes a disease model that enhances our understanding of E18-induced encephalitis and provides a valuable platform for evaluating therapeutic interventions and developing vaccines.IMPORTANCEE18 represents an important pathogen in infectious diseases, with potential neurological complications that warrant further investigation. However, due to ethical and technical limitations, its neuropathological mechanisms have long remained unexplored. This study presents a novel encephalitis model using 7-day-old hFcRnTg mice. The integration of MRI, histopathology, and multi-omics analysis elucidated the molecular mechanisms of viral neural invasion, offering critical insights into pediatric viral encephalitis and potential therapeutic strategies. This animal model provides a valuable platform for understanding E18-induced encephalitis mechanisms and evaluating potential therapeutics and vaccines.
authors: Li F, Huang J, Fu Y, Huang L, Zhang H, Wang Y, Jia L, Xie Z, Chen X.

title: BK virus-neutralizing antibodies converge on a shared site of vulnerability on VP1.
abstract: BK virus is a human polyomavirus that infects approximately 80% of adults and establishes lifelong latency. Although primary infection is typically asymptomatic, viral reactivation in kidney transplant recipients can cause BK virus-associated nephropathy, leading to graft dysfunction and rejection. Despite the clinical severity of viral reactivation, antiviral treatment options remain limited. Notably, high serum titers of BK virus-neutralizing antibodies are associated with reduced BK virus DNAemia in kidney transplant recipients, suggesting an important role for humoral immunity in controlling viral replication. Here, we curated a comprehensive database of human antibodies targeting the major capsid protein VP1 by integrating previously reported sequences with newly generated data. Sequence analysis revealed only limited convergence among these antibodies. Nevertheless, functional and biochemical characterization showed that most neutralizing antibodies compete for overlapping epitopes, indicating convergence on a common antigenic site within the receptor-binding cleft of VP1. Together, these findings define an immunodominant site of vulnerability on the BK virus capsid and provide a mechanistic basis for the rational design of vaccines and antibody-based therapies.ImportanceBK virus (BKV) reactivation is a common complication in kidney transplant recipients, yet no approved antivirals are currently available. The standard of care consists of reducing immunosuppressive therapy, which carries an inherent risk of graft rejection. Antibodies represent promising therapeutic agents for the prevention and treatment of viral infections, particularly when effective vaccines are unavailable. Elucidating the dominant mechanisms of antibody-mediated protection is crucial for guiding the design and optimization of antibody-based therapies. In this study, we identify novel potent neutralizing antibodies against BKV, compare them with previously reported monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), and demonstrate that they compete for binding. Our findings show that most neutralizing mAbs converge on the receptor-binding cleft of VP1, identifying this region as both a major site of vulnerability and a hotspot for immune-driven viral escape, with important implications for therapeutic design.
authors: Vinyals-Sales D, Foglierini M, Schelling R, Winiger RR, Burton I, Perez L.

title: An Indole-3-Acetic Acid-Amido Synthetase, GmGH3.2, Negatively Regulates Salt Tolerance in Soybean.
abstract: Soil salinization severely restricts soybean growth and productivity. Therefore, uncovering salt-tolerance genes and their regulatory mechanisms is critical for breeding salt-tolerant soybean varieties. In this study, a genome-wide association study (GWAS) was conducted across four environments, and 7 quantitative trait locus (QTLs) associated with salt-tolerance traits were identified. Furthermore, the candidate gene GmGH3.2 was cloned at qSTG2-1, which encodes an indole-3-acetic acid-amido synthetase. Functional analyses revealed that interfering with expression of GmGH3.2 in soybean hairy roots significantly enhanced salt tolerance, as evidenced by an increase in total root length, surface area, volume, and tip number. Conversely, the overexpression of GmGH3.2 markedly inhibited root growth under salt stress when compared with the control. Additionally, GmGH3.2 negatively regulates salt tolerance by influencing K+-Na+ homeostasis and the expression of six salt tolerance-associated genes (GmSOS1, GmNHX1, GmSALT3, GmAKT1, GmHKT1, and GmSKOR). Moreover, GmGH3.2 interacts with GmKH1 in the nucleus and may collaboratively participate in the regulation of salt tolerance. In summary, our findings establish GmGH3.2 as a negative regulator of salt tolerance in soybean, providing valuable theoretical insights and genetic resources for molecular breeding of salt-tolerant cultivars.
authors: Zhang J, Wang Y, Wang L, Yu Y, Fu N, Shen A, Guan X, Zhang D, Kan G, Huang F, Xu X, Yu D, Huang Z, Yang Y.

title: Protecting host mitochondria with vitamin B3 preserves bioenergetics and thermogenesis during antibiotic treatment
abstract: Antibiotics that target bacterial translation can also impair mitochondrial function because mitochondria retain bacterial-like ribosomes. As antibiotic resistance continues to increase and the use of several broad-spectrum antibiotics has been limited by their mitochondrial toxicity, there is a growing need to understand their off-target effects in host physiology, and to identify strategies that can mitigate antibiotic-induced mitochondrial dysfunction. We demonstrate that antibiotic chloramphenicol (CA) induces a dose-dependent reduction in mitochondrial respiration and mitochondrial thermogenesis in Drosophila S2 cells, human HEK293T cells and in developing Drosophila larvae. In vivo, CA exposure triggers female-biased aberrant innate immune activation of hosts carrying naturally occurring mitochondrial rRNA variants. Metabolomic profiling revealed alterations in vitamin B3 metabolism in Drosophila during and following CA exposure. Among the vitamin B3 vitamers examined, nicotinamide (NAM) exhibited the strongest protective effect, mitigating the CA-induced impairments in mitochondrial respiration and thermogenesis, as well as aberrant immune activation. We identify mitochondrial thermogenesis as a previously unrecognized target of antibiotic-induced mitochondrial perturbation and a sensitive marker of mitochondrial stress. Furthermore, we demonstrate that co-supplementation of CA with NAM mitigates antibiotic-induced mitochondrial toxicity through evolutionarily conserved mitochondrial pathways. Finally, we establish Drosophila as a powerful model for investigating antibiotic-induced mitochondrial dysfunction and for developing therapeutic strategies to protect host mitochondria during antibiotic treatment.

title: Genetic effects on serum and urine metabolites across ancestries and their links to disease
abstract: Genome-wide association studies of the metabolome have predominantly examined European-ancestry populations using a single biofluid, constraining both the discovery of metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs) and the resolution of causal variant finemapping. Here, we report a multi-ancestry genome-wide association study of 1,955 serum and urine metabolites in 4,431 European American and African American participants from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study. We identify 969 mQTLs for 553 metabolites, 30% unreported in studies of matched biofluid and ancestry, and replicate 91-99% of testable mQTLs in two independent cohorts. In the African American sample with balanced sample sizes, 36% of metabolites with mQTLs are serum-specific, 39% urine-specific, and 25% shared, demonstrating complementary genetic architecture. Only 23 of 632 candidate ancestry-specific mQTLs show heterogeneous effects beyond variant availability and power, yet allele frequency differences expose functional variants such as an SLC28A1 splice variant, virtually absent in Europeans, that increases urine uridine excretion, implicating impaired CNT1-mediated renal nucleoside reabsorption. Multi-ancestry finemapping improves credible set resolution, and colocalization with the Million Veteran Program phenome links the catalog to cardiometabolic, kidney and liver traits consistent with prioritized gene function. Integrating biofluids and ancestries enhances genetic discovery and mechanistic characterization of the human metabolome.

title: Bacterial-Mimetic Membranes Reveal Hopanoid-Associated Domain-Like Lateral Heterogeneity
abstract: Bacterial membranes are increasingly recognized as laterally heterogeneous assemblies whose local organization can regulate transport, stress adaptation, and interactions with membrane-active compounds. However, the physical principles by which bacterial lipid composition generates spatially distinct membrane environments remain poorly understood, partly because experimentally tractable models that reproducibly exhibit lateral segregation and permit quantitative characterization are limited. Here, we show that a multicomponent, hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membrane spontaneously self-organizes into laterally distinct physical environments that are consistently resolved in experiments and molecular simulations. Giant unilamellar vesicles prepared from a lipid mixture inspired by lipid classes found in hopanoid-producing bacteria, including Methylorubrum extorquens, exhibit stable micron-scale lateral segregation, which is independently reproduced in compositionally matched coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. The resulting membrane environments differ in composition, packing, order, mobility, and mechanical properties. Hopanoid-associated domain-like regions are more condensed, more ordered, and less mobile, whereas PE-rich non-domain regions remain more laterally expanded and exhibit faster lipid diffusion. At the global level, the bacterial-inspired membrane displays greater bending rigidity than a fluid phosphatidylcholine reference, while ATR-FTIR measurements independently support increased lipid-chain ordering and denser membrane packing. Together, these findings establish that hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membranes can spontaneously generate coexisting physical environments whose distinct local properties collectively determine global membrane behavior. The resulting experimental-computational framework provides a quantitative basis for investigating bacterial-like membrane heterogeneity and how local composition, dynamics, and mechanics govern responses to membrane-targeting perturbations.
authors: Rzycki M, Kucharski M, Szulc N, Drabik D.
