title: Unravelling the Temporal and Geographic Patterns of HIV-1 Cases in Libya: Demographic Trends and Spatial Clustering.
abstract: Abstract  Background  The epidemiology of HIV-1 in Libya has evolved substantially since the first major recognized outbreak in Benghazi during the 1990s. Although previous investigations have separately described the national geographic distribution of HIV infection and the molecular diversity of circulating HIV-1 strains, integrating these perspectives provides a broader framework for understanding the changing epidemic landscape. This study aimed to characterize the spatial and temporal distribution of reported HIV-1 infections in Libya and to examine the geographic distribution of major HIV-1 genetic subtypes. Methods  A retrospective nationwide analysis was conducted using routinely collected HIV surveillance records covering 1993–2017. A total of 8,015 newly diagnosed HIV cases with geographic information were included in the epidemiological analysis. Temporal changes in regional distribution and demographic characteristics were examined. Molecular findings were integrated from a previously characterized set of 159 HIV-1 strains obtained from 814 HIV-positive individuals across four Libyan regions between 1995 and 2010. HIV-1 subtypes were determined using molecular sequencing and phylogenetic analysis. Spatial patterns were interpreted by comparing regional case concentrations with the geographic distribution of characterized viral subtypes. Results  Among the 8,015 reported cases, 5,327 (66.5%) were male and 2,688 (33.5%) were female. Individuals aged 25–34 years represented the largest age group, with 2,965 cases (37.0%), followed by those aged 35–44 years, with 1,892 (23.6%). The geographic distribution changed markedly over the study period. The eastern region represented the major concentration during the earlier period, including 1,180 reported cases during 1998–2002, whereas the western region recorded 1,449 cases during 2010–2017. Central and southern regions also became increasingly represented during the later period. The molecular dataset comprised 117 (73.6%) subtype B strains, 29 (18.2%) CRF02_AG strains, and 13 (8.2%) subtype A strains. Subtype B was detected throughout the country and was particularly represented in the northern region; CRF02_AG was more frequently represented in the eastern region, whereas subtype A was observed particularly in western and southern areas. The combined epidemiological and molecular evidence indicates increasing geographic heterogeneity of HIV-1 across Libya over time. Conclusions  The Libyan HIV-1 epidemic demonstrates substantial spatial, temporal, demographic, and molecular heterogeneity. The epidemiological pattern evolved from an early concentration of reported infections in eastern Libya to a broader national distribution, while molecular surveillance demonstrated the circulation of multiple HIV-1 lineages with distinct regional patterns. These findings support the value of integrating molecular surveillance with national epidemiological and spatial monitoring
authors: Daw MA.

title: Advances in Microbial Production of L-Malic Acid.
abstract: L-Malic acid is an important organic acid widely used in food, pharmaceutical, and chemical industries. Compared with traditional chemical and enzymatic production methods, microbial fermentation offers a more sustainable route for producing optically pure L-malic acid from renewable resources. This chapter summarizes the properties, applications, production methods, biosynthetic pathways, strain improvement strategies, and downstream processing of L-malic acid. Special attention is given to Aspergillus niger, which is a promising host for L-malic acid production due to its strong organic acid secretion ability, robust metabolism, and good industrial tolerance. Recent strategies, including metabolic engineering, adaptive evolution, stress tolerance improvement, and utilization of low-cost substrates, are discussed to highlight future directions for efficient and economical L-malic acid production.
authors: Xu Q, Chen SY, Xu SS, Zhang C, Huang H.

title: The dual role of protein glycosylation in HBV infection: facilitating viral pathogenesis and shaping host defense.
abstract: Hepatitis B is the most prevalent chronic viral infection worldwide, posing a serious threat to global public health. Protein glycosylation, a critical post-translational modification, regulates diverse physiological processes. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is associated with altered glycosylation of both viral and host proteins, which influences viral entry, immune evasion and disease progression, while HBV infection remodels host glycosylation. Given the sensitivity of glycosylation patterns to pathological perturbations, it is particularly relevant to examine how HBV exploits host glycosylation machinery to facilitate viral persistence and pathogenesis. This review is organised around a dual-role framework: one arm covers the proviral functions of glycosylation (viral entry, envelope protein folding, processing, assembly and secretion, persistence, immune escape and disease progression), the other the host-protective functions of the same pathways (glycosylation-dependent restriction factors, glycan-dependent ER quality control and ERAD, cellular stress responses and immune regulation). This exploration provides insights into the glycan-dependent mechanisms underlying HBV infection and their implications for developing novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.
authors: Yang J, Sun Z, Li H, Zhao Y.

title: Doxycycline and Nitazoxanide as a Candidate Immunomodulatory Combination for the Early Management of Ebola Disease Caused by Bundibugyo Virus
abstract: As of 5 November 2026, Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo had produced 10,741 confirmed cases and 5,230 deaths, with close to two of every three deaths in an earlier WHO reporting interval occurring in communities rather than treatment centres. No vaccine or treatment is approved for this species, and the agents in trials are monoclonal antibodies and direct-acting antivirals. In 2021 I proposed reclassifying COVID-19, Ebola virus disease and Nipah virus infection as a novel acute onset immune dysrhythmia syndrome. Read through it, the pathology now described in Bundibugyo-infected macaques points to two arms: fatal animals showed a myeloid hyperinflammatory profile with raised interleukin-6 and myeloperoxidase, survivors transcripts of an intact T cell response. Basing on that convergence I propose doxycycline and nitazoxanide as an early immunomodulatory combination, each acting on a different arm. Doxycycline inhibits matrix metalloproteinases at exposures achievable in man, and nitazoxanide amplifies the RIG-I and PKR arm the virus suppresses. To be noted that none of this establishes efficacy in Bundibugyo disease. What it offers is a mechanism worth testing in two licensed, oral, inexpensive drugs on the shelf, with the host-directed concentration still unmeasured. I therefore ask for species-specific work: activity in relevant cells and in the macaque model, the unbound concentration-response relationship, and a two-by-two factorial evaluation, preclinical and clinical, powered for the interaction. I strongly believe the search for safe immunomodulators is the one most likely to end in a drug available on the day it is needed.
authors: Kelleni MT.

title: Polymorphic In Vitro Assembly of a Bacterial Microcompartment Shell Protein.
abstract: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are self-assembling protein nanocages involved in metabolic compartmentalization in bacteria. They consist of hexagonal and pentagonal protein subunits that tile the facets of polyhedral shells. BMCs can assemble a variety of morphologies, making them attractive platforms for engineering synthetic biomaterials and organizing catalysis. Here, a single 99-amino-acid hexameric shell protein from the BMC of Haliangium ochraceum is shown to self-assemble in vitro into a range of nanoscale and mesoscale architectures, including flat lattice sheets, nanorolls, single-walled nanotubes, and nanospheres. The assembly morphology can be controlled by modulating the ionic strength of the assembly buffer, which influences the anisotropic interactions between subunits. These structures represent model platforms for engineered synthetic nanoreactors and provide a framework for exploring the emergent physical, mechanical, and chemical properties of protein-based crystalline materials.

title: Sphingomyelin-cholesterol synergy facilitates conformational maturation of the cytolysin A pore.
abstract: Bacterial pore-forming toxins breach host barriers by converting water-soluble monomers into transmembrane pores extracellularly, among the most radical transitions in structural biology. We show that synergy between host sphingomyelin (SM) and cholesterol (CHOL) facilitates the conformational maturation of Cytolysin A (ClyA), lowering the energetic barrier to membrane insertion. Combining vesicle and suspended-lipid-bilayer assays, molecular dynamics simulations, cell permeabilization and biophysical measurements, we demonstrate that SM-CHOL synergy selectively lowers the barrier for unfolding the membrane-bound β-tongue motif-the critical step in ClyA maturation-generating a reactive molten-globule intermediate, and directs its refolding into the α-helical conformation required for pore formation. Conserved lysines K175 and K206 are the cationic anchors for this interaction; anchor mutants uncouple membrane binding from conformational maturation, distinguishing this specific lipid-mediated folding event from bulk membrane order. As assembly proceeds, the toxin reciprocally remodels the membrane and dismantles liquid-ordered domains, coupling folding to disruption of host lipid organization. These findings establish a paradigm of lipid-mediated conformational catalysis, revealing how pathogens might have co-evolved to exploit host lipid complexity to overcome membrane-insertion barriers.
authors: Sannigrahi A, Chakraborty D, Moral R, Rai VH, Kulshrestha A, Maity D, Challil MV, Ayappa KG, Paul S, Roy R.

title: Nipah virus in Asia: A persistent zoonotic threat.
abstract: We conducted a narrative review of the literature on Nipah virus (NiV) in Asia indexed in PubMed through August 31, 2026. NiV is a highly pathogenic zoonotic paramyxovirus with pandemic potential, causing recurrent outbreaks in South and Southeast Asia since 1998, with reported case-fatality rates of approximately 40-75%. Recent outbreaks in Bangladesh and India between January 2025 and June 2026 underscore the continued public health threat posed by this emerging pathogen. Two genetically and epidemiologically distinct strains exist: NiV-Malaysia (NiV-M) and NiV-Bangladesh (NiV-B). Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic infection to rapidly progressive encephalitis, sometimes accompanied by areflexia, segmental myoclonus, and brainstem dysfunction. Respiratory involvement, including acute respiratory distress syndrome, has been prominent in NiV-B outbreaks. Diagnosis relies on reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and serological testing; magnetic resonance imaging may reveal multiple brain lesions, predominantly involving the subcortical white matter. No licensed vaccines or specific antivirals exist. Treatment remains supportive. In vitro findings and studies in animal models have identified potential therapeutic candidates, including the monoclonal antibody m102.4 and remdesivir. However, evidence of efficacy in non-human primates does not establish clinical benefit in humans, and the effectiveness of these interventions in patients remains uncertain. Prevention strategies focus on reducing bat-human contact, behavior change interventions, and strict infection control in healthcare settings. The absence of licensed medical countermeasures and the potential for pandemic spread necessitate urgent acceleration of vaccine and antiviral programs alongside strengthened One Health approaches to prevent spillover events.
journal: Journal of microbiology, immunology, and infection = Wei mian yu gan ran za zhi
authors: Lai CC, Liu JW, Lee PI, Chang SY, Huang SE, Yang JY, Hsueh PR.

title: Targeting PLAGL2 in hepatocellular carcinoma and metabolic liver injury: molecular mechanisms and pharmacological opportunities.
abstract: PLAGL2 is a C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factor increasingly recognized as a potential pharmacological target in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and metabolic-inflammatory liver disease. Although PLAGL2 has traditionally been studied as an oncogenic regulator, recent evidence links it to therapeutically relevant adaptive programs in HCC, including the PLAGL2-EGFR-HIF-1/2α signaling loop, non-coding RNA-mediated PLAGL2/HIF-1α regulation, C-MET/STAT3-associated survival signaling, macrophage recruitment, extracellular matrix remodeling and resistance to targeted therapies. In parallel, hepatocyte-specific Plagl2 deficiency has been shown to alleviate metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) by limiting MYD88-licensed inflammasome activation, pyroptotic signaling and IL-1β-associated macrophage activation. These findings suggest that PLAGL2 may operate at the interface of hepatocyte stress, inflammatory remodeling and tumor adaptation. Recent development of PLAGL2-directed small molecules, including compounds that suppress PLAGL2 transcriptional activity or target its DNA-binding domain, further raises the possibility that this transcription factor is pharmacologically approachable. This review critically evaluates PLAGL2 as an emerging therapeutic candidate in liver disease, focusing on hypoxia-linked signaling, inflammasome activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, therapeutic resistance and early pharmacological targeting strategies. We also discuss the attractive but still unproven hypothesis that PLAGL2 contributes to the MASH-HCC continuum.
authors: Pastwińska J, Karwaciak I, Sałkowska A, Bachorz RA, Dastych J, Ratajewski M.

title: Title: Topoisomerase I Inhibition Serves as a Tumor Vaccine by Inducing the ERVs-dsRNA-Interferon Pathway.
abstract: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) can activate potent anti-tumor immunity, but its clinical translation remains challenging. We sought to identify clinically applicable strategies to induce endogenous dsRNA and enhance anti-tumor immune responses. Here, we integrated genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening data with the Therapeutic Target Database (TTD) and identified Topoisomerase I (TOP1) as a potential inducer of dsRNA. Mechanistically, we found that TOP1 was associated with suppression of endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) in an enzyme activity-dependent manner, and this was accompanied by "viral mimicry" through the induction of dsRNA. Pharmacological inhibition of TOP1 using Irinotecan (CPT-11) triggered dsRNA accumulation across cancer models, including patient-derived organoids (PDOs), activating the RIG-I/MDA5-MAVS pathway and antiviral interferon responses (Type I/III IFNs, ISGs). scRNA-seq revealed that CPT-11 remodeled the tumor microenvironment, promoting infiltration of dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and T cells. Combining CPT-11 with PD-1 blockade in "cold" tumors dramatically improved survival. CPT-11 also generated a potent in situ vaccine effect, establishing immunological memory that prevented tumor rechallenge. Moreover, tumor cells pretreated with CPT-11 in vitro were also able to exert a vaccine-like effect, inhibiting the growth of subsequently inoculated tumors. Collectively, our findings support the repurposing of TOP1 inhibitors such as CPT-11 to harness dsRNA-mediated immune activation for more effective cancer therapy.

title: The calcium signaling links to fungal pathogenicity by a dual-action regulator.
abstract: Candida albicans is a clinically important opportunistic fungal pathogen with a strong capacity to sense and adapt to fluctuating host microenvironments. Although transcription factor Crz1 is well established as a central regulator of calcium (Ca2+) homeostasis, accumulating evidence points to the involvement of additional factors. Through a large-scale genetic screen, we identified transcription factor Cas5 as a previously unrecognized regulator of Ca2+ homeostasis in C. albicans. Mechanistically, Cas5 directly represses the expression of protein kinase Tpk1, thereby influencing the dephosphorylation, nuclear localization, and downstream signaling activity of Crz1 to maintain Ca2+ balance. Furthermore, we show that calcineurin-dependent virulence requires Cas5 independently of Crz1, addressing a long-standing gap in understanding calcineurin-mediated pathogenicity. Collectively, our findings identify Cas5 as a dual-functional regulator coordinating Ca2+ homeostasis and pathogenicity in C. albicans, advancing our understanding of into its survival and virulence strategies within the host.
authors: Wang Y, Wu Y, Zhang L, Liu J, Liu S, Gao N, Huang X, Xue W, Dong Y, Huang J, Ying C, Zhong L, Xue X, Chen C.

title: Formononetin disrupts MRSA biofilm via potential SarA-associated regulatory modulation.
abstract: Biofilm formation is a crucial aspect of Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) pathogenesis and contributes to its resistance against conventional antibiotics. This study reports the identification of a bioactive molecule, formononetin, from Glycyrrhiza glabra L., that is effective against MRSA. Formononetin significantly inhibited biofilm formation, disrupted sessile biofilm, and reduced the hemolytic activity of MRSA in a dose-dependent manner. Formononetin also increased the survival rate of MRSA-infected G. mellonella larvae by decreasing the bacterial load and increasing melanization. The combination of formononetin with antibiotics, like oxacillin, ampicillin, and streptomycin, showed a fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) ≤ 0.5, which indicates a synergistic effect. Molecular docking studies showed formononetin can bind to the global regulator, SarA, with an estimated binding score of -6.176 kcal/mol. Further, the aspartate residue (D20) in SarA was identified as a binding site for formononetin. Microscale thermophoresis and electrophoretic mobility shift assay of the SarAD20A mutant showed reduced affinity towards formononetin without affecting its DNA-binding activity compared to its wild-type counterpart. Further, proteomic profiling of MRSA upon treatment with formononetin showed significant modulation of SarA and SarA-related pathways, such as scdA and agrC. Our findings suggest that formononetin holds promise as a natural agent for combating MRSA biofilm.
authors: Borah A, Jena JP, Vijay M, Okram A, M G, P N, Barbuddhe SB, Hegde NR, Rawool DB, Srivastava A.

title: SARS-CoV-2 variants and cardiovascular complications - Implications for surveillance and vaccination: A narrative review.
abstract: COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, is linked to both acute and lasting cardiovascular complications. This review synthesizes 165 studies from MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library to summarize cardiovascular outcomes, underlying mechanisms, and implications for variant surveillance and vaccination. Clinical evidence reveals increased risks of arrhythmias, ischemic and inflammatory heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular events, and thromboembolic disorders even after the acute phase, including in non-hospitalized patients. These risks are higher following more severe infections. Proposed mechanisms include direct viral injury, endothelial dysfunction, complement activation, dysregulated inflammation and coagulation, and disruption of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Experimental studies show spike mutations alter viral entry and antibody escape, though their impact on cardiovascular outcomes is still unclear. Vaccination is associated with fewer cardiovascular events and post-acute sequelae, despite offering incomplete protection. Ongoing genomic surveillance, vaccination efforts, and cardiovascular follow-up are crucial to inform preventive strategies and manage the long-term cardiovascular burden of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
authors: Nappi F.

title: Probiotic-mediated reduction of detectable cypermethrin residues in milk: Effects on oxidative stress, DNA damage, and blood biochemistry in rats.
abstract: The use of pesticides is vital for increasing agricultural production to meet global food demand and combat harmful insects. This study has investigated the impact of probiotics (bacteria and yeast) on cypermethrin pesticide residues in milk, both in vitro and in vivo. Heat processing reduced detectable residues by 19-22%, whereas fermentation with mixed starters [Lb. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, St. thermophilus, Lcb. casei, Lsb. reuteri and B. bifidum (ST4), and the same yoghurt starter plus S. boulardii (ST5)] reduced detectable parent cypermethrin by up to 98% under a high-exposure fortification of 10 ppm. Yoghurt prepared with ST4 and ST5 showed acceptable physicochemical properties and retained viable probiotic bacteria and yeast during 21-days of refrigerated storage. In vivo, liver enzymes (GOT, GPT, and ALP) increased in the unfermented 10 ppm milk group (T1) to 192, 43, and 450 IU/L, respectively, relative to the untreated control (TC). The DNA-damage marker 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) rose to 108.72 µmol/mL in T1 versus 86.66 µmol/mL in TC, whereas T2-T5 values were 87.35, 87.76, 71.59 and 75.17 µmol/mL. Antioxidant enzymes (SOD, GST-px, and CAT) increased in T4 and T5 and decreased in T1; relative liver and kidney weights increased only in T1. These findings show that the selected starter cultures can lower detectable parent cypermethrin and are associated with improved oxidative and biochemical markers in a controlled high-exposure model. They do not demonstrate metabolic detoxification: metabolites were not profiled, so conversion to toxic transformation products or simple cell-wall adsorption cannot be excluded. LOD and LOQ were not determined, so the lowest reported residuals (∼0.2 ppm) should be read as indicative rather than fully validated concentrations. The 10 ppm model far exceeds milk MRLs (typically 0.05-0.1 mg/kg), a pesticide-free yoghurt control and histopathology were not included, and source milk was not screened for aflatoxin M1 or other co-contaminants. Repeating the work at environmentally realistic levels, preferably in a multi-dose design, is required before any food-safety application is considered.
journal: Journal of environmental science and health. Part. B, Pesticides, food contaminants, and agricultural wastes
authors: Niamah AK, S Raheem W, Al-Dahmoshi HO, Murdas IA, Al-Sahlany STG, Verma DK, Patel AR.

title: Illumination of anguillid herpesvirus 1 transmission in European eels reveals the importance of host developmental stage and agonistic social interactions.
abstract: The European eel has a complex life cycle involving various developmental stages and migrations through marine and freshwater environments. It is critically endangered and therefore a flagship species for conservation efforts. The European eel is also an important fish species in aquaculture. One of the major pathogens contributing to the decline of the European eel is thought to be anguillid herpesvirus 1 (AngHV-1). In this study, we used in vivo bioluminescent imaging to study the ability of AngHV-1 to infect the various developmental stages of the European eel, and to investigate virus transmission between eels. Our results highlight that eels become sensitive to AngHV-1 infection only when they become yellow eels (a freshwater stage prior to maturity), with the gills and the periodontal mucosa acting as the first sites of replication after inoculation by immersion in virus-containing water. Also, multifocal cutaneous bioluminescent signals appeared in grouped eels, but not in isolated eels. These observations suggested that the virus might be transmitted through biting between fish. In support of this hypothesis, experiments based on single artificial bites occurring between infected eels and naïve eels led to the infection of all exposed subjects. The biological relevance of AngHV-1 transmission by biting was further supported by observation of the instability of virion infectivity in water and fish mucus. Our study thus challenges the current paradigm that fish viruses are transmitted mainly via water acting as an abiotic vector. It demonstrates that, as in air, so in water, social interactions matter.IMPORTANCEFish viruses have devastating effects on wildlife and severe economic impact on aquaculture. The current paradigm is that they are transmitted via water acting as an abiotic vector. Here, we used in vivo bioluminescent imaging to study the ability of anguillid herpesvirus 1 (AngHV-1) to infect different developmental stages of European eel and to investigate virus transmission between eels. The major findings were that (i) eels become sensitive to AngHV-1 infection only when they become yellow eels, with the gills and the periodontal mucosa acting as the first sites of replication after inoculation by immersion in virus-containing water; (ii) AngHV-1 is efficiently transmitted between fish through biting, thereby avoiding virion instability in water and mucus. Our study thus challenges the current paradigm that fish viruses are transmitted mainly via water acting as an abiotic and protective vector. It demonstrates that, as in air, so in water, social interactions matter.
authors: Delrez N, Zhang H, Denoël M, Ovidio M, Nzau Matondo B, Larbanoix L, Dotto-Maurel A, Davison AJ, Donohoe O, Vanderplasschen A.

title: Characterization of herpes B virus isolated from wild cynomolgus macaques and its pathogenic effects in captive hosts.
abstract: Despite the high seroprevalence of herpes B virus (BV) among wild macaques, it remains unclear why BV is rarely transmitted to humans who live alongside macaques in their natural habitats. We investigated disease progression, host immune responses, viral shedding, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry of tissues after BV injection in cynomolgus macaques. BV was isolated from a wild Thai cynomolgus macaque living in southern Thailand and intramuscularly injected into four captive macaques (two males and two females) housed at the Animal Biosafety Level 3 facility. Over 49 days, all macaques remained clinically healthy but showed enlarged lymph nodes. IgM was detected on 9 days post-infection (dpi) and peaked at 13 dpi, while IgG appeared on 11 dpi and peaked at 28 dpi. No viral DNA was detected in oral, urogenital, or rectal swabs throughout the 49 day study period. However, viral DNA was identified in the spleen, sublingual gland, and trigeminal ganglia. Histopathology revealed tissue damage in the spleen and trigeminal ganglion, with BV immunoreactivity in the spleen. Overall, BV injection induces localized lymphoid and immune responses without causing clinical symptoms or viral shedding in natural macaque hosts. This may help explain why natural macaque hosts remain healthy and why human BV infections associated with wild cynomolgus macaques have rarely been documented.IMPORTANCEHerpes B virus (BV) isolated from a wild cynomolgus macaque was inoculated into captive macaques in an experimental setting. BV infection triggers localized lymphoid and immune responses (IgM and IgG) without causing clinical symptoms or viral shedding. Viral DNA was detected in the spleen, sublingual gland, and trigeminal ganglia. These insights improve our understanding of how BV interacts with its natural macaque hosts and shed light on the rare transmission of BV from wild macaques to humans.

title: Genome characterization of cluster B4 mycobacteriophages LittleDigger and Renkei (Caudoviricetes).
abstract: Bacteriophages LittleDigger and Renkei were isolated from soil in Miami, FL, USA using Mycobacterium smegmatis mc² 155. Their genomes are 70,752 and 70,746 bp long, respectively, both encoding 98 predicted genes. They are assigned to the actinobacteriophage B4 cluster and revealed a siphoviral morphology by transmission electron microscopy.

title: The pks gene clusters modulate the pathogenicity of Klebsiella pneumoniae by impairing neutrophil extracellular traps.
abstract: The pks gene clusters, crucial virulence-associated gene clusters in Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae), have been verified to exacerbate disease severity in infected hosts. During the early stage of pks-positive K. pneumoniae infection, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are produced by neutrophils to capture and eliminate pathogens. However, neutrophils struggle to completely eliminate bacteria via NETs. To confirm the role of the pks gene clusters in infection, we performed a bacterial survival assay to assess neutrophil dysfunction. NET structural damage was confirmed via scanning electron microscopy observation and NET staining. The DNA breakage was verified by γH2AX staining and Western blot. In the mouse sepsis model, immunofluorescent staining and histological analysis were used to verify pathogenic changes induced by the pks gene clusters. Data were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test or the Kruskal-Wallis H test. Results showed that the pks gene clusters were associated with DNA damage. The pks gene clusters disrupted the mesh-like structure of NETs, which resulted in NET dysfunction. In vivo, pks-positive K. pneumoniae affected the bactericidal capacity of NETs. In the mouse model, pks-positive Klebsiella pneumoniae is more prone to inducing liver abscess formation. In conclusion, the pks gene clusters impair NET function, reducing NETs' ability to capture and kill bacteria, and increasing the risk of liver abscess formation.IMPORTANCEThis study elucidates the interplay between the pks gene clusters of Klebsiella pneumoniae and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). Our observations underscore the impact of the pks gene clusters on NETs' functionality, and we further investigate its implications on murine pathogenicity and virulence. These findings offer novel insights into the clinical management of Klebsiella pneumoniae infections.
authors: Luo C, Chen Y, Shi Y, Chen S, Lin Y, Yang B.

title: Molecularly imprinted polymer thin-film solid-phase microextraction for biomarkers of anaerobic metabolism of BTEX by microorganisms involved in bioremediation and in microbially influenced corrosion.
abstract: A molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP) composed of 2-vinylpyridine and 1-vinyl-3-ethylimidazolium acetate (FMs) imprinted with homophthalic acid (a pseudo-template (T)) was fabricated directly on a stainless-steel substrate for the selective adsorption of mono- and dicarboxylic acid metabolites of light aromatic components of petrogenic oil from complex aqueous samples. The analytical method features multiplexed sample processing, which yields high-throughput extraction and desorption (≥45 samples in 2.7 h or -1 and limits of quantitation (LOQs) of 0.1-0.5 ng mL-1 with excellent linearity (R2 > 0.998) over 2-3 orders of magnitude for monocarboxylic acids (e.g., 0.1-500 ng mL-1 for salicylic acid and 0.5-1000 ng mL-1 for o-, p-, and m-toluic acid) and for dicarboxylic metabolites (e.g., 0.5-500 ng mL-1 for phenylsuccinic acid and 0.1-500 ng mL-1 for benzylsuccinic acid). The accuracies from spiked samples ranged from 84.4 to 108% with a %RSD of 1.6-13% for seawater and from 83.6 to 114% with a %RSD of 1.3-10.5% for produced water.
authors: Nwachukwu TO, Akhoondi R, Bottaro CS.

title: Stratification of Gastric Cancer Based on Methylation Status of Enhancer Regions and Effects on Transcriptional Regulation.
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus-positive gastric cancer (EBV(+) GC) shows extensive DNA hypermethylation in gene promoter regions. DNA methylation induced by EBV infection contributes to carcinogenesis through tumor suppressor gene inactivation. Whereas aberrant DNA methylation in enhancer regions might reportedly contribute to carcinogenesis, its impact has not been fully elucidated. Therefore, we here performed DNA methylome analysis on clinical samples, including GC and normal gastric mucosa, using the Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip array to evaluate the epigenome in the enhancer regions. We stratified GC cases into three subclusters using hierarchical clustering analysis based on the methylation status of enhancer regions; EBV(+) GC samples were classified into the most extensively methylated subcluster. We identified genes with promoters unmethylated but enhancers aberrantly methylated in EBV(+) GC. Such methylated genes included Inositol polyphosphate-5-phosphatase A (INPP5A), which is associated with the phosphoinositide 3-kinase/Akt signaling pathway and cell proliferation and survival, and showed lower expression levels in EBV(+) GC compared with normal mucosa and other GC samples. We infected GES1, an immortalized gastric epithelial cell line, with EBV in vitro, and demonstrated the induction of aberrant DNA methylation in the INPP5A enhancer region and the downregulation of its expression. These findings indicate that EBV(+) GC exhibits a specific DNA hypermethylation phenotype in enhancer regions, and EBV infection in gastric cells could induce aberrant DNA methylation in enhancer regions, involving dysregulation of cancer-related gene expression.
authors: Okada T, Usui G, Okabe A, Seki M, Fujiki R, Abe H, Rahmutulla B, Fukuyo M, Morikawa T, Ushiku T, Kaneda A.

title: Sucrose signaling regulates theanine accumulation via the CsYABBY2-CsMYB5-CsPDX2.1 module in tea plants.
abstract: Theanine is a specialized non-protein amino acid that determines the quality of tea (Camellia sinensis), yet the regulatory mechanisms controlling its hydrolysis remain unknown. Here we show that sucrose acts as a signal to modulate theanine accumulation by regulating a transcriptional repressor module that suppresses the theanine hydrolase gene CsPDX2.1. Using a yeast one-hybrid screen, we identified two transcription factors, CsYABBY2 and CsMYB5, that directly bind to distinct cis-elements (TAATGATT and TAACCA) in the CsPDX2.1 promoter. We demonstrate that CsYABBY2 and CsMYB5 interact to form a complex, and that co-expression of both proteins synergistically enhances repression of CsPDX2.1 transcription. Functional analyses via virus-induced gene silencing and transient overexpression confirmed that this module negatively regulates CsPDX2.1 expression and positively controls theanine accumulation. Importantly, exogenous sucrose suppresses CsYABBY2 and CsMYB5 expression, thereby derepressing CsPDX2.1 expression and reducing theanine levels, suggesting that sucrose functions as a regulatory factor affecting this pathway. Our findings reveal a sucrose-responsive (CsYABBY2-CsMYB5-CsPDX2.1) module that mediates theanine accumulation, providing a molecular basis for understanding varietal differences in theanine content.
authors: He Y, Zhong Q, Song S, Li M, Liu B, Ma S, Zhuang J, Wang Y, Chen X, Han R, Liu S, Li X.

title: A Human Tumor Virus Recruits HSP70 Chaperone to Remodel Its Replisome on DNA
abstract: Human Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCV) large T (LT) protein functions as a replication helicase analogous to the cellular MCM complex but requires a second MCV protein, small T (sT), for efficient LT-initiated replication. Both LT and sT encode highly-conserved DnaJ domains that bind to the cellular refolding molecule, heat shock protein 70 (HSP70). Using single-molecule imaging and FRET, we find that sT recruits dimeric HSP70 to serve as a molecular bridge between sT and LT on DNA and that this complex facilitates remodeling LT into a functional double-hexameric helicase. Disruption of LT-HSP70-HSP70-sT interaction with HSP70 inhibitors or by mutations to the LT-sT DnaJ domains collapse the LT-HSP70-HSP70-sT complex, abolishing sT-enhanced LT dodecamerization and ATP-dependent DNA unwinding. Assembly of virus-free mammalian MCM3, MCM4 and MCM6 in nuclear extracts similarly recruits HSP70 to DNA suggesting that Hsp70 remodeling is used for efficient eukaryotic assembly of the multi-protein replication machinery.
authors: Wan L, Li X, Vittot P, Brodsky J, Wipf P, Moore PS, Chang Y.

title: Intraspecific lineage divergence in Aegilops umbellulata Zhuk.: its association with variation in morphological and reproductive traits
abstract: Abstract    Aegilops umbellulata  Zhuk. is a wild diploid wheat species (UU genome) native to the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East. To characterize the natural variation, 202 accessions were analyzed across their distribution ranges at the molecular and phenotypic levels. Population structure analysis revealed two major genetic lineages, UmbL1 and UmbL2. UmbL1 was further divided into western (UmbL1w) and eastern (UmbL1e) sublineages, whereas UmbL2 was restricted to the far west. Two additional groups, Intermediate-w and Intermediate-e, were genetically and geographically intermediate between UmbL1w and UmbL2 and between UmbL1w and UmbL1e, respectively. Among the 24 morphological and phenological traits, flowering time, awn length, trichome level, and seed-related traits showed clear lineage-associated variations. The UmbL1w accessions tended to flower later and had longer awns, higher trichome levels, and smaller seeds, with more spikelets per spike, whereas the UmbL1e accessions tended to flower earlier and produced larger seeds with fewer spikelets. The UmbL2 accessions showed intermediate flowering times and broad seeds with few spikelets. Genome-wide association analysis identified loci potentially associated with the trichome level, and comparative analysis highlighted a candidate gene on chromosome 3U. These findings provide insights into the diversity of  Ae. umbellulata  and its potential use in bread wheat breeding.
authors: Son I, Kasazumi N, Takumi S, Yoshida K, Matsuoka Y.

title: Pharmacological enhancement of 20S proteasome-mediated degradation exposes a vulnerability in human papillomavirus (HPV)-driven cervical cancer
abstract: Abstract  Abstract: Despite the availability of prophylactic vaccines against human papillomavirus (HPV), infection and subsequent cervical cancer remain a significant global health problem. HPV viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 drive oncogenesis, in part through disruption of cell growth control pathways via degradation of the tumor suppressors p53 and pRB, respectively. These proteins contain intrinsically disordered regions that enable interactions with multiple cellular targets but also complicate the development of conventional therapeutics. While these proteins have previously been associated with a ubiquitin-dependent clearance mechanism through the 26S proteasome, we show that these HPV viral proteins can be degraded in a ubiquitin-independent method through the 20S proteasome alone. We also show that the small molecule-enhancement of this protease reduces HPV E6 and E7 protein levels across high-risk strains of the virus in a proteasome-dependent and transcription-independent manner. 20S proteasome activation suppressed HPV-driven phenotypes, including reduced proliferation and restoration of cell-cycle regulatory signaling. Whole cell proteomic analysis revealed remodeling of cancer-associated pathways including shifts consistent with reduced proliferative and oncogenic metabolic signaling. Collectively, these findings identify a previously unrecognized vulnerability of HPV oncoproteins and establish 20S proteasome activation as a potential therapeutic strategy for HPV-associated cancers.
authors: Tepe J, Cartwright S, Le L, Carranza A, Hartnett K, Ghaffari B, Dou Y, Konduru G, Kumar P, Zhang T.

title: Molecular Detection of Spotted Fever Group Rickettsia in Ticks Collected From Wildlife Carcasses at a Bushmeat Market in Ghana.
abstract: Despite extensive bushmeat consumption in Ghana, data on tick-borne zoonotic risks remain limited. This study investigated ticks collected from wildlife carcasses at the Atwemonom Bushmeat Market in Kumasi from April 2020 to April 2021 to assess the presence of zoonotic pathogens. Ticks were morphologically identified using standard taxonomic keys and screened for selected bacterial pathogens using PCR and Sanger sequencing. A total of 211 ticks were recovered from the 46 wildlife carcasses, with Ixodes aulacodi (49.76%) as the predominant species. Ticks were pooled (total pools = 94) by species and host; pool sizes ranged from 1 to 7 (Median 2). Rickettsial DNA was detected in 10.64% of tick pools, including Rickettsia africae and Rickettsia massiliae, whereas Coxiella burnetii was not detected. These findings highlight an underrecognized wildlife-human interface for potential rickettsial transmission and underscore the need for integrated surveillance and diagnostic capacity. This study establishes an essential epidemiological baseline that may inform future research and evidence-based vector and disease management strategies.
authors: Amoako EK, Addo SO, Malm RO, Danso-Coffie CK, Agbobli EA, Yeboah R, Offih-Kyei W, Behene E, Kwofie KD, Kwarteng SA, Bimi L, Gyan BA, Oduro D.

title: Harnessing plant redox networks and bacterial modulation for next-generation abiotic stress resilience in crops.
abstract: Abiotic stresses such as drought, salinity, heavy metals, heat, and cold disrupt cellular redox homeostasis, resulting in the excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative damage that negatively affect plant growth and productivity. Under controlled conditions, lower level of ROS act as signaling molecule, whereas, at elevated levels with biotic and abiotic stress factors, causes cellular damage. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms involved in redox homeostasis in plants, including both enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant systems. The integrated roles of phytohormone signaling and plant growth-promoting bacteria (PGPB) in regulating ROS metabolism, boosting antioxidant capacity, and enhancing abiotic stress tolerance are further discussed. Mechanistic insights into plant stress adaptation are provided by evaluating recent advances in transcriptional regulation, epigenetic modification, and redox-associated regulatory networks. Moreover, we review the contributions of multi-omics approaches toward understanding redox regulation and identifying key molecular components involved in stress resilience. Finally, emerging applications of synthetic biology and artificial intelligence are explored as potential tools for engineering redox regulatory networks to accelerate the development of climate-resilient crops. Overall, this review provides an integrated mechanistic framework outlining how redox biology, PGPB interactions, and next-generation engineering strategies can be combined to enhance crop resilience and sustainable agricultural productivity under future environmental shifts.
authors: Sarkar RK, Bhattacharyya A, Sarkar S, Pramanik B, Dutta S, Debnath S, Paul A, Bhattacharya K, Upadhyay SK, Rani A, Koolman L, Panneerselvam P, Santoyo G, Mitra D.

title: Emerging Biological Threats in the Twenty-First Century: A Narrative Review Integrating One Health, Genomic Surveillance, and Laboratory Biosecurity for Pandemic Preparedness.
abstract: The frequency of emerging infectious diseases has risen over the twenty-first century, driven by anthropogenic pressures including wildlife trade, rapid urbanization, deforestation, and climate change, which increasingly force human, animal, and environmental systems into closer proximity and create conditions favorable to zoonotic spillover. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed vulnerabilities in global health infrastructure while also catalyzing advances in genomic epidemiology and medical countermeasure platforms. This narrative review synthesizes recent peer-reviewed and policy literature (see Search Strategy) on pathogen emergence, the operationalization of the One Health framework, and the intersection of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) with viral outbreaks, including the well-documented rise in empirical antibiotic use and secondary multidrug-resistant infections during acute respiratory pandemics. We also review gaps in laboratory biosecurity, including governance of Dual-Use Research of Concern (DURC), the expansion of high-containment laboratories, and emerging cyberbiosecurity risks. Building on this literature, we propose an integrated preparedness framework organized around three pillars-One Health surveillance, genomic and environmental surveillance, and laboratory biosecurity and governance-with AMR and artificial intelligence (AI) treated as cross-cutting considerations, and with particular attention to the constraints facing low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and fragile, conflict-affected settings. We argue that strengthening global biosecurity will require decentralized genomic surveillance, sustained local laboratory capacity, and equitable international cooperation, while noting that the feasibility of these measures depends on financing, governance, and workforce constraints that are not yet fully resolved in the literature.
authors: Hassan SA, Guled BA, Omar AI.

title: Rapid electrochemical genosensing platform for direct detection of CTX-M-15 ESBL gene.
abstract: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) producing Enterobacteriaceae, particularly CTX-M-15-harboring strains, present significant diagnostic challenges due to limitations of conventional phenotypic and molecular methods. Here, we report a rapid electrochemical genosensing platform for direct CTX-M-15 detection using gold-electrodeposited screen-printed carbon electrode (SPCE) following solution-phase probe-target hybridization. A 22-mer probe targeting conserved CTX-M-15 regions was designed through sequence alignment and validated by Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST), primer mapping, and thermodynamic analysis. Probe specificity was confirmed by fluorescence in-situ hybridization (FISH) and fluorescence spectroscopy. Electrochemical characterization and detection were performed using square-wave voltammetry (SWV), enabling discrimination between complementary DNA, denatured DNA, and non-target species. Optimization of probe-to-target ratio, hybridization time, methylene blue volume, and SWV frequency established a 15 min assay with a linear range of 2 pM-20 μM (R2 = 0.98) and a detection limit of 2 pM. The sensor exhibited high specificity toward CTX-M-15 over different bacterial strains. It was further clinically validated using clinical isolate samples, showing complete agreement with PCR and disc diffusion results. These findings demonstrate its potential as a rapid, low-cost platform for AMR diagnostics.
authors: Shukla M, Yadav N, Newaskar V, Zala D, Bhatt V, Cinti S, Tripathi S, Pandya A.

title: Proteome-wide profiling reveals compartment-specific RNA buffering of protein aggregation during stress
abstract: Cellular adaptation to stress requires extensive remodeling of RNA metabolism. The rewiring of the RNA-protein interaction landscape and the assembly of biomolecular condensates are central to this response, yet the global stress-induced reorganization of macromolecular RNA-protein assemblies remains incompletely characterized. Here, we apply R-DeeP, a density gradient approach coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry, to profile the RNA-dependent sedimentation behaviour of the  Saccharomyces cerevisiae proteome during heat and salt stress. We demonstrate that stress triggers a profound, stress-specific reorganization of the RNA interactome. Many proteins undergo pronounced, selective shifts into high-molecular weight fractions, indicative of aggregation. RNase treatment markedly exacerbates this aggregation, consistent with the model that RNA acts as a general chaperone that keeps proteins with intrinsically disordered regions soluble. Strikingly, our data demonstrate that this protection is compartmentalised. Nuclear proteins are partially shielded from stress-induced aggregation. This protection coincides with the nuclear accumulation of RNA caused by a block of RNA export during stress, and RNase treatment abolishes this protection. Nuclear RNA retention may therefore act as a buffer that actively increases the local chaperoning capacity of the nucleus. In contrast, cytoplasmic proteins, including translation factors and ribonucleoprotein granule components, exhibit increased aggregation under stress. Fluorescence microscopy confirmed that increased biochemical aggregation in density gradients reflects changes in assembly state  in vivo . For many stress-induced aggregators, these changes are visible as spatial reorganisation in stressed cells, such as the formation of foci. Our findings suggest that cells use subcellular RNA distribution to tune the condensation and/or aggregation threshold of proteins in a compartment-specific manner.

title: Draft genome sequence of Escherichia coli ECMC01 isolated from clinical bovine mastitis in Malaysia.
abstract: The draft genome sequence of Escherichia coli ECMC01 isolated from bovine mastitis in Malaysia is reported. The 5.13-Mb genome encodes 4,967 predicted protein-coding genes, 92 RNA genes, and multiple determinants associated with antimicrobial resistance and virulence.
authors: Alam RS, Rosli NFS, Hera BMFH, Chen Z, Ramanoon SZ, Bhassu S, Tan GYA, Muthukrishnan S.

title: Human Metapneumovirus in the Post-pandemic Era:: A Multicenter Comparative Study With Respiratory Syncytial Virus in Argentina, 2022-2025.
abstract: BackgroundHuman metapneumovirus (hMPV), identified in 2001, is an important cause of acute lower respiratory infections (ALRI) in children worldwide and is generally considered the second most frequent viral cause after respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Comparative data between hMPV and RSV in the post-pandemic period remain scarce in Latin America, particularly after the introduction of maternal RSV immunization.MethodsWe conducted a prospective multicenter surveillance study in 5 tertiary pediatric hospitals in Argentina between 2022 and 2025. Children hospitalized with reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction-confirmed hMPV or RSV-associated ALRI were included. Epidemiologic characteristics, clinical presentation, respiratory support requirements, outcomes and seasonal patterns were compared. Independent predictors of hMPV versus RSV infection were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression.ResultsAmong 19,021 ALRI hospitalizations, 661 (3.5%) were hMPV and 2397 (12.6%) were RSV cases. hMPV patients were older (median 10 vs 8 months; P ConclusionsThis emerging respiratory virus demonstrates distinct epidemiologic and clinical characteristics, predominantly affecting older children with respiratory vulnerability. In the era of RSV prevention strategies, hMPV may represent an increasingly important contributor to the residual burden of severe pediatric ALRI, highlighting the need for development of preventive interventions.
authors: Gentile A, Juarez MDV, Lucion MF, Gregorio G, Lopez O, Pejito MN, Falaschi A, Zuzel P, Lobertti S, Gioiosa A, Fernandez T, Lopez L, Guarnieri C, Ensinck G, Bakir J.

title: Designing Antimicrobial Peptides Against Resistance: From Molecular Mechanisms to AI-Driven Discovery
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short, mostly cationic and amphipathic molecules that constitute an evolutionarily ancient arm of innate immunity in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans, and they have re-emerged as leading candidates against antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This review integrates the biosynthesis, structure–function relationships, molecular mechanisms, pharmacology and biomedical translation of AMPs. AMPs can be classified according their biosynthesis and structures: Ribosomally synthesized peptides—including classical host-defence peptides, ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs), bacteriocins and non-ribosomal peptides assembled by modular megaenzymes (non-ribosomal peptide synthetases -NRPS. Activity is governed less by a fixed sequence than by a tunable balance of cationicity, hydrophobicity and amphipathicity that jointly determine potency and selectivity. Mechanistically, AMPs act through membrane permeabilization (barrel-stave, toroidal-pore and carpet models) and, as is increasingly recognized, through intracellular targets such as lipid II, nucleic acids, the ribosome and chaperones, as well as through host immunomodulation. The principal barrier to systemic use is due to unfavorable pharmacokinetics, proteolytic lability, rapid clearance and serum sequestration. Therefore, extensive peptide engineering (D-amino acids, cyclisation, lipidation, peptidomimetics) and most recently, machine learning and generative artificial intelligence (AI) to navigate an astronomically large sequence space toward multi-objective optima are used to develop new AMPs. Clinically validated AMPs (nisin, daptomycin, polymyxins, gramicidin, bacitracin) cluster where pharmacokinetic constraints are least binding, while antifungal, antiviral, antibiofilm, immunomodulatory, anticancer and antibiotic-resensitizing applications are advancing. With a comparatively high genetic barrier to resistance, AMPs are positioned as a complementary—not a replacement—class within the response to the AMR.
authors: Islek Camadan EE, Kocagoz T.

title: Gene regulatory architecture in antibiotic resistance is optimized for specific dynamic regimens
abstract: Cellular responses to antibiotics face a fundamental trade-off: resistance must be deployed quickly enough to prevent the accumulation of drug inside the cell, but expression of resistance genes is costly in the absence of the drug. Therefore, antibiotic responses are typically regulated, controlling not only whether resistance is expressed, but also when, how strongly, and for how long. These regulatory strategies are implemented through the strength and arrangement of promoters and operators. However, it is still not clear how the dynamics of drug exposure select for specific regulatory strategies. Here, we develop a dynamical model of a typical antibiotic response, where a transcriptional repressor senses the drug and regulates expression of a resistance protein, coupled to the effects of the drug on cell growth and gene expression. We define a cost function that weighs the different burdens imposed on the cell over the course of the response, and perform  in silico optimization of the regulatory parameters under different selective pressures for three architectures of increasing complexity: constitutive expression of resistance, repression by a constitutively expressed repressor, and repression by a self-regulated repressor. We find that strong drug exposures favor constitutive expression of resistance, high costs of basal expression favor repression by a constitutive repressor, and self-regulation of the repressor is favored only when the response must provide protection while also restraining overexpression of resistance. Stochastic simulations further show that self-regulation of the repressor protects cells against fluctuations in repressor levels, which cause unnecessary induction of resistance before exposure and failed induction after exposure. This framework links the dynamics of the environment to the evolution of gene regulation, providing a basis to predict which regulatory strategies are expected to arise under specific selective pressures.  Significance  Bacteria regulate the expression of antibiotic resistance genes to avoid the costs of producing resistance when it is not needed. However, regulated responses take time to activate, which can be fatal when cells are suddenly exposed to large drug doses. Here, we use a mathematical model of antibiotic responses to identify which regulatory strategies are optimal under different selective pressures. We show that the choice between constitutive and regulated expression of resistance, and the use of self-regulation by the repressor, depend on the dynamics of drug exposure and on which costs dominate the response. Noise in gene expression further favors self-regulation of the repressor near the limit of tolerable drug exposures. These results help explain the diversity of regulatory architectures found in natural resistance mechanisms, and the frequent loss of regulation in pathogens exposed to antibiotic treatments.
authors: Geng H, Schultz D.

title: A hybrid nature-based ecological restoration system stabilizes water quality and food-web recovery in a continuous nutrient-loaded pond.
abstract: Small water bodies are important hotspots for nutrient transformation but are highly vulnerable to persistent anthropogenic loading. Ecological restoration is often evaluated by short-term pollutant removal, whereas the processes that sustain water quality and ecological function under continuing external inputs remain less understood. Here, we implemented a hybrid nature-based ecological restoration system integrating ecological floating beds, microbial electrochemical system-enhanced floating beds (ECOFB-MES), submerged macrophytes, and ecological revetments in a 2600-m2 shallow rural pond continuously receiving secondary treatment effluent and rainfall-driven runoff. Across pronounced seasonal variability (5-36 °C), the water quality consistently met the surface water Class III standard (GB 3838-2002) and effectively prevented eutrophication. Water-quality persistence was accompanied by aquatic-community recovery, characterized by declining phytoplankton abundance and increasing zooplankton and benthic macroinvertebrates. Increasing sediment ORP coincided with increased Fe(III) abundance and phosphorus fraction redistribution, indicating a shift toward stronger phosphorus retention and a lower potential for internal phosphorus release. Microbial-community restructuring, electrochemically mediated electron transfer, plant nutrient assimilation, and sediment stabilization provided complementary pathways for nutrient transformation and retention. Greenhouse-gas measurements further indicated potential carbon-related co-benefits. These results demonstrate that sustained improvement in nutrient-loaded small water bodies can emerge from coordinated regulation of the water column, sediment-water interface, and aquatic biological community. This study provides field-scale evidence for advancing small-water-body restoration toward integrated ecological stabilization under persistent anthropogenic pressure.
authors: Li J, Liu G, Tian Y, Liu Y, Qiu Y, Feng Y.

title: Genetically Predicted Plasma Lipid Metabolites and Immune-Cell Phenotypes in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: A Two-Sample Mendelian Randomization Study with Exploratory Reverse and Mediation Analyses.
abstract: PurposeTo evaluate associations of genetically predicted plasma lipid metabolites and immune-cell phenotypes with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and assess candidate immune-mediated lipid-COPD pathways.MethodsWe conducted two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses using genome-wide association study summary statistics for COPD in 458,440 individuals of European ancestry (26,274 cases and 432,166 controls), 179 plasma lipid metabolites in 7,174 Finnish participants, and 731 immune-cell phenotypes in 3,757 Sardinian participants. Genetic instruments selected at P-5 were linkage-disequilibrium clumped, harmonized and screened for instrument strength. Inverse-variance weighting (IVW) was the primary estimator, with robust adjusted profile score (MR-RAPS) used for sensitivity analysis. Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction was applied separately across the complete lipid and immune-cell test families. Reverse MR of 13 selected lipids, cross-ancestry analyses using an East-Asian COPD outcome, and two-step MR of 18 previously selected candidate pathways were exploratory. Indirect effects were estimated, and complementary multivariable MR with conditional F-statistics were evaluated separately; BH correction covered the reverse and indirect-effect families.ResultsTwenty-one lipid metabolites and 48 immune-cell phenotypes showed nominal IVW associations with COPD (PConclusionThe primary European analyses provided limited evidence for multiplicity-adjusted associations of the evaluated plasma lipid metabolites or immune-cell phenotypes with COPD, and none of the candidate indirect effects was statistically supported. Reverse-MR signals should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating and require validation in independent cohorts and experimental studies. The present findings do not support clinical risk prediction or diagnostic application.

title: Prevalence and Immune Impact of HBV, HCV, EBV, and Syphilis Coinfections Among People Living with HIV in Hubei Province, China (2019-2023).
abstract: Introduction/objectivePeople living with HIV (PLWH) are disproportionately affected by viral coinfections, including hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and syphilis, each capable of compounding immune impairment and increasing morbidity. Despite effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), the integrated burden of these coinfections and their immunological impact among PLWH in China remains incompletely characterised, particularly across the COVID-19 pandemic period.MethodsThis retrospective cross-sectional study analysed routinely collected surveillance and laboratory data from five sites in Hubei Province, China, across three periods: 2019, 2022, and 2023. A total of 788 PLWH aged ≥18 years with confirmed HIV infection were included. HBV coinfection was defined by HBsAg positivity, HCV by anti-HCV seropositivity, EBV by detectable plasma DNA (>400 copies/mL), and syphilis by Treponema pallidum antibody seropositivity. Immune status was assessed using the CD4+/CD8+ ratio and T-cell subset indices. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of each coinfection and of immune impairment. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS, with significance set at p ResultsThe cohort was predominantly male (83.6%) and aged ≥50 years (52.3%). ART coverage was 92.4%, and virological suppression was achieved in 383/626 participants with available viral-load data (61.2%; 48.6% of the full cohort, N = 788). The overall prevalence of HBV and/or HCV coinfection was 25.9%; HIV-HBV was identified in 13.5%, HIV-HCV in 16.1%, and triple HIV-HBV-HCV in 3.7%. HIV-EBV coinfection was detected in 4.3% and syphilis seropositivity in 24.2%, the highest coinfection burden (T. pallidum antibody, not confirmed active infection). Coinfection prevalence differed significantly across surveillance periods; anti-HCV seroprevalence increased from 1.1% in 2019 to 21.3% in 2023, and syphilis seropositivity increased from 23.9% to 40.2% (both p DiscussionA high burden of viral coinfections that differed across surveillance periods of differing cohort composition was identified among PLWH in Hubei Province across 2019-2023, with syphilis representing the most prevalent coinfection. EBV was the only coinfection independently associated with immune impairment after adjustment for ART and demographic factors.ConclusionIntegrating syphilis screening and evaluating EBV monitoring alongside routine hepatitis surveillance warrant further investigation in this region.
authors: Mei F, Naz W, Cheng D, Chen T, Khan S, Sun G, Li J, Yousaf T.

title: Thermotolerance of natural Arabidopsis thaliana demes growing under salinity.
abstract: Climate change is intensifying abiotic stresses, with salinity and short-term heat stress emerging as constraints on plant growth and productivity. Although individual stress responses are well studied, plants frequently experience multiple stresses simultaneously. Natural genetic diversity plays a key role in shaping plant resilience under these conditions. Here, we investigated natural variation in thermotolerance under moderate salinity among Arabidopsis thaliana demes from Catalonia, where inland sites experience higher temperatures than coastal sites. Two screenings of 18 demes revealed divergence in heat tolerance that was not explained by the main axes of population structure, and demes were exposed to combined heat and salt stress. Under moderate salinity (25 mM NaCl), the inland deme A1 maintained relative biomass and photosystem II performance after heat shock, together with greater induction of HSFA2, HSP101, and HSP60-2. This advantage was attenuated at 50 mM NaCl, where heat increased leaf Na+ in A1 and reduced induction of root SOS1 and HKT1;1. In contrast, the coastal deme SFG matched A1 in relative biomass at 50 mM NaCl and showed the lowest leaf Na+ and highest K+:Na+ ratio after heat, coinciding with maintenance of SOS1 and HKT1;1 expression. Sequence analysis of 53 HSPs and 23 HSFs identified synonymous, missense, and regulatory-region variants differentiating tolerant and sensitive demes, while a genome-wide FST scan identified candidate regions. Together, these findings show that natural variation within a gene pool is associated with contrasting physiological and molecular responses to combined heat and salinity stress, with candidate mechanisms involving proteostasis and ionic homeostasis.
authors: Giordano D, González-Cobo C, Bartak M, Poschenrieder C, Busoms S.

title: Impacts of Longwall Mining-Induced Goafs on Sulfate Generation and Biogeochemical Transformation in a Multiaquifer System: Insights From C, S, O, and H Isotopes.
abstract: Longwall mining disrupts overlying strata and creates goafs, altering groundwater conditions and the chemical composition of affected aquifer systems. In arid and semiarid regions, understanding how deep coal extraction influences sulfate biogeochemistry is essential for assessing mining-related groundwater degradation and protecting scarce groundwater resources. This study combined major-ion chemistry, water isotopes (δD and δ18Owater), sulfate isotopes (δ34S and δ18OSO4), δ13CDIC, and Bayesian isotope mixing analysis to investigate sulfate sources and transformation in the multiaquifer system and goaf of the Jinjie Coal Mine, China. The results reveal a marked contrast between sulfate generation in the goaf and its subsequent transformation in the Jurassic aquifers. Pyrite oxidation and associated carbonate dissolution dominate sulfate and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) production in goaf water, whereas Bayesian source apportionment identifies pyrite oxidation as the principal sulfate source in most goaf-water samples. The spatial variation in source contributions is consistent with differences in the thickness and continuity of the Baode aquitard. Mining-induced fracturing, locally extending to the surface, facilitates the exposure of pyrite-bearing strata to oxygenated water and air, promoting sulfate generation in the goaf. The resulting sulfate subsequently enters the Jurassic aquifers, where relatively confined and reducing conditions favor bacterial sulfate reduction. Sulfate depletion, enrichment of residual sulfate in heavy sulfur and oxygen isotopes, and relatively depleted δ13CDIC values provide complementary evidence for this transformation. These findings provide a process-based framework for understanding sulfate evolution in mining-affected groundwater systems.
journal: Water environment research : a research publication of the Water Environment Federation
authors: Yang Z, Fang J, Zhao Y, Zhang Y, Wang C, Zhang W.

title: From sliding clamp to stationary repressor: how clamp-locking proteins convert KorB into an effective long-range gene silencer.
abstract: Transcriptional repression in prokaryotes is typically achieved by repressor proteins that bind close to, or within, the core promoters they control. KorB, a plasmid-partitioning protein essential for stable plasmid inheritance that additionally acts as a transcriptional repressor, poses a puzzle for this canonical view: it can control promoters located kilobase distances from its DNA binding site. This spatial discrepancy motivated three decades of competing models for KorB-mediated repression, and none of the emerging theories of polymerisation along DNA and/or long-range DNA looping proved entirely satisfactory. The present mini-review discusses recent work demonstrating that KorB instead solves this problem dynamically: it is a self-loading, CTP-dependent DNA-sliding clamp protein that entraps DNA and diffuses away from its loading site to reach distal target promoters. Acting alone, KorB is a poor repressor, confounded by the spatiotemporal limitations of 1D-diffusion. Effective, site-specific silencing instead relies on a second class of protein, exemplified by KorA and, more recently, the paralogous protein TrbA. These clamp-locking proteins lock the sliding KorB in place at target promoters, dramatically increasing repression. The present mini-review details the structural basis of this clamp-locking interaction, its consequences for transcriptional initiation, and the broader questions this sliding-clamp-to-repressor strategy raises for long-range gene regulation, plasmid biology, and the spread of antimicrobial resistance.
authors: McLean TC.

title: The Rcs System Is Required for Virulence and Colonization of the Poplar Canker Bacterium Lonsdalea populi.
abstract: Unlike traditional two-component systems, the Rcs system is an atypical multicomponent phosphorelay. It represents one of the most complex signalling networks in bacteria, regulating vital physiological processes; however, its function in the poplar canker bacterium Lonsdalea populi remains unclear. By combining RNA sequencing, electrophoretic mobility shift assays and pathogenicity assays, we identified two novel RcsB target genes: the pectate lyase gene pelE and the TolC-family outer membrane channel gene omeP. Unphosphorylated RcsB can directly regulate pelE expression to promote host pectin degradation. As PelE degrades the plant cell wall, it activates host immune responses and triggers a burst of reactive oxygen species (ROS). We propose that the transmembrane kinase RcsC senses these stimuli and, via RcsD, transfers phosphate to RcsB, consistent with the conserved Rcs phosphorelay. Phosphorylated RcsB enhanced binding affinity, thereby strengthening transcriptional regulation of omeP and enhancing the tolerance of the pathogen to ROS. This study shows that the Rcs system coordinately regulates omeP and pelE expression to establish an infection pathway, hence promoting L. populi colonization. It highlights a core strategy of woody plant pathogens to degrade host barriers and withstand stress, offering new insights for targeted control.
authors: Yang R, Guo Y, Wang Y, Wang Y, Li A.

title: Single-Step Sample-Activated Alternating Sequential Flow Enables Autonomous Multistep Electrochemical Lateral Flow Detection of Mpox Virus DNA.
abstract: The 2022 multinational mpox virus (MPXV) outbreak and continued cross-border transmission have highlighted limitations of laboratory-confined PCR diagnostics. Here, we report an alternating lateral flow architecture (ALFA) that transforms traditional single-pass lateral flow into a programmable platform for autonomous multistep electrochemical nucleic acid detection following a single prepared-sample introduction. By regulating passive fluid delivery, ALFA enables sequential molecular processing and in situ signal generation without external intervention. Coupled with Ag(I)-mediated mismatch DNA nanocomplexes (MDNs), the system provides electrochemical signal amplification without nucleic acid amplification. ALFA detected MPXV DNA with a limit of detection (LOD) of 1.55 pM and a linear range of 101-105 pM. In urine and saliva spiked with structurally intact viral particles, the lowest statistically distinguishable concentration was 10 copies mL-1. Clinical evaluation of 50 PCR-characterized lesion swab samples yielded 92.11% sensitivity, 100% specificity, and 94.0% accuracy. The platform also maintained stable performance over an estimated 112 days. ALFA therefore provides a programmable lateral flow framework for rapid, amplification-free, decentralized nucleic acid diagnostics.
authors: Lapee-E V, Phimdee P, Jung HI, Pasomsub E, Yakoh A.

title: Label-Free and Strain-Resolved Characterization of AI-2 Associated Quorum Sensing Functional Phenotypes in Bacterial Isolates Using Single-Cell Raman Spectroscopy and Deep Learning.
abstract: We evaluated the relationship between Raman spectral profiles obtained by single-cell Raman spectroscopy (SCRS) and autoinducer-2 (AI-2)-associated quorum sensing (QS) functional phenotypes using experimentally measured relative BB170 reporter responses as functional reference values. Based on this relationship, this study provides a rapid, label-free SCRS-based model for characterizing AI-2-associated QS functional phenotypes in bacterial isolates. The optimized residual neural network (ResNet) achieved an R2 of 0.8351 under spectrum-level 10-fold cross-validation, while strain-level aggregated evaluation showed good agreement with experimentally measured responses within the represented dataset (R2 = 0.8840). In an independent-isolates set of 21 strains from multiple sources spanning the No-, Low-, Medium-, and High-response categories, the model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.092, a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.148, an R2 of 0.805, and an overall category accuracy of 80.95%. Reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) detected luxS expression in all 21 independent isolates, providing complementary evidence for their potential AI-2-associated signaling capacity. In addition, furanone C-30 treatment of W37 resulted in concordant decreases in experimentally measured and model-estimated relative BB170 reporter responses, further supporting the responsiveness of the captured spectral phenotype to within-strain functional perturbation. Integrated Gradients (IG) analysis highlighted coordinated Raman spectral regions associated with proteins, lipids, polysaccharides, nucleic acids, and sulfur-containing groups, suggesting that model estimates were based on multiband spectral patterns rather than a single characteristic feature.
authors: Zhang H, Wang Y, Su Y, Zheng X, Cai B, Ge J.

title: Aptamer-Based Fluorescent Assays for Detection of the Host-Response Viral Biomarker 3'-Deoxy-3',4'-Didehydro-Cytidine.
abstract: Improved viral diagnostics are urgently needed to strengthen pandemic preparedness and combat antimicrobial resistance, highlighting the importance of 3'-deoxy-3',4'-didehydro-cytidine (ddhC), a host-derived, pan-viral biomarker that addresses key limitations of PCR-based diagnostics. Current methods for ddhC measurement rely on liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) or nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, which are accurate but costly and impractical for rapid or point-of-care testing. Here, we report the development of aptamer-based fluorescent assays for selective ddhC detection. Low-micromolar-affinity DNA aptamers were isolated using capture-systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) and characterised by isothermal titration calorimetry. Using a common core aptamer sequence, three fluorescence assay formats-strand displacement, molecular beacon, and dye displacement-were developed and evaluated. Independent LC-MS analysis demonstrated a strong correlation between creatinine-normalised urinary and serum ddhC concentrations in inpatient samples (R = 0.98, p <0.0001), supporting urine as a non-invasive matrix for ddhC detection. Among the three aptamer-based formats tested, the dye displacement assay exhibited the lowest functional Kd but was limited in urine by inner filter effects, whereas a Cy5-labelled strand displacement assay overcame this limitation and detected ddhC in patient urine with moderate correlation to LC-MS (R = 0.76, p = 0.001). Together, these results establish aptamer-based sensing approaches for ddhC and demonstrate their feasibility in clinical urine samples, providing a foundation for further optimisation toward accessible, non-invasive, and rapid detection of acute viral infection.
authors: Mehta R, Ben-Aissa S, Yang K, Chekmeneva E, Valdivia-Garcia M, Maslen L, Ferris T, Skirlo K, Mills E, Sgro V, Sriskandan S, Cass AEG.

title: IMSS: An Integrated Mass Spectrometry Strategy for Targeted Discovery of CyclopeptidesExemplified by Phakellicyclins from the Marine Sponge Phakellia fusca.
abstract: Cyclopeptides (CPs) represent a structurally diverse class of bioactive natural products but remain analytically challenging due to their high structural similarity, low abundance, and complex matrices. Herein, we report an integrated mass spectrometry strategy (IMSS) enabling selective detection, annotation, and targeted isolation of CPs from marine organisms. The workflow incorporates: (1) multiplexed diagnostic neutral loss and precursor ion (NL/PI) scanning based on the six most frequent amino acid residues (Pro, Ile/Leu, Val, Tyr, Phe, Trp) identified from 16 reference standards; (2) de novo sequencing-assisted spectral validation via CycloNovo; (3) dual dereplication combining GNPS molecular networking with a curated library of 538 marine CPs; and (4) MS-triggered automated purification for target-oriented isolation. When applied to the marine sponge Phakellia fusca, IMSS afforded 23 candidate CPs and allowed targeted purification of two unknown cyclooctapeptides, phakellicyclins A and B, featuring rare dioxindolylalanine and β-3-oxindolylalanine residues, respectively. Both compounds exhibited potent anti-inflammatory activity through selective inhibition of interleukin-6 (IL-6) production without obvious cytotoxicity. This study establishes a robust and reproducible MS workflow for the targeted discovery of Pro/Ile/Leu-enriched marine CPs, with demonstrated potential for adaptation to other CP classes.
authors: Wu Y, Yu J, Li R, Xu J, Zhang Y, Liu L, Sun F, Lin H, Wang S.
