title: Ecophysiological effects of continuous substrate vibrations on two bivalve species: The great scallop and the Pacific oyster.
abstract: Anthropogenic noise became a growing concern for marine ecosystems, due to the increase of diverse human activities such as ships, pile driving, drilling, underwater explosions, and seismic testing. Establishing meaningful reference values in underwater noise risk assessment is therefore essential to support decision-making and regulatory frameworks. In this study, we assessed the ecophysiological responses of two benthic species (Pecten maximus and Crassostrea gigas) exposed to four levels of continuous substrate vibrations (0, 0.05, 0.10 and 0.15 m/s2, RMS) at 20 Hz during 48 h in laboratory. Whole-organism behavioral and physiological responses (i.e. valve opening, respiration and filtration rates) were recorded during the experiments. At the end of experiments, proteomic differences between vibration levels were compared together with the assay of a global measure of oxidative damage (protein carbonyls) to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying responses to substrate vibrations. Our study showed behavioral, physiological and molecular responses varied with vibration acceleration levels, although patterns differed among endpoints and species. Especially, oxidative damage increased significantly in P. maximus at 0.10 m/s2, whereas no significant effect was observed in C. gigas. Significant differences in valve closures (0.10 and 0.15 m/s2) and filtration rates (0.15 m/s2) were observed in both species, but only through interactions with other factors for C. gigas. Several potential candidates for biomarkers were also identified, requiring further investigations. Finally, reference values were proposed for both species to improve underwater noise risk assessment.

title: Epigenetic age acceleration in the brain and blood of people with epilepsy and in a mouse model of focal cortical dysplasia: a retrospective cross-sectional study.
abstract: BackgroundPeople with epilepsy have reduced life expectancy and more age-related comorbidities, suggesting a link to faster biological ageing. Direct molecular evidence has been scarce.MethodsWe applied DNA-methylation-based epigenetic clocks to brain and blood samples from 324 unique individuals with structural or genetic epilepsy and 65 non-epilepsy controls, and to an in utero electroporation mouse model of somatic mTOR pathway activation (etiocopy of human FCD type 2) sampled before and after seizure onset. Epigenetic age acceleration was defined as the residual from a robust regression on chronological age, sex, cell-type composition, and array type. Relative telomere length was measured in the mouse model to independently validate biological ageing.FindingsIn brain, epigenetic age acceleration was consistent across structural lesion types (median +7.3 years, p InterpretationAccelerated epigenetic ageing is a consistent feature of the epileptic brain in drug-resistant structural epilepsies and a candidate pathway for disease modification. The contribution of systemic ageing remains unresolved, and generalisability to other aetiologies will need to be further tested.FundingElse Kröner Fresenius Stiftung, German Science Foundation, L'Institut pour la Recherche en Santé Publique, Interdisziplinäres Zentrum für Klinische Forschung, Czech Science Foundation, Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic, Ministry of Education, Youth and Sports of the Czech Republic, Research Foundation-Flanders FWO.

title: Loss of DUSP2-RPA signaling enhances virtual memory T cell-mediated innate-like antiviral immunity.
abstract: Virtual memory CD8+ T (TVM) cells are antigen-inexperienced cells with rapid effector potential, but how their differentiation and antiviral activity are regulated remains unclear. Here, using an autoantibody-based screening strategy, we identify the phosphatase DUSP2 as a key regulator of TVM cell responses. Dual-specificity phosphatase 2 (DUSP2) deficiency enhances CD8+ T cell-dependent antiviral immunity and promotes the expansion of a highly activated CD44super-high TVM subset. Upon viral challenge, these TVM cells respond rapidly without antigen recognition and display enhanced effector and cytokine programs, supporting an innate-like mode of antiviral immunity rather than conventional antigen-specific recall. Mechanistically, DUSP2 interacts with the replication protein A (RPA) complex to regulate RPA2 phosphorylation and chromatin association. Disruption of the DUSP2-RPA axis promotes R-loop accumulation and increases chromatin accessibility, which in turn activates Eomesodermin (EOMES)-associated transcriptional programs, eventually promoting TVM cell differentiation. T cell-specific deletion of RPA1 phenocopies these effects, leading to spontaneous TVM cell accumulation and rapid effector-like responses upon viral challenge. Together, our findings establish a DUSP2-RPA-R-loop axis that restrains TVM cell development and innate-like antiviral immunity.
authors: Tian W, Qiu Y, Wang W, Xing X, Feng Y, Xu C, Liu L, Tie L, Wei Y, Lu D.

title: Integrative Network Pharmacology and Transcriptomic Analysis Prioritizes CCR1 and C5AR1 as Candidate Thromboinflammatory Targets Shared by Panax notoginseng Saponins and Stroke-Relevant Drugs in Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: Thromboinflammation is a central pathological process contributing to secondary brain injury after ischemic stroke (IS). Panax notoginseng saponins (PNS) exert pleiotropic anti-inflammatory, antithrombotic, and vascular effects, but the molecular convergence between PNS-associated pharmacology and stroke-relevant conventional agents remains incompletely characterized. We integrated network pharmacology, bulk transcriptomic datasets, single-cell RNA sequencing, regulatory-network analysis, and structure-based molecular docking to prioritize candidate targets shared by PNS and an exploratory screening panel of 16 stroke-relevant pharmacological agents. Predicted drug and PNS targets were intersected with IS-associated differentially expressed genes (DEGs), followed by network analysis, independent cross-dataset expression assessment, gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA), transcription-factor (TF) prediction with co-expression analysis, myeloid-cell sub-clustering, and GNINA docking. The screening framework yielded 79 shared predicted pharmacological targets and 10 disease-associated candidates: ITK, CDK2, C5AR1, VDR, S1PR2, KIF11, CCR1, FAP, PRKCD, and MAOA. CCR1 and C5AR1 were prioritized because they combined high network connectivity with consistent disease-associated expression across the analyzed datasets and strong links to thromboinflammatory pathways. BATF2 and SPI1 expression positively correlated with both C5AR1 and CCR1 in GSE56267. Myeloid sub-clustering further showed that C5ar1 was broadly distributed across stroke-associated microglial and monocyte/macrophage states, whereas Ccr1 was more restricted to activated inflammatory and infiltrating myeloid populations. GNINA docking of all fourteen network-defined receptor-ligand systems identified five complexes with docking affinity scores between - 8.06 and - 10.94 kcal/mol (ginsenosides Rd and Re at CCR1; notoginsenoside R1, ginsenoside Rg1, and ginsenoside Rd at C5AR1). Collectively, these analyses prioritize CCR1 and C5AR1 as convergent candidate thromboinflammatory nodes shared by PNS-associated and stroke-relevant pharmacological target spaces. The findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish pharmacological synergy, direct receptor coupling, or causal therapeutic mechanisms.
authors: Chen G, Ye Y, Zheng R, Xie Q, Li F, Yang W.

title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics define a C3-centred multicellular ecology in colorectal liver metastasis.
abstract: Colorectal liver metastasis (CRLM) develops through malignant-cell plasticity and microenvironmental remodeling, yet the spatial principles by which epithelial, stromal, vascular and myeloid states assemble remain poorly defined. We integrated a 136,995-cell single-cell atlas, four spatial transcriptomic sections and bulk-cohort survival analysis. cNMF resolved three recurrent malignant programs-C1 Proliferative-biosynthetic, C2 AP-1 stress-inflammatory and C3 Secretory-invasive immune-like-which recurred across donors (with a rare, patient-associated tuft/chemosensory component in C3) and followed a pseudotime-associated C1-to-C2-to-C3 ordering rather than a demonstrated temporal progression. C3 cells, rare overall and of donor-dependent abundance, showed epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invasive features, and in exploratory analyses their signature was associated with shorter recurrence-free survival. Continuous RGS1/CTSL programs captured macrophage heterogeneity more robustly than discrete subclusters. Spatial deconvolution revealed recurrent Fib-COL10A1-Endo-GJA5 proximity and variable C3 integration, with focal CTSL-program macrophage interfaces; MAPK and VEGF pathway activity was higher in C3-rich regions, although this association depended on how C3 was measured. An INHBA-CST6-LBH-FSTL3 score, which aggregates C3 and stromal expression, was associated with recurrence in TCGA, with partial external support in GSE39582 and no demonstrated gain over clinical variables. Virtual knockout of CST6 and LBH and LINCS screening prioritized MEK inhibition (PD-0325901) as a candidate for reversing the C3-associated transcriptional state; no target-engagement claim is made. Together, these findings define a spatially variable, C3-centred multicellular ecology in CRLM and provide a testable computational framework nominating recurrence-associated signatures and network-level candidates for experimental validation.
authors: Ma F, Yu Y.

title: <sup>1</sup>H, <sup>13</sup>C and <sup>15</sup>N Resonance assignments for YdbL from Escherichia coli in both its apo state and in complex with the C-terminus of YnbE.
abstract: The interaction between AsmA-like protein YdbH and YnbE constitutes one of the main putative phospholipid transport systems driving outer membrane (OM) biogenesis in Escherichia coli. YdbH is anchored to the IM via its N-terminus and extends into a long, periplasmic domain composed of stacked β-sheets which generates a hydrophobic groove to shield phospholipids from the aqueous periplasm. It forms a continuous cell-envelope spanning complex via its interaction with OM lipoprotein YnbE. YnbE is highly self-multimeric and forms complexes with YdbH of unknown stoichiometry. YdbL, encoded within the same operon as YdbH and YnbE, is a soluble periplasmic protein that acts in a chaperone-like role to modulate YnbE multimerisation and mediate efficient YdbH-YnbE complex assembly. NMR revealed a direct and highly conserved interaction interface between YdbL and the C-terminus of YnbE, supporting the hypothesis that YdbL can directly tune YnbE behaviour. In this report, we present the 1H, 13C and 15N resonance assignments for YdbL in both its apo state and in complex with a peptide derived from the C-terminus of YnbE. Analysis of the chemical shift data reveals the interaction interface for YdbL with YnbE does not result in significant changes in secondary structure but does appear to increase stabilisation of interacting α-helices. Overall, chemical shift changes observed for YdbL upon complex formation are reflective of side chain rearrangements in the peptide binding site and the interaction is confirmed with direct peptide-YdbL NOEs. Peptide-peptide short and medium range NOEs, and analysis of Hα chemical shifts, provide evidence that the bound YnbE peptide adopts an α-helical fold as predicted by in silico modelling of the interaction of full-length YnbE with YdbL. Together, these results strengthen directly related work underpinning YdbL function in controlling YnbE multimerisation to ensure correct complex formation with YdbH.
authors: De'Ath C, Isom GL, Redfield C.

title: Persistent infection is associated with divergent evolution of T cell repertoires.
abstract: In chronic infection, T cell clones recognizing the same epitope are variably expanded, with some clones evolving to become dominant, while others are lost. Clonal expansion and changes in the repertoire reflect both T cell receptor-intrinsic (TCR-intrinsic) and -extrinsic factors, yet the individuality of TCR repertoires makes it difficult to disentangle how TCR sequence shapes clonal behaviors. To address this, we exploited the observation that TCRs can be grouped into clusters based on sequence similarity. Using complementarity-determining region 3β (CDR3β) sequencing data derived from lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus-specific CD8+ T cells from mice infected early and late in the course of chronic infection, we identified CDR3β clusters ubiquitously shared by all mice. The pattern of CDR3β cluster abundance was highly similar between mice at the early time point in both self-limiting and persistent infection models. Over the course of chronic infection, the pattern of cluster abundance diverged between mice and dominant clones emerged that did not share sequence similarity between mice. This repertoire divergence was not observed in self-limiting infection, where the pattern of cluster abundance established early in infection was stable between mice beyond resolution of infection. In chronic infection, the repertoires of stem-like and exhausted antigen-specific T cells remained similar over time within individual mice, suggesting clonal selection acts on the stem-like pool. Our findings suggest that antigen-specific CD8+ T cell clones expanded early in infection have CDR3β motifs that are shared between mice, supporting a role for TCR structural properties in determining the repertoire structure. Divergent patterns of repertoire composition later in chronic infection suggest that these shared CDR3β motifs are less important in patterning the repertoire than during the initial response and there is greater complexity in factors that sculpt the repertoire over the course of persistent antigen exposure.
authors: Chang DY, Bravi B, Malik S, McGuire DJ, Ahmed H, Antia R, Ahmed R, Ghorani E.

title: Ecosystem Determinants of Therapeutic Resistance in Pancreatic Cancer: Implications for Precision Oncology.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains highly lethal despite advances in systemic and biomarker-directed therapy. Treatment resistance reflects not only tumor genotype but also desmoplasia, vascular dysfunction, immune suppression, metabolic adaptation, and evolutionary plasticity. This review integrates signaling dependency, ecosystem architecture, and adaptive evolution into an ecosystem-adaptive framework to explain therapeutic failure in PDAC and proposes four candidate ecosystem states: desmoplastic exclusion, myeloid dominance, hypoxic-metabolic adaptation, and immune-interface organization. These dynamic states may influence therapeutic exposure and resistance beyond conventional molecular classification. Prospective validation could support biomarker development, therapeutic stratification, rational treatment combinations, and treatment sequencing in pancreatic cancer.
authors: Shahiwala AF.

title: Selenium-Containing bioactive peptides attenuate spinal cord injury by inhibiting Blood-Spinal cord barrier disruption and neuronal ferroptosis.
abstract: BackgroundSpinal cord injury (SCI) triggers a devastating cascade of secondary damage characterized by blood-spinal cord barrier (BSCB) disruption and neuronal ferroptosis, for which effective therapeutic interventions remain limited. Selenium-containing bioactive peptides derived from Spirulina platensis (SeSP) have emerged as potential neuroprotective agents. However, their therapeutic efficacy and underlying molecular mechanisms in the context of SCI have not been fully elucidated.MethodsTo address this, we utilized a clinically relevant rat model of T10 contusion SCI to evaluate the restorative effects of SeSP. We systematically assessed neurological function recovery and employed a combination of immunofluorescence, western blotting, and biochemical assays to investigate BSCB integrity, neuroinflammatory responses, oxidative stress markers, and ferroptosis regulatory networks within the injured spinal cord.ResultsSeSP administration significantly promoted locomotor recovery and preserved BSCB integrity by restoring the expression of key tight junction proteins (ZO-1, Occludin, and Claudin-5) and suppressing matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) activity. Furthermore, SeSP treatment attenuated neuronal loss, inhibited microglial activation, and reduced the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Mechanistically, SeSP mitigated lipid peroxidation and DNA damage while exerting a potent anti-ferroptotic effect, as evidenced by the upregulation of GPX4, FTH1, and SLC7A11, and the downregulation of TXNIP, ACSL1, and DMT1.ConclusionOur findings demonstrate that SeSP exerts robust neuroprotection in SCI primarily by maintaining BSCB integrity and inhibiting oxidative stress-driven neuronal ferroptosis. These data identify SeSP as a promising therapeutic candidate for mitigating secondary injury and enhancing functional recovery following spinal cord trauma.
authors: Kuang N, Xiao Z, Liu W, Yu X, Wei Q, Wang Y, Ma T, Chen M, Zheng Z, He H, Su M.

title: Molecular Determinants of Treatment Resistance in Cervical Cancer: A Systematic Review and Integrative Bioinformatic Analysis of Publicly Available Datasets.
abstract: Treatment resistance remains a major challenge in cervical cancer management, particularly among patients undergoing chemoradiotherapy. Despite increasing knowledge of resistance-associated molecular pathways, clinically validated biomarkers capable of predicting treatment outcomes remain limited. This study combined a systematic review of clinical and preclinical studies with an integrative bioinformatic analysis of publicly available transcriptomic datasets. Gene expression profiles from cervical cancer models exposed to chemotherapeutic agents and epigenetic modulators were analyzed to identify treatment-response-associated transcriptional signatures. Candidate genes were subsequently evaluated in clinical datasets comprising normal cervical tissue, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, and invasive cervical cancer. Functional enrichment analysis, protein-protein interaction network construction, and survival analyses were performed to assess biological relevance. A total of 38 genes demonstrated concordant expression changes across independent treatment conditions. Clinical evaluation revealed progressive dysregulation of several candidates during cervical neoplastic progression and invasive disease development. Functional analyses indicated enrichment of pathways related to extracellular matrix organization, metabolic regulation, and p53-associated signaling. Network analysis identified lumican (LUM) as a candidate gene occupying a relatively high connectivity within the constructed interaction network. No statistically significant association between LUM expression and overall survival was observed. This integrative approach identified reproducible treatment-response-associated transcriptional signatures that may participate in biological processes relevant to therapeutic adaptation in cervical cancer. LUM emerged as a prioritized candidate for future investigation. However, its biological and clinical significance remains exploratory and requires validation in independent treatment-annotated cohorts and functional studies.
journal: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research
authors: Bereza K, Kukiełka A, Trojnarska D, Grabarek BO, Zmarzły N, Bereza B.

title: Integrated Multi-omics Reveals Molecular Signatures of Rett Syndrome, Informing Future Biomarker Discovery.
abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder primarily caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene. Despite numerous clinical trials being conducted, there are limited disease-modifying options available for individuals with RTT. This paucity of effective treatments can in part be attributed to the lack of clinically useful biomarkers that can objectively assess treatment response. Moreover, diagnosis of RTT continues to be clinical, when clinical manifestations are apparent, precluding early therapeutic approaches. Thus, clinical biomarkers of disease stage could improve diagnosis and enable real-time monitoring of response to treatment, providing the earliest possible indications of therapeutic efficacy. Given MeCP2's role as a key regulator of gene transcription, we used an untargeted omics approach to evaluate transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolic profiles in blood from individuals with RTT (n = 9) and age- and sex-matched controls (n = 8). In addition to characterising differential expression at each omic layer, to understand the shared biology and coordinated molecular signals across all omic datasets, we used the unsupervised machine learning framework Multi-Omics Factor Analysis version 2 (MOFA2). The individual omic data consisted of a robust upregulation of genes involved in ribosomal structure and translation together with a downregulation in vesicle trafficking genes. An upregulation in ribosomal machinery and mitochondrial function together with a concomitant downregulation of critical epigenetic regulators, immune-signalling molecules, and cytoskeletal structural anchors was observed in the proteomics, which was supported by the phosphoproteomics. Notably, plasma metabolomics pointed towards alterations in energy substrates and lipid/cholesterol handling, suggesting systemic downstream consequences of primary intracellular disturbances. The integrated MOFA2 data supported the individual omic data revealing a central disease axis principally shaped by the proteome and transcriptome and supported by the metabolome and phosphoproteome, identifying potential biomarkers, including latent biological processes that distinguish RTT from controls (Latent Factor 1) and correlates of clinical severity (Latent Factor 2). Overall, our data reveal a distinctive 'disease state' molecular signature that distinguishes individuals with RTT from controls, where the findings in RTT blood cells are consistent with previously reported altered translational and mitochondrial function and disrupted chromatin regulation, cytoskeletal dynamics, and metabolic signalling. Our integrated multi-omics analyses revealed that PBMC's LTN1, ATRX, CHD8, SPTB, DMTN, PRF1, CD40LG, and PTPRCAP and plasma glutamate are the most promising disease-state (complementary diagnostic) candidate biomarkers while sphingomyelin, RTN3, and MMP1 appear to be the most suitable biomarkers of disease severity. Here, we demonstrate that blood from individuals with RTT reflects the molecular systemic consequences of MeCP2 dysfunction.
authors: Issar JK, Hertzog A, Pang I, Graham ME, Aryamanesh N, Riley LG, Piras IS, Hansen NP, Finney CA, Shvetcov A, Gloss B, Bandodkar S, Dale RC, Sun Q, Ellaway C, Tolun AA, Ho G, Kaufmann WE, Gold WA.

title: A cohesin acetylation complex that recognises nicked DNA
abstract: Eukaryotic DNA replication products are held together by cohesin to enable their faithful inheritance during cell division. The establishment of stable sister chromatid cohesion requires replication-coupled acetylation of two conserved lysines on the cohesin Smc3 ATPase head. Here, we use AlphaFold 3 to predict the existence of a budding yeast cohesin acetylation complex, consisting of the replication protein PCNA, the cohesin subunit Pds5 and the Eco1 acetyltransferase. The predicted complex specifically contacts nicked DNA, a replication fork determinant that controls acetylation. Furthermore, cohesin engagement results in predicted conformational adaptations that bring acetyl-CoA in striking distance of the Smc3 target lysine. We perform biochemical and genetic experiments that confirm anticipated features of this reaction trajectory. Related cohesin acetylation complexes are predicted to form in other eukaryotes, including humans. Our study combines AI-assisted structure predictions and wet-bench experimentation to reveal the likely mechanism of replication-coupled cohesin acetylation during sister chromatid cohesion establishment.
authors: Bouchoux C, Uhlmann F.

title: Transcriptome profiling reveals gene regulatory network governing seed size in Brassica napus
abstract: Seed size is a critical trait influencing yield and quality in oilseed crops such as  Brassica napus . Despite their economic importance, the genetic and molecular mechanisms regulating seed size remain unclear, particularly in polyploid species, such as  B. napus . To deepen our understanding of seed size regulation, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis across four developmental stages (heart, torpedo, green, and mature) and three distinct seed organs: the seed coat, embryo, and endosperm. Differential expression analysis between  B. napus var. Zhongshuang (ZS11) and  B. napus cv. Ragged Jack (RJ) was performed to uncover regulatory networks involved in seed size control. Our results uncovered dynamic gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and pinpointed key regulators, including well-established factors like  ABI5 and  BRI1 , as well as novel candidate genes such as  KNAT5 ,  ARF11 ,  SUS2 ,  UGT72B1 ,  UGT89A2 , and  SBT1.7 . The present research provides an understanding of the regulatory networks governing seed size in  B. napus . These findings not only enhance our knowledge of seed biology but also offer valuable resources for future breeding strategies aimed at optimizing seed size and yield in polyploid oilseed crops.
authors: Zoclanclounon YAB, Siles L, Woolfenden H, Morris RJ, Kurup S.

title: Transcriptomic and Metabolomic Analysis of the Caudate and Putamen in ADHD
abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly heritable, heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder that typically manifests in childhood; however, transcriptomic studies have inadequately accounted for age of onset and subtype, with cohorts largely comprising of adults. To address this gap, we established a stringently phenotyped ADHD cohort (up to 19 years; clinically diagnosed combined and inattentive-type ADHD) and integrated postmortem caudate and putamen bulk RNA-seq, LC-MS metabolomics, MEGENA gene co-expression analysis, and cross-study comparison. We identified 279 up- and 35 downregulated DEGs in the caudate and 110 up- and 89 downregulated DEGs in the putamen. The combined caudate-putamen metabolomic analysis revealed dopamine dysregulation (1.68-fold reduction) and dysregulation of four additional metabolites. Enrichment analysis revealed shared molecular signatures involving immune responses, ATP metabolism and calcium ion-dependent signaling, with region-specific differences in the direction of alteration. Neuronal homeostasis, and protein stress showed suppression in the putamen, along with activation of neurotransmitter reuptake, whereas CSF circulation and ECM organization were activated in the caudate, with suppression in CNS myelination, and signs of ventricular perturbations. MEGENA identified 26 ADHD-associated caudate modules and 33 putamen modules. These modules captured canonical synaptic and neuronal-circuitry pathways alongside cellular differentiation, metabolism, and cell-survival processes. FGD1 emerged as a candidate caudate hub gene among the neuronal modules. Cross-study comparison analysis suggested that molecular alterations in ADHD may be age-dependent. Additionally, assessing levels of 76 potential risk genes identified by a large ADHD GWAS study one ARTN exhibited dysregulated levels in putamen and none in caudate. Together, these findings reveal brain-region-specific molecular dysregulation in ADHD across pathways extending beyond canonical neurotransmission to immune, differentiation, and energy-metabolic processes, along with novel evidence of perturbations in the understudied lateral ventricles.
authors: Patel R, Wang S, Deshmukh E, Fajen S, Williams J.

title: Quantitative trait loci mapping identifies genetic loci modifying MafAS64F-mediated dysglycemia
abstract: Increasing evidence has shown the role of genetic background on the penetrance of monogenic diabetes. A missense mutation of the pancreatic β-cell-enriched transcription factor MafA co-segregates with diabetes (MafA-MODY) and non-syndromic insulinomatosis. We recently investigated the effects of genetic background on MafAS64F-driven dysglycemia in genetically diverse mice harboring this mutation. Here we leveraged the effects of genetic background on phenotypic penetrance to map quantitative trait loci (QTL) potentially modifying glycemia in response to this variant. We investigated MafaS64F/+ mice from an F2 intercross of the C57BL/6J and SJL/J genetic backgrounds through oral glucose tolerance testing at 4, 5, 6, and 8 weeks of age to evaluate glucose tolerance and glycemic trajectory. All F2 mice were genetically monitored for single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) between the C57BL/6J and SJL/J backgrounds, allowing us to identify modifying loci on 6 chromosomes (2, 126 Mbp; 3, 59 Mbp and 103 Mbp; 7, 47 Mbp; 11 45 Mbp; 13, 4 Mbp; and 16, 85-97 Mbp), containing 172 candidate genes. For example, known MODY genes Abcc8 (Sur1) and Kcnj11 (Kir6.2) are within the QTL region on chromosome 7 and contain polymorphisms between backgrounds that may impart combinatorial effects on the phenotypic penetrance of MafAS64F-mediated dysglycemia
authors: Maurer M, Johnson L, Lee D, Yandell BS, Keller MP, Cha J.

title: Amino acid clustering and epistasis guide sequence-based prediction of phenotype modulation
abstract: Protein sequences encode the molecular information necessary for their biological function. As functional adaptation often emerges from combined effects of multiple positions, understanding how sequence variation gives rise to functional differences remains a central challenge. Here, we developed an improved strategy to identify phenotype modulating positions and use them to predict phenotypes, by relating amino acid identity to experimentally measured quantitative properties across families. Using family-specific sequence-phenotype datasets, our results show that epistasis plays a crucial role in phenotype modulation. Position specific amino acid clustering further improved performance indicating that key functional information is often captured by broad physicochemical amino acid classes, with hydrophobicity playing a crucial role in phenotype modulation. Our identified phenotype modulating positions involve both proximal and distal sites relative to functional sites. While the former is captured by individual positions, the latter is captured when epistasis is taken into account. Comparison with experimentally identified positions showed partial recovery of known functionally relevant residues, while at the same time revealing candidate positions that may contribute to phenotypic variation. Taken together, these results suggest that quantitative phenotypes are often governed by a network of interacting amino acid residues and may be engineered by a limited amount of sequence modifications. This finding highlights the potential of our framework to deepen our understanding of protein function, evolution, and adaptation, providing new targets for the rational modulation and engineering of protein phenotypes.
authors: Hernandez Berthet AS, Sanchez IE, Noguera ME, Roman EA.

title: Allele-selective knockdown of mutant DNAJB6 improves molecular features in a primary mouse myotube model of LGMDD1
abstract: Dominant variants in DNAJB6 cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy D1 (LGMDD1), a progressive myopathy associated with disrupted protein homeostasis. Because complete loss of DNAJB6 is embryonic lethal in mice, we evaluated allele-selective knockdown as a strategy to reduce mutant DNAJB6 while preserving wild-type protein. We generated a knock-in mouse carrying an N-terminal 3xFLAG tag on the wild-type Dnajb6 allele, allowing endogenous wild-type and F90I DNAJB6, the murine equivalent of human F89I, to be measured within the same sample. Flag-LGMDD1 mice recapitulated the functional, myopathological, and biochemical features seen in other LGMDD1 models and in human disease. F90I DNAJB6 was more abundant and degraded more slowly than wild-type DNAJB6, and LGMDD1 muscle and primary myotubes showed altered protein handling at baseline and following proteostatic stress. Comparative proteomic analyses identified DNAJA4 as a candidate marker responsive to pathogenic DNAJB6 activity. A two-stage mismatch screen identified a lead candidate siRNA with 264-fold selectivity for F90I DNAJB6. In primary Flag-LGMDD1 myotubes, this siRNA selectively reduced F90I DNAJB6 and shifted several baseline and stress-dependent molecular abnormalities involving p62, HSP70, DNAJA4, and markers associated with unfolded protein response signaling toward control values. These findings establish cellular proof of concept for allele-selective knockdown in LGMDD1.
authors: Vohra A, Haller M, Paing MM, Dam ABL, Daw JA, Bengoechea R, Pittman SK, Wang T, Yuede CM, Miller TM, True HL, Harper SQ, Chou T, Weihl CC, Findlay AR.

title: Regional Vulnerability to Brain Metastases Reflects Structural, Metabolic and Genetic Organization of the Healthy Brain
abstract: Background:  Brain metastases (BMs), the most common intracranial tumor, do not distribute uniformly throughout the brain, but instead preferentially localize to specific regions. Building on known associations with perfusion and the gray-white matter junction, we hypothesized that regional vulnerability to BMs also reflects the cellular and molecular organization of the healthy brain. Methods: In a discovery cohort of 1,406 patients, we generated a voxelwise map of BM distribution and compared it with normative atlases of brain microstructure, vasculature, metabolism, cell-type composition, and gene expression. Associations were tested for replication in an independent multicenter validation cohort of 1,209 patients. Results: In the discovery cohort, BM frequency was higher near the gray-white matter junction and in regions with greater cerebral perfusion, glucose metabolism, and mitochondrial density. At the cellular level, BM frequency was inversely related to astrocyte and microglial transcriptional signatures. Using normative gene expression maps derived from postmortem healthy brain tissue, we identified 17 genes spatially associated with BM vulnerability and specific to metastases relative to other intracranial lesion types. These associations replicated in the validation cohort. The immune checkpoint gene LAG3 ranked among the ten genes most positively associated with metastatic vulnerability across all genes tested (r = 0.40-0.45, p Conclusions: These findings suggest that BM vulnerability reflects healthy brain organization and identify LAG-3, a clinically targetable immune checkpoint, as a candidate link between regional brain immune biology and metastatic colonization.

title: Safety and tolerability of RJx-01 to maintain muscle integrity in patients following hospitalisation with an acute exacerbation of COPD (MINT-COPD): protocol for a phase IIa randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial
abstract: Introduction:  Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is one of the leading causes of global disability and disability-adjusted life years. One of the key systemic features of COPD is impaired skeletal muscle mass and function, termed sarcopenia. The recognition of skeletal muscle dysfunction as a treatable trait in COPD opens a therapeutic avenue for pharmacological development, with the aim of improving physical function and reducing healthcare utilisation. A novel combination drug, RJx-01, was identified as a candidate therapy for sarcopenia based on preclinical evidence. The primary aim of this study is to evaluate the safety and tolerability of RJx-01 compared with placebo following hospitalisation with an acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD), when acute deterioration of skeletal muscle integrity is observed. Exploratory efficacy analyses will assess differences in muscle function, mass, and multi-omic-derived outcomes.  Methods and analysis The MINT-COPD trial is a phase IIa, single centre, randomised controlled trial (RCT). Eighty participants admitted to hospital with AECOPD will be randomly assigned 1:1 to receive either oral RJx-01 or placebo, once daily for 24 weeks. The primary outcome is safety and tolerability of RJx-01 compared with placebo in COPD patients. Exploratory objectives aim to assess the preliminary effects of AECOPD-associated hospitalisation and RJx-01 treatment on muscle mass, function, and fatiguability, as well as patient reported symptoms and frailty. The optional skeletal muscle biopsy sub-study aims to assess the effects of AECOPD on proteomic and transcriptomic markers of skeletal muscle.

title: Cholinergic modulation engages a CHRM1-IL-17 neuroimmune axis to promote diabetic wound repair
abstract: Chronic non-healing wounds are a major complication of diabetes, where persistent inflammation fails to transition into effective tissue repair (1-3). Here we identify cholinergic modulation as a mechanism that promotes productive inflammation and diabetic wound healing. Using a healing-associated fibroblast signature derived from single-cell profiling of human diabetic foot ulcers (3), we identified the acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitor metrifonate as a candidate inducer of reparative wound programs. Topical delivery accelerated healing in diabetic mice and increased acetylcholine availability within the wound. Complementary receptor pharmacology identified muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 1 (CHRM1) as the principal receptor mediating the reparative response. Transcriptomic and cellular analyses revealed early induction of IL-17-associated inflammatory programs and enrichment of CHRM1⁺NK1.1⁺ innate lymphocytes. Depletion of NK1.1⁺ cells or neutralization of IL-17A abolished the pro-healing effect, whereas spatial transcriptomics revealed treatment-associated organization of NK cells within vascular niches. Localized treatment further promoted repair in diabetic porcine wounds and human skin models. Together, these findings identify a CHRM1-IL-17 neuroimmune axis linking cholinergic modulation to diabetic wound repair and establish local AChE inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy for chronic wounds.

title: FACT frees Ubp10 from nucleosome sequestration after rapid H2B deubiquitination
abstract: Chromatin-modifying enzymes must engage their substrate, act on it and release it, but which step limits their turnover is unclear. Using three-color single-molecule fluorescence, we directly visualized the yeast deubiquitinase Ubp10 removing ubiquitin from H2B on individual nucleosomes. Ubp10 cleaved the mark within seconds of binding, without detectable DNA unwrapping, yet it did not let go: ~80% of nucleosomes remained bound after 45 minutes, and unmodified nucleosomes formed similarly long-lived complexes. Ubp10 turnover is therefore limited by release rather than catalysis. The histone chaperone FACT relieved this bottleneck by accelerating Ubp10-nucleosome dissociation. In living yeast, nuclear depletion of the FACT subunit Spt16 increased the slowly diffusing, chromatin-bound fraction of nucleoplasmic Ubp10. These findings identify FACT-dependent release as a likely mechanism for recycling Ubp10 on chromatin. More broadly, a nucleosome can sequester the enzyme acting on it, making enzyme release a step at which chromatin modification can be controlled.
authors: Merino-Urteaga R, Zaehringer J, Nune M, Wolberger C, Ha T.

title: Parasitic manipulations may determine the fate of ecosystems
abstract: The ecological importance of parasites has been increasingly recognized. Beyond effects on host survival and longevity, parasites induce phenotypic changes in their hosts that alter species interactions. Such changes are often called parasitic manipulations, a common phenomenon in which parasites alter the phenotypes of their hosts to increase their own fitness. In my manuscript, I introduce the idea that parasitic manipulations can determine the fate of ecosystems by directing them towards alternative stable states. Starting from a solitary, stochastic infection event, parasitic manipulations can generate positive feedback loops that practically irreversibly push an ecosystem along divergent developmental pathways. The specific path taken depends on the transmission strategy of the manipulative parasite colonizing the naïve community first. Using three ecologically realistic scenarios, I demonstrate how particular manipulative strategies can drive the assembly of communities that are virtually resistant to the invasion of alternative manipulative strategies. Furthermore, I outline how ecosystems, which I call ‘naïve to parasites’, arise and explain why such scenarios are likely to become more frequent in the Anthropocene, making parasitic manipulations increasingly important drivers of ecosystem dynamics. I then discuss possible empirical tests of this hypothesis and its potential limitations. Finally, I position my hypothesis within established ecological theory such as ecosystem engineering, regime shift theory, and the manipulative microbiome hypothesis.
authors: Gopko M.

title: Design, Additive Fabrication, and Prototype Validation of 3D-Printed PETG Microalgal Curtain- Wall Modules with Embedded Control
abstract: Abstract  Building-integrated photobioreactors require façade components that reconcile geometric adaptability, manufacturability, liquid containment, modularity, and operational monitoring. This study develops a 3D-printed PETG microalgal curtain-wall module integrating parametric design, additive fabrication, embedded sensing, and prototype operation. Nine Rhino/Grasshopper-generated variants (150 × 150 mm) exhibited closed-mesh areas of 707.0–729.4 cm² and predicted filament demand of 29.75–30.54 g (CV 0.87%). Recorded printing times ranged from 100 to 125 min (CV 7.87%). A continuous single-wall spiral-vase strategy enabled transparent reactor prototypes for liquid filling and circulation. An STM32-based system provided multi-source sensing and rule-based pump actuation. Prototype tests showed liquid containment, pump-driven circulation with Spirulina (Arthrospira) culture medium, and preliminary multi-module assembly. The results establish the prototype-level building-engineering feasibility of additively manufactured bio-reactive curtain-wall modules while identifying the requirements for future façade-scale performance validation.
authors: Sheng B, Guo Y, Feng M, Chen Y, Zheng X, Chen L, Bardón CC, Chao Z, Bao D, Valladares OP.

title: Endophytic colonization by Beauveria bassiana induces steroidal glycoalkaloids accumulation in tomato and suppresses Tuta absoluta performance
abstract: Abstract    Beauveria bassiana  is widely used as an entomopathogen in sustainable pest management, and its endophytic colonization has been increasingly recognized as a potential means of priming plant defence against herbivores. Here we show that root drenching of tomato with  B. bassiana  substantially reduced the fitness of  Tuta absoluta  : larval development was prolonged by 2.1 days, fourth-instar larval weight dropped by 34%, pupal weight by 22%, and pupation rate, emergence rate and female fecundity all declined significantly. Foliar spray application produced weaker effects, affecting only pupal weight and emergence rate. No  B. bassiana  was re-isolated from insect bodies, ruling out direct infection and pointing to a plant-mediated mechanism. Transcriptomic profiling of  T. absoluta  larvae feeding on colonized plants revealed the upregulation of detoxification-related metabolic pathways, particularly cytochrome P450 genes. To test whether this response was triggered by steroidal glycoalkaloids (SGAs), we fed larvae on tomato mutants with reduced or elevated SGA content. Larvae feeding on SGA-knockout mutants showed no changes in detoxification enzyme activity or development relative to controls, whereas those feeding on SGA-overexpressing mutants exhibited strong developmental inhibition and a marked increase in cytochrome P450 activity. These results demonstrate that endophytic  B. bassiana  primes tomato defence against  T. absoluta  specifically through SGA induction. Our findings establish a mechanistic basis for integrating entomopathogenic fungi with plant innate immunity in pest management.
authors: He L, Chen H, Yan G, Wang Z, Liu W, Liu H, Wang Z.

title: Glabranin counteracts MAFLD by stimulating liver lipid catabolism via the PKA-AMPK axis
abstract: Abstract    Background:  Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) is the most prevalent chronic liver disorder worldwide and remains without effective pharmacological interventions capable of targeting the underlying metabolic dysfunction. Here, we investigated the therapeutic potential and molecular mechanisms of action of glabranin, a prenylated flavanone isolated from  Glycyrrhiza glabra  leaves, in complementary  in vitro  and  in vivo  models of steatosis.  Methods:  Steatosis was induced in HepG2 cells by exposure to oleic and palmitic acids, and in  Drosophila melanogaster  through high-fat diet feeding. The effects of glabranin on lipid droplets accumulation and metabolic homeostasis were evaluated using integrated phenotypic, proteomic, and kinome analyses.  Results:  Glabranin markedly reduced intracellular lipid droplets accumulation in oleic/palmitic acid-overloaded HepG2 cells, as well as in Huh7 cells. Integrated proteomic and kinome profiling revealed robust activation of the cAMP-PKA-AMPK signaling axis, accompanied by coordinated induction of lipid-catabolic pathways. Mechanistically, glabranin enhanced lipolysis and lipophagy, promoted mitochondrial β-oxidation, and stimulated NRF2-dependent antioxidant responses, thereby restoring metabolic flexibility and reducing lipotoxic stress. The metabolic benefits of glabranin were confirmed in  vivo  using a high-fat diet-induced  D. melanogaster  model. Glabranin supplementation significantly decreased lipid accumulation, restored locomotor performance, and improved survival, demonstrating efficacy across evolutionarily conserved metabolic pathways.  Conclusions:  Our findings identify glabranin as a previously unrecognized metabolic modulator that reprograms hepatic lipid metabolism through activation of the cAMP-PKA-AMPK network. By simultaneously enhancing lipid droplets clearance, mitochondrial fatty acid utilization, and antioxidant defense, glabranin effectively counteracts steatotic state in both  in vitro  and  in vivo  models. These results position glabranin as a promising candidate for the prevention and treatment of early-stage MAFLD and provide a strong rationale for its further preclinical development.
authors: Moukham H, Spandri G, Beghelli D, Santoro V, Serio S, Piccinelli AL, Maffioli E, Tedeschi G, Labra M, Schrul B, Tripodi F, Coccetti P.

title: HDAC1 K438 Lactylation is Associated with NF-κB-related Microglial Inflammatory Activation in Alzheimer’s Disease
abstract: Abstract    Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is characterized by persistent microglial activation, yet how metabolic stress contributes to inflammatory reprogramming remains unclear. This study investigated the role of histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) lactylation in microglial inflammation. HDAC1 and global protein lactylation were examined in human AD prefrontal cortex and 5×FAD mice, alongside human single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic analyses. Proteomic and lactylomic profiling of BV2 microglia exposed to hypoxia and lipopolysaccharide (LPS-Hy) was used to characterize inflammatory reprogramming and identify candidate HDAC1 lactylation sites, followed by molecular docking and mutagenesis. HDAC1 lactylation and global protein lactylation signals were elevated in IBA1-positive microglia in human AD tissue and 5×FAD mice and associated with activation markers. Transcriptomic analyses revealed no corresponding increase in HDAC1 mRNA in AD microglia, implicating post-translational modification in HDAC1-associated inflammatory regulation. Lactylomic profiling identified K438 as a major HDAC1 lactylation site, while molecular docking suggested structural compatibility between lactate and the HDAC1 catalytic pocket. Wild-type HDAC1 enhanced LPS-Hy-induced  Il1b  and  Nos2  expression, whereas the K438R mutant abolished detectable HDAC1 lactylation and lost this enhancing effect, accompanied by altered total p65 abundance. Cross-dataset integration identified a conserved immune–metabolic microglial module across human AD, Aβ-positive microglia, and LPS-Hy-treated BV2 cells, with HDAC1 as a highly connected network hub. Together, these findings support a role for HDAC1 K438 lactylation in regulating microglial inflammatory responses under metabolic and inflammatory stress, highlighting a potential non-histone post-translational mechanism linking cellular stress to immune-metabolic reprogramming and a candidate target for further investigation in AD.
authors: Fei X, Wang X, Zhang J, Liu F, Zhu L, Ma C.

title: Development of a General Academic Written Chinese Word List: A Corpus-Based Approach
abstract: Abstract  This study developed the General Academic Written Chinese Word List (GAWCWL) as a supplementary vocabulary resource for Chinese for Academic Purposes (CAP). A 9.95-million-token corpus was compiled through stratified random sampling of texts published between 2012 and 2022 across ten disciplines and four written academic text types. Word selection used a five-dimensional procedure: Jieba segmentation (candidate extraction), full exclusion of Hanyu Shuiping Kaoshi (HSK) Levels 1–6 words, frequency and range thresholds, and Discipline Measurement (DM). The resulting list contained 487 entries and accounted for 8.58% of tokens in the development corpus, compared with 7.66% for the Chinese Academic Vocabulary List and 4.86% for the General Academic Chinese Vocabulary List after HSK vocabulary was excluded from all three lists. Across the four text types, GAWCWL coverage ranged from 7.22% to 9.56%, with a coefficient of variation of 12.2%. In supplementary external evaluation, the GAWCWL covered 8.79% of tokens in an independent corpus of aquatic science journal articles and 2.74% in a science-fiction corpus, indicating higher coverage in the academic than in the non-academic texts examined. The GAWCWL provides a corpus-informed reference for vocabulary support beyond the specified HSK baseline in written academic Chinese. Its broader applicability and instructional effectiveness require further investigation.
authors: Jiang Y, Tongpoon-Patanasorn A.

title: Synthesis, DFT study, molecular docking and antibacterial evaluation of a nitrophenyl-thienochromenone azo ligand and its Mn(II), Co(II) and Fe(II) complexes
abstract: Abstract    The nitrophenyl-substituted azo-thienochromenone ligand 3-amino-1-[(E)-(4-nitrophenyl)diazenyl]-4  H  -thieno[3,4-c]chromen-4-one (  2  ), obtained by diazo coupling on 3-amino-4  H  -thieno[3,4-c]chromen-4-one prepared via a modified Gewald cyclisation, was reacted with MnCl₂·4H₂O, CoCl₂·6H₂O and FeSO₄·7H₂O to give three new complexes,  3  (Mn),  4  (Co) and  5  (Fe), characterised by HRESI-MS, UV-Vis, FT-IR, multinuclear/2D NMR and powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD), which together established bidentate coordination of the ligand through the lactone carbonyl oxygen and the deprotonated aromatic amine nitrogen, leaving the azo bridge and nitro group uncoordinated. DFT calculations (B3LYP/6-311 + + G(d,p)) showed the HOMO-LUMO gap narrowing on complexation in the order  4  (1.679 eV) 5  (2.085 eV) 3  (2.513 eV) 2  (2.737 eV), with  4  showing the highest electrophilicity index (ω = 16.143 eV). Molecular docking against E. coli DNA gyrase (7AB4), S. aureus DNA gyrase (1MWT) and P. aeruginosa lectin LecB (4NG2) ranked  3  as the most promising candidate, outperforming ciprofloxacin on 7AB4 and 1MWT, and broth microdilution confirmed this trend, with  3  giving the lowest MICs of the series (16 µg/mL against E. coli and S. aureus) while  5  was the only bactericidal compound against P. aeruginosa (MBC/MIC = 1). Overall, complexation of  2  with Mn(II), Co(II) and Fe(II) consistently enhanced antibacterial activity relative to the free ligand, with the manganese complex  3  standing out as the most active and computationally consistent candidate, supporting azo-thienochromenone metal complexes as a viable platform for antibacterial drug development.

title: Systems Integration of the SARS-CoV-2 ORF7b–c-Myc–PVT1–miR-145/214–HIF-2α–TFRC–CCL2 Axis in Long COVID Pathobiology and Epigenetic Reversal
abstract: Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC), clinically designated as Long COVID, affects over 400 million individuals globally, presenting as a multisystem disorder characterized by chronic microvascular endotheliitis, exertional exhaustion, pathological cardiac remodeling, and systemic autoimmunity [1–3]. While acute COVID-19 is primarily initiated by viral entry via ACE2, persistent post-viral sequelae are driven by sustained expression of viral accessory factors and host transcriptional hijacking [1,2,4]. Here, we establish a comprehensive systems-biology framework demonstrating that SARS-CoV-2 accessory protein Orf7b overexpression drives high-amplitude transactivation of master oncogene c-Myc, which hypertranscribes long non-coding RNA PVT1 [1,2]. The resultant multi-isoform surge of PVT1 linear, circPVT1, and ecDNA transcripts acts as a high-capacity competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) network that sequesters protective host microRNA-145-5p (miR-145-5p) and miR-214 [1,2]. This dual microRNA depletion initiates a secondary derepression cascade involving hypoxia-inducible factor-2α (HIF-2α / EPAS1) and Transferrin Receptor 1 (TFRC / TfR1) [1,2,4,5]. Dense TFRC accumulation accelerates diferric transferrin endocytosis, expanding the intracellular labile iron pool, driving ROS-dependent transcription and secretion of chemokine CCL2, and provoking concentric cardiac hypertrophy, microvascular endotheliitis, ACE2-independent viral entry, and TLR7-regulated TFR1-driven B-cell autoimmunity [1–6]. Crucially, we demonstrate that this entire pathological network can be reversed upstream by host-directed p53/NRF2-based epigenetic shielding via miR-145-5p transactivation, 3'-UTR transcript cleavage, and mitochondrial cristae restoration [1,2,7].
authors: Lakshmanane B.

title: Room temperature lysis incubation improves DNA yield in the Norgen Plant/Fungi DNA Isolation Kit across multiple plant species.
abstract: PremiseCommercial plant DNA extraction kits typically include a 65°C lysis incubation step, inherited from cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB)-based methods. Recent work suggests that cooler lysis temperatures can improve DNA purity in CTAB extractions; whether this also improves yield in CTAB-based column kits has not been tested.Methods and resultsWe compared room temperature (RT, ~25°C) and 65°C lysis incubation using the Norgen Plant/Fungi DNA Isolation Kit (CTAB-based lysis buffer) across six plant species in a paired split-tissue design (n = 59 pairs). RT incubation significantly increased Qubit fluorometric DNA yield by 47% overall, with a significant treatment × species interaction. RT-extracted Cucurbita pepo DNA was compatible with genotyping-by-sequencing. In a focused generalization test, the modification did not improve yield with the Qiagen DNeasy Plant Mini Kit, whose lysis buffer uses the anionic detergent sodium dodecyl sulphate, indicating that the effect is specific to kit lysis chemistry.ConclusionsFor the Norgen kit, omitting the heating step is a zero-cost modification that significantly improves DNA yield and the ratio of absorbance at 260 nm and 230 nm (A260/A230 purity ratio) for most eudicot species tested, with no loss of downstream compatibility. This benefit appears specific to CTAB-based lysis and should be validated for each kit and species before adoption.
authors: Ohali S, Abu-Nassar J, Shalit-Kaneh A, Draru E, Oren E.

title: Development of Virus-Mimicking Artificial Positive Controls for TaqMan® real-time PCR assays.
abstract: TaqMan® real time PCR is the gold standard for virus detection, yet laboratories face challenges with acquiring positive controls, due to biosecurity restrictions and limited supply. Building on virus-mimicking artificial positive controls (ViMAPC) used in endpoint PCR, we have developed ViMAPCs for TaqMan® PCR. We utilize a sister virus taxon to create a positive control template which contains the target virus primer and probe sequences. As a proof-of-concept the novel strategy has been tested using both RNA and DNA viruses. ViMAPCs were tested in parallel with targeted virus-infected material with cross-verification tests carried out in a second laboratory and all met preset equivalence criteria. The technology provides highly reproducible positive controls for virus diagnostics allowing for the use of TaqMan® PCR when the procurement of true positive controls is difficult, such as a new incursion or biosecurity breaches.
authors: Atanda H, Stainton D, Osundahunsi B, Sierra-Mejia A, Singh S, Tzanetakis IE.

title: Ciprofol protects against hypoxia/reoxygenation-induced injury in cardiac microvascular endothelial cells via the DYRK1A/PI3K/AKT signaling pathway.
abstract: ObjectiveMyocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury is a major complication following revascularization therapy for ischemic heart disease. Ciprofol (CIP) has been proven to protect cardiomyocytes from I/R-induced apoptosis, yet its role and underlying molecular mechanisms in vascular endothelial cells under hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) conditions remain incompletely elucidated. This study aimed to investigate the protective effects of CIP on I/R injury and its associated molecular mechanisms.MethodsC57BL/6 J mice were subjected to myocardial I/R injury. An in vitro H/R model was established in HUVECs to mimic myocardial I/R injury. The histopathological analysis was conducted by H&E staining. After H/R stimulation and/or CIP treatment, multiple cellular biological functions and molecular markers were assessed: cell viability and proliferation were detected via CCK-8 assay and EdU staining; colony formation ability was evaluated by cell cloning assay; cell migration capacity was measured through wound-healing assay; apoptosis was analyzed using TUNEL staining and Annexin V-FITC/PI flow cytometry; DNA damage was assessed by detecting the expression of ATM, ATR, γ-H2AX, and PARP1; cell cycle progression was determined by the expression of Cyclin B and cdc2; and the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptotic pathway was examined via the expression of Bcl-2, Bax, and Caspase-3. RNA-seq and untargeted metabolomics were conducted to identify the potential therapeutic mechanisms of CIP. DYRK1A, a key candidate gene, was validated by RNA-seq, metabolomics, and qRT-PCR. Overexpression and knockdown experiments were performed to confirm the role of the DYRK1A/PI3K/AKT signaling axis in CIP-mediated protection against H/R injury.ResultsThe levels of cardiomyocyte apoptosis and myocardial enzymes were decreased in CIP-treated mice compared with the H/R group. In H/R-injured HUVECs, CIP dose-dependently restored cell viability, enhanced EdU incorporation, and accelerated cell invasion ability. Simultaneously, CIP reduced apoptosis and suppressed activation of caspase-3. Meanwhile, CIP alleviated DNA damage responses, shown decreased levels of γ-H2AX, ATM, and ATR, and restored PARP1 expression. Mechanistically, CIP significantly modulated tyrosine metabolism and downregulated DYRK1A expression, leading to the activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway. Notably, overexpression of DYRK1A abolished the protective effects of CIP, whereas DYRK1A knockdown reversed H/R-induced cell injury and further potentiated the protective function of CIP, confirming that the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway is a critical mediator of this process.ConclusionCIP promotes proliferation, migration and invasion, while inhibiting apoptosis, in H/R-injured HUVECs by regulating the DYRK1A/PI3K/AKT signaling axis. These findings highlight CIP as a promising endothelial-protective agent for the treatment of I/R-related vascular disorders.
authors: Duan L, He X, He G, Zhou T, Sun M.

title: Predicting chlorination reaction kinetics via a substructure token-based pre-trained model.
abstract: Prediction of chlorination reaction kinetics is essential for understanding the transformation of organic pollutants during water treatment, but model development is constrained by the limited availability of experimental kinetic data. Here, we developed SPEBERT, a pre-trained chemical language model employing substructure-level tokens, and integrated it with an artificial neural network (ANN) to predict second-order chlorination rate constants (kapp) for 257 organic compounds. Among all evaluated frameworks, SPEBERT-83M-ANN achieved the best performance (Rtest2=0.75, RMSE=1.00, MAE=0.73) and showed better generalization than frameworks without pre-training. Applicability-domain (AD) analyses further showed that prediction performance was associated with both structural and kinetic response coverage of the training set. SHAP analysis identified substructures related to predicted chlorination reactivity and revealed that their SHAP contributions varied with their local bonding environments. Application to 642 river-basin contaminants prioritized seven primary candidates within the AD for subsequent investigation of DBP formation. These results demonstrate the utility of the substructure token-based pre-trained molecular representations for chlorination kinetics prediction under limited data. The framework also provides an interpretable approach for chlorination kinetics prediction and a practical strategy for the prioritization of candidates for subsequent DBP formation investigation.
authors: Li R, Liu Q, Xie Y, Du C, Lin L, Wang D.

title: Comparative cytotoxic, apoptotic, cell-cycle, gene-expression, and antioxidant effects of lutein and cabbage extract in AGS gastric cancer cells.
abstract: Gastric cancer remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, underscoring the need to investigate potential therapeutic candidates. Lutein, a naturally occurring dietary carotenoid, has demonstrated biological activities of interest in cancer research. This study evaluated the effects of lutein on cell viability, apoptosis, cell-cycle distribution, selected cancer-related gene expression, and total antioxidant capacity in AGS gastric cancer cells, using GES-1 non-malignant gastric epithelial cells as a comparator. Cabbage extract was evaluated separately to assess its cellular effects. Lutein and cabbage extract were tested individually. Cell viability and half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC₅₀) were assessed using the MTT assay. Apoptosis was evaluated by Annexin V-FITC/propidium iodide staining and flow cytometry, and cell-cycle distribution was analyzed by propidium iodide staining and flow cytometry. The expression of ERBB2, CCND1, MICAL2, PAK1, and MCC was measured by RT-qPCR. Total antioxidant capacity (TAC) was assessed using an ABTS-based assay. Lutein reduced AGS cell viability in a dose- and time-dependent manner, with an IC₅₀ of approximately 12.5 µg/mL after 48 and 72 h of treatment. Neither lutein nor cabbage extract reached an IC₅₀ in GES-1 cells within the tested concentration range. Flow-cytometric analysis showed that late apoptosis in AGS cells reached 87.4% following lutein treatment, compared with 38.0% following cabbage extract treatment. Lutein treatment was also associated with an increase in the S-phase population in AGS cells to 49.5%, compared with 33.5% in the PBS-treated control. RT-qPCR analysis showed reduced mRNA expression of ERBB2, CCND1, MICAL2, and PAK1 and increased MCC mRNA expression in lutein-treated AGS cells. Furthermore, lutein significantly reduced the measured TAC value in AGS cells, whereas no statistically significant treatment-related differences were detected in GES-1 cells. Under the experimental conditions tested, lutein produced more pronounced antiproliferative and apoptosis-associated effects in AGS cells than cabbage extract. These responses were accompanied by altered cell-cycle distribution, changes in the expression of selected cancer-related genes, and reduced measured total antioxidant capacity. However, the study did not establish the specific apoptotic pathways involved, validate the observed transcriptional changes at the protein level, or determine whether redox modulation causally contributed to the cellular effects. Further studies using additional cell models, protein-level validation, pathway-specific assays, and in vivo models are required to clarify the mechanisms and assess the broader relevance of these findings.
authors: Shirazi M, Shahanipour K, Monajemi R, Yazdanpanahi N.

title: The virulent milRNA Foc-milR87 manipulates host hormone signaling to promote root infection by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense.
abstract: Banana (Musa spp.), a critical global staple and cash crop, is facing severe threats from Fusarium wilt caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense Tropical Race 4 (Foc TR4). Deciphering the molecular pathogenesis of Foc TR4 and its immune regulatory network with the host is essential for developing novel control strategies targeting host resistance genes. Foc-milR87 is a virulent milRNA that targets the banana AP2/ERF family transcription factor MaPTI6L, but how it regulates downstream immune network in banana is still mysterious. Here, we analyzed transcriptomic data from banana roots infected with wild-type Foc TR4 (XJZ2) and Foc-milR87 knockout mutant (ΔFoc-milR87) to investigate Foc-milR87's regulatory role in pathogenesis. Knockout of the Foc-milR87 precursor significantly impaired Foc TR4's root infection and colonization capability. Transcriptomic analysis and experimental evidence revealed that Foc-milR87 modulates banana salicylic acid, ethylene, and abscisic acid pathways to promote root infection. Bioinformatic analysis identified numerous transcription factors from AP2/ERF, WRKY, and bHLH families as potential downstream targets, suggesting that Foc-milR87 manipulates these regulators to reprogram the host transcriptome and disturb plant immunity. This study elucidates the molecular role of fungal milRNA in early pathogenesis, offering novel insights for banana wilt resistance breeding.
authors: He C, Cheng S, Gan R, Huang R, Kong G, Xi P, Jiang Z, Situ J, Li M.

title: Structural dynamics and energetic basis of conserved ACE2 binding across SARS-CoV-2 variants.
abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD) mediates viral entry through binding to the human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor. Since the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, numerous variants have accumulated mutations within the RBD, particularly among Omicron sublineages. Here, molecular dynamics simulations and molecular mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann surface area (MM-PBSA) calculations were used to investigate RBD-ACE2 interactions across SARS-CoV-2 variants, including Alpha, Gamma, Delta, Epsilon, Kappa, Mu, and Omicron subvariants BA.1, BA.2, BA.3, BA.4/BA.5, BA.2.12.1, BA.2.75, BA.4.6, BA.5.9, XBB.1.5, XBB.1.16, EG.5, BA.2.86, JN.1, NB.1.8.1, and XFG. Global structural properties, including backbone stability, compactness, and solvent accessibility, were highly conserved across variants. In contrast, residue-level flexibility was concentrated within the receptor-binding motif (RBM), with Omicron subvariants exhibiting greater heterogeneity than earlier variants. Essential dynamics analysis indicated that variant evolution primarily modulates the extent of conformational sampling along a conserved dominant mode of motion. Hydrogen bond analysis showed that substitutions at residue 493 altered local RBD-ACE2 hydrogen-bonding networks while preserving a conserved set of interface-stabilising interactions. MM-PBSA analysis demonstrated that binding was primarily driven by favourable electrostatic interactions localised to key RBM residues, particularly in early Omicron subvariants. However, these gains were largely offset by opposing polar solvation penalties, resulting in only modest variation in predicted ACE2 binding affinity. Together, these findings indicate that SARS-CoV-2 evolution maintains RBD-ACE2 binding through compensatory structural and energetic changes despite extensive mutation of the RBD.
authors: Liang JJ, Karagiannis TC.

title: Integrated multi-omics identifies PTGDS-enriched mature oligodendrocyte state remodeling in paraquat-associated Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Paraquat (PQ) is an environmentally relevant herbicide associated with neurotoxicity and Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, yet the key molecular determinants linking PQ exposure to PD and the cellular states in which these alterations occur remain incompletely understood. We integrated network toxicology, human PD transcriptomics, machine learning, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics, virtual perturbation, model-inferred protein analysis, molecular docking, and tissue validation to characterize PQ-associated molecular and cellular remodeling. Integrating PQ-associated targets with PD-related genes identified 293 candidates, among which prostaglandin D2 synthase (PTGDS) was consistently prioritized by random forest, XGBoost, and LASSO, with its PD-associated expression pattern reproduced across the discovery and independent validation cohorts. Single-cell analysis localized Ptgds expression predominantly to oligodendrocytes and identified two PTGDS-enriched mature oligodendrocyte (MOL) states with PQ-associated compositional patterns. CytoTRACE placed these PTGDS-enriched populations among relatively mature oligodendrocyte states. Functional analyses revealed distinct state-specific programs, with Ptgds+Mag+ MOL associated with myelin-associated programs, axon ensheathment-related programs, cholesterol metabolism, and lipid transport, whereas Ptgds+Il33+ MOL was linked to neuron-interaction-related programs, synaptic organization, cell adhesion, and neuron-glia communication. Ligand-receptor inference and spatial analyses supported state-specific changes in neuron-glia communication and spatial relationships. Spatial metabolomics showed significantly increased phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin signals in regions with higher inferred representation of Ptgds+Mag+ MOL states. Virtual Ptgds perturbation and scTranslator-based protein prediction further suggested state-specific myelin-lipid and neuron-interaction programs, while molecular docking provided preliminary structural predictions regarding a potential PQ-PTGDS interaction. Immunofluorescence further confirmed PTGDS localization in mature oligodendrocytes within the substantia nigra. Collectively, these findings identify PTGDS-enriched mature oligodendrocyte states as cellular contexts associated with PQ-related brain remodeling and extend our understanding of PQ neurotoxicity beyond classical neuron-centered mechanisms. This integrative framework provides mechanistic insight into how an environmental neurotoxicant may reshape myelin-lipid homeostasis and neuron-glia interactions in the context of PD-related brain pathology.
authors: Zhang Y, Pan R, Zhang Z, Lin J, Zheng F, Hu H, Yu G, Shao W, Guo Z, Li H, Wu S.

title: Dimensional Synthesis of Spherical Stephenson III Linkages for Upper-Limb Rehabilitation Devices
abstract: Robot-assisted shoulder rehabilitation benefits from mechanisms that guide the arm along physiological paths about a Remote Center of Motion (RCM) aligned with the shoulder. Single-actuator spherical linkages are an attractive low-cost option, but their dimensional synthesis is hindered by branch, circuit, and order defects. This paper proposes a design-optimization procedure for an actuated spherical Stephenson III linkage used as a single-drive upper-limb rehabilitation device. The displacement problem is decoupled into a base four-bar loop and a closing dyad, solved by two nested quadratic equations that give exactly the four assembly modes in closed form. The two discriminants are shown to coincide with the singularity conditions of the velocity equations, so a single positivity test detects both branch crossing and toggle configurations, while a two-bit label tracks one assembly mode along the workspace. Velocity coefficients, expressed in closed form via triple products, provide a dimensionless manipulability index for discarding candidate designs. The procedure is applied to a reaching task, and yields a defect-free, compact device with smooth velocity profiles and is compared with a previously published optimization-based synthesis of the same mechanism.
authors: Di Gregorio R.

title: Apigenin Attenuates Lipopolysaccharide-Induced Endothelial Activation and Injury-Associated Phenotypes in Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells.
abstract: BackgroundSepsis represents a severe challenge in critical‑care medicine. Protecting endothelial function and alleviating microvascular inflammation and oxidative stress help reduce sepsis‑associated mortality. Apigenin, a natural flavonoid, exerts anti‑inflammatory and anti‑oxidant effects; its mechanisms against endothelial injury relevant to sepsis remain unclear.PurposeThis study combined computational biology and in‑vitro assays to explore potential targets of apigenin against lipopolysaccharide‑triggered endothelial dysfunction.MethodsNetwork pharmacology was performed for target screening followed by GO and KEGG enrichment. Transcriptomic profiles were analyzed. Molecular docking and 100‑ns molecular dynamics simulations predicted apigenin‑protein interactions. An LPS‑stimulated HUVECs injury model was established. qRT-PCR, ELISA, flow cytometry and fluorescent probes were used to evaluate inflammation, apoptosis, reactive oxygen species and monocyte adhesion.ResultsA total of 104 intersecting targets were identified. AKT1, HSP90AA1, EGFR, ESR1 and HIF1A were potential core candidates, with PI3K‑Akt, TNF and HIF‑1 signaling possibly involved. Simulations predicted relatively stable apigenin‑protein complexes. At 40 μM, apigenin mitigated LPS‑provoked inflammatory response, oxidative stress, apoptosis and monocyte adhesion in HUVECs.ConclusionApigenin protects HUVECs from LPS‑induced endothelial injury possibly via multi‑target and multi‑pathway patterns. This study provides preliminary computational and in vitro evidence for further investigation of apigenin against LPS-triggered endothelial injury, with potential implications for sepsis-associated vascular damage that requires further in vivo validation.
authors: Wen J, Hong S, Lai J, Chen K, Li L, Jiang S.

title: Deoxycholic Acid-Grafted Carboxymethyl Chitosan Nanomicelles Embedded in Alginate Microspheres for Oral Mangiferin Delivery in Experimental Colitis.
abstract: PurposeTo develop a hierarchical polysaccharide formulation combining nanoscale loading of hydrophobic mangiferin (MGF) with microscale gastrointestinal protection, and to evaluate it in dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis.MethodsCarboxymethyl chitosan grafted with deoxycholic acid (DA-CMCS) was self-assembled with MGF into nanomicelles (MGF/DA-CMCS SNM), which were embedded by electrospray into Ca2⁺-cross-linked alginate microspheres (MGF/DA-CMCS@SA MS). It was assessed by physicochemical characterization, sequential pH release and gastrointestinal stability, carrier fluorescence imaging, cell assays, a DSS proof-of-concept model, 16S rRNA and RNA sequencing, and short-term compatibility tests.ResultsThe nanomicelles measured 120.7 ± 0.9 nm, with a PDI of 0.342 ± 0.019, a zeta potential of -24.2 ± 1.0 mV and an apparent encapsulation efficiency of 88.03% ± 0.58%; the microspheres measured 110.3 ± 2.6 µm. Alginate encapsulation suppressed release at pH 1.2 and accelerated it at intestinal pH, consistent with microspheres remaining intact in simulated gastric fluid and disintegrating in intestinal fluid. In vitro, the system scavenged radicals, lowered intracellular ROS, protected cells from oxidative injury and attenuated inflammatory macrophage activation. After oral administration, Cy5-labeled microspheres gave stronger intestinal fluorescence than nanomicelles alone; as Cy5 labeled the carrier, this reports carrier distribution, not tissue MGF concentration. In DSS colitis, it attenuated body-weight loss, DAI, colon shortening and histological damage, and was associated with epithelial barrier-marker changes and microbiota and transcriptomic shifts, with short-term in vitro and in vivo compatibility.ConclusionThe nanomicelle-in-microsphere system provides proof-of-concept intestinal pH-responsive oral delivery for MGF. Direct pharmacokinetic measurement, carrier-only controls, morphometric histopathology, mechanistic validation, longer-term safety testing and process-scale characterization remain necessary.
authors: Liu C, Li Y, Jiang N, He W, Xu Z, Zhang Y, Wu X, Jiang J, Zheng B, Lin C, Xiang Y, He Y, Xu C, Liang Z, He J.
