title: A Topology-Feature Disentangled Deep Clustering Method for scRNA-seq Based on Graph-to-MLP Distillation
abstract: AbstractMotivationGraph neural networks (GNNs), owing to their ability to model topological relationships between cells, have gradually emerged as a mainstream approach in the clustering analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. However, their practical application still faces the following challenges: (1) excessive smoothing undermines cellular heterogeneity; (2) pre-constructed graphs introduce end-to-end dependencies; (3) large-scale cellular graph computations are computationally intensive.ResultsTo fully utilise the expression profiles and topological information contained within scRNA-seq data and overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a Graph-to-MLP (G2M) knowledge distillation method incorporating AdaBoost principles, and builds upon this to develop a graph-disentangled single-cell clustering framework—scAdaG2M. This framework utilises a GNN teacher model to learn higher-order topological relationships and local neighbourhood structures between cells on a cellular graph, whilst multiple lightweight MLP student models perform feature learning in an ungraphed setting. By combining this with an AdaBoost-style dynamic reweighting strategy, the framework enhances the model’s ability to characterise cells that are difficult to distinguish, cells with blurred boundaries, and potentially rare cell populations, thereby mitigating the dilution of cellular heterogeneity caused by over-smoothing. At the same time, this framework effectively decouples graph-based modelling from graph-free reasoning, reduces the end-to-end reliance on pre-constructed graphs, and significantly reduces the computational overhead associated with large-scale cellular graphs.AvailabilityAll datasets used in this study are publicly available. Detailed information about all the single-cell datasets analyzed in this paper is provided in Supplementary Table 1. The source code is available at https://github.com/gxl1110/scAdaG2M and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21512950.Supplementary informationSupplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: ROOF: Robustness-Oriented Optimal Factorization for Fluorescence Crosstalk Correction
abstract: AbstractMotivationFluorescence bleed-through (spectral crosstalk) compromises the accuracy of signal interpretation, quantification, and visualization in multi-band fluorescence microscopy. Existing correction methods rely either on experimental calibration or blind spectral unmixing, but often suffer from limited robustness to biological variability, overcorrection artifacts, or the need for manual parameter tuning. We propose ROOF (Robustness-Oriented Optimal Factorization), a semi-blind framework that unifies calibration-based modeling with data-driven spectral unmixing. It formulates crosstalk correction as a diagonally normalized nonnegative matrix factorization problem regularized by a reference crosstalk matrix obtained from single-labeled control samples. The regularization parameter is estimated automatically via maximum likelihood, eliminating manual tuning while adapting to specimen-specific variations.ResultsExperiments on synthetic and real four-band fluorescence images demonstrate that ROOF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art crosstalk correction methods. ROOF achieves higher correction accuracy, suppresses overcorrection artifacts, preserves biologically meaningful fluorescence colocalization, and is computationally efficient. These results highlight ROOF’s robustness, efficiency, and practical value for reliable quantitative fluorescence imaging.Availability and implementationThe codes are available at https://github.com/baobabking/ROOF with DOI:10.5281/zenodo.21872937.

title: The role of nitrogen and phosphorus limitation in controlling cellular saxitoxin quotas in the harmful cyanobacteria, Dolichospermum and Aphanizomenon
abstract: Toxin production by cyanobacteria that cause harmful algal blooms (CyanoHABs) can be influenced by nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), yet little is known regarding how the macronutrient balance affects their saxitoxin (STX) content. Here, we report on the influence of N and P limitation on cellular STX quotas of multiple strains of the freshwater cyanobacteria, Dolichospermum circinale and Aphanizomenon gracile. Strains were grown semi-continuously and exposed to different concentrations of N and P after which growth rates, photosynthetic efficiency, N2 fixation rates, alkaline phosphatase activity (APA), and STX cell quotas were quantified. Despite diazotrophic capabilities, growth rates of the cyanobacteria could be limited by low levels of N or P. For all strains, low P conditions (0–1 μM orthophosphate; 0–31 μg L−1) led to significant and up to five-fold increase in STX quotas and APA, indicating that P limitation within this range of P concentrations increased cellular STX quotas. N2 fixation rates were also significantly reduced by P limitation. There were differential responses to P limitation across strains, with D. circinale strain ACMB05 exhibiting greater reductions in growth rate and photosynthetic efficiency at low P, whereas growth rates of D. circinale strain ACBU02 and A. gracile changed less despite increased STX quotas and APA. Low P conditions increased the abundance of the saxitoxin congeners GTX2, STX, and dcGTX2, which are among the more potent congeners, thereby further enhancing total toxicity of cells under low P conditions. This study demonstrates that, although N or P availability can constrain the growth of these diazotrophic cyanobacteria, P limitation consistently increased their cellular STX quotas. While mitigation of P may restrict CyanoHABs proliferation, this study identifies a potential trade-off between bloom biomass and cellular toxicity under low P conditions.

title: Exposure of Salmonella Enteritidis to ovotransferrin under egg-white conditions: cytoplasmic-membrane depolarization and increased pspG promoter activity
abstract: Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis is a major food-borne pathogen associated with the consumption of eggs and egg products. This association reflects the ability of S. Enteritidis to survive in egg white despite the presence of a large number of antimicrobial factors. One such factor is ovotransferrin, which plays a key role through its iron-chelating activity, although membrane-perturbating activity has also been observed. This study aimed to assess the membrane-damaging activity of ovotransferrin against S. Enteritidis and its contribution to egg-white antimicrobial activity. We investigated ovotransferrin’s ability to depolarize the cytoplasmic membrane of S. Enteritidis and its effect on pspG promoter activity. The pspG gene belongs to the phage shock protein (Psp) system, a membrane stress response involved in maintaining membrane integrity and proton motive force. Experiments were conducted under egg-white-like conditions using a synthetic medium mimicking the ionic composition at pH 7.9 and 9.3 (as encountered in egg white just after laying and a few days after, respectively). The effect of temperature was also investigated to consider conditions supporting bacterial growth (30 °C) or rapid bacterial killing (45 °C) in egg white. Membrane depolarization was monitored using the fluorescent probe DiSC3(5) and pspG promoter activity was assessed using a transcriptional fusion in the presence of 10% egg white. Ovotransferrin induced membrane depolarization in S. Enteritidis and increased pspG promoter activity, as did 10% egg white. While membrane depolarization was similar at both temperatures, it was enhanced at alkaline pH, whereas pspG promoter activity was reduced under combined heat and alkaline stress. Overall, this study shows that ovotransferrin contributes to egg-white-induced membrane perturbation in the S. Enteritidis strain tested and reveals that two key environmental factors (temperature and pH) modulate the bacterial stress response to egg white. These results provide new insights into the mechanisms involved in the response of S. Enteritidis to egg white conditions, including how environmental factors influence membrane perturbation and pspG promoter activity. They thereby improve our understanding of the physiology of S. Enteritidis in egg white, a major food-safety concern.

title: Responses of microbial colonies, rice growth, and yield performance to salt stress under different substrate conditions
abstract: Salt stress is one of the major abiotic stresses limiting rice production, and substrate conditions play a key role in salt stress response. The substrates in this study included S1 (river sand); S2 (river sand: laterite: peat moss = 8:1:1); S3 (river sand: laterite: peat moss = 6:2:2); S4 (river sand: laterite: peat moss = 4:3:3); S5 (laterite: peat moss = 1:1); S6 (laterite). Each bucket contained the same volume of substrate and the same mass of NaCl with fresh water as a control. In this study, yield was significantly positively correlated with thousand seed weight, setting rate, nutrient content (total phosphorus, total nitrogen, total potassium, and organic matter), significantly negatively correlated with pH, and not significantly correlated with Na+ and Cl− content. Under salt stress, the richness and diversity of the microbial communities in S1 and S4 were significantly reduced compared with their respective non-salt controls, while no significant changes occurred in S2 and S5. Salt stress increased the relative abundance of “stress tolerant” phenotypes in the S1 substrate, and Ellin6067 and MND1 had a high contribution to this phenotypes in TY1. This study provides a theoretical basis for optimizing the microecology of saline soil and salt tolerant cultivation of rice.

title: Fermentation of black wolfberry juice using a mixed culture and compound substrate: screening of lactic acid bacteria, process optimization, and quality analysis
abstract: BackgroundThis study aimed to enhance the quality of black wolfberry juice through fermentation with mixed lactic acid bacteria (LAB) and a composite substrate.MethodsOptimization identified a synergistic blend of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, and Lacticaseibacillus casei, along with a substrate consisting of black wolfberry, Potentilla anserina, and isomalto-oligosaccharide.ResultsCompared with unfermented juice, this process significantly increased total sugar and total phenolic contents by 45.16% and 43.96%, respectively, and markedly boosted antioxidant activity, with DPPH and ABTS+ radical scavenging rates improving by 48.58% and 59.47%, respectively. Multi-omics analysis revealed significant positive associations between the relative abundance of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum and specific flavor-related metabolites as well as lipid profiles, and led to distinct remodeling of lipid and triterpenoid profiles.ConclusionThe multi-omics integration systematically elucidated the potential metabolic pathways underlying the quality improvement, thus providing a theoretical reference for laboratory-scale process optimization of fermented black wolfberry juice.

title: Gut microbiota–insulin signaling axis mediates the therapeutic effects of TJZY decoction against PMOS
abstract: Introduction:TiaoJing ZhongYu (TJZY) Decoction is a traditional Chinese medicine formula used in the management of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). The molecular basis for its effects in PMOS, however, remains incompletely understood. This study assessed the therapeutic effects of TJZY Decoction in an obese rat model of PMOS and explored associated mechanisms using gut microbiome profiling, network pharmacology, and molecular biology approaches.MethodsAn obese rat model of PMOS was established using a high-fat diet and letrozole. Rats were assigned to Control, Model, low-dose TJZY (TJZY-L), high-dose TJZY (TJZY-H), and metformin (Met) groups. Body weight, estrous cyclicity, glucose tolerance, serum lipids, sex hormones, and liver and kidney function were assessed. Ovarian histopathology was evaluated by hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. 16S rRNA sequencing characterized gut microbiota and predicted functional profiles. Ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with Q exactive tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-QE-MS/MS) identified TJZY Decoction constituents, while network pharmacology predicted therapeutic targets. Real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), Western blotting, and immunohistochemistry (IHC) assessed insulin signaling and the PI3K/AKT pathway.ResultsTJZY Decoction attenuated weight gain, improved glucose tolerance and dyslipidemia, restored estrous cyclicity, and ameliorated polycystic ovarian histopathology in PMOS rats. Compared with the Model group, TJZY-H reduced serum testosterone (T) by 13.8% (P < 0.0001) and decreased the luteinizing hormone/follicle-stimulating hormone (LH/FSH) ratio by 46.1% (P < 0.0001). Treatment was associated with increased Shannon and Simpson diversity indices and altered gut microbial composition. Mean relative abundances of Allobaculum and Treponema changed from 7.74% to 13.07% and from 14.08% to 0.15%, second is an increase in the proportions of Lactobacillus and Collinsella. UHPLC-QE-MS/MS annotated 93 putative constituents, and network pharmacology linked 32 candidate constituents to 67 shared targets. TJZY-H was also associated with increased ovarian PI3K and AKT phosphorylation and reduced expression of gluconeogenesis- and inflammation-related genes.ConclusionTJZY Decoction improved reproductive and metabolic abnormalities in rats with obesity-related PMOS. These effects may involve gut microbiota remodeling and enhanced insulin/PI3K/AKT signaling; reduced expression of gluconeogenesis- and inflammation-related markers was also observed. These findings associate TJZY Decoction treatment with gut microbiota remodeling and altered ovarian insulin/PI3K/AKT signaling; a causal link between them remains to be established.

title: Phenome-wide genetic analysis of EBV EBNA1 and ZEBRA seroreactivity identifies divergent disease associations and candidate inflammatory pathways
abstract: IntroductionEpstein–Barr virus (EBV) infects most adults worldwide, but the disease relevance of host responses to distinct EBV antigens remains incompletely characterized. We compared disease associations of seroreactivity to the latency-associated antigen EBNA1 and the immediate-early lytic antigen ZEBRA and explored candidate host pathways.MethodsWe performed phenome-wide genetic screening of 1,075 phenotypes using UK Biobank summary statistics from 408,961 participants, followed by two-sample Mendelian randomization using FinnGen R11 data. Literature mining analyzed SemRep-derived subject–predicate–object (SPO) triples from 42,392 PubMed abstracts to map EBV-related diseases, genes, and therapies. Host genes were prioritized through summary-data-based MR of anti-ZEBRA GWAS and GTEx v8 eQTL data, GeneCards disease-gene intersections, and protein interaction analysis. Experiments used an ovalbumin-induced mouse asthma model and B95-8 and Raji cells.ResultsPhenome-wide screening prioritized 40 antibody–phenotype pairs. Of the 34 pairs evaluated by Mendelian randomization, 21 reached nominal significance and 19 remained significant after false discovery rate correction. Genetically proxied anti-ZEBRA seroreactivity showed positive associations with type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, nasal polyps, asthma, and hypothyroidism. In contrast, genetically proxied anti-EBNA1 seroreactivity showed inverse associations with several overlapping autoimmune phenotypes and a positive association with multiple sclerosis. Literature mining yielded 62,334 triples, with autoimmune disease concepts less frequent than malignancy or infection concepts. Frequently cited EBV-linked genes were enriched in inflammatory pathways, including NF-κB signaling. Integrative analyses identified 55 shared candidate genes, with NFKB1 showing the highest connectivity in the resulting interaction network. Lung tissues from the murine asthma model showed reduced cytoplasmic p105 and increased nuclear p50. BZLF1 overexpression in B95-8 and Raji cells was associated with reduced whole-cell p105 and increased nuclear p50. In B95-8 cells without BZLF1 overexpression, NFKB1-targeting siRNA reduced p105 abundance and was associated with higher EBV DNA levels.DiscussionEBNA1 and ZEBRA seroreactivity exhibited distinct genetically supported disease-association patterns. Integrative analyses and experimental observations prioritize NFKB1 as a candidate hub within ZEBRA-associated inflammatory pathways, providing a basis for further mechanistic investigation.

title: RIG-I–MAVS–IFN–NOXA axis coordinates antiviral innate response and apoptosis during parahenipavirus infection
abstract: Gamak virus (GAKV) is a recently identified shrew-borne paramyxovirus belonging to the genus Parahenipavirus, which also includes the zoonotic Langya virus (LayV). Despite the growing recognition of shrew-associated paramyxoviruses, the host pathways that detect infection and regulate antiviral responses remain poorly understood. In this study, we characterized host responses to GAKV infection using integrated in vitro and in vivo approaches. GAKV infection induced robust innate immune responses in A549 cells, characterized by activation of interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) and signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1), together with induction of type I interferon (IFN) and interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). Transcriptomic analysis further revealed coordinated enrichment of antiviral and intrinsic apoptosis-associated pathways, suggesting a link between innate immune signaling and apoptosis during GAKV infection. Genetic analyses identified retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) and mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) as essential mediators of antiviral signaling and apoptosis during GAKV infection. Furthermore, disruption of type I IFN-STAT1 signaling attenuated apoptosis. NOXA knockdown reduced apoptosis and enhanced viral replication. Consistent with these in vitro findings, intranasal GAKV inoculation in six-week-old female immunocompetent BALB/c mice was associated with viral RNA detection in lungs and induction of antiviral responses without overt disease. Together, these findings identify a RIG-I–MAVS–IFN–NOXA signaling axis that integrates antiviral and apoptotic responses during GAKV infection, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding host defense against parahenipaviruses.

title: Structure-guided engineering of eukaryotic Fanzor-ωRNA system enhances in vivo gene editing for dystrophin restoration in a Duchenne mouse model
abstract:
Background
                     Eukaryotic Fanzor (Fz) proteins are compact RNA-guided endonucleases homologous to prokaryotic TnpB/Cas12, offering theoretical advantages for single AAV delivery. However, their low editing efficiency and poorly defined specificity in mammals have hindered therapeutic development.
                  
                     Results
                     Here, we perform structure-guided engineering of Spizellomyces punctatus Fanzor1 nuclease (SpuFz1) to enhance its utility for in vivo genome editing and identify several Fanzor variants whose efficiencies are comparable or only slightly lower than widely-used miniature enAsCas12f1 and large-sized SpCas9. We demonstrate that catalytically dead dSpuFz1-v4.2 can be repurposed for CRISPRa-mediated transcriptional activation in a proof-of-concept manner. Genome-wide PEM-seq in mice reveal low translocation frequencies (below 0.05%, much lower than the background threshold set by the PEM-seq protocol), with no detected events attributable to off-target editing. GUIDE-seq analysis also confirms genome-wide low off-target profile for SpuFz1-v4.2 in human cells, with small amounts of off-target editing due to 3’ terminal sequence tolerability. Embryonic mRNA injection efficiently generates mutant mice. Crucially, single AAV9 delivery of SpuFz1-v4.2 in a humanized Duchenne muscular dystrophy model induces targeted exon skipping, restores dystrophin expression to ~ 10% of wild-type levels, and improves muscle contractile force.
                  
                     Conclusions
                     Structure-guided optimization overcomes the activity barrier of eukaryotic Fanzors while maintaining low off-target effect. The engineered SpuFz1-v4.2 retains the hypercompact size necessary for single AAV packaging, establishing a robust platform for in vivo gene editing. This work positions Fanzor by a preliminary proof-of-concept therapeutic study as a viable, miniature alternative to CRISPR-Cas systems for genetic disease intervention and functional genomics.

title: Chemical warfare in the rice plant rhizosphere: Diverse Pseudomonas antagonize the green alga Chlamydomonas
abstract: Algae and bacteria form dynamic partnerships that shape diverse ecosystems. The model green microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is often found in paddy rice fields, where the diversity and functional characteristics of its bacterial partners remain largely unexplored. Here, we isolated 12 bacterial strains from the rice rhizosphere and its surrounding soil. Phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA gene sequences revealed that eight isolates belong to the genus Pseudomonas. Three Pseudomonas rhizosphere strains exhibited antagonistic effects against C. reinhardtii, negatively impacting its growth, pigmentation and cell morphology. Close physical associations between the three antagonistic Pseudomonas strains and C. reinhardtii were observed in liquid cultures. Whole genome sequencing identified the antagonistic strains as Pseudomonas alloputida, Pseudomonas tohonis, and Pseudomonas asiatica. The three bacterial genomes encode several factors well-known for mediating chemical warfare. Notably, P. tohonis bears a gene cluster encoding the phenolic toxin, 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol (DAPG). DAPG inhibits the growth and alters the cell morphology of C. reinhardtii. These findings expand our understanding of the diversity of bacterial partners associated with C. reinhardtii and highlight the role of Pseudomonas rice rhizosphere-associated bacteria as potent green algal antagonists. They harbor a reservoir of common functional traits that negatively influence green algal population dynamics.
authors: Yang, X., Shetty, P., Vajrangi, B., Ul Haq, I., Mittag, M.

title: Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses
abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA-sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus- and tissue-specific regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways.
authors: Badonnel, K., Cokelaer, T., Turc, E., Monot, M., Manuguerra, J.-C., Ermonval, M., Gallo, G.

title: Sedimentary ancient DNA expands bioarchaeological evidence and interpretation at Roman Harelbeke
abstract: Sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) can expand archaeological research by recovering broad biological signals from small amounts of sediment. Here, we apply shotgun sedaDNA metagenomics and target capture (also known as hybridization capture) to disused Roman wells from the vicus of Harelbeke, Belgium, dated to ca. 160-300 CE, and integrate the results with existing bioarchaeological datasets. Moving beyond individual introduced taxa as proxies for Roman influence, we reconstruct community-level profiles spanning consumption-related, synanthropic, and environmental organisms. SedaDNA reproduced most established bioarchaeological signals, including cultivated plants and domestic animals, while also recovering additional environmental taxa that established methods underrepresented. Mitochondrial target capture strengthened selected faunal detections and enabled phylogenetic placement of a pig (Sus scrofa) within the European mitochondrial lineage. The predominance of previously established consumption-related taxa is consistent with subsistence continuity and selective adoption of Roman-introduced resources, although taxon counts alone cannot establish their relative importance. Analytical-effort modeling further indicates that batch-based sedaDNA workflows can provide broad biological profiles at lower cost and time investment than established archaeological methods. Overall, sedaDNA complements conventional bioarchaeology by broadening taxonomic recovery, supporting scalable sampling, and providing a broad-spectrum approach to reconstructing settlement ecology, subsistence, and human-environment interaction.
authors: Özdogan, K. T., Furni, F., Nota, K., Erven, J., Aal, J., Reurings, S., den Boef, L., van Mousch, R., de Groot, G. A., Plets, G.

title: Ecological and genomic insights into seaweed-associated Verrucomicrobiota from the Gulf of Mannar.
abstract: Members of the phylum Verrucomicrobiota are increasingly recognized for their ecological versatility and capacity to degrade complex polysaccharides across diverse marine and freshwater ecosystems. In this study, we recovered 11 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) affiliated with the orders Puniceicoccales and Verrucomicrobiales from seaweed-associated microbiomes in the Gulf of Mannar, India. Verrucomicrobiota constituted 0.6%-2.9% of the total bacterial community across the analyzed algal samples, indicating their consistent presence but low abundance in these habitats. Five high-quality MAGs (JB022, JB024, JB025, JB027, JB023; completeness >90%, contamination Verrucomicrobiota families, expanding the known diversity of this phylum in marine algal ecosystems. Comparative genomic analysis showed that these genomes encode diverse biosynthetic gene clusters and a rich repertoire of carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) and sulfatases, suggesting adaptation to the degradation of polysaccharides typical of seaweed substrates. These binned genomes also possess genes related to fermentative metabolism, nitrogen fixation, and partial denitrification, indicating metabolic versatility and potential contributions to nutrient cycling within algal holobionts. These findings reveal that seaweed-associated Verrucomicrobiota from the Gulf of Mannar represent phylogenomically distinct and functionally specialized lineages with ecological relevance in carbon and nitrogen cycling in coastal marine ecosystems. This study provides the first genomic insights into seaweed-associated Verrucomicrobiota from India, representing potential new taxa and underscoring their potential roles in polysaccharide degradation and holobiont functioning.ImportanceCoastal biomes harbor a rich diversity of microorganisms, and only a few studies have focused on the diversity and functional role of members of the phylum Verrucomicrobiota. Despite their low abundance, members of the phylum Verrucomicrobiota can play an important role in regulating the fate of carbon within marine ecosystems. This study presents the first identification of novel Verrucomicrobial taxa from India, particularly from the Gulf of Mannar, a marine biodiversity hotspot with limited prior microbial investigations. Through metagenome-resolved genomic analysis, this work infers the potential ecological role of these newly discovered Verrucomicrobiota members and suggests their probable role in the carbon cycling and ecosystem processes.
authors: Ramudu B, Sreya PK, Vighnesh L, Biswas R, Mahima D, Sushmita M, Hari Naga Papa Rao A, Sasikala C, Venkata Ramana C.

title: IBD is associated with species-specific changes in gut microbial gene diversity.
abstract: Intra-species genomic variation provides the raw material for natural selection and can reflect the recent diversification history of microbial populations. Environmental stress may be regarded as the ultimate accelerator of the evolutionary process, especially for microorganisms, which can alter their DNA if presented with nutrient limitation, toxins, or pathogen attack. Chronic intestinal inflammation, as in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), represents prolonged environmental stress for gut commensal bacteria, bringing many enteric species down to undetectable levels. However, it remains unclear how microbes that colonize IBD patients actually respond to IBD-associated stressors and whether stress-driven bacterial dynamics may be identified at the population level from the bacterial gut metagenome. To investigate IBD-associated strain-level population dynamics, we performed metagenomic analyses focusing on measuring within-individual bacterial diversity for a panel of gut commensals present across IBD patients and Controls. First, we found species-specific differences in genome-level bacterial diversity. Then, we found that certain genes and functions may harbor different levels and kinds of genetic divergence within the same species across IBD patients and Controls. Functions that were enriched in IBD with both neutral divergence and functional divergence were associated with motility and iron-scavenging, among others. These results may point toward functions that are under selection in the context of IBD stress and could inform future mechanistic work, exploring previously unknown routes of bacterial diversification and adaptation to stress in the gut microbiome.ImportanceInflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is characterized by profound alterations in the gut microbiome composition, and most research so far has focused on changes in species-level abundance to understand gut microbiome contributions to disease dynamics. However, investigating strain-level variation has the potential to uncover previously unknown factors underlying bacterial persistence during gut inflammation, hence revealing key aspects driving gut dysbiosis. Here, we showed that IBD is associated with species-specific changes in gut microbial population-level genetic diversity and identified individual genes and functions that seem to harbor differential genetic diversity within IBD-associated strains. More broadly, our results highlight how intra-species population- and gene-level diversity could be used as sensors of environmental stress in the gut microbiome, and further studies could follow up on the functions highlighted in this work to establish causal links between gut inflammatory conditions and processes of bacterial adaptation to stress.
authors: Mazzoni C, Yassour M.

title: Longitudinal Multiomics Reveals Core Microbiome Disruption and Potential Keystone-Associated Recovery Following Pesticide Exposure.
abstract: Pesticides have become indispensable in modern agriculture, serving as a primary tool to minimize crop loss amid increasing human population pressures. While the negative effects of pesticides on the soil microbiome have been reported, the temporal dynamics of soil microorganisms under pesticide use remain underexplored. Specifically, limited knowledge exists regarding how the soil microbiome responds to pesticides before and after the manufacturer-labeled 'safe period' of 21 days after application. We conducted a longitudinal microcosm study to investigate the temporal impacts of herbicide, fungicide, and insecticide on soil microbial diversity, composition, network complexity, and functional pathways across five time points. Our results show that soil microbial communities are negatively impacted by pesticide applications, but there is a trend of recovery after 21 days. We found a significant impact of the temporal persistence of pesticides on both bacterial and fungal community composition, with a stronger effect on fungi. Network analysis revealed that core microbiome networks were negatively impacted by pesticide applications, with the core microbial nodes, raw associations, and modularity declining in pesticide-treated soils, and this negative effect was particularly strong for pyrethroid insecticides. We identified several differentially abundant taxa, including Xanthobacteraceae and Vicinamibacteriales among bacteria, and Mortierella, Mytilinidales among fungi, which could serve as useful biomarkers for pesticide-affected soils. Results from microbial co-occurrence network analysis revealed that one ASV assigned to the Methyloligellaceae family consistently emerged as a keystone taxon in pesticide-treated soils. Using genome-resolved metagenomics, we assembled the genomes (MAGs) of Methyloligellaceae members and found these taxa harbor putative genes associated with pesticide degradation and antimicrobial resistance, suggesting their possible role in community recovery. Given the remarkably dynamic nature of soil microbial communities, our findings bridge an important knowledge gap regarding the short-term dynamics of microbial structures and functional pathways in response to major pesticides.
authors: Chakraborty D, Vanderhyde M, Camuy-Velez L, Saha B, Fayshal MA, Elvers R, Dragt H, Rodriguez S, Xu J, Iskander SM, Banerjee S.

title: Antimicrobial Peptides in Marine Bivalve Mollusks: Family Diversity, Immune Expression, Mechanisms of Action, and Biotechnological Translation.
abstract: Marine bivalves encounter high microbial loads in seawater and depend on humoral innate defenses, including antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). This review brings together evidence on bivalve AMP families, evolutionary diversity, expression responses, and mechanisms of action. The synthesis connects these biological findings with peptide preparation, production research, and biotechnological development. Genomic studies associate family diversity, including defensins, mytilins, and myticins, with duplication, recombination, and selection. The functional consequences still require peptide-specific validation. AMP transcripts in immune and barrier tissues vary with development, pathogen exposure, and environmental conditions, while mature-peptide abundance and activity have been studied less extensively. Studies of characterized bivalve AMPs identify mechanisms beyond membrane permeabilization. These include inhibition of lipid II-dependent cell-wall synthesis, teichoic acid-associated nanonet formation, bacterial DNA interactions, and changes in reactive oxygen species homeostasis. Some members also inhibit biofilms or regulate host immunity through chemotaxis and phagocytosis. The evidence supports several antimicrobial and immune-regulatory roles for bivalve AMPs, but endogenous defense, exogenous efficacy, and production feasibility have been validated to different extents. A major gap remains between candidate sequences, verified mature-peptide functions, and reproducible production under use-relevant conditions. Research should therefore connect functional validation with folding, stability, scalable preparation, safety, and application-specific testing.
authors: Shen C, Wang Y, Huang Q, Cai X, Guo Y, Zuo Q, Lin X.

title: Identification of ebastine and ceritinib as effective inhibitors of Fusobacterium nucleatum FtsZ.
abstract: The role of microorganisms in cancer is not a new concept-bacteria, parasites, and viruses have all been implicated in cancer development. Fusobacterium nucleatum, a member of the oral microbiota, has emerged as an important cancer-associated bacterium. Unbiased global genomic analyses have demonstrated that F. nucleatum is enriched in human colorectal cancer (CRC) tissues compared with noncancerous colorectal tissues, underscoring the urgent need for specific antimicrobial agents targeting F. nucleatum for CRC prevention and treatment. In this study, structure-based virtual screening successfully identified ebastine and ceritinib as antimicrobial agents targeting Fusobacterium nucleatum FtsZ (FnFtsZ). Their potent anti-F. nucleatum activity was confirmed through in vitro assays, including minimum inhibitory concentration determination and microscopic observation of filamentous morphology. Both ebastine and ceritinib exhibited significant antibacterial effects. Enzyme activity and polymerization assays demonstrated that their mechanism of action involves inhibition of FnFtsZ GTPase activity and disruption of FnFtsZ polymerization. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and light microscopy further confirmed that these compounds effectively disrupt cell division, leading to abnormal or halted division and inhibiting F. nucleatum proliferation. Overall, our findings identified ebastine and ceritinib as potential drugs against F. nucleatum proliferation, although further structural optimization is required. Additionally, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of an integrated computational-experimental approach targeting bacterial cell division in microbiome-associated pathologies.ImportanceColorectal cancer (CRC) is strongly driven by the enrichment of the oncogenic bacterium Fusobacterium nucleatum in gut lesions. However, the lack of targeted anti-F. nucleatum drugs significantly limits microbe-related interventions for CRC. In this study, we repurposed two clinically approved drugs, ebastine and ceritinib, as highly effective inhibitors of FnFtsZ, the key protein responsible for bacterial cell division. We demonstrated that both drugs inhibit bacterial proliferation by suppressing FnFtsZ function and disrupting the cell division process. Our work offers safe, readily available candidate agents for controlling CRC-associated pathogenic bacteria and establishes a reliable computational-experimental workflow to screen division-targeted antimicrobials for microbiome-related cancers.
authors: Fang H, Shu Y, Zhou Z, Li Y, Gong T, Yang M, Zhang B, Jin Y, Liu Y, Wang C, Zhao L, Liu Y, Chen P.

title: Assembly of host-specific bacterial and fungal communities from soil by diverse subaerial green algae
abstract: Green algae recruit microbes from their environment to the phycosphere, a region closely surrounding algal cells which is analogous to the rhizosphere of land plants. Recent work showed that subaerial green algae can recruit and assemble their phycosphere microbiota from soil-derived bacteria. However, how widespread this ability is among diverse green algae, whether host identity shapes community composition, and whether soil-borne fungi can be recruited to the phycosphere remained unclear. Here, we show that subaerial green algae spanning Chlorophyta and Streptophyta assemble distinct phycosphere communities from soil-derived bacteria and fungi, with host identity as the primary driver of phycosphere composition, both in natural soil and in a liquid mesocosm. In soil, bacterial communities were strongly reshaped by algal hosts, whereas the fungal communities responded more weakly and less consistently. In liquid system, bacterial community composition was correlated with host phylogeny. Phycosphere communities included taxa known to associate with land plants in the rhizosphere, supporting the finding that some microbial taxa associate with a wide range of photosynthetic hosts. Our findings demonstrate that the green algae capacity to assemble distinct phycosphere communities possibly predates the divergence of Chlorophyta and Streptophyta. The stronger effect of host identity on bacterial than fungal community mirrors patterns observed in land plant microbiota, suggesting that principles of host-microbe interactions are conserved across evolutionarily distant photosynthetic hosts.
authors: Slawinska MW, Melkonian B, Melkonian M, Flores-Uribe J, Durán P, Garrido-Oter R.

title: Microbial lineages and metabolic capacities associated with mercury methylation in supraglacial cryoconite.
abstract: Supraglacial cryoconite concentrates mercury (Hg), but the transcriptionally active putative Hg-methylating lineages and their metabolic organization remain poorly resolved. We combined an 8 h in situ HgCl2 perturbation with metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, expression-based functional prioritization, and genome-resolved analyses. Initial post-dose total Hg (THg) was positively associated with endpoint methylmercury (MeHg) after controlling for sampling site (within-site ρ = 0.749, permutation P = 0.0002). hgcA transcripts were detected in 29 of 30 treatment units across all six treatment levels, with prominent contributions from Bacteroidota and Desulfobacterota. We recovered 512 HgcA-like sequences, including 258 with conserved cap-helix motifs. Among 34 candidate metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), 26 had same-contig HgcAB support and 32 reached ≥ 90% genome breadth in at least one 2023 DNA sample. Functional prioritization highlighted corrinoid, heme/siroheme, and amino-acid/C1 metabolism. Their recurrence in candidate MAGs, together with model-predicted cobalt, iron, and amino-acid uptake, defines cofactor, methyl-donor, and cellular redox capacities relevant to established HgcAB biochemistry. These findings resolve transcriptionally active putative Hg-methylating lineages and their metabolic organization in glacier-surface ecosystems.
authors: Xu Y, Chen Z, Capo E, Kang S, Guo J, Wang S, Zhang W, Liu G, Chen T, Zhang B.

title: Mechanisms of unique chaotropic resistance and biocalcification in a halophilic Virgibacillus isolated from ephemeral microbial mats of the calcium-rich Don Juan pond in Antarctica.
abstract: IntroductionDon Juan Pond (DJP), located in the McMurdo Dry Valleys of Antarctica, is one of the most extreme cold aquatic environments on our planet and most similar to Mars due to its CaCl₂-rich brines, low water activity, exceptional chaotropicity, average annual subzero temperatures and intense solar radiation during the Antarctic summer. Although the central DJP brine is considered anathema to life, the surrounding basin seasonally hosts temporary streams, ponds, and, very rarely, ephemeral microbial mats.MethodsIn this study, we investigated the diversity of these microbial mats and attempted to cultivate Ca2+-tolerant bacteria and analyze the phenotypic and molecular characteristics of the most promising isolates. To understand the molecular mechanisms underlying their adaptive strategy, further analysis of their genomic potential, adaptive epigenetic transformations and differential transcriptomics was conducted. Predicted functions were verified through physiological experiments.ResultsThe most calcium-tolerant isolate, Virgibacillus flavescens DJP025-4, was studied in detail, including its adaptive physiology and, in particular, its remarkable tolerance to varying calcium concentrations, unmatched by other prokaryotes. DJP025-4 cells were able to survive and remain cultivable after 3 months of exposure to 3.0 M Ca2+, corresponding to a water activity of approximately 0.63 and total chaotropicity value of +276.6 kJ kg-1, conditions well below the current limit for life survival equivalent. Transcriptome analysis revealed that the primary metabolic response of strain DJP025-4 to Ca2+ stress includes enzymatically induced urease-independent CaCO3 precipitation, enhanced uptake of external compatible solutes, and activation of cell surface structures biosynthesis, including peptidoglycan metabolism, biofilm matrix formation, and cellular appendage assembly, which finally increase the cell surface area and the number of Ca2 + precipitation centers on it. Whole-genome analysis revealed a high degree of genetic plasticity in this bacterium, involving natural transformation with genetic material acquired from the bacterial community and adaptive epigenetic mechanisms of gene regulation.DiscussionAmong the key findings, it is worth noting that, in addition to developing remarkable adaptation mechanisms to withstand and thrive in a harsh, calcium-rich environment, strain DJP025-4 appears to remain dependent on the presence of external compatible solutes. We hypothesize that within the DJP stream ecosystem, it is able to survive at high Ca2+ concentrations by utilizing trace amounts of such substances produced by other organisms, specifically, moderate halophiles inhabiting surface microbial mats in lower-salinity zones, which release dissolved organic matter and osmolytes into the environment.
authors: Marturano L, La Cono V, Smedile F, La Spada G, Crisafi F, Selivanova EA, Ignatenko ME, Mudaliyar M, Ghosal D, Messina E, Modica A, Reva ON, Gavrilov SN, Yakimov MM.

title: Plant growth-promoting traits and biocontrol mechanism of three Pseudomonas strains against Geotrichum citri-aurantii.
abstract: BackgroundPlant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) play essential roles in improving plant growth performance and enhancing plant disease resistance. Pseudomonas species are widely recognized as promising beneficial microorganisms owing to their excellent plant growth-promoting and biocontrol potential.MethodsThree bacterial strains, MBJ003, MBJ016 and MB1046, were isolated from potato and tomato rhizosphere soils collected in Guangdong Province, P.R. China. Taxonomic identification was performed based on morphological characteristics, physiological and biochemical profiles, as well as phylogenetic and whole-genome analyses. Genomic features, plant-growth promoting traits and antifungal activities against Geotrichum citri-aurantii were characterized, and the function of the type VI secretion system (T6SS) in strain MB1046 was explored.ResultsStrain MBJ003 was identified as Pseudomonas paraeruginosa, MB1046 as Pseudomonas palmensis, and MBJ016 represents a novel Pseudomonas species. Whole-genome sequencing uncovered abundant and diverse secondary metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) underlying biocontrol capacity. Additionally, strain MB1046 harbours 17 type VI secretion system (T6SS) components. All three strains exhibited multiple plant-beneficial traits including phosphate solubilization, siderophore synthesis and IAA production, while strain MBJ003 additionally showed protease activity. The three strains displayed strong antagonism toward G. citri-aurantii. Their cell-free fermentation supernatants exerted antifungal effects, with MBJ003 showing the strongest inhibition. In vitro inoculation assays confirmed that these strains effectively control citrus postharvest disease caused by G. citri-aurantii. We further provided insights into the T6SS-mediated antagonism of MB1046 against G. citri-aurantii.ConclusionThis study systematically characterizes the plant-growth-promoting properties and antifungal mechanism of three Pseudomonas strains. These strains are valuable microbial candidates for developing biocontrol agents to manage crop postharvest diseases.
authors: Wang C, Mao L, Zhu B, Liu X, Xv X, Zhuo J.

title: Herbicide-based control of Spartina alterniflora disrupts microbial functional potential in a coastal wetland.
abstract: Herbicide-based control of invasive plants is increasingly implemented in coastal wetlands, yet the ecological consequences of herbicide residues for sediment microbiome-mediated biogeochemical functioning remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how herbicide exposure associated with Spartina alterniflora management reshapes sediment microbial communities and biogeochemical potentials in Hangzhou Bay, China. Using metagenomic sequencing and a microbe-based Index of Functional Integrity (M-IFI), we quantified alterations in microbial potentials involved in methane, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur cycling. Higher concentrations of haloxyfop and imazapyr were detected in areas subjected to herbicide-based management. Treated sediments exhibited lower α-diversity of methane-cycling genes, and more than 65% of reconstructed biogeochemical pathways had lower relative abundances, with reductions in methanogenesis-associated genes. Nitrogen and sulfur cycling pathways underwent extensive restructuring, whereas phosphorus acquisition, transport, and utilization potentials were broadly impaired. Genome-resolved analyses recovered 300 metagenome-assembled genomes and revealed distinct patterns of functional specialization and metabolic complementarity among microbial populations. Complete methane, nitrogen, and sulfur cycling potentials were sustained through community-level metabolic cooperation, whereas phosphorus cycling was disproportionately supported by a limited number of metabolically versatile populations. Herbicide exposure markedly decreased M-IFI values, with over 70% of treated sediments classified as moderately or severely disturbed. Collectively, our findings reveal that chemical control of invasive plants can impose hidden belowground ecological costs by disrupting microbiome-supported biogeochemical networks and reducing microbial functional integrity, highlighting the need to incorporate microbiome-based indicators into sustainable coastal wetland management.
authors: Zhao X, Sun Y, Ding J, Fei F, Gu W, Qu X, Wang B, Jiang X.

title: Beneficial microbes in plant salt stress tolerance: mechanisms, antioxidant defense, and multi-omics insights.
abstract: Salinity stress represents a significant environmental challenge that affects plant growth, resulting in adverse impacts on crop productivity and overall yield. Salt accumulation in plants affects cellular homeostasis and provokes osmotic and ionic imbalance. It stimulates higher reactive oxygen species (ROS) production leading to oxidative stress damage and eventual cellular dysfunction. Beneficial microorganisms like plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, endophytic fungi, and rhizosphere-associated microbes have recently emerged as resources for sustainable solutions to enhance plant resiliency against salinity stress. Their effects can involve osmotic adjustment, ion sequestration, oxidative-stress mitigation, phytohormone regulation, and rhizosphere-mediated stress buffering. The mechanisms to impart such benefits may include improved nutrients acquisition, assist in osmotic regulation, modulation of phytohormones signaling, and maintenance of cellular ion homeostasis. Often, beneficial microorganisms carry the potential to trigger both enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant defense mechanisms. These responses contribute to oxidative-stress mitigation, yet, their interpretation requires contemplation of fine balance between oxidative damage and plant responses. For example, selected microbial inoculation studies have reported changes in the activity of crucial antioxidant enzymes, like superoxide dismutase, ascorbate peroxidase, catalase, and glutathione reductase. However, the magnitude and the direction of these responses are context dependent. Multi-omics approaches, including amplicon and shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, host transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, have expanded our understanding of the taxa, genes, transcripts, proteins, and metabolites associated with plant-microbe interactions under salinity. Therefore, here an effort has been made to present the evidential support for reported microbial effects and their proposed mechanisms of salt tolerance, with a focus on enzymatic and non-enzymatic defense mechanisms and the learnings of multi-omics studies. Frontier integrative mechanisms, including microbiome engineering, synthetic microbial consortia, and systems biology frameworks, are discussed for cultivating climate-resilient crops and sustainable agricultural systems in the salt-affected environments.
authors: Shree S, Chaudhary A, Kumar S, Singh K, Dubey N.

title: Compound microbial intelligent membrane fermentation reshapes the bacterial community and reduces antibiotic, metal, and biocide resistance genes and virulence factors in duck litter.
abstract: BackgroundContaminated duck litter is a leading cause of flock disease and a bottleneck for the sustainable development of large-scale dry-rearing systems.MethodsWe applied shotgun metagenomics to litter from four positions within each of three independent compound microbial intelligent membrane fermentation beds, with unfermented litter from the same three batches as the control. We investigated the bacterial community alongside the abundance of antibiotic, metal and biocide resistance genes (ARGs, MRGs and BRGs) and of virulence factor genes (VFGs).ResultsFermented litter was consistently enriched in thermophilic and thermotolerant taxa and in beneficial genera such as Paenibacillus and Bacillus, while opportunistic pathogens including Streptococcus, Mycobacterium and Escherichia were clearly reduced. The total burden of the ARG and VFG classes fell in every fermented position, and representative determinants were consistently depleted: floR, qacEdelta1 and sul2 among the ARGs, ruvB among the MRGs, mexF, ideR and sodA among the BRGs, and htpB, clpV and katA among the VFGs. A small number of genes, tet(L), fexA and bacA among them, rose in the most active zones, indicating structural remodeling of the resistance reservoir rather than uniform removal. Fermentation was not spatially uniform: the upper and edge layers were more active, and the center-lower layer remained closest to the unfermented control.ConclusionIntelligent membrane fermentation reduced the overall abundance of resistance and virulence determinants in the litter microbiome, and spatial uniformity is important for the process. Because these data are DNA-based, they describe the abundance of resistance and virulence determinants and not resistance or virulence phenotypes.
authors: Sun T, Mei G, Li M, Mo J, Zhang C, Ma Y, Zhao J, Peng S, Lin F, Chen JL, Li Z.

title: Isolation, genomic and comparative proteomic characterization of three lytic Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteriophages from wastewater in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso
abstract: Abstract    Background.  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  is a leading cause of opportunistic and healthcare-associated infections and is listed by the World Health Organization among the pathogens for which new therapeutic options are most urgently needed. Lytic bacteriophages are one of the few alternatives that can be deployed rapidly and at low cost, but phage collections and phage genome sequences remain very unevenly distributed geographically, and West Africa is particularly under-represented. Wastewater, which combines high bacterial densities with continuous inputs of faecal, hospital and industrial effluent, is the most productive environment for recovering phages that are locally adapted to circulating clinical strains. We therefore set out to isolate lytic phages active against clinical  P. aeruginosa  isolates from wastewater in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso, and to characterize their genomes. Results.  Twenty-eight lytic phages were isolated from five wastewater sites using six  P. aeruginosa  host strains, and screened against a panel of eleven clinical and reference strains. Host ranges were broad: eleven isolates lysed at least ten of the eleven strains and three lysed all eleven, while only two isolates were restricted to four strains. Five phages were selected for whole-genome sequencing and three yielded complete, high-quality assemblies. All three belong to the class  Caudoviricetes  . vB_PaeM_CM0001 (57,614 bp; 63.5% GC; 88 CDSs) is a member of the family  Mesyanzhinovviridae  , subfamily  Bradleyvirinae  , genus  Abidjanvirus  . vB_PaeP_CM0002 (43,491 bp) and vB_PaeP_CM0003 (43,177 bp), each encoding 65 CDSs with 62.3–62.6% GC, belong to the family  Autographiviridae  , subfamily  Krylovirinae  , genus  Phikmvvirus  . Intergenomic similarities indicate that vB_PaeM_CM0001 is a new isolate of an existing  Abidjanvirus  species, whereas vB_PaeP_CM0002 and vB_PaeP_CM0003 represent two new  Phikmvvirus  species. The two  Phikmvvirus  genomes share 91.9% nucleotide identity and 62 orthogroups and are fully collinear with each other and with their closest relatives; their divergence is confined to nucleotide substitution and to a single 2.0 kb region spanning the tail fibre locus. vB_PaeM_CM0001 shares no detectable orthogroups with them. Conclusions.  These three genomes are the first  P. aeruginosa  phage genomes reported from Burkina Faso. Two of them represent new species. Their broad host ranges, strictly lytic gene repertoires and absence of resistance determinants make them credible starting points for a national phage bank and for future therapeutic evaluation.
authors: Gnada K, Silga EW, Essoh CY, Yao RK, Sanou AQ, Ouangraoua A, Gomgnimbou MK.

title: DIA quantitative proteomics reveals the regulatory mechanism of aroma-producing yeast on the formation of Xuanwei ham flavour: microbial fermentation and protein degradation.
abstract: To clarify the regulatory effects of three aroma-producing yeasts (Rhodotorula mucilaginosa, Yamadazyma triangularis, and Debaryomyces hansenii) on microbial community structure and muscle protein expression during Xuanwei ham fermentation, this study used Xuanwei ham inoculated with the three yeasts as the research material. High-throughput sequencing was applied to analyze changes in microbial community composition and diversity. Data-independent acquisition (DIA) quantitative proteomics was used to identify differentially expressed proteins, combined with Gene Ontology (GO) functional enrichment, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway, and protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analyses. The results showed that inoculated yeasts significantly reshaped the bacterial and fungal communities of ham, markedly inhibited the overgrowth of Aspergillus, and enriched functional microorganisms such as Staphylococcus and Serratia, with significant differences among groups (P < 0.05). A total of 3401 proteins were identified, were screened. These proteins were mainly enriched in pathways including carboxylic acid metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, myofibril depolymerization, mitochondrial energy metabolism, and regulated muscle protein degradation and flavour precursor formation through the core protein interaction network. These findings indicate that aroma-producing yeasts improve the quality of Xuanwei ham by optimizing microbial community structure and regulating muscle protein metabolism, providing a scientific basis for the development of starter cultures suitable for dry-cured ham and precise quality control.
authors: Ren R, Zhou N, Xun W, Li J, Du Y, Yang Y, Tan J, Tang S, Yang K, Weng C, Dong H, Pu E, Liao G, Wang G.

title: Host control and regulation of human anellovirus persistence
abstract: SUMMARY  Anelloviruses are the most abundant and diverse eukaryotic viruses known to infect humans and can persist throughout our lifetimes. Despite their ubiquity, the host factors governing their physiologic distribution and abundance remain poorly understood. Here, we construct a viral pangenome of 2,023 strains to quantify anellovirus DNA in >1.1 million participants spanning three genetic biobanks. Genome-wide association studies identify 121 loci linked to viral persistence, predominantly via immune regulation by NF-κB signaling. Further, we associate variable anellovirus detection with conditions characterized by immune dysfunction, including lymphoid malignancies. By screening 3.2 petabases of human single-cell sequencing data, we identify myeloid progenitors in the bone marrow as a prominent site of anellovirus transcription in vivo. Finally, Perturb-seq of anellovirus proteins reveals that anellovirus ORF2, particularly from Alphatorquevirus, attenuates TNF-α-induced NF-κB signaling, connecting host genetic variation, cellular context, and viral immunomodulation to characterize the persistence of the eukaryotic human virome’s most abundant component.
authors: Gutierrez JC, Ali TA, Honeycutt CC, Neo JH, Helmsauer K, Nyeo SS, Le A, Vela AJ, Kida LC, Varela AA, Ardy RC, Metzner E, Ulirsch JC, Dhindsa RS, Fiziev PP, Chikhi R, Norman TM, Dey KK, Lareau CA.

title: Investigations into the Virome of Grasses Growing in the Environment of Sugarcane in Florida.
abstract: Samples of 26 plant species and the aphid Melanaphis sorghi were collected in the Everglades Agricultural Area (South Florida) from 2017-2019 to investigate the virome of grasses growing in the environment of sugarcane. Leaf samples were obtained from cultivated as well as from wild species. Detection and identification of the viruses present in 388 plant and 11 aphid samples were performed using the virion-associated nucleic acid (VANA)-metagenomics approach. Twenty-four viruses were identified, and 12 plant species and the aphid were infected by at least one virus. Fourteen of these 24 viruses were known viruses whereas 10 were putatively new virus species, including an alphaendornavirus (family Endornaviridae), an alphanucleorhabdovirus (Rhabdoviridae), an amalgavirus (Amalgaviridae), a marafivirus (Tymoviridae), a mastrevirus (Geminiviridae), and a sobemovirus (Solemoviridae). The highest number of viruses was detected in Columbus grass and sorghum (10 and 11, respectively). Sugarcane mosaic virus (SCMV; Potyvirus sacchari, Potyviridae) and maize chlorotic dwarf virus (Waikavirus zeae, Secoviridae) were the most widespread viruses, occurring in nine and seven plant species, respectively, and were also detected in the aphid. In a phylogenetic tree constructed with partial genome sequences (4,000 nt) of SCMV obtained from GenBank and herein, virus isolates from eight plant species were distributed in three different lineages, thus suggesting significant diversity of this virus in Florida. Only two Saccharum-infecting viruses, SCMV and sugarcane yellow leaf virus (Polerovirus SCYLV, Solemoviridae) were detected in sorghum and other grasses. These plants may, therefore, serve as putative reservoirs for the causal agents of two sugarcane diseases in Florida.
authors: Rott PC, Filloux D, Daugrois JH, Fernandez E, Julian C, Galzi S, Beiriger R, Odero DC, Sood SG, Roumagnac P.

title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of four foodborne Vibrio harveyi: Insights into antimicrobial resistance, secretion systems, and ecological fitness.
abstract: Vibrio harveyi is a prominent marine and seafood-borne pathogen that poses a significant threat to global aquaculture and public health. To better understand its adaptive evolution, four V. harveyi isolates recovered from Chinese seafood markets were comprehensively characterized using an integrated framework of whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomics, and phenotypic profiling. The genomes ranged from 5.7 to 5.8 Mb and exhibited high overall genomic conservation, with ANI values exceeding 98%, but substantial variation was observed in accessory genomic regions. Phylogenomic analysis separated the isolates into three major lineages, with Vh1067 showing the greatest divergence from the other isolates. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing revealed widespread resistance to β-lactams, while Vh1067 displayed a multidrug-resistant phenotype associated with blaVEB-1, tet(C), sul2, floR, ereA, and multiple aminoglycoside resistance determinants within a Tn3-type transposon. All isolates exhibited optimal growth at 2-3% NaCl and retained both swimming and swarming motility, whereas biofilm-forming capacity varied substantially among strains. Comparative analysis identified extensive diversity in T6SS, T3SS, Rhs-associated systems, toxin-antitoxin modules, and other virulence-associated determinants. All isolates exhibited bactericidal activity against Escherichia coli, with Vh2287 and Vh2376 showing the strongest competitive effects. This study highlights substantial genomic variation among the four seafood-associated V. harveyi isolates and underscores potential associations between secretion system features, antimicrobial resistance, and environmental adaptability.
authors: Hui M, Li B, Huang X, Ding F, Liu H, Wang X, Jiang X, Lu P, Chen K, Zeng P, Dong N, Chen S, Cheng Q.

title: Dehalobacter-mediated reductive dechlorination of the organophosphorus insecticide chlorpyrifos in mangrove sediments.
abstract: Mangrove sediments are important sinks for organic contaminants, including the widely used chlorinated organophosphorus insecticide chlorpyrifos (CPF). Although CPF degradation under oxic conditions has been extensively studied, its anaerobic transformation in reducing coastal environments remains poorly understood. Here, a mangrove sediment-derived anaerobic enrichment culture achieved nearly complete transformation of 10 mg L-1 CPF within 10 days. Ultraperformance liquid chromatography-Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry (UPLCOrbitrap-HRMS) revealed the formation of a mono-dechlorinated CPF product, which was tentatively assigned as O,Odiethyl O-(3,5-dichloro-2-pyridinyl) phosphorothioate based on tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) evidence and density functional theory (DFT) calculations of C-Cl bond dissociation energies. The enrichment culture also reductively dechlorinated 3,5,6-trichloro-2-pyridinol (TCP), a common CPF transformation product, primarily to 5,6-dichloro-2-pyridinol, with Ecological Structure-Activity Relationships (ECOSAR) modeling predicting lower aquatic toxicity for the dechlorinated products than for their parent compounds. 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and metagenomic analyses revealed marked enrichment of Dehalobacter during active CPF transformation, strongly implicating this organohalide-respiring lineage in CPF dechlorination. A high-quality Dehalobacter metagenome-assembled genome harboring 39 rdhA homologs was recovered. Integrated metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic analyses further prioritized four candidate reductive dehalogenases (CPF-RDH1/2/3/9), with CPF-RDH2 showing the strongest proteomic support. Together, these findings uncover an overlooked anaerobic transformation route of CPF through direct reductive dechlorination and highlight the potential role of Dehalobacter-associated organohalide respiration in the environmental fate of chlorinated organophosphorus contaminants in mangrove sediments.
authors: Li J, Zhong Y, Yang S, Wu J, Zhang Y, Zeng Y, Song J, Zhu X, Li D, Ling J, Yu Z, Häggblom MM, Peng P.

title: Genome-based reclassification of Streptosporangium sandarakinum Kämpfer et al. 2013 as a later heterotypic synonym of Streptosporangium nondiastaticum Nonomura and Ohara 1969 (Approved Lists 1980).
abstract: A comparison of 16S rRNA gene sequences between Streptosporangium sandarakinum GW-12028T and Streptosporangium nondiastaticum IFO 13990T revealed a sequence similarity of 98.8%. The genus Streptosporangium includes 33 species with validly published names. The type strains S. sandarakinum GW-12028T (=DSM 45763T=LMG 27062T) and S. nondiastaticum IFO 13990T (=ATCC 27101T=DSM 43848T=JCM 3114T=KCTC 9434T=NBRC 13990T=VKM Ac-1299T) were both isolated from soil. Whole-genome data were used to clarify the taxonomic assignment of these two closely related Streptosporangium species. Overall genomic relatedness index analyses indicated that S. sandarakinum GW-12028T and S. nondiastaticum IFO 13990T shared average nucleotide identity and digital DNA-DNA hybridization values >95% and >70%, respectively, exceeding the thresholds for bacterial species delineation. Additionally, S. sandarakinum GW-12028T and S. nondiastaticum IFO 13990T displayed near-identical phenotypic and chemotaxonomic profiles. Based on the 16S rRNA gene phylogenetic tree and the core-genome phylogenomic trees, S. sandarakinum GW-12028T and S. nondiastaticum IFO 13990T phylogenetically form a separate, tight cluster apart from other Streptosporangium species. Based on this combined evidence, S. sandarakinum Kämpfer et al. 2013 is proposed as a later heterotypic synonym of S. nondiastaticum Nonomura and Ohara 1969.
journal: International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology
authors: Cruz A, McLaughlin RW, Elshahed MS, Lawson PA, Miller SL.

title: Elevation Amplifies Carrier-Type Differences in Nitrogen Cycling and N2O Dynamics in Lake Biofilms.
abstract: Lake biofilms are microbial habitats for nitrogen transformation, but how carrier type and elevation influence N2O dynamics remains unclear. We examined abiotic- and biotic-carrier biofilms from 12 lakes spanning 4-4272 m using anoxic incubations, 15N tracing, selective inhibition, isotopocule analysis, and metagenomics. Net N2O emission potential increased with elevation in both carrier types, with the largest carrier contrast at high elevation, where biotic-carrier biofilms showed the highest net N2O emission potential. 15N partitioning showed a marked shift in emission sources. At low elevation, heterotrophic nitrification dominated abiotic-carrier biofilms (∼91%), whereas denitrification contributed ∼57% in biotic-carrier biofilms. At high elevation, denitrification accounted for 67-97% of net N2O emission across both carriers, and bacterial denitrification dominated the total denitrification rate potential. Metagenomic profiles provided mechanistic support: high-elevation biotic-carrier biofilms showed higher relative representation of genes for dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium and nitrogen fixation, but had few nosZ-carrying genomes, indicating weak terminal N2O reduction capacity. Overall, carrier type and elevation jointly shape nitrogen transformation pathways. High-elevation lake ecosystems, particularly those with abundant biotic substrates, may harbor disproportionately important biofilm N2O hotspots under global change.
authors: Xue Y, Li L, Wang Y, Xiong Y, Deng M, Song K.

title: Gut microbiota composition of India's Baiga tribe: Insights from an indigenous particularly vulnerable tribal group.
abstract: The transition from traditional foraging lifestyles to modernized urban environments is associated with reduced human gut microbiome diversity. To examine this shift within the Indian subcontinent, we used shotgun metagenomics to compare the gut microbiota of 50 adults: 25 from the indigenous, foraging, and particularly vulnerable Baiga tribe and 25 from an urban population in Bhopal, Central India. The Baiga maintained a diverse ecosystem enriched with fiber-degrading bacteria such as Roseburia and Faecalibacterium, forming networks suited to complex carbohydrate fermentation. The urban microbiome showed lower phylogenetic diversity and evenness, with higher relative abundance of Prevotella copri and dairy-adapted taxa. Functionally, the tribal gut retained pathways for environmental sensing and complex plant metabolism, whereas the urban gut was enriched in pathways associated with potential inflammation. These findings identify the Baiga as a reservoir of preserved human microbial diversity relevant to metabolic health.
authors: Kallapura G, Prakash AS, Prasad R, Josphine I, Maurya M, Dhar D.

title: Microbiome-targeted strategies for Alzheimer's disease: multi-omics signatures, mechanistic links, and intervention evidence.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasingly studied in relation to gut microbial mechanisms because microbial metabolism, mucosal barrier function, and peripheral immune activation may influence neuroinflammation and host metabolic stress. This review evaluates microbiome-linked evidence in AD with emphasis on studies that combine metagenomics, metabolomics, inflammatory markers, neuroimaging, cerebrospinal fluid or blood biomarkers, and cognitive phenotyping. Current data support several recurring but not yet causal axes, including bile acid transformation, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), bacterial product-related inflammatory signaling, and barrier dysfunction. We also review microbiome-targeted interventions, including diet and prebiotics, strain-specified probiotics and synbiotics, oligosaccharide-based agents, gut-restricted antimicrobials, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). The strength of evidence differs substantially across these strategies: sodium oligomannate has been tested in a phase 3 trial, whereas many probiotic, antimicrobial, and FMT approaches remain early clinical, preclinical, or mechanism-generating. Future trials should define a priori microbial, metabolite, immune, and brain biomarker endpoints; control diet, medication, and comorbidity confounding; and validate candidate signatures across independent cohorts before using microbiome profiles for screening or treatment selection.
authors: Huang X, Zhang X, Zhu Q.

title: Chromosome-level assembly of Lemnamoeba sinaloensis gen. nov. et sp. nov. (Apofilosa) reveals dynamic genome evolution in Rhizaria.
abstract: BackgroundRhizaria is a eukaryotic supergroup including many amoeboid protists. Despite harboring a large diversity and many ecologically important species, the genomes belonging to this supergroup remain poorly explored. With only a handful available genome sequences, most of low contiguity, little is known about overall architecture, characteristics, and evolution of rhizarian genomes.ResultsWe provide a highly contiguous genome assembly of an undescribed marine rhizarian amoeba formerly known as M6MM. The assembly revealed a small (27 Mb; 8704 genes) and compact genome (84% genes, 10% repeats, 6% intergenic regions), and was almost fully captured in six contigs confirmed cytologically to represent chromosomes. The genome contains a very large amount of simple-sequence repeats (SSRs), particularly of the AC:GT dinucleotide class (206 loci/Mb), in total covering almost 2% of the assembly. We also obtained the complete mitochondrial genome, which is reduced and devoid of ribosomal protein genes similarly to some other rhizarians. Some of these "missing" mitochondrial-encoded genes are found in the nuclear genome and are predicted to be targeted to the mitochondrion. In our 18S rDNA phylogenetic analysis, M6MM loosely groups with environmental sequences and the amoeboflagellate Viscidocauda repens. However, this amoeba is phylogenetically distant from any described species and expresses a unique pseudopodial morphology, prompting us to erect the novel genus and species Lemnamoeba sinaloensis gen. nov. et. sp. nov. Environmental data show that L. sinaloensis has a wide marine distribution and can mostly be found between the surface and 100 m depths.ConclusionThis study adds another genus to the hitherto taxonomically poor Apofilosa, provides one of the highest-quality rhizarian genome assemblies to date, and reveals an abundance of SSRs in the genome, highlighting the complexity of eukaryotic genomes in underexplored parts of the tree of life.
authors: Hiltunen Thorén M, Onuț-Brännström I, Zlatogursky V, Pardasani Y, Pecková H, Karlíková A, Holzer AS, Burki F.

title: Systematic analysis of MYB transcription factors in lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) reveals NnMYB48 as a positive regulator of aporphine alkaloid biosynthesis.
abstract: Aporphine alkaloids in lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) are medicinally significant compounds, and their biosynthesis is orchestrated by a complex network involving various transcription factors (TFs). MYB TFs constitute one of the most critical classes, yet their specific functions in lotus aporphine alkaloid biosynthesis remained largely unexplored. Using the newly assembled lotus telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome, we systematically characterized the full complement lotus MYB genes and identified 126 R2R3-MYBs, 57 1R-MYBs, five R1R2R3-MYBs, and one 4R-MYB. Phylogenetic and gene duplication analysis revealed 63 collinear NnMYB gene pairs and 15 tandemly arrayed gene clusters, indicating that both whole-genome and local tandem duplication events collectively drove the expansion of the NnMYB family. Correlation analysis between gene expression and aporphine abundance identified 44 NnMYB candidates potentially involved in aporphine biosynthesis. Among them, NnMYB48 was predominantly expressed in the lotus leaves and showed a rapid transcriptional response to methyl jasmonate (MeJA). Transient overexpression of NnMYB48 in lotus petals markedly upregulated multiple aporphine biosynthetic genes and increased the accumulation of major aporphine alkaloids. Further dual-luciferase reporter assays, yeast one-hybrid, and electrophoretic mobility shift assays confirmed that NnMYB48 directly binds to the promoters of NnTYDC and NnCYP80G, thereby activating their transcription and promoting alkaloid biosynthesis. Collectively, these findings provide critical insights into the evolution trajectory and functional diversification of the NnMYB family in lotus.
authors: Zhang M, Yang Z, He R, Zhang Y, Huang Z, Liu J, Sun H, Li J, Yang M, Deng X.

title: Bacteriophage associated liver injury in a person with cystic fibrosis and prior liver transplantation.
abstract: A 27-year-old man with cystic fibrosis, prior liver transplantation for advanced cystic fibrosis related liver disease, tacrolimus immunosuppression, multidrug resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, recurrent drug induced liver injury, and intolerance to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor underwent matched bacteriophage therapy. Intravenous phages were administered at 109 plaque forming units per dose and nebulised phages at 5 × 109 plaque forming units per dose twice daily. Within two days, marked elevations in alanine transaminase, aspartate transaminase, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma glutamyl transferase developed, prompting treatment cessation. Peak alanine transaminase reached 494 U/L and alkaline phosphatase 527 U/L were observed, while bilirubin and coagulation parameters remained normal. Extensive investigation, including magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography and medication review, identified no alternative cause. Rechallenge with nebulised phage therapy alone resulted in recurrent liver enzyme elevation after eight days, again resolving following discontinuation. Temporal correlation was demonstrated between liver function test abnormalities and detection of phage DNA in serum and sputum. No bacteriophage neutralisation, bacterial DNAaemia, development of phage resistance, or significant bacterial genomic change was observed. Despite early cessation, lung function improved over the subsequent six months.
journal: Journal of cystic fibrosis : official journal of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society
