title: Upgrading yeast-based low-carbon biomanufacturing by harnessing a universal in vivo evolution system.
abstract: Non-conventional yeasts are emerging as key cell factories in low-carbon biomanufacturing, but unlocking their full potential requires optimizing complex traits, such as substrate utilization and high-level protein expression, through in vivo genome-wide evolution. To address this, we developed a universal plasmid vector deploying a DNA Helicase-Activation-Induced Cytidine Deaminase (Helicase-AID) for genome-wide base editing. This system enables cross-species mutagenesis in diverse yeasts, including Yarrowia lipolytica, Pichia pastoris, and Kluyveromyces marxianus. We demonstrated that MCM5-AID base editing efficiency in Y. lipolytica is time-dependent, achieving a cumulative mutation rate of 3.13 × 10-5 mutations per base pair (bp-1) over 432 hours. Using this system, we evolved Y. lipolytica variants exhibiting a 37.77% increase in maximum specific growth rate on acetate, alongside altered starch production ranging from -92.96% to 17.45%. Crucially, we utilized this platform to activate the silent expression of heterologous proteins, overcoming a persistent bottleneck in microbial strain engineering. Evolutionary, transcriptomic and genomic analyses showed that evolved Y. lipolytica variants exhibited enhanced accumulation of Cas13x, a naturally difficult-to-express protein, via reduced proteolytic degradation. In contrast, evolved P. pastoris variants gained the ability to express previously silent thaumatin through significant transcriptional upregulation, enhanced protein folding, and increased amino acid biosynthesis. Ultimately, this universal in vivo evolution system provides a robust platform for genome-directed evolution across diverse industrial yeast species, accelerating the systematic exploration of their potential in low-carbon biomanufacturing.
authors: Duan S, Shi Z, Wang X, Rong W, Peng G, Yun L, Liang S, Chen Q, Xiao A, Liu S, He H, Abuhena MD, Liu W, Ma H, Lin Y, Liao X, Wang G.

title: Comparative mitogenomics of Hippophae reveals conserved gene content, repeat-mediated structural variation, and limited phylogenetic resolution.
abstract: Plant mitochondrial genomes retain conserved coding content but evolve rapidly in structure. We assembled mitogenomes of four Hippophae taxa from long reads and compared them with four published mitogenomes. Gene content and codon usage were largely conserved, whereas the assemblies of closely related taxa differed by up to four inversions and two translocations. Long reads spanning repeats of 1.3-9.6 kb supported both assembled and recombinant arrangements, and allowing for repeat-mediated isomers removed all inversions among the seven records compared. RNA-seq identified 80-262 candidate editing sites per taxon, and mitogenome-plastome homologous fragments made up 12.54-12.77% of each assembly. A 31-gene phylogeny supported Hippophae monophyly but weakly resolved relationships within the genus (16 parsimony-informative sites). Only nad4 showed a Hippophae-specific increase in ω; its fixed C-to-T substitutions and intron loss point to retroprocessing rather than positive selection. Most structural differences among Hippophae mitogenomes can be explained by repeat-mediated isomerization.
authors: Zeng Z, Zhang H, He J, Nima C, Ouzhu D, Qiong B, Dolma D, Wang R, Bacuo C, Ma N, Qiong, Wang J.

title: Legume root nodule endophytes belonging to Agrobacterium, Bacillus, Paenibacillus, and Pseudomonas possess the nitrogen-fixing (nifH) gene similar to rhizobia.
abstract: BackgroundLegume root nodules, the site of biological nitrogen fixation, are inhabited by diverse microsymbionts. Consequently, as part of our ongoing work to discover the nitrogen-fixing microsymbionts, the present study aims to identify nodule endophytes possessing the nitrogen fixation (nifH) gene.Methods and resultsRoot nodules of Mucuna prurita, Vigna umbellata, and Vigna unguiculata were collected for microsymbiont isolation. Isolation resulted in fifty-one bacterial isolates; of these, initial screening detected eighteen nifH-positive isolates. To identify the species, 16 S rRNA was amplified and successfully sequenced for sixteen isolates. Analysis of the 16 S rRNA sequence revealed that ten isolates were rhizobia, including Rhizobium and Bradyrhizobium, while the other 6 isolates were identified as non-rhizobial endophytes (NRE) from the genera Agrobacterium, Bacillus, Paenibacillus, and Pseudomonas. Diversity in morphological and biochemical characteristics was observed among the nodule endophytes. All sixteen endophytes produce the phytohormones auxin and gibberellic acid, although they lack the phosphate solubilisation activity. To identify representative bacterial strains, random amplified polymorphic DNA (RAPD) was performed. The nifH gene from the selected bacterial strains was sequenced, and a phylogenetic tree was constructed. The nifH phylogenetic tree grouped the rhizobia and NRE, indicating a shared ancestry of their nifH gene.ConclusionThis study confirms that NRE are common members of the legume root nodule microbial community, and some of them carry nifH genes similar to those of rhizobia, providing molecular evidence for their potential nitrogen-fixing ability.
authors: Pongener B, Paul A.

title: Large-genome phages encode diverse proteins associated with host cell envelope functions
abstract: Abstract  Huge phages (or jumbo phages, > 200 kilobases) encode extensive protein repertoires, yet their functional diversity and potential roles in host physiology remain poorly understood. Using protein structure-based analyses of dominant protein families across 7,187 non-redundant genomes of huge phages, we uncovered pronounced phylogenetic and habitat-associated diversification. Notably, we identified diverse proteins associated with bacterial cell envelope functions, particularly in human gut-associated huge phages. These included previously unreported phage-encoded sortase B, whose putative substrates contain signal peptides and cell-wall sorting signals, suggesting a potential route for displaying phage proteins on bacterial surfaces. Phage-encoded phage shock protein A (PspA) was distributed across diverse lineages and frequently neighbored genes associated with membrane organization and transport, implicating potential roles in membrane physiology. We also identified 1,603 β-barrel outer membrane proteins (OMPs) across 1,303 huge phages from diverse ecosystems. These OMPs exhibited structural diversity and associations with predicted host taxonomy, habitat, and neighboring envelope-related genes. Metatranscriptomic analysis supported expression of representative phage-encoded PspA and OMP genes in natural communities including the human gut. Together, these findings reveal bacterial cell envelope processes as a previously underappreciated potential interface for huge phage–host interactions.
authors: Chen L, Yuan L.

title: Genomic and phenotypic analysis reveals taxonomic and biosynthetic diversity in desert-derived Saccharothrix
abstract: Abstract    Rare actinomycetes represent an underexplored source of bioactive natural products, yet their taxonomic diversity and biosynthetic potential remain incompletely characterized. Here, ten  Saccharothrix  strains isolated from the Gurbantunggut Desert in Xinjiang, northwestern China, were investigated using phylogenomics, comparative genomics, biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) mining, and antimicrobial assays. Genome-based analyses identified two lineages that may represent novel species. A total of 413 BGCs were predicted across the ten genomes. Comparative BiG-SCAPE analysis grouped 1,461 BGCs from the ten study strains, reference  Saccharothrix  genomes, and MIBiG into 735 gene cluster families (GCFs). Only three of the 19 GCFs containing MIBiG reference BGCs also included BGCs from the study strains, indicating limited overlap with characterized BGCs. Antimicrobial activity was detected in 89 of 300 strain–medium–indicator combinations, with positive results more frequent against fungal than bacterial indicators. Notably, the strain with the largest number of predicted BGCs did not exhibit the broadest antimicrobial spectrum. These findings reveal taxonomic and biosynthetic diversity among desert-derived  Saccharothrix  and provide a basis for prioritizing strains and biosynthetic pathways for further natural product discovery.
authors: Li S, Dong L, Wang Z, Wang X, Bobushova S, Tian C, Duixiannale A, Chen X, Zhang W, Fang B, Liu Y, Li X, Li W.

title: Whole genome sequencing of Curcuma xanthorrhiza Roxb. reveals ploidy-driven speciation and divergent specialized metabolite biosynthesis in the genus Curcuma.
abstract: Curcuma xanthorrhiza Roxb., commonly known as javanese turmeric (temulawak), is a rhizomatous herb with significant ethnobotanical and nutraceutical importance, valued for producing curcuminoids and xanthorrhizol. Despite its considerable medicinal and economic value, the genomic basis underlying these important traits has remained largely uncharacterized. This study presents its first whole-genome assembly, generated through a hybrid sequencing strategy utilizing 21.82 Gb of PacBio HiFi and 21.46 Gb of Illumina short-read data. Independent k-mer profiling and assembly-based analyses converged on a triploid genome architecture, resulting in a 579.07 Mb contig-level assembly (N50 = 1.48 Mb) with high completeness (BUSCO: 94.5-97.7%), 42,169 annotated protein-coding genes and a PSAURON score of 98.4. Comparative phylogenomic analysis across the Zingiberaceae revealed that while C. xanthorrhiza diverged from its sister taxon Curcuma caesia Roxb. recently (~ 1.76 Mya), it exhibits profound macrosynteny disruption, a net gene-family contraction, and the most compact gene complement among the sampled species. Genome-wide mining of biosynthetic gene clusters identified 26 candidates, including a paralogous pair of curcuminoid loci, though further validation by RNA-seq co-expression is needed. Additionally, genome-wide homology-search identified AC50XY_029945 as the strongest candidate (S)-β-bisabolene synthase for xanthorrhizol biosynthesis, proposed as a trans-acting, dispersed pathway architecture involving 51 candidate CYP71 cytochrome P450s, an SDR oxidoreductase, and co-located WRKY/ERF/MYB transcription factors. These results establish the first nuclear genomic resource for C. xanthorrhiza, highlighting the role of ploidy-driven genome instability in driving rapid-speciation and secondary metabolite diversification in the genus Curcuma.
authors: Rahmat E, Hutabarat JT, Anindita L, Sianipar NF, Assidqi K, Faizal A, Kang CH, Kang Y, Ansori ANM, Trinugroho JP.

title: Evaluation of full-length 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing using Oxford Nanopore Technologies for diversity surveys of understudied microbiomes.
abstract: The use of long-read sequencing is becoming increasingly popular in the study of host-associated microbiomes. However, its application has not yet been optimized for characterizing understudied microbiomes, such as those in marine environments. We evaluated the accuracy and consistency of long-read sequencing of full-length 16S rRNA genes for diversity surveys of symbiotic dinoflagellate (family Symbiodiniaceae) microbiomes. When comparing long-read amplicon sequencing of the full-length bacterial 16S rRNA gene with short-read sequencing of the V4 hypervariable gene region using a known microbial community, the former recapitulated the bacterial taxonomic composition more accurately. Long-read sequencing performed using Oxford Nanopore Technologies was also highly consistent between sequencing runs and flow cells. Long-read sequencing technologies enable microbiome surveys using the full-length 16S rRNA gene, achieving higher accuracy and resolution. This work validates long-read sequencing as a robust approach for resolving microbiome composition in understudied marine systems, thereby supporting ecological and evolutionary investigations of host-microbe associations.
authors: Li VY, González-Pech R, Lera-Lozano D, Román-Reyna V, Medina M.

title: [Characterization of the caries-associated oral microbiome across age groups based on global metagenomic species-level genome bins data].
abstract: Objective: Based on the analysis of global multicenter metagenomic species-level genome bin (SGB), this study aims to identify core cariogenic SGBs across all age groups and provide a basis for the precise diagnosis and age-stratified prevention and treatment of dental caries. Methods: Eight published studies available in the National Center for Biotechnology Information database before August 2024 were included, with a total of 496 oral metagenomic samples enrolled. Samples were stratified into saliva and dental plaque groups across three age segments (Results: Analysis at the SGB level revealed that 652 SGBs were detected in plaque samples and 931 SGBs in saliva samples. Specific core SGB clusters were identified in each age group (50%). Differential analysis indicated that caries was accompanied by marked ecological dysbiosis. These differential patterns were highly age-and sample-specific. Saliva samples in the group agedStreptococcus enrichment versus Capnocytophaga in the healthy group. Notably, in the≥13-year-old group, the caries-associated microbiome shifted to anaerobic Prevotella species alongside Streptococcus. Heatmap analysis confirmed clear ecological turnovers across all ages, with the sharpest demarcation found in the youngest age group. Conclusions: Analysis at the SGB level unveils microbial dysbiosis patterns with greater precision than traditional species-level profiling, providing a novel theoretical basis for the precision diagnosis and age-specific management of dental caries.

title: Roots through time: dynamics of the rhizosphere microbiome and its nutrient-cycling potential in Zostera marina meadows with implications for microbiome-based restoration.
abstract: The seagrass rhizosphere microbiome is critical for sedimentary nutrient turnover, yet the spatiotemporal dynamics of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur cycling across Zostera marina developmental stages remain poorly understood. Leveraging metagenomic sequencing and 147 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), we resolved functional gene profiles in rhizosphere and bulk sediments across three discrete developmental stage (vegetative, reproductive and dormant). Temporal variation (i.e., sampling period) explained 48.1-57.4% of the variance in nutrient-cycling-associated microbial community composition, whereas spatial partitioning between rhizosphere and bulk compartments accounted for 11.6-20.0%. Carbon fixation genes were significantly enriched in the rhizosphere during reproduction but reached peak abundance in bulk sediments during dormancy. Nitrogen fixation and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) genes were enriched in the rhizosphere during both vegetative and dormant stages. Phosphorus mobilization-associated genes displayed parallel enrichment patterns, with the regulatory two-component system gene phoR broadly conserved across MAGs. Sulfur oxidation genes were enriched in the rhizosphere during vegetative and dormant stages, yet exhibited higher relative abundance in bulk sediments during reproduction. Critically, multiple Desulfobacterota MAGs co-occurred with nitrogen fixation and sulfate reduction genes, and the alkaline phosphatase gene phoD was identified in several of these genomes. Together, these findings reveal developmentally orchestrated shifts in microbial nutrient-cycling potential, underscoring the importance of protecting the native rhizosphere microbiome in eelgrass restoration, while considering site-specific biogeochemical constraints, particularly nutrient availability and sulfide conditions.
authors: Sun J, Zhao X, Yan WJ, Li WT, Sun WL, Zhang PD.

title: Clavispora mexcalensis sp. nov.: a novel Mexican yeast species isolated from mezcal must with promising polyol and ethanol production from lignocellulose hydrolysates.
abstract: Yeasts are micro-organisms with high biotechnological potential for various industrial processes. Non-conventional yeasts offer advantages over classic Saccharomyces yeasts, such as the ability to assimilate pentoses natively. This project aimed to describe and characterize a new yeast species isolated from mezcal must in Oaxaca, México. For its identification, whole-genome sequencing was performed. Phylogenomic analyses (BUSCO, OrthoFinder and IQ-TREE) indicated 99.0% genome completeness of included 2,319 orthologs. Comparative genomic analyses were performed using average nucleotide identity (ANI), calculated with FastANI and core-proteome phylogenomics, complemented by average amino acid identity (AAI) comparisons. Additionally, macro- and micro-morphological analyses (the latter by scanning electron microscopy) were performed. l-arabinose assimilation and thermotolerance were also assessed. The uptake of various sugars, including xylose and arabinose, was evaluated, and the corresponding metabolic pathways were confirmed through experimental and genomic analyses. Phylogenomic analysis, together with FastANI and complementary AAI values, confirmed that, despite its close relationship to Clavispora lusitaniae and Clavispora paralusitaniae, this strain represents a novel species, for which the name Clavispora mexcalensis sp. nov. is proposed. The strain exhibits marked thermotolerance, maintaining substantial growth at 48 °C. It assimilates glucose, d-xylose, l-arabinose and cellobiose as sole carbon sources, and produces xylitol, ethanol and arabitol. Macro- and micro-morphological characteristics are consistent with those of other members of the genus Clavispora, although some cells exhibit numerous bud scars. These results expand the known diversity of yeasts associated with mezcal and indicate that Cl. mexcalensis sp. nov. is a potential candidate for biotechnological applications requiring high-temperature tolerance or the bioconversion of unconventional sugars.
journal: International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology
authors: Lara-Meléndez A, Hernández-García JA, Ponce-Noyola T, Villa-Tanaca L, Ramos-Valdivia AC, Barrera-Cortés J, Salgado LM.

title: Genome-Wide Analysis of C2H2 Transcription Factors in Phoebe bournei and Functional Characterization of PnC2H2-14 in Cold Tolerance.
abstract: Low temperature is a major abiotic stress that severely restricts plant growth, development, and geographical distribution. Although C2H2 zinc finger proteins have been widely implicated in regulating plant growth and responses to environmental stresses, their biological functions in Phoebe bournei remain largely unexplored. In this study, a total of 61 C2H2 genes were identified from the P. bournei genome and grouped into five phylogenetic clades. Comparative analyses of conserved motifs and exon-intron organization demonstrated that members within each clade share highly similar structural characteristics. Promoter analysis indicated that PnC2H2 genes are associated with stress- and hormone-responsive elements. PnC2H2-14 was strongly induced by cold stress and predominantly expressed in leaves. Subcellular localization confirmed that PnC2H2-14 is a nuclear protein, while yeast assays demonstrated that it possesses no intrinsic transcriptional activation activity. Functional characterization revealed that ectopic expression of PnC2H2-14 in tobacco markedly improved cold tolerance by limiting reactive oxygen species accumulation, enhancing antioxidant enzyme activities, and alleviating membrane injury during cold exposure. In addition, several antioxidant-related genes were significantly upregulated in transgenic plants. These results suggest that PnC2H2-14 positively regulates cold tolerance by enhancing antioxidant defense and maintaining ROS homeostasis. This study provides insights into the evolution and function of the C2H2 gene family in P. bournei and identifies candidate genes for improving cold resistance.
authors: Yang Y, Zhou S, Zhu Y, Fei Y, Hu D, Yang Y, Cheng Z.

title: Outer Membrane Vesicles as a Potential Pathway for Antibiotic Resistance Transfer between Cyanobacteria and Bacteria.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) have profoundly exacerbated environmental risks to public health, evolving into a pressing ecological dilemma. Distinct from traditional pathways, outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) are emerging as important vectors for horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in aquatic environments, yet their role in inter-phylum ARG dissemination remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that OMVs mediate bidirectional HGT of ARGs between the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 and Escherichia coli DH5α. Co-incubation experiments confirmed that OMVs derived from either strain could associate with the other, accompanied by successful functional expression of transferred resistance genes. In simulated aquatic environmental conditions, OMVs supplementation increased HGT frequency by 1.49-2.27 folds compared to the control group on day 5. Metagenomic analysis further revealed that OMVs carrying resistance genes induced subtle shifts in coastal microbial community composition. Our findings establish OMVs as mobile genetic packages that enable ARGs exchange between cyanobacteria and heterotrophic bacteria, highlighting a previously overlooked pathway for environmental dissemination of ARGs and providing a theoretical basis for mitigating antibiotic resistance risks in aquatic ecosystems.
authors: Yang Y, Zhang W, Ma Y, Zhang Y, Liu J, Niu Z.

title: A Sargassum-associated phage slows Vibrio alginolyticus persistence on macroalgal surfaces.
abstract: Macroalgal surfaces harbour dense and metabolically active microbial consortia in which Vibrio alginolyticus exhibits marked ecological plasticity, spanning from mutualistic to opportunistic lifestyles. In these structured biofilm habitats, phages play a central role in shaping bacterial population structure and metabolic interactions. Here, a lytic phage vB_ValP-R39Z (R39Z) and its V. alginolyticus host were isolated from the surface of Sargassum hemiphyllum. Phage R39Z displays a podovirus morphotype, with a latent period of ~50 min and a burst size of 109 p.f.u. per cell, a narrow host range restricted to its original host, and stability across environmentally relevant conditions (pH 7-9 and 4-35 °C). R39Z harbours a 71.8 kb dsDNA genome (37.7 mol% G+C), encoding 83 ORFs, and is distinct from established genera, representing a previously unclassified genus. Functionally, R39Z significantly reduced biofilm biomass in vitro, and in an ex vivo assay using Sargassum blades, it reduced the viable cell abundance of V. alginolyticus ZS10 on blade surfaces by ~99%, as determined by c.f.u. enumeration. These findings demonstrate that R39Z efficiently disrupts biofilm formation and suppresses Vibrio colonization on macroalgal surfaces, underscoring its ecological relevance and potential for targeted biocontrol in algal-associated microbiomes.
authors: Zuo Z, Jiang H, Zhu P, Zhang Q, Li M, Zou L, Zhang R, Yang Y, Yang Y.

title: Antimicrobial resistance in environment and wastewaters of a swine slaughterhouse - tracking ESKAPE bacteria and ESBL-/carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli.
abstract: IntroductionThis study investigated the occurrence, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profiles, and genomic features of selected ESKAPE bacteria and ESBL-/carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli isolated from wastewater and floor swabs in a swine slaughterhouse in Central Italy.MethodsBy integrating microbiological and genomic analyses across different operational phases, the study observed persistence and dissemination of antimicrobial resistant bacteria (ARB) within the abattoir environment.ResultsE. coli was the most prevalent species (39.6%) across all matrices, confirming its role as an indicator of fecal and environmental contamination. Despite cleaning and depuration, few ARB and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) persisted, particularly in wastewater, reflecting the partial efficacy of conventional sanitation and treatment measures. The antimicrobial susceptibility tests revealed high resistance against ampicillin (47.2%), tetracycline (41.2%), and trimethoprim (34.0%), with multidrug resistant isolates occurring in nearly one-third of samples. Whole-genome sequencing identified the resistome, e.g., bla TEM, bla CTX-M, and bla OXA-48 genes. The detection of bla NDM in treated wastewater underscores the potential for environmental dissemination of carbapenemase producers. Phylogenetic analyses revealed clonal persistence of OXA- and ESBL-producing E. coli and Acinetobacter baumannii across samples, while livestock-associated MRSA ST398 indicated localized contamination events.DiscussionThese findings demonstrate that slaughterhouse ecosystems can function as active reservoirs and transmission nodes for AMR.
authors: Manfreda C, Guarneri F, Ferri G, Di Vittori C, Olivastri A, Piccioni MA, Ianieri A, Alborali GL, Vergara A.

title: Genome mining and comprehensive molecular characterization of feline Panleukopenia virus reveals distinct VP2 mutational signatures and evolutionary divergence.
abstract: Feline Panleukopenia Virus is a highly contagious, systemic, and environmentally stable virus that primarily targets leukocytes and affects cats of all ages. Despite its clinical and epidemiological importance, limited molecular surveillance studies have been conducted in the densely populated downstate region of New York. The objective of this study was to investigate the molecular and serological prevalence of FPV among shelter cats in this region and to isolate and genetically characterize circulating strains. Samples, including swabs and sera, were collected from 108 shelter cats and tested using quantitative PCR (qPCR) and immunofluorescent assay (IFA), respectively. Results showed that 25.0% (27/108) of the cats were FPV-positive by qPCR, while 39.8% (43/108) were positive by IFA, indicating active viral circulation within the tested populations. Viral isolation was successfully performed using Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) cells. Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) confirmed the detection of a newly characterized FPV isolate (Accession: PZ251627) circulating within the tested shelter cat population. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated high nucleotide similarity with previously reported FPV strains, including MH165482 (99.3%), MN127781 (99.2%), and MH165481 (99.2%). Analysis of the VP2 gene also revealed close similarity with isolates OQ615264, KT899746, and PVMRFD, along with two amino acid substitutions, Ile101Thr and Glu411Ala. Spatial interpolation analysis identified a higher occurrence of FPV-positive cats in western downstate New York, emphasizing the importance of continued surveillance and monitoring programs.
journal: Infection, genetics and evolution : journal of molecular epidemiology and evolutionary genetics in infectious diseases
authors: Hemida MU, Moawed N, Shah AU, Burgos M, Levitan D, Poonsuk K, Vagra C.

title: Rhodotorula mucilaginosa DM2025 ameliorates obesity through cholesterol binding and the gut mycobiome-BAT PPARγ/UCP1 axis.
abstract: Obesity is a major global health challenge, necessitating safe and effective therapies. Although probiotics are promising for obesity management, research has focused on bacteria, leaving non-Saccharomyces yeasts underexplored. Here, we investigated the anti‑obesity mechanisms of Rhodotorula mucilaginosa DM2025, isolated from the healthy murine gut. To test whether benefits depend on viable cells, high‑fat diet‑fed mice received either live yeast or its cell‑free supernatant, followed by integrated physiological, genomic, and metabolomic analyzes. Live yeast, but not supernatant, significantly reduced body weight gain, improved serum lipids, and was associated with activation of brown adipose tissue thermogenesis (upregulated PPARγ, PGC1α, UCP1). Though the supernatant lowered total cholesterol, it failed to affect weight or thermogenic genes, indicating cholesterol‑lowering and weight reduction are distinct processes. Live cells were enriched in propionate, indole, and carotenoid‑related metabolites, with genomic support for their biosynthesis. Live yeast reshaped the gut mycobiome, promoting Basidiomycota/Rhodotorula dominance; this fungal restructuring was absent in HFD controls. These findings suggest that R. mucilaginosa DM2025 anti‑obesity efficacy relies on the continuous metabolic activity of live cells, producing thermogenesis‑associated metabolites that may contribute to BAT activation. Additionally, physical cholesterol binding to the yeast cell surface provides a complementary cholesterol‑reduction mechanism. Thus, R. mucilaginosa DM2025 represents a promising live probiotic candidate for obesity intervention.
authors: Jing Y, Xiang Y, Zafir OC, Sun Q, Chen B, Cao X, Hou J, Li H.

title: Elevational Adaptation in the Moth Thitarodes xiaojinensis: HSP60A-Mediated Thermal Tolerance Evolution Under Gene Flow.
abstract: Climate warming intensifies thermal selection on high-elevation species, yet the molecular mechanisms enabling rapid adaptation under ongoing gene flow remain poorly understood. We examined differentiation between High-elevation (High) and Low-elevation (Low) ecotype samples of Thitarodes xiaojinensis, an endemic ghost moth of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, using SLAF-seq, RNA-seq profiling and survival experiments. Phylogenetic analyses confirm the two ecotype samples are conspecific, and they differ in forewing phenotype. Population structure at K = 2 uncovers elevation-correlated clustering despite weak genome-wide structure (optimal K = 1). Genome-wide F ST scans (Weir & Cockerham) identify HSP60A as a prominent outlier locus (F ST = 0.391, top 1.4% of genome-wide windows). Targeted PCR amplification and sequencing confirmed a nonsense mutation (Glu378*) in the HSP60A coding sequence. This derived allele was carried by 80% (4/5) of Low individuals and by none of 5 High individuals (0 of 10 chromosome copies, one-sided 95% upper bound on allele frequency ≈ 26%), suggesting that it is associated with incipient ecological divergence between the two ecotypes. Co-expression network analysis grouped the chaperone genes into two systems with divergent thermal responses. The small HSPs were induced 2.3-fold from 8°C to 16°C, whereas the classical chaperones were not induced, and HSP60A was consistently placed within the latter (median biweight midcorrelation +0.56 with classical chaperones versus -0.27 with small HSPs, p = 3.5 × 10-9). Across the three temperatures the Low ecotype expressed HSP60A at lower levels than the High ecotype, significant under log2(TPM + 1) (p = 0.020) but not under the other two scales, and survived better at 16°C (p = 0.0342). These results link a coding variant at HSP60A, its lower transcript level in the Low ecotype and the better survival of that ecotype at 16°C, and identify HSP60A as a candidate locus for ecotype-informed conservation of the Ophiocordyceps sinensis host insect.
authors: Wei Q, He Y, Pang S, Chen S.

title: Genome-Wide Identification of the CpG2-like Gene Family in Zucchini (Cucurbita pepo) and the Functional Characterization of CpG2-like74 in Fruit Peel Pigmentation
abstract: Zucchini (Cucurbita pepo L.; 2n = 2x = 40) is an economically important vegetable crop worldwide. G2-like transcription factors, members of the plant-specific GARP superfamily, play important roles in chloroplast development and photosynthetic regulation. However, the G2-like gene family and its functions in zucchini remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, 98 CpG2-like genes were identified and classified into nine subfamilies based on phylogenetic analysis. Nine members clustered with AtGLK1, AtGLK2, and AtAPRR2, which are associated with chloroplast biogenesis and chlorophyll accumulation. Comparative qRT-PCR analysis of different tissues from two zucchini lines with white and dark green fruit peels identified CpG2-like74 as a candidate gene potentially associated with fruit peel coloration. Heterologous overexpression of CpG2-like74 in the Arabidopsis thaliana glk1 glk2 double mutant resulted in greener tissues, improved chloroplast ultrastructure, and increased chlorophyll and carotenoid contents. Subcellular localization analysis showed that CpG2-like74 localized to the nucleus. Yeast one-hybrid and dual-luciferase assays further indicated that CpG2-like74 bound to the promoters of CpCAB7 and CpCAB8 and activated their transcription. In addition, dual-luciferase assays supported its ability to activate the promoters of CpCAB7 and CpCAB8, which encode light-harvesting complex proteins. Collectively, these findings suggest that CpG2-like74 contributes to the regulation of chloroplast development and pigment accumulation and may be involved in fruit peel coloration in zucchini. This study provides a foundation for further investigation of the molecular mechanisms underlying fruit peel color variation and for the potential application of CpG2-like74 in zucchini breeding.
authors: Wang G, Zhang K, Yang Q, Wang Y, Wang C, Qu S.

title: Co-occurring divergent arbitrium receptors outside canonical prophage regions in bacterial genomes.
abstract: Arbitrium signaling enables peptide-mediated communication among bacteriophages and regulates lysis-lysogeny decisions through diverse genetic architectures. Here, we identified two divergent AimR-like receptors in each of the alkaliphilic bacteria Alkalihalobacterium alkalinitrilicum DSM 22532 and Caldalkalibacillus mannanilyticus JCM 10596, with within-genome amino acid identities of 30.6% and 27.4%, respectively. All four receptors occurred outside predicted prophage regions, with distinct genomic neighborhoods and a putative aimP-like gene adjacent to one receptor. Despite substantial sequence divergence, structural comparisons revealed conservation within aligned regions of the AimR fold. Associations with mobile genetic elements suggest possible genomic mobility, although the evolutionary origins and functional roles of these receptors remain unresolved. These findings highlight the diversity of co-occurring AimR-like receptors in bacterial genomes.
authors: Balcázar JL.

title: Electrode-associated growth reveals structure of OmcZ-type cytochrome nanowires in anaerobic methanotrophic archaea.
abstract: Anaerobic methanotrophic (ANME) archaea are key regulators of methane emissions in anoxic environments, yet their physiology remains poorly understood due to the lack of axenic cultures. Here, we show that cultivation on poised electrodes yields near-axenic cultures (95.8% relative abundance) of a freshwater ANME, for which we propose the name 'Candidatus Methanoperedens vercellensis'. We identified key physiological properties of 'Ca. M. vercellensis': doubling times of 4.6 days at 30 °C, menaquinone as respiratory electron carrier, the inability to oxidize ethane, and preferential reduction of iron oxides over nitrate after cultivation on electrodes. A 3.3 Å cryo-electron microscopy structure of filaments displayed on the archaeal surface revealed polymerized OmcZ-type cytochrome nanowires, which are homologous to OmcZ nanowires essential for long-range (>10 μm) extracellular electron transfer (EET) in Geobacter sulfurreducens. The archaeal OmcZ-type nanowires include dense, collinear stacking of protected hemesakin to bacterial OmcZ nanowires, but with post-translational modification, thus yielding morphology distinct from bacterial OmcZ nanowires. Notably, in contrast to bacterial OmcZ, archaeal OmcZ-type nanowires do not form interconnected networks, and hemes are less solvent-exposed, which can protect them from the environment. Surprisingly, these archaea assemble OmcZ into nanowires even in the apparent absence of prolyl isomerase involved in folding bacterial OmcZ. This work establishes a model system for molecular understanding of nanowire-mediated EET in archaea.
authors: Wissink M, Shen C, Wang J, Egas RA, Smid P, Elling FJ, Becker KW, Pabst M, Jetten MSM, Liu J, Malvankar NS, Welte CU.

title: PFBS exposure alters gut microbial functional potential and colon immune responses: an integrated metagenomic and transcriptomic analysis.
abstract: PER: and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental contaminants of global concern, yet the impacts of short-chain substitutes such as perfluorobutanesulfonic acid (PFBS) on gut microbial functional potential and host intestinal responses remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated metagenomic sequencing and transcriptomic profiling to investigate the effects of PFBS exposure in C57BL/6 mice administered PFBS through drinking water for 30 days. PFBS exposure increased serum PFBS concentrations and was associated with colon shortening, reduced goblet cell numbers, and decreased mucus-associated staining. Metagenomic analysis revealed alterations in gut microbial composition and functional profiles, including enrichment of sulfate-reducing bacteria, particularly Desulfovibrio species, and increased abundance of sulfate reduction-associated genes. Colon transcriptomic analysis identified 51 differentially expressed genes, with enrichment of pathways including complement and coagulation cascades. Immune cell abundance estimation and F4/80 immunohistochemistry indicated increased macrophage-associated signals in the PFBS-exposed group. Notably, Desulfovibrio abundance was positively correlated with macrophage-associated scores and the expression of complement genes C1qa, C1qb, and C1qc, whose upregulation was further confirmed by RT-qPCR. Increased hydrogen sulfide concentrations in colon contents were also observed following PFBS exposure. Together, these findings suggest that PFBS exposure was associated with coordinated alterations in Desulfovibrio abundance and colon immune-associated gene expression, highlighting potential microbiota-host interactions relevant to the intestinal effects of short-chain PFAS.
authors: Zhu Y, Wang K, Qin F, Zhang Q, Shen W, Pu C, Li M.

title: Joint species distribution modelling of insect microbiota: Time to jump onto a new opportunity.
abstract: How microbes and insects influence each other is a topical question in insect science. With this contribution, we highlight joint species distribution models (JSDMs) - which model all microbial taxa in a community jointly rather than one at a time - as a statistical framework particularly well suited for resolving the drivers of host-microbe associations. While JSDM has been widely applied to microbiota of organisms other than insects, only a handful of studies have applied them thus far to insect systems. To encourage insect microbiota researchers to catch up with the benefits of JSDM, we outline the statistical and ecological basics of JSDM and give flesh to the modelling framework by reviewing how it has so far been applied to insect microbiota. We highlight the power of JSDMs in separating host, environmental and microbial drivers of community assembly, and in generating hypotheses about how different microbes influence each other. We further propose a predictive framework for identifying and characterizing five ecological categories of insect-associated microbes: (1) obligate nutritional symbionts; (2) facultative endosymbionts; (3) specialized gut associates; (4) transient microbes; and (5) pathogens and parasites. In particular, we hypothesize how the ecological characteristics of these different microbial categories are reflected in the statistical signatures recovered by JSDMs. We further suggest how JSDM can be applied to address the phylogenetic and ecological scales at which microbiome patterns are structured and to uncover how global environmental changes may reshape insect microbiota.
authors: Ovaskainen O, Łukasik P, Roslin T.

title: Microbiota-dependent biofunctionality of sulfated fucans from Saccharina japonica during intestinal epithelial development in juvenile mice: Limosilactobacillus reuteri L11 as a microbial responder.
abstract: Previous studies have demonstrated that sulfated fucans from Saccharina japonica (SJ-FUC) promote intestinal epithelial development in juvenile mice. However, whether this biofunctionality depends on the gut microbiota and which microbial responders contribute to this process remain unclear. Here, we integrated in vitro anaerobic fermentation, metagenomic analysis, antibiotic-mediated microbiota depletion, bacterial isolation, and juvenile mouse intervention to investigate the microbial basis underlying the intestinal biofunctionality of SJ-FUC. In vitro fecal fermentation showed that SJ-FUC markedly remodeled the gut microbiota derived from both conventional and SJ-FUC-adapted mice and selectively enriched specific bacterial taxa. Limosilactobacillus reuteri exhibited a consistent response to SJ-FUC, with a higher baseline abundance in adapted microbiota and further enrichment after fermentation. In antibiotic-treated mice, microbiota depletion markedly attenuated SJ-FUC-induced intestinal stem cell-associated responses, epithelial proliferation, and secretory lineage differentiation, demonstrating that the intestinal effects of SJ-FUC are largely microbiota-dependent. A strain of L. reuteri, designated L11, was subsequently isolated from the SJ-FUC fecal fermentation system and functionally evaluated in juvenile mice. Both viable L11 and its cell-free supernatant upregulated the intestinal stem cell markers Lgr5, Olfm4, and Ascl2, enhanced Wnt/β-catenin-related gene expression and epithelial proliferation, and promoted secretory lineage differentiation. Overall, these findings establish the gut microbiota as an important contributor to the intestinal biofunctionality of SJ-FUC and identify L. reuteri L11 as a functional microbial responder associated with these effects. This study provides new insight into how an edible-algae-derived sulfated polysaccharide influences juvenile intestinal epithelial development through interactions with the gut microbiota.
authors: Wei B, Sun H, Wang Y, Luo Y, Xie T, Chang Y, Wang Y, Tang Q.

title: Symbiotic and commensal root microbes are key determinants of plant responses to rising CO₂
abstract: Rising atmospheric CO₂ stimulates plant growth, but this effect is often constrained by nutrient availability. While beneficial soil-derived microbial symbionts such as nitrogen-fixing rhizobia and mycorrhizal fungi are known to mitigate this limitation, the role of plant commensal microbiota remains unclear. Here, using a gnotobiotic growth system and the model legume Lotus japonicus, we show that the magnitude of plant responses to elevated CO₂ is largely explained by the composition of its root-associated microbial community. Axenic plants exhibited limited physiological responses to increasing CO₂ but inoculation with symbiotic and commensal microbes significantly amplified this effect. Commensal bacteria alone, while not increasing overall biomass, shifted plant carbon allocation belowground. Microbial abundances in roots increased with atmospheric CO₂, even when normalized to plant DNA. The strongest plant and microbial responses were observed when rhizobia, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, and the commensal bacterial community were all present. These findings indicate that multi-partner microbial associations will shape both plant growth and the allocation of carbon belowground as atmospheric CO₂ concentrations continue to rise.
authors: Cotta MS, Kajdewicz P, Anastasopoulos L, Duran-Ballesteros C, Huang J, Kübler K, Göbel M, Trumbore S, Schulze-Lefert P, Garrido-Oter R.

title: Efficacy, Safety and Gut Microbiome Characteristics of Fecal Microbiota Transplantation and immunotherapy for Lung Cancer with Brain Metastases
abstract: Abstract    Objective  The blood-brain barrier (BBB) and central immunosuppressive microenvironment impair the efficacy of immunotherapy in lung-cancer patients with brain metastases (LCBM). Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) remodels intestinal microecology to regulate central immunity via the gut-brain axis. This study aimed to explore the collaboration of FMT and immunotherapy in LCBM, and the potential mechanism by which FMT reshapes gut microbiota to improve intracranial therapeutic efficacy. Methods  Patients with LCBM who received FMT and immunotherapy at Changzhou Second People’s Hospital between May 2024 and April 2026 were enrolled in this retrospective study. Intracranial and extracranial lesion responses were assessed according to RECIST version 1.1. Survival analysis was conducted using the Kaplan-Meier method, and safety was evaluated based on CTCAE version 5.0. Fecal metagenomic sequencing was performed for one representative patient with prominent clinical benefit to characterize shifts in gut-microbiota composition and function before and after FMT. Results  The final follow-up date was August, 2026, with a median follow-up of 10.5 months. The median age of enrolled 16 patients was 68 years (range 49–81 years); 68.75% (11/16) were male. Adenocarcinoma accounted for 93.75% (15/16). 56.25% (9/16) of patients had an ECOG-PS score ≥ 2. 75% (12/16) received one FMT session, and 50% (8/16) were treated in third-line or later settings. The intracranial objective response rate (ORR) was 37.5% and disease control rate (DCR) was 100%, with a median intracranial progression-free survival (iPFS) of 6.1 months. The extracranial ORR was 25.0% and DCR was 93.75%, with a median extracranial progression-free survival (ePFS) of 7.2 months. No significant efficacy difference was observed between patients with EGFR-TKI resistance and those without EGFR mutations. Most FMT-related adverse events were grade 1–2 self-limiting gastrointestinal reactions. Microbiota analysis of the beneficiary patient revealed severe baseline gut dysbiosis characterized by over-enrichment of Firmicutes and near-depletion of Bacteroidetes. After FMT, microbial diversity was restored and elevated; the  Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes  ratio reached a balanced status.  Phocaeicola  ,  Bacteroides  and butyrate-producing beneficial bacteria were markedly enriched while pathogenic bacteria were effectively suppressed, accompanied by substantial improvement in anti-tumor metabolic capacity of the gut microbiome. Conclusion  FMT is safe and feasible for patients with LCBM. By remodeling intestinal microecological balance, FMT achieves promising and durable intracranial disease control when combined with immonotherapy.
authors: Qin L, Li D, Wang C, Qian D, Wei Y, Qi Y, Tao L, Chen P, Jiang H, Geng Q.

title: Parenteral CHIKV mRNA Vaccination Reshapes the Gut Microbial, Metabolic, and Immune Landscapes.
abstract: The gut microbiota is increasingly recognized as a critical modulator of vaccine efficacy. However, how parenteral vaccines-particularly those against non-enteric viruses-reshape the intestinal microenvironment remains poorly defined. Here, we investigated the impact of two validated CHIKV mRNA vaccines on gut microbial composition, metabolic activity, and immune features in rhesus macaques. Using a longitudinal multi-omics approach, including metagenomics, metabolomics, and proteomics, and comparing with CHIKV-infected animals, we assessed whether systemic vaccination alone, in the absence of intestinal viral replication, was associated with changes in the gut microenvironment. We demonstrate that vaccination induces reproducible shifts in gut microbiota composition, notably enriching Segatella copri, similar to infection-associated changes. These alterations are accompanied by remodeling of purine and bile acid metabolism, with persistent increases in xanthine and uric acid. Upon viral challenge, vaccinated animals exhibit reduced intestinal viral burden, attenuated pathology, and elevated expression of proteins related to antigen presentation, immunoglobulins, and epithelial barrier function. These findings provide direct evidence that systemic CHIKV mRNA vaccination is associated with changes in the gut microbial, metabolic, and immune landscapes, highlighting the gastrointestinal tract as an active and responsive target of parenteral vaccinations.

title: L-carnitine conjugation: a previously unrecognized pathway proposed for anaerobic benzo(a)pyrene biodegradation by Alicycliphilus sp. T452 under nitrate‑reducing conditions.
abstract: Anaerobic respiration of microorganisms is a key process driving the degradation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in contaminated environments. However, the mechanism underlying the anaerobic breakdown of benzo(a)pyrene remains poorly understood, limiting our knowledge of the fate and natural attenuation potential of this hazardous compound. Here, we report a novel nitrate‑reducing bacterium, Alicycliphilus sp. T452, isolated from PAH‑contaminated river sediment, which degrades benzo(a)pyrene under anaerobic conditions with a degradation ratio of 40.6% ± 2.9% over 100 h. Using UHPLC‑QTOF/MS‑based metabolite profiling, 18 potential intermediates were putatively identified, including four L‑carnitine‑conjugated intermediates, of which two were supported by deuterium labeling. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses revealed that specific clusters containing genes encoding Pfam L-carnitine dehydratase bile acid/inducible protein were specifically upregulated during benzo(a)pyrene degradation, providing multi-omics evidence supporting the proposal of a L‑carnitine‑conjugated pathway. This L‑carnitine conjugation likely enhances the solubility and intracellular transport of hydrophobic benzo(a)pyrene‑derived metabolites, representing a proposed microbial strategy to overcome bioavailability constraints. In addition, L‑carnitine is naturally present in anoxic environments, and its conjugation may represent a general microbial adaptation to hydrophobic organic contaminants. Our findings thus expand our understanding of the anaerobic fate of PAHs and offer mechanistic insights into their natural attenuation in contaminated environments.
authors: Deng T, Dong M, Geng C, Ren K, Xu M.

title: Computational functional annotation and structural modelling of hypothetical proteins in Stenotrophomonas maltophilia NCTC10958.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance represents a significant global health challenge, specifically concerning the escalation of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia has emerged as a prevalent pathogen affecting immunocompromised patients in intensive care units. Its incidence has notably increased, particularly during the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic, complicated by resistance mechanisms such as enzymatic degradation and biofilm formation. Despite its clinical importance, the functional roles of many genomic regions remain obscure. This study aimed to characterize 61 hypothetical proteins from S. maltophilia NCTC10958 to elucidate their involvement in virulence and adaptation. Functional annotation revealed that a significant proportion of these proteins are membrane-associated enzymes and transporters essential for environmental adaptation. Key findings include the identification of putative virulence factors involved in biofilm formation and motility, such as phosphoglycerate mutase and type IV pilus assembly proteins. Crucially, the analysis uncovered key functional determinants, including a ComEC/Rec2 family competence protein involved in DNA uptake and a mycobacterial membrane protein large family transporter linked to cell envelope processes and transport. Structural modelling validated high-confidence tertiary structures for these targets, confirming their biological feasibility. These insights provide a foundation for understanding the pathogenicity of S. maltophilia NCTC10958 and highlight specific HPs as promising candidates for therapeutic intervention.
authors: Alnaqshabandy IHF.

title: Genome annotation and population genomics reveal adaptive signatures in the Japanese seahorse (Hippocampus mohnikei) based on whole-genome resequencing.
abstract: The Japanese seahorse (Hippocampus mohnikei) is a fish species of significant commercial and ecological value in East Asia. However, its genomic structure and adaptive mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we performed structural annotation of the available genome and conducted a systematic population genomic survey of four geographic populations (WH, LZ, QD and XM) from coastal waters of China. The results show that the Japanese seahorse has 24,595 annotated protein-coding genes, and evaluations combining BUSCO (83.05%-92.92%), OMArk (91.95%), and transcriptomic validation (base-level precision of 77.40%) suggest a moderate-to-high completeness and structural accuracy of this gene set. A total of 5,569,533 SNPs were initially identified, and 604,542 high-quality SNPs were retained after stringent filtering and LD pruning for downstream population genomic analyses. Population genomic analysis revealed that the observed heterozygosity (Ho) was moderate (0.2419-0.2756), but nucleotide diversity (π) remained consistently low (~ 0.0030), suggesting that a putative population expansion or bottleneck event may have occurred recently. Adaptive scanning analysis identified 118 candidate adaptive loci, primarily concentrated on two contig-level genomic regions (331 and 557). Functional analysis of the 515 associated candidate genes revealed an enrichment in cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) pathways, MAPK signaling, and neurodevelopmental genes, which are putatively associated with environmental stress responses. These findings suggest that the local adaptation of the Japanese seahorse may potentially involve stress-responsive pathways. This research offers fundamental genomic insights for elucidating the adaptive evolution of seahorses.
journal: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part D, Genomics & proteomics
authors: Liu C, Lv W, Yuan T, Wang K, Su X.

title: Environmental media-based microbial source tracking enables source identification of antimicrobial resistance in urban rivers.
abstract: Urban rivers receiving treated wastewater remain hotspots for antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), yet quantitative source attribution remains challenging. Conventional microbial source tracking (MST) cannot distinguish ARG contributions from treated effluent, untreated sewage, and environmental reservoirs such as sediments. Here, we developed an environmental media-based MST (EM-MST) framework integrating source-enriched microbial markers to quantify ARG sources in an urban river impacted by two wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) and combined sewer overflow (CSO). From fifteen screened markers, NOB-16S (effluent-enriched nitrite-oxidizing bacteria), dsrA (sediment-enriched sulfate-reducing bacteria), and crAssphage (sewage-associated) were selected using qPCR validation and multivariate analysis. Combined with shotgun metagenomic profiling of 676 ARGs and a non-negative least squares mixing model, these markers enabled source attribution. During dry weather, WWTP effluent accounted for the largest source proportion (81.5-93.1%), with efflux pump, sulfonamide, macrolide, and aminoglycoside ARGs. During the sampled CSO event, untreated sewage accounted for 91%-100% of the estimated source contribution, delivering β-lactam, macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin, and tetracycline ARGs associated with gut microbiota. River sediments showed greater resistome similarity to WWTP effluent, consistent with an effluent-associated ARG reservoir, while the estimated sediment contribution remained minor (3.0 ± 5.3%). The EM-MST enables quantitative differentiation of ARG sources in wastewater-impacted urban rivers.
authors: Sabar MA, Than VH, Sugie Y, Wada H, Zhao B, Matsuura N, Ihara M, Watanabe T, Tanaka H, Honda R.

title: Potential of foaming events in reshaping vertical distribution of waterborne antibiotic-resistant human pathogens and signaling public health risks in surface waters.
abstract: While pathogens in surface waters frequently cause epidemic outbreaks and millions of annual deaths worldwide, their association with natural aqueous foaming, a common yet overlooked phenomenon, remains unexplored. This study investigated whether foaming is associated with changes in the distribution and potential risk of antibiotic-resistant human pathogens (ARHPB) in surface waters, challenging the traditional view that sediments are the primary sink for waterborne pathogens. The surface foam layer was found to coincide with selective transport of bacteria (particularly, the potential priority multidrug-resistant genera like Acinetobacter and Enterobacter) from benthic sediments into the water column via bubble adhesion, a mechanism linked to the bacterial virulence trait of motility. Meanwhile, bacteriophages were predominantly distributed in the water column, where genes associated with immune modulation were more abundant. Metagenomic analysis reveals that the relative abundance of potential human-pathogenic bacteria harboring co-localized antibiotic resistance genes and mobile genetic elements was greater in the water column during foaming (from near-zero to markedly higher levels) than under unfoamed conditions, suggesting enhanced potential for horizontal gene transfer. However, foamed and unfoamed samples were collected in July and October, respectively, and the temporal confound prevented causal attribution to foaming alone. Nevertheless, consistent patterns across four independent water bodies indicate that foaming events are among the covarying factors for the elevated potential ARHPB relative abundance and deserve further exploration as potential sentinels for public health risks. Inclusion of foam monitoring in aquatic risk assessment frameworks warrants consideration, pending prospective validation.
authors: Zhang M, Liu J, Shen Y, Chen J, Li J, Fang Q, Huang J, Zhang S, Shao Z, Yang J, Luo Y, Zhang D, Imanmadi D, Pan X.

title: Unveiling Microbial Gene Functions in Maize Cultivars With Varying Drought Resistance.
abstract: The rhizosphere microbiome is recognized as a "biological tool" for mitigating drought stress on plant development. However, the functional genes involved in plant-microbe interactions, particularly in drought-sensitive and drought-tolerant cultivars, remain poorly understood. This study comparatively evaluated the functional gene set of the maize rhizosphere microbiome in Monsanto DKC 72-70 (drought-tolerant) and CRN-3505 (drought-sensitive) maize genotypes at water holding capacity (WHC) values of 60, 80, and 100% via shotgun metagenomics. The findings revealed that both cultivars contained a variety of microbial taxa, such as Actinobacteria, Alphaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacilli, with plant stress tolerance genes. The analysis of beta diversity indicated significant differences between drought-stressed (60% WHC) and well-watered (100% WHC) conditions in both cultivars (R ≈ 0.57, 0.58; p < 0.01), which implies that the functional gene composition is different and that there are intermediate patterns at 80% WHC. In terms of functional responses, drought-sensitive maize presented increased expression of genes related to sulfur oxidation (soxA, soxB, soxD) and osmoprotectant synthesis (BetI, betC, CHCH), indicating a reactive stress response. Conversely, drought- tolerant maize presented regulated expression of the nitrogen metabolism (glnA) and iron homeostasis (FUR) genes in all the WHCs, thus indicating efficient adaptation. In addition, the drought-tolerant maize cultivar selectively expressed stress-response genes (SigB, AhpC) and protein protection genes (dnaJ, dnaK), whereas the drought-sensitive maize cultivar constitutively expressed these genes across conditions. This study provides novel evidence of cultivar-specific functional microbial signatures and demonstrates how microbial gene functions underpin drought tolerance in maize under varying water availability conditions.
authors: Molefe-Madlaliso RR, Amoo AE, Babalola OO.

title: Parasites of parasites: Herbaria as archives of hidden ecological interactions.
abstract: Hyperparasitism, the infection of parasites by other parasites, is among the least explored ecological interaction types. Ampelomyces, intracellular fungi that infect the plant diseases causing powdery mildews, form a naturally occurring parasite-on-parasite system that is both widespread and poorly understood. This tripartite association among plants, pathogens and hyperparasites provides a powerful model for studying multi-trophic interactions and the evolution of host specialization. Using DNA from herbarium specimens collected across 28 countries over the past 150 years as well as those available in NCBI GenBank, we revealed previously hidden ecological and evolutionary patterns in the Ampelomyces-powdery mildew system. Historical collections allowed us to detect hyperparasites that cannot be easily observed, uncovering multiple novel lineages and global patterns of host association. A global reassessment of all publicly available sequences showed that 13% of entries labelled as Ampelomyces are misidentified, revealing a major issue with uncurated, public databases. To resolve this, we developed a curated, voucher-linked phylogenetic framework in T-BAS to serve as a reference for future ecological, genomic and biocontrol studies. Together, our results demonstrate that herbaria function as large-scale ecological observatories, capable of revealing cryptic interactions across continents and providing a strengthened framework for future ecological and evolutionary research on hyperparasitism.
authors: Thomas J, Paul A, Crouch U, Braun U, Takamatsu S, Németh MZ, Kiss L, Carbone I, Mitchell J, Cotter HVT, Bradshaw M.

title: Discovery of New Quinoxaline, Tetracyclic-Quinoxaline, and Imidazo[2,1-a]isoindole Derivatives as Potent Antibacterial Candidates Targeting DNA Gyrase and Topoisomerase IV With Molecular Modeling Simulations.
abstract: Developing new antibacterial agents is crucial for combating antibiotic resistance, which has predominantly emerged due to the overuse and misuse of antimicrobial agents. In this study, a new series of quinoxaline-based compounds and imidazo[2,1-a]isoindole derivatives were synthesized through the reaction of 1,2-diaminobenzene with carbonyl-rich compounds. The structures of these derivatives were confirmed through various spectroscopic analyses (IR, mass spectra, and 1H/13C NMR) and elemental analysis. Furthermore, their antibacterial activities were evaluated in vitro. Antibacterial efficacy was assessed against three gram-positive (Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus pneumoniae, and Bacillus subtilis) and three gram-negative bacterial isolates (Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa); compounds 3, 9, and 14 demonstrated significant inhibitory activity against all tested isolates, with comparable MIC and MBC values. To further explore their antimicrobial potential, these three active synthesized compounds were assessed for their antibiofilm activity as anti-infective agents against S. aureus (MDR224) and P. aeruginosa (MDR225). Notably, three compounds demonstrated superior bactericidal activity compared to ciprofloxacin (CIP), with undetectable resistance frequencies. Additionally, their potency for inhibiting DNA gyrase and DNA topoisomerase IV was found to be significantly promising, with low IC50 values ranging from 6.75 ± 0.82 to 8.27 ± 1.2 µM and from 8.79 ± 0.24 to 10.33 ± 0.81 µM, respectively, in contrast to CIP, which exhibited IC50 values of 47.68 ± 0.17 and 35.4 ± 0.55 µM. The in silico ADME, pharmacokinetic properties, docking simulations, and DFT calculations of the most promising candidates, 3, 9, and 14, demonstrate significant antibacterial activity and considerable potential for future development.
authors: Ragab A, Basseem M, Aboul-Magd DS, Kronek J, Kroneková Z.

title: Nitrogen availability modulates soil microbial carbon fixation in wetland through community and metabolic remodelling.
abstract: Excess agricultural nitrogen (N) from farm drainage and runoff causes wetland water N pollution and destabilizes soil carbon (C) sinks, however, how this N enrichment regulates wetland soil microbial autotrophic C fixation remains unclear. Here, we combined field experiments, 13CO2 continuous pulse labeling, DNA-stable isotope probing and metagenomics to investigate the dose-dependent effects of N input on soil microbial community assembly, co-occurrence networks, C-fixation pathways, and soil physicochemical properties in Songnen Plain saline-alkali wetlands of China. The results indicate that N input exerts a threshold regulation on microbial C fixation, with distinct depth-dependent responses. Intermediate N input (N2, 10 g N m-2 yr-1) alleviates soil microbial N limitation, elevates RubisCO and hydrolase activities, optimizes soil CN-phosphorus stoichiometry, and promotes the accumulation of mineral-associated organic C. Such intermediate N input remodels microbial community structure, increases microbial diversity and network stability, and enriches key C-fixing taxa including Cyanobacteriota and Alphaproteobacteria, thereby upregulating six core autotrophic C-fixation pathways. In contrast, excessive N (N4, 24 g N m-2 yr-1) input induces soil acidification and nutrient imbalance, disrupts microbial network stability, declines functional C-fixing microbiota and suppresses C-fixation gene expression, ultimately reducing soil CO2 assimilation and organic C accumulation. Structural equation modelling and random forest analyses further reveal soil microbial biomass N and RubisCO activity are the primary drivers of microbial C fixation, mediated by soil microbial C metabolic pathways and community diversity. This work reveals mechanisms of wetland soil C fixation under agricultural N pollution and informs wetland nutrient management and C-sink conservation.
authors: Luo S, Song Y, Zhao Y, Zhang H, Ren J, Zhang J, Song C.

title: cgMLST typing reproducibility is maintained across diverse whole-genome sequencing workflows in a multi-country HERA2 surveillance pilot.
abstract: IntroductionWhole-genome sequencing (WGS) has become indispensable in infectious disease surveillance, yet its implementation across laboratories remains heterogeneous. Six laboratories from four European countries participated in 2023 in a pilot ring trial as part of the HERA2 project, using a standardized panel of 25 bacterial isolates representing five public health-relevant species. The aim was to assess the comparability and reproducibility of laboratory-specific WGS workflows and to determine whether workflow-related variability affected cgMLST-based interpretations relevant for routine surveillance and outbreak investigations.MethodsParticipating laboratories applied their established wet-laboratory workflows, including different sample-processing, DNA-extraction and library-preparation methods and sequencing platforms. Illumina sequencing was performed by all laboratories, while Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing was available in two. To specifically evaluate variability introduced by wet-laboratory procedures, all raw sequencing data were centrally processed using the same bioinformatic pipeline. Reproducibility was primarily assessed using cgMLST allelic distances to the Lab 1 Illumina comparator assembly and concordance of cluster assignments, complemented by analyses of sequencing and assembly variability.ResultsDespite substantial differences in wet-laboratory workflows and technical sequencing characteristics, retained Illumina records showed only small cgMLST allelic differences across laboratories (0-2 alleles) and concordant cluster assignments. Sequencing and assembly metrics varied according to laboratory, species, and technical factors, but this variability did not prevent concordant Illumina-based cluster interpretation among records meeting predefined minimum quality requirements. ONT results were more species-dependent, and several records, particularly for Salmonella enterica, did not achieve the required cgMLST target completeness. These ONT findings should be interpreted in the context of the technology available at the time of the 2023 ring trial.ConclusionsOur results suggest that complete standardization of wet-laboratory workflows may not be required to achieve comparable Illumina-based cgMLST results across laboratories. Rather, laboratories may retain validated local workflows provided that the resulting sequencing data meet appropriate minimum quality requirements. This supports a pragmatic approach to multi-laboratory genomic surveillance that prioritizes data quality and fitness-for-purpose over uniformity of individual wet-laboratory procedures.
authors: Cabal Rosel A, Galanopoulos AP, Polemis M, Henczkó J, Pappa O, Karligiotou E, Malliarou M, Chochlakis D, Hyden P, Daza Prieto B, Stöger A, Polzer D, Ungvári E, Tóth Á, Ruppitsch W, Juric D, Ferencak I, Tabain I.

title: Feed additives as systems-level modulators of the ruminant host-microbiome interaction: a multi-omics perspective on efficiency, resistance, and reproduction.
abstract: Ruminant livestock face converging pressures from climatic variation, antimicrobial agents, and the imperative for sustainable intensification. However, the molecular imprints through which nutritional interventions modulate host-microbiome interactions across physiological contexts remain fragmented across disciplinary themes. Here, we synthesize evidence from metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metabolomics, and host transcriptomics to propose that feed additives operate as systems-level modulators of a functionally integrated rumen-liver-immune-reproductive axis, rather than acting on isolated metabolic pathways. Prevotella, Butyrivibrio, Ruminococcus, and Fibrobacter recurrently emerged across studies to be associated with feed efficiency, immune modulation, resistome dynamics, and reproductive fitness. However, their relationship is context dependent and not causal. Furthermore, hepatic transcriptomic and microRNA (miRNA)-mediated regulatory networks could serve as a molecular bridge connecting ruminal fermentation events to systemic phenotypic outcomes. The ruminant resistome may also represent a potential interface with public health rather than an isolated ecological phenomenon, given the capacity for horizontal gene transfer through mobile genetic elements, although the extent of transmission to humans remains to be quantified. Early-life microbial programming and reproductive tract microbiome composition also represent tractable intervention windows for precision management. This integrated framework could reframe feed additive research from a single pathway to a systems-level perspective, offering a basis for precision ruminant production.
authors: Fijabi O, Morenikeji OB, Ivey SL, Loest C, Idowu M, Ashley R, Ogunade IM, Taiwo G.

title: Isolation and characterization of novel Klebsiella phages from Benin and their antibiofilm activities on multidrug resistant and hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae strains.
abstract: Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae represents a growing clinical threat, particularly where multidrug resistance limits treatment options. This study aims to characterize Klebsiella phages isolated in Benin and evaluate their efficacy in reducing bacterial cell growth, biofilm inhibition and biofilm disruption. To achieve this objective, we isolated Klebsiella phages by enriching samples of hospital effluent, pig droppings, and stool, using clinical multidrug resistant and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae strains as hosts. These phages were characterized using transmission electron microscopy, whole-genome sequencing, and biological assays. Then, we evaluated their antibiofilm activity and stability under harsh conditions (pH and temperature) in vitro. So, we report the isolation and characterization of three novel lytic phages from Benin (Kp1Bj_HH11_M23, Kp2Bj_LN294_M23, and Kp10Bj_LN54_14). These Myoviruses, belonging to the genera Marfavirus and Jiaodavirus, display broad host range activity against multidrug resistant and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae strains with various capsular serotypes including KL114, KL53, KL8, KL62, KL64, KL124, KL102, KL57, KL39, KL48, KL17, KL20, KL2, KL30, KL51, KL105, KL146, KL28, KL122, KL38, KL3, and KL163. Genomic analysis confirmed the absence of virulence and antimicrobial resistance genes. The phages exhibit rapid adsorption, short latency periods (5-10 min), and high burst sizes (119-2208 PFU/cell). All three phages have significantly biofilm disruption effect in vitro (Kp1Bj_HH11_M23, biofilm disruption rate of 98.46 %, p-value = 0.0170; Kp2Bj_LN294_M23, biofilm disruption rate of 65.56%, p-value p-value = 0.003). Their stability across a wide range of temperatures and pH further supports their potential for therapeutic development. Together, these data highlight the value of locally sourced phages as candidates for tackling region-specific antimicrobial resistance challenges.

title: Camptothecin transformation in plant-associated Sphingobium lineages is linked to a plasmid accessory region.
abstract: Specialized plant metabolites impose strong chemical constraints on plant-associated microorganisms; however, the bacterial pathways that enable transformation of complex alkaloid scaffolds remain poorly understood. Here, we show that plant-associated Sphingobium lineages transform camptothecin (CPT) and that this phenotype is associated with a plasmid accessory region. Strain OP1, isolated from the rhizosphere of the CPT-producing plant Ophiorrhiza pumila, transformed CPT into a transient product, M1, which retained the E-ring lactone and subsequently decreased during incubation. OP1 also transformed 10-hydroxycamptothecin, whereas transformation of 7-ethyl-10-hydroxycamptothecin was delayed or limited, indicating substrate selectivity. Genome-based taxonomic analyses placed OP1, NN19, and KJ09 in one putative novel Sphingobium species-level lineage and IROP2 in a related but distinct lineage. Comparison of NN19 with its non-transforming derivative NTG18 resulted in the identification of GAP2, a 97.8-kb region of plasmid pNN19-1 absent from NTG18 and enriched in redox, hydrolase, transport, regulatory, oxygenation, and ring-cleavage functions. A rearranged pIROP2 module retained homologs of the core GAP2 oxygenation and ring-cleavage candidates, whereas IROP2 generated oxygenated products from CPT analogs. RNA sequencing during growth of NN19 with CPT as the sole added carbon source prioritized the same early module, including monooxygenase and dioxygenase candidates. The collective phenotypic, chemical, genetic, comparative-genomic, and expression evidence supports a model in which a plasmid accessory module contributes to CPT transformation.
authors: Takeda H, Takahashi N, Kakiura KSI, Suzuki H, Kijinami T, Horiuchi M, Wakana D, Sudoh H, Hosoe T.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance at Slaughterhouse and Meat-Processing Interfaces in East Africa: A One Health Review of Contamination Pathways, Occupational Exposure and Control Strategies
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major One Health challenge because resistant microorganisms and resistance determinants can circulate among humans, animals and the environment. Slaughterhouses and meat-processing facilities represent important interfaces within this interconnected system. Animals carrying resistant bacteria may introduce them into slaughter environments, where contamination can occur through gastrointestinal contents, hides, carcasses, workers’ hands, knives, equipment, water and processing surfaces. These pathways may expose workers and consumers while contributing to the wider environmental dissemination of resistant microorganisms. This review examines evidence concerning AMR at slaughterhouse and meat-processing interfaces in East Africa, with emphasis on contamination pathways, occupational exposure, bacterial resistance patterns, genomic evidence and feasible control strategies. A targeted narrative literature search was conducted using PubMed-indexed records, PubMed Central, publisher platforms, institutional repositories and international policy sources. Relevant evidence was identified from Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and Ethiopia. Studies from western Kenya have demonstrated resistant bacteria in slaughterhouse environments, carcasses and workers, while investigations in Tanzania have identified antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli in goat meat and meat-handler-associated isolates. Evidence from Ethiopia has documented Salmonella and Staphylococcus aureus contamination across carcasses, workers and processing environments. A 2026 investigation in southwestern Uganda additionally reported antimicrobial residues and resistant bacteria in beef samples. Genomic investigations from Tanzania have identified extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing E. coli, including isolates carrying blaCTX-M-15 and multidrug-resistance-associated plasmids. However, the available evidence is geographically uneven, methodologically heterogeneous and insufficient to establish the direction or frequency of transmission between animals, workers, meat and environmental compartments. Important limitations include inconsistent sampling designs, variable antimicrobial susceptibility testing, limited genomic surveillance and a lack of longitudinal studies linking antimicrobial use, slaughterhouse contamination and human colonization. A coordinated One Health response should combine antimicrobial stewardship in livestock production, ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection, hygienic slaughter practices, worker protection, water and waste management, food-chain surveillance and genomic epidemiology. Strengthening these measures through regional collaboration could improve food safety and reduce opportunities for the dissemination of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in East Africa.
authors: Habiyakare JdD, Niyonsaba D, Munezero V, I. Mudahunga O, Uwonkunda D, Dushimumubyeyi A, Ineza Singizwa A, Mutimukeye L.
