title: Human cognitive performance-associated gut microbiota influences learning and memory in mice through arginine and pterin metabolism.
abstract: The human gut microbiome undergoes changes across the lifespan and has been implicated in age-related decline. The symbol digit modalities test (SDMT) is a measure of information processing speed and is sensitive to mild cognitive impairment. Here, we assessed SDMT scores and fecal shotgun metagenomics in older individuals from the Imageomics cohort (n = 867) and performed fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from human donors to male C57BL/6 mouse recipients. In mice, we evaluated cognitive performance using the Morris water maze (MWM) and measured neurone density, fecal shotgun metagenomics, hippocampal metabolomics, and cortical gene expression to identify microbial-derived functional properties related to cognitive performance. In humans, both microbial species composition and functional profiles were associated with cognitive performance. FMT from high-SDMT donors improved cognitive performance and increased neuronal density in recipient mice compared with FMT from low-SDMT donors. In both humans and mice, higher cognitive performance was associated with arginine and proline metabolism and pterin-related pathways. In mice receiving microbiota from high-SDMT donors, cortical gene expression showed enrichment of dopamine receptor pathways and reduced dopamine reuptake and catecholamine biosynthesis. Our findings highlight the potential role of the gut microbiome in cognitive performance among older individuals, particularly information processing speed, and identify potential mechanisms involving alterations in arginine and pterin metabolism. Integrating human and mouse data supports a model in which microbiota-associated metabolic remodeling influences cognitive performance.

title: Orf virus early genes ORFV113 and ORFV114 are individually dispensable for replication in vitro but required for full virulence in vivo.
abstract: Orf is a highly contagious zoonotic disease caused by Orf virus (ORFV), resulting in significant economic losses to the livestock industry. ORFV113 and ORFV114, located in the terminal variable region of the ORFV genome, are putative virulence-associated genes. To elucidate their biological functions, we characterized the transcription kinetics of both genes and generated single-gene deletion mutants by homologous recombination, using transfer plasmids carrying flanking homology arms and an enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) reporter cassette. Lamb testis (LT) cells transfected with the recombinant plasmids were infected with the parental ORFV-JS strain; recombinant viruses were enriched by limiting dilution, purified by consecutive rounds of plaque isolation, and verified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Both genes are highly conserved among ORFV isolates (92-100% nucleotide identity) and are transcribed with early kinetics. The genetically stable deletion mutants, designated ORFV-Δ113 and ORFV-Δ114, were successfully generated. Deletion of either gene did not significantly alter viral growth kinetics or cytopathic effects (CPE) in LT cells. In a rabbit skin scarification model (n = 4 per group), however, both mutants induced markedly milder macroscopic lesions with lower cumulative clinical scores (P < 0.05), and viral loads in scab tissue were reduced 17-fold (ORFV-Δ113) and 10-fold (ORFV-Δ114) relative to the wild-type strain (P < 0.01). Thus, ORFV113 and ORFV114 are dispensable for viral replication in vitro but are required for full virulence in vivo. The resulting deletion mutants provide valuable tools for dissecting virus-host interactions and are promising candidates for the rational design of live-attenuated ORFV vaccines.
authors: Zhou W, Hu J, Wang X, Wang N, Cheng Z, Cheng A, Pang F.

title: Coordinating substrate accessibility with indigenous microorganisms functionality to enhance medium-chain fatty acid production from waste activated sludge.
abstract: Efficient medium-chain fatty acid (MCFA) production from waste activated sludge (WAS) depends on both substrate accessibility and microbial conversion. To clarify their roles in chain elongation (CE), three pretreatments were evaluated in a two-stage fermentation system with indigenous microorganisms retained or inactivated. Thermal-alkaline pretreatment achieved the highest MCFA production (4973.9 ± 274.2 mg COD/L) by improving substrate accessibility, although its relatively low selectivity indicated that greater precursor availability did not necessarily favor carbon allocation to MCFA. Retaining indigenous microorganisms increased MCFA production by 35.8-76.9% compared with corresponding autoclaved reactors and altered ethanol consumption and short-chain fatty acid dynamics, suggesting their involvement in intermediate utilization. Community analysis associated effective CE with complementary hydrolytic, acidogenic, and chain-elongating populations, including Macellibacteroides, Romboutsia, Clostridium, and Caproiciproducens, rather than the enrichment of chain-elongating bacteria alone. Metagenomic analysis of the thermal-alkaline system indicated differences in genetic potential for substrate degradation, glycolysis, electron transfer, acetyl-CoA formation, and reverse β-oxidation. These results suggest that coordinating pretreatment-driven substrate supply with indigenous microbial conversion capacity is essential for improving sludge-derived MCFA production.
authors: Tan L, Mei J, Song X, Bai X, Chen B, Wang Y, Shi J, Xu X, Jiang Z, Liu Z, Liu W, Yue X, Zhou A.

title: Genomic epidemiology and transmission dynamics of Acinetobacter baumannii: Comparison of clinical and wastewater isolates.
abstract: This study characterized the epidemiological, phenotypic, and genomic dynamics of Acinetobacter baumannii across inpatient, outpatient, hospital environmental, and diverse wastewater habitats from January to December 2025. Bacterial detection exhibited pronounced seasonal variations and habitat heterogeneity, with wastewater showing the highest prevalence and summer marking the peak period. High-touch surfaces represented the core hospital contamination nodes, and healthcare workers faced potential risks of carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) colonization. Notably, CRAB and multidrug-resistant strains appeared confined to clinical niches, where the dominant ST2Pas and ST164Pas clones stably harbored abundant carbapenemases, disinfectant resistance genes, and virulence factors. Anthropogenic antibiotic and sanitizer selective pressures likely drive their high multiple antibiotic resistance index (MARI) phenotypes. Conversely, wastewater strains were predominantly pan-susceptible (MARI < 0.2) but enriched with novel sequence types (STs) and rare resistance genes, suggesting their role as a natural reservoir for genetic diversification. Core-genome SNP transmission networks indicated high-density intra-hospital cross-transmission and occult inter-hospital dissemination, while capturing potential bidirectional cross-habitat spillover events. Mechanistically, conjugative plasmids, insertion sequences (IS256/IS3/IS66), and active prophages mediated resistance and virulence recombination in clinical strains. Meanwhile, wastewater strains might utilize the ISNCY family to undergo environmental adaptation, with integrons playing a minor role in resistance spread. This study uncovers the divergent evolutionary pathways of A. baumannii, providing critical genomic evidence for integrated clinical-environmental management to mitigate the cross-niche dissemination of antimicrobial resistance.
authors: Wang X, Zhang Y, Liang Y, You S, Xu T, Xu Y, Qiu Y, Wang Y, Feng J, Zhao B, Shen Y, Ren L.

title: SNAT2-mediated amino acid import maintains osmotic balance to restrain macrophage metabolic reprogramming and inflammasome activation.
abstract: Macrophages undergo metabolic reprogramming during inflammatory responses to microbial infection, in part because of activation of the transcription factor HIF-1α (hypoxia-inducible factor 1α). Here, we identified regulators of HIF-1α-dependent gene expression during immune activation induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and during the hypoxic response using genome-wide CRISPR screens in cultured mouse macrophages. The small neutral amino acid transporter SNAT2 (encoded by Slc38a2) was a key inhibitor of HIF-1α activation and metabolic reprogramming in cultured and bone marrow-derived mouse macrophages in response to LPS but not to hypoxia. Inflammatory stimulation increased SNAT2 protein abundance and dynamically expanded intracellular amino acid pools in a largely SNAT2-dependent manner. Consistent with the role of intracellular amino acids as osmolytes, SNAT2 deficiency resulted in osmotic imbalance and aberrant activation of NFAT5, a central transcriptional regulator of osmotic stress responses. In turn, NFAT5 promoted nitric oxide- and HIF-1α-dependent metabolic reprogramming and augmented NLRP3 inflammasome activation under hyperosmotic conditions. Supplementation with organic osmolytes mitigated both the excessive metabolic reprogramming and hyperosmotic inflammasome activation in SNAT2-deficient macrophages. Consistent with the heightened inflammatory phenotype in vitro, myeloid-specific deletion of SNAT2 reduced bacterial burden in mice infected with Listeria monocytogenes. Together, these findings identify SNAT2 as a negative feedback regulator that restrains macrophage metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory activation by maintaining amino acid availability that supports osmotic homeostasis.
authors: Yasukura S, Yoshinaga M, Tsugawa H, Tse KM, Aoki M, Nishioka K, Kajiya A, Takeuchi T, Harada H, Tsujikawa A, Bassik MC, Arita M, Takeuchi O.

title: Microbial hydrocarbonoclastic responses to extreme marine environments: adaptive strategies of psychrophilic and halophilic microorganisms.
abstract: The biological remediation of complex petroleum waste streams suffers from severe performance bottlenecks in industrial and marine settings due to the simultaneous thermal, osmotic and mechanical stress. In these hypersaline and multi-extreme matrices, such as produced water, coastal oil spills, and refinery lagoons, conventional mesophiles succumb to rapid plasmolysis, catalytic deceleration, and metabolic uncoupling. Halophilic microorganisms offer indispensable advantages for remediating these hostile environments; their specialized adaptations including acidic proteomes that resist salting-out, compatible solute accumulation that maintains cellular turgor, and cell-bound biosurfactant secretion preserve biocatalytic integrity where conventional degraders fail. This review provides a detailed overview of recent advances in the structural biology of extremophilic enzymes, biosurfactant-mediated interfacial bioavailability changes and genome-scale regulatory networks regulating hydrocarbonoclastic psychrophiles and halophiles. This article integrates structural insights, e.g. localized molecular flexibility of cold-active oxygenases and surface acidity stabilizing salt-tolerant biocatalysts, with functional multi-omics workflows that trace carbon flux from dynamic stress-sensing mechanisms to complete hydrocarbon mineralization. In addition, this paper discusses particular eco-physiological challenges of oil spills in the open ocean, such as the spatial compartmentalization of deep-water plumes, the dynamics of marine oil snow formation, and the metabolic trade-offs imposed by synthetic chemical dispersants. Also, this review discusses how the integration of high-throughput multi-omics data with artificial intelligence pipelines and predictive machine learning algorithms can accelerate strain engineering and bioprocess optimization. Finally, it offers a strong data-driven systems biology approach to move next-generation extremophilic bioprocesses from exploratory laboratory concepts to scalable, field-reproducible industrial realities.
authors: Ahmed A, Kumar A, Hazarika J, Geed SR.

title: Satellite DNA landscape in the alpaca genome and comparison with other camelids.
abstract: Satellite DNAs (satDNAs) are among the least resolved components of telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assemblies despite recent advances in long-read sequencing. Among mammals, camelids provide an excellent system to study satDNA evolution because of their exceptional karyotypic conservation despite more than 11 million years of independent evolution. Here, we systematically characterize the satDNA landscape of the chromosome-level alpaca reference genome VicPac4 by combining bioinformatic reference-guided repeat identification, PCR validation, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Cross-species PCR analysis of 13 candidate satDNAs revealed two major conservation patterns: six families amplified across all camelids, whereas seven were restricted to South American camelids (SACs). FISH further demonstrated distinct chromosomal organization of nine satDNA families: four showed widespread chromosomal distribution; three localized near centromeres of a subset of chromosomes; one was primarily associated with chromosome 26 but had lower copy number on additional chromosomes, and one exclusively mapped to chromosomes 27 and 36 in all SACs. The latter displayed consistent and prominent copy number differences between species, individuals and homologous chromosomes, suggesting naturally occurring variation in satellite array expansion. This satellite amplified by PCR across Camelidae, whereas FISH detected expanded arrays only in SACs, suggesting differences in satellite organization between SAC and Camels. Beyond satDNA identification, the proposed workflow facilitated the discovery and comparative analysis of pseudogene-rich repetitive blocks in the alpaca genome and their absence in Camels' genome assemblies. These findings substantially expand the alpaca satDNAs catalogue and provide a cytogenetic framework for future T2T genome refinement and comparative studies across Camelidae.
journal: Chromosome research : an international journal on the molecular, supramolecular and evolutionary aspects of chromosome biology
authors: Mendoza-Cerna MN, Anderson HC, Fox CR, Aranda E, de Anda Pulido E, Davis BW, Raudsepp T.

title: Catabolite activator protein and quorum sensing cross-control group behaviors in Vibrio campbellii.
abstract: Vibrio species adapt to different niches by sensing and responding to environmental signals such as nutrients, host cues, and quorum sensing autoinducers. Vibrio campbellii uses the master quorum sensing transcription factor LuxR to control the expression of hundreds of genes at high cell density. Furthermore, many gamma-proteobacteria use the global transcription factor catabolite activator protein (CAP) to control numerous physiologically relevant pathways, many of which are also modulated by quorum sensing, such as competence, biofilm formation, and carbon metabolism. However, the extent to which these two global transcription factors overlap to co-regulate gene expression and bacterial behaviors is understudied. In this work, we used chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled with high-throughput Illumina sequencing (ChIP-seq) and RNA-seq to determine the individual and combined regulons of CAP and LuxR in V. campbellii. We found that CAP and LuxR co-occupied 11 promoters to synergistically or antagonistically co-regulate genes involved with metabolism, respiration, and virulence. It was previously proposed that CAP and LuxR both bound the bioluminescence (luxCDABE) promoter to co-regulate these genes, and our RNA-seq data showed that these were indeed the most strongly co-regulated genes. However, our ChIP-seq data revealed that only LuxR bound the luxCDABE promoter in vivo. This pattern of co-regulation-where both CAP and LuxR strongly impact transcription, but only LuxR binds the promoter-was the most common mechanism observed. Our model for bioluminescence regulation is that CAP indirectly activates luxCDABE expression through the regulation of an intermediate factor. This study established new connections between the global gene regulatory networks underpinning nutrient sensing and population sensing.ImportanceVibrio bacteria (vibrios) colonize and infect diverse marine hosts, including corals, fish, oysters, and shrimp, and can also cause life-threatening human infections, all of which are rising annually due to increasing ocean temperatures. To develop effective treatments against Vibrio infections, it is critical to understand the global gene regulation mechanisms vibrios use that enable pathogenic lifestyles. Signal transduction systems in bacteria are well-characterized; however, how vibrios coordinate global gene expression changes in response to multiple environmental inputs is understudied. Here, we determined how the aquaculture pathogen Vibrio campbellii regulates global gene expression in response to bacterial population signals and nutrient availability signals. Our findings help contextualize how vibrios respond to their fluctuating environments in nature.
authors: Mullins CM, Ball AS, Geyman LJ, Lukich LK, Hermann LK, Podicheti R, Ren Z, Wang X, Rusch DB, van Kessel JC.

title: Melanoidins Suppress Cucumber and Tomato Diseases Incited by Pathogens that are Oomycetes, Bacteria and a Virus
abstract: We recently reported that solutions of the nitrogenous compounds melanoidins (M), that are formed during the final stages of the Maillard Reaction, are inducers of plant resistance (Elad et al. 2026). M promoted immunity and induced disease resistance through an effect on the transcriptome, primarily through the salicylic acid pathway. Here we tested the effect of M on plant diseases that are caused by Oomycetes, bacteria and a tobamovirus. Drench and spray of M suppressed Pythium aphanidermatum damping off in cucumber, cucumber downy mildew (Pseudoperonospera cubensis), tomato late blight (Phytophthora infestans), bacterial speck (Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato), bacterial canker (Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. michiganensis) and the Tobamovirus Tomato brown rugose fruit virus (ToBRFV) in tomato. In various experiments control was achieved by concentrations of 0.03 and 0.1% and on older and younger leaves and even in long term experiments where the M was applied for ca 11 weeks. It can be concluded that the disease resistance inducer M can suppress soilborne and foliar diseases that are caused by Oomycetes, bacteria and a virus of the genus Tobamovirus, in addition to the fungal pathogen Botrytis cinerea reported earlier.
authors: Elad Y, Rav-David D, Tsechansky L, Graber ER.

title: Epidemiological Investigation and Genetic Evolution Analysis of Feline Calicivirus during 2025–2026 in Shandong Province
abstract: Abstract  Feline calicivirus (FCV) is a major viral pathogen associated with feline respiratory diseases. To characterize the epidemiological and evolutionary features of FCV in Shandong Province, China, 656 clinical feline specimens were collected during 2025–2026. RT-PCR was used to screen for common feline viral pathogens, and FCV-positive samples were subjected to virus isolation, purification and whole-genome sequencing. The overall FCV-positive rate was 1.67% (11/656). Co-infections predominated among FCV-positive specimens, with feline parvovirus (FPV) as the most frequent co-infecting agent. Eleven local FCV strains were isolated; genogroup analysis showed that both GI (six strains) and GII (five strains) were circulating. Four high-confidence recombination events were identified. Notably, strain F1481 (genogroup GI) originated from inter-genogroup recombination between a GII-type isolate (F1506) and a GI-type isolate (F1498), providing bioinformatic evidence for natural inter-genogroup recombination between GI and GII FCV strains. These findings indicate that recombination and antigenic drift are important evolutionary forces shaping local FCV populations and provide empirical evidence for regional disease control and the development of geographically matched vaccine candidates.
authors: Wang Y, Tian A, Wei K, Yang S, Zhao L, Qi L, Lin X, Sun W, Ma F, Fang L, Zhang L, Wu J.

title: PlasmidCall: predicting whether resistance genes in short-read assemblies lie on plasmids or chromosomes, tested in 432 carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales
abstract: Abstract  Antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) can lie on the bacterial chromosome, where they are passed on mainly with the host strain, or on plasmids, which can move them between bacteria. Most bacterial genomes are sequenced with short reads, which assemble into many fragments (contigs), so whether a contig, and any ARG on it, comes from a plasmid or from the chromosome usually has to be predicted. Plasmid classifiers are software tools that make this prediction for each contig from different kinds of evidence, and each tends to fail on different contigs. PlasmidCall v1.2-General is a logistic-regression model that combines the plasmid or chromosome calls of twelve such classifiers into one decision. Four gradient-boosting models, fitted on a larger training set, combine some or all of these calls with features of the contig, its neighbours in the assembly graph and its isolate. The five models were tested without refitting on 432 carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales isolates from one hospital, none used in model development. For each isolate, a hybrid assembly built from long and short reads provided reference labels (plasmid or chromosome) for 30,986 of its 35,805 short-read contigs of at least 1 kb, whether or not they carried an ARG. PlasmidCall v1.2-General gave a decision on every contig: 94.9% of its plasmid calls were correct (precision 0.9491; 95% CI 0.8915-0.9642, resampling clusters of closely related isolates), and it found 91.8% of plasmid contigs (recall 0.9184). Its precision was 0.028 lower than a previously reported estimate; the two 95% intervals overlapped when clusters of related isolates were resampled, but not when single isolates were. The gradient-boosting models found 98.9-99.2% of plasmid contigs at precision 0.887-0.922. On contigs carrying ARGs, v1.2-General had precision 0.935 and recall 0.969, and on the 383 contigs carrying the carbapenemase gene blaKPC (post hoc), 0.994 and 0.970. PlasmidCall can therefore place resistance genes, including blaKPC, on a plasmid or the chromosome from short-read data alone, with a choice between higher precision and higher recall.
authors: Piranfar V.

title: Salicornia: a halophyte with unique salt-tolerant genes for developing future climate-resilient crops, high-value bioproducts and saline land utilization.
abstract: Salicornia, a stem-succulent halophyte, grows naturally in coastal areas with high salinity and can complete its life cycle in extreme environmental conditions due to its high adaptability to salt, drought, and temperature stress. It survives in saline environments through morpho-anatomical modifications, ion homeostasis, biochemical changes, osmolyte accumulation, and antioxidant defense mechanisms. Its growth and adaptation to salinity are further supported by a variety of rhizospheric and endophytic microbes. Salicornia is a valuable source of herbal salt, food, feed, medicines, and biofuel due to its high content of essential fatty acids, minerals, and bioactive compounds. Its large-scale cultivation on coastal and saline wastelands contributes to sustainable blue and green economies by aiding in soil reclamation and carbon sequestration. The Salicornia derived genes and biomass offer significant potential for developing climate-resilient crops and value-added bioproducts. Recent genomic and transcriptomic advances, including chromosome-scale and telomere-to-telomere genome assemblies, have provided valuable resources for understanding molecular adaptation to salinity. Several transcription factors (TFs), transporters, and stress-responsive genes have been identified and studied to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying salinity tolerance across different Salicornia species, and few of these genes have been functionally validated using transgenic techniques demonstrating enhanced salinity, drought, or osmotic stress tolerance. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of current knowledge on the distribution, genetic diversity, cultivation, economic importance, and multi-level mechanisms underlying salinity tolerance in Salicornia, while highlighting recent genomic resources, functional validation studies, plant-microbe interactions, and their potential application in developing salinity-resilient crops.
authors: Agarwal PK, Choikunnumil MK, Gupta A, Rajan A, Agarwal P, Salvi JA.

title: Butyrate Deficiency due to Microbial Dysbiosis Promotes Anxiety.
abstract: Individuals with diabetes frequently suffer from anxiety; however, the mechanism for this association remains incompletely understood. Diabetes-associated genes have been implicated in the control of central nervous system (CNS) disorders. In the current study, we observed a marked down-regulation of secretagogin (SCGN) across multiple organs in diabetic mouse models, and Scgn knockout (Scgn -/-) mice developed diabetes, confirming SCGN as a diabetes-associated gene. Behavioral analyses revealed that Scgn -/- mice exhibited anxiety-like phenotypes compared to wild-type (WT) mice. Notably, germ-free (GF) Scgn -/- mice did not manifest these behavioral abnormalities, suggesting that SCGN influences anxiety through gut microbiota-dependent mechanisms. Subsequent shotgun metagenomic sequencing confirmed gut microbiota dysbiosis in Scgn -/- mice. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from Scgn -/- donors into GF mice recapitulated the anxiety-like phenotypes. Given the established roles of microbial metabolites in gut-brain axis signaling, we identified a substantial depletion of butyrate, a key neuroactive metabolite, in fecal and plasma samples from Scgn -/- mice. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed neural overactivation, as reflected by c-Fos expression in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of Scgn -/- mice, which was corroborated by metabolomic profiling indicating dysregulated tryptophan metabolism in this region. Mechanistically, up-regulation of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) and kynureninase (KYNU) led to excessive production of quinolinic acid, an NMDA receptor agonist that increased pyramidal neuron excitability in the mPFC, thereby promoting anxiety-like behaviors in Scgn -/- mice. Supplementation with Odoribacter splanchnicus, a butyrate-producing bacterium, could reverse this abnormal signaling pathway and alleviate anxiety-like behaviors. Critically, butyrate administration mitigated this anxiogenic cascade in vivo and in vitro, as validated by electrophysiological recordings. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that SCGN deficiency induces gut dysbiosis, reduces butyrate availability, and promotes excitotoxicity in the mPFC, at least in part, through disrupted tryptophan metabolism, ultimately leading to anxiety. This SCGN-modulated gut-brain axis highlights potential new therapeutic targets for the treatment of diabetes-associated anxiety.
authors: Zhou L, Zang Z, Zhang H, Fei X, Zhu G, Mu Y, Jiang P, Wang X, Zhao M, Ai Z, Cao X, Liu Z, Yin H, Li L, Tian J, Yang H, Fan X, Tan S, Li S.

title: Integrating PCR and sequencing for the identification of pathogenic fungi on formalin-fixed tissues: a systematic review toward a pragmatic histomolecular solution.
abstract: Although histopathology is a gold standard for the diagnosis of invasive fungal infections, the morphological analysis does not provide an accurate genus and/or species identification. Because this specific identification is required for antifungal therapy prescription, the implementation of molecular techniques to identify fungi on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue in practice is crucial, especially when specimen has not been simultaneously sent to the mycology laboratory. However, such approaches/procedures remain heterogenous. The objective of this systematic review (PROSPERO: CRD420261420594) was to gather data from the literature to support future efforts toward the standardisation of diagnostic practices for fungal identification on FFPE tissue. Among the 1,550 records found on MEDLINE-PubMed and Google Scholar, 57 studies were included. Thirty-two, 27, and 10 studies investigated the use on FFPE tissue of taxon-specific fungal PCR (n = 1421 FFPE samples tested), panfungal PCR followed by Sanger sequencing (n = 1647 FFPE samples tested), and targeted next-generation sequencing/massive parallel sequencing (NGS/MPS) or untargeted metagenomics (n = 408 FFPE samples tested; some studies reported several techniques), respectively. The sensitivity and specificity of the techniques, according to pre-analytical, histopathological, and molecular criteria were reported and discussed. Advantages and limitations of each technique are presented. While taxon-specific fungal PCR are widely available and highly sensitive, sequencing-based techniques have a broader spectrum for identification purpose. Finally, because of the contamination of tissue sections and the presence of fungi belonging to microbiota on samples, the molecular identification should always be correlated to the pathogenic fungi's morphology, to ensure an accurate and reliable integrated histomolecular diagnosis.

authors: Trecourt A, Gorkiewicz G, Adle-Biassette H, Rabodonirina M, Cathomas G, Langer R, Devouassoux-Shisheboran M, Menotti J, Hofman P, on behalf the Infectious Diseases Pathology Working Group of the European Society of Pathology (ESP).

title: Mining and engineering novel staphylococcal lysostaphins as species-specific antibacterial agents.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) presents a serious global healthcare challenge, with staphylococci, especially Staphylococcus aureus, being the main cause of deadly infections. Peptidoglycan hydrolases, particularly lysostaphins, are highly promising alternatives to traditional antibiotics, collectively termed enzybiotics, due to their specific lytic action against the bacterial cell wall. To thoroughly explore their therapeutic potential, we performed comprehensive genome mining of 118,127 staphylococcal and 500 closely related mammaliicoccal genomes. Ultimately, we discovered 19 unique lysostaphin sequences, divided into four distinct evolutionary clusters. By characterizing five novel lysostaphins alongside known references, we observed diverse lytic activities and species-specificities. Notably, we identified a novel lysostaphin variant from Staphylococcus simulans, Lys-Ssim, representing a previously unknown evolutionary cluster, which exhibits unmatched substrate promiscuity and an unprecedented lytic activity that extends beyond staphylococci. Additionally, structural modeling and site-directed mutagenesis revealed that peptidoglycan hydrolysis by these M23 metalloproteases depends on highly flexible conformations of the binding cleft. Using these structural insights, we successfully engineered lysostaphins with significantly improved enzyme selectivity for S. aureus while nearly eliminating activity against the skin commensal S. epidermidis. We also demonstrated the potential to engineer lysostaphins active against species other than staphylococci. Our findings show that natural staphylococcal lysostaphins are a rich, highly specialized resource for developing rationally engineered, microbiota-friendly antibacterial agents.
authors: Bukowski M, Zhydzetski A, Jankowska A, Chlebicka K, Zarta DM, Malerczyk J, Włudyka F, Tossavainen H, Antenucci L, Permi P, Świderska K, Drąg M, Władyka B.

title: Alternative sigma factor σ54 (RpoN) of Vibrio fischeri is required during initial squid light organ colonization but its continued induction is not required for maintenance.
abstract: Animals depend on bacterial symbionts that provide functions essential for host physiology and fitness. The marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri establishes a mutualistic association within the light organ of the Hawaiian bobtail squid Euprymna scolopes, where bacterial bioluminescence enables a host camouflage behavior. Successful colonization of the light organ requires the alternative sigma factor σ54 (RpoN), which activates genes involved in biofilm formation and motility that are essential for bacterial entry into the host. However, whether σ54 remains important after the initial stages of colonization has been unclear. Here, using an IPTG-inducible rpoN expression system, we demonstrate that induction of rpoN is required for initial entry into the light organ, but continued inducer exposure is not required for subsequent maintenance of colonization and bioluminescence production. Transcriptomic analysis of RNA-sequencing of low-cell-density cultures identified σ54-dependent expression of genes involved in flagellar motility, chemotaxis, nitrogen assimilation, molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis, and formate metabolism. We further show that the bacterial enhancer-binding protein VF_1401 activates genes required for Moco biosynthesis and formate metabolism but is not required for light organ colonization. Together, these findings define the temporal requirement for σ54 during symbiosis establishment and reveal a previously unrecognized role for σ54 in regulating molybdenum-dependent metabolism in V. fischeri.IMPORTANCEMany bacteria encode the alternative sigma factor σ54 (RpoN), which enables selective activation of specific cellular processes in response to environmental signals. Our findings refine the conditions under which σ54 contributes to host colonization by a bacterial symbiont, providing new insight into the context-dependent roles of this conserved regulator. In addition, our transcriptomic analysis identifies a previously unrecognized link between σ54 and molybdenum assimilation, revealing a potential mechanism by which σ54 coordinates trace element homeostasis with bacterial physiology. These findings broaden our understanding of σ54 regulatory networks and may inform future strategies to manipulate the physiology of beneficial bacterial symbionts.
authors: Muriel-Mundo CA, Miyashiro TI.

title: PCB-Exposed Gut Microbiota Recapitulate Neurobehavioral Deficits and Reprogram Hippocampal Transcriptomic Signatures
abstract: ABSTRACT  Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are persistent environmental pollutants associated with developmental neurotoxicity and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, whether PCB-induced alterations in gut microbiota contribute to neurodevelopmental toxicity independently of direct chemical exposure remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether transplantation of PCB-associated gut microbiota produces early neurobehavioral alterations and disrupts brain molecular pathways in offspring. Gut microbiota from conventional dams exposed to the Fox River PCB mixture (FRM; 6.0 mg/kg/day) or vehicle were transplanted into germ-free recipient females without direct PCB administration. At postnatal day 7 (P7), offspring underwent ultrasonic vocalization (USV) testing, whole-brain RNA sequencing (n = 4/sex/group), and untargeted serum metabolomics. Untargeted serum metabolomics were also performed in donor dams. PCB-associated fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) significantly reduced offspring USVs, reproducing effects observed following direct maternal PCB exposure. Brain transcriptomics in offspring identified substantially more differentially expressed genes in males (9,339) than females (1,082), including 512 shared genes. Concordantly regulated genes revealed downregulation of neurotransmitter signaling and ion channel pathways alongside upregulation of RNA processing pathways. Male-associated responses involved altered protein synthesis and neuronal signaling, whereas female-associated responses involved DNA repair and extracellular matrix remodeling. Despite these molecular differences, behavioral responses showed no significant sex-dependent effect. Maternal metabolomics revealed increased bile acids and decreased indole-3-propionic acid, highlighting potential AhR-NFκB and bile acid-associated signaling mechanisms. Offspring metabolomics further identified alterations in lipid-associated metabolites and metabolic profiles. Collectively, these findings show that transferring PCB-exposed microbiota reproduces early neurobehavioral alterations and induces shared and sex-biased molecular responses, identifying the maternal gut microbiome as a candidate mediator linking PCB exposure to developmental neurotoxicity.
authors: Suh YP, Wilson RJ, Breese NM, Lein PJ, Lehmler H, Cui JY.

title: PP271, a novel bacteriophage primase-polymerase, enables Primer-Free DNA Amplification
abstract: Primases are essential enzymes that initiate DNA replication by synthesizing  de novo primers for replicative DNA polymerases, which ensure accurate genome duplication owing to their high specificity, fidelity, and processivity. PrimPols have emerged as versatile DNA-initiating enzymes that are widely distributed across diverse replication systems, from bacteriophages to humans.  In this work, a novel PrimPol enzyme, PP271, encoded by bacteriophage vB_EfaS-271, was characterized. PP271 belongs to the archaeal–eukaryotic primase (AEP) superfamily and contains the conserved catalytic core, together with a C-terminal PriCT domain. Enzymatic analysis demonstrated that PP271 functions as a  bona fide PrimPol, i.e. a DNA primase capable of synthetizing short DNA primers. PP271 priming activity is strongly stimulated by  ADP , which serves as the preferred initiating nucleotide. Additionally, PP271 exhibits relaxed specificity for selecting the priming site, compared to other PrimPols with more restricted template preferences.  TruePrime™ amplification technology combines the  Thermus thermophilus PrimPol and the highly processive Phi29 DNA polymerase to achieve primer-free DNA amplification. While highly efficient, further improvements in amplification yield, fidelity and product complexity remain possible. Here, we show that DNA primers synthesized by PP271 are efficiently extended by Phi29 DNA polymerase, enabling their coordinated action. Moreover, the short primers generated by PP271 are expected to minimize the contribution of primase-derived errors to the final amplification product while allowing efficient DNA synthesis across a broader range of sequence contexts. Altogether, these findings identify PP271 as a promising alternative for improving primase-dependent DNA amplification.  Key points  Bacteriophage EFAS271 encodes PP271, a DNA-dependent DNA primase-polymerase PP271 preferentially uses  ADP as the initiating nucleotide during primer synthesis  PP271 enables primer-free isothermal DNA amplification with Phi29 DNApol
authors: Jiménez-Mejías A, Guerra-González S, Olmos R, Lázaro I, Blanco L, Martínez-Jiménez MI.

title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.
authors: Sharma C, Översti S, Stass R, Lucaci AG, Audet J, Safronetz D, Zhao L, Lythgoe K, Katzourakis A, Bowden TA, Lytras S, Ghafari M.

title: CRISPR-Based Metabolic Engineering of Microbial Cell Factories for Sustainable Bio manufacturing: A Systematic analysis of 1,000 Studies (2012–2026)
abstract: Abstract  CRISPR genome editing and microbial metabolic engineering now work hand in hand. That pairing has changed sustainable bio manufacturing in real ways. This review pulls together 1,000 peer-reviewed articles from 2012 to 2026. They come from 201 journals. We mapped how the field evolved, how the technology diversified, which host chassis researchers prefer, what product classes they target, and where in the world the work gets done. Our approach mixed bibliometric, feature engineering, and multivariate statistics. That includes principal component analysis, hierarchical clustering, co-occurrence network analysis, and correlation mapping. We tracked the CRISPR variant landscape, host chassis distribution, product class priorities, and geographic concentration of research output. The temporal analysis shows a shift. Early work explored many CRISPR variants. Recent work focuses on applications. Mean CRISPR variants per article dropped from 2.42 in 2018 to 1.40 in 2026. Our findings give a quantitative roadmap of where the field is heading. They also point to emerging opportunities in non-conventional yeast, filamentous fungi, and cyanobacterial chassis for sustainable bio manufacturing.
authors: Zeeshan N, Afzal T, Ahmed Z, Abid I.

title: Genome-Informed Development of a Highly Specific Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification Assay for Detection of the Laurel Wilt Pathogen in Avocado.
abstract: Laurel wilt, caused by the ambrosia fungus Harringtonia lauricola (HL), threatens Lauraceae forests and avocado production. Rapid and accurate diagnosis is critical for disease management, but current methods are often slow or difficult to implement directly from field-collected wood samples. A published loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay targeting the HL β-tubulin (β-tub) gene enables rapid detection but lacks extensive validation for avocado tissues and may produce ambiguous amplification products when applied to non-target fungi and crude plant extracts. This study evaluated the specificity, sensitivity, and inclusivity of the β-tub assay and developed a novel HL-specific LAMP marker (HL_0354) through comparative genomic analyses. Both assays were validated using fungal isolates, diverse HL strains, and naturally and artificially infected avocado wood samples. The β-tub assay produced late nonspecific amplification products with several non-HL species and consistently detected HL at 5 pg DNA. In contrast, HL_0354 showed no reproducible amplification from non-target fungi and reproducibly detected 0.5 pg of HL DNA in crude avocado DNA matrices (0.05 ng/µl), with amplifications typically occurring within 5-12 min. Inclusivity testing confirmed detection of all HL strains evaluated despite minor annealing-temperature variation among Southeast Asian isolates. When applied to field samples, HL_0354 achieved a true-positive rate of 97% and an overall diagnostic accuracy of 98%, outperforming the β-tub assay (90% and 94%, respectively), without false-positive detections. Coupled with a simple Chelex-based extraction protocol, HL_0354 provides a rapid, sensitive, and field-deployable approach for detection of H. lauricola in avocado wood samples, supporting laurel wilt surveillance and management.
authors: Díaz-Valderrama JR, Navia-Urrutia M, Weber S, Padmanabhan C, Cano LM, Cárdenas DE, Manosalva P, Gazis R.

title: Isolation, identification and whole genome sequence analysis of influenza B virus from Shanghai during 2023-2024.
abstract: Influenza B virus, a member of the Orthomyxoviridae family, is a significant contributor to global respiratory infections alongside influenza A virus. This study investigated the prevalence and genomic characteristics of influenza B virus during the 2023-2024 season in Shanghai, China. Among 174 clinical samples collected from the Nanxiang Branch of Ruijin Hospital, the positivity rate for influenza B virus was 62.36%. Genomic analysis revealed that all characterized isolates belonged to the B/Victoria lineage and were classified within subclade C.5.7, corresponding to the legacy designation V1A.3a.2. No B/Yamagata lineage strains were detected. Comparative genomic analysis further revealed close genetic similarity between the Shanghai isolates and strains from Shanxi Province, suggesting a potential geographical or evolutionary relationship. These findings highlight the substantial activity of influenza B virus in Shanghai during the study period and underscore the importance of continued genomic surveillance to monitor viral evolution and inform public health strategies.
authors: Ashraf MA, Yue L, Raza MA, Shen B, Xu H, Amjad MN, Din GU, Chen L, Hu R, Tian Y, Bhutto AA, Dai A, Yan H, Hu Y.

title: Root exudate flux as a quantitative language of phytobiome assembly and stress resilience.
abstract: Climate change threatens crop productivity and soil function, increasing reliance on rhizosphere microbiomes that support plant nutrition, stress tolerance and disease suppression. Plants shape these communities through root exudation, which transfers an estimated 13.4 Pg C yr-1, about 9% of global gross primary productivity, belowground. Yet most studies report exudate composition rather than the concentrations and rates microorganisms perceive. This review synthesises the literature, with particular emphasis on studies published between 2015 and 2026, especially those from 2020 onwards, while incorporating foundational earlier studies. It proposes a quantitative signalling framework in which absolute concentration, release flux and spatial gradient influence microbial responses at defined activation thresholds. Exudate chemistry, biosynthesis, transport and uptake are first examined, distinguishing passive diffusion sustained by the microbial sink from transporter-mediated release, root re-uptake and phytosiderophore-mediated iron acquisition. Sampling and analytical approaches, including HRMS-based metabolomics, stable isotope tracing, imaging and kinetic modelling, are then evaluated, separating relative from absolute quantification. Because most high-precision flux data derive from hydroponic or sterile systems, where wheat phytosiderophore release exceeds that in soil by about 50-fold, in situ microdialysis, corrections for sorption and degradation, and minimum reporting standards are proposed. Signal-response modules and allelochemical signalling at the root-microbe-soil interface are discussed, followed by multi-omics integration, where static metabolite pools and transcripts cannot resolve flux unless anchored by pulse labelling with LC-MS, stable isotope probing and NanoSIMS. Stress-induced quantitative reprogramming of exudation is interpreted within this framework. Exudation measured in soil is concluded to be a net flux, and unresolved compound-specific thresholds remain the principal barrier to predictive rhizosphere manipulation.
authors: Elias EM, Benny CM, Thomas T.

title: Shinella sp. LB1 remediates acetamiprid-contaminated soil by coupling NHase- and amidase-mediated dual-pathway biodegradation with nitrogen‑cycle regulation.
abstract: Microbe‑mediated biodegradation offers a promising strategy for acetamiprid (ACE) removal. Although nitrile hydratase (NHase) and amidase from distinct microbes constitute the two main enzymatic routes, dual-enzyme degraders are rare, and their nitrogen-cycle modulation in soil bioremediation remains unclear. Here, we enriched a microbiota DCM (dominated by Shinella, Achromobacter, and Agrobacterium) from ACE-contaminated cowpea soil, and isolated a novel degrader Shinella sp. LB1, the first reported member of its genus capable of utilizing ACE as the sole carbon and energy source, with an exceptional degradation rate of 27.10 ± 0.55 mg·L-1·h-1. Genomic analysis, heterologous expression and LC-MS/MS analyses demonstrated that strain LB1 uniquely harbors both NHase (1635 bp, chromosome) and amidase (2713 bp, plasmid 3) gene clusters, enabling dual-pathway conversion of ACE to N-amidoamide derivative (IM 1-2) via hydration and to N-methyl-(6-chloro-3-pyridyl) methylamine (IM 1-4) via N‑deacetylation, respectively. Comparative genomics suggested that NHase may be vertically inherited across 77.19% of Shinella spp., whereas the amidase, flanked by an ISPps1 transposase, is likely exclusive to LB1 via horizontal transfer. Soil microcosm experiments revealed that ACE contamination enriched nitrifiers (e.g., Nitrosospira), depleting NH4+-N and accumulating NO3--N. Bioaugmentation with LB1, which lacks a complete nitrate‑reduction pathway, not only accelerated ACE dissipation by 54.12% but also selectively recruited indigenous nitrate reducers (e.g., f_Comamonadaceae), enhancing soil catalase, urease, and nitrate reductase activities and promoting NO3--N to NH4+-N conversion. These findings provide novel insights into the metabolic diversity and evolutionary dynamics of ACE-degrading bacteria, offering a sustainable bioaugmentation strategy for ACE-contaminated soil remediation.
authors: Wu Z, Leng S, Fu X, Wu J, Qian Y, Liu B, Fu X, Ni H, Huang Y, Long ZE, Zou L.

title: Born in the wild: the ecological roles of key Enterobacteriaceae virulence factors.
abstract: Many Enterobacteriaceae family pathogens are not truly human adapted but are instead opportunists able to thrive in various different niches. Survival in environments outside human hosts provides a means for transmission and also represents an important selective pressure shaping the evolution of these bacterial species. Pathogens such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae benefit from highly diverse genomes and horizontally acquired virulence or host fitness factors that collectively determine infection type and severity. These same "virulence" factors can also drive environmental survival. Here we will review current knowledge of the environmental roles of canonical host fitness factors of opportunistic pathogens, including capsule, siderophores, curli, and type VI secretion systems. These systems are primarily known for their roles in protection, nutrient acquisition, and intermicrobial competition within the host but can also make dramatic contributions to environmental survival. Investigating these roles can give us new perspectives on how these factors may function within the host and help us to understand the evolutionary forces shaping bacterial pathogens.
authors: Nunez C, Howells GA, Short FL.

title: Decentralized Biosynthesis of the Spiro-DKP Alkaloid Chevalinulin A Enabled by Nonclustered P450 and Intermolecular [4 + 2] Cyclase.
abstract: Intermolecular Diels-Alder (DA) cycloadditions are pivotal for constructing complex polycyclic architectures. However, biological catalysts performing this transformation on diketopiperazine (DKP) cores remain largely unidentified. Here, we report a decentralized biosynthetic pathway in the deep-sea cold-seep sourced fungus Aspergillus chevalieri CS-122 that assembles chevalinulin A, a spiro[bicyclo[2.2.2]octane]-DKP alkaloid. This pathway involves two nonclustered enzymes, CalO and FadA. CalO is a cytochrome P450 that furnishes an essential exocyclic olefin, while FadA represents the first FAD oxidoreductase-like Diels-Alderase that catalyzes an intermolecular, endoselective [4 + 2] cycloaddition between neoechinulin B and 3,4-trans-cyclohexadiene. These enzymes function downstream of a conserved gene cluster, effectively decoupling core scaffold assembly from late-stage functionalization. This strategy likely underpins the extensive structural diversity of fungal DKP alkaloids. Notably, CalO and FadA were identified via an integrated transcriptomic and structure-guided computational pipeline, rather than sequence homology, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in mining functional catalysts from genomic "dark matter". Mutational analysis indicates that residues M193, Y226, Y315, and D446 are critical in FadA activity. This study reveals a decentralized biosynthetic paradigm linking clustered core assembly with dispersed diversification, establishing a general framework for engineering complex alkaloid scaffolds.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
authors: Meng LH, Wang LY, Ying Z, Li XM, Li X, Yan LH, Wang BG.

title: SEARCHLIGHT: A Modular Workflow for High-Resolution Viral Single-cell Genomics.
abstract: Single-cell viral genomics is limited by low viral abundance and incomplete genome recovery. We developed SEARCHLIGHT (scRNA-seq-enabled acquisition of mRNA and consensus haplotypes linking individual genotypes and host transcriptomes), a modular workflow that improves recovery of viral cDNA from standard 10× Genomics 5' single-cell libraries, preserving barcodes for cell-level genome reconstruction. The core Basic Protocol uses virus-specific primers during cDNA synthesis to recover viral sequences from single cells. Two optional modules extend the workflow: SEARCHLIGHT + Kinnex, which increases sequencing depth through cDNA concatenation, and SEARCHLIGHT + Twist + Kinnex, which incorporates hybrid capture to enrich viral cDNA before long-read sequencing. Together, these modules expand recovery from moderate to low-abundance infections and support high-resolution analysis of viral diversity across diverse sample types. SEARCHLIGHT provides a flexible framework for balancing sensitivity, throughput, and cost in single-cell viral genomics. Published 2026. This article is a U.S. Government work and is in the public domain in the USA. Current Protocols published by Wiley Periodicals LLC. Basic Protocol: SEARCHLIGHT core workflow (single-cell viral genomics) Alternate Protocol 1: SEARCHLIGHT + Kinnex Alternate Protocol 2: SEARCHLIGHT + Twist + Kinnex.
authors: Dábilla N, Mastroianni I, Dolan PT.

title: Co-dissemination of anti-phage defence systems and multidrug resistance is associated with the seventh-pandemic Vibrio cholerae defensome.
abstract: Anti-phage defence systems in Vibrio cholerae are recognized as cargo on mobile genetic elements carrying antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and virulence genes, but a population-scale view of how the V. cholerae defensome partitions between the pandemic O1 clade and the environmental non-O1 reservoir has been missing. We analysed 1,740 RefSeq V. cholerae genomes (773 O1, 967 non-O1) sampled from 1934 to 2022 across 60 countries. Cataloguing defence systems with DefenseFinder, we found that the non-O1 reservoir harboured 283 subtypes and 55 families absent from any O1. This asymmetry persisted after collapsing each core-genome lineage to a single representative, although it partly reflected the greater diversity of non-O1. O1 favoured abortive infection systems (36.8% vs 14.1% in non-O1; P<0.001). Defence and prophage burden were inversely related within O1 (R=-0.15) but weakly positive in non-O1, and a five-decade reconstruction revealed mirror trajectories of rising defence diversity and declining prophage burden in O1, coincident with SXT/R391 integrative conjugative element-borne AMR. A bipartite network identified strong defence-AMR associations (Phi up to 0.80), nominating AbiE, AbiJ, AvcID, Menshen, Retron-I_A and Lamassu-Fam as candidate co-acquired cargo; though much of this is clonal, the strongest associations falling to 0.51 to 0.68 after de-duplication. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection clustering resolved seven defensome lineages, and a Random Forest classifier trained on defence profile predicted multidrug resistance status with cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.96, generalizing across O1 (0.92), non-O1 (0.93), decades (0.88) and regions (AUC=0.92); a five-system signature (AbiE, BREX-I, CBASS-II, AvcID and AbiJ) achieved AUC=0.91. Together, these data show that the pandemic defensome has expanded in step with the AMR-bearing mobilome rather than with prophage burden, with defence and resistance genes co-inherited on seventh pandemic El Tor elements. Their association reflects shared lineage history rather than a causal or mechanistic link, and the defensome serves as a descriptive genomic correlate of multidrug resistance.
authors: Hoque MM, To J, Leo D, McDougald D, Matson JS, Espinoza-Vergara G.

title: Long Noncoding RNA LINC00941 Links Oncogenic KRAS Signaling to Aggressiveness, DNA Repair, and Chemoresistance in Pancreatic Cancer.
abstract: Oncogenic KRAS mutations are the primary drivers of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but the noncoding landscape downstream of KRAS remains to be fully elucidated. Here, by integrating PDAC RNA sequencing and exome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), we identified 49 long intergenic noncoding RNAs (lincRNAs) differentially expressed according to KRAS mutation status. Among these, LINC00941 emerged as a primary candidate, as its expression is regulated by KRAS in both loss- and gain-of-function models and is significantly upregulated in PDAC tumors. Analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing and clinical datasets (TCGA/ICGC) revealed that LINC00941 is significantly enriched in PDAC malignant epithelial cells and correlates with poor PDAC patient prognosis. Functional assays demonstrated that LINC00941 knockdown impairs PDAC cell migration and invasion. Notably, LINC00941-depleted cells exhibit delayed DNA repair following irradiation, as shown by the slower resolution of radiation-induced DNA strand breaks, and increased sensitivity to gemcitabine-induced apoptosis. Transcriptomic and RT-qPCR analyses associated the loss of LINC00941 with a significant reduction in key DNA repair and survival-related genes, including BACH1, TOP2A, and BIRC5. These findings suggest that LINC00941 is required to maintain genomic stability and promote survival under therapeutic stress in KRAS-driven cells. In conclusion, our study identifies a novel KRAS/LINC00941 axis that supports a pro-survival and chemoresistant phenotype in PDAC, positioning LINC00941 as a mediator of the DNA damage response and a potential therapeutic target in PDAC.

title: A recall-rescue fuzzy layer over paired Z-DNA Hunter scans for fast Z-DNA detection.
abstract: Accurate detection of Z-DNA-forming regions is limited by the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity in sequence-based methods. We present Z-DNA-Fuzzy Hunter 1.1.0-a fast and interpretable protocol that extends Z-DNA Hunter through a dual-scan strategy combined with a fuzzy expert layer. A permissive scan (model 2, minimum length 6 bp, threshold 30%) captures a broad candidate set, while a stringent scan (model 2, minimum length 10 bp, threshold 60%) provides high-confidence support. These outputs are integrated using fuzzy inference incorporating sequence signal, cross-scan support, genomic context, and bias penalties. On the audited 385-locus Shin analysis, the protocol achieves balanced accuracy 0.883 (recall 0.862, specificity 0.904), comparable with the published Z-DNABERT operating point, while alternative modes increase specificity to 0.973. The paired scans are combined by a transparent, configurable prioritization layer with an adjustable recall-specificity trade-off. The local workflow requires only a FASTA (Fast-All sequence alignment format), sequence and transcription start site annotation. The tool is freely available at https://github.com/mifo123/zdna-fuzzy-hunter.
authors: Petrovič M, Trenz O, Kledus F, Brázda V, Šťastný J.

title: Dietary carbohydrate structure affects the gut microbial diversity, succession, and compartmentalization in black soldier fly larvae.
abstract: Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) plays a pivotal role in bioconverting organic wastes into high-value biomass by gut microbiota. However, how dietary carbohydrate structure modulates gut microbial assembly remains unclear. Here, we characterized the gut bacterial communities across developmental stages and gut regions of BSFL reared on wheat bran (fiber-rich) and cassava (starch-rich) diets using 16S rRNA sequencing. Alpha-diversity analysis revealed that wheat bran diet significantly enhanced species richness (ACE, Chao) and diversity (Shannon), with progressive increases across larval stages, whereas cassava diet only increased richness without improved evenness. Dietary substrate was the primary driver of gut microbiota composition (PC1: 32.5% variance), followed by developmental stage. Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Bacteroidota, and Actinobacteriota were the predominant bacterial phyla across both diets. Firmicutes dominated the wheat bran group (52.34%) with a successional shift from Proteobacteria-enriched early stages to Firmicutes-enriched later stages, while Proteobacteria prevailed in cassava group (79.27%) throughout development. The wheat bran group was dominated by the genera of Klebsiella (20.17%), Bacillus (18.17%), Providencia (10.15%), whereas cassava group by unclassified_f_Enterobacteriaceae, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Providencia, and Morganella. Specially, Bacillaceae prevailed in the anterior gut and the hindgut and Lachnospiraceae in the hindgut under wheat bran diet, indicating sequential fiber degradation. Cassava diet exhibited a homogeneous Enterobacteriaceae dominance across all regions. LEfSe further identified Firmicutes-affiliated taxa enriched in wheat bran and Dysgonomonas-associated taxa in cassava. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that dietary carbohydrate structure dictates the taxonomic composition of the BSFL gut microbiota, offering practical guidance for optimizing waste bioconversion stratˇegies based on feedstock characteristics.

title: The Chlorella Cell Wall From Structural Diversity and Biosynthesis to Disruption and Biotechnological Applications.
abstract: Chlorella is an important microalgal platform for sustainable biotechnology, but its chemically resistant and structurally heterogeneous cell wall can restrict genetic transformation, intracellular product recovery, digestibility, and biomass utilization. This review synthesizes current knowledge of cell walls in Chlorella and related Chlorella-like algae, integrating taxonomic and phylogenetic context with composition, architecture, biosynthesis, developmental and environmental remodeling, analytical considerations, disruption strategies, and applications. Reported walls contain variable proportions of glucose-, rhamnose-, mannose-, and glucosamine-containing polymers, proteins, and, in some lineages, highly resistant outer components. Their architecture and physicochemical properties vary among species, strains, growth phases, and cultivation conditions, affecting rigidity, permeability, and extractability. Genomic and biochemical evidence suggests that wall formation involves broadly conserved glycan-related and secretory functions together with lineage-divergent glucan-, glycoprotein-, and chitin-chitosan-related machinery, although most candidate biosynthetic and remodeling enzymes remain functionally uncharacterized. Interpretation of wall composition requires careful distinction among intact cells, whole biomass, isolated walls, and extracted fractions, because monosaccharide composition alone does not establish polymer identity. Enzymatic permeabilization is generally most compatible with viable-cell transformation, whereas chemical, physical, enzymatic, and hybrid treatments can improve intracellular product recovery, with efficiencies strongly dependent on species and process conditions. Wall-rich residues may also serve as sources of fermentable carbohydrates, biosorbent surfaces, and functional materials. A strain- and lineage-resolved understanding of wall structure and biosynthesis will be essential for developing tunable wall properties that balance cultivation robustness with downstream accessibility.
authors: Lee H, Nam S, Choi BY, Park S, Son M, Shin CH, Yamaoka Y.

title: Assessment of microbiome-UV interactions in a physiological ex vivo human skin model.
abstract: IntroductionThe cutaneous microbiome is increasingly recognized as a modulator of skin physiology and UV responses, yet mechanistic studies in human models remain limited by the lack of model systems that preserve physiologically relevant skin architecture and microbial communities.MethodsWe used the physiological Perfex ex vivo human skin explant system to assess microbiome-UV interactions. Abdominal skin explants from three donors were inoculated with donor-specific cheek microbiomes or vehicle, and, after 24 h, exposed or not to a single UV irradiation. Assessments were performed 48 h after inoculation. Bacterial survival and transfer were evaluated by culture-based CFU enumeration and 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Cutaneous responses were assessed by RT-qPCR for 29 genes involved in oxidative stress, inflammation, skin hydration, barrier function, and epidermal differentiation. Cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs), 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG), oxidized proteins, and NRF2 were quantified by immunohistochemistry.ResultsPerfex explants supported short-term persistence of donor-derived skin microbiota for up to 48 h, although cultivable bacteria decreased by approximately 90% over this period, including upon UV irradiation. 16S profiles confirmed donor-specific microbiome transfer but also revealed residual bacterial DNA in uninoculated controls, limiting interpretation of UV effects on microbial composition. Assessing expression changes in 29 epidermal genes examined, four-GPX1, IVL, LOR, and KRT1-exhibited UV-induced expression patterns that differed according to the presence or absence of the microbiome. By contrast, microbiome inoculation markedly attenuated UV-induced CPDs, 8-OHdG, protein oxidation, and NRF2 induction.DiscussionDespite substantial limitations in microbial engraftment, viability, and temporal resolution, the Perfex system provides a physiologically relevant ex vivo platform in which a transplanted human skin microbiome could modulate UV-induced oxidative and genotoxic damage. These proof-of-concept data support further refinement of this model for mechanistic microbiome-UV studies.
authors: Matarrese P, Percoco G, Patatian A, Guéré C, Fitoussi R, Vié K, Poulet V, Ngari C, Seyer D.

title: Polyextremotolerant lignocellulolytic bacteria from contrasting halo-alkaline habitats as sources of extremozymes for rice husk saccharification and biofuel applications.
abstract: RationaleLignocellulosic agricultural residues represent an enormous and largely untapped feedstock for second-generation biofuels, yet their structural recalcitrance remains the central bottleneck for cost-effective bioconversion. Conventional mesophilic enzymes lose much of their activity under the high-salinity, alkaline and thermally stressful conditions that define industrial biomass processing- a gap that microorganisms from naturally halo-alkaline ecosystems are well positioned to fill. Rice husk, generated in massive quantities as a by-product of rice milling across South Asia, remains an underutilized substrate whose silica-rich, lignin-shielded architecture makes it an appropriate and demanding test case for halotolerant biocatalysts.MethodsThree ecologically distinct saline habitats were sampled: Poovar Lake, a brackish mangrove estuary in Kerala (pH 6.92, salinity (chloride concentration) 1.90 g/L), Varkala Beach, a high-chloride concentration coastal site (pH 8.24, salinity (chloride concentration) 31.16 g/L), and Sanjay Lake, an anthropogenic inland lake in Delhi (pH 9.25, salinity (chloride concentration) 0.42 g/L). Using selective enrichment on halophilic media at 40 °C across a salinity range of 3-9% (w/v) NaCl, 29 halotolerant isolates were recovered and screened for xylanase, cellulase, lipase, amylase and protease activity using plate-based zone assays. The four most active cellulase- and xylanase-producing isolates, identified by 16S rRNA gene sequencing as Priestia flexa (XBL51), Bacillus proteolyticus (XBL61), Bacillus paralicheniformis (XBL66) and "Vibrio neocaledonicus" (XBL71), were then evaluated for their ability to hydrolyze alkaline-pretreated rice husk (1.5% (w/v) NaOH, 60 °C, 90 min) under saline-alkaline stress (4.5% (w/v) NaCl, pH 8.5, 40 °C). Growth kinetics and reducing sugar release were monitored over 6-days, and post-degradation structural changes in the biomass were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM).ResultsAlkaline pretreatment significantly disrupted the crystalline architecture of rice husk, reducing the crystallinity index (CrI) from 49.31% to 33.93%, thereby loosening the structure and substantially improving substrate accessibility for enzymatic attack. Among individual isolates, monoculture of XBL61 and XBL71, as well as XBL51 + XBL66 + XBL71 showed the strongest growth on pretreated rice husk as the sole carbon source. Reducing sugar release across the top-performing isolates and consortia ranged from 1.69 to 1.97 mg/g over the 6-day incubation. Monocultures XBL61 and XBL66 emerged as the most effective isolates, exhibiting sustained sugar production. Among the two-isolate consortium, XBL51 + XBL71 exhibited synergistic growth and hydrolysis activity. Post-incubation, XRD analysis showed that XBL61 alone raised the CrI marginally to 52.10%, suggesting reduction of amorphous regions, including non-cellulosic components such as hemicellulose and amorphous cellulose. By contrast, the XBL51 + XBL71 consortium reduced the CrI to 49.07%, reflecting more extensive and balanced structural deconstruction. SEM corroborated these findings, revealing a clear progression from the intact, tightly laminated surface of untreated biomass through the fissured, loosened layers of the pretreated material, to the deeply porous, honeycombed morphology left following consortium-mediated degradation.ConclusionThese results demonstrate that halotolerant bacteria isolated from contrasting saline habitats, particularly when used as rationally designed consortia, can effectively deconstruct alkaline-pretreated rice husk under conditions that would substantially inhibit conventional mesophilic cellulases. The inherent stress tolerance of these isolates makes them promising candidates for lignocellulosic biorefinery processes where elevated salinity and alkaline pH are unavoidable operational realities. Enzyme-level characterization and fermentation coupling of these isolates represent logical next steps toward translating these findings into scalable platforms for second-generation biofuel production.
authors: Gupta A, Pandey S, Agrawal A, Chauhan A, Huang KW, Karan R.

title: Bacterial interfaces and surface chemistry shape hydroxyapatite mineral architecture during microbially induced calcium phosphate precipitation.
abstract: Calcium phosphate biomineralization plays a crucial role in the formation of geological deposits, biological materials, and environmental remediation. While microorganisms are known to influence calcium phosphate precipitation, the relative contributions of bacterial cell surfaces and extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) remain poorly defined. This study presents the first microscale investigation of the distinct roles of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial cells and EPS in regulating hydroxyapatite (HAp) mineralization, employing abiotic, EPS-mediated, and bacterial precipitation systems. Zeta potential measurements and Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) revealed that both bacterial cells and isolated EPS provide negatively charged, chemically distinct interfaces capable of interacting with dissolved Ca2+ ions. Solution chemistry demonstrated greater phosphate and calcium ion depletion in biotic systems, consistent with enhanced crystal precipitation compared to abiotic controls. Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) and Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) analyses showed that biological interfaces produced distinct crystal morphologies and surface characteristics. X-ray diffraction (XRD) revealed significant differences in phase composition: abiotic precipitation produced mixed calcium phosphate phases, whereas EPS-mediated precipitation promoted nucleation but remained dominated by precursor phases. In contrast, whole-cell systems favored HAp formation, with Sporosarcina pasteurii producing phase-pure crystalline HAp and Pseudomonas fluorescens producing HAp-dominant precipitates. Acid dissolution experiments further confirmed the increased stability of biogenic precipitates. These findings demonstrate that the spatial organization of bacterial surface functional groups, rather than surface charge alone, governs hydroxyapatite phase evolution, crystal growth, and mineral stability. While localized metabolic activity may contribute to microenvironmental conditions, the results highlight the importance of bacterial cell surfaces and EPS as key determinants of hydroxyapatite biomineralization, providing a mechanistic basis for the design of biologically mediated mineral materials.
authors: Toprak P, Rodriguez-Navarro C, Mukherjee A, Pring A, Dhami NK.

title: Impacts on water chemistry and the non-target microbial community following application of a novel chemical control strategy for Karenia brevis.
abstract: Environmental impact is a critical factor when considering potential control of Florida red tide (Karenia brevis). A combination of ammonium (50 μM) and putrescine (85 μM), hereafter "NP", was formulated to control K. brevis growth in laboratory culture. However, effects of NP on water quality and non-target organisms in complex microbial communities require investigation. To assess potential impacts, mesocosms containing non-red tide microbial communities were treated with NP and compared to Controls over seven days. Putrescine had a residence time of two days while total ammonia increased to toxic levels following NP application. Dynamics in oxygen, pH, and turbidity implicated microbial heterotrophy in the removal of putrescine and release of ammonia. Except on Day 5, chlorophyll a was not significantly different between treatments. However, accessory pigment analysis and eukaryotic metabarcode profiling revealed that NP treatment restructured phytoplankton and heterotrophic microeukaryote communities. NP-treated phytoplankton communities experienced reductions in abundance and diversity of dinoflagellates, and increases in relative abundance of other phytoplankton groups, including diatoms and chlorophytes. Metabarcoding showed that heterotrophic microeukaryotes increased over time regardless of treatment, and became the majority of metabarcode reads in NP-treated communities. Heterotroph community composition was distinguished by relatively abundant eukaryvores in Controls, and bacterivores in NP-treated mesocosms. Thus, NP had complex interconnected impacts on water quality and the microbial community, with an increase in the relative abundance and diversity of heterotrophs and beneficial phytoplankton species, while also resulting in elevated ammonium and sustained decreases in pH.
authors: Johnson GI, Burris DS, Miller C, Wetzel DL, Wang Y, Lovko VJ, Coyne KJ.

title: Metatranscriptomic insights into PCB biodegradation enhanced by an endogenous Rpf-associated secretion fraction and recombinant Rpf.
abstract: Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are persistent organic pollutants whose biodegradation can be constrained by the transition of indigenous PCB-degrading microorganisms into a viable but non-culturable (VBNC) state. Although resuscitation-promoting factors (Rpfs) can reactivate dormant microorganisms, the multistep production and purification of recombinant Rpf may constrain its practical application. Here, a crude autocrine Rpf-associated fraction (ca-Rpf) secreted by Achromobacter sp. HR2 was compared with recombinant Rpf (re-Rpf) for enhancing PCB biodegradation. Both treatments enhanced PCB degradation during acclimation and generated enriched cultures that retained improved degradation capacity without further Rpf supplementation. At 40 mg/L Aroclor 1242, PCB degradation efficiencies on day 18 reached 60.8% and 53.6% in the ca-Rpf- and re-Rpf-enriched cultures, respectively, compared with 40.1% in the control. Enhanced degradation was accompanied by increased Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and cytochrome P450 activities. Metatranscriptomic analysis revealed treatment-dependent changes in the expression of genes associated with central carbon metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, aromatic-compound degradation, and dormancy-related processes. The ca-Rpf-enriched cultures exhibited stronger transcriptional responses in several catabolic pathways, accompanied by shifts in the relative representation of putative PCB-degrading taxa, including Pseudomonas, Stenotrophomonas, and Azospirillum. These findings link enhanced PCB biodegradation to microbial community remodeling and catabolic gene transcription, highlighting the potential of endogenous Rpf-associated preparations for bioremediation.
authors: Yu W, Sun F, Dong F, Shen C, Su X.

title: Vitamin levels in consumers: is diet, dissolved vitamins or vitamins produced by gut microbiota the most important source?
abstract: Vitamins are continuously required for organismal metabolism. They are produced by phytoplankton, bacteria, and fungi and the general notion is that aquatic consumers, such as zooplankton and fish, obtain them from the diet. The focus here is on vitamin B1, called thiamine or thiamin, and the observation that concentrations of this vitamin decline with increasing trophic level. The mechanisms leading to this pattern are not well understood but we argue that it could be a sign of lower mass-specific metabolic demand for thiamine in larger compared to smaller consumers. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential for alternative pathways of vitamin provision to consumers, apart from diet, including contributions from gut microbiota, or less likely, from the pool dissolved in water. How vitamins move through the food web as well as the metabolic demand of vitamins in differently sized consumers are essential factors to quantify to understand why top consumers, such as many salmonid species across the Northern Hemisphere, periodically develop thiamine deficiency, resulting in massive mortality.
authors: Hylander S, Ejsmond MJ.
