title: MdMYB1R1 Activates MdMAPKKK18 and Additional Defense Pathways to Confer Resistance to Woody Fungal Pathogens in Apple.
abstract: Trunk diseases caused by woody plant pathogens, including Valsa mali and Botryosphaeria dothidea, represent a major threat to global apple production; however, the molecular basis of host resistance remains largely elusive. In this study, we employed TMT-based quantitative proteomic profiling to compare necrotic and uninfected twig tissues of apple following V. mali inoculation, identifying 904 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs). Among these, the MYB transcription factor, MdMYB1R1, exhibited a pronounced induction in response to pathogen infection. Subcellular localization and transactivation assays revealed that MdMYB1R1 localizes to the nucleus and acts as a transcriptional activator. Transient overexpression of MdMYB1R1 in Nicotiana benthamiana potentiated reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and activated MAPK signaling, correlating with enhanced resistance against Sclerotinia sclerotiorum. Stable overexpression of MdMYB1R1 in apple markedly enhanced resistance to both V. mali and B. dothidea, whereas silencing of MdMYB1R1 impaired disease tolerance. Through DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq), yeast one-hybrid (Y1H), electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA), and dual-luciferase reporter assays, we demonstrated that MdMYB1R1 binds to the promoter region of MdMAPKKK18 and activates its transcription, a gene encoding a mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase involved in MAPK signaling. Genetic epistasis analysis further revealed that overexpression of MdMAPKKK18 only partially rescued the compromised resistance in MdMYB1R1-RNAi plants. Collectively, our findings identify MdMYB1R1 as a key positive regulator of apple resistance against trunk fungal diseases, acting at least in part by directly activating the MdMAPKKK18-mediated MAPK cascade and by regulating additional defense pathways, thus providing a promising candidate for breeding disease-resistant apple cultivars.
authors: Liu H, Chen S, Zhang Q, Du Y, Gao X, Xu L, Huang L.

title: Cross-Sectional Association between Fiber Intake and Gastrointestinal Inflammation is Dependent on FUT2 Secretor Status in Healthy Adults.
abstract: BackgroundGut microbes consume mucins in the absence of dietary fermentable fiber. People with non-secretor alpha-1-2-L-fucosyltransferase 2 (FUT2) genotypes produce gastrointestinal (GI) mucins that lack terminal fucose and have increased risk for inflammatory bowel disease.ObjectivesThis study aimed to determine whether associations between fiber intake and subclinical GI inflammation and/or microbiome function are modified by FUT2 genotype in healthy adults.MethodsWe assessed interactions between fiber intake, FUT2 genotype, and GI inflammation markers in a cross-sectional observational study of healthy adults. Participants with 24-h dietary recalls and food frequency questionnaires to characterize recent and habitual diet, respectively, and fecal samples, plasma samples and/or shotgun metagenomes (n=297) were included in this analysis. Differences in microbiome composition between secretors and non-secretors were analyzed using PERMANOVA and machine learning. A custom-designed TaqManTM probe was used to genotype a single nucleotide polymorphism (rs601338) to determine secretor status. ELISA was used to measure fecal calprotectin, myeloperoxidase, and neopterin, as well as plasma lipopolysaccharide binding protein. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were measured in fecal samples. Relationships between fiber intake, FUT2 genotype and outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed effect models.ResultsHigher energy-adjusted total recent fiber, total habitual fiber, and soluble fiber intake was associated with lower calprotectin levels in secretors, but not in non-secretors. Overall microbiome composition did not differ by secretor status. However, the ratio of mucin-degrading to plant-degrading enzymes, Muc2Plant, in the gut microbiome was positively associated with increased fecal calprotectin in secretors, but not in non-secretors. There was no interaction between dietary fiber intake, the FUT2 genotype, and fecal SCFAs.ConclusionThe association of higher dietary fiber intake with lower subclinical GI inflammation and lower mucin-degrading enzymes was observed in secretors, but not in non-secretors. Clinical trials in nutrition are needed to determine if non-secretors are less responsive to dietary fiber.
authors: Bouzid YY, Oliver A, Blecksmith SE, Wilson SMG, Alkan Z, Huang L, Bennett BJ, Kable ME, Stephensen CB, Lemay DG.

title: CRISPR, mRNA, and Beyond: Nucleic Acid Therapeutics in Allergy and Immunology.
abstract: The management of allergic and immunologic diseases has long centered on symptom management rather than disease modification. Conventional pharmacotherapy controls manifestations of the immune dysregulation but does little to treat the underlying cause. Newer monoclonal and small molecule therapies target downstream effectors of the type 2 inflammatory cascade, and allergen immunotherapy, while disease-modifying, requires years of administration for effect. Nucleic acid therapies represent a different approach that intervenes at the level of genetic information itself, at the DNA, RNA, or protein-production step. This includes mRNA treatments that direct cells to produce therapeutic proteins or modify allergen-specific immune responses; antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNAs that selectively silence disease genes; adeno-associated viral vectors for sustained gene delivery; and CRISPR-based systems that permanently edit the genome. Several technologies have advanced to clinical proof of concept including a CRISPR gene-editing therapy (lonvoguran ziclumeran) that reduced hereditary angioedema attacks by 87% compared with placebo in a randomized controlled trial. An inhaled DNAzyme targeting the intracellular transcription factor GATA3 attenuated allergen-induced late asthmatic responses by 34% in humans, and CD19 CAR-T cell therapy induced drug-free remission in severe autoimmune disease. As of 2025, 24 oligonucleotide therapeutics have received FDA approval, including donidalorsen, the first RNA-targeted prophylactic therapy approved for hereditary angioedema. This review examines each therapeutic technology, its mechanism and delivery strategy, and the evidence relevant to allergic and immunologic disease. Persistent challenges, including delivery beyond the liver, immune responses to viral vectors, and the need for long-term safety data, are addressed alongside a proposed integration with existing treatment paradigms.
journal: Annals of allergy, asthma & immunology : official publication of the American College of Allergy, Asthma, & Immunology
authors: Schauberger EM, Phillips JA.

title: Perfluorooctane sulfonate impairs propionate-to-methane carbon transfer by disrupting syntrophic electron and thermodynamic coupling during sludge anaerobic digestion.
abstract: Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) accumulates in sewage sludge, yet the metabolic step most sensitive to PFOS during anaerobic digestion remains unclear. Here, substrate-specific activity tests, 13C3-propionate tracing, redox and thermodynamic measurements, metagenomics, and microbial network analysis were combined to investigate how PFOS disrupts propionate-to-methane conversion. At 5.0 mg/L PFOS, cumulative methane production decreased by 12.2%, whereas the maximum propionate degradation rate declined by 47.8%. Under the same exposure, acetoclastic and H2/CO2-dependent methanogenic activities decreased by 18.0% and 21.0%, respectively. The propionate fraction in residual volatile fatty acid‌ (VFA) increased from 22.6% to 51.8%. 13C tracing showed that 13CH4 recovery fell from 41.6% to 13.9% and carbon-transfer efficiency from 45.7% to 26.1%. PFOS also caused H2 accumulation to 4.9 × 10-4 atm, reduced ATP and ETSA by 42.8% and 39.9%, and shifted the ΔG of propionate oxidation to - 1.9 kJ/mol. Metagenomic and network analyses further showed losses of propionate oxidizers, hydrogenotrophic methanogens, related functions, and syntrophic connectivity. PFOS therefore primarily destabilized anaerobic digestion by decoupling syntrophic propionate oxidation.
authors: Kuang Y, Chen S, Ma D, Zhao J, Wang H, Sun Y, Wang J.

title: Highly effective removal of trichloroethylene in groundwater by modified nano zero-valent iron coupled with microbial degradation.
abstract: Trichloroethylene (TCE) contamination in groundwater poses a serious environmental concern due to its persistence, toxicity, and potential risks to human health. Although nano-zero-valent iron (nZVI) coupled with microbial degradation has shown promise for TCE remediation, the limited stability, aggregation, and potential microbial toxicity of nZVI remain major challenges. In this study, a carboxymethyl cellulose-stabilized nZVI (CMC-nZVI) coupled with an aerobic microbial consortium was developed to enhance TCE removal and improve the compatibility between nZVI and microorganisms. The effects of CMC modification on nZVI stability, microbial activity, and TCE degradation performance were systematically investigated. Results demonstrated that CMC modification improved the dispersion stability and environmental compatibility of nZVI, thereby promoting synergistic interactions between nZVI and microorganisms. The optimized CMC-nZVI coupled system containing 4% microbial inoculum and 1.0 g/L CMC-nZVI achieved 83.21% removal of 100 mg/L TCE within 5 days and maintained sustainable degradation performance during the subsequent degradation cycle. CMC-nZVI reduced the accumulation of toxic intermediates and facilitated a more favorable TCE transformation pathway. Furthermore, metagenomic analysis indicated that the coupled system caused limited disturbance to microbial community richness while enriching potential TCE-degrading genera and enhancing the abundance of functional genes associated with pollutant transformation. These findings provide direction for further elucidating the mechanisms of coupled dehalogenation processes, optimizing coupled systems, and advancing in-situ remediation.
authors: Zheng Y, Zhi L, Wang T, Gao X, Yu H, Teng Y.

title: Geninthiocin promotes RIG-I-mediated anti-RNA viral signaling responses.
abstract: RIG-I, the core RNA sensor of RIG-I-mediated type I IFNs (IFN-I) signaling, induces the innate antiviral response through recognizing RNA viruses. Upon RNA virus infection, RIG-I undergoes autophagic degradation to attenuate host innate immune response for immune evasion. Thus, we sought to discovery the lead compounds that promote RIG-I protein stability to enhance host antiviral ability. Natural compounds have a rich history for contributing to new therapeutic candidates. Up to now, there is rarely reported that natural compounds enhance RIG-I to clear RNA virus. By screening a natural compound library, we identified that Geninthiocin, a natural thiopeptide from a marine Streptomyces, potentiates RIG-I-IFN-I signaling to enhance IFN-I and antiviral ISGs expression through inhibiting RIG-I autophagic degradation. Both in human and murine cells, Geninthiocin promoted RIG-I-mediated IFN-I and antiviral ISGs expression upon Influenza A virus PR8 (IAV) infection or RNA mimics Poly(I:C) stimulation. In vivo, we observed that Geninthiocin significantly suppressed IAV PR8 induced death and enhance the expression of IFN-I and antiviral ISGs in C57BL/6 J mice. By performing molecular docking and biotin pull down assay, we observed that Geninthiocin interacted with RIG-I. Further, Geninthiocin repressed RIG-I autophagic degradation to positively regulate RIG-I-IFN-I signaling response. Together, we reveal the novel function of Geninthiocin in anti-RNA viral innate immune response by enhancing RIG-I-IFN-I signaling activation, which provides new insight in developing therapeutic strategy for IAVs or other RNA viral infectious diseases.
authors: Cui J, Liu J, Chong W, Bi W, Zhou X, Chen M, Wan Q, Pan M.

title: A heavy molybdenum reservoir in Neoarchean seawater tracks extensive iron oxidation.
abstract: The lead-up to the Great Oxidation Event (GOE; between 2.5 and 2.2 Ga) was arguably as consequential as the event itself, yet substantial uncertainties remain regarding the timing and magnitude of oxygen rise in early Earth's oceans. Heavy molybdenum isotope compositions (δ98Mo) in Neoarchean marine sediments have traditionally been interpreted as evidence for adsorption of dissolved Mo onto iron oxyhydroxides [e.g., ferrihydrite; Fe(OH)3] and manganese oxides (MnO2) formed in oxygenated marine environments, implying at least regional surface oxygen accumulation immediately prior to the GOE. Here, we propose an alternate explanation in which these isotopic signatures arose in a largely anoxic ocean. Analyses of Neoarchean banded iron formations (BIFs) deposited at 2.57 to 2.51 Ga reveal a broad range of δ98Mo values, which are best explained by the combined effects of Mo adsorption onto primary ferrihydrite, followed by its diagenetic incorporation into Fe(II)-Mo(IV)-sulfides. After accounting for isotopic fractionation during adsorption, we estimate that Neoarchean seawater δ98Mo maintained a relatively stable composition between 1.5‰ and 1.6‰. A newly developed Mo isotope mass balance model further indicates that only a minor MnO2 sink was required to generate these heavy δ98Mo values. Instead, the dominant control was likely removal of isotopically light Mo via adsorption to settling ferrihydrite particles in ferruginous seawater. Given the lack of oxygen indicators for cyanobacterial photosynthesis, we posit that anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria (photoferrotrophs) were the primary drivers of ferrihydrite precipitation during BIF deposition. Together, these findings imply that the Neoarchean Mo isotope record reflects anaerobic biological oxidation of Fe(II) rather than pervasive surface seawater oxygenation preceding the GOE.
authors: Wang C, Dong F, Dong Z, Robbins L, Zhang L, Li J, Stüeken E, Kendall B, Konhauser K, Wan B.

title: Genetic architecture of the egg size-number trade-off in the Pacific oyster, Crassostrea gigas.
abstract: The trade-off between egg size and number is a fundamental concept in life-history theory, yet its genetic underpinnings remain poorly characterized in marine invertebrates. In this study, we investigated the genetic architecture of reproductive traits in the Pacific oyster (Crassostrea gigas) using quantitative genetics and genome-wide association analyses. Reproductive traits were measured in 650 offspring, and 220 ripe females were randomly selected for genotyping followed by genome-wide association analysis. We found negative phenotypic and genetic correlations between egg size and egg number. Notably, two variants in the 5' UTR of the TRIM71 locus exhibited opposite allelic effects on the two traits, suggesting a candidate regulatory locus contributing to variation in reproductive allocation. By integrating GWAS with stage-specific transcriptomic profiles, we prioritized candidate genes associated with each trait and identified distinct temporal expression patterns: genes linked to egg size were more highly expressed during early developmental stages, whereas those associated with egg number showed elevated expression during gametogenesis and gonadal ripening. These findings reveal that the egg size-number trade-off in C. gigas is associated with both allelic variation at specific loci and temporally separated expression programs during reproductive development, providing novel insights into the molecular basis of reproductive allocation in marine invertebrates.
authors: Ma H, Yang B, Wu D, Shi C, Chen C, Lu Z, Wang T, Li Q, Liu S.

title: Growth on human serum albumin drives large genomic inversion in Porphyromonas gingivalis.
abstract: Insertion sequence transposable elements can bring about breakage and rejoining of chromosomal DNA in inverted orientations. Genomic inversions are a type of chromosomal rearrangement that significantly influence gene expression, yet our understanding of what conditions and processes drive these rearrangements remains unclear. Importantly, these inversions are typically reversible and therefore dynamic. Using long reads to evaluate genome structure, this study revealed that populations of some strains of the oral anaerobe Porphyromonas gingivalis have two distinct genome arrangements, and the large 1.5 Mbp inversion resulting from these rearrangements is controlled by matching ISPg2 transposase elements. Strains that can rearrange their genomes undergo early autolysis when grown on human serum albumin (HSA) as a substrate, yet the strains lacking the matching ISPg2 elements do not. Intriguingly, a subset of cells within the population survives after lysis, and the inverted sub-population orientation becomes dominant. We propose that P. gingivalis maintains different genotypic subpopulations with varying phenotypes within its population as a bet-hedging strategy, where some of the cells will continue to persist after most of the cells lyse, thereby improving overall survival. The findings presented here provide further confirmation of striking differences between P. gingivalis strains and new insights into the impact of genome rearrangement on P. gingivalis physiology by using HSA as a biologically relevant substrate for growth.ImportanceIn bacteria, some regions of chromosomal DNA (called insertion sequence transposable elements) can exchange with each other and cause large sections of a genome to flip around in the opposite direction. This study identified a dynamic 1.5 Mbp chromosomal inversion in Porphyromonas gingivalis mediated by ISPg2 elements. Triggered by growth on human serum albumin, this rearrangement modulates autolysis while allowing a resilient subpopulation to dominate. Our findings highlight a bet-hedging strategy as a vital mechanism for P. gingivalis persistence, offering new insights into how genomic plasticity drives survival in biologically relevant growth conditions.
authors: DiSalvo B, Ko YK, Kim H-M, Tang J, Cugini C, Yu M, Davey ME.

title: Orientia tsutsugamushi genotypes associated with severe scrub typhus in South India.
abstract: BackgroundOrientia tsutsugamushi is an obligate intracellular bacterium with a complex genome, causing mite-borne scrub typhus in many parts of Asia. We determined O. tsutsugamushi genotypes in chigger mites, small mammal hosts and human fever cases to explore genotype-specific virulence.MethodsWe enrolled scrub typhus patients from two hospitals in Tamil Nadu, India. Chigger mites were collected from small mammals trapped in 25 rural villages located within the catchment areas of the hospitals. Samples underwent screening for Orientia with real-time PCR followed by nested PCR of the partial tsa56 gene and Sanger sequencing. Phylogenetic trees were used to group sequences into clades, labelled according to the nearest reference genotypes.ResultsWe determined 138 tsa56 sequences from 1165 blood samples from human fever cases, 63 sequences from 762 chigger pools, and 58 sequences from 874 small mammals. Sequences were grouped into nine genotypes. The two most common genotypes in chiggers and small mammals were never found in human scrub typhus cases, while genotypes common in humans were rare in chiggers. There was a positive relationship between the human-to-chigger genotype prevalence ratio and the genotype-specific proportions of human infections that were severe (r= 0.87, p= 0.011). Two genotypes, labelled Kato-Vellore and TA763-Vellore, caused 72% of infections involving shock and all five observed deaths. The genotype-specific risk of shock was closely associated with the prevalence of eschar skin lesions (r= 0.84, p= 0.017).ConclusionO. tsutsugamushi genotypes differed strongly between chiggers and human fever patients and showed marked variation in clinical severity.
authors: Schmidt WP, Alexander N, Makepeace BL, Castaneda Sastre E, Khoo JJ, Salje J, Abhilash KPP, Alex R, Chandramohan D, Devamani C.

title: LOca-1: A minimal calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase from the Loki’s Castle hydrothermal vent field
abstract: Orthocaspases are prokaryotic homologs of metacaspases within the C14 family of cysteine proteases, yet their biochemical properties and cellular roles remain poorly understood. Here, we report the discovery and comprehensive characterization of LOca-1, a metagenome-derived orthocaspase from the Loki’s Castle hydrothermal vent field. LOca-1 consists primarily of a single, conserved p20 catalytic domain and undergoes calcium-dependent activation through cleavage at a conserved arginine residue. Once activated, LOca-1 displays strict arginyl-specific proteolytic activity and strong selectivity for residues surrounding the cleavage site. The enzyme is both thermoactive and thermostable, exhibiting maximal activity at 65 °C and a melting temperature of approximately 72 °C. Structural modelling revealed conservation of the catalytic core relative to plant metacaspases despite substantial sequence divergence. To our knowledge, LOca-1 is only the second biochemically characterized orthocaspase and the first reported from a deep-sea hydrothermal vent environment. LOca-1 expands the known biochemical diversity of prokaryotic metacaspase homologs and provides insights into the properties of a minimal p20-domain orthocaspase. Together, our findings establish LOca-1 as a thermostable, calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase and provide a foundation for future studies of orthocaspase function in prokaryotes.
authors: Arsın H, Hribovšek P, Urich L, Fedøy A, Stokke R, Mak P, Kaczorowska A, O’Donoghue AJ, Kaczorowski T, Steen IH.

title: SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and vulnerability of human blastocysts during in vitro preimplantation development.
abstract: Human preimplantation embryos express the SARS-CoV-2 entry factors ACE2, TMPRSS2 and BSG (CD147) on trophectoderm (TE) cells, suggesting susceptibility to infection. Likewise, SARS-CoV-2-pseudotyped reporter viruses induced cytopathic effects in blastocysts, while the zona pellucida (ZP) appeared to confer partial protection. The impact of authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection on embryonic lineage specification and developmental competence has not been established. Here, we exposed cryopreserved human embryos, donated under ethics approval and informed consent, to authentic SARS-CoV-2 (B.1.617.2, Delta variant). While embryos with an intact ZP remained uninfected, laser-assisted hatching rendered 19/21 (90.5%) of embryos susceptible to infection, as confirmed by detection of viral dsRNA. Moreover, SARS-CoV-2 infection had a pronounced effect on blastocyst development with a possibly fatal outcome. Compared to mock-treated embryos (n = 47), infected blastocysts (n = 48) showed a significantly reduced surface area (p = 0.0003), reduced total cell number (p = 0.0139), and reduced NANOG+ epiblast cell numbers (p = 0.0054) 24 hours post-exposure, while the number of GATA4+ primitive endoderm cells remained unaffected (p = 0.5255). Intriguingly, despite viral replication being largely confined to the trophectoderm (TE), this selective epiblast reduction suggests a disruption of TE-derived paracrine signaling required for epiblast specification. Finally, prolonged viral replication resulted in embryonic lysis and death. Digital transcriptomic profiling (mock, n = 29 embryos; SARS-CoV-2, n = 28 embryos; each in n = 5 minipools) revealed upregulation of innate antiviral and inflammatory genes, including IFIH1, IRF7, NOD2, and TNFRSF1A, as well as the recently identified SARS-CoV-2 entry factor TMEM106B, alongside altered developmental signatures concerning genome activation, pluripotency, and lineage-specific programs. These findings show that ZP disruption makes human blastocysts susceptible to productive SARS-CoV-2 infection, with adverse consequences for lineage allocation and direct implications for biosafety and virological counselling in medically assisted reproduction practice.
authors: Kumpanenko Y, Tryfonos M, Essahib W, De Munck N, Van Weyenbergh J, Alpizar YA, Dallmeier K, Van de Velde H.

title: Batch, Prefetch, Skip, Orient, Squeeze: Faster, Smaller k-mer dictionaries via the Spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform
abstract: Looking up k-mers in an index is a core operation in genomics, underlying read mapping, metagenomic classification, and many other tasks. Queries are often streaming: the k-mers come from a longer sequence such as a sequencing read, and consecutive k-mers overlap. The fastest index for such queries is currently the hashing-based SSHash; indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) are competitive in space but slower. We show how to make SBWT indexes both faster and smaller. First, we process queries in small batches and prefetch the memory each will need next, hiding the latency of the dependent random accesses that dominate a lookup; together with a new rank structure that reads one cache line per query, this makes k-mer lookups about seven times faster than unbatched SBWT search. Second, we extend batching to streaming search and show that one failed lookup can rule out many k-mers of a read at once, which removes the need for the longest common suffix array. Third, we build an SBWT that stores only one orientation of each k-mer, thereby halving its size, with a modified search that exploits how rarely the orientation changes along a read. Finally, we adapt a compact subset rank structure to batched search. On the collections of the SSHash benchmark, and on two collections up to 15 times larger, our fastest index answers streaming queries for 31-mers faster than SSHash on every read set, by up to 4.9 times, using 12 bits per canonical k-mer against SSHash's 7.4-11.1. We also show that a 6.1-bit index is still faster than SSHash on most read sets, and that our smallest index needs about 4 bits per canonical k-mer. Unlike that of SSHash, the space of our indexes barely varies across collections. Our code is available at https://github.com/anadis504/sbwt-squeeze-rs.
authors: Diseth AC, Alanko JN, Mackenzie J, Puglisi SJ.

title: gyrB-BASED MOLECULAR IDENTIFICATION AND PHYLOGENETIC RELATEDNESS OF UROPATHOGENIC Klebsiella quasipneumoniae IN TWO TERTIARY HOSPITALS IN SOUTHWEST NIGERIA
abstract: Abstract    Background  Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most frequent bacterial infections worldwide and pose a major public health problem.  Klebsiella  species are primary causes of UTIs and are often associated with drug resistance. In this study, we sequenced and compared the  gyrB  gene of uropathogenic  Klebsiella  spp. isolates from two tertiary hospitals in southwest Nigeria with reference strains of the  Klebsiella  pneumoniae complex available in GenBank to determine their phylogenetic relatedness and bridge the knowledge gap on the genetic relatedness of uropathogenic  Klebsiella  spp. in southwest Nigeria. Methods  We collected 227 urine samples from University College Hospital Ibadan and Federal Medical Centre Abeokuta, Ogun State, Nigeria, and biochemically identified  Klebsiella  spp. Sequencing of the  gyrB  gene was conducted on 7 isolates based on resistance patterns. Phylogenetic analysis was done by NGPhylogeny.fr, and the phylogenetic tree was visualized by Interactive Tree of Life (iTOL). Results  Of the cultured samples, 96 colonies appeared morphologically as  Klebsiella  spp-like on Eosin Methylene Blue agar (EMB). Biochemical identification revealed that  K  .  pneumoniae  (42) and  Klebsiella oxytoca  22 made up the  Klebsiella-like  isolates, with the remaining (32) being  Enterobacter  spp. Seven randomly selected  Klebsiella pneumoniae  isolates were identified as  Klebsiella quasipneumoniae  using the  gyrB  gene sequence. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the isolates from the two hospitals clustered closely with reference strains, indicating shared evolutionary lineages. Conclusion  The uropathogenic  Klebsiella  spp. isolates from the two hospitals in southwest Nigeria are closely related to members of the K. pneumoniae complex. These findings underscore the importance of continued molecular surveillance and suggest that conserved transnational lineages are involved in proper taxonomic classification.
authors: Sadiq SO, Ike WE, Oloyede AR, Ojo OE, Adewole AI.

title: Bacterial Preconditioning Differentially Reshapes Neuronal Responses to Intermittent and Continuous Hypoxia-Like Stress
abstract: Abstract    The microbiota–gut–brain axis exposes the nervous system to microbial information, but whether such exposure becomes part of the biological history that shapes later neuronal stress responses remains unknown. Here, we tested whether transient direct exposure to live  Lactiplantibacillus plantarum  (  L. plantarum  ) alters how differentiated B35 neuronal cells subsequently respond to hypoxia-like metabolic stress. We compared two trajectories combining chemical HIF stabilization with nutrient restriction: an intermittent, sublethal condition with recovery periods (MHX), relevant to recurrent vascular insufficiency, and a continuous severe condition (SHX). These trajectories generated distinct structural, metabolic and transcriptional states. Prior  L. plantarum  exposure was associated with higher MTT-derived metabolic viability after MHX but not SHX, and induced broader transcriptional reorganization under MHX (167 versus 64 differentially expressed genes), engaging signaling and cytoskeletal programs together with pathways linked to negative regulation of apoptosis and oxidative-stress-induced cell death. Only one bacterially responsive gene was shared between the two stress trajectories. Thus,  L. plantarum  did not impose a fixed neuroprotective program. Instead, prior microbial exposure acted as a biological input whose consequences depended on the subsequent stress trajectory. These findings establish neuron–bacteria communication as history-dependent and define an adaptive range in which microbial signals can influence neuronal responses before metabolic stress becomes overwhelming—a principle relevant to preventive intervention during recurrent vascular stress.
authors: Leaño-Hinojosa A, Lombardo-Hernandez J, Benitez-Cruz J, Rapetta I, García-Esteban MT, Murciano-Cespedosa A, Juan-Llamas C, Serrano-Regal MP, Geuna S, Cocolin L, Herrera-Rincon C.

title: Metagenomic assessment of airborne and surface viral signals and worker acceptability during a partial-lid intervention in a Cambodian live bird market
abstract: Abstract  Mechanical defeathering can disperse viral material in live poultry markets, but interventional machine modifications must fit routine work. This nonrandomized field study evaluated partial lids on defeathering machines at Orussey Market, Cambodia, across six sampling days, three with lids and three without. Targeted RT-qPCR and target-enriched metagenomics characterised viral RNA in air samples collected during a three-hour air-sampling period and in nearby surface samples collected before and after that period, while work questionnaires assessed usability. Sequencing detected 73 poultry-associated viral taxa. Influenza A virus, avian coronavirus and rotavirus G together accounted for over 80% of relative metagenomic abundance in 14 of 18 air samples. In air samples, RT-qPCR cycle thresholds correlated inversely with metagenomic relative abundance for avian influenza virus and Newcastle disease virus (Spearman’s ρ = −0.645 and − 0.684, respectively). Airborne richness was descriptively lower on days with lids, but targeted viral detections did not change consistently, and composition profiles overlapped. Surface profiles changed from before to after the air-sampling period on days with and without lids; the study did not establish a lid-associated difference in these changes. All five workers reported discomfort and perceived slower work; none wanted to use the lid in its tested form, although three would continue if it were permanently integrated into the machine. With only three sampling days per condition, the study did not establish a consistent reduction in airborne or surface viral contamination associated with lid use. Future studies should evaluate lids redesigned with workers alongside complementary measures addressing ventilation, hygiene, and clean water and waste management to reduce occupational exposure.

title: Structure-function analyses of the O<sub>2</sub>-dependent dimer-monomer transition in the FNR transcription factor.
abstract: About 2,5 billion years ago, oxygenic photosynthesis favored the evolution of gene expression regulatory strategies to respire atmospheric O2 in many anaerobic organisms. One such strategy was the evolution of the Fumarate Nitrate Reduction (FNR) regulator from a cAMP-binding transcription factor. The activity of FNR is regulated by a [Fe4S4] cluster-dependent dimer-monomer transition. The dimeric FNR responds to O2 through cluster degradation, which causes monomerization and loss of binding to its palindromic DNA receptor sites. Despite extensive structural and functional characterization, the molecular mechanism underlying signal transmission from the cluster to the DNA-binding domain and the dimer interface remains unclear. Here, we used a series of specific variants to explore this process both functionally, through stopped-flow and in vivo activity tests, and structurally, by exposing FNR crystals to O2 and three-dimensionally determining its effects. The emerging picture consists of three clearly interconnected major steps: cluster degradation, breaking of two intermolecular salt bridges, and bending and separation of the two dimerization α-helices. We also performed a preliminary analysis of FNRs belonging to different bacterial classes and concluded that their variable cysteine-based cluster coordination motifs might influence signal transmission.
journal: Journal of biological inorganic chemistry : JBIC : a publication of the Society of Biological Inorganic Chemistry
authors: de Rosny E, Volbeda A, Amara P, Rohac R, Darnault C, Chenavier F, Fontecilla-Camps JC.

title: The changing epidemiology of multidrug-resistant bacteria in hospitals: from high-risk clones to clinical impact.
abstract: Multidrug-resistant bacteria (MDRB) have become a major challenge for healthcare systems, representing a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections worldwide. The hospital environment provides ideal conditions for the emergence and dissemination of these microorganisms due to intensive antimicrobial use, the concentration of vulnerable patients, frequent invasive procedures, and opportunities for cross-transmission. The epidemiology of MDRB is dynamic and varies according to geographic region, healthcare practices, and local antimicrobial selective pressure. This review briefly summarizes the current epidemiology of MDRB in hospital settings, focusing on the ESKAPE pathogens. Special attention is given to the emergence and international dissemination of the so-called high-risk clones, which have played a central role in the global spread of antimicrobial resistance. The review also addresses the principal epidemiological risk factors, transmission routes, the role of environmental reservoirs and colonized patients, and the contribution of intensive care units as major amplification points for MDRB transmission and maintenance. Moreover, infections caused by MDRB are associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and higher healthcare costs. Continuous surveillance, rapid microbiological diagnosis, infection prevention and control measures, and antimicrobial stewardship programs remain essential to limit their spread and clinical impact. New genomic surveillance approaches are improving our understanding of transmission dynamics and supporting more potentially effective control strategies.
journal: Revista espanola de quimioterapia : publicacion oficial de la Sociedad Espanola de Quimioterapia
authors: Gijón-Cordero D, Ruiz-Garbajosa P, Cantón R.

title: Gut microbiota, immune cell traits, and infectious mononucleosis: a two-sample mendelian randomization and mediation analysis.
abstract: Infectious mononucleosis (IM) is an acute disease caused by the Epstein-Barr virus. This study assessed the causal association between the gut microbiota (GM) and IM and how the immune cells are mediators of this process through Mendelian randomization (MR). Two-step, two-sample MR was used to test the overall causal impact of GM on IM, the impact of GM on 731 immune cell characteristics, and the indirect effect of GM on IM. GM summary statistics (207 taxa, 7,738 Dutch participants), immune cell genome-wide association studies (GWAS, 3,757 Sardinians), and IM data (3,838 cases/486,087 controls, FinnGen R12) were used. P10 were used as the criteria in selecting instrumental variables. Bidirectionality MR and mediation MR with 1000 bootstrap replications were done to determine reverse causality and proportional mediation effects. MR analysis revealed 12 GM taxa with protective effects against IM and three taxa associated with an increased risk of IM. G__Lachnospiraceae_noname increased IM, and o__Burkholderiales.f__Oxalobacteraceae and g__Oxalobacter_formigenes had protective effects. IM had no impact on GM composition, and 22 immune cell characteristics were causally associated with IM with 10 risk-enhancing and 12 protective traits. The increased absolute count of hematopoietic stem cells (HSC AC) mediated 10.4% and the reduced percentage of CM CD8br %CD8br mediated -13.3% of the protective effect of o__Burkholderiales.f__Oxalobacteraceae. The results offer an important piece of information on microbial and immunologic targets of IM prevention.
journal: Brazilian journal of medical and biological research = Revista brasileira de pesquisas medicas e biologicas
authors: Wu G, Wang M, Si Y, Wang X, Li H, Wang L, Wang R.

title: Therapeutic and Prophylactic Agents for Viral Diseases: Current Status, Challenges, and Future Prospects.
abstract: Viral diseases remain a major global health challenge despite substantial advances in vaccination, antiviral therapeutics, and public-health interventions. However, current antiviral strategies are still constrained by important gaps, including rapid viral evolution, limited broad-spectrum efficacy, immune escape, antiviral resistance, incomplete durability of protection, and inequitable global access to prevention and treatment. This review provides a comprehensive and integrated overview of contemporary antiviral prevention and therapeutic strategies, spanning vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, direct-acting antivirals, host-targeted therapies, immunomodulators, RNA-based therapeutics, gene-editing technologies, and cellular immunotherapies. We discuss the mechanistic foundations, clinical applications, pharmacologic considerations, and translational challenges associated with each modality across major human viral pathogens, including HIV, HBV, HCV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, Ebola virus, arboviruses, and herpesviruses. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging innovations such as long-acting prophylaxis, Fc-engineered monoclonal antibodies, nanoparticle and mucosal vaccine platforms, CRISPR-based antiviral systems, and broadly protective host-directed approaches designed to overcome resistance and enhance pandemic preparedness. In addition, we highlight the growing importance of real-time genomic surveillance and equitable global deployment strategies in shaping future antiviral responses, collectively underscoring that the next generation of antiviral medicine will depend on the convergence of universal immunization strategies, durable therapeutics, precision immune modulation, and rapidly deployable platform technologies capable of addressing both endemic and emerging viral threats.
authors: Khan S, Nisar A, Li X, Yu H, Qadeer A, Mehmood SA, Lamraoui I, Liu S, Zhu L, Deng X, Kong B, Zhong K, Xia Z.

title: CRISPR Technology: From Bench to Bedside Applications.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas genome editing represents one of the most transformative advances in modern molecular biology, enabling programmable site-specific genetic modification that has revolutionized functional genomics and precision therapeutic development. Beyond canonical Cas9 nucleases, the CRISPR toolkit has diversified into precision base editors, prime editors, CRISPR-associated transposases, and Cas12/Cas13 RNA-targeting effectors, each with distinct mechanistic properties. Clinically, ex vivo CRISPR therapies for hemoglobinopathies have secured regulatory approval, while base editing, prime editing, and in vivo Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T candidates are advancing through trials for a broad spectrum of hematologic, oncologic, and rare genetic disorders. However, existing reviews largely address technical innovation or clinical translation in isolation, lacking a holistic, up-to-date synthesis of the full bench-to-bedside trajectory of CRISPR technology. This review systematically dissects the molecular mechanisms, advantages, and limitations of core CRISPR editing platforms; summarizes pivotal clinical data across hemoglobinopathies, CAR-T immunotherapy, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cardiometabolic diseases and rare monogenic diseases; evaluates delivery systems including lipid nanoparticles and viral vectors; and discusses key translational barriers such as off-target genotoxicity and immunogenicity alongside emerging optimization strategies. This work provides a holistic bench-to-bedside framework for CRISPR research, offering critical insights to advance next-generation precision genetic medicine.

title: The synthetic biology frontier: engineered oncolytic viruses and viral vectors for next-generation cancer therapy and gene delivery.
abstract: Viruses are no longer used merely as naturally occurring tools for gene transfer or as blunt cytolytic agents. Researchers are rewriting their genomes, capsids, tropisms, regulatory elements, and payloads to create therapeutic systems that sense disease, execute conditional programs, and remodel pathological tissue. In oncology, engineered oncolytic viruses (OVs) can combine tumor-selective replication with immunogenic cell death, antigen release, and local immune stimulation. In parallel, viral-vector engineering, particularly AAV and LVs, is addressing central limitations of gene delivery: the prevalence of pre-existing neutralizing antibodies, the difficulty of systemic administration and repeat dosing (AAV), and the manufacturing bottleneck of ex vivo cell therapies (LV). The clinical record is encouraging but uneven: T-VEC has shown that an engineered herpes simplex virus can improve durable responses in selected melanoma lesions, while G47Δ/teserpaturev and newer armed HSV platforms provide evidence of feasibility, safety, and occasional durable responses in difficult solid tumors. Lentiviral vector-based in vivo CAR-T cell generation, exemplified by KLN-1010/inMMyCAR and related first-in-human programs, signals a paradigm shift away from ex vivo manufacturing. However, the broader field has not converted its large preclinical literature into a proportional number of clinically meaningful, systemically deployable medicines. The main bottlenecks remain delivery, tumor heterogeneity, immune clearance, suboptimal pharmacodynamic biomarkers, manufacturing complexity, resistance, and the difficulty of proving benefit for products with delayed or immunologically mediated effects. This review examines the synthetic biology toolkit for programmable viral therapeutics through a unified engineering framework that integrates OVs, AAV, and LVs by design principle rather than by vector class. We discuss tumor-selective promoters, microRNA detargeting, retargeted capsids and ligands, attenuation, genome-scale assembly, immune-stimulatory payloads, bispecific and trispecific engagers, logic-gated circuits, safety switches, serodivergent AAV capsids, biomimetic cloaking, cell carriers, biomaterial delivery systems, and in vivo CAR-T generation. Our central thesis is that the next generation of viral medicines will be selected not by the most elaborate genome, but by the most coherent alignment of five measurable success factors: tumor selectivity, immune remodeling, delivery and biodistribution, controllable safety, and manufacturability. The emerging paradigm is therefore programmable viral therapeutics: context-sensitive biological medicines designed to operate within the constraints of human tumors and human immunity.
authors: Alsharedeh RH, Aljabali AAA, Obeid MA, Alqudah A, Gammoh O, Qnais E, Mishra V, Mishra Y, El-Tanani M.

title: Synthetic Community Driven by a Keystone Rhizosphere Bacterium Suppresses Whitefly-Mediated Begomovirus Transmission via the Jasmonate Signaling Pathway in Tomato.
abstract: Tomato production is threatened by the combined stress of whiteflies and the whitefly-transmitted Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV). Although the rhizosphere microbiome plays a critical role in plant defense, the rational assembly strategy and underlying mechanisms of a synthetic microbial community (SynCom) targeting this insect-virus complex remain unclear. Here, leveraging the beneficial soil legacy induced by Beauveria bassiana, we constructed an eight-strain synthetic community through multi-omics analysis, soil incubation, and root exudate chemotaxis assays. One-strain knockout experiments confirmed that strain N2 is the keystone species driving the biocontrol function. Through supernatant cross-culture assays, we further refined this consortium into an optimized synthetic community (OptSynM) consisting of the single keystone strain and four helper strains. Bioassays demonstrated that OptSynM significantly reduced whitefly fitness and suppressed TYLCV accumulation in tomato plants. Within the consortium, the helper strains enhanced the rhizosphere colonization of N2 by promoting its growth and biofilm formation. Mechanistically, OptSynM activated host systemic immunity via the jasmonic acid signaling pathway. Furthermore, OptSynM maintained robust biocontrol efficacy in pot trials conducted with natural agricultural soil. Our findings highlight the practical promise of microbiome-based interventions and provide a strategic framework for using synthetic microbial communities to facilitate sustainable agricultural practices.
authors: Zhao J, Wang Y, Yan G, Chen H, Xie Y, Wang W, Liu H.

title: Reduced methoxine formation by a sulfhydrylase variant identified through adaptive laboratory evolution of engineered Methylorubrum extorquens.
abstract: Streamlining metabolic pathways in microbes is a key strategy in metabolic engineering, often intended to channel evolution toward predictable outcomes. Here, Methylorubrum extorquens PA1 was rationally engineered by deleting redundant formate dehydrogenase operons (fdh234) to focus adaptive laboratory evolution on the remaining formate oxidation step under methanol stress. Genome sequencing identified a MetY-1 Y57D substitution in all five endpoint isolates from one evolving population, while the retained formate dehydrogenase operon carried no detected mutation. In vitro biochemical assays with purified MetY-1 showed that Y57D shifted the methoxine dose-response relative to the wild-type enzyme; at 5% (v/v) methanol the wild-type enzyme accumulated 0.386 ± 0.085 µM methoxine, whereas methoxine remained below the 0.025 µM detection limit for Y57D. A homocysteine-equivalent thiol signal, measured with Ellman reagent, remained detectable for both enzymes under the tested conditions. These results support a fine-tuning model for the product specificity of MetY-1 under methanol. The findings identify this specificity as a candidate point at which methanol toxicity may be mitigated; the contribution of the Y57D substitution to cellular growth was not tested here.
authors: Lee GM, Song DU, Ryu H, Kim J, Park S, Lee H, Kim D.

title: Characterization of EHV-1 viral genes at the respiratory tract using a tracheal explant culture model.
abstract: Equine herpesvirus 1 is the cause of respiratory disease, abortions, and equine herpesvirus myeloencephalopathy (EHM) in horse populations worldwide. Current vaccines do not prevent EHM. Several viral genes have been implicated in systemic dissemination and viral transfer to the CNS, but their roles during early respiratory events remain unclear. This study employed an equine tracheal explant culture model to characterize the role of selected EHV-1 genes in viral replication, infectivity, and innate immune activation during early respiratory infection. Tracheal explants were collected from respiratory healthy horses and inoculated with EHV-1 Ab4 WT or EHV-1 Ab4 recombinant viruses containing deletions or substitutions in genes involved in neuropathogenesis. Viral infection was evaluated using complementary approaches including immunohistochemistry, quantitative PCR, TCID₅₀ assays, and RT-qPCR analysis of innate immune genes. Deletion of ORF1 resulted in increased viral antigen detection, elevated viral DNA levels, enhanced production of infectious virus, and induction of innate immune markers (TLR3, IRF7, IRF9, CXCL9, CXCL10, CCL2, IL-6) supporting the role of ORF1 in modulating epithelial immune responses during early infection. Deletion of ORF2 increased antigen detection and showed limited regulation of chemokines (CXCL9, CCL5). Deletion of the gI-gE heterodimer reduced infectious virus production despite limited effects on viral genome presence, while increasing the expression of TLR3, IRF7, and CXCL9, highlighting its importance in cell-cell spread at the respiratory epithelium. Additionally, gB4, gD4, and the N752 variant exhibited WT-like replication with only subtle immune effects. Collectively, these findings provide insight into viral determinants that shape early epithelial infection and may influence downstream disease outcomes.
authors: Vázquez GB, Giessler KS, Sharma S, Osterrieder N, Kiupel M, Azab W, Hussey GS.

title: Visual Detection of Foodborne Viruses in Leafy Greens Using an AsCas12f-Split-G-Quadruplex Sensor.
abstract: Foodborne viruses are responsible for a substantial burden of disease worldwide, with fresh produce serving as the most abundant vehicle for transmission. However, rapid detection in solid produce, such as leafy greens, remains underdeveloped, as conventional methods often require labor-intensive sample preparation and specialized instrumentation. Herein, we present a colorimetric CRISPR-split-G4 biosensor for rapid viral surveillance in leafy greens that combines reverse transcription recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-RPA), AsCas12f-mediated trans-cleavage, and a modular split-G-quadruplex (split-G4) reporter system. In this system, target recognition activates the trans-cleavage activity of AsCas12f, resulting in degradation of a blocker strand and subsequent assembly of a catalytically active G4-hemin DNAzyme that generates a visible signal easily detectable by the naked eye. Using norovirus as a model pathogen, the platform exhibited high analytical sensitivity and specificity, enabling reliable detection of viral particles with minimal instrumentation. To evaluate practical applicability, the assay was coupled with a simplified leaf-disk extraction workflow and successfully applied to contaminated romaine lettuce and baby spinach samples without requiring viral nucleic acid purification. The platform achieved detection limits of 1000 and 5000 viral copies per 100 mg of romaine lettuce and spinach tissue, respectively. From sample processing to visual readout, the entire assay was completed in approximately 2 h. By integrating isothermal amplification, CRISPR-based target recognition, and instrument-free signal generation into a streamlined workflow, this strategy provides a promising platform for decentralized food safety monitoring and establishes a flexible framework for the on-site detection of viral pathogens in complex food matrices.
authors: Kasputis T, Landivar M, Yuan L, Wright RC, Zhang C, Chen J.

title: Host and anatomical filters prevent microbiome convergence in avian scavengers.
abstract: How host-associated microbiomes assemble under intense environmental microbial exposure remains a central question in microbial ecology. Vultures represent a unique natural system because these species differ markedly in feeding ecology and carcass use. We characterized bacterial communities across four anatomical niches (facial, buccal, tracheal, and cloacal) in 155 individuals spanning all four European obligate vulture species (subfamily Gypaetinae: Gypaetus barbatus, Neophron percnopterus, and Aegypiinae: Aegypius monachus and Gyps fulvus) and the facultative scavenger Milvus milvus. Microbiome composition was jointly structured by host species and anatomical niche, with host identity explaining more variation than anatomical compartment and a significant interaction indicating that interspecific differentiation depended on body site. Each niche supported distinct bacterial assemblages and core microbiomes: Cloacal communities were enriched in anaerobic gut-associated taxa, whereas facial and tracheal communities contained more environmental and respiratory-associated bacteria. Host-specific taxonomic signatures persisted within anatomical niches despite recurrent exposure to the same carrion-associated microbial pool. Age further influenced community composition, whereas sex had little detectable effect. The facultative scavenger showed the same broad anatomical compartmentalization observed in obligate scavengers, although taxonomic signatures differed among species. Thus, sustained exposure to a shared, microbially rich resource was insufficient to produce a common scavenger microbiome. Instead, microbiome assembly reflected hierarchical filtering by host identity, anatomical environment, and ontogeny. These findings distinguish microbial exposure from microbial persistence, establishing avian scavengers as a natural model for understanding how host-associated communities remain differentiated, despite recurrent exposure to shared environmental microbial reservoirs across ecological and anatomical scales in vertebrate hosts.
authors: Margalida A, Castellano-Hinojosa A, Oliva-Vidal P, Boutin S, María Martínez J, Braun M, Sauer-Gürth H, Schulze-Hagen K, Wink M.

title: Beyond association: pathogenesis models reveal ecological drivers of vaginal dysbiosis.
abstract: Despite its critical importance to health, our understanding of the vaginal microbiome lags far behind other mucosal sites, reflecting both the distinct biology of the human vaginal microenvironment and the historic neglect of women's reproductive health in biomedical research. Recent investment in this area, coupled with the widespread use of high-throughput omics technologies, has greatly expanded our understanding of vaginal microbiota states and their associations with health and disease. However, associative studies that correlate community composition with clinical outcomes are limited in their ability to define causal, modifiable host-microbe relationships that support a protective microbiota. Consequently, broad probiotic strategies based on descriptive findings show limited success in restoring lasting homeostasis in the female reproductive tract. Murine infection models provide tractable systems for identifying evolutionarily conserved physiological processes that influence microbial growth. Here, we highlight studies across pathogenesis fields that leverage murine models to identify ecological factors controlling infection susceptibility in the vaginal microenvironment. Rather than treating pathogen colonization as an endpoint alone, we emphasize how genetically tractable microbes reveal the resources, barriers, and immune responses mediating microbial persistence, ascension, and inflammation. Where possible, we integrate these findings with clinical observations to assess their relevance to human reproductive health. Together, these studies illustrate how imperfect but tractable models reveal causal drivers of vaginal dysbiosis in women and help ground large-scale associative studies in a more clinically relevant way.
authors: Radlinski LC, Bäumler AJ.

title: Reducing bacterial resistance evolution through antimicrobial peptide modifications.
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional antibiotics, yet bacteria can evolve resistance toward them through mechanisms that are poorly understood. Here, we selected a well-characterized antimicrobial peptide, melittin, as a model peptide that was shown to induce high levels of resistance in the human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus. We hypothesize that the physicochemical properties of AMPs might play a role in resistance development. To explore this hypothesis, we used computational approaches to design melittin derivatives with diverse physicochemical characteristics. A data set of 191 melittin-derived sequences (8-26 amino acids long) was analyzed to identify representative peptides spanning diverse physicochemical clusters. Selected peptides were synthesized and tested in an experimental evolution assay. Resistance dynamics, cross-resistance patterns, and cytotoxicity were evaluated in parallel. Full-length melittin with an amide or carboxylic acid C' terminus and highly hydrophobic derivatives [e.g., Mel(2-22)] showed high resistance occurrence, whereas Mel(5-24), a truncated variant, maintained antimicrobial activity while eliciting minimal resistance development. Whole-genome sequencing of endpoint populations revealed that melittin-evolved strains accumulated convergent mutations most prominently in pmtR, whereas Mel(5-24)-evolved populations converged only on ydbT, with no mutations in canonical resistance loci, suggesting fewer accessible adaptive pathways against the truncated peptide. Our results indicate that peptide hydrophobicity and chain length correlated with resistance fold change, whereas coil propensity showed a negative correlation. Notably, Mel(5-24) displayed reduced cross-resistance to other peptides and lower cytotoxicity toward mammalian cells than melittin, suggesting a broader therapeutic window. Overall, our findings indicate that tuning peptide hydrophobicity and chain length along with structural propensity can mitigate the evolutionary pressure driving resistance while maintaining antibacterial potency. Rational modulation of such physicochemical properties may provide a practical route for designing AMPs with improved selectivity and lower resistance potential.
authors: Cohen Tzemach H, Maron B, Malach E, Hayouka Z.

title: The protection of chronic cerebral ischemia by Hua-Feng-Dan involves the modulation of hippocampal transcriptome and gut dysbiosis.
abstract: The protective effects of Hua-Feng-Dan recipes against chronic cerebral hypoperfusion-induced ischemia were examined; RNA-seq and 16 S-rRNA-seq were used to explore the molecular mechanisms. Male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent unilateral common carotid artery ligation surgery to establish chronic cerebral hypoperfusion (CCH) models. Then, the CCH rats were treated with various Hua-Feng-Dan recipes in diet for 20 days. Finally, behavioral tests were performed, followed by histopathology. Hippocampal RNA was isolated for RNA-seq and RT-qPCR analyses; Colon bacterial DNA was isolated for 16 S rRNA-seq and bioinformatics. The CCH rats exhibited cognition deficits evidenced by Behavioral tests. The neurons in the hippocampus CA1 area were damaged. Hua-Feng-Dan recipes as Reduced_H (0.5 g/kg), Original, and Nonferment improved behavioral deficits and morphological changes, while Reduced_L (0.25 g/kg) was ineffective. RNA-seq revealed distinct gene expression pattern among groups. Ingenuity pathway analysis of differentially expressed genes revealed Hua-Feng-Dan recipes ameliorated Canonical pathways involved in cytosolic Ca2+ overload, disruption of IGF homeostasis and Neutrophil degranulation; attenuated CCH-activated Upstream regulators such as IL1B, IL6, TNF, IGF1, and glucose metabolism. CCH-decreased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio were recovered by Hua-Feng-Dan recipes. CCH-increased Prevotellaceae and decreased Lachnospiraceae were attenuated; CCH-increased ASV1 and decreased ASV39 were brought to normal after Hua-Feng-Dan treatments. Similar to the efficacy against CCH, Reduced_L was ineffective in transcriptome and gut microbiota analysis. Hua-Feng-Dan recipes (Reduced_H, Original, and Nonferment) are effective against CCH-induced chronic cerebral ischemia, while Reduced_L was ineffective. The mechanisms of the protection are related to transcriptome regulation in the hippocampus, and modulation of CCH-disrupted gut dysbiosis.
authors: Liu B, Huang B, Xu Y, Liu J.

title: Impacts of algal community structure on algae-derived phosphorus concentrations in Lake Taihu, China, from 2021 to 2025
abstract: Abstract    Phosphorus control remains a critical challenge for managing eutrophication in Lake Taihu, yet quantitative assessments of algae-derived phosphorus (ADP) and its response to community shifts remain scarce. Based on monthly data from 20 entire-lake stations during 2021–2025 and an experimentally determined cellular phosphorus content for  Microcystis  spp. (1.46×10  − 10  mg/cell), we estimated cell-specific phosphorus for 113 algal species by cell-volume conversion and quantified ADP and phylum-level contributions. Annual mean total algal density decreased from 1.2×10  8  cells/L in 2021 to 6.9×10  7  cells/L in 2025, with marked turnover:  Microcystis  spp. fell from 83.6% to 32.4% of total density, while diatoms, cryptophytes and chlorophytes rose significantly. Annual mean ADP ranged from 0.015 to 0.022 mg/L (33.4% of TP) and was dominated by cyanobacteria, diatoms and chlorophytes. Cyanobacteria supplied over 65% of ADP during 2021–2022, declining markedly after 2023, while diatom and chlorophyte contributions rose. Notably, an algal rebound in December 2024 (density up 79.3% year-on-year) coincided with a 25.0% ADP decrease, because a large gain in small-celled cyanobacteria was outweighed by a much smaller loss of large-celled diatoms containing seven to eight times more phosphorus per cell. These findings show that ADP is a key component of TP in Lake Taihu and is governed by two mechanistically distinct controls: algal biomass (quantity) and the community-weighted cell-specific phosphorus content set by the assemblage cell-size structure (quality), which can act in opposite directions. Algal community structure thus acts as an active regulator of lake phosphorus and must be considered alongside algal density in phosphorus management.
authors: Yang Z, Zhu B, Zhang J, Dai X, Zhang H, Xu Y, Song T, Zhuang Y.

title: Long-term organic fertilizer amendment improves citrus yield and quality in calcareous soil mainly by shaping the microbiome and mobilizing soil phosphorus
abstract: Abstract    Background and aims  Citrus, the largest fruit globally, often encounters nutritional imbalances, notably phosphorus (P) deficiency, when cultivated in calcareous soil. Although organic fertilizers outperform inorganic alternatives in citrus production, their specific impacts and the microbiome’s role in calcareous soil remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of rapeseed cakes (RC) and cow manure (CM) on citrus plant-soil performance and their correlations with microbiome composition and functional profiles. Methods  We conducted a 5-year long-term positioning field experiment on citrus under calcareous soil conditions. Field experiments combined with amplicon and metagenome sequencing were employed to analyze differences in plant-soil performance and rhizosphere microbiome traits under RC and CM treatments. Isolation-culture verification was further performed to validate the function of key differential microorganisms. Results  RC and CM supplementation enhanced fruit yield and quality while facilitating P utilization in calcareous soil, with CM showing a better improvement effect. Both organic fertilizers induced significant alterations in rhizosphere microbiome composition and function. The genus  Cupriavidus  was significantly enriched in rhizosphere under organic fertilizer treatments. Isolation-culture verification confirmed it enhanced soil P availability by secreting organic acids, alkaline phosphatases and other enzymes, serving as plant-growth-promoting rhizobacteria for citrus. Conclusion  Our findings clarify the effects of rapeseed cakes and cow manure on citrus growth and soil P activation in calcareous soil, and reveal the key role of the rhizosphere microbiome represented by  Cupriavidus  in this process. This study advances our understanding of microbiome-mediated improvement of citrus growth and P utilization via organic fertilizer application.
authors: gong k, wang h, you c, zheng c, Qian W, Pang Y, yang w, yin h, Li q, zeng y, peng l, wang n, Chun C.

title: Epigenetic and Post-Transcriptional Regulation of Autophagy in Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), principally comprising Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), encompasses chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disorders of the gastrointestinal tract. Genome-wide association studies have identified hundreds of susceptibility loci associated with IBD. Recent studies have highlighted the critical importance of autophagy in maintaining intestinal epithelial homeostasis, regulating host-microbiota interactions, coordinating immune responses and restricting microbial pathogens. Furthermore, emerging evidence indicates that classical epigenetic mechanisms and post-transcriptional regulators may influence autophagy-related pathways in IBD and thereby shape intestinal inflammatory responses. This review critically evaluates current evidence linking epigenetic and post-transcriptional regulation to autophagy in IBD, distinguishes established mechanisms from indirect associations and discusses their mechanistic and translational implications.
authors: Liu Y, Jiang W, Zhou J, Xun F, Li H, Li Y, Zhang J, Qian Y, Wang H.

title: Genetic mechanisms underlying feeding behaviour in silkworm larvae.
abstract: The silkworm, an economically important insect that feeds almost exclusively on mulberry leaves, has emerged as a pivotal model for understanding the genetic basis of feeding behaviour in herbivorous specialists. Recent advances have begun to unravel the complex molecular networks that enable efficient host plant recognition, nutrient intake and metabolic adaptation. Feeding behaviour in silkworm larvae is governed by a multi-layered regulatory system that coordinates peripheral detection, internal organ sensing and neuroendocrine regulation. Key players include gustatory and odorant receptors, odorant-binding proteins, odorant-degrading enzymes, neuropeptides and transcription factors, all functioning in a coordinated, tissue-specific manner. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of these genetic mechanisms within an integrative framework that links peripheral chemosensation and internal organ sensing to neuropeptide regulation and ultimately to behavioural output. We further discuss how comparative and evolutionary perspectives illuminate the genomic and adaptive evolution of mulberry specialization. We also consider emerging regulatory layers, including epigenetic modifications and the microbiota-gut-brain axis, which have been implicated in feeding behaviour in other insects but remain largely unexplored in the silkworm. Finally, we highlight emerging technologies that will advance research in this field, providing a foundation for improving artificial diet-based sericulture.
authors: Jiang D, Tong X, Dai F, Zou Y.

title: Unraveling the Genetic Architecture of Sclerotinia Basal Stalk Rot Resistance in Cultivated Sunflower Through Genome-Wide Association Mapping.
abstract: Sclerotinia basal stalk rot (BSR), caused by the necrotrophic fungal pathogen Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, is an economically important disease of cultivated sunflower (Helianthus annuus L.). Resistance to BSR is quantitative and genetically complex, and although biparental mapping studies have identified genomic regions associated with resistance, knowledge of the broader genetic architecture of BSR resistance in diverse cultivated sunflower germplasm remains limited. In this study, genome-wide association studies were conducted to understand the genetic architecture of BSR resistance using two independent panels. The Sunflower Association Mapping (SAM) panel was evaluated under greenhouse conditions with two S. sclerotiorum isolates differing in aggressiveness, BN166 or NEB-274, using two disease traits: mean days to death and area under the mortality curve. An open-pollinated variety (OPV) panel was evaluated across four field environments after inoculation with isolate NEB-274 and scored for disease incidence. Genotyping datasets comprised 3.2 and 3.5 million single nucleotide polymorphisms for the SAM and OPV panels, respectively. The study identified 20 significant associations in the SAM panel and 7 in the OPV panel. No overlapping associations were detected between panels or isolates, indicating isolate- and environment-specific genetic architecture despite moderate positive correlations between isolates (r ≈ 0.74). Eight loci co-localized with previously reported BSR quantitative trait locus intervals. Candidate genes included a protein kinase at the strongest association, a receptor-like kinase, a glutathione S-transferase, and members of the WD40 repeat protein family detected in both panels. These findings provide genomic resources for marker-assisted selection and resistance breeding.
authors: Angidi S, McNellie JP, Henning S, Pasche JS, Hulke B, Underwood W.

title: Improving Talaromycosis Infection Diagnosis and Prognosis with Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing.
abstract: BackgroundEarly diagnosis and timely initiation of appropriate antifungal treatment are critical for improving the prognosis of talaromycosis infection. We aimed to test whether metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), versus conventional microbiological testing (CMT), improves talaromycosis diagnosis and management in HIV-negative patients via higher sensitivity and faster detection.MethodsWe retrospectively investigated the clinical data of patients with Talaromyces marneffei (T. marneffei) infection in six hospitals in Fujian, China, between July 2015 and June 2024. The diagnostic performance and clinical impact of mNGS were compared with those of CMT.ResultsSeventy-four patients were included, with 38 cases in the mNGS group and 36 cases for CMT group, based on the method that established the definitive diagnosis. The median duration from hospitalization to confirmed diagnosis was significantly shorter in the mNGS group than in the CMT group (5.0 vs 12.0 days, p p p = 0.033; 26.3% vs 5.56%, p = 0.025). The mNGS group has a trend of lower mortality compared with the CMT group (18.4% vs 38.9%, p = 0.072). In addition, the length of stay was significantly shorter in the mNGS group than in the CMT group (14.5 days vs 21.0 days, p = 0.007).ConclusionmNGS facilitates rapid diagnosis and improves administration of targeted antimicrobial therapy, thus improving the prognosis of T. marneffei infection. The clinical utility of mNGS for talaromycosis in at-risk populations should be investigated in prospective and large studies.
authors: Zhang L, He X, Xu L, Xiao J, Lin J, Song B, Chen L, Chen G, Liu K.

title: Aldehyde-dependent β-aminocarbonyl chitosan/Ag composites: Linking chemical structure, silver loading, and antibacterial performance.
abstract: In this study, β-aminocarbonyl chitosan (BACC) derivatives were synthesized through Mannich modification using different aldehyde precursors and subsequently incorporated with Ag to investigate the relationship between chemical structure, Ag loading, and antibacterial performance. The resulting materials were characterized by FTIR and UV-Vis spectroscopy, while Ag incorporation was quantitatively determined using atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS). Antibacterial activity was evaluated against bacteria associated with fresh chicken meat using the total plate count (TPC) method at concentrations of 1000 and 2500 ppm after 0, 3, and 7 days of refrigerated storage. FTIR analysis indicated interactions of Ag species with nitrogen- and oxygen-containing functional groups, while the evolution of surface plasmon resonance bands supported the formation and stabilization of Ag species. AAS revealed structure-dependent Ag loading, with values of 1.25%, 0.93%, 0.80%, 0.73%, and 0.53% for BACC-Sa/Ag, BACC-OV/Ag, BACC-F/Ag, Ch/Ag, and BACC-P/Ag, respectively. BACC-Sa/Ag achieved the highest bacterial reduction of 96.39 ± 0.39% at 2500 ppm after 7 days, while BACC-F/Ag reached 96.27 ± 0.59% under the same conditions. Notably, BACC-P/Ag achieved 95.40 ± 0.42% reduction after 3 days at 1000 ppm despite having the lowest Ag loading. These results demonstrate that antibacterial performance was governed by the combined effects of aldehyde-derived functionality, Ag incorporation, concentration, and storage time rather than Ag loading alone. The results demonstrated their potential to suppress microbial growth, highlighting the applicability of these materials as candidates for further development in antibacterial food-preservation systems. Nevertheless, additional investigations involving film fabrication, silver-ion release, migration, and safety assessments are necessary before their suitability for food-contact packaging applications can be established.
authors: Ismiyarto, Shafika FN, Ressa FK, Wahyuni AP, Amanah PN, Ngadiwiyana, Sarjono PR, Bajracharya GB, Muhtar H.

title: Ecological commissioning links microbial succession to treatment stabilization during managed aquifer recharge.
abstract: Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) systems require ecological as well as hydraulic commissioning, yet when attached microbial communities become spatially organized and associated with stable treatment remains unresolved. We operated duplicate 10 m sand-column trains supplied with River Lek water for 12 months and tracked water quality and bacterial communities monthly at 1, 5, and 10 m and in the effluent. Removal trajectories for dissolved organic carbon, Fe²⁺, Mn²⁺, NH₄⁺, and NO₂⁻ and bacterial diversity showed little sustained directional change after approximately 5 months, while distance-associated communities became evident after month 6. At month 12, ASVs shared with 10 m sand accounted for 69.7% of effluent sequence abundance. Only 11.6% of shared influent-sand sequence abundance was consistent with neutral expectations, whereas sand-to-effluent neutral-model fit increased to R² = 0.60. We define this coordinated transition as ecological commissioning: a months-long process in which environmental selection organizes attached communities, spatial zones emerge, and terminal-zone dispersal increasingly shapes produced-water microbiology. Although timing is system specific, this framework identifies start-up and terminal aquifer zones as targets for MAR treatment verification and biological water-quality management.
authors: Zhai Y, Wang X, van der Meer W, van Loosdrecht MCM, Zhu Y, Qiu Q, Liu G, Pabst M.

title: SiTIFY9 enhances salt stress tolerance and promotes early flowering in foxtail millet.
abstract: Soil salinity severely limits plant growth and productivity through osmotic stress, ion toxicity, and excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Although TIFY proteins regulate plant responses to environmental stresses, their roles in salt tolerance in foxtail millet (Setaria italica) remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized SiTIFY9 (Seita.9G51810) through phylogenetic analysis, expression profiling, subcellular localization, transcriptional activation assays, stable overexpression, physiological measurements, and transcriptome sequencing. SiTIFY9 clustered with rice OsTIFY11a/OsJAZ9, localized predominantly to the nucleus, and exhibited no autonomous transcriptional activation activity in yeast. Under salt stress, SiTIFY9-overexpressing plants showed reduced hydrogen peroxide and malondialdehyde accumulation, increased catalase and peroxidase activities, and enhanced proline accumulation compared with wild-type plants. Overexpression also restricted Na+ accumulation, promoted K+ retention, and increased the K+/Na+ ratio, indicating improved ionic homeostasis. Transcriptome analysis revealed extensive transcriptional changes associated with stress responses, redox regulation, ion transport, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, and secondary metabolism. RT-qPCR further confirmed altered expression of genes involved in ion transport, osmoprotection, transcriptional regulation, and stress defense. Independently, SiTIFY9-overexpressing plants flowered 14-16 days earlier than wild-type plants under non-saline conditions, suggesting an additional role in flowering-time regulation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that SiTIFY9 overexpression enhances salt tolerance by improving antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, and ionic homeostasis, accompanied by transcriptional reprogramming of stress-responsive pathways. Furthermore, its association with earlier flowering suggests a potential developmental function. This study identifies SiTIFY9 as a promising candidate for further investigation of salt-stress tolerance and flowering-time regulation in foxtail millet.
authors: Terfa GN, Hu L, He C, Fu Q, Nasim A, Su J, Pan W, Nie X.
