title: Integrative transcriptomic and in silico analysis identifies novel long non-coding RNAs associated with BCL6 and SPARC in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
abstract: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common and clinically heterogeneous subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, marked by extensive transcriptional dysregulation and variable therapeutic outcomes. While protein-coding alterations are well characterized, the regulatory role of the non-coding transcriptome remains incompletely defined. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) modulate gene expression through cis/trans transcriptional control, RNA-RNA interactions, and RNA-protein scaffolding. However, DLBCL-specific lncRNAs remain largely unexplored. We applied an integrative in silico framework using RNA-seq datasets from the Sequence Read Archive and The Cancer Genome Atlas, incorporating quality control, alignment, quantification, TPM normalization, differential expression, principal component analysis, multi-level filtering, cis-annotation, survival analysis, functional enrichment with STRING network construction, mutation profiling, RNA-RNA interaction prediction (IntaRNA), and RNA-protein interaction analysis (catRAPID) with structural modeling. With this approach we identified three previously uncharacterized lncRNAs, namely lnc-SPARC-2:3, lnc-FXYD2-1:5, and lnc-ADAMTS1-2:1. These consistently overexpressed lncRNAs in DLBCL were validated by semi-quantitative PCR. In silico thermodynamic modeling supported stable RNA-RNA duplex formation with neighboring mRNAs, and protein interaction analyses predicted high-confidence binding to BCL6 protein. These lncRNAs are predicted to participate in lncRNA-mediated attenuation of BCL6 and may disrupt germinal center regulatory programs, impair B-cell lineage commitment and promote microenvironment-dependent signaling, alongside enrichment of ECM proteoglycans indicative of stromal remodeling, accompanied by marked upregulation of SPARC mRNA. Correlation analyses across the SRA and TCGA cohorts supported the IntaRNA-predicted interactions of lnc-ADAMTS1-2:1-ADAMTS5, lnc-FXYD2-1:5-FXYD6, and lnc-SPARC-2:3-ATOX1, revealing consistent positive associations that remained supported after adjustment for cohort and stromal score. Notably, the observed survival trend for lnc-FXYD2-1:5 did not reach statistical significance; nevertheless, it is suggested as a candidate biomarker with potential prognostic relevance that merits further investigation in larger independent cohorts. Collectively, this study provides a systematic computational framework supported by experimental validation for the presence of the shortlisted lncRNAs. However, further experimental validation is required to establish their functional roles, which may support their investigation as potential therapeutic targets in future DLBCL studies.
authors: Arun SM, Roy U, Desai S, Choudhary B, Raghavan SC, Devaki NS.

title: Intrinsic replication advantage of a Hepatitis B Virus genotype C strain is independent of the basal core promoter A1762T/G1764A mutation.
abstract: This study aimed to isolate and characterize individual hepatitis B virus (HBV) strains from a patient co-infected with genotype B and C, and to directly compare their intrinsic replication capacities. HBV DNA was isolated from a chronic hepatitis B patient. Genotypes were determined by genotype-specific polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and full-length genomes were cloned. Two clones representing subgenotype B2 (c17) and C1 (c21) were selected, sequenced and transfected into HepG2 cells. Viral replication was assessed via Southern blot and quantitative PCR. The role of the common Adenine (A)1762Thymine (T/)Guanine (G)1764A mutation in the C1 clone was investigated by site-directed mutagenesis. As a result, the genotype C1 clone exhibited significantly higher replication capacity than the B2 clone. Counterintuitively, reverting the A1762T/G1764A mutation in the C1 clone to wild-type further enhanced its replication, indicating this mutation was not the primary driver of its high replicative fitness. In conclusion, HBV genotype C1 possesses a greater inherent replication capacity than B2, independent of the classic basal core promoter (BCP) mutation, providing a virological explanation for its association with severe disease outcomes in co-infection.
authors: Xiao Y, Chen X, Li Z, Lei S, Chen Z, Cai J, Cui X.

title: Cell-Cell Communication Network Analysis of Tertiary Lymphoid Structures in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer.
abstract: Tertiary Lymphoid Structures (TLS) are associated with a favorable prognosis in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC). However, the mechanisms governing their formation, particularly the existence of breast cancer subtype-specific critical cell communication networks, remain unclear. This study aims to systematically decipher the specific cellular interaction networks associated with TLS in TNBC and Estrogen Receptor-positive Breast Cancer (ER+ BC). Public spatial transcriptomics (TNBC: GSE210616; ER+ BC: 10x Genomics public Visium dataset) and single-cell transcriptomics (GSE176078) data were integrated to attribute TLS-associated genes to their cell-type origins and infer intercellular communication. TLS regions were independently identified by two pathologists based on H&E images (TNBC: 7 TLS; ER+ BC: 12 TLS), followed by differential expression analysis. Using single-cell data, a dual-criterion (expression rate ≥20% and average expression level ≥ upper quartile) was employed for cell-type expression attribution, with sensitivity analysis across thresholds. Cell-cell communication network inference and quantitative analysis were performed based on an expanded ligand-receptor database (CellTalkDB, 3,398 pairs), and the core findings were cross-validated using CellChat. TLS in TNBC exhibited a far more active transcriptional state compared to ER+ Breast Cancer (ER+ BC), with 198 vs 29 differentially expressed genes. Interaction network analysis revealed that in TNBC TLS, fibroblasts (cancer-associated fibroblasts, CAFs) constituted the dominant core signaling hub (net signal output strength: +458.7), whereas endothelial cells were the predominant net signal receiver (net output: -808.6). In contrast, TLS in ER+ BC were characterized by interactions predominantly involving fibroblasts (dominant output, +261.1) and plasma cells (dominant reception, -127.0). Cell-type expression attribution further confirmed that TLS-associated signals in TNBC predominantly originated from fibroblasts (70.3% of core TLS genes). Our intercellular communication analysis reveals a stark subtype-specific landscape: TLSs in TNBC are predominantly characterized by a fibroblast (CAF)-centered signaling hub, whereas TLS in ER+ BC features a fibroblast-plasma cell axis. The association between the TLS-related transcriptional signature and immune cytolytic activity was further supported in the independent The Cancer Genome Atlas breast cancer cohort (r = 0.747, P < 0.001). However, as these inferences are drawn from transcriptional correlations in public datasets, further mechanistic studies-such as ligand-receptor functional assays or in vivo perturbation models-are essential to determine whether this TNBC-specific hub actively contributes to TLS formation or merely reflects the local immune microenvironment. This study identifies a TNBC-specific fibroblast (CAF)-centered communication hub as a prominent feature of TLS-associated intercellular networks, offering prioritized candidate axes warranting further functional validation for potential immunotherapy development.
authors: Meng M, Li Y.

title: Structure-based binding pocket conservation analysis identifies 9-OH urolithin dehydroxylase candidates across phylogenetically diverse bacteria.
abstract: Urolithins are polyphenolic compounds produced by gut microbiota from dietary ellagitannins and ellagic acid, with urolithin A being the most bioactive and associated with a range of pharmaceutical activities like anti-aging and anti-inflammatory effects. Despite these benefits, the number of known urolithin A-producing bacteria and their corresponding enzymes is very limited. In this study, we combined conventional sequence-based homology search with structural modeling to identify novel bacteria potentially harboring 9-OH urolithin dehydroxylases, primarily characterized in the Enterocloster genus, that catalyze a key dehydroxylation step essential for urolithin A production. Using three Enterocloster references, a sequence database search coupled with subunit co-occurrence screening was performed. AlphaFold 3 was then employed to model the three-dimensional structures of the candidate multi-subunit complexes. Based on these models, comparative analysis was conducted to screen for candidate enzymes that share closely conserved three-dimensional structural characteristics and conserved core residue architectures within their active-site pockets. The resulting non-Enterocloster candidates, including Aromatoleum sp. and Dehalobacter restrictus, exhibited high predicted functional similarity to the reference enzymes based on conserved binding pocket architectures. This study demonstrates that binding pocket structural signatures help the identification of novel potential urolithin dehydroxylases and previously unrecognized urolithin A-producing bacteria.
authors: Piroozmand F, Kaushik R, Kawashima H, Yamaguchi T, Mizuguchi K, Mohammadipanah F, Re S.

title: Seasonal variation in the spatial distribution, community assembly, and associated factors of antibiotic resistance genes in tropical drinking water reservoirs of Hainan, China.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) have been widely investigated in temperate and subtropical reservoirs but remain poorly understood in tropical drinking-water reservoirs. We sampled four drinking-water reservoirs in Hainan during both winter and summer, integrating physicochemical, heavy-metal, and metagenomic data to investigate the diversity, spatiotemporal patterns, and assembly of ARGs, mobile genetic elements (MGEs), and microbial communities. ARG composition and community structure differed significantly by season and reservoir. Contig-based analysis identified ARG-MGE arrangements in diverse putative hosts; sul1 and qacEdelta1 co-occurred with integrases and transposases, demonstrating MGE co-localization. Null-model analysis indicated reservoir-specific ARG assembly in winter but predominantly stochastic assembly in summer, whereas microbial community assembly was deterministic in both seasons. Mantel and Spearman analyses showed seasonal variation in ARG relationships: stronger correlations with environmental factors in winter and more positive correlations with MGEs in summer. Summer co-occurrence networks were larger and more connected, with more positive ARG-MGE-microbial genus associations. Partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) showed positive MGE-ARG associations in both seasons, whereas microbial community composition was negatively associated with ARGs only in winter. These results characterize seasonal ARG variation and its associations with MGEs and microbial communities in tropical reservoirs, providing a baseline for monitoring regional drinking-water sources.
authors: Huang L, Chen B, Liu X, Guo Z, Zhang G, Li J, Fu Q.

title: Temperature-dependent regulation of persistence and virulence genes in Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1 on oak leaf lettuce and indications for root internalization.
abstract: Increasing evidence of Pseudomonas aeruginosa on fresh plant-based foods raises food safety concerns, particularly under changing environmental conditions. Temperature changes may affect plant microbiota and human pathogen presence on fresh produce. This study investigates the temperature-dependent gene expression of P. aeruginosa PAO1 on oak leaf lettuce as a model system and explores the potential for root internalization by P. aeruginosa PAO1. Therefore, temperature-dependent transcriptomic changes of P. aeruginosa PAO1 were assessed by analyzing differentially expressed genes following plant inoculation and incubation at 18 and 22 °C. Moreover, oak leaf lettuce was cultivated in soil inoculated with P. aeruginosa PAO1_sfGFP_UHH07, and internalization was analyzed using confocal laser scanning microscopy. Transcriptomic analyses showed that a moderate temperature increase shifted bacterial gene expression, with virulence-associated genes upregulated at 22 °C and persistence-associated genes predominating at 18 °C. Results provide preliminary evidence that P. aeruginosa PAO1 may internalize into the roots of oak leaf lettuce, whereas no GFP signal indicative of translocation into the leaves was detected. The findings indicate that temperature changes could influence the transcriptional emphasis on virulence- and persistence-associated genes of P. aeruginosa PAO1 present on oak leaf lettuce and provide a basis for further investigation under more complex environmental conditions.
authors: Griese J, Hoffmann T, Peal J, Weiss A.

title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain.
abstract: Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables the development of deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants.

title: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain.
abstract: Direct measurement of chromatin states together with transcription is essential for understanding how cell-type-specific regulatory programs are established and maintained in the adult human brain. Here, we present a large-scale single-cell multimodal atlas by jointly profiling the transcriptome with active (H3K27ac) or repressive (H3K27me3) histone modifications across 18 adult brain regions. We targeted over 750,000 nuclei spanning 160 cell types and integrated these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, 3D genome architecture, and spatial transcriptomes. This framework resolved chromatin states for over 500,000 candidate regulatory elements, identified enhancer-gene links and regulatory programs, revealed Polycomb-associated ultra-long-range contacts, and uncovered brainwide epigenomic heterogeneity. We further developed a sequence-to-function model to predict cell-type-specific effects of candidate neurological disease variants. Finally, comparative analyses across species reveal conservation in active regulatory programs but divergence in repressive programs. Together, this study provides a comprehensive epigenomic reference for interpreting regulatory principles and epigenetic memory underlying human brain organization and disease.

title: Multimodal single-cell epigenomic and 3D genome atlas of the human basal ganglia.
abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) underlie motor control, reward processing, and many neurological and psychiatric disorders, yet cell-type-resolved epigenomic and 3D genome maps of the human BG remain limited. Here, we present a multimodal single-cell atlas of DNA methylation (261,331 nuclei) and 3D chromatin conformation (229,286 nuclei) from eight subregions, harmonized under the BG consensus taxonomy and integrated with matched data across multiple regulatory layers. We identify millions of differentially methylated regions across cell types, enriched for distinct transcription factor motifs, and link them to disease-associated heritability. We characterize the POU6F2+ STR D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neuron (SPN) subtype, with concordant signatures across multiple modalities, and reveal region-specific methylation and contact gradients. Integrative gene regulatory networks (GRNs) predict cell-type-resolved enhancer-promoter interactions, nominating candidate regulatory mechanisms for Parkinson's disease (PD) risk variants at SNCA. Finally, multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) profiling combined with cross-species Patch-seq identifies a neuronal subtype, STR FS PTHLH-PVALB GABA, with electrophysiological differences across the striatal matrix-striosome (MS) boundary.

title: Taxonomic descriptions of Tessaracoccus zhenghani sp. nov., Tessaracoccus pujii sp. nov., Tessaracoccus luoxuelianae sp. nov. and Tessaracoccus yangjingae sp. nov.
abstract: Eight Gram-stain-positive, non-spore-forming, non-motile, oxidase-negative novel bacterial strains with oval- to rod-shaped morphology designated Y36ᵀ, Y1639, Z1128ᵀ, Y1544, Y1736ᵀ, W1776, G1721ᵀ and Y1940 were isolated from the in situ coal and coal mine dust matrices in Shanxi Province, PR China. Phylogenetic analysis of the 16S rRNA gene and 813 core genes revealed that these 8 strains belong to the genus Tessaracoccus. 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis revealed that strain Y36T exhibited the highest similarity to Tessaracoccus lubricantis KSS-17SeT (98.42%), while strains Z1128T, Y1736T and G1721T showed the highest similarities to Tessaracoccus aquimaris NSG39T (98.61%, 98.47% and 97.64%, respectively). Average nucleotide identity (ANI) and digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH) values between these four novel species and all members of the genus Tessaracoccus were below species thresholds (95-96% for ANI and 70% for dDDH). Anteiso-C15:0 was the predominant cellular fatty acid in all eight isolates. Summed feature 3 (C16:1ω7c/C16:1ω6c) was also a major component in strains Z1128ᵀ, Y1544, Y1736ᵀ, W1776, G1721ᵀ and Y1940. Strain Y1736ᵀ additionally contained anteiso-C17:1ω9c as a major fatty acid. All novel type strains had MK-9 (H4) as the sole respiratory quinone. The major polar lipids of strains Y36ᵀ and Y1736ᵀ were diphosphatidylglycerol and phosphatidylglycerol. Strains Z1128ᵀ and G1721ᵀ contained diphosphatidylglycerol, phosphatidylglycerol, phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylinositol mannoside as their major polar lipids. Strains Y36ᵀ and G1721ᵀ contained ribose as the sole cell-wall sugar. Strain Z1128ᵀ had ribose and glucose, while strain Y1736ᵀ harboured rhamnose, ribose and glucose as the major cell-wall sugars. The cell-wall peptidoglycan contained ʟʟ-diaminopimelic acid as the diagnostic diamino acid. Based on genotypic, phenotypic, phylogenetic and biochemical properties, the eight uncharacterized strains represent four novel species in the genus Tessaracoccus, for which the names Tessaracoccus zhenghani sp. nov. (type Y36T=GDMCC 1.5638T=KCTC 59558T), Tessaracoccus pujii sp. nov. (type strain Z1128T=GDMCC 1.5727T=KCTC 59595T), Tessaracoccus luoxuelianae sp. nov. (type strain Y1736T=GDMCC 1.5728T=KCTC 59596T) and Tessaracoccus yangjingae sp. nov. (type strain G1721T=GDMCC 1.5729T=KCTC 59594T) are proposed, respectively.
journal: International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology
authors: Gao F, Chen Y, He Y, Zhao L, Xie J, Du X, Yang Q, Liu T, Yang C, Kang Z, Du X, Pu J, Zheng H, Xu J, Dong K.

title: Brassinosteroid and Light Quality Synergistically Regulate Aroma Biosynthesis via the CmBES1-4-CmDof13 Module in Postharvest Oriental Melon (Cucumis melo).
abstract: Brassinosteroids and light quality regulate secondary metabolism in fruits, yet the synergistic control of volatile aroma biosynthesis in oriental melon (Cucumis melo var. makuwa) remains unclear. In this study, we used volatile metabolomics, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), and DNA Affinity Purification Sequencing (DAP-seq) methods to show that red light combined with brassinosteroids effectively increased total volatiles, particularly esters, at day 6 after harvest. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA) identified a module strongly associated with ester content, in which the brassinosteroid-responsive transcription factor CmBES1-4 co-occurred with CmDof13 and the downstream target genes CmLOX18 and CmAAT1. DAP-seq analysis revealed that CmBES1-4 bound E-box and BRRE motifs genome-wide, thereby directly targeting CmDof13. Dual-luciferase, yeast one-hybrid, and EMSA assays confirmed that CmBES1-4 activated CmDof13 expression via E-box binding. These findings identified a novel light/BR-CmBES1-4-CmDof13-ester biosynthesis regulatory module, which provided theoretical insights for improving postharvest aroma quality in oriental melon.
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
authors: Zhang C, Ju M, Wang Z, Pang H, Zhang Y, Chen Q, Wu X.

title: l-Arginine Ameliorates IBS-D by Modulating the Ligilactobacillus murinus-LCA-FXR/eNOS Signaling Axis.
abstract: l-Arginine is a semiessential amino acid with diverse metabolic functions and has been implicated in gastrointestinal health through interactions with the gut microbiota; however, its therapeutic potential in diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) remains unclear. Here, an IBS-D mouse model was established in C57BL/6J mice, and multiomics analyses combined with in vivo and in vitro validation were performed to investigate the mechanisms underlying l-arginine-mediated protection. l-Arginine supplementation significantly alleviated IBS-D-like symptoms and improved intestinal barrier function. Transcriptomic analysis revealed the activation of the FXR/PI3K/AKT/eNOS signaling pathway, which was associated with enhanced nitric oxide production. Integrated metagenomic and transcriptomic analyses identified Ligilactobacillus murinus (L. murinus) as a key microbiota component associated with bile acid metabolism and eNOS expression. Furthermore, L. murinus transplantation reproduced the beneficial effects of l-arginine, and metabolomic analysis identified lithocholic acid (LCA) as a microbiota-derived metabolite involved in this process. In vitro experiments demonstrated that LCA alleviated lipopolysaccharide-induced epithelial inflammation and barrier dysfunction via FXR/eNOS activation. Collectively, these findings reveal that l-arginine ameliorates IBS-D through microbiota remodeling, LCA-mediated bile acid regulation, and activation of the colonic FXR/PI3K/AKT/eNOS axis, highlighting its potential as a microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategy.
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
authors: Zheng X, Ying Y, Yang J, Liu X, Ye H, Dong Z, Zhang Y, Tan X, Zhang W.

title: Synbiotic of 2'-FL and B. longum subsp. infantis BXY2 Alleviates Colitis in Toddler Microbiota-Associated Mice: Potential Involvement of Gut Microbial Arachidonic Acid Metabolism.
abstract: Increasing inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) incidence in toddlers requires safe interventions. We developed a synbiotic combining 2'-fucosyllactose (2'-FL) with Bifidobacterium strain and evaluated its protective efficacy against DSS-induced colitis in toddler microbiota-associated (TMA) mice. Among 30 Bifidobacterium strains, Bifidobacterium longum subsp. infantis BXY2 and Bifidobacterium. breve BG4 utilized 2'-FL in vitro. However, only the 2'-FL and BXY2 synbiotic significantly alleviated colitis. The 400 mg/kg 2'-FL and BXY2 synbiotic showed the greatest protective effect, restoring body weight and colon length, reducing disease activity and histological scores, improving barrier function, attenuating inflammation. Compared with 2'-FL or BXY2 alone, the synbiotic enhanced goblet cells and barrier proteins. Metagenomics revealed enrichment of B. longum subsp. infantis and Phascolarctobacterium faecium. Metabolomics showed reduced fecal arachidonic acid (AA). These results indicated that gut microbial AA metabolism might be involved in alleviating colitis in TMA mice. Thus, this synbiotic is a promising preventive strategy for toddler IBD.
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
authors: Jing Y, Bai X, Li J, Feng X, Gu Y, Ji Y, Zhai Z, Hao Y.

title: [The impact of Cirbp knockout on the expression of immune-related genes in the cortex of developing mice].
abstract: Objective To investigate how cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (Cirbp) knockout affects the expression of immune-related genes in the cerebral cortex during postnatal development. Methods Wild-type (WT) and Cirbp knockout (Cirbp-) C57BL/6 mice were euthanized at postnatal day 21 (P21), and cortical tissues were collected. Western blot was used to detect CIRBP protein expression in cortical tissues. Transcriptome sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs), thereby facilitating the identification of key immune-related genes. Candidate genes were validated using real-time quantitative PCR. Results Western blot confirmed the absence of CIRBP protein expression in the cortex of Cirbp- mice. Compared with the WT group, transcriptomic analysis identified 268 DEGs in the cortex of Cirbp- mice, of which 118 were upregulated and 150 were downregulated. Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis showed that the DEGs were mainly enriched in biological processes including signal transduction, transmembrane transport, and positive regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis indicated that the DEGs were predominantly enriched in the cytosolic DNA-sensing pathway, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) signaling pathway, and Toll-like receptor signaling pathway. REACTOME pathway enrichment revealed that the DEGs were mainly enriched in signal transduction, peptide ligand-binding receptors, and downstream signaling pathways of G protein-coupled receptors. In the protein-protein interaction (PPI) network, the identified immune-related genes in the cortex included interleukin 6 (IL-6), C-C motif chemokine ligand 4 (CCL4), CCL5, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 10 (CXCL10), cellular communication network factor 1(CCN1), and cluster of Differentiation 274 (CD274). Real-time quantitative PCR validation showed that the mRNA expression levels of these key immune-related genes were consistent with the RNA sequencing results. Conclusion Cirbp knockout significantly alters the expression of immune-related genes in the cortex of developing mice, providing candidate targets for subsequent investigations into the protein-level underlying CIRBP-mediated neuroimmune regulation.
journal: Xi bao yu fen zi mian yi xue za zhi = Chinese journal of cellular and molecular immunology
authors: Zheng M, Li M, Guan R, Liu X.

title: Lipophilic Redox Mediators Reprogram Intracellular Electron Flow to Promote Arsenic Methylation in Soil Fermentative Bacteria.
abstract: Anaerobic arsenic (As) methylation by fermentative microorganisms, particularly Clostridium-related populations, controls As speciation, mobility, and volatilization in flooded paddy soils, yet the mechanisms promoting this process remain poorly understood. Here, we reveal that phenazine- and phenoxazine-like redox mediators can enhance anaerobic As methylation via reshaping the intracellular electron allocation in a representative As-methylating fermentative bacterium. We integrated As speciation analysis, metabolite profiling, proteomics, and metabolic-flux modeling to determine how resazurin, as a represenative lipophilic redox mediator, reshapes fermentative metabolism and methylated As (MeAs) formation. The membrane-permeable redox mediator resazurin increased the apparent rate constant of MeAs formation by up to fourfold relative to the hydrophilic mediator anthraquinone-2,6-disulfonic acid (AQDS). Unlike AQDS, resazurin enhanced dimethylarsine formation while establishing a more reducing intracellular environment by diverting electrons from hydrogen evolution, indicating altered intracellular electron disposal. At the proteomic level, resazurin induced coordinated increases in As(III) methyltransferase (ArsM) and proteins involved in S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) biosynthesis, representing the primary molecular responses associated with enhanced As methylation. Proteins involved in amino-acid-fueled energy conservation and redox homeostasis were also enriched, potentially creating favorable cellular conditions for SAM-dependent As methylation. In a paddy-soil-derived fermentative consortium, resazurin likewise enhanced MeAs production and increased transcript levels of Clostridium-associated arsM and the SAM synthetase gene (metK). These findings identify lipophilicity-dependent, redox-compound-mediated intracellular electron flow reprogramming as a previously underappreciated control on anaerobic As methylation and provide a mechanistic basis for predicting MeAs formation in flooded soil environments.

title: Electron Transfer at Microbe-Mineral Interfaces: From Molecular Mechanisms to Ecosystem-Scale Biogeochemical Cycling and Remediation.
abstract: Microbe-mineral electron transfer (MMET) drives key microbial processes and biogeochemical cycling, but linking these microscopic interactions to ecosystem-scale dynamics remains a major challenge. MMET couples intracellular metabolism to extracellular mineral transformations. The resulting changes in mineral redox state and reactivity can, in turn, influence microbial energy conservation and metabolism. MMET flux could therefore provide a quantitative link between nanometer-scale electron exchange and larger-scale biogeochemical processes. In energy-limited and contaminated environments, electroactive microorganisms may transfer electrons to or acquire electrons from redox-active minerals, depending on their metabolic capabilities and local redox conditions. These interactions can support energy conservation, mitigate toxic stress, and generate localized zones of high biogeochemical activity. As their effects accumulate across space and time, microscale electron transfer may influence ecosystem-scale elemental cycling, microbial community succession, organic carbon stabilization, and contaminant fate. Building on established modeling approaches, we suggest that integrating individual-based models (IBMs) with genome-scale metabolic models (GSMMs) could translate spatially heterogeneous, genome-informed microbial responses into collective MMET fluxes across scales while accounting for key thermodynamic and kinetic constraints. More broadly, progress requires characterizing electroactive microbial diversity and mechanisms, engineering microbe-mineral interfaces through computational design and synthetic biology, and translating MMET principles into scalable environmental applications.
authors: Liu J, Wu Z, Feng X, Shi L, Rosso KM.

title: Epigenome, Microbiome, and Metabolites: Unraveling the Complex Pathogenesis of Celiac Disease.
abstract: Celiac disease (CeD) is a chronic autoimmune disease triggered by gluten consumption in genetically susceptible individuals, primarily those with HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 haplotypes. Although these genetic factors are responsible for a substantial portion of disease risk, they do not fully explain disease heritability or the rising incidence observed worldwide. Recent clinical studies highlight epigenetic modifications-including DNA methylation, histone modifications, non-coding RNA regulation, and RNA methylation-as critical mediators bridging genetic susceptibility and environmental influences, such as gut microbiota dysbiosis, dietary patterns, early-life exposures, infections, and pharmaceutical interventions. These epigenetic mechanisms modulate immune responses, intestinal barrier function, and inflammatory pathways, contributing to the loss of gluten tolerance and perpetuation of mucosal damage. Key players, including tissue transglutaminase 2 (TG2) and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), form amplifying feedback loops that exacerbate pathogenesis. Bacterial metabolites and lifestyle factors further influence epigenetic landscapes, offering reversible targets for intervention. This review synthesizes current evidence on epigenetic alterations in CeD, emphasizing their interplay with microbiota and metabolites, tissue-specific patterns, and potential as biomarkers. It also explores implications for novel therapeutic strategies beyond the gluten-free diet, including epigenetic modulators and microbiota-targeted approaches, to advance personalized prevention and management of CeD.
authors: Atoom AM, Allela OQB, Nayak PP, Arora V, Singla S, Athab ZH, Urazbaeva D, Usmanov R.

title: A Bacterial Extracellular Matrix Protein Forms a Supramolecular Metallogel.
abstract: The microbial extracellular matrix (ECM) is a complex network of self-secreted biopolymers that unite cells in biofilms, providing them with structural integrity and protection from antimicrobials. Made of fibrillar proteins interspersed with polysaccharides, ECM material is often implicitly held responsible for biofilms' hydrogel-like mechanical signature; the exact molecular mechanisms of the ECM assembly and their link to hydrogel formation, however, remain enigmatic. Here, we discover that in the presence of zinc ions, TasA, the major ECM protein of Bacillus subtilis, forms hydrogels that recapitulate the mechanical properties of whole biofilms. Electron and atomic force microscopies as well as small-angle X-ray scattering showed that cross-linking with zinc ions induced a transition in the TasA architecture from one-dimensional fibers to two-dimensional nanosheets. Electron paramagnetic resonance and X-ray diffraction data link this dramatic morphological shift to molecular changes in the coordination environment of zinc ions and protein structure. This study provides the first example and a novel molecular mechanism of supramolecular metallogelation by a native bacterial protein. Bridging between molecular processes, mesoscopic structure, and macroscopic material properties, it not only advances the fundamental understanding of ECM assembly in situ but also establishes artificial ECM-based (metallo-)hydrogels as matrix mimics for bacterial infection studies.
authors: Ghrayeb M, Ashman A, Mukhopadhyay S, Fellig A, Jopp J, Levi-Kalisman Y, Raviv U, Bertinetti L, Politi Y, Zaburdaev V, Ruthstein S, Chai L.

title: Associations of self-reported and actigraphic sleep with gut microbiome composition and diversity among older adults.
abstract: Study objectivesPoor sleep is linked to adverse health outcomes. Animal studies suggest the gut microbiome may influence sleep, but human findings remain inconsistent. We examined associations of self-reported insomnia symptoms, daytime sleepiness, and actigraphy-measured sleep with gut microbiome diversity and composition in older adults.Materials and methodsWe studied 869 Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging participants with self-reported sleep and shotgun metagenomic sequencing; 332 also had actigraphy. We tested associations of sleep with alpha diversity, beta diversity, and species composition using regression, PERMANOVA, and ANCOM-BC2, adjusting for age, sex, BMI, physical activity, education, and depressive symptoms.ResultsParticipants had a mean age of 70.7 years; 54.8 per cent were female and 66.9 per cent white. Trouble falling asleep ≥5 times/week was associated with higher Shannon diversity (β = 0.41 SD; 95% CI: 0.09, 0.73) and Pielou's evenness, but not richness metrics. No actigraphy-measured sleep variables were associated with alpha or beta diversity. Beta diversity analyses suggested excessive sleepiness (1-2 or 3-4 times/week) was associated with a different microbial composition, though the variance explained was small. In species-level analyses, frequent insomnia symptoms or excessive sleepiness were associated with depleted or undetected Eubacterium sp. CAG:251. In exploratory actigraphy models, each doubling of sleep efficiency was associated with higher Eubacterium sp. CAG:251 prevalence (PR = 2.15; 95% CI: 1.47, 3.14), while each 30-minute increase in wake after sleep onset was associated with lower prevalence (PR = 0.49; 95% CI: 0.29, 0.81).ConclusionsGlobal diversity findings were limited and inconsistent, whereas subjective and objective sleep disturbances converged on Eubacterium sp. CAG:251. These findings are exploratory and require longitudinal replication.
authors: Tilves C, Holingue C, Wanigatunga SK, Chia CW, Zhao N, Wu MN, Schrack JA, Simonsick EM, Ferrucci L, Tanaka T, Spira AP, Mueller NT.

title: Genome-wide selection signatures and candidate genes in Tanzanian indigenous chickens across contrasting agro-ecological environments.
abstract: Sub-Saharan African indigenous chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus) have been shaped by long-term selection in tropical production environments, but the genomic basis of their adaptation is still poorly understood. We sequenced 196 Tanzanian indigenous chickens (TICs) from 12 populations across four contrasting agro-ecological zones, with 40 birds from five Chinese indigenous breeds as a cross-continental reference. We detected selection signatures using pooled heterozygosity, runs of homozygosity (ROH), and a three-statistic directional scan (FST, XP-EHH, and the π ratio). TICs showed weak differentiation among populations (mean FST = 0.021) but were clearly separated from the Chinese breeds (0.104). Inbreeding was low and came almost entirely from short ROH, with mean FROH of 0.053 to 0.076 across zones (runs ≥ 300 kb). Candidates fell into two main classes by breadth of sharing. The first, shared across most analysis groups including the Chinese populations, may represent ancestral or domestication-related signals. These include LIPE on GGA14, both chicken α-amylase paralogs on GGA8, and VSTM2A on GGA2, which has also been reported in Botswanan, Arabian, and Chinese indigenous chickens. The second comprises zone-specific candidates from the directional scan, of which four were robust to jackknife resampling: AGMO in the Central Plateau, SUGCT in the Coastal Lowland, and TSHR and the EYA3 interval, which also contains PTAFR, in the Eastern Plateau. TSHR and LIPE have both recently been reported in the Nigerian scan as heat-stress candidates. ZFHX4 on GGA2, recovered by pooled heterozygosity, gave the strongest multi-window signal in the warmer pool, and its top window contains a SNP suggestively associated with Newcastle disease response in Rwandan indigenous chickens, reported on the same assembly. Because the agro-ecological zone was used to structure sampling and was not tested as an environmental variable, these loci are candidates for functional validation and not proven targets of climatic adaptation. Low inbreeding and shallow structure nonetheless support in situ conservation of these populations.
authors: Pius L, Zheng S, Yang P, Thomas K, Kusza S, Liu M, Xu D.

title: Integration of genotyping by sequencing and machine learning for genome-wide identification of informative markers for body weight in broiler chickens.
abstract: Identifying associations between single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and economically important traits is fundamental to modern poultry breeding programs. However, genome-wide studies based on commercial high-density SNP arrays are often prohibitively expensive, particularly for large populations and in resource-limited settings. Therefore, this study employed a cost-effective genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS) approach combined with two ensemble machine learning algorithms, Random Forest (RF) and Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), to identify informative markers of body weight (BW) at hatch, 3 weeks (BW3), and 6 weeks (BW6) of age in broiler chickens derived from reciprocal crosses between the commercial Arian line and native Urmia chicken. A total of 368 birds were genotyped using GBS, and 312 second-generation (F₂) birds with complete phenotypic records were utilized for genomic screening and machine learning analyses. The hyperparameters of both machine learning algorithms were optimized using a grid search with three-fold cross-validation. The combined application of RF and GBM identified several informative SNP markers located on chromosomes 1, 4, 13, 17, 19, 20, and 24. Positional candidate genes located within these genomic regions included platelet-derived growth factor D (PDGFD), KIRRE-like nephrin family adhesion molecule 3 (KIRREL3), ETS proto-oncogene 1, transcription factor (ETS1), acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 1 (ACSL1), diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 2 (DGAT2), and selenophosphate synthetase 1 (SEPHS1). Gene Ontology enrichment analysis indicated that these genes are involved in biological processes related to the regulation of protein degradation, immune responses, and lipid metabolism. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating cost-effective GBS with machine learning approaches to identify genomic regions and informative markers for body weight in broiler chickens, providing valuable genomic resources for future breeding and genetic improvement programs.
authors: Bani Saadat H, Vaez Torshizi R, Masoudi AA.

title: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing improves pathogen detection in culture-negative infections: a diagnostic performance study.
abstract: The conventional microbiological diagnosis is frequently insensitive, time consuming and targeted. Patients with underlying immune suppression and those who have recently been on antibiotics often have culture-negative infections. In recent years, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) has emerged as a novel, pathogen-agnostic diagnostic approach. A total of 136 clinical specimens were submitted for metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) between August 2022 and January 2024. Of these samples, 86 from 73 patients were included in this retrospective study. Thirteen patients had more than one specimen included in the study. All specimens were processed using conventional microbiological methods and analyzed using mNGS technology, either by using Illumina next-generation sequencing technology or Oxford Nanopore long-read technology. The diagnostic performance characteristics, including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV), were calculated for both methods. The agreement between the two methods was evaluated using Cohen's kappa coefficient. The paired comparisons were made using the McNemar test. The areas under the ROC curves for both methods were calculated, and the multivariable logistic regression analysis was used to identify the variables that were independently associated with mNGS positivity. Here, conventional microbiology identified pathogens in 16.3% of samples, whereas mNGS identified pathogens in 45.3% of samples. The sensitivity and specificity of mNGS were 57.1 and 84.2%, respectively. By McNemar testing, there was significant detection of pathogens by mNGS (p = 0.0015). The agreement between two methods was poor (kappa = 0.20). The ROC curve for mNGS results showed moderate diagnostic accuracy with an AUC of 0.71. By multivariable logistic regression, immunocompromised status (OR 2.8, 95% CI 1.3-6.0, p = 0.018) and positive imaging findings (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.4-6.9, p = 0.010) were independently associated with mNGS positivity. mNGS is able to identify more pathogens in culture-negative cases than conventional methods. There is scope for mNGS to be used in a complementary fashion, whilst relying on conventional methods as the primary tool for diagnosis of infections. Notably, the greatest additional information will come from the use of mNGS in immunocompromised patients.
authors: Tayeb HT, Abouelhoda M, Alqasabi A, Magrashi A, Nafe G, Alzahrani T, Alzeer S, Bakheet R.

title: Engineering mRNA-Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines against multidrug resistant bacteria: current and future prospects
abstract: AbstractThis review highlights the significant potential of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology for application in bacterial vaccines, with a long-term goal to provide critical tools in controlling problematic microbial infections regardless of their antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profile. The current landscape of bacterial vaccine development, including methods for identification of candidate antigens, are discussed along with emerging design principles for LNP delivery systems. We focus on mRNA-LNP systems for delivery of bacterial vaccine antigens in large part due to their extensive clinical validation, compatibility with reverse vaccinology, and growing prominence in modern vaccinology. Attention is also given to emerging opportunities to develop effective tools to combat severe infections, particularly those caused by AMR bacterial infections. Specific advantages and challenges of RNA-based vaccine platforms and LNP delivery systems compared to other vaccine modalities including strategies are highlighted, with a focus on particular strengths in conserved antigen identification via genome sequencing and recent advances in optimizing LNP composition for induction of strongly protective immunity for vaccine delivery. We argue that mRNA-LNP technology combined with reverse vaccinology approaches has the potential to improve and accelerate bacterial vaccine development, particularly for broadly protective immunity less dependent on bacterial strain surface composition and which are entirely dependent on host immunity, making them agnostic to the issue of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Multi-stress tolerant Bacillus from salt-affected arid soil
abstract: AbstractSalinity, drought, and heat severely constrain microbial activity in arid soils. This study investigated whether multi-stress tolerance in Bacillus isolated from the rhizosphere of Suaeda vera is associated with a genomic complement of stress-response and plant growth-promoting genes. We isolated 150 bacterial isolates from this rhizosphere soil at saline sites (16–32 dS/m) of Sehb El Mesjoune, central Morocco. Among these isolates, 65 were classified as multi-stress tolerant, as they grew in culture media under salinity (1.7–3.4 M NaCl), drought (10–20% PEG), and elevated temperatures (≥47°C), with Bacillus (33%) as the dominant genus. Out of these isolates, five Bacillus strains were selected for further analysis. Whole-genome sequencing revealed a genomic architecture with multiple abiotic stress tolerance mechanisms, including KtrABCD transporters, Na+/H+ antiporters, the opuABCD pathway, and the stressosome sensory complex, with operons for biofilm formation (epsA-O, tasA, bslA) potentially relevant to root association. Comparative ortholog analysis detected 444 orthogroups common to the strains from Sehb El Mesjoune and the saline reference B. halotolerans ZB201702 but absent from the non-saline reference B. velezensis FZB42. Of these, 81 were annotated as stress tolerance or plant growth-promoting genes, a pattern that may reflect environmental filtering, although species-level ancestry cannot be excluded. Additionally, in vitro assays and SEM imaging confirmed these traits were functionally expressed, resulting in Bacillus strains attaching to wheat seeds. These findings suggest that the five selected Bacillus strains represent promising candidates for future greenhouse and field testing as bacterial inoculants for crops grown in salt-affected arid soils.

title: M2iOR: a quantitative, context-resolved atlas of insect odorant receptor-odorant interactions
abstract: AbstractOlfactory detection in insects relies on interactions between odorant molecules and odorant receptors (ORs) expressed in olfactory sensory neurons. Although numerous studies have characterized insect OR-ligand interactions, these data remain scattered across the literature and heterogeneous in terms of species, experimental systems, and reporting standards, limiting their systematic analysis. Here, we present the Molecule to Insect Odorant Receptor database (M2iOR, https://m2ior.chemsensim.fr/), a curated, publicly accessible resource designed to centralize and standardize odorant-receptor interaction data. In its current release, M2iOR compiles 35 891 bioassay experiments describing 30 348 distinct insect OR-molecule pairs, extracted from 41 peer-reviewed publications and public databases. The resource integrates ligand structures, receptor sequences, species names, mixture information, and detailed experimental metadata. M2iOR provides flexible query tools allowing users to retrieve activity profiles for individual molecules or compound sets, and identify agonists and nonagonists for specific insect ORs, enabling comparative analyses across receptors, species, or bioassay systems. Advanced filtering based on curated metadata and batch search functionality support high-throughput analyses. For each query, users can visualize and download a curated aggregation of experimental results, including a binarized combinatorial representation of olfactory coding suitable for downstream computational studies. M2iOR provides a comprehensive framework for data-driven research in insect olfaction and comparative chemosensory biology.

title: Evo2VED: a database of DNA large language model-derived scores for variant interpretation
abstract: AbstractThe Evo2 Variant Effect Database (Evo2VED; https://dnallmved.org/) is a publicly accessible resource cataloging precomputed Evo2-derived variant effect scores, defined as allelic score differences, for 6.48 million human variants common in the gnomAD non-Finnish European population. Evo2VED includes scores from the 7B and 40B models under three scoring schemes, alongside annotations of variant function, evolutionary constraint, allele age, and disease associations. It integrates genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from UK Biobank, FinnGen, and the Million Veteran Program. Three complementary modules support variant-level interpretation, regional and region-set exploration, and trait-level analysis through flexible queries, interactive visualizations, and downloadable results. Evo2VED also catalogs associations between Evo2 annotations and per-SNP heritability across thousands of traits from these biobanks. A guided workflow connects GWAS with associated regions and individual variant evidence. Case studies of hypertension and depression illustrate how regional comparisons of Evo2 scores and GWAS signals can guide candidate variant prioritization. Evaluations using massively parallel reporter assays, molecular QTLs, fine-mapping probabilities, and clinical annotations assess associations with Evo2 scores alone and their added value beyond conservation and regulatory annotations. By providing accessible scores, contextual annotations, and comparative analyses, Evo2VED facilitates exploration and application of genomic language model predictions in human genetics research.

title: The Biodiversity Cell Atlas database: a curated resource for comparative single-cell genomics across the eukaryotic tree of life
abstract: AbstractSingle-cell genomics has transformed the study of cellular diversity, but the resulting atlases are scattered across publications, formats, and annotation standards. Efforts to make these data findable and interoperable have focused largely on aggregating and harmonizing existing model organism datasets. The Biodiversity Cell Atlas database is an open resource that addresses this gap by uniformly (re)processing, curating, and comparing whole-organism single-cell atlases sampled across the eukaryotic tree of life. Starting from raw sequencing data, each dataset is processed through a consistent workflow and enriched with standardized quality-control metrics, metacell-level aggregation, gene co-expression modules, and phylogeny-based orthology and functional annotation, enabling both gene- and cell type-centric exploration within species as well as principled comparisons between them. The portal currently hosts 39 datasets across 33 species spanning 13 eukaryotic phyla, and offers multiple levels of access, from raw and filtered count matrices to normalized, aggregated, and analysis-ready data layers. These are accessible through an interactive web interface (https://portal.biodiversitycellatlas.org) and a documented REST API (https://portal.biodiversitycellatlas.org/api/v1/). All data, code, and infrastructure are continuously released and maintained under open licenses, providing a curated and reusable foundation for comparative single-cell genomics.

title: ADMETatlas: an online database of peptide ADMET evidence toward peptide therapeutic development
abstract: AbstractPeptide therapeutics are expanding rapidly, yet poor permeability and limited in vivo stability still decide whether a candidate reaches the clinic. Judging these properties is difficult, because one sequence can be studied as different molecular forms or products, and reported values carry different experimental contexts. Despite the continuous accumulation of measurements of peptide absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET), few open-access resources keep each value attached to the material tested and its assay context. Herein, we present ADMETatlas, a curated peptide ADMET, safety, and developability database. Currently, ADMETatlas contains 39 641 measurements at 17 measured end points across 37 467 canonical peptide identities, 110 drug products, and 10 computed descriptors. Each measurement retains its value, unit, formal end point, assay context, and primary reference. Peptide identities, molecular forms, and products are cross-linked at the resolution each source supports. In addition to browsing and retrieval, a developability module profiles single candidates and compares several side by side. Applications to GLP-1 receptor agonists and polymyxin B show how route and formulation change the reading of peptide pharmacokinetics. We hope that ADMETatlas will prove useful in evidence-based peptide optimization and condition-aware modeling. ADMETatlas is freely available, without registration, at https://admetatlas.scbdd.com/.

title: VastDB 2.0: a multispecies atlas of alternative splicing profiles, evolution, and function
abstract: AbstractVastDB is a widely used resource for the systematic exploration of alternative splicing, integrating quantitative splicing profiles with gene expression, genomic features, evolutionary conservation, and protein impact. Here, we present VastDB 2.0, a major expansion of the database in phylogenetic breadth and functional information. VastDB 2.0 covers 26 animal species spanning the major bilaterian clades and Cnidaria, comprising 7769 RNA-seq samples across diverse cell types, tissues, developmental stages, and other physiological contexts. Exon-level evolutionary relationships have been substantially expanded, enabling comparative analyses of exon conservation, gain, and loss across a larger phylogeny. In addition, VastDB 2.0 introduces a manually curated functional classification of alternative splicing events comprising 12 476 annotations from primary literature, which follows a standardized nomenclature and facilitates both biological interpretation and experimental prioritization. The web interface has also been redesigned with improved visualization and updated computational annotations. Together, VastDB 2.0 provides a comprehensive comparative framework for investigating the regulation, evolution, and functional impact of alternative splicing across Metazoa. VastDB 2.0 is freely available at https://vastdb.crg.eu.

title: DIANA-miRGen v5: TSS characterization and transcriptional regulation of miRNAs in human and mouse
abstract: AbstractCharacterizing microRNA transcriptional regulation is challenging because primary microRNA transcripts undergo rapid nuclear processing, leaving full-length molecules poorly represented in conventional transcriptomic data. DIANA-miRGen v5 addresses this annotation gap by combining Capture Long-read Sequencing (CLS) data, generated within GENCODE to improve non-coding RNA annotation, with GENCODE reference gene and transcript annotations to resolve miRNA host contexts. For human, the database provides experimentally informed, transcript-anchored host and promoter annotations for 1560/1918 pre-miRNA loci (81.3%), represented by 1302 distinct reference transcripts. CLS-derived human transcription start sites (TSSs) are accompanied by overlap information from FANTOM5 CAGE, ENCODE PRO-cap, and RAMPAGE. Transcription factor (TF)-filtered ChIP-Atlas data annotate candidate TF occupancy within windows extending 10 kb upstream and 2 kb downstream of selected host TSSs, yielding 4 901 330 human gene-level host-window overlap records. For mouse, annotations cover 994/1227 loci (81.0%), comprising 785 distinct reference transcripts. Mouse TSSs obtained from CLS include FANTOM5 CAGE overlap information, while ChIP-Atlas analysis yielded 2 378 918 gene-level host-window overlap records. The redesigned interface supports linked gene- and transcript-level exploration, interactive genome visualization, contextual tracks, bulk downloads, and open access through a REST API. DIANA-miRGen v5 is freely available without registration at http://microrna.gr/mirgenv5/.

title: TransCirc 2.0: a multi-species resource for translatable circular RNAs and cognate translation products
abstract: AbstractTransCirc is an evidence-integrated database for evaluating the translation potential of circular RNAs (circRNAs) and their putative products. Here, we present TransCirc 2.0, a major update that expands this resource from a primarily human-focused database to 10 vertebrate species, comprising more than 2.8 million circRNAs and increasing coverage by approximately 10-fold through the integration of standardized full-length circRNA sequences. Within the original multi-evidence framework, we incorporate additional evidence, including translation initiation sites, internal ribosome entry sites, N6-methyladenosine, ribosome/polysome association, and mass spectrometry (MS), together with circRNA-specific open reading frame and sequence-composition annotations. In light of recent advances in AI-based RNA modeling, we further incorporate multiple regulatory features predicted by TranslationAI and LAMAR. The circRNA-encoded proteins are further annotated for degron-associated stability and degradation properties, while MS-supported peptides are evaluated for potential MHC-I presentation. Collectively, these updates establish a cross-species framework linking full-length circRNA sequences with multi-level translation evidence and downstream product annotations, supporting systematic evaluation of circRNA translation potential and putative translation products. TransCirc 2.0 is freely available at https://www.biosino.org/transcirc/.

title: RiPPs in functional laboratory medicine: translational opportunities and class III lanthipeptides as a comparative case study
abstract: Ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) are genetically encoded natural products that undergo diverse enzymatic modifications to generate structurally constrained molecules with broad biological activities and substantial engineering potential. Their defined biosynthetic origins, target-recognition properties, structural stability, and genetic encodability make RiPPs attractive molecular resources for both natural product research and emerging function-oriented applications in laboratory medicine. In this review, we summarize the biosynthetic logic and structural diversity of RiPPs, with particular emphasis on class III lanthipeptides as a representative and underexplored subgroup of structural and biosynthetic innovation. We curate 19 structurally characterized and experimentally validated class III lanthipeptides and compare their taxonomic origins, biosynthetic gene cluster organization, precursor peptide features, LanKC-mediated modifications, ring topologies, maturation routes, and reported biological functions. The analysis reveals a strong representation of Actinobacteria, a predominance of Lab-containing architectures, considerable diversity in maturation strategies, and a substantial proportion of functionally unresolved members. Beyond this comparative analysis, we discuss the emerging potential of RiPPs in mechanism-informed antimicrobial susceptibility testing, functional molecular diagnostics, microbiome functional-state assessment, engineered molecular probes, and precision anti-infective strategies. Because most of these applications remain exploratory or preclinical, we further propose a six-level evidence framework that distinguishes BGC presence, transcriptional activity, mature product detection, target engagement, biological activity, and clinical validation. By integrating the diversity of class III lanthipeptides with the broader translational potential of RiPPs, this review provides a framework for linking biosynthetic information, structural innovation, molecular function, and future applications in functional laboratory medicine.

title: A novel gellan gum-degrading glycoside hydrolase from the hyperthermophile Fervidibacter sacchari
abstract: Fervidibacter sacchari is an aerobic hyperthermophile within the phylum Armatimonadota that degrades various polysaccharides. Its genome encodes 117 putative glycoside hydrolases (GHs), including two assigned to GH family 50 (GH50). In this study, a multidomain GH50 enzyme, Fsa11540Gus, was expressed, purified, and functionally characterized. Despite most GH50s being known as β-agarases, Fsa11540Gus was optimally active on gellan gum, followed by β-glucan, with lower activity on carboxymethyl (CM)-curdlan and agarose. Nanostructure-initiator mass spectrometry (NIMS) analysis of degradation products of gellan gum indicated β-1,4-endoglucuronidase activity at the glucuronate-glucose bond. Mutation of either conserved active-site glutamic acid with proposed roles as acid/base catalyst and nucleophile to alanine (E409A or E575A) or amino acids with predicted roles in substrate recognition and distortion (N408A, F630A, and E646A) decreased enzyme activity. These results rule out gellan lyase activity and confirm Fsa11540Gus as the first known glycoside hydrolase to degrade gellan gum. NIMS analysis of other degradation products revealed β-1,3-endoglucanase activity on oat β-glucan and CM-curdlan and likely β-1,4-endo glycoside hydrolase activity on the galactose-3,6-anhydrogalactose-galactose bond in agarose. The enzyme was active on gellan gum from 70 to 95 °C, with optimal activity at 80–90 °C and rapid deactivation at 100 °C. AlphaFold 3 computed structure models predicted a monomeric structure, which was confirmed by native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. The enzyme has a predicted N-terminal Sec translocase/signal peptidase I signal peptide, an N-terminal domain of unknown function, a GH50 domain, and a large C-terminal domain annotated as COG1572/pfam07705. Phylogenetic analysis of Fsa11540Gus and other GH50 enzymes revealed a monophyletic clade in the genera Fervidibacter and Caldisaccharidevorator with these distinctive N- and C-terminal domains, suggesting recent vertical evolution but a dynamic deeper evolutionary history involving domain swapping and changes in protein localization. This study shows that Fsa11540Gus is the first known enzyme with glycoside hydrolase activity on gellan gum and expands our understanding of the GH50 family and polysaccharide metabolism by Armatimonadota.
authors: Brian P. Hedlund

title: Comparative analysis of gut microbiota structure in the Xinjiang (China) population of children with mild-to-moderate and severe autism spectrum disorder
abstract: BackgroundAutism spectrum disorder (ASD) exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity; however, the relationship between gut microbiome features and ASD severity remains incompletely understood.MethodsWe enrolled 88 children with ASD from Xinjiang, China, and characterized gut microbial profiles using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. α and β diversity were compared between children with mild-to-moderate ASD (MM-ASD) and severe ASD (S-ASD), and their associations with Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) scores were assessed. Differential abundance analyses were performed using ANCOM-BC2, LinDA, and LEfSe. Predicted functional potentials were inferred using PICRUSt2. A nested cross-validation framework with random forest models was applied to evaluate the discriminative performance of microbial features.ResultsNo significant differences were observed in overall α or β diversity between the MM-ASD and S-ASD groups, and CARS scores were not significantly associated with microbial diversity metrics. By integrating results from ANCOM-BC2, LinDA, and LEfSe, five candidate genera with consistent enrichment patterns were identified: Angelakisella and CAG-83 were enriched in the S-ASD group, whereas Terrisporobacter, Lactobacillus, and Adlercreutzia were enriched in the MM-ASD group. The relative abundances of Angelakisella and CAG-83 showed positive correlations with CARS scores, while Adlercreutzia exhibited a negative correlation with CARS scores. PICRUSt2-based analysis suggested differences in predicted energy metabolism-related functional potentials; however, these functional inferences remain hypothetical and require validation using direct functional assays. In nested cross-validation, the microbial feature-based model demonstrated limited discriminative performance (AUC = 0.579) compared with the baseline model (AUC = 0.521).ConclusionIn this small, single-region, cross-sectional cohort, gut microbial characteristics were not robustly associated with overall ASD severity. Future multicenter, larger-scale longitudinal studies integrating multi-omics approaches and standardized clinical assessments are warranted to further clarify the relationship between gut microbiome features and ASD severity.
authors: Rena Maimaiti

title: Candidatus Pannonibacter alzirae sp. nov. isolated from a septic immunocompromised patient in Brazil
abstract: Pannonibacter species. are non-fermentative Gram-stain-negative bacteria, with rare reports of human infections primarily affecting immunocompromised patients. Here, we report the genomic and phenotypic characterization of a novel Pannonibacter species, isolated from a bacteremia episode in a pediatric patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia in Brazil. Initial characterization of the isolate (here named CBAS 1226) by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry and 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing identified it as Pannonibacter sp., most closely related to P. phragmitetus. However, comparison of its MALDI-TOF spectrum with a commercial reference library revealed compatibility with only two of the five main spectra profiles for P. phragmitetus. This discrepancy motivated comprehensive genomic, biochemical, morphological, and antimicrobial resistance profiling of CBAS 1226. Genomic analysis revealed that Pannonibacter sp. CBAS 1226 is phylogenetically distinct from P. phragmitetus and other known species, with ANI and dDDH values below species delineation thresholds, supporting its proposal as Candidatus Pannonibacter alzirae. It forms small, non-hemolytic, grayish-white colonies on blood agar, similar to its closest relatives P. phragmitetus and P. indicus. Phenotypically, it is distinguished by positive - and {beta}-glucosidase activity, along with the utilization of citrate, L-proline, and 2-ketoglutarate. It is negative for alkaline phosphatase and unable to utilize D-fructose, D-melibiose, esculin, or L-arginine. The isolate exhibited higher MICs for {beta}-lactams, whereas carbapenems and fluoroquinolones showed low MICs. The isolate is capable of forming biofilms and tolerates alkaline conditions, a wide range of temperatures, and different oxygen concentrations. Altogether, this report emphasizes the relevance of additional proteomics- and genomics-based approaches to clarify unusual bacterial infections and describes a new Pannonibacter species with distinct features and the potential to cause opportunistic infections.

title: Ultra-small bacteria and their phages discovered through metagenomics in a sub-arctic degrading permafrost ecosystem
abstract: Patescibacteriota is a diverse bacterial phylum characterized by ultra-small cell size, streamlined genome, incomplete metabolism and episymbiotic lifestyle. While Patescibacteriota have been detected across a wide range of ecosystem types, their phages are not widely described. We utilized metagenomics to explore these less characterized parts of the microbiome in a sporadic permafrost ecosystem, with samples from palsa and peat soils, small ponds and streams. We retrieved 33 high-quality metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) of Patescibacteriota, mainly from the classes Minisyncoccia and Saccharimonadia. Minisyncoccia was a dominant class in the thawing soils and thaw ponds, whereas the Saccharimonadia was more abundant in the frozen palsa soil layers. The distribution of the Patescibacteria classes was also reflected in their metabolic potential. For example, gluconeogenesis pathway was complete only in MAGs from the class Minisyncoccia, whereas cytochrome o ubiquinol oxidase was mainly found from the MAGs of the class Saccharimondia. The viral community analysis yielded 16 354 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), which represented mainly tailed dsDNA viruses from the class Caudoviricetes. Based on genome size, 16 vOTUs were qualified as jumbophages and one as a megaphage. Similar to the bacterial community, the viral community composition differed across sample types. The most common hosts for bacterial viruses were phyla Pseudomonadota, Acidobacteriota and Actinomycetota. A further 196 vOTUs were in silico linked to Patescibacteriota hosts. The Patescibacteriota phages were diverse, with only two vOTUs representing the same genus. The relative abundance of Patescibacteriota-associated phages was especially high in frozen palsa soils, largely following the same pattern of abundance as Patescibacteriota.
authors: Tuomela, N., Demina, T., Thomas, D. N., Kaartokallio, H., Hultman, J.

title: Virucidal Star Polymer Disrupts Alphavirus Infection in Aedes Mosquitoes
abstract: Mosquito-borne alphaviruses represent an increasing global health threat, yet there are currently no antiviral interventions capable of targeting both the vertebrate host and mosquito vector. Here, we investigated the antiviral potential of the heparan sulfate proteoglycan-mimicking zwitterionic polymer ZP12 against alphavirus infection in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. ZP12 exhibited potent antiviral and virucidal activity against Ross River virus (RRV) and Semliki Forest virus (SFV) in C6/36 mosquito cells. Antiviral activity was retained in ex vivo mosquito gut cultures, where both high (100 g/mL) and low (0.5 g/mL) concentrations significantly reduced RRV replication, with viral titres reduced by up to five orders of magnitude at peak infection. Delayed-treatment studies demonstrated that ZP12 retained antiviral activity after infection had been initiated, although efficacy declined as treatment was delayed. To evaluate prophylactic delivery, mosquitoes were exposed to ZP12 through sugar feeding prior to viral challenge. While this approach did not directly protect against subsequent gut infection, follow-up experiments demonstrated that ZP12 remained biologically active within the mosquito, suggesting that limited delivery to the midgut rather than loss of antiviral activity restricted efficacy. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that ZP12 is a potent antiviral and virucidal agent against alphaviruses in mosquito cells and tissues and supports its further development as a transmission-blocking strategy for arboviral control.
authors: Macleod, S.-L., Van Langendonck, M., Rase, N., Rosales-Rosas, A. L., Jones, S. T., Delang, L.

title: Strain-specific early, host-shaped late: the rhizobial transcriptome across symbiosis
abstract: The two ends of the rhizobial symbiotic trajectory have only been described separately. Here we report strand-specific RNA-seq of bacteroids of two strains, each against free-living cells of the same strain and alongside its flavonoid response: Sinorhizobium fredii HH103 from soybean (Glycine max), Glycyrrhiza uralensis and Lotus burttii, and Rhizobium tropici CIAT 899 from common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) and L. burttii, the one legume both strains nodulate. Between 1877 and 2284 genes respond per strain-host combination, and most of that response is host-common: 1171 of 2855 genes respond in all three hosts of HH103 and 1664 of 2703 in both hosts of CIAT 899. What distinguishes the remainder is host identity rather than nodule type, since HH103 bacteroids from the indeterminate-nodule G. uralensis resemble those from L. burttii more than either resembles those from soybean, its natural host. Nitrogen fixation and the stress response are over-represented in every bacteroid and motility is almost entirely repressed, yet the shared core of CIAT 899 is the only repression-dominated gene set here and its translational machinery is induced where that of HH103 is repressed. Dismantling of the early programme is selective: in HH103 the type III apparatus is switched off, the Nod factor operons are attenuated but retained, and the fixABCX operon under a nod box is amplified, so a nod box does not by itself mark a gene as early. CIAT 899, lacking a type III system and placing no nif/fix gene under flavonoid control, keeps that block flat until the nodule, then engages 26 of its 30 genes. Across genera, 26% of responding orthologue pairs are shared in the bacteroid against 5% in the flavonoid response: each bacterium negotiates entry in a dialect of its own and converges on a shared end state whose amplitude, rather than content, the host modulates.

title: Flexible phosphorus allocation to the phosphoproteome underpins diatom regulatory adaptations to fluctuating phosphate supply
abstract: Diatoms are major drivers of marine phosphorus (P) cycling and are highly adapted to cope with variable P supply. P-starved diatoms can sense increases in P availability within seconds, accumulating this limiting resource through luxury polyphosphate (polyP) storage. Yet, how diatoms coordinate such responses is unknown. Protein phosphorylation is a core mechanism for environmental signal transduction in eukaryotes, but how cells balance investment in protein phosphorylation against competing physiological demands during P limitation is poorly understood. Here, we characterise system-wide remodelling of the Phaeodactylum tricornutum phosphoproteome in response to P deficiency and subsequent resupply. We identify widespread proteome dephosphorylation across 44% of phosphosites, revealing a previously unrecognised P-sparing strategy in marine phytoplankton. Following P resupply, diatoms orchestrate extensive phosphoproteome reprogramming within minutes. We characterise previously unrecognized components for early recovery from P limitation, including a novel environmentally prevalent intracellular H+/phosphate transporter strongly conserved in diverse diatoms. We also identify a vacuolar Ca2+-dependent protein kinase (CDPK) associated with polyP-storage granules. Mutant and inhibitor analyses demonstrate a role for Ca2+- and CDPK-signalling in the regulation of luxury polyP accumulation. Our findings reveal that recovery from P starvation is mediated by rapid phosphoregulatory control of intracellular P trafficking, organellar ATP generation coupled with luxury P storage, enabling diatoms to exploit newly available P and thrive in fluctuating P regimes. Collectively, our study uncovers the phosphoproteome as a flexible intracellular P reservoir and establishes mechanistic links between intracellular P budgeting, signalling and the marine P cycle.

title: Infection-dependent antibiotic response phenotypes emerge during chronic airway adaptation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Objectives Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infections can persist for years despite intensive antibiotic therapy guided by standard antimicrobial susceptibility testing. While this technique captures the emergence of resistance, it does not reproduce many features of the infection environment, where adaptation acquired during chronic infection may alter bacterial responses to antibiotics in ways that are not fully reflected by conventional susceptibility testing. Here we investigated antibiotic responses of longitudinal clinical isolates under standard laboratory conditions and in an airway epithelial infection model. Methods Six longitudinal pairs of P. aeruginosa isolates from people with cystic fibrosis were analysed. Changes in bacterial growth following exposure to tobramycin, ceftazidime and ciprofloxacin were quantified under standard laboratory conditions and compared with changes in bacterial burden after treatment measured in differentiated airway epithelial cultures maintained under air-liquid interface (ALI) conditions that reproduce key features of the airway infection environment. Representative phenotypes were visualized by confocal microscopy and interpreted in the context of available whole-genome sequencing data. Results Major resistance phenotypes identified by conventional susceptibility testing were largely reproduced in the ALI model. However, concordance between phenotypes observed under standard laboratory and ALI conditions differed between antibiotics. Several isolates classified as susceptible according to conventional susceptibility testing displayed substantial survival in the ALI model, and these discordant phenotypes were observed predominantly among those isolates recovered after prolonged airway persistence. Genomic analyses identified mutations associated with both classical resistance mechanisms and chronic adaptation. Conclusions Phenotypes observed under conventional laboratory conditions do not uniformly predict those observed in the ALI airway conditions. Discordant phenotypes were most apparent among chronically adapted isolates and varied between antibiotics, suggesting that adaptation acquired during chronic infection can alter antibiotic responses in ways that are not fully reflected by conventional susceptibility testing.
authors: Laborda, P., Cebrian-Sastre, E., La Rosa, R., Molin, S., Johansen, H. K.
