title: Coupling Complementary Pathways in a Bacterial Co-culture Enables 4-Aminophenol Removal during Paracetamol Degradation
abstract: Pharmaceutical biodegradation can generate potentially toxic metabolites that persist after the parent compound has been removed, posing additional risks to aquatic environments. Microbial co-cultures offer a promising strategy to address this challenge by combining complementary metabolic capabilities to remove both pharmaceuticals and their harmful transformation products by coupling complementary degradation pathways. Here, we investigated a two-species co-culture combining the paracetamol-degrading bacterium Delftia P1 with Microbacterium lacus to enable subsequent 4-AP removal. While Delftia P1 efficiently degraded paracetamol, it accumulated 4-AP as a dead-end metabolite. M. lacus was selected to complement this metabolic limitation because its genome contains a homolog of sadB, a monooxygenase gene involved in 4-AP transformation. The relative abundance of the two strains strongly influenced 4-AP removal, with the highest efficiency achieved at a Delftia P1:M. lacus cell-density ratio of 1:100, corresponding to an OD600nm ratio of 1:10. At this ratio, the co-culture achieved complete removal of paracetamol and 4-AP within 6 and 24 h, respectively. Its capacity was tested in wastewater, where 100% of paracetamol were removed within 4 h and no accumulation of 4-AP was observed within 24 h. These findings demonstrate the potential of cocultivating bacteria with complementary metabolic capabilities to address both pharmaceutical contamination and transformation-product accumulation. Moreover, the highest 4-AP removal was achieved when M. lacus was present at a 100-fold higher cell density than Delftia P1, highlighting the importance of considering relative cell densities when designing co-cultures.
authors: Demaria, F., Schaffter, M., Zimmardi, C., Suleiman, M., Junier, P., Corvini, P.

title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of northern dragonhead, Dracocephalum ruyschiana L., 1753
abstract: We present a chromosome-level genome assembly for the vascular plant northern dragonhead, Dracocephalum ruyschiana. The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes, hap1 and hap2, of 661 Mb and 681 Mb, with 93.6% and 92.5%, respectively, scaffolded into seven chromosomes each - in line with the known karyotype. Assembly quality was high, with conserved single-copy ortholog completeness scores of 97.9% and 97.8%, combined k-mer completeness of 98.1%, and 38,141 and 38,617 annotated protein-coding genes for hap1 and hap2, respectively. This assembly provides a high-quality genomic resource for future research and conservation of northern dragonhead, as well as the endangered northern dragonhead sap beetle, which depends on the plant for reproduction and whose genome assembly is described in a complementary genome note.

title: Systematic benchmarks reveal DNA polymerase combinations for high-quality genome assembly
abstract: Background: A fundamental challenge in biodiversity genomics is generating long-read sequencing data and high-quality genome assemblies from samples lacking gold-standard flash-frozen tissue, including ethanol-preserved specimens, minimally invasive biopsies, and small-bodied organisms. Amplification-based library preparation enables long-read sequencing of such samples, but assembly quality critically depends on the polymerase used for amplification. Results: We present a systematic benchmark of eleven long-range DNA polymerases for PacBio HiFi sequencing and genome assembly across three taxonomically diverse species: a springtail, a sea slug, and a bat. We show that polymerase choice substantially affects assembly contiguity and gene completeness, primarily caused by polymerase-intrinsic GC-dependent amplification bias and read coverage heterogeneity. Five polymerases consistently produced assemblies with comparatively high contiguity and completeness, with some enzymes outperforming the polymerase currently used in the PacBio Ampli-Fi protocol. Importantly, combining reads amplified with different polymerases frequently resulted in superior assemblies, because polymerases complement each other by covering regions where others drop out. Combining reads amplified with different polymerases, we generated haplotype-resolved assemblies of the ~1 Gb giant springtail and ~2 Gb bat genome and improved the sea slug reference genome. Using the human GIAB benchmark, we further show that optimized amplification strategies improve variant-calling accuracy, highlighting their utility in medical and clinical research. To facilitate polymerase benchmarking across additional taxa, we provide the polymeval pipeline (https://github.com/casparbein/polymeval), which automates the computational workflow. Conclusion: Our study demonstrates that optimized amplification-based HiFi sequencing generates assemblies with >1 Mb contig N50 and >90% gene completeness, providing a toolkit to produce long-read genome assemblies from challenging samples.

title: Elucidating Bat SuperImmunity: Insights from the Bent-Wing Bat Genome Assembly and Multi-Omics Analysis
abstract: Bats have evolved a range of unique adaptations, including powered flight, echolocation, and exceptional longevity. They have also attracted considerable scientific attention, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic, due to their association with a broad diversity of viruses and their potential role in zoonotic transmission and emerging infectious diseases. Despite hosting numerous viruses, bats often exhibit limited clinical manifestations of infection, suggesting the evolution of distinctive mechanisms of immune regulation and tolerance. Understanding the molecular basis of these mechanisms has become a major focus of current research, with genome-wide analyses providing important insights into the genetic adaptations underlying bat immunity. Nevertheless, the regulatory complexity of bat genomes, particularly the contribution of non-coding RNAs and post-transcriptional RNA editing, remains comparatively underexplored. Here, we present an integrated multi-omic framework for the common bent-wing bat (Miniopterus schreibersii), combining a contiguous chromosome-scale genome assembly with multi-tissue transcriptomic profiling, long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) identification and synteny analysis, endogenous viral elements (EVE) mapping, and same-individual RNA editomic analyses. This study provides a comprehensive resource for investigating genome organization, transcriptional regulation, evolutionary relationships, and post-transcriptional modifications in this species. In particular, it offers an opportunity to explore the potential contribution of non-coding regulatory elements and RNA editing to the molecular mechanisms underlying viral interactions and immune regulation in bats. Collectively, these resources provide a valuable foundation for advancing our understanding of bat genome evolution and the regulatory mechanisms potentially associated with their distinctive responses to viral infections.
authors: Herrera-Ubeda, C., Zawisza-Alvarez, M., Catalan-Rabaneda, M., Serra-Cobo, J., Garcia-Fernandez, J.

title: MicroDUET: a dual-headed genomic foundation model for pathogen surveillance
abstract: Pathogen genomic surveillance works from raw reads, assembled genomes and alignments, representations that are slow and costly to compare at scale. Compact embeddings from genomic language models offer an alternative, but surveillance requires resolving both evolutionary ancestry (phylogeny) and phenotypic capability (function) - which need not co-vary. Here we present MicroDUET, which adapts a 26.6-million-parameter ProkBERT backbone with two 3.5-million-parameter adapter heads: a phylogeny head trained contrastively on genome windows from the same microbes, and a function head trained to identify genes across taxa. On held-out retrieval benchmarks, the phylogeny head returned the correct species for 80.3% and 66.6% of cellular and viral queries, and the function head the correct gene family for 97.3% and 97.2%, reaching 74.4% accuracy on an independent antimicrobial resistance-class benchmark. Across all three benchmarks MicroDUET outranked 17 other genomic encoders. Without training on lineage, clade or drug-susceptibility tasks, MicroDUET identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis and mpox virus lineages and clades (0.965, 0.975 accuracy), discriminated rifampicin resistance without lineage adjustment (AUROC 0.985), and retrospectively identified an emerging mpox lineage as anomalous (AUROC 0.974). MicroDUET operates 10^3 - 10^4 times faster than single-threaded sequence-based alignments. MicroDUET therefore provides a compact, reusable representation for scalable pathogen surveillance and sequence triage.
authors: Barber, M., Suster, C. J. E., Lei, J., Getchell, M., Wulandari, S., Sintchenko, V., Pronyk, P. M.

title: Tropical peatland microbiomes as a One Health nexus: linking soil, plant, and climate health across land-use transitions.
abstract: The One Health framework recognizes the intrinsic connections among environmental, plant, animal and human health. While soils and soil microbes have received substantial attention in the recent years, tropical peatlands still remain largely overlooked despite representing globally important reservoirs of carbon, biodiversity, freshwater. Microorganisms are central regulators of peat accumulation, nutrient cycling, greenhouse gas exchange and ecosystem resilience, yet their role as mediators of One Health outcomes has received limited attention. Emerging evidence from tropical peatlands demonstrates that land-use change, drainage, fire and agricultural conversion substantially alter microbial community composition and function, with cascading effects on ecosystem processes. In this Perspective, peatland microbiomes are proposed as critical but neglected One Health nexus linking soil health, vegetation dynamics, wildlife habitat quality, climate regulation and human wellbeing. Considering, oil palm plantations that produce the most consumed vegetable oil in the world, cover substantial portion of tropical peatlands, tropical peat also plays a crucial role in food security and safety. The perspective argues that microbial communities should move from being considered ecological indicators to becoming policy-relevant components of peatland governance. Furthermore, incorporation of microbiome informed indicators into restoration, carbon accounting and ecosystem health frameworks is proposed as a necessity. By integrating microbial ecology with One Health principles, tropical peatlands can serve as an impactful model system for understanding how belowground biodiversity underpins ecosystem services and planetary health.
authors: Dhandapani S.

title: Beyond the membrane: the overlooked nuclear localization of the prion protein.
abstract: Although the prion protein (PrP) is best known as a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored cell surface glycoprotein lacking canonical nucleic acid-binding domains, accumulating evidence indicates that it can be localized in the cytosol and nucleus and exhibits a remarkable ability to interact with both RNA and DNA molecules. A wide range of nucleic acids have been identified as PrP interactors, including cellular and viral RNAs, genomic and mitochondrial DNA, as well as highly structured nucleic acid motifs. For instance, G-quadruplexes and DNA hairpin aptamers, often display particularly high affinity for PrP. These observations suggest that PrP's nucleic acid binding property is a potentially overlooked part of PrP biology, with possible implications for its physiological functions and pathological roles, including the formation of biomolecular condensates. While such condensates might participate in the spatiotemporal organization of PrP biological activities, their aging into less dynamic, gel- or solid-like assemblies could also contribute to pathological protein aggregation linked to prion disease pathogenesis. Herein, we review the literature about nuclear-associated PrP and discuss its molecular features relevant to nucleic-acid binding. Furthermore, we argue that PrP might harbor previously underappreciated nuclear functions as supported by microscopy and biochemical evidence reporting intranuclear and perinuclear PrP. We propose that this understudied nuclear localization of PrP might stem from the historical focus on membrane-associated PrP, and we call for renewed attention to its potential nuclear activities.
authors: Juliani Do Amaral M, Freire MH, Rodrigues MPMD, Cordeiro Y.

title: Unveiling novel therapeutic targets and potent hits to combat antimicrobial resistance in Bacteroides fragilis.
abstract: The opportunistic anaerobic bacterium Bacteroides fragilis is an important human pathogen associated with a variety of infections, including intra-abdominal abscesses, peritonitis, bacteremia, lung abscesses and surgical site infections. The growing number of strains that are multidrug-resistant (MDR) in B. fragilis has raised attention to identify new therapeutic targets and discover potent antimicrobial drugs. An integrative computational approach was used in this study to highlight promising inhibitors against B. fragilis and identify potential therapeutic targets. The present study identified 18 essential proteins from the B. fragilis proteome that contribute to virulence and pathogenicity and play critical roles in bacterial survival. Furthermore, protein-protein interactions (PPI's) network analysis, functional annotation, and enrichment analyses identified tetraacyldisaccharide 4'-kinase (LpxK) as the most promising druggable target, owing to its essential role in lipopolysaccharide (LPS) biosynthesis in Gram-negative bacteria. Structure-guided drug design identified five high-affinity LpxK inhibitors. DFT and molecular dynamics analyses confirmed stable binding and conformational stability. Furthermore, these findings provide a theoretical basis for the rational development of targeted antibacterial agents against multidrug-resistant B. fragilis towards infectious disease control, and lay the foundation for future experimental evaluation and optimization.
authors: Sureshan M, Vundavalli DS, Sanjay A, Srikanth S, Ulaganathan V, Mani U, Dhanaraj P, Trivedi RK.

title: Shared host-genetic architecture between gut microbiota and internalizing psychopathology.
abstract: It is unknown whether gut microbial composition causally influences mental illness. Using genetic variants as instruments (Mendelian randomization, MR), we tested the genetically predicted effects of 211 gut microbial taxa on nine psychiatric and psychopathology-related phenotypes. Of 1,898 valid tests, seven taxon-outcome associations (five clades) passed false-discovery-rate correction (FDR < 0.05). All involved depression, neuroticism or insomnia, the three most precisely estimated outcomes. The strongest, a protective association of the Mollicutes/Tenericutes clade with depression (odds ratio 0.93 per SD of log-abundance, p = 1.5 × 10-6), survived every multiple-testing correction. The associations persisted with weak-instrument-robust estimators, stricter instrument selection and leave-one-out analysis, and reverse-direction MR found no effect of psychiatric liability on these taxa. In independent samples, the depression association had the same direction but was weaker and non-significant (one-sided p = 0.13), and the neuroticism and insomnia associations, tested with limited power, did not replicate. Bayesian colocalization (posterior probability of a shared variant < 0.05 at every locus) and CAUSE (0 of 45 pairs causal) did not support causation at individual loci. In factor-level MR within a Genomic SEM model, Mollicutes/Tenericutes was associated with a latent internalizing factor, and Butyrivibrio and Negativicutes/Selenomonadales with internalizing-specific variance beyond a general psychopathology factor. Psychotic-factor estimates were null but imprecise, and specificity relative to less well-powered phenotypes remains unresolved. Selected gut taxa and internalizing psychopathology appear to share host-genetic influences, and the evidence does not support direct effects of these taxa on the disorders.
authors: Velez-Pardo P, Solano RJ, Quinchia-Figueroa AM, Montoya Monsalve R, Moratto-Vasquez NS.

title: From qualitative to quantitative: Real-Time HSV kinetics enable smartphone-based multiplex LAMP for microbial source tracking.
abstract: Identifying the source of fecal contamination in the field requires assays that are multiplexed, quantitative, and portable-capabilities that current colorimetric isothermal assays do not yet offer in combination. Here, we present a smartphone-integrated multiplex loop-mediated isothermal amplification (mLAMP) platform that combines a primer-immobilized polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) microwell chip with real-time hue-saturation-value (HSV) image analysis for quantitative detection of five microbial targets, including Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, Salmonella typhimurium, and human- and dog-associated Bacteroidales markers. Instead of conventional endpoint RGB analysis, the platform continuously monitors colorimetric amplification and derives an Amplification Signal Threshold (AST) from the kinetic HSV profile for objective quantification. Spatial separation of lyophilized primer sets in individual microwells minimizes primer interference while enabling simultaneous multiplex detection on a single chip. Using plasmid DNA standards, AST-based calibration spanned input pDNA concentrations from 106 to 1 copy/μL, with positive amplification detected at an input concentration of 1 copy/μL (corresponding to 0.4 expected copies per microwell) for selected targets. HSV-mLAMP estimates were consistent with quantitative PCR (Pearson's r = 0.977). The portable system successfully detected fecal indicator bacteria and microbial source tracking markers across multiple environmental matrices, demonstrating its applicability for rapid, field-deployable multiplex microbial monitoring and source tracking.
authors: Li L, Bae S.

title: HiEGP: An environment-informed genomic prediction framework that facilitates soybean genebank germplasm evaluation and climate-smart breeding.
abstract: The biodiversity preserved in gene banks drives crop improvement and strengthens climate resilience for feeding the future. However, only a limited fraction of germplasm has been well characterized, because phenotyping remains low-throughput and costly, especially for region-specific yield-related traits. This gap hinders the utilization of gene bank biodiversity in breeding, particularly for photoperiod and temperature-sensitive crops like soybean. Here, we constructed a multi-environment soybean dataset integrating phenotypes, genotypes, and environmental covariates for 1,421 diverse soybean germplasm accessions. It includes six key breeding traits collected across nine locations (latitudes 28.53°-45.64°), along with bioclimatic and soil data. We developed HiEGP (High-dimensional Environmental Factor Integration for Genomic Prediction), a feature-engineered hierarchical G×E prediction framework that integrates environmental main effects, genotype-specific environmental responses, genomic background, and environmental similarity. HiEGP achieved high predictive performance under both validation settings, reaching average trait-wise pooled correlations of 0.871 for predicting untested genotypes in observed environments and 0.775 for predicting untested genotypes in unobserved environments, outperforming the evaluated methods overall. In the external USDA soybean panel, HiEGP showed stable prediction for 100-seed weight, with environment-wise correlations ranging from 0.70 to 0.81. HiEGP enabled environment-response genome-wide association studies, recovering known maturity loci and identifying 175 candidate regions associated with environmental-response patterns. Phenotypic evidence from ethyl methanesulfonate mutants supported the prioritization of selected candidate genes. HiEGP supported regional adaptation assessment under the observed environmental conditions. This capability offers a scalable strategy to improve the characterization and breeding use of underexplored gene bank germplasm for environment-informed soybean breeding.
authors: Che Y, Li H, Jin X, Zhao C, Wang Q, Qiu H, Huang W, Zhao Q, Liu L, Wang X, Xing G, Hu G, Guo S, Shuang L, Hawkesford MJ, Varshney RK, Hoogenboom G, Li YH, Qiu LJ.

title: Multimodal Integration Identifies C16orf74 as an EMT Regulator With Prognostic Relevance in HNSCC.
abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is an aggressive malignancy characterized by marked intratumoral heterogeneity and poor clinical outcomes. Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) promotes metastasis, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance. However, the key molecular determinants underlying EMT-associated malignant states remain incompletely defined, and their translation into clinically accessible tools is challenging. In this study, we performed an integrative multiomics analysis to dissect malignant epithelial heterogeneity in HNSCC. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) identified a highly malignant EMT epithelial subpopulation characterized by elevated genomic instability and terminal malignant states. Furthermore, an ensemble of machine learning algorithms prioritized C16orf74 as a key EMT-associated malignant regulator. Spatial transcriptomics localized C16orf74 spatially concentrated at invasive-front and transitory regions associated with distinct tumor microenvironmental niches. Gain- and loss-of-function assays confirmed that C16orf74 regulates EMT activation, migration, invasion, and tumor-sphere formation in HNSCC cells. Mechanistically, integrative regulon, transcriptomic, spatial, and functional analyses identified high-mobility group AT-hook 2 (HMGA2) as a candidate downstream mediator of C16orf74-associated EMT. To translate these biological insights into clinical practice, we developed an EMT-based pathomics prognostic model using hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images, which achieved robust prognostic stratification. Notably, high-risk group interpretably exhibited a positive correlation with C16orf74 expression, EMT enrichment, an immunosuppressive microenvironment, and resistance to standard chemotherapeutic agents. Collectively, our findings identify C16orf74 as a putative EMT regulator and develop a clinically accessible pathomics model for prognostic and therapeutic stratification in HNSCC.
authors: Huang Z, Anzai T, Lu J, Fukawa Y, Ushio A, Ishimaru N, Podyma-Inoue KA, Watabe T.

title: A Python GUI for integrated regional analysis of GWAS-identified QTLs.
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify genomic regions associated with complex traits, but interpreting these regions requires further analysis of local linkage disequilibrium (LD), marker-trait relationships and multilocus genotype patterns. In this study, a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) was developed to integrate regional post-GWAS analyses and provide a button-driven alternative to command-line workflows. The platform includes PLINK-based regional marker extraction, LD calculation, LD decay visualisation, exploratory regional SNP-trait analysis, candidate LD region detection, graph-based LD clustering and pairwise genotype-combination analysis. As a proof of concept, the workflow was applied to publicly available genotype data from the Bengal and Assam Aus Panel and grain iron (Fe) concentration data from the same population. The analysis focused on a previously reported quantitative trait locus (QTL) located at approximately 29.28 megabase pairs (Mbp) on rice chromosome 7, near the candidate gene nicotianamine synthase 3 (OsNAS3). The GUI extracted 4894 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) from a 1-Mbp interval and generated 11,973,171 pairwise LD comparisons. Exploratory regional SNP-trait analysis evaluated 4448 eligible SNPs. Because the GUI screening procedure did not account for population structure or relatedness, the regional SNPs were additionally evaluated using a mixed linear model incorporating five genome-wide principal components and a genomic kinship matrix. The adjusted analysis identified 133 Bonferroni-significant and 1635 Benjamini-Hochberg-significant SNPs, including marginal adjusted signals within the genomic neighbourhood of OsNAS3. At the specified clumping parameters, all 133 Bonferroni-significant SNPs were assigned to a single clump indexed by SNP 7:29285763, and no residual association remained significant after conditioning on this lead marker and correcting for multiple testing. Among 43,639 SNP pairs separated by no more than 1000 base pairs (bp), 22,952 had r2 ≥ 0.6. These strong-LD pairs were summarised as 116 candidate LD regions using interval-based aggregation and 339 graph-based LD clusters using connected-components analysis. Of the 22,952 strong-LD SNP pairs, 21,646 met the genotype-call eligibility criteria for pairwise genotype-combination analysis. Although exploratory pairwise analysis of variance (ANOVA) identified numerous corrected genotype-phenotype differences, nested-model comparisons provided no corrected evidence that any two-locus genotype combination explained additional phenotypic variation beyond its better constituent single-marker model. These findings reflect the extensive LD within the selected QTL interval and represent regional prioritisation rather than identification of causal variants. Overall, the GUI provides a reproducible framework for characterising GWAS-derived QTL intervals, regional LD patterns and genotype-phenotype relationships. Its broader applicability should be further evaluated using additional traits, populations, genomic regions and organisms with compatible PLINK genotype data.
authors: Talukdar P, Martin M.

title: Natural Variation in ZmASB1 Links Tryptophan Metabolism to Root Growth and Drought Tolerance in Maize.
abstract: Root amino acid metabolism is important for maize adaptation to water deficit, but the genetic mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. We profiled 18 free amino acids in the roots of 192 diverse maize inbred lines and integrated genome-wide association analyses with root transcriptome data. This approach identified 118 metabolite QTLs and prioritized ZmASB1, which encodes the β-subunit of anthranilate synthase, as a candidate regulator of tryptophan (Trp) accumulation. A cis-regulatory locus in the ZmASB1 promoter was associated with variation in ZmASB1 expression and root Trp abundance. Functional analyses indicated that ZmASB1 promotes Trp accumulation and root growth through Trp-dependent auxin biosynthesis. ZmASB1-overexpressing lines showed enhanced root development and drought tolerance, whereas the mutant exhibited the opposite phenotypes. Exogenous Trp or auxin partially rescued the root-growth and drought-sensitive phenotypes of the mutant. We identified a 5-bp insertion/deletion (InDel-178) in the ZmASB1 promoter that affects promoter activity by altering the binding of the transcription factor ZmDOF17. The favorable ZmASB1InDel+ allele was enriched in modern maize inbred lines relative to teosinte and landraces. Together, these findings identify a natural cis-regulatory mechanism controlling ZmASB1 expression and support a ZmASB1-tryptophan-auxin module that contributes to root development and drought responses in maize seedlings.
authors: Yang X, Wang H, Zhang X, Wang Y, Tian Y, Wang B, Zhu T, Fang S, Li W, Rui W, Zhang Y, Sun D, Gao H, Li Y, Jia Z, Yang Z, Xu C, Li P.

title: SadA gene copy number variation and subtype-associated sulfonamide transformation in Paenarthrobacter sp. R1: insights from multi-omics and molecular dynamics.
abstract: Microbial degradation is crucial for eliminating sulfonamide antibiotics (SAs) from environments, yet the contributions of gene copy number and subtype diversity to SA transformation remain unclear. Here, we characterize Paenarthrobacter strain R1, a hyper-degrader exhibiting rapid, broad-spectrum SA biotransformation. Genomic analysis revealed an expanded sadA repertoire comprising six copies (one Type I and five Type II), suggesting a potential gene dosage effect on SA degradation. Transcriptomic analysis revealed preferential induction of Type II-associated sad genes during sulfamethoxazole transformation, with little or no induction of Type I-associated genes. Heterologous co-expression assays revealed distinct subtype-associated transformation profiles. The Type II strain rapidly transformed sulfamethoxazole and sulfadiazine, whereas the Type III strain, carrying a variant from another SA-degrading Paenarthrobacter strain, achieved more extensive sulfamethazine transformation. In contrast, the Type I strain showed no significant SA transformation under the tested conditions. Molecular dynamics simulations and free-energy calculations suggested that differences in SA transformation may be associated with the precise spatial alignment of substrates relative to the FMN cofactor, rather than merely overall predicted binding affinity. Type II and Type III variants exhibited distinct residue-interaction networks involving polar anchoring and hydrophobic confinement that may favor catalytically relevant substrate geometries for specific SAs. Conversely, Type I exhibited greater conformational fluctuations, potentially affecting productive substrate positioning. This study integrates multi-omics and structural dynamics to propose a biotransformation model highlighting the potential contributions of sadA copy number, subtype diversity, and structural determinants to substrate-dependent SA degradation.
authors: Chen J, Guo Y, Zhan Y, Liu J, Lin Y, Zhang Y, Xie S, Qian Q.

title: Outdoor-aging of biodegradable mulch film alters humification and microbial assembly during swine manure composting: A trade-off between carbon provision and microbial selection.
abstract: Biodegradable mulch films (bio-MFs) have been promoted as alternatives to polyethylene (PE) films, but their behavior during co-composting with livestock manure remains poorly understood. In this study, swine manure was co-composted with outdoor-aging bio-MFs, non-aging bio-MFs, and aging PE-MFs. Outdoor aging disrupted the polymer structure of the bio-MFs. The aging bio-MF treatment showed a lower final dissolved organic carbon (DOC) content (10.63 g kg-1) than the PE-MF treatment (16.52 g kg-1), and both BM and NBM reached comparable final germination indices (96.46% and 95.98%). This response coincided with the early enrichment of low-molecular-weight UVA humic-like C4 (114.70 R.U. on day 2). Microbial analysis showed that aging bio-MFs were associated with stronger synergistic interactions among bacterial phyla involved in organic matter degradation. Non-aging bio-MFs were associated with stronger microbial selection, as indicated by a higher relative abundance (RA) of Firmicutes in NBM (78.15%) than in CK (20.70%) and BM (19.80%), and a 3.64- to 4.95-fold lower Proteobacteria RA in NBM (7.80%) than in BM (28.37%), CK (37.19%), and PEM (38.63%) at the end of the composting. These contrasting responses indicate a trade-off between carbon provision and microbial selection. These results show that outdoor aging was associated with mature compost quality and may be a promising pretreatment for bio-MF co-composting.
authors: Ren J, Chen Z, Yun Z, Si M, Wen Q.

title: Tumor-mimicking brain parenchymal granuloma with molecular detection of Mycobacterium xenopi by metagenomic sequencing and targeted PCR: a case report.
abstract: Central nervous system infection caused by Mycobacterium xenopi is exceptionally rare and may mimic intracranial neoplasia. A 60-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes presented with progressive headache and left homonymous hemianopia. Magnetic resonance imaging showed an irregularly enhancing right occipital mass-like lesion with marked edema and tumor-like magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Stereotactic biopsy demonstrated chronic granulomatous inflammation without neoplasia; periodic acid-Schiff, Gomori methenamine silver, and acid-fast stains were negative. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing of sterile, unfixed lesional brain tissue detected 2347 species-specific reads assigned to M. xenopi, with a negative laboratory control. Targeted mycobacterial PCR performed during the diagnostic work-up on remaining biopsy-derived brain tissue was also reported positive for M. xenopi, providing concordant molecular support. Because tissue was limited, no separate specimen was submitted for culture or susceptibility testing. The patient received oral rifampicin, ethambutol, clarithromycin, and moxifloxacin. Headache resolved within 2 weeks, bedside visual-field assessment suggested partial improvement, and available records documented treatment for more than 6 months without clinically apparent adverse events. One-year non-contrast computed tomography showed right occipital encephalomalacic evolution without an obvious persistent mass-like lesion or mass effect. This case highlights the value of tissue-based molecular testing in tumor-mimicking central nervous system granulomas when conventional staining is nondiagnostic, while underscoring the continuing importance of culture, susceptibility testing, and prolonged objective follow-up.
journal: Journal of infection and chemotherapy : official journal of the Japan Society of Chemotherapy
authors: Luo Y, Chen J, Ye F, Zhang M, Zhang Y, Zhan Z, He Y, Zhu Z.

title: Recent advances in the molecular pathogenesis of Epstein-Barr virus-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a major etiologic factor in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Although persistent latent EBV infection has traditionally been viewed as central to NPC carcinogenesis, recent evidence has broadened our understanding of the dynamic interactions between EBV and host cells. Host genetic and epigenetic alterations may precede EBV infection, establishing a cellular environment permissive for viral persistence. Within this permissive context, latent EBV gene products activate oncogenic signaling, with their effects further reinforced by genomic instability and epigenetic reprogramming. This evolving evidence has also challenged the conventional view that EBV in NPC is predominantly restricted to a latent state. Abortive or partial lytic infection may coexist with latency and contribute to malignant phenotypes, while emerging evidence indicates that productive viral replication can occur in a subset of NPC cells and clinical tumors. In parallel, advances in genomic, epigenomic, single-cell, and spatial technologies have uncovered additional mechanisms, including EBNA1-mediated chromosomal instability, EBV-induced three-dimensional chromatin reorganization, and intricate interactions between EBV-infected tumor cells and the immune microenvironment. Collectively, these findings support a dynamic model in which host susceptibility, evolving EBV infection states, and subsequent genomic, epigenomic, and immune remodeling interact to shape NPC development and progression. This review synthesizes recent advances in the molecular pathogenesis of EBV-associated NPC, with particular emphasis on epigenetic reprogramming and the emerging contribution of EBV lytic infection.
authors: Kondo S, Dochi H, Komura S, Nakagawa T, Kawasaki H, Hirai N, Kano M, Mizokami H, Matsumura K, Uno D, Ogawa M, Endo K, Misawa K, Kaneda A, Yoshizaki T.

title: Acquired antimicrobial resistance in clinical and hospital-environment isolates in onco-haematology: Detection of blaVIM-4/blaPER-1 in Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and aac(6')-Ib-cr/sul2/dfrA1 in Burkholderia cepacia.
abstract: AimsStenotrophomonas maltophilia and Burkholderia cepacia are opportunistic saprophytic bacteria that have emerged as important pathogens in immunocompromised patients. The objective of this study was to characterize antimicrobial resistance determinants in clinical and environmental isolates of S. maltophilia and B. cepacia and to assess their potential clinical relevance.Methods and resultsA total of 71 clinical isolates of S. maltophilia and B. cepacia, collected between 2018 and 2022, and 25 environmental isolates collected in 2023, were identified using the Analytical Profile Index 20NE (API 20NE). Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed by the disc diffusion method and the Epsilometer test (E-test). The double-disc synergy test screened for extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) activity; resistance genes were detected by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and the genetic context of blaVIM-4 was investigated by whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A total of 51 S. maltophilia and 12 B. cepacia strains were resistant to at least one antibiotic. An ESBL phenotype was detected in 34 S. maltophilia and six B. cepacia strains. We report the detection of blaVIM-4 and blaPER-1 in S. maltophilia, and of aac(6')-Ib-cr, sul2, and dfrA1 in B. cepacia. Genomic analysis suggested a probable chromosomal location of blaVIM-4 within a class 1 integron, alongside aac(6')-II, dfrA1, and sul1, flanked by TnpR- and TnpA-family transposases, in an ST78 S. maltophilia strain.ConclusionsAlthough the S. maltophilia species is intrinsically resistant to carbapenems, the detection of blaVIM-4 highlights the importance of further investigation to study the potential mobilization and horizontal transfer of this gene to susceptible species in clinical settings.
authors: Mohamedhen Vall M, Frigui S, Raddaoui A, Ammeri RW, Chebbi Y, Achour W.

title: Protocol for the production of high-yielded research-grade AAV vectors in transiently transfected HEK293T cells.
abstract: Adeno-associated vector is a platform of choice for delivering genome-editing toolkits, due to its transient and robust expression. Here, we present a protocol for viral production for in vivo use. We describe steps for transfecting producer cells, harvesting virus, and purifying/concentrating viral particles. We then detail procedures for estimating viral titers. This protocol ensures high viral yields and transduction competency and is scalable to meet user-customized production needs. For complete details on the use of this protocol, please refer to Kantor et al.1.
authors: Duke L, Kantor B.

title: Identification and characterization of a divergent reptarenavirus in an Amazon coral snake (Micrurus spixii [Wagler, 1824]).
abstract: Reptarenaviruses are viruses belonging to the genus Reptarenavirus within the family Arenaviridae, which infect snakes and cause inclusion body disease (IBD), a fatal condition characterized by behavioral abnormalities and wasting. Although many reptarenaviruses have been identified thus far, the phylogenetic gaps between reptarenaviruses and the other arenaviruses suggest the existence of yet-to-be-identified reptarenaviruses filling the gaps. In this study, we identified a reptarenavirus from publicly available RNA-seq data derived from an Amazon coral snake (Micrurus spixii) and tentatively named it Amazon coral snake virus 1 (ACSV-1). We identified four ACSV-1 contigs containing the putative full-length open reading frames of the NP, GP, and L genes, as well as the partial Z gene. Phylogenetic analyses showed that ACSV-1 is highly divergent from reptarenaviruses assignable to currently recognized species. The NP, GP, and L genes showed maximum nucleotide sequence identities of 45.7%, 37.7%, and 43.0%, respectively, to these viruses. Based on the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) species demarcation criteria, ACSV-1 can be assigned to a novel species of virus within the genus Reptarenavirus. This study expands our understanding of the diversity and evolution of reptarenaviruses.
authors: Onishi A, Kishimoto M, Horie M.

title: Mechanistic Study of the Role of Obesity and Muscle Strength Factors in Recurrent Patellar Dislocation Based on Multi-Omics Data.
abstract: BackgroundRecurrent patellar dislocation (RPD) is primarily associated with anatomical predisposition, but obesity-related and muscle-related traits may modify susceptibility and clinical consequences. This study used Mendelian randomization (MR) together with genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and single-cell data to investigate the relationships of obesity- and muscle-related traits with RPD and to explore candidate molecular signals.MethodsBidirectional MR analysis was performed to assess the relationships between RPD and obesity-related traits (birth weight, childhood BMI, body fat percentage) and muscle-related traits (hand grip strength, walking speed, appendicular lean mass). Summary-data-based MR (SMR), proteomic data, and single-cell sequencing data were subsequently integrated to prioritize and characterize candidate molecular factors associated with RPD.ResultsGenetically predicted birth weight, childhood BMI, and body fat percentage were associated with increased susceptibility to RPD, whereas the muscle-related traits examined were not associated with increased RPD risk. Reverse MR suggested that RPD was associated with reduced walking speed and appendicular lean mass and increased body fat percentage. SMR enrichment highlighted lipid metabolism-related processes, and integration with rat proteomics prioritized DBI. Single-cell analysis indicated that DBI may contribute to RPD by affecting tenocyte function.ConclusionGenetically predicted obesity-related traits, particularly childhood BMI and body fat percentage, may increase susceptibility to RPD, although established anatomical abnormalities remain the primary determinants of recurrent patellar instability. DBI was identified as a candidate molecular factor associated with RPD, but its biological and therapeutic relevance requires further functional and clinical validation.
authors: Shi W, Li Z, Wu M, Liu S, Chen H.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of CHMP4C in colorectal cancer: associations with Genomic instability and the tumor microenvironment.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is shaped by complex genomic and tumor microenvironmental interactions. Charged multivesicular body protein 4 C (CHMP4C), a core ESCRT-III component involved in cytokinetic abscission and vesicular trafficking, has been implicated in chromosomal stability and cancer biology, but its relevance to CRC remains incompletely understood. We integrated cBioPortal genomic analyses, TCGA-COAD transcriptomic data, pathway and enrichment analyses, immune/stromal deconvolution, public proteomic datasets, and experimental validation in CRC specimens. CHMP4C alterations, predominantly amplifications and copy-number gains, were significantly enriched in chromosomal-instability categories, particularly CIN-HR and CIN-LR, and were comparatively uncommon in hypermutated tumors. Although altered tumors showed a directional representation within MSS and pMMR categories, neither MMR nor MSI status was significantly associated with CHMP4C alterations after multiple-testing correction. Higher CHMP4C expression was associated with reduced immune and stromal representation and an immune-excluded transcriptional phenotype. Pathway analyses placed CHMP4C within modules related to ESCRT-dependent cytokinetic regulation, endosomal remodeling, vesicular trafficking, and regulated cell-death processes. Proteomic findings were not uniformly concordant across independent datasets, whereas experimental analysis confirmed elevated CHMP4C expression in CRC tissue. CHMP4C alteration status was not consistently associated with conventional survival outcomes. CHMP4C alterations are associated with an amplification-enriched, CIN-associated genomic context, while elevated CHMP4C expression is associated with reduced immune and stromal representation. These findings support CHMP4C as a candidate marker of CIN-associated CRC biology and a hypothesis-generating link between genomic instability and immune exclusion. Functional and spatial studies and larger molecularly stratified cohorts are required to establish its mechanistic and clinical significance.
authors: Shaghaghi Shahr R, Hoseini SM, Nematollahi A, Salimzadeh J, Mazaheri M.

title: An overview of grapevine trunk disease pathogens newly reported in Montenegro.
abstract: Grapevine trunk diseases (GTDs) represent an increasing problem in viticulture worldwide; however, their etiology in Montenegro has so far remained largely unexplored, and symptoms have traditionally been attributed solely to esca. During surveys conducted in 15 vineyards comprising multiple grapevine cultivars, typical esca symptoms as well as other GTDs-associated symptoms were recorded. A total of 319 fungal isolates were obtained and grouped into 13 morphotypes, from which 20 representative isolates were selected for preliminary molecular identification.The isolates belonged to 15 genera commonly associated with GTDs. Nine isolates were identified to the species level based on morphological characteristics and multilocus phylogenetic analyses (ITS, LSU, act, tub2, tef1a, rpb2, cal, and his). For the first time in Montenegro, the association of Cadophora luteo-olivacea, Diaporthe eres, Seimatosporium vitis viniferae, and four Botryosphaeriaceae species (Botryosphaeria sp., Diplodia mutila, Diplodia seriata, and Neofusicoccum parvum species complex) with grapevine trunk diseases is reported. In addition, Biscogniauxia mediterranea is reported for the first time in Europe in association with grapevine disease symptoms. Pathogenicity tests confirmed the ability of selected isolates to induce necrotic lesions, with varying levels of aggressiveness. The frequent presence of multiple pathogens within the same trunk indicates possible co-infections contributing to symptom expression. This study represents the first comprehensive overview of GTDs fungi in Montenegro and expands existing knowledge of this disease complex in southeastern Europe.
authors: Kandic B, Mondello V, Latinovic J, Fontaine F, Latinovic N.

title: Porphyromonas gingivalis TonB2 is required for protease maturation and cell surface remodeling.
abstract: TonB-dependent transport systems are essential for nutrient acquisition in Gram-negative bacteria. Although Porphyromonas gingivalis, a major periodontal pathogen, encodes multiple TonB-dependent receptors (TBDT), the identity and function of its TonB energy transducers remain poorly understood. Here, we identified three putative TonB proteins encoded by PG0633 (TonB1), PG0785 (TonB2), and PG2185 (TonB3), and generated a TonB2-deficient strain to investigate its biological role. Bioinformatics analyses revealed that TonB2 possesses unique structural features conserved within members of the Cytophaga-Flavobacterium-Bacteroides (CFB) group while retaining a C-terminal domain homologous to well-characterized TonB proteins from Helicobacter pylori and Escherichia coli. Both protein sequence similarity and genomic organization further support the conservation of TonB2 among members of the phylum Bacteroidota. Loss of TonB2 resulted in extensive proteomic remodeling, including increased abundance of proteins involved in gene regulation, translation, protection against oxidative and nitrosative stress, and glycosylation, accompanied by decreased levels of proteins associated with polysaccharide export, efflux systems, and lipoprotein biogenesis. Phenotypic analyses demonstrated that the TonB2-deficient mutant was impaired in heme accumulation at the cell surface, exhibited reduced gingipain activity, and displayed diminished capsule production. Furthermore, although the mutant adhered to and invaded host cells more efficiently than the wild type, its intracellular survival was significantly compromised. Collectively, these findings reveal an unexpected role for TonB2 in cell surface biogenesis, virulence-associated functions, and host-pathogen interactions, expanding our understanding of TonB system versatility and suggesting functional crosstalk between the TonB and Tol energy transduction systems.ImportanceThe TonB system is a major energy-transducing complex in Gram-negative bacteria, but its functions outside classical nutrient acquisition remain poorly understood, particularly in the phylum Bacteroidota. Here, we show that Porphyromonas gingivalis TonB2 plays a role distinct from canonical TonB-dependent transport. Rather than primarily supporting iron uptake, TonB2 contributes to gingipain maturation, capsule production, cell surface organization, and interactions with host cells. These diverse phenotypes suggest a broader role in coordinating cell envelope biogenesis and integrity. We propose that TonB2 has been adapted to couple energy transduction with envelope maintenance, revealing an unexpected functional diversification of TonB proteins that supports virulence and cellular homeostasis.
authors: Rostami S, Belvin BR, Lewis JP.

title: APOBEC3 antagonism fully explains HIV-1 Vif essentiality in THP-1 cells under interferon and differentiation conditions.
abstract: HIV-1 virion infectivity factor (Vif) counteracts APOBEC3 (A3) proteins by targeting them for proteasomal degradation, thereby preventing lethal G-to-A mutations and loss of infectivity. However, Vif also degrades additional cellular proteins, raising the possibility that its essential role in infectious virion production may extend beyond A3 antagonism, particularly under inflammatory or differentiation conditions. Whether such conditions reveal additional essential Vif targets remains unresolved. Here, using interferon (IFN)-stimulated or phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA)-differentiated THP-1 monocytic cells, we directly addressed this question. Although type I IFN and PMA markedly suppressed viral production through Vif-independent mechanisms, ΔVif viruses produced from stimulated parental cells exhibited severely reduced infectivity. In contrast, disruption of A3A-A3G fully restored ΔVif infectivity to wild-type levels under all conditions tested. G-to-A mutations were attributable exclusively to A3 proteins under both IFN and PMA stimulation, whereas IFN-induced, A3-independent blocks to reverse transcription were not antagonized by Vif. Moreover, Vif-mediated degradation of the non-A3 targets PPP2R5 family proteins did not measurably contribute to virion infectivity under these conditions. Across diverse HIV-1 strains, the requirement for Vif in this experimental system was strictly dependent on A3 family proteins. These findings indicate that, under the conditions examined here, the essential role of Vif is fully explained by antagonism of A3-mediated restriction. Our results further suggest that counteracting A3-mediated restriction and mutagenesis represents a major evolutionary pressure shaping Vif.IMPORTANCEA3 proteins are potent intrinsic antiviral factors that restrict HIV-1 by inducing lethal mutations and impairing reverse transcription. The viral protein Vif counteracts A3-mediated restriction, yet it also targets additional host proteins, raising questions about whether its essential role extends beyond A3 antagonism under inflammatory conditions. Myeloid cells mount interferon (IFN) responses and undergo transcriptional reprogramming upon differentiation, environments in which additional Vif functions could emerge. Using an A3A-A3G-null monocytic cell model, we show that even under IFN stimulation or phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA)-induced differentiation, the requirement for Vif in maintaining HIV-1 infectivity is due to A3 proteins. In contrast, Vif does not counteract IFN-induced, A3-independent restriction pathways, highlighting functional specificity. These findings establish the A3-Vif axis as the central determinant of Vif dependency and suggest that counteracting A3-mediated restriction and mutagenesis represents a major evolutionary pressure shaping Vif. Targeting Vif may therefore expose HIV-1 to intrinsic inactivation, even in inflammatory environments.
authors: Shimizu R, Jonathan M, Terasawa H, Saito A, Monde K, Ikeda T.

title: Integrative Transcriptome- and Proteome-Wide Analyses Prioritize Candidate Genes for Eczema Susceptibility.
abstract: Eczema is a common inflammatory skin disease. Although genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified multiple eczema susceptibility loci, the underlying effector genes and molecular contexts remain incompletely resolved. This study aimed to integrate transcriptomic and proteomic reference resources to prioritize candidate genes with cross-panel molecular support. Primary discovery combined cross-tissue transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) using the sparse canonical correlation analysis-aggregated Cauchy association test (sCCA-ACAT) with single-tissue TWAS across 49 Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) v8 tissues. Candidates were further evaluated using whole-blood and adipose TWAS, brain proteome-wide association study (PWAS), and exploratory PWAS with brain proteomic prediction weights derived separately from male and female reference samples. Summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), heterogeneity in dependent instruments (HEIDI) testing, and blood expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) colocalization were used for genetic prioritization. Cross-tissue and single-tissue TWAS identified 50 and 164 genes, respectively, at a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05. Of the 35 overlapping genes, 16 were retained after conditional and joint analysis. Integration with peripheral TWAS and brain PWAS prioritized LIME1 and TRAF3. LIME1 showed significant but oppositely signed associations in whole-blood TWAS and brain PWAS, whereas TRAF3 showed support in adipose TWAS and brain PWAS, together with SMR and blood-eQTL colocalization support. PWAS using male-derived brain proteomic weights additionally identified ASTN2. Overall, TRAF3 showed the most complete evidence profile, whereas LIME1 remained a cross-panel candidate with discordant association directions. These analyses provide gene-prioritization evidence.
authors: Zhang K, Wang Y.

title: Impact of Ruminococcus gnavus on lipid metabolism via isoCDCA.
abstract: The gut microbiota is increasingly recognized as a regulator of host lipid metabolism, yet the specific strains and effector metabolites driving hyperlipidemia remain poorly defined. Here, we identified Ruminococcus gnavus (R. gnavus) as a candidate contributor to cholesterol-related dyslipidemia and delineated its metabolic mechanism. Comparing individuals with high versus normal TC/LDL-C (HTL vs NTL) in both normal-weight and overweight populations, we found that fecal R. gnavus was enriched in HTL individuals regardless of BMI stratum, a finding validated by species-specific qPCR in an independent cohort (n = 488). Administering R. gnavus to mice fed a normal or high-fat diet induced alterations in circulating lipids and liver function markers, accompanied by hepatic steatosis. Hepatic transcriptomics and targeted bile acid profiling converged on bile acid metabolism: R. gnavus downregulated key hepatic genes (Cyp7a1, Cyp8b1, Ldlr, and Ppara) and elevated isochenodeoxycholic acid (isoCDCA) levels both in vivo and in vitro. In vitro, R. gnavus directly converted chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) to isoCDCA. Clinically, serum isoCDCA was elevated in HTL individuals in an independent cohort (n = 1,137) and was positively associated with TC, TG, and LDL-C. Functionally, oral isoCDCA supplementation reproduced key lipid disturbances in mice, and isoCDCA downregulated lipid metabolism genes and promoted lipid accumulation in hepatocytes; heterologous expression of R. gnavus hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases conferred isoCDCA-producing capacity on E. coli and elevated circulating TC and LDL-C in colonized mice. These findings nominate isoCDCA as a microbial effector metabolite linking R. gnavus to hepatic lipid dysregulation and identify the R. gnavus-isoCDCA axis as a potential target for the prevention and treatment of hyperlipidemia.
authors: Peng YL, Xiao YY, Yin SJ, Zhou HH, Zhang W, Zhu P, Li Q.

title: Learning from Hi-C reveals nuclear dynamical reorganization in budding yeast across the cell cycle
abstract: Hi-C contact maps provide population-averaged measurements of chromosomal contacts. Converting these measurements, however, into three-dimensional structures and associated dynamics remains an underdetermined problem. Existing approaches broadly fall into two classes. Data-driven reconstruction methods that infer either a consensus structure or an ensemble of conformations, but do not inform on chromosome dynamics. Physics-based models, which generate dynamical trajectories, but require prior assumptions about nuclear geometry, chromatin mechanics, tethering, or molecular interactions. Here, we bridge these approaches using the Full-Inversion Chromatin model, a data-driven whole-genome polymer framework that learns an effective force field directly from Hi-C contact probabilities; integrated with Serpentine, a tool to quantify contact-map discrepancies while accounting for differences in sequencing coverage and sparsity. This generates structural ensembles of chromosomes and effective chromatin dynamics. We apply this method at 5-kb resolution to  Saccharomyces cerevisiae in G1, mid-S, S/G2, G2/M, anaphase, and quiescence. Without explicitly imposing the spindle pole body, centromere or telomere tethering, predefined chromatin states, or nuclear-envelope interactions, the inferred ensembles recover these major features of yeast nuclear organization. Importantly, although dynamical information is not used during model training, the resulting polymer trajectories reproduce the subdiffusive scaling and chromosomal variations of independently measured chromatin motion. The model further predicts heterogeneous mobility along chromosomes and a distinctive telomere-dependent dynamical organization. Thus, population-averaged Hi-C contacts contain sufficient information to infer not only three-dimensional genome organization, but also effective, locus-dependent chromatin dynamics.
authors: Oliveira AB, Contessoto VG, Mozziconacci J, Onuchic JN, Scolari VF.

title: Probiotics with cranberry extract and vitamin C in women with recurrent urinary tract infections: a randomized controlled trial
abstract: Abstract    Introduction and Hypothesis  : Recurrent urinary tract infections (rUTIs) pose a significant clinical burden in women and contribute to antibiotic use. This study investigates the probiotic properties of  Lactiplantibacillus plantarum  KABP062 and KABP063, and their efficacy combined with cranberry extract and vitamin C in reducing rUTIs recurrence.  Methods  : Probiotic functionality and safety were assessed using  in vitro  and  in silico  approaches, including antimicrobial activity against uropathogens, gastrointestinal tolerance, enzymatic safety, and genomic screening for bacteriocin and biogenic amine biosynthesis genes. Clinical efficacy of the multi-component formulation was investigated in a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving women with active or recent rUTIs. Participants received daily capsules containing probiotic strains (≥ 10  8  colony forming units, CFUs), cranberry extract (240 mg) and vitamin C (40 mg), or placebo for six months. The primary endpoint was the proportion of women with physician-confirmed recurrences. Secondary outcomes included number of recurrences, antibiotic use (days), vaginal microbiota, and safety.  Results  : Both  L. plantarum  strains inhibited multiple uropathogens, including  Escherichia coli  , and showed gastrointestinal tolerance and a favorable safety profile. A total of 106 women were randomized. After six months, the proportion of participants experiencing at least one UTI did not differ between groups (p = 0.689). However, the active group was associated with a lower number of UTIs compared to control group (p = 0.013). Antibiotic use was also significantly reduced (p = 0.031) in active group vs control, alongside decreases in seven UTI-associated genera in the vaginal microbiota, including  Escherichia/Shigella  . Adverse events were comparable between groups. Conclusions: The multi-component formula was safe. Although the primary endpoint was not met, the intervention was associated with a lower number of UTIs and reduced antibiotic use, together with potential reductions in the vaginal uropathogen reservoir.
authors: Martin LL, Barea VM, Suárez JB, Gómez GM, Bregante JFE, Ibaigar-Pedraza I, Guerrero-Bonmatty R, Carrillo-Norte JA, Perez M, González-Enguita C.

title: Natural genus-exclusive four-position VP24 configuration in Bundibugyo virus links host interferon tone to a testable cell-type ordering
abstract: Abstract  Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) causes outbreaks with lower case-fatality than Ebola virus (EBOV); its VP24 carries the only BDBV-specific functional difference mapped to date. That difference was defined in an engineered virus. Here, we integrate a sequence census, a human cell-type expression atlas, and a reanalysis of public infection data to connect the natural BDBV VP24 configuration to host interferon (IFN) tone and derive a testable cell-type ordering of post-entry IFN-mediated restriction. All 31 full-length BDBV VP24 records and all 36 complete 2026 outbreak genomes carried S83/Q135/H140/A141; none of the other five orthoebolavirus species assessed carried the complete set. Two consensus-only single-position departures occurred among 860 callable copies in the surveillance data. Δ, a baseline IFN-tone score, tracks the IFN-stimulated level attained by a cell and predicts the strength of IFN-mediated suppression of viral RNA accumulation in cells infected with BDBV carrying the VP24 defect: high Δ denotes stronger suppression, low Δ weaker. Across 154 human cell types, Δ was higher in surface epithelia and circulating myeloid cells (enterocytes 1.28; monocytes 1.00) than in retinal and testicular cells (retinal pigment epithelium − 1.02; Sertoli cells − 0.68). A competing importin-α model predicted exemption in the 47 cell types with high Δ but low importin-α, including enteric epithelium and hepatocytes. In the HIV-1 restriction panel, Δ discriminated restricted from permissive cells (area under the curve (AUC) 0.87), whereas importin-α was at chance (AUC 0.47–0.50); functional data therefore descriptively support Δ.

title: Biosynthesis, Characterization, and Antimicrobial Activity of Gold Nanoparticles Using Chitosan Isolated From Portunus Sanguinolentus Shells
abstract: Abstract    Marine bio-nanotechnology has emerged as a promising field for developing eco-friendly nanomaterials with biomedical applications. This study reports the biosynthesis, characterization, and antimicrobial evaluation of chitosan-gold nanoparticles (CHS-AuNPs) using chitosan extracted from the exoskeleton of  Portunus sanguinolentus  (three-spot swimming crab). Chitosan was successfully isolated from crab shell waste through sequential demineralization, deproteinization, decolorization, and deacetylation processes. The Chitosan-mediated AuNPs were characterized using UV-Visible spectroscopy, FT-IR, XRD, SEM-EDX, HR-TEM with SAED, DLS, and AFM techniques. UV-Vis spectroscopy revealed a characteristic surface plasmon resonance band at 529 nm, confirming the formation of gold nanoparticles. FT-IR analysis indicated the involvement of hydroxyl and amine groups in the reduction and stabilization of nanoparticles. XRD patterns confirmed the face-centered cubic crystalline structure of metallic gold, with Bragg reflections from the (111), (200), and (220) planes. SEM and HR-TEM images revealed predominantly spherical, polydisperse nanoparticles with sizes ranging from 8–10 nm (AFM) to 51.43 nm (DLS hydrodynamic diameter). EDAX analysis confirmed the elemental composition with a strong gold signal. The antimicrobial activity of CHS-AuNPs was evaluated against six bacterial strains (  E. coli  ,  Enterobacter  ,  P. aeruginosa  ,  K. pneumonia  e, S. aureus, and  E. faecalis  ) and four fungal strains (  A. niger  ,  Penicillium  ,  Rhizopus  , and  A. flavus  ) using the agar well diffusion method. The Chitosan-mediated AuNPs exhibited significant dose-dependent antibacterial activity, with the maximum zone of inhibition against S. aureus (22 ± 0.77 mm) and  P. aeruginosa  (22 ± 1.47 mm) at 40 µg/mL. Antifungal activity was highest against  Penicillium  (15 ± 0.57 mm) at the same concentration. The Chitosan-mediated AuNPs demonstrated superior antimicrobial efficacy compared to chitosan alone, highlighting their potential as promising therapeutic agents in biomedical applications, particularly in drug delivery and infection control.
authors: Sangeetha B.

title: Nebulized Covalent Killing of Macrolide-Resistant Mycoplasma pneumoniae: Computational Target Prediction and Design of a Proximity-Triggered Phosphorus(V) Conjugate
abstract: Abstract    Macrolide-resistant  Mycoplasma pneumoniae  (MRMP) has reached crisis prevalence—97.1% of 421 isolates in a 2023–2024 multicenter survey in China and more than 90% across twenty provinces—while the pediatric formulary remains confined to three antibiotic classes that all act on intracellular housekeeping machinery. No mechanism-diverse drug exists for this pathogen, in part because covalent anchoring strategies have lacked trigger-site knowledge for bacterial surface proteins. Here we address that gap computationally through a proteome-scale tyrosine-trigger screen of thirteen  M. pneumoniae  surface proteins (82 qualifying hits), corroboration against experimental cryo-electron-microscopy structures (PDB 8A9A and 9GVG), antibody-epitope and pocket mapping, and conservation analysis across four complete genomes spanning both dominant P1 genotypes (P1-1 and P1-2). The screen identified the essential lipid-acquisition protein P116 as the sole Tier-1 target. Four trigger tyrosines (Tyr671, Tyr566, Tyr188, Tyr206) display phenol-hydroxyl solvent-accessible surface areas of 35.2–43.5 Å² in the physiological dimer, and Tyr398 resides inside a validated monoclonal-antibody epitope (residue SASA 52.4 Å² on the isolated P116 chain of the 9GVG complex; 31.9 Å² in the antibody-bound state). A 533 Å³ subsidiary pocket lies only 2.7 Å from Tyr671, but its entrance aperture measures only 4.0–4.5 Å—too narrow for any aromatic ring (in-plane widths: benzene 7.02 Å, naphthalene 7.36 Å)—which forced an architecture inversion: the recognition group was moved from the anchor end of the conjugate to the leaving-group side of the electrophilic warhead, so that binding occurs in a solvent-side groove without crossing any aperture. The resulting lead, K2 (C₂₉H₂₇FN₂O₈PS⁻, monoisotopic mass 613.1215 Da; two-carbon tether), achieves a qualifying docked-pose fraction of 0.85 (range 0.80–0.90 across four random seeds; 0.78 on an independent seed set), with a median warhead-P···Tyr671-OH distance of 5.60 Å, whereas the warhead-inactivated control K2-N scores 0.00 and the two top-scoring compounds by docking score (− 10.62 and − 10.45 kcal/mol) produce zero qualifying poses—motivating ranking by pose fraction rather than docking score. Successful exchange of K2 is predicted to generate a + 375.0421 Da covalent adduct, a proposed intact-protein mass-spectrometry readout. All eighteen trigger sites are invariant across the four genomes. Because the organism colonizes the airway lumen extracellularly, the design is compatible with nebulized local delivery at the site of infection. This work proposes the first proximity-triggered covalent antibacterial strategy and delivers a conservation-anchored target map together with synthetically tractable, architecture-inverted conjugate designs, providing a defined experimental path toward mechanism-diverse agents against MRMP.
authors: Shen C, Li D.

title: Genome-Wide Pleiotropic Analyses Characterize the Genetic Etiology Shared between Cardiovascular and Gastrointestinal Tract Diseases
abstract: Abstract    Background  This study aimed to investigate the shared genetic etiology between gastrointestinal tract and cardiovascular diseases, and to identify shared genomic loci, genes, and pathways.​  Methods  Using aggregated genome-wide association statistics from public data sources, a genome-wide pleiotropic association study was conducted. Multiple statistical genetic approaches were applied to sequentially explore pleiotropic associations across genome-wide single-nucleotide variations, genes, biological pathways, and gut microbiota. The potential shared genetic causes among 7 gastrointestinal tract diseases and 11 cardiovascular diseases were analyzed.​  Results  A total of 350 pleiotropic loci were identified. Colocalization analysis detected 95 shared causal loci across disease pairs. Multiple gene pathways were found to be closely associated with these diseases, and key biological processes—including cell signal transduction and T-cell activation—exhibited significant correlations across the studied diseases. A robust pleiotropic association was observed between gastrointestinal tract and cardiovascular diseases, suggesting that these diseases may cross-influence each other in the context of different immune cells and tissues, while sharing common immune response mechanisms. Several immune cell populations, such as CD103⁺ CD11b⁺ dendritic cells, CD8⁺ splenic lymph node DCs, and γδ T cells, showed cross-disease correlations, highlighting the critical role of the immune system in the pathogenesis of both gastrointestinal tract and cardiovascular diseases. Multitrait colocalization analysis via HyPrColoc identified 6 pleiotropic loci harboring shared microbiota, underscoring the significant involvement of gut microbiota in disease pleiotropy.​  Conclusions  This study establishes a genetic and mechanistic framework for the shared etiology of gastrointestinal tract and cardiovascular diseases, with pleiotropic variants, inflammatory pathways, and gut microbiota interactions as key drivers. These insights not only deepen our understanding of cardiovascular-gastrointestinal comorbidities but also lay the groundwork for precision medicine strategies targeting shared biological mechanisms.
authors: Qiu Z, Li Z, Wu Y, Chong J, Chen C, Li J, Yang Y, Lu Z, Yuan X, Zhu Y, Chen T, Ma J, Li Y.

title: Challenges of Microalgae Integration in Recirculating Aquaculture Systems: Bridging Potential and Practice
abstract: Abstract    Microalgae offer various benefits to aquaculture, serving as biofilters, immunostimulants, and nutrient‑rich feed additives that enhance water quality, growth, and disease resistance in recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS). Their ability to assimilate dissolved nutrients, capture CO  2  , oxygenate water, and proliferate rapidly without arable land or freshwater renders them environmentally attractive. In aquaculture, microalgae can partially replace conventional protein sources while providing omega-3 and omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), reducing dependence on conventional feeds. Despite variability in biochemical composition and high production costs, incorporating microalgae into formulated feeds and  in situ  cultivation for direct grazing have been widely investigated. Recent advances in cultivation, nutrient recovery, reactor design, and techno-economic assessment have renewed interest in integrating microalgae into RAS. However, existing reviews focus on wastewater treatment, biomass production, or aquafeeds, rather than assessing the feasibility, economic viability, and scalability of  in situ  cultivation in commercial RAS. This review therefore evaluates current evidence on integrating live microalgae into aquaculture and RAS from technical, economic, and sustainability perspectives. Microalgae simultaneously enhance nutrient recovery, reduce aeration requirements, generate valuable biomass, and support animal health; however, evidence remains largely limited to pilot-scale studies. High light and energy demands, self-shading, and biofouling limit the photosynthetic efficiency of microalgae. Costly harvesting processes, instability among microalgal species, and water clarity management constrain consistent biomass production and scalability. Without advances in continuous, efficient harvesting, strain robustness, microbial control, and process economics, commercial adoption in RAS is likely to remain limited to niche applications rather than becoming a broadly viable strategy.
authors: Tiwari SP, Mudimu O, Mannott I, Lang I, Schulz C.

title: Efficient Bioproduction of Citric Acid in Aspergillus niger.
abstract: Citric acid is the most widely produced organic acid in industrial biotechnology, with a global annual output exceeding 2 million tons and broad applications across the food, pharmaceutical, chemical, and environmental sectors. Despite more than a century of industrial development since the discovery of citric acid fermentation by Aspergillus niger in 1917, current production systems are approaching critical bottlenecks in strain performance, process efficiency, and environmental sustainability. Increasing evidence indicates that citrate overproduction is not governed by a single metabolic pathway but emerges as a multi-constraint-driven systems phenomenon involving coordinated regulation of metabolism, cellular physiology, and environmental conditions. Recent advances in systems biology and synthetic biology have enabled a paradigm shift from empirical optimization to rational and programmable biomanufacturing. The integration of multi-omics data with genome-scale metabolic models has substantially deepened the understanding of citrate overflow metabolism. In parallel, the development of CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing, dynamic gene regulation systems, and promoter engineering has enabled precise and multiplexed rewiring of metabolic networks. Targeted engineering strategies focusing on carbon uptake, mitochondrial metabolism, citrate transport, and morphology regulation have demonstrated that high-level production requires coordinated multi-layer optimization rather than single-gene modifications. At the process level, emerging strategies, including immobilized fermentation, in situ product recovery, and the utilization of alternative non-food feedstocks, are being increasingly integrated with engineered strains to enhance productivity and sustainability. These advances collectively point toward a transition from conventional fermentation to a multi-scale, integrated biomanufacturing framework. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent progress in citric acid biomanufacturing, covering the evolution of industrial A. niger strains, systems-level mechanisms of citrate accumulation, synthetic biology-enabled tool development, rational chassis engineering strategies, and process intensification approaches. Finally, we discuss future directions, including dynamic metabolic control, artificial intelligence-assisted design, and circular biorefinery systems, aiming to establish a fully integrated, intelligent, and sustainable paradigm for next-generation citric acid production.
authors: Zheng X, Sun J, Zheng P.

title: Mitochondrial antiviral signalling protein (MAVS) in cardiovascular diseases (CVD): a novel pharmacological target.
abstract: Mitochondrial antiviral signalling protein (MAVS), also known as interferon-β (IFN-β) promoter stimulator 1 (IPS-1), virus-induced signalling adaptor (VISA), and CARD adaptor inducing IFN-β (CARDIF), has emerged as a regulatory node linking mitochondrial stress, innate immune signalling, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) pathogenesis. In the cardiovascular system, MAVS is activated not only by viral RNA sensors such as retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) and melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5), but also by endogenous danger signals. This activation promotes transcription of NLR family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) and pro-inflammatory cytokines, and facilitates NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and cytokine maturation, processes implicated in myocardial inflammation, remodelling, and dysfunction in conditions such as myocardial hypertrophy, atherosclerosis, and cardiomyopathy. Beyond inflammasome activation, MAVS intersects with multiple cell death and homeostatic pathways relevant to CVD, including apoptosis, autophagy, and, potentially, ferroptosis. Preclinical studies show that genetic ablation of MAVS, or pharmacological interventions that limit mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), mitochondrial double-stranded RNA (mtdsRNA) release, or downstream innate immune signalling, can attenuate MAVS-associated inflammation, oxidative stress, and metabolic remodelling, thereby slowing disease progression in experimental cardiovascular models. MAVS, however, also performs essential protective functions, particularly in antiviral defence and maintenance of cardiac homeostasis, underscoring the need for context-specific, cell-type-restricted, or pathway-selective modulation rather than indiscriminate inhibition. Collectively, these findings position MAVS as a promising therapeutic target in CVD, warranting further investigation into MAVS-associated signalling pathways and their modulation in cardiovascular contexts.
authors: Mayamba BS, Chaurembo AI, Chanda F, Zheng X, Liang YT, Deng WH, Liu Y, Huang ZF, Lin YF, Xing N, Liu PP, Lin HB.

title: Sepsis in 2026: from bundles to biology. A critical review.
abstract: Sepsis remains associated with a substantial burden of morbidity and mortality despite more than two decades of Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) recommendations. The 2026 update reinforces early recognition, resuscitation, timely antimicrobial therapy, source control, and reassessment, yet the benefit of increasingly intensive implementation of standardized measures may be approaching a ceiling. A central limitation is treating sepsis as a homogeneous entity despite the wide variation in etiologies, host susceptibility, immune responses, and clinical trajectories. Artificial intelligence, host-response biomarkers, rapid microbiological diagnosis, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic optimization provide new opportunities to shorten the time to effective intervention. In parallel, transcriptomic, genomic, and routine clinical data can identify subphenotypes and endotypes associated with different prognoses and potentially different treatment responses. Secondary analyses of clinical trials illustrate how an intervention that is neutral overall may be beneficial in biologically defined subgroups. The next step should combine SSC bundles with biological stratification, adaptive trial designs, and point-of-care tools capable of matching treatment to patient profile in real time. This review proposes a transition from standardized sepsis management toward precision medicine: the right treatment for the right patient at the right time.
journal: Revista espanola de quimioterapia : publicacion oficial de la Sociedad Espanola de Quimioterapia
authors: Estella Á, Candel FJ.
