title: Beyond the Infection: The Immunopathological Cascade and Novel Therapeutic Avenues in Viral Myocarditis.
abstract: Viral myocarditis (VMC) is an inflammatory disease of the myocardium induced by infection with cardiotropic viruses. Its pathogenesis encompasses direct virus-induced myocardial injury and excessive host immune-mediated pathological responses. This review systematically delineates the dynamic progression of VMC, from viral invasion and immune activation to chronic myocardial remodeling. Special emphasis is placed on pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) in sensing viral components, and how mechanisms like cytokine storms, autoimmunity, and macrophage polarization imbalances drive myocardial injury and fibrosis. Furthermore, we summarize current and emerging therapeutic strategies-highlighting etiology-guided stratification based on myocardial viral genome status. For virus-positive cases, direct pathogen-targeted antivirals (e.g., interferon-beta [IFN-β], telbivudine), viral entry decoys, mitochondrial protectants, novel antiheart failure agents (SGLT2 inhibitors, ARNI), and blood component apheresis (TPE/IA) offer promising avenues. Conversely, immunosuppressive regimens, CAR-Treg therapies, and cytokine antagonists (e.g., IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-17) are strictly indicated for virus-negative inflammatory cardiomyopathy. The clinical translation potential and challenges in these multitarget interventions are discussed in detail. Despite advances in elucidating VMC immunopathology, precise management remains ch.allenging due to difficulties in balancing antiviral defense and inflammatory injury. Future research should leverage multiomics technologies and personalized multitarget approaches to improve clinical outcomes.
authors: Chen Y, Liu M, Wu J, Li Y, Wan Z, Cheng S, Chen M, Luo G, Chen H.

title: Therapeutic Targeting of the Cancer Microbiome and Metabolome: Ongoing Trials and Future Directions for the Surgical Oncologist.
abstract: The role of the human microbiome in cancer development, progression, and response to therapy has moved from correlative curiosity to demonstrated impact on tumor biology. This represents a critical factor for surgical oncologists as they not only resect these tumors, but also direct perioperative antimicrobial exposure and increasingly co-manage neoadjuvant and surveillance pathways in which microbial state may predict and modify response. This review summarizes the basis for therapeutic modulation of the cancer microbiome and metabolome in a contemporary clinical-trial landscape across four broad strategies: additive (fecal microbiota transplantation, defined consortia, and live biotherapeutic products), subtractive (targeted antimicrobials), dietary and metabolome-directed interventions, and engineered or next-generation platforms. Particular attention is given to subtractive approaches in colon and rectal cancer and to the underexplored perioperative interface between the microbiome and surgical outcomes such as anastomotic leak. We outline the principal methodological and translational obstacles, including low-biomass contamination, causal inference, unintended antibiotic effects, and product standardization. Looking ahead, we propose roles for surgeons across the care continuum, from biospecimen stewardship and trial referral to integration of microbiome and circulating tumor DNA signals in surveillance.
authors: Nachman EJ, Neilson T, White MG.

title: ALDH2 Deficiency Promotes Mitochondrial Oxidative Stress and Adverse Limb Outcomes via VDAC-HSP60 Signaling.
abstract: The ALDH2 rs671 variant, which is frequent in East Asian populations, markedly reduces mitochondrial aldehyde-detoxifying capacity and thereby increases vulnerability to reactive aldehydes, including 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), during ischemic stress. We show that impaired ALDH2 activity perturbs endothelial mitochondrial proteostasis through an ALDH2-4-HNE-HSP60-VDAC1 pathway. In Aldh2 knock-in mice and endothelial cells exposed to oxygen-glucose deprivation, ALDH2 deficiency was accompanied by 4-HNE accumulation, mitochondrial DNA injury, loss of membrane potential, increased mitochondrial ROS, mitochondrial fragmentation, and apoptosis. Analysis of transcriptomic data highlighted HSP60 (HSPD1) as a downstream candidate. LC-MS/MS, covalent docking, co-immunoprecipitation, and proximity ligation analyses supported 4-HNE modification of HSP60, while native electrophoresis indicated disruption of higher-order HSP60 assembly. HSP60 redistribution to the cytosol was predominantly dependent on VDAC1. Activating ALDH2 with AD-5591, or suppressing VDAC1 genetically or pharmacologically, preserved HSP60 homeostasis, mitochondrial integrity, and endothelial function. In a prospective cohort of 227 patients with peripheral artery disease, the rs671 variant was associated with a higher incidence of major adverse limb events. These data position HSP60 proteostasis downstream of ALDH2-dependent aldehyde detoxification and identify the ALDH2-4-HNE-HSP60-VDAC1 pathway as a potential therapeutic target in ischemic vascular disease.
authors: Lin YC, Wu NC, Hong CS, Hsu PC, Yang WJ, Chang YC, Chen CH, Chang WT.

title: Root Microbiota Reprogram Aboveground Metabolite Allocation Across Tea Plant Tissues.
abstract: Tea quality is determined by the composition and spatial distribution of specialized metabolites, such as amino acids, catechins, and caffeine, which vary across tissues and developmental stages. However, the mechanisms underlying metabolite allocation among tissues remain unclear. Plant-associated microbiota, particularly root communities, play important roles in regulating plant metabolism, yet their coordinated effects across plant compartments are poorly understood. Here, we combined metabolomic and microbiome analyses to investigate metabolic-microbial interactions in the white tea cultivar Zhenghe Dabai. Metabolite-associated microbial taxa identified from leaves were linked to root-derived isolates, and two synthetic communities (SynCom1 and SynCom2) were constructed and applied to the rhizosphere. Both SynComs enhanced flavan metabolite accumulation, especially proanthocyanidins, but exhibited distinct regulatory patterns. SynCom1 increased stem-enriched proanthocyanidins and multiple amino acids, including theanine, while SynCom2 promoted specific flavan derivatives and amino acids such as glutamate and tryptophan. Transcriptomic analysis revealed differential activation of flavonoid biosynthesis and amino acid transport pathways, with SynCom1 upregulating the transporter gene CsCAT1. Overall, our results demonstrate that root microbiota can differentially regulate host metabolism and metabolite allocation, providing new insights into microbiome-mediated quality formation in tea and highlighting the potential of synthetic microbial communities for crop improvement.
authors: Xin W, Zhang J, Tian W, Ren L, Zhu Z, Chen Z, Ye M, Yang L, Liu Y, Zhou J, Zheng C, Tang W.

title: Genetic and regulatory architecture of meat yield traits in commercial pig populations.
abstract: BackgroundLean meat percentage (LMP), longissimus muscle area (LMA), and longissimus muscle depth (LMD) are critical carcass traits that directly impact meat yield and the economic efficiency of swine production. Although genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified numerous loci associated with these traits, the functional characterization of candidate quantitative trait loci (QTLs) and their regulatory mechanisms is still limited and poses significant challenges. Here, we conducted GWAS in 4593 pigs from three commercial populations (Yorkshire, Landrace and Duroc) to identify loci associated with LMP, LMA and LMD. We further integrated integrative chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, chromatin interaction information, and dual-luciferase reporter assays to identify candidate QTLs with potential regulatory functions. Candidate genes were subsequently prioritized using single-nucleus RNA sequencing, Phenome-wide association analysis, and Mendelian randomization.ResultsThis multi-layered approach prioritized candidate regulatory QTLs associated with LMP, LMA and LMD, and identified high-confidence candidate genes potentially involved in the regulation of meat yield traits. For LMP, WWOX and ABL1 showed the strongest evidence in Yorkshire and Landrace population, respectively. For LMA, PHB1 and BAZ2A showed the strongest evidence in the Yorkshire and combined-population, respectively. SLC16A7 was specifically associated with both LMP and LMA in Landrace. For LMD, ENSSSCG00000045482 and RSPO4 showed the strongest evidence in Yorkshire pigs, while XPO4 was identified in the combined-population analysis. These genes may influence muscle metabolic homeostasis, muscle proliferation, hypertrophy, and atrophy through interactions with myogenic transcription factors and key signaling pathways such as PPAR-RXR and Wnt/β-catenin.ConclusionsThese findings provide new insights into the genetic and regulatory basis of meat yield traits in pigs and highlight candidate regulatory QTLs and genes for future functional validation and precision breeding applications aimed at improving pork yield.
authors: Huang Y, Wang M, Zhou M, Xiao S, Zhang Z.

title: Identification of genetic loci enhancing heterologous protein production in Ogataea minuta by restriction enzyme-assisted insertional mutagenesis.
abstract: Methylotrophic yeast Ogataea minuta has been utilized as a host for heterologous protein production and genetic engineering has been used to develop this capacity further. To identify genetic loci whose disruption improves the performance of O. minuta as a heterologous protein production host, restriction enzyme-assisted insertional mutagenesis was applied to its genome. High-producing clones were isolated by colorimetric screening using ScPho5 acid phosphatase expression, driven by the TDH1 promoter, as a reporter. Upon applying a two-step screening process to approximately 5000 mutants, 16 candidate strains producing ScPho5 at high levels were selected. The insertion sites in two of these strains were identified in TDA3 and GDH2, the disruption of which was confirmed to enhance ScPho5 production. Enhanced production was further confirmed by reintroducing the mutations into alternative reporter systems expressing ScPHO5 under the AOX1 promoter and CLuc under the TDH1 promoter. These findings show that the TDA3 and GDH2 genes play important roles in heterologous protein production in O. minuta. This study demonstrates that restriction enzyme-assisted insertional mutagenesis combined with the ScPho5 reporter assay provides an effective strategy for identifying genetic loci that enhance heterologous secretory protein production in O. minuta.
authors: Nakatani Y, Tsuda M, Baba S, Nonaka K, Yoko-O T, Chiba Y.

title: Global phylogeny and biogeography of the nematode-trapping mushroom genus Hohenbuehelia.
abstract: Hohenbuehelia is a genus of wood decaying fungi in the phylum Basidiomycota that has evolved the ability to capture and consume nematodes (nematophagy). Nematophagy has evolved multiple times across the kingdom Fungi as well as in Oomycota (Chromista). Hohenbuehelia is unique in that it has evolved diverse strategies for nematophagy in different species through the production of adhesive knobs on its hyphae (predatory strategy), on germinated conidia or basidiospores (parasitoid strategy), or both (intermediate strategy). However, the evolutionary path for the development of these strategies remains enigmatic. In this study, we present a comprehensive global multigene phylogeny of Hohenbuehelia, including descriptions of three novel species from North America, and we investigate the evolution of nematophagous strategies. We infer that the ancestor of Hohenbuehelia was a "predator" that possessed adhesive knobs only on its hyphae, which have subsequently been lost in several lineages as conidia with adhesive knobs have evolved repeatedly. Some "intermediate predators" possess adhesive knobs both on hyphae and conidia, while "parasitoid" forms produce only adhesive conidia. Transitions between predators, intermediate predators and parasitoids reflect shifts in mechanisms of nematophagy and dispersal, with potential consequences for sexual reproduction. We investigated the temporal and spatial contexts of diversification by performing molecular-clock analysis and biogeographic reconstruction, which suggest that Hohenbuehelia may have originated in the Holarctic realm approximately 160 million years ago.
authors: Prabhu PP, Bradshaw AJ, Consiglio G, Setti L, Thorn RG, Hibbett DS.

title: Occurrence, Potential Sources, and Microbial Associations of Microplastics in the Puzhehei Lake Watershed, a Karst Region of Southwest China.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are emerging contaminants of global concern, yet their potential sources, distribution across environmental media, and associations with sediment microbial communities in karst lake watersheds remain poorly understood. This study investigated the occurrence, potential sources, multimedia distribution, and microbial associations of MPs across surface water, groundwater, and sediments in a representative karst region of Puzhehei Lake watershed in southwestern China. The results indicate that MPs were widely detected in all environmental media, with average abundances of 21.26 items L-1, 31.25 items L-1, and 4415.32 items kg-1 in surface water, groundwater, and sediments, respectively. Although groundwater exhibited a higher mean MP abundance than surface water, the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.225). MPs were predominantly fragments (55.79%-58.21%) and dark-colored particles (black, gray, and brown), with particle sizes mainly concentrated at ≤0.05 mm. The major polymer types identified were polystyrene (PS), polypropylene (PP), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET). Positive matrix factorization (PMF) analyzed three factors tentatively associated with agricultural activities (40.65%), tourism (34.00%), and domestic activities (25.35%), respectively. Further analyses suggested potential associations among the MP characteristics, sediment bacterial communities and predicted nitrogen-cycling functional groups. Although several correlations involving MP morphology, color, and particle size were nominally significant, none remained statistically significant after false discovery rate correction. These findings provide preliminary insights into the potential relationships between MPs and sediment microbial communities in karst environments. However, these microbial associations should be regarded as exploratory and hypothesis-generating because of unmeasured environmental covariates and the possibility of residual spatial confounding. This study provides insights into the potential sources and environmental distribution of MPs and offers a basis for pollution management in ecologically vulnerable regions.
authors: Wu Y, Zhou X, Fu C, Wang R, Song W.

title: Choline attenuates lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation in the BV-2 microglial cell line via the α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor/nuclear factor kappa-B signaling pathway.
abstract: ObjectiveThis study aimed to investigate the potential mechanisms by which choline (CHO) attenuates lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced neuroinflammatory responses in BV-2 microglial cells through network pharmacology-based prediction and in vitro experiments. These neuroinflammatory responses are implicated in the pathophysiology of sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE).MethodsPutative CHO targets were retrieved from PubChem, the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD), and SwissTargetPrediction, while SAE-associated genes were sourced from OMIM and GeneCards. Overlapping targets from both datasets were subjected to protein-protein interaction (PPI) network construction, along with Gene Ontology (GO) functional annotation and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment, to identify core candidate genes and key signaling cascades. The predicted outcomes were subsequently verified by in vitro experiments, including cell viability assays, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), immunofluorescence, quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), and Western blot.ResultsAn intersection of 672 SAE-associated genes and 109 CHO-responsive genes yielded 24 common targets. Among them, TNF, IL10, IL6, MMP9, and IL1B were identified as potential hub therapeutic targets. KEGG enrichment analysis revealed the involvement of multiple pathways, with the nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) cascade being particularly notable. In cell-based assays, CHO administration reduced the levels of pro-inflammatory mediators (TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) and concurrently increased those of anti-inflammatory markers (IL-4, IL-10, and CD206). Furthermore, CHO elevated α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR) expression while suppressing IκBα and NF-κB p65 phosphorylation. Treatment with the α7nAChR antagonist methyllycaconitine citrate (MLA) reversed these effects.ConclusionsCHO may inhibit microglial neuroinflammation and promote anti-inflammatory polarization, potentially via the α7nAChR/NF-κB signaling pathway.
authors: Xia Z, Wang D, Qiu X, Huang S, Wen Y, Huang Y.

title: Rare recovery of reassortants between contemporary clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 viruses and human influenza A viruses in vitro.
abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) pandemics can arise when animal-derived and human-adapted IAVs exchange genome segments; however, whether contemporary clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 viruses can generate viable reassortants with human IAVs is unclear. Here, we tested the reassortment potential of two clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 viruses with human-adapted H1N1 and H3N2 IAVs using a biosafe reassortment system. Across multiple coinfection conditions, we genotyped 2,698 plaque-purified viral clones and recovered 20 reassortants (0.74%). Polymerase assays identified human IAV subunits, particularly H1N1 PA or H3N2 PB2, that increased H5N1 polymerase activity. Thus, contemporary clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 viruses can reassort with human IAVs, but factors beyond polymerase compatibility may limit their recovery.
authors: Ankerhold J, Kessler S, Petric PP, Jakob C, Beer M, Schwemmle M, Reuther P, Ciminski K.

title: Erdosteine Enhances Tobramycin Activity Against a Tobramycin-Resistant Clinical Isolate and PAO1 Reference Strain of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
abstract: BackgroundChronic respiratory infections caused by pathogens including Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) pose a major therapeutic challenge in patients with pulmonary diseases such as cystic fibrosis (CF) and non-CF bronchiectasis, where treatment efficacy is limited by the formation of biofilms, the emergence of multidrug resistant pathogens and a shortage of new and effective antibiotic classes. One approach to address this problem involves the use of "antibiotic enhancers", which are compounds that potentiate the activity of existing antibiotics without possessing direct antimicrobial effects of their own. The mucoactive thiol-based prodrug erdosteine, currently approved for the treatment of acute and chronic respiratory diseases, has been reported to exhibit anti-adhesive activity against respiratory pathogens, suggesting a clinically relevant contribution to the prevention of bacterial colonisation. Furthermore, in addition to reported anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities, erdosteine has demonstrated the ability to potentiate the activity of various antimicrobial drugs. However, to date, whether erdosteine can enhance the activity of tobramycin, an antibiotic widely used to treat pathogens in the respiratory tract, has not been investigated. In this study, we investigated the ability of MET-1, the primary active metabolite of erdosteine, to enhance the activity of tobramycin against P. aeruginosa strains using a panel of both in vitro and in vivo assays.MethodsThe activity of both mono- and combination therapies was measured in planktonic P. aeruginosa (strains RP73 & PAO1) using in vitro microdilution assays including chequerboard analysis and time-kill assays, whilst activity against biofilms were analysed using microtiter plate assays with readouts including total biomass, metabolic activity, and bacterial enumeration. Combination therapy of 40 mg/kg tobramycin and 100 mg/kg erdosteine was also assessed in vivo using a murine model of chronic pulmonary infection induced by P. aeruginosa.Results10 mg/L MET-1 significantly enhanced the antimicrobial activity of tobramycin in planktonic cultures of RP73 at 24 h and PAO1 at 4 h, leading to a greater than 2 log10 reduction in bacterial numbers compared to tobramycin monotherapy, despite MET-1 demonstrating no intrinsic bactericidal activity. In mature biofilms, MET-1 substantially enhanced tobramycin activity, reducing the biomass-derived IC₅₀ by approximately 18-fold in RP73 and 13-fold in PAO1. Finally, combination therapy of 40 mg/kg tobramycin and 100 mg/kg erdosteine was associated with a lower pulmonary bacterial burden in a murine model of chronic pulmonary infection.ConclusionsOur in vitro and in vivo studies highlight the ability of erdosteine to potentiate the activity of tobramycin suggesting that erdosteine has the potential to reduce the burden of long-term antimicrobial therapies in patients with chronic respiratory infections and thus improve clinical outcomes.
authors: Ramsden B, Cigana C, Gugliandolo D, Rossano M, Bragonzi A, Page CP, Amison RT.

title: Reading and rewiring natural-product biosynthesis in microbial hosts with genetically encoded biosensors.
abstract: Covering: 2000 to 2026Natural products (NPs) are structurally diverse bioactive molecules with broad applications in pharmaceuticals, nutraceuticals, cosmetics, and other high-value sectors. Microbial cell factories provide programmable platforms for NP production, but their performance is often constrained by dynamic bottlenecks that are not readily inferred from end-point titers, including limited precursor or cofactor supply, toxic intermediate accumulation, inefficient heterologous enzyme function, and competition with host metabolism. Genetically encoded biosensors translate NP molecules, pathway-relevant metabolites, or cellular states into measurable, selectable, or regulatory outputs. Here, we critically examine biosensor design principles and distinguish the variable detected, recognition modality, output, and implementation format. We then assess how direct product sensing, pathway-state monitoring, dynamic regulation, enzyme screening, genome-wide perturbation, and growth-coupled evolution can support microbial NP engineering. Emphasis is placed on the correspondence between sensor output and the intended engineering objective. This framework clarifies when biosensors can provide actionable information for rewiring NP-producing microbial hosts.
authors: Ki M, Eun H, Park J, Prabowo CPS, Kim D, Lee SY.

title: Allicin attenuates diet-induced obesity in association with gut microbiota remodeling, fecal butyrate, and hepatic PPAR signaling in rats.
abstract: Obesity is associated with gut microbial dysbiosis and impaired intestinal barrier function. Allicin, a garlic-derived organosulfur compound, has shown anti-obesity effects, but the links between its effects on gut microbial metabolism and hepatic gene expression remain unclear. This study examined the metabolic effects of allicin and associated gut-liver responses using microbiota profiling, targeted short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) metabolomics, hepatic transcriptomics, network pharmacology and quantitative PCR. Male Sprague-Dawley rats received oral allicin at 60 or 80 mg kg-1 day-1 for 4 weeks after 8 weeks of high-fat diet (HFD) feeding. Compared with HFD controls, both doses reduced body weight gain, improved glucose tolerance and serum lipid profiles, and lowered serum markers of hepatic injury. Allicin treatment also remodeled the gut microbiota by enriching Ligilactobacillus and Akkermansia and reducing Escherichia-Shigella, and increased fecal butyrate concentrations. These changes were accompanied by increased colonic expression of barrier-related and SCFA receptor genes and lower serum lipopolysaccharide concentrations. Hepatic transcriptomics and network pharmacology both implicated peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signaling, with qPCR supporting expression changes in selected genes. Correlation analyses identified positive associations of fecal butyrate concentrations with the relative abundances of Ligilactobacillus and Akkermansia and with colonic barrier-related gene expression. Together, these findings support a proposed microbiota-butyrate-hepatic PPAR framework for further investigation of allicin as a potential functional food ingredient, while causal links among these components remain to be established.
authors: Zhang S, Ding L, Yao J, Cheng X, Zhang Y, Hou Y, Ding W, Li X, Wang Z.

title: Modulation of the general stress response impacts protein expression, energy economy, and heterogeneity in virtually non-dividing yeast cultures.
abstract: Microbial cells adapt their physiology when growth is restricted by nutrient limitation, balancing survival with the capacity to produce proteins. Here, we investigated this adaptation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae by comparing retentostat cultures, in which specific growth rates reached below 0.001 h⁻¹, of a reference strain (ScNTi001) and a ∆msn2∆msn4 mutant (ScNTm001). We show that general stress-response transcription factors Msn2 and Msn4 are crucial for maintaining energy efficiency and for survival under this extreme calorie restriction. Their absence increased population heterogeneity and reduced viability, underscoring a role beyond merely stress resistance. To understand (heterologous) protein expression dynamics, we monitored how a stress-inducible promoter (PHSP12) and a constitutive promoter (PTEF1) impacted protein levels. The PHSP12 remained active at moderate to low growth rates, but expression sharply dropped below 0.001 h⁻¹, whereas the PTEF1 sustained protein expression, with activity linked to specific glucose uptake rates rather than growth rate. This decoupling revealed a trade-off: although PTEF1-driven ymNeongreen-specific production rates were 70% higher in the absence of ∆msn2∆msn4, overall product yields were 13% lower.ImportanceThis study demonstrates how Msn2 and Msn4 govern cellular robustness under extreme nutrient-limited conditions at near-zero growth rates. It also guides promoter selection strategies for growth-independent production processes. More broadly, this study shows that retentostats can be used as a valuable tool to dissect stress-response pathways, survival mechanisms, and growth-independent expression systems in microbial cell factories.
authors: Temelli N, Raats SAC, Lucheti PR, Weusthuis RA, Bisschops MMM.

title: A dual endogenous selectable marker system for Aspergillus flavus and its application in characterizing nsdD function in development and aflatoxin biosynthesis.
abstract: Aspergillus flavus poses a significant threat to global food security and public health, as it not only triggers severe mold spoilage in staple crops like peanuts and corn but also produces aflatoxin, a potent carcinogen. However, genetic manipulation of this fungus is notoriously challenging due to its inherent insensitivity to conventional antibiotics. To overcome this barrier, we established a robust, fully endogenous genetic transformation system for a highly toxigenic wild-type strain, A. flavus-SD, using polyethylene glycol (PEG)-mediated protoplast transfection with two selectable markers: pyrG (uracil auxotrophy/5-FOA counterselection) and a β-tubulin E198A point mutation (carbendazim resistance). We successfully constructed the tool strains with a ΔpyrG mutation, which were used for gene knockout and overexpression, and the β-tubulin E198A mutant was used for gene complementation. To validate the operational efficacy of this platform, we performed knockout, complementation, and overexpression of the nsdD gene as a test case. This study provides a reliable technical foundation for elucidating the molecular mechanisms governing aflatoxin biosynthesis and pathogenicity, thereby facilitating the identification of novel targets for A. flavus control.ImportanceThis study established a novel genetic transformation system for a highly toxigenic wild-type strain, Aspergillus flavus-SD, utilizing fully endogenous selectable markers: pyrG (uracil auxotrophy/5-FOA counterselection) and a β-tubulin E198A point mutation (carbendazim resistance). This platform eliminates the need for heterologous antibiotic resistance cassettes, thereby reducing biosafety concerns while enabling iterative genome editing through marker recycling. Using this system, we demonstrated its efficacy by validating the expected phenotypic changes upon nsdD manipulation, revealing a previously unrecognized trade-off between sclerotia formation and aflatoxin biosynthesis. This work provides a valuable, compliance-friendly resource for the fungal research community and lays a foundation for identifying novel targets to disrupt fungal persistence and mycotoxin production in agricultural settings.
authors: Zhao X-L, Zhang Q, Li P-W, Luo C-X.

title: Draft genome sequence of Bacillus licheniformis strain TCCC11148 isolated from unused sanitary pad.
abstract: Bacillus licheniformis is an environmentally widespread, spore-forming bacterium with industrial and ecological importance. Here, we report the draft genome sequence of a B. licheniformis isolate recovered from an unused sanitary pad in Ogbomoso, Nigeria. The assembled genome comprises 4.1 Mb in 12 contigs with a GC content of 46%.
authors: Oladipo EK, Elutade OA, Oluwasanya GJ, Onyeaka H, Olatunde SK.

title: The Phosphatidylserine Synthase (pssA) Mutant of Agrobacterium fabrum Exhibits Membrane Lipid Remodeling, Altered Physiological Traits, and Reduced Plant Infectivity.
abstract: Agrobacterium fabrum is a plant pathogen that induces tumor formation through the genetic transformation of infected plant tissues. Its pathogenicity is strongly influenced by the composition and structural organization of bacterial membranes. In this study, we characterized a mutant defective in the phosphatidylserine synthase gene (pssA), which encodes a key enzyme in the phosphatidylserine/phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthetic pathway. The lipid profile of the mutant was analyzed using thin-layer chromatography and high-resolution electrospray ionization mass spectrometry. The mutant lacked phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and PE methylation intermediates and exhibited extensive lipid remodeling, including altered levels of phosphatidylglycerol, cardiolipin, and ornithine lipids compared with the wild-type strain. We also examined the physiological traits of the mutant, including resistance to environmental stressors, motility, and plant infectivity, all of which were markedly impaired. To investigate the global consequences of membrane lipid disruption, we performed transcriptomic analysis. A total of 283 genes were differentially expressed in the mutant relative to the wild-type strain, with a predominance of upregulated genes associated with carbohydrate, amino acid, inorganic ion, and lipid transport and metabolism, particularly genes encoding ABC transporters. In contrast, genes involved in flagellar assembly, chemotaxis, signal transduction, and transcription were strongly downregulated, consistent with the observed motility defect. Genes encoding components of several two-component regulatory systems and transcription factors were also downregulated, suggesting that membrane lipid remodeling affects global regulatory networks.
authors: Żebracki K, Choma A, Mazur A, Koper P, Swatek A, Pastuszka A, Suśniak K, Smirnova Y, Komaniecka I.

title: Histoplasma capsulatum Strains from the American Regions Displayed Different Virulence Strategies According to Their Phylogenetic Species.
abstract: Virulence strategies from distinct phylogenetic species of the Histoplasma capsulatum complex have been scarcely documented. Using assays for intracellular replication of H. capsulatum yeasts, induction of cytokine production in yeast-infected human cell-lines (pneumocytes A549 and differentiated macrophages THP-1), and determination of lethal dose 50% (LD 50%) in yeast-infected male BALB/c mice, we characterize virulence strategies of four H. capsulatum strains from the American regions. Yeast replication in human cell-lines expressed by colony-forming units/mL at 2, 6, 24, and 48 h postinfection, supported that EH-315 and 60I strains (NAm 3 and LAm A phylogenetic species, respectively) developed major ability to survive intracellularly. Cytokine production by infected host cell-lines was mainly detectable at 24 and 48 h postinfection. The A549 cells only produced high values for CCL2 and CXCL8 chemokines when infected with EH-315 and 60I strains, whereas the THP-1 cells showed high values for CCL2, CCL5, CXCL8, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 cytokines when infected with each fungal strain tested, highlighting the results for EH-315 and 60I strains. Likewise, LD 50% data showed that the NAm 3 strain (EH-315) was the most lethal. Thus, the obtained findings could differentiate virulence strategies depending on the genotypes of H. capsulatum strains studied.
authors: Rodríguez-Arellanes G, Tenorio EP, Betancourt-León O, Ramos-Martínez I, Muñoz JAR, Ramírez JA, García-Pérez BE, Fusco-Almeida AM, Mendes-Giannini MJS, Zancopé-Oliveira RM, Taylor ML.

title: Structural basis and regulatory mechanisms of interferon regulatory factor 9 (IRF9) in immunity and disease.
abstract: As the DNA-binding subunit of the interferon-stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3) complex, interferon regulatory factor 9 (IRF9) plays an indispensable role in type I and type III interferon-mediated antiviral innate immunity. In response to type I interferon stimulation, IRF9 assembles with phosphorylated STAT1 and STAT2 to form the ISGF3 complex, which translocates to the nucleus, binds ISRE elements, and drives the transcription of hundreds of ISGs to establish the cellular antiviral state. However, research over the past two decades has revealed that the functions of IRF9 extend far beyond this. Here, we summarize and discuss the discovery, structural basis, and regulatory mechanisms of IRF9 in both canonical and non-canonical JAK-STAT pathways. We further detail its multifaceted roles in antiviral immunity, autoimmune diseases, intestinal inflammation, metabolic regulation, cardiovascular diseases, and tumors, summarize viral immune evasion strategies targeting IRF9, and offer future perspectives. Together, we present a complete picture of IRF9's evolution from an obscure IRF to a multifunctional transcriptional regulator.
authors: Li Z, Zheng H, Miao Y, Yuan Y.

title: Modular assembly of mitochondrial complex III from a dynamic matrix domain pool
abstract: Mitochondrial complex III is a central component of the cellular energy metabolism. It is an obligate dimer of catalytic and accessory subunits that are encoded by two genomes. How its large matrix domain, formed by the core proteins Qcr1 and Qcr2, is built and joined to the membrane part and during assembly is not known. Here we show that Qcr1 and Qcr2 preassemble independently of complex III into matrix domain modules. Cryo-EM structures from a cardiolipin-deficient yeast strain and of recombinant protein resolved single, double and triple matrix domains, which are linked by the C-terminal tail of Qcr1. In the mature complex III, the same tail binds cytochrome b and cardiolipin. The modules form a dynamic pool, in which assembly species interconvert and exchange subunits. Mutations at the module interfaces, including mimics of human disease variants, reshape this pool and deletion of the Qcr1 tail impairs respiratory growth. Substitution of a tyrosine residue linked to parkinsonism exposes a conserved cysteine residue to oxidation. A cryo-EM structure of an assembly intermediate shows a cap of two matrix domains bound to a monomeric membrane module of cytochrome b, Qcr7, Qcr8 and cytochrome c1. We propose that complex III receives its matrix domain from a dynamic pool of prebuilt modules, which organizes the dimerization of the complex.
authors: Jimenez-Niebla J, Jha R, Wirth C, Busto JV, Feignier A, Cosenza-Contreras M, Ruoff K, Dorer M, Babic R, Drepper F, Kraft C, Huesgen PF, Wiedemann N, Kao W, Hunte C.

title: Dual-reporter assay for selective small molecule inhibition of expanded toxic huntingtin
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in exon 1 of the human huntingtin gene (HTT). The resultant pathogenic allele (mHTT) produces a mutant huntingtin protein (mHtt) containing an expanded polyglutamine tract. Because mHtt drives neurodegeneration while wildtype huntingtin (Htt) remains critical for regulation of gene transcription and cell survival, an ideal therapeutic would specifically downregulate mHtt expression while preserving Htt. Small molecules are attractive candidates for HD given their ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier and amenability to oral dosing, but there remains no high-throughput platform that reports both efficacy and allele selectivity. Here, we present a bacterial assay in which exon 1 of HTT and mHTT, each fused to spectrally distinct fluorescent proteins, are co-expressed in the same cell, allowing simultaneous quantification of their expression in the presence of small molecules. This high-throughput assay isolates the effect of small molecules on huntingtin expression without confounding factors present in mammalian cells, such as endogenous Htt or human RNA-binding proteins. To validate this assay, we evaluated two previously reported CAG repeat binding compounds and used circular dichroism spectroscopy and cell-free protein synthesis to investigate their underlying mechanisms. Furamidine exhibited reproducible, sequence-dependent effects, altering the structural stability of HTT RNA and selectively decreasing the wildtype Htt expression (a selectivity profile opposite to what is therapeutically required). In contrast, myricetin did not affect HTT RNA stability and its decreased signal in the dual-expression assay was due to fluorophore artifacts. This highlights the importance of complementary workflows in distinguishing genuine modulators from reporter-specific artifacts. Collectively, these findings establish the dual-expression assay as a screening platform for CAG repeat-targeting small molecules and demonstrate the importance of determining which allele reported compounds preferentially affect.
authors: Kraichely EA, Kim S, Wang J, Jung KW, Chung P.

title: Viperin deficiency in CD4⁺ T cells enhances protective immunity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection
abstract: Abstract  Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains a major global health threat. CD4⁺ T cells are indispensable for protective immunity against Mtb infection. This study defines the T-cell-intrinsic role of Viperin (encoded by Rsad2) during Mtb infection. We utilized T cell-specific Viperin knockout (Rsad2cko) mice and adoptive transfer models into Rag1-/- hosts to assess outcomes following aerosol Mtb infection. We found that Viperin deficiency in CD4⁺ T cells significantly reduced bacterial burden and pathology in Mtb-infected lungs. This enhanced protection was associated with an increased frequency and activation of Mtb-specific CD4⁺ T cells. Viperin-deficient CD4⁺ T cells exhibited enhanced early activation, proliferation, and a bias towards differentiating into short-lived effector memory (Tem) over central memory (Tcm) cells. Furthermore, these cells showed a pronounced skewing towards a Th1 phenotype, with robust IFN-γ production, both in vivo and under Th1-polarizing conditions in vitro. Viperin-deficient CD4⁺ T cells displayed reduced apoptosis and increased activation of the PI3K-Akt-mTOR and PKC-θ-NF-κB pro-survival pathways upon T cell receptor (TCR) stimulation, accompanied by transcriptional downregulation of the pro-apoptotic mediator Bbc3 (PUMA) and the proliferation brake Gadd45a in vivo. Collectively, our study reveals that Viperin intrinsically dampens CD4⁺ T cell function by restraining Th1 differentiation, proliferation, and survival, thereby identifying Viperin as a potential immunotherapeutic target for enhancing T cell-mediated defense against TB. These findings also highlight a context-dependent duality of Viperin, which is protective in viral infection but detrimental in Mtb infection, underscoring its role as a homeostatic regulator of T cell immunity.
authors: Zhou X, Liang Y, Lin L, Li H, Niu H, Han Z, Xu M, Wen Q, Zhou L, Zhou C, Ma L.

title: Longitudinal BCR repertoire dynamics reveal the evolution of broadly binding antibodies following heterologous SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and breakthrough infection: a single-donor case study.
abstract: Continued SARS-CoV-2 antigenic drift and the persistent risk of zoonotic sarbecovirus spillover highlight the need for broadly protective countermeasures. Here, we longitudinally profiled the B cell receptor (BCR) repertoire of a single volunteer who received heterologous booster vaccination followed by Omicron BF.7 breakthrough infection, integrating bulk BCR sequencing with single B cell culture and antibody binding analysis. Breakthrough infection was associated with broadened serum neutralization across SARS-CoV-2 variants and related sarbecoviruses, consistent with recall of antibodies targeting conserved epitopes. Repertoire analysis revealed stage-specific remodelling, with high-affinity binding antibodies shifting from an IGHV1-46-enriched profile after vaccination to preferential representation of IGHV3-30-3 after infection. Isolated monoclonal antibodies exhibited nanomolar-to-picomolar binding affinities to diverse animal-derived sarbecovirus spikes, with broad binding commonly, but not universally, associated with CDRH3 lengths of 14-16 amino acids. Phylogenetic and sequence analyses defined divergent evolutionary trajectories for IGHV1-46 and IGHV3-30-3 lineages, highlighting candidate genetic features that warrant validation in larger cohorts. Together, these findings describe how sequential heterologous antigen exposures can reshape the humoral repertoire in one individual and generate hypotheses for future pan-sarbecovirus antibody and vaccine studies.
authors: Qiao R, Chen X, Zhang X, Shao Y, Zhang L, Yang L, Mi Y, Lu Y, Li J, Chen Y, Yu H, Wang Y, Zhao X, Wang P.

title: Pantoea Species Isolated from Onion Plants and Bulbs Across Different Regions of Chile.
abstract: Onions are one of the main vegetables cultivated in Chile. In recent years, changing climate conditions have favored the emergence of new bacterial diseases, where Pantoea species have been reported as causal agents of onion leaf blight and bulb rot in central Chile. The objective of this work was to study the abundance of Pantoea spp. isolated from symptomatic onion plants sampled in different regions of Chile. The identification of Pantoea species was determined based on gyrB, leuS and rpoB genes sequences, revealing Pantoea agglomerans as the most frequently isolated species, followed by Pantoea ananatis and Pantoea eucalypti. Pathogenicity tests were performed. Only three of the 20 isolated strains showed clear symptoms of bulb damage, with P. ananatis exhibiting the most severe symptoms. The complete genome of a pathogenic strain of each identified species was sequenced. These genomes were used for the implementation of PCR-High Resolution Melting-based system determining characteristic profiles of each species in order to facilitate the identification of the isolates in onion samples. Six primer pairs of housekeeping genes previously used in multilocus analysis were used to test their ability to differentiate between Pantoea species. The primer pairs gyrB and leuS showed the greatest discrimination among the Pantoea species. In this study, the identification of Pantoea species isolated from onion crops in Chile, revealed that only a small proportion were pathogenic, even in diseased plants. This highlights complex plant-bacteria interactions and suggests PCR-HRM as a useful tool to study these populations and better understand disease development.
authors: Calderón G, Muñoz-Quiroz V, Vásconez IN, Seeger M, Guajardo J, MacLellan MP, Dutta B, Guajardo V, Valenzuela M.

title: Evolution-Inspired Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Protein Engineering.
abstract: Protein engineering requires efficient navigation of vast sequence spaces under limited evaluation budgets, especially when multiple properties must be optimized simultaneously. We developed evolution-inspired multi-objective Bayesian optimization (EvoMOBO), an active-learning framework that integrates path-dependent sequence generation, global candidate competition, and explicit multi-objective optimization, enabling efficient prioritization of high-value variants without exhaustive library enumeration. Compared with state-of-the-art methods on complete steroid receptor DNA-binding domain (DBD) and ParD3 antitoxin landscapes, EvoMOBO achieved greater target-region enrichment while maintaining sequence diversity across two- and three-objective tasks. In the DBD landscape, optimization guided by simulation-derived geometric descriptors enriched variants with satisfactory experimental performance without experimental labels. Building on this validation, we applied EvoMOBO to two enzyme-engineering tasks using mechanistic descriptors, with experiments reserved for final validation. For an old yellow enzyme from Geobacillus kaustophilus, probabilities of substrate binding and reaction preorganization guided optimization of a non-native oxidative dehydrogenation, yielding a variant that increased substrate conversion from 17.5% to 95%. For a formate oxidase from Aspergillus oryzae, stability-related descriptors identified aggregation-resistant variants that nearly doubled diethyl phthalate degradation in a photoenzymatic cascade. Together, these results demonstrate robust multi-objective optimization by EvoMOBO and show that mechanism-derived descriptors can effectively guide protein engineering toward experimentally improved functions.
authors: Wen K, Wang S, Sun Y, Li S, Wang M, Liu H, Li Q, Zhu J.

title: Adaptive laboratory evolution of Cupriavidus necator to sodium salts as a whole cell engineering strategy for enhanced trehalose production.
abstract: Trehalose is an important compatible solute with diverse applications in the pharmaceutical, food, and cosmetic industries. In Cupriavidus necator, trehalose biosynthesis is naturally associated with osmotic stress, but typically retained intracellularly as an osmo-protectant. In this study, adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) was used as a whole cell engineering strategy to adapt C. necator H16 to increasing osmotic stress. ALE was performed with independent lineages and gradually increasing concentrations of NaCl and Na₂SO₄, reaching stable growth at up to 500 mM NaCl or 400 mM Na₂SO₄. In selected single colonies of the adapted cultures, the SetA sugar efflux transporter from Escherichia coli was expressed to enable trehalose secretion. Moderate concentrations of Na₂SO₄ were identified as most effective osmotic trigger, balancing growth and trehalose production. Under the selected production conditions the best-performing adapted isolate produced 11.5 g/L trehalose from 20 g/L fructose, corresponding to 60.5% of the theoretical maximum yield, compared to 7.4 g/L and 42.1% in the parental strain. Genome sequencing revealed mutations affecting transporters, membrane structure, metabolism and regulators. These mutations are considered contributors to the observed osmoadaptive phenotype, while individual effects on trehalose production were not resolved. Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of ALE as a whole cell engineering strategy for generating C. necator isolates with improved extracellular trehalose production under defined conditions.
authors: van der Sande L, Müller M, Aliyu H, Kaster AK, Holtmann D.

title: Multi-Omics Mendelian Randomization Identifies DDX17 as a Potential Mediator Linking Gut Microbiota-Immune-Metabolism Axis to Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: IntroductionThe gut microbiota-immune-metabolism axis has been implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis; however, the key host molecular targets linking peripheral dysregulation to central neurodegeneration remain elusive.MethodsIn this study, we systematically integrated large-scale GWAS data covering 1,903 gut microbiota taxa, 14,696 immune cell features, and 34,843 metabolite features with AD GWAS summary statistics, using two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) to identify causal genes. These genes were intersected with differentially expressed genes from three GEO datasets, followed by protein-protein interaction network construction using four Cytoscape algorithms (MCC, EPC, DMNC, Degree) and feature selection via three machine learning methods (Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, LASSO). Single-cell transcriptomics (GSE188545) localized key gene expression, Support Vector Machine virtual knockout (scTenifoldKnk) analyzed downstream regulatory networks, with in vitro validation performed in okadaic acid-treated SH-SY5Y cells using RT-qPCR and Western blotting.ResultsMR analysis revealed multiple causal associations among microbial taxa, immune phenotypes, metabolites, and AD. Integration of MR causal genes with DEGs, PPI network analysis, and machine learning refinement prioritized six key genes: BYSL, DDX17, HSPA6, RRN3, C4B, and NCKAP1L. Among them, only DDX17 showed robust expression in AD-associated neuronal populations in single-cell transcriptomics, whereas the other five genes showed low expression and may act through non-cell-autonomous mechanisms. Virtual knockout predicted that the PI3K/AKT pathway was the most significantly enriched downstream of DDX17 perturbation. In vitro, DDX17 was significantly upregulated in an OA-induced AD cell model, and siRNA-mediated knockdown partially reversed tau hyperphosphorylation (total P-tau and P-tau Thr217), while restoring AKT phosphorylation at Thr308 and Ser473.ConclusionThese findings suggest that DDX17 is a potential downstream host candidate linking peripheral dysregulation to tau pathology in AD, partially through PI3K/AKT pathway modulation. However, these results are primarily hypothesis-generating, and direct mechanistic and in vivo validation remain essential.
authors: Xiao Z, Qin Y, Dong M, Wei S, Ma Q, Luo C, Li Y, Chen F, Wu G, Wei P, Hu R, Huang Z, Liu C.

title: Anti-osteoclastogenic statins from the deep-sea-derived fungus Penicillium commune.
abstract: Three new 11,15-seco-15-O-methyl statins (1-3) were isolated from the deep-sea-derived fungus Penicillium commune MCCC 3A00122, along with 28 known compounds. Their structures were established through comprehensive spectroscopic analyses, including NMR, HRESIMS, OR, and ECD. Compounds 2 and 11 exhibited potent inhibitory activity against RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis in bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMMs) at concentrations of 0.25-1.0 μM. Furthermore, compound 2 markedly disrupted F-actin ring formation and downregulated the mRNA expression of osteoclast-specific marker genes. RNA sequencing identified 308 differentially expressed genes following compound 2 treatment, including 207 upregulated and 101 downregulated genes. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses linked these transcriptional changes to osteoclast differentiation, bone resorption, inflammatory responses, and cytokine signaling. Protein-protein interaction analysis and molecular docking further nominated osteoclast-associated receptor (OSCAR) as a candidate target. Collectively, these findings identify compound 2 as a promising anti-osteoclastogenic candidate and provide a basis for further mechanistic and in vivo investigations.
authors: Yu HY, Guo YQ, Zou ZB, Meng DL, Yang XW, Xie CL.

title: First molecular detection and phylogenetic characterization of herpesviruses in Sri Lankan bats.
abstract: BackgroundHerpesviruses are highly diverse and widely distributed pathogens infecting a broad range of animal hosts, including bats. Despite this wide distribution, they are typically extremely species-specific in their host associations. To better understand herpesvirus diversity in Sri Lankan bats, we screened 391 oral swab samples collected from five different bat species inhabiting Wavulgalge cave, Wellawaya (Uva Province, Sri Lanka) during three sampling periods (March 2018, July 2018, and January 2019) for herpesvirus DNA. A nested PCR assay was used, targeting the DNA polymerase gene of Herpesviruses.ResultsIn total, 152 samples (38.87%) were tested positive, within five bat species (Hipposideros speoris (9/22), Hipposideros lankadiva (2/4), Miniopterus phillipsi (61/224), Rousettus leschenaultii (18/46), and Rhinolophus rouxii (62/95). Statistical analysis indicated no significant difference in overall detection rates among species (p > 0.05), whereas prevalence varied significantly across sampling periods (p ConclusionsNotably, sequences did not cluster by host bat species, suggesting limited host specificity among the Sri Lankan bat species examined. The high prevalence across multiple species highlights the complex host-virus dynamics. Overall, this study provides the first characterization of herpesviruses in Sri Lankan bats, contributing to global knowledge of bat virology.
authors: Perera T, Schwarz F, Muzeniek T, Siriwardana S, Becker-Ziaja B, Perera I, Handunnetti S, Weerasena J, Premawansa G, Premawansa S, Yapa W, Nitsche A, Kohl C.

title: PDCD6 reduces iridovirus SGIV infection via regulating apoptosis and immune response in Epinephelus coioides.
abstract: Programmed cell death 6 (PDCD6) is a key regulator of apoptosis and innate immunity. In this study, two novel PDCD6, PDCD6-1 and PDCD6-2, were identified from Epinephelus coioides, an important cultured marine fish in China. Both of PDCD6-1 and PDCD6-2 sequences contain three conserved EF-hand domains, and share high homology with PDCD6 from other teleosts. PDCD6 is distributed in both the cytoplasm and nucleus, and can be detected in all of ten tissues examined with the differential expression levels. The mRNA levels of both isoforms were significantly downregulated during Singapore grouper iridovirus (SGIV) infection, one of the most important viral pathogens of marine fish. Overexpressing PDCD6 significantly inhibited SGIV-induced cytopathic effects (CPE), the transcription of viral core genes (e.g., ICP18, LITAF, MCP, and VP19), and progeny virus produces. Overexpressing PDCD6 could promote the transcriptional activity of NF-κB and AP-1 promoters, and the expression of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α and IL-1β) during SGIV infection. Furthermore, PDCD6 promoted SGIV-induced apoptosis by activating the caspase-3 pathway, as evidenced by the upregulation of proapoptotic genes (p53 and Bax) and the downregulation of the antiapoptotic gene Bcl-2. However, knockdown PDCD6 occurred the opposite effects. These findings suggested that PDCD6 could act as a positive regulator of antiviral immunity in groupers, providing novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying fish resistance to iridovirus infection.
authors: Yang WF, Huang W, Zou SM, Zeng WD, Deng ZF, Lan YM, Wang TF, Qin QW, Sun HY.

title: Novel RNA viruses and differences in viral composition between summer and winter collections of a Portuguese Drosophila suzukii population.
abstract: Insect-associated RNA viruses are important modulators of host physiology, immunity, and population dynamics. Factors such as host ecology, geographical niches, and seasonal variation may influence virus-host interactions and shape virome composition. Characterizing viral communities across populations and host contexts is therefore essential for understanding the ecological and evolutionary drivers of viral diversity. The spotted-wing drosophila (Drosophila suzukii), an invasive pest of soft fruits, provides an ideal system to study insect-associated viruses due to its global spread and its presence in the field throughout the year. Here, we used high-throughput RNA sequencing to characterize the RNA virome of a Portuguese population of D. suzukii, analysing flies collected at a single site in summer (July 2021) and the following winter (January 2022). We identified nine viruses, including four putative novel viruses (DsuNV1, DsuViV1, DsuPhV1, and DsuRV1) and five previously described viruses reported in D. suzukii or related Drosophila hosts. Viral detection, prevalence, and abundance differed between the two collections, with some viruses identified in only one sampling period. The observed variation highlights the dynamic nature of viral communities in natural populations and expands the known diversity of viruses associated with this economically important pest. Additionally, the differences in viral repertoires observed between sampling periods suggest that dispersal, local ecology, and seasonal factors may contribute to shaping the D. suzukii virome, providing a foundation for future studies on virus-host interactions.
authors: Costa-Santos M, Santos C, Herrero S, Hernández-Pelegrín L.

title: Structure-guided optimization of the A58 DNA aptamer targeting the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein through integrated computational analysis.
abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein plays a key role in RNA recognition, genome packaging, and replication. Its RNA-binding domain is an attractive target for the development of nucleic acid-based antiviral and diagnostic strategies. The A58 DNA aptamer is an experimentally derived high-affinity aptamer that targets the nucleocapsid protein via its N-terminal RNA-binding domain to form a defined complex. However, the dynamic stability and binding energetics of this complex remain unexplored. Hence, in this computational study, a structure-guided strategy was employed to investigate the optimization of a 20-nucleotide A58 DNA aptamer. The original nucleotide sequence of the A58 aptamer was mutated to generate a library of 255 non-parental mutated variants at positions 9-12 while preserving the experimentally characterized 5'-TCGGAT-3' loop. The 3D structures were predicted using AlphaFold 3 and docked against the nucleocapsid protein using HADDOCK2.4. The top four best-affinity variants, Apt66, Apt123, Apt17, and Apt94, were selected after docking and subjected to molecular dynamics simulations for 200 ns along with the original PDB structure of the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein with the A58 aptamer taken as a reference. After a comprehensive post-simulation analysis, Apt94 was identified as the most favorable computationally prioritized candidate, followed by Apt123, Apt17, and Apt66, indicating that mutations at the targeted nucleotides in the A58 DNA aptamer can remodel its dynamic and energetic behaviors. This study provides a rational framework for identifying potential aptamer variants with distinct structural, dynamic, and energetic signatures for subsequent experimental affinity, specificity, and functional evaluation against the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein.
authors: Ul Haq A.

title: PLEKHG5 promotes equine herpesvirus type 1 replication and is associated with changes in cellular autophagy.
abstract: Equine herpesvirus type 1 (EHV-1) is an important equine pathogen that causes respiratory disease, abortion, and neurological disorders, posing a significant threat to the equine industry worldwide. Cellular autophagy plays important roles in viral infection; however, the involvement of PLEKHG5 in EHV-1 infection and its relationship with autophagy remain poorly understood. In this study, baby hamster kidney-21 (BHK-21) cells and Syrian golden hamsters were used to investigate the role of PLEKHG5 in EHV-1 infection. The results showed that PLEKHG5 expression positively correlated with EHV-1 replication. PLEKHG5 overexpression promoted viral genome replication, titers, and protein expression, whereas PLEKHG5 knockdown significantly inhibited viral replication. Changes in PLEKHG5 expression were accompanied by alterations in the autophagy-related markers LC3 and p62 and in autophagy-related structures. Confocal microscopy revealed spatial overlap of PLEKHG5 with p62, mRFP-LC3, and LAMP1, suggesting an association with autophagy- and lysosome-related compartments. In vivo experiments demonstrated that PLEKHG5 knockdown reduced viral loads in multiple tissues and alleviated inflammatory responses and tissue damage. Collectively, these findings suggest that PLEKHG5 promotes EHV-1 replication and is associated with changes in autophagy-related processes, providing new insights into host-virus interactions.
authors: Yu T, Ge L, Lv S, Duan Z, Wang B, Tang L, Yang L, Li Z, Shi H, Fu Q.

title: Multi-Omics Integration Reveals Key Genes and Potential Metabolic Mediation Mechanisms in Atopic Dermatitis.
abstract: ObjectiveTo integrate expression quantitative trait locus-based Mendelian randomization (eQTL-MR), spatial transcriptomics, summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), mediation MR, and exploratory virtual knockout to prioritize candidate genes and potential metabolic mediation pathways in atopic dermatitis (AD).MethodsWhole-blood eQTL and AD genome-wide association study data were analyzed by two-sample MR, followed by intersection with differentially expressed genes from lesional versus non-lesional AD skin spatial transcriptomics, SMR, and the heterogeneity in dependent instruments (HEIDI) test. MR of 1,400 plasma metabolomic traits was integrated with gene-metabolite and gene-AD estimates. Spatial expression and scTenifoldKnk applied to spot-level expression matrices were used for exploratory functional interpretation.ResultsMR identified 1,671 candidate genes; 66 overlapped with spatial transcriptomic differentially expressed genes, and 13 were prioritized by SMR/HEIDI. Eighty-six metabolites and 198 of 1,118 gene-metabolite tests were nominally associated (IVW P ConclusionThese computational findings suggest candidate gene-metabolite relationships in AD. The mediation paths did not survive correction for multiple testing. Interpretation of the spatial expression and virtual-knockout results requires additional methodological validation and independent experimental confirmation.
authors: Zhang C, Zhang T, Du K, Xue W, Wang Z, Du Y, Wang Z.

title: MicroRNA regulation of fruit development genes in contrasting Prunus persica varieties differing in harvest date.
abstract: Harvest date is a key agronomic trait in peach and nectarine production, strongly influencing market availability and economic value. Although fruit harvest timing can vary by up to three months among varieties, the transcriptional regulatory mechanisms underlying this trait remain poorly understood. In this study, we analyzed two nectarine varieties contrasting in harvest date: the early-ripening variety 'Early Juan' (EJ) and the late-ripening variety 'Super August' (SA). Agronomic traits and mesocarp cell wall composition were evaluated at four developmental stages, together with transcriptomic and microRNA (miRNA) profiling using three biological replicates per variety and stage. A total of 24 mRNA and 24 small RNA libraries were sequenced using Illumina HiSeq X (100-bp paired-end) and HiSeq 2500 (50-bp single-end) platforms, respectively. RNA-seq reads were aligned to the Prunus persica reference genome using STAR, while known and novel miRNAs were characterized using Bowtie and miRDeep-P. Differential expression was assessed using DESeq2 with an adjusted P-value/FDR ≤ 0.05 and |log2FC| > 1. Despite displaying similar agronomic characteristics, both varieties differed in mesocarp cell wall composition, with distinct temporal patterns of cell wall remodeling. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that developmental stage was the main source of variation, while variety-specific transcriptional divergence became more evident as fruit development progressed. A similar pattern was observed in miRNA profiles. A total of 380 novel miRNAs were identified, with the greatest number of differentially expressed miRNAs observed at the late developmental stage (T3). Regulatory network analyses identified three ppe-miR156 isoforms negatively correlated with members of the SPL transcription factor family, associated with abscisic acid and auxin signaling pathways. Additionally, ppe-miR858 was negatively correlated with CSLC12 and MYB20, genes linked to glucan biosynthesis and lignin-associated transcriptional regulation. Together, these findings identify the ppe-miR156-SPL and ppe-miR858-MYB20/CSLC12 modules as candidate regulators associated with harvest timing in nectarine and provide a molecular framework for future functional validation studies.
authors: Lillo-Carmona V, Fuenzalida-Valdivia I, Covarrubias MP, Guzmán-Belmar L, Arancibia N, Rothkegel K, Martínez-Almarza C, Zaviezo C, Pérez-Donoso AG, Turner A, Figueroa CR, Meneses C.

title: The relevance of genetic disease in kidney transplantation.
abstract: Purpose of reviewGenetic disease is an increasingly recognized, but undiagnosed, cause of kidney failure. This review examines how genetics informs the evaluation and management of kidney transplant candidates and recipients.Recent findingsMonogenic disease accounts for 10-20% of adult chronic kidney disease. In kidney transplantation cohorts, diagnostic yield increases with clinical selection, from 11% among waitlisted patients tested after excluding those with a documented genetic cause of kidney disease, to 23% in unselected kidney transplant recipients including polycystic kidney disease, to 33-54% in highly selected cohorts. Genomic testing reclassifies the cause of kidney failure in about one-third of genetically diagnosed recipients, most often correcting focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, or chronic kidney disease of unknown cause. Because recurrence tracks disease mechanisms rather than histology, a molecular diagnosis distinguishes nonrecurrent intrinsic kidney disease from recurrent circulating-factor and complement-mediated disease. It also identifies conditions that recur but are preventable, such as primary hyperoxaluria and adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency.SummaryGenetic testing, by targeted phenotype panels, comprehensive kidney-disease panels, or exome and genome sequencing as appropriate, should be integrated to the assessment of selected kidney transplant candidates and recipients, interpreted within a multidisciplinary team, and supported by periodic reanalysis.
authors: Arnaldi M, Connaughton DM.

title: Neoepitope prediction integrated with DNA repair gene profiling for precision oncology.
abstract: BackgroundTumors with defective DNA-repair machinery accumulate somatic mutations at a high rate, and some of these mutations give rise to neoantigens, short peptide fragments that the immune system can recognize as foreign elements. While the connection between repair deficiency and tumor immunogenicity is well established, few analyses ask which missense neoepitopes encoded by mutations in the repair genes themselves are generated by more than one mutation, and where such shared peptides sit between fully personalized and off-the-shelf vaccine designs.MethodsWe curated 1419 missense mutations across 29 DNA-repair genes from three TCGA cohorts: invasive breast carcinoma (BRCA), colorectal adenocarcinoma (COAD), and ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma (OV). For each variant, we generated 8-11mer mutant peptides and ran them through a consensus prediction pipeline (NetMHCpan 4.1, MHCflurry 2.0, and pVACseq), restricted to eight population-frequent HLA class I alleles. Peptides were ranked using a composite score that combined binding affinity (IC50), mutant-versus-wild-type fold change, the number of distinct mutations that produce the same peptide, and gene-level oncogenic relevance. A bipartite mutation-epitope graph was then projected onto the peptide layer to study connectivity. The analysis is purely in silico, covers only missense substitutions, and uses a population-based HLA panel rather than patient genotypes.ResultsThe pipeline yielded 33,405 unique candidate neoepitopes from 429,464 peptide-HLA predictions. About one in six (5420, 16.2%) were produced by more than one mutation, and the resulting network had a heavy-tailed degree distribution. We identified 836 hub peptides (2.5% of nodes) linked to more than five mutations, and 342 peptides linked to more than ten; the most connected are nested TP53 windows shared by 71 recurrent calls at a single genomic site. Hub and non-hub peptides did not differ meaningfully in predicted affinity (median best IC50 16,774 nM versus 16,671 nM; Cliff's delta -0.02; P = 0.26, Mann-Whitney U), and within the binding subset (IC50 ConclusionsTreating the missense neoepitope landscape as a mutation-peptide network identifies peptides shared by more than one mutation, concentrated at TP53 hotspots. These shared peptides illustrate design options between fully personalized and off-the-shelf vaccines, but all results are predictions from a population HLA panel and require experimental and patient-level validation.
authors: Shravya RS, Pallavi B, Singh TR.

title: Circulating Quiescin Sulfhydryl Oxidase and Risk of Cardiovascular Disease: A Mendelian Randomization and Post-GWAS Analysis.
abstract: BackgroundTo systematically evaluate the causal associations between circulating quiescin sulfhydryl oxidase (QSOX) family enzymes and cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) using Mendelian randomization (MR) and post-Genome-Wide Association Study (post-GWAS) analyses.MethodsThe authors integrated protein quantitative trait locus (pQTL) data for plasma QSOX from the INTERVAL and deCODE studies with CVD GWAS summary statistics from large‑scale biobank datasets and disease‑specific consortia. Discovery MR analyses were followed by meta-analysis and independent replication. Post-GWAS annotation using the FUMA platform was performed to delineate the pQTL architecture of circulating QSOX2 and to prioritize likely causal variants. Summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) was applied to confirm direct effects of QSOX2 on CVDs and to characterize its regulatory networks at individual cis and trans pQTLs.ResultsInitial pan-MR analyses suggested risk-increasing associations of circulating QSOX2 with several CVDs, but showed substantial SNP-level heterogeneity. Regional and functional annotation identified pleiotropic signals originating from distal and trans regions, and prioritized the missense variant rs12380852 as the leading causal candidate, predicted to impair QSOX2 structural stability and enzymatic activity. Notably, cis-MR and SMR analyses restricted to the QSOX2 locus revealed consistent protective effects against atrial fibrillation (AF) and heart failure (HF). Summary‑data-based Mendelian randomization on trans pQTL rs3184504 (a SH2B3 missense variant) linked SH2B3‑mediated inflammatory pathways to QSOX2 trans regulation.ConclusionThe authors' findings suggest a protective role of circulating QSOX2 in AF and HF. The prioritized causal variants and identified trans-regulatory pathways may serve as targets for future functional validation and druggable design. #Xinyu Che, Ao Chen, and Yan Xia contributed equally to this work.
authors: Che X, Chen A, Xia Y, Yang Z, Shao X, Yu B, Lu D, Ma J, Chen Z, Qian J, Ge J.

title: Next-Generation Mycobacterium tuberculosis Diagnostics: A Systematic Review of Molecular, CRISPR, and Biosensor Technologies.
abstract: IntroductionTB (tuberculosis) due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis continues to be a significant worldwide health issue. Timely and reliable diagnostic tests will improve treatment outcomes and reduce the spread of disease. Traditional TB diagnostics currently available, such as smear microscopy and culture, have significant limitations with regard to sensitivity and turnaround times, especially for smear-negative cases and for tuberculosis in extrapulmonary locations.ObjectivesThe purpose of this review is to analyze the evolution of TB diagnostics from traditional microbiology to new molecular diagnostic methods (including CRISPR, biosensor technology, and microfluidic methods), including an assessment of their diagnostic testing performance, feasibility, and potential for the future.MethodsThe systematic narrative review aimed to systematically assess literature published from 2020 to 2025 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The review was carried out according to the PRISMA guidelines and included 89 studies after screening and assessing for eligibility. The data were analysed qualitatively (i.e., through thematic analysis) by comparing data from conventional, molecular, and next-generation diagnostic methods.ResultsMolecular tests (e.g., GeneXpert, Line Probe Assays, PCR, and Whole Genome Sequencing) provide greater sensitivity and specificity than traditional methods and allow for faster diagnosis. Additionally, newer CRISPR-based tests, biosensors, and microfluidic devices hold promise for rapid, portable, point-of-care diagnosis of tuberculosis.DiscussionThe findings indicate that molecular diagnostics improve rapid detection and drug-resistance profiling, while CRISPR and biosensor platforms offer potential for rapid point-of-care testing. However, affordability, infrastructure, clinical validation, and scalability remain important barriers.ConclusionThe use of molecular diagnostic testing, CRISPR technology, biosensors, artificial intelligence, and portable platforms will dramatically enhance existing TB surveillance systems and strategies for controlling the disease globally.
authors: Gomase VS, Nimje HM, Kale S, Midathada A, Dhamane SP.

title: Overcoming hurdles in developing a reliable and reproducible biofilm model of Malassezia applied to M. furfur, M. pachydermatis, M. sympodialis and M. slooffiae.
abstract: Yeasts belonging to the Malassezia genus represent the predominant fungi of the human skin microbiota. Their involvement in various pathologies is notably associated with their ability to form biofilms. However, knowledge regarding these structures remains limited due to culture constraints related to lipid dependence. This study aimed to develop a reliable in vitro model for studying mono- and multispecies Malassezia biofilms, using M. furfur, M. pachydermatis, M. sympodialis, and M. slooffiae. To overcome the natural aggregation of cells, a sonication protocol was optimized to obtain homogeneous suspensions without affecting cell viability. A correlation between optical density at 600 nm and cell concentration enabled the rapid standardization of Malassezia inocula. The comparative study of planktonic growth kinetics revealed generation times ranging from 7 to 15 h depending on the species, with M. sympodialis exhibiting the fastest growth. No difference was observed for M. furfur and M. sympodialis grown in single or mixed culture in planktonic conditions. Biofilm development was monitored over 168 h by quantifying biomass and metabolic activity. M. furfur, M. pachydermatis, and M. sympodialis showed a significant increase in both parameters, typical of mature biofilms. In contrast, M. slooffiae exhibited an increase in metabolic activity without a significant increase in biomass, suggesting an unusual biofilm phenotype requiring further investigation. This study proposes a standardized biofilm model for the evaluation of mono- and multispecies biofilms suitable for the different species of Malassezia. This model represents a relevant tool for studying interspecies interactions and for the development of new antifungal strategies targeting Malassezia biofilms.
authors: Porcheron JE, Nalet L, Crapart S, Girardot M, Imbert C, Cateau E.

title: RecA protein activates the E. coli topoisomerase III catenation function: essential role of the RecA ATPase.
abstract: RecA protein loaded into lesion-containing post-replication gaps must engage in strand exchange utilizing DNA substrates with no free ends, a process that is topologically constrained. The process can be mimicked by examining RecA-mediated DNA strand exchange between a circular ssDNA and a partially homologous circular supercoiled DNA. RecA protein can pair these substrates but cannot promote a net strand exchange. On its own, topoisomerase III promotes little reaction with the same two substrates. However, the two proteins together promote a robust reaction that rapidly, within 1-2 min, converts the substrates quantitatively to catenanes and hemicatenanes. The results reveal an important new functional interaction for bacterial topoisomerase III. The reaction is tightly coupled to RecA-mediated ATP hydrolysis. The rate of RecA-promoted ATP hydrolysis controls not just the extent but also the rate of the catenation/hemicatenation reaction. The ssDNA substrate is also required. Post-replication gaps are created in essentially every replication cycle and can be lethal if left unresolved. Given the need for rapid gap amelioration prior to the arrival of a new replication fork, the strong enzymatic and topological collaboration between RecA and topoisomerase III may have been a major evolutionary driver for the RecA ATPase activity.
authors: Phan KL, Dunbar EL, Cox MM.

title: Rational engineering of a thermophilic xylose reductase for efficient galactitol biosynthesis in Yarrowia lipolytica.
abstract: To develop an efficient whole-cell biocatalytic system for galactitol production through rational engineering of a thermophilic xylose reductase (XR) and construction of an engineered Yarrowia lipolytica cell factory. Three thermophilic fungal XRs were screened for d-galactose reduction, and the XR from Thermomyces lanuginosus (TlXR) exhibited superior catalytic activity and thermostability. Multiple rational engineering strategies, including dimer-interface engineering and consensus-guided mutagenesis, were applied to improve TlXR performance. The superior mutant M3 (F204W/G222S/S274N) showed enhanced catalytic activity toward d-galactose and significantly improved thermostability, retaining 66.8% residual activity after incubation at 50°C for 12 h, whereas the wild-type enzyme retained only 17.6%. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the F204W mutation enhanced dimer-interface interactions, while G222S and S274N strengthened NADPH binding within the catalytic pocket. The optimized TlXR-M3 was subsequently introduced into Y. lipolytica through multi-copy genomic integration to establish a whole-cell biocatalytic system. The engineered strain S-Tl2 achieved 25.2 g l-1 galactitol from 40.0 g l-1  d-galactose, corresponding to a conversion yield of 63.0%. This study successfully developed an engineered thermophilic XR and an efficient Y. lipolytica whole-cell platform for galactitol biosynthesis. These results provide a promising strategy for sustainable production of rare sugar alcohols using thermophilic reductases and engineered yeast cell factories.
authors: Zhu Y, Deng L, Jiang S, Li J, Men Y, Yang J, Sun Y.
