title: De Novo Design of Multi-Mechanistic AIE Photosensitizer for Broad-Spectrum Bacterial Eradication.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance poses a serious threat to human health. Inspired by the clinical practice of employing drug combinations to achieve combined effects, we hypothesized that integrating multiple mechanisms into a single molecule could address drug-resistant bacterial infections. Based on a propeller-modification strategy and dual alkyl-chain engineering, we de novo designed and synthesized a C2-symmetric propeller-shaped aggregation-induced emission photosensitizer. After iterative screening, the optimized compound MeOTDP-2 exhibits broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, enabling efficient eradication of planktonic bacteria, drug-resistant strains, polymicrobial infections, biofilms, and persister cells, with no cellular invasiveness and negligible cytotoxicity. Mechanistic studies revealed that MeOTDP-2 achieves chemo-photodynamic combined antibacterial therapy by targeting and disrupting bacterial membranes and DNA, alongside light-mediated intracellular reactive oxygen species accumulation. Furthermore, in mouse models of MRSA-induced skin abscess and full-thickness skin wound infection, MeOTDP-2 demonstrated superior therapeutic efficacy to vancomycin. This strategy, integrating dual targeting with multiple mechanisms, offers new promise for overcoming bacterial resistance.
authors: Li ZH, Sun YQ, Li D, Zhu KW, Chen S, Xue L, Liu X, Li R, Kong H, Li YC, Zhang E.

title: Magnaporthe oryzae chrysovirus 1-A confers QoI fungicide tolerance in host conidial development.
abstract: Rice blast caused by Pyricularia oryzae (syn. Magnaporthe oryzae) is a major fungal disease of rice, and QoI fungicides are widely used for its control. Here, we established a conidium-based assay for evaluating mycovirus-associated fungicide responses using Magnaporthe oryzae chrysovirus 1-A (MoCV1-A)-infected and virus-free isogenic isolates. The conidial development of the two isolates was compared in the presence of azoxystrobin (AZ). MoCV1-A infection significantly reduced sensitivity to AZ at the conidial stage, although infected isolates remained susceptible at higher AZ concentrations. Quantitative RT-PCR showed that transcript levels of genes associated with mitochondrial respiration, cAMP-PKA signaling, and melanin biosynthesis were maintained in MoCV1-A-infected conidia following AZ treatment. The ATP levels of MoCV1-A-infected conidia also were consistently higher than those of virus-free conidia before and after AZ treatment. These results suggest that MoCV1-A infection reduces QoI sensitivity by maintaining cellular energy homeostasis under fungicide stress through a mechanism distinct from target-site mutations.
authors: Goto K, Komatsu K, Moriyama H.

title: In vitro susceptibility of antimicrobial resistant strains of Escherichia coli isolated from the urine of dogs to pivmecillinam and fosfomycin.
abstract: BackgroundMultidrug resistant (MDR) and extended spectrum beta-lactamase-producing (ESBL) uropathogenic Escherichia coli are a cause of urinary tract infection (UTI) in dogs. Limited antimicrobial options are available for these infections.Hypothesis/objectivesDetermine the in vitro susceptibility of MDR and ESBL urinary E. coli isolates to pivmecillinam and fosfomycin using isolates collected from dogs with either UTI or subclinical bacteriuria. The secondary aim was to compare 2 susceptibility test methods for pivmecillinam: agar dilution and gradient strip testing.AnimalsThirty-four banked frozen urine isolates stored at the University of California, Davis Microbiology Laboratory collected from 33 dogs.MethodsGradient strip tests and agar dilution were used to evaluate E. coli susceptibility to mecillinam, the active form of pivmecillinam. Median paired mecillinam minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) differences by the 2 test methods were compared. For mecillinam resistant isolates, genomic sequencing was performed to determine resistance genes. Fosfomycin MICs were determined by gradient strip susceptibility testing.ResultsAll isolates were susceptible to fosfomycin (34/34) and most isolates were susceptible using mecillinam agar dilution (31/34) and gradient strip (32/34), respectively. The paired log2-transformed mecillinam MIC results were significantly higher for agar dilution compared with gradient strip testing (V = 21.5, r = -0.91).Conclusions and clinical importancePivmecillinam and fosfomycin are potential antimicrobial treatment options for dogs with MDR or ESBL E. coli UTI. Agar dilution is the preferred testing method for mecillinam susceptibility.
authors: Pohlmann M, LeCuyer TE, Woerde D, Palm C, Westropp JL.

title: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Palindromic Repeats-Cas Genome-Editing Systems in Filamentous Fungi: Current Tools, Optimization Strategies, and Future Perspectives.
abstract: Filamentous fungi are important microbial cell factories for producing antibiotics, organic acids, enzymes, and other valuable products, with broad applications in food, agriculture, and medicine. However, inefficient and imprecise genome editing remains a major bottleneck limiting rational strain engineering. This review summarizes major genome-editing tools in filamentous fungi, including Cre-loxP, TALENs, and CRISPR-Cas systems, with emphasis on their mechanisms, advantages, and limitations. We highlight CRISPR-Cas9 as the predominant platform and discuss optimization strategies involving sgRNA design, engineered Cas9 variants, promoter engineering, AMA1-based replicative plasmids, and ribonucleoprotein delivery. Emerging technologies, including base editing, prime editing, Cas12a, and Mad7, are also discussed for their potential to broaden editing capabilities. Finally, we outline future perspectives focusing on extending the application of existing genome-editing systems in filamentous fungi and discovering novel genome-editing tools from large-scale omics data sets. This review will accelerate the development of filamentous fungi as versatile platforms for biomanufacturing.
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
authors: Du R, Wang W, Xie J, Li Y, Wu N, Xu Q.

title: Non-Linear Epigenetic Aging Clocks: A Case Study in Atlantic Halibut (Hippoglossus hippoglossus).
abstract: Age information is fundamental in population biology. In fisheries management, robust and effective stock assessment models depend on accurate estimates of fecundity, survival rates, and other life-history traits, many of which vary with age. Consequently, reliable age determination is essential for understanding population dynamics and supporting informed management and conservation decisions. Age in fish is generally estimated by counting otolith growth rings, a labor- and time-intensive approach that requires lethal sampling and highly specialized, species-specific expertise. To supplement current otolith-based aging efforts, we developed a DNA methylation approach for aging Atlantic Halibut. We conducted whole-genome methylation sequencing on 106 wild-caught individuals with otolith-derived age estimates, ranging from 4 to 29. CpG loci were evaluated as candidate age predictors using elastic net regression and a generalized additive model, with the latter allowing for the incorporation of non-linear relationships between CpG methylation and age. Age-associated loci identified by elastic net regression were primarily located in likely subtelomeric and intronic regions. Importantly, inclusion of older individuals in the data set led to changes in the selected CpG sites but not in their respective chromosomal regions, suggesting that it is the methylation patterns in the chromosomes, rather than specific CpG sites, that correlate with age. The sex-separated generalized additive model (GAM) performed better than the elastic net regression as it exhibited the lowest per-age median error (MAE < 1 year, or < 2% of the average Atlantic Halibut lifespan). Our framework for epigenetic clock calibration allows for robust, system-specific clock calibration, which can be used for other non-model organisms under exploitation and conservation concern.
authors: Weise EM, Nemeczek CM, den Heyer CE, Flemming JM, Ruzzante DE.

title: High-Throughput Dual-Optical Droplet Screening for Quantitative Functional Bacterial Selection.
abstract: Droplet microfluidics enables ultra-high-throughput biological screening, yet most platforms rely on single-parameter optical detection, limiting the information available for selection and analysis. Here, we present a high-throughput droplet screening and sorting platform that integrates simultaneous fluorescence and absorbance (scattering) detection with acoustic actuation for robust, kHz-rate operation. By combining complementary optical modalities within a single device, we enable multi-parameter characterization and sorting of droplets based on both molecular and cellular properties. We first validate the system using model droplets containing defined combinations of fluorophores and absorbers, achieving on-demand sorting of multiple sub-populations with efficiencies exceeding 97% at kilohertz rates. We then demonstrate biological functionality by quantifying bacterial growth via optical density (scattering/absorbance) and protein expression via green fluorescent protein (GFP) fluorescence within the same droplets. This dual readout enables simultaneous assessment of cell proliferation and gene expression and allows normalization of fluorescence signals to cell number, providing single-cell-level insight within droplets. Importantly, we observe a temporal delay of ∼42 min between growth and fluorescence signals, highlighting the dynamic relationship between cell proliferation and protein expression. The ability to resolve and exploit such multi-parameter dynamics enables more precise selection of functional phenotypes, including differentiation of sub-populations based on growth and expression characteristics. This integrated acoustofluidic platform provides a versatile and scalable approach for multi-parameter droplet analysis and sorting, with applications in microbiology, diagnostics, and directed evolution, where simultaneous measurement of the cellular state and function is critical.
authors: Richter ES, Link A, Sparrow R, Franke T.

title: A Hyaluronic Acid-Stabilized Zinc-Loaded Probiotic Mitigates Nanoplastic Toxicity across the Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis.
abstract: Nanoplastics are emerging stressors that perturb host physiology across the gut-immune-brain continuum, yet scalable interventions remain limited. Here, we engineer ZG@EcN@HA, a biohybrid living system created by vacuum-assisted intracellular loading of zinc gluconate into Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) followed by an outer hyaluronic acid (HA) shell. This architecture preserves probiotic culturability under gastric challenge and supports sustained zinc availability in intestinal conditions. In zebrafish chronically exposed to polystyrene nanoplastics, we observe reproducible neurobehavioral impairment coupled with inflammatory activation, redox imbalance, barrier stress, neurotransmitter dysregulation, and multiorgan histopathology. ZG@EcN@HA yields the most coherent rescue compared with single-component controls, restoring behavioral outputs and realigning immune-redox-neurochemical readouts. ASV-based profiling shows recovery of microbial diversity and a shift toward a control-like community structure, including reduced dominance of inflammation-linked taxa. Intestinal transcriptomics and integrative correlation analyses further support normalization of barrier/metabolic programs and attenuation of innate inflammatory signaling. Together, the data identify a materials-enabled strategy for microbiota-gut-brain protection against chronic nanoplastic stress.
authors: Zhao J, Zhang K, Fang Y, Tao R, Xu H, Yi J, Yu H, Chen R, Wang H, Wu W, Yang Q, Sun D.

title: Utilizing collateral effects of antibiotic resistance to sustain antibiotic efficacy and addressing current barriers to translation.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) results from acquiring mutations or genes that allow microbes to withstand antimicrobials. These genetic modifications can also cause non-selected changes in other cell phenotypes, such as fitness and susceptibility to antibiotic classes different from the one under selection. These collateral effects of AMR acquisition could be exploited to improve treatments. This is increasingly important in light of AMR as a major global health problem, associated with 4.71 million deaths worldwide in 2021, with 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to AMR. Additionally, the lack of development of novel antimicrobials active against resistant infections continues to compound the crisis. Even if new antimicrobials are developed, resistance will most likely emerge through adaptive evolution. Therefore, it is imperative to explore strategies to maintain the efficacy of new and existing antibiotics and limit the acquisition of AMR to continue to treat infections successfully. Understanding the impact of resistance acquisition on the bacterial phenotype, including collateral effects, has the potential to improve therapeutic outcomes. In this perspective, we will summarize the collateral effects of resistance acquisition, including fitness costs, collateral susceptibility networks, mutant selection windows and the probability of establishment of bacterial populations, and explore how these may be exploited to enhance the effectiveness of existing antibiotics. We will also discuss how challenges such as genetic background, polymicrobial infections and the environment are current barriers to the translation of these principles into the clinic.
authors: Kashif S, James BA, Domingo-Sananes MR, Hubbard ATM.

title: Phage-Based Biofilm Control in Engineered Water Environments.
abstract: Biofilms represent a predominant bacterial lifestyle and contribute to the ecological stability and biochemical functioning in water systems. Paradoxically, excessive biofilm formation threatens water security and public health by causing biofouling, harboring pathogens, and facilitating the transmission of antimicrobial resistance. Phage treatment offers a promising strategy for the targeted regulation of biofilm microecology without generating harmful disinfection byproducts. However, its performance in environmental settings can be constrained by spatiotemporal heterogeneity, suboptimal phage exposure, and the evolution of phage resistance in bacteria, creating additional challenges for engineering applications. Here, we synthesize phage-based biofilm control as a multilevel intervention paradigm organized by biological bottlenecks. We examine strategies that improve transport and host access, enhance targeting and productive lysis, induce biofilm disruption through prophage activation, and perturb biofilm communities through keystone-centered interactions. We then align these intervention principles with distinct biofilm scenarios and operational constraints in engineered water environments. Emerging technologies are evaluated according to their roles in target identification, validation under application-relevant conditions, and treatment monitoring. Finally, we propose a closed-loop framework encompassing system diagnosis, intervention design and validation, monitored deployment, and adaptive management. Overall, this Review provides an integrated roadmap for advancing scalable and sustainable phage-based biofilm control in engineered water environments.
authors: Zhang X, Ruan C, Balcazar JL, Liao J, Shen H, Shen Y, Alvarez PJJ, Yu P.

title: Purple Phototrophic Bacteria as a Novel Platform for Coenzyme Q10 Production from CO2, Syngas, and Sulfur Waste Byproducts.
abstract: The efficient conversion of CO2 and industrial waste streams into value-added products remains a critical challenge for sustainable microbial processes. Here, we present the first systematic demonstration of purple phototrophic bacteria (PPB) as platforms for the autotrophic valorization of CO2 and industrial off-gases or sulfur byproducts into valuable metabolites. Genome-guided screening combined with experimental validation identified strains capable of coupling photoautotrophic growth with the production of CoQ10 and carotenoid pigments. Among them, Rhodospirillum rubrum DSM 467 and DSM 107 exhibited the highest performance, maintaining stable CO2 and H2 consumption under semicontinuous operation and accumulating up to 9.6 ± 0.2 mgCoQ10 gbiomass-1 under CO2/ H2 conditions, comparable to engineered production systems. In addition, R. rubrum DSM 467 efficiently oxidized CO from syngas via the water-gas shift reaction, displaying hierarchical substrate utilization driven by energetic constraints. In contrast, Marichromatium purpuratum simultaneously oxidized H2 and thiosulfate (S2O32-), enabling parallel electron input into the photosynthetic electron transport chain and enhanced growth. Overall, these results establish PPB as robust and metabolically flexible biocatalysts for converting CO2 and industrial waste streams into high-value chemicals with direct applications in the pharmaceutical and nutraceutical industries.
authors: Huang-Lin E, Lebrero R, Cantera S.

title: Let sleeping dogs lie? Domestic carnivores as potential sentinels for One Health surveillance of antimicrobial resistance: the example of Réunion Island.
abstract: ObjectivesExtended-spectrum β-lactamase- and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (ESBL-E and CP-E, respectively) are global public health threats, prioritized by the WHO for urgent action. We assessed prevalence, risk factors and genomic context of ESBL-E and CP-E carriage in domestic carnivores on Réunion Island and compared resistant isolates with human isolates to evaluate pets' role in islandwide antimicrobial resistance transmission.MethodsCombining the methods of classical microbiology (selective culture, MS identification, disc-diffusion antimicrobial susceptibility testing) and WGS (using in-house Nanopore technology), we compared 55 ESBL-E isolates originating from 881 domestic carnivores obtained in an island-wide cross-sectional survey with 40 human isolates obtained through an existing ESBL surveillance network and from healthy volunteers. We evaluated the risk factors for ESBL-E carriage in domestic carnivores by fitting multivariate generalized linear models applied to data from anamnestic questionnaires.ResultsThe prevalence of ESBL-E/CP-E carriage was 6% in carnivores (dogs: 8%; cats: 3%). The dominant ESBL gene across hosts (dogs, cats, humans) was blaCTX-M-15, followed by blaCTX-M-27. Three carbapenem-resistant isolates were detected in dogs, including the blaNDM-1 gene. Risk factors for animal ESBL-E/CP-E colonization included intact reproductive status, recent antibiotic therapy and free-roaming behaviour. Animal-originating ESBL-producing Escherichia coli exhibited greater genetic diversity than human-origin isolates, suggesting multiple introduction sources and environmental influences.ConclusionsOur findings suggest that domestic carnivores should be routinely included in surveillance networks, as their lifestyle and close contact with humans may allow trends in their enteric antimicrobial-resistant flora to foreshadow trends in the human resistome.
authors: Rabaly C, Wilkinson DA, Miltgen G, Belmonte O, Etheves A, Maurines-Carboneill C, Sellier A, Doizy A, Rieux A, Garrigos T, Squarzoni C, Albrechtova K.

title: LESS-PseU: A Language Model-Enhanced Semistacking Framework for RNA Pseudouridine Site Prediction.
abstract: Accurate prediction of RNA pseudouridine (Ψ) sites remains challenging because existing models often struggle to integrate interpretable handcrafted features with high-dimensional contextual representations from pretrained genomic language models. To address this issue, we propose LESS-PseU, a language model-enhanced semistacking framework that fuses the predicted probability features of primary learners with DNABERT2 embeddings for multiple species Ψ site prediction. Specifically, we first built three primary learners based on three kinds of hand-crafted features, including one-hot, k-mer, and nucleotide chemical property features. Instead of training a primary learner based on the embeddings extracted from DNABERT2, the embeddings were directly concatenated with the predicted probabilities of the three primary learners as the input features for a Logistic Regression meta-learner for final prediction. Under a leakage-aware cross-validation setting, our model was validated on the training sets of three species. Furthermore, on independent test sets from human, mouse, and yeast, LESS-PseU achieved AUC values of 0.9069, 0.8833, and 0.8820, respectively, which were higher than those of the compared models. A Friedman test indicated an overall difference (p = 0.029). Paired DeLong tests further showed that the AUC improvements over Meta-PseU were significant for the human and mouse data sets, while those over PseU-ST were significant for all three species. Ablation analysis, fusion-strategy comparison, and pretrained language-model comparison further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Additional evaluations on m5C and m7G benchmarks provided preliminary evidence that the framework may be applicable to other RNA modification prediction tasks.
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
authors: Yang H, Cheng Z, He S, Zhang Y, Zhu X.

title: Synbiotic Kefir-Yacon Drink Ameliorates Hypertension by Modulating Antioxidant and Anti-Inflammatory Pathways.
abstract: Hypertension is associated with oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and gut microbiota dysbiosis. This study evaluated whether a fermented kefir-yacon synbiotic beverage could improve hemodynamic parameters in a hypertension model through its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and gut microbiota-modulating effects. Spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) and Wistar rats were divided into four groups: Wistar treated with vehicle (W), SHR treated with vehicle (SHR), SHR treated with unfermented yacon (SY), and SHR treated with the kefir-yacon beverage (SKY). Treatments were administered orally for 8 weeks. Hemodynamic parameters, oxidative stress markers, transcription factors, antioxidant enzymes, pro-inflammatory cytokines, cardiac hypertrophy, and selected fecal bacterial populations were assessed. The synbiotic beverage significantly reduced systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial pressure, restoring values comparable to those of normotensive animals (p < 0.05). Heart rate and cardiac hypertrophy were also reduced. In cardiac tissue, the beverage increased Nrf2 expression and antioxidant enzyme activities (SOD and CAT), while reducing lipid peroxidation (TBARS) and NF-κB expression. Plasma TNF-α and IL-6 concentrations decreased (p < 0.05). Fecal counts of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus increased, indicating modulation of gut microbiota. The fermented kefir-yacon beverage demonstrated antihypertensive, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory effects, suggesting its potential as a complementary nutritional strategy for managing hypertension.
authors: Moraes FSA, Fragoso MC, da Silva CL, Dutra KA, Gonçalves LGDS, Campelo LA, Melo Junior AF, Bissoli NS, Amorim GAB, Lima EM, Andrade TU.

title: Enhancing Ethanol Yield and Flavor Profile in Simulated Baijiu Solid‑State Fermentation via Cobalt Ferrite Nanozyme: An Innovative Nanozyme-Driven Strategy.
abstract: This study explored the application of cobalt ferrite (CoFe2O4) nanozyme as a novel biocatalyst to enhance the solid-state fermentation of baijiu. Results showed the nanozyme exhibited SOD-like and CAT-like activities, effectively reducing ROS levels in Saccharomyces cerevisiae induced by H2O2 and ethanol. In S. cerevisiae fermentation, supplementation with 500 µg/mL of the nanozyme significantly increased ethanol production by 22.15%, and transcriptomic analysis further revealed that the nanozyme upregulated genes involved in carbon utilization, ROS scavenging, and ethanol biosynthesis in S. cerevisiae. Based on the results, the CoFe2O4 nanozyme was introduced into fermentation grains of the simulated baijiu solid-state fermentation. Addition of the nanozyme (7.5 mg CoFe2O4 per 350 g of fermented grains) increased the total concentration of flavor compounds in fermented grains by 18.62%, and the alcohol by volume of distilled baijiu reached 15.15%vol. High-throughput sequencing of fermentation grains showed that nanozyme addition increased the relative abundances of Bacillus, Enterobacter, Saccharomyces, and Thermoascus. These genera were positively correlated with major flavor compounds. Moreover, metabolic function profiling demonstrated significant upregulation of genes involved in carbohydrate metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and detoxification. Collectively, this study presented an innovative nanozyme-based strategy to improve ethanol yield and flavor complexity in baijiu production. This strategy provided a promising route to optimizing microbial fermentation performance. It could further promote the technical progress of traditional fermented‑beverage production.
authors: Li Y, Xia M, Gao Y, Liu H, Hou C, Wang Q, Wang YZ.

title: Evidence of Putative Mitonuclear Incompatibilities in the Bullock's and Baltimore Oriole Hybrid Zone.
abstract: Mitonuclear incompatibilities are genetic mismatches between mitochondrial and nuclear genomes that initially arise through hybridization. Although these incompatibilities can reduce hybrid fitness and contribute to reproductive isolation, they remain poorly understood in most avian hybrid zones. To investigate mitonuclear discordance in the extensively studied hybrid zone between Bullock's (Icterus bullockii) and Baltimore Orioles (I. galbula), we used whole-genome resequencing and mitochondrial haplotyping to assign mitochondrial ancestry to 136 individuals previously characterized for their levels of nuclear genomic admixture. We detected a narrow mitochondrial cline across the hybrid zone and strong asymmetry in mitochondrial inheritance, with 83% of putative F1 hybrids having I. galbula mitochondrial ancestry, a pattern consistent with predictions from Darwin's corollary to Haldane's rule involving uniparentally inherited loci. Genome-wide association analyses revealed nonrandom associations between mitochondrial haplotype and autosomal nuclear loci, notably including candidate genes with mitochondrial functions. Population-specific signals of positive selection at these loci further suggest differential selective pressures linked to mitochondrial ancestry. Together, our results provide evidence that mitonuclear interactions may contribute to asymmetric introgression and the maintenance of species boundaries in this classic avian hybrid zone.
authors: Goch LP, Khalil S, Butcher B, Lovette IJ, Walsh J.

title: Integrated Multi-Omics Analyses Reveal Causal DNA Methylation-Breast Cancer Associations Mediated by Plasma Proteins.
abstract: Although aberrant DNA methylation is implicated in breast cancer (BC) pathogenesis, establishing causality is difficult and the downstream mediators are unclear. We investigated the causal role of blood DNA methylation and its proteomic mediators. Differentially methylated positions (DMPs) were identified from a genome-wide blood methylation dataset, and two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) was performed using methylation quantitative trait loci for the significant DMPs together with BC genetic data from two independent consortia (FinnGen and the Breast Cancer Association Consortium), applying inverse-variance weighted and generalized summary-data-based MR with validation by Bayesian colocalization and PheWAS. Proteome-wide mediation and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analyses explored downstream pathways. We identified 19,169 DMPs, and MR revealed 95 CpG sites with consistent, MR-supported associations with BC. Meta-analysis confirmed three high-confidence loci (cg15146122, OR = 0.91; cg01529201, OR = 1.14; cg24704912, OR = 1.11), with colocalization support for two of them. Mediation analysis identified 203 BC-associated proteins, the three CpG sites influencing 41-314 proteins involved in immune regulation, apoptosis and lysosomal pathways and scRNA-seq localized the mediator proteins to specific cell populations of the tumour microenvironment. Blood DNA methylation is therefore associated with BC risk in an MR-supported manner through specific plasma proteins, highlighting candidate epigenetic biomarkers.
journal: Journal of cellular and molecular medicine
authors: Wang W, Cheng Z, Liu R, Cheng X, Chen H.

title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals coordinated microbial, metabolic, and ovarian immune responses to dietary quercetin in aged laying chickens.
abstract: Ovarian aging is associated with declining laying performance, but the short-term physiological and molecular responses of aged laying hens to dietary quercetin remain incompletely characterized. In a 30-d feeding trial, 180 Hy-Line White hens (480 d old) received diets supplemented with 0, 200, or 600 mg/kg quercetin (6 cages per treatment; 10 hens per cage). Egg production was recorded by cage, and ovarian, biochemical, and molecular endpoints were assessed at day 30. Cecal microbiota, serum metabolomics, and ovarian transcriptomics were compared between the control and 600 mg/kg groups (n = 6 hens per group). Compared with controls, hens receiving 600 mg/kg quercetin had a higher four-week mean laying rate (90.67% vs. 87.74%), more small white follicles, and increased hepatic and ovarian antioxidant enzyme activities. ANCOM supported a difference in only one genus-level taxon (DEV114). Untargeted metabolomics selected 552 exploratory features based on nominal significance criteria, including elevated signals for features putatively annotated as tryptophan- and indole-related metabolites. Ovarian analyses showed increased CYP1B1 expression, reduced NLRP3 protein abundance, altered immune- and apoptosis-related transcripts, and lower TUNEL positivity in SWFs. Cross-omics associations did not remain significant after false discovery rate correction, limiting inference about independent microbiota-metabolite-ovary relationships. Together, these findings provide an integrated characterization of short-term reproductive and molecular responses to dietary quercetin in aged laying hens and highlight candidate metabolic and immune signatures for targeted mechanistic investigation.
authors: Yang Z, Dong J, Cai X, Yuan Q, Xiao Y, Gao W, Zhang C, Mi Y.

title: Site-specific ecological risk assessment of a historically contaminated site: Integrating environmental DNA and species sensitivity distributions for multi-trophic soil communities.
abstract: Ecological risk assessment of historically contaminated soils remains challenging because conventional species sensitivity distribution (SSD) approaches largely depend on standardized laboratory toxicity data derived from a limited number of test species. In this study, an environmental DNA (eDNA)-based SSD framework was explored to characterize multi-trophic community responses, evaluate site-specific risks, and estimate ecological thresholds across different land-use scenarios at a retired coking site. eDNA metabarcoding revealed substantial shifts in the composition and co-occurrence network structure of multi-trophic soil communities, including bacteria, fungi, protists, metazoans, and plants, along the contamination gradient. Five dominant contaminants, including naphthalene, indeno(1,2,3-cd)pyrene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and 1,2-xylene, were identified as major drivers of community responses. Concentration-response relationships between operational taxonomic units (OTUs) and contaminant concentrations were subsequently fitted, and SSD models were constructed using the estimated OTU-based EC50 values. Based on joint probability curves (JPCs), probabilistic ecological risks decreased in the following order: indeno(1,2,3-cd)pyrene, naphthalene, 1,2-xylene, toluene, and ethylbenzene. The derived hazardous concentration (HCx) ranges for naphthalene, indeno(1,2,3-cd)pyrene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and 1,2-xylene were 3.54-6.66, 0.250-0.589, 2.24-7.45, 5.00-10.0, and 0.184-1.57 mg kg-1, respectively, across parkland, residential, and industrial land-use scenarios. Overall, despite uncertainties inherent in eDNA methodology, this study suggests the feasibility of integrating eDNA-based community profiling with SSD modeling for in situ ecological risk screening at historically contaminated sites.
authors: Li X, Wan J, Guo Y, Chen Q, Lu X, Cai Y, Li W, Jiang J, Wang G, Long T.

title: Identification of environmental conditions favourable to Pseudo-nitzschia bloom occurrence along the Portuguese Atlantic coast using satellite-derived predictors.
abstract: Pseudo-nitzschia (Pn) diatoms pose recurrent risks to coastal ecosystems and shellfish harvesting along the Portuguese Atlantic coast, where operational forecasting of bloom occurrence can support monitoring programmes by enabling earlier and targeted management responses. Here we develop and evaluate a machine-learning framework to identify environmental conditions favourable to Pn bloom occurrence along the Portuguese Atlantic coast, using exclusively satellite-derived predictors and a validation strategy designed to closely mimic real-world forecasting conditions. Predictive models were developed for the core study region (the shellfish production zones L1-L2), a long-standing hotspot for Pn and domoic acid events, using a decade-long matched dataset (2013-2023; 1440 observations) combining sea surface temperature, an upwelling index, chlorophyll-a, and plankton functional types. Across multiple model classes and feature configurations, Pn habitat suitability proved moderately predictable. Ensemble tree-based methods achieved the strongest discrimination: Random Forest reached 0.74 ± 0.05 with environmental predictors; Extra Trees reached 0.77 ± 0.06 with biological variables added. Feature-importance analyses revealed that seasonal structure, spatial context, and lagged environmental conditions dominate model decisions, while biological indicators refine bloom likelihood within physically favourable periods. The framework demonstrates operationally relevant skill for satellite-supported HAB early-warning systems along eastern boundary upwelling coasts.
authors: Bnoussaad A, Cherif EK, Pinto L, Neves R, Silva AD, Bernardino A.

title: Double-probe rolling circle amplification with lateral flow readout for highly specific detection of the phytopathogenic and keratocutaneous pathogen Fusarium proliferatum.
abstract: Fusarium proliferatum is a soilborne phytopathogenic fungus that poses a serious threat to global crop production owing to its broad host range, strong toxigenicity, and wide distribution. Beyond its agricultural impact, this fungus has also emerged as an opportunistic pathogen capable of infecting human cornea and skin, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Rapid and accurate on-site detection is critical for early disease intervention. In this study, we adapted and optimized a dual-probe rolling circle amplification integrated with lateral flow assay (dpRCA-LFA) for the specific detection of F. proliferatum, building on previously reported dpRCA-LFA principles. The main contributions of this work are the design of F. proliferatum-specific probes and the optimization of the reaction system for soil and field sample testing. The conventional single padlock probe was redesigned into two probes (long probe and short probe), establishing a dual-recognition mechanism that substantially enhances specificity. Under optimized conditions, the lowest concentration at which a visible positive signal was observed was 6.6 × 10-4 ng μL-1 for genomic DNA and 2.7 × 102 copies μL-1 for recombinant plasmid containing the TEF-1α. These values represent the detection end-points under the tested conditions rather than statistically established limits of detection, and correspond to a 100-fold improvement over conventional PCR-AGE in the tested dilution series. Specificity testing against 19 fungal strains yielded positive signals exclusively for F. proliferatum. The assay exhibited robust anti-interference performance, with consistent detection even when target DNA constituted only 1% of total DNA. In artificially inoculated soil samples, dpRCA-LFA achieved a 10-fold higher sensitivity than PCR-AGE. In field samples, dpRCA-LFA identified five positive samples versus four detected by PCR-AGE. Given the limited number of field samples, this difference is presented as a preliminary observation rather than a demonstration of superior field performance. The entire process, from amplification to visual result interpretation, can be completed within 90 min without requiring specialized equipment. Collectively, dpRCA-LFA offers a rapid, sensitive, and specific tool for the detection of F. proliferatum in fungal cultures and soil matrices, with potential utility for decentralized screening after suitable DNA extraction and controlled reaction processing. Clinical application remains a future direction.
authors: Liu F, Xia W, Wu H, Wang Y, Zhang Y, Li X.

title: Fermentative valorization of edible algae: nutritional potential, food applications, safety considerations, and industrial challenges.
abstract: Edible algae, including microalgae and macroalgae, are recognized as sustainable aquatic bioresources for future food systems, with high areal productivity, low reliance on arable land and freshwater, and rich nutrients including proteins, polyunsaturated fatty acids, pigments, minerals, vitamins and functional polysaccharides. Yet their wider application in mainstream foods is limited by low digestibility, rigid cell walls, marine off-flavors, variable safety and high processing costs. This review examines the nutritional potential, food applications, fermentation strategies, safety considerations and industrial bottlenecks of edible algae, focusing on fermentation-mediated valorization as an enabling strategy beyond conventional preservation. Lactic acid, alcoholic and mixed-culture fermentation can boost shelf stability, release intracellular nutrients, modulate sensory attributes, generate bioactive metabolites, and support circular use of residual algal biomass. Meanwhile, advanced technologies like enzyme-assisted extraction, non-thermal extraction, microfluidics and nanoencapsulation help enhance ingredient functionality and bioactive delivery. The review also notes that the future value of algae-based foods relies on matrix-specific formulation, standardized safety control for heavy metals and iodine, strain improvement, biorefinery integration and consumer-oriented sensory design. Overall, fermentative and precision-processing strategies offer a promising route to transform algae from niche supplements into safe, palatable, multifunctional ingredients for sustainable food innovation.
authors: Ma D, Xia C, Jia A, Zhang G, Zhao Y, Ren H, Liu X, Li F, Li L, Jia R, Li K.

title: Metagenomic insights into carbon and nitrogen cycling functions in an integrated rice-crayfish farming system with straw return.
abstract: Straw return is an important strategy for agricultural residue utilization, and functional microbial communities are known to play a pivotal role in straw decomposition and nutrient cycling. Nevertheless, the decomposition dynamics and associated microbial functional outcomes in rice-aquaculture systems remain poorly documented. This study established a rice-crayfish integrated system with straw return and assessed the mechanisms of straw decomposition and the resulting improvement on soil fertility through soil physicochemical characterization, enzyme activity assays, and metagenomic sequencing. Soil samples were obtained in July (PF7, the rice transplanting stage following the crayfish farming period) and November (PF11, the post-harvest field drying period), with surrounding ditches as controls (CK7 and CK11). The results showed that straw was effectively decomposed, releasing potassium and nitrogen nutrients, while urease and cellulase activities were markedly increased in the paddy field. Metagenomic analysis revealed that Pseudomonadota was the dominant phylum, whereas Euryarchaeota and Nitrososphaerota exhibited the most pronounced changes, with their abundances in PF11 being 0.23-fold and 10.57-fold of those in CK11, respectively. In the C cycle, C degradation was the most abundant pathway, in which amino acid degradation (primarily derived from crayfish farming) dominated, followed by aromatic compound degradation (associated with straw decomposition). For the methane metabolic pathway, the greenhouse gas emission potential was reduced, as evidenced by lower mcrA abundances in PF than in CK. N cycling was primarily mediated through organic N metabolism (81.63-84.14%), with the remaining fraction dominated by nitrification and denitrification. Furthermore, the relevant analysis consistently indicated that C cycling genes occupy more central positions and TN showed a negative effect on these genes. Collectively, this integrated system was associated with straw decomposition, facilitated terminal organic C and N mineralization, while greenhouse gas-related functional potentials were reduced, supporting sustainable straw utilization in rice-crayfish agroecosystems.
authors: Wang F, Chen Z, Zhou X, Liu X, Jiang Y, Fang G, Su Y, Rong C, Ji S, Hou G.

title: Iron-oxidizing bacteria-mediated Fe(II) organo-mineralization drives arsenic and microplastics co-immobilization.
abstract: The increasing coexistence of arsenic (As) and microplastics (MPs) in acid mine drainage (AMD) environments poses amplified ecological risks to aquatic ecosystems. However, the mechanisms underlying their co-immobilization remain poorly understood. Here, quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation monitoring, molecular dynamics simulations, and microanalytical techniques were integrated to investigate Fe(II) organo-mineralization mediated by Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans, a typical iron-oxidizing bacterium, and its role in As-MPs co-immobilization. The results show that A. ferrooxidans promoted organo-poorly crystalline Fe-As minerals (organo-PCFAMs) formation, whose organic components including lipids, free fatty acids, and/or saccharides, facilitated their adhesion to polyethylene (PE)- and polystyrene (PS)-MPs primarily through van der Waals interactions. Meanwhile, hydroxyl radicals generated during Fe(II) bio-oxidation, continued organo-PCFAMs accumulation and transformation intensified MPs surface damage with their size reduction, and increased organo-PCFAMs loading capacity. These coupled processes enhanced As-MPs co-immobilization, achieving removal rates of 61-98% for As and 73-97% for MPs, with PS-MPs immobilized more effectively than PE-MPs owing to stronger interfacial interactions. Overall, this study elucidates molecular-to-microscale mechanisms by which A. ferrooxidans-mediated organo-mineralization generated mineral bridge to drive As-MPs co-immobilization, advances understanding of their coupled biogeochemical cycling, and provides a strategy for mitigating As-MPs co-contamination in AMD environments.
authors: Xia X, Zhou YH, Xia JL, Nie ZY, Liang YT, Yang K.

title: Microplastics and cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms: Mechanistic pathways, cyanotoxin dynamics, and quantitative evidence from polystyrene (PS)-Microcystis interactions.
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) and cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (HABs) are widespread aquatic stressors that threaten ecosystem health and water quality. Their co-occurrence may further alter bloom dynamics, cyanotoxin production, and associated exposure risks. However, inconsistent findings hinder mechanistic understanding. This review synthesizes evidence from pure-culture experiments, mixed-community studies, field and environmentally realistic observations, and cyanotoxin-focused research, with an emphasis on freshwater cyanobacteria. We have conducted a focused meta-analysis of polystyrene (PS) effects on pure cultures of Microcystis aeruginosa, selecting this polymer-species pair to reduce polymer-related variability. PS exposure had an overall inhibitory effect, reducing M. aeruginosa growth by approximately 27%, although substantial heterogeneity persisted. Across the broader literature, outcomes depended on polymer identity, particle size, concentration, surface chemistry, and aging state. MPs may indirectly modify bloom development through extracellular polymeric substance production, aggregation, biofilm and plastisphere formation, and nutrient-mediated interactions. They may also affect cyanotoxin synthesis, extracellular release, adsorption-desorption, and secondary exposure pathways. Overall, MPs are not universal promoters of HABs but context-dependent modulators of bloom development, toxicity, and ecological risk, with considerable variability even within a single polymer-species system.
authors: Lv H, Liu H, Shan S, Xu Y, Liu S, Zhang X, Lopez C, Li D, Zhang Y, Li B.

title: Molecular diagnostics in immunocompromised patients: promises, pitfalls, and practical strategies.
abstract: Infections remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in immunocompromised patients, frequently presenting with atypical clinical manifestations and a broad spectrum of potential pathogens. Advances in molecular diagnostics, particularly multiplex PCR panels and metagenomic next-generation sequencing, have substantially improved pathogen detection rates and reduced time to diagnosis. Nevertheless, their routine clinical implementation remains challenging. Key limitations include: the inability to reliably distinguish colonization from active infection, high costs, and the risk of over-interpretation in the absence of clinical correlation. This mini-review provides an etiological framework for infections in immunocompromised hosts, critically examines the indications and limitations of current molecular diagnostic platforms, and proposes integrated multimodal strategies to optimize clinical decision-making and antimicrobial stewardship.
journal: Revista espanola de quimioterapia : publicacion oficial de la Sociedad Espanola de Quimioterapia
authors: Rua M, Pina-Sánchez M, Candel FJ, Del Pozo JL.

title: Syndromic diagnosis and precision medicine in severe infections.
abstract: The implementation of syndromic PCR panels has transformed the management of severe infections, including bloodstream, lower respiratory tract, and central nervous system infections, by enabling rapid pathogen identification and earlier optimization of antimicrobial therapy. As regulatory, technical, and interpretative challenges are overcome, unbiased shotgun metagenomic next-generation sequencing is expected to complement these platforms and become integrated into routine clinical practice, offering comprehensive, hypothesis-free detection of known and emerging pathogens in a single assay.
journal: Revista espanola de quimioterapia : publicacion oficial de la Sociedad Espanola de Quimioterapia
authors: Clari MÁ, Carbonell N, Navarro D.

title: Microbial manganese oxidation links aquatic biogeochemistry to water treatment performance.
abstract: Microbial manganese (Mn) oxidation converts dissolved Mn(II) into Mn(III/IV)-bearing solids and generates biogenic Mn oxides (BioMnOx) that shape nutrient and contaminant fate. This review addresses three questions: what evidence identifies microbial Mn(II)-oxidation pathways; how do environmental conditions and mineral properties regulate these pathways and subsequent reactions; and which measurements link mechanistic activity to water-treatment performance? We synthesize studies on Mn-oxidizing microorganisms, catalytic mechanisms, environmental regulation and community interactions, coupling with carbon and nitrogen cycling, and BioMnOx reactivity in natural and engineered waters. Direct routes involving multicopper oxidases, heme peroxidases, and catalase-peroxidases operate alongside ROS-mediated and microenvironmental pathways, with their relative contributions shaped by oxygen availability, nutrient supply, physiological state, and community composition. BioMnOx provide reactive, mixed-valence interfaces that retain metals and metalloids and transform nitrogen species, organic contaminants, and natural organic matter. Groundwater biofiltration is the most established application, while Mn-redox-driven nitrogen removal and micropollutant treatment are emerging configurations. Translating these processes into reliable treatment requires comparable activity metrics, paired aqueous and solid-phase Mn measurements, spatially resolved Mn/O2 profiles, and long-term evaluation in realistic water matrices.
authors: Liu Y, Li F, Zhou H.

title: Cytosolic DNA sensing through the cGAS-STING pathway contributes to neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neuron loss in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Current therapies for Parkinson's disease (PD) relieve symptoms but do not slow neurodegeneration. Chronic neuroinflammation driven by innate immunity is increasingly implicated in dopaminergic neuron loss, and the cytosolic DNA sensor cGAS and its adaptor STING are candidate mediators. cGAS-STING converts misplaced self- or pathogen-derived double-stranded DNA into type I interferon and NF-κB responses. We summarize the signaling cascade and its structural basis, and review evidence from post-mortem tissue, genetic studies and animal models that mitochondrial DNA leakage, lysosomal dysfunction and α-synuclein pathology activate cGAS-STING in microglia and astrocytes. We propose an Aging-BBB-virus-cGAS-STING hypothesis to explain delayed onset and selective nigral vulnerability. Finally, we evaluate natural compounds, autophagy enhancers and STING inhibitors, and argue that brain penetration and combination approaches will determine whether cGAS-STING inhibition becomes disease-modifying.
authors: Sun Y, He L, Peng Q.

title: A microbiome-guided foliar Bacillus SynCom couples photosynthetic growth with low-toxicity cadmium accumulation in Solanum nigrum L.
abstract: Cadmium (Cd) phytoextraction often requires balancing metal accumulation with plant growth, yet Cd toxicity constrains photosynthesis and biomass production. Here, we developed a microbiome-guided foliar Bacillus synthetic community (SynCom) for Solanum nigrum, combining Bacillus megaterium NCT-2 with a leaf-derived Bacillus isolate, LE45, selected from the NCT-2-responsive leaf microbiome. SynCom inoculation enhanced leaf colonization, increased leaf fresh weight, Cd concentration, and leaf Cd accumulation by 41.35%, 35.33%, and 91.24%, respectively, and improved magnesium (Mg) accumulation, SPAD and photosynthetic rate. It also reduced chloroplast starch granule accumulation while increasing soluble sugars and amylase activity. Cd partitioning shifted towards cell wall and soluble fractions and away from organelles, accompanied by less labile chemical forms. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses revealed coordinated changes in Mg transport, sugar metabolism, cell wall remodeling, Cd transport and stress-related pathways. Together, these results demonstrate that this simplified two-member SynCom couples Mg-associated photosynthetic activation and carbon remobilization with low-toxicity Cd accumulation, providing a controllable and leaf-centred framework for improving aboveground Cd phytoextraction.
authors: Chi Y, Wu S, Ma X, Wang J, Chen X, Chu S, Zhang S, Zhou P, Zhang D.

title: Molecular Architecture and Control of Enterococcus faecalis biofilms: Implications for Anti-virulence Therapy.
abstract: Enterococcus faecalis is a major opportunistic pathogen found especially in healthcare settings and is responsible for persistent and recurrent infections. Its remarkable survival and virulence can be attributed to its capacity to form robust biofilms on host tissues and medical devices. Biofilm-associated growth confers enhanced antibiotic tolerance, protects against host immune responses, and facilitates long-term colonization. The molecular mechanisms underlying E. faecalis biofilm development, encompassing the sequential stages of surface attachment, microcolony formation, maturation, and dispersal, have been of particular interest for therapeutic interventions. Key surface-associated factors, including enterococcal surface protein (Esp), endocarditis- and biofilm-associated pili (Ebp), aggregation substance, and Microbial Surface Components Recognizing Adhesive Matrix Molecules (MSCRAMMs), collectively mediate adhesion to biotic and abiotic surfaces and promote intercellular aggregation. The growth of the biofilm is mainly driven by enterococcal polysaccharide antigen (EPA) and extracellular DNA, both of which are critical for structural integrity and antimicrobial tolerance. Autolysis-dependent eDNA production, carried out by extracellular proteases, i.e., gelatinase (GelE) and serine protease (SprE), under the regulation of the Fsr quorum sensing (QS) system, is crucial for biofilm development in E. faecalis. Several global regulatory networks linked to stress adaptation, cell envelope homeostasis, and antimicrobial resistance could also affect biofilm physiology in E. faecalis. Several of these factors and regulatory pathways have been the target of emerging anti-biofilm strategies. These strategies might include small molecules, antimicrobial peptides, nanoparticles, and bacteriophages. Since biofilm development and sustainability are multifactorial processes, understanding their regulatory architecture will aid the development of effective therapeutic approaches against persistent enterococcal infections.
authors: Goel D, Kumar S.

title: The infectious unit of influenza A virus is a population of particles, not a single virion, as shown by absolute particle quantification
abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) populations are characterized by a high prevalence of non-infectious virions, with particle-to-plaque forming unit (PFU) ratios typically ranging from 10 to 1,000. While "multiplicity reactivation" -the process by which incomplete viral genomes (IVGs) establish productive infection through co-infection- has long been hypothesized, its quantitative nature has remained elusive. In this study, we utilized a digital influenza assay to achieve absolute quantification of IAV particles, allowing us to define the particle-based multiplicity of infection (pMOI) for precise evaluation. We combined this approach with a single-cell infection assay using microcompartmentalized containers and machine learning-based automated cell classification to accurately assess infection outcomes across a wide range of pMOIs. Our analysis of the A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (H1N1) revealed a count-to-plaque forming unit (PFU) ratio of approximately 400, meaning only a tiny fraction of particles possesses infectivity. Remarkably, the infection rate in single-cell infection experiments followed a sigmoidal curve and reached saturation at a pMOI of only 5 to 10. This demonstrates that under high-pMOI conditions, productive infection is predominantly driven by genome complementation among incomplete particles rather than solely by fully infectious virions. On the other hand, mathematical model analysis based on these findings suggested that the functionality of each of the eight genomic segments within a virus particle follows a stochastic process, resulting in a probability distribution for the number of functional segments per particle. This mechanism proved exceptionally robust across multiple strains despite a 20-fold variation in CTPR values. Ultimately, these findings indicate that incomplete particles are not merely biological noise but active contributors to the infection process, significantly enhancing the infectivity and evolutionary flexibility of IAV. This study will provide a more refined understanding of influenza transmission dynamics and risk assessment, particularly in environments where multiple virus particles are present within a single respiratory droplet.
authors: Kawahara, Y., Tamao, K., Fujioka, Y., Yamayoshi, S., Ohba, Y., Kawaoka, Y., Noji, H., Tabata, K. V.

title: bofasa enables high-quality orthology inference across diverse multi-species bacterial genome sets
abstract: Bacterial species can be separated by billions of years of evolution. However, studies of such ancient relationships often rely on methods developed for eukaryotes, which are less diverse. Such methods can regard instances of horizontal gene transfer as contamination, rely heavily on a species phylogeny when partitioning paralogs, and fail to account for the multi-domain architectures of some genes. Here, we introduce, showcase, and benchmark bofasa, a software for high-quality and automated inference of ortholog groups across distantly related bacterial species. bofasa employs a recursive algorithm to split coarse homolog groups into paralogous subsets and first establishes domain-level ortholog groups prior to assessing evolutionary relationships between entire proteins. In comparison to other methods commonly used for multi-species bacterial comparative genomics, bofasa is substantially more conservative in predicting orthology yet can often recover the largest single-copy core genome. Beyond orthology inference, the software also features several additional utility functionalities, including assessment of which ortholog groups are commonly found on mobile genetic elements or possess variable genomic contexts.
authors: Salamzade, R. A., Yaffe, E., Kottapalli, A., Kalan, L. R., Relman, D. A.

title: Exploring taxonomic diversity in the genus Suberites Nardo, 1833: Insights from microbial, phylogenetic, and morphological analyses
abstract: Marine sponges (phylum Porifera) are a highly diverse and polymorphic group of marine invertebrates whose taxonomic delimitation is often challenging due to high intraspecific variability and the scarcity of diagnostic morphological characters. Their close association with microbial symbionts also makes them an important source of secondary metabolites, some of which may contribute to sponge colouration. Here, we use morphological characters, molecular phylogenetic markers, and 16S metabarcoding of the symbiont community to understand speciation in a common Mediterranean sponge lineage. We collected 43 specimens of the genus Suberites from the Mediterranean Sea and the North and South Atlantic Oceans, between 55-150 m depths, and sequenced two barcoding genes, cytochrome c oxidase I and 28S rDNA, as well as studied their spicular complements. We identified five closely-related species: S. domuncula, S. ficus/pagurorum, S. dandelenae, S. ambulodomus, and a new species of Suberites from the Balearic Islands, Suberites sp. nov. The latter represents a potential new pseudo-cryptic species closely related to S. domuncula, because of their strong morphological and molecular affinities. The potential new Mediterranean species exhibits six colour morphotypes (yellow, gray, orange, brown, red, and blue), and the microbiome analyses of the symbiotic communities revealed significant differences in bacterial community composition among colour morphotypes, specially of bacteria that produce different pigments which potentially give the sponge is colouration. These results provide valuable insights into species boundaries and evolutionary relationships within the genus Suberites and support a role for the microbiome in sponge colouration.

title: RAMP-Seq: a single-tube nanopore workflow for co-amplifying full-length 16S rRNA and antimicrobial resistance genes for integrated taxonomic and resistance profiling
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance needs workflows that both identify bacteria and detect resistance genes from a single sample, but current targeted nanopore assays typically split these steps into separate reactions or library preparations. We introduce RAMP-Seq (Rapid AMR Profiling by Sequencing), a workflow that simultaneously amplifies the full-length 16S rRNA gene (~1,500 bp) together with eight resistance determinants (~600 - 700 bp) in a single multiplex PCR and then sequences the resulting mixed-length amplicon pool as a single nanopore library. The eight-primer pair set targets dominant alleles of {beta}-lactamase, carbapenemase, quinolone-resistance and silver-resistance families. Read-length distributions confirmed that both size classes were co-amplified evenly using a single, non-equimolar primer pool. From extracted DNA to the first taxonomically classified reads took 8.2 {+/-} 0.6 h. Full-length 16S sequencing of an eight-member mock community identified all anticipated taxa, and the observed abundances closely followed the expected log-scaled composition (Pearson's r = 0.879). The full nineplex amplicon assay was subsequently tested on three distinct matrices: pooled clinical isolates, spiked human blood, and environmental water samples. Using an equal-mass pool of genomic DNA from eleven multidrug-resistant clinical and repository isolates, the full assay produced genus-level and resistance-gene profiles that were consistent across biological replicates (r = 0.998 and r = 0.824), and it specifically identified all seven panel targets present, confirmed by Illumina whole-genome sequencing. After carbonate-based host DNA depletion, Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from spiked human blood at every titration down to 102 CFU/mL, as were all five panel targets carried by that strain. Across five water-sampling sites from a sewage treatment plant (STP) to a connected lake system, microbial communities and resistance-gene profiles were site-specific: influent and effluent communities overlapped little, while the lake inlet and outlet were similar. Target resistance genes were most numerous and abundant in STP influent, fewer in effluent, and rare or absent in lake and well samples. Because bacterial identification relies on amplification of the conserved, near-universal 16S rRNA gene, rather than on species-specific primer sets, RAMP-Seq can detect and taxonomically classify bacteria in a design-agnostic manner. The same single-tube chemistry therefore serves sample types as different as clinical specimens and environmental water and is extendable to longer ribosomal targets and further resistance-gene families.

title: Development of African Swine Fever Virus Pseudotype Systems for Ba71v and Georgia 2007 strains
abstract: African swine fever virus (ASFV) is a large, complex DNA virus that causes a severe haemorrhagic disease in domestic swine and Eurasian wild boar. Due to its high pathogenicity, research involving ASFV is restricted to high-containment laboratories, which significantly limits investigations into its biology, host interactions and the development of effective control measures. To overcome these limitations, this study utilised pseudotyped virus (PV) technology to identify ASFV proteins involved in cell entry. Candidate proteins were identified through bioinformatic analysis and a review of the published literature, incorporated into PVs, and subsequently assessed for their ability to facilitate cellular entry. This approach identified a combination of three ASFV proteins that, when combined, resulted in the most efficient cell entry. This work represents the successful generation of the first functional ASF pseudotype system for both Ba71v and Georgia 2007 strains, enabling the safe study of ASFV entry mechanisms under containment level 2.

title: Chromatin accessibility predictions reveal lineage-structured effects of noncoding variants across hematopoiesis
abstract: Background. Noncoding variants account for over 90% of genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings, but their mechanisms are often unclear. Sequence-to-function models provide one approach to variant interpretation by predicting the effects of genetic variation on molecular phenotypes. ChromBPNet predicts variant effects on chromatin accessibility, but how these predictions are organized across differentiation hierarchies and relate to orthogonal predictions remains unclear. Results. We trained ChromBPNet models for 17 hematopoietic cell types and scored 302,830 variants. Of 242,307 variants accessible in at least one cell type, 5.6% were predicted to alter chromatin accessibility. Variants active in more cell types had larger predicted effects. Predicted effects also reflected hematopoietic lineage structure, with sharing declining with lineage distance while effect direction was preserved in 99.6% of parent-child comparisons. ChromBPNet predictions agreed with GWAS fine-mapping but largely identified distinct variants. Fine-mapping-only variants were enriched for coding and transcript-associated variation, whereas ChromBPNet-only variants were enriched for regulatory elements, accessible chromatin, and trait-relevant activity. In K562 CRISPRi datasets, predicted accessibility gain showed limited association with target-gene validation. Regulatory elements containing CTCF motifs were less likely to have validated target genes, consistent with a role in chromatin organization rather than gene activation. Conclusions. ChromBPNet and fine-mapping provide complementary information about variant function. Predicted accessibility effects identify the cell types in which noncoding variants are likely to act and capture relationships across the hematopoietic hierarchy, but provide limited information about the genes they regulate. All predictions are available at: https://bloodnnet.ccbr.utoronto.ca/.
authors: Kazemi, M., Morris, J. A.

title: A p32 family RNA editing factor acts in mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis
abstract: AbstractBiogenesis of mitochondrial ribosomes (mitoribosomes) in the unicellular parasite Trypanosoma brucei requires an exceptionally large toolkit of assembly factors, identified in stable precursors of large and small mitoribosomal subunits (mtLSU and mtSSU) by cryoEM. Here, using genetic modifications and proteomic characterization of the immunoprecipitated assemblosome, the earliest characterized mtSSU precursor, we determined that a cap of its distinctive protrusion of hitherto unknown composition consists of a p22 homotrimer. This protein was previously implicated in the uridine-insertion editing of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit II transcript. Our functional analysis confirmed this role but revealed that its ablation also causes a loss of mtSSU and a systemic reduction in mitochondrial translation, phenocopying the depletion of established mitoribosomal assembly factors. Consequently, the oxidative phosphorylation system and mitochondrial function are compromised. The p22 protein belongs to the p32 family. We showed that five of its six trypanosomal members are involved in mtSSU biogenesis. Notably, p32 proteins are associated with mitoribosomes in two other distant eukaryotic lineages. A eukaryote-wide mapping of p32 proteins documented that their presence correlates with the retention of mitochondrial genomes. Together, our findings redefine trypanosomal p22 as a dual-function coordinator of mitochondrial gene expression and reveal that the ancestral role of the p32 family is associated with mitochondrial translation.

title: A conserved tetrapolar mating system permits sexual hybridization and recombinant host phenotypes in wheat- and barley-adapted Puccinia striiformis
abstract: AbstractHost specialization can restrict gene flow in fungal pathogens, yet sexual compatibility may persist when mating occurs on a shared alternate host. We tested this possibility by crossing wheat-adapted Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici and barley-adapted P. striiformis f. sp. hordei on Berberis vulgaris. Despite contrasting host specialization and genome-wide sequence differentiation, reciprocal crosses produced 18 viable aeciospore-derived progeny. Chromosome-scale parental assemblies revealed physically unlinked homeodomain (HD) and pheromone receptor (PR) mating-type loci, consistent with a conserved tetrapolar mating system. All progeny inherited one HD haplotype from each parent, representing all four parental HD haplotype combinations. Phenotyped progeny displayed host-interaction profiles distinct from either parent, including compatibility with selected genotypes of both wheat and barley. These findings demonstrate that host-associated differentiation in P. striiformis can coexist with incomplete intrinsic reproductive isolation between the tested parental isolates, allowing sexual hybridization to generate novel host phenotypes.

title: Fungal stress responses from the view of transcriptome vectors.
abstract: Transcriptomic approaches are widely used to study the stress biology of fungi or other (micro)organisms. When three or more transcriptomes are compared, considering their relative positions can clarify their relations. Here we represent transcriptomes as points in an N-dimensional space (transcriptome space), where dimensions measure the transcriptional intensities of genes. In this space stress responses correspond to vectors from the pretreatment transcriptome to the transcriptome altered by the treatment. This approach enables us to create simple definitions that let us focus on the data measured in the experiment. In addition, we show (1) the importance of kinetic studies in comparing stress responses, especially when examining responses to changes of different magnitudes; (2) how a reference transcriptome with genes expressed near the upper and lower ends of their transcriptional range constrains stress responses; (3) why the pre-treatment difference between transcriptomes makes the evaluation process difficult. We also show that comprehending the results of combinatorial stress response experiments is disproportionately challenging because of the cumulative nature of the problems mentioned above in these experiments. We propose that considering the relations of transcriptomes as points in the transcriptome space provides a view that complements the standard gene-centered analyses. Developing a model that describes the processes resulting in the observed relative position of transcriptomes can help reduce the risk of misinterpreting transcriptional changes at the level of individual genes or gene groups.
authors: Antal K, Pócsi I, Emri T.

title: Phytohormonal regulation of plant immunity under biotic stress: Mechanisms, crosstalk, and sustainable management strategies.
abstract: Biotic stress caused by pathogens and herbivores remains a major constraint on crop productivity. Plant immunity is regulated by an interconnected hormonal network in which salicylic acid, jasmonic acid, and ethylene interact with abscisic acid, auxin, cytokinins, gibberellins, brassinosteroids, strigolactones, and peptide hormones. This review synthesizes evidence on hormonal control of receptor-mediated immunity, reactive oxygen species, secondary metabolism, pathogen manipulation, and growth-defense trade-offs. Three conclusions emerge. First, hormonal effects are conditional on pathogen lifestyle, infection stage, tissue, dosage, genotype, and environment; therefore, individual hormones cannot be assigned universally protective or susceptibility-promoting roles. Second, pathogens exploit hormonal crosstalk, while constitutive defense activation can reduce growth, fertility, yield, or abiotic-stress tolerance. Third, omics, biosensors, spatial profiling, and genome editing can identify regulatory nodes, but their agricultural value depends on causal validation and field performance. We propose phytohormonal immune architecture as a framework for integrating these processes. Effective deployment should prioritize inducible, tissue-specific, and dose-controlled regulation through priming, beneficial microbes, breeding, promoter engineering, and targeted delivery. Hormone-based strategies should complement established crop-protection practices and be evaluated jointly for pathogen restriction, productivity, environmental stability, and physiological cost.
authors: Younas MU, Jamali ZH, Qasim M, Ahmad I, Korai SK, Zulfiqar U, Alotaibi MS, Gururani MA.

title: Mechanistic Characterization of a Multiproduct Sesquiterpene Synthase for Triquinanes and Quadranes from Streptomyces pathocidini.
abstract: Through genome mining, a sesquiterpene synthase from Streptomyces pathocidini was discovered and shown to generate a mixture of multiple products. Isotopic labeling experiments and DFT calculations were performed for detailed insight into its complex cyclization mechanism. Enzyme engineering through site-directed mutagenesis gave access to four additional products, one of which occurred as a minor constituent in the wild-type enzyme.

title: Accumulation of Polyphosphate Inhibits Biofilm Formation in Mycobacteria by Activating RegX3 to Reduce Intracellular c-di-GMP Levels.
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can persist in the host for prolonged periods. Biofilm formation represents a key strategy that promotes bacterial persistence, enhances antibiotic resistance, and facilitates immune evasion. Thus, targeting biofilm formation holds significant therapeutic potential for tuberculosis. Exopolyphosphatase 1 (PPX1), highly conserved among mycobacteria, hydrolyzes inorganic polyphosphate. Although changes in polyphosphate levels are known to influence mycobacterial biofilm formation, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. In this study, using a Mycobacterium smegmatis model strain, we found that the level of polyphosphate in the Δppx1 mutant significantly increases, concomitant with impaired biofilm formation. Further investigation revealed that elevated polyphosphate enhances the transcriptional activity of the transcription factor RegX3, which in turn represses biofilm formation. Mechanistically, activated RegX3 directly binds to and upregulates the dcpA gene, encoding a bifunctional enzyme that lowers intracellular cyclic di-GMP levels. This reduction ultimately perturbs cell wall lipid synthesis and compromises biofilm formation. In summary, this work reveals a signaling pathway through which polyphosphate governs biofilm formation in M. smegmatis.
authors: Huang T, Zhen J, Le TTT, Yan Y, Huang F, Xie J.

title: Fungal Phosphatase-Dependent Induction of Host Cell Pyroptosis by Candidalysin.
abstract: Fungal infections pose a major public health threat and can cause host cell damage through diverse forms of regulated cell death. However, our understanding of how fungal pathogens interact with host to elicit pyroptosis remains in its infancy. Here, we show that candidalysin, the cytolytic peptide toxin of Candida albicans, induces cell type-specific pyroptosis in epithelial cells and macrophages through GSDME and GSDMD activation, respectively. Dynamic dual transcriptomic profiling of host-fungal interaction suggested associations of candidalysin-induced pyroptosis with CCND1 in macrophages and BHLHE40 in epithelial cells, together with shared changes in phosphatase-related genes in C. albicans. In vivo, C. albicans infection induced a biphasic pyroptosis in kidney, characterized by early Caspase-3-GSDME and later Caspase-1-GSDMD activation. Candidalysin deficiency reduced pyroptotic responses and increased host CCND1 expression, whereas CCND1 knockdown enhanced pyroptosis. Furthermore, PHO100-mediated phosphate regulation contributed to fungal growth and hyphal development under phosphate limitation and influenced host pyroptotic responses. Together, these findings highlight a potential role for fungal phosphate-related regulation in candidalysin-associated pyroptosis and C. albicans pathogenicity.
authors: Hong YM, Wang XL, Wang L, Xiong SC, Zhou JA, Zhang TY, Sun YY, Wu D, Mao Y, Ma YJ, Cheong IH, Kozlakidis Z, Wu WJ, Chen CB, Liu NN, Wang H.

title: Mapping Protist Export to Deep-Sea Sediments Reveals Decoupled Export and Transfer Patterns.
abstract: Gravitational particle sinking is the main mechanism for carbon export in the biological carbon pump. However, the connectivity of particle-associated protist communities from the surface to the seafloor remains poorly resolved. We used 18S rRNA gene metabarcoding to characterise exported protist communities within sinking particles and deep-sea sediments in subtropical and subantarctic waters of the southwest Pacific Ocean. Sinking particles were collected with multi-depth formalin-fixed and preservative-free (live) particle interceptor traps and compared against the water column community (upper: 5-40 m; lower: 70-500 m). Amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) from upper water column samples accounted for a 2- to 4-fold higher proportion of reads and ASV richness compared to lower water column samples in fixed trap and sediment samples, suggesting a stronger surface protist contribution towards export. Tracing differential abundance patterns of ASVs in upper water column and fixed trap samples revealed taxa-specific decoupling between ASV export potential across the mixed layer and transfer potential to the upper mesopelagic. These export patterns, similarly suggested by taxa-specific decrease in ASV richness between fixed and live traps, remained comparable across biogeochemically contrasting water masses. This suggests that the drivers of particle-associated protist loss during export might be linked to characteristics consistent across environmental conditions, such as specific microbial interactions or cell properties. Transfer potential was a strong indicator of ASV detection in deep-sea sediments, emphasising that tracing export at multiple depths across the pelagic-benthic continuum is critical to identify protist taxa driving long-term carbon sequestration.
authors: Ong DRY, Gutiérrez-Rodríguez A, Bilewitch J, Nodder SD, Stukel MR, Décima M, Kelly TB, Lopes Dos Santos A.
