title: Antagonistic Activity of Endophytic Bacteria From Stress-Tolerant Plants Against Two Strains of Fusarium oxysporum.
abstract: Endophytes as microorganisms that colonize internal plant tissues without causing apparent disease symptoms under the conditions studied. The research focused on studying the soil profile of the host plants Phoenix dactylifera, Hemerocallis fulva, and Abutilon indicum selected for the isolation of PGP and stress-tolerant endophytes and their antagonistic activities of endophytic bacteria derived from the stress-tolerant plants. These isolates were assessed for their potential to promote plant growth (PGP). Following this, the screened isolates underwent further testing for their ability to tolerate salt stress (ranging from 2% to 16% salt concentration) and heavy metals. Additionally, their antagonistic effects against the plant pathogen Fusarium oxysporum strain MTCC 1755 and MTCC 8609 were examined. Samples for this study were collected from the Kangra district in Himachal Pradesh. It was found that twelve isolates have shown antagonistic activity against the phytopathogen MTCC1755, whereas 10 isolates have shown antagonistic activity against MTCC 8609. Two isolates, DL3R2 and A1S1S, promoted plant growth, enhanced stress tolerance, and showed antagonistic activity. Isolate A1S1S exhibited the highest level of inhibition against Fusarium oxysporum strains MTCC8609, with inhibition zones of 0.47 ± 0.13 cm, and DL3R2 with 0.42 ± 0.07 against MTCC1755, respectively. A1S1S, identified as Pelomonas aquatic (OP984335), and DL3R2, as Solibacillus silvestris (OP854919), showed promising biocontrol potential against Fusarium oxysporum, suggesting potential for practical applications with further research.
authors: Kaur M, Sharma V, Karnwal A, Alatar AA, Abdel-Salam EM, Faizan M, Faisal M.

title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia.
abstract: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here, we generated a single-cell multi-omic atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical human donors. This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis-regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia. Integration with matched MERFISH spatial transcriptomics further uncovered regional heterogeneity in epigenomic and transcriptional programs. Finally, we used this atlas to interpret noncoding risk variants associated with neuropsychiatric disorders and to construct a deep-learning model that predicts gene regulatory activities and variant effects. Together, this work provides a multimodal regulatory framework for understanding human basal ganglia organization, evolution, and disease genetics.
authors: Chang L, Li K, Xie Y, Zhong G, Rink JA, Báez-Becerra CT, Lie A, Indralingam HS, Loe T, Dong K, Gao X, Wang Z, Zu S, Kern JC, Zhao Z, Boone E, Flores J, Monell A, Olness J, Barragan C, Osgood E, Owens W, Schenker-Ahmed N, Zhang W, Liu D, Barcoma AS, Willier JK, Knutson KW, Russo KG, Liu J, Cho S, Arzavala J, Young CK, Sundaram GV, Manning AC, Sanchez Y, Bikkina A, Berry JV, O'Connor C, Liem M, Marrin MV, Rose C, Alt SN, Zhu C, Zemke NR, Ding W, Klein A, Fu Y, Johansen N, Bakken TE, Hodge RD, Keene CD, Lein ES, Li D, Zhu Q, Wang T, Xu X, Ecker JR, Behrens MM, Ren B.

title: Nucleic Acid Aptamers in Bacteriology: Mapping the Landscape, Exploring Bioimaging Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is becoming increasingly widespread, underlining the importance of rapid, accurate identification of bacterial infections for effective diagnostic, clinical, and environmental management. While next-generation sequencing excels at genetic characterization, it falls short in real-time, in situ detection, a critical gap where nucleic acid aptamers emerge as a compelling alternative. These synthetic oligonucleotides enable direct, low-cost, and versatile detection of bacterial targets without requiring DNA extraction or amplification. Their portability supports point-of-care diagnostics, while their molecular precision enables integration into advanced bioimaging platforms for non-invasive, real-time, spatial, and functional monitoring of pathogens in biological environments. This perspective explores the potential of aptamers for bacterial bioimaging, assessing the landscape of bacterial-targeting aptamers, zooming in on aptamer-based bioimaging approaches for bacterial detection, addressing key challenges, and outlining future opportunities, such as real-time dynamic infection imaging and theranostics, polyclonal/multivalent aptamers, multiplex imaging, aptamer-based biosensors, and AI-driven detection.
authors: Mezouarhi C, Benhassou HA, Ouadghiri M, Fechter P, Choulier L.

title: Tribovoltaic Effect-Driven Contact-Electro-Catalysis at a MoS2-Water Interface.
abstract: Contact-electro-catalysis (CEC) enables mechanically driven interfacial redox reactions through contact-induced charge transfer. Most CEC systems rely on dielectric or insulating materials, whereas the role of semiconductor carrier dynamics remains largely unexplored. Here we establish a tribovoltaic effect-driven CEC mechanism at a MoS2-water solid-liquid interface, where mechanical contact dynamically modulates semiconductor carriers and interfacial electron transfer. Electrical measurements and in situ Raman spectroscopy reveal that contact electrification and tribovoltaic carrier modulation synergistically regulate the interfacial electronic state. This coupled charge-transfer process promotes oxygen reduction to H2O2, which is subsequently activated to generate highly reactive •OH. Notably, under identical experimental conditions, the MoS2-based tribovoltaic-CEC system exhibits approximately 88-fold higher •OH production from H2O2 than conventional FEP- and PVDF-based CEC systems. Radical trapping, theoretical calculations and in situ fluorescence imaging further establish the relationship between interfacial charge transfer, oxygen activation and reactive oxygen species generation. Under ultrasound-assisted conditions, the system achieves approximately 90% degradation of tetracycline and efficient bacterial disinfection in real lake water. Our findings reveal the tribovoltaic effect as a potential mechanistic contributor to semiconductor catalytic activity, offering a new perspective on and a potential strategy for dynamically tuning solid-liquid interfacial catalysis through mechanically regulated carrier transfer.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
authors: Liu XY, Hu Q, Hong CZ, Zhu T, Sun YL, Li H, Jiang P.

title: A paper-based colorimetric biosensor for detecting African swine fever virus DNA in contrived whole blood.
abstract: African swine fever virus (ASFV) poses a major transboundary threat to global swine production, creating a need for timely molecular detection closer to the point of need (PON) to support rapid outbreak-control decisions. Here, we report a paper-based colorimetric quantitative loop-mediated isothermal amplification (qLAMP) biosensor targeting highly conserved ASFV viral protein 72 (VP72) gene for analytical detection of ASFV DNA in contrived whole blood samples. We evaluated paper LAMP assay using digital polymerase chain reaction (dPCR)-quantified synthetic VP72 plasmid DNA spiked into swine whole blood diluted to 5% (v/v) in 5% D-mannitol, and determined a limit of detection (LOD) of 25 copies per reaction, equivalent to approximately 67 copies per μL of original whole blood. In a separate cross-reactivity assessment using diluted plasma, we observed no amplification with nine common swine pathogens. The paper LAMP assay achieved 100% analytical sensitivity and specificity during in-house testing and 90% and 92% analytical sensitivity and specificity respectively in an external laboratory evaluation. The complete paper LAMP assay was performed within 60 min using a portable heating and imaging platform. Together, these results demonstrate the analytical feasibility and inter-laboratory transferability of a paper-based ASFV DNA detection workflow in a complex blood matrix, providing a foundation for future validation with virus-containing and naturally infected specimens toward point-of-need ASFV testing.
authors: Raut B, Palla G, Rafiq N, Wang J, Kumar V, Kamel MS, Nguyen DV, Lanka S, Maddox CW, Ragland D, Pasternak JA, Verma MS.

title: Serum isthmin-1 levels in chronic hepatitis B: association with viral replication and hepatic dysfunction.
abstract: IntroductionChronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health problem, underscoring the need for biomarkers that reflect viral replication and liver function. Isthmin-1 (ISM-1), an immunometabolic adipokine, has not been adequately studied in chronic HBV infection. This study evaluated serum ISM-1 levels in patients with chronic HBV to assess its potential as a complementary marker of viral activity and hepatic dysfunction.MethodologyIn this cross-sectional study, 100 patients with histologically mild chronic hepatitis B and 60 healthy controls were enrolled. Serum ISM-1 levels were measured using a commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kit alongside comprehensive virological and biochemical assessments.ResultsSerum ISM-1 concentrations were significantly lower in patients with chronic HBV than in healthy controls (102.74 ± 15.64 vs. 194.62 ± 187.59 pg/mL; p ConclusionsSerum ISM-1 levels are significantly reduced in chronic HBV infection and are inversely associated with viral replication. The positive correlation with direct bilirubin may reflect an adaptive cellular response to hepatocellular stress rather than simple dysfunction. Despite its limited specificity, the high sensitivity of ISM-1 suggests that it could be a valuable complementary tool for monitoring disease progression and viral status in clinical practice.
journal: Journal of infection in developing countries
authors: Öner P, Şenol FF, Aytaç Ö, Afşar Karatepe B, Aşçı Toraman Z, Algül S.

title: New Citrinin and Coumarin Derivatives from a Marine-Derived Penicillium sp. RCDB006.
abstract: One new citrinin derivative (1) and four new coumarins (2-5), along with seven known compounds, were isolated from a deep-sea-derived fungus Penicillium sp. RCDB006 in the sediments of the Diamantina Fracture Zone, the second deepest trench in the Indian Ocean. Comprehensive spectroscopic analyses (NMR and HRESIMS) established the planar structures. Furthermore, the absolute configurations of compounds 1-5 were assigned by comparing experimental and calculated ECD data, alongside X-ray crystallographic analysis. These compounds were evaluated for antibacterial and antiproliferative activities against a panel of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, as well as two cancer cell lines. Compound 9 exhibited modest bactericidal activity and also inhibited the growth of human acute myeloid leukemia (MV4-11) and colorectal cancer (SW620) cells with IC50 values of 34.36 and 36.50 μM, respectively.
authors: Li Q, Ruan W, Zhao Y, Pan Y, Lin L, Wu W, Huang W, Wang X, Deng G, Wang J, Yang CG, Chen Y, Wang MW.

title: A climate-driven mechanistic transmission model to characterize dengue epidemiology in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
abstract: Dengue is a major public health concern in tropical and sub-tropical areas of the world. Dengue virus is transmitted to humans primarily by female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and its epidemiology is heavily influenced by the climate. We developed a mechanistic compartmental model to characterize how climate and the evolution of population-level immunity influence changes in the epidemiology of dengue. The model explicitly incorporates aquatic and adult stages of the mosquito vector and cross-immunity (to another serotype) to better represent the transmission of dengue compared to previous models. It incorporates parameters related to mosquito development, behaviour, and mortality that are dependent on temperature, rainfall, and humidity. We calibrated the model to available dengue seroprevalence estimates for Dhaka, Bangladesh as it is a well-observed densely populated endemic area for dengue and will be strongly impacted by climate change. We then simulated dengue epidemiology for the period of 1995-2014 and compared the simulation output with available epidemiologic data. The model produced repeating annual outbreaks of dengue with strong seasonality, as observed in the dengue case reports for Dhaka. The median number of annual dengue infections produced by the model was 1.6 million (IQR: 0.6-2.3 million) and the median of the annual daily peak size of dengue infections was 24,121 (IQR: 7,807-39,308) across the simulations. These figures while exceeding reported cases in Dhaka, which do not include asymptomatic infections or cases not seeking healthcare, align with previous estimates. The modelled seroprevalence of 62% (IQR: 58-75%) aligned with survey results from Dhaka. In most model simulations, dengue infections occurred during August to December with the median peak occurring in October. The model outputs demonstrated a high degree of conformity to the reported data in terms of seasonality, and seroprevalence, indicating that the model provides a good representation of overall dengue epidemiology in Dhaka. By accounting for climate variables, host immunity, and their interplay, our model is well-suited for evaluating the long-term impact of climate change on dengue transmission in Dhaka and other settings where climate and epidemiological data are available.
authors: Paul KK, Regan DG, Green DL, Macadam I, Gray RT.

title: Risk assessment of ciguatoxic fish species in the French Antilles: scientific evidence for regulatory decision-making.
abstract: Ciguatera poisoning (CP) is a significant public health concern in tropical regions, caused by consumption of reef fish contaminated with ciguatoxins (CTX) produced by benthic dinoflagellates. Residents of the French Antilles (Guadeloupe and Martinique) who consume reef fish are regularly affected by CP. This study aimed to identify fish species responsible for CP in the French Antilles and to develop an evidence-based risk classification to inform updates to fish commercialization regulations. We analyzed surveillance data (2002-2021) from the General Directorate for Food and the National Reference Laboratory for Marine Biotoxins, including 74 fish samples associated with 133 human cases of CP. Fish species were identified using DNA analysis (63/74 specimens). A systematic review of PubMed and Scopus (from the earliest available records to June 2024) identified additional at-risk species in the Caribbean. Species were classified by confidence level based on CTX confirmation and documentation. DNA analysis identified 22 species from local poisoning cases and revealed 24% discordance with morphological identification (15/63 specimens). The literature review added 45 species. In total, 67 species were classified as posing CP risk, including 13 groupers (Serranidae), 9 jacks (Carangidae), 14 snappers (Lutjanidae) and 2 bigeyes (Priacanthidae). Comparison with the 2002 Guadeloupe prefectural order banning certain fish species highlighted regulatory gaps. Among 133 cases, digestive symptoms occurred in 71%, neurological in 57%, and pruritus in 49%. Imputability assessment showed 90% were probable or very probable. This assessment provides evidence to support updating regulatory frameworks in the French Antilles.
authors: Maillot A, Nicolas M, Dechraoui Bottein MY, Arnich N, Sinno-Tellier S, de Haro L.

title: miR-144-3p amplifies MAPK-dependent host responses to Eimeria tenella through dual-specificity phosphatase 1 repression.
abstract: Eimeria tenella (E. tenella) elicits pronounced inflammatory and cytopathic responses in chickens, but how post-transcriptional regulation shapes these host responses remains poorly understood. Whether infection-responsive microRNAs (miRNAs) are merely signatures of infection or active regulators of host-parasite interactions are particularly unclear. Here, we identified miR-144-3p as a key infection-associated miRNA by validating candidates derived from chickens with divergent susceptibility to coccidiosis in an independent E. tenella-challenged population. miR-144-3p was strongly associated with inflammatory, oxidative, and cecal pathological phenotypes and was markedly induced by sporozoite stimulation in DF-1 cells. Gain- and loss-of-function analyses showed that miR-144-3p increased the proportion of sporozoite-positive cells, enhanced inflammatory cytokine production and apoptosis, and impaired cell viability and proliferative capacity. Mechanistically, miR-144-3p directly bound the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of dual-specificity phosphatase 1 (DUSP1) and suppressed its protein expression. DUSP1 exerted reciprocal effects on these cellular phenotypes and restrained phosphorylation of p38, JNK, and ERK. miR-144-3p overexpression relieved DUSP1-mediated suppression of MAPK signaling, whereas restoration of DUSP1 partially reversed miR-144-3p-induced MAPK activation, inflammatory responses, apoptosis, and loss of cell viability. Collectively, these findings establish a miR-144-3p/DUSP1/MAPK regulatory axis through which post-transcriptional repression of a MAPK phosphatase amplifies sporozoite-associated inflammatory and cytopathic responses. This study provides a mechanistic framework linking miRNA-target interaction to MAPK-dependent host responses during E. tenella infection.
authors: Tang J, Dong L, Tang M, Zhang J, Zhang T, Zhang G, Xie K, Dai G.

title: NLRP3<sup>+</sup> Macrophages: Central Inflammatory Nodes of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm and Potential Cellular Target of Omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids.
abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a fatal inflammatory vascular disease without effective clinical treatments. Dietary patterns regulate aortic inflammation, and Mediterranean diet-derived omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (ω-3 PUFA) exert anti-inflammatory effects, yet their cellular targets in AAA remain unclear. We integrated three single-cell RNA-seq cohorts (12 AAA, 3 controls) and constructed a human aortic cell atlas with 64,258 cells. Pseudo-bulk analysis and CoVarNet multicellular network analysis revealed a core remodeling axis: protective FOLR2+ resident macrophages were depleted, while a unique AAA-enriched NLRP3+ inflammatory macrophage population (M08_Mph_NLRP3) formed the hub of pathological inflammatory networks. Three bulk transcriptomic cohorts and five complementary enrichment approaches verified this signature. An LPS/OX-LDL/IL-1β-stimulated THP-1 model recapitulated AAA macrophage pathological changes including NLRP3 inflammasome overactivation, enhanced proliferation and migration. Further functional tests demonstrated ω-3 PUFA markedly blocked inflammasome cascade, reduced IL-1β/IL-18 release and reversed all macrophage pathological phenotypes. This study identifies M08_Mph_NLRP3 as the important inflammatory mediator of AAA and provides single-cell and in vitro functional evidence supporting ω-3 PUFA as a candidate nutritional agent targeting NLRP3-driven vascular inflammation.
authors: Wang Y, Pan H, Rong H, Zeng Y, Li Y, Li X, Liang Z, Wang J, Fang L, Li P, Dai X.

title: Cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COX1) protects against hypoxic-ischemic injury in HT22 neurons by inhibiting oxidative stress and apoptosis through the Nrf2/HO-1 signaling.
abstract: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive oxidative stress, and neuronal apoptosis. Cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COX1), the catalytic core subunit of mitochondrial complex IV, is particularly susceptible to reactive oxygen species-mediated damage and may influence neuronal survival under hypoxic-ischemic conditions. However, the role of COX1 in HIE and its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. HIE related genes were screened by intergrating data from the GEOGSE144456 and GSE112137 dataset​s . An oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) injury model was established in HT22 cells. COX1 expression was quantified using reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and western blotting. Cell viability, proliferation, and apoptosis were assessed using Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assays, 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) assays, and annexin V/propidium iodide flow cytometry, respectively. Bioinformatic analysis identified COX1 as a candidate HIE-related target. OGD markedly reduced COX1 expression in HT22 cells. COX1 overexpression increased cell viability and proliferation, reduced apoptosis and cleaved caspase-3 expression, decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, increased glutathione (GSH) content and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, and upregulated nuclear factor-erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) and heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) expression. These effects were attenuated by the Nrf2 inhibitor ML385. COX1 may protect against oxygen-glucose deprivation-induced neuronal injury by activating the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway, reducing oxidative stress, and suppressing apoptosis.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10616-026-01105-5.
authors: Yu X, Zheng R, Han W.

title: DNAH5-Associated Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia With Natural Paternity and Advanced Bronchiectasis.
abstract: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a rare inherited disorder of motile cilia that may remain unrecognised until adulthood. We report a 43-year-old lifelong non-smoker with recurrent respiratory infections since childhood, chronic rhinosinusitis, situs inversus totalis, advanced bilateral bronchiectasis, severe non-reversible airflow obstruction, and chronic hypoxemic respiratory failure. His course was complicated by chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infection and frequent exacerbations. Despite a characteristic Kartagener phenotype, he had fathered six biological children conceived without assisted reproductive techniques. Whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous pathogenic frameshift variant in DNAH5 (NM_001369.3:c.5563dup; p.(Ile1855Asnfs*6)), establishing the molecular diagnosis. This case highlights the reproductive phenotypic variability of DNAH5-associated PCD and emphasises that natural paternity does not exclude PCD or justify delaying molecular genetic evaluation.
authors: Momchilovikj S, Debreshlioska A, Mustafa R, Angelovska I, Dimitrijevikj K, Omerova B.

title: Asymmetric bond modulation at electronically coupled Bi/SnS heterointerfaces enables high-rate and durable sodium-ion storage.
abstract: The conversion- and alloying-type materials are promising anode candidates of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) due to their high theoretical capacities. However, they still suffer from trade-off between structural stability and reaction kinetics, which limits the practical applications of SIBs. Herein, we report an efficient strategy to break such trade-off by asymmetric bond modulation. A Bi/SnS heterostructure encapsulated in N,S co-doped carbon frameworks (Bi/SnS@NSC) is designed and constructed. Metallic screening predominantly localizes the electronic perturbation on the SnS side. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and crystal orbital Hamilton population (COHP) analyses reveal that the interfacial charge polarization weakens SnS bonds, maintains stable BiBi interactions, and effectively reduces the diffusion barriers of Na+. In situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) characterization further confirms highly reversible multistep phase evolution of both components during sodiation/desodiation. As a result, Bi/SnS@NSC delivers a high capacity of 358.9 mAh g-1 at 40 A g-1, and maintains 310.6 mAh g-1 after 2500 cycles at 20 A g-1. This work provides an effective way to achieve a synergistic enhancement in the electrochemical performance and stability of SIBs by modulating the metal-semiconductor structure to control interfacial charge distribution.
journal: Journal of colloid and interface science
authors: Tan W, Chen J, Wen L, Guo D, Zhao J, Hao B, Zhang D, Han L, Qu X, Xiong Z, Huang R, Li X.

title: Protective effects of endophytic fungus Neopestalotiopsis clavispora against whole body γ-radiation: Modulation of oxidative stress, anti-inflammatory, and genoprotective actions.
abstract: BackgroundIonizing radiation induces reactive oxygen species (ROS) that lead to oxidative stress, haematological suppression, inflammation, DNA damage, and cell cycle perturbations. The identification of effective natural radioprotectors is therefore important for mitigating radiation-induced injuries during radiotherapy and accidental exposures. Natural endophytic fungi represent a promising source of bioactive metabolites with antioxidant properties as an alternative to synthetic agents for protecting against these effects.MethodsThe radioprotective potential of Neopestalotiopsis clavispora (N. clavispora) extract was investigated in Swiss albino mice exposed to whole-body γ-radiation (2 Gy, 60Co source, 3.58 Gy/min). Mice were pretreated orally with N. clavispora extract (100 mg/kg body weight) and ascorbic acid (100 mg/kg, reference standard) for 5 consecutive days prior to irradiation. Radiation-induced changes in haematological indices, oxidative stress markers (MDA, GSH, TAC, thiols), serum enzymes (SGPT, SGOT, ALP), cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-4), micronuclei, DNA damage (comet assay), and cell cycle were assessed 24 h post-irradiation.ResultsIrradiation significantly reduced RBC (7.09 ± 0.70 × 106/μL) and WBC (2.41 ± 0.42 × 103/μL), elevated MDA (2.51 ± 0.38 μM/L), depleted GSH (0.89 ± 0.11 μg/mL), increased SGPT (7.30 ± 0.92 IU/L), TNF-α (8.62 ± 0.96 pg/mL), IL-6 (21.77 ± 0.18 pg/mL), mnPCE (0.15 ± 0.00), OTM (7.88 ± 0.54), and reduced G0/G1 phase (41.54 ± 1.29%) versus controls. N. clavispora pretreatment restored these parameters comparably to ascorbic acid (e.g., RBC 8.01 ± 0.98 × 106/μL; MDA 1.24 ± 0.09 μM/L).ConclusionN. clavispora extract exerts potent radioprotective effects consistent with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and genoprotective actions.
journal: Applied radiation and isotopes : including data, instrumentation and methods for use in agriculture, industry and medicine
authors: Swaroopa S, Gnanasekaran TS, Kedilaya VR, Naregundi K, Lolajaksha AB, Murshed NMF, Poonacha SK.

title: Identification of m6A-Associated mRNAs, lncRNAs, and m6A Regulators in Endometriosis.
abstract: BackgroundEndometriosis (EMs), which causes significant pain and infertility, continues to affect women of reproductive age, yet its molecular mechanisms remain inadequately defined. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification is the most prevalent post-transcriptional modification in mammalian mRNA, and recent studies have increasingly focused on elucidating the relationship between m6A and EMs, to provide theoretical insights for clinical prevention and treatment.MethodsUsing human m6A-mRNA and lncRNA epigenomic microarray techniques, functional and pathway enrichment analysis, protein-protein interaction network (PPI), and R packages, we conducted exploratory analyses to identify mRNAs and lncRNAs with differential methylation, as well as important m6A regulators associated with EMs. These findings were verified using external databases, along with RNA extraction and quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR), immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence techniques.ResultsSpecifically, our analysis revealed 1631 hyper-upregulated, 219 hypo-upregulated, and 6483 hypo-downregulated differentially methylated and expressed genes (DMEGs). Additionally, we identified 8 candidate hub genes-RHOA, KCNA2, BDNF, CACNA1C, FGFR1, IL18, KCNIP2, and RPL17-and characterized their enriched pathways. Furthermore, we observed 6 significantly hypermethylated and 14 significantly hypomethylated lncRNAs in EMs. Our screening identified two key m6A regulators, WTAP and RBM15, which may represent candidate molecules worthy of further investigation in the context of EMs.ConclusionThis exploratory screening analysis delineates aberrant expression signatures of m6A regulators and their associated mRNAs and lncRNAs in endometriosis tissues, yielding preliminary molecular profiles that merely reflect correlations rather than causal or definite functional relationships.
authors: Ren C, He Y, Qu Y, Zhao Y, Zhang G.

title: Genetically Predicted Circulating Protein-to-Protein Ratios and Osteoarthritis Risk: A Mendelian Randomization Study with Pilot Experimental Assessment.
abstract: ObjectivesTo investigate associations between genetically predicted circulating protein- to-protein ratios (PPRs) and osteoarthritis (OA) and assess whether additional genetic analyses support their interpretation.MethodsTwo-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) screened 2,821 PPRs against two OA datasets. Nineteen candidates underwent reverse MR, instrument-location annotation, and regional colocalisation. Separate STAMBP and WWP2 MR analyses were compared with the STAMBP/WWP2 MR analysis. Functional annotation and pilot assessments of serum and cartilage in DMM mice provided biological context.ResultsNineteen PPRs showed nominal associations with concordant directions across datasets. None of 38 reverse associations survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Most prioritized instruments were trans to both component genes. STAMBP showed a positive association with GCST90038686, whereas STAMBP/WWP2 showed an inverse association; WWP2 showed no nominal association. RNF41/WWP2 and RNF41 colocalised with GO_AllOA in one discovery region under default priors, but support was prior-sensitive and not consistently replicated. STAMBP/WWP2 showed no strong regional colocalisation support. DMM mice had a lower serum STAMBP/WWP2 ratio and reduced staining for both proteins in cartilage.DiscussionCross-dataset consistency supports further investigation of the prioritized PPRs. However, predominantly trans instruments, prior-sensitive colocalisation, and differences between human genetic analyses and mouse expression measurements limit ratio-specific causal interpretation.ConclusionThese exploratory findings prioritize PPR-related signals for further investigation but do not establish ratio-specific causality, a mechanistic role in OA, or clinical utility.
authors: Xing M, Zhang Y, Zhao M, Song XY, Li L, Li X, Men X.

title: From gas exchange physiology to barrier biology and egg quality: a text-mining synthesis of avian eggshell pore-system research, 1953-2026.
abstract: Avian eggshell pores connect embryonic respiration, water balance, microbial defense and egg quality, but the evidence is distributed across physiological and production disciplines. We combined quantitative literature mapping with biological synthesis. We assembled a query-defined corpus of 445 publications from Web of Science and Scopus searches, including taxonomically relaxed and structure-function searches. Species-masked title-abstract text was analyzed by non-negative matrix factorization, with five topics retained for interpretation. Controlled dictionaries supplied complementary species, function, structure and technology annotations. The themes covered cuticle-mediated barriers, egg quality and storage, nest humidity and water loss, hatchability and breeder traits, and gas diffusion. Across completed years through 2025, publication activity increased by an estimated 40.7% per decade (incidence-rate ratio 1.407; 95% confidence interval 1.293-1.536). In the selected five-topic model, linear analyses showed declining gas-diffusion weights and increasing cuticle/barrier and quality/storage weights. Period means nevertheless showed nonuniform trajectories. Eleven enriched function-structure associations included microbial defense with cuticle/pore plugs (31 records; lift 4.22). Fifteen illustrative primary reports connected these patterns with effects of shell transport, barrier integrity, incubation conditions and storage interventions. The synthesis supports joint assessment of shell exchange, microbial protection and egg quality under defined species and production conditions. Retrieval history, imperfect dictionary annotation and topic-initialization sensitivity limit generalization beyond the mapped literature.
authors: Yonar H, Beşoluk FÇ.

title: Antibiotic removal and antibiotic resistance gene modulation in a pyrite-based bioelectrochemically enhanced constructed wetland.
abstract: Antibiotic residues and the environmental dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) pose persistent threats to aquatic ecosystems and public health. A pyrite-based bioelectrochemically enhanced constructed wetland (PBE-CW) was developed to evaluate the removal of enrofloxacin (ENR) and sulfamethoxazole (SMX), responses of resistance-related genetic elements, pyrite interfacial transformation, plant responses, and microbial functional potential. At 1.2 V, ENR and SMX removal efficiencies reached 87.33 ± 3.13% and 99.85 ± 0.32%, respectively. Independent batch experiments showed that applied voltage enhanced ENR and SMX transformation in the pyrite system, accompanied by stronger 1O2 signals and multiple intermediates. During long-term operation, pyrite surface oxidation was accompanied by Fe/S dissolution and migration, enrichment of genera associated with electroactivity, Fe/S transformation, and antibiotic degradation, and increased abundances of genes related to extracellular electron transfer (EET), Fe/S cycling, and aromatic compound transformation. Meanwhile, target ARGs and intI1 generally showed lower absolute abundances in the anoxic zone and lower relative abundances in the aerobic zone. Overall, PBE-CW enhanced antibiotic removal and showed potential for modulating resistance-related risks through the integration of pyrite, bioelectrochemical processes, and rhizosphere interactions.
authors: Peng J, Ailijiang N, Mao Q, Chang J, Zhang Z, Abulake A, Zhang Y, Tu X.

title: Identification of Candidate Targets and Immune Characteristics of Salvianolic Acid E Against Ulcerative Colitis via Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis and Machine Learning.
abstract: IntroductionUlcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with a complex pathogenesis. This study aims to systematically investigate the mechanism of Salvianolic acid E (SAE) in treating UC by identifying its core molecular targets.MethodsPotential target genes of SAE against UC were screened via differential expression analysis of datasets. Integrated approaches including machine learning algorithms, network pharmacology, molecular docking, immune infiltration analysis, and experimental validation were employed to investigate the binding interactions between SAE and target proteins.ResultsA total of 13 potential target genes were identified. Machine learning further refined these to five core genes (SLC23A1, SLC6A14, LCN2, PLA2G2A, and CASP1) as key regulatory factors. Among them, SLC23A1 was significantly downregulated, whereas the other four were significantly upregulated. Molecular docking showed putative interactions between SAE and the target proteins. Immune infiltration analysis revealed strong correlations between the core genes and immune cells such as M2 macrophages, neutrophils, and resting mast cells. Cellular-level validation confirmed the expression patterns of these key genes.DiscussionThese five core genes constitute a coordinated pathological axis underlying UC progression, which sequentially involves impaired epithelial barrier function, activated innate immune response, amplified pro-inflammatory lipid signaling, and caspase-1-mediated pyroptosis. The stable binding of SAE to these target proteins supports a multi-target synergistic mechanism: SAE may concurrently correct dysregulated solute transport, suppress pro-inflammatory enzymatic activities, and modulate the colonic immune microenvironment. In particular, the strong associations of core genes with neutrophils, M2 macrophages, and resting mast cells suggest that immunomodulation may serve as a critical potential dimension of SAE's therapeutic efficacy against UC. Our integrated analytical strategy also provides a replicable paradigm for deciphering the pharmacological mechanisms of multi-target natural compounds.ConclusionThe five candidate regulatory genes and the putative binding of SAE to its key targets provide critical insights into the therapeutic mechanism of SAE in UC, offering novel directions for future UC treatment development.
authors: Liu Y, Guo B, Yu L, Tang Y, Han C, Zhou Z, Zhang S, He Y.

title: Dynamic hormonome and transcriptome landscapes during maize seed filling and dehydration.
abstract: High yield and direct-harvest suitability are key goals in modern maize production but are constrained by limited seed-filling efficiency and dehydration rate. However, the genetic basis of these processes remains poorly understood. Here, we generated a high-resolution hormonome and transcriptome atlas of maize inbred line B73 during seed development, spanning 15 stages from filling to dehydration, using LC-MS/MS and RNA-seq. In total, 70 hormone compounds and 24,194 genes were identified, of which 1,495 genes, including 162 transcription factors, exhibited distinct seed- and developmental-stage-specific expression profiles. Weighted gene co-expression network (WGCNA) and gene regulatory network (GRN) analyses reveal that auxin, jasmonic acid (JA), brassinosteroid, abscisic acid, and ethylene signaling pathways jointly modulate grain dehydration. Genes encoding late embryogenesis abundant (LEA) proteins, heat shock proteins (HSPs), and aquaporins were enriched in dehydration-associated modules. Exogenous application of the JA inhibitor salicylhydroxamic acid significantly accelerated grain drying, reducing moisture content from 30.22% to 27.72% with minimal effect on grain dry weight. Integration of GRN, WGCNA, and meta-QTL analyses identified ZmbZip3 as a candidate regulator of grain dehydration. Functional validation confirmed that knockout of ZmbZip3 accelerated grain dehydration and did not compromise yield potential. Together, these results provide a comprehensive view of the hormonal and transcriptional regulation of maize seed filling and dehydration, offering valuable targets for breeding and chemical regulation of direct-harvest maize.
authors: Wang W, Ren Z, Jiang C, Li L, Zhou Y, Zhang M, Li Z, Cheng J, Yi F, Duan L.

title: Identification and validation of serum EPHB2 as a candidate biomarker for colorectal cancer and precancerous lesions.
abstract: This study identifies and validates serum EPHB2 as a non-invasive candidate biomarker for early detection of colorectal cancer (CRC) and precancerous adenomas. Through integrative analysis of multi-cohort transcriptomics, pan-cancer databases, and single-cell RNA sequencing, EPHB2 was identified as a CRC-specific marker predominantly localized to malignant epithelial cells, with expression progressively elevated from precancerous lesions through advanced carcinoma. Clinical ELISA validation in prospective local and independent external cohorts, supported by tissue immunohistochemistry, demonstrated robust diagnostic performance across both cohorts: serum EPHB2 achieved AUCs of 0.794-0.839 for adenoma detection and 0.816-0.897 for distinguishing CRC from healthy controls, and effectively discriminated neoplastic from benign inflammatory lesions (AUCs of 0.817-0.874). Mechanistic analyses further revealed that EPHB2 expression is associated with Wnt/β-catenin signaling activation in colorectal tumorigenesis. Collectively, these findings establish serum EPHB2 as a promising candidate biomarker that warrants further prospective evaluation for early detection of colorectal neoplasia.
authors: Zhang D, Wang J, Pan H, Zhao S, Jin X, Lu W, Ji C, Cui R, Ying H, Wang J, Li B, Jin H, Wang L, Yang J, Kang N, Huang X, Xu C, Xie X.

title: Discernible phenotypic alterations following linc-10 knockout in Caenorhabditis elegans.
abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are regulatory molecules that play vital roles in various cellular processes. Although the loss of function of most annotated lncRNAs in several model organisms does not result in severe phenotypes, suggesting they are not essential for survival or reproduction, lncRNAs may still act as responsive elements under diverse physiological and pathological conditions. In this study, we investigated the role of the linc-10 gene in Caenorhabditis elegans and found that its deletion is associated with altered gene expression and impaired reproductive fitness. Knockout (KO) mutants of linc-10 exhibited mild but notable abnormalities, including reduced brood size, altered developmental trajectories, and increased sensitivity to stress, along with occasional sterility and a slightly elevated male ratio. We characterized the expression patterns of linc-10 across developmental stages and performed high-throughput sequencing to detect differentially expressed genes (DEGs) following linc-10 deletion. We found that several immune-related genes were dysregulated. Notably, linc-10 mutants showed increased susceptibility to Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 infection and other stressors. Small RNA sequencing further revealed alterations in piRNA and miRNA profiles after linc-10 deletion. Importantly, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated insertion of a Plinc-10::linc-10 rescue transgene into a neutral intergenic site partially rescued the reduced brood size and stress-sensitive phenotypes of linc-10 mutants, supporting the functional relevance of the linc-10 transcript. Together, these findings suggest that linc-10 contributes to reproductive fitness, immune homeostasis, and stress resilience in C. elegans.
authors: Zhou C, Sun X, Wu R, Wu Z, Chen H.

title: Jiangtang Pill for Type 2 Diabetes: Network Pharmacology and Transcriptomics.
abstract: IntroductionThis study computationally explores the polypharmacological mechanisms of Jiangtang Pill (JTP) in treating Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) using an integrated in silico approach.MethodsActive compounds of JTP and predicted pharmacological targets were extracted from databases. Protein-protein interaction networks identified core hubs, which were intersected with DEGs from a T2DM transcriptomic dataset (GSE15932). Functional mechanisms were evaluated via GO and KEGG analyses. Immune infiltration was assessed using CIBERSORT. Molecular docking and 100-ns Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations were performed to evaluate the predicted binding interactions and dynamic behavior of key ligand-protein complexes.ResultsAKT1, MAPK3, STAT3, and TNF emerged as candidate targets supported by the integrated network and transcriptomic analyses. Functional enrichment highlighted the PI3K-Akt, AGE-RAGE, and MAPK pathways. CIBERSORT analysis indicated a lower estimated abundance of CD4+ memory activated T cells in T2DM, which was inversely associated with the expression of selected targets. The 100-ns MD simulations showed that the four ligand-protein complexes remained dynamically associated throughout the trajectories, with distinct RMSD, RMSF, compactness, and hydrogen-bonding profiles for β-sitosterol and kaempferol.DiscussionBy integrating network pharmacology, clinical transcriptomics, and structural analyses, this study supports a hypothesis that JTP may influence metabolic and immune-related pathways involved in T2DM.ConclusionThese findings provide a testable computational framework for the potential multi-target actions of JTP and warrant further experimental validation.
authors: Liu R, Zhang M, Zhao Y, Dong H, Si H, Niu Y.

title: Placental Glycolysis-Related Transcriptional Features in Early-Onset Preeclampsia Complicated by Fetal Growth Restriction.
abstract: BackgroundPreeclampsia (PE) is a severe obstetric complication characterized by the new onset of hypertension and proteinuria after 20 weeks of gestation. However, bulk transcriptomic approaches cannot resolve cell type-specific alterations within the heterogeneous placenta. Single- cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables gene expression profiling at individual-cell resolution, thereby revealing cellular heterogeneity and identifying cell populations and pathways potentially involved in disease processes.MethodsThis exploratory study integrated scRNA-seq data from one EOPE-FGR placental sample and one healthy control sample with bulk RNA-seq data. The Seurat and limma packages were used for single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analyses, respectively. Gene set enrichment analysis and differential expression analysis were performed to identify candidate pathways and genes. RT-qPCR was used to examine candidate gene expression, whereas the Cell Counting Kit-8 assay was used to assess the effect of FLT1 knockdown on cell viability under hypoxia/reoxygenation conditions.ResultsExploratory scRNA-seq analysis identified ten major placental cell types. In the two analyzed samples, the EOPE-FGR sample showed a higher observed EVT proportion, whereas EVT cells displayed sample-specific glycolysis-, interferon-, and immune-related expression patterns. These single-cell observations were treated as exploratory. An exploratory intersection of bulk disease- versus-control differentially expressed genes with genes identified from the EVT high- versus low-glycolysis-score comparison prioritized 11 candidate genes: FLT1, PROCR, INHA, CST6, HTRA1, C12orf75, FSTL3, INHBA, CDA, EBI3, and PRG2. In supportive in vitro experiments, eight selected genes showed increased expression under hypoxia/reoxygenation conditions, and FLT1 knockdown was associated with an increased CCK-8 signal. The CCK-8 assay did not directly assess glycolytic activity.DiscussionBulk RNA-seq analysis identified glycolysis-related enrichment in EOPE-FGR placentas, whereas the single-cell datasets provided exploratory observations of EVT-associated expression patterns. Given the limited scRNA-seq sample size, these observations should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger independent cohorts.ConclusionThe integrated analyses prioritized candidate genes associated with bulk disease-related and within-sample EVT glycolysis-score-related expression patterns. These exploratory findings do not establish a causal relationship between FLT1, glycolytic activity, and immune alterations and require validation in larger cohorts and through direct metabolic assays.
authors: Zhang R, Peng Y, Gao Y, Kong W, Lin B, Deng M, Chen Z, Liu Y, Liu Q.

title: OJIP kinetics and JIP-test parameters reveal species-specific PSII responses of microalgae to phenanthrene and polystyrene nanoplastics.
abstract: Phenanthrene (Phe) and polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPs) occur together in aquatic environments, but their combined effects on photosystem II (PSII) photochemistry remain insufficiently characterized. We examined OJIP fluorescence transients and JIP-test parameters in Chlorella sp. and Isochrysis galbana exposed for 24-96 h to nominal Phe concentrations of 0.5-2.0 mg L⁻¹ in the absence or presence of 1 mg L⁻¹ PS-NPs. The same three independent culture flasks per treatment were sampled repeatedly over time. At 96 h, ΦEo and Area showed pronounced treatment-associated variation, although the magnitude and statistical support differed between taxa. Energy-flux parameters showed limited statistical separation among treatments, and PIabs was retained as a secondary result because its interpretation was constrained by high variability, negative exported values and loss of statistical support after endpoint-level multiplicity adjustment. Repeated-measures analysis further showed that treatment, exposure time and their interaction contributed differently to variation among PSII parameters. In the complete-data analysis, one matched Area comparison in Chlorella sp. was significant after multiplicity correction, but this comparison was not robust to conservative exclusion of a flagged record. The absence of a PS-NPs-only treatment also prevents separation of an independent particle effect from a Phe-dependent interaction. These findings characterize species- and parameter-dependent PSII photochemical responses during short-term exposure. Because growth, pigment composition, oxidative stress and cell viability were not measured in parallel, the fluorescence responses cannot be interpreted as direct evidence of whole-cell toxicity or population-level effects.

title: ClpB-mediated modulation of GroEL-bound luciferase and subsequent refolding by DnaK chaperone system.
abstract: In prokaryotes, DnaK-DnaJ-GrpE (KJE), GroEL-GroES (ELS) and the AAA+ disaggregase ClpB constitute the major ATP-dependent chaperone systems involved in protein quality control machinery. Although the individual functions and interplay of KJE and ClpB systems have been extensively studied, the role of ClpB with ELS during KJE-mediated substrate refolding is still elusive. Here, we investigated the role of ClpB in KJE- and ELS-mediated refolding of chemically and heat-denatured luciferase. Simultaneous presence of KJE, ELS and ClpB significantly enhanced the refolding of chemically denatured luciferase, whereas the combination of KJE and ClpB resulted in a higher refolding yield of heat-denatured luciferase. The inhibitory effect of ELS on KJE-mediated refolding of luciferase was significantly reduced when KJE, ELS and ClpB were present simultaneously. Sequential chaperone addition experiments showed that ELS-bound heat-denatured luciferase was refolded to 24% and 36% of its native activity by KJE and ClpB respectively, whereas the KJE-ClpB chaperone system further enhanced refolding to 43%. ClpB alone did not enhanced the refolding of ELS-bound chemically denatured luciferase, while subsequent addition of KJE or KJE-ClpB restored 36% and 44% of the native activity, respectively. Turbidity assay showed that the KJE system effectively suppressed heat-induced luciferase aggregation, whereas ClpB alone exhibited no anti-aggregation activity. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that ClpB cooperates with the KJE chaperone system to enhance substrate refolding and rescue ELS-stalled substrate proteins, thus providing insights into the coordinated action of ATP-dependent chaperone systems in the maintenance of cellular protein homeostasis.
authors: Varsha, Pandey P, Priya S, Sharma SK.

title: The ssDNA-binding protein MEIOB sustains synaptonemal complex integrity by stabilizing recombination intermediates during male meiosis.
abstract: The synaptonemal complex (SC) is fundamental to meiotic recombination and crossover formation between homologous chromosomes. In yeast, the SC is assembled and sustained by the ZZS complex (Zip2-Zip4-Spo16). However, how ZZS components are recruited and stabilized at chromosomes, and whether their mammalian orthologs (SHOC1-TEX11-SPO16) play similar roles, remain poorly understood. Here, we report that germ cell-specific ablation of the meiosis-specific single-stranded DNA-binding protein MEIOB in mice causes premature chromosomal desynapsis in early pachytene spermatocytes, leading to their elimination before mid-pachytene. Mechanistically, MEIOB associates with SPO16 in vitro, and Spo16-deficient pachytene-like spermatocytes display comparable premature desynapsis and severely reduced MEIOB foci on chromosomal axes. Moreover, the recruitment of another ZZS component, TEX11, to recombination intermediates is markedly diminished in Meiob knockout pachytene spermatocytes. Together, our findings suggest that the MEIOB-SPATA22 complex may cooperate with SPO16 to support SC integrity and crossover formation during mammalian meiosis.
authors: Feng H, Jiang B, Gao Y, Zubair M, Hu L, Wang H, Wang X, Li M, Luo M, Sun J, Huo L, Liu D.

title: Effects of DNA Supercoil Handedness on Catalytic Inhibition of Mycobacterial Gyrase by Gepotidacin.
abstract: Gepotidacin, the first-in-class triazaacenaphthylene antibacterial, kills bacteria by stabilizing DNA cleavage complexes and inhibiting the catalytic activities of the type II topoisomerases, gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Mycobacterial species encode gyrase as their sole type II topoisomerase, meaning that inhibition of this enzyme blocks several essential cellular functions through a single target. Unlike fluoroquinolones and spiropyrimidinetriones, which inhibit gyrase by inserting two drug molecules, one at each of the cleaved scissile bonds, gepotidacin intercalates a single molecule into the intact double helix between the two scissile bonds within the enzyme active site. To determine how the distinct binding mechanism of gepotidacin affects its inhibitory profile, we examined the ability of the drug to inhibit decatenation, supercoiling of relaxed DNA, and relaxation of positive supercoils catalyzed by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacteroides abscessus gyrase. Gepotidacin inhibited decatenation and supercoiling at comparable concentrations but required higher concentrations to inhibit relaxation of positively supercoiled DNA, a pattern distinct from fluoroquinolones and spiropyrimidetriones. Similar results were observed with GSK000, a Mycobacterium tuberculosis gyrase inhibitor that also intercalates into intact DNA in the gyrase active site. Using mutant gyrase enzymes capable of relaxing both positively and negatively supercoiled DNA, we found that gepotidacin and GSK000 inhibited relaxation of negative supercoils at substantially lower concentrations (∼13-fold on average) than relaxation of positive supercoils. This sensitivity to supercoil handedness was markedly higher than observed for nonintercalative drugs (moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin, zoliflodacin, and novobiocin). These findings suggest that the intercalative binding mechanism of gepotidacin confers heightened sensitivity to DNA supercoil handedness.
authors: Armenia JF, Osheroff N.

title: Schisantherin B Preserves Cochlear Function and Hair Cell Integrity in Aging by Restoring Mitochondrial Homeostasis via eEF1A2-Beclin-1-Mediated Mitophagy.
abstract: BackgroundAge-related hearing loss (ARHL) represents one of the prevalent degenerative conditions in the elderly worldwide, characterized by progressive auditory dysfunction that impairs quality of life. Currently, no approved pharmacotherapies are available to prevent.MethodsIn vitro protective effects of STB were assessed by cell viability and Senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal staining) in D-galactose-induced senescent mouse cochlear explants and HEI-OC1 cells. In vivo auditory function and cochlear injury were examined by hearing threshold detection and histological analysis of hair cells, ribbon synapses, and spiral ganglion neurons in SAMP8 and C57BL/6J mice. RNA sequencing was used to identify STB-mediated transcriptional changes. Immunofluorescence and Western blotting were performed to investigate the molecular mechanisms.ResultsSTB pretreatment reduced cell loss and senescence in vitro. In vivo, STB attenuated low-to-mid frequency hearing threshold shifts and cochlear degeneration. Mechanistically, STB upregulated eEF1A2, which promoted Beclin-1-mediated mitophagy, reduced ROS accumulation, and suppressed caspase-3-dependent apoptosis. RNA-seq confirmed that STB modulated Beclin-1 expression via eEF1A2.ConclusionThese data confirm the significant protective effect of STB against ARHL, highlighting its potential as a natural candidate for ARHL intervention and verify that it exerts its effects by regulating cellular autophagy via the eEF1A2-Beclin 1 pathway.
authors: Tang G, Gao Z, Ma T, Liu M, Xie J, Yang P, Shu Y, Zhang T.

title: Polymer dynamics reveal stage-wise unfolding and homologous pairing of chromosomes in fission yeast.
abstract: During meiosis, the exchange of genetic material ("recombination") is essential to bring about genetic variation in offspring. To carry out the recombination, homologous pairs of DNA have to come into proximity and align, which is inherently a polymer dynamics problem. In fission yeast, this is accomplished by the extensive nuclear oscillation that applies a pulling force on the chromosome polymers. In this work, we investigate the competition between the pulling force that tries to facilitate the alignment and the intra-chromatin interactions that assist the chromatin folding. The crucial role played by the intra-chromatin interaction for a range of pulling forces and loci locations is highlighted here. Upon comparing our results with the experimental findings, we not only reaffirm the enhancement of contact probability with loci-dependent pulling but also get a meaningful interpretation of the chromosome unfolding and pairing at different stages of movement.
authors: Kumar S, Padinhateeri R, Thakur S.

title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes.
abstract: Astrocytes shape synapses and circuits, yet their diversity within the human basal ganglia remains poorly defined. Integrating single-nucleus transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with spatial transcriptomics, we identify three anatomically organized astrocyte subgroups-striatal gray matter (GM), extra-striatal GM, and white matter (WM)-distinguished by neurotransmitter transporter expression and synapse-associated programs that reflect afferent input. These molecular distinctions generalize brain-wide, separating telencephalic from non-telencephalic astrocytes, with LHX2 marking telencephalic astrocyte identity across species. Within the striatum (STR), dorsal and ventral populations align with distinct microcircuits; a ventral population maps to the nucleus accumbens mediodorsal shell alongside specialized neuronal subtypes, a pattern conserved in nonhuman primates. A deep learning sequence model identifies subgroup-specific enhancer codes and recovers established transcription factor motif logic from published enhancer-AAV datasets, providing a foundation for targeted viral vector design. These findings define intersecting axes of human astrocyte specialization and offer a framework for cell-type-specific dissection of basal ganglia circuits.

title: Cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia.
abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are conserved brain regions essential for motor control, learning, emotion, and cognition and are implicated in neurological and psychiatric disease, yet a unified cross-species taxonomy of BG cell types is lacking. We present a multiomic consensus atlas of 1.8 million nuclei from humans, macaques, and marmosets spanning eight BG structures, integrating gene expression, open chromatin, and spatial profiling. Alignment across species and to mouse and human whole-brain atlases identifies 61 homologous cell types conserved over 76 million years. Dorsal-ventral spatial identity is more conserved than D1/D2 receptor or striosome/matrix identity, and striatum (STR) D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neurons have distinct molecular, electrophysiological, and morphological features. Cis-regulatory analysis reveals conserved sequence grammars that encode cell identity and inform viral targeting, and cell-type-resolved mapping localizes psychiatric and neurodegenerative risk to specific BG cell populations. This work provides a foundational resource for BG evolution, function, and disease.

title: Rationally Designed TLR2-QS-21 Liposomal Adjuvant Enhances Immunogenicity while Reducing Reactogenicity in Subunit Vaccines.
abstract: Potent vaccine adjuvants often link strong adaptive immunity with excessive inflammation. Here, we developed BQS01, a liposomal adjuvant that replaces the TLR4 agonist monophosphoryl lipid A (MPL) with a synthetic TLR2 agonist (BXY-14) while retaining QS-21. BQS01 induced a TLR2-associated transcriptional profile, enhanced dendritic cell activation and T-cell priming, and was associated with increased IL-10 production. In ovalbumin and varicella-zoster virus mouse models, BQS01 generated antibody responses comparable to an AS01b-like MPL/QS-21 comparator and durable polyfunctional cellular immunity, while reducing systemic weight loss, local inflammation, and TNF-α accumulation. These findings suggest that innate signaling architecture, rather than inflammatory magnitude alone, contributes to adjuvant performance and may guide the design of next-generation vaccines with an improved immunogenicity-reactogenicity balance.
authors: Ma W, Tang R, Wang H, Jia H, Wang Y, Zhou S, Lv T, Wang X.

title: A specialized microbiome enriched in nitrification and halogen cycling potential resolved from multi-omics investigation of a Caribbean suboxic and acidic marine sinkhole
abstract:
Background
                The Luymes Sinkholes, located on the Luymes Bank northwest of Saba, represent a unique marine environment characterized by distinct biogeochemical gradients. Most noticeable is an acidic (pH ≈ 6.25) and suboxic (O2 < 60 µmol/kg) submerged ‘lake’ at ~ 220 m depth exhibiting extreme deviations from standard oceanographic patterns, including elevated inorganic carbon, nitrate, and phosphate, and a lower temperature (20.3 ºC vs 26.4 ºC). To determine how the microbiome within the submerged acid lake adapted to these unique conditions, we collected 59 coupled samples of size-filtered (0.22 µm) planktonic microbes for shotgun metagenomics and solid-phase extracted dissolved organic matter for untargeted metabolomics from 21 stations at depths ranging from 2 to 600 m during a 10-day research cruise in December 2019.
              
                Results
                We identified a distinct microbial community within the submerged acid lake different from the non-acidic sinkholes, with increased abundances of Nitrospinota, Thermoproteota, Planctomycetota, and Actinobacteriota. We also found three enriched classes of dissolved compounds within the submerged acid lake: (1) large, (2) low-polarity, and (3) halogenated metabolites, including iodides and halobenzoic acids. Correlations between microbial taxa and metabolite classes show potential links between nitrifying archaea and halogenated compound cycling. We further supported these findings using the functional annotation of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and protein clusters showing enrichment of nitrification and halogen cycling genes, suggesting the presence of specialized degradation and biosynthetic pathways, directly connecting microbial metabolism to the observed geochemical conditions.
              
                Conclusion
                These findings demonstrate that the submerged acid lake contains specific microbially driven biogeochemical processes under acidified and low-oxygen conditions, providing a natural model for future extreme ocean acidification scenarios. With this multi‑omics approach, we were able to connect the microbial metabolism with this unique environment, thereby expanding our understanding of how both are interconnected.

title: Low-abundance taxa are associated with a refined rumen microbiome–resistome interplay in high-yielding dairy cows: an absolute abundance-based metagenomic perspective
abstract:
Background
                     The rumen microbiota undergoes dynamic shifts in response to fluctuations in physiological stages and host-related factors, and has been associated with productive traits including milk yield, feed efficiency, and methane emissions. However, the ecological mechanisms underlying the relationship between microbial relative abundance, absolute abundance, and shifts in microbiota structure, and their connection to host production performance, remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize the rumen microecological features across cows with divergent lactation performance, with particular emphasis on linking microbial absolute abundance, mobile genetic elements, and antibiotic resistance genes to productivity in high-yielding cows. In this study, rumen fluid was collected from 8 high-yielding cows and 8 low-yielding cows selected from 90 mid-lactation Holstein cows. Shotgun metagenomics with spike-in-based absolute quantification and untargeted metabolomics were employed to investigate the characteristics and potential associations and transmission patterns of rumen microbial communities and ARGs in cows with different milk yields.
                  
                     Results
                     We observed that high-yielding cows exhibited stronger carbohydrate metabolism capacity, higher Chao1 and ACE indices, and lower total microbial absolute abundance. Moreover, high-yielding cows displayed reduced absolute abundances of bacteria and viruses, increased relative abundances of archaea and eukaryotes, and a more intricate microbial network architecture. These shifts were accompanied by a reduction in ARGs prevalence, particularly within peptide, elfamycin, and fluoroquinolone antibiotic categories, and were accompanied by a streamlined ARGs interaction network. Furthermore, the attenuation of ARGs was associated with reduced levels of MGEs, especially those linked to replication, phage activity, genetic transfer, and defense functions. These findings suggest potential associations among microbial structure, MGEs, and ARGs in the rumen ecosystem.
                  
                     Conclusion
                     These findings indicate that complex microbial networks involving low-abundance taxa, together with a streamlined ARGs ecosystem, are associated with high milk yield in dairy cows. This perspective offers valuable implications for mitigating antibiotic resistance risks in intensive livestock systems and advancing efficient, healthy dairy production.

title: Multi-locus pairing expands the functional repertoire of two-peptide bacteriocins
abstract: Two-peptide bacteriocins are generally viewed as self-contained systems whose peptides are encoded at the same biosynthetic locus and co-expressed to form an active antimicrobial pair. Here, we show that functional pairing extends beyond this organization. Comparative genomic analysis revealed frequent co-occurrence of putative two-peptide bacteriocins encoded at distinct chromosomal loci in streptococci. Testing pairwise combinations of 47 peptides produced by cell-free protein synthesis identified 54 combinations with enhanced antimicrobial activity, with inter-locus combinations more frequent than intra-locus combinations. In Streptococcus mitis strain C22, four dispersed bacteriocin loci are coordinately expressed during exponential growth despite regulation by partially independent signaling pathways, providing an opportunity for inter-locus pairing. Split-luciferase complementation assays showed that active peptide pairs associate and that these interactions depend predominantly on amino acid sequence. Using a bacteriocin-free S. mitis background, we further show that components produced by distinct bacterial cells can act together to increase producer competitiveness in co-culture with S. pneumoniae. These findings reveal a modular organization in which peptides encoded at different loci can form functional combinations, including when produced by separate cells. This flexibility expands the antimicrobial repertoire available to individual strains and provides a mechanism for bacteriocin diversification while retaining functional compatibility.
authors: Lanca, J., Borralho, J., Sa-Leao, R.

title: The FraA adhesin and Ebp pili mediate Enterococcus faecalis adhesion under fluid flow
abstract: Enterococcus faecalis is a frequent cause of infective endocarditis and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI). Successful colonization is challenged by blood and urine flow and relies on a strong and resilient bacterial attachment. Here, we identify molecular determinants that enable E. faecalis to maintain adhesion under flow, notably the flow-related adhesin (FraA), a previously uncharacterized adhesion factor encoded by OG1RF_11764. Transcriptomic analysis revealed increased fraA expression in surface-attached bacteria exposed to shear stress. Structural predictions identified an N-terminal region with homology to characterized Gram-positive adhesins, followed by tandem CLIPPER repeats with putative isopeptide-bond-forming residues and a C-terminal cell-wall sorting signal. Using microfluidics and single-cell tracking, we found that deletion of fraA accelerated detachment from hydrophobic abiotic surfaces under fluid flow. In line with this finding, loss of fraA reduced catheter colonization in a murine CAUTI model. Analysis of 9,192 E. faecalis genomes identified FraA in 50.8% of isolates, spanning clinical and non-clinical sources, with sequence type-associated variation in CLIPPER repeat number. Another determinant, Ebp pilus, enhances adhesion at high shear stress and contributes to a shear-enhanced adhesion pattern. Collectively, these findings identify FraA as an adhesion factor contributing to medical-device colonization and together with Ebp pili support attachment across different hydrodynamic conditions. Identifying these adhesion mechanisms could inform strategies to prevent colonization of medical devices exposed to fluid flow.
authors: Antypas, H., Roch, M., Ng, K. K. F., Silva Rosa da Luz, B., Wen, R. T. J., Thomas, R. Z., Filloux, A., Kline, K. A.

title: Mechanical unloading and exercise volume differentially modulate the gut microbiome and intestinal gene expression in mice
abstract: Mechanical unloading and physical activity can influence the gut microbiome and intestinal physiology, but the effects of exercise volume and prior hindlimb suspension remain incompletely understood. This study investigated how hindlimb suspension, different exercise volumes, and exercise following hindlimb suspension affect gut microbial composition and intestinal gene expression in mice. Mice were assigned to five groups: control (C), hindlimb suspension (HL), high-volume exercise (HE), low-volume exercise (LE), and hindlimb suspension followed by exercise (HLE). Cecal microbiota composition was characterized using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, followed by alpha- and beta-diversity analyses and LinDA differential-abundance analysis. Jejunal gene expression was assessed by quantitative PCR for markers related to oxidative stress, inflammation, metabolic signaling, and epithelial function. Hindlimb suspension reduced microbial richness, as indicated by the Observed, Chao1, and ACE indices, and was associated with a significant difference in overall microbial community composition compared with controls. It was also associated with reductions in Streptococcaceae/Streptococcus and Spirochaetota. Low-volume exercise produced the most extensive phylum-level differential-abundance findings, whereas high-volume exercise showed no significant phylum-level differences from controls. Both exercise groups (HE and LE) exhibited increased intestinal expression of GPX1, HMOX1, NFKB1, and SOD2. HE also increased IGF and MUC2 expression, whereas HLE reduced IGF expression compared with controls. Community composition did not differ significantly between HLE and HL, and LGR5 expression did not differ significantly among groups. In conclusion, hindlimb suspension was associated with reduced microbial richness and selective taxonomic changes, whereas low-volume exercise produced the most extensive phylum-level alterations in microbial composition. Exercise volume was also associated with distinct intestinal transcriptional responses, while exercise following mechanical unloading did not produce a microbial community composition significantly different from that observed following unloading alone. These findings highlight the context-dependent effects of mechanical unloading and exercise on gut microbial composition and intestinal gene expression.
authors: Hundam, S., Al-Zghoul, M. B., Ogiliat, S., Makableh, D., Abu-Haniyeh, L. A., Shahatit, S.

title: Pathological effects of NETs: seed and soil hypothesis for inflammation spread by primed neutrophils.
abstract: AbstractThe ability of activated neutrophils to release decondensed chromatin as neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in response to stimuli is conserved throughout evolution. Although NETs support host defense by forming physical barriers against microbes, their toxicity can cause tissue damage. Large NET networks, generated through the activation of NLRP3 inflammasome, the citrullinating enzyme peptidylarginine deiminase 4, and neutrophil-derived enzymes, are central to the pathogenesis of numerous diseases. Chronic disorders often originate at a localized site, for example, the joints in rheumatoid arthritis, or after a major inflammatory event before progressing to distant organs, such as the heart. In this perspective, we hypothesize that circulating primed neutrophils represent the "seeds" of chronic disease that adhere to activated vessels, the "soil" of susceptible organs. We explore the mechanisms underlying NET formation and discuss animal and human evidence supporting our hypothesis.
authors: Wagner DD, Heger LA.

title: Global research landscape on the brain-gut axis in early life: a bibliometric and visualized study.
abstract: IntroductionBackground: the brain-gut axis was recognized as a bidirectional communication system linking the central and enteric nervous systems through neural, hormonal, immune, and metabolic pathways. It played a pivotal role in early-life neurodevelopment, immune programming, and gastrointestinal function. Although the field had grown rapidly, a comprehensive bibliometric evaluation of global research trends, hotspots, and collaborations was lacking. Methods: we conducted a bibliometric and visualized analysis of publications on the brain-gut axis in early life from 2004 to 2024, using the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) database. CiteSpace was used to generate co-authorship, institutional collaboration, keyword co-occurrence, and co-citation networks, as well as burst detection, timeline views, and dual-map overlays. Results: a total of 1,429 publications were analyzed. Research output increased steadily from 2015 and peaked in 2023, reflecting growing global interest. The United States and China were the most productive countries, with strong collaborative ties observed among institutions in North America, Europe, and East Asia. University College Cork, University of California System, and Harvard University were the leading institutions, while J. F. Cryan, T. G. Dinan, and G. Clarke were the most influential authors. Early studies focused on anatomical and developmental aspects, while recent hotspots included autism spectrum disorder, intestinal permeability, fecal microbiota transplantation, and psychological stress. Mechanistic keywords highlighted short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolism, vagus nerve signaling, and microglia-immune interactions. Conclusions: this study provided a comprehensive bibliometric overview of early-life brain-gut axis research over the past two decades. It revealed dynamic thematic evolution, expanding interdisciplinary collaboration, and the emergence of translational opportunities. These findings offer a valuable reference for future research directions in pediatric neurogastroenterology and microbiota-based interventions.
authors: Hu Z, Xu J, Jiang F, Liu Y.

title: A pH-responsive GelMA-KerMA hydrogel delivering luteolin-loaded PLGA nanoparticles promotes myocardial repair via Akt/Bad signaling and multitarget regulation.
abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) triggers cardiomyocyte apoptosis, oxidative stress imbalance, ventricular fibrosis, and impaired angiogenesis. Luteolin, a natural flavonoid compound, possesses antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and cardioprotective properties, making it a promising candidate for MI treatment. However, its poor water solubility, low bioavailability, and chemical instability severely hinder its clinical translation. To address these limitations, we developed a photo-crosslinked composite hydrogel delivery system using gelatin methacryloyl and keratin methacryloyl (GelMA-KerMA). Luteolin-loaded poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanoparticles were uniformly dispersed within a three-dimensional gel network to achieve pH-triggered local drug delivery. The covalent GelMA-KerMA network retained structural integrity under both pH conditions. In the weakly acidic infarct microenvironment, acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of PLGA ester bonds was the primary driver of accelerated luteolin release, whereas the network mainly acted as a sustained-retarding reservoir. The incorporation of KerMA endowed the patch with enhanced mechanical stability and cytocompatibility, enabling better mechanical matching with the infarcted myocardium. The composite hydrogel promotes myocardial repair and functional recovery through the coordinated regulation of the rapid Akt/Bad phosphorylation cascade. It also sustains MAPK/Rap1-dependent transcriptional reprogramming. It inhibits mitochondrial apoptosis, scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), suppresses fibroblast activation, and promotes neovascularization. This study presents a protein-based delivery platform that integrates tailored physicochemical and mechanical properties with multi-pathway myocardial repair capabilities, offering a biomaterial strategy for minimally invasive local drug delivery in ischemic MI.
authors: Jiang D, Li J, Hu J, Jiang D, Yang W, Huang W.
